Guess who just got back today?

Them wild-eyed boys that’d been away;

Haven’t changed, had much to say,

But man, I still think them cats are crazy;

They were askin’ if you were around,

How you was, where you could be found;

Told ‘em you were livin’ downtown,

Drivin’ all the old men crazy;

The boys are back in town...



- “The Boys Are Back in Town” Thin Lizzy, 1976



Wednesday 1st September 1976

As far as Remus could tell, getting clapped on the back by James Potter while having three fractured ribs was a lot like throwing yourself in front of an oncoming train. There was no waving or conventional “hellos” to be had, just a single upright dog-pile as James and Peter charged up from behind on the busy station platform. With a great hurrah they grappled him by the shoulders and he nearly threw his mother’s white trunk across the station cringing in pain. Thankfully the excitement didn’t last long; the moment the other two rounded him and got a decent look at his front their delightful expressions vanished.

“Lupin, what the hell happened to your face?” James exclaimed.

Remus knew he looked rough. Still yellow under the eyes from the bruising and with a scabby cut over the bridge of his nose that extended all the way up into his eyebrow, his appearance shocked anyone who got too close. Fracturing his ribs meant that he hadn’t gotten a decent breath-in in weeks, though his nose had healed in a relatively straight line and the stitches were finally gone. The doctors said he’d probably have the scar forever, just another more permanent reminder of his refusal to play by his father’s rules. If Lyall Lupin had hated the sight of him before, he detested it now.

“Football accident,” Remus said flatly. He’d been practising the lie for most of August while he’d slummed around the estate, whining and wincing without Tomny’s downers. “I guess I make a pretty poor goalkeeper.”

James winced and Peter called it “hard cheese”, nearly making Remus laugh out loud at the thought of Vint’s last and only words to him; but at least they hadn’t badgered him for more. Like Giles (who’d had more than enough to say after picking Remus up and driving him straight to the hospital) the boys rarely overstepped boundaries, even ones never explicitly said aloud. Remus suspected it was a de facto result of being friends with Sirius for so long.

“So where’s Black?” He asked, glancing around the busy train platform just in case Sirius was getting ready to spring up and break the rest of his ribs.

“He’s already at school,” James said. “Reg made prefect this year so they had to come a day early.”

“Oh.”

“Yeah, his train would’ve come through yesterday. But c’mon, let’s go claim a carriage before they’re all full.”

Once on the train, Remus was pleased to find that that year he’d be riding in a private carriage with air con and windows working latches. As Peter and James busied themselves with a round of cards, he planted himself by the window with a book. He’d been thinking a lot about Sirius lately—or at least, more than usual. It had started when the butlers finally brought him the letters, which he’d read while bedridden and half-delirious from the pain in his face and chest. They were well-written of course, with that same Sirius Black wit that Remus had grown so used to, only now accompanied by his perfect penmanship as well.

Tucking them into the pages of his book so his friends wouldn’t see, Remus scanned the letters, reminded of the bit of guilt he’d been carrying ever since he first plucked up the courage to open them. There was one for nearly every week of the summer holiday, but Remus had read them so many times he could’ve almost recited them off by heart.



Dear Moony,

(After a summer away Remus still cringed at the nickname.)

Summer’s shit, but what else is new. Dad’s away in London most of the time at least, but mum found the couple of albums I got the bloke in the kitchen to stash away for me and tossed them into the salon’s fireplace. Such a bloody waste—I didn’t even get to play them! At least now the salon stinks so badly that we don’t do afternoon tea in there anymore. I figure they’re going to be airing the place out for weeks to get rid of the smell of burnt PVC.

James says he can’t ring you. I thought you said your family didn’t do holidays?

I know you don’t understand the romantic and sophisticated past-time that is letter writing and your handwriting is pretty shit, but if you get this one, post me back.

Sirius.



Dear Moony,

Where do you think is the most effective spot for hiding a body? I’m about ready to murder Reg’s damn dog. He’s only an ugly little thing, so I figure the flower beds in the front garden would be a safe bet, though Mum would just as quickly bump me off for disturbing the begonias.

You and James don’t know how good you’ve got it. Brothers are a nightmare. I’d give anything to trade Reg for Simeon—at least he’s good for something other than whinging like a girl. I’m pretty sure Reg pays Kreacher in bacon to piss in my shoes.

You’ve got dogs, where do you bury them? The front or back garden?

Write soon.

Sirius.

PS: I swear I really do like dogs. Most of the time.



Moony,

I’m starting to wonder if your dad’s as strict as mine or if you’re just illiterate. I know the second can’t be true because you’re never without a bloody book in your hand, so I’m just going to put your lack of return-correspondence down to you being a lazy arse.

If it is the first one though then you should write a song. A great, bloody fuck you to dear ol’ dad. Wouldn’t that be something? I’ll write one too, then we can compare in September.

I’ve been trying to write actually. All of it’s shit, but even the best wrote shit sometimes right? “The Laughing Gnome” must still plague Bowie, I swear.

Heard any good music since school ended? Andy’s all over this group called the Ramones lately, but they’ve only got one album out and I haven’t heard it.

Hope you’re enjoying the heat.

Sirius.



He was half right at least; Remus was a lazy arse, but he was also without so much as a sophisticated or romantic bone in his body, and a few of the ones he did have were broken, so that was a decent enough excuse right?

At first Remus told himself the neglect was because he felt so damn horrible all the time; after all he’d barely left his bedroom for the last month of holiday, but eventually he had to put his lack of correspondence down to plain nerves. Even if he did write Sirius back, what would he say?

‘Hey, summer’s been peachy. Got beaten to a pulp and might’ve lost all my friends but did you catch that last episode of the Pops?’

Lord.

When he finally did write Sirius back, it was nearly the last week of summer holiday. After he’d explained that the letter was going to a school friend in Bath, Giles agreed to post it and get it expedited, but there was no telling if the letter had made it to Sirius since he hadn’t written anything else back.

It didn’t matter, Remus told himself. It was just a short thing anyway—hardly a Nobel Prize in literature. He and Sirius could just catch up at school, and if the other boy wanted to pummel him for ignoring him all summer Remus would at least request that he avoid the nose.

“Oi, Lupin,” James called from the other bench, “put down the bloody book and come help me whip this tosser in rummy.”

“Not even Lupin can’t save your sorry arse, Potter,” Peter grinned evilly, expertly twirling the stack of cards around in his hands.

Snapping his book shut over the letter, Remus turned back to his friends and smiled. “Fine,” he said, “but we’re playing aces high this time.”





* * *





“Everyone got your room keys? Come get your schedules if you haven’t got ‘em already!”

Kenny, the new Godric dorm monitor, was doing his best to holler over the group of year 7 boys as they mulled about on the front lawn of the dorm, looking distinctly small and nervous after moving from the western primary half of campus to the bigger upper-secondary half where they’d be expected to spent the rest of their menial youth.

James waved at Kenny as they passed, both of them being on the football team, and Peter elbowed Remus, almost dropping one of his trunks in the process.

“Do you reckon you were ever that short, Lupin?” He teased, pointing at the kids.

“You reckon you’ll ever be any taller?” Remus asked, and Peter knocked his trunk into the back of his legs in retaliation, nearly buckling his knees.

“Hurry up or they’ll start thinking we’re part of the welcoming party,” James chastised, carrying two of his trunks in one hand and another over his shoulder.

They made their way up the steps of the dorm, passing the plaque depicting the Godric griffin and through the front doors. Immediately they were met with the familiar woody scent of the pine-panelled hallways and the smell of fresh tea coming from the kitchenette across the hall. Other boys were mulling around with bags in hand same as them, and even more were in the common room, greeting friends and exchanging stories of their holidays.

All three boys peered into the main rooms as they went, just in case they could spot Sirius, but he was nowhere to be found on the dorm’s lower levels, so they trudged on to the stairs.

“You go on without me,” Peter moaned just as they reached the third floor landing. “I can’t do it anymore.” He dropped his trunks in the middle of the staircase, slumping over them dramatically.

“You’re not even the one carrying the stereo,” James quipped, ignoring his friend and continuing up the stairs.

“Is there no sympathy for a man who just lugged three trunks across the biggest campus in the Highlands?”

“Not when he’s blocking the stairs,” Remus said, gently nudging his friend in the heels until he got moving again.

The sight of their dorm room after two months away was as familiar now as that of Tomny’s flat. It wasn’t like his room at the estate, empty and wide and quiet. The walls were as bare as they’d left them last June and the room was clean and untouched but in less than twenty-four hours it’d be filled with pictures and posters and all the things he and his friends loved. Eventually there’d be dishes waiting by the door for someone to take them downstairs, and stray slacks and socks would begin to pile up on the floor until one of them—usually James—picked them up. There would be chatter and snores to fill the in between moments and of course there would be the boys those noises belonged to. It was something to look forward to. Usually.

“Dear god!” James groaned as he made his way into the room, dropping his trunks to wave a hand across his face and fend off the smell from the thick haze that had enveloped the room. “What’d you do, Black, hot-box our room with your grandmother’s moth balls?”

“No, I asked your mum for hers.” Jumping up from his bed eagerly, Sirius plucked a fat cigar from his lips and tapped its end on an ashtray he’d obviously nicked from the common room downstairs. “Alright, lads?”

“Alright!” James answered, as Remus lugged the rest of his things into the room. His chest burned so horribly that he had to stop to lean up against one of his bed posts, and even worse—it seemed as though seeing Sirius again had knocked more than a few ribs loose. Sirius had returned to school with a newly chiselled jaw, no longer that belonging to a growing boy but a man. His dark hair still curled just past that jawline and he’d gotten taller but somehow avoided the lanky-limb syndrome that plagued Remus. It was so bloody unfair.

In an attempt to break himself out of his daze, Remus coughed around the room’s smoke and sent himself into a spasm of pain while James and Sirius flew forward, grappling each other in a ferocious hug.

“You okay, Remus?” Peter croaked, still breathless and red in the face. Remus waved him off and clutched an arm across his tender ribs as he slid to the floor next to his trunks.

With a delightful yell James picked Sirius up off the ground and spun him, only releasing him once Sirius had caught his feet on one of his bed posts and pushed off it, nearly toppling them both. The cigar had been thrown halfway across the room, spilling ash everywhere, but their expressions remained like that of the sun after a spring storm, bright and elated; two brothers reunited after a bitter fate had sought to try to separate them.

Never wanting to be left out, Peter surged forward to receive a hug of his own, one that was just as vigorous and ended with Sirius grinding his knuckles into the top of the poor boy's head for good measure. As Peter wailed and batted at him, Sirius looked over and finally noticed Remus, still sprawled among his trunks and trying not to wince. The smile he gave him was only that of amusement at first—like a kid who’d discovered a toy he’d forgotten about—but like everyone else so far, the shock and realisation dawned as he got a better look at Remus’ face.

“Fucking hell.” Releasing Peter, Sirius leapt forward and dropped down into a squat, staring like he was watching a monkey in a zoo. “What chewed you up and spat you out again?”

Sirius reached out as though he might grasp him by the chin, but he was already too close and Remus felt more aware of the other boy than he normally was. He smacked Sirius’ hand away and cleared his throat before answering; “It was an accident.”

Sirius clicked his tongue in judgement. “This the reason why you ignored my letters all summer then?”

“Knew you wouldn’t let that one go.”

“ ‘Course not.” Sirius bit his lip over a smile, the expression almost endearing.

Almost.

“So, you bloody lunatic,” he continued, “what the hell did you do?”

“It was a football accident,” Remus said, enunciating each syllable. “Sorry to say I won’t be trying out for the team this year either.”

Sirius snorted but finally fell back and popped up to his feet, extending an arm to help him up. Remus took it and stood up, straightening his shirt.

“You got taller,” Sirius said once they were both standing, squinting at him a bit.

“So did you.”

“Yeah but you’re going to have to duck to get through doorways soon, you giant.”

“And you’ll have to turn sideways just to fit that fat head through them,” James chimed in, opening the window between his and Sirius’ beds to air out some of the cigar smoke.

“Probably true,” Sirius said, before licking his lips and slowly extending his arms out to the side like he was waiting for a hug. It took Remus all of three seconds before he realised he was expecting a hug from him.

“C’mon,” he said wryly, “the least you can do after ignoring me all summer is give a little cuddle.”

Remus shook his head and slipped away. “I’m an injured man, keep your mitts off.”

“Aw, where you going, Moony? I’m not gonna hurt you!”

“That nickname isn’t funny anymore!”

“But touch is the language of love, Moony!”

“You speak enough languages for all of us, Black.”

Sirius let his arms clap back against his sides. “Fine. But one day when I’m dead and gone you’re going to regret not hugging me.”

“I would agree,” Remus said, dragging a trunk toward his bed, “but then we’d both be liars.”

After Sirius had put out the cigar he’d apparently stolen from his father’s office and the room was at least semi-breathable again, James and Peter began regaling them with tales of their joint summer. They’d spent most of it at their families’ neighbouring summer homes, located in some charming sea-side town in Devon. The two of them took turns narrating the same story, interjecting when the other forgot something or when they had a differing opinion on how a scene had played out. Having already unpacked the rest of his things, Sirius seemed content to listen to them yammer while setting up his stereo and turntable, the first thing that had emerged from James’ heavy trunks.

It was with great pride that Remus used the empty wall space over his side table to blu-tack the Queen poster Lee had presented him with in early July. Over his bed he pinned pictures of other bands like The Stones, Deep Purple, and of course The Who. Once he’d finished with the stereo Sirius came over to admire them.

“Looks great,” he said.

“But I’m still missing the best part,” Remus answered wryly, before leaning forward and tacking Sirius’ Shrieking Shack photograph to the wall for all to see. Sirius scoffed immediately and crossed his arms over his chest.

“Yeah well, you’re a bleeding hypocrite if you think any of these toffs are any less fruity than Bowie.”

Remus sighed. “If I throw a stick, will you chase it and leave me alone?”

“Do you have a stick?”

Remus shook his head and reached for the remaining posters on his bed. “Potter, Pete, here.” Unfolding them carefully, he proudly presented his friends with posters of their own—The Kinks for James and Cream for Peter, the latter of which had been hard to procure since the band had broken up before they’d even hit puberty. Remus was half-sure Lee had simply ripped it off a record shop’s wall.

“Think of them as belated birthday gifts,” he said as James and Peter shared giddy looks and thanked him.

“Here’s yours,” Remus said, handing Sirius his own poster. Sirius eyed him with a slightly raised brow before unrolling it.

“Oh, bless ya, Moony!” Turning, Sirius happily showed off Bowie’s Aladdin Sane image to the rest of them.

“Maybe his fruitiness will add some colour to the room,” Remus said as Sirius rushed to his side of the dorm to hang the poster up.

“You’re right, it does add some colour,” Sirius said, standing back to admire it.

“There’s also this.”

A little more shyly, Remus handed him the copy of The Count of Monte Cristo that Tonya had let him keep after the summer. She’d marked little notes into the margins of her favourite scenes and he’d yet to get tired of reading through them, but he knew Sirius would appreciate the story.

“Is it my birthday or something?” Sirius asked as he plucked the book from his hands and skimmed through its pages.

“It’s just ‘cause you liked Dumas’ other stuff,” Remus said, sticking his hands in his pockets.

“So what, you annotate your books now?”

“No, not me. It belonged to a friend.”

Sirius looked up, another perfect eyebrow raised; “Lily?”

“Er… no.”

“So vague.” Smiling a bit, Sirius closed the book and tapped its spine against the centre of Remus’ chest. “Can’t wait to read it. Cheers.”

Nodding sheepishly, Remus turned away only to find James standing directly behind him with a stack of records in his hands and a sly grin on his face.

“Five quid says he doesn’t read it.”

“I read!” Sirius huffed. “More than you anyway, you thick jock.”

Snatching the albums from him, Sirius set them down on his bed with the rest of his collection before setting a vinyl up on the turntable and dropping its needle onto the surface. Remus recognised the opening beat of Diamond Dogs before Bowie had so much as uttered his first line, and Sirius smirked back at him, winking while they listened and enjoyed the company of friends they’d been missing all summer.

“Moony, want to help me organise these?” Sirius asked, turning back to the pile of albums scattered about his bed.

Remus looked back. “What am I, your maid?”

“So you won’t do it?”

“Ugh… move over, tosser.”





* * *





The rumours about the muggings, the unfortunate fencing mishap, and even the Ibiza helicopter accident could’ve all been tolerated, but Mary’s pestering about the secret BDSM sex cult that practiced knife throwing in the nude was really beginning to weighing on Remus’ mental well-being. Of course he’d been expecting all of it—not many well-to-do kiddies returned to school looking like they’d lost a knife-fight with a blind bag lady—but he would’ve at least thought the rumours would have remained more grounded in reality. The truth might’ve been less surprising to the general student body than some of the other things that were being said, but Remus wasn’t quite that desperate yet.

Despite her riveting summer spent travelling around the country’s coastline while her parents compiled a new reference guide on seaside flora and her older sister Petunia hogged the phone to dial-up her boyfriend, Lily’s newest impassioned topic of interest became Remus’ face the moment she’d laid eyes on him. He could hardly fault her for it though—everyone stared, though Remus actually had to give it to Crouch for coming up with ‘scarface’ and ‘scratching post’ all on his own.

“Remus, please just tell me what happened,” she begged, leaning down over her breakfast and attempting to look him in the eye. They were sitting with James on one end of their usual dining hall table while the rest of their friends compared beginning-of-term homework lists on the other and Mary gave Sirius his first manicure of the year.

Expertly avoiding Lily’s gaze, Remus continued spooning the bran cereal he’d mistakenly picked up in the cafeteria line-up into his mouth. He’d already had to pour enough sugar into it to make James grimace just to make the taste bearable. “I told you,” he mumbled, mouth full, “football accident. Broke my nose.”

“That’s rubbish,” Lily snapped, astute as always. “You hate football. And you look like you got hit by a bus.”

“Your love really knows no bounds, Evans.”

James leaned in to interrupt, looking at Lily rather pointedly; “Daisy, just let the man be.”

“You butt out,” Lily instructed, blazing past the nickname that made Remus momentarily pause his cereal-spooning in surprise. “All summer and not a single phone call—I didn’t even know if you were coming back. Then you show up looking like this. Now I want the truth,” she ordered, “or I’ll… I’ll give you detention!”

The corners of Remus’ mouth turned up. “Sounds like abusing your prefect-powers, Evans.”

“And here I thought Remus was the only one immune to your viciousness,” James added, sharing in his entertainment.

“Secrets hurt people,” Lily whined. “Just look at his nose!”

Remus pushed away his empty cereal bowl. “Well, my nose doesn’t hurt anymore, however my feelings are certainly taking a beating.”

Lily gave him a glare that said she’d very much like to prolong said beating, but relented and finished her own breakfast in grudging silence.

“Want some more tea?” James asked her eventually.

Lily nodded. “One sugar, please.”

“I know. Fancy a cuppa, Lupin?”

“Yeah, four—”

“You’re getting two,” James said, snatching his mug and standing up.

“Like the bloody sugar police,” Remus grumbled as James crossed the dining hall. Lily turned around in her seat as he did, chewing on her thumb nail absent-mindedly. Watching her, a suspicious feeling began to bloom in Remus’ gut and after a few seconds he rapped his spoon on the table top, making Lily jump and spin around again.

“Nice view?” He drawled.

Lily’s eyebrows knit together in the centre. “What?”

“I asked if you liked the view.”

“What view?”

“Of Potter’s arse.”

Lily turned beet-red. “Don’t be ridiculous. He has a stain on his trousers, that's all. I was going to tell him when he got back.”

“Oh, of course."

"He did!"

"Yeah, okay. And this ‘Daisy’ stuff? What’s that about?”

“It’s just a stupid nickname. He does it because he knows it bothers me, that’s all.”

“Mhm, sure.”

“I will give you detention.”

Before she could make good on her threat, Sirius dropped down on the bench in James’ spot and clapped his hands to the top of the table, fingers splayed and painted in a pattern of red and black.

“It’s some of Macdonald’s best work!” He declared, grinning. “And look!”

With one hand, Sirius pointed to his eyes, and Lily’s eyebrows rose to her hairline.

“Is that eyeliner?”

“Yeah! Mary did it like hers,” Sirius said, looking extremely pleased. Between that, the nail polish, the earring, and the silver chain tucked just under his collar that Sirius had apparently taken to wearing over the summer, he looked about as close to a rock star as Remus had ever seen him.

“Why are you wearing eyeliner?” Lily asked.

“ ‘Cause it’s cool,” Sirius said, snootily. “Jagger wears it.”

“Does Jagger wear it at eight in the morning on his way to organic chemistry?”

“I’m not even sure Jagger would know what organic chemistry is,” Remus said, finding his voice for the first time since Sirius had sat down. The dark-haired boy smirked back at him and a moment later James slid in next to Remus with three cups of tea in hand, organising them on the table in front of himself. Finally he glanced up at Sirius and gave an impressed smile.

“Well, don’t you look spiffing.”

“See,” Sirius drawled, rolling his head toward Lily, “at least someone can appreciate true artistry.”

“Slughorn’s going to write you up for sure,” Lily said, shaking her head as she reached for her tea. Remus noted with slight amusement that she was smiling though.

“Nah. Blind bat would have to stop his fluttering and focus on my face for longer than three seconds to do that.”

“At least he remembers your name. He called Davey, ‘Mr. Crumpet’ the other day.”

“That’s not even close to ‘Gudgeon’,” Remus said.

Sirius smirked. “It’s ‘cause he can’t be bothered to remember anyone’s name outside of his silly club.”

“So what does he call you?” Remus asked. “ ‘Mr. White’?”

“Just ‘Black’ actually. James and I got the notice at the end of last year—an invite into Sluggy’s inner circle.”

James nodded, and Lily’s mouth dropped open. “No way. Both of you got an invite to the Slug Club?” She narrowed her eyes at James, who gave a sorry smile and a shrug.

“It was supposed to be a surprise?” He said in a guilty voice.

Remus, who was thankful every day that he did not take chemistry, peered at them questioningly; “Not to be dim or anything but what the bloody-fuck’s a ‘Slug Club’?”

“It’s Professor Slughorn’s private chemistry group,” Lily explained. “It’s as close as we’ll get to an official academic association before university and it’s very good to have on applications, especially Oxford and Cambridge since he taught there.”

“Yeah, well I don’t plan on filling out any of those,” Sirius said, examining his manicure.

“So you’re not going?” Lily asked.

“No, I’ll go.”

“Why does that sound suspicious?”

It was impossible for any of them to miss the look that passed between Sirius and James, and Remus answered for them; “Because it is.”

As James lifted his tea to his lips, Lily gave a groan and opted to do the same rather than prolong the conversation. Before Remus could reach for his own, Sirius stretched across the table and scooped up the last mug.

“Just think about it this way, Evans,” he started, waving the cup around, “you’ve got two of Hawkings’ finest by your side every club meeting, though I do warn you that I plan to marry Potter for his money, so you’d better back off.”

Both Lily and James coughed into their tea and Sirius smugly sipped his own before gagging and nearly dropping the cup. “Fucking hell Moony, your taste in tea really is murder.”





* * *





Thursday 9th September 1976

Peter wasn’t very happy to hear that they’d lifted the headphones from the AV room the year before, but they were already one week into the school year and Sirius’ musical habits were definitely starting to get old. It had taken some convincing on Remus’ part, but once Sirius had progressed to playing The Zombies’ “Tell Her No” on repeat just to be annoying, Peter had finally caved.

“Here,” he said, emerging from the AV room with a pair of headphones in hand. He passed them to Sirius, who strung them around his neck happily.

“It’s more for our benefit than his, Pete,” Remus promised, as Peter locked the door behind himself.

“I’m still distinctly under the impression that you lot won’t miss one measly set of speakers,” Sirius said, casually holding his hands behind his head.

“Your stereo is loud enough on its own!” Peter snapped, making a point of ensuring that the door was locked tightly behind them. Sirius blew his tongue at him as they all turned down the hall and made their way out of the building. Outside, other students were mulling around, taking in the remaining summer heat and enjoying themselves before the term’s inevitable worries of homework, tests, and studying set in.

“Seems like kind of a shame though,” James surmised as they emerged onto the pavement; “I mean, waiting for Halloween to have any fun?”

“You’re as bad as Sirius,” Peter huffed. “We’re not playing more Led Zeppelin in church—Francis would never believe me a second time!”

“Get your knickers out of a knot, Pete,” Sirius scoffed. “Playing the same joke two years in a row would be shameful. There’s got to be something we can pull out of our four gobs that’ll kick off the year right.”

“Didn’t you already ask Bobby to make us more fireworks?” James asked.

“Oh, because those turned out so great the last time,” Remus groaned.

“Really Moony, between you and Pete I don’t know which is the worse stick in the mud,” Sirius said, letting out a yawn just as they passed Castle Hall. Suddenly he slammed to a halt in the middle of the pavement, letting Remus walk right into him.

“Oi, watch where you’re—”

“When was the last time either of you lot paid a visit to our dear Headmistress?” Sirius asked out of the blue. Following his gaze to the top of Castle Hall’s staircase, Remus spotted Headmistress McGonagall talking to a few teachers.

“She called me in early last year,” he answered.

“And I had to talk to her about the team’s trip to the tournament,” James added, “but Lily visits her office all the time for prefect’s stuff.”

Remus smirked a little at the back of Sirius’ head. “I’m sorta surprised she didn’t haul you in last year, Sirius. You know, after that red mark in History. I thought the Blacks were supposed to be perfect in everything.”

Sirius turned around, looking scandalised. “Is that our Remus Lupin, bragging?”

“Can’t be,” James agreed.

Remus shrugged innocently. “What was it you said last year, Black? ‘Every dog’s allowed an off-day’?”

“Well, it might interest you to know that I didn’t actually fail that exam,” Sirius mused, equally as innocent.

A moment of silence passed between all of them, then; “What?”

“The kid who sat behind Potter and I—Langston Hobbs—he paid me to take the test for him so he’d pass the class. He wrote my name on the top of his exam while I wrote his name on mine. It was good money too, more than enough for a few drinks at some dingy Scottish pub show.”

There went the metaphorical rug, and Remus began to piece everything together. “So… your poor mark…”

“Yup.”

“And… the money at the end of the year…”

“Uh-huh.”

“And my beating you in history…”

“Mhm.” Sirius looked back at Remus, his expression so smug it was sour. “You actually beat Langston, not me. Sorry, Moons.”

It took a clap on the back from James to stir Remus out of his stunned silence. Once his daze was broken, he let out an incredulous laugh. “You fucking wanker! You let me believe I actually beat you in a class for a whole summer?”

“Maybe if you’d written me back I would’ve had time to fess up.”

Never underestimate a Black.

“What a bitch,” Remus said to James and Peter, who were sniggering at the both of them. “I’m gonna get you,” he swore. “This year all bets are off.”

“Bring it on, Lupin,” Sirius said. “But in the meantime, how up to snuff are your lock-picking skills?”

Instantly sobered of his humour, Peter moaned; “Lord have mercy.”

But the plan had already been hatched; Remus could tell from a single that the practical joke gears were already turning inside Sirius’ skull.

“What are you thinking, Black?” James asked, kicking his ankles playfully.

“Nothing,” Sirius said simply, “just that McGonagall must be feeling lonely after a whole summer apart from all her favourite students. Maybe we should pay her office a little visit? You know, like any good group of Hawkings students…”



Chapter End Notes

Rummy is a card game.

A 'bag lady' is a homeless [woman] who carries her belongings around in various bags.

Really excited to give you the next chapter. Pranks are the best to write ^^





Chapter 32: Prongs


Chapter Summary

The boys do some good ol' fashioned breaking n' entering. 'Prongs' is born.



Chapter Notes

Impulsively posting this because it's a fun chapter, enjoy!



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Band on the run, band on the run,

And the jailer man and sailor Sam,

Were searching everyone;

For the band on the run, band on the run,

For the band on the run…



- “Band on the Run” Wings, 1973



Castle Hall was imposing enough during the daytime with its stone columns and endless front steps, but come nightfall the building really took after its namesake, appearing as a daunting stone palace that looked as though it housed more than a few blood-sucking creatures. Situated at the very heart of Hawkings’ campus, the only building older than the hall was the church itself, which had been built before the boarding school for Britain’s most well-to-do children had even been conceptualised. The only modern-looking thing about it was the flat roof, which made for very good pranking as far as Sirius was concerned.

“It always looks so creepy,” James said as they skirted around the bushes lining the driveway and made their way up the pavement.

“I think I saw someone in the window!” Peter whimpered, pointing to one of the old stained-glass windows. All the windows were sitting dark, as the hall normally was past sundown.

“Pretty sure it was just your torch’s reflection, Pete,” Remus said. Peter looked down at the metal flashlight in his hand and clicked it off for good measure.

“No one’s around, you ninny,” Sirius hissed, the first one on the steps and zipping up them with about as much energy as a jackrabbit on dexys.

Peter scowled after him bitterly. “If Filch catches us I’m letting him skin you first.”

All four of them went up the stairs together, their trainers scuffing across the stone until they made it to the top flagstones. Bending down in front of one of the double doors, Remus snapped his fingers at Sirius until he handed him the hairpins.

“You think Mary’s going to start noticing she’s missing a few of these?” He asked, bending them into the right shape before sliding the bits of metal into the lock.

“Nah,” Sirius said, leaning back against the wall next to him and clicking the spring of his lighter; “girls always have an endless supply of ‘em.”

“Yeah but you plucked those ones right out of her hair today,” James mused.

“I know. Thought she was going to murder me when her hair puffed up like that.”

James and Sirius shared a cheeky fist-bump before James turned his back to the front doors while he kept watch of the front lawn. Peter did the same, though he appeared distinctly more nervous about the whole affair; it was one thing to break into an empty church or his own AV room after hours, another to bust into the Headmistress’s office when anyone could just happen upon them.

The thrill should’ve bothered him—he didn’t have time to spend another month in detention if he was going to beat Sirius come exam time—but Remus was too delighted by the idea of the prank to care all that much for nerves. It was a simple task really, apart from the manual labour, and no one would get hurt so even if they were caught the punishment couldn’t be that bad. Right?

“Jesus, Lupin, I thought you said you were an expert on breaking and entering?” Sirius huffed when Remus failed to get the door open after several minutes.

“I never said anything about being an expert,” he shot, “you just always assume whatever’s most convenient! Why don’t you stop your whinging and get me some light?”

Instead of reaching for Peter’s torch, Sirius bent down next to him and clicked the lighter on, holding it next to the door handle where he was working. It was a pathetic attempt but Remus knew without even seeing his face that he was just being an ass anyway.

“Should we try another way in?” James suggested, turning to peer over Remus’ shoulder. “There’s gotta be a back door right?”

“There is but it leads down into the boiler room, and the door up to the rest of the building is locked from the other side,” Remus answered.

“What’d you do, go around trying every door on campus?” Asked Sirius.

“No… maybe.” Clumsily, Remus’ fingers slipped and he lodged one of the pins deep into the lock, jamming it instantly. “Shit,” he cursed, trying to wrench it free only to be thwarted by the sweat that had collected in his palms.

“Let me.” Ushering him out of the way, Sirius grasped the door handle and the end of the pin. He yanked hard but the metal was slippery and didn’t give.

“Here,” James said, trying his best to get the pin out.

Peter chuckled, slapping his palm with the head of his torch. “How many lads does it take to get a pin out of a lock?”

“Two less than it takes to whoop you one, Pete,” Remus quipped, standing up to give his knees a break while James continued to work at the stuck lock. Taking a moment to wonder if he might have a chance at the lock in the boiler room, Remus stepped up to the other door and grasped the handle, turning it. “Do we have another pin—?”

There was a crisp click and the door opened, falling toward Remus as James and Sirius stared in shock.

“It’s fucking open?” Peter cried. “You mean you didn’t even check to see if it was locked in the first place?"

Sirius shot upwards, clapping Remus on the shoulder. “Good job, Moony. Knew you’d get the job done!”

“Bunch of numpties, you lot are!” Peter grumbled as they all slipped inside, leaving the stuck pin behind. “Is no one even slightly worried over why the front door might be unlocked in the first place?”

“If I see anyone, I’ll ask,” Sirius said, making his way down the hall and toward the main staircase.

“There could still be teachers around!”

“It’s nearly midnight,” Remus whispered. “I doubt anyone’s around.”

“And if they are, Pete, you were just saying earlier that you needed help with some homework!” James finished, patting his friend comfortingly on the back.

While Peter used a harsh whisper to outline the impracticability of asking for help with maths during a break-in, they made their way up the stairs, trying their best to keep their footsteps quiet on the ancient staircase.

“Maybe time to cut back on the cigs, hey Moony?” James teased as they made it to the top and Remus stopped to muffle a cough with his elbow. It made his chest twinge and he leaned against the railing for support while his friends stopped to wait for him.

“If I did, you lot would just badger me until I got more,” he rasped. “Bunch of chain-smoking drunkards, you are.”

Sirius flicked his zippo on and off as he waited at the top of the stairs. “Messers, tramps, numpties, chain-smoking drunkards, what do you figure’s next? The Three Musketeers?”

“There’s four of us,” Peter pointed out.

“Read a book, Pete?” Remus sighed, before finishing the rest of his climb and emerging at the top of the staircase next to Sirius. “But alright, I’ll indulge you. Which Musketeer are you then?”

Even in the darkness of the hallway he could see the cheeky glint in Sirius’ eye. “Obviously I’m D’Artagnan. None of you are romantic enough to carry an entire story.”

“I call Athos then,” James chimed, making Sirius nodded in agreement.

“Pete’s obviously Porthos, and you my dear Moony, simply scream Aramis. I just know you’re waiting to run out on us, you sneaky bastard.”

“Okay, walk on then, you poof,” Remus scoffed.

“What, don’t tell me you’re offended? You know I’m right!”

Rather than answering him, he gave Sirius a little shove that had him nearly tumbling over a decorative chair left outside an office doorway. It was amusing to watch the normally graceful Sirius catch himself on the seat of the chair and bounce back, knocking into a hutch set next to the chair and almost toppling the vase of fresh flowers sitting on top. James caught it at the last second and Sirius straightened up, shoving Remus gently in return while they cackled.

"That was very graceful, Black, good show," Peter snickered.

"I try," Sirius scoffed lightly, shooting a squinted smile in Remus' direction.

Once they’d staunched their laughter and James returned the vase to its rightful spot they continued on to the end of the hall, stopping outside the Headmistress’s office.

“I’ve always wondered what ‘O.M. First Class’ meant,” James said, peering at the plaque next to the door.

“Well, maybe you can ask the old bird herself.” Reaching up, Sirius grasped the heavy, lion-shaped door knocker and slammed it down onto its base—once, twice, three times. Each bang echoed down the dim hallway, making the rest of them seize up in alarm. They were all deadly silent for a long moment after, just waiting for the sound of footsteps or an office door being opened. When nothing came, three pairs of shoulders slouched with relief.

“It’s like you want us to be caught!” Peter hissed, and just Sirius winked as he grasped the door handle. It fell open under his grip, also unlocked.

“Pete,” he started, as though he were lecturing a child, “we’re going to be lifting half of her furniture and leaving it on the roof—if you haven’t already prepared yourself for the chance of being caught then you’re not a proper Musketeer.”

Stepping inside the grand office, Sirius waited until they’d all filed in before taking Peter’s torch and lighting up the room. The air was warm to the point of being stuffy but smelt softly of freshly cooked biscuits, with various novelty items, odd plants, and heavy books crowding every surface.

“Isn’t much one for interior design, is she?” Peter said, staring into the face of the grandfather clock leaning up against the wall closest to him. As if on cue, the clock struck midnight and Peter flew backward into James who had to clap a hand over his mouth to keep from laughing. Delighted, Sirius began to trail a hand over the red velvet sofa in the middle of the sitting area.

“Oh I don’t know,” he said happily, once the chiming had ceased, “it sorta looks like our salon back home, only with more… ambiance? No—character.”

Remus glanced at the fireplace and imagined throwing a record into a lit fire, watching it melt and smoke and fill the room with the scent of burnt plastic. If he’d written back to that letter of Sirius’ he might’ve told him to put Walburga’s curtains in the flames for good measure, or smash her best china. No album deserved such a nasty end—not even disco.

“Barely any dust though,” James said, standing on the opposite side of the room and trailing his fingers over one of the bookshelves, rubbing them together.

“Someone’s been cleaning,” Peter observed, pointing his torch at a small trolley of cleaning supplies on the far side of the room.

“We’re not moving all of it, right?” Remus asked, lifting a small snow globe off of the table in front of the fireplace.

“No, just enough for it to be noticeable,” Sirius said, testing the weight of an armchair.

“Good, because that desk must weigh a thousand pounds,” James said, pointing further into the office. Sirius followed his line of sight and nodded slyly.

“Moony, think you can work on getting the door to the roof open?”

“If it’s not already open,” Peter scoffed.

Remus set the globe down. “Yeah I can do it.”

Plucking another pin from his own hair this time, Sirius tossed it to him and he fumbled to catch it in the dark, looking away before he started staring at the way Sirius’ dark waves tumbled down over his pale forehead.

Leaving his friends to take stock of the room, Remus borrowed the torch and crept down the quiet hallway by himself. He made it to the short staircase that led up to the little doorway letting out onto the roof and bent down in front of it, getting to work. The door was indeed locked but he managed to get it open in decent time—Take that, Black—and after a quick peek out onto the roof, Remus made his way back to the office and slipped inside, shutting the door behind himself. Rather than casing the room for furniture that could be hauled up to its new home, he found Sirius sitting on top of the desk with several file folders in hand while James slouched back in McGonagall’s leather chair, spinning around and staring at the ceiling as though he were intentionally trying to make himself sick. Peter was lounging on the sofa in front of the fireplace, chin propped up against one hand and half-asleep already.

Remus cleared his throat; “Thought we were moving stuff out, not moving ourselves in.”

“We’re just taking a little break before the back-busting work begins,” Sirius said, licking his thumb before flipping the page in the file he was reading. “Barty Crouch really is a bloody idiot. Who fails art in year ten? Oh, wait—his final project was a collage of nudie magazine clippings. That’s actually kind of funny.”

“I want to see,” Peter said, jumping up and joining James over Sirius’ shoulders, leaving the sofa’s pillows significantly skewed.

“Oh! And here’s his dad’s phone number. How do you reckon he’d react if someone from the Communist Party of Great Britain called looking to 'thank Barty for his ongoing support'?”

I live with highly educated idiots, Remus thought as he went to right the pillows, keenly aware that they were only there to leave things a mess in the first place. As he sorted out the cushions the same cat statue he’d seen on the fireplace’s mantle when he first arrived in the Headmistress’s office caught his eye—only now there were two of them. An unperfect pair, the first cat was a striped grey and distinctly tall and noble in appearance while the second appeared the colour of dust and little more than a shaggy skeleton in the dim light of the room. Though unlike the other statue its eyes were distinctly lifelike, catching the light of Peter’s torch as he waved it about the room.

“Oi, guys look what I found.”

Leaving the cats in peace, Remus crossed the office to join his friends as Sirius pulled another file from the cabinet behind McGonagall’s desk.

“Who’s is that?” James asked, looking up from a different file—his own.

“Evans’,” Sirius grinned, using the file to fan himself as James launched himself to his feet.

“You should put that one back.”

Sirius gawped. “Put it back—don’t you want to know what dirt McGonagall’s got on your favourite ginger?”

James shook his head firmly. “Nope, don’t need to.”

“Why not?”

" 'Cause!"

" 'Cause'? Are you joking?"

Remus reached over Sirius and snatched the file from his hand. “Leave Lily out of your pranks. I thought we had a job to do?”

Sirius rolled his eyes. “You two really need to stop licking the bottom of Evans’ boots.”

“Can we just get on with this?” James blagged.

“Yeah, it’s school tomorrow,” Peter added, stifling another yawn.

After a bit more griping from Sirius they returned the files to what they hoped were the right places and began to move about the room, sliding things closer to the door as quietly as they could. Carrying their heavy loads, they made their way down the hallways one by one and from there, up onto the roof, which was open to the stars and without any light at all. The only other way off the roof was a fire escape leading down to the ground at the back of the building, which was so old they couldn’t tell if it was painted red or just entirely rusted over.

“Watch the pipes,” James warned, carefully stepping over a vent while carrying a potted plant in his arms. Of course Remus immediately got his foot caught, going to the ground in attempts to save the lamp he was carrying.

“Fuck,” he hissed, as his friends stifled laugher behind their shirt sleeves.

“S'like a newborn giraffe,” Sirius mocked, helping him to his feet.

A half-hour later, and they’d managed to move almost half of the office’s contents up to the roof. Remus did his best to keep his feet under him, which was easier said than done after Sirius had decided that the sofa would be next.

“Knew we should’ve made Potter lift this one,” Sirius grunted, holding the bottom end as Remus walked backward up the roof’s stairs.

“He’s sorting the desk!” Remus reminded him, slumping at the top of the stairs to catch his breath.

“They always make it look so easy on TV. Just a cut-to and all the furniture’s sitting pretty on the roof.”

“Less lip and more lift,” Remus ordered, wiping the sweat from his forehead before grabbing hold of the bottom of the couch once more. His ribs were screaming but it would’ve felt like too much of a pansy excuse if he told his friends about the full-extent of his injuries in the middle of a prank. And that would just lead to more questions he didn’t care to answer.

After a bit more grunting and griping, the two boys finally set the sofa down in the middle of the roof, listening to the tiny gravel crunch under their feet.

“Just give me a second,” Remus huffed. He collapsed onto the sofa and dropped his head back while slinging an arm over his eyes, gritting his teeth to stave off the pain. A moment later he felt a gentle kick at the sole of his trainer before the sofa dipped and he lifted his arm back to find Sirius next to him, staring up at the sky.

“You see that star, the really bright one?” He pointed up, and Remus squinted before nodding. The star seemed to twinkle with a dozen different colours, blinking like it was watching them back. “The Egyptians associated that star with at least a dozen gods,” Sirius continued. “They used it to mark their New Year and built temples and pyramids aligned to its rising and falling. They call it the Morning Star, because you can see it best at dawn. Wanna guess its other name?”

Remus frowned. “Something Egyptian?”

“No,” Sirius laughed, “Sirius. I’m named after that star.”

Remus squinted more, though he didn’t have to. The star was brighter than anything else for miles. Not even the busy city lights of London would’ve been able to drown it out. “Suddenly the insufferable god-complex makes much more sense,” he said.

“I’ll push you off the roof,” Sirius quipped.

“I’ll take you with me.”

Chuckling, Sirius readjusted himself on the sofa and propped his feet up on McGonagall’s matching ottoman. As he did his hand just barely brushed Remus' pinky, but Sirius didn’t seem to notice. “Everyone in my family’s named after some star or whatever. Just another stupid tradition to rope us in. Reg’s got two stars actually, and Andy’s got an entire galaxy out there.”

“Sounds like you’ve been chipped then. I mean, only one star? That's chump change.”

Sirius glanced over sharply, smiling. “Rich coming from a guy whose name is essentially ‘Wolf Wolf’.”

“Dickhead,” Remus chuckled, looking down at his hands. When he glanced back up again Sirius’ eyes were on the sky and he was bobbing his head, quietly humming a tune just for the two of them;

“Hmm… Hmm… 'Star baby… flashy little shiny little two timin’ mama singin’… Star baby—shiny little flashy little lovin’ machine…' " Pressing his chin to his shoulder, Sirius smiled to himself. “That’s the only bit I know, but I think The Who got it right with that one.”

Remus punched him lightly in the shoulder. “That’s The Guess Who, you numpty. Thought you were supposed to be a musician.”

“Ow, Moony!” Sirius moaned, half-laughing. “I was only kidding.”

“Then that bruise is your own fault.” Remus stood up and flexed his sides gingerly. “C’mon, I’m tired and this mess was your idea, so see it through.”

“Ooh—yes, sir.”

Sirius popped up from the sofa and together they crossed back to the stairs, taking them two at a time until they’d made it back into the hall. It was still quiet, but by the time they’d made it back to the office they could hear Peter’s familiar whining.

“You nob, we weren’t supposed to break anything!”

Stepping inside, Remus immediately spotted the deer in the headlights on the other side of the office—or more accurately, he saw James clutching the stag’s head that should’ve been hanging over McGonagall’s desk, while Peter shone an accusatory torch on him.

“Oops,” James said, holding the deer in one hand and the plaque it normally hung on in the other.

“You two destroying personal property now?” Sirius called, scampering over to the desk to join him.

“It’s hollow inside!” Squinting in the light of Peter’s torch, James peered down into the stag’s head before tipping it back and dropping it down over his shoulders like a Halloween mask. It looked ridiculous—the body of a boy with a full snout and antlers to boot—which meant everyone was laughing instantly, even Remus.

“It suits you, Pot,” Sirius said, reaching up to pet James’ furry nose; “Snug fit?”

“Yeah,” James said, voice muffled by the mask as he swung his head back a bit and nearly took out a row of books on the shelf behind him. “Bloody stinks in here too.”

“What does it smell like?” Peter asked.

“Like plastic and death.”

Sirius grabbed hold of one of the antlers. “I wanna try.”

“Hold on, I’m not done yet. Anyone got a camera?”

Shaking his head hopelessly, Remus glanced about the room. So far they’d managed to move the sofa, its matching ottoman, two side tables, a floor lamp, several random bits and baubles, and even the fireguard screen from in front of the fireplace. They didn’t have much hope in hell of moving the desk, he figured, but at least when the Headmistress returned to her office the next morning she’d definitely notice something was off.

While the others continued to amuse themselves by testing how high James could reach with his antlers (he knocked several books off of the bookshelves doing this, but Sirius seemed to have just as much fun catching them as they fell), Remus turned back to the fireplace. For the most part all of the furniture that could be moved by them alone was already up there, and he didn’t fancy messing with the student records and shelves of paperwork—that would just be making a mess no one would be laughing at. A few more bits and bobs though, now that couldn’t hurt.

Using an empty magazine rack, Remus piled several more things into his arms before remembering the cat statues—or rather, the statue. When he went to retrieve them he found only one left; the noble, grey tabby. Scooping it up, he tucked it into the crook of his arm before turning to the door. He’d only just gotten it open when he looked up to the wall shelf hanging above it and nearly dropped everything he was carrying as he gasped in alarm.

The second scraggly little statue was there, resting on the top of the shelf like a little spy and staring down at them with those glowing eyes.

Remus turned, his heart still hammering in his chest. “Who left the—”

“Watch the antlers, Potter!” Sirius cried, moving around the desk as James followed him, arms outstretched as he stumbled along blind. In an attempt to steer clear of him, Sirius crashed into Peter, who went down with a great ‘omph', letting his torch skitter across the floor and momentarily blind Remus as it spun to a stop in his direction.

“Bunch of toffs,” Remus mumbled, turning his face away as yellow spots filled his vision. He reached for the statue, thinking it was best to take the pair together. Only, he hadn’t expected it to reach back.

Quick as lightning, the cat extended a single paw and swatted at him, hissing as it left three long claw marks across the back of his hand. The noise of surprise that left Remus’ mouth was more akin to a dying goat than a sixteen year-old boy. He leapt back from the door, nearly dropping everything he was holding while two boys and a stag turned toward him in shock.

“It’s alive!” He exclaimed. “I-I mean—it’s a cat!”

Retrieving his torch, Peter raised the light to where Remus was pointing and paled instantly.

“Oh shit—it’s Mrs. Norris,” he squeaked as the feline licked her lips.

“Who?” Remus demanded.

“Filch’s cat!”

“And just what kind of freaky cat doesn’t fucking move when you’re staring right at it?”

Suddenly Remus heard a voice echo up from the stairs through the open door ahead of him.

“Mrs. Norris, are you up there my sweet?”

“No!” Sirius called in a high-pitched voice, making every one of his friends—including James the deer—turn toward him in horror. At least he had the gall to look regretful.

"Oops."

“WHO’S UP THERE?”

“Time to go!” Peter yelped, rushing past all of them and out into the hall with his torch in hand. Desperately, Remus looked around for a place to get rid of the statue and the magazine rack before Sirius appeared at his side, taking half the load from him and tossing it aside with a loud clatter.

“You heard Pete,” He said. “Potter, come on!”

“It’s stuck!” James said, scrambling to get hold of the bottom of the deer head.

“What do you mean it’s stuck—stop playing around.”

“I’m not!”

As Sirius grabbed hold of the antlers to yank the taxidermy head off his best friend’s real one, Remus went to the door. He could hear the heavy thumps of Filch’s footsteps coming up the stairs while he continued wailing at them.

“Blimey, it really is on there,” Sirius grunted, yanking with both hands now.

“Ow! You’re going to break my glasses. And my face!”

“WHERE ARE YOU, YOU LITTLE BUGGERS?” Filch roared, even closer now. Any second he’d emerge on the top of the landing and cut off their only escape.

Remus turned back around and grabbed Sirius by the shirt collar, yanking him toward the door. “Just bring it.”

“What?” James shouted, but it was already decided. Guided by Sirius’ hold on his antlers, he was dragged from the office and forced to keep up as they booked it down the hall, passing the staircase and Filch, whose torch light could already be seen flickering up from the floor below.

“I HEAR YOU! STUDENTS OUT OF BED! STUDENTS IN THE CORRIDOR!”

They made it to the stairs, where Peter was waiting and appeared about ready to faint. After shoving James through, Remus slammed the door behind them and emerged on the roof next to his friends.

“Now where do we go?” Peter moaned helplessly.

“The fire escape.” Sirius took off across the roof, still dragging James behind him and Remus and Peter followed. Avoiding the scattered bits of furniture, they swung themselves onto the rusty bit of metal, taking the stairs two at a time and nearly toppling onto each other in their urgency to escape. As if to announce their presence, James’ antlers ratted off every bar on the way down;

Ding-ding-ding-ding-ding-ding-d-d-d-d-ding!

“This is horrible!” He screeched. Following from behind, Remus briefly wondered if he was crying under his furry helmet.

“Shh—! Shut up, James!” Peter said.

”I can’t!”

“Fucking—STOP!” Sirius, the leader, slammed to a halt just at the bottom of the metal staircase, and Remus nearly took an antler to the eye as he crashed into James’ back.

“Why are we stopping?” Peter barked.

“Ran out of stairs.”

Looking over the edge, Remus saw that Sirius was right—the fire escape ended several feet off the ground over a small pit of gravel, probably to deter students from doing exactly what they’d caught themselves in.

“Some bloody emergency exit,” Peter moaned.

“WHEN I CATCH YOU I’M GONNA HANG YEH FROM THE CHURCH STEEPLE BY YER FRONT TEETH!”

They all looked up, apart from James, who was hooked on a hole in the grate of the stairs overhead. Remus almost thought he could see the light of Filch’s torch flitting around the sky. He didn’t think the headmistress would let Filch make good on his threats, but they’d also just finished moving most of her belongings up onto the roof.

“Are you gonna jump or not?” Remus hissed.

Sirius turned around to gape, before a tenuous smile split across his face. “Did I hear you right, Lupin? You said we should jump?”

“Unless you’d rather I push you.”

Unfazed, Sirius shrugged. “All for one and one for all, right?” He said, before launching himself off the bottom of the stairs. James thrust his arm out at the space his best friend had been occupying just a moment before, waving it around like he could catch him.

“Sirius?!”

“Bend your knees, Potter,” Remus said, before giving his friend a shove from behind. With a strangled wail, James toppled over the edge and before he could let himself look too long at the ground, Remus jumped after him. Surprisingly Peter wasted no time with his own free-fall and all four boys found themselves in one bruised pile at the bottom, half lying on each other as they wiggled to get free.

“Bloody hell, I think Prongs here got me,” Sirius moaned, holding his side as he rolled away from them and staggered to his feet. James did the same, though now missing an antler thanks to their crash-landing. The groan that came out of Remus as he flipped himself over and got to his feet would’ve made the rest of them wince had they not been nursing injuries of their own. At least the gravel had been round little stones and not like the nasty, gritty stuff that was on top of the roof.

A loud clanging came from above—Filch was banging his torch on the bars at the top of the fire escape.

“I HEAR YOU! YOU STAY RIGHT THERE!”

“Not bloody likely,” Peter chirped, scrambling in the stones and taking off across the lawn at a full sprint.

“You see that little bugger run?” Sirius said, still rubbing his ribs.

“No,” James said. “I can’t see ANYTHING!”

“Shut up!” Remus lashed, gathering hold of the remaining antler and giving a sharp tug. The head stuck firm, earning him only another grunt from James.

“WHERE ARE YOU?”

Remus released the antler, and tsked. “Guess you’re running home like that, Potter.”

”WHAT?! NO WAY!”

“Oh-ho-ho! Fuck yeah!” Sirius cried, shoving James forward and breaking into a run. Despite his dire straits, James dashed on and soon all three of them were taking off across the campus after Peter, Filch’s torch shining after them like a flimsy spotlight.

“GET BACK HERE!”

“Yes, yes, yes! Suck it Filch!” Sirius screamed as they ran, as though it had all been part of his plan all along. They took turns pushing the man-deer between them to make sure he stayed running in a straight line rather than veering off into a tree. It didn’t take long to catch up to Peter and eventually they all made it back to House Lane, collapsing onto the front lawn of their dorm as they wheezed and howled with laughter.

Well, all of them apart from James.

He was too busy crying under his new hat.



Chapter End Notes

A torch is a flashlight.

'Dexys' are slang for the stimulant drug, dextroamphetamine.

This chapter was suuuuper fun to write. One of my favourite to date, hope you enjoyed! And yes, The Who and The Guess Who are two different bands ;)





Chapter 33: Sheila


Chapter Summary

Remus' connection to Hawkings hits closer to home than he thought.



Chapter Notes
