Eleanor Rigby,

Picks up the rice in the church where a wedding has been,

Lives in a dream;

Waits at the window,

Wearing the face that she keeps in a jar by the door,

Who is it for?





All the lonely people,

Where do they all come from?

All the lonely people,

Where do they all belong?

- "Eleanor Rigby" The Beatles, 1966



Monday 20th September 1976

“So… what do you think?”

Remus lowered the notebook, eyebrows raised. “Mm? Oh, yeah. It’s… good. This part, ‘moon, star, acoustic guitar’, yeah that bit’s good…”

“It’s shit.”

“What? No. No… Well… Maybe… But not all of it.”

Huffing, Sirius gave a grumpy strum on his guitar, legs tucked up beneath him on his bed. Remus sat across from him on the floor, back pressed against the edge of James’ bed as he flipped through the notebook Sirius had kept with him over the summer. Like his letters promised, he’d been trying to write, but most of the songs ended up being a reflection of how being at home made him feel. Either horrendously gritty or intensely dark, with many that involved setting fire to the house or giving his mother a rather (gruesome) piece of his mind. Not all of it was terrible though—several of the lyrics had promise, and Remus quite liked the lines that went;

Loving you is how it feels to be done dirty,

Without you I was clear and now all I’ve got are all these worries;

I never asked for none of it,

But you were always generous,

‘Cause love and kind and worry are just so fucking effortless.

It felt like real rock and roll, or in the very least, melodramatic, which was Sirius’ favourite brand of rebellious sentiment anyway.

“Have you shown James?” He asked, turning the next page, which was mostly just a scribble of crossed out lines than anything else.

“No. I wanted you to be the first.”

“O-oh?” Remus’ licked his lips and forced a chuckle. “Why? ‘Cause it doesn’t matter what I think?”

Sirius looked up from his guitar very quickly. “No. ‘Cause you’re harder to impress. James is too nice. Even if it was all shit he’d never say so—but you would. Makes me want to work harder, I think.”

“Oh…” Remus suddenly found the scribbled page very interesting, staring down at it to avoid Sirius’ intense gaze.

“Besides, can’t hardly ever get the dumb idiot to slow down nowadays. Did you know that before you got back to the room, he blasted out of here so fast he didn’t even give himself time to dry his hair. Looked like he got hit by lightning.”

“So not much different from usual then?”

Sirius tossed his head back and forth a bit in cheeky consideration. “No, not by much. Gotta love him, that Prongs.”

“That’s your worst nickname yet,” Remus said, thinking back to the weekend before, when they’d nearly had to cut the stag head in half with a pair of kitchen scissors just to get James out of it. Now it hung on a peg inside their bathroom, looking distinctly worse for wear and now missing not only an antler as but one of its eyes as well. Despite that fact, Remus still felt like he was being watched every time he took a shower or did his business, but Sirius insisted on keeping the ugly thing as some sort of horrendous trophy.

“Does this mean you’re coming around to ‘Moony’?” Sirius asked.

“No—never. Not unless you want to be ‘Starman’.”

“Well—”

“Shut up, forget I said anything.”

“You’re no fun,” Sirius grumbled lightheartedly, before mercifully returning to his guitar. Remus smiled to himself and flipped to another page in the notebook. It only had four lines, like a fleeting thought Sirius put down on the page and immediately forgot about.

Couldn’t ring you,

Couldn’t swing you;

There’s too much distance,

Haven’t found that path of least resistance.

Because he was selfish, Remus immediately thought of Tomny. It had been nearly a month of school and there hadn’t been any attempts on making good of that promise they’d made to one another over the summer. They’d talked once while Remus was recuperating at home, but even then Tomny’s answers had been short and tame in comparison to the boy he’d used to be. Not Tonya though; halfway through the call she’d stolen the receiver from her boyfriend and regaled Remus of her everyday—which was pretty much the same from dawn till dusk, and yet somehow she still managed to make it sound fascinating.

There had been no word since then though, despite the fact that Remus double-checked that they had the dorm’s direct phone number and made Tomny swear to call before letting him hang up. Of course it made more sense for Remus to phone him first, but that felt a lot like plunging off the deep end, and he was half sure he’d rather take another spill off Castle Hall’s fire escape. Plus he felt indignant; Tomny was a big boy—he needed to make good on his own promises.

Sort of like him.

Now, he’d never actually promised to write over the summer, or even pick up the phone when James or Peter called, but he did commit to other things; like taking Sirius around London one day, and playing Hope’s records. And since he’d done neither…

There’s too much distance,

Haven’t found that path of least resistance…

“Sorry I never wrote,” Remus mumbled.

Sirius’ fingers stopped on the Rickenbacker’s strings; he’d been practising an Elton John song, one Remus only recognised thanks to Tonya’s affinity with the colourful musician.

“What do you mean you’re sorry?”

“I’m sorry I never wrote back,” Remus said, more firmly. “You wrote a lot—clearly, but I—”

“But you did write, Moony.”

Remus looked up. “Huh?”

Reaching for his guitar case, Sirius began sorting rifling through the small pocket on the lid. From between the countless music sheets he pulled out a small envelope, covered in with postage stamps and yellow expedited stickers. Sirius opened the envelope and pulled out the letter, unfolding it and clearing his throat.

“ ‘To Sirius, sorry I haven’t written much, summer’s been buzzy’—‘buzzy’ Moony, really?”

“Don’t!” Remus surged forward and tried to snatch the letter away, but Sirius just rolled backward on his bed, leaving the guitar abandoned between them like the Berlin Wall.

“Don’t be rude, Moony, I’m not done reading. Now where was I? Ah yes. ‘Sorry to hear about Reg’s dog—that is if you’ve already bumped it off. The garden is a good bet though, as long as—’”

“Give me that!” Remus climbed up onto the bed after him but Sirius was too quick, slipping off its end to bounce across the room.

“It’s not even embarrassing!” He insisted. “And look you made me lose my place again! Let’s see… ‘you write too much, Black.’ That’s funny coming from someone who can devour ‘War and Peace’ in a week.”

“I’ve never even read ‘War and Peace’! No one has!”

Sirius ignored him. “ ‘You’re lucky you haven’t seen any of the ‘Pops’—it’s all disco nowadays. I swear, if I have to hear ‘Shake Your Booty’ one more time I’ll put my foot through the telly’.”

Scrambling up from the bed, Remus chased after Sirius, who soared across Peter’s, keeping enough distance between them that he could still wave the letter back and forth like a dog with a bone.

“Why did you keep that in your bloody guitar case?” Remus demanded, reaching over the bed to swat at him. Sirius danced just out of reach, grinning like a hyena.

“To read it to you of course! Sort of thought I’d get the chance to do it with the other lads around, but I guess an audience of one is better than an audience of none—ooh, think that could be a lyric, Moony?”

“Sod off!” Remus threw himself over the bed for one last go, making his chest twinge in pain, but Sirius only cackled and ran around it, diving across James’ bed and upsetting the pile of laundry James had obviously neglected to put away before racing out of the room.

Hauling himself to his feet, Remus picked up one of the pillows he’d knocked off Peter’s bed and tossed it after Sirius with more force than was probably necessary—unfortunately he’d never had the best aim. The pillow sailed across the bedroom and slammed into the front of the stereo, making it clatter backward on the hutch. Both of the boys froze, almost afraid it would topple sideways from the collision, but by some miracle the hi-fi remained upright, and a moment later a faint click sounded as the tape inside the stereo came to life with a faint whirring.

‘Well, Annie’s pretty neat,

She always eats her meat;

And Joe is awful strong,

Bet your life he’s puttin’ us on;

Oh lordy!

Oh lordy!’

Remus couldn’t help himself. He sank down on top of Peter’s bed, pressing his face into the covers to smother his laughter and the sweet relief that came along with it.

The letter had made it to Sirius, all his worrying and he hadn’t even mentioned it until now, the tosser. But Sirius had gotten the letter—and he’d kept it. He’d kept it just to torture Remus later—he’d bet on it. He’d hoped for it.

When Remus had finally laughed enough that he was able to raise his head up again, he found Sirius there, leaning over from the bed’s other side, the corners of his eyes pinched with a smile.

‘I saw you watchin’ from the stairs,

You’re everyone that ever cared;

Oh, lordy!

Oh, lordy!’

“You could take it back,” Sirius said, holding out the letter, “but I bet you won’t.”

Remus gave him a long look, grinding his teeth together behind a haggard smile.

This bloody tosser.

Using the back of his hand, he smacked the letter away and pushed off the ground. “Fine, keep it then.”

Smugly, Sirius stepped back and neatly folded the letter back up, crossing back to his side of the room and carefully tucking it into its envelope. Remus watched, suddenly struck by how alike the back of Sirius’ head was to Tonya’s. They could’ve passed as siblings. Both of them shared the same black waves and pouty lips—they were pretty and they knew it.

Woah—uh-uh, you miserable toff.

Remus let out a deep breath and returned to his own bed, throwing himself onto it and staring up at the ceiling. Sirius had already tucked himself back up on his own, the Rickenbacker over his lap, but he let the rest of the song play.

‘John, I’m only dancing,

She turns me on;

But I’m only dancing,

She turns me on;

But don’t get me wrong,

I’m only dancing;

Dancing,

Won’t someone touch me?

Touch me…’

"Hey, Moony?"

"Yeah?"

"Reckon you'll ever write any songs of your own? Like for real?"

"Who says I'm not writing them right now?"

"Are you?"

"... No. 'Course not."

There was a short pause. "Well, if you ever did, I'd sing them."

Remus stared up at the roof of his bed. He was thankful Sirius couldn't see his face from there. The smile on his face would've only tripled his ego.



* * *





Friday 24th September 1976

Now that he was no longer waking up so stiff and sore, Remus would’ve thought that carrying Lily’s bag would’ve been easier, but he was half sure she carried every textbook she owned with her everywhere she went. Either that or she had a secret brick collection she’d neglected to share before passing the satchel over.

“What’s the kid’s name again?” Remus asked Mary, who was walking on his left while Lily walked on his right. He was somehow carrying her bag as well as his own after the girls had swindled him into holding them when they’d disappeared into the loo and then just never taken them back. Clearly their feminist agenda was just mere performance activism.

“Georgina Irene,” Mary sighed. “It’s a horrid name.”

“So you nicknamed her ‘Gigi’?”

“Only because I thought it would piss off Kara-Ann.”

Mary said her step-mother’s name with such visceral repulsion that even Lily made a sour face. Neither of them could blame her though, Remus wasn’t sure how he’d react if Lyall came home with a wife only eight years older than he was. Thankfully, his father was a frigid bastard, averse to anything apart from his work and his dogs.

“How was I supposed to know that she was going to love it? God, all summer it was ‘Gigi this’ or ‘Gigi that’. I’m never going on holiday with my family again.”

“New York was nice though?” Lily asked.

“Pete’s been to New York,” Remus said.

“I thought he went to Florida?” Mary shook her head, swinging her umbrella with it and nearly taking out Remus’ eye. “Whatever. The city was wonderful, très éblouissante, and the shows were amazing. I could really see myself living there—but the crying. I swear, I’m never having children. I told you they didn't bring the nanny along, yeah? So whenever Daddy and that witch went out I got stuck playing babysitter! Pretty sure the kid started throwing up just because she thought it was funny to see me squirm! I never thought I’d say it but I’m glad to be stuck up here in the middle of nowhere. At least I have you guys, and it also puts me I’m far, far away from ‘Kara-Ann’—I told you she insists on being called the full thing? Just ‘Kara’ is ‘completely unacceptable’. ”

Lily glanced up at Remus like she was used to the spiel already, but there really wasn’t any stopping Mary once she started a rant. Luckily, they had James to do it for them.

“Hey guys,” James said, approaching them from across the pavement after appearing from behind the Galilei Block. He was slightly out of breath like he’d been running and both his dark hair and glasses were speckled with rain. Lily tipped her umbrella out for him to join her as he jogged to a stop in front of them and James smiled thankfully, taking it from her to hold up over the both of them.

“Black not with you?” Remus asked, adjusting Lily’s hefty school bag on his shoulder.

“Nope. Slughorn had to give him detention after he put the dry ice from today’s lesson in a water bottle and left it under Snape’s lab stool until it exploded.”

Lily gave a sharp gasp and James had to swallow an obvious smile. “I didn’t do it,” he insisted. “Made quite the boom though.”

“I knew leaving you three alone in chemistry this year would be a mistake.”

“Does that mean you’re interested in transferring in?”

“No,” Lily said haughtily, “then I’d have to drop psychology. You and Sev are just going to have to learn to get along on your own.”

“Not that this ‘finally talking to one another’ thing isn’t cute and all,” Mary said, “but I’m starving, so could we please go to dinner? Private study just about killed me.”

“You guys go ahead,” Remus said ducking out from under Mary’s umbrella (she never held it high enough to shield him from the rain anyway) and sliding the girls’ bags off his shoulder. “I’ll meet you later. I’ve got to get more strings from Buchanan. I broke one this morning.”

“It’s all the practising you and Sirius have been doing,” James said.

Mary beamed very suddenly. “Oh! Are you two writing your own songs yet? You could always write about—”

“No, we’re not,” Remus cut in mercilessly. At least he wasn’t.

“Well, say hello to Mrs. Buchanan for us,” Lily said, reaching to take her bag back. James intercepted her easily.

“I got it,” he said, taking the book bag and slinging it over his own shoulder. Lily let him, biting her lip and looking like she was fighting a blush.

“See Lily?” Mary said, taking her bag from Remus. “I told you blokes were good for something.” Grinning, she held the bag out to James.

“Cheers, Macdonald,” James sighed, obediently taking the bag. With three bags plus the umbrella he looked a lot like a human pack-animal.

“Good luck, Potter,” Remus saluted, and Mary gave him a cheeky wink as James waved him off dismissively. He didn’t appear at all displeased, though—Remus could see the puckered dimples standing out on his cheeks.

He left his friends outside the science block, turning and setting off across the campus to the Bellchant building. The rain, which had started as a regular autumn drizzle, quickly turned to a full-blown downpour and by the time he made it to the musical arts building he was soaked through to his undershirt. Sticking his head inside the classroom door, Remus found the music room empty, and the lights in Mrs. Buchanan's office off. He would’ve left all together had he not heard a clatter and a rather colourful string of curses coming from the storage room at the very back.

“Jesus F. Chopin! Ugh.” Another clatter came, louder this time, and then a little more defeated; “Shit..."

Stepping inside, Remus approached the storage room, its door slightly ajar, and knocked on the outside. “Er… Mrs. Buchanan?”

Sheila appeared in the doorway, pushing the door open so quickly it nearly sent him toppling back against the side of the orchestra risers.

“Remus! Oh, I’m sorry!” Mrs. Buchanan rushed up to him wearing a blue dress covered in white flowers and a pair of red wellies. She had her rain hat on too but was missing a jacket, making her look quite odd indoors. "You just spooked me a bit. Here, let me help you."

"It's okay." Righting himself before Sheila could apologise too much or touch him, Remus straightened up and took a peer into the storage room to find it a mess of toppled boxes and books. His teacher seemed to pick up on the awkwardness and quickly shut the door behind herself with a short chuckle.

“Oh, ignore that, I was just trying to find something but now I’m running late. I’ll have to save tidy-up for Monday.”

Remus glanced at the clock on the music room wall. “You’re leaving this weekend?”

“Yes,” Sheila sighed, giving a small smile, “my train leaves soon, but I should make it to the station in time as long as the rain hasn’t completely ruined the roads.”

She passed him by in a hurry, crossing the classroom to her podium where a large briefcase sat, open and stuffed to the brim with books and other class marking. Her raincoat was draped on a stool behind it, just as bright a red as her boots. Some of her hair had come untucked from beneath her hat in little muddy-brown wisps that fell across her face. It should’ve made her look as tired and haggard as any other teacher at the end of a long school week, but Sheila remained as bright as a summer morning. She always looked like that; it was her eyes, which would’ve been a completely unremarkable, ordinary shade of brown if they weren’t always smiling so kindly at you.

“Is there something I can do for you, Remus?”

Snapping out of his short daze, Remus crossed the classroom after her, taking his time to skip across the risers as he’d gotten used to doing over the past year. “I broke a string again,” he said reluctantly, “I know it’s the second since term started but—”

“Nonsense, you just have to work on not tightening them so much,” Sheila dismissed. “But it also means you’ve been practising, good boy.” She hummed a bit before abandoning the podium and walking to the far wall of the room, where she unlocked one of her cabinets and began rifling around for the right strings for the Fender.

Remus waited patiently, grinding the tip of his trainer into the bottom riser before realising it left a smudge of mud behind. He stopped immediately, not wanting to muck-up Sheila’s precious space. In it nearly every day, though usually tired through the morning, Remus had come to appreciate the music room. Like an eternal paradox, it was constantly calm and hectic all at once. You were almost always guaranteed to hear some sort of moaning, banging, or squeaking from some sort of instrument, but no matter who was making the noise or acting out, Sheila was as kind as she was indulgent. Remus could remember thinking on their first day of forms that year, that not a single other person in the entire British Isles would’ve been able to handle the class. Sheila was the only one who was both patient and firm enough to control the group of snobby trouble-makers. He’d heard the worst of the class—Barty Crouch included—say terrible things to her during a fit or a foul mood, but no matter how badly they deserved a good beating for it, Sheila was never cross. It was always ‘one more chance’ with the humble music teacher, and when that chance was up, she loved her students enough to give them another. It was almost fascinating.

“There,” Sheila said, closing the cupboard doors. She returned to his side and held out the package of strings. “Here you go. Do you need any help tuning it?”

“No, I'm okay. Thanks,” Remus said, taking them and tucking them into his bag.

Sheila watched him, before clicking her tongue. “Remus, you’re soaked to the bone, where’s your raincoat?”

“Oh. Forgot it at the dorm.”

“You’re going to catch a cold.”

“I run warm,” he said, and though it was true, he could still feel the autumn chill licking up his spine.

Sheila chuckled before turning back to her podium, sliding her keys onto her wrist with a springy bracelet cord. “I think we’ve gotten rather lucky this year, actually. When I was a student here—about a million years ago—it used to rain all through autumn, and then you had to deal with the snow—and then the rain and snow. It was nearly unbearable.”

Remus was stunned. “You went to school here?”

“I did,” Sheila mused, “and somehow Professor McGonagall still managed to convince me to come back. She was my history professor back then, you know.”

“My mum went to Hawkings.” The words came out automatically, like they sometimes did when he was least expecting to say anything at all. How many months had it been since he’d thought about it? Not enough. Not when he would still catch himself lying awake at night in their dorm, wondering if she’d belonged to Rowena House like Lily and the girls, or if she’d sat in the same classroom—the same seat. The Bellchant building was over a hundred years old, it had acoustics from the turn of the century; she could have stood right there where he was standing, she could have—

Remus’ face snapped to the piano. It couldn’t be the same, but watching Sirius sit at the bench, practically drooling over the keys but never playing, it was like trying to remember his mother’s piano. So close and yet not there.

Feeling suddenly guilty though he had no reasonable reason to be, he looked back to his teacher. His jaw was clenched so tightly that he could feel the ache in his nose, which had healed weeks ago. The look Sheila was giving him was musing, not her normal, big smile, but instead something shyer.

“I know,” she said. “I knew your mum actually. Hope Lupin. ‘Course, she was Hope Howell when I knew her.”

Remus felt his mouth go dry. “You did?”

“Mhm. We were the same year even. Her family was from Cardiff, right, but both of us went to Hawkings for our entire childhood. We grew up here. Neither of us were very close with our parents because of it, but it was nice to find family in each other.”

Remus reached up and wrapped his fingers around the strap of his book bag, strangling it in his grasp. It felt like he was waiting for Sheila to burst out laughing like, ‘psyche! You should’ve seen your face!’ but she kept smiling, her eyebrows more upturned than usual.

“Do you know a lot of students’ parents?” He blurted out.

Sheila nodded a bit. “Some. It’s not uncommon for alumni to send their children to a school like Hawkings. This college is known for a lot of things you know, not just being damp and cold.” Sheila tried a more comforting smile, but Remus was too rattled to return it. It was ironic really, that he had to travel the length of the entire country to learn more about his mother from strangers than he had in his own home.

“I’m sorry if I’ve upset you, Remus,” Sheila said, reading his silence expertly. “I didn’t want to make you uncomfortable. I thought it might be a hard thing to talk about, given that Hope’s passed on.”

“So you know she died then…” Remus forced himself to swallow.

It was Sheila's turn to be quiet. Finally, she nodded. “Yes. I recieved an invitation to her funeral, but... I couldn’t attend due to some personal issues. I’m sorry, Remus.”

You were invited to the funeral?

The idea socked him in the gut, but was almost laughable. Before coming to Hawkings he’d never even heard of a ‘Sheila Buchanan’—how many strangers had attended his mother’s wake? Lyall hadn't let him go—claimed he was too young for such things. Too distraught. Bad for public image.

Sheila had been invited though. This school friend Hope had never so much as mentioned. Why? Why her?

How come you got to know her and I didn’t?

He needed a cigarette. Or to punch something. Probably both. He could hit the drums at the back of the room, or that horrible gong Barty was always having a go at in morning forms, but that wouldn’t do anything. His hand would just bounce back. They’d just make noise. He wanted to break something.

A teacher for almost as many years as Remus had been alive, Sheila read his distress like an open book, and seemed to opt for a distraction rather than de-escalation.

“Remus,” she said, glancing quickly down at her watch, “will you come with me for a moment?”

Forcing himself to release his strangled bag strap, he managed a stiff nod. Sheila wasted no time. Snapping her briefcase shut and gathering her coat over one arm, she ushered him out of the music room and into the hall.

“It’s just down here,” she said reassuringly, leading him past music rooms number #3 and #4. Like the rest of the Bellchant building, the hallway’s walls were lined with photographs. Some were portraits of famous composers—Bach, Beethoven, Debussy, Schubert, even Sheila’s favourite, Chopin—and other frames contained class photos, each labelled with a year and filled with a collage of previous music students who’d come and gone from the school.

Remus realised what was happening before his and Sheila’s shoes stopped squeaking on the tile.

“This is the one,” his teacher said, looking up at a frame at least three feet across. The golden plaque beneath it read, Mr. Derry’s year 13 Music Class, 1954-55.

The photos encased behind the glass were scattered about one another, all elegantly framed into little boxes. Students grinned back at him around the lips of trumpets, slammed mallets down onto huge bass drums, concentrated as they were caught mid-song on their violins. Most of the photos were without colour, but none were faded. The kids could’ve been practising their instruments the day before, for all he knew. Even the uniforms remained much the same, only the faces were different.

One was familiar though.

A Sheila, twenty years younger than the one he was standing next to now, was bent over mid-laugh with a violin tucked under her chin and her bow poking into the shoulder of the girl next to her. The crest on the breast-pocket of her uniform was for Bronte House, and she had an excessively large hair bow pressed to the top of her head. Remus would’ve bet all his cigarettes for the year that the colour of the bow was similar to the bright, showy patterns Sheila wore as a teacher.

“That’s you,” he said, pointing up at a photo in the top-most corner of the frame.

“Mhm. That’s me the year I graduated from Hawkings,” she hummed. “And just there, that’s your mum.”

Remus clamped down on his bottom lip with his teeth. Sheila reached up with her long fingers and touched the bottom of her photo, right below where the girl sat in front of a grand piano. The instrument was mostly out of frame, but she was turned around on its bench, caught mid-laugh just like Sheila’s younger self. Her blonde hair was pinned back from her face in pretty curls and her fingers hovered over the keys, just barely brushing them.

The photo could’ve been staged; they looked that happy.

The last time Remus had seen Hope’s blonde hair, it had been spread out over the pillow of her hospital bed. Her blue eyes—grey and squinty with humour in the photograph—were tired, with heavy purple bags painted underneath like bruises. She’d been quiet, haunted almost, and when she did speak she hadn’t laughed, she’d cried.

He hadn’t, but that was probably just because of the chaos that was thundering through his mind. A part of him would never forgive her for what she'd told him that day, for the pressure she'd left on his shoulders, but then she'd gone and died and the anger had snowballed anyway. He sometimes wished he'd asked her more questions, but at the time they'd scared him. She'd scared him.

“Remus, are you alright?” Sheila asked softly.

“Yeah. Yeah I’m—” In realisation, Remus slapped a hand to his cheek and his fingers came away wet. Ashamed, he ran his still-damp shirt sleeve over his entire face and sucked in a sniffle, coughing to clear his throat. “I’m fine,” he said forcefully, his voice cracking slightly. “Thanks, Sh—Mrs. Buchanan. I think I’m gonna go now. Sorry if I kept you from your train.”

Sheila cupped both hands in front of her over her briefcase handle. “Don’t be sorry, love. I’m the one that’s always keeping you, after all.”

Remus nodded and turned away.

“Oh and Remus,” Sheila called, making him turn back so sharply he made her jump. “If you ever need anything,” she said, deflating in the shoulders as the surprise left her, “I’m always here to talk. I know I’m gone on some weekends, but if you ever need me, you can phone from the office. The secretarial ladies will have my number.”

He stared at her openly. “You want me to call you, while you’re not at school?”

“Only if you want to talk,” she said simply, with another warm smile. "You... well, I only mean to stay that if you ever want to talk more about Hope, I'd be glad to answer any questions I can. I know she loved you very much."

Almost bitterly, Remus touched his tongue to the inside of his cheek. “Okay. Goodbye, Mrs. Buchanan. Be… be safe on the road.”

“Goodbye, Remus. I hope you have a good weekend.”

Turning back around, he left her there in front of the photographs, the deafening echoes of his squeaking trainers chasing him all the way out of the building. The rain had stopped now, of course, and the sun was just peeking through the clouds above him. Remus stared up at it dejectedly, a hand over his eyes. He hated the rain, always had, but at least if it were still raining then there might’ve been a chance that someone else at Hawkings would’ve felt as miserable as he did.

Chapter 34: Courante


Chapter Summary

Remus gets a phone call, and then runs into someone unexpected. The boys plan a devilish prank.



Chapter Notes

CW: References to drugs/distribution of illegal substances. Blood/gore trigger, nothing violent, just a gag. Also references to cut wrists in concurrence with the blood trigger. This is toward the very end of the chapter, so please beware if you're sensitive to it <3



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Surprise, surprise,

The boys are home;

My guardian angel,

Run down my telephone;

The heats on, Mister,

Can’t you hear them scream,

What ever happened to the teenage dream?

- “Teenage Dream” T. Rex, 1974



Thursday 21st October 1976

“Oi, Lupin! Phone call!”

The muffled shout came with a sharp banging on their dorm room door. Hearing it, Remus launched himself up out of bed so fast he nearly tripped on the stack of books Sirius had pulled out of his hutch earlier that morning. He hadn’t even taken a book, just left a mess. Remus was starting to suspect he did it on purpose just so he could watch him put them all back into order again.

“Moony, bring back tea!” Peter called as he threw the door open.

Taking the stairs two at a time, he might’ve slammed right into Sirius, who was making his way up to their room with a large duffle bag slung over one shoulder, had the other boy not pressed himself against the railing as Remus sailed past.

“Where’re you going in such a rush?” Sirius demanded.

“Be right back!” He called, nearly slipping on the third-floor landing as he went.

Only one of the three Godric House phones was free, but he’d gotten lucky and it was the last phone on the left, meaning that he could pull the cord taunt and swing into the other hallway for a bit of privacy.

Remus slowed as he approached the phone and readjusted his school jumper, eyeing the receiver that had been left off its hook for him to retrieve. His heart was slamming against his rib cage and his palms were clammy, but it felt stupid to hesitate, so he forced himself to scoop up the phone as casually as he could and leaned back against the wall, tucking himself around the corner so no one could watch him slowly raise the speaker to his ear.

“Hello…?”

Please God, just this once—don’t let it be Giles.

“Hey, Lu.”

Remus let out a sigh like he’d just run a marathon but his vigour returned instantly along with a sudden surge of anger. “ ‘Hey, Lu’? Two months and all I get is ‘hey, Lu’?”

“Helloooo, Remus, my darling. That better?” Tomny said from the other end, making Remus scrunch his nose up with an embarrassed smile.

“Hey, Tom,” he sighed.

“Jesus, if I’d have known you’d get so up in arms I would’ve waited another month.”

“Sod off. You already took your damn time. It’s almost Halloween—my friends are already concocting some sort of plan for it.”

“Ooh, I’m sorry, am I interrupting then? Were you busy making up your costumes? I bet you’d look really good as a little cat or something.”

“Yeah, about as good as you’d look in a fairy dress.”

“I missed your snappy attitude, Lu.” His voice came out crackly as the connection faded every now and then, but it was about as good as it got so far up in the Highlands.

“Say, who was it who picked up the phone earlier?” Tomny asked.

“What? Oh, well, the phones here are sorta communal. One rings and whoever’s closest picks up and shouts out a name.”

“Like prison?”

“Yeah, like prison.”

“Jesus Christ. Maybe we do need to come save you.”

“How’s home?” Remus asked, anxiously thumbing the phone’s cord.

“Wet,” Tomny said, “but it’s not as hot anymore, thank fuck. The humidity’s killer though.”

“It’s pretty gross up here too,” Remus answered.

“I’ll bet.”

There was a bit of silence between them, just enough for Remus to wonder why they were talking about the bloody weather. They never talked about the weather, not unless—

“You tweaking, Tomny?”

“Aw shit, Lu. Can’t even look me in the eye and ya still manage to see right through me.” There was a short laugh that ended with a muffled cough, before Tomny got back on the line. “Tonya’s trying this ‘holistic healing’ thing. Between you and me it’s all bullshit, but she got rid of everythin', even the hash. Told her it didn’t make a lick ‘a sense, while doing what—well, what we do, but she won’t have it. Lee’s almost been banished from the flat twice.”

“So what, you runnin’ drugs now, Tom?” Remus asked, though he already knew the answer. He made sure to lower his voice though, just in case. “It’s drugs now?”

“Ha, it’s always been drugs, Lu. You’re smart enough to know that. S’just where you get ‘em that’s changed.”

Remus licked his lips. Over the summer he’d watched Tonya do upwards of three or four lines a day, really hardcore stuff, and even when he’d wondered where Tomny had gotten the blow and how much his girlfriend’s habit was costing him, he’d never asked. Back then it was just about keeping his head down and shutting up so Tomny wouldn’t throw him out. Guess that didn’t matter much anymore though. He wasn’t sure quitting cold turkey was the best approach, but at least it was something.

“How is Tonya?”

“She’s good—napping. I can wake her up if you’d—”

“No! I mean, I want to talk to her, yeah, but you first.”

There was a bit of silence from Tomny’s end, and Remus wished he really could see him, but Tomny had never been much of a chatterbox while strung-out anyway. “Okay… What do you want to talk about? You wanna tell me about school? You gettin’ good grades?”

“God, you sound like Giles,” Remus scoffed.

“Who’s Giles?”

“Oh… dad’s chauffeur.”

“You mean the big bloke who’s always coming to get you from Aldgate?”

“You knew he was coming to get me?”

“Sorry to break it to you, but you’re not as sneaky as you think you are. You’re just lucky Lee and the others are decently thick in the head.”

Remus laughed. There obviously wasn’t much point in lying anymore, since Tomny clearly knew everything. “Yeah well, that’s him.”

“He act like your mum, then? Always pestering?”

“Fuck, yes,” Remus laughed, “I don’t think my father would remember I existed if Giles weren’t around to remind him.”

“Want me to rough the old guy up? I’ll meet him in Aldgate.”

“Nah,” Remus smiled, “Giles is good. Better than most.”

“Better than us? Then your boys?”

“No. Impossible. No one better.”

Tomny gave a satisfied, “Mhm,” and Remus heard a faint voice in the background. “I should call you more often, Lu,” he said, “you make me sound so good.”

“I’m not your stooge,” Remus said.

“No, you’re not, that’s—” there was a short clatter; “Bloody hell woman, would you give me a second?”

Straightening up against the wall, Remus pressed both hands to the receiver as Tomny tussled for the phone on his end.

“Fine, fine! Lupin—the old bird wants a turn. I’ll talk to you soon, yeah?”

“Yeah!” Remus called. “Yeah, anytime, Tom.”

“It’s my turn,” a voice grumbled, and a moment later Tonya was shouting down the other end of the line; “REMUS, MY SWEET LOVE! HOW ARE YOU?”

He flinched away from the receiver and faintly heard Tomny say something crude about phone etiquette in the background.

“I know how to use the phone, Tomny. You’re the caveman,” Tonya chided. “Sorry love, just got excited. I’ve been trying to convince Tomny to call all this time, you know, but I think he just got a little nervous. Dunno why—it’s only ‘little ol’ Lu’. But you know how he is.”

“I will cut that phone line, woman!” Tomny warned in the background, making Remus smile.

“It’s nice to hear from you, Ton.”

“Oh, it’s so nice to hear from you too, darling. Have you been eating well? That school feeds you enough right? I bet you pay out the back-end for tuition, so they’d better.”

“Food’s fine. How about you?”

“Oh yeah, we’re eating fine, but these bleeders still won’t eat a fucking mushroom, can you believe that?”

“Lupin doesn’t like mushrooms either!” Tomny called, and Tonya gasped.

“Remus!”

“They’re a fungus!” He said, defensively.

“They’re good for you! Lots of fibre.”

“They grow in shit!”

“Everything grows in shit! It’s a shit-eats-shit kind of world!”

Remus clapped a hand over his eyes, even though he knew Tonya wouldn’t be able to see it, luckily she was as clever as she was erratic.

“What was that about it being nice to hear from me?” She said, cheekily.

“Well it was,” he shot back, before softening; “It is. Heard you emptied the flat of all the magic medicine.”

“I did,” she said indignantly, “and any and all artillery. We’re turning a new leaf over here. I’ve been trying to tell Tomny to stop shitting where he eats.”

“Tonya, so much shit-talk today.”

“Ooh, I better be careful or I’ll become a bad influence on our little angel.”

“I’m not an angel,” Remus said, dismissively, then more quietly; “I’m a messer.”

“A what?”

“Nothing. Say, listen to this, I lent one of my roommates your book, ‘The Count of Monte Cristo’—”

“Oh? Did he like it?”

“—Hasn’t finished it yet, but he’s started writing some song about it, something about how Dantès was wrongfully imprisoned without trial and how it's all just a metaphor for making our own luck or something.”

“Your friend writes songs?”

“Well, yeah, but—”

“Are you writing songs, Remus?”

“No—! I mean, no, definitely not.”

“I think it would be sort of brilliant if you were,” Tonya said, and Remus imagined her combing her long, black hair over one should the way she did when she got into one of her quietly excited moods.

“I’m not the musician,” he mumbled, “Sirius is.”

“Well I’m not talking about Sandy or whatever his name is—you’re taking music lessons again at school, right?”

“Yeah.”

“Then you’re a musician.” Of course Tonya said this so matter-of-factly that there was no room for argument. “Don’t sell yourself short, sweet love. It’s such a waste of time. You’re at school, you’re young—”

“You’re young too, Tonya.”

“Hm.” There was some silence, then; “Be a musician, Remus. If that’s what makes you happy. Or be a circus clown—or a rice farmer, or—”

As Tonya rambled on, Remus had to force himself to release the phone cord before it snapped; he hadn’t realised he’d been twisting it so tightly around his wrist.

“What makes you happy, Tonya?” He asked, interrupting her. She went quiet again, then spoke more softly;

“I’ll tell you at Christmas.”

Remus perked up a bit. “Christmas?”

“Yeah. You’re coming home right?”

“Well…” Home to the estate, maybe, but Remus was pretty sure Tomny had been serious: no more East End. Still, he couldn’t help the sliver of hope that bloomed in his chest. “I hope to,” he confessed.

“Brilliant. I’ll cook, we’ll do presents. It’ll be good.”

“You don’t need to get me anything.”

“Shut up, Christmas is Christmas. You’re getting a present.”

“Fine, but I’m going to get you something too.”

“I hope so. I take a size four-carat diamond.”

“Hah.”

Tonya giggled into the other end before sighing. “I should go now, love. These toll calls are atrocious, but I’ll call again, even if Tomny wants to be a little girl about it.”

“Okay. I’ll talk to you guys later then.”

“Okay. Goodbye, sweetheart.”

“Bye.”

The line clicked dead and Remus dropped the phone to his side, sagging back against the wall with his eyes closed. It was easy to replay the entire conversation in his head—he did that all the time when he couldn’t sleep—but it was harder to imagine what else he could’ve said over a phone call. Maybe things would be better by the holiday, maybe he actually could get away with visiting the flat again. His nose wouldn’t thank him and neither would Tomny, but if he already had Tonya rooting for him then at least he had a chance.

“Um, excuse me?”

Remus jolted sideways away from the sudden voice, only to be yanked back slightly by his hold on the receiver. Another boy was standing a few steps away, looking nervous as he stared up at him. Finally he pointed to the phone in Remus’ hand while shyly sucking on his lower lip.

“Are you done with the phone?”

“Oh,” Remus looked down at the stretched cord and stepped forward, dropping the receiver back down on the stand. “Yeah, s’all yours, mate.”

While the mousey boy squeezed in between him and the wall, Remus stepped away and rubbed at the back of his neck. It didn’t feel right to head directly back to his room where he’d certainly find it difficult to hide such an odd mood from his friends, so instead he walked out the front doors of the dorm, wearing only his jumper. The late October air was crisp but at least it wasn’t raining. He drifted up the pavement of House Lane, kicking rocks or pinecones that had fallen from the trees out of his way as he went.

The phone call had left him both lighter in the chest and foggier in the head; Tomny hadn’t said anything about letting him visit for the holidays, that was all Tonya, and Tonya wasn’t the one who’d kicked him out. She didn’t know the truth either, or at least, he thought she didn’t. The realisation that Tomny might’ve told the others who he really was and where he’d actually grown up hit harder than those kids who’d beat him in the alley. He tried telling himself that he had no real reason to believe Tomny had told anyone else—both he and Doss had kept things so hush that even Remus had been fooled—but now that he was on the outs by default, there really was no need for them to keep lying to the other lads. It wasn’t loyal and it wasn’t Tomny.

It would’ve been a lie to say that he wasn’t angry about being forced out. Lee and Doss had been in plenty of fights—Seesaw had nearly gone blind during a nasty row before Remus had even known him—but he gets cornered once and that’s it; you’re out. Do not pass go, do not collect a decent reputation in London’s roughest neighbourhood.

Remus touched his hand to his nose. The nasty gash he’d gotten when bone had broken skin had healed weeks ago, and now he was just left with an angry red scar. It would fade some eventually, but every time he looked in a mirror he was met by a reflection only a mother could love. And he didn’t have one of those.

The boys had been good about it mostly, never bringing up the injury again after that first day, and always quick to offer a beating to kids like Crouch or Snape when they made their snide comments. Those Remus could handle, especially after discovering how powerful a look from ‘scarface’ could be when he was feeling particularly venomous. Crouch had nearly pissed his pants in the second week of forms when he’d made a jab at Sirius for his colourful nails (courtesy of Mary, of course) and Remus had slammed a fist down on a symbol behind his head, making the whole class jump and stare. Besides the fact that Crouch was a git for no reason at all, Remus had come around to Sirius’ painted nails. They’d been a cherry-red that week, and Remus had zoned out watching Sirius strum on his guitar until the polish was chipped and worn.

Sirius had chosen blue next. Mary offered to paint Remus’ too—a matching colour of course—but he’d refused. It was enough to just watch Sirius’ fingers and pretend as though he had a fraction of the talent. He was getting better though, as Sheila spent every class assuring him, and Remus decided to give her the benefit of the doubt because it made him feel better.

It had been easy to assume that things would be awkward after the encounter with his music teacher, but Sheila remained a force to be reckoned with. The following Monday they’d all reconvened in forms as always and though Remus had done his best to avoid her gaze, she’d made no indication that anything was wrong. She called his name for registration, smiled as always and even took time out of her morning to help him and Sirius work out the bridge to “Like a Rolling Stone”. It was completely and utterly normal, not like anything he’d been expecting after she’d revealed that she’d not only known Hope, but that they were close friends. Close enough to have a photograph of the pair of them hanging up for twenty years where everyone could see. He hadn’t sought out the photo since Sheila had shown it to him, but he couldn’t get the image out of his mind anyway; they’d looked so happy, absolutely lit up with joy. Remus wasn’t sure he’d ever seen his mother look like that.

He couldn’t remember deciding that his destination was going to be the Bellchant building, yet his feet had carried him there anyway. It was a Sunday and Sheila had been absent from Communion earlier that morning which likely meant she was off campus again for the weekend. It seemed that the music teacher was spending most weekends away nowadays. It made Remus kick himself for not taking the chance when they were alone to ask where it was she was always disappearing to. He’d been understandably distracted at least.

The Bellchant building was always quietest on the weekends, and he and Sirius had made good use of it to sneak away and practice toward the end of the year 11. They were rarely interrupted, and more than once he’d had to hide his cigarettes to keep Sirius from lighting up right there on the risers. He didn’t think it was fair to sully the only classroom in the entire campus that he enjoyed being in with ash and smoke. It wasn’t as though Sirius wanted to desecrate the hall of music and artistic expression, just that he took any and all chance to stick it to the ruling powers. Though Remus hadn’t been around to see it, Sirius had once lit one of their hand-rolled cigarettes off a bunsen burner in the middle of chemistry and Slughorn gave him detention carrying all the empty propane canisters from the classroom to the school’s rubbish centre. According to him, it had been worth it to see the dopey look on the professor’s face though.

Remus turned around halfway to music room #2, feeling a bit stupid. Dinner was going to start soon and he’d hoped to finish his Literacy homework beforehand. He hadn’t brought the Fender or his cigarettes and it wasn’t like he had the stomach to ‘visit mum’ either, so the walk had been a waste. But just as he was making his way back to the music hall’s main doors, the faint sound of a violin drifted toward him. It was coming from one of the private lesson rooms across the hallway—a pretty melody with a quick tempo, like something you could dance to.

Shifting his weight in front of the main doors, Remus’ curiosity won out and he turned back, creeping up to the doorway of one of the private rooms—the only one with any light peeking through its frosted-glass window. Leaning his ear against it to listen, he was reminded of the songs Sheila would sometimes play for them at the beginning of class. Hers were always chipper and upbeat or otherwise beautiful and calming, but as he listened, Remus felt the song grow sadder, like its composer had experienced some great loss in the middle of writing it.

Perhaps it was because he was feeling sentimental after his phone call, or maybe he was just becoming too curious for his own good; either way the door clicked open and Remus peeked inside to find Regulus Black standing with his back to the door, a violin tucked under his chin. The far side of the practice room was covered in mirrors, reflecting Regulus' gentle movements as he played. His eyes were closed and the expression on his face was serene, leaving him looking younger than he normally did while wearing his usual stoic frown. Regulus’ entire body moved with the song like the violin was an extension of himself, dark Black-family waves falling down across his forehead as he swayed.

Remus watched him for a long time, utterly entranced. There was a music stand set up in front of Regulus, but his eyes never opened; it was almost like the song was flowing out of him rather than off the page. It was exactly like Sirius, he thought, when he got lost in his strumming and just let his body take over.

The song’s abrupt end caught Remus by surprise. He was still watching, captivated by Regulus’ movement even more than the melody, but he didn’t miss it when the dark-haired boy opened his eyes and straightened up, catching sight of him in the mirror.

“What are you doing in here?” Regulus demanded.

“Sorry!” Remus balked. “Didn’t mean to eavesdrop, I just heard you and—”

“I booked this as a private room.”

“Yeah, sorry,” Remus rubbed his arm awkwardly, unaware that any of the rooms could be booked by students in the first place. “I’m Remus, I know Sirius and—”

“I know who you are,” Regulus snapped, bending down to throw open the violin case. “You’re one of my brother’s roommates.”

“Yeah…”

“The one who busted his face punching a cop.”

Remus’ mouth dropped open. “What? No, I never punched any cop. Who said that?”

“He did—my brother. Barty overheard him in your forms.”

Remus let out a bark of laughter. “I’m gonna kill that numpty.”

Apparently not all that entertained by Remus’ shock, Regulus snapped his violin case shut and began gathering his music sheets up off the stand. Feeling slightly guilty for interrupting, Remus squeezed the door handle and bit his lip. “That was really good,” he said, “whatever you were playing.”

Regulus glanced up at him in the mirror with an irritated expression, but answered anyway. “Violin Partita number two in D minor. Courante."

“I have no idea what that means,” Remus said, automatically.

"Well that's no surprise," Regulus scoffed, snapping his music folder closed and tucking it up under one arm as he scooped the violin case up off the floor. When he rounded and approached the door, he gave Remus a haughty look with the same grey eyes as Sirius. "Are you going to move, or are you going to punch me too?"

"Wha—?"

Regulus shoved past, disinterested.

“It was just a football accident actually,” Remus called. “I never punched anyone.” That was true, at least.

Pausing a few steps away, the younger boy glanced back. “My brother isn’t as clever as he thinks he is. If he were, he’d know when to keep his mouth shut.”

Before Remus could even begin to wonder what it was that he actually meant by the remark, Regulus made his way to the front doors of the Bellchant building and pushed them open, stepping out into the sun.





* * *





When he returned to his dorm room, tea tray in hand, Remus found James and Sirius sitting on the floor, their laps covered in rope and black tarping. Along with the ominous supplies, sat the rather sorry-looking stag’s head (fur now slightly matted thanks to the steam from their showers), a bucket, a box of safety matches, and a megaphone they’d surely lifted from Ms. Hooch.

“Do I even want to know?” Remus said, shutting the door behind himself with his foot.

Sirius looked up pointedly. He had a notebook open in front of him on the floor with a scribbled list of bullet points. “Where have you been, you slacker?”

Remus carefully adjusted one of the mugs of tea on his tray. “Nowhere. Now what is it I’ve been slacking off from?”

“You were supposed to be here helping us plan and prepare for our Halloween prank extravaganza!”

“Extravaganza? Halloween is almost two weeks away.”

“That’s why we gotta plan!" Sirius insisted. "Just you wait—this is gonna totally blow every other prank out of the water.”

Shaking his head hopelessly, Remus crossed the room and carefully sat down across from them, setting the tea tray on the floor. “So what? No pumpkins or baseball bats this year?”

Sirius bent back over his notes. “Nope, that’s kids stuff. We have matured some, Moony."

“And so naturally you resort to what appears to be a rather unorthodox murder plot.”

While Sirius snickered, James continued tying knots in the bundle of rope. “You’ll think it’s brilliant when you hear it, Lupin. We’re including the girls too.”

“Lily and Marlene agreed to be in on a prank?” Remus asked in disbelief.

“No,” Sirius snorted, “they’re going to be the ones getting pranked, a’course.”

“Lily’s going to give you detention for the rest of your sorry lives. If she doesn’t kill you first, that is.”

“Whose is whose?” James asked, disregarding the threat and glancing at the tea tray, giving each cup its own sceptical look.

“This one’s yours.”

“One sugar?”

“Yes, Mum,” Remus drawled, and James took the cup from him, smirking. “I ran into your brother today,” he said to Sirius, passing him his own cup.

“Oh, yeah? How is the dear little git?”

“Fine. Though he told me you’ve been going around telling people I punched a bloody cop.” James snorted into his tea at that, and Sirius gave a guilty grin.

“I’m just trying to add to your mystique, Moony. No one’s going to be afraid of you if they find out you broke your face on a football.”

“Who says I want people to be afraid of me?” Remus demanded.

“You do—every day when you go around brooding.”

“You’re such an ass, Black.”

“You remember what you do with asses though right? You kiss them.” Sirius stuck his lips out at him, but Remus only rolled his eyes and reached for his tea.

“So what’s this plan of yours?”

To answer him, Sirius spun his notebook around and pushed it towards him. Remus scanned the page. “Bonfire? Ghosts? James dies? What the hell is this?”

“It’s history in the making,” Sirius sang giddily.

“When did you even have time to come up with this?”

“During maths, mostly. Potter helped in chem though.”

Shaking his head, Remus looked at the list again. “Oh my god… they’re actually going to murder you.”

“ ‘Us’, Lupin,” Sirius smirked, “murder us.”

Remus scoffed and pushed the notebook back before raising his tea to his lips. “So where’s Pete?”

On cue, Peter burst out of the bathroom, his arms dripping blood up to his elbows. “I did it! It worked!” He cried, thrusting his hands out ahead of him and spattering their bedroom floor with red gore.

“Bloody hell!” Remus sputtered in alarm, upsetting his cup and spilling tea down the front of his jumper.

Peter beamed. “Good pun, Moony!”

Hissing, Remus peeled hot tea-soaked fabric away from his chest, gaping up at his friends in horror. “Pete, what the fuck did you do? Slit your own wrists for fun?”

“Calm down, Lupin,” James said, stifling a laugh, “s'only fake blood.”

“Yeah, just a bit of corn syrup and food colouring,” Peter supplied, while noticing the mess he was leaving on the floor.

“But if it’s making you react like this, then Halloween’s going to be fucking amazing,” Sirius beamed.

It was James who got up first, walking up to Peter and wiping a bit of the fake blood off of his forearm, testing its stickiness between his fingers and then tasting it. He grimaced a bit, then said; “Still better than Lupin’s tea.”

“It looks so real,” Sirius observed from his place on the ground. “The girls are going to shit themselves.”

“Please no more shit talk today,” Remus mumbled to himself.

“It’s just meant to be funny,” James warned Sirius, coming out of a bathroom with a towel for Peter; “We’re not trying to traumatise them.”

“Speak for yourself.”

For James, Remus reached forward and took a swipe at Sirius’ shoulder. “Think of poor Prongs’ feelings. He’ll never get Lily’s hand in marriage if she drops dead of fright first.”

“It’s not like she’s actually his girlfriend,” Sirius said in his own defence, making James purse his lips sourly. “In fact until November first she’s just another target. So Moony, fancy a trip back to the Shrieking Shack?”
