Mary nodded eagerly and James dropped down to her level, barely flinching as she ran the pencil across his lower lash line. When she’d finished he stood up again, turning around to Sirius and Lily, who had cuddled up next to each other in anticipation. “What do you think?”

“Er, sure—”

“Blimey, Mary, I knew you had girlfriends but I didn’t know you were into girls,” Bryan snorted.

James whirled around, but it was Remus’ turn. He stood and held a hand to James’ chest as he stepped past him, stopping over Bryan and Mary’s couch and holding out his hand. “Mary, may I?”

Without any hesitation, Mary passed the eye pencil over and Remus pressed it to the corner of his eye, drawing a very poor line across his lid with a shaky hand before doing the same to the other. Eyes watering like James’, he passed the pencil back and glared down at Bryan again, who hadn’t moved but had straightened up slightly on the couch. “I think it’s time for you to leave, Bry,” he ordered. “This is actually a private party.”

Bryan scoffed. “I was invited.”

“And now I’m uninviting you.”

“Oh yeah? Fine then.” He looked at Mary. “Guess we should get out of here, babe.”

“I think I’m gonna stay actually,” Mary said, while casually examining her nails. “You know, visit with my friends before we all go home for two weeks.”

“Yeah, you should totally go though. Don’t think we have any Pink Floyd to play anyway, and to be honest, I’m just not sure you’re girlish enough for me, Bry.”

Affronted, Bryan drew back and looked around the room, then up to Remus, who was still staring him down. Finally he smacked his beer down and stood up, putting them nearly chest to chest. Remus wrinkled his nose—he smelt like a mixture of sour aftershave and cheap cigars.

Acting on instinct, Remus flinched forward like he might lunge at him and Bryan just about jumped out of his skin before scoffing and stomping out of the common room. They heard the dorm’s front doors slam shut and instantly everyone began snorting in laughter.

“I think he about pissed his pants just then!” Sirius guffawed.

“Yeah well, you’re not allowed to pick your own boyfriends anymore,” he said to her. Mary just shrugged innocently, blowing him a cheeky kiss as he returned to his own couch next to Marlene.

“I think you missed a few spots,” Marlene observed, licking her thumb and wiping it across his eyelid. By the time they’d gotten through both sides of Pet Sounds they were all reasonably gassed and giggly and had come to the collective conclusion that wherever Lottie and Mickey had taken that spliff, they were unlikely to return.

“At least we know some of us are getting some,” Sirius observed, raising his beer toward the two remaining couples in the room. Moira blanched and Peter flipped him off, but James had the privilege of being closer and just shoved Sirius for the comment. Unfortunately, Sirius had been sitting on the back of the couch. He toppled backwards—drink and all—straight into the turntable’s stand. There was a record-scratching stop and the turntable went down with a bang as Sirius gave a low groan.

“Oh shit!” James yelped, jumping up. “Sorry, mate!”

Remus set his beer aside. “Yup.”

“Why me? Get your man to do it.”

“C’mon, Black,” Lily said, jumping up from the couch and reaching across it to grab Sirius by the elbow, leading him toward the dorm’s kitchenette. As they went Marlene withdrew her legs from Remus’ lap and stood up.

“Lead the way.”

Remus pushed up from the couch and together they unwound themselves from the circle, heading for the stairs. On the second floor, Marlene let out a loud groan.

“I forgot you guys lived on the fourth floor,” she sighed, before her foot came out from underneath her and she nearly slipped down the stairs they’d already climbed. Grabbing her forearm, Remus waited until she was steady again before letting go. “Sorry,” she half-laughed, “it’s like I’ve got two left feet when I’m drinking.”

“Better than me. I’ve always got two left feet, drunk or not.”

“I’ve never been in a boy’s dorm room before,” she admitted, taking in the posters and discarded socks scattered about the room.

“It’s not that bad. Much better than my brothers' rooms when we were growing up,” Marlene hummed. She’d stopped in front of his Queen poster and admired it with her hands locked behind her back. “This one your bed?”

“Mhm.”

Marlene bent down and picked up one of the books from the pile on his nightstand. “Oh, I’d wondered where this one went.”

“Sorry. You can take it back if you want.”

She set the book down. “No, it’s fine. You take your time with it.”

“Thanks.”

Remus shrugged. “Bryan’s a dick.”

“I guess not everyone can be as sensible as you, Marls.”

Marlene dropped her finger from the dial. “You think I don’t like boys?”

Remus froze. “No—er—that’s not what I meant—”

“I do,” she insisted, “but I sort of think it’s the person that counts, not their… gender…”

“Well, that makes sense.”

“You really think so?” Marlene asked.

“Sure,” he said dimly, “shouldn’t you like someone as a person first? Before you—you know, date them?”

She considered. “I like you, Remus. As a person.”

“Oh.” He released the wires and stepped back from the stereo a bit. “I like you as a person too.”

He suddenly felt like he was holding his breath. “One or two people.”

“I’ve never kissed anyone,” she confessed.

“It’s really not all that.”

“It’s not?”

“No, I lied,” he said, quickly. “But I guess it feels better if you… like them as a person first.”

Marlene pressed her lips together and nodded slowly. She had such big blue eyes. Remus’ palms felt sweaty; he was still lashed. When had she gotten this close? She smelt like beer, but also sort of fruity.

“Are you going to kiss me?” She asked.

It lasted maybe only a few seconds before Marlene pulled away, cheeks tinged with pink. They stared at one another, and Remus licked his lips, tasting her lip gloss.

“Tastes like cherry.”

“Huh?”

“Your lipstick.”

“Oh.” Marlene held a hand to her mouth before smiling behind her fingers. “Yeah. It’s Mary’s actually.”

“Cool…” Letting out a breath, Remus drummed his fingers on top of the hi-fi.

“Yeah, sure. Here, you want to carry this?” Grateful for the distraction, Remus grabbed Sirius’ turntable and passed it to her before hastily disconnecting the rest of the stereo’s wires and lifting it into his arms. With the sound system between them it was hard to imagine they’d been so close only seconds before.

Marlene smiled sweetly, still blushing, and turned to leave the room. They didn't say anything on the way down, eyes glued to the stairs so they wouldn't slip, and by the time they made it down to the ground floor Remus had managed to shake off most of his jitters.

“Disliking pop music is not the same thing as misogyny,” Sirius argued, passing her a drink.

“You like The Faces, but what is Rod Stewart on his own? He’s a pop star.”

“He writes ballads!”

“You’re delusional.”

“Moony!” Sirius shouted when he spotted them. Shooting across the room, he halved Remus' burden when he grabbed hold of the other side of the stereo. “Save me! They want to play more disco-pop.”

“Disco?” Remus echoed sorely.

“It’s party music,” Mary called. She raised a Bee Gees album and Marlene’s face lit up. Remus watched her, tongue pressed to the inside of his cheek, and slowly cracked a small smile.

“Maybe it is time we diversify, Black. After all, what is glam rock if not disco?”

Sirius’ mouth dropped open. “No, don’t tell me they’ve gotten to you too? I can’t handle losing three mates in one day.”

“I only said they’re kind of R&B,” James scoffed.

“And funk is kinda fun,” Peter added.

Sirius moaned and dropped his forehead down on top of the hi-fi in Remus’ arms.

“Oh c’mon, you whiner,” Mary cackled as Marlene brought her the turntable; “It’s good to leave your options open in life. You never know what sort of fun you’ll find if you do.”





* * *





Remus was thrilled to be going home. Not only was he going to get to see the rest of his friends, but this was the perfect way to reset the clock. No more jealousy or whinging—or incidents—just good friends and good music and good times. That is if Sirius ever got on the bleeding bus.

“C’mon, Black, they’re going to leave without us!”

“You say that as if it’s a bad thing.”

Remus danced from foot to foot. How was he supposed to explain to Sirius, who held such a strong distaste for going home, that it was a bad thing. Missing the bus and having to catch a later train would only mean less time spent at the flat, and therefore less time with the friends he’d only recently learned he’d get to see again.

“If you don’t come now I’ll never tell you what I got on the geography exam," he threatened.

“Alright, alright, don’t get your knickers in a twist.” A moment passed and Sirius gave a great ‘a-ha!’ from inside the bathroom. He came out with his trunk in one hand, his chain necklace in the other. “Sucker must’ve fallen behind the toilet when I was showering last night.”

“Peachy, can we go now?”

Sirius shook his head and dusted the necklace off on his shirt before popping his top button and stringing it around his neck. As he did so, a charm on the end of the necklace caught Remus’ eye.

“That a pick?”

Sirius perked up and then glanced down before touching his collarbone. “Oh yeah,” he held up the guitar pick, which was strung on the chain as though it were some holy cross. “Put it on there myself. You like it?”

“Yeah,” Remus said, “it looks cool.”

Sirius smiled and then bit his lip before taking the chain off again and holding it out to him. “Here.”

“What?”

“Take it.”

“No, it's yours,” Remus scoffed.

“Only half. The other half’s yours technically.”

Remus looked at him, confused, and Sirius pinched the pick. “It’s the pick from last year. You gave it to me just after exams, remember? Guess it’s my turn to give it back.”

Remus was quite honestly stunned. He hadn’t even remembered doing that, and yet Sirius had been carrying the cheap and thoughtless gift around with him everywhere. “Still, it’s your necklace. You should keep it.”

“You really think it’s that tacky?”

“No, of course not! But it's clearly important to you—”

Sirius came forward quickly and grabbed Remus’ hand, folding the necklace into his palm. “Mum actually tried to take it last time she saw it. I’d rather you have it than lose it to her. Just think of it as an early Christmas gift.”

“I haven’t gotten anything for you,” Remus said slowly, staring down at the chain. It was warm to the touch, or maybe that was just Sirius.

“Good thing I’ve already thought up what you can give me,” Sirius said, strolling back to his abandoned trunk.

“And what’s that?”

He jutted his thumb toward Remus’ bed, clicking his tongue; “When you gonna make good on that promise of yours?”

It took Remus a moment to understand but once he did he glanced to his right, where Hope’s records sat quietly beneath the bed. Untouched and unplayed. “You want the records? Well… you can just have them, I suppose.”

Sirius sighed. “I don’t want to take them from you, dummy, I want to listen to them with you.”

“Oh.”

“Yeah. If you… want to, that is.”

“You sure that’s what you want for Christmas?” Remus licked his lips. “They’re just records.”

Sirius shrugged. “They’re important to you. I think it’d be cool if they could be important to all of us.” He smirked. “For now though, I’ll settle for you fessing up over that exam.”

Remus tucked the chain into his pocket and considered. “Okay. I got a sixty-five.”

“You—a sixty-five?!”

“Yup. Let’s go.” Remus turned and shot out of their room.

“Lupin!”

Sirius only managed to catch up with him on the ground floor, which was nearly empty now that most students were already down by the buses. James and Peter had gone on ahead to collect their girlfriends, both of which were accompanying them. Between them and the other girls, Remus expected the compartment was going to be rather crowded.

“I don’t need the ‘but you studied’ lecture. I already got it from Lily,” Remus insisted as he and Sirius made their way down the path short-cut to Castle Hall, breath visible in the chilly December air.

“Bet mine would be way funnier though,” Sirius said, knocking his trunk into Remus’ thigh. He paused afterwards to let out a low groan, holding his stomach and still clearly feeling the effects of the hangover he’d sworn he didn’t have.

“You should’ve avoided that whisky,” Remus told him.

“I paced myself.”

“Uh-huh, whatever you say. Just make sure you sit next to James on the train. I’m not wearing your breakfast for nine hours.”

“You’re right. And you can sit with Evans. I don’t need to witness another show like last night’s lovefest anyway.”

Remus smiled as he recollected the shift in James and Lily’s outward affection the moment hard liquor had made an appearance. “They weren’t that bad. Nothing compared to you on the pull.”

“So you’ve been paying attention!” Sirius laughed. “Good. This must mean we’re okay.”

“Why wouldn’t we be okay?” Remus asked, slowing his strides a bit.

“Oh don’t give me that. You’ve been acting funny, and I think I know why.”

“You do?”

“Yup. You were upset I was spending so much time with James. We got caught up with the music and sort of forgot about you. So I’m sorry.”

“Oh, that.” Remus let out a breath of relief. “Don’t worry, I’m over it.”

“So you were mad?”

“More like ‘casually irritated’. But it’s fine now. James sounds really good for a beginner. You’re a great teacher.”

Sirius lit up and skipped forward until he was walking backwards in front of him. “Nah, it’s all him, I swear! He’s gonna take Andy’s guitar home for Christmas to practice too. Bet he'll come back sounding like Robert Johnson or something. Give his soul for God's own talent.”

Remus smiled. “Careful, he might just come back next term sounding better than you.”

“I wouldn’t put it past the wanker. He’s just got this magic in his fingers or something! Evans’ is a lucky gal.”

“Ugh, don’t be gross.”

“What? Oh c'mon, I know you’re a bit of a prude, Moons, but one day you’re gonna get over that and when you do you’ll see that—”

“I kissed Marlene.”

Sirius stopped dead in his tracks and Remus had to side-step to avoid running into him.

“What?”

“Last night,” he confessed. “In our room.”

Sirius blinked at him before looking around with a shocked sense of bewilderment. Remus could almost see the gears turning in his head, while just a little further down the road a crowd of teachers and kids stood shuffling around in front of a long row of buses.

“What the fuck,” Sirius said finally; “Marlene? Why her?”

“Why not?” Remus rebuked.

“It’s just… since when?”

“Since when what?”

“Since when have you liked her?!”

“I’ve always liked Marlene.”

Eyes widening again, Sirius huffed and muttered under his breath; “Jesus Christ… So what, this gonna be a thing now?”

“I don’t know. Why are you getting so pissy?”

“She’s our friend.”

“Lily’s our friend too, and you didn’t seem to have much of a problem with it when you propositioned me to get her to fall in love with James last year."

"I didn't ask you to get her to fall in love with him!"

"Okay, and what about you and Mary the year before that?”

“That’s different. Marlene’s…”

“She’s what?”

Sirius pressed his lips together in a sour line. “Never mind. Let’s just go.” He turned and stalked away, trunk in hand, and Remus was left to stare after him. There hadn’t been much time since the kiss to worry about what it meant for their friend group, and though he had expected some teasing, Sirius’ reaction left a bad taste in his mouth.

“Hey, hold on!” Remus used his long legs to catch up with Sirius, who was nearly to the buses now. “Are you really this angry that I kissed a girl when you—”

“Shh!” Sirius smacked a hand to the centre of Remus’ chest to silence him.

"Don't shush me!"

"Shut up then! And bloody look!”

Following his gaze, Remus spotted Snape staring down the rest of their friends as they waited to board the bus. "Oh fuck," he sighed. "Gotta hand it to the slimy git, he never really cares much about being outnumbered."

Sirius didn't respond, only set off across the berm with his trunk in one hand. Following closely on his heels, Remus met his friends and pulled to a stop next to Mary and Marlene, who were both scowling with their arms crossed over their chest. Sirius barely glanced at Marlene, and went straight to Mary’s other side, nudging her.

“What’s Snivellus want?” He asked.

Mary whispered back; “He’s upset Lily’s taking our train.”

“Why would you want to get off at Doncaster?!” Snape demanded loudly, making James huff at Lily’s side.

“It’s none of your business, Snivellus.”

“Wasn’t talking to you, skiver.”

“Stop that,” Lily snapped from behind her muffler. “Sev, I’m sorry, I just thought it might be okay to take the other line this time.”

“You don’t have to explain yourself to him every time he comes whining,” James said.

“Shush. Sev, I really am sorry. You should come with us!”

“You're sorry? Sorry for what—lying to me?!”

“I didn’t lie, I just didn’t—”

“Tell me!” Snape howled. “You didn’t tell me! Just like you didn’t tell me you spent our last night before holiday at their dorm!” He jabbed a finger at James.

Lily’s eyes widened. “Who—”

“Bryan had some things to say when he got back!”

Remus resisted rolling his eyes. Did they put all the insufferable assholes in Salazar?

“Really,” Snape blagged on, “walking home so late—or should I say early? People are going to get the wrong idea, Lily. You don’t want anyone thinking you’re a slag do you?”

“Him?!” He shrieked at Lily. “You—HIM?!"

“Go ahead, keep talking, see what happens!” James growled, drawing an even bigger crowd.

“Gentlemen!” Sheila shouted, sliding through a few Byron House students who’d stopped to watch. “Oh, Jesus F. Chop—are we going to have to have this conversation again, you two?! Because I was under the distinct impression that we’d finished this last year! Mr. Potter—release Mr. Snape this instant!”

James immediately dropped Snape’s collar, and the other boy staggered back as their teacher stepped between them. Dressed in a bright blue parka, Sheila looked more like a blueberry than a teacher, but her threat cut through her wardrobe as per usual. “Whose bus is this?” She demanded.

“Ours,” Lily answered, earning her an extra-nasty glare from Snape. Sheila turned on him.

“Mr. Snape, is this your bus?”

“… No.”

“Where is your bus?”

Snape begrudgingly gestured down the line.

“Then shouldn’t you be standing next to it?”

Jaw clenched bitterly, Snape shot one last look at Lily and James before he marched off. They all watched him go and Sheila checked her watch. “Right, well, buses will be leaving soon. I want the rest of you on board. Now.” She looked at James and gave him a pointed ‘go on’ wave.

Nodding, James turned and walked back to Lily. “Sorry, I think I messed up,” he mumbled, and Lily sighed sadly before taking his gloved hand and giving it a squeeze. He smiled faintly, and together they climbed onto the bus followed by a rattled-looking Peter and Moira.

Remus turned to Sirius, fully expecting a quip at Snape’s expense, but he wasn’t there, and when he looked back to the bus doors he found Sirius climbing the steps behind Mary with hands in his pockets.

“C’mon, Remus,” Sheila said, smiling at him. “Don’t want to miss your bus.”

Awkwardly, Remus nodded and set his trunk down with the rest where the driver was busy packing them in the bus’s boot. He made his way to the stairs and turned back to find Sheila waving at him. “Have a happy Christmas,” she called, before turning to say the same to any other student who looked her way.

“Happy Christmas, Mrs. Buchanan,” he said quietly, before boarding the bus.





* * *





Sirius did not talk to him the entire ride to the station. He took a seat near the back of the bus with Sandy Herron from music and left him to sit with Lottie, who was apparently ‘immensely sad’ to be separated from Mickey for the holidays but ‘uber-excited’ to go home to do some proper shopping and visit her other girlfriends. A seat ahead, James and Lily leaned into one another, apologising quietly and comforting each other over the fight. Remus knew Snape was a touchy subject between them, but he hoped letting the cat out of the bag would finally put his and Lily’s dying friendship to rest.

By the time their bus pulled into the train station Remus had to wee so badly he was practically dancing in his seat. Unfortunately bad road conditions on the way there meant there was only time to grab their bags and rush to the platform or risk missing the train all together. They piled into a compartment—only seven of them since Peter had gone off to join Moira—and played musical chairs until they all fit. The entire time Sirius stayed as far from Remus as he could, more content to let James sit with one asscheek on his lap than to even glance in his direction. If it’d just been the four of them Remus would’ve demanded they have it out right there, but with the girls around he felt less willing to poke holes in their veiled friendship. So, as the train pulled away from the platform he resigned himself to the reality that the next time he spoke to Sirius might just be in 1977.

Feeling extra-stuffy and really needing to go now, Remus finally excused himself from the compartment and set off down the aisle, looking for the bathroom.

“Remus? Wait up!” Someone called after him. He turned to find Marlene, slipping out of the compartment after him.

“Oh hey, Marls. Sorry but I really gotta—”

“I just need a second,” Marlene insisted, reaching him and unlacing her scarf from her neck with one hand. She was tightly fisting a book to her chest with the other, her knuckles white. “I needed to say this before I lose my nerve.”

“Marlene McKinnon lose her nerve? Imposs—”

“I wanted to apologise.”

Remus stopped bouncing from foot to foot and cleared his throat a bit. “Apologise? Apologise for what?”

Marlene winced a bit. “For forcing you to kiss me last night. We were pretty drunk—or at least I was—and I let this thing Lily said go to my head—”

“Marlene, you didn’t force me to kiss you.”

“I didn’t?”

“No. I…” Remus shook his head, searching for the right words, “I kissed you too. It was fine.”

“Oh…”

“I mean it was more than fine—it was good.”

Marlene bit her lip. “Oh.”

“Yeah, so—don’t apologise.” Sirius’ words echoed through his memory. “You’re not any different from anyone else. S’normal to kiss. Or at least, that’s what I’ve heard…”

“Cool.” Blushing a bit, Marlene reached up to tuck a lock of her hair behind her ear. “Because I didn’t want you to think that I expected anything.”

Remus straightened up. “Oh no. Never.”

“Or that you had to—”

“Mm-mm, nope.”

“But if you were interested, then I would, maybe—”

“Maybe—?”

“If you thought that—”

“We—”

“Yeah?”

“Yeah!”

“Are we talking about the same thing?”

Remus pursed his lips. “What are you talking about…?”

“Um—us?”

“Oh, yeah! Totally.”

“Really?”

He gulped. “Mhm. Sure, I suppose?"

Marlene clapped her hands together lightly. “Great. So—um—I’ll call you? Over Christmas? Or—or you can call me… of course.”

Remus thought instantly of the flat. “How about I call you,” he suggested.

Marlene nodded instantly, biting her lip. “Okay. Here.” She pulled a little slip of paper from inside her book. “Glad I have that now—felt a bit silly, but it’s my family’s number. You can call it and just ask for me.”

“Brilliant.” He took the note and stared at it lightly before tucking it into his pocket. “I’ll… I'll call you then!”

“Brilliant,” Marlene said firmly. They stood there a moment until she gestured down the aisle with her book. “I guess I should let you go now.”

“Huh?”

“Weren’t you going somewhere?”

Remus chuckled awkwardly. “Oh, yeah. Just the loo.”

“Okay,” Marlene smiled shyly. “Well, I’ll meet you back with the others.”

He nodded and she turned away, moving back down the train corridor to their overstuffed compartment. Watching her go, Remus got that familiar squirmy feeling in his gut before realising it was just his bladder screaming in distress. When he finally returned to the compartment he walked in to find all of his friends playing poker and betting with a bag of peanuts from the snack trolley.

“All I’m saying is that you and Mickey were gone for a long time last night,” Mary said. “Care to fill us in?”

“If you must know,” Lottie drawled while sorting the cards in her hand, “there are two reigning factors in why you were so sorely missing my exuberant presence last night. First, I knew I was going to get stuck with you lot for nine hours on a train today, so who needed the extra party? And second, our room was completely empty. So don’t act so surprised when one of us takes advantage of such an opportunity.”

“Oh Lot,” Lily moaned while the rest of them laughed.

“Hey, you could’ve tried Potter’s room,” Lottie shrugged innocently.

Marlene glanced up at Remus then, cheeks pink, and they shared a silent smile before she made room on the bench next to her for him.

“Want me to deal you in, Remus?” Lily offered as he drew the door closed behind him.

“Yeah, I need you,” James said. “Sirius won’t play and I'm horribly outnumbered. I can't win back our stolen dignity from Black's birthday all on my own.”

“Fat chance anyway, Potter,” Mary cackled, glancing at Lottie’s hand.

Lottie turned it over; “Straight flush. Next you’ll be streaking through the entire train, boys.”

James groaned in defeat while all the girls giggled and Remus slid in beside Marlene. He spared a chance look across the carriage but Sirius was turned away, jacket pulled up to his ears and head leaning against the window, eyes closed as though he were asleep.

Chapter 44: Christmas, 1976


Chapter Summary

Remus goes home. Then he goes home, home.

This chapter is dedicated to maraudmoons, who said they'd preform a sacrifice for me just to get some more of the silly words inside my head. Instead of that, I hope you (and everyone else) snuggles up with some fuzzy socks, your favourite tea, and enjoys this chapter. It's a happy one.

(Or you can just read it on toilet or the bus like the fan-fiction gremlins I know we all are. <3)



Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes



Subway’s no way for a good man to go down,

Rich man can ride and the hobo, he can drown;

And I thank the Lord for the people I have found,

I thank the Lord for the people I have found…

- “Mona Lisas and Mad Hatters” Elton John, 1972



Nothing could be trusted to stay stagnant forever, not even the dour Lupin Estate. Though little had changed in actuality. The ground was still painted in damp rather than fresh wisps of snowfall, and Lyall Lupin’s preference for keeping an ever-revolving array of staff hadn’t waned, though Remus was pleased enough to find that the maid who brought him tea in the morning wasn’t as stingy with the milk and sugar as the last had been.

A new litter of pups had been born in late-November to the even-tempered Zenyatta and a stud from some breeder in the Midlands. Remus knew better than to name them without his father’s consent, but the runt of the litter was grey all over with a spotted nose and reminded him of Dusty. Secretly he dubbed the pup Smokey.

Ever man’s bestest friend, Dusty still greeted him with enthusiasm—Giles even more so. They spent his first night back loosing to each other in cards and Remus had a great lie-in the following morning. Outside of that, the halls were quiet and the house was calm. The only agitation came at supper time, when Remus took his meals in the dining room with his only father for company. Those were usually quiet too.

On the rare occasion Lyall would put down whatever document he was pouring over and acknowledge his son's existence. Mostly Remus wished he wouldn't, but that was probably one of the only reasons he did.

"How are your classes?"

"Fine."

"I hope they’re teaching you proper politics.”

"What does that even mean?"

His father answered with another question. "Are they still pushing the socialists’s agenda?” He asked. “Or have they moved onto things that might actually be useful in life?"

Remus stubbornly pushed his peas around his plate. "They teach us history."

"That'll be a no then."

A roll of the eyes, and; "Whatever you say, Dad..."

Lyall raised a brow and set his empty glass down, wiping his hands on the cloth napkin.

"I'll be returning to the office early. Goddamn Labour Party has ordered a thirty million pound cut to public expenditure, meaning that the whole bloody country's about to go up in flames. It's like those lunatics in office want a crisis. There'll be strikes in the streets next, I expect. As if we need the traffic. I’ll be staying in the city for the duration. You'll remain here with Giles. Use the time to study. I don’t want you running around the streets—not when you're about to return to school. Do you understand me?"

"Was that a rhetorical question?"

"Do you understand?"

Remus set his jaw. "Yes, sir."

Eyeing him sourly, Lyall pushed his chair back from the table and stood, gathering a fistful of documents. Remus saw it coming before it happened—he would stride from the room without another glance and wouldn't look at him until another inevitable dinner the following evening. No, 'goodnight son' or 'have a good day tomorrow'. Certainly no 'I love you's. It irked him, but not because he needed any of that. He didn't want Lyall's attention, but the urge to scream in his face—Look at me!—it was so strong. Maybe it was just acknowledgement that he wanted.

"My literacy professor liked my final paper," Remus said suddenly, before his father could leave. "He said it was the best in the entire year. That I could probably be published one day."

Lyall glanced up at him. "So now they're filling your head with nonsense. Do I really need to tell you how much a freelance author makes in this economy? And that's if you even manage to find work. Not many would hire someone who can't even manage a few measly exams. Tell me, Remus, how could someone who's 'best in the entire year' achieve a mere 'satisfactory' on three out of seven exams?"

"It was a mistake," Remus grumbled, throwing himself back in his chair.

"You mean your teachers incorrectly marked their own exams?"

"No! I was... distracted."

"Do you think that is an adequate excuse? I didn't send you to Scotland to be distracted. What could be so interesting as to keep you from your only job?"

Remus ground his teeth together. "Never mind."

"There is nothing decent in life for 'satisfactory' people. Unless you'd prefer to live penny-to-penny, with some damn labour union waiting to snatch the food from your family's mouths every time the government denies them new gloves for the winter, I suggest you learn to ignore your distractions."

"Are you a Tory, Dad?"

"I'm a realist, Remus. I think you'll find they make more money. Now don't be bothering Giles. If you need anything—sort it out yourself."

Straightening up, Lyall adjusted his collar and strode from the room. Remus watched him go. "Merry Christmas to you too, Dad," he swore, before turning around in his seat and throwing his fork across the dining hall. He'd hoped it would miraculously stick in the wood, but it only landed with an empty clatter.

He almost ran off that night, but then—as if reading his mind—Lyall ordered him to help their head dog trainer, Sebastian, wean the new puppies onto solid food. It was a tedious affair; the dogs had to be fed every three hours and even then they still screeched for their mother's milk, but Remus appreciated the work. It kept him busy, and dogs were better company than people most days anyway.

"They're a scrappy bunch, these'uns!" Sebastian declared. The dog-trainer had a thick Norfolk accent and Remus was lucky if he could decipher every third word. "Best watch yoour fingers with Whistlejacket thurr. She'll tairke 'em roight off. Oi pity the poour bastard who's got 'er. But yow know yoour father—payment up front."

"You mean they're already sold?" Remus held Smokey close to his chest. He wasn't supposed to baby the dogs, but they were puppies. Barely four weeks old. Sebastian wouldn't rat on him.

"Yes sair, got all their pairpers sorted this mahrnin'. They'll be riddy to goo by end 'f Jan-oo-ary, oi figure. But doon' worry, we'll still 'ave plenty 'a beasts around for yow to 'alp me with. Navver a shortage of work 'ere."

Outside of caring for the dogs, he spent ample time catching up on the shows and music he’d missed while at school. Disco was officially in full-swing—it was all Top of the Pops was playing—and a sober Remus would have normally been less-likely to entertain it, but there was nothing else to do apart from listen, sleep, read, and make the trek across the damp lawn to the doghouse. He could've called James or Peter, but they were sure to be busy with their own families. Marlene had given him her phone number, but that too felt awkward. What would he even say? He hadn't read anything of substance since most of his books had gone with him to school. She would probably appreciate hearing about the puppies, but then wouldn't the sensible thing be to invite her over to see them? Remus had never had a friend over to the estate before. But then again, most of them didn't even know it existed.

There was Giles to distract him, of course. And despite what Lyall had to say, the old man was all too happy to accept a round of cards or an extra set of hands. Then, when he wasn’t running his normal errands or fixing something around the house like a driver-turned-handyman, Giles could always be found in the parlour in the same burgundy armchair that had been dubbed his for as long as Remus could remember. If it was before lunchtime he’d have that morning’s paper in hand. Between lunch and dinner it was the same paper, though he’d most certainly moved onto the daily crossword. After dinner it was a glass of his favourite brandy, which always smelt okay but tasted horrible. Not that Giles had ever let Remus try the drink. That would be completely irresponsible.

There were a lot of memories attached to that chair; one of them being a faint stain on its left armrest leftover from a time when six year-old Remus had knocked a vase off its shelf in the library and split his hand open trying to piece it back together. He’d balled and went straight to the old man who just lifted him calmly into his lap and pressed the sleeve of his own jacket against the cut to staunch the bleeding until Remus was coherent enough to explain what had happened. He couldn’t remember so much as touching the chair, just the comfort that came with being drawn into Giles’ lap. Afterwards the stain remained; enduring the years in the shape of half of a tiny hand print, splayed wide as it reached for comfort.

Now Remus was looking for comfort again, but he wasn't six years-old anymore.

It took almost three days to persuade Giles to let him leave. He could’ve just left on his own of course—had been doing it for nearly half his life now—but something about that Christmas felt different. It was as though there was a fog hanging over him.

What if Lee had been wrong?

What if Tomny never meant to have him back?

What if he got angry?

It was like knowingly placing a bet on the wrong horse. Tomny had been ready to let him go that very first September he’d been shipped off to the Highlands; only Remus had been blind to the fact, and he’d dumbly forced himself back into his life again and again just like a bad cold. He’d already learned to stop feeling guilty over the phone calls—those felt safe because of the distance it kept between them—but showing up again, it felt dangerous. Remus wasn’t sure he could handle being forced to leave a second time, but as muddled as everything felt, those nights spent back at the estate passed as though he were racing the clock. He had a little more than a week until his return to school. So few days to do all the things he wanted.

And so, Remus did all in his power to convince his oldest friend and caretaker that he was an upstanding citizen, totally capable of keeping himself out of trouble while home. He did this mostly during the evenings, hoping that the brandy would butter-up Giles’ sense of rationality, and eventually he got what he wanted.

On the morning of Christmas Eve, Giles drove him to Aldgate himself. He was quiet for most of the ride, despite Remus’ excited (or nervous—he couldn’t decide which) energy seeping out from the backseat, but that didn’t mean he wasn’t going to lecture.

“Sounds to me like you’re just running from your problems,” Giles said, after they’d passed through Bermondsey and started across the Tower Bridge. He was chewing on a toothpick, something he’d picked up to help kick his bad snuff habit.

“Has he even asked to see me since he left?”

There was no need to mention Lyall's name. Giles was quiet in the front seat of the Rolls.

“Well, then I’ll do what I want.”

“The dogs miss you.”

“I’ve seen them.”

“The ladies in the kitchen miss you.”

“I’ve seen them too.”

The driver was quiet again for a bit, then pulled the toothpick from his mouth; “Remus, son—I know you two don’t always get on, but your father is just looking out for your best interests. You like that school, yeah? Well he sent you there. Tried to make it work for you after all the rest didn’t.”

Remus didn’t bother to add how Lyall had neglected to mention that his mother had also gone to Hawkings. Perhaps he honestly didn’t know, or had forgotten in the last twenty years since they were married—or maybe he just didn’t care. Either way, he wouldn’t be getting a thank you from him.

“I’ll still call you,” he promised, “but I want to go. At least for a few days. I have people waiting on me too, you know.”

Giles glanced back at him in the car's mirror. “It’s important to have friends, lad. No one likes being lonely, but try to take things seriously.”

“That would be becoming boring, Gil."

“What’s that?”

Remus smiled to himself. " ‘If you can’t be good, be smart’. It's good advice—wonder who gave it to me.”

Giles could only shake his head hopelessly.

Remus kept the exchange in the back of his mind for the rest of the drive. He wasn’t sure going back to the End was the smart thing—it’d certainly never been the good thing by anyone’s standards—but the rest of his school friends were enjoying their holidays with the people they loved. He wanted to, too, all nerves aside.

Luckily, it turned out that Lee was true to his word after all.

As Remus dragged his feet across the cracked pathway that led up to the flat’s steps, he heard someone shriek his name from above and looked up to find Tonya on the balcony, wrapped up in a robe and waving frantically. Even from three floors up he could see the dark circles under her eyes, the hollowness of her cheeks, and yet when she smiled at him it was as though all the worst parts of the world simply vanished.

Tonya immediately tossed the cigarette she’d been smoking over the railing and dashed back inside the flat, only to come flying out the building’s front door a few seconds later. She tackled him in a hug so fierce he almost fell over, but she was a small woman, and he used the momentum of her love to swing her around in a big circle.

“Oh, Remus, my love, I’m so happy to see you!” She gushed in his ear, before yanking back to get a look at him, hands moving from his shoulders to his cheeks. “You’ve grown! Look at how handsome you’ve gotten!” Her thumb brushed his scar. “And so devil-may-care.” She wiggled her eyebrows suggestively and Remus squirmed in her grip, embarrassed as he batted off her hands.

“C’mon Tonya, what are you, my mother?”

“Leave him be, Ton. He’s come home from school, not war,” Tomny called. He’d apparently followed her and was leaning in the building’s doorway, arms crossed over his broad chest. Remus immediately dashed up the steps and they grappled, hugging with a tight hand on the neck while clapping each other on the back.

“Happy to see you, Lu.”

“You too, Tom,” Remus said as he pulled back. His heart was slamming against his ribcage and he felt so happy that if Tomny had asked, he would've burst into song right there on the front steps. Luckily the older boy only smiled, showing off a handsome dimple.

“Glad Lee got a hold of you," Tomny said. "Been a bit busy around 'ere, sorry we haven't called much."

“It's fine—totally fine. But Lee—he said you wanted me… well that I should come by.”

Tomny nodded. “It’s Christmas, and no one pays attention around the holidays 'nyway. Not when s'brass monkeys outside and the whole country’s eatin' gingerbread and drinkin' themselves into a stupor.”

“Yeah,” Remus nodded. “But you don’t have to worry, Tom. I’ll only stay for a few days—less if you want. Promised I’d be back soon anyway.”

Tomny’s smiled tightened and he lifted a hand to cup the side of Remus’ neck again. “Yer a good lad, but don't worry too much. We missed you.”

Remus could've cried. Happiness or relief, it didn't matter.

“C’mon now,” Tonya said, appearing at his side and rubbing his arms comfortingly, “it’s freezing. Let’s get you inside and warmed up.”

Tomny took the bag he’d brought with him and they went in together, arm in arm. Everywhere in the building was drafty but the flat was still warm thanks to the amount of bodies filling it up. Remus was instantly bombarded by his friends—Doss and Lee, who tackled him with happy grunts of hello, Seesaw and Vint who nodded and bumped his fist cordially. Just like the estate there were new faces, including Lee’s younger brother Ian, who shook his hand so wildly Remus felt his shoulder pop.

“Don’ mind him,” Lee started, “ 'e’s always bouncing off the walls. We’re pretty sure s‘cause he was conceived on poppers.”

"You're so embarrasin'!" Ian shoved him and ended up in a headlock. “Ugh—gerroff, Lee!”

“Oi—watch out everyone he’s gonna blow!”

The brothers began to tussle and Remus stood back, laughing with everyone else as Ian inevitably lost—unable to break Lee’s hold around his neck. He could definitely see the family resemblance in their lanky frames and mess of freckles, but really it was their smiles that made them brothers.

“Oh fuckin’ hell—now what's this?"

Tomny’s cuss cut through the room, making everyone straighten up or jump as though a gun had gone off. Remus whipped around to find Tomny staring at him, eyes hard and suspicious. He stepped forward and the other guys parted around him like a ship at sea, following his back as though they were readying for a fight.

“Reckon you’re bein' funny, do ya?” He asked in a low voice, looking Remus up and down.

Remus blinked. “I… what?”

“Explain, now.”

“Tom, I don't know what you're…”

Tomny scoffed his laughter and raised a hand. Everyone watched him, deadly still, though instead of a fist Tomny just flattened his fingers and measured his own height. He passed over himself and then forward until his hand knocked against the top of Remus’ forehead.

“You went and got taller than me didn’t you, you lil' git.”

Remus opened and closed his mouth, stupefied, then; “Maybe you just shrunk in your old age.”

Tomny stared at him hard, until his mask cracked and a grin shone through. He began to laugh, and the tension visibly drained from the room. It was a bit unnerving how quickly it'd came and went, but Remus had no time to bask in it. Before he could say anything else, Tomny had him in his own headlock.

“Cheeky, Lu!”

"Fuck Tomny—get off!"

“He’s right though, Tom,” Lee added, “I think I see a few grey hairs even!”

“If I’ve got any greys it’s because I’m always lookin’ after dirty bleeders like you!”

“Ha-ha, yes, so funny!” Remus heard Tonya snap her fingers several times as he fought against Tomny’s bicep. “Now let me through, you nobs. I have a surprise for Remus.”

“Sorry Ton, Lu’s a bit busy at the moment,” Tomny said.

“Let me go!” Remus wailed.

“No can do, sweetheart. You’re just going to have to live with it.”

“Don’t be a dick, Tomny. Remus, look!”

With a grunt, Remus managed to lift his head. Tonya stood before him, smiling radiantly in her robe, and from behind her back she produced a brand-spanking-new album;

Queen: A Day at the Races.

“Happy Christmas, Remus.”





* * *





The initial bonhomie of his arrival had worn off by the next morning, replaced instead by the meager excitement that took hold of everyone come Christmas Day. Remus didn't mind in the slightest. It'd taken him all of one hour to realise just how badly he'd been missing the gentle existence of the shabby London flat. The humble two-bedroom had been left with its usual occupants, plus Ian, who according to Tonya had started coming around regularly after his and Lee’s mum had gotten back with their step-dad. The guy had a penchant for double-malt whisky as well as speaking with his fists and taking his anger out on sixteen year-olds with lippy mouths. And there were more than enough of those to go around.

It’d only taken one phone call from Ian for Lee to nearly put the prick in the hospital, which seemed only fair to the rest of them, since after all, Lee had spent most of his childhood playing punching bag for the rest of his mum’s piece-of-shit boyfriends.

Ian’s arrival wasn’t the only new development within the group though; Doss had a girlfriend now who worked in a Debenhams across the city and was always hopping on the tube to go visit her. The others tried to rag on him for it of course, but they were rebuked by Tonya, who was apparently the only one he’d permitted to meet the girl so far. Remus could tell that Doss must've really liked her—his usually cool and collected expression turned shy and embarrassed at mere mention of her name—and he was happy for him. Happier still that he’d been there a whole night and not sensed a single hint of animosity from any of his friends. It soothed the fear he’d secretly been carrying ever since Tomny revealed he knew everything about his real life and family. But it was obvious—Tomny had said nothing. Doss probably didn't even know that Remus knew, and it was enough. If he had to carry the secret for the rest of his life just to ensure his friends would stay this happy, he would gladly do so.

It was late on Christmas Day when they’d all finally woken and gathered together. Tomny sat in his armchair while Lee and Ian split the other sofa and Remus relaxed on the same couch he’d woken up on. Seesaw offered him a puff of his morning spliff but he declined, too busy watching Doss and Vint help Tonya prepare breakfast. It was funny seeing the two largest guys among them squeeze into such a tiny kitchen, only to gingerly move around Tonya as though she were a grizzly bear and not simply a girl who barely came up to their chins. The telly was playing some holiday special but no one was really paying any attention. There was too much to say.

“You jammy bastard," Lee hissed, "you set off a bomb?”

“Not a real bomb. Just these stink bombs my roommates concocted.”

“Wicked. Do you remember the recipe?”

“Oh no!” Tonya shouted from the kitchen. “Remus John, don’t you dare say another word. I will not allow stink bombs anywhere near this place. Not in my house.”

“Oh c’mon, Ton,” Lee tried, “we’ll only do it outside.”

“Bien essayé, dickheads.” She emerged from the kitchen waving a spatula threateningly. “Now come get your breakfast.”

Tonya had truly outdone herself. She presented them with dutch pancakes and poached eggs, bubble and squeak and crumpets, even homemade hollandaise. In true formal fashion, they devoured the spread while sitting on the living room floor.

“Blimey, didn’t even know you could roast a plum,” Ian said as he licked his fingers.

“Those were figs,” Tonya laughed.

“Well they were fig-tastic.”

Tonya got up to collect their plates but Tomny just exchanged her seats. “Nah, I’ve got it,” he said, pressing a kiss to her temple as he passed.

Tonya smiled and dropped down into the recliner, draping her legs over one side. Remus caught her gaze and she winked before mouthing something. Unsure, he perked up and she leaned in to whisper to him. “Go help him.”

Remus nodded automatically and shot up from his seat, scuttling into the kitchen and collecting a few more empty plates as he went. He found Tomny standing over the sink, suds halfway up his forearms.

“Ah, some indentured help,” he said cheerfully; “Good. I’ll wash, you dry.”

Remus set the plates down and took up a rag, taking the next dish from him as he handed it over. "You guys seem like you're doing good."

“Mhm. Winter's are slow mostly. The others are glad you came back by the way,” Tomny said and Remus glanced at him, before dropping his gaze, a bit haughtily.

“Don’t think you’re beating around the bush hard enough, Tom. Might need a bigger stick.”

Tomny huffed in that way that meant he was laughing and Remus felt a little shudder run up his spine as he set the dried dish aside and picked up another.

“You always did have a mouth on you,” Tomny started again, “but you’re right. And I’m glad too—really. Though, I did wonder though whether you’d actually show if I wasn’t the person to tell you to come.”

“You mean this was all a fuckin' test?”

“Mm. Tonya and I took bets actually.”

“You utter asshole. Fine—what’d you bet on then?”

Tomny just smiled down at the dish water. “I don’t mind, you know—how much Tonya likes you. I don’t mind.”

Remus blinked. “Well why would you? She’s in love with you.”

“Yeah. S’pose she is. Feels good to be with the people you love during the holidays, don’t it?”

“Yeah, it does," he answered, ears burning.

“You haven’t been smoking as much,” Tomny said casually. “You quit?”

“No,” Remus answered, reaching to put a stack of plates away, “just cut back a bit. We roll our own at school.”

“Guess I should’ve gotten you something other than fags for Christmas then. Though I suppose I just ruined the surprise.”

“No, it’s fine! It’ll give my fingers a break for a while. Siri—I mean, my friends at school suck at rolling so it’s always me. And our fence has high rates—shit’s expensive up north.”

Tomny chuckled. “You got some books too, I think—and records. Don’t tell the other lads I told you, but Tonya picked it all out mostly. She's the only one with taste.”

“You didn’t have to get me anything,” Remus protested.

“That mean you have nothing for us, then?”

“No…” In truth, Remus’ bag was stuffed with several badly wrapped presents, most of which were recycled from Lyall’s extensive wardrobe. He had reasoned that it wasn’t stealing since all of it had been cleared out by the maids as part of their yearly household purge and would’ve been sent to the local refuse anyway. Most of the clothes were going to be too big on them, apart from maybe Doss, but they were clean and warm and it made Remus happy to be able to give his friends something in exchange for their generosity.

“Oh, yeah? Never gotten a gift from a blue-blood before,” Tomny said snidely, and Remus shouldered him gently for it.

“If you’re worried about how much I paid you can relax. They’re gifts of practicality.”

“Practical—? Honestly, what is that school teachin' you? ‘Practicality’, pish.”

Remus snorted just as Tonya appeared in the kitchen behind them. “Hey, we can finish clean-up later. Doss wants to visit Felicia and I’d like to do presents before he goes.”

“Okay, we’re coming,” Tomny answered, turning off the tap and wiping his hands. Remus put away his last dish and together they wandered back into the living room, Tomny’s arm looped around his shoulders.

Watching Doss exchange his battered belt and boots for new ones while Tomny tugged a new jumper over his head felt like the best gift he could’ve gotten. Lee made a crack that he’d never owned a jacket that didn’t already need to be patched in the elbows, while Vint gave Remus an approving nod for the fresh slacks, which thankfully didn’t look entirely out of place with the rest of his get-up.

“We’re like new men,” Tomny chuckled, running his hands across the jumper's soft wool.

Lee popped his jacket collar. “Hold on Tom, you sure Lu didn’t give you a frilly skirt to match? Could’a sworn I saw one.”

“Yeah and s'up your arse.”

“Gentlemen!” Tonya called from down the hallway. “Drumroll, please!”

Immediately Tomny threw himself down in his recliner and began slamming his hands down on its arms while the rest of them smacked every available surface. A moment later Tonya emerged from the hallway in a sweeping white dress made top-to-bottom out of a delicate lace. Remus hadn't realised it, but it tied daintily at the wrists and neck, making her look like some fairytale princess. She was barefoot, despite the cold that seeped up through the floorboards, and glowing as she spun around in a circle and let the skirt billow outwards.

“How do I look?” She called, twisting her dark hair up into a bun and holding it in place. “Like a proper lady?”

“Simply gorgeous!” Doss announced.

“Elizabeth Taylor would be shamed to know her!” Lee added enthusiastically.

Blowing them both a kiss, Tonya turned to Remus. “Well? What do you think, love?”

Remus’ mouth went as dry as paper.

I think you’re the prettiest girl I’ve ever seen, he thought.

“Looks… nice…” he said.

“Oh no,” Lee started, “you broke him.”

Still smiling, Tonya rolled her eyes lightly and Tomny slid in front of her, cupping her waist. “I think you look amazing.”

“Oh yeah?” Tonya dropped her arm, letting her hair untwist down her back as Tomny kissed her.

“Oi, get a room, you two,” Doss shouted as Ian and Lee gave a whistle. Tonya just wrapped her arms around her boyfriend’s back while Tomny shot them the bird, leaving them all laughing and nudging one another.

Remus sat back on the sofa, fiddling with one of the books he’d been gifted. He tried not to stare, but seeing Tonya emerge in all white had stolen the air from his lungs. The dress had been a lucky find really—lucky that the maids had found it in some back closet and decided to toss it and luckier still that the tags had still been attached and he couldn’t recall any memories of seeing Hope wear it. He wasn't entirely sure what qualified as 'tacky' but gifting someone his dead mother's clothes was probably not far off.

Before any of them had to bear further witness to more public displays of affection, Tonya sharply pulled back from Tomny and pointed at Remus with a devilish grin. She had a little slip of paper tucked between two of her fingers. “Oh Remus, I found this on the bedroom floor—think it must’ve fallen out of your bag. It’s got a phone number on it.”

Before he could take it, Tomny reached over and plucked the paper from her fingers, unfolding it. “ ‘Hope you have a Happy Christmas’,” he read; “ ‘Call me when you can’. Oh and look, there’s a little heart.”

“Give me that!” Remus grunted, jumping up to snatch the paper. Tomny was faster, and he yanked his arm back.

“Now who’s givin' you notes with little hearts on ‘em?”

“No one you know!”

“Well we should change that,” Tonya said, giddily. “Someone get the phone.”





* * *





Of course none of them would drop it. Each of his friends had an addictive personality in their own way—after latching onto something they never let it go until each and every joke or wise-crack had been wrung dry, and in this case, the joke was Remus’ current relationship status.

“I’m not calling her on Christmas,” he insisted, after he’d managed to steal Marlene’s phone number back and stash it out of sight.

“Why not?” Tonya whined. “She gave you her number hoping you would call! Haven’t you left the poor girl waiting long enough?”

“You’re blowing this way out of proportion!”

“Aw, look—he’s blushing,” Tomny teased. Remus swat at him with the towel he was using to dry the rest of the dishes.

Tonya got between them. “You have to call her tomorrow. It’d be cruel to wait any longer.”

Reaching over her, Tomny handed him a freshly-scrubbed cooking pan; “Yeah, and don’t you worry, Lu, we’ll be right here for moral support.”

That was how he ended up dialling Marlene’s house on the evening of Boxing Day with several of his friends behind him, craning their ears to listen in. They never stopped sniggering and Remus quickly began to pray that no one would pick up and he’d just get the machine instead. Too bad he had shit luck.

“Shhh! Guys, shut up!” He snapped.

The line clicked to life. “Hello?”

“Er—hi. Is Marlene around?”

“Speaking.”

"Call her something sweet!" Tonya hissed. "Make it unique! Tell her she’s lovely! She sounds lovely! Ooh—what colour are her eyes?”

"Tonya—shut up!"

"Hello...?"

“Oh! Hey there, er—Cherry. It's Remus.” He winced the moment the words left his mouth, and both Lee and Tomny burst into snorts of laughter while Tonya smacked her forehead. Mortified, Remus swatted the air in their direction as Marlene chuckled lightly into the other end.

“ 'Cherry'? That my nickname now?”

“Too weird?” He sighed.

“No,” she answered, “I think I like it. In goofy way. So what’s going on, you numpty? Have a good Christmas?”

“Yeah, was great. You?”

“Wonderful. It’s really nice to hear from you. I talked to Lily yesterday, has she rung you yet?”

“Er—no, but that’s not really her fault.”

Lee nudged him. “Psst, Lu—ask her if she’s got any fit girlfriends looking to boff.”

“Piss off,” Remus grumbled.

“What’s that?” Marlene asked from the other end.

“Oh—not you! S'nothing, just some idiot shouting in my other ear.”

“You got family visiting?”

“Nah, just some friends.”

“Wish I could see our friends right now,” Marlene sighed. “Might be a nice break. It feels like mum invited an entire village for the holidays. I have to bunk with my nan and aunt Rosie.”

“Damn.”

“Yeah, I know. But it’s not so bad actually, most of them leave tomorrow. Just wanted to whine a bit. My brothers are visiting so that’s been nice.”

“Oh yeah, two right? Michael and—what’s the other?”

“John. His wife Anna’s actually pregnant, announced it yesterday morning. I’m gonna be an aunty.”

“Wow. Congrats.”

“Thanks!”

“Psst, Lu—”

“Shut up, Lee—”

“Sounds like you’re having fun,” Marlene said.

“Something like that,” Remus grunted, pushing Lee away from the phone by the face.

“Look, Remus," Marlene started, her tone turning very serious, "I wanted to know if I could talk to you about something before we went back to school?”

Remus switched ears with the receiver uneasily. Tonya instantly pressed her head to the other side. “Oh. Or I mean—oh yeah...?”

“Yeah. I know we kind of talked on the train, but I really don’t like leaving things muddled like that. Mary says it's how people go from liking each other to switching their shampoo for hair-removal cream."

"She's done that?"

"Oh, I suppose you weren't around after she and Darby Ellis broke up in year ten."

"Fuck, that's insane."

"Oh yeah, it totally was!” Marlene stopped suddenly and cleared her throat. “But like I was wondering… What do you think of… ehm—‘us’?”

Tonya gave a sharp gasp but clapped her hand over her mouth the moment Remus shot her a glare.

“ ‘Us’?” He echoed. “Well, we’re good aren’t we?”

“Oh sure, but I didn’t really mean just… friends ‘us’.”

“Oh.”

Tonya drew back and slapped Remus in the shoulder. “Don’t make her do all the work!” She hissed quietly.

Marlene spoke again; “I just mean that it might be nice, you know, to try it out. In the beginning I thought Lily was crazy—like we’re such good friends already—but she and James seem to be doing alright so I figured that maybe...”

Tonya slapped him again and the words tumbled out. “Thatweshoulddate?”

"Fuck yeah!" Doss shouted suddenly. Remus threw a hand up to ward off their laughter, but it didn't stop Lee from touching his shoulder and making a sizzling sound.

“You think we should?” Marlene asked.

“Sure," he bumbled. "As long as you want to.”

“Yeah, sure—I mean—yes. I think it’d be cool. An 'us'.”

Remus nodded. “Cool. 'Us' it is then."

“Wow. Mary’s gonna totally lose her head,” she giggled after a moment. “Lily too, since she called it and all. Though I suppose you’ll know all about that.”

Remus thought of Sirius, and how he’d reacted that last day on the train.

“They’re not the only ones.”

“Well, that’s great then! Us! So I’ll… see you on the train?”

“Yeah, ‘course.”

“Cool. Well, I should go probably. Mum needs help with dinner and all that, I’m sure. Ta then?”

“Yeah, ta.”

There was a final moment of nervous silence and then line clicked dead and Remus slowly pulled the receiver away from his ear. His friends all stared back at him, each of them looking right chuffed and proud.

“Holy fuck,” Tomny started. “Did our Lu actually just get 'imself a girlfriend?”

“I think 'e did,” Doss confirmed, crossing his arms.

“Not sure how smooth 'e was about it,” Lee shrugged, “but I guess it did the job.”

“He was brilliant!” Tonya declared, throwing her arms around Remus in a hug. Lee joined her, then Doss, and Tomny, and even Ian, who’d only just walked in the door with Seesaw and Vint, carrying enough booze to intoxicate an army.

“What we all huggin' for?” Ian asked after-the-fact.

“We’re huggin' to congratulate this spiffin’ tosser!” Tomny shouted, squeezing even tighter.

“You’re all crushing me!” Remus wailed.

"It's the weight of our love, Lu!"

“Alright, off,” Tonya laughed, and the boys released them. She turned and reached into Ian’s paper bag, withdrawing a large bottle of brandy. “Tonight we’re celebrating.”

Chapter 45: Tempo Rubato


Chapter Summary

Remus battles his greatest enemy; time. 1976 comes to a close with love, and the barest hint of what may lay ahead.

That was one of the good nights.

Tonya liked to dance. It didn’t matter who her partner was or if she was alone, she would dance anywhere, anytime. The summer before Remus had watched her skip or sway home more times than she’d walked, and once when they’d come across a pair of buskers outside the local market she’d tossed her shopping aside and danced and spun to their music until she’d fallen into his arms, dizzy and glowing like the sun.
