He froze slightly, before robotically picking up the chunks and rising back up to his feet, tossing them into the sink with another clatter. Tonya watched him sadly, face half-covered, but he didn’t miss the blood this time.

“They say seeing red where you want white is a bad sign,” Remus mumbled, tugging the towel away away from her. Tonya let him, fingers holding onto empty air as he took in the sight of blood smudged beneath her nose.

“Yeah, well I always thought red was a nice colour on me,” she said, almost attempting a laugh before snatching the towel back and wiping her face. “S'fine, it’ll stop soon.”

“Anything I can do?”

“Nope.” She tipped her head back and pinched the bridge of her nose. “Actually yes—pour me another drink?”

“We were just crying in the living room and you want another drink?”

“Oh, were you crying?”

“Now who’s being the dick?”

Tonya dropped the towel and smiled into the mirror. She had blood in her teeth that she sucked away with her tongue. “Tea, then.”

Remus nodded and stepped away from the door, biting his lip. He turned to go, before something inside won out and he stopped just outside that little sliver of yellow bathroom light to watch her. “Tonya, why do you take so many drugs?"

She looked to him, pretty face still stained with her own blood, and sighed. "Same reason as everyone else, I suppose. They help me forget myself for a little while."

"What's there to forget?" She was so beautiful, he couldn’t ever imagine wanting to forget her.

"Oh, sweet love." Tonya smiled again—sadly—and his heart ached.

"Are you at least... happy then?”

Just like last time, the question caught her off guard. “What do you mean, love?”

“I mean… are you okay?”

She didn’t respond right away, just looked him up and down before gently rapping her knuckles against the porcelain sink three times. Remus felt his breath hitch, and she nodded softly, mouthing to him, ‘I’m okay’.

Squeezing the bathroom doorknob tightly, Remus couldn’t think of anything else to say. “Alright, Ton…” He made to step away.

“Remus, what makes you happy?” Tonya asked suddenly.

Pausing, he bit his lip, then; “I’ll tell you next Christmas.”

Tonya’s smile broadened and she shook her head with a light laugh. “Cheeky. Fine. Call me when tea’s ready.”





* * *





In the end he'd left her there, cleaning up the mess that would exist even if he didn’t, and made the tea. They took it in the living room ("Rod Stewart is totally soft rock.") and when their friends finally returned, only a few minutes shy of midnight, Tonya somehow found it in herself to welcome them with open arms. No one mentioned the ragged looks, or the desperation with which they chugged their booze and pills, and things were normal. As normal as they could be. In a time as tumultuous and unsure as 1976, you’d have been hard-pressed to find a single person without an addiction, whether it be drugs or alcohol or cigarettes or football or porn rags. Everyone owed their day-to-day to some habitual dependency, and maybe that was why Remus didn’t say anything.

Love was blind, after all.

Years down the road, in another haphazard radio interview he’d let Gideon talk him into and wouldn’t even remember the next day, Remus would recall that the only things to do in the seventies were get high and listen to music. They didn’t have fancy electronics like VHS tapes or boomboxes and it would be years before the Average Joe was carrying around his own cell phone. The only football matches that were shown on TV were the championships or highlighted Match of the Week, and if you wanted to watch a film you had to go to the cinema and cough up a couple of quid just to sit in the dark for a few hours and forget the rest of the world existed at all. That was all right and good, but whether you were in London and poor or Scotland and rich, your options were limited.

At school he made and played music and eventually he would get real good at it too. The whole thing had mostly started as a joke—just another way to distract themselves or else skive-off studying for A-Levels. None of them knew it then but that joke would turn into the rest of their lives, messily intertwining with relationships, money, fame, and personal introspection. Things would go wrong just as many times as they went right and people would come and go until no one was surprised by anything anymore. Some things were predictable of course, like James and Lily, though they had their own fair share of surprises in store too. They should’ve seen the first big mess coming—there would be many—but even then they were young and stupid and Peter was hardly the only one at fault. Marlene was less shocking; by their last year of school it was clear she was never going to wait for anyone to simply hand her happiness to her. Lottie was more simple, but still brave. It took Remus a while to realise just how much he admired her for it. And Mary had also done well for herself, even if it had taken her a while to pick up the pieces.

But then there was Sirius.

Sirius and his ever-damning belief that being able to live through your suffering was just further proof that you were alive. Remus had never bought much into the idea, but what did he know? For most of his life he’d looked at everything the wrong way; upside down or backward. He was like a cup half empty. A guitar with no strings. Where others saw sunshine he saw rain. And he fucking hated the rain. It was quite pathetic—but made for a few damn good songs in the end.

The radio interview had come after most things, during that bit where he was just floating, using what was left of his talent to collaborate with friends like the Longbottoms and write cheap pop ditties for the likes of Gilderoy Lockheart. He never let the studio put his name on any of them, even though Sirius would teasingly tell him to be proud of the work. They weren’t together then but they talked nearly every day, saw one another every other day, and occasionally fucked on the couch. It was an unspoken rule that the bed was off-limits until they figured out what it was they were doing. Only, Remus wasn’t sure they’d ever really known what they were doing.

Eventually he would came to learn that there was a technique in music that felt a lot like this, called ‘tempo rubato’. It involved speeding or slowing the traditional tempo of a song to invoke new feeling, as beautiful representation of freedom that relied completely on the discretion of the musician. If done incorrectly the technique could effectively butcher a thing of beauty—but if done right, it could award complete and utter freedom over the most expressive art known to man. That rubato was the thing one heard when an orchestra conductor briefly slowed a key moment in a classical piece. It was that breath at the end of a love ballad where your very heart felt as though it was shattering. It was responsible for every moment of emotion felt by conscious beings capable of hearing a music note played aloud.

Tempo rubato meant ‘robbed time’. That was the name humans gave to the concept. Like a word, time could not be captured, so people did the only thing they could, they attempted to defy it. They used surgeries to fix the physical flaws that came with age, and took photographs to help them remember a moment otherwise lost. People defied time by naming it. They called the past ‘memories’ and the future ‘what’s yet to pass’. They called hopelessness ‘rubato’, and in doing so, they granted themselves the illusion of controlling time.

At least, that's how he'd described it whenever someone cared enough to ask.

But still, it remained a comforting thought. If someone could speed up or slow down something as uncapturable as music—as pure emotion—then maybe time really was within their control. But everyone knew it wasn't possible. Not really. Whether as a conscious realisation or an inherent knowing, the answer was clear; time passed with or without people. With or without photographs or tempo. It always did, and it was easy to look back and desperately want to cling to it. Natural even, because what was behind was clear—it'd already been lived. It was the unknown ahead that scared people.

At sixteen Remus couldn’t have told anyone what a ‘tempo rubato’ was, but he’d been unknowingly experiencing it all his life. Being at school felt like the traditional, fast-moving tempo of the piece, and those few precious moments in the flat were his rubato. There he couldn’t play or make music, he could only listen and live. Conversations were without any real goal, the days blurred into one another, and the nights felt endless but not hopeless. There was very little action or adventure and that was how he liked it. The flat was rubato, one he’d never find anywhere else. There would be others, yes, but none the same. If he’d known then maybe he would’ve taken more pictures and less drugs so he could better commit them to memory.

But that’s the thing about memories—in the moment they’re not memories at all. They’re not even time.

They’re just life.



Chapter End Notes

'Chuffed' means proud.

'Skive-off' means skip out on something.

The song they dance to is “Teo Torriatte” by Queen, off their 1976 album ‘A Day at the Races’. It’s the final song on the album, and is otherwise known as “Let Us Cling Together”, which seems to work perfectly in this bitter-sweet situation.

So the after bit at the end feels very lethargic to me, but I've always wanted to better hint at the future, especially that of the band! (You may catch a few references to some characters you’ve been wondering about, lol) I cannot wait to give it to you. See you all in 1977!





Chapter 46: Healing


Chapter Summary

Back to Hawkings, January 1977. Remus has a plan. Sirius has a secret.



Chapter Notes

CW: Scars and allusions to child abuse.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



So where are you going to, I don’t mind,

If I live too long I’m afraid I’ll die;

So I will follow you wherever you go,

If you offered hand is still open to me;

Strangers on this road we are on,

We are not two, we are one…

- “Strangers” The Kinks, 1970



Monday 3rd January 1977

Three days at home after visiting the flat would’ve normally sobered him, but even as his stomach squirmed and his eyes twinged from the smoky smell of the burning tar that always seemed to accompany London train stations, Remus made his way through Kings Cross feeling as though every vein had been electrified. He’d just finished the best Christmas of his teenage life, and though he was heading back to school, things were sure to be different. His luck was shifting, and he’d already made a list of ways things were sure to improve;

He had a plan for a prank, courtesy of Seesaw.

He was going to fix any poor marks, probably courtesy of Lily.

He had a girlfriend.

He was going to apologise to Sirius.



The last point was certainly the most contentious, but things with Sirius had ended on a poor note and Remus couldn’t stop thinking about it, despite the fact that he wasn’t entirely sure what they’d fought over in the first place. It was bad enough that Lily and James’ argument had divided them the year before, he couldn’t imagine what living in the same room would be like if things between them were still foul after the holiday. After Remus had spent first term sour as a grape, James and Peter would have no choice but to take Sirius’ side, they owed each other such loyalty. There was another thing too; he’d promised Tonya that he would find the words, and starting off with an apology sounded like his best bet.

By the time he made it to the correct platform there were only a handful stragglers left to board. He glanced through a few windows, hoping to spot the other boys, but as the train’s first warning whistle cut through the station Remus threw himself up into one of the cars and began moving toward their usual section of the train. The other passengers were mostly students of course, and he waved to the occasional friendly face as he made his way down the corridor, trunk bumping between the wall and his knees.

As expected, he found all three of the other boys sitting towards the back of the train in one of the more spacious compartments and tugged the door open, plucking the toothpick he’d stolen from Giles that morning from his mouth; “Wotcher.”

“Hi-ya, Remus!” James called. “Thought you were going to miss the train.”

“It’s called being fashionably late, Potter, look it up.” He nodded to Peter. “Hey, Pete.”

“Hey there, Lupin.”

Remus swallowed. “Hey, Black.”

Sirius turned back from the window he’d been focused on and looked him up and down. Across his lap sat Andy’s acoustic guitar, which he was plucking absent-mindedly with his legs stretched out in front of him and crossed at the ankles. He was wearing his suede jacket over a white button-up and he had to toss his dark waves out of his eyes to get a good look at him. Add in a few cigarettes and a glass of scotch left abandoned on the windowsill and he could’ve been on an album cover.

“Hey, Moony,” Sirius answered coolly.

It was as though the entire apologetic script Remus had been rehearsing in his head for the last three days had evaporated into thin air, and he was left to smile awkwardly and nod. Returning the toothpick to his teeth, he closed the door after himself and lifted his trunk up onto the overhead shelf with the others’ before taking a seat between Peter and the window.

“You have a good Christmas?” James asked. He had Andy’s empty guitar case tucked up between his legs and was gently rapping his knuckles against the painted leather.

“Yeah, brilliant.”

James raised both eyebrows. “Anything exciting happen?”

“Er—not much.”

“You got a haircut. Looks nice.”

“Thanks, Prongs.”

“Okay enough with the pleasantries, let’s just spit it out already,” Sirius said. “How long did you think you could keep such a dirty little secret?”

Remus balked a bit. There was no way they could’ve found out about Tomny and the others, not unless Marlene had somehow figured out how to trace phone calls—oh!

“You mean that,” Remus sighed before moving the toothpick to the other side of his mouth with his tongue. He hadn’t expected Sirius to bring Marlene up so quickly—or at all, really—but he supposed getting it out in the open sooner was better than later.

“Yeah,” Sirius drawled, “when were you gonna tell us about Olga?”

“I’m sorry—who?” Peter snorted.

“The mail-order bride Lupin’s dad got from Russia—you know, to ensure that prestigious Lupin line of theirs continues.”

It took a second for all of them to realise Sirius was joking, but when they did James and Peter snorted while Remus let out a breath and then a laugh.

“You dickhead,” he said, using one foot to reach across and knock him in the shin. Sirius smiled smugly and just like that any hint of animosity between them melted away.

“No, but seriously,” James started, “when were you going to tell us you’re dating Marlene?”

“You’re dating MARLENE?” Peter shouted, loudly enough to make Remus flinch away. “Since when?!”

“Not very long! We’ve all been on holiday and—”

Another loud whistle blew, indicating the train’s incoming departure and Remus bit down on the toothpick.

“I’m surprised Lottie didn’t tell you, Pete,” James said, making Peter roll his eyes.

“She never tells me anything. She left last week to see Mickey and I had to find out from mum after they’d already dropped her at the station.”

“She taking the other line to school then?”

“Mhm.”

Remus cut a glance across to Sirius, who had turned to tuning the guitar, expression neutral. “Oi, Sirius,” he started, just as the compartment door flew open and Mary and Marlene stood there, half-panting on the threshold.

“Made it,” Mary said, tugging her trunk inside and collapsing on the bench next to Sirius. She looked different, he realised. Her natural hair which she was always pinning in place with gel or pins was now done up in braids so close to her scalp that Remus was sure it’d hurt to get them done. She had big hoops dangling from her ears too, but the same merry-Mary smile.

“You guys look like you ran here,” Peter said.

“We wouldn’t have had to if this one hadn’t bothered to stop and flirt with the train attendant,” Marlene huffed, drawing the door closed after her. She looked the same, save the fact that she was wearing a leather jacket over her clothes that was so big it could’ve fit Doss.

“He looked just like Jermaine Jackson from the Jackson Five,” Mary defended, “I had to tell him!”

“You did a lot more than just tell him.”

“If he’d looked like Andy Gibb you’d have been asking for his autograph.”

Marlene rolled her eyes and began trying to lift her trunk up onto the shelf.

“Here, I got it,” Remus said, standing. She let him take the trunk, smiling as she lifted a satchel from her shoulder.

“Thanks, Remus."

When the trunk was securely stowed, they sat down together to find the rest of their friends staring and wearing the same shit-eating grins on their faces.

“What?” Marlene snapped, nervously tucking a piece of hair behind her ear.

“Nothing,” James and Mary said in unison. It made Marlene blush terribly, and Remus shot them the bird just as the final whistle blew and the train rumbled to life beneath them.

“Hope the trolley comes by soon,” Peter mumbled.

“My mum packed us some samosas if anyone’s hungry,” James offered.

“Oh, yes please,” Mary said; “Forgot to eat breakfast.”

While Sirius continued tuning his guitar, James produced a bin full of homemade goods courtesy of his mum and Marlene pulled her bag onto her lap.

“Remus, I got a few new books for Christmas. Would you like to see?"

“Sure."

“I’ve already read this one—devoured it, actually—but you might like it too.” She withdrew a copy of Mrs. Dalloway and passed it to him. As Remus flipped the cover open to have a look, he realised he couldn’t get past the first line. Instead his attention was being drawn across the carriage to Sirius as he pensively traced the strings of his guitar up and down. It was an odd gesture for him—for Sirius who was always looking to expel endless energy.

As the train shook and trembled beneath them on the tracks, Remus could hear Marlene distantly explaining the synopsis of the novel, but he was too distracted to do more than nod along. Instead he watched, transfixed, as Sirius’ long fingers gently plucked a few chords. He kept his left hand pressed to the top of the strings to mute their sound, and Remus felt the agony of the silenced notes like a red-hot poker in his gut.

Play, he silently pleaded. Please play something.

Finally, Sirius lifted his right hand high, ready to strum, but the moment he flexed his wrist his hand seized as though he were in pain and he clapped his fingers over the strings, gagging the life out of them. Remus sucked in a short gasp, and though there was no way he could’ve heard him over the noise of the train and their friends, Sirius’ eyes shot to his and for a split second they were alone in the world.

Find the words.

There wasn’t time.

Just as quickly as their eyes had met, Sirius looked away, setting one elbow atop the guitar’s body and leaning his chin on his hand to stare out the train window in silence as the clamour of London’s city-life drifted away.





* * *





It took a few days, but eventually Remus had grown sure in his suspicions that Sirius had indeed injured himself somehow. When they were finally talking without giving each other strange looks he tried bridging the subject, but Sirius just passed over the question with simple denial. Still, Remus remained unconvinced by the blasé attitude. Sirius wasn’t playing anything in their dorm or in music class, and whenever anyone tried to prompt him he would also dismiss their interest with some lazy excuse. Not even James could get him to play, though Sirius hadn’t cut him off completely. He let James regale him with everything he’d practiced over the holiday, supplying lukewarm congratulations and corrections where necessary as though he’d lost all interest in the art. But that wasn’t even the most startling part; since returning to school Sirius hadn’t played a single album.

Not one.

In fact, he hadn’t even reconnected the hi-fi after they’d brought it downstairs for their end of term party. Remus hadn’t realised until he went to play something himself and found the cords hanging abandoned behind Sirius’ hutch.

“He’s just in a slump,” James said. They’d just gotten out of maths and were on their way to meet Lily and Marlene for lunch. So far having a girlfriend had consisted mostly of walking one another to and from classes and meeting for meals, which to Remus didn’t feel all that different from having friends. The only new bit was the kissing, which if he was being honest, they’d only done a few times and usually only as a fleeting goodbye.

“It happens sometimes,” James continued, “usually when he comes back from holiday or after his parents call or something.”

Remus glared at the ground. “I don’t fucking get it. Why do they care so much if his dad’s such a dick and his mum’s a right hag?”

“Pete and I’ve been asking ourselves that since we met him. Miles was better with it, I think. His grandfather was a mean old coot, so he could relate better than we could or—I don’t know, maybe he just had better advice..."

Remus shook his head. He knew why Sirius hadn't told them, it was why Marlene refused to let her girlfriends visit her in Southwark. James and Peter both had perfect home-lives as far as anyone like Sirius could be concerned, how could he ever expect them to relate?

“So Miles had family problems too then?”

“Kinda," James murmured. "His mum left when he was really young and his dad went a bit berserk after so he was raised by his grandparents. We never met 'em though. They were old and didn’t like making the trip up here, even when we were little. Miles always said it was the damp, made it hard on his grandfather since he was injured in the war or something. They were pretty strict though, never let him watch TV or call us up over the holidays.”

“Is that why you haven't spoken to him since he left?"

"Yeah. We tried sending letters, but never heard anything back."

"You don't think he could've..."

“Died?"

Idiot!

Remus halted in the middle of the pavement, and James stopped with him, crossing his arms over his chest.

"Sorry, Prongs! I-I didn't mean to..."

"It's fine," James said. "But do us a favour and don't mention it when Sirius is around. It upsets him, and we can't know for sure what happened, so best just let it lie."

Remus nodded solemnly, and bit his lip. “Yeah... yeah, alright. My bad... Think I’m just looking too far into things anyway. I never met Miles, but Sirius, he… something’s up with him.”

“Always is, after the holidays. I'm sure he’ll be back to normal in a few days.”

"But it's never been this bad before. Maybe he just needs a change of pace."

“Dunno where he’s gonna get that. Hawkings has existed the same way for hundreds of years, and it’s not about to change just because we want it to.”

“Never took you for a pessimist, Potter.”

“Call it the age-old January blues.”

With a shared smirk, they began walking again. But Remus' mind was still reeling.

“Still... Doesn’t have to be a big change or anything... Maybe we could just...” He trailed off, reaching up to thumb his shirt collar. Just beneath Remus could feel the silver chain and pick, strung together just like Sirius had meant for. Meanwhile James began peering at him suspiciously through his round glasses.

“Okay, you went quiet real fast... What're you thinking, Lupin?”

“Just that I never got Sirius anything for Christmas.”

“Well in that case, you never got me or Pete anything either.”

Remus began laughing, and shoved his friend lightly.

“Tosser.”

He’d spent the rest of their walk explaining his idea to James, who turned out to be pleasantly surprised. Sirius had asked for only one thing before holiday—to listen to Hope’s albums, and if they could be the thing that broke him out of his musical funk, well then maybe this was exactly what Remus had been waiting for. For so long he’d let those damn records hang over his head like a suicide note, when really they were just bits of plastic with grooves impressed into them. Break them, play them, it didn’t matter, she wasn’t going to come back for them. So might as well put them to some use before the memories they represented decayed any further.

Later that evening he enlisted James and Peter’s help to set up the stereo while he pulled out Hope’s trunk. There were fresh cracks along its corners, water damage leftover from the prank on Sirius’ birthday, and he ran his fingers along them as though they were fresh joints in the trunk's history.

“He’s gonna be so excited,” James chimed, half-stretched out under his bed to plug everything in.

“It’s gonna nearly double his collection,” Peter agreed. “How could he not be happy?”

“Just remember it’s about his happiness when he starts blaring the volume at all hours again,” Remus said happily, lifting the trunk up onto his bed. He had the key already in hand but the moment he heard the tiny lock click open something in his chest sank and he had to ask Peter to sort through them while he escaped under the guise of needing to take a piss.

The click had been the trigger. For a split second it sounded identical to the latch on the door of the estate’s stables and he’d seen a flash of Hope as she led him across the hay-strewn floor toward her own mare, Georgina. Remus had always disliked horses, even at five. They could sense nervous energy and fed into it with their own agitation. He’d cried, not wanting to go in, but Hope insisted because they’d come all the way from the house for a visit and pulled him into the pen anyway. Terrified, he’d thrown a screaming fit in the middle of his stall and Georgina matched it, nearly cracking his mother in two with a swift kick. The stable hand who’d found them had to have assumed she was half-dead thanks to all the blood, but Hope just wobbled around holding her bloodied head in her hands and ranting about how it wasn’t the horse’s fault and that they couldn’t put her down.

Remus didn’t learn until much later that the horse hadn’t been Georgina at all, but an unbroken stallion Lyall was housing for a friend. The real Georgina had been Hope’s horse as a little girl and had been dead for more than a decade. Silly me, she'd said later, I must've forgotten.

Remus splashed cold water on his face to help him shake the worst of it off. Perhaps the records weren’t such a good idea, after all there was a reason he’d kept them shut away for so long—but he’d been so confident they would be the thing to help Sirius. Yes—he could do this. They were just bits of flattened PVC.

“Moony, which album did you want to play first?” James called through the door. Towelling off his face and neck, Remus walked out and avoided looking him in the eye.

“Nah, play whatever you want.”

“Okay. Cheers!”

James had of course found the only Kinks record in the collection and put it on. A few minutes into it the front door finally opened and Sirius strode in quickly as though he were already on a mission.

“Hey mate!” James called eagerly from his bed.

“Hey,” Sirius responded, entirely oblivious to the fact that his own stereo was playing and instead surging toward the jacket he’d left hanging up on his peg and rifling through its pockets. “Oh Potter, did you see where I left that twenty quid?”

“You used it as a bookmark,” Remus called first and Sirius pointed at him fondly, winking, before rushing to the foot of his bed and sifting through the stack of books he’d left there—most of which belonged to Remus in the first place.

“Hey,” James tried, “we have a surprise for you.”

“Cool. Can’t wait to see it.”

James and Peter exchanged a look.

“It’s a good surprise,” Peter added.

“I’ll bet.”

James stood up from his bed. “What are you doing?”

“Sorry, just in a bit of a rush. Lupin, which book was it?”

“Maths text…”

“Ah.” Sirius whipped his head back and forth before spotting the textbook on his bedside beneath an empty tea mug. He ripped the bill free and shoved it into his pocket. “Kay, see you guys later then.”

James stopped him halfway to the door. “Oi, what’s your rush?”

“I’m meeting Xeno.”

“For what?”

Sirius waved the twenty pound note in the air. “What else? Don’t worry, I promise I’ll share.”

“But Remus has a gift for you,” James said pointedly. Pausing, Sirius glanced Remus' way and he bit his lip before ever-so-slightly gesturing to the hi-fi with his chin. Sirius followed his gaze before his eyes finally settled on the stack of albums left piled on top of his bedspread. Slowly he made his way toward them and began to gently sift through, as though they might disintegrate should he be too rough.

“These…” Sirius started, before looking up, “these your mum’s?”

Remus nodded. “Thought we could mix them in with the others… if you’d like.”

Sirius looked back to the pile and flipped through a few more, stopping on Jimi Hendrix’s Electric Ladyland. “Wow,” he said, “guess your mum did have some taste.”

“More than mine, all she listens to is polka,” Peter said, making them all smile.

Sirius straightened out the album stack and patted his hands on his trousers. “This is great, thanks Moony. Would you—erm—would you mind sorting them in with the rest? I… told Xeno I’d meet him and I’m already late.”

James visibly deflated, but very secretly, Remus was relieved. He’d been having second thoughts the entire time, but Sirius’ nonchalance had saved him from having to gush and play pretend-sentiment over it all. “Yeah, no problem,” he said and Sirius flashed him a grateful smile before slipping out of the room. He took with him the hopeful mood and James immediately collapsed back onto his bed as Ray Davies serenaded him through the hi-fi’s speakers.

"What the fuck was that?" He wailed. "You would'a thought we offered him jellied eels for dinner and not three dozen fresh-fucking albums for his collection."

Remus crossed over to James' bed and set a comforting hand on his friend's shoulder. "Don't worry, we'll figure something else out, Prongs."

"Like what? If Hendrix can't solve his problems, who can?"

“Maybe his tastes have changed?” Peter suggested. “Maybe he’d just more into country now.”

James and Remus cringed at the same time.

"Pete, not all thoughts are meant to be voiced aloud, mate."

Despite the surprising failure, James only grew more invigorated than ever to break Sirius’ bad spell. He sought his best friend out one-on-one most times, but James was too kind and every time he tried to get into the nitty-gritty with him Sirius would expertly distract him by asking about the new football kit he got for Christmas or some latest win by Arsenal. When he did manage to get anywhere, Sirius would turn stony and James would have no choice but to back off. So, the term trudged on, wet, muddy, and grey, until the entirety of dorm 4A felt about as exciting as a cancer clinic.

“The rest of us have noticed a difference too, you know,” Marlene said, as she chugged from a water bottle. He’d dropped by the indoor pitch to walk her back from practice and was sweating more than she was, dressed up in his full winter garb.

“You have then,” Remus confirmed. He knew it wasn’t just them.

“Yeah. Black's been quieter lately, especially in class. I think he even let Flitwick get through an entire lecture the other day without tossing a paper airplane over his head.”

“God, he’s sicker than I thought.”

“I hope that’s supposed to be funny,” Marlene said with an arched brow. “I wish I could offer better advice but if he’s been like this for—how long did you say?”

“Almost two weeks. Since we got back from holiday.”

“That long, huh? Well I’m sorry, Rem, but I’m not sure what you should do. No one else was there with him.”

At that moment, a lightbulb went off in his head. Remus shot up from the sports bench, suddenly very enthused. “That’s it! Oh my god, Cherry, you’re a genius!”

“I am?”

“Yes!” He jumped over a few scattered footballs and kissed her cheek. “Sorry, I’ll walk you home tomorrow, promise—I just gotta check something!”

Pausing to cough up half a lung—he’d made a mistake smoking that fag on his way to the football pitch—Remus took a deep breath and marched up the front steps of the dorm. Salazar House was decidedly less dank and dreary-looking with the lights on, and like its fellow dorm counterparts was decorated according to its House colours of silver and forest green. “Well, look at what we have here,” he called; “a wolf’s fallen into the snake pit.”

“Come to try out Salazar’s fangs, Lupin?” Barty sneered. “I warn you we’re a bit more dangerous in the daytime.”

"Reg—"

“Oi Loony, how’s the new girlfriend?” Barty tried, casually flipping over a card. “You know—the tall one who acts likes a bloke. Reckon she’d be prettier if she weren’t so worried about stretching pennies? I didn’t know we were still supposed to date within the same caste.”

“You should get out of our dorm,” Regulus said dismissively, sipping his tea.

“Yeah,” Travers sneered, “I think you’re starting to stink up the joint.”

“Nah, that’s just Loony’s natural pheromone. Attracts all the little scrubbers and bag ladies to him.”

“His arm. He fell out a window.”

“He always has to push everything,” the younger boy said lowly. “Nothing’s ever good enough—he always has to pick a fight. Can’t even go a few weeks without running his stupid mouth.”

“Sirius doesn’t pick fights for no reason,” Remus replied cuttingly. “If you pushed him then that’s your fault.”

Regulus looked up sharply. “We haven’t been brothers for a long time.”

Wrenching himself free, Regulus stomped away and Remus let out a long sigh, holding his forehead. He’d always known that Sirius’ issues with his brother went deeper than the typical sibling spats, but he couldn’t help agreeing with everything Reg had said. Sirius did run his mouth, but he also chose his family, just like Remus did, and nothing had ever felt better than that chosen family.

“Weren't you listening?! No, he didn’t!” James sighed and shook his head. “Sorry, Moons. Don't mean to snap."

"S'okay."

James looked around, clearly frustrated, and moaned again. "Damn it—I promised Pete I would help him and Francis move the AV room stuff out. They’re getting that new clubroom they requisitioned. You staying in?”

“Yeah.”

James nodded, looking more relieved. “Kay. He’s a sulker, but if you just leave him be he’ll get over it eventually. Maybe just check on him in a bit.”

“See you in a few.” Before he left James held out his fist and Remus bumped it in farewell. He thought about stopping him—telling him what Regulus had said, but in the end he let James go. Perhaps they all needed the space.

After the door closed behind him the dorm room felt eerily quiet, and Remus cast his eyes to the bathroom. “Always picking a fight,” he tsked, before shedding his jacket and falling down on his own bed.

Already ahead on homework thanks to Lily (#2 on his list was progressing nicely) he picked up the latest book Marlene had lent him. It was fine so far—some gothic parody by one of her newest obsessions, Margaret Atwood. Its plot felt maybe a bit long-winded but he suspected the bit about the feminist poetry and the main character faking her own death to flee to Italy had appealed to something inside Marlene. He’d really only agreed to read it on the promise that she would read his newest favourite, a book he’d been gifted for Christmas. It was called Carrie , a horror-thriller novel by some debut-writer from America. He’d originally thought the concept to be rather baseless and simple but it had hooked him enough that he’d read it twice before passing it on to Marlene, who appeared less than excited as she skimmed its pages.

When he finally dropped his book to stare at the bathroom door again it’d been nearly an hour. Sirius hadn’t made a single peep in all that time, and glancing at the clock, Remus began to feel antsy. Sitting up, Remus started toward the bathroom and gently rapped the tip of his knuckles against the door.

No answer.

He knocked harder this time, and still nothing.

“Oi,” he called, “Black, open up.”

He knocked again—nothing.

"Sirius? Sirius!"

He pounded.

“Sirius! Open the door!”

Sirius did not answer and quickly Remus felt his heart rise into his throat. He slammed his fist against the door until he heard its hinges begin to squeak. He used both hands, hammering until he felt as though he were punching cement.

Finally the door flew open.

“JAMES FUCK OFF—!"

Remus froze as Sirius gaped up at him. Remus gaped right back. In nearly a year and a half of living side-by-side, he'd never seen Sirius without a shirt on. For so long he'd chalked it up to insecurity; everyone was insecure about something—even self-satisfied works of art like Sirius Black. But this—he'd never expected this.

Sirius was shirtless, wearing only his pyjama pants as though he’d started getting ready for bed only to stop halfway, but his skin was far from bare. Lacing up the left side of his torso were patches of pink flesh pulled taunt over muscle, rippling with age and imperfection as though his body was a classical painting that’d been through a botched restoration. The scars stretched up across his chest and shoulder, interlacing with one another like tiger stripes, but the expression on Sirius’ face was neither fierce nor undaunted. He stared back at Remus as though he were simply the edge of the world, and he was ready to tip over the edge and be swallowed by nothingness.

But Remus was just a boy, and so Sirius’ shock broke and he spun around, whipping his shirt up off the floor from behind him and tugging it over his shoulders with sharp, furious motions. The scars disappeared out of sight—they were burns, Remus realised; old and healed by time but not erased entirely.

“I thought you were James,” Sirius said gruffly, not looking at him.

“Sorry,” he mumbled. “You didn’t come out and I just… I’d wondered if you drowned in the tub or something.”

Sirius fumbled with his shirt buttons. “Yeah, well, obviously not.”

Twinging red in the face, Sirius did his shirt up to the last button and then they stood there, facing each other down but unsure of what to say next. Remus half expected the door to slam in his face, but before Sirius could, words came tumbling out. “I know a trick, you know. For—for when you’re in the bath or just want to be left alone.”

Sirius glanced up at him and raised an eyebrow expectantly.

“It’s this.” Swallowing, Remus raised his fist gently and knocked his knuckles against the doorframe once. “It means I need help.”

“Help?” Sirius echoed. "How could that mean help?"

"Well it's... It's for when all you have left in you is a single knock. One knock is still better than nothing, you know."

"I don't get it. Sounds useless."

“Maybe, but two—” he knocked twice; “Two means, ‘I’m okay’.”

Sirius’ eyes shifted to the door frame and Remus' bruised knuckles. “And three?”

Remus shook his head. “There is no three. Just ‘okay’ and ‘not’. No knocks at all means ‘I’m already dead, bury me with white roses’.”

“Why white roses?”

“Because they’re… pure?”

Exhaling like he'd been longing for a different answer, Sirius started to close the door.

“Sirius, wait—” Remus jammed his foot in the way. “I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to—to walk in on you or pry or anything.”

Sirius sagged backward slightly. “I don’t care if you see,” he griped, though Remus got the feeling it wasn’t the truth. If it was, Sirius wouldn’t have spent so long hiding the scars under long-sleeved shirts and pyjamas. They didn’t seem like the kind one got while jumping out a window, but he knew asking right now would just make him shut down completely.

“I had an idea for a prank,” Remus tried instead. “I flagged Darby Harrison down on the train at the beginning of term—he’s been an altar boy since seventh year, right? Well, he told me that the ministers rarely check what it is they’re putting in those thuribles before communion. I brought a lot of hash back with me, and I thought that maybe it might be funny to test that theory about Jesus and weed.”

“You mean hotbox the entire church?”

“Or... try to, at least," he shrugged. "I have a friend back home who managed it when he was twelve. He tried to do it again but his friend thought it would be funnier to put gunpowder in instead. Nearly blew the priest’s arm off.”

Like a lightning flash, Remus saw the corner of Sirius’ mouth quirk up. “That’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve heard.”

“Ha, maybe…”

Sirius looked down to the ground, then back up through those dark lashes. “Do you want to listen to something later?”

Remus’ heart jumped. Oh yes. Oh dear god, yes. “Yeah, anything. Whatever you want.”

“Okay,” Sirius said, and then he closed the door.

Remus stood there for a long moment, staring at the dark wood. Had he done it then? Had he found the right words? How would he know if he had—would Sirius open the door again?

He breathed in and held it, waiting, but then exhaled when nothing happened. Perhaps he was wrong, then.

“Stupid,” he muttered to himself, turning away. But before he moved, there was a gentle knock, followed by another. Two.

I’m okay.

Remus bit his lip over a small, grateful smile. “Okay,” he whispered. “You’re okay.”



Chapter End Notes

Andy Gibb was the younger brother of the Bee Gees trio and a certifiable heartthrob in the mid-70s. He passed away in 1988.

The book Marlene lends Remus is "Lady Oracle" by Margaret Atwood (1976). It's a good read Marlene would've absolutely loved.

Also, “Mrs Dalloway” totally isn’t a queer-coded novel… not at all…

"Strangers" is an absolutely under-appreciated Kinks' song, and frankly I'm appalled that I've never seen a Marauders edit for it. Heresy. Go stream it and you'll understand.

Chapter 47: Band of Marauders


Chapter Summary

Remus eases into the dating life, whilst also juggling his friends and their many, many mishaps.



Chapter Notes

CW: Brief references to smoking/weed and sexual themes. Mostly cheeky fluff, which you deserve!



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Johnny told his Mama,

"Hey Mama, I'm goin' away;

I'm gonna hit the big time,

Gonna be a big star someday;"

Mama came to the door,

With a teardrop in her eye;

Johnny said, "Don't cry Mama,

Smile and wave goodbye..."

- "Shooting Star" Bad Company, 1975



Remus liked kissing Marlene. She was tall enough that he didn’t have to bend down and risk neck injuries the way James always seemed to be doing with Lily (not that he ever complained of course). She was also honest about the things that she liked and disliked; for example she liked it when Remus greeted her with a kiss on the cheek but didn’t when there were enough people around to draw attention, and she enjoyed holding hands but always preferred to let go before things got too clammy. She always smelled good—like fabric softener and mint toothpaste—and even when they were so close that her face blurred together like an Impressionist painting, he always found her pretty.

The actual dating part turned out to be easier than he’d expected too. Perhaps it was just an upside of finding a partner within the same friend group, but hanging out with Marlene as boyfriend and girlfriend didn’t feel all that different from how they’d hung out before. Living at school full-time meant they couldn’t just pop off to the cinema or ice cream parlour for a casual date, so like the rest of the couples at Hawkings, they had to find other ways to preoccupy themselves outside of homework or music or Marlene’s football practices. After playing matchmaker for most of first term, Remus had expected Lily to put her efforts to rest once it came out that he and Marlene were indeed an item, but she’d always been an overachiever.

“I just think it’s so cute!” She would gush—often. It was a taxing affair, but luckily he and Marlene were alike in more ways than one.

“We’re not golden retrievers, Lils. Why don’t you give it a rest already?” She would complain—equally as often.

The boys were just as bad, though their preferred method of teasing tended to involve betting on how many times he and Marlene had bunked up already. Remus finally knew how Peter was always feeling.

“C’mon, Moony! Four times? Five times? At least tell me if I’m getting close! Am I really that far off the mark?”

“You’re so far off you might as well be floating in space, you arse!”

“You mean it’s more than that? Ooh, you slag!”

“Oh piss off,” Remus grumbled, kicking his leg up on the coffee table in front of him. Sirius smirked from across the common room and leaned forward to continue his rag-fest but James beat him to it;

“If Lupin wants to share then he will. Not everyone’s as ripped-and-ready as you, Black. Sometimes people like to take care with… special matters like this.”

“Nah, Moony’s sneaky. Bet he’s got the leg over twice as many times as you and Evans since term started.”

Lily threw a couch pillow at Sirius from her spot next to James, and he snatched it out of the air. “It’s lucky for McKinnon really,” he started. “For a while there it was beginning to look as though she wasn’t going to be able to find a bloke who could see over her head. And you, Moons—with that grumpy attitude of yours—I was beginning to think I was going to have to set you up with one of my cousins. Although I’m not sure how they’d take to dating a tree.”

“Get a haircut, hippy,” Remus quipped.

“Beanstalksaywhat?”

“What?”

“HA!”

“I’d date Remus,” Lily surmised, barely glancing up from the day-timer she was flipping through. Her omission instantly sobered Sirius of his laughter and he coughed a bit before clearing his throat.

“You already have Potter.”

“James would date Remus too.”

Sirius turned on James, who shrugged amicably. “Well, wouldn’t you? He’s just so cute.”

“Hey,” Marlene smiled, tucking herself into his side.

“Hey.” He kissed her.

“Really, why is that so hard to find?” Mary demanded, after watching them. “Just a simple little love—that’s all I want! One I can grow old with and retire to the countryside where we can let creamed spinach drip down our wrinkly chins in peace!”

“Oui! But there is a difference between grandiose and tacky.”

“It’s Lance.” Mary crossed her arms. “And he’s been taking pointers from you apparently. Today in class he tried singing that ‘Mary Mary’ song to me acapella.”

“I was there,” Marlene said to Remus, “it really was awful.”

“I broke up with him on the spot!” Mary cried. “But he wouldn’t stop bloody singing so who knows if he even heard me! I think I’m going to have to do it again tomorrow at lunch.”

“Shall I serenade you with a half decent song in the meantime?” Sirius offered.

“No, I’m taking a break from lead singer types actually. So, Remus, is there any chance you and Marlene are looking for a third?”

Remus squirmed a bit. “Like polygamy? Ain’t that an American thing?”

“Not polygamy—it’s called polyfidelity. Hippies do it in communes all the time.”

“Well, no offence Mary, but I think one girlfriend is enough.”

“Yeah,” Sirius said, “Lupin’s a dog person didn’t you know? He wouldn’t know what to do with two pussies.”

Sirius had never outrightly admitted to hurting himself over holiday, but the day after their interaction outside the bathroom, Remus had told James what Regulus said and James had practiced a bit of tough love on his best friend. He’d marched right up to Sirius in the dining hall that same morning and clamped his hand over his wrist until he yelped and confirmed their suspicions.

“You’re a right idiot, you know that?” James had snapped, as he lovingly wrapped a tensor bandage around Sirius’ wrist. After a quick visit to Ms. Pomfrey’s medical room the injury turned out to be just a nasty sprain, but it at least gave Sirius reason enough to slack-off in class. He ended up milking the injury until Professor Bilshin threatened to give him detention cataloguing his extensive collection of foreign newspaper clippings if he so much as tried to get another student to write his next paper for him.

As if by magic, Sirius' wrist had been miraculously healed the following day and he was back to his regular wisecracking self. The teasing was not exactly pleasant, but Remus tolerated it. It wasn’t as though he was the only one feeling it and getting defensive would only lead to questions as to why he hadn’t bunked off with his girlfriend yet. They were teenagers living at a religious private institution in the bum-fuck backyard of Britain, with the only neighbours for miles being sheep and cattle—the only thing hornier was a travelling businessman or a Catholic priest. And yet they’d done little more than a bit of heavy petting.
