Marlene shifted closer to Remus on the grass, leaning her head on his shoulder. “I can’t believe she didn’t tell me,” she whispered sadly. “I mean, me? My family doesn't have money or influence or...”

“She might’ve just been embarrassed.”

“Maybe…”

A rumbling sound came from above them, and they all looked up to see James poke his head out. “Moony, she wants you.”

Remus blinked. “Me?”

James began climbing out the window. Slowly, Remus stood and changed places with him, clambering up the side of the dorm and swinging himself over the window ledge with a groan. Inside, he found Lily tucked up on Marlene’s corner bed, hugging one of Lottie’s fuzzy pink pillows and clutching a fistful of tissues.

“Hey… you…” Remus started, lowering the window whilst feeling extremely awkward.

“You can sit, Remus,” Lily said, her voice tight with congestion. He did so, gingerly taking a spot at the foot of the bed while Lily blew her nose. “Thanks for coming up.”

“ ‘Course. Are... you okay, Lils?”

She nodded at first, but then descended into a rigorous head-shake, covering her face with the pillow. “I’m just so embarrassed.”

“Of what?”

“Of everything! You guys tried to tell me I couldn’t fix things with Sev but I just thought that he’d listen to me eventually. I didn’t mean for it all to go to crap like it did.”

“Trust me,” Remus promised, “it was definitely not your fault.”

Lily blew her nose again. “I don’t mean to cry, but I can’t help it. Sev’s right.”

“Well, Snape’s a dick—” Remus caught himself; “I mean, it’s fine to cry. Everyone cries.”

“Do you cry, Remus?”

“Er—yeah, sometimes..."

Lily nodded in consideration. “I guess everyone knows about my scholarship now.”

“Yeah… but it’s nothing to be ashamed of, you know.”

“It just sucks sometimes to be in a place full of one sort of people and still be different. I didn’t mean for the secret to go on as long as it did, but one year turned into two and then I got top student and then prefect—I just didn’t want to be known as the ‘scholarship swot’.”

Remus rubbed the side of his neck. He understood better than Lily would ever know, just how it felt to keep a lie going with all your friends. “Well what about Marlene? She’s not rich or anything.”

“I know,” Lily sighed, “but she’s so much better at handling it than me. She’s actually really tough.”

“Oh I know,” he said, and Lily gave a small smile.

“I wish I had told them and not just Snape.”

“He shouldn’t have done that,” Remus said firmly. “I don't care how angry he was, you don’t just go shoutin' someone’s secrets out for the whole world to hear, and especially not like that. He was talking like you have something to be ashamed about, but it’s actually bloody impressive. You got into Hawkings without anyone’s help but your own—you set the curve Lily. No one else could’ve done it but you. Not me, not James, not Sirius. You.”

Lily glanced down at Marlene’s bed covers shyly. “Wow, Remus.”

“I only meant to say that you should be proud,” he said sheepishly. “Don’t let tossers like Snape or anyone else take away from your achievements. You’re better than that, Lils.”

Lily pulled a fresh tissue from the box near her feet and used it to wipe a bit of stray peanut butter from his shirt. “You’re pretty good at this,” she said. “You should start a club or something—offer relationship advice. Bet you could even charge for it.”

“Ha. Very funny.”

“I’m serious—well, partly. But you do actually give really good advice, Remus. Like James.”

“And I’m sure he’s much better with this stuff than me.”

“You’re both good, but I did chew him out again for going after Snape, just you know."

"I wouldn't expect any less, to be honest."

"Still, I’m lucky to have both of you. All of you.”

Remus smiled. “Does that mean you’re feeling better then?”

“Well… I don’t feel any worse, so I suppose yes, I must be.”

“Good.”

Lily returned his smile as another rock hit the bedroom window. Remus stood up and crossed the room, lifting it and sticking his head out.

“Is she feeling better yet?” Sirius asked. “Because the sun is gone and we’re freezing.”

“They can come in,” Lily sighed, tossing her tissues away and smoothing back her mussed curls.

One by one the rest of them climbed inside. The girls instantly dove on Lily, doing everything from coddling her with baby talk to kissing her cheeks. She batted her hands at them but eventually hugged back, and James let out a sigh of relief.

“Seems a shame to go home,” he said, rubbing the back of his head sorely. “Maybe I should stay.”

“You don’t care about getting caught?” Remus asked.

“Nah. I’ve already got detention for a month, who cares.”

Remus smiled slightly before glancing around the room. “Say, Prongs, do you remember Xeno’s room—what they did with all the beds?”

James glanced around, and then perked up as though a lightbulb had gone off. “Ah, now that’s not a bad idea, Moony.”

Nudging Sirius and Peter, they filled them in and began pushing furniture out of the way one by one, while the girls looked on in question;

“What are you doing with our furniture?” Mary asked.

“You’ll see,” James grunted, shoving Lottie’s bed toward Marlene’s. Eventually the girls got it, and no one objected as they set the four beds side by side against one wall. Blankets and pillows came out in full force, scattering between them for ultimate comfort and they all settled in next to one another in a row. Remus didn't argue as Mary and Marlene pulled him down between them, but did catch Sirius giving him an odd look before he tucked in on Mary's other side.

“A slumber party!” Lottie cheered. “On the last day before holiday, how brilliant!”

“We don’t have to stay the whole night,” Remus said, setting his hands behind his head, “we’ll fix it in a bit.”

“Don’t bother,” Lily said, “I sort of like it.”

“You want us to leave your room looking like you’re about to have a massive orgy?” Sirius said aloud, earning himself an elbow in the gut from Mary. “Ow! Sorry, sorry, I know.”

They all laughed, staring up at the roof of the beds until one of them hit the lights. Mary muttered that they could’ve used some music, but none of them wanted to bother setting up the stereo, so instead they just talked. It went on like a game of telephone, each of them recalling a story or a short anecdote until another interjected with something else. Lily talked a bit about why she’d hid her scholarship for so long and Remus could tell they all understood. Mary ended up confessing to already dumping Grayson, who was still too hung up on some girl he knew from back home to be of any real interest. Sirius made James congratulate himself for finally being able to tell the difference between rake and sweep picking and Peter told them all about his Uncle Morris, who had given him lessons on the drums when he was a little kid. Both Sirius and James were floored—then ecstatic. Finally Peter had managed to surprise them.

When it was his turn, Remus’ friends let him sit in silence for a while, mulling over all the secrets he’d kept and coveted in his short seventeen years of life. One secret leapt out glaringly, but Remus had never said that one aloud before, not even to himself. For so long he’d held onto the hope that as long as he kept silent then that horrible thing wouldn’t be true—couldn’t be true. And though he loved his friends more than ever in that moment, Remus was afraid that letting go of that hope now would doom him forever. And so he distracted himself with the one thing he knew would do the trick.

Tomny.

The moment he started talking about the London boys Remus knew he’d made the right decision. His friends were ecstatic. The room was instantly alight with a flurry of questions, until it seemed like nothing was off limits. Luckily he had his secret-keeper there to reel them all in.

“One at a time, you lunatics!” Sirius cried. “Let the man breathe!”

“I knew it!” James practically shouted over him; “I knew that gang rumour wasn’t all rubbish! You should’ve heard him the first time we went to see Xeno, Sirius! He was talking like the bloody Godfather!”

“A gang? That’s how you broke your nose?!” Lily hollered after James.

“Imagine that,” Peter mused, “my friend, Remus, a drug dealer.”

Marlene put her hands together in prayer. “Our Father who thou art in heaven, please forgive Remus for his past sins. He was being stupid—just a great big fucking idiot.”

"Hear, hear!"

Once they’d managed to move past the illegal drabbles of the East Enders, the girls grappled onto any tidbit of Tonya, especially the stories Remus relayed about her travels and every man, bloke, and beggar she’d managed to swindle along the way.

“She sounds like a real queen bitch,” Mary said, and Remus hesitated before figuring that it must be a good thing.

And that was it. When he was done talking, his friends simply stopped. It was obvious there were more questions, but there was also more time. It was as though they trusted him enough to know that he wasn’t just going to run off and leave them hanging. And for Remus, who had done nothing but run for the last six years, it was peace.

As they cycled on to new talks of Easter plans and travels home, Remus lapsed into a bout of quiet tranquility. No one questioned it. Marlene held his hand and Mary’s shoulder pressed up against his own fondly. He was happy. Just like with music, his friends’ voices put him so at ease that before he knew it, Remus had fallen asleep.





* * *





Maybe it was the chatter, or the fact that he’d been operating on little more than glimpses of shut-eye lately, but whatever it was, Remus had never slept so soundly. They’d left the window open so the girls’ room was still cool, and Marlene’s hair smelt good even as it tickled his nose. She must’ve changed her shampoo—instead of fresh linens and hints of lemon Remus detected sandalwood and the sort of burnt-sugar aroma that came along with hand rolled cigars. Smiling lightly to himself, he shifted and Marlene gave a muttered groan—only it was a much lower noise than he’d ever heard her make. Masculine almost.

Oh god.

Remus’ eyes shot open.

No. No way.

He was pretty sure the last time he’d seen Marlene her hair was pin-straight and blonde, not a mess of pitch-black waves that looked like spilt ink on a pillow. He was also sure that Sirius had been lying on Mary’s far side, and yet he was right there next to him, dozing with a relaxed expression. This close, Remus could almost count every one of his eyelashes. It was horrifying. His heart was hammering so loudly he was half-convinced Sirius would hear it and wake up. He could already imagine his eyes whipping open—that split-second of seeing himself reflected in their pooly grey colour before everything came crashing down.

Desperate, Remus made to pull away only to freeze again when someone nuzzled him from behind. It was Marlene, he realised. At some point while sleeping he must’ve rolled away from her toward Sirius, banishing his peace from the evening before. With his best friend at his front and his girlfriend at his back he was utterly trapped. If he dared move so much as a single muscle, he was sure Sirius would wake and they’d have to acknowledge the closeness. And then something would change. Their relationship would shift again. Like a barrel over a waterfall.

Remus tried to mentally reason with himself; Sirius wasn’t—okay maybe he was—but he wasn’t!

But who was he kidding? The girls, the squirmy sensation he got in his gut when they were alone together—the bloody incidents? It was undeniable. A change so subtle it’d become as natural as breathing before he’d even realised it. Maybe that’s why it took so long to notice. Feeling almost light-headed, Remus looked down again. Sirius' lips were gently parted in his sleep. His own felt dry and chapped, but Sirius' looked pillow-soft. And they were right there. All he'd have to do was reach across that short space and—

Squeezing his eyes shut, Remus went rigid as a board, refusing to even breathe in Sirius' direction. He waited for what felt like hours until mercy finally shone on him. With a little grunt, Marlene turned over onto her other side in her sleep and he seized his opportunity immediately, flipping over and breathing in until linen and lemon drowned out all hints of Sirius. It helped some, but still his mind wouldn’t shut off. He and Sirius were friends, best friends even. They were each other's secret keepers—future bandmates. They both had girlfriends who they liked and they stayed up late listening to each other's favourite music, comforting one another when reality got to be too much. Sirius knew how to push boundaries just enough to make him feel better but not so much as to make everything bad again. And things were never bad around Sirius because Sirius made everything good. Sirius didn't think that about himself, but Remus knew it. Sirius was good. He was funny and handsome and infuriating and Remus loved—

He loved Sirius.

Oh no.

I love Sirius?

It was like a punch to the gut, and Remus' eyes flew open. Of course. That was it. That was everything. Everything wrong with him and everything so, so right. Sirius Black with one of his bestest friends in the world, and Remus was also indisputably—irrevocably—in love with him.

Well, the voice in his head said, good luck with that one, mate.

Chapter 55: Detach


Chapter Summary

The return home before Easter holiday, 1978.



Chapter Notes

moonyfrog told me to take a break from my mental health and finish this, LOL (all jokes—shoutout to them) so you can... "thank" them for this chapter, hehe. Wanted to post it early because it's a shorter one, next chapter will still be out sometime this weekend.

PS: For those of you on tik-tok, the opening of this chapter reminds me a lot of "Wake up Gromit! C'mon Gromit, we've got to hide the body! There's no cheese and crackers in prison, Gromit!" and it just makes me chuckle.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Tommy, can you hear me?

Can you feel me near you?

Tommy, can you see me?

Can I help to cheer you?

Oooh, Tommy,

Tommy,

Tommy,

Tommy…

- “Tommy Can You Hear Me?” The Who, 1969



“HOLY FUCK, WE’RE SO LATE!”

Remus shot upright in bed. All around him, his friends awoke in varying states of distress. There was no time for any of them to wonder how Sirius and Mary had mysteriously changed spots—there was no time for anything. In some sick show of comradery, all of them had fallen asleep in one massive pile, and now they were late for their bus home.

"Fuck—fuck—fuck." James continued to curse as he flew off the bed, bouncing across the room to collect his trainers. It was his incessant internal clock that saved them, which meant there had to be at least one upside of having a morning person for a best friend.

"How much time do we have?" Lily demanded, all while rubbing her eyes, which were still red and puffy from the day before.

"Not much!" Peter answered, white-knuckling Lottie’s alarm clock. "Has anyone seen my other shoe?!"

Still slightly dazed, Remus got up after Mary and immediately bungled it, tripping over the corner of Lottie's shag rug. He sprawled with a great ‘omph!’, knocking both his elbow and head sharply against the floorboards. While his ears rung, he became aware that someone was calling his name, but only snapped to when he come face-to-face with Sirius, who had bent over to help him up.

“C’mon, Moony. We don’t have time for your theatrics, we’re gonna miss the bus!”

Remus was a deer in headlights. His toes curled. His mouth dropped open. And then he remembered.

I like Sirius Black.

The thought crashed into him like a freight train. He wanted to flee—to find the deepest hole he could, crawl into it, and never come out again. Sirius looked so perfect, he couldn't take it! All sea-stone eyes and sleep-mussed hair and—

No! Bloody-fuck no! This is insane! Who thinks like this?!

Sirius was his friend—dammit! He didn’t have the time or willpower for this. How had he even managed to fall back asleep? Was it sheer nerves? Had he simply passed out in shock instead?

“Moony? Earth to Moony!” Sirius grumbled, irritated that Remus had laid there like a dead fish rather than take his hand.

He's calling you, that cursed, sing-song voice said. Maybe snap out of it, hey?

"MOOOONY!"

“Okay!” Remus wheezed, grappling onto his arm and letting Sirius swing him back up to his feet. James and Peter were already outside, having left through the window while Remus was still having his internal melt-down. Sirius promptly followed them, before looking back at Remus with an odd look.

"Are you okay? You look more freaked out than usual."

"I'm fine," Remus grunted, not meeting his eye.

"Did you actually hit your head?”

"No! Now go on!"

Sirius looked him up and down once more before swinging his leg over the window ledge and gracefully dropping down onto the electrical box below. Stomach in knots, Remus hesitated. Would he be able to survive nine hours on a train like this?

“Fuck, my hair!” Mary wailed from behind. “Has anyone seen my sleeping bonnet?”

“You left it in the bathroom,” shouted Lottie.

“… WHO GOT IT WET?! IT’S SILK!”

Screw the train, he wouldn't survive another thirty seconds in here. Practically holding his breath, Remus swung both legs over the window.

“Remus!” Marlene called, just before he could throw himself off the ledge. While the rest of the girls flew about their bedroom collecting last minute packing, she scuttled forward. “I meant to ask you something yesterday.”

“LUPIN!” James barked from outside; “LEG IT OR LOSE IT!”

“I’m coming!” Remus lashed. When he turned back he caught an eyeful of Mary as she whipped off her shirt without a shred of hesitation. Moaning, he quickly covered his eyes to preserve both their modesties. “Look Cherry, can this wait until we’re on the train or something?”

"Well, I meant to ask yesterday but with everything going on—"

"LUPIN?!"

"HOLD ON!"

“I just didn’t want to put you on the spot in front of everyone!”

That got his attention. He peeked out between his fingers and Marlene relaxed, adjusting the rumpled school shirt she’d neglected to change out of the night before.

“I wanted to know if you’d consider coming to mine for Easter?” She asked quickly. "You don't have to! S'just a thought really...."

Remus opened and then closed his mouth in surprise. “Oh. You mean like your house… with your family?”

“Yeah, I don’t think the drive is too far from yours in Blackheath, and my dad already offered to fetch you himself if you’d like. Really, it was my mum's idea. She was the one who suggested you come by for dinner. They… They really want to meet you, is all.”

“MOONY!” Sirius wailed behind him. “I personally don’t mind staying but unless you want to camp out at school for the next week, get your arse down here!”

“Alright!” Remus cleared his throat a bit. He hadn’t really considered what he was going to do to pass the time while at home. Under normal circumstances he would’ve gone straight to Tomny’s, but it’d been weeks since the telephone line had been disconnected, and a part of him was afraid to find an empty flat. And now with this Sirius-headache, he needed to find a new distraction or he would surely go insane.

“I’ll come,” he promised, and Marlene smiled with relief. It instantly made him feel guilty. First for considering his girlfriend a distraction, and second for every thought he’d ever had about Sirius.

“Cool, okay, we can talk more about it on the train then.”

“Okay, see you there.”

“Don’t be late,” she chuckled, waving as he dropped down onto the grass outside.

They ran back to their dorm, just to stumble across the bedroom’s threshold and continue the race to collect their things. Remus had only enough time to change his clothes and grab his trunk before James was ordering them out again and they were weaving down the staircase along with a few other lagging students. On their way out, he distantly heard one of the phones ring, and then his name was called.

“Lupin, wait up! Phone’s for you!”

James hit the breaks just as he made it to the front door, jacket sagging on his shoulders. “Oh bloody hell—Lupin, the bus leaves in twenty minutes!”

“So I have twenty minutes then?”

“It takes fifteen just to walk to Castle Hall!”

“Then I’ll run,” Remus reasoned, despite the cramp already forming in his side. “Don’t worry, it’s probably just Giles making sure I’m getting on the bloody thing.”

“Give us your bag then,” Sirius said, taking his trunk from him.

Remus handed it over, and his fingers brushed against Sirius’. A shiver shot up his arm, like an electric shock and suddenly he was drowning all over again.

I like Sirius Black. Sirius fucking Black.

"Moony, hand your bag over!"

He pushed the thought away. Now was not the time for another freak-out.

“Sorry! I—I mean, thanks,” he stammered. “I’ll... I'll be right behind you! Just don’t let the bus leave without me.”

Another strange look from Sirius. He was forming a collection, it seemed.

While his friends all nodded and threw themselves out onto Godric’s front lawn, Remus hastily turned back to the phone. He found it unhooked and waiting for him and quickly raised it to his ear, smoothing out his hair while he cleared the lump from his throat.

“Yes? Hello, what is it?”

“Hey, Lu.”

Another shiver ran up Remus’ spine, this one much different from the one the gentle brush of Sirius' hand had given him. With a shaky breath, he glanced around himself, as though it were a cruel joke and someone was waiting in the corner to jump out and scare him. Finally he switched the receiver to the other ear, hands trembling slightly.

“Tom...?”

“Yeah," Tomny's familiar brogue answered. "Haven’t heard from you in a while. Er... How've ya been?”

“How have I…?” He began to sputter. “What the fuck Tomny!”

“Oh, damn..."

Remus felt his temper flare. “Haven’t heard from me—how ‘bout haven’t heard from you! What the hell happened to your phone line?”

“Was jus' down for a while,” Tomny mumbled, completely apathetic.

“I thought you were dead!” Remus lashed. “Instead you just—what—couldn’t bother to pay the damn bill?!”

Tomny sighed into the other end. “Wasn’t like that. Sorry to worry you.”

“Fuck your sorry,” Remus grumbled, though his anger was already waning. This many emotions so early in the morning—he wasn't going to make it to lunch. “What’s been going on then? I’m about to come home, dammit. My bus leaves in a few minutes.”

“I won’t keep you then.”

“Shut up. Just say what you want and I’ll gas you for the rest when I get back.”

“Okay. Tonya’s gone.”

He'd had a response ready—another vicious insult—but suddenly all coherent thought fled his mind.

“What...?” Remus held his stomach. “What do you mean she’s gone?”

“She left.”

“Left... where?”

“Left the flat, Lu.” Tomny’s voice had an edge to it. “It was a while ago. February.”

Remus looked down at his shoes. The last time he’d talked to Tonya was February. Then everyone had gone radio-silent.

“Do—Do you know where she went?”

“No. She didn’t say goodbye actually. Didn’t leave much behind either. Jus' this letter for you.”

“For…” Remus trailed off in disbelief. “You sure it’s for me?”

“S’got your name on it. I can post it, if you give me your school’s address or whatever.”

“O—Or I could come and get it?”

“I’d rather just post it,” Tomny said. “Don’t really want it around 'ere anymore, ya know?”

“Yeah. Yeah, okay. You... got a pen then?”

He waited until Tomny was ready before relaying the school’s address. He’d expected him to say something stupid about the dorm's name or the fact that the street the school was technically on was called ‘Bell End Road’, but Tomny was quiet the entire time.

“Well, I’ll post it when I got the time,” he said finally.

“Okay. Are you… alright, Tom?”

“Mm. Jus’ fine.”

“You don’t sound fine.”

“I’m excellent then. Tonya’s old hat anyway. Sorry you’re just finding out now.”

“Yeah, but it’s okay,” Remus said, trying his best to sound upbeat, “I’ll come by and we can talk about—”

“I don’t think that’s such a good idea.”

“… What?”

“I don’t think you should come by the flat anymore, Lu. Lots of stuff’s happened. Ian cut a guy last month and we're still cleaning up the mess. Don’t think it’s such a good idea for other people to start comin’ round again.”

"You mean he... killed someone?"

"Well, it was'na exactly a knick."

“Holy fuck.” Remus forced a breath in through his nose. “O-Okay, but maybe once things have calmed down a bit we can meet and talk. Tonya said some stuff when she and I talked—”

“God fucking dammit,” Tomny said lowly. “Don’t you get it, Remus? I don’t want you comin' around! No one does—me, the boys, we got shit goin' on. Can’t sit around pretending things are fine and dandy jus' ‘cause you got a holiday from school. So you jus' stay away, and life’ll bloody go on like it always has, okay?”

Remus had never felt so fragile. Tomny never yelled at him—not unless he really deserved it. Hearing him say he didn’t want him around was like a sucker-punch to the gut.

“Did you—” Tomny coughed sharply before letting out a staggered breath. “Did you hear me?”

“Yeah Tom…” Remus whispered, head down, “I heard you.”

There was silence, then Tomny coughed again to clear his throat. “Good. I’ll post the letter, just… we’ll talk later.”

A lie. “Okay, Tom.”

“… Bye, Lu.”

The line clicked dead and Remus felt cold all over. He dropped the phone from his ear and leaned his forehead against it, sucking in a breath so sharp it sounded as though he were in pain. Then he realised—he was in pain. The cold became an ache, one he hadn't felt in a long time. When he finally realised what he was doing, he had no idea how long it’d been since James and the others had gone on ahead. Wiping his face, Remus hung up the receiver and turned, staggering out the front of the dorm toward the short-cut that led to Castle Hall. The reality that Tonya was gone and Tomny had finally said the words he’d been dreading most didn’t really hit him until he was walking across the pavement, staring as James waved his arms frantically for him to hurry.

“He’s here!” Remus heard him holler at the bus driver. When he turned back, James’ expression went from irritated to concerned. “Blimey mate, you okay? You look like your dog just died or something.” James’ eyes widened suddenly. “Your dog didn’t just die, did it?”

That would really be the cherry on top, Remus thought bitterly. He shook his head.

Gingerly, James pat him on the back and together they stepped aboard, the bus doors squeaking closed behind them. Going on ahead, James sat down next to Lily while Marlene waved at him from the seat behind her and moved her bag so he could sit. Remus lumbered down the aisle toward her, feeling strangely disconnected from his surroundings. He almost sat, before spotting Sirius near the back, tucked up tight next to Chastity.

"Remus...?"

He looked down. There was concern on Marlene's face.

“Sorry,” he said, clutching the back of the seat until his knuckles went white; “I just really need to talk to Sirius right now. See you on the train?”

“Yeah, sure,” she answered lightly, obviously reading his expression.

The bus was already moving by the time he’d made it down the aisle to Sirius. Chastity noticed him first, glancing up from her window seat and muttering something under her breath to her boyfriend, who looked up with a smile that made Remus’ heart lurch.

“Oh, hey Moony, glad you made it. Thought you were gonna have to mail yourself back to London.”

“Can I talk to you?”

Sirius’ smile disappeared in an instant. He looked to Chastity, before leaning in and whispering something in her ear.

“Noooo,” Chastity started to pout, but Sirius only cupped her cheek and murmured some more, still wearing that handsome look that not even Remus could refuse. Finally she rolled her eyes and stood up, squeezing out inside the aisle. She made sure to shoot Remus a nasty glare, before stalking off down the aisle.

“It’s fine,” Sirius said, standing up and indicating for Remus to take the window seat, “I’ll find her on the train.”

Remus slid in ahead of him and was instantly thankful. Each limb felt as though it were made with lead and he felt sick, like the rumbling motion of the bus had knocked something inside of him loose. Dropping down next to him, Sirius glanced around to make sure no one was listening in. Remus instantly loved him for it.

“So what’s up—who was on the phone? Was it…?”

As per usual, Sirius was already inside his head. “Yeah,” he croaked, “it was Tomny.”

“Well, about time. What did he say? Did he at least have a half-decent excuse for disappearing off the face of the earth?”

Remus turned away, rubbing his face. His eyes stung, and he didn’t want Sirius to see him cry. “He said Tonya left.”

“Oh…" Clearly it wasn't what Sirius was expecting. "Damn... She just left home?”

“Yeah. In February. Maybe right after we talked.”

“Do you know that for sure?”

“… No.”

“Then don’t say that.”

Remus felt a sob well up in his throat. What makes you happy? If he’d said he would tell her on Easter, would she have stayed?

"Hey," Sirius tried, leaning in close, "what's all this? It's okay. You're gonna be okay. You just need to see Tom, right?"

“No," he whimpered. "He told me not to come back, Sirius. He said don't come back to the flat.”

Anger bloomed on Sirius' face. "That sodding git—he’s blaming you?!”

“No, I just—I dunno. Someone died. Not anyone I know, but… God, I bet it’s a mess.”

“And he’s blaming you,” Sirius said again. “Man, fuck him.”

Remus flinched and Sirius pulled back. “Sorry,” he mumbled, before slowly placing his hand on his arm. “I’m sorry, Moony.”

“It’s what I get,” Remus murmured, “for thinking I could play both sides.”

“Aw, you poor idiot. You weren’t playing both sides, you were just existing. What’s wrong with that—with just being happy?”

But Remus wasn’t happy. For nearly two years he’d been torn, never fully in one place. And now Tonya was gone and Tomny had outgrown him and he had no way of catching up to either of them.

"I wish we weren't going home," he breathed.

"Trust me," Sirius said softly, "where we're going? It ain't home."

Oh, Sirius.

With his head in hands, Remus bent forward, and finally the tears came. It was like opening the floodgates. The rumble of the bus hid all noise, but it was like a thunderstorm had hit inside his chest.

“Aw, Moons,” Sirius said, rubbing his back. “It’ll be okay. It just sucks for a little while. I know, I know.”

Just the day before, Lily had asked him if he cried. He'd hesitated then. But now, with Sirius doing his best to cover him from view, Remus wasn't sure he would ever be able to stop.



Chapter End Notes

Chapter 56: Easter, 1977


Chapter Summary

Remus returns to London for Easter, short a few friends. Luckily the McKinnons have invited him for dinner.



Chapter Notes

This chapter took a while to edit, so it's out a little later than I would've preferred. Hope you enjoy it though!

CW: 'F' word used in smoking context. Brief mention of sexual content. Some not so nice undertones of homophobia and vague references of suicide.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Yesterday,

All my troubles seemed so far away;

Now it looks as though they’re here to stay,

Oh, I believe in yesterday...

- “Yesterday” The Beatles, 1965



Number twelve, Grimmauld Place of Widcombe, Bath, stood three hours away by train and a little more than four by car. Remus knew this because he’d spent his first day back in London measuring the distance out on the maps Giles left tucked in the seat pockets of the Rolls. It was as though he needed to convince himself on paper that simply running away to Sirius was not a feasible option. Even if he did make it all the way to Bath, Sirius wasn't even permitted to use the phone over holidays—Remus doubted he’d be allowed so much as a glimpse of his friend if he went. Though, the rebel in him couldn't help but imagine throwing stones at Sirius' window, then climbing some trellis until they were nose to nose and he could look him in the eye as he asked him to run away together. He knew without a second thought that Sirius wouldn't hesitate. They'd climb down that trellis with little more than the clothes on their backs and they'd be off. They could busk on street corners for pennies like they'd always talked about, and stow away in freight trains to warmer weather the moment it grew cold again. Sirius would never complain, too busy enjoying the moment, and that gave Remus courage.

Except it was only ever a fever dream, and foggy London mornings culled those quick enough.

Maybe if he'd had Sirius he would've been able to pluck up the courage to visit James or Peter’s—but alone, Remus couldn’t even pick up the phone, let alone accept invitations to mother-made suppers or Piccadilly Circus. He knew James and Peter would understand if he told them, but the mere idea of trying to explain what Tomny had said made him sick to his stomach. They would feel sad for him, then rage as Sirius had, but it would be misplaced. They didn't know what had gone on before, not really—how he'd lied to everyone and stuck his nose in where it didn't belong. How he'd used Tomny as an outlet for all the anger he felt for his parents, and Tonya as a comfort. How he'd fallen in love with both of them and then treated it all like a vacation from a life without any real hardship. It was guilt beyond measure—and James and Peter would never understand. Sirius came the closest. He already knew the 'before' stuff, which made the 'now' bits easier. But Sirius wasn’t around.

On his second day, Remus wrote a letter.





Dear Sirius,

I called the flat again from my house. I know you told me not to, but I did it anyway. I was hoping the line would be dead again, but it rang and someone picked up. I think it was Ian, but I couldn’t really be sure because I hung up the moment they said hello. I guess a part of me wanted to think that things would stop for them too. But Tomny was right. Life just goes on.



In the end he didn’t post it. Instead Remus shoved the letter in a bottom drawer with the rest of his things; books, albums, cigarettes—everything that’d ever come out of the flat. He told himself that he would burn it. That way there wouldn’t be anything left and he could truly put it all behind him.

When he’d reappeared on Tomny’s doorstep last Christmas it’d been thanks to a sliver of hope that Tomny hadn’t truly meant what he’d said when he’d gotten hurt in August. Now that sliver was inflamed. Infected and slowly poisoning the rest of him with anger and hurt and bitterness, enough to drown out some of the guilt. Tomny had given up, and wherever she was, Tonya had given up too. They weren’t his friends, maybe they never had been. What sort of friends ran away or gave up on one another so easily? Sirius wouldn’t have given up—James or Peter neither. The phrase ‘give up’ didn’t exist in any dictionary they owned, and you’d probably have to break a few legs to get any of them to leave you behind. It made Remus wonder where he fell on that spectrum. He didn’t want to give up either, but if Tomny hated him so much, what else was there to do?

The only calls he took were from Marlene, his girlfriend and possibly the most reliable person he knew. She made things easier, even if he did feel guilty every time he so much as thought of Sirius in her presence. If Tomny’s phone call had done anything, it’d distracted him from the sudden Sirius revelation. The distance felt good too, in that way. Surely Sirius couldn’t occupy his every waking thought all the way from Bath.

Marlene visiting the estate had been Remus' idea, surprisingly enough. They had several days before he was due to visit hers for dinner and he’d suddenly grown antsy in the absence of his friends. Unlike James and Peter, Marlene knew some bits about Tomny—mostly the innocent stuff—and so confessing to her what had him so rattled was easier too. Always making sure to invite her over on the days Lyall was at the office, he sent a car and Marlene became the first friend he’d ever had over to his childhood home.

“Bloody big enough, isn't it?” She said, staring up at the looming ceilings of the foyer. Suddenly, as if remembering where she was, Marlene clapped her hand to her mouth. “I-I mean, it’s beautiful.”

“You don’t have to do that,” he smiled; “You can just be yourself, Cherry.”

She seemed grateful for that at least, and truthfully, he was grateful for her. They took their time walking the grounds, where Marlene met all the dogs and laughed when they leapt up to lick her face. She seemed to like the horses best, and though Remus had no personal interest in, he enjoying seeing the way her face lit up outside the stable.

Giles loved her, naturally. He’d grown up in Battersea not far from hers and was more than delighted to discuss how the area had changed since he was young. Other topics of conversation included football matches they both followed and of course Remus himself—though he was pretty sure Giles was making up most of the embarrassing stories he was able to ‘suddenly remember’. It was almost startling how well the two of them got on. Marlene had that sort of quick and witty disposition Giles admired, and the second time she’d come to visit, he went himself to pick her up.

Eventually Marlene had the idea that they should go and see a show. It was just by happenstance that her local cinema was showing the film version of Carrie, and though she seemed less than excited over the content, Mary had suggested to her that they should catch a movie at least once as a couple before they headed back to school for the rest of term. Mary was actually supposed to meet them there with some guy her cousin had introduced her to, but at the last second she’d declared him a creep and bailed on their plans.

“I don’t know what’s wrong with her,” Marlene grumbled as they paid for their tickets. “It’s like she’s gone completely off the rails. She hops from guy to guy like there’s a prize to be won—except the only prize I can think of is being called a slag. I don't know how she gets away with it.”

“She doesn't sleep with all of them, does she?”

“No, but that hardly matters—they’d just lie and say they did get with her. Most boys are disgusting that way.”

After the usher ripped their tickets they made their way inside and Marlene left him to go to the toilet while Remus got in line for the concession. When it happened he was mostly spaced-out, staring at the movie poster showing Carrie’s actress bathed in blood on the wall next to the theatre hallways. Another movie had just gotten out, and a small crowd of people were shuffling toward the doors, scattering bits of popcorn on the floor as they went. He saw a flash of familiar golden-brown and abandoned his place in line immediately, shooting toward him with his hand outstretched.

“Tomny! Tom!” He called, hardly believing that he’d spotted his friend in some tiny picture house in East Dulwich of all places, but as he clasped his hand on the guy’s shoulder, he turned and Remus realised that it wasn’t Tomny at all, just a guy who slightly resembled him from the back.

“Sorry, mate,” he breathed, “thought you were someone else.”

The guy just looked at him funny before shambling off with the brunette girl he was with, and Remus had the bitter thought that Tonya was much prettier.

“Remus?”

He turned to find Marlene, her blue eyes wide with concern.

“Sorry, I… got distracted.”

“It’s okay,” she said kindly. “Did you still want that popcorn?”

The theatre was dark, which Remus was grateful for, and Marlene spent most of the film with her face turned into his shoulder, jumping every time the music clashed or anything moderately gruesome appeared on screen. He tried his best to focus on the film, but the incident with the almost-Tomny had him too rattled to really enjoy it—which was a shame too, since he’d heard the filmmakers had used actual pigs’ blood in the finale.

Giles was waiting to drive Marlene home when it was over. She sat in the front and used her extensive vocabulary of ‘ibles’ (‘horrible’, ‘terrible’, ‘incomprehensible’, that sort of thing) to regale the driver with her impression of the film while Giles interjected with tidbits such as how Remus used to be afraid of everything from pigeons to his own shadow.

“You had your eyes covered during that part!” Remus protested from the back seat, after Marlene complained about the way Carrie effectively cut two students in half like ground beef by slamming them in a door.

“Says you,” Marlene laughed. “You were staring at the wall for most of it! What, starting to rethink this whole interest in horror and gore?”

He let her have it, only because he didn’t want her to think he was too distracted to have a good time with her.

When they made it back to Marlene’s house—a very modest-looking row home on a very modest-looking street—he got out and walked her to the door. Giles was watching them and Remus had to turn around and wave an arm at him in exasperation to get him to drive up the street a bit, which he did, only after honking obnoxiously.

“I like Giles,” Marlene said; “I see where you get your sass from now.”

“Yeah, he’s good,” Remus said, putting his hands in his pockets.

Marlene looked down at her shoes. She was wearing trainers and a pair of flared jeans, which had shocked him at first since he’d grown so used to seeing her in her school clothes. She had no makeup on and her hair was in a plain ponytail, but she’d worn these jangly bracelets on her wrists and a large flowy wrap-shirt which made her look a bit like Stevie Nicks.

“I had fun tonight,” she said shyly. “It was nice to go out on a real date.”

“Yeah it was,” he shrugged. “Too bad we can’t really see movies at school.”

“Yup.”

Marlene opened her mouth like she was going to say something else, but just closed it again, smiling. “Well, I guess I’ll see you tomorrow.”

Remus nodded. “You’re sure I don’t need to bring anything? I could always—”

"What thing?"

"The 'Remus worry'."

Remus managed a genuine smile. "The what?"

"You fret like an old woman, Remus. Sometimes I wonder if you're a teenage boy at all."

She shrugged innocently. "I'm serious, though. Mum’s a little pushy but if you just be yourself, you’ll be fine. Maybe polish up your table manners a bit though, they’re a bit lax.”

Turning, Remus made his way back down to the pavement and up the street to where the Roll’s brake lights were shining. If he were back at Hawkings he’d probably have heard crickets chirping, but it was just London, so all that could be heard were the nearby sounds of late-night traffic. Giles tucked away the paper he’d been reading under the car lamp as he slipped into the backseat. It was the same one he’d read cover-to-cover that morning, which meant he hadn’t been reading it at all and had definitely been spying instead.

“Ready for home?” He asked.

“Yeah,” Remus said, “let’s get back.”

That night he wrote Sirius another letter.

Sunday 10th April 1977 — Easter Sunday

He brought flowers because Giles said he couldn’t turn up empty-handed to meet Marlene’s family. He combed his hair because Giles said he looked like a yob when he didn’t. He’d almost worn a tie because Giles said so, but had drawn the line there and shoved the thing in a bush on the way up to the front door to ring the bell.

Marlene answered, looking pretty in a blue dress and matching barrettes in her hair. “Don’t you look spiffing,” she said. “And you brought flowers. How cute.”

“Giles’ idea,” Remus said bashfully.

Marlene smirked. “Well, you came all this way, might as well come in.”

“Wow, thanks.”

He passed her the bouquet and took off his shoes in the tight entryway as Marlene hollered down the hall to announce his arrival; “Mum, Remus is here! And he brought flowers!”

“How nice!” Mrs. McKinnon hollered back from deeper inside the house.

"Dining room's this way," Marlene said, gesturing down the hall.

"Hey," Remus asked quietly, stopping her before she could lead him further into the house, "your family isn't gonna, like... ask me about football and stuff, are they?"

"That's what you're worried about?" Marlene sniggered.

"That and other things. It just would be great if they didn't."

"Well, no promises," she smirked. "Now c'mon.” Looking far too pleased with herself, Marlene turned and led him down the yellow-papered hallway and into a dining room. The table was made up for eight, set with floral-covered china dishes and a lacy table cloth. The dining room's walls were scattered with pictures and photographs of the McKinnons and their family, along with several holy crosses and a large portrait of Christ.

There was a short clatter and Marlene's mother appeared through the doorway separated the dining room from the kitchen. “Oh, there he is!” She cried, while wiping her hands on a dishcloth. Apart from being shorter than Marlene, she was almost the spitting image of her daughter, all fair and rosy. “It’s so nice to finally meet you, Remus,” Mrs. McKinnon said, immediately pulling him into a rib-cracking hug. “Marlene’s told us all about you, of course, but she never said you were so tall, my oh my.”

“It’s a pleasure to meet you too, Mrs. McKinnon,” Remus winced. She had a grip like iron.

“What good manners. We can set them in the middle of the table. Now, dinner’s almost ready, so I’m going to get the boys. They’re out back smoking. Gracie, will you go check on Danielle? Her feet were feeling sore so she laid down in John’s old room.”

“Kay,” Marlene said, taking his hand while Joyce turned and retreated back into the kitchen. “Do you wanna see my room?”

“Sure,” he shrugged, and Marlene led him back out into the hall, dodging a rather large china cabinet and a second painting of Jesus nailed to the cross. “They call you Gracie?” He asked, absent-mindedly staring at Marlene’s hand in his as she led him up the staircase.

“Yeah,” Marlene said, “since I was little. 'Grace' is my middle name.”

“Oh. Right.”

“I was named after my dad’s aunt Gracie actually—the one who paid for my school and all that. Only you guys call me Marls.”

They stopped outside the first bedroom on the second-floor landing and Marlene knocked before poking her head in. There was a bit of mumbling, but she came back out with a smile. “Danielle’s my brother John’s wife. She’s six months pregnant and apparently has had a pretty miserable pregnancy so far, so I’m pretty sure everything still sucks for her right now.”

“And I suppose everything’s gonna suck for John too, in about three months.”

“Shhh!” Marlene hissed, but she was still smiling. “C’mon, my room’s just down here.”

They kept going, the floorboards creaking beneath their feet. Everything was tight in these sort of row homes, he knew, but Marlene’s house felt more lived-in than any of those he’d visited with Tomny in their early days. Each room seemed to smell of candles or cloves and every surface had some sort of crochet doily draped over it. Remus had never met any of his grandparents, but it made him wonder if this was what their homes might've looked like. The feel of a grandmother's doily, the smell of a grandfather's cigar—that sort of thing.

Down the hall, Marlene's bedroom was tiny, with only a closet, desk, and a single bed decorated with pink and blue flowers. There wasn’t much else apart from a few bits and bobs here and there and some old photographs of her and her family. She had a more recent photo of her and the girls framed on the desk and a small cross hung on the wall over her bed, but it was clear that the space was only occupied for about four months out of the year; Marlene’s school jumper was draped on the back of her desk chair, next to a stack of books and assigned reading.

“You don’t have to be sorry,” he murmured. "You're my girlfriend..."

Her humour worked, and Remus relaxed slightly, hearing the bed squeak beneath him. “If I’m a cranky old man then you’re a crazy old bat.”

“Both, I suppose.”

Marlene chuckled and leaned forward, hugging him tightly while pressing her face to the side of his neck. Letting out a sigh, Remus reached up and cupped the back of her head. It hit him then that this was all he ever wanted from her. Her laughter—her acceptance. Except he was pretty sure boyfriends were supposed to want more from their girlfriends.

Another thing to appreciate about Marlene, she always cut out the torturous bits.

Remus stood.

The swift sound of clanking silverware followed as everyone dug in, spooning themselves generous helpings from the large dish ware. As he robotically did the same, Remus felt his mind begin to float. More laughter, then Marlene leaned her head on his shoulder. “It’s sort of a relief—not dating you anymore.”

Remus covered his eyes dramatically. “And there goes my pride.”

“Fragile jessy,” she said, pinching his arm. “You’re the one who broke up with me.”

“You agreed!”

“As I was saying, it’s a relief to just be your friend again. I like you, Remus, but I’m not sure relationships are for me. Maybe I’m weird too.”

“Nah, you’re great.”

“Aw. You poof.”

“You might actually be the meanest person I’ve ever met,” Remus exclaimed happily. “And I’ve met Snape!”

“Ooh, do I get a prize?”

"Only my love."

“Ha. You are a poof. And I love you too. As a friend, of course.”

"Naturally."

They smiled at one another, before Marlene sighed and grabbed his neck, drawing him toward her. Their foreheads knocked together, and Remus felt calm wash over him.

“You know,” Marlene murmured, “I’m coming to realise something else about myself too.”

“What’s that?”

She hummed a bit. “I think I’m going to keep it to myself for a little while longer, if that’s okay.”

“Oh. Yeah, I understand.”

Pulling back, she cupped his face, stroking her thumbs across the bit of stubble on his jaw. “Knew you would.” She kissed him on the cheek and pat his thigh before swinging her legs over his and standing up. “Guess we should get dressed if we’re not going to shag, then. Unless you wanted to try break up sex?”

“I thought it was ‘make up sex’?”

She shrugged, then tossed him his shirt, tugging her own over her head as she made her way to the wall next to the door. “Got anything else to say before I turn the lights back on and we’re officially broken up?”

“Is that the signifier?” Remus snorted, then; “Nah, I’m good.”

Marlene smiled, but her hand stilled as she reached for the light switch. “Remus, do you think I could ask one more thing of you before we break up?”

“ ‘Course. Anything.”

Hesitating a moment longer, she bit her lip. “Will you still call me Cherry even if we’re broken up? You’ll think it’s silly, but it sort of… makes me feel pretty. Like how Mary feels when her boyfriends give her nicknames.”

“Of course I’ll still call you Cherry,” he said, like it was the easiest thing in the world. And really, it was.

Marlene’s shy smile returned. “Thanks,” she murmured.

“Oh, and Cherry?”

“Yeah?”

“You’ve always been pretty.”

“Oh Remus. In another world…"

Then she turned the lights on, and just like that, they were broken up.

Chapter Summary

Remus Lupin is a free man. Free to date, or not date and just fret over how good his best friend looks when he's doing... well, anything at all, really. Dammit.

No, one voice swore.

She pointed.

“Oh. You’re right. It is a bloody leprechaun.”

She laughed, and it was like sunshine after rain. But that was the thing about Scotland; no matter how many sunny days you got, there was always sure to be a coming storm.

The letter came on an inconspicuous Thursday. There was absolutely nothing about the day that had felt any different from the last. It’d rained in the morning, and by the afternoon the rain had stopped. He had taken four sugars in his tea at breakfast, three at lunch, had homework in two classes, and once that was finished, had made plans to practice with Sirius and James in the music room. Even Peter was going to join them, still sceptical over the drums but finally willing to try as long as Sirius agreed to go at his pace and not push too hard. By all accounts it was a good day. Remus mourned it the moment the letter slipped under their bedroom door.

It had taken its time to arrive, that was for sure. Maybe it was just the slow post, or maybe Tomny had had second thoughts about sending it. He knew the latter could be true, as the top edge of the envelope had already been ripped before being hastily taped back together.

It was strange to see Tonya’s pretty handwriting juxtaposed with Tomny’s poor scrawl. All she’d committed to was his name, ‘Remus John Lupin’ in the centre of the envelope’s back. It’d been Tomny who’d scribbled the school’s address beneath, though he’d misspelled ‘Hawkings’. Remus found himself thanking whatever lucky stars he had that it hadn’t been lost along the way, which he hated himself for a second later. Perhaps it would've been better off lost. After all, this wasn’t just a letter updating him on her journey, or a postcard from some tiny hillside village in the south of France, this was Tonya's goodbye. He wanted to tear it in half—to shred it into little pieces just like she'd done with his heart. But he didn’t because it was also an explanation, and that was more than he’d ever gotten from anyone else.

He waited until he was alone in the dorm to read it, then he peeled back the tape and slowly unfolded the thin paper.

The words hit like a train.



Remus,

I know you won’t understand why I’m writing this to you, but words are all I have left and I know you deserve them. I feel sorry I can’t give as much to Tomny, but he wouldn’t know what to do with a letter and no matter how hard I tried, I could never bring myself say them aloud. I think it's because I knew that if I had, he’d have just smiled at me and I’d have never left. But I have to leave. I never even meant to stay, you see. I haven’t spent this much time in one place since I was fourteen and when I asked myself why that is, I couldn’t find the answer.

I suppose that’s just it though, I want to find the answer. I know that’s vague, but I’ve spent half my life looking for it and I didn’t find it in London. I’m sorry if it's selfish, but I want you to know that seeing you at Christmas made me so undeniably happy. I love you so dearly, Remus. In fact, I heard a song on the radio the other day that reminded me of you. I didn’t catch its name, but I know you would’ve liked it. It made me think that there are lots of things out there that we might like that we don’t even know about because we’ve missed them or because someone couldn’t remember the name or the words or what it smelt like or how it felt to run their hands across it. But I ’m rambling now, and this was the only piece of blank paper I could find in the entire flat without any coffee stains so I should probably stop wasting it.

I want you to know that I loved Tomny, I did. But I’ve never really considered love to be the end-all-be-all. Love to me has always felt like an ongoing method of life, not the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Love should be eclectic—diverse and transformative just like people. When it isn’t—when it becomes something that is required of life, that’s when I feel myself drifting away. This time I drifted away with drugs, but it wasn’t even the first time. I’ve also drifted away with alcohol, work, religion, (did I ever tell you about the time I joined a cult? Wild times, man) and each time it left me emptier than before. I suppose it’s a lot like how you treat music. But I advise you not to make it that terrifying end-all-be-all. Don’t let it be the only way you can communicate with others, otherwise it’ll lose all its meaning. And when our vices lose their meaning we really don’t have much left, do we?

I’ll stop trying to give you advice now. I know you probably don’t want it. You’re probably very angry with me. Tomny too. And I want you to know I understand. You can be angry, but I’ll still love you. I’ll always love you. Even when you’re wasting away as a bank teller or a rice farmer or a rock star, you’ll always be loved by me. Oh, look at that—I’ve used the whole front and back and still this page is too short. I should’ve written in pencil so I could erase all my bad advice and only list the ways that I love you.

These aren’t all of those ways, but here are a few:

I love you like you love Queen, Remus—only much more because you started loving Queen on Christmas last year and I’ve loved you since the moment we met. I love you the way Tomny loves Lee, Doss, Seesaw, Vint, and all the rest—only I’m a girl and much better looking so naturally my love’s much more desirable. I love you like the sky meets the sea, forever and endless no matter how far you go to meet it. I love you enough to write cheesy lines like that. I love you like springtime. Like a second snowfall but not the first because it’s always unexpected and I always expected to love you. I love you like a soulmate, which says a lot because I don’t believe in soulmates. Instead I like to think that our souls are made for more than just one thing, but I’m so lucky because my soul was made to love yours.

I love you. I love you. I love you. I really, really love you.

Don’t let Tomny stay angry. I love him too. I loved him enough to stay but I love him even enough to leave. And I’m sorry I couldn’t give him anything. It’s just not how we work. He’ll understand what I mean.

I have to go now, sweet love. Be safe, be healthy, and please be happy, whatever that means. And don’t let anyone—ever—tell you what that means.

Love forever,

Tonya.

Sirius lowered the letter.

“Damn.”

Remus couldn’t help it. He laughed. He kept laughing until it’d become sad and weepy and pathetic, and Sirius had moved over against the wall of the astronomy room to press their shoulders together. He’d rushed from the dorm before even finishing the front half of the letter—unwilling to remain where anyone could find him. When he’d failed to show up for band practice, Sirius had been the one to come looking. He was grateful that he’d come alone—any attempt from James and Peter to comfort him would’ve felt unbearable. But when Sirius put an arm around him and pulled him in close, Remus was so, so pleased. He felt inconsolable, fragile and even a little broken—if this was what brokenness was—but having Sirius close numbed some of it—allowed him some perspective. Tonya was the loss he’d been mourning for weeks now, the letter was just the finality of it. The last string to be cut.

“She really doesn’t pull her punches, does she?” Sirius said, and Remus choked on another laugh-turned-sob.

“No… no, she does not.”

“Just straight to the throat. No mercy.”

“Ha… yeah.”

“Is there anything I can do?”

Remus sighed. There were plenty of things Sirius could do, but none he could ask of him.

“Tell me a story?” He asked instead. Begged.

“What kind of story?”

“A happy one.”

Sirius clicked his tongue. “Those are hard to come by, but I suppose I’ll see what I can do…” Sirius lifted his thumb nail to his mouth, nibbling on it while he thought. “Huh…” he started; “Okay. Once upon a time—”

“Oh bloody hell, here we go.”

“Oi, do you want the story or not?”

“… Proceed.”

Sirius cleared his throat. “Once upon a time, there was a musician—”

“You?”

“Shh! Shut up—there was once a wonderful musician and... he was known throughout the world for his musical compositions."

As Sirius lapsed into gentle prose, Remus found himself relaxing. He slid back against the cool wall of the astronomy room and let his head rest next to Sirius'. Not touching, just close enough to feel his radiating warmth.

"He could play any instrument—any style," Sirius recited, "and was revered as a master of the art. Some called his abilities, ‘a gift from God’. Others whispered that he’d made a deal with the Devil, as no one could comprehend how any normal person could possess such a talent. So, along with his small band, he travelled the world for many years, playing to not just noblemen and ladies but also those without a penny to their name. He did it all for free too, because he thought that if his talent was God-given, then it should be shared with everyone.

“Well one day, while he was playing a concert for some King’s court, a man stepped forward, interrupting the music. He was wearing simple clothes, nothing fantastical at all, and yet when spoke, everyone listened. He said that he didn’t believe one man could create such sweet music all on his own—that it must’ve been some sort of trick or a lie. Naturally, the humble musician stood up for himself—of course it wasn’t a lie, his music was his to possess and to share.”

“This guy sounds like a right dick.”

“Yes, well, he was—and he wasn’t convinced! He asked for proof of the musician’s talent. He told him to set aside his accompanying bandmates and play in the middle of the hall for all to see. Of course the musician agreed, though he was unaccustomed to others challenging his talent. First he played the piano, but that was deemed too grand—there were plenty of places one could hide a trick or lie within a piano. So instead he played the harp, but by some chance, the strings snapped the moment his fingers touched them. Next he tried the violin, but those strings snapped too. Frustrated with his bad luck, he borrowed the brass horn of his bandmate, but its keys were mysteriously rusted in place. It was unplayable, and he blamed the man for neglecting his instrument. He took the drum of another, but its hide ripped the moment he set palm to it, and he was left embarrassed. Finally he reached for his own brass flute, the very first instrument he’d ever learned how to play. But when he took up the flute and blew into it, no sound came out.

"Disappointed, the musician insisted that he could play, and demanded that another instrument be presented to him. It was then that the same man who'd challenged him presented a reed flute to replace the musician’s very own. Now, this flute was a dinky little thing—and the audience whispered about how it was too simple an instrument to be played in a King's court. But the musician accepted it anyway, and when the flute was played, it produced the most beautiful music. Satisfied, the musician continued to play, pleased that he was finally able to show-up the nasty challenger—and with his own instrument, no less. 'There, now you see what I can do,' he told the man. And the stranger bowed and said, 'Yes, you truly have no rival'. And so the musician finished his concert to many applause, returned the man's flute, and went home.

The next day the musician was due to give a second show. He arrived back at the hall with his band in tow, feeling even more victorious than before. Confident, he took up his instrument and began to play, and only then did he find that he no longer could carry a tune at all. Not on any instrument, big or small. Grand or simple. It was as though his very fingers had forgotten what it was to play music. When he looked to his music sheets it was as though his eyes no longer worked—he couldn't read the very notes he himself had written. Devastated, the musician looked to the crowd, who were all staring on in disappointment. He did not see the man who had challenged him. One by one his bandmates abandoned him, unable to support a master who could not lead them to greatness. Repulsed by the horrible noise, the King ordered him from his hall and as word spread of the musician's failure, not even the common folk wanted to hear his ruins. So, he wandered the world, returning to the same places he’d once played to crowds of hundreds, hoping that one day the mysterious stranger with the reed flute would reappear and challenge him again. But he never did, and no matter what instrument the musician played or however many sheets of music he gathered, he could never play or read a single note ever again. The end.”

Sirius let out a long breath, sounding almost tired, and though he’d successfully lost himself in the story—lulled by Sirius’ easy voice—Remus tipped his head back against the wall and stared at him in question. “Is that the end?”

“... Yep.”

"Actually?"

"Yeah, but don't you get it? It's about vanity. The man wasn't a man at all, he was a reflection of pride. By giving into pride the musician lost everything—his talent, his friends, his admirers."

Remus' mouth dropped open. “Okay but, fucking hell—I thought it was supposed to be a happy story not some bloody cautionary tale about being a pompous nob!”

The corners of Sirius' mouth twisted and he nodded in silent agreement. “Maybe, you're right. I thought it was happy when I first remembered it, but then I guess it does sorta fall off at the end there.”

“You are a sociopath,” Remus laughed incredulously. “Couldn’t you have just—I don’t know, made a fairy appear that forgave him and gave him back the bloody flute?”

“I guess I could’ve, but somehow that doesn't sound as genuine, does it?”

Remus wiped the corners of his mouth, still shaking his head. “You really know how to cheer someone up.”

“Does that mean you’re feeling better?” Sirius asked merrily.

“Better than that musician guy, I’ll bet.”

“Oh good, then you’re welcome.”

Remus looked down at the ground. Sirius’ arm was still around him and his shoulder felt warm where it met his. But then again, everything felt warm around Sirius.

“Who told you that story?” He asked.

“Hm, maybe the second or third governess after Gisela? Now that I think about it, she was probably just trying to scare me out of being a massive cunt. I was thirteen and thought that anyone less than Schubert was a hack.”

“Someone should tell her she failed. You're totally a massive cunt.”

“Ha! C'mon now, I’d say I have at least few more years before that story really becomes applicable. Can't be revered as a ‘master of the art’ until I got people in Japan and South America shouting my name.”

Remus cracked a smile and wiped his face on the back of his sleeve. “Do me a favour and send me a postcard.”

“Don’t need to—you’re gonna be there with me. Royalties, remember?”

“Eh, I dunno, maybe I’ll be a rice farmer instead.”

Sirius chuckled. “Okay, whatever you say. But I’ll tell you what though, Moons, that letter was pure shite. Like ‘run down your leg—ruin your trousers type-a shite.”

”I get the picture.”

”My point is… I’ll never love you enough to leave you.”

Remus’ breath caught. “Yeah…?”

“Yeah,” Sirius said, beaming at him in the dark.

With nothing else to do but cry, Remus closed his eyes. For a moment he could see it—standing next to Sirius on stage, James and Peter right there with them. It would be nice if something as good as music was the only thing that mattered. It would be really nice.

Slowly he folded up Tonya’s letter and held it out to Sirius. “Will you keep this for me? I just… I don’t need something else to keep me up at night.”

Sirius took the letter without a shred of hesitation and tucked it into the inside pocket of his coat. “Of course, Moons,” he said, “anything.”

They locked eyes for a moment and Remus let himself wonder if maybe… but no.

“Alright,” he said, untucking himself from Sirius’ side and getting up, “your story might’ve sucked arse, but I’m not nearly as weepy anymore.”

“Hey, I worked hard on that story! My delivery was very authentic!”

“Work smarter, not harder, Black,” Remus smiled, holding out his hand. Sirius took it eagerly and he pulled him to his feet.

“Is there anything you’d like me to tell the others? You know, about your shitty gangster mates and their bad taste in women,” Sirius asked as they made their way to the exit.

“No,” Remus answered blithely, “I sort of like being a little mysterious.”

“In that case, I'll never have to say anything to anyone. You’ve already got the market cornered in ‘mysterious’.”

Again, Remus thanked his lucky stars for giving him Sirius.

Walking back together, they met James and Peter on Godric’s front steps, hailing the pair of them as they were about to make their way inside. It was cooler out now that the sun was going down, and the wind was blowing just enough to excuse how close together they'd been walking, but then their friends called out they naturally sprung apart, though the look Sirius gave him afterwards appeared almost reluctant. Remus told himself to ignore it. No use giving in to nonsense assumptions.

“There you are!” Peter moaned. “Thought you’d gotten lost in the woods or something.”

“Nah, not the woods, just the little girls room,” Sirius smirked, shouldering Remus as they made their way up the path.

James set the bottom of Andy’s guitar case on the ground and leaned his chest against its top. “So much for practice, hey lads?”

“Sorry, my fault,” Remus said. "Wasn’t feeling all that good.”

“You go see the nurse?”

“No, he slunk off on his own like a dying cat,” Sirius said mercilessly.

James sighed sadly. “Oh, Moony, Moony, Moony.”

“I wasn’t feeling that bad!” Remus scoffed, shooting a glare at Sirius.

“Anything to do with Marlene?” Peter asked pityingly.

“Er—yeah, sure, whatever.”

James reached over and clapped him on the shoulder. “Don’t worry mate, we’re here for you. We ain't afraid of a few tears. You can just let it all out if you need to. We'll hold ya.”

“Thank you, Prongs. What would I do without you.”

It was sarcasm, but James smiled anyway.

“Look at him blush,” Sirius said suddenly, reaching to pinch Remus on the cheek. “Do you need a pick-me-up, Moony?”

“Fuck off.”

“No—I’m serious! ‘Cause I had this great idea for a prank—”

“You’re still paying off your detentions from your last ‘great idea’,” Peter pointed out.

“Wormy—where’s your sense of adventure?”

“It’s up yours.”

James and Remus both snorted. Sirius blazed past it; “I was only wondering, how do you think the professors would fair if we just switched all the coffee in the teacher’s lounge for decaf?”

“If they find out they’d be likely to let Filch lynch you,” James said, but he was holding his chin in that way of his that meant he was already on board. Sirius knew it too.

“Okay, so step one—we leave a few of Bob’s firecrackers outside the building, light them all off with a fuse—that should clear the room long enough for us to make the switch.”

Listening to steps two, three, and so on, Remus leaned back against the dorm’s metal handrail and crossed his legs at the ankles. Sirius always tended to talk with hands, but it was particularly bad when he was excited. He held his fists up, waving them about as Peter and James peppered him with questions about this or that. Content to watch, Remus was smiling until he spotted someone moving up the street in front of their dorm.

“Don’t look now, Black," he mumbled, "but your girlfriend’s coming.”

Sirius straightened up immediately, and they all turned just in time to spot Chastity as she swept up the dorm’s front path.

“Sirius!" She called sweetly; "C’mon, darling, it's almost dinner and you promised we’d eat with the girls today!”

Waving back awkwardly, Sirius replied; “Yeah, just one moment, babe.”

James and Peter began to chortle quietly, and even Remus couldn't resist a tease. “Oh,” he said smugly, “well, don’t be late on our account, darling. The girls are waiting, after all.”

Sirius whipped his head around and glared at him while James picked up the guitar case and turned toward the door. “S’okay, Sirius. Go and join her, we can talk more about your prank idea after dinner.”

Sirius sighed, clearly irritated, and Remus felt a spark of satisfaction. It vanished the moment Sirius stepped down the stairs, casually waving goodbye as he crossed the lawn toward his girlfriend. As he reached her, Chastity immediately grappled onto his arm, and Peter turned to follow James inside, holding the door open.

“You coming, Moony?”

“Yeah...” he murmured, when in reality Remus was caught. I'll never love you enough to leave you, that's what Sirius had said. But he couldn't expect that. Sirius wasn't his. Sirius was a friend and a guy and—and Remus was... Well, quite frankly Remus was sure what he was! But it was something, wasn't it? How could a feeling like this be nothing? How could he be forced to stare at their backs as they got further away? Before when he'd watched Sirius disappear across the grass to the Chastity's dorm he’d begged fate to bring him back, and fate had laughed at him, but now Sirius was only a few feet away. All it would take was a few measly words—if he could only figure out what they were.

"Come back..." Remus whispered, because he had nothing else. "Come back."

The words were but a breath of a wish on the wind. He couldn't even bring himself to say them any louder. You have my letter, he pleaded silently. You have my everything. Please come back.

He didn't think he would. Remus had never believed in magic, but watching Sirius turn—like he could actually hear him—that was nothing short of a miracle.

When their eyes finally met, Remus’ lips parted, and for a moment his heart stopped all together. A second later, Sirius had drawn his long strides to a halt at the edge of the lawn as if he too were frozen. If Remus could've looked anywhere else he might've seen how Chastity's mouth moved in the shape of her boyfriend's name while she tugged on his arm, but he could not see her. He only saw Sirius. He saw him as his expression became torn, as he looked to the girl that claimed to love him, and then back to Remus. It was as if he were searching for a reason to stay. Remus wished he could give it to him, and wished harder still when Sirius licked his lips and he swore he could taste it. All of it was pure torture in the span of a few seconds.

“Moony, lad, you okay?” James called, reappearing in the door next to Peter and snapping Remus out of all of it.

“Yeah—Yeah, m’coming,” he croaked, forcing himself to look away. Moving stiffly, he crossed the front step to the door, but just as James was stepping aside for him, a shriek of girlish contempt echoed from across the lawn;

“What?!”

They all spun round to find Chastity standing before Sirius, hands fisted in front of her and a look of utter disbelief on her face. As Chastity wailed her displeasure, Sirius only shrugged, speaking more quietly than she, with his hands now rid of hers and pressed into his jacket pockets.

"You really—?! Tell me you're not serious!" Chastity howled.

Next to Remus, James leaned in and murmured; "Five quid he says something like 'I'm always Sirius'."

"No bet," Peter snarked, just as Chastity lifted her arm and slapped Sirius clean across the face.

“Ooooh!” The boys winced together, recoiling backward in surprise.

“FUCK YOU, SIRIUS BLACK!” Chastity roared, whirling around and stomping off. They all watched her go, still frozen in place while Sirius started back toward them, rubbing his cheek sorely.

"Man, that girl should try out for the olympic boxing team," he winced, approaching the bottom set of stairs. "She's got an arm to rival Muhammad Ali." Shaking the sting off, Sirius let out a heavy breath and glanced up at them. His cheek was positively glowing red, and yet Remus had never seen him looking so happy.

“What did you bloody say to her?” James ogled.

“… Who?”

“CHASTITY!” They all wailed together.

“Oh!"Sirius grinned broadly; "Y’know, just that we should probably try and see other people and all that.”

“You dumped her?” Peter demanded.

“Sure—if that's what you want to call it.”

“What else would you call it?”

“Amicable separation, maybe?”

“Mate,” James clapped a hand to his forehead in disbelief; “there was absolutely nothing amicable about that.”

Sirius shrugged, appearing completely unbothered. “You win some, you lose some.”

“You’re something else, Black. Really.”

Sirius started up the stairs and squeezed between them, taking the guitar from James and slipping through the front door. They all followed him, one by one, but James caught up first.

"So what, you're just gonna be single now?"

"Why not? More fun that way anyway." Sirius glanced back at Remus, giving him a wink that turned his insides to water. “Now Moony and I can be single blokes together. Wolves need a pack, right?”

He began to howl mockingly, and Remus made a strangled noise in the back of his throat. “You—! You did not just dump your girlfriend to make that terrible joke!”

“HA! No, but it felt pretty good anyway. Now when do you reckon we should forcibly switch our dear teachers to a decaf diet—tomorrow at lunch?”

“Can’t,” Remus huffed, following his friends inside, “got a lunch date."

"With who?" Sirius snorted sardonically.

"Marlene."

Slamming to a halt, Sirius glanced back at him sharply, staring as though his soul were leaving his body. “WHAT?” He exploded. “But I thought the two of you broke up?!”

“We did,” Remus said innocently and suddenly a lot less frazzled. “Don’t tell me you guys don’t go out on dates with your friends?”

Sirius puckered, actually turning red, and in a final hurrah, James hugged him from behind. “Don’t worry, Sirius, I’ll take one for the team and take you out. Now where is it you'd like to go for lunch, darling?”
