Saturday 21st May 1977

Sirius might’ve not been as impressed by his new nickname, but the girls certainly were. They spent the several hours of the following afternoon laughing over it, plus the fact that Sirius had to walk the entire way home with cow shit between his toes before washing off under the hose outside their dorm. The boot, sadly, could not be saved, as they never recovered it from wherever Sirius had thrown it in the field.

“So you’re not gonna go back to look for it?” Lottie asked, popping a grape into her mouth.

“Nah, let the cows keep it,” Sirius grumbled. He had an arm draped over his eyes as he laid back on the picnic blanket, and his head was propped up on Mary’s shin. It was just after dinner and all eight of them were currently crammed on the single blanket, making up a single messy knot of limbs. Occasionally one of them complained of a knee to the back or shifted and crushed someone’s hand, but it was the first nice day in weeks since the April rain had fled, and there was a real sweetness on the breeze that made everyone want to be outside.

“I wish you’d taken a picture,” Marlene laughed.

“It happened too fast, was much too dark,” James sighed. “It exists now only in our memories.”

“It wasn’t that funny,” Sirius said. “Lupin just took the lazy-way out and picked a dog’s name and these numpties pretended it fit. It’s practically slander.”

“You’re just lashed because it is funny,” Peter snorted.

“It’s not funny!”

“Oh yes, it is.”

“Okay, if we don’t talk about something else right now I’m gonna go mental,” Sirius warned.

“Did you ever settle on the name for your band then?” Lily asked, flipping through Peter’s sketchbook. She’d had to practically wrestle it out of his hands, but after promising to correct his maths homework, he finally handed it over.

“Oh, that’s still a thing?” Marlene asked after her.

“Yup. Naw'stop movin', Cherry, m'almost done.” Remus said around the hair bobble in his mouth. He hadn't meant to be roped into doing her hair, but really, he didn't mind.

As Marlene straightened her back for him, Mary lifted her sunglasses up. “So you can all suddenly play instruments now?”

“What do you mean ‘suddenly’?” Sirius asked. “The four of us have been practising together for weeks now—me and Moony, for years.”

She shrugged. “Calvin keeps me busy.”

Sirius grimaced and word of Mary's latest beau. “You’re still dating that guy? He looks about thirty-five.”

“He’s only a year older than us.”

“He’s got chewing gum for brains,” Marlene added, grimly.

“Yeah, but he’s got just the right amount of opinions to make him tolerable and his dad runs a hedge fund, so who cares. Plus, he's not all that bad in the sack,” Mary smirked.

Remus couldn't see it, but he got the sense that Marlene was rolling her eyes.

“Are you guys actually any good with those instruments of yours?” Mary asked.

“It’s a work in progress,” Sirius said staunchly. “Elvis wasn’t born a musical genius, you know.”

“Even if Sirius was,” James snickered. Sirius saluted him.

“Well, have you written any songs yet?” Lottie asked.

“Not entirely,” Peter answered.

“Do you even have a name?” Marlene drawled.

“YES!” All three boys answered together, before Sirius cleared his throat and answered; “The Marauders!”

Remus looked up. “You mean that was official?”

“Unless you’ve got any better ideas, name-giver-extraordinaire,” Sirius ragged. He took a moment to look him up and down, but Remus just returned to his task at hand—braiding Marlene’s hair. Too bad all it took was one glance away for him to lose his place and get all muddled up.

“I messed it up again,” he sighed, releasing Marlene’s blonde plaits and letting them unravel down her back.

“S’okay, you gave it your best shot,” Marlene giggled, before crawling across the checkerboard blanket to Mary and plopping down in front of her expert fingers.

“Where’d you get the idea for ‘Marauders’?” Lily asked. Remus looked down at the sketchbook in her lap to find she was looking through several beautiful sketches of Moira. She wasn’t facing the viewer in any of them, which meant Peter must’ve done them without her knowing.

“From Mrs. Buchanan, actually,” James said, leaning back on his hands next to Lily. “She sprung us from Filch after a failed prank. It was one of the words she used to threaten us out of doing it again.”

Lily smirked down at the sketchbook lightly. “Fitting.”

“I think it sounds a bit naff actually,” Mary said, the picture of honesty.

“Gee, thanks. Does that mean you've got any bright ideas under that big hair of yours then?” Sirius asked, reaching over to poke at Mary’s hair, which was so big it nearly blocked out the sun. Her choice to ditch the braided hairstyle she’d been sporting since Christmas had left her with an afro to rival Diana Ross, but Mary had the confidence to pull anything off, so of course it looked good.

“Paws off, Padfoot,” Mary hissed, batting Sirius away while she continued to braid Marlene’s hair. “I just mean that no one’s gonna get it. It’s funny to you, sure, but to everyone else? Nu-uh, it’ll be a missed opportunity.”

“A missed opportunity for what?” Peter asked, pulling his t-shirt away from his neck to fan himself.

“To make a statement, of course! ‘The Marauders’—no, way too many syllables. Don’t you want people to remember you? Well, people are stupid, and they ain’t gonna if your name don’t roll off the tongue."

"I didn't think choosing a band name would come with so many conditions," Remus said sarcastically, while stretching out his back.

"Of course it does. It's like the cover of a book—it tells people what you're about. Take Sirius’ favourite pop band for example, Small Faces—”

Sirius scoffed; “They’re a rock band.”

“Shush. What I’m saying is, is that they may have had a few hits as ‘Small Faces’ but they didn’t really get good until they were just calling themselves ‘Faces’. And how about ‘T. Rex’? Could you imagine shouting ‘we want Tyrannosaurus Rex at a concert? No, you shout for T. Rex.”

“So you don’t like it at all?” James asked. “Because our backup was 'The Vaudeville Pantsers'.”

“No, I—” Mary grimaced; “Actually I don’t even want to know where you were going with that one.”

“Read it off a gum wrapper,” Sirius snorted, nudging Lottie with his elbow.

“The name is fine,” Mary clarified, “almost great even. You just need to lose one little detail.”

“And that is?”

“Duh—lose the ‘the’! No one’s about to go and pay to see a group declaring themselves as ‘The Marauders’ like some cheesy daytime comedy sketch. But ‘Marauders’, maybe—so just refer to yourselves directly and move on with it.”

“But that’s just bad grammar,” Sirius insisted.

“And since when do you care so much about grammar?” Marlene asked, smugly.

“I think Mary’s right,” Lottie declared. “Shorter might not always be ideal, but I think it’s acceptable in this instant.”

“Lottie’s filthy mind aside, I actually think Mary’s right too,” Lily added, before glancing up from the sketchbook. “You do have a lot of sketches of Moira in here, don’t you, Peter?”

Peter shot forward and snatched up the sketchbook. “I told you not to go that far!”

“They’re beautiful though,” Lily said kindly, turning back to the rest of them; “I guess the question the problem begs is this—are you describing yourselves as a collective or a concept?”

James squinted at her; “Huh?”

“Well ‘The Marauders’ implies that you’re all a singular marauder forming one unit, but ‘Marauders’ is more like a statement. Like ‘The Beatles’ are each a singular ‘Beatle’ on their own, I suppose, but the members of ‘Led Zeppelin’ aren’t all claiming to be flying lead balloons.”

“Exactly!” Mary agreed, getting so excited she almost dropped the tail of Marlene’s braid before she could tie it off. “Plus ‘the’ isn’t sexy.”

“You’re all nutters,” Sirius said. “There’s nothing wrong with ‘the’.”

“Should we put it to a vote then? All those in favour of ‘Marauders’—the concept—raise your hand.”

All four girls raised their hands, and eventually so did James and Peter. Sirius gaped at them. “You didn’t have any complaints yesterday when we let Pete paint ‘The Marauders’ across the side of Andy’s guitar case!”

James grinned at him and shrugged. “ ‘The’ ain’t sexy, mate.”

Done deliberating, Remus also raised his hand. “I’m with the girls.”

“There’s a shocker,” Sirius huffed.

Remus just smiled at him. “C’mon Black, you don’t want to be a Marauder, or even ‘the’ Marauder. That name feels too tangible for you—too touchable. Wouldn’t you rather be un-touchable? Be a concept people have to work to understand? What even is ‘Led Zeppelin’? It’s a million different things because no one pictures a concept the same way.”

Sirius drew back a bit, and Mary rocked her head in his direction, pointing back at Remus. “I’d listen to him if I were you.”

Sirius peered at him for a long time, but then finally relaxed, as if all the fight was draining out of him, one cheeky quip at a time. “ ‘Marauders’,” he echoed, before sighing, “alright, you’ve convinced me, but it better be a bloody good concept.”

“ ‘Cause how could it be any worse than ‘Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot, and Prongs’,” Lily smiled.

“Har, har, you’re so funny, Evans,” Sirius said, but he too was smiling.

“I don’t know why you’re so upset about the nickname in the first place, Sirius,” Mary said, fiddling with the end of Marlene’s braid. “Us girls don’t even have them and you don’t hear us whinging.”

“Actually we do,” Marlene said.

“We do?”

“Well, Lily and I do.”

“What’s yours then—you mean ‘Marls’?”

“No, it's ‘Cherry’,” Remus said automatically, before catching Marlene’s eye. Blushing a bit, she gave him a cheeky wink before sipping out of her water bottle.

“And here’s ‘Daisy’,” James grinned, jutting a thumb toward Lily, who cupped his chin and pulled him in close to plant a kiss on his cheek.

Mary turned on Lottie. "And you?"

Lottie considered. “Well, strickly speaking, I’m fine with ‘Lot’. After all, ‘Lottie’ is already a nickname. Though Mickey did used to call me ‘Barbie’ sometimes.”

Peter grimaced. “Oh bloody hell.”

“What the fuck?” Mary demanded. “You mean to say that I’m the only one here without a nickname?”

“Well, ‘Mary’ is already pretty short, ain’t it?” Marlene offered.

She scowled at her. “Sirius is right, you guys are lazy twats.”

“You mean you don't like 'Macdonald', Macdonald?” Sirius teased.

“Up yours, Black. A surname’s not a nickname.”

“Okay, then how do you fancy ‘Nymph’?”

Mary paused; “Like a fairy?”

“No, I was thinking more like ‘nymphomaniac’.”

Snatching Marlene’s water bottle from her, she tossed it at Sirius, who flinched and caught it in the stomach with a groan.

“ ‘Fairy Mary’ does sound kind of cute though,” Lottie suggested.

“Do not encourage him.”

Beaming very suddenly, Sirius clutched the bottle to his chest. “Oh, I know,” he started, “how about ‘Mingy Mary’? Or ‘Suzy Snatch’ if you want a bit of ambiguity. Or even better yet, just Snatchy? Gotta make it short and snappy so all the stupid people can remember it, right?”

After taking a second to glance around and see if there was anything else she could throw at him, but turning up empty, Mary settled for a venomous glare. “I hate you.”

James chuckled. “Well, if Padfoot here can be named after an unsavoury memory as well as one of Lupin’s dogs, then why not try that? Moony—what was your favourite dog’s name back home?”

Remus felt like he was walking into a trap. “Er… Dusty.”

“That’s PERFECT!” Sirius exclaimed. “Dusty Snatch!”



Chapter End Notes

'Twelfth of Never' and 'Tibb's Eve' are idioms to express something that'll never happen.

'Harrods' is a London department store.

'Naff' means lame or unfashionable. Can also be used to tell someone to "f*** off".

I really like this chapter, especially the beginning. Felt a lot like a character study into who Remus is right in this moment. To me, Remus and Sirius' behaviour is also very telling of what they're feeling on the inside, and just react in different ways. Sirius is very external, while Remus internalises everything. Chapter 61: Liar's Dessert


Chapter Summary

Remus Lupin wants two things: a distraction from how aware he is of his best friend, and to pass his exams. Lucky for him Barty Crouch can help with at least one of those things.



Chapter Notes

CW: Mentions of suicide and homophobic language. Brief violence, and a generally not-so-happy Remus.

I'm so tired, but happy I got this out! If you can't tell by the end, I'm really ramping up for some new developments, so I hope you enjoy <3

Wednesday 25th May 1977

Sirius was terrible with anything spicy.

Remus knew this because more than once he’d watched him dip his sticky fingers into one of James’ regular care packages, only to complain for the next several hours that he’d never be able to taste anything ever again. Now, with only a month shy from the end of term, Euphemia Potter had sent her famous homemade chocolates as an early exam reward. Only thanks to having more kick than your average sweet, the chocolates felt more like a punishment rather than a reward.

“Maybe it is a punishment,” Peter said, staring down at the tin and its unassuming tissue paper. “Like a warning—fail your exams and she’ll force-feed you the fire-chocolate.”

“She makes ‘em with bhut jolokia seeds,” James explained. “Ghost peppers. Evil stuff. But the salsa and vindaloo are great. If you've have the stomach for it, that is.”

“Which ninety-nine percent of the population does not. One bite is like licking the bottom of Satan’s flamin’ ball sack,” Sirius said, already pale.

Despite being under the impression that putting anything in chocolate that might bite back was a terrible shame, Remus couldn’t resist clapping Sirius on the shoulder. “Well, Padfoot, your name was on the card too, and I’m sure you don’t want to disappoint ‘mum’, so go ahead—give it a go.”

“You’re mental if you think I’m going anywhere near that stuff. My eyes are watering just with the bloody lid open.” Taking the chocolates from Peter, Sirius snapped the lid shut and slid the tin beneath James’ bed.

“They only get spicier with time, you know,” James said, grabbing his school bag. “Dad calls ‘em the ‘fine wine of chocolate’.”

Sirius held up a hand. “Out of sight, out of mouth, Potter.”

It was just as hard in forms not to tease him, so Remus didn’t bother practising much self-control. They sat around the room in a staggered formation in desks that Sheila had brought in for studying in preparation for their exams, which would commence the following week. She had the radio going as well, letting the quiet classical music drift across the classroom to 'stimulate their minds' and 'help wake them all up'. Rather than getting much studying done himself, Remus spent most of the short period watching Sirius, who was concentrating on the sheet music he’d propped up on a music stand next to his desk, scribbling and erasing notes while he hummed a tune to himself.

“Who would’a thought that the great Sirius Black would be frightened by a little chocolate,” Remus said quietly, eyeing Sheila, who was lounging across the room and doing class marking while wearing a dress so vibrantly purple she probably could’ve been seen from Mars.

“I didn’t see you jumping at the bit to take a bite either,” Sirius shot back, pulling one foot up onto his chair and nibbling on the end of his pencil as he glared at his work.

“What’s that?” Remus asked, pointing at the song.

“I’m calling it ‘Wag the Dog’. Just wish I could remember how this bit went when I wrote it.” He turned his glare toward their teacher. "Bloody Sheila. It's a music classroom—we should be playing music, not studying for maths."

“Does it have any lyrics?” Remus asked quietly, more intrigued than before.

“Mhm. Back at the dorm. You can have a look later if you want.”

“Okay, cheers.”

Sirius gave him a sideways glance. “Have you managed to write anything?”

Remus stared down at his English book a little harder. “A little. Not much though. It’s felt a little harder since… well, you know.”

Sirius nodded in understanding. “Okay. You just let me know if you want to collaborate again or something.”

Encouraged by Sirius’ calm response, Remus looked up again. “I might have this one song.”

“Oh yeah?”

“It’s... er—kinda sappy though.” And not at all about you, so don't look too far into it.

“That’s alright,” Sirius smiled, “every rock band needs a few ballads.”

“And a few poofs too, I suppose,” called a nasally voice from behind.

Remus turned around in his seat, instantly soured. “You know, eavesdropping’s actually considered a sin, Crouch.”

Barty sneered at him; “You’d know all about that then, wouldn’t you, fudge packer?” Beside him, Yaxley gave an ugly chortle and held out his palm for his friend to smack.

“You want me to lock you in the broom cupboard again, you little shit?” Snarled Sirius.

Ignoring him, Barty turned to Remus, looking him up and down with an evil look. “I heard something interesting from my dad the other day, Loony. You see, he’s a politician too, only he works for the Crown, making sure all those sleazy, two-bit politicians are doing their job. And get this, he went 'round a new office the other day and happened to pick up on a familiar name. Now I'm no expert on genealogy, but unless there's more Lupins running 'round London than I thought, then I'd say he found your dad.”

“Wow! You’re so obsessed with Lupin that you’re already telling your parents about him?” Sirius said. “Careful Bartemius, your own closet’s turning a bit see-through.”

Barty did not laugh this time. He ignored Sirius’ quip and kept his eyes trained on Remus like a predator waiting to strike. “You wanna know what my dad heard at that office?"

"No really," Remus drawled, "but I'm sure you're going to tell us anyway so why don't you just get on with it?"

"—He heard that Lupin senior’s got himself a bit of a wild child at home!" Barty hissed. "That he's so embarrassed of you he won't even let himself be seen with you in public! That you’ve been tossed out of so many schools, Hawkings was the only place left to send you.”

Remus shared a look with Sirius. “Yeah, and...?”

Barty laughed like he'd gotten them. “Ha! So you admit it then? You admit you’re a complete loser—a waster and a disgrace of a son?!”

Sirius clicked his tongue bitterly; “Shit! I thought I was the disgrace, Moony? You’re supposed to be the phoenix rising from the ashes—the one turning his life around.”

“He’s certainly not!” Barty said smugly. “My dad said he’s a no-good waste of space that wouldn’t amount to anything, and that Lyall Lupin’s just waiting for the day he can dump your arse.”

Remus turned to Sirius, feigning relief and delight. “Black, did you hear that, Barty says my dad’s finally gonna kick me to the curb—can you believe it?”

“If only I were given such a gift!” Sirius declared. “Ah, woe is me. Whoever spanked you with that lucky stick, spanked you hard, Lupin!”

Remus snorted, but Barty had already realised they were just making fun of him. He leaned forward in his chair, practically foaming at the mouth.

“I heard other stuff too,” he seethed, “like how you bashed up your face running with thugs and then they got tired of you and jumped you, leaving you for dead. That’s why you look like a cat used your face as a scratching post!”

“The drama!” Sirius gasped. “Moony, you told us it was a football accident.”

“I guess the pain made me block it out,” Remus shrugged. “Why Barty, were you looking for a way in? I’m not sure if anyone back home’s recruiting but with your face I’m sure they’ll think you look the part already.”

“You’re still laughing but that’s not all I heard, Loony,” Barty said very slowly. “A little birdy told me a rumour's been going around about you. Guess the nickname make more sense now that I know your—”

Interrupting him, Sirius waved a friendly hand; “Okay, Crouchie, go ahead. Just admit you’re in love with dear Lupin, here, so we can all move on and get our work done.”

Barty’s eyes shot wide. “What the fuck? I’m not—”

“Don’t feel bad for falling head over heels for the handsome chap, it’s okay. Most people can't help it. Moony’s a hot-ticket item, didn’t you know?”

“That's disgusting! You’re mental!”

“And you’ve absolutely pictured him naked. C’mon Crouch, just admit you’re in love with him.”

Sputtering, Barty launched himself to his feet, his chair toppling behind him. “I’m not in love with him!” He shouted. Everyone turned to look and a few kids began to snigger while Barty fumed, but before either Remus or Sirius could respond, Sheila cut the music.

“Mr. Crouch,” she called, standing up from her chair and straightening her dress. “I was just about to take a walk to deliver today’s attendance sheet, care to gather your things and join me?”

Barty turned his vicious glare on their teacher, and though it was obvious there was more he wanted to say, the giggling had spread. As though that weren't enough, Sirius held up his hands and drew a heart in the air, before blowing Barty a kiss to finish it all off. The younger boy looked about ready to snap as the class’s sniggering rose to even further heights, but either out of embarrassment or sheer lack of a clever response, he snatched up his school bag and obediently followed Sheila to the door.

“You didn’t have to say that,” Remus said after they'd gone and the class's chittering had died down. He knew his cheeks red with embarrassment, but Sirius only turned back to his song with a haughty expression.

“I say call a spade a spade. If he’s gonna play dirty, then so will we.”

Remus sat back with a huff. Making fun of Barty’s arrogant spiel had been fun, but as he reopened his book to the correct page, he was left with the gut feeling that it wasn’t the last they’d be hearing from Barty or his father.





* * *





Friday 27th May 1977

Remus wasn't exactly sure what for, but between their spat in forms and the following morning, Barty had somehow procured himself a set of detentions that left him unable to attend forms for most of the week. This meant he did not arrive in class the next day or the day after, and Remus allowed himself a sigh of relief. At least this way he could study in peace. AS-Levels were not taken as seriously as O or A-Levels, nor did their exam period last as long, but that didn't mean Lily wasn't completely losing her head over them. She flitted about campus, handing out detention slips to any rowdy students who much as dared to get within twenty feet of her while she had a textbook open, and once actually considered giving Peter a pink slip for merely mentioning the word 'fail' in her presence.

Remus didn't really mind. Lily had always been the best out of his friends to study with, and he preferred quizzing her than himself anyway. Though sometimes her particular brand of 'dramatic crazy' did bridge on Sirius-territory.

“How do they all keep disappearing?” She demanded, scrambling desperately through her book bag.

“It’s nice to see you’ve finally figured out how to relax during exams,” Remus drawled, busy flipping through his notes.

Lily looked up, hair frazzled and a pencil stuck behind each ear. “Wha—?”

“Not even sarcasm can reach you,” he sighed, before reaching over and plucking both pencils from behind her ears. “Here.”

Looking distinctly embarrassed, Lily took them and pressed her knuckles to her warm cheeks. “You’re right, I need to calm down or else I’ll just start bursting into tears on the spot.”

“Eugh. Do me a favour and hold out until Potter crosses the berm,” Remus said, pointing to where James and Sirius were making their way toward their picnic table, food trays in hand.

“Bit early for dinner, isn’t it?” Lily said, collecting a few of her library books to make room for them as they flopped down on the bench.

“We missed lunch,” Sirius answered, shovelling half a sandwich into his mouth. “Final detention for poisoning Snape.”

“Ah.” Lily smiled to herself as she set to tapping a stack of papers into order. “I at least hope some of the punishment sunk in?”

Sirius started to refuse around the mouthful of sandwich, but James just smacked him in the gut, making him cough. “Yes, definitely. I’m ready to get back on the pitch.”

“And pass your exams?”

“Yes, well, those too.”

Lily smiled and passed him a few papers. “There’s the history notes you wanted.”

Talking them, James gave them a quick once-over. “Ah, perfect! Thanks, Daisy.”

“Don’t thank me, thank Remus. I borrowed them from him.”

Both James and Sirius raised an impressed brow, and Sirius swallowed his sandwich. “And how is your studying going, Moony?”

“Fine,” Remus answered lightly.

“Just fine?”

“Swell.”

Sirius smirked. “Hm. Guess we’ll see how swell once exams are finished.”

Remus returned the expression. “Guess we will, Pattycake. When I beat you, that is.”

Flashing him the bird, Sirius took another bite of his sandwich. He liked to play the nonchalant genius, but Remus knew that he'd done more than just crack a textbook in the last several weeks. Sirius wasn't much of a studier, but he could be trusted to pull his own weight when his pride was on the line. It almost humbled Remus to think that the entire reason Sirius was taking exams seriously was just to ensure he didn't whip his arse too badly, but Remus was also determined. He expected he had a real chance of being first in year for History, maybe close to that in Modern Lit, but even breaking the top ten for MFL and geography would be enough to hold over Sirius' head. That's right, Remus Lupin was going to come out on top this year. This time, he wasn’t going to let anything or anyone throw him off his game.

Or, that had been the plan anyway.

“Oi, Loony!” Barty called, making his way across the lawn toward them with his hands in his pockets, moving at a pace that he must’ve thought was quite swaggy, except only made him look like a club-footed duck instead. He had a line-up behind him; Yaxley, Travers, who were both wearing expressions that made them appear as though they went around frying bugs with magnifying glasses for fun. Bringing up the rear was none other than Regulus, who held his nose high but at least looked the most adverse to be there.

“Oh joy, the gang’s all here,” Sirius said, holding his fork between his teeth and pretending to look bored. “Seriously, Crouch, we don't see you for three days and you miss us so badly you have to hunt us down on our lunch break? Pfft, get a hobby.”

"He has a hobby," James said wryly. "Pretty sure I caught him burning ants with a magnifying glass last week."

"Oh yes, I even like to name them first," Barty added. "Potter Jr. made such a lovely sizzle."

“What do you want, Barty? I really don't think you need another detention, but I'll oblige you if you insist on carrying on,” Lily shot, leaning protectively over her books as though she feared they’d get splattered with peanut butter.

“Lupin and I have unfinished business,” Barty answered, stopping a few feet away and spitting into the grass. “You too, Black.”

Sirius waved cheerily.

“Having unfinished business with Remus sounds a lot like a death sentence,” James called in a lofty voice, but instead of looking unnerved, Barty’s face only split into a grin.

“Have some experience there, Potter? Though I suppose you would, being friends with such a nasty bloke.”

“Actually, I don’t have any business with you,” Remus said firmly. “In fact, if I could, I’d get a refund for every minute I’ve had to spend looking at your miserable face, so if you wouldn’t mind—piss off already.”

The enemy boys all exchanged looks, ranging from scornful to impressed, while Regulus just looked away as though the whole thing were beneath him. Remus supposed that that was exactly what he thought, being who he was. Regulus had never been nice, but he wasn't known for being a bully. His relationship with his roommates had always felt like a friendship of convenience at best.

“You always did have a bad mouth on ya, Loony," Yaxley grunted.

“Better than bad teeth. When was the last time the lot of you visited the dentist?”

That got the boys to scowl at least.

“You should hear the things they say about you Lupins," Barty tried.

“Can’t be all that bad compared to what all the year eleven girls say about you,” Sirius interjected. He was talking to Barty, but he couldn’t take his gaze off his brother. “And what about you?” Sirius asked loudly, forcing Regulus to look at him.

“Got nothing to do with me,” Regulus said arrogantly.

“You’re here.”

“So are you.”

“You think this makes you cool?” Sirius snapped.

“You think I care what you think is cool?”

“I think you care an awful lot, actually.”

Regulus’ glare could’ve cut glass. “I don't care what you think at all. If I could, I'd put you out on the curb myself. You’re the same as him anyway." His eyes slid to Remus.

Launching himself to his feet, Sirius slammed his hands down on the table, rattling his dishes. “You foul little git! What’s that supposed to mean?”

“It makes sense," Barty said. “Two fucked-up tossers, teaming up. You make the perfect pair—both loathed by your own parents? With naught but a five pence piece to rub between you on your own."

Sirius scoffed mockingly. "If you think you're going to get a rise out of me with crap like that, you've another thing coming, you shitty twat. Now why don't you turn around and run back to Mummy before I have to spank you myself."

"Ooh, that's cheeky. You offer that to all your enemies?"

"Only the ones that I feel are particularly desperate for it."

Barty's smile was feral. It might've been enough for him had he come for Sirius, but he was the wrong target.

"Speaking of Mummy..." Like some evil little doll, Barty's bulging frogs-eyes shifted to Remus. "Lupin, is it true you have trouble sleeping?”

Remus set his jaw. “What’s it to you, Barty?”

“Oh nothing, really, it's just—" Barty gave an exaggerated sigh; "I get it, you know. I’m sure it’s mighty hard to fall asleep without Mummy around to tuck you in at night. At least you've got the summer and Christmas. But oh, wait... you don't have a mummy, do you, Loony? Hm. Sad.”

While Remus bristled, James shot to his feet next to Sirius. “You shut your dirty trap! That’s got nothing to do with you!”

“Yeah, why don’t you move on to someone who wants to hear you blow rubbish everywhere!” Lily fumed, pointing her pencil at the other boys in a very threatening manner.

“My Loony, the peanut gallery’s awfully loud today, ain’t it? Reckon you could shut them up for a little bit so we could chat?” Barty crooned.

Remus gripped the edge of the table until his knuckled turned while. “I told you Crouch, we’ve got nothing to talk about. It's time you pissed off.”

“Aw, don’t be like that.”

“Barty, I’m gonna give you and your shitty band of cronies one last chance to move on,” Sirius hissed, “after that I’ll—”

“You’ll what—sing us a song?"

"Can we at least pick the tune?” Travers added enthusiastically.

Having had enough, Remus stood from the table and strode straight up to Barty, who balked slightly when he realised just how much height Remus had on him at such a short distance.

“Barty, I know your English marks are shit, but do me a favour, and read my lips. I'm done with you. You hear me? You’re pathetic, and you’re done. Now fuck off.”

Barty let out a high trill from the back of his throat and smiled again, eyes wide as saucers. “Oh I’m pathetic, am I? Well, at least I’m not so terrible that my mum had to go and kill herself.”

There was a small gasp from behind him—Lily—but Remus was frozen. The words had hit him like a bucket of ice water, and Barty quickly grew giddy off his shock.

“Yeah—Yeah!” He cackled, dancing backward a few feet to hide amongst his friends. “Dad confirmed it for us, ha! Apparently your old man's got as big a reputation as you—did you know that, Loony? A right bastard, they say he is! There's rumour he offed his wife himself! But really, who could blame him? Not when he's got a missus with one foot in the grave, the other in the loony bin, and a kid who's hell-bent on serving at her majesty's pleasure! Ohhhh, the stories they tell about you... Tell me, Loony, how'd he get you a place here, huh? How many strings did Dad have to pull? Did he finally offer that old bat McGonagall the shag she'd been missing all her life?"

“You sick fuck!” Sirius shouted, culminating all of his friend's horror with a few words. Unfortunately his anger only served to egg Barty further on.

"No? A sob story then, maybe? Don't tell me you cried to her. How'd it go? Maybe like—'Please Professor, please let me in to school, I'm sure my dad'll beat me if he catches me on the pipe again! He's afraid I'll end up like me ma, hanging myself in the closet'!" Barty stopped to cackle some more, and nudged Yaxley to the left of him. "Oi, none of you would happen to have a picture of the old bird, would ya? Loony's good for a laugh, but I’ve always wanted to see real crazy in the flesh.”

With a scream, Lily ripped herself up from the picnic table and threw herself toward Barty. Only James stopped her—catching her round the middle as she kicked out at them. "Just get away!" She screeched. "How dare you say such vile things!"

"Get the fuck out of here, Crouch!" James hollered over her shoulder.

“Oh c’mon, don’t tell me you guys didn’t know?" Barty crowed. "I mean surely you all knew! You’re ‘friends’, right? Any real friend would want to know that they're living in the same room as mental-made-flesh! Any of you got any juicy details so we can fill out the story a bit more? I heard it was actually the pills that done 'er in, but was it more Hollywood than that? Drowning? Oh! Did she throw herself off the parapets? Now c’mon, don't be shy, we'll be sure to get everything right when we pass the story along!”

"REG, PUT MUZZLE ON YOUR FUCKING FRIEND!" Sirius cried, making Regulus actually jump backward.

"Muzzle yourself!" Regulus hissed, before grabbing Barty by the arm. "Barty, let's just go."

"But I ain't done!" Barty announced. "Lupin's been awful quiet, and I wanna hear him make some noise. Am I not speaking the right language, Loony? Shall I try a bark? Woof! Woof! Arf!"

Emboldened by their friend's nerve, Yaxley and Travers began to bark too, crowding in until they were but an arm's length away. Remus couldn't react to the mocking, he could barely even speak—all he felt was the white-hot coils of rage. He sensed his friends at his back, each of them pulled taut as a string as they hurled obscenities back at the nasty boys. Barty only laughed. So did his friends. Regulus wrapped his arms across himself and rolled his eyes. In the beginning, the shock had been enough to make Remus feel and see white, but now as he watched Barty’s face contort into bouts of hideous laughter that only left his ears ringing, he saw red.

“Say, Lupin, who is it you take after, mum or dad?”

Stop.

"I’ll bet it’s mum."

Stop it.

"Did you get to see the body after they dragged her out? Did you get to keep the rope?"

STOP IT!

"Did she even love you?" Barty frowned. "Seemed in a real rush to get out. Bet you don't even care."

Remus’ fist came up in a single fluid motion. All it took was a single punch for Crouch to hit the ground.





* * *





By the time Remus came back to himself, he was sitting outside the Headmistress’s office with a bag of ice taped over his hand. His knuckles stung, but it was nothing compared to how he felt inside. Barty’s words had hit like Tonya’s, only where he’d had time to prepare himself for hers, Barty’s were all too unexpected. They’d made him feel as fragile as glass but as cold and numb as stone.

It’d been a while since he’d lost himself like that. Punching Mickey back in January had been an instinct, but this was pure rage. He’d wanted to hurt Barty. It was smart of James and Sirius to hold him back. If they hadn't, Barty wouldn't have been able to walk the next day. Remus would've done ten times worse than what had happened to him in that alley last summer. And he would've enjoyed it. Perhaps that was the worst part.

There'd been a lot of shouting, and eventually Lily had gone for a teacher, but the only thing Remus clearly remembered from the heated moment was a pair of grey eyes. Not Sirius', but Regulus'. Remus hadn’t had the time or sense to discern what sort of expression he was making with the rest of his face, but it was certainly shock mixed with something else. Regret or fear, maybe both.

The office door clicked open, and Barty emerged, looking spiteful as he held a sack of ice to his own jaw. He’d been lucky not to bite his tongue, but Remus could still hear the sound of his teeth snapping together like an echo in his head.

Barty paused outside the door and they glared at one another until Sheila finally appeared behind him, looking tired and unimpressed. “You may go back to your dorm, Mr. Crouch,” she said, and Barty turned to stalk down the hall, stubbornly dragging his feet the entire way.

After watching him go, Sheila finally turned on Remus. “Alright, mister, your turn.”

Pushing up from the chair, he followed her inside and flopped down in a seat opposite to the Headmistress, who had her hands folded neatly in her lap. Sheila stood behind her, wisps of chestnut hair slipping out of her bun. Just seeing her made everything worse—the ringing in his ears, the trembling in his hands. It was as though an elephant was sitting on his chest.

“I’m not talking,” Remus said staunchly.

“Well, that’s surely a shame,” McGonagall answered, “as we have much to talk about.”

“Expel me then, I don’t care.”

“Remus, don’t say that,” Sheila sighed, but he just tore his gaze away, refusing to look at her.

Professor McGonagall cleared her throat. “I told you at the beginning of last year, Mr. Lupin, that we take violence very seriously here at Hawkings. You've been doing very well here, all things considered, but I must enforce upon you the seriousness of what you have done. Student on student barbarity is not tolerated in any form, under any circumstances.”

“Then expel me.”

They were all quiet for a little bit, and the headmistress sighed, but before she could speak again, a loud clattering sounded in the hall. With a spectacular cry, Sirius, James, and Lily burst forth across the officer threshold, each of them out of breath before they'd even begun shouting.

“Professor McGonagall, you can’t expel Remus!” Lily yelled.

“It was Barty’s fault!” James said. “He started the fight when he showed up spewing all kinds of bullsh—all kinds of nonsense!”

“Minnie, you can’t!” Sirius shouted. “Lupin’s the best we’ve got and if you can’t see that then you’re blind!”

Very calmly, McGonagall held up a hand to silence them; “I understand your compassion and distress, but right now I need to speak with Mr. Lupin.”

Lily threw out her arms. “But professor—!”

“Remus doesn’t deserve this!”

“What Crouch said was—”

“Ah, ah.” McGonagall shook her head. “That’s quite enough, thank you. I will hear all I need to from Remus.”

“Okay,” Sirius heaved, “but what’s gonna happen to him?”

The Headmistress’s smile was kind at least. “Go and be well, Mr. Black. Remus will rejoin you when he is ready.”

All of them deflating in various levels of relief, his friends turned and slowly shuffled reluctantly from the office, trying their best to offer him comforting waves as they went. The last to leave, Sirius grasped the door handle and pulled it closed behind them, but before he slipped out of sight he flashed Remus a wincing smile and a quick thumbs up.

Almost more tired now, Remus sunk further down into his seat and squeezed his face in his hands.

“It’s good to see that someone cares about whether you’re expelled or not. Enough to storm all of Castle Hall it seems,” McGonagall said. She had an amused expression, but even as he peeled his fingers away, Remus only stared at the floor.

“Professor,” Sheila started, biting her lip. “I wonder if you might let Remus and I take a walk together. I think it's best he be allowed to rest a bit more before the three of us chat and you decide on a course of action.”

Eyes squinted in consideration, the Headmistress glanced at him, mouth razor thin. “Yes, I believe that might be a good idea, Mrs. Buchanan. A bit of fresh air might do us all some good.”

Sheila smiled and gathered up her white frock coat, coming around the table and gently prodding Remus in the arm. “C’mon Remus,” she said quietly, jutting her head toward the door. “Let’s take a tour of the grounds, shall we?”

“I don’t want to,” he grumbled.

“I don’t care.”

Remus looked up sharply, but Sheila was still smiling. “Walk with me," she said kindly.

Every cell in his body wanted to scream in protest—be stubborn, tell the crazy lady to fuck off!—but that would just mean staying in the office, where they could poke and prod at him until he really lost it. So, Remus grudgingly pushed himself to his feet and followed her out. A part of him wondered if his friends would be waiting, but he saw no sight of them even as he was led out the back doors of Castle Hall and down the pavement toward the school’s rose gardens. The flowers were already in full-bloom, casting a beautiful colour across the lush gardens and filling the air with a scent that made Remus' nose itch.

Sheila sighed happily, breathing it all in. “Ah. Much better being outside, don’t you think, Remus?”

“I’m still not gonna talk," he answered stubbornly.

“Okay, we’ll just walk then.”

It irritated him that she was using the same method of de-escalation she’d used on Barty just a few days before—that she’d even consider putting them on the same scale—but as he stomped along, Mrs. Buchanan just walked quietly next to him, hands tucked behind her back. She wasn’t a short woman, but he was still taller, and he wondered briefly if that imitated her at all—if she was worried to be alone with him like he knew other teachers at other schools had been.

But then as if to answer his unasked question, she started to whistle a cheery tune and Remus knew for sure that Sheila Buchanan had nerves of steel.

“You know sometimes, Remus, bad things happen to good people," she told him, after a good long while. "Don't misunderstand, good things can also happen to bad people, and okay things to just okay people. They say life’s a circle, but that’s not what I’ve found. Instead I think it’s rather more like a spider’s web, connected with all these different paths, and we’re constantly arriving at new crossroads, wondering which is the best path to take—which will get us out of the web fastest or safest or with the best possible outcome. We’re built to believe the concept that one path is always better than another—that if we fail at something, we've failed for good, because there was only one right path and we missed it. We missed our way out. But I know now that that's all utter shit." She smiled up at him. "Sometimes things are just hard, and we must face them however well we can.”

Remus looked anywhere but at his teacher. They’d reached the centre of the gardens and were just passing a trio of girls sat on a bench and comparing photographs in an album. Sheila paused her story long enough to say hello and greet each girl by name—she always knew everyone’s name—before swinging her hands out from behind her back and returning her gaze to him once more.

“I know some things are hard, Remus, and I’m not going to tell you more crap like ‘life isn’t fair’ or ‘some people have been to war’, though it might make a funny joke. Instead, would you like to tell me what was hard about today?”

No.

“Not really.”

“How about yesterday then?”

He almost refused her again, but then remembered he’d managed to rip a hole in his trousers during second period. The story came tumbling out before he could stop it, and Sheila began laughing before he was even finished, holding her stomach and pushing the hair from her eyes. “That is unfortunate. I do hope that your trousers can be mended.”

“I don’t think so, Mary already declared them a lost cause. Which is sorta funny, considering I don't think Mary knows how to sew.”

Sheila lit up again. “Mary Macdonald, right? Ah, you're right, she’s a funny girl. Are you two close?”

“Sort of… We’re friends.”

“Well, it makes me happy to hear that.”

Remus dug his nails into his palms. They were alone in this half of the garden at least. “My mum was sick but she didn’t kill herself,” he confessed all at once, feeling the words leave his body like a single breath.

Sheila gave a breadth's pause. “I know. I know what happened to Hope."

As if urged on further by her words, Remus stopped dead in the middle of the path and put his head in hands. “She didn’t kill herself,” he ground out again.

“I know.”

“She didn’t!”

“I understand.”

He moaned through his teeth, before sucking in a shaky lungful of air. Sheila approached him from the side, like one might an injured animal, and placed a hand gently on his arm.

“Remus, I have something for you. I’m a bit worried it might make things harder, but if it at all helps, then I think you should have it.”

It took a moment, but finally he pulled his hands away and sniffed. “What is it?”

“It’s... Well, it's your mother.” Slowly, Sheila reached into her jacket pocket and withdrew a small book—a pocket bible. From within its pages, she pulled out a single photograph, black and white and faded in some places, but still clear enough.

“It took me a while to find this. It is over twenty years old now, which makes me feel terribly old,” Sheila said, chuckling faintly as she carefully handed it over, “but I managed to uncover it during my last trip home to visit Colin, and I thought you might like to see it.”

Remus turned the photograph around and stared down at three people no older than he was now. It was Sheila, young and wearing her school uniform, along with Hope in hers, and another boy. They were all smiling, arms tucked around each other as they crowded into the lens. Along the bottom of the photo was a date, April 23rd 1954.

“Mum’s birthday,” he murmured.

“That’s right," she said. "We were around seventeen here, I believe. That’s your mum, and me, and our friend Thaddeus. Thaddeus Dean. We all grew up together—here at Hawkings. Thaddeus loathed his full name though, so everyone called him Tad. We really had so much fun at school.”

Remus’ hold tightened on the photograph. Tad.

“I’ll understand if this is too much,” she said, watching him cautiously, “but there’s one more.”

Prying his eyes away, he looked down to find her holding a second photograph, this one of a baby in colour. Taking it, he stared at the infant’s big blue eyes, before slowly turning it over. On the back was printed, Remus John Lupin, born March 10, 1960. 2.9 kgs.

“I…” Remus immediately looked up, fixing his gaze on a rose bush across from him. “You… have my baby photo…”

“I do,” she said softly. “Your mum and I were still very close when you were born. I'd just moved to London with Colin, and when she brought you to see me, it was wonderful. You were so were frightfully small then—a far cry from now—but I was so pleased to see that you’d been born healthy.”

Unsure of what to do, Remus passed the photo back, and Sheila took it, looking at him before tucking it back into her bible. “I’m sorry if this was strange or… or odd, Remus. I just wanted you to know that I understand, as much as I can. I miss your mother very much. She was very dear to me, and it’s alright to be upset sometimes, but you have a responsibility as a student here, and I know you know what that means. Your friends treasure you, and there’s nothing more valuable than that.”

He grunted—there weren't the words—but Sheila didn't seem to mind. She just clutched his baby photo in a tight grip, before wiping her eyes and smiling at him once more.

What mistakes have you made then? Remus thought. Eyes still downcast, he made to pass the first photo back, but Sheila pressed it back toward him.

“You can keep that one, if you’d like.”

It was her kind way of telling him to take it, and because he didn’t have it in him to argue anymore, he tucked the photo into his breast pocket, feeling it’s featherweight like a bolder against his chest. It struck him then how much easier things might’ve been if he’d been born Sheila's son rather than Hope’s. But then a feeling of instant self-loathing overcame him.

What a horrible son, the nasty voice sneered. How could you even think that about your own mother?

Remus suddenly felt sick, but Sheila was still watching him, her expression strangely concentrated—he had to say something.

Clearing his throat awkwardly, Remus smoothed his hand over the pocket with the photo. “Thank you, Mrs. Buchanan,” he mumbled, “for… being my teacher.”

Sheila's smile softened. For a moment another emotion flitted across her face. It felt like longing.

“You’re welcome, Remus.”





* * *





When he finally returned to the dorm, his friends were waiting for him. James and Lily were both busy pacing ahead the length of the room while Sirius laid upside down on James’ bed, tossing a hand ball up and down thoughtlessly. In reality Remus really only got a split-second image of the scene before he'd stepped inside and all three of them had rushed him.

“What they gonna do to you?” Sirius demanded.

“They’re not gonna expel you, right?” James pleaded.

“It wouldn’t be fair!” Lily added, though Remus was pretty sure she’d never once been under the impression that life was fair in the first place.

He shut the door and shook his head. “McGonagall says she’s withholding judgement. And punishment.”

“What the bloody hell does that mean?” Sirius demanded. "You shouldn't even be getting a bleedin' punishment in the first place—didn't you tell them what Barty said?!"

He shrugged. “I dunno what she's gonna decide, but they sent me back so…”

“So you’re not expelled!” Lily cried, before letting out a heavy sigh of relief and throwing her arms around his neck. “Oh, Remus, I’m so sorry! Barty had no right to say what he did!”

“I know. It's fine.” He pat her gently on the back—a sign that he wasn't interested in being fret over anymore—before pulling away. Lily withdrew shyly, and James stepped up to cup her shoulders as Remus stepped past all of them and strode to his bed.

“How are you feeling then?” James asked.

“I told you, I'm fine.”

James glanced sceptically at Sirius, who instantly began to seethe; “That git, Crouch. He knew exactly what he was doing coming at you! We can’t let him get away with it. We have to get the bastard back.”

“Sirius, Remus just got let off the hook—he could’ve been expelled!" Lily said. "Let's not push it, okay?”

“We didn’t do anything when the git and everyone else was coming after you for your scholarship,” Sirius pointed out, “so where’s the line then? When is enough, enough?”

Remus sat down on his bed and rubbed his eyes. Hearing Sirius come to his defence might've felt nice any other time, but right then he was too tired to think of revenge. The photo Sheila had given him was boring a hole in his pocket and all he wanted to do was sleep.

“Barty just wanted to start something, you said it yourself earlier,” James reasoned. “He knew he could hurt Remus by saying it like that so he did, but he’s just a stupid kid.”

“And we’re not about to listen to someone as pathetic as Barty anyway. Besides, Remus’ mum passed when he was little, you'd have to be ten-feet thick in the head to even consider that he could’ve had anything to do with it,” Lily finished.

Sirius gave a low moan; “Why aren’t we asking Moony what he wants to do? He should be the one who decides! Barty used his mum’s suicide as canon fodder! He can’t just get away with—”

Suddenly on high-alert, Remus tore his hands away from his face. “My mum didn’t commit suicide!”

All three of them froze, opening up the circle they’d gathered in to gape at him. Sirius, who'd been cut-off in his rant, looked the most horrified. He stared at Remus as though he'd just told them that he was a bloody wizard and could cast magic spells.

“Oh, Remus…” Lily tried; “We didn't…”

He shot to his feet; “She died of pneumonia for Christ’s sake—of fucking cancer! What, don't tell me you all actually believed some stupid rumour that's been going around?”

The stunned looks on his friends’ faces were enough to tell Remus that yes—yes they did believe it.

“How long have you guys thought this?” He demanded.

None of them answered.

“How long?”

“You never talk about it,” Sirius said. “We… We just assumed that...”

“That she fucking killed herself?!”

The dots were starting to connect; the way they gingerly stepped around all mention of his mother, how they never asked about the records or about the estate—even Marlene’s mum on Easter.

It’s so hard when a family member just refuses to get better.

They’d all thought it then—believed some rumour and talked about it amongst themselves too. Remus suddenly found it hard to breathe, and when Lily stepped toward him with those big green eyes of hers, he staggered back so quickly that he knocked almost everything off his bedside table. The lamp clattered to the floor by his feet and he stared at it. The bulb had cracked.

“Remus.”

When he looked back, he found Sirius just in front of him.

“We’re sorry.”

“You’re sorry?” He echoed. "You're fucking sorry?"

“Yes, we’re sorry. I’m sorry.”

"FUCK YOUR SORRY!" He howled. "You never even bothered to ask me what had happened! And don’t you dare say ‘would you have wanted to’—anything is better than this!”

Sirius licked his lips. “I understand how you feel. Can you really blame us for not asking, though? You just... You never talk about this stuff, Moons.”

He wasn’t sure if this was Sirius’ way of inviting him to fight—to get it over with—but he took the chance anyway. “Well, what about you?” He snarled. “You never talk about anything unless you can make a joke out of it. So what’s your trauma then, your mum? Those burns on your chest? You said it was boiling water—what, misjudge your bath temperature, genius boy?!”

He didn’t mean to be so vicious. His words made even Lily flinch, but Sirius took the anger in stride.

“I guess you could say it was both, actually. It started with a kettle. Mum and I got into it in the kitchen one day—something about Reg. All I remember is she hit him and he was crying, so I got between ‘em. She didn't like that, you see, so she went and grabbed the kettle right off the hob. I guess it burnt her so she went to throw it, but Reg was... He was right there. It was a mistake, but the consequences stuck around, obviously.”

Sirius spoke so pragmatically, so unembellished and detached, that Remus could’ve believed it was a story he’d read off-hand in a paper.

“I was eleven,” he finished finally. “Same age as you when your mum died. But I mean hey, could’ve been worse, right? At least my scars missed my face.”

“F-Fuck you,” Remus hissed. It didn’t make him feel any better. Smiling sadly, Sirius held his gaze, brave and stoic and beautiful.

“I’m sorry, Moony."

No, they're not.

Lily stepped forward. There were tears in her eyes. "We're sorry, Remus."

They just pity you. Those are tears of pity.

"We really are sorry, Moony," James finished. "We didn't mean it. Please believe us."

Gritting his teeth, Remus squeezed until he could feel the pain in every inch of his jaw. Then finally, he slumped forward, hanging his head in acceptance.

None of them spoke for a long time, but when Remus covered his face again to hide any tears that might have squeezed their way out, Sirius stepped forward and enveloped him in a strong hug.

“We’re sorry, Moony,” he said.

“We love you, Remus,” Lily sniffled, grappling for the both of them with fingers that were tender and solid. James was next, and though his hands were rougher, they weren’t any less gentle.

"We wouldn't trade you for the world, Moons. You're our best mate. We love ya, man."

And because he loved them too, Remus hugged his friends.



Chapter End Notes

Being 'jumped in' refers to the beatings that youth gangs sometimes give to make sure an initiate is tough enough to join a gang.

'Serving at her majesty's pleasure' is an idiom for serving a prison sentence.
