21st July 1977

“Break—the break! USE YOUR BREAK!”

Remus let out a bark of laughter as he slammed on the Roll’s brake pedal, the car lurching to a halt just ahead of the estate’s driveway. Still clinging to the door handle for dear life, Giles tugged the cap from his head and used it to dab the sweat from his receding hairline. They’d been driving up and down the back roads around the estate for nearly a month now, and Remus was quite pleased with his progress, even if Giles was more cynical.

“You are going to be the death of me,” he cursed.

“C’mon Gil, it wasn’t that even bad!” Remus said, throwing the car into park.

“Oh really? Try telling that to that lead foot of yours. I think you all but murdered that bush of rhododendrons back there.”

“Eh, they’ll grow back.”

“But the paint on the Rolls won’t!”

Grinning, Remus drummed his fingers on the steering wheel. “Whadda'ya say—one more whip around?”

Giles shook his head, unbuckling himself from the seat. “Sorry lad, I've got to get the car cleaned up to take your father to his next meeting."

"You mean his next date."

"Don't be a snot."

"Why won't you tell me where he's been going? Who's 'S'? I saw it written down in his calendar for tonight. 'Dinner with 'S'—seven o'clock'."

"Dammit, Remus—I thought I told you to stop going into his office? Your father's books aren't for you to stick your smarmy nose in."

Remus shrugged, unbothered. "I wasn't trying to stick my nose into anything—I was looking for his whisky. He always keeps some in the bottom drawer, and the bar cabinet was looking a bit dry."

Giles reached over and swatted him upside the head.

“Ow! What was that for, ya old fart?! You can't just hit me anymore, I'm not a kid!"

"Having to say that you aren't a kid just proves that you are, you little fart. Now c’mon, turn us around and let’s get this thing parked. Tomorrow I’ll take you out in one of the other cars, teach you on a manual."

“I’d rather drive to China,” Remus grumbled, sliding the gear shift out of park.

Giles chuckled; “This sort ‘a steel don’t float, son. And besides, a man’s got to be able to drive a manual else he can't call himself a real man.”

"I thought I was just a 'kid'."

"Yes, one that's too smart for his own good. Now let's get going."

After he'd crept the car back up the estate’s drive, Remus shut the engine off, handed Giles the keys, and got out. The air around him smelt of clean breeze and freshly mown grass and the warm July sun immediately began to beat down on the back of his neck as it got ready to set over the horizon. It was like any other summer afternoon, except that Remus was angry. He didn't want to be there, and yet he couldn't find the right excuse to leave. The driving lessons were only a short reprieve from his every day, which were spent doing pointless things like marching up and down the lawn with Dusty, or reading books that he immediately forgot the moment he shut them, or listening to the same albums over and over and over again. He'd left the house enough times, mostly to go to the record shop and brush up on all the music he'd missed over the last school year. As a result he'd accumulated quite the collection for himself, but without Sirius to write to, or the flat as an escape, he had no one to share them with. Of course there was Marlene, though she'd left for Morocco a week ago. James and Peter were there too, and he'd already gone out with them a handful of times, but they were always trying to get him to come over to their houses for this or that—mostly band practice. Eventually Remus had grown good at giving excuses to avoid visiting. After the fiasco with Marlene's family on Easter he was too hesitant, not that he believed that anyone who could raise a James Potter could be all that bad.

No... really, it just came down to wanting to spend all of his time wallowing and feeling sorry for himself. Outside of that, all he wanted to do was go out and get utterly pissed. He wanted to run the town as he once did, smashing bottles and knocking over rubbish bins—just become that great idiot without a care in the world. He wanted to wake up hungover on a dingy sofa only to stumble to the toilet, throw up the entire contents of his stomach, before choking down some eggs and waiting for that second wind so he could do it all over again. He wanted to go back to the flat. But that wasn't an option anymore.

At least Giles was happy. It was the first holiday in years that he wasn't driving around the city at all hours, picking Remus up off of random street corners. He didn't have to wait by the phone anymore—a fact that made Remus feel guilty when he realised how often he'd done it. Nope, now Giles was free to play nursemaid, which he did passionately—never allowing Remus to sleep past noon. More than once Remus had found himself wanting to snap viciously at him for it, but he had so few people left in his corner... and chasing off the one man that had been around longer than he could remember didn't seem like the best course of action.

So, he put up with it. But sticking around and accepting Giles' badgering also came with a few more annoying stipulations.

"How did it go today, Giles?" Lyall asked, standing at the top of the estate's stairs, busy adjusting the cuffs on his suit jacket. It was so hot, Remus couldn't wrap his head around how he stood it.

"Good!" Giles called. "I figure he'll be ready for the roadway soon, though he's gotta work some on his stop-and-go. Still a bit sharp, that. Wouldn't want someone to ram into him from behind."

Lyall shifted his measuring gaze to Remus as he made it to the top step. "And how do you feel it went?"

Remus scoffed lightly; "You mean you're actually asking me?"

"Don't be dramatic. Just say if you're not ready."

"It's fine."

"Hm." Lyall stopped fiddling with his cuffs. "I'm going out tonight. Tell the cooks when you're hungry. And clean up your room, it looks as though an animal lives there, not a boy."

"Sure thing. And you have fun on your 'date'. That's what it is, right?"

It might've been a trick of the light, but Remus could've sworn he saw the corner of his father's eye twitch. But then he'd turned away, marching down the front steps and down the path toward the dog house. "Giles, I'll be with the dogs until we leave. Call Sebastian or Jeffrey and send them over to the kennels."

As his father kept on, Giles nodded and flashed Remus a friendly wink before heading in the opposite direction, toward the staff's quarters. Remus just glared after his father.

"Hope you stink all through dinner," he muttered, pushing open the front doors and marching grumpily inside. He'd just reached the main staircase when a butler intercepted him and presented a letter. For a moment Remus was elated—was this finally it?!—but then he turned it over the envelope, revealing Jillian’s bubbly handwriting and the kiss mark she'd left in red lipstick.

His heart sank. Jillian had been writing to him at least twice a week since the summer holiday had started, and yet there hadn't been so much as a postage stamp from Bath. It made Remus want to tear his hair out. Every novel-length letter from his ex-biology partner could’ve been confirmation that Sirius was fine and not in fact upset over what had happened between them on their final night at school. After so long without any word, Remus had half a mind to jump on a train just to shake some sense into Sirius himself. Always a step ahead where his friends were concerned, James claimed to have already bought the damn ticket—but somehow Lily and Peter had convinced him not to go. If Sirius couldn't write, then it must've meant he was already in deep shit, and having his 'no-good, prankster friends' show up on his family's doorstep wouldn't help nullify that.

"This is Sirius Black we're talking about," Peter insisted, the last time Remus had seen them, "he's basically indestructible. He's always been able to take what his family threw at him and shove it right back tenfold. Just you wait, he's gonna show up at school even more smug than before. He'll probably even ask for a medal of valour. Sirius will be just fine."

You're wrong, Remus had thought arrogantly, none of you know what I know.

Pfft, you don't even know what you know.

This better not be what going crazy feels like. If I'm to listen to a stupid, unhelpful inner voice for the rest of my life, then can someone please just off me now.

Everyone's got an inner voice, mate. Some are just louder than others.

Sirius Black was not indestructible. He was vain and easily-influenced, and sensitive and brash. He went about his days not caring what anyone thought of him, while simultaneously caring far too much. But he also wasn't afraid to cry, had a penchant for justice—no matter how misguided—and never let anyone get down on themselves when he could help it. And he was so soft. So fucking soft...

Damn it.

Remus missed him. He couldn't help it. Missing Sirius came as easily as breathing. He just wished that it made more sense; how he could miss Sirius as he had been—want him like he did—and yet not be queer. The thought had crossed his mind countless times that perhaps he was just in denial, but every time he was out with Marlene he felt giddy to be by her side. Would that cute girl across the shop think he was desirable because he was out with her? Would those pretty university birds sitting on the public library's front steps look twice at him because he was tall and had another girl on his arm? He liked the attention, though none of them were Sirius, so the desire to act on it was simply not there. Or maybe it was, since he’d made plenty of moves already and none of them on a man—it was complicated. But the girls got his heart racing the same way Sirius did, and the more it happened, the more Remus began to realise that it was the same feeling—Sirius just invoked it more often.

Maybe it would've been better if he was queer. Certainly would've answered a few questions. He liked girls because they were generally kind, and he found them pretty. Sirius was pretty too, but Remus had never looked at another bloke and thought that they were handsome or that he wanted to be with them. For him, Sirius was the exception. He was set apart from the rest—othered. Not a girl, but not like other blokes either. Remus wondered if this 'othering' of his best friend made him a bad person. He knew intrinsically that he liked girls, but liking Sirius wasn't a choice, it was just a part of being human. He was so beautiful that people naturally gravitated toward him, whether because they wanted him for themselves or because they hoped some of his beauty would rub off on them. Remus didn't want to be gravitationally beautiful, so he supposed that it only left the former.

Thoughts like these made Remus want to do something drastic—an urge he'd already acted on several times since summer's start. It almost always involved dragging James or Peter along to some pub or elsewhere, but they were seventeen too, and short of cheating on their girlfriends, they were willing to do almost anything to have a good time.

It'd all started with that girl they'd met in that corner pub in Bethnal Green. She'd had grey eyes like a storm cloud, and knew about Queen and Deep Purple and Neil Young. Remus hadn't been anticipating going home with her, but he was already four pints in by the time she'd introduced herself. After her it was the girl he'd met while watching James play a round of scrimmage football out in East Finchley. Her name had been Mei, which she'd said meant beautiful. He only remembered because he'd used it as a cheesy pick-up line straight after, which he honestly hadn't expected to work. As it turned out he only met up with Beautiful Mei that one time, and then a week later it was that freckled brunette who'd approached him by the bally-hole tables. She'd seemed a bit squirrelly at first but she'd had the loveliest hands. Remus had been showing her how to use the machine's knobs to score a proper shot when the next thing he knew they were kissing.

Kissing girls was easy now. He'd done it enough times that he'd already sworn to himself that the next time he saw Marlene he'd apologise for being so frigid while they'd dated. But as easy as it was to sweet-talk his way into an evening of trivial fornication, and as beautiful and as pretty and as soft as the girls were, they were never Sirius.

Later that evening, after his father and Giles had left for the meeting with 'S', Remus called James up and invited him out. James had just gotten back that morning after spending two weeks at Lily's in Liverpool, and was obviously still tired from the train, but after a quick nod over on Peter's line, he phoned Remus back and said they were both in. Since his friends lived all the way in Finchley, Remus agreed that they should meet up in the middle, and hopped a cab over to the nearest tube station where he rode the line all the way into Westminster. It was just getting dark by the time he arrived, but it was still hot out so he rolled the sleeves up on his t-shirt and strolled confidently into the pub. The place was more of a hole in the ground than a restaurant, but Remus had come to like the set-up thanks to its penchant for playing live music and the fact that the bartender only ever bothered Peter over his age. As promised, a band was playing as he walked in, and he found James and Peter already set up at a table with a pint each and one more for him.

"Hey lads."

"Hey yourself, stranger," James said, raising his glass as Remus sat. Remus took the pint Peter slid toward him, sipping it as he watched the band. They didn't look all that much older than they were, and they had no singer, which meant their music was ornamental to the pub at best. They were playing a Beach Boys cover, but it wasn't one of their more-known hits so they were having trouble capturing the audience's attention. Remus thought condescendingly that they could've played in every grimy pub from there to Newham and would probably still never get anywhere.

"So... how was seeing the girlfriends?" He asked, his entire attitude rather lacklustre.

"Great," James answered. "We had to sleep in separate rooms, obviously, but Lily's parents are real friendly. Her older sister... a bit less so."

"Yeah, but you already knew that going in," Peter teased. "I got lucky. Moira's an only child. And her house is massive."

"Hm. Sounds nice."

James sipped his beer, before setting the glass down and wiping his mouth. "What'd you get up to then? You seem... different."

"Yeah, looking a bit beefy there, Moony,” Peter razzed. “You going to the gym now? Jazzercise maybe?"

"Piss off, ya dickhead," Remus chuckled. "Giles has got me working around the house a bit. Yesterday I helped him rebuild part of the fence that'd fallen in. Mostly I just faffed around."

"Get any of your summer homework done?" James asked.

"Nah. Might not do it, to be honest."

"But you're a prefect now," Peter said. "Are you allowed to just not do your homework?"

"Guess we'll find out..." Feeling suddenly restless among all the noise, Remus cast his gaze around the room. He spotted on a girl sitting by her lonesome at the bar top. She wasn't looking at him, but after a few seconds she reached for a napkin further down the bar and caught his eye.

James leaned in; "So, uh… have you given any more thought about coming to Devon with us at the end of the week?"

"Mm... yeah, no—totally."

"Christ, whatchu looking at now—" James turned around in his seat. "Oh. I see the appeal."

Remus smirked slightly, but the girl had looked away. Blimey, that's a short skirt.

"We just got here," Peter complained. "And what's this one supposed to be, number sixteen? Does Marlene know how lively you've become these last few weeks?"

"Marlene's in Africa," Remus snapped; "And besides, we're not dating."

Peter raised his hands in defeat. "Could'a fooled me, what with how often you were seeing her before. Exes get back together all the time, just saying."

"We're friends, Wormtail, that's all..." Remus glanced back to the girl. She was watching him now—in that way girls did when they wanted to be noticed but didn't want it to seem obvious that they were the ones doing the noticing. "You guys feel like another pint...?"

James looked down at his not even half-empty glass. "Fuck, just go talk to her then, numpty."

"Yeah, see you in an hour," Peter scoffed. "Or more."

"I'm coming back… But just in case I don't." Smiling, he slapped a few quid down on the table for the beers, before standing up and unweaving himself from the table.

The pub was busy, but not so busy that Remus had trouble making his way to the bar. He stopped on the far end, two stools away from the girl, who'd quickly turned back into her drink. It was a martini—a far cry from the drinks normally served in places like this one—and he watched out of the corner of his eye as she began stirring it with the olive skewer. When the bartender approached him, Remus ordered another pint of whatever they had on tap and stopped to wait, quietly drumming his hands on the bar top. He feigned interest in the band for a while, and when he got his drink he paid and turned lazily back the direction he'd come. He hesitated at the last second, and turned to the girl, leaning in ever so slightly.

"Is the music always this bad here?" He asked.

She looked up, a small smile playing at her lips. "No. Normally it's worse."

"Oh shit."

"You're pretty tall, you know."

Remus almost smiled. They always said he was tall. "Thanks. That's a nice top."

She peeked down at the flouncy shirt she was wearing. It was jewel-blue and cut deeply down the middle, tying off just above her waist. "Guys don't normally notice my clothes," she said, sounding amused. "How old are you?"

"Nineteen," he lied. "I'm Remus."

He extended a hand and she took it, smiling. "Remus... Never heard that sort of name before. Is it a family name?"

"Not really."

"Oh. Well, I'm Lucy."

"Like the Beatles song?"

"The what?"

"You know, 'Lucy in the Sky with...' Never mind." Remus cleared his throat. “Say, don't the girls who normally come here just get a beer or something? I didn't even know they made drinks like that." He slowly began to close the gap between them, stopping until only a single stool separated them. Lucy watched every move with blue eyes the same colour as her top.

"Guess I just like to stand out." She raised the olive spear from her martini glass and held the olive between her teeth, slowly sliding it off the toothpick before chewing. "You here with your mates then?"

"What? Oh... yeah."

"They seem interesting."

"Nah, they're just—" Remus peeked back at James and Peter, only to find the pair of them staring openly over the rim of their pints. He straightened up, shooting his friends a nasty look—cut it out!—to which James and Peter just laughed and turned back around.

"Funny too," Lucy chuckled.

"More like funny looking."

"Well, your one friend does have a lot of gel in his hair."

"It's just something he's trying out. Pretty sure he wants to look like Elvis."

"You should tell him to wash it out. I'll bet it looks way better natural. Sorta like yours." Smoothly, she reached up and gently pawed at one of Remus' curls, her gaze never leaving his face.

Remus swallowed thickly. "Are you here with anyone?"

Lucy's eyes wandered slightly, but then she shook her head. "I know a few people in the back, but they're all busy playing cards."

"You don't play?"

"Not really. Never been very good at it so they left me behind. S'just me tonight, I'm afraid."

"Do you want to grab a booth together?"

"Hm... Buy me another drink first?"

Remus had never ordered a martini before, so he simply told the guy to remake Lucy's last drink and drop it off at one of the booths near the back. The lights were purposely dimmer there, and as he and Lucy cuddled together on one of the padded benches, Remus found that the dizzy feeling had returned.

"You're a really good kisser," Lucy said between bouts of snogging.

For some reason the compliment stung. "Worth kissing more than once...?"

She gave him a funny look, and answered with more tongue. Remus didn't mind; she was a good kisser too. And she smelt good—like vanilla. Her lips were slightly salty from the martini, but the rest of her was sweet. She had long black hair that she kept having to sweep out of her face like a curtain and her grip felt solid and real on the side of his neck. She kept herself flush against his thigh, occasionally slipping a hand down his chest and lower. It was just so easy to get lost in it, even the band's piddling music faded away; no silly counting games, no Marauders, no secret kisses in the toilet—certainly no Sirius.

Remus was just considering asking Lucy to leave with him—as if he could've actually brought her back to the estate—when a furious grip came down and latched viciously along the collar of his t-shirt. His throat made the most pathetic choking sound as he was yanked backward and out of the booth, missing his feet completely and crashing to the floor on his back. Before he'd even had time to breathe, a thug wearing a plain white singlet and a pair of track pants was screaming at him.

"WOTCHER THINK YOR DOIN' WIV YOR TONGUE DOWN ME GIRLFRIEND'S THROAT, YOU LITTLE PRICK?!"

Remus was stunned. As he finally got his feet under him and managed to stand, the skinhead kept screaming at him, wailing his obscenities while Lucy shot up from the bench, shrieking and grappling her boyfriend by the arm. "Matty! Matty, please! He's just some stupid kid!"

"I'LL KILL YA!" He barked, taking a swing that Remus had to jump back to avoid. "I'LL BREAK YOR LEGS, YA CHEEKY FUCKER!"

"I didn't know she was your girlfriend!" Remus shouted. “She—!"

The guy took another swing, this one barely missing by a hair. Remus had to throw himself back onto an empty table just to evade it, which only made Matty angrier. Brushing Lucy off, he advanced on Remus, who scrambled to get back on his feet again.

"GET OVER 'ERE, YOU RAT-ARSED BASTARD! I'LL GIVE YOU—"

"WOAH—WOAH! Just hold on a second!" James cried, getting between the two of them. "Look mate, I think this is all just a big misunder—"

Matty's fist came up deadly-quick, catching James in the side of the jaw and making his head snap back painfully. As Lucy screamed blue murder, James crumpled to the floor with Matty standing over him and barking his insults again.

"LIKE SUM 'A THAT, BITCH?!"

Other people around the pub were already moving. Obviously used to the havoc, the bartender had emerged from behind his booth, while several old codgers who had just stopped in to enjoy themselves a beer were on getting to their feet. They might've done something about it, had he given them a chance to do so, but Remus had just seen one of his friends take the fall for him. Instantly his ears thrummed with blood. He wanted a taste of it too.

With only that driving him, Remus threw himself at their attacker head-on. Now, Remus Lupin may have been tall, but he was still only about ninety pounds sopping wet. Despite that fact, he mustered all the force he could manage and grappled the skinhead around the middle, forcing him back against the edge of booth's table with a nasty thump. The surprise shot had succeeded in stunned him temporarily, but the moment Matty recovered he began wailing down on Remus' back with both fists, knocking the air straight from his lungs. After that a knee came up, slamming painfully into his cheek as he held him. Body screaming in pain, Remus released the thug's middle on instinct only to take another shot to the ribs. He couldn't hear anything over Lucy's screams, but as long as he was the one getting hit then it meant James was safe.

In the end he got a few decent shots in—one just below the chin that left the guy's teeth rattling, and a few in the chest and shoulders, but by the time the pub's staff was hauling them apart and tossing Remus out onto the street, it was clear he'd just had his arse handed to him. Ushered by Peter, who was nowhere to be found during the actual brawl, he and James stumbled down street after street. They kept going until they were sure no one had followed them, making sure to stick to the more brightly-lit corners until they finally made it back to the station.

"D-Don't want to get jumped just as we're a-about to get on the t-train," Peter stammered, pacing nervously back and forth in front of the entrance to the underground. "James, a-are we going then? I think we should g-go."

"Yeah, one second," James sighed, before turning back to Remus. His cheek had swollen up to the side of a golf ball on the way from the pub, and Peter had been yammering about how badly his mother was going to lose it when she saw, but James had been quiet the entire way. "Moony—"

"I am so sorry, mate," Remus started immediately. "I didn't mean for all that to happen."

"I know you didn't, and I'm not upset."

"But your cheek... and your glasses!"

James raised the mangled eyeglasses meekly. Sometime during the scuffle they'd gotten knocked off of his face and trampled under boot. "S'fine. I got a spare back at home."

"Your mum's still gonna kill you," Peter murmured.

"Thanks, Wormtail." James let out another long sigh. "Moony, are you sure you're okay?"

Remus straightened up, swallowing a wince. His back ached, but he wasn't going to whine in front of the friend who'd just taken a beating for him. "Oh yeah. Don't think it should be too bad—dick barely got me."

"Tell that to your black eye," Peter said.

"Pete." James shoved the busted frames into his pocket. "Moony, I just mean are you okay-okay? 'Cause you haven't been acting like yourself for a while now, and... We're worried."

"Don't you worry about me, Prongs. I'm fine."

"You don't seem it. Is this about Sirius? 'Cause you said it yourself, that he's gonna be—"

"It's not about Sirius!"

Both James and Peter flinched back when he shouted, and Remus instantly felt more foul than he had all summer. Good going, fuck-head, even the friends that are here are freaked out by you now.

"I'm just trying to be less like myself," Remus swore. "You know, to make things easier on you guys."

"Why would we want that?"

Remus hugged his arm. Why, indeed.

"I think you should come to Devon with us," James said. "It'll be good to get away. Get some fresh air—walk along the beach a bit. There's plenty for you to read, and Mum's a great cook. We can make trips into town whenever we want, and even take the canoes out when the tide's in. It's nice."

"I dunno... I just don't think that stuff's for me. It's your family."

"You're our best friend, Remus," he sighed, then; "At least promise that you'll think about it."

"... Alright."

James gave him a tight smile, before reaching out and fondly patting him on the shoulder. Remus winced when he did it, and they all began to laugh—even Peter.

"You're sure you're okay getting home?" James asked later, as he and Peter started for the open doors of their train.

"Yeah. I'll be good. S'not that far."

"Kay. We'll call you tomorrow then, see about Devon."

Remus waved goodbye as his friends' train pulled away. He only had a few minutes until his own would be by, but when it came roaring down the tracks, it was as though his feet had frozen to the tile. He didn't want to go home. But he couldn't go where it was that he really wanted to be, so instead he just walked.

First it was aimless, just up and down the borough's dark streets—into Mayfair and back. It wasn't cold, even without a jacket, and the humidity kept up even with the late hour. A few cabs stopped along the road thinking he wanted a ride, but those stopped once he'd crossed over into Lambeth and began to take the backstreets. It occurred to Remus then that he was in the prime position to be mugged, but either thanks to whatever luck he maintained or because anyone he passed determined that he didn't have anything worth taking, no one bothered him.

It was close to one in the morning when he realised that he'd drifted south into Peckham. All the shops were shut up for the night, and when he stopped for a much-needed fag, he managed to spot a few kids tagging a shop's metal window covers with spray paint. The sight made him a bit nostalgic, and he watched until they'd finished and moved on to tag something else.

Well, here you are. Out on the town, running the streets again. Feel good?

Fuck off.

And where would I go? I'm you.

Remus knew any sane person in his position would've hailed a cab or found the nearest phone booth and called their personal driver, but if he couldn't be Moony of Marauders or Lu of the East End, then he certainly didn't want to be Remus Lupin.

He spent the night on a park bench in Deptford, like a true bum, and was awoken early the next morning by the rising sun and the sound of cars as parents arrived to drop their kiddies off at the nursery across the lawn. Feeling a lot like he'd been hit by a bus, Remus hauled himself to his feet and stumbled the rest of the way home. He was just checking his pockets to make sure no one had robbed him of his zippo and fags as he'd slept—they hadn’t—when the front door flew open and Giles was dragging him inside.

"And just where have you been all night?!" He howled.

"Nowhere—stayed over at James'."

"You mean to say that you stayed out at your friend's place all night and then came flouncing home at seven in the morning? I think not!"

Remus bristled, snatching his arm away with an indignant grunt. Honestly, you start coming home every night for a few weeks in a row and everyone begins to think it's the new normal.

"What's it matter?" He snapped. "I'm back, aren't I?"

"You've been fighting—don't deny it, you're beat to shit and you're walking like you spent all day hunched over in a coal mine. Now where were you?"

"I told you, at James' house!"

"Did you fight with him?"

"Fuck—no! Now will you piss off, Giles?!"

Giles frowned deeply, and Remus wanted to swear at him again. He'd thought a night out on the streets would leave him less angry when he'd returned. Apparently not.

"Honestly, son... I thought that this 'staying out all hours' business was behind us. What's there possibly to go back to around Aldgate?"

"I didn't go back there," Remus growled.

"Then how'd you get so beat up?"

He couldn't do it anymore. He didn't want to hear Giles' speech about how it'd felt to pick him up half-dead after he'd been jumped in the alley with Tonya last summer—he'd been there! He was the one who'd gotten utterly curb-stomped and beaten to a pulp in the first place! Why was it that other people made it so easy to feed him their pain, but never stopped to consider his?

Practically snarling, Remus shoved past the old man and headed directly for the stairs. He didn't want to think about Tomny, or the flat, or any of it! Fuck... he just wanted to sleep.

"Hold on there, young master," Giles called after him. "Your father wants you on the hunt today. It'll just be the two of you, and he's been waiting until you returned."

Remus whipped around again—fast enough to make his back twinge. "What—why? He hasn't wanted me to go with him in years."

"Maybe it's for some father-son bonding then. Lord knows the two of you could use it."

"I can't go trouncing around some bleedin' forest right now, I'm hurt."

"How hurt? Do you wanna talk about it?"

So it was a punishment then.

Fuck it.

Remus turned, carrying back up on the stairs and stomping with his every step.

"I've already laid out your things!" Giles hollered. "Shower fast and get changed, or I swear you won't leave your room for a week!"

It hurt to shower, hurt even more to maneuver himself into the stupid get-up and heavy bush boots that Giles had set out for him. Remus was at least sure nothing was broken—a small silver-lining—but as he made his way back downstairs and found his father and Giles waiting for him by the front door along with another swath of servants, every twinge became a throbbing ache.

"Since when is July hunting season?" He grumbled, refusing the gun case that was held out to him.

"I've a colleague who has given me leave to shoot on his property out near Tonbridge," Lyall said, busy inspecting each rifle as it was set in its case.

"Is that even legal?"

"No, not that one... the Remington model—yes, that's it... Well, Remus—" Lyall paused, staring openly at the bruise that'd bloomed just above his son's cheek bone. "What’s happened to your face?"

"Got in a fight," Remus said finally, with an air of superiority.

"Did you win?"

He didn't answer right away and immediately regretted it as Lyall turned away. "Pointless then, wasn't it? Anyway, I think you'll find that the closer you study the law, Remus, the easier it is to work around it."

Remus rolled his eyes. Typical.

They didn't take the Rolls, not wanting to mar its tires on the dirt roads, and so instead Giles drove them in a Chrysler which he coveted for its rear-wheel drive. They were followed by a small lorry that was carrying the dogs, who Lyall would've never gone hunting without, and Remus spent the entire ride glaring out the window, leaving as much space in the back seat between himself and his father as possible.

"Can we at least put the radio on?" He'd complained.

"No," Lyall answered straight away, too busy flipping through some document for work to even look up; "It won't kill you to have some silence."

"Do you ever stop working?" Remus said, scowling at the papers.

"It's called having a work ethic, Remus."

"That what you tell your girlfriend?"

Lyall didn't so much as blink. "I said silence, didn't I?"

Remus resumed his window-brooding.

When they finally reached their destination, a crop of forest surrounding a vast man-made lake, Remus piled out of the sedan and rushed over to the lorry, where all of the dogs were already busy barking their heads off. They could obviously sense that they were in a new place, and when he and the driver opened the back hutch, five large coonhounds came rushing out.

"Return for us in two hours," Lyall instructed, taking his rifle and ammo pack from Giles. He didn't bother giving one to Remus, who hadn't shot anything in years, and instead forced him to carry the game bag. Remus did so, squirming only slightly when he remembered that the bag would soon be full of dead waterfowl. After that they set off into the trees, the dogs so close they were nearly underfoot. Padfoot and Seabiscuit were the senior dogs now, having already sired litters of their own and calmed down some in their old age, but the puppies, Ruffian, Red Rum, and Eclipse, raced in and around Remus' legs as they made their way from path to path, noses pressed to the earth as they searched.

"Why didn't you bring Sebastian or one of the other trainers with you?" Remus asked eventually.

“I wanted it to be just the two of us today,” Lyall answered.

"Why?"

"You're my son. Do I really need a reason to want to spend time with you?"

"You've always needed one before."

Apparently Lyall didn't have much to say to that. He stayed quiet for a while, simply plunging on ahead through the trees, eyes trained above and below for any sign of a pheasant or grouse. "How are things at school?" He asked finally.

"Fine."

"And your marks?"

"Wonderful."

"Good. You're smart, even if you'd like to pretend otherwise."

Remus mumbled out of the corner of his mouth; "Only around you..."

"How do you feel about the school as a whole?" Lyall asked. "Is it worth your time? I wonder sometimes, what with you so far away."

"It's a great school," Remus said firmly. "Better than anything in London. Our exam marks are top of the country, and the teachers are good too."

"That is good to hear. And your free time? How is that spent?"

"Studying... and with friends..."

"Like that boy—James Potter? Giles was telling me, and so I had him looked into. His father runs his own firm, is that right? It's impressive. They've obviously done well for themselves, especially for immigrants. Who are the rest?"

Remus couldn't believe that Lyall had actually looked into his friends' families to ensure he was mingling with the proper sort. Or he could—he just wasn't sure which made him more angry.

"The rest of your friends, Remus," Lyall prompted. "What are their names?"

"Peter Pettigrew... a few girls..."

"Girls? I do hope you're behaving."

"I am!" Remus said, suddenly embarrassed. He'd never once talked about girls or dating with his father before, at least not aside from the general "don't be foolish" lecture. That had all been done with Giles. "And there's also another... his name's Sirius Black."

Lyall whipped his face around. "A Black? As the Blacks?"

"You know them?"

"There isn't a person of substance in all of England who doesn't know that family." Lyall's cool expression returned and he continued on, leaves crunching beneath his boots. "If he's really who I think he is, he could be worth having around. Be careful not to upset him. You're the last person who should be dealing with the wrath of that family."

Remus scowled. It bothered him that his father could even consider that he might have the faintest idea of who Sirius was, purely based on his family's name. It was the same reason Barty thought he knew anything about their family when his father started gossiping. Pure rubbish.

As he followed, Red Rum began snapping at Remus' ankles in attempts to get him to play. He brushed the pup off at first, but the baying was too cute. Cracking a small smile, he bent down to pat him.

“Do NOT—!” His father roared suddenly, making Remus flinch and rip his hand back.

"It's a bloody dog! He's bound to want to—"

“They’re working—learning to be obedient," Lyall scolded, before clicking his tongue in distaste. "I see you’re still just as soft with them, uncaring whether your ruin progress someone else has worked hard at. Here, make yourself useful and plant these for the pups to find.”

He passed Remus the bag of already dead fowl, freshly killed that morning at the estate, and lifted a whistle to his lips. Its silent sound drew every one of the dogs to him with utter compliance and when he was sure they were at attention, Lyall turned and set off through the trees, not even bothering to check whether the dogs were following. They did of course, with their tails upright and wagging the entire time.

"That's not obedience," Remus hissed to no one in particular, "that's brain-washing."

Taking the bag, he began marching in the opposite direction, stopping every time he found a downed tree or root hovel he should shove some dead fowl into. He tried not to gag as he pulled them from the bag, stuffing their limp bodies into the hiding spots for the puppies to "hunt". It was a disgusting task—some of the birds were still wet and they stunk to high-heaven—but it was a thoughtless one. Every now and then he'd hear a shot followed by a flurry of barking, but it was always a long ways off.

When Remus had finally managed to rid himself of the last game bird, he started back the way he'd come, following the distant sound of barking until he finally made it to the edge of the property's lake. There he found Lyall peering through the scope of his rifle, with Seabiscuit and Padfoot sitting loyally at his side, both panting in the July heat. Across the water, perhaps a hundred or so yards away, was a large family of ducks, swimming about innocently, completely unaware of the predators eyeing them from the shore. The puppies were nowhere in sight, probably already hunting down dead bird carcass.

“We’re going to be having a guest for dinner tonight,” Lyall said, without looking at him or lowering the gun.

“So that’s what you wanted to talk about,” Remus said dryly. "Knew it."

“Your behaviour of late has been satisfactory. I expect it to continue throughout her visit.”

“Her?” Remus could hardly believe it. He'd been right?! His own miserable father was actually seeing someone and now she was coming to their house?! He couldn't even remember the last woman he'd seen at the estate that wasn't a part of the staff. Probably some dippy wife of a random government official there on business.

“Her name is Sandra," Lyall said. "She's a good woman. She only wants to meet you. And you will behave yourself.”

“So what’s she to you?” Remus demanded. "Is she really your girlfriend or something?"

This time Lyall did look at him, sideways and measuring. “She's important.”

“Ha, I get it. You’ve finally cracked—realised that not even you can stand your own company.”

“Say what you wish now, but you will not embarrass me."

“As if I cared enough to make embarrassing you a hobby.”

Bringing it to his lips, Lyall gave a short blow on the whistle and both dogs at his side barked viciously, instantly scattering the waterfowl. As the birds took to the air he let loose a single shot, its bang echoing out across the forest like the crack of thunder. The downed duck smacked the lake’s surface and Padfoot was gone instantly, racing into the water to fetch it for his master.

Lyall lowered the gun, already squinting into the morning sun. “Maybe that’s the problem, Remus. You don’t care.”





* * *





He wanted to hate her—god, did he want to—but even Remus could deny it.

Sandra was nice.

She wasn't spectacular or even particularly loathsome like he’d hoped she would be, she didn't even mention the black eye—she was just nice. It sucked.

Rather than letting Lyall send Giles or someone else to fetch her, she'd driven on her own, in a fancy midnight-blue Bentley that made the Rolls look like a matchbox car. When the car pulled up, he'd found himself expecting some great beauty queen with hair big enough to block out the sun, but Sandra's hair wasn't big at all. It was combed modestly and perfectly coif, and her smile as she shook his hand was genuine. It was all certainly a surprise, but what had ended up shocking Remus the most was not her car or hair or generally pleasant disposition, but how—well—how old she was.

She wasn't old old, but she certainly wasn't young. And wasn't she supposed to be young? Was that not the main draw for a man who decides to date again so late in life—that said date would be fresh enough out of the baby bassinet that her youthful energy would surround everything and leave him feeling spry and virile again? Every other coffin-dodger with money refused to chase girls who weren’t young enough to be their daughter, but Sandra couldn’t have been that far off from Lyall's age at all. She had blonde hair that was streaked with the faintest signs of white and lines at the corners of her mouth and eyes that meant she must’ve smiled a lot. She even showed up to dinner wearing a fitted pantsuit and loafers. She was the complete opposite of everything Remus had been expecting.

It was still awkward, especially when she went to shake his hand, but Lyall had already threatened to take away his driving lessons if he didn’t make it through dinner without incident. So, while his father and Sandra sat at one end of the table, Remus sat at the other and ate without objection.

“Remus, your father tells me you go to school in Scotland,” Sandra said, trying to be personable despite the stilted atmosphere. "Hawkings College, right? I had a cousin who went there before transferring to King’s Canterbury.”

Remus nodded, wordlessly chewing on his braised spinach.

"Is it a good school?"

"... Yup."

"Lots of fun things to do?"

"Oh yeah, loads."

"Like what?"

Remus set his jaw and looked up. "My friends and I recently recreated a scene from a horror film."

"Oh?"

"Yeah. Made a real mess too—blood everywhere. A few students even passed out seeing it."

A look of pure fury flitted across Lyall's face, but Sandra remained unfazed. "Was it for a school play?"

He considered keeping up the nastiness, but Lyall's warning gaze was deterrent enough. "Yeah... something like that..."

"That sounds great then. I'd have loved to read the script. Do you like to read, Remus?"

“Sometimes.”

"It's all he does," Lyall amended. "Even when I'm trying to get him to do other things, he always has his nose in a book. It's where he gets all of those spunky retorts of his."

Sandra beamed. “So you’re a bookworm then?”

“No, not really," Remus ground out.

“Oh, but if you were—I should let you know that my family has a wonderful library on our property. You could borrow whatever you liked.”

“My school's library is fine, thanks.”

“I’ll bet. Hawkings is older than dust, isn’t it?”

“Some of the teachers are too.”

She smiled again, though Remus hadn’t really meant the quip in a friendly way. He began stuffing his mouth with baby potatoes, eating around the steak on his plate. It was too easy to picture the way the game birds had flopped around in his hand earlier that afternoon.

“Your father also tells me you’re fond of dogs,” Sandra started.

Remus looked up, meeting his father’s reproachful eye across the table. “Wow, guess he really has been chatty.”

Lyall’s upper lip twitched, but Sandra blazed past it. “I love animals too. My family actually breeds race horses—it’s how I met your father. There's plenty of crossover between the hounds and horses. I could even take you to one of the races sometime. The biggest ones happen during the fall and winter, but there’s always something going on. And perhaps when you’re back for Christmas we could make a day of it?”

Remus almost choked on a potato. Christmas?! She expected to be around for that long?

Elsewhere in the house, the phone rang and Remus felt suddenly apprehensive in his seat. Swallowing, he shook his head. “No thanks, Sandra, I’m not the biggest fan of horses actually.”

“Oh, that’s too bad," she said. "Would that mean you wouldn’t be interested in joining me for a ride sometime? I promise we don’t have to race if you don’t want to.”

“No—”

“He’d love to,” Lyall answered for him. “It’ll get him out of the house.”

“That’s funny considering you had an issue with how often I was gone before,” Remus shot back.

“Watch your temper.”

“It’s okay he doesn’t have to,” Sandra said kindly, before turning back to him, “but I can promise, Remus, that it won’t be like any ride you’ve had before.”

Rather than answering her, he leaned back in his seat and sipped his wine—it was the horribly bitter kind his father insisted on having with all meals. Before Lyall could object to his stubborn silence, a butler appeared in the room, bowing his head lightly.

“Who was on the phone then, Carsten?” Lyall asked, running his tongue across his teeth. “Was it McCarron with those stats I asked for?”

“Actually sir, the phone call was for the young master.”

Remus perked up in his seat and Lyall regarded him from the end of the table. “One of your school friends again, I expect,” he said sourly. “You’d think they’d have respect for proper meal times. You may call them back later.”

“Please let me take it,” Remus said stiffly, “Dad.”

“No, it can wait until after supper."

"But I told them I was going to call, and we were out with the dogs all day. I should get it now, it could be important."

"You're children. What could possibly be so important for children?"

"Please—"

"I've already said no. Now you’re being rude to our guest.”

Sandra reached out and covered Lyall’s hand with her own. “I don’t mind, love. Remus and I can talk again tomorrow, perhaps... on that ride of ours?”

It was sneaky and he didn’t like it, but Sandra was smiling broadly and he knew he was caught. Finally he nodded and Lyall raised his head before bringing his wine glass to his lips.

“Fine, you’re excused.”

Jumping up from his chair, Remus all but ran from the room, passing the butler in the hall and making his way to the salon to pick up the line.

“Hello?”

“Hey Moony, it’s me,” James’ cheery drawl echoed through the phone.

“God, you don’t know how good it is to hear your voice,” he moaned into the receiver.

“Miss me that much, do you?”

“Family dinners suck, mate.”

“Ha. I get that. But you know where you wouldn't have to sit through any of those? In Devon."

Remus sighed. "Prongs, you know I love ya, but I just don't think that..."

"I understand," James said. "It'd be a month away from home, and we only just got back from school. I don't like that you'll be on your own though. Maybe if Marlene weren't away in Africa, and Mary weren't in Paris—"

"Hey, I'll be fine. Besides, if Sirius could last every summer on his own out in bum-fuck Bath, then how hard could it be for me here?"

"Hm. Promise you'll come over when we're back then? Mum and Dad won't bite."

"Cross my heart and hope to die, stick a needle in my—!"

"Alright! I believe you..." James let out a big sigh, and Remus got the distinct feeling that there was more to be said.

"Prongs...?"

"I wasn't just calling to talk about Devon," James said all at once. "There's something else too. It's got to do with Sirius."

Remus' breath caught, and he switched the receiver to the other ear. "Have you heard from him then? Has he said—"

"No, Moony," James mumbled, “it's my letters. They've bounced—they were sent back. 'Return to sender' stamped all across the front."

It was as though the bottom had dropped out from Remus' stomach. He fell into the lounge chair by the phone, pulling the chord so taunt he nearly toppled the entire thing. "But—But I haven't gotten any of my letters back."

"Maybe they just haven't come yet..."

"You don't think they could've actually moved do you?"

"No way. His family's lived in that house for generations. Most likely they're keeping him shut up and he can't get to the mail anymore."

"Fuck." Remus bit down on his thumb nail. "Reckon he's alright?"

"Yeah, but I've got a bad feeling..."

“He’s brave, Prongs," Remus said quickly, suddenly determined to be optimistic enough for both of them; "He’ll be okay. Sirius said so himself—just a few more weeks and we’ll be back at school. Then he'll turn eighteen, get his inheritance from Alphard and he’ll never have to go back.”

“You’re right,” James said grimly. “You’ll still let me know if he contacts you though? I can’t be sure that he’d remember to write to the summer house.”

“I’ll call the second I hear from him. Cross my heart."

“Thanks Moony, I’ll see you in a few weeks then. You can come over for a barbecue or something—see Pete’s new drum kit, too.”

“Blimey, it’s not even his birthday!" Remus said in awe. "His parents actually went for it then?”

“Yeah, surprised him with it today. Pretty sure it was mostly thanks to Simeon, I guess he can be pretty convincing when he wants to be. The kit looks great though—a Premier five piece.”

“Nice. Can’t wait to jam.”

“Me neither.”

“Cool… I’ll see you then?”

“Okay... Bye, Moons.”

James hung up and Remus sat there, listening to the dial tone and twisting the receiver in his hands. When it came to Sirius it was easy to put on a brave face for his friends, but he couldn’t help but spend every other waking moment fretting through his teeth. If they'd always been able to get word through before, but now suddenly letters were being sent back, then what had changed?

That night Remus wrote two more letters. One being to Jillian—a short, polite thing since he’d neglected to answer the last four that she’d sent, and the other to Sirius, begging him to send word. In it he told him that they’d accept a smiley face scribbled on the back of a gum wrapper, anything that would tell them he was okay. Anything that could tide them over until September. He wasn't even sure Sirius' letter would get through, but when he handed the letters off to Giles the next morning to be posted, he sent with them all of the positive karma he'd managed to accumulate in his brief seventeen years of existence. He prayed it would be enough.

Only... Remus did not expect what would come next.





* * *





Sandra hadn't been kidding when she said her family raced horses. After arranging for Giles to drop him off at her family’s track, which boasted stands big enough to seat over fifty-thousand people, she'd waited personally for Remus to arrive, standing out front of the stadium with a grand smile on her face. Apart from the two of them, the only other people inside the racecourse was the team of construction workers he and Sandra had passed on their way inside.

“We’re doing some reconstruction over the summer so everything will be ready for the fall season,” she explained, while pointing out different parts of the building as she went. “I’m going to have an atrium put in the South wing with a glass ceiling, that way people can take the air even when rain hits.”

Remus just nodded along, entirely overwhelmed just being there, but as they made their way out onto the top of the stands, it occurred to him that Sandra wasn’t exactly dressed for horseback riding. She had boots on, but other than that she was wearing jeans and a simple blue button-up. He hadn’t dressed for the occasion either, but only because he’d planned to stay as far from the horses as possible under the guise of ‘just wanting to watch’.

“Well, here we are,” Sandra said, smiling over the track, which might’ve been beautiful had the green not been ripped up and left as dusty brown dirt instead. “We’re resurfacing the turf,” she said as if it was a funny joke, “but I figured this would be perfect for our ride.”

She started down the stairs toward the top of the stretch, and Remus scrambled after her. “Sandra, I think this is the part where I tell you that I don’t actually know how to ride."

“Oh, that’s fine, dear.”

"Yeah, I know all proper boys would've known how to ride back in your day but—"

" 'Back in my day'? Wow, thank you so much for that, Remus."

“Sorry! I just—I-I don’t know what my dad’s told you but I’ve never ridden—actually I hate horses!”

“That won't be a problem.”

"Really I'm terrified of them! I piss my pants every time one so much as looks me in the eye."

"Ha! This isn't a punishment, you know, Remus."

"I know—!" He babbled. "It's just—no offence, but I only came because—”

“Because your father told you to. I don’t mind, honestly.”

“I swear, Sandra—I’ll probably just fall off and break something! Or everything. I've done it. Just like a few days ago, even.”

They’d reached the bottom of the stands, and Sandra whirled around, still grinning broadly. “I don’t think you’ll have any issues with falling unless you want to stick your head that far out the window.”

Temporarily stupefied by the sentence had just been strung together for him, Remus simply blinked at her, and Sandra began to laugh before pointing just down the track. He followed it, and instead of finding a starting gate lined with horses, he saw only a fancy sports car waiting in the middle of the track, with its chrome freshly shined and cherry red paint-job glinting in the sun.

“I told you,” she said, “it’s not like any ride you’ve ever had before.”

And that was how Remus ended up strapping himself into the passenger seat of a Jaguar E-type sports car. He had never really been much for cars, but seeing the thing up close and feeling the purr of the engine beneath them had him positively giddy.

“Turf’s no good for cars,” Sandra said from the driver's seat; “but dirt? That’s what drag racing was made for.”

Remus gasped; "Yeah mean we're actually gonna race this thing?"

"Only if you're not worried about making a mess of your pants. Because that might ruin the leather."

He laughed, and shook his head. Maybe Sandra was cool. She raced cars, and she didn't even care about messing up the paint!

“How fast can it go?” He asked, peeking at the speedometer.

“How fast do you want to go?” Sandra said, before pulling a pair of sunglasses from the visor and passing him a white handkerchief. “Drop that out the window when you’re ready.”

“Why?”

She put on the sunglasses and shrugged; “It’s symbolic.”

Hiding a smile, Remus turned and threw the handkerchief out the window. Before it'd even had time to hit the ground, Sandra let loose a wild cry—WOO-HOO!—and slammed her foot down on the accelerator. Instantly Remus found himself slammed back against the seat as the back wheels of the car spun into a fishtail. He almost thought they'd never go forward, but then the rubber caught on soft earth and they were off—speeding down the track like lightning. With the windows down, the stagnant summer heat slammed him in the face mercilessly, but as they hurdled toward the first bend, Remus had never felt so exhilarated. When they hit the curve he slid against the door, clinging to the window’s edge as a mixture of terror and delight was ripped from his throat. Sandra was clearly an expert; she allowed the car’s rear to drag just long enough to kick up the dust before levelling everything out and leaving them to fly down the straight faster than any horse ever could.

In less than thirty seconds they'd hit the second corner and rounded onto the home-stretch, as wind ripped through Remus' hair and euphoria sang in his veins. When Sandra finally pulled the car to a skidding stop just past the start line, Remus was thrown against his seat belt and smacked back into the chair behind him while his heart still thrummed wildly in his chest.

“So,” she said, lifting her shades, “what’d you think?”

Remus let out a heavy breath, nearly panting. “I think that Giles is going to be so jealous!”

Sandra threw her head back and laughed. “I know, right? Don’t get me wrong, I love horses—have since I was a little girl—but there’s nothing like driving along with the wind gently blowing through your hair.”

“You call that gentle?”

She laughed again, light and happy. “I’m glad you came with me today, Remus. Thank you.”

The air suddenly felt heavy with unsaid promises, and Remus shifted uncomfortably in his seat. He almost wished they were driving again, but Sandra just sat there watching him until it was obvious that she wasn't going to make another move. The ball was in Remus' court now.

“So…" he pandered, "how long have you known my dad...?”

“Ah, I was waiting for that question actually.” Sandra put the Jaguar in park and stretched her arms out ahead of her. “I’ve known your father for quite a few years, in fact. He was a business consultant for my late husband, Paul, who passed just over a year ago. Lyall was a great friend to him.”

“There’s a first,” Remus mumbled out of the corner of his mouth.

“Ah, I have heard that you and your father find it hard to get along,” Sandra said lightly, “and I know it’s not any of my business, but I can’t help but be a little jealous. Paul and I never had any children. We were each other’s only family beyond our parents, you see.”

“You didn’t want kids of your own?”

“Oh, children? No, nasty little buggers.” She smirked. “I’m only kidding. I can’t have children actually. But Paul and I were happy on our own for the most part. Saved time for other things. This was his car, in fact.”

Remus trailed his hand across the window edge, feeling the soft white leather under his fingertips. “S’a nice car.”

"Yes, it is. He didn't get the chance to take it out much before he passed, so I always make sure I have the most fun I can while driving it."

"That's too bad. Nice of you, though."

“Thank you. Does that mean you want to go again?”

Remus raised his eyes to Sandra's in an instant. “Hell yes.”

“I was hoping you'd say that,” she beamed, grabbing the gear shift. “And who knows, maybe if you’re lucky I’ll let you take her for a few spins yourself.”

Remus looked from her to the track as the engine revved. Then they were off again and it was pure bliss. He’d never felt so weightless.

After that they spend the entire afternoon just sailing around the track—Sandra could even do the circuit in reverse. Remus never got tired of it, not for a second. He could’ve lived with the wind in his hair and the roar of the engine dulling each of his senses. There was no space to worry or panic while the car was moving, and it was the most relief he'd felt in months.

Sandra was true to her word in the end and even let him take a turn behind the wheel, which practically vibrated under his grip. It was intimidating at first, having that much power under his thumb, but all it took was a single lap for Remus to find that same euphoric thrill as when Sandra was driving. Every loop brought more confidence, until eventually he was pushing almost one hundred miles an hour on the straight-aways. Once they’d managed to reduce most of the petrol in the tank, Remus’ found that his hearing was severely diminished but he didn’t even mind. He’d even agreed to call Sandra ‘Sandy’—at her insistence of course.

On the way home Remus found himself excited all over again. He couldn’t wait to tell his friends. The ringing in his ears felt the same as it did after seeing that band play their first year together. He knew Sirius would’ve absolutely loved it of course, and he imagined the pair of them whipping around the track together after they’d finished school. Sandra had told him that they redo the turf regularly to combat wear on the turf, perhaps then.

Dusty waylaid him on the way in the door, slobbering across the front of his trousers; not that he cared much—they were already covered in a fine layer of dirt and grim from the track. As Remus bent down to scratch at the dog’s stomach, he heard the phone rang distantly. He waited for his father or someone else to answer, but then a butler appeared—Gregory, he thought his name was.

“The phone, sir,” the maybe-Gregory said.

"Who is it?"

"Another young man. He's asked for you by name."

It was James again then. Remus got to his feet with a nod.

“I’ll be right there,” he told him, before patting Dusty on the stomach and watching as the hound turned over. “C’mon boy! Let’s go get the phone—let’s go get the phone!”

He raced Dusty to the salon and they skidded in together. Though not as nimble as he once was, the old dog turned at the last moment, upsetting a small end table with his tail and nearly knocking a vase of flowers to the ground. Diving to the ground, Remus caught it at the last second—a save that would’ve left even James impressed—and sighed as Dusty congratulated him by licking his face.

“This is what they mean when they say animals resemble their owners,” he grumbled, before righting the vase. “Sit,” he told him. Dusty didn’t, but that was more Remus’ fault than his anyway.

“Dozy dog,” he muttered, before walking to the phone and picking up the receiver where the butler had left it sitting off the hook. “Prongs, I'm so glad you called! You'll never guess what I just did. Dad's girlfriend, Sandy, she—”

“Moony.”

Remus’ knees nearly buckled. He had to sit down before he could speak again, clutching onto the receiver with both hands.

“Sirius… is—is that you?”

“Yeah, s’me.”

For a second he didn’t have a single thought in his head at all, apart from how tired Sirius sounded. Each syllable was stretched, like it took every ounce of his energy to get them out. Remus cleared his throat, suddenly more nervous than ever.

“We… We haven’t heard from you in weeks!” He chittered. “Blimey, are you okay? Where are you—who’s phone is this?”

“Moony,” Sirius said again, like he was begging, “I just really need your help…”

Chapter 66: Per Aspera Ad Astra


Chapter Summary

Honestly, these boys. What are we to do with them?



Chapter Notes

CW: References to abuse and neglect as well as smoking.

A/N: Gotta be honest, I was NOT expecting such a reaction from that cliff-hanger, hah! I suppose it might be because I don't commonly feature them within this fic, but ya'll were reeeeeeeling. Naturally, I loved it ofc, but I swear I wasn't trying to edge you with this long wait!
