See the end of the chapter for more notes



How can I try to explain?

When I do he turns away again,

It’s always been the same, same old story;

From the moment I could talk,

I was ordered to listen;

Now there’s a way,

And I know that I have to go away…

- “Father and Son” Cat Stevens, 1970



When Sirius called and asked for his help, Remus made the split-second decision that he would go to the ends of the earth to reach him. Luckily he only had to go as far as Dover.

The little port town was just over an hour from London, which meant he could leave and meet him before it even got dark. There was only one problem.

He had no way of getting there.

Sirius hadn't divulged much, but he did admit to swiping another passenger's ticket to get aboard the ferry across the Channel, unable to pay the ticket fee himself. Remus could tell he felt bad, but his current lack of funds meant that hopping a train into the city wasn't an option on his own. The attendants would catch him and since he wasn't legally an adult, he would be held until his parents came to retrieve him. Sirius didn't need to extrapolate further. Remus considered taking the line down himself with enough fare to pay both their ways back, but it'd twice as long, and something in Sirius’ voice had made him exceedingly nervous—like if he didn’t reach him as soon as possible, he’d never see him again.

It stung later, mostly when he was being shouted at, but he hadn’t even stopped to consider asking Giles for help. It would take too long—would mean too many questions. Sirius needed him and he needed him now. Going from the phone, to his bedroom, to the car, had taken less time than it took for Giles to polish off his evening brandy. Remus didn’t even remember swiping the keys off the parlour table—it was all a blur. The Roll’s front seat felt a lot bigger without the old driver sitting in there with him, but he didn't hesitate to turn the car on and begin rolling it down the rocky driveway. Flashing his high beams so the gateman wouldn’t recognise him, Remus did his best to look bulky under Giles’ jacket and cap, which he’d stolen off one of the pegs by the kitchen door. He’d always maintained the opinion that he wasn’t a thief, but for Sirius he’d be anything.

The nerves didn’t really set in until he was driving down the M20 motorway, white-knuckling the steering wheel and trying not to drift out of his lane. As wildly anxious as he was for Sirius, he couldn't bring himself to drive any faster than the speed limit. Getting himself pulled over wasn't going to help Sirius anyway. Most cars just sped on past, not paying the Rolls any mind, and Remus was almost able to relax until a lorry triple his size ran up from behind and gave a honk so blaringly loud that he nearly launched himself into the sedan’s roof.

What are you doing, a voice said, you don’t even have a driving license!

Without room for reason, he pushed back; I ain’t eighteen either but that didn’t stop the bloke in the bar from serving Pete, James, and me those pints two weeks ago.

A Ford raced past him in the next lane, so close they could’ve kissed mirrors and Remus struggled to not veer into the barrier.

You’re gonna die, you stupid fucking idiot!

“Oh shut up,” Remus grumbled, flicking on the radio.

The music helped some—soothed him at least—but even if he were a seasoned driver he still would’ve been distracted. Sirius’ short phone conversation replayed over and over again in his head, becoming more terrifying with each iteration. Remus struggled to stay calm. Sirius wasn't dying, he just needed help, and now help was coming. He'd been calm too—tired-sounding, mostly—but still eerily calm.

“I’m in Dover,” he’d said, after asking for his help.

“Dover?” Remus had exclaimed; “What the bloody fuck are you doing there?”

“You know where it is then?"

"Yes, I know where fucking Dover is!"

"Good. Can you come get me?”

“Can I... Of course I can come, but what—”

“I’m at the port, the one with all the ferries. Can you find that?”

“Yes, but Sirius—you have to tell me what’s going on!”

“Can’t," Sirius sighed; "there's too much to tell. I dialled your number wrong the first time, and I already had to bum the money to pay for this one. If you come, I promise to tell you everything once you get here. You can get here, right? Just you?”

“Just...? Aw, fuck Sirius—"

“—Please insert two pound fifty for another three minutes.”

There was a bang, like Sirius had punched the machine. “Damn tourist rates.”

“Sirius,” Remus tried again, “are you sure you're okay?”

Sirius was quiet for a few precious seconds, but finally he answered, low and more tired than before; “I will be once you get here.”

Then the line had cut and Remus’ life had gone from leisurely morning drives to unhinged grand theft auto. Lyall was going to have him strung up when he found out. Probably cut him up and feed him to the dogs. And Giles might just let him—there was no way he hadn’t noticed the absence of his vexing ward and precious car.

It doesn’t matter, he told himself, Sirius called, which means he’s not dead in a ditch somewhere. And it means he wasn't ignoring your letters. Maybe.

A sharp ding echoed from the dashboard, knocking him free of his thoughts, and Remus looked down to find the petrol meter had fallen into the red.

You dickhead—you didn’t even stop to check if you had any gas?!

Nervous all over again, he took the first exit off the motorway and limped the car long until he managed to find a fill station just off the side of the road. He pulled the Rolls up to an empty pump and turned the car off, taking a moment to compose himself before making his way inside the station. Wiping his sweaty palms on the sides of his trousers, Remus waited in line for his turn at the counter, keeping a careful eye on the Rolls through the window.

"Next," the station attendant called lazily, as the man in front shambled off. Remus jumped to, stepping up to the counter and pulling his his wallet out of his pocket. He nearly fumbled it, but when he looked up at the attendant he found him scratching his neck and yawning disinterestedly. Really, he couldn’t have been much older than Remus was, judging by the amount of acne across his forehead.

“Ten on pump five,” Remus said, as casually as he could.

The guy began to ring him up. “Nice car,” he said over a second yawn, gesturing lazily to the window.

Instant panic. “It's, uhm—it’s a rental,” Remus stammered.

“Hm. You said you wanted ten on five?”

“Er—yes.”

The attendant hit a few more buttons on the register, which popped open with a dull clatter, and Remus passed him a ten pound note before looking down at the large sweets display across the counter’s front.

“These too,” he said quickly, dropping several chocolate bars on the countertop.

The guy raised a brow, but took the sweets. Remus swallowed.

“And a pack of Embassy Number One’s.”





* * *





Remus streaked down the pavement, dodging the crowd as they mulled from the ferry terminal toward the bus loop and car park. The last boat had just gotten in, bringing with it the smell of salt and sea, with just a hint of summertime and rotting fish. Remus had never been to the sea before; seeing its vast waters as they stretched out all the way to the horizon made him feel calm at first, but also like he was running out of time.

Just beyond the docks the sun was setting, lighting up the entire sky with a bright orange glow. Seagulls crooned overhead and the leaving ferries blared their loud horns, but Remus paid no attention to any of it. He was too busy scanning every face for a hint of familiarity; a cheeky smirk, a straight nose, a pair of storm-grey eyes. Instead all the noses were too wide or too curved, the grey eyes without that tell-tale glint of mischievousness. He went as far down the wharf as he could, throwing himself at the railing and staring out over the ocean as people unloaded from the ferry. No one so much as paid him a second glance.

With Sirius nowhere in sight, Remus finally stopped a ferry attendant, patting him hurriedly on the shoulder while nearly out of breath.

“Have you seen a guy—a—a boy. My age, about this tall—with long black hair?”

The attendant reached up to scratch beneath his cap, beads of sweat dripping down his temple. “ ‘fraid not son. You see lots of people on the wharf, gets too hard to distinguish 'em all. Have a look around if ye' want, but best be getting on soon. Terminal’s closing in a few minutes.”

Huffing, Remus spun away and scanned the crowd again. It was thinner now, most people having moved on, but there was not a hint of raven-black among them.

"C'mon Sirius..." He moaned under his breath. "Where are you?"

He circled the wharf once more, and then checked all the bus stops. Even tried swinging over the rail to get a peak at the barnacle-covered rocks below, thinking Sirius might have slipped away to avoid being noticed. Nothing.

"I swear to god, if you let yourself be kidnapped because you thought it'd make a funny joke, then I'll..."

There.

Remus thought he might throw up. The relief was immediate—all that had happened was a single man with a briefcase stepped aside and he finally caught a glimpse of someone sitting alone on a stone bench, head tipped back and feet crossed at the ankles. He didn't see his face—Remus didn't have to. He would know Sirius Black anywhere.

“Sirius!” He shouted, starting forward. Sirius’ head snapped up, blinking in the evening light until finally he noticed him. Almost stumbling on the pavement, Remus raced to him. Sirius was slow to get up, but it didn’t matter. He reached him in a few short strides and clapped his arms around him, squeezing so tight that Sirius gave a little gasp.

“You crazy tosser!” Remus wailed. “What’s happened to you?”

An echo of a sigh brushed his ear, but Sirius still hugged him back. “Hey, Moony.”

He pulled away, glaring at him while his eyes began to burn with unshed tears. “ ‘Hey’? You're gonna 'hey' me now? Sirius, what are you doing here?”

“Oh, jus’ went for a little vacation, s’all,” Sirius said, giving him a smile that didn’t reach his eyes. Most of his hair was tucked up in a cap and he had a faint bruise on his left cheek, with dark circles under both eyes. The clothes he was wearing were unsettling—a stiff grey button-up that looked itchier than hell and matching slacks. The whole thing made him looks as though he'd just gotten out of prison. Blimey, maybe he had.

“Where were you?” Remus pushed.

“France. Belgium before that.”

His eyes bulged. “Belgium? Bloody—why?!”

“It’s a long story.”

“You promised you’d tell me.”

“I know, but can we do it somewhere else? Please Moony, I’m really tired.”

With a pang in his chest, Remus sighed and looked around. Hardly anyone was left on the wharf, and those who were, were bustling by with bags in hand, not paying them any mind. Sirius had no bags, just the clothes on his back.

“Okay,” he said. “C’mon, the car’s this way.”

Leading the way back to the carpark, Remus opened the Roll’s door for Sirius and watched as he stood back and raised an eyebrow.

“Don’t tell me this is yours?”

“No, it's not,” Remus scoffed. “So bloody get in before a bobby starts sniffing around.”

Sirius looked at him and Remus saw the briefest hint of a smile on his face as he slid into the front seat. Lord how he'd missed that smile. Stomach in knots, he closed the door after him and went around to the driver’s seat, strapping himself in and starting up the car. It was immensely hard—like holding back an atom bomb, really—to not just simply explode on Sirius with all his questions, but doing that would probably just make Sirius retreat further. As they pulled out of the car park and left the port behind, Sirius kept his head to the window, watching it until everything passed out of sight. Only then did he finally look relieved.

They drove in silence for the first bit. Remus tried hard to focus on the road, but if there was only a single distraction in the world, then it was going to be Sirius Black. What with his quippy jokes, bobbing leg, snapping or strumming fingers—except now Sirius wasn’t doing any of it. Utterly still and silent as a grave, it was like all the life and energy had been drained out of him. Remus was reminded of last January, when Sirius had returned to school cold and distant. Now the twilight reflected poorly off his pale skin, turning him as grey and muted as his clothes.

As the evening road lights of the M20 began to flicker across their faces, Remus remembered the chocolate bars and smokes he’d picked up from the petrol station. Licking his lips, and he gestured to the glove box.

“There’s some chocolate and smokes in the glove compartment.”

Sirius looked back from the window, blinking a bit. “Chocolate and cigarettes? How much more ‘Remus Lupin’ can you get?”

“Just eat. Chocolate might be a bit melted now though.”

Bending forward, Sirius opened the glovebox and pulled out a bar and the pack of Embassys. Always the dramatic, he went for the cigarettes first, popping the top of the carton.

"I see you didn't bother to wait," he smirked, putting one of the remaining cigarettes between his teeth.

"I paid for them. And 'sides, you still owe me for the last round."

"Mhm. Don't worry, I'm good for it. I mean, look at me—simply dripping in wealth."

Remus smiled a bit, reassured by the joke. With one hand on the wheel, he shimmied his lighter out of his pocket, holding it up and flicking the flame to life. Sirius came forward and lit his smoke, before cracking the Roll’s window and exhaling in relief.

“God, that’s better,” he moaned, ripping open a chocolate bar and taking bites between puffs. “You’re actually quite good,” Sirius said over a full-mouth, once he’d gotten some energy back. Remus looked to him in question and Sirius gestured to the road with his cigarette.

“What? Oh, you mean driving. Yeah, told you I was getting lessons.”

“No, you didn’t.”

“Yeah, I did. Said so in my—”

Remus stopped abruptly, remembering how he hadn’t gotten a single written response from Sirius all summer. Sirius, clever as he was, caught up easily. He swallowed a mouthful of chocolate and caramel and carefully licked the stickiness from his fingers before pulling another drag.

“If you wrote me any letters, I never got them,” he said, exhaling.

“Figured as much,” Remus mumbled. He sounded disappointed, but really it was a relief. He’d been so worried that Sirius wasn’t writing to him because of what had happened in the bathroom on their last day of school, as though things had suddenly changed between them—that they weren’t friends anymore. His only reassurance that he wasn’t the only one being frozen out had come when Sirius hadn’t responded to any of James or Peter’s letters either, though that had hardly been cause for celebration.

“Do you want to tell me what you were doing in Belgium now?” Remus asked.

Sirius kept his face to the window. “It was mum’s idea, I think. I couldn’t tell what it was, but things were different when I got back."

"Different how?"

"Different like... they didn't notice me. At first I thought it was a punishment—the ignoring. Mum's never been able to do it before, she always wants the last word, but this time it was like I... wasn't even there anymore. None of them talked to me for the first two weeks."

"Not even Regulus?”

"He did... a little. I tried apologising for the prank, but he didn't care. Not that he should have to. It was... bad. You know, what I did to him... Pretty sure mum told him not to talk to me too. I didn't realise it then, but she was cutting ties—just waiting for everything to be ready." Sirius laughed dryly. "For the fucking paperwork to come through."

"I don't understand..."

Sirius took another drag, but he must've inhaled straight into his lungs because it left him coughing. "Guess she'd—" cough; "—She’d heard about this school that supposedly could straighten out even the worst benders." Cough, cough; "... She probably thought it would work on me too.”

Remus stared at him in alarm, before snapping his eyes back to the road. Benders?

“You mean she knows about you and—er… other… guys?”

“Ha—” Sirius paused to clear his throat. "I just mean she wanted her problem solved—me solved. I turn eighteen this year, so they had to send me away before then if they had any chance of getting me committed.”

“Committed?!”

“I know, right? Turns out crazy runs in my family too. We’ve so much in common, you and I.” Sirius laughed half-heartedly, then frowned very deeply. “Sorry… Didn’t mean that.”

Remus hardly cared. If there was a time to be mad at Sirius Black, it wasn’t now.

“So weren't they… gonna let you come back to school?” He asked.

“Nope. The school runs all year round, and if you're really good—summers too. Hah... Guess we know now what Reg was on about when he talked to you before.”

Putting two and two together, Remus grew suddenly furious. “You mean the little bleeder knew that they were gonna send you away and he still didn’t say anything? At all?!”

“Can't hardly blame him,” Sirius said, uncharacteristically apathetic. “I was a right bastard, and he was just trying to save his own skin. Probably figured that he’d get sent away too if he tried saying anything against it.”

That’s no excuse, Remus silently seethed. Sirius was right, Regulus had no loyalty to anyone.

“So how’d you end up in Dover then?” He asked finally.

“The school—they call it a school, but it’s more like an institution. Kids from all over, most of us didn't even speak the same language, not that they allowed much interaction. It's all about 'healing' or some crap. 'Healing the mind through constraint of the body'—pretty sure they got their slogans from the Mansons... So it goes like, you've got your crazy kids—I'm talking the kind that use their own shit to draw on the walls. Then there's your 'problem kids', like moi for example, though I'm pretty sure I was small fry in comparison. A couple of them had already been to prison, though none of them could roll a joint like you."

"You had weed with you?"

"There's a mule everywhere, Moons. But yeah... got the strap for that one. And everything’s grey—the clothes, the beds, the walls, and there’s bars on most of the windows. It's like a real prison. It was in Ghent. I’m still not exactly sure what part—didn’t stop to ask—but at least it was in the city and not in some nowhere part of the countryside. Then I would've been really fucked.”

Remus stared at the road. He hated the Blacks. Who could do that to their own son?

“And... how long were you there for?”

“A week, maybe? What’s the date anyway?”

“It’s the twenty-second.”

Sirius swore. “Almost two then.”

“Fucking—How could you not know what day it was?”

“They have an ‘isolation room’. You get sent there if you lip off too much. Guess I was in there longer than I thought.”

Remus’ hands tightened on the wheel. “Jesus…”

“Yeah, but you should’a saw it when I started swearing at them in German—then French! They understood that, ha. They probably thought I was just some dumb English prat—they got all angry and nasty and this big woman—I’m talking built like a fridge, bint was massive—she screwed up her face real and tight and she… well, she…” Sirius trailed off. “Doesn’t matter. When they let me out I managed to sneak out through a second floor window when one of the crappy matrons left her office open. Thought they’d know better actually.”

“You and bloody windows.”

Sirius smirked and held up his hands. “No injuries this time, promise. Anyway, after I got out I hitchhiked across the border into France with this old farmer. He only spoke Dutch, but seemed nice enough. Kept showing me this picture of his wife he kept in his wallet. I think she was dead. But he got me all the way to Calais, and I walked the rest of the way toward the ferry.”

“Fuck... Hitchhiking...?" Remus took a breath. "Mary’s in France, why didn’t you just call her?”

Sirius grimaced slightly. “I thought about it, but explaining everything to her with her family around sounded horrible, and besides, Paris is south of Calais. I wanted to go north.”

“Did you even fucking sleep at all?”

“No, but it’s fine now, you’re here.”

Remus pressed his lips together in a thin line. He wished they had the radio, but this part of the highway was like a radio dead-zone. At least it was finally dark out, and eventually the yellow road lamps had fallen away. The only light came from their headlights and those of passing cards on the other side of the motorway.

“Want me to take over for a while?” Sirius asked casually.

“Do you even know how to drive?”

“No, but it can’t be that hard. You’re doing it.”

“Sod off. I’m fine,” Remus said. “You should sleep. There’s a jacket in the back you can use for a blanket if you want.”

Flicking his cigarette stub out the window, Sirius turned around and pulled Giles’ jacket over him, settling back against the car door. Remus watched him subtly, and Sirius’ eyes eventually slid closed.

“… Moony?”

“You’re supposed to be sleeping.”

“I know, it’s just… Don’t crash.”

Remus smiled to himself. “Sleep.”

He heard Sirius chuckle, but turned quiet after that, too tired to keep his eyes open any longer. Remus drove on in silence, occasionally sneaking a glance to his right. As always, Sirius looked best in the moonlight. No longer grey, but luminous again. Funny how friends and laughter could do that. The flat cap he was wearing still hid most of his hair but a thick lock had come loose just behind his ear, draping down his neck like a curtain.

Around twenty minutes later, as they were nearing Bexleyheath, the radio gave a crackle. Picking up the station he’d lost on his way to Dover, it cut into a song mid-way and suddenly the radio was playing the Beatles over the Roll’s dull roar;





‘—comes the sun, do, do, do,

Here comes the sun,

And I say, it’s alright…’



Not wanting to wake Sirius, Remus reached out to turn the volume down, when suddenly a voice croaked out; “Don’t.”

He froze, glancing between the road and Sirius, who was peering at him over the shoulder of the jacket.

“It’s okay,” Sirius murmured, “I like it.”

Slowly, Remus pulled back and gave a nod; “Alright, then.”

Sirius smiled, and when the next verse picked up again he began to sing along, more than a weak murmur than anything else. Remus loved it.





‘Little darling, the smiles returning to the faces,

Little darling, it seems like years since it’s been here;

Here comes the sun, do, do, do,

Here comes the sun,

And I say, it’s alright…’



Remus relaxed in his seat, leaning one arm against the window as he drove. By all accounts he’d had a good summer so far, but now that Sirius was there, all else paled in comparison. That was what love was, he supposed—even if Sirius had asked him to forget all of it, he couldn’t. It would’ve taken everything he had to do that.

But it took nothing to sing along, so as Sirius murmured the lyrics, sleepy and finally at peace, he did too.





* * *





He knew Giles was going to be mad, but this was something else. At nearly midnight, Remus had pulled up to the Lupin estate’s front gates in the Rolls. Sirius had already squeezed himself into the foot space between his seat and the glove compartment, and with the jacket draped over him it was as though he weren’t there at all. The gateman still gaped at Remus as he pulled up, but he just held a finger to his lips and the guy eventually let him in.

“The Latin on the gate,” Sirius said, flipping the jacket off of him after they’d driven through; “ ‘Homo homini lupus est’—does it mean what I think it means?”

“Oh you mean you don’t know? Thought you were taking Latin for an A-Levels.”

Sirius gave him an unimpressed look and Remus smirked.

“It means, ‘a man is a wolf to his fellow man’.”

“Ew. That your family motto?”

“Guess so.”

“Well, I suppose it’s still better than mine.”

Remus made sure to pull up tightly to the house, next to the kitchen entrance and just out of view from the main windows. “What’s yours then?”

“ ‘Toujours pur’—always pure.”

“Damn French people.”

“D’accord.”

Releasing their seat belts, they got out together and briskly scuttled up the front steps, careful to remain as inconspicuous as possible. There were no lights on inside, which made for some relief, and using Giles’ keys Remus was able to open the front door and let them inside.

“Wow. Guess you Lupins do pretty well for yourselves,” Sirius said, gazing around at the grand foyer. “Hard to believe a bloke as hard as you grew up in a place like this.”

Remus pushed him toward the stairs. “I know you’re just saying that, and I hate you for it. Now move on already.”

Sirius opened his mouth to make another jab, but instead all that came out was a; “HAVE YOU LOST YOUR GODDAMN MIND?!”

“Crikey!” Sirius gasped, as they both practically fell over in shock. More quick to the draw, Remus shoved him the rest of the way up the stairs and then promptly stumbled back down them on his own, ready to head Giles off as he stormed out of the hallway. The old driver appeared not half a second later, face red up to his hairline, with his fists raised as though he were about to go several rounds with Muhammad Ali.

“STEALING A CAR?” He roared, halting in the middle of the foyer. “YOU ACTUALLY STOLE THE CAR?”

“Have you told my dad?” Remus asked automatically.

“HAVE I—no, but I bloody well should have! I thought I’d raised you better! I mean, really—what were you THINKING?!”

I wasn’t, Remus told himself. And it was true—it had all been about getting to Sirius. Not that he could tell Giles that. As good as Giles was, he couldn’t trust that he wouldn’t try and send Sirius back home. Adults were like that, always assuming they knew best. Well, he was the one who knew Sirius best.

“I’m sorry,” he said honestly. “Would you believe me if I told you it was important?”

“What could be so bloody important that a seventeen year-old has to commit grand theft auto?!”

“I…” Remus looked down, then his eyes slid to the second floor, where Sirius was still hidden out of sight. “… I can’t tell you.”

“Can’t you at least lie then?” Giles snapped.

“You really want me to lie?”

“Of course not! Might make me feel better though!”

“And here I thought you’d raised me better than that.”

“Ooh, you cheeky…” Giles sucked in a deep breath, growing big in the chest and puckering his mouth like a balloon ready to explode. “So what?” He grunted. “You’re not gonna tell me where it is you were?”

It hurt, but no, he couldn’t. Remus shook his head. “I didn’t go to the End though,” he added quickly, “I swear.”

“I bloody-well know you didn’t go to the East End! If you had, the Rolls would be down a tire and its back window would be smashed in!”

“But they’re not!” He agreed. “So that means everything’s okay…?”

“Everything is most definitely NOT OKAY!”

Remus winced. “Alright, I can tell you're mad—"

"Try FURIOUS!"

"—But can you at least wait to punish me until tomorrow? I promise to do whatever you say without any complaints.”

It wasn’t enough, not by miles, but the old man had clearly run out of steam. He deflated with another unsatisfied grunt and thrust out his open palm. Remus stared at it a moment, before understanding. Quickly, he stepped forward and handed over the keys. Giles snapped them up like hot coal and promptly dropped them into his pocket.

“Fine, go,” he lashed; “Get to bed before I put you over my goddamn knee. And for your sake, you best haven’t put a scratch on ‘er!”

Remus couldn’t help it; he threw his arms around Giles and squeezed tight. “Thanks, Gil. Knew you’d understand.”

For all his anger, Giles did not push him away. He did, however, sputter a bit in surprise; “Er—don’t think this means you’re suddenly fancy-free! I’m gonna work you for all you’re sodding worth, starting first-thing tomorrow!”

“Whatever you say,” Remus said, not the least bit bothered.

Once the hug had long overstayed the usual Remus’ level of welcome, Remus let go and started up the stairs, an extra spring in his step.

“Don’t you forget—tomorrow morning, seven AM!” Giles called after him. “You’re going to scrub that car until I can pick my teeth in its bumper!”

“Oh goodie, so I only have to scrub enough for three teeth then?”

“What’d you say?”

“Nothing!”

“Yeah, just get going, ya little blighter! And be quiet already, it’s bleedin’ midnight!”

As Giles fell away behind him, Remus obediently raced up the rest of the stairs and swung himself around the banister. He was aiming for the hall, ready to tell Sirius that they’d actually gotten away with all of it when he nearly tripped over him instead. Sirius, who was crouching behind the railing like a spying child, looked up at Remus as he skidded to a halt just before his shins.

“So that’s Giles,” Sirius sniggered; “Seems like a decent enough bloke.”

“You’re a dirty eavesdropper,” Remus said lightly, before reaching down and taking his arm. Hauling Sirius to his feet, they quietly scuttled down the hallway to his bedroom, and soon enough they were both slipping inside.

“Sorry for the mess. I mostly tell the maids not to come in here,” Remus said as he got the lights. They came on all at once, illuminating the scattered piles of books, records, and unfinished summer homework, as well as all of the laundry and dishes he’d neglected to clear away. Among them was a breakfast tray from several days ago, still sitting by the door and now looking decently mouldy. Snatching up a dirty t-shirt from the floor, Remus quickly covered it while Sirius watched him from the corner of his eye, looking amused.

“Nah, s’fine,” he said, taking the room in and appearing almost mesmerized by the grand space. “Though I’d be lying if I said I weren’t surprised. You’re so neat at school.”

Remus put his hands in his pockets and shrugged. “This ain’t school, I guess…”

“Got that right.” Sirius stopped to right an old tea mug, which had fallen from atop a stack of books at the foot of his bed. “Your room's pretty huge though. You could fit like… thirty marauders in here.”

“You’re telling me yours ain’t bigger?”

“No, it is.” Sirius kept looking around. At the heavy velvet curtains, the dour wallpaper, the ancient rugs. “I dunno, maybe it’s me, but it just doesn’t feel like you…”

“It's a stranger’s room,” Remus agreed, following him in. “I know. Never cared for it much myself.”

“Mine neither,” Sirius said, looking at him softly. Remus returned the look, and suddenly the urge to kiss him was so great he could feel his mouth begin to water. Luckily Sirius was too enamoured by the room to notice. He’d already moved away again, spotting Andy’s guitar, which Remus had left leaning up against the far side of his bed.

“This I remember,” he grinned. “Thought James took it for the summer?” Throwing himself over the bed, Sirius reached for the instrument and sat up, slinging it across his lap. He took a moment to pluck a few strings before wincing. “Ooh, out of tune.”

“Well, that would be my fault,” Remus said, coming forward to lean casually against the bedpost. “James actually got his own. He lent me yours so I could try practising on it, but I’m not very good.”

“He got his own guitar?” Sirius echoed with delight. “And you’re playing now?”

“I only gave it a shot, yeah, but it’s really James you should hear. He’s been practising every day—oh, and Pete got his own drum set!”

“Actually?”

“Yeah! I haven’t seen it myself but James says it’s positively ace. Guess there’s a lot you gotta catch up on, Padfoot. Heh.” He’d meant it as a joke, but Sirius looked down to the guitar, gently patting its body with his hand and Remus knew it’d been the wrong thing to say.

“Sirius, I didn’t mean—”

“No, it’s okay,” Sirius said quickly, “s’normal… the summers. Used to suck more when we were kids, but ya get through it. Like Christmas. I'd rather you catch me up anyway.”

“Y-You would?”

“Yeah, James and Pete take forever to tell a story, but you’re much more streamlined. And besides, they’re off at the summer house anyway, right? I don't think I can handle listening to them go on about the same damn beach. It's always the same—sandy.”

“Oh yeah, right. Heh...” Remus bit his lip over a smile. “We should tell them that you’re here actually. And what happened. They’re really worried.”

“Nah, it’s late,” Sirius said, shaking his head adamantly. He was still wearing that ugly cap. “Besides, I don’t want to ruin their holiday.”

“You wouldn’t ruin it. They’d be thrilled—not the Belgium part, the part about you being alright…”

“Yeah, they’d be thrilled, alright. So thrilled they’d hop the first train back to make sure you’re telling the truth. Trust me, I know James.”

“So… what? You just want to wait until they get back? That’ll be almost a month from now.”

Sirius looked up at him in earnest. “Would that be a problem? I just… Sorry... I know you didn’t exactly ask your family if I could visit.”

Remus was quick to correct his mistake; he didn't want Sirius to think he was unwelcome. “Shut up. Do you really think I ask permission to do things?”

Sirius chuckled quickly. “You’re right. I think tonight is case in point enough. But I still don’t want to intrude.”

“Why? Intruding’s never bothered you before.”

Sirius shrugged, then played a few more sad notes.

Almost frowning, Remus reached out and grabbed hold of the head of the guitar. “I’m kidding—it’s fine, Sirius. You can stay here. For… For as long as you want.”

Sirius looked to his hand on the guitar, licking his lips. “Thanks, Moony.”

“Don’t thank me anymore, you would’ve done the same.”

“Obviously.” Sirius smiled and Remus sheepishly let go of the guitar.

“Are you… Are you hungry then?”

“Nah, jus’ tired. I could use a shower though.”

“Yeah, you do smell a bit like a sewer.”

“Ow. A sewer of roses, maybe.”

Remus pointed to the far wall. “Toilet’s there. Should have everything. Use whatever you want, just make sure you lock the other door. Sometimes the maids make night rounds for the dirty towels and they’re pretty shite at knocking.”

Setting the guitar aside and popping to his feet, Sirius wiggled his eyebrows suggestively. “Oh, I dunno… Maybe I’ll just leave the door open a crack. See who wanders in.”

“I wouldn’t. Most of them are old enough to be your grandmother. And you're supposed to be hiding.”

Sirius laughed, then reached out to put a hand on Remus’ shoulder. “You’re a real friend, Moons. Don't know what I did to deserve you.”

That makes two of us.

Taking a breath, Remus nodded and then watched while Sirius turned and slipped into the bathroom. As the door clicked shut, a puzzled feeling fell over him, and he glanced at the guitar suspiciously. It almost felt like he’d missed a punchline. Was his comedic timing off? No, never. Not unless…

“Wait…” he murmured as the shower turned on, “did he mean leave the door open in case… I wandered in?”

The guitar said nothing, and Remus suddenly felt very, very stupid.

“AUGH!” He cried, smacking the bed covers like a tantruming child. “What the hell?!”

Missed your shot, did ya, Romeo?

“What?! No! No way! Ugh—there is absolutely no way he could’ve actually meant me.”

He was looking at you when he said it, wasn’t he?

“Yeah—and he was joking!”

Believe it or not, but I don’t actually think that toilet conjugal visits are beyond him.

“But he called me a friend! A bloody friend!”

Hey, I’m on your side here. Get it in already or fucking get out, ya moron.

Remus scowled. I hate you.

Determined to stifle the infernal voice in his head, Remus set off to do the thing he should’ve gotten out of the way days ago—cleaning. Collecting all of the dirty dishes, he snuck out and carried each armful down to the kitchens, trying his best not to make too much noise as he left them to soak in the sink. While he was down there, he grabbed a few day-old scones for Sirius and filled up a large glass of water before making his way back upstairs. No one bothered him, it being so late, and he could still hear the gentle rush of the shower as he walked inside.

You could try the door, see if he left it open.

Ugh… Sod off already, why don’t you!

Gathering up his dirty laundry, Remus threw it all into the hamper next to the bathroom before fighting with his bed covers and shoving them in too. He was still a seventeen year-old boy, which meant he hadn’t changed them since returning for the holiday, but he thought Sirius might appreciate some clean sheets after what he’d been through. The books and records he left alone, because Sirius would also appreciate them.

Just as he had finished tucking the blanket’s corners in, the man of the hour finally emerged from the steaming bathroom. Sirius was still wearing the trousers he’d arrived in, but his chest was bare, and he had a towel over his head which he used to rub the dampness from his hair.

“I’ll get you something to sleep in!” Remus called, trying not to make eye contact with his half-naked roommate as he rushed to the wardrobe. “Bed’s clean, by the way. You can take the left side. Or the right—doesn’t really matter to me.”

Sirius looked up, keeping the towel around his head. “It’s fine. I’ll take the sofa over there.”

Remus froze. “Oh! Er…”

“Sorry,” Sirius said, quickly padding over to the small chaise lounge that sat in the corner of the room. “It’s just… It’s your bed, innit? And I really don’t want to be any more of a bother.”

“You wouldn’t be! But—ehm…” Remus bit down hard on his tongue as he slowly pawed through the clothes in his wardrobe; “Sorry, I just assumed, but… Sorry… It’s fine. Just um… here.” Picking out a pair of winceyette pyjama bottoms, he crossed the room and awkwardly handed them over.

“Thanks,” Sirius said, taking them. He reached up to remove the towel, before stopping midway and gesturing meekly to the trousers. “Sorry, do you mind?”

“Oh! No, go ahead.” Remus cleared his throat. “I’ll just… get you a blanket.” Streaking away, he snatched the fresh quilt off of his bed and began bunching it up in his arms. He hadn’t been able to avoid looking at Sirius’ scars—the shiny, pink layers of skin that pulled taut over his shoulder like wax—but they’d hardly mattered. It was really everything else that had intrigued him so badly. Not that any of that was a good idea. Stupid, stupid, stupid!

“Can I take one of these, then?” Sirius said, appearing at his elbow with the towel still hanging over his head. He’d really only been gesturing to the pillows, but it still made Remus leap about a foot into the air. “Jesus! You feeling alright?”

“Er—yeah!" Remus winced. "Sorry, just tired too. You go ahead. My casa or whatever…”

“Cool.” Sirius plucked a pillow off his bed. “Oh and by the way, it’s ‘mi casa’.”

“… What?”

“The saying—‘mi casa, es su casa’.”

“Oh. Right.” Remus swallowed thickly, before handing him the blanket. Sirius took it, and his fingertips brushed the back of Remus’ hand, making goosebumps sprout all the way up to his shoulder.

Stop being such an idiot, you sleep in the same room for most of the year, don’t you?

This is different. He’s in my room—with his shirt off!

“You sure you’re okay, Moons?” Sirius asked, peering at him.

“I'm fine—it should be you we're worried about! Not that—er... Sorry. I can… I can take that towel from ya now.”

Sirius reached up to bundle either side under his chin like some Russian grandmother. “I’m good. Hair’s still kinda wet. But hey, thanks for the blanket. And the trousers, though… they are a bit long.”

They both looked down, and Remus noted the bunched up fabric around Sirius’ ankles. Sirius would’ve never called himself short, so he was obviously doing it to make Remus feel better. And it did work some.

“I left some water and a few scones for you on that table there,” Remus said in what he hoped was a kindly way. “I know it’s late and all, but they shouldn’t be rock-hard yet.”

“Yum. You’re the best.” Tucking the pillow and blanket under one arm, Sirius gave him a friendly nudge to the shoulder with his fist before walking over to the chaise. As he went about turning the lounge into an acceptable bed, Remus drew the curtains and got the light. His ears still felt hot, but it was manageable.

“Moony?” Sirius called, after they’d both finally settled down under their covers. His voice felt so far away in the big room—completely unlike the comfort of their dorm.

“Yeah…?”

“Thanks.”

Staring up at the roof of his bed, Remus felt his heart flutter again. It was horrible.

“I told you—stop saying thanks.”

“I mean it though,” Sirius insisted; “You really saved me back there.”

Remus turned over in bed. Through a crack in the curtains, he could just make out the moon, full and bright. Hopeful.

“See you in the morning, Sirius."

“... Okay, Moony.”





* * *





The next morning, Remus served his punishment and then some for stealing the Rolls and taking it for his so-called “joy ride”. He scrubbed and scrubbed until his fingers were prunes and the car shone with a million sun-kisses twinkles. When Giles could see his every pore in its reflection, he continued his discipline by making Remus polish the floor of the foyer, hang all of the laundry, clean every window in the ground floor, and finish it all off by washing his dishes from the night before—plus any that had been procured from breakfast that day. The kitchen ladies seemed to find it all quite comical, but rewarded him for his efforts with heaping trays of breakfast.

“Gots to feed the growing boy,” one of the cooks—an old Romanian woman named Imena—said, after insisting he take a fifth piece of toast. Remus didn’t argue. He was eating for two stomachs today.

Punishment finally finished with, Remus made a quick pit-stop to pick up a certain someone before sneaking the food up to the second floor. He’d almost toppled both glasses of orange juice several times by the time he stopped outside his own bedroom, but after knocking twice, then twice again—their code, ‘I’m okay’ —Remus stuck his head in.

“Sirius, you up? Snuck you some breakfast.”

“Yes! Absolutely famished,” Sirius cried, tossing a random book aside as he shot upright. He was already dressed, all in borrowed clothes, and had folded the blanket and pillow up on the back of the little sofa like any good house guest.

Remus grinned and got ready to open the door wide. “Good. ‘Cause the ladies in the kitchen hooked us up. Also... I might have a surprise."

"Ooh. I love surprises. What is it?"

"Don’t freak out, but I brought someone to see you.”

Sirius froze a bit, like he was afraid James was about to come thundering into the room, but the moment Remus opened the door fully and allowed a single excited coonhound to race inside, a huge grin bloomed across his face.

“Oh shit—dog!”

It was all Sirius had time to say before Dusty had zoomed across the room and bowled right through his middle. “OOF—! Down boy! Jesus. Excitable bugger, aren’t you?” Sirius began scratching the speckled dog behind the scruff of his neck. “Now, who might you be? Hold on, this can't be the legendary Dusty, can it?”

Eyeing the glasses of juice precariously to avoid spilling, Remus came in and shut the door behind him with a little jerk his foot, before crossing the room and setting their breakfasts down on the coffee table in front of the chaise. “Padfoot, meet Dusty—Dusty, meet Padfoot.”

“Well, Dusty I—oh! That’s right, you have another Padfoot here! Where is he? I should like to meet such a distinguished gentleman.”

Remus shrugged. “He’s probably in the kennel—it’s one of the big buildings on the other side of the lawn. Only Dusty comes into the house.”

“And how’d you get so lucky, huh?” Sirius grabbed Dusty round the snout, leaning in and making a shameless kissy-face at the end of his nose. Obviously thrilled by the attention, Dusty retaliated by surging forward again, slamming his snout into Sirius’ chin and making his head snap back sharply.

“Agh, fuck! Man, I think he rattled my brain.”

Sirius pressed a hand to his forehead, careful to avoid the brim of his hat. It was the only thing he’d brought from Belgium that he insisted on keeping, despite the fact that it made him look like a charity advert.

“Why are you still wearing that thing?” Remus asked, busy arranging their breakfast trays on the table. “Weren’t you the one who said that all hats are a menace to good hair?”

Sirius grunted, trying to shove Dusty off of him as he desperately lapped at the side of his face. “I’m just… c'mon boy... Just—trying to bring back the style!” He declared. “Why? You mean to say that you’re suddenly into fashion?”

Remus just looked at him.

“There then," Sirius said, as Dusty practically bowled him over on the chaise. "It’s a statement, just like Marauders. You’re just—ngh—behind the times, Lupin.”

Remus shook his head, before pulling Dusty off of his friend and passing Sirius a fork. Sirius took it eagerly, and immediately began shovelling huge bites into his mouth as though he were actually starving. Remus realised with a pang that he might be.

“Fuck, I missed fry-ups,” Sirius moaned. “Mum hates anything greasy. I swear, she’s probably made of porridge at this point. Porridge and hatred.”

“I can get you more later if you’re still hungry,” Remus promised, fiddling with a sausage. Dusty began to whine until he caved and fed it to him. “And we can visit the dogs as long as we’re careful. I don’t think they’re doing any training today anyway.”

"Thought I was supposed to be hiding?"

"You are... but I could lie. Say you're a friend. S'not like you'll have to meet my dad or anything."

Sirius gave him a wry look, which was stifled only by his giant mouthful of egg and toast. “Ah, don’t you fret over me.”

“I’m not fretting.”

“You are. It's like your default setting. Mooning Moony."

“I just don’t want you to feel cooped up in here.”

Swallowing, Sirius waved him off. “Oh no, I’ve got plenty of entertainment. You, the guitar, your astounding collection of books lacking any and all plot—and now Dusty!”

“My books have plot.”

“If you count eternal damnation and self-loathing as plot, then sure. But oh, that’s right… I’m forgetting the really scurrilous stuff. You tried to hide it, but I’ve a nose for things like these. I snuffed you out, you sneaky tosser.”

Remus shrugged, assuming that Sirius was talking about the small bit of weed he’d hidden in the bottom drawer of his dresser. “You can have it, but I wouldn’t smoke it in here. Pretty sure Giles can smell burning hash from a mile away.”

“I didn’t mean the weed—though I did find that too.”

“Then what?” He glanced at the bookshelves. “A book? I dunno which one it could be then. I may have a copy of ‘Frankenstein’ lying around if you’re that desperate, but I’d hardly call Mary Shelley ‘scurrilous’.”

“So you admit they have no plot!” Sirius smirked devilishly, and then suddenly whipped a letter out from under a pillow, torn open on its top; “No, it’s not Frankenstein, my poor Watson. What I found was much more interesting.” He turned it over, holding the letter up to the side of his face and puckering directly next to the kiss mark on its back.

Oh shit.

“Sirius, don’t—!”

“You never told me Jillian Stewart had a thing for you, Moony! And blimey, judging by the length of this love letter, she is absolutely smitten!”

“You asshole!”

Remus lunged across the table for the letter, nearly scattering the dishes, but Sirius only let out a bark of laughter and sat upright on the sofa, waving the letter in the air as if to taunt him with it.

“Don’t be too embarrassed, Stewart really does have a way with words! I mean, just listen to this prose—‘kinder than mother Theresa, the smartest boy in our year, eyes like the sea—oh fuck, Moons! She got your eye colour wrong! What a shite girlfriend.”

“Sirius, I’m gonna kill you!”

Coming around the table, Remus dodged his gangly dog and threw himself forward. He ended up missing the letter and falling against the plush edge of the chaise while Dusty barked frantically and Sirius slid away, grinning maniacally.

“You should frame it—put it in a museum! Call it ‘les désespérés et les dégénérés’!”

“Give it back!”

“No way—I’m gonna frame it!” Peeling the letter free from his envelope, Sirius tossed the extra paper away and slipped further from Remus. He used one hand to unfurl the letter and kept the other pressed to the top of his head to hold his post boy’s cap down. “ ‘Dear Remus’,” he read; “ ‘I’ve only just arrived in Bordeaux’—she’s in France? Did you tell her to look Mary up?”

“Give it to me!”

“No! Finder’s keepers, Moons! Now—where was I?”

Grabbing him by the ankle, Remus gave a single viscous tug and Sirius flopped directly down onto his back with a yelp. The noise was almost too satisfying, and Remus fought a grin as Sirius scowled defiantly. Giving him a sharp push, Sirius made to turn over and shimmy away but Remus stopped that too, pinning his leg in place.

“Gotcha,” he said smugly. “Now give that back.”

Sirius smirked. “In your dreams, Lupin. Dusty—here boy, come and get the treat!”

Instantly Dusty was there. He swiped the letter from Sirius’ outstretched arm like it was another sausage and shot across the room with it.

“So NOW you listen?!” Remus moaned. Pushing up, he started scrambling to get away, but Sirius was faster. He brought his knee up at the last second, catching Remus in the gut and making him sag back into the sofa. Sitting up, Sirius laughed at him—the git—and made to turn, but Remus wouldn’t have it.

“Right… that’s it!”

He lunged again, grappling his friend and pinning him back onto the velvet. This time Remus didn’t stop until he was straddling Sirius round the waist. Sirius fought back of course, almost like he did with James, and soon enough they were really scrapping. Struggling to keep his hold, Remus grunted—Sirius was like an eel, twisting every which way in attempts to escape. He had to squeeze his thighs just to keep him in place and took several light jabs to the chest for it, but Sirius’ smack was like the gentle kiss of butterfly wings compared to some of the rounds he used to go with Doss and Lee. His legs were deadly enough, but with those pinned, Remus was obviously the winner. Almost laughing—I’ve got you!—he used his hands to cage Sirius in, pressing them to the sofa on either side of his face and leaned forward to—what? Punch him? Kiss him?

Not that it mattered.

Before Remus could decide what it was he was about to do, Sirius wrapped a hand around his wrist and shoved it directly off the edge of the sofa. With all of his weight leaning on his hands and nothing keeping him from diving head-first into Sirius’ nose, Remus dipped forward and let out a sharp squawk of surprise. He was a hair’s distance away from smacking their foreheads together when he managed to catch himself, and as his chest heaved, he looked up to find the both of them nose-to-nose. Staring back at him, Sirius’ lips also parted in shock.

Kiss him!

The thought was almost like a punch to the head. It hit Remus all at once, and he let out a second noise, this one a mixture of what sounded like a gag and grunt. It broke Sirius’ spell, and his face split into a grin as he began to laugh at him.

“Ha! You’re a real shit boxer, Moons. Wouldn't last ten seconds against Prongs.”

Remus couldn’t even comprehend enough to laugh. He was too busy reeling—still stuck on that little ring of pure blue he could see encircling both of Sirius’ pupils.

Kiss him, you great quaking idiot!

“I…”

Do it! He’s already kissed you!

“I’m… what?”

"Moons? You good...?"

"I—er... uhm... ngh...?"

WOOF!

That’s right… that’s your best friend—the best friend that you should’ve kissed, you blithering pansy!

Resisting a moan, Remus stubbornly shoved all thoughts of kissing away. He’d hoped that after everything with James and Peter, and then with the girls, that things might feel clearer; and yet there he was, dripping in anxiety the moment Sirius so much as glanced at him. Fuck. How was he ever going to survive the summer?

I’m not gay. I’m not gay, he told himself. He’s just impossible not to notice. It’s like his job. Him and that annoyingly stupid-horrible-beautiful face—no! Think of something else—think of the stupid hat!

Dusty barked again—WOOF!—as Remus reached him. He was sitting proudly by the foot of the bed, the remains of Jillian’s letter scattered in a slobbery circle around his feet.

“That’s a damn shame,” Sirius called, as Remus bent down to scoop up the shredded pieces. “Can it not be saved at all?”

“I-I don’t need to save it,” Remus huffed, collecting every scrap into his palm and quickly moving to stuff it into the waist basket beside his desk. He’d just gotten all the spines to face the right way when Sirius appeared at his side, toeing the bin with Jillian’s letter.

“Sorry I got your love letter shredded.”

Remus smacked the book he was holding down onto the desk. “Don’t you listen to anything? I said it’s not a love letter!”

“Hm…” Sirius pressed his lips out into a curious pout. “Have you written her back at all?”

"No."

"Liar. You're too nice to not have."

Remus scowled. “… A few times. Only a few.”

“So you must like her then?”

“No! Jesus Christ—you said it yourself, I only answer to be polite!”

“But you still wrote her. C’mon, lover-boy, I’m not an idiot. You wrote to her knowing that it’d give her hope, and now she’s swooning at your curls, and dotting her ‘i’s with tiny hearts, and—”

“Well at least she wrote me!” Remus snapped viciously, before immediately regretting it. Sirius’ face fell, and instead of laughing he pressed his lips into a thin line, looking away dismissively.

“Yeah, well… sorry for that.”

“No,” Remus moaned, catching Sirius by the arm, “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean it. It wasn’t your fault. You were… ”

“I was deposed,” Sirius finished. “Packed up, forced onto a train, then a boat, then another train… But hey, my bad. Next time I’ll try and get you the address.”

Fuck. Remus sighed, before forcing a smile. “How ‘bout we just agree that there won’t be a next time, okay?”

Sirius looked up at him through those thick lashes, and finally he nodded.

Feeling slightly at a loss over what to do next, Remus pushed the stack of books away and cleared his throat. “We should go somewhere. Get out of here for a while. I hate this house. Maybe not as much as you hate yours but… It just sucks the life out of you.”

“Makes you miserable,” Sirius agreed. “I get it. This mean you’re gonna be my tour guide around London?”

“I’d probably be shit at that too, but yeah, I’ll do it. Where do you want to go?”

Sirius shrugged. “Anywhere. London’s my oyster.”

“I thought it was ‘the world’s your oyster’.”

“The world’s too vast right now, Moons. We start with London, and then we take the world. More realistic that way.”

Remus smiled, and he felt better. “Let’s at least finish breakfast first.”

Sirius’ eyes flitted away. “Yeah… dunno about that one.” He pointed, and Remus spun around to find Dusty with his head bent over a clear plate that had held half of a full English breakfast not five minutes before.

“Augh! Goddammit, Dusty!” He groaned as Sirius began to laugh from behind him. Marching up to the dog, he grabbed him by the collar, hauling him away from the table just as he was reaching for the rest of the toast. “You bloody—”

They were cut off by a sharp knock coming from the door. Already trained, Sirius all but dove behind the bed. It was smart of him too, since Remus was pretty sure he’d forgotten to lock the door. Instantly on edge, he forced Dusty to sit and cleared his throat.

“I’m changing, don’t come in!”

“It’s Carston, sir,” the butler said through the door; “Your father has asked that you meet him in his office.”

Remus huffed. “Bloody ruins everything… Alright! I’ll be there in a moment!”

“Very good, sir.”

Releasing Dusty’s collar, Remus crept toward the door and waited several seconds before opening it and peering out. All he heard was the sound of the butler’s footsteps receding down the hall, and let out a sigh of relief.

“Dad’s office, huh?” Sirius drawled, now lounging on the bed. “Someone's in trouble... Heh—kidding. I know what that’s like.”

Remus shut the door quickly. “Are you gonna be okay in here?”

“Oh yeah, don’t worry about me or Dusty-man. We’ll be waiting right here for you when you get back. In fact, bring more eggs.”

WOOF!

Remus rolled his eyes. It was with love. “Fine. Be back in a jiffy then. Make sure you lock the door behind me.”

Sirius saluted, and Remus opened the door again, slipping out.

The main hallway was as quiet as normal. There was only the gentle patter of his feet on the wood as he walked, occasionally joined by the distant sounds of a maid moving about, most likely dusting some old china or changing the untouched linens on every unused bed. It all felt so pointless. A huge house, and for what? No one came over. No one slept in the beds. There was Sandra now… but Remus doubted it would actually last. She would realise eventually that Lyall was never going to put her before his work. She’d be lucky to make par with the dogs. She’d find out things that girlfriends ought not want to know, and then she’d decide none of it was worth it and whatever rose-tinted honeymoon she was living in would end. It was what had done-in Tomny and Tonya. Their ugly bits got a bit too ugly and then… poof.

Remus still wondered about Tomny. Couldn’t help it really. He wished he could talk to him about Sirius. For someone who’d grown up without any real role models, Tomny sure gave good advice. He’d probably have found the whole thing hilarious—rich boy is sent abroad and promptly runs away to live in his best friend’s closet. It would be funnier only because Sirius’ unusual antics were almost tame compared to people Tomny knew; the one difference was money and pride. Tomny would’ve told Orion and Walburga Black to take their ancient and noble lineage and shove it right up their arse.

Yeah… he missed Tomny.

But Sirius was there now, and they hadn’t resorted to hiding in closets yet, though as Remus stopped outside his father’s office, it occurred to him that perhaps they’d already been found out. For all they knew, Lyall could be preparing to have Sirius dragged home in chains. Inviting him alone to break the news was just his pathetic way of saving face. Remus would never let it happen—he’d force Sirius to call James first. Or Peter, or Lily, or even that cousin of his in Islington—Andy. She’d already been disowned for having her daughter out of wedlock. Didn’t even help that she’d married the guy after—he was far too poor. And if not Andy, then someone. James’ parents… an eccentric aunt… someone. Someone would help. They had to.

“You called for me?” Remus called, as he strode into the office without bothering to knock. If they were already caught then there was no need to stand on ceremony. Unexpectedly, he found Lyall not at his desk but across the room at the bar cabinet, pouring himself a scotch.

“A little early for drinking, innit?”

“The correct phrasing is, ‘isn’t it’,” Lyall said dryly, capping the scotch and carrying the glass back to his impossibly large oak desk. “Get yourself one if you wish,” he told him, “but close the door.”

Remus didn’t, but he did close the office door, only slightly bewildered by his father’s unnervingly blasé attitude. As he approached the imposing desk, Lyall sipped his scotch and turned to admire the large painting that hung on the wall behind him. It was of a beach somewhere in Wales. He and Hope had gone there on their honeymoon. The Lupins had had enough money to go anywhere in the world when they’d married, and Hope had chosen there. Lyall had had the painting commissioned as a birthday gift a few years before that. Remus wasn’t sure why he kept it around.

“Are we gonna talk or are we gonna just stand here?” He said, taking a deep breath to soothe his frayed nerves. Maybe Lyall didn’t know about Sirius. Maybe he just wanted to lecture.

Turning away from the painting, Lyall set the scotch down and opened one of the finely crafted boxes on his desk and withdrew a cigar. Instead of setting it between his teeth, he offered it to Remus expectantly.

“No, I’m fine."

Lyall gave him a hard look. “Just take it.”

Huffing lowly, Remus stepped up to the desk and took the cigar. Lyall lit a match and held it to one end, letting Remus puff on the other until it glowed orange. Instantly the peppery smoke had him coughing, and he drew back as Lyall lit one for himself, a ghost of a smile on his lips.

“Glad to know there’s some things you haven’t tried.”

Scowling, Remus held the cigar away from him, but didn’t put it down. He didn’t want to give Lyall the satisfaction. Casually, his father waved out the match and sucked back his own cigar, before breathing out the smoke and finally dropping down into his leather throne.

“I got a letter from your school today,” he said.

A flicker of hesitant hope bloomed in Remus’ chest. So it wasn’t about Sirius then… but what else?

“What did it say?” He asked, doing his best to remain aloof.

“That you’ve been asked to be a school prefect.”

It was not the answer Remus had been expecting.

“Well?" Lyall raised a brow. "Is it true?”

“… Yes.”

“And you’ve accepted?”

Thinking back to the silver prefect pin sitting on top of his dresser, Remus took a deep breath. “Yes…”

Lyall sucked in another lungful of cigar. “Good. Then I will inform the school that you’re looking to enter university right away. Your classes will have to be switched. Can't have anything unnecessary clogging up your schedule.”

Eyes blown wide, Remus stepped forward, nearly dropping his cigar. “My classes?! You can't just—”

“Your current choices are unacceptable,” Lyall snapped. “I’ve read the sylabuses. Medieval History, Pre-colonial Africa, the Life and Works of Shakespeare—music. None of these things are going to help you in the real world.”

“Who bloody said I wanted to live in your so-called ‘real’ world?”

“That’s a child’s answer. No one gets a choice in the end, but the choices you make now will make or break how you navigate it.”

“You’re not changing my classes!”

“No, you will. That is as long as you wish to attend that school.”

“You’re the one who sent me there in the first place!”

“And you’ve done well for yourself, all things considered. Don’t let it all be for nothing.”

“Why?” Remus wailed. “Why are you so bloody miserable all of the time? And why must I always be miserable with you?!”

“You’re fortunate,” Lyall said sharply; “don’t presume to pretend otherwise. People would kill for the things you have—the opportunities I’ve given you.”

“I never asked for any of that!”

“Yes, and I never asked—!” Lyall drew up short, raising his cigar in a firm dismissal. “That’s enough.”

“No, go ahead,” Remus taunted. “Say what you meant to say.”

“Not another word, Remus," Lyall warned. "Or mark mine, you won’t be going back to that school. It’s a few useless classes in exchange for a real future. One day you’ll thank me.”

Torn between fury and fear of losing everything left dear to him, Remus bit his tongue. Was this how it felt for Sirius? Or was it much worse, considering his family never gave him a choice? Goddammit.

Clearing his throat, Lyall lifted his scotch to his lips and finished it in a single gulp. “We can talk more about this later,” he said after; “For now, I have something else we must discuss.”

“Must you be so fucking formal about everything?” Remus said scornfully. Lyall eyed him, but said nothing until he’d tapped the ash off his cigar into the ashtray in front of him.

“I’ve asked Sandra to marry me.”

Remus felt his ears pop. “What?”

“And she’s accepted.”

“What... the fuck...?”

“Please, Remus, try to maintain some decorum.” Lyall raised his chin. “Truthfully there isn’t much to discuss. Everything’s already decided. The ceremony will take place in September.”

“How could this already be decided?” He demanded. “How long have you even been dating her?”

“Don’t be a child,” Lyall scoffed, making Remus’ temper flare even more. “The two of you had a good time together yesterday, didn’t you?”

“So?! Tolerating one measly day together doesn’t mean I want to live with her!”

“Do you want to live here at all, Remus?”

The question caught him like a slap. “No,” he ground out.

“Then I suggest you return to school, attend your classes, and then continue on to a good university so that you might support yourself outside these walls one day. God knows that it isn’t that hard.”

“I won’t call her mother.”

“I don’t believe she asked you to.”

“I won’t love her! ... I’ll hate her—and I’ll make her hate me too.”

Lyall levelled his gaze. It was scornful—no, unimpressed.

“Seventeen years of practice, and that’s all you can muster?” He drawled. “A single bit of hatred? I would’ve expected more from you.”

Remus couldn’t help it—he threw the cigar, letting it sail over Lyall’s shoulder and spatter ash against the painting of his mother’s beach. It didn’t matter. It was worth about as much as every other painfully mundane landscape hanging up in the estate. Remus hated all of them.

“You’re losing control again,” Lyall warned from his chair.

“Oh shut up!” He roared, slamming his hands down on the front of the desk. “You know what you used to tell me when she lost control—when she went off the rails?!”

“You’re making this about her, but it has nothing to do with your mother.”

Remus wondered how Lyall could be so wrong. This had everything to do with her.

“ ‘Remus, go to your room’—‘Remus, go to bed’!” He howled; “And when I refused, you’d ask me, ‘Remus, why are you such a brat?’—‘Remus, why don’t you ever listen?’ But you never gave me a chance, not one! I was just her son, and you were waiting for me to go off the rails too—I always knew it! ... And when it eventually happened—well, me you’d just have committed, because—oh, you’d already learned your lesson!”

Utterly still, Lyall didn’t even blink at him. “How world-weary you’ve become in just a few years at that school. Perhaps you should be committed, if this is how you insist on behaving—stark-raving mad and still just a child.”

Enraged, Remus grabbed the empty scotch glass and threw it against the wall. It shattered into a million tiny pieces and yet he didn’t feel even the slightest bit better.

“You hate me! Just admit it—JUST SAY IT! Say what we both know to be true! Say it, so all of this can be OVER WITH!”

But Lyall said nothing. Even as Remus heaved with the effort of his shouts, his father gave him nothing.

You could just say it yourself, you know, the vicious Moony sneered. If you really had the balls you’d finally come out with it. You never told the lads at school because you were afraid it would make you lesser—you never told Tomny because it would make you the same. And no matter how much you wanted to be one of them, you always needed to be special.

No...

Oh yes… But maybe it’s not about them at all. Maybe it’s about him. Lyall... Dad... You’re afraid he won’t care. And you want him to care, you always have. He could pull you from that school, ship you off to Belgium, and you’d still care. You can’t help it.

With an immense cry of frustration, Remus slammed his fist down onto the desk. He didn’t so much as dent the surface, but the pain stifled some of the thoughts.

“I know, you know,” he growled—dared. “I’ve known for years and I know you have too... But that doesn’t make me the coward, I was just a kid—you’re the one who can’t say it!”

A muscle twitched in Lyall’s jaw. Remus seized it. If this pain so demanded to be felt, then Lyall would feel it too.

“Yeah—you,” Remus hissed. “The adult—the father... How could I ever be ashamed of it—me? I can’t. Not when you’re bad enough for the both of us… What’s a’matter, can’t admit to yourself? Afraid that that would mean she never actually loved you...? Well, I’ll tell you one thing, Dad—you touch my classes and I’ll tell Sandra everything. I’ll call the damn papers—your bloody boss—anyone who cares enough to gossip... To hell what happens to me.”

It was enough. Lyall dropped his brow, hands fisted in his lap. “Get. Out.”

“What? Is it harder to hide from your ghosts when they’re still alive?”

“OUT!”

Remus exhaled. His eyes burned and his limbs felt heavy, but he’d gotten what he wanted, and now he needed to be anywhere else.

“Yeah, alright,” he sighed, slowly moving backwards to the door; “But hey, good luck on the marriage. Congrats—really! You don’t deserve her…”

Pushing open the door, Remus emerged in the hallway and slammed it behind himself. He was still breathing hard, his heart beating loud enough that it echoed in his temples like an ache. He considered just screaming, but before he even had time to fill his lungs, he heard the familiar click of another door behind shut a short ways away. Perking up, he followed it, dragging his feet until finally he found himself outside the room no one ever entered. Not since he was eleven, anyway.

Hand practically trembling, Remus reached for the door’s handle. It fell open under his touch, revealing a vast music room, every table and chair covered in a white sheet to protect it from dust and light. As he looked around, it struck him how he used to be afraid of this room, back when Hope would just sit by the window in her wheelchair and stare at nothing, as though she were already dead. Then she’d died and it was just empty again. Or at least it had been before.

Across the room, at the piano he must’ve uncovered himself, Sirius sat alone. He was still wearing the cap, but had rolled up the borrowed shirt and trousers at his wrists and ankles just to make them fit. He’d never looked less like himself, but Remus would’ve still recognised him blind. It was a relatable feeling, that blindness. As he advanced into the room, every step Remus took felt soundless, as though he’d gone deaf out of fear alone. He must’ve, because he could see Sirius playing and yet heard no song. It wasn’t until he was standing directly behind him, watching the gentle movement of his hands, that Remus realised that there was sound. Sirius was playing so tenderly that the music was like a whisper. You had to want to listen to hear it.

Slowly, he slid in beside Sirius on the bench, watching his slender fingers softly dance up and down the tops of the keys. He wanted desperately to take one of those beautiful hands in his own, but everything was so raw at that moment that Remus was half-sure he’d have simply ceased to exist if he acknowledged the pain long enough to do it.

“You were listening,” he said. Sirius stopped playing immediately and carefully tucked his hands into his lap.

“… Yeah.”

“You shouldn’t have done that.”

“Sorry.”

“Someone could’ve seen you.” Taken you from me.

“They didn’t,” Sirius promised.

Remus swallowed; “Good,” but his voice cracked and he hated himself for it.

“He shouldn’t have talked to you like that.”

“… Don’t worry about it.”

“He threatened to take you out of school.”

“He won’t. It would mean keeping me here, and he’s too desperate. My staying would ruin everything. He wants to start over… That’s why he’s marrying that woman.”

“Is she…” Sirius took a breath. “Is she bad?”

“No,” Remus answered, “she’s good.”

“Oh… m'glad.”

Neither of them said anything for a while, just staring at the black-lacquered surface of the piano. Remus could see his reflection as though he were looking into a mirror. Eventually Sirius reached out again with a single hand, playing a few somber notes like the closing to a chapter. Remus recognised them immediately, and gave a weak chuckle—just air blowing out his nose.

“ ‘Any way the wind blows’…”

Sirius withdrew his hand and instead of returning it to his lap, he slid it beneath Remus’ own, lacing their fingers together so tightly it felt as though not a single atom could've fit between their palms. It didn’t even make him nervous like he’d thought it would. In the end Sirius was still his friend.

“I’m happy you’re here, Remus,” Sirius said.

And then Remus sighed, in relief and thankfulness. Because thank god for Sirius Black.

“Do you want to get out of here?” He asked. “Just go somewhere—anywhere?”

“Yes,” Sirius told him. “Anywhere with you.”
