Chapter 67: City Lights, London Nights


Chapter Summary

They take the city, and maybe just a little bit... the city will take them.



Chapter Notes

CW: Spitting, smoking, and just general tomfoolery (lol). 'F' slur used ONLY in a smoking context. Sexual content (non-graphic) that could be considered important to the plot. Read whatever makes you most comfortable.

There's a lot of subtext in this chapter, especially within Remus & Sirius' conversation outside the cinema. I hope it's clear enough, but they really are just scared boys, and love and sexuality are as scary as it gets sometimes. Love them as they are when possible <3



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Waterfall,

Don’t ever change your ways;

Fall with me for a million days,

Oh, my waterfall…

- “May This Be Love” Jimi Hendrix, 1967



Most people who grew up in London had a hard time seeing the magic in it. Like Remus, they saw the Underground only for its horrible rush hour and poorly-lit stations. They thought of streets like Carnaby as crowded tourist-traps and never really got excited about much of anything. But for newcomers like Sirius, who were just itching to sink their teeth into anything street-cultured, London might as well have been the promised land. It was all new, from the shops and streets, to the people that filled them. It went without saying that Sirius had never been on the tube before. He’d also never hailed a cab for himself, or gotten lost on a backstreet. Sirius had never had to step over a morning drunkard’s vomit outside a Chinese place that looked scummy but actually had amazing wonton soup. He’d never scattered pigeons in Hyde park, or eaten a kebab from a street vendor along Portobello, or haggled amongst the stalls of Brick Lane, and he’d certainly never strolled into a random pub to catch a pint and a friendly game of snooker.

For all intents and purposes, Sirius was a complete city-virgin, but perhaps the strangest thing to Remus was that Sirius had never spat on the pavement.

“I just don’t get it. What’s the appeal?” Sirius asked, as they made their way down the street. Row houses rose up on either side of them, decorated with brick and iron fences, all overgrown with ivy and ragged thorn bushes. They’d just crossed over into Clifton Hill after walking a good twenty minutes from the station. Neither of them made a fuss, for a young boy in 1977, anything under five miles wasn’t worth the whinging.

“I can’t just tell you,” Remus said, “it’s like a cultural thing. You do it with the lads.”

“Sounds like a more disappointing jerk-circle.”

Remus shoved him, making Sirius lurch sideways into the road as he sniggered. Stopping to wait for him, Remus dodged a young mum pushing her baby in a pram and crossed his arms over his chest. “Go on, try it then,” he prompted.

Sirius eyed the pram that had just passed. “You mean now? In public?”

“S’long as it doesn’t offend your pretty little manners.”

Sirius scowled and Remus waved the comment off. “Here, watch me.” Stopping in the middle of the pavement, he hocked back a large wad of saliva and spat it in the direction of the road. He managed to clear about ten feet—almost a new personal record—and when he turned to Sirius he found him clapping blithely.

“And who says the hooligan doesn’t have any talents.”

“You go then,” Remus urged. Sirius sighed and reached up to scratch his head beneath his cap, before making a noise deep in his throat as though he were trying to clear it.

“That’s it,” Remus said, “gotta dig deep. Doss always told me to imagine like you’d just swallowed a spoonful of cough syrup. But you’re going for distance not size, so—”

Sirius turned on him. “Can you shut up, I just swallowed it!”

Remus backed away. “Sorry, my bad. Take your time.”

Taking a deep breath, Sirius wiggled his jaw around, looking distinctly concentrated. When he threw his head back Remus almost thought he was gonna do it, but what came out was a pitiful spit wad that just barely cleared the tip of his trainers.

“Sirius, that was… Well, it was just sad actually.”

Sirius wiped his mouth. “It’s gross.”

“Nah—well, maybe—but you’re not getting enough momentum. Come ‘ere.”

Turning around, Remus grabbed hold of the rusty iron fence that let into one of the row houses’ front garden. Sirius joined him a moment later, looking slightly intrigued and a bit perturbed all at once.

“Try ‘n put your whole body into it,” Remus instructed, before leaning backwards. Using the fence, he propelled himself forward and launched the spit wad so far that it landed in the scraggly, heat-ravaged pushes beneath the house’s front windows.

“Damn.” Sirius shook out his shoulders, even cracking his neck as though he were getting ready to run a hundred metre dash. “It’s a cultural thing…” he murmured to himself, before hawking back enough to make Remus’ throat twinge, and rocking back on his heels to shoot a winner spit glob directly over the fence. It sailed a few feet before hitting the grass, and Remus jumped up in celebration.

“Brilliant! Maybe you are a natural after all.”

“Bet I could get it further than you,” Sirius said, looking suddenly smug.

“Oh yeah? Try it.”

Grabbing hold of the fence again they both began hacking, but before they could expel another wad of phlegm, the front door of the house flew open and an old man came thundering out in only his robe, waving that morning’s paper around like a bat.

“Oi! Stop spitting on my lawn!”

Remus swallowed the wad of spit, and together he and Sirius dashed away down the street, laughing together.

“Did you see his face?” Remus asked once they’d finally stopped on the next corner. “He looked as mad as Filch that night we set the firecrackers off.”

“Thought the old codger was going to flash us, to be honest,” Sirius agreed, stretching his arms up over his head with a low moan. For all the walking they’d already done, it was still early, but that just meant there was plenty left to see.

“Haven’t we made it yet?” Sirius asked, glancing around.

“Almost. Should be just one more street up.”

They kept walking, hands in their pockets and knocking the odd stone out of their path. Remus had just pulled his cigarettes from his pocket and passed them along to Sirius when they turned the corner onto the zebra crossing and Abbey Road finally fell into view. Sirius drew to an abrupt halt, actually fumbling his cigarette and leaving Remus to pick it up.

“Holy fuck!” He cried. “It’s bloody real!”

“ ‘Course it’s real,” Remus smirked, tucking the cigarette into the corner of his own mouth and lighting the end. All around them were scattered tourists, snapping photos and using the striped crossing to recreate their own version of the photo off of the Beatles’ most infamous album.

“George Harrison walked here,” Sirius prattled; “John Lennon walked here.”

“They recorded right over there too, if you’re interested,” Remus said, pointing further up the street, where more people were mulling around outside the gates of the EMI recording studio.

Sirius’ mouth fell open. Then snapped shut. “I think I might pass out.”

As Sirius continued fawning over the iconic musical landmark, Remus settled back against the brick pony wall along the side of the road and continued smoking his cigarette. He’d been to Abbey Road twice before. Hope had taken him when he was maybe nine, right after he’d first shown interest in her favourite group of mods-turned-rockers. The second had been with Tomny, mostly to rewrite the memory of the first. Tomny hadn’t even been able to name a single Beatle, but he'd still played at being excited for Remus' sake. A bit pointless now, but third time’s the charm… probably.

“I could find a camera—snap your picture,” Remus drawled, when Sirius kept playing at getting closer to the crossing. He eased in slowly, looking out of place amongst the sightseers in his borrowed, oversized clothes and ragged shoes and cap.

“Nah,” Sirius dismissed, reaching down to pull the cigarette carton from Sirius’ breast pocket himself; “I think I’m content to watch. Wouldn’t want any evidence of myself dressed like this anyway.”

Remus held up his lighter, and Sirius leaned in to catch the flame with the end of his fag. Looking down at him, he couldn’t help but notice that Sirius’ lashes were still endlessly long. It reminded him of that day in the girls’ room when they’d woken up next to each other, and because it wasn’t exactly a pleasant memory, Remus pushed it away.

“Shall we find you some new clothes then?”

After leaving Abbey Road behind, they hopped a tram and made their way back into the heart of the city, toward Mayfair and Soho. Remus considered taking Sirius to Selfridges or C&A but Sirius had been to a department store before—better to give him an experience that was wholly new.

“I’ve never owned anything second-hand. Unless you count Andy's guitar,” Sirius said, as they scooted round the street corner and slipped inside the charity shop. It smelt of dust and old leather inside, just as Remus remembered, and the shop staff was little more than a teenage girl sitting behind the counter, flipping through a magazine. A few others mulled about lackadaisically—an old man picking through the chinaware, a scholar-type pulling old books down from the shelves, a young mum carefully sifting through the children’s section with a sleeping baby against her shoulder. All of them living their own lives, completely separate from the two of them. If there was anywhere you could be a complete unknown, then it was a second-hand shop in Soho.

As the door chimed behind them, Remus gaze fell on a shoe rack overflowing with ragged books and trainers. On top sat a beaten up pair of red Chuck Taylors, which were inexplicably, just his size.

"You should get them," Sirius said, when he'd finished ogling long enough to catch Remus staring.

"Nah, we're here for you."

"But they'd look good on you."

Remus bit the inside of his cheek, before tossing Sirius a cheeky glance. “Come on, let’s get you dressed.”

He steered Sirius toward the rows and rows of clothing racks along the back, walking past badly dressed mannequins and abandoned furniture. They stopped at the first aisle, which was mostly shirts, and Remus had Sirius go down one side while he took the other. There was bound to be something among the endless stockpile of fabric that was halfway decent and could suit the posh boy.

“Sorta smells like a library in here… Like mouldy books,” Sirius observed as they quietly pushed the wire hangers from right to left. “They probably do it to attract your sort.”

Remus raised an eyebrow. “What d’you mean by ‘my sort’?”

“You know, the ‘old before their time’ types. The romancers who think they’re no good at romance. The gifted kids who squander everything on booze, fags, and records.”

“Wow. You should write a song. Dick.”

Sirius smirked down at the clothes, and then plucked a garish-looking caftan big enough to house an elephant off of the rack and held it up with two fingers.

“I think it’s your colour,” Remus snarked.

Sighing, Sirius dropped the hanger back on the rack. “Come on, Moony, what are we doing here? I wanna see the sights!”

“And we will, but first you need some decent clothes.”

“I have clothes.” Sirius gestured to himself pointedly.

“I meant clothes that actually fit. You look like some orphan straight out of Dickens.”

Sirius defiantly tipped the rim of his post-boy cap toward him. “You sound like James.”

“Trust me, I don’t. Just try and think of this as a new experience. Have you even been in a charity shop before?”

“Obviously not.”

“Well, then there’s a first for everything.” He held up a brown collar shirt, which Sirius grimaced at. “So picky,” he huffed, returning it to the rack. Moments like these were when Remus was most reminded of his friend’s privilege. His own, too, if he were being honest. The Blacks probably would’ve locked Sirius in a box and dropped him in the sea before letting him march into a high street second-hand shop, and Lyall would’ve been right there with them.

“Do you really shop here?” Sirius asked, pausing to study a suede vest, before apparently deciding against it.

“Sometimes…” Remus kept his gaze on the clothes. “It was easier to walk through the End when I wasn’t dressed like—”

“A rich prat?” Sirius was eyeing him pointedly.

“Uhm… yeah. A new coat’s kinda a giveaway down there, and since I went there all the time I learned how to not be noticed. Not that it matters anymore anyway…” Remus took a breath, trying for a cheerier tone. “But hey, sometimes you can find some really cool stuff in here. Got my favourite Stones’ shirt right in this very shop.”

“You mean the one with holes in both armpits?”

He ignored him, shucking the wire hangers down their rows until he found something promising. “Here,” he said, holding up a plain white t-shirt. Sirius reached over the rack and took the garment from him, turning it around for inspection.

“Oh goodie, only two stains… Do they have anything in black?”

Remus snatched the shirt back and hung it on the rack. “It’s dead summer, do you want to sweat to death?”

“If I’m gonna go out, I might as well go out in style.” Sirius looked off to his left and did a double take. “Oh, look Moons! Real cowboy boots!”

“I don’t understand how your sense of fashion works,” Remus started, but Sirius had already rushed off, abandoning him in the middle rows. Sighing, he turned back around and continued sorting through the assembled hoard. A few more shoppers who had wandered in from the heat were meandering silently around him, but the shop was pleasantly cool thanks to the rattling fans set up in each corner. Just over their noise, Remus could hear the sound of a radio going, playing its top ten hits.



‘I’m your boogie man, I’m your boogie man,

Turn me on;

I’m your boogie man, I’m your boogie man,

Do what you want…’



It wasn’t a good song per say, but it was easy to mindlessly bob his head along with. Remus was just considering what the odds were that Sirius would agree to a lime green polo shirt when the sharp sound of a feminine giggle caught his attention. He looked up from the rack and found a pair of girls two rows over, faces bent closely to one another as they whispered behind a handful of clothes. If their knowing smiles were anything to go by, then they must’ve been there for some time. Remus looked down, pushing a few more hangers aside arbitrarily, and when he glanced back up again one of the girls was staring straight at him. She waved and flashed him a pretty smile, before her friend grabbed her wrist urgently and squeaked something that sounded a lot like ‘what are you doing?!’

As the girls descended into another giggle fit, Remus reached up and rubbed the back of his neck. He’d already told himself that he wasn’t interested in any more casual flings. Sirius’ sudden entrance had more than scared the promiscuity right out of him. But still, one last peek couldn’t hurt…

“Oi, Moony—”

Remus jumped on the spot, whirling around to find Sirius next to him.

Speaking of sudden entrances…

“Damn,” Sirius chuckled, “didn’t mean to sneak up on you, space cadet.”

“I was concentrating,” Remus clipped.

“Oh yeah? On what?” Sirius leaned in, but another tell-tale giggle made him look up. “Ooh, I get it.”

“Sirius, don’t.”

Sirius waved him off, and leaned forward on the clothes rack, whistling sharply. “ ‘Ello, ladies, nice day for a shop, innit? You two pretty things come ‘ere often?”

The girls glanced at each other and then began to laugh behind their hands, quickly shooting off in the other direction. Obviously soured by their lacklustre response, Sirius turned back around. “Hmph. Must be deaf.”

“No, I think they heard you,” Remus mocked. “It’s not a bar, Sirius, it’s a charity shop. And who were you trying to imitate anyway, Michael Cain?”

“No, it was you from our first year together—any’un got ‘a light? Can’t imagine why that would turn ‘em off.”

“Must’ve been the clothes then.” Flicking the rim of Sirius’ cap, Remus went back to the rack and pushed aside several tops, eventually coming across a half-decent button up. “What do you think? This one doesn’t have ruffles on the collar at least.”

Sirius shook his head adamantly. “Nah, s’not really ‘me’—but check this out!”

He raised his other arm, showing off a beaten-up leather jacket that looked as though it weighed forty pounds and had survived both World Wars. Remus ogled it.

“It’s summer!”

“I know it’s summer, but this thing’s killer, Moons! Someone real cool owned this jacket once, I can tell. You can practically smell the history on it.”

“Actually that’s just cat piss.”

Sirius rolled his eyes. “Found these too.” He held up a pair of blue jeans that once touched revealed themselves to have had just enough wear and wash to turn the fabric soft as butter.

“Those aren’t terrible,” Remus said, giving them a once-over. “We should find you some new shoes too, yours are falling apart…”

Sirius nodded, and then his face lit up and he reached past Remus, toward the shirts. “Oh yes, this is it! This is the one.”

“Lemme see.” Remus turned the top around. “… You’ve got to be kidding me.”

“I’m all about blending in with the locals,” Sirius sniggered, ripping the shirt off its hanger.

Not five minutes later, Remus found himself sitting outside of a fitting room on a fuzzy electric-blue footstool, twiddling his thumbs while he waited for Sirius to try on the clothes.

“Jeans are a bit tight around the family jewels,” Sirius called over the door, “but my arse looks fantastic.”

Remus felt his heart jump. “Hurry up, you’re burning daylight.”

“Coming!” The fitting room door flew open and Sirius strutted out, wearing the faded jeans and t-shirt he’s picked off the rack. It might’ve been nice, had the front of the shirt not bore the words, ‘Who’s “Big Ben” and why’s everyone looking for him?’

“Well?” Sirius grinned; “How do I look?”

Remus slouched back against the fitting room wall. “You’re so embarrassing.”

“Meh. Dans une grande âme tout est grand.” Sirius turned around to get a look at his backside in the mirror. “I mean, just look at my arse, Moony!”

“No thanks.”

“No, seriously, have a look! Jeans fit like a glove.”

Remus sighed and glanced up. Sirius was right, they did look good. And familiar… As Sirius spun around admiring himself and chortling at the stupid tourist’s shirt, Remus leaned in to get a better look. On one of the back pockets of the jeans he spotted the small outline of a heart, as though several rhinestones had once adorned it and had since chipped off. He racked his brain.

“Hey… doesn’t Mary have a pair of jeans she always claims makes her butt look spectacular?”

“Hm? Oh yeah—wears ‘em on every date.”

“Did you know if they happened to have anything on the back pockets?”

Sirius paused. “Yeah… a little heart or something.”

Remus squinted harder, just to be sure, but yep—definitely a heart. He snorted. “Padfoot… I hate to say it, but I think you’re wearing women’s trousers, mate.”

“What?” Sirius reached around, attempting to peek at the faded tag. “Shit. What are the odds? Guess that explains it though, Mary’s never wrong about these kinds of things.”

Remus shook his head hopelessly, then; “You should get them. Your arse… does look fantastic.”

“Ha! Knew you looked.”

Looking a little too pleased, Sirius ducked back into the fitting room. As he did, Remus swallowed the lump that had formed in his throat and peered out around the corner to the rest of the shop. He didn’t see the girls from earlier, perhaps they’d moved on.

“What shall I do with the shirt and slacks you leant me?” Sirius called through the door.

“Just leave ‘em,” Remus said, now busy picking a hangnail. “They’re too small for me anyway.”

“Ha. That’s just your under-handed way of calling me short.” A second later Sirius had strolled out, now donning the leather jacket. The sight of him caught Remus’ attention straight away, and he watched as Sirius began strutting in front of the mirror again, flapping the leather collar with supreme confidence. “So? What do we you think of the jacket?” Sirius inquired. “I think it looks ace.”

“It’d look better without that stupid hat, I’ll bet,” Remus said. Sirius looked at him in the mirror, before gently smoothing his hands over the brim.

“Nah… the hat adds to it.”

“You’re going to sweat to death.” Remus stood; “Just take it off.”

“No, I’m fine.”

“C’mon Padfoot, I’m sure you’ll be alright without—” Before he’d even finished his sentence, Remus had made a grab for the cap, and Sirius spun around like a cornered dog—one that was ready to take his hand off at the wrist.

“DON’T—!”

Remus yanked his arm back. “S-Sorry! Was only teasing…”

Retaliation dawned, and Sirius paled slightly before shrinking back from him like a school boy about to receive the strap. “Nah, m’sorry. Didn’t mean to snap at ya.” Sirius licked his lips. “I… haven’t taken it off really.”

“Why not?”

Sirius’ eyes dipped to the floor. “It’s… my hair? It kinda… got cut.”

Remus stepped forward again, not quite so much as to invade Sirius’ space, but enough to peek under the brim at the flaccid locks of dark hair pasted to his forehead beneath. “You still look like you got hair.”

“It’s the side here.” Sirius gestured languidly at his head. “The matron came at me with these clippers, but I wouldn’t have it. So she yanked me, and I yanked back. Hurt like a bitch for a while.”

“You mean she…?”

“Yeah. Hair’s gone.”

Remus suddenly felt very fidgety. “Well, I… I’m sure it doesn’t look that bad.”

“It doesn’t look good. You’d laugh if you saw it.”

“No, I wouldn’t.” He gave Sirius a very hard, genuine look. “I wouldn’t.”

The look made Sirius falter a bit, and he shrugged. “It’s not that fascinating anyway.”

“Would you show me?”

Sirius clenched his jaw like he might say no, but after several seconds of anguish, he finally stepped back and whipped the hat off his head. Locks of sweaty hair promptly tumbled down to just below his jaw, looking lanky and sad, but Remus didn’t really see the issue until he glimpsed the other side of Sirius’ head in the mirror. Horrified, he grabbed his friend by the shoulders and spun him. There, just behind his ear, Sirius had a small bald patch, as though whoever had grabbed it had held on until the hair had torn out from the root.

“Those fucking—” Remus sucked in a sharp breath. He’d nearly reached out to touch it but then Sirius turned back around and fit the cap back over his head, tucking in the leftover pieces of hair.

“Whatever, it’s done,” he said dismissively. “Don’t even hurt anymore either. I just don’t want others to see, so I’ve been covering it up… Didn’t exactly have time to see a barber in Calais.”

“Well, we could—” Remus scrambled for a solution, “we could hide it some other way maybe?”

“Oh yeah?” Sirius asked sarcastically. “Started carrying makeup and wigs around with you? Too bad Mary’s in France, could’ve used her.”

“Don’t be an idiot,” Remus said. “We could tie it back. Should hide the worst bits at least.”

“Nah, tried that already. You still see where the hair's missing, plus it kinda hurts... Don’t worry though, m’sure it’ll be fine soon enough.”

“How about braiding it then? I could do it. I mean, I’m not that great, but I could try.”

The offer had clearly surprised Sirius, who raised both eyebrows. “You want to braid my hair?”

“Just for now, jackass," Remus snapped, feeling flushed. "You don’t even have to keep it in for long. Anything’s better than that hat.”

Sirius’ lips quirked upwards. “So many nasty comments about my choice of dress today.”

“Just trying to look out for you.” Glancing around himself, Remus reached into a bin of spare clothes next to the fitting room. He withdrew a single unpaired trainer and quickly unravelled its lace.

“What are you gonna do with that?” Asked Sirius.

Remus held the shoelace up. “I’m gonna tie your hair back. Might be a bit rough but no one’s gonna notice. Now go on, have a seat.”

Looking only a little reluctant, Sirius popped a squat over the shaggy purple stool and Remus took up his spot behind him. His hands began to feel clammy as he began to gather Sirius’ hair back away from his face, and he worked carefully to avoid touching any other part of him.

“I thought you don’t steal, Moons,” Sirius mused, watching him in the mirror.

“I don’t.”

“You gonna pay for that shoelace then?”

Remus rolled his eyes, before glancing around to make sure the teenage shopkeeper hadn’t set upon them. “Fine, I will knick one shoelace. Happy? Now shut up and let me concentrate.”

Sirius smiled, but was quiet after that. Wiping his palms on his trousers, Remus cleared his throat and tried to ignore the way Sirius’ reflection was staring at him in the mirror, while attempting to recall the girls’ lessons. Bring sides under the middle—or was it over? Christ.

His fingers felt slow and clumsy, but after the first two or three ruined attempts, Remus finally got into the swing of it. Sirius never complained, simply waited until he’d woven the braid all the way down the back of his head and tied it off with the shoelace. He snatched his hands away again when Sirius tipped his head back to smile at him.

“There…” Remus mumbled; “All finished.”

Getting up from the little stool, Sirius peered into the mirror. Turning his head this way and that to admire Remus’ work, he pulled a few pieces free around his face and finally straightened up. “Wow. You really never cease to amaze me, Moons.”

“S’just a braid…”

“Do I look okay?”

“Huh? Oh… yeah! Y-You look great! Or I mean—you can’t see the bald spot at all.”

Sirius began fiddling with the stubby end of the braid. “It doesn’t look too… girlish?”

“Ha. Since when have you ever worried about ‘looking girlish’?”

He laughed again, and straightened up. “You’re right. Thanks, Moons.”

Remus looked away. “Don’t mention it… Shall we finish finding you a shirt then?”

“Whaddya mean? I’ve got a shirt right here.”

He looked at the tourist atrocity clinging to Sirius’ frame. “You can’t really be planning to wear that around the city.”

“Why not?”

“You’re gonna look like one of those tourists from Abbey Road. Like an American.”

“Well, can’t have that, can we?” Sirius said, making no move to remove the shirt. “Perhaps I should work on my accent, eh gov’na? Can’t have the yanks going crackers thinking I’m one ‘a them, can we? It’d all be straight dog’s dinner from there!”

“Yeah… so I’m gonna go find you those shoes now.” Remus turned and began strolling away. “… Bloody idiot.”

Sirius just chased after him. “What, you don’t like that one? Alright, how ‘bout I commit to the bit. Now how’s it go again… Maybe like—hey, I’m wah’kin’ here! Oh shit, that was pretty good! Right, Moons? … tch… Moooons!”





* * *





Remus had started keeping a mental list in his head of all the things he’d learned about the institution in Belgium;

They aided and abetted in kidnapping kids from their own homes.

And then when the kids arrived they dressed them in itchy grey suits, like convicts.

And when they misbehaved they locked them in isolation rooms for days on end.

And encouraged corporal punishment.

And withheld food.

And ripped their fucking hair out!

Lyall would’ve loved it, surely. A fact that only made him more pissed off. The matron who’d tried to shear Sirius’ hair off had better hope that Remus Lupin never made it as far as Belgium. If he did, nothing was gonna stop him from burning her miserable school to the ground.

“Turn this way, Moons.”

Luckily, Sirius didn’t seem as intent on stewing over the bad.

Remus turned to him when bid, and Sirius slipped a pair of sunglasses up the bridge of his nose. He inspected them for a moment, before ultimately shaking his head and returning them to the table stand they’d stopped at.

“You’ve got such a big head, you dwarf all of them,” Sirius mused, perusing through the frames with clever interest. He’d already picked out a pair for himself, and the wayfarers sat balanced on the top of his handsome head. Remus had just about melted when he’d put them on. Pretty fuck.

As Sirius fit a second pair on him, this one in the shape of a cat-eye (for his own amusement, surely), Remus lifted an arm to check his watch. They’d left the charity shop ages ago, and had since been up and down the city streets, dipping into various neighbourhoods like Camden High Street, making faces at the mods and punks and catching trolleys up and down for no good reason. It would’ve been faster to get around using the tube, but staying above ground meant better views and Sirius was just dying to ride one of the double-decker buses anyway. A by-product of that, they were now waiting to catch a short hop-on tour from Fitzrovia to Trafalgar Square, so Sirius could check ‘punting a pigeon’ off of his bucket list.

“Did you still want to go to the museum?” Remus asked, busy flipping through a sightseeing map as Sirius fit his dozenth pair of sunglasses on him. He’d already given up on not looking like a tourist. “Says here they’ve got a big exhibit on music. Classical music, but still.”

“I’d rather go play that game you mentioned,” Sirius said absent-mindedly. “Shoot ‘n toot or whatever.”

“It’s ‘Shoot ‘em up’. It’s a video game—like remember ‘Pong’? They’ve got this crazy place in Burlington, s'called an arcade. James and I went with Pete at the beginning of summer. Pretty sure he’s gone there every day he’s been home.”

Sirius picked up a new pair of glasses. They’d been standing and chatting for so long that the stand owner had begun to eye them suspiciously, but Remus quelled him well enough when he passed over a few quid for Sirius’ glasses.

“I can’t decide which John you should be,” Sirius said, holding up two pairs on either side of Remus’ face. “Are we to go with Elton, or Lennon?”

Remus arched his brow. “Seriously?”

“You’re right. Has to be Lennon.”

Tossing the ginormous, bedazzled square-rims aside, Sirius opened the round tea-shades and shoved them onto Remus’ face. Remus didn’t fight it—he just paid the stall guy and they carried on.

“Sorry I’m costing you so much today,” Sirius said, casting a glance around the busy street as they crept closer to the trolley stop.

“Nah, spend away. It’s only my dad’s money.”

“I’ll pay you back, swears,” Sirius said anyway. “Once I get my inheritance from Alphard. I’m almost eighteen. Soon we’ll be able to rent out a flat or something.”

“I see. Have you picked out where it is you want to live then?”

“Still shopping around. Soho’s nice though. It’s got a drug-dealer on every corner, right?”

“Only if you know where to look.”

Sirius grinned. “It’s gonna be so nice to have a place of our own.”

Our?

Remus grabbed the side of his neck awkwardly. “James and Pete’ll be there too… right?”

Sirius gave him a funny look. “As opposed to being…?”

“Uh…” Glancing away, Remus pushed the sunglasses further up his nose. “Right, I just meant that—”

“Quick, Moons,” Sirius interrupted; “Trolley’s here.”

So, Remus was once again saved from his own stupidity. Sirius wasted no time rushing to the top floor of the bus, taking up an empty set of seats near the very back. As he sat down next to him, Remus silently cursed himself. It was time to get a grip. Sirius wasn’t there because he was in love with him, Sirius was there because he’d needed help, and Remus had been the closest—the most convenient. That wasn’t to say that Remus was ungrateful, he would’ve helped Sirius even if all they’d done since was fight, but he wasn’t any more special to him than James, or even Peter. He was just there.

Well, if there was all he could be, then that’s what he’d do.

As the open-air bus made its way down the street, full to the brim with tourists and people from all over, Sirius stood up on his seat and whooped at the sky—just a great hoorah! It made Remus cringe a bit while the other passengers laughed, and soon enough one of the tour-leaders had come storming up the stairs to lambast him for ‘committing unsafe acts while the bus is in motion’. Sirius attempted to give lip, but Remus just pulled him back into his seat and they laughed together.

“Think we could get everyone here in on a game of bumps?” Sirius suggested not two minutes later.

“Do it and I’ll throw you over the side,” he warned, but the next time the bus hit a pothole, Sirius jabbed Remus in the arm and suddenly they were scrapping again right there in their seats. That was the last straw for the tour-leader, who demanded to know where their guardians were. Without any parents to be found, they bid the bus goodbye and made a hasty exit along Shaftesbury Avenue, about five stops too early. Weaving through the theatre district’s tight alleys, each filled with tiny cafes and boutiques, they made their way through Chinatown toward Soho, nearly the exact route Remus had taken on a trip out with Marlene weeks before. By then they were starving, and so Remus stopped to get them both a basket of chips, which they ate while they walked.

“Imagine living down here!” Sirius declared, stuffing his face as he stared up at the towering rows of flats and shops. They’d been out for hours and he still hadn’t lost an ounce of awe. “We gotta find ourselves a place somewhere like this,” he said around bites; “Somewhere big enough for all of us.”

“That’s gonna cost a pretty penny—fitting all four of us into one flat,” Remus said.

“Five. Can’t count out Evans.”

Remus laughed in surprise, dodging a woman walking her dog as they made their way down the street. “Here, gimme these,” he said, before taking Sirius’ empty to-go container and tossing it in a public bin. “You know… you’ve been oddly ‘team Evans’ for a while now, Padfoot. It’s odd. Did something happen between the two of you?”

“What makes you say that? I’m just assuming that Evans is the only one of us who can actually cook.”

“She’d lash you for saying that.”

“I know,” Sirius said with a guilty smile.

“Nice try, now fess up,” Remus prodded, even poking him in the shoulder. “You’ve been a little too friendly ever since that crap with Snape. So what is it that she’s got on you?”

“Nothing!”

He poked him again. “Come on!”

“Evans and I just came to a mutual understanding s’all! We talked over Easter and—”

“You talked?”

“Letters,” Sirius dismissed; “She sent me a letter. I sent one back, s’all.”

“Well, what was in it? What did you… talk about?”

“Normal stuff—her sister being a prat, Reg being a nob. I think she was just checking in. Making sure I didn’t off myself. Said something about Prongs needing his best friend back come April.”

They’d stopped along with a small crowd at a pedestrian crossing and Remus leaned in. It secretly pleased him to be able to do that; he hadn’t realised it until Sirius had taken the hat off, but he must’ve grown some more. Now he could see right over the top of Sirius’ head. He tried not to be too smug about it.

“So…?” Remus prompted. “What’d you say back?”

Sirius looked away, almost bashful. “I… I thanked her! I was expecting word from you and the lads, but Evans had never sent a letter before. It just felt genuine, I guess. She’s actually pretty funny once you get to know her, you know.”

He said this last bit very wryly, and Remus shook his head, endlessly amused. “Oh my god, you’ve gone soft for Lily.”

“Shut up,” Sirius pouted as the traffic changed and they began across the street. “Did you know her middle name was ‘Juniper’? And her sister is ‘Petunia Marigold’? I almost pissed my pants laughing reading that.”

“Her parents are botanists. And yes, I did know that. You’re not the only one Lily’s fond of, ya know.”

Sirius smiled. “Is that Remus Lupin, bragging? Hah. You’re right though, I wager you’re the only one who has a chance of swooping her out from under Prongs’ feet.”

“Nah,” Remus said very quickly; “Lily’s just a friend.”

Sirius shrugged again. “Suit yourself. But she liked you when she still hated the rest of us, so… I can’t be all wrong. Maybe she had a crush.”

He shrugged indifferently. "It's one of them."

“I’d meant to have the hay dropped off here, but they must’ve mistaken the kennels for the stables,” Sandra said, dropping the bale down outside the stables’ grand white doors and dusting her hands. “Dunno how…” he wheezed; “the dogs are… so noisy…”

“I thought the same thing!” Tipping her head back so she could see past the brim of her hat, Sandra squinted up at the impressive building. The entire thing was built out of pine, creating a long ‘L’ shape along the estate’s eastern side. It was more out of the way than the garages or kennel, and Remus liked it that way. Inside he could hear the horses’ normal baying and the occasional whinny. The Lupins didn’t have many horses, but money was old, and horses would always be money. Lyall’s mother, Remus’ grandmother, had supposedly kept many more, but they’d been sold off to other more interested buyers when she’d passed on. Though that had been ages before Remus was born.

“Are you… looking to expand the stables then?” He asked. There was another fresh pile of lumber sitting next to the stable’s outer wall, and several feet of grass had been dug up and replaced with new posts as thick as two men put together.

“I am!” Sandra replied. “Your stables are beautiful, but I’m afraid not all of my girls would fit, and I wouldn’t want to get rid of any of your horses.”

“Not my horses.” He didn’t even know most of their names. “Get rid of ‘em if you want. Or sell them. It’s whatever…”

“Oh no, I couldn’t do that. This is their home.” She gestured for the stable door. “Shall we go in then? Say hello?”

Remus shook his head. “Still don’t like horses much.”

Sandra dropped her arm immediately, accepting the boundary he’d given her without the slightest thought. He could tell though that he’d upset some sort of plan. Clearly there was more on her mind than just a stable expansion and a few stray bales of hay.

“Did you know, Remus,” she started, “that horses can hear a human heartbeat from as far as four metres away? It’s why they call them the mirrors of the soul—they feel your every intention before you even know what it is yourself.” Smiling wistfully now, Sandra lifted one foot and placed it on the edge of her hay bale, leaning into it. “When I was a little girl, my father taught me two things—or three, I suppose. How to drive, how to swing a hammer… and to bring a horse with me whenever I made a deal that had a chance of running sour.”

“I at least hope the last one was useful.”

“Ha! Yes, actually. I took my favourite mare with me the day I signed the deed to my first house. We ended up having to do it in the front garden, and that’s when I realised the entire foundation was rotted… heh, s’a bit silly… But my point is—horses always know when you’re being truthful. They see it inside you. Turn you honest.”

Because he wanted to be difficult, Remus said; “I dunno, just sounded like dumb luck… noticing the foundation, that is.”

Sandra just smiled again, perhaps even a bit wider this time. God, why did she have to be so nice?

“Alright, I see what you mean, and I’ll stop going on about horses, but I’m still left wondering… if the two of us can be honest with each other?”

Oh. Right then… It was one of those conversations. It’d be a lie to say that Remus hadn’t been expecting it. Adults never talked to kids or teenagers just to ‘talk’, there always had to be some sort of catch… some bloody lesson.

“This about you and my dad gettin’ hitched?” He asked. The least he could do was make her slightly uncomfortable too.

Sandra nodded her head in earnest. “It is. What do you think of it?”

Remus almost didn't have an answer. Lyall never asked his opinion on anything, things just simple were, and it was up to him to get with the program or be left behind. He usually didn't mind it as much, but if being left behind meant he wouldn't get to go back to Hawkings, then he might as well be honest.

“Truthfully? I don’t give a rat’s arse," he said. "Marry whoever you want.”

It obviously wasn’t the answer she’d been looking for, but Remus suddenly didn’t feel much like pandering. Disappointed, Sandra paused for a moment before meeting his eye again. “I see. Well, I appreciate your honesty. But I want you to know that I won’t change anything without your permission either. It’s still your home, Remus.”

“You’re moving in without my permission, aren’t you?”

“Oh.” Sandra let out a stilted laugh. “Alright, so that is quite the change, I'll agree that you have me there. Let me rephrase then—I won’t… or… I will try to keep things the same. I don’t want you to think that I’m coming in here to upset everything you and your father have. I simply want to add to it. But if you veto something—that’s it, it’s gone. No need for an explanation, I won’t even question it. I’m not trying to replace your mother.”

Because he was cruel, Remus said; “You couldn’t.”

She nodded earnestly. “I understand. Hope was very kind, you know. I didn’t know her all that well, just the odd lunch-in. But she was always such a glowing woman. She spoke about you a lot—to anyone who’d listen. About her little boy... When we heard she’d grown sick we were all so upset.”

Remus said nothing. ‘We were upset’? He didn’t even know who ‘we’ was.

“Did you really drag me out here to talk about my dead mum, Sandra?”

“Oh… no. I’m sorry.” Sandra knotted her fingers together with unease. “There was more to it, but I won’t keep you. I just… I would really like it if we could be a family, Remus. You and your father, I’ve grown very fond of you both.”

Remus let out a sigh, pushing himself to his feet. How was he to tell her that they hadn’t even been a family before? That there was no ‘you and your father’?

“Could we do that?” Sandra asked again. “Could we try to be a family? ... Would you let me be a part of your family?”

Remus pinched the bridge of his nose. “Look Sandra—Sandy, whatever… I really don’t care. Change what you want, make your family, I just want to be left alone.”

Sandra sighed quietly, upset, and Remus had to fight the urge to feel guilty. Whatever pain this is, keep it. I've enough of my own.

“You’re a good boy, Remus,” she said, almost surprising him. “Thank you for your kindness.”

He’d been anything but kind, but Sandra hadn’t really meant it that way anyway. What she’d really meant was, thank you for making things clear.

Remus dug the toe of his trainer into the soft bed of sand that surrounded the stables. “Is there anything else then…?”

“No, I believe I’ve got it from here. Boys should be arriving soon with the lorry. And thank you for your help with the hay. I’m much obliged, and so are the horses, I’m sure.”

Avoiding her gaze so as to not permeate the air with further awkwardness, Remus gave Sandra a single polite nod and stepped past her, back up the path toward the main house. He only got a few feet before he turned back around again. He couldn’t help it—he had to know.

“Why did you fall in love with him? … Him? Of all people?”

Sandra turned around, and then she looked at him. Or into him. He wasn’t sure.

“Your father feels things very intensely, Remus,” she said. “I can tell that you have that in common. You’re like two lost ships, drifting along aimlessly, just looking for their lighthouse.”

“And are you supposed to be that lighthouse or something?”

“I can’t be sure,” she said softly. “But Remus… forgiveness is a gift you give to yourself.”

Remus’ eyes began to burn. He should’ve known.

“Tell me, Sandy, would you forgive a man who forced you to call him ‘father’, but would never call you his son?”

The question had been part metaphor, part truth. Not knowing what Sandra knew, he wasn’t sure if she’d caught the double-meaning. Not that it mattered. He did not wait to hear her answer anyway.

Mid-August 1977





Remus didn’t need a lighthouse. He had a lightbulb. And not just any lightbulb—a lightbulb that shone with all the ferocity of the brightest star in the night sky. Sirius was his lightbulb. He just knew it. It was mid-August now, which meant that they’d been hiding out together for just over three weeks. Soon it’d be a month. An entire month, and no one was the wiser. Remus was almost inclined to rub it in his father’s face.

Remember that ineffable House of Black? While I’ve got their eldest son in my bedroom—in my bed! How’s that for keeping him happy, eh Dad?

He didn’t of course, because that would be ludicrous. But Lyall still wasn’t bothering to hound his every step anyway, so Remus just went back to focusing on what they had—enjoying it. Which might’ve been easier, had another deadline not been looming.

“So… school?” Remus had asked that very same morning. It was Sunday again, their third together, and they had no plans. It was wonderful.

Across from him on the bed, Sirius did not even glance up from the joint he was fiddling with. “Ugh. Do you think I’ll ever get better at rolling these damn things?”

"Sirius... I'm talking about school."

"Mhm... Oh bollocks... Will you roll it then?"

Remus sighed. Foiled again. “Hand it here.”

Sirius did so, and Remus expertly shimmied the loose hash into the centre of the paper, licking its side and rolling it up.

“Ace,” Sirius commended, taking the spliff and adding it to a jar with several others.

“James and Pete are coming back from Devon soon,” Remus attempted instead. “I’m supposed to meet them.”

“How nice.” Sirius began glancing around for the jar’s lid.

“You’re going to go with me, right?”

“Sure. Eventually. No need to rush.”

“They come back soon,” Remus said again. “Like soon, soon. Like three days soon.”

Sirius found the lid amongst the bed covers and quickly jammed it onto the jar’s top, before tossing the whole thing up in the air haphazardly. “How nice,” he said again.

“Sirius.” Remus caught the jar out of the air. “I’ve ignored seven calls from James since you got here. Seven.”

“Nice number, seven. You know what’s even better than seven though? Eight.”

“No, no more joking. We have to tell them.”

“Do we though?” Sirius pouted. “Would it not be enough to just let them know that you heard from me?”

“It would be a lie.”

“Just a tiny one, wouldn’t hurt much. And then in a few days we can go see them together and all’s well again!”

Remus set the down with a huff. “I don’t understand why you’re being so difficult. They’re your best friends.”

“I’m not being difficult. I just would rather savour this.” Sirius looked leaned back on his arms. “I wanna see them, course I do, but rushing back there would mean all this has to stop, wouldn't it? And I… I don’t think I want that.”

Later they both snuck down to the parlour and Remus rang James’ summer house. He knew Sirius didn’t mean to be cruel to his friends on purpose; he simply resided under the impression that if they were going to worry somewhere, then it might as well be from the comfort of their summer homes.

“I still think you should still talk to him,” Remus pushed one final time, as he flopped down into one of the salon’s arm chairs and pulled the phone towards him.

“Then he’d know I’m here,” Sirius grumbled stubbornly.

“And safe. Is that really such a bad thing?”

“Look, I know James. You tell him I’m here and he’d rush out onto the road to hitchhike.”

“It’s not about that, you git. I just don’t need him or Pete coming home early to weep over me.”

“How do you know they’d weep? At this point I think James is just as likely to sock you one,” Remus pointed out. “And hey, if he does come back maybe he’ll get you out of my hair for a while.”

“I’ve not even done anything yet!”

“Hey, Moony…? You still there?”

“Oh! Yeah—fine! Just dealing with the—er… dog!”

“Arf!” Sirius barked, before clapping his hand over his mouth to avoid bursting into laughter.

“You stupid—” Remus swallowed thickly. “Hey James, reckon I could call you back later? I’m just in the middle of something here and I sorta think I need both hands for it.”

“Oh sure, Moons. We’re going back to the village tonight for Simeon’s birthday dinner but I can catch you whenever. Let me know if Sirius writes again. Or better yet, maybe I should just post him from here. You think he’ll—”

Remus couldn’t wait anymore. “Let you know—got it! Bye now!”

With a gasp of relief, he slammed the receiver back down on the phone before turning to glare at the handsome boy kneeling between his legs.

“I could kill you.”

Sirius grinned evilly, barely restraining his eager fingers. “You could. Or you could tell me why you were so desperate not to go to Devon with them in the first place.”

“ ‘Cause I hate the beach. And because I didn’t really feel like intruding on their only family holiday of the year.”

“Hm. Is there anything you do like?”

Their blissful existence together came to an end too quickly. Remus had blinked and most of August had come and gone. Soon he’d be expected to return to school not just as any old student, but a prefect. And then after that? Well, he just had to figure out what it was he was to do with the rest of his life. Remus wasn’t sure if knowing that made him feel triumphant or horrified. It was an odd feeling to know that the person you liked most in the world knew every dark inch of you. Or well, most of you.

"You have to tell them," Remus said quietly. "James would want to know."

"Maybe, but..."

"Do you think he'd pity you? Because—"

“No, it's not pity. James is too good for that."

"Then why is it hard? I won't know unless you tell me."

"It’s just different with James,” Sirius said, murmuring into his hair. He was hugging Remus from behind, something he'd started doing whenever he didn't want Remus to see his face. They hadn’t talked much that day—the last day. Instead they'd just laid next to each other with the radio playing and watched the sun rise and fall in the sky outside their window. Eventually the blue summer sky had given way to a majestic sunset, casting a warm orange glow over the entire room. Tomorrow their friends would be back and Sirius could go see them... if he wanted.

“How so?” Remus asked, because he knew it would help Sirius answer.

“He’s so good, Moony. If James were a colour he’d be pure white. Like a cloud. A great white cloud... What if I stain him?”

Remus slid a hand up to his chest, where it found Sirius' and he could lace their fingers together. “You said his parents were good. What if they’re able to help?”

“Yeah. I promised James, and well… I’m not quite ready to give you up just yet.”
