He held out a hand to help Sirius up, and together they gathered the rest of their things and set off. Leaving Primrose Hill behind, they made their way back over the train tracks toward the market in Camden Lock. Along the way they passed the Roundhouse, so named for the circular stage that occupied its interior. The building itself had originally housed a railway turntable, and then later used as a warehouse for old railway cars, but now attracted bands from all over the world to perform to intimate crowds hand-picked from London’s finest and most passionate fans.

“Everyone’s played there,” Remus said, when Sirius stopped to hand off the chain link fence surrounding the venue. “Jimi Hendrix, Pink Floyd, the Doors… The Who. Even David Bowie.”

“Yes,” Sirius said with a wistful smile. “And one day it’s gonna be us.”

Remus didn’t bother questioning the finality with which Sirius made his statement. Even if they had a snowball’s chance in hell of actually making it onto the Roundhouse’s stage—or any stage, really—it was his dream too now.

Carrying on, they followed the tracks until they found themselves skirting around the market, its stalls piled high with various antiques and handmade jewellery. Sirius stopped outside one of them to admire a table piled high with chunky silver and brass rings. The woman selling them was set up behind the table on a mattress of several oriental-looking rugs, eating a salad that looked more like the grass of Primrose Hill than lettuce. Her entire outfit seemed to be made of various silk scarves and the smile she gave them when they approached felt similar to the rest of the traders in the market; just a hungry artist looking to make a buck.

“My dad has one of these,” Sirius said, plucking a large signet ring out of the heap. “Family heirloom. Had the Black family crest on it and everything. Was supposed to be mine when I turned eighteen. Suppose it’ll go to Reg now.”

“Good riddance?” Remus suggested meekly.

“Yeah,” Sirius agreed. “Always thought it was an ugly old thing anyway. Though, at least his was real silver.”

The stall-woman gave them a vexing look and Remus quickly took the ring from Sirius, replacing it and steering him away. The next few stalls were packed with fresh cooking and hungry market-goers, and Remus had to muscle his way to the front of the line where he ordered döner kebab for both of them. Lamb for himself, beef for Sirius.

“Ohhh… I think I’m gonna marry this sandwich,” Sirius moaned, already several bites in as they made their way out of the market thoroughfare.

“Are you now? Didn’t you once say that you’d never get married?”

“… I’m going to fuck this sandwich.”

Remus grinned, taking a large bite of his own. “It’s called kebab, you tourist.”

Sirius just nodded, eyes closed in reverence. “I want to make a pun, but I can’t think of any, so I’m just going to enjoy this.”

Mouths stuffed, they made their way along, eating while walking and hindered only by their sparse possessions. People passed them in the streets without so much as a glance. Maybe one day, when they were christening stages like the likes of the Roundhouse or Dingwalls, the reaction would be different. But for now they were just two nameless idiots with half a pack of fags and an old beat-up guitar.

“Which was back to the station?” Sirius asked around another bite of kebab. Throwing his wrapper in a roadside bin, Remus wiped his mouth on the back of his hand, already looking on ahead.

“It’s just—”

Remus’ eyes shot wide.

Could it be? … Really? Agh… ah fuck.

Oblivious, Sirius looked up at him with a cheeky expression. He reached for his cheek. “Oi babe, I think you’ve got a little something right—eugh!”

Grabbing Sirius by the collar of his shirt, Remus quickly hauled him into an alleyway that they’d just passed. Surprised by the sudden yank, Sirius dropped the rest of his kebab on the way and appeared fully ready to throw a quality fit, but something on Remus’ face must’ve given him reason to pause. Instead he slowly peeked around him and peered out onto the street, obviously unsure what to look for.

“Moons…?”

It was as though Remus’ heartbeat had moved from his chest into his ears. It’d been so long, he almost glossed over them entirely, but Vint was a large guy who wore his leather jacket more often than Sirius, and Seesaw was never without his signature shades. But still they looked different. Their heads were shaved… their faces more flat and square. Remus could remember thinking they’d all looked grown last Christmas, but this was something else. Gone were the boyish features he’d known, replaced by stoney looks that deterred any passerby from getting too close. They weren’t alone either—they had a gaggle of other guys with them, some younger and freckled, others with leftover scars from acne or one-too-many fights. He couldn’t recall any of them as familiar, but he searched every one of their faces desperately. For a hint—a chance.

No dice. Tomny was not among them.

“Moons?” Sirius said again, grabbing his arm. “You good…?”

Remus said nothing, just ushered Sirius further into the alley. The group was almost upon them, and he couldn’t bring himself to look when they passed. He didn’t want to be noticed—he couldn’t be noticed, what would he even say? Hello? Hello and goodbye? I’m sorry? Dammit.

In whatever capacity to feel that he had left, he was grateful for Sirius. The other boy didn’t say anything else, and simply waited until the pack of boys-turned-men had long passed. A few of them were in the middle of conversation—laughing. Remus couldn’t tell what about, it was so quick, but caught wind of Seesaw’s lazy drawl as he quipped a quick reply and it was enough to send him sprawling back to those days at the flat. He’d thought he’d mourned them all. Guess not.

“I knew them,” Remus said later, when he’d finally had the courage to exit the alleyway and continue on.

“You mean those guys?” Sirius clarified. “The ones that looked fresh outta the chokey?”

He glanced over his shoulder like the boys might reappear holding switchblades and brass knuckles.

“They didn’t look like that when I knew ‘em,” Remus murmured. “They were my f-f… my friends. They know Tomny.”

Sirius’ expression became a glower. He still had not forgiven Tomny for the way he’d ended things, though it was entirely on Remus’ behalf. “You should’ve said hello,” he told him; “Asked them where Tomny was so we can go kick his arse.”

Even in his raw state, Remus found it within himself to smile. “You’d actually pick a fight with Tomny for me?”

“Hmph. Can’t be that tough, not if he’s weaselling out over the phone like a little bitch.”

The snipe did not make Remus feel better, but Sirius was quick to rectify it. He leaned in close as they walked and wrapped a friendly arm around Remus’ shoulders.

“Hey, don’t think about it. Those guys are the ones missing out, not you. After all, you’re Remus Dean, you’re gonna play the Roundhouse one day. Then the 100 Club, and the Astoria, and Wardour Street… you’re amazing, you are.”

“Careful,” Remus replied meekly, “any more ‘a that and m’gonna start thinking you’re trying to charm your way into my trousers.”

“Don’t be silly. I’ve already done that twice over.”

That you have.

With a sigh caught between relief and longing, Remus wrapped his own arm around Sirius’ shoulders. It was just a friendly gesture—no one would’ve mistaken them for being anything other than a pair of lads out on the town, but it meant more because it was Sirius. Sirius would always mean more.

“Ah! I know just what’ll cheer you up!” Sirius declared not five minutes later. They were only a street over from the station and it was getting late into the afternoon, but that didn’t deter him from steering Remus directly toward the record shop the moment he spotted it.

“Retail therapy’s always helped me,” Sirius instructed, pushing the door open and letting the bell overhead chime.

“Especially when it’s someone else’s money,” Remus added.

“Precisely!”

It was a small shop, with yellow overhead lights all cracked in various places and crates upon crates of old vinyl stacked all the way to the ceiling. There was music playing, and a few other shoppers weaved amongst the rows, browsing quietly while an animated clerk attempted to charm some girl over the register’s counter. “Hey-up,” he called halfheartedly, as the two of them ambled inside. Sirius returned the lame hello with a wave.

“Think they got any Sex Pistols?” He asked Remus.

“Only one way to find out…”

With tapes on one side and records on the left, they promptly got to work.

“Do you think we’ll ever be rid of disco?” Sirius asked, standing across from Remus and haphazardly flicking through the shrink-film wrapped albums.

“Could be worse. Could be synth.”

“You think synth's worse than disco?”

“Obviously. At least disco uses some real instruments. Synth is all machines making music—nasty. You lose the human aspect of it, the part that makes it rich and… I dunno, alive.”

“You’re such a music snob,” Sirius laughed. “I love it.”

Remus smirked down at the row of albums in front of him. How easily Sirius could banish a bad spell. All thoughts of Tomny and the flat gone, a giddy feeling had come over Remus, like the sort that made screams of triumph build up in your chest. Before he could lose it completely, he shoved the albums back into their place and cleared his throat.

“Gonna go ask the guy if he’s got any Sex Pistols.”

Sirius just nodded, bobbing his head to the shop's music as rummaged through the stacks.

As Remus broke away, he slipped around the few other shoppers and stopped a short ways away from the cash counter. The shop clerk was still heavily engrossed in conversation with the girl—or that was to say, she was still heavily engrossed in conversation with him. Remus had to wait several minutes while the guy went on and on about the marvels of bands like Bad Company and Cheap Trick, not so subtly pausing every third word to peek down the front of her shirt as she leaned half her torso across the counter. Remus didn't care much to listen in, but his mouth-breathing was hard to ignore.

"Yeah, so ya see, Black Sabbath was completely unlike anything on the scene at the time. Their blues-rock was pure sludge music—either ya hated it or loved it.” He shrugged nonchalantly. “I personally prefer their earlier stuff meself, but ‘Technical Ecstasy’ wasn’t bad.”

Impossibly, the girl leaned even further over the counter. “Wasn't their lead singer supposed to have sold his soul to the devil?”

“That’s jus' Oz being Oz. He created this whole ‘Prince of Darkness’ thing to wake people up. You know, make rock faster by slowin' it down.”

“Wow.”

Grimacing slightly, Remus glanced at his wrist, wishing he’d remembered his watch. “Uh, s’cuse me…”

“Be right with you, pal,” the clerk responded, without so much as glancing Remus’ way. “Have you listened to their debut album?”

The girl shook her head.

“Oh man, you’re really missing out. It’s just got these—these tones to it, ya know?! It’s doom, but it’s also hope, and—and—ya know, their guitarist used to lower his string tension all the time to get these really low, grovelly notes. I’m talking like, almost out of tune here!"

Remus rolled his eyes. "Uhm..."

"Yeah, hold on a sec, mate. Anyway, he did it so he could mix rhythm riffs with lead guitarist right there in studio. He hated editing his sound in the booth. Said it ruined—”

“No, he didn't,” Remus cut-in mercilessly, “he did it because he was missing the tips of two fingers on his right hand.”

Both the girl and the clerk looked up at him very sharply. “Excuse me?”

“Tony Iommi,” Remus said. “He lost them while working at a sheet metal factory when he was seventeen. That's why he played low.”

The clerk squinted at him critically. “Who?”

“The… The guitarist…? Of Black Sabbath?” Remus glanced around as though he were being chaffed. “Were you not just talking about him?”

Looking more than a little affronted, the clerk cleared his throat and began to nod briskly. “Right. Iommi. Class act, him… er—Right!” He lifted his hands into the shape of an air-guitar and began mimicking the fretboard while the girl watched. “Lost his fingers! Total devastation time. Imagine fretting a guitar with half your hand!”

“Well, actually—” Remus pointed to the guy’s other arm; “Iommi plays left-handed so it’d be your other hand.”

The clerk gave a sharp huff and dropped his arms. “Orright, kid, whatchu want?”

“Do you have the Sex Pistols’ new single?”

“You sure you’re old enough for that kind of stuff?”

The girl giggled and Remus puckered slightly. “You sure you’re not too old to be hitting on teenage girls?”

Apparently the joke was not a hit. “Don’t got it,” the clerk retorted.

“Could you double-check?”

“Look, even if I did have it once upon a time, you’re about the tenth guy I’ve turned away already. Try checking back next week.”

“Gee, thanks,” Remus replied, not at all thankful. He turned away and the clerk promptly launched back into another rant—“Where was I? Oh right, actually Sabbath’s pretty much old-hat now anyway. It’s punk that’s in now. You’ve heard of the Ramones?”

Making his way back across the shop, he found Sirius going through a milk crate of LPs that were on-offer.

“Ever cared much for the Allman Brothers, Moons?”

“Nah, too American.”

“Too right.” Sirius dropped the LP back into the crate. “What’s the verdict then? We gettin’ high to ‘God Save the Queen’ tonight?”

Remus shook his head. “They don’t got it.”

“Bollocks.”

“We could always check in Finchley. James said there’s a decent shop not too far from his place.”

“Right, right—he’s told me about it. But hey, I found these!” Crossing over to the centre aisle, Sirius began showing off several more albums—good albums. Marvin Gaye. Joni Mitchell. King Crimson. Even a few he didn't know.

“What’s ‘Kraftwerk’?” Remus asked, holding up one of the albums curiously.

“Dunno,” Sirius said; “I’m trying to diversify. I think they’re German—but look, one of these songs is over twenty-two minutes long!”

“Jesus... and they say Queen's bad. Alright, give ‘em here then.” Gathering the albums from Sirius and tucking them under one arm.

"Oh, you don't have to get all of them," Sirius said quickly.

"Sure, I do. Call it an advance on your birthday gift."

Sirius smiled shyly, fingering his sunglasses.

As they turned for the cash counter, the door behind them opened and chimed to allow other customers inside. Neither of them paid any mind. “You think you’re ready to head on to James’ now?” Remus asked.

“Good as,” Sirius said. “Can’t keep ‘em waiting forever, now can we?”

“Not if you want this band of yours to actually work out. Any more of this nonsense and James might actually kill you. And then what would we do without our notorious Sirius Black?”

Sirius grinned. “ ‘Notorious’, huh? I like the sound of that.”

“You would.”

“Gotta find you a new stage name too. How 'bout the Rakish Re—"

"No."

"No? Alright, then maybe, Majestic Moo—"

"Keep trying."

Sirius huffed. "Fine, then how about the Spectacular—"

“Sirius…?!"

The name had not come from Remus or Sirius' mouth. Instead it’d echoed from behind—from the woman who’d just walked into the shop. Already half-facing Sirius, Remus saw her first; she was quite short, but no one they knew from school, with hair the colour of coffee with just a bit too much cream. At her temples were two twin streaks of purple and she wore a collared necklace around her throat like a second belt. Heavy beaded hoops hung from either ear and dark coal rimmed her eyes—a punk if Remus had ever seen one. But as striking as she was, Remus was instantly horrified. He hadn’t counted on anyone recognising Sirius before they were even due back to school. Almost a month of pure secrecy coupled with hiding out in his bedroom and here was this random stranger off the street, waltzing in and shouting his name out of nowhere. There couldn’t be that many Siriuses in London, surely. And none that could’ve been mistaken for Sirius Black.

Remus felt like saying, Don’t turn around. Just run. Run and I’ll distract them! But they were not characters on a daytime drama with finite answers and endings. They were just two boys with a strong affinity for irony, and there was nothing else to do aside from watch as Sirius spun around to face the potential threat. Face her and… hug her?

Lost in his own surprise, Remus stood by dumbfounded as Sirius’ face split into an inexplicable expression of disbelief and utter joy. “ANDY!” He cried, throwing himself forward and forcing the woman to catch him. She did—barely—and then stood back to get a better look at him.

“Oh my god! It is you, Sirius! Holy fuck—what are you—How are you—?!" She whipped her head around. “Ted! Ted, it’s Sirius! It’s my cousin.”

Another guy stepped forward. Remus hadn’t the gall to notice him until he did, but what he found was a man nearly twice Andy’s height, with an eyebrow piercing, wearing a creased t-shirt with the words ‘Vive le Rock’ across its front. His hair was spiked up with gel and he wore leather cuffs on both wrists. Despite the rough-looking dress, he appeared friendly enough as he extended a hand toward Sirius, tucking a cigarette behind his ear as he did so.

“I’m Ted,” he said with a lazy smile. “Pleasure to meetcha. Heard lots from Andy.”

Sirius shook Ted’s hand, still entirely starstruck. “I-I’m sorry,” he managed, “but is this really happening right now? I mean—what are you doing here? Where’s Dora?”

Andy looked Sirius up and down slowly, like she still couldn't believe it was him. “Dora’s with grandma. The Grateful Dead’s just released a new album, and we—we know the owner… What are you doing here? Have you really moved to London?”

Appearing unsure, Sirius glanced back at Remus. “Er... Something like that…”

Andy didn’t miss the look. For the first time Remus felt as though she’d noticed his presence; giving him the same once-over, she paused just long enough for him to begin worrying again—but the next moment she was smiling, and all the anxiety instantly melted away. Her eyes weren’t the same grey as Sirius’, more of a mottled brown, but they had the same shape, the same little wicked crinkle at the outer corner.

“Oh, who cares?!” She exclaimed. “You’re here. And you have my guitar!”

Sirius perked up, raising the colourful guitar case high. “Yeah, a‘course! Couldn’t leave it. It’s the best gift I’ve ever gotten.”

Looking like she might cry, Andy let out a little whimper of happiness and pulled Sirius into another hug. “It’s been too long—you’ve grown so much… oh… I missed you, little brother.”

Unable to see his face, Remus couldn’t be sure what expression Sirius was making, but if he knew him at all, then it was bound to be something very close to luminous.

They’re like mirrors of each other, Remus thought later, as the four of them made their way up and down the borough’s busy streets together. From behind, the Black cousins could’ve been closer to siblings. They both had that willowy look about them—pale skin, dark eyes, with legs up to their necks and hair to match. Then there was the part where they both spoke with their hands; the more excited they got, the more they jumped over one another in conversation until eventually they were finishing each other’s sentences with ease.

“You do know that Bella—”

“Got married? Oh yeah, Cissy still sends me the occasional letter. Did you—”

“Go to the wedding? Nah, as if mum would ever let me. It was in April anyway. But I saw the photos! ... Almost feel bad for Bella, too. Her unibrow might be worse, but nothing’s as bad as his—”

“His teeth! Oh my god, I remember the teeth. Like a fucking horse!”

It was good to hear Sirius laugh at someone else’s jokes. He and Andy walked on ahead, leaving Remus and Ted to trail behind like the leftover partners they were. They had no real destination, but the sudden reunion was too wonderful an opportunity to pass up. No one complained, after all Andy and Sirius hadn’t done more than send letters and talk over the phone in almost five years. Since that time, Andy had found out she was pregnant, had the baby out of wedlock with a lower-class boy from Tottenham, and was promptly ejected from the family of Black—an experience the cousins now shared.

“I don’t know why you didn’t just call me!” Andy lashed, after Sirius reluctantly told her how he’d ended up in London in the first place.

“What was I supposed to say? ‘Hey Andy, mum sent me to prison in Belgium, can you come pick me up?’ ”

“Yes! Exactly that!”

Sirius waved the answer off, but Remus could tell he was secretly pleased. It was a foreign feeling to him—cousins. Remus didn’t have any. Both Hope and Lyall had been only children, and well… there was no way of knowing what went on within his more distant relations.

“They look alike, don’t you think?” Ted asked suddenly, pulling Remus back down to earth. “Think it’s the eyes. Like a gene lottery. Though I suppose I’m the lucky one, really.”

Me too, Remus thought.

Smiling, Ted turned to look at him while they walked. “Sorry, I never caught your name?”

“Oh, my bad. It’s Remus.”

“Pleasure. You Sirius’ friend then?” Ted offered a hand, which Remus shook. It was firm, his palm a bit rough, like Giles' or any other working boy. Briefly, Remus wondered what Ted thought of his palm. It was probably smooth enough to assume that he'd never done a day of work in his life.

“Er… yeah," he answered. "He’s been staying with me for a while.”

“You from London then?” Ted asked.

“Mhm. Blackheath.”

“Nice. From Tottenham, meself, but we’re over in Islington now. The two of you should drop in sometime! I’d love to get Sirius to jam out with us. You play anything?”

“Bass.”

“Oh, champ! Don’t tell Andy I said this—but the bass is where it’s really at.”

Remus smiled. He liked Ted, he’d decided. He was friendly without asking too many questions, and he was tall enough that Remus didn’t feel gangly or out of place. Plus, he looked bloody cool. A bit fit, even—but that was queer thought, so he pushed it away.

“Sirius said you used to be in a band?” He asked.

Ted nodded. “A few years ago. Almost got a contract even, but then everything went tits up when our lead singer skipped town for America. Thought he would make it big in L.A, ‘cept now he buses tables while his boss busts his balls.”

“Oh. Bad luck, that.”

“Eh, didn’t matter really. I quit not long after anyway—when Dora was born. Gotta feed the family somehow, right?” Ted chuckled. “Not that I’m complaining! Got a whole new outlook on life. I look back now and I’ve realised that I was just drifting before, y’know? Andy didn’t just give me a family, she gave me a purpose.” Without any prompting, Ted popped a tattered wallet out of his pocket and flipped it open. Aside from a sparse few paper notes and his driving licence, it held only a handful of photographs, mainly of Andy holding a chubby baby girl.

“This is the most recent,” he said, thumbing through and producing a small photo of his daughter covered in paint and brandishing a paintbrush like a sword. He showed the photo off with all the eager glee of a loving father, almost a complete paradox to his hard, punk-like exterior. “Cute, huh?”

Remus nodded firmly until Ted had tucked the photo away again. He couldn’t imagine giving up everything for something as trivial as family. But maybe that was just because his family had never given anything up for him.

“I wish we could’ve talked for longer, but Dora turns into a real riot act if we’re even a minute late,” Andy said, after their twentieth turn around the block had ended outside the entrance to the Underground. “We’re still not sure who taught her how to read a bloody clock at only four years-old, but I’m gonna wring their neck when I find out.”

“Reckon she’s just gifted,” Sirius said, “like me.”

“Don’t say that. Can’t afford to let my kid take after a bruiser like you.” Andy ruffled his hair fondly, loosening the braid Remus had done himself that morning. “You’ll come and visit us before heading back to school then?”

“Sure, sure,” Sirius smiled.

“I mean it. If you don’t I’ll kick your arse.”

“C’mon Ands, we’re not kids anymore. You couldn’t kick my ass if you tried,” he scoffed, leaning in to taunt her. Andy socked him one for it—right in the stomach—and Sirius folded around her fist like a piece of paper.

“You were saying?”

“Ugh… alright, I yield, Ands—uncle, uncle!”

After that they hugged, and Remus held back to shake Ted’s hand once more.

“Take care of him, Remus,” Andy said, just as they were about to part ways. It was only about the third thing she’d said to him directly, the first being ‘so you’re the Remus I’ve been hearing so much about!’ and the second, ‘blimey, you are tall’. Remus didn’t really mind; Sirius was usually the subject of attention, but this time around he deserved it.

“I will,” he promised her.

“We take care of each other!” Sirius interjected, hitting Remus with the tip of his guitar case and poking his tongue out in Andy’s direction.

“Don’t be a stranger then!” Andy called, taking Ted’s hand and already backing down the pavement. “You come visit too, Remus, and bring James and Peter as well! We’ll catch a show—or have one! Perhaps both!”

They waved, the happy couple, and Remus and Sirius returned it in kind. Neither of them moved until Andy and Ted’s forms had faded far into the distance, and when they finally turned to head down onto the platform, Sirius did so with a revived spring in his step.

“Absolutely mental—seeing Andy again!” Sirius said, as the next train to Finchley rumbled into the underground station and they boarded. “She was pissed off that I didn’t give her the bell a'course,” he went on; “Or tell ‘er I was in London, but it was… Blimey—amazing. She looks the exact same.”

“Real fates at work,” Remus agreed, as they took two seats near the back of the train car. “You gonna go visit her then?”

“Yeah, should, shouldn’t I? ... ‘sides, I’d like to see Dora, and Ted’s supposedly still got all of his old equipment in storage. I told you once that Andy was the only other one Alphard left money to? It’s how they bought the house in Islington! You could come—we could all go! ... Ha, oh hell. James is going to be so pissed off that we’re this late.”

Remus shrugged. “Day ain’t over yet, he’ll understand once we explain everything.”

“Yeah—yeah, he's good like that, that Prongs. He’ll understand. Can’t wait to tell him about Andy.”

“You never told me that Andy calls you ‘brother’,” Remus said, because he could tell Sirius wasn’t done talking about her.

“Picked up on that, did you?” Sirius beamed, still babbling along. “Jus’ something we did as kids. All I had was Reg, and she liked her sisters well enough, I guess, but we were always the odd ducks. Pretending it was just the two of us made things more bearable. Sucked when she left though. But hey—we’re both better for it, we’re both here now! Totally free and livin’ life.”

“That’s right,” Remus said, then; “I don’t have any cousins.”

“None?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Sounds a bit lonely.”

“Hm. Maybe… I had the dogs though.”

Suddenly going very quiet, Sirius bit his lip. “Er—that’s right, what am saying?! You’re not really missing out on much anyway. In fact, I hate most of my cousins! They're all racist, right-wing Tories who'd rather get with each other than marry someone of a lower class. ‘Cept for Andy of course.”

Remus chuckled lightly. “Thanks for trying to make me feel better. Andy seems pretty rad.”

“Oh yeah, she is. Sorry I never really introduced you properly—got a bit excited.”

“S’okay. Next time.”

Smiling, Sirius glanced down at his hands. The anticipation of ‘next time’ was written all across his face, and Remus was glad for him. In the exposed space of the train car, he wished he could have leaned his head on Sirius’ shoulder in comfort, but he couldn’t, so instead he set his bag across their laps and slid one hand beneath it, reaching for Sirius’ lovely fingers.

If Remus hadn’t turned to face the train window to hide his own guilty blush, he might’ve noticed the smile on Sirius’ face become that much wider.





* * *





“Moony?” Sirius asked, as they made their way down the street from the station. It was already late afternoon, almost evening, and they were most certainly late, but Remus still couldn’t bring himself to rush.

“Mhm?” He responded, busy staring at the passing houses.

“Don’t hate me, but I think I’m still sort of nervous…”

“It’s just James, Sirius.”

“It’s not though. It’s the Potters. I’ve only ever visited that one time, and when I showed up, it took about five minutes for them to start calling me their son. It was… indescribable.”

“Wow, you’ve really convinced me. They sound horrible—guess we should go home!”

Halting in the middle of the pavement, Remus made a sharp about-turn and Sirius laughed, immediately pulling him back by the arm. “Alright, I get it. I’m being a pansy.”

“You are,” Remus agreed. “And I’m tired of putting up with it, so let’s just getchu on home to Prongs, okay?”

Sirius sighed. It was with love. “Okay, Moony.”

Like they had on the train, Sirius reached for his hand. Remus let him at first—he’d almost grown used to it after a month—but as they began to walk, he noticed a young couple down the lane pushing a pram ahead of them and quickly pulled free of his grasp. Sirius’ fingers flexed at the sudden absence, but he said nothing about it. Cringing with slight regret, Remus held his breath until the couple passed, but even then he couldn’t bring himself to reach back out again. He told himself not to be bothered—Sirius understood.

On the way they discovered that the walk from the station to the Potters’ was a decent one. They passed through several different neighbourhoods and suburbs until the townhouses gave way to detached homes, and then detached homes with a driveway, and then detached homes with a driveway and a garden and a path and then some. They really only got lost once, but after stopping a passerby for directions, they eventually found themselves walking down a private driveway lined with rich growth and birch trees. They had to pass a country club to find the house, but finally made it to the proper start of the Potters’ drive after a few more minutes of walking.

“Bloody hell,” Remus murmured, when he first spotted the house. He was used to the vast finery of the Lupin estate, but Potter Cottage was something else.

“I know, right?” Sirius said back, still taking it all in himself.

Just beyond an unlocked gate made of solid brass was an elegant driveway that stretched all the way up to a stunning three-floor Tudor home. It’s sprawling front garden was covered in blooming colours and fully-grown trees of birch and oak. Each window was made of stained glass, and flowering ivy crawling up its exterior walls. The lawn was perfectly manicured, with thriving rose bushes that dotted the lane leading all the way up to the home’s front door. Everywhere they looked there was more greenery, more life, but none of it felt stifling or uniform. Grass grew where it chose to grow, and the weeds were tidy but not eliminated all together. It felt a bit arbitrary to call such a fine house a 'cottage', but the home wasn't so needlessly large as to avoid any real character in favour of blatant wealth. It was warm and happy—it looked happy.

“Hasn't changed a lick,” Sirius said, trailing his fingers across the bars of the gate. Taking the initiative, Remus pushed it open for him and together they started up the drive where they eventually passed Mr. Potter’s sensible, yet still flashy, Aston Martin sedan.

"Giles would be jealous," Remus said, peeking in the window. "Look, it's got a built-in cassette player!" He glanced up, but Sirius had already moved on, having set his guitar case down on the front stoop to wring his hands nervously. Remus followed, and Sirius turned to him, taking a deep breath.

“Alright. So how should we do this?”

“How ‘bout like this.” Remus rang the doorbell.

“Moons, I wasn’t ready!”

Already fretting, Sirius ducked behind a shrub while a great thundering started inside the house. It sounded to Remus like frantic footsteps, and he was proven right when James burst forth out the front door, looking wide-eyed and utterly delighted to see him.

“Moony!” He declared, already hugging Remus fiercely. “About time, mate! I told you to ring me when you got to the station so Dad and I could come pick you up!”

“S’okay, I enjoyed the walk,” Remus smiled, patting James on the back in return.

Releasing him, James stepped back into the doorway. “Made it alright then? I hope your dad didn’t give you much trouble. Mum says she’ll still call if he’s got a problem with you staying over.”

“Nah, he don’t care. Got enough on his plate to not be worried about me.”

Nodding understandably, James began to usher him inside. Already Remus could smell the comforting scent of fresh baking. “Come on in then, Mum’s just in the kitchen making lunch. Pete’s gonna be by soon too! He’s just the lane over.”

Biting his lip over a smile, Remus dug his heels in and hesitated on the door mat. “Well, there’s one thing you probably know first, Prongs…”

“What’s that?”

With a great cry, Sirius burst out from behind the shrub, a single leaf caught in his fringe. “TA-DA!” He announced, as James’ jaw fell open. “Miss me, Prongsie?”

If James did, Sirius never heard about it. After snapping his head back and forth between them for a few shocked seconds, James Potter let out a furious war cry and threw himself out of the doorway, making Sirius turn-tail and run out of sheer alarm.

“OH—GOD! SOMEONE CALL ANIMAL CONTROL," Sirius wailed. "WE’VE A PRONGS ON THE LOOSE!”

“YOU WANKER!” James screamed, chasing his best friend all across the lawn, shouting and waving his fists as he ran. “GET BACK ‘ERE—I’M GONNA THROTTLE YOU!”

“MOONY! OH, MOONY—AUGH GOD—HELP ME!”

Remus shook his head. “Told you he’d be mad!” He called, just as James threw himself forward and managed to tackle Sirius from behind. With a great ‘omph!’ they went down into a single pile and began to roll across the lawn like two thrashing crocodiles. No surprise, it was James who came up on top, pinning Sirius on his stomach as he rubbed his smug face into the grass.

“YOU BASTARD! YOU CHEEKY FUCKING BASTARD! DO YOU EVEN KNOW HOW WORRIED I WAS?!”

Sirius made a grunting noise that might’ve been something akin to ‘no, why don’t you tell me?’ and James finally let him up to breathe.

“OUT WITH IT! WHERE HAVE YOU BEEN ALL THIS TIME?!”

“Oh, you know…” Sirius began spitting foliage. “Around…”

With another cry, James thrust his face back down into the turf and Remus just sighed, crossing his arms. He might’ve gone to break the tussle up himself, had someone else not stepped out onto the stoop with him.

“What the devil is going on out here?”

Remus spun around to find a woman standing in the doorway, holding a hand to her forehead as she peered out at the pair of wrestling boys on her front lawn. He knew instantly that it was James’ mum—she had his almond-shaped eyes and brown complexion, with the same high ridged nose and angular cheeks. She appeared a bit older than he’d imagined, but still clearly a pretty woman, with her hair methodically pinned back from her face and an intricate golden earring dangling from each ear.

“James, what are you doing? Get up this instant!” Mrs. Potter ordered. She had a light accent which James lacked, but there wasn’t a hint of anger in her voice. “Honestly, what does that boy think he’s up to?”

“Just a bit of dog training,” Remus quipped out of the corner of his mouth. She caught it and turned on him. For a moment he had the good sense to be frightened—Euphemia Potter was said to be a generally kind woman, but her temper was not one to be prodded.

“You must be Remus,” she said, and then rather than reprimanding any of them, she smiled kindly and offered her hand.

Remus relaxed. “I'm pleased to meet you, Mrs. Potter,” he said, taking it.

“Oh please, do call me Effie.”

He wouldn’t, but nodded anyway. “You, ehm… have a wonderful house... spectacular garden.”

“The garden’s not my doing I’m afraid,” Mrs. Potter said wistfully. “That’s all Monty. I’ve the brown thumb in the family, but James has told us a lot about you, Remus. He’s been oh so eagerly awaiting your arrival…” She cast her eyes back out across the lawn, where James was still busy grinding Sirius’ face into the dirt. “Though now he seems a bit distracted.”

Remus laughed nervously. “Party my fault I think. I hope you don’t mind, but I brought a spare.”

“Oh, not at all.” Mrs. Potter squinted at the pair. Then she huffed good-naturedly and raised her chin to shout; “James Fleamont Potter, if you know what’s good for you then you’ll release that poor boy at once—!”

Spurned by his mother’s words, James gave Sirius’ back one more shove for good measure before at last rolling off him. He was laughing now—Sirius too—and when they stood up they slung an arm over the other’s shoulder, grinning as they made their way back back up to the front door.

“I think you knocked a tooth loose,” Remus heard Sirius say.

“You sure it wasn’t something in your brain?” James replied.

More laughter, and Mrs. Potter’s eyes shot wide as she finally realised who it was.

“Is that—it can’t be,” she gasped; “Mr. Sirius Black!”

Sirius looked up, and his face was instantly aglow with joy.

“Hi, Mum!” He cried, and Mrs. Potter opened her arms wide, letting him run to her and scooping him up in a hug so fierce it nearly pulled him off his own feet.

“It’s been so long, dear!” She cheered, squeezing him tightly. “James didn’t tell us you’d be coming!”

“Yeah well, James didn’t know!” James shot, stopping next to Remus on the doorstep.

“Ah, no matter, you’re both here!” Mrs. Potter smiled, releasing Sirius and patting Remus on the shoulder. The gesture was friendly but Remus still baulked a bit. At least she hadn’t tried to hug him too.

“Come in then,” she insisted; “I’ve got lunch ready and Monty’s just out in the back garden reading the paper.” Still grinned ear-to-ear, Mrs. Potter flitted back inside, and Remus heard her holler across the house; “MONTY—the boys are here!”

“The boys?!”

“Yes! Ring the Pettigrews, let Peterbird know they’ve arrived! And put out the lemonade! They’re probably parched, the poor dears.”

“I think she’s happy to see you,” James said, taking Sirius’ guitar from him.

“Not as happy as I am to see her,” Sirius said, with a subtle wink in Remus’ direction.

Letting James take the backpack from him too, Remus followed his friends inside, taking off his shoes in the entryway. A long hallway extended the length of the house, emptying out into what appeared to be a salon and fine dining room. Around the rich artwork, which ranged from impressionist paintings to clay statues and carven wooden figurines, rows and rows of photographs hung on every wall, each of them filled with happy memories from James’ childhood.

“Look at the handsome tyke,” Sirius razzed, pointing out a photo of a much chubbier-looking James in a baby bonnet.

“I’d like to see some of your baby photos,” James scoffed. “That hair and nose? You probably looked like a rat.”

“Au contraire, I was a very handsome baby. In fact, it was the only time my mother ever bothered to show me off. Apparently it all went downhill the moment I learned how to talk.”

“That I believe.” James paused to look Sirius up and down. “By the way, what are you wearing?”

Sirius glanced down at his ill-fitting outfit. He still had his arse-clinging jeans on, but his shirt was about three-sizes too long for his torso and combined with the oversized leather jacket he was absolutely swimming in fabric.

“What, don’t like my new look, Prongs?” He sniffed haughtily.

“Didn’t say that, it’s just different s’all.”

“Shirt’s mine,” Remus professed, much to Sirius’ apparent displeasure.

James peered on him, before looking back to Sirius and lifting the edge of his jacket sceptically. “Why’re you wearing Moony’s clothes—and how did you even get here?!”

At that, Sirius and Remus exchanged another glance.

“It’s… a long story,” Sirius said.

“Well,” James started, looking more tense than he had a moment ago, “you can tell me over lunch, I s’pose. Mum made kheer—it’s like a rice pudding. And a trifle too.”

“Ugh,” Sirius moaned happily, almost as though the very mention of dessert had soothed all of his troubles; “Prongs, your mum wouldn’t happen to be single, would she?”





* * *





Remus’ earlier assessment of Potter Cottage turned out exactly right—it was warm. The interior of the home was just as grand as its out, and every room felt rich with character. The mahogany floors of each hallway were swathed in vibrant rugs and lush plants sat in every corner. The furniture was all of quality—solid wood that looked as though it’d been carved by only the finest artisans. Eager to get his friends settled in, James showed them around to each room on the ground floor, including the salon, where the family kept their shrine. It sat in its own corner of the room, a large table covered in a silk cloth and decorated with images of deities, fresh flowers, incense dishes, and other silver and brass instruments meant for prayer.

“This is where Mum and Dad conduct Aarti,” James said. “It’s worship—sort of like communion but we can do it at home. They sent me to Hawkings for the education, but we’re technically Hindu.”

“Nothing technical about it,” Mr. Potter called, drifting into the salon with his hands held lazily behind his back. There was no way to not mistake him for James’ dad; they looked almost identical, from the wild thatch of black hair on their heads down to the dimples on their cheeks. The only differences at all were the thick streaks of silver lacing through Mr. Potter’s hair and the square tortoise shell glasses he wore.

“James is right,” Mr. Potter continued, “we sent him to a British school to receive a British education, but he is still a good Gujarati boy. Most of the time, anyway. Just don’t tell your mother about the rest.” Mr. Potter winked, and James and Sirius shared a small snigger.

“Sirius,” he called after, fondly extending his arms, “it is so good to see you, my boy.”

Sirius didn’t hesitate; he rushed Mr. Potter with all of the same enthusiasm as he did his wife and let himself be held.

“It’s good to see you too, Pops.”

“James here was getting desperate. Couldn’t very well sit still these past few weeks. I think perhaps he thought you’d forgotten him. Replaced him with a newer model.”

“Dad,” James moaned.

“Never,” Sirius promised, pulling away and letting Mr. Potter ruffle his hair. Then he turned to Remus and held out a hand.

“Remus, I presume?”

Remus nodded and took the hand, only to be pulled into a great bear-hug of an embrace. He didn’t fight it, but when Mr. Potter released him with a hearty laugh, he couldn’t help the nervous chitter that followed. “It’s nice to meet you, sir...”

“ ‘Sir’ was my father, call me Monty,” Mr. Potter said, waving him off kindly before clapping his hands together. “So, boys, what are your plans for evening? I’ve got the nets set up in the back garden. How ‘bout we have a friendly game of—”

“Monty!” Mrs. Potter clipped from the salon’s doorway; “Didn’t I tell you to set out the lemonade?”

“Yes, yes, dear. Be right over.” As his wife turned to leave Mr. Potter leaned over to Remus and murmured; “Scary, that one. But she does make the most wonderful suppers.”

While his parents set to preparing the table for lunch, James led them on a tour of the back garden, which did indeed boast a near full-size football pitch along with a large oak cradling a treehouse that appeared bigger than some flats Remus had been to in the East End. On the door was a small sign bearing the words ‘James’ Place – only smiles allowed’. Along with the vast field and heavy oak, Mr. Potter kept an immaculate lawn, which he decorated with various fruit trees and a porch big enough to entertain dozens of people.

After the backyard, they finally ventured up to the second floor, where James showed off his father's office, which doubled as a library, Mrs. Potter's studio (she was on leave of work for the summer), and several impressive guest rooms. Each was large enough to house a king-size bed and every door seemed to open up to a room more lively and large than that before it.

“We have family come and stay with us lots,” James said, after showing them the third bathroom. “You’d love my cousin Ajay, he’s got great taste in music, but he’s living in Boston right now. Going to Harvard.”

“Hey, you still got that picture of Farrah Fawcett pinned to the ceiling over your bed?” Asked Sirius.

“It’s a movie poster!”

“Yeah. Of her tits.”

“Now why would that be hanging over your bed, Prongs?” Remus added with a smirk.

Rolling his eyes, James led them down the hall to his own bedroom, which was easily four times the size of their dorm room Hawkings. Every wall was plastered with photographs, Arsenal team banners, and posters showcasing his favourite bands. The second-hand guitar he’d received that same summer was leaning proudly up against his desk, and above that hung the framed Kink’s album Something Else, which was amazingly signed by the entire band. Mr. Potter had picked it up at auction a few Christmases ago and Remus had been infinitely jealous when he’d heard about it, but James never took the thing off the wall even to bring it to school, too worried it’d get ruined.

“Mum says you guys can take whatever guest room you’d like,” James said, sitting on his bed. “Pete’s gonna stay over too so it’ll be just like school. You are staying, right?”

Remus nodded. “Giles gave me a week or so.”

“And you?” James looked to Sirius sternly. “You gonna tell me what’s been going on—why I haven’t heard from you all summer and then you just suddenly turn up on my doorstep with Moony?”

Sirius rubbed the back of his neck like Remus did when he was feeling guilty. “I’d rather wait until Pete gets here. Don’t really want to go over it twice…”

James looked like he wanted to argue, but in the end he only nodded in agreement. “You’re okay though?”

Sirius chanced a glance at Remus. “Yeah, m’okay.”

Staring at his best friend a moment longer, James eventually turned his gaze on Remus, who smiled comfortingly. He looked down, but just then Mrs. Potter’s voice carried up to them from the ground floor; “Boys, lunch! And Peterbird’s here!”

“ ‘Peterbird’?” Sirius echoed wryly.

“Don’t you say anything,” James groaned. “Mum’s been calling him it forever, but I know he hates it.”

“Heh—couldn’t imagine why.”

Shaking his head, James jumped up from the bed and slid his arm around Sirius’ shoulders. “C’mon then,” he said, “let’s eat.”

After Peter had had his turn to sputter and gape at Sirius’ arrival, they took lunch under one of the apple trees in the backyard, laying out a blanket and sitting around one another as the summer breeze tousled their hair. Peter staunchly remained in the shade, still nursing a terrible sunburn he’d gotten on holiday, and Sirius restrained himself and only teased him for the nickname twice.

While they’d been setting up, Remus had caught Mrs. Potter staring at them while she set the porch table for herself and Mr. Potter. It took him a while to realise that she was in fact staring at Sirius; the look on her face simultaneously worried and baffled, as though she were simply waiting for him to disappear in front of her eyes. It was obvious that she knew something was wrong—maybe that was just what it meant to be a mother—but she always held her tongue, pinching Sirius’ cheeks every time he turned to her. On the other hand, Mr. Potter didn’t seem all that interested in prying. Out of all of them, Peter was the least subtle. He eyed Sirius’ clothes and general lack of belongings like the whole thing were a puzzle he’d yet to solve, and when Sirius brought Andy’s guitar out he couldn’t help but blurt;

“I thought Moony had the guitar?”

“I did,” Remus surmised automatically, “but it’s Sirius’ guitar.”

“So he was with you then?” Peter asked, not missing a beat.

Thankfully, it was Sirius who answered; “I called Moony a little while ago,” he said. “He helped me out, made sure I could get here.”

“Why didn’t you call me first?” James demanded. “No offence, Moony.”

Remus waved him off, picking at one of Mrs. Potter’s homemade sausage rolls.

“I couldn’t remember the number for the summer house,” Sirius said. It was a lie, Remus knew. Sirius didn’t forget things easily, especially not his best friend’s phone number. James however, didn’t seem to make the connection. He slumped back on his spot on the blanket and glared down at his lemonade grudgingly.

“So… what happened then?”

Strumming gently on the guitar, Sirius sucked on his lower lip. “Got disowned.”

“Your parents threw you out?!” Peter gasped, with as little bedside manner as usual.

“Not exactly. They sent me away. To this school… in Belgium.”

James and Peter’s reactions were not all that different from how Remus’ own had been. Their jaws dropped and they looked around, blinking as though they were waiting for each other to make sense of it.

“B-B-BELGIUM?!” Peter ended up sputtering. “What the bloody hell were you doing there?!”

“Like I said, it was a school,” Sirius continued. “Got sent there for ‘bad behaviour’, but I managed to break out and hop a train into France.

“France?!” James cursed. “You mean you just casually hitchhiked through two countries?!”

“Not really. After the train I caught a ferry to Dover, and then Moony picked me up. Been staying at his place ever since.”

“For how long?” Asked Peter.

“A… few days.”

“A few DAYS?!” James shouted, before turning on Remus. “You had a few days with him and you couldn’t be bothered to pick up the phone and let us know? You knew he was okay and you didn’t say anything?!”

“I told him not to, Prongs!" Sirius insisted. "I didn’t want to ruin your guys’ holiday.”

“Holiday-schmoliday! I thought you were dead—or—or at least in trouble!”

“He was in trouble, haven’t you been listening?” Remus lashed, suddenly more annoyed. “They tried to disown him and then sent him out of the bloody country! You were in Devon—what was he supposed to do?!”

“Moony,” Sirius said, placing a hand on Remus’ thigh; “it’s okay. They didn’t know.”

“Everything alright, boys?” Mr. Potter called. He and his wife were sitting across the lawn on the patio, but James had certainly been yelling loud enough for them to hear. The sudden attention made Remus spring upright, and gently nudge Sirius’ hand from his leg.

“Yeah, Dad, everything’s fine,” James called before huffing and turning back to the pair of them. “This is fucking mental,” he said in a low voice; “You know this is fucking mental, right?”

“Yeah,” Remus and Sirius said together.

“Great, now that we're all on the same page… You’re gonna to tell us what it is we ‘don’t know’?” Still glaring at them, James snatched up a roll and bit into it fiercely, as though his mother’s home cooking could calm him.

Sirius shifted uncomfortably on the blanket before setting the guitar beside himself. “I’m not going back to school.”

“Not going back?” Peter echoed, perhaps his millionth question since the entire conversation started. “Why, ‘cause you were disowned?”

Sirius nodded.

“Couldn’t you ask your parents to take you back—convince them to change their minds? Maybe if you say you’re sorry, they’ll take you back.”

“Of course he’s not gonna say sorry!” Remus snapped. “Don’t you know what they’ve done to him? They’re monsters—how could you even think that, Pete?”

“Well, at least then he could go back with us,” Peter said sorely. “School’s almost starting anyway—he won’t even have to see them soon!”

“You mean you’d actually support him going back there? Just like they want? What the fuck, Peter?!”

“Okay,” James started, throwing his arms out, “so going back home isn’t an option then, but you can’t just drop out!”

“I can’t access Alphard’s inheritance until at least November,” Sirius said, “that’s too late for tuition.”

“I bet you could talk to McGonagall,” Peter reasoned. “Get a payment plan or something. Maybe she could make you a scholarship student—like Lily!”

Sirius scoffed sarcastically; “If by some miracle, McGonagall agreed to let me come back without any incentive, she’d still have to tell my parents.”

“Why don’t we just pay your tuition?” James said.

Instantly Sirius turned stony. “No. No way.”

“Why not? Any one of us has the money, we just gotta ask our parents. You can stay here too—until school starts. My parents won’t mind, they love you.”

Sirius’ grip tightened on the neck of the guitar. This was the conversation Remus knew he’d been dreading the most—and Remus had been dreading it because just like James, he couldn’t understand why Sirius wouldn’t accept the help he was definitely owed.

“I love them too,” Sirius said, “but I still can’t accept.”

James smacked a hand down defiantly. “You’re telling me that after a decade of friendship and enough bullshit to sink the bloody Titanic, you can’t accept a bit of money to come back to school with us?”

“It’s not just the money,” Sirius said stubbornly. “If you tell your parents what happened they’d have to tell somebody and then I might get sent back.”

Sticking his hand into his lemonade, Peter brought an ice cube up to cool his sunburned forehead. “I thought you said you were disowned? Why would they even want you back?”

"Watch the tone, Pete," Remus snapped.

"I didn't mean it like that!"

Sirius scratched his head. “I guess I don’t know for sure if I've been disowned, but I’m also not really looking to find out. I just need to get by until I’m eighteen and then I’ll never have to worry about it again. Moony’s right, I won’t go back to them.”

“Then come back to school—with us!” James pushed. “My parents aren’t just gonna let you walk back into that place, not if you explain everything! I’m sure there’s something my dad could do legally, and then it wouldn’t matter what your raving mother has to say.”

“And what would I tell them? Your parents?”

“The truth! Tell them they sent you fucking Belgium.”

“It’s just a school. It’d be like Moony’s dad sending him to Hawkings—nothing against the law there.”

“Tell them you’ve been mistreated then,” Peter supplied. “I mean you have been, haven’t you?”

“It’d just be my word against theirs,” Sirius said. “And they’ve got the influence, while I’ve got no proof.”

“Yes, you do.”

The words had come out before Remus could stop them, but he didn’t regret them—not even when Sirius’ sighed and dropped his head.

“You have your scars,” Remus said firmly, grabbing Sirius by the shoulder and forcing him to look at him. “You could start telling people what happened. Show them. It’s proof.”

“They’re six years old, no one’s gonna care.”

“But they might if you tell them your parents forcibly sent you out of the country to an institution that tried to cut your hair and beat you when you wouldn’t let them!”

Sirius scowled bitterly, like he’d been betrayed, but Remus didn’t have it in him to worry about it. He wanted Sirius to come back to school just as badly as the others did, and if he had to play bad cop to do it, he would.

“They really tried to cut your hair?” James asked.

“Yeah, and then they ripped it out,” Remus answered for him, while Sirius just glared.

“Show us your hair, Sirius,” James said firmly.

Huffing, Sirius broke away from their staring contest just long enough to reach up and rip the elastic from his hair. After a bit more finessing, the braid he’d been sporting for several weeks fell apart around his fingers. For a long time he didn’t move, staring at the gingham picnic blanket. It was obvious he was reluctant to put his pain on display, but it was too important to back out now.

Willing to be brave enough for the both of them, Remus reached over and took Sirius’ arm, squeezing it comfortingly. “Hey, it’s just us,” he murmured.

Sirius eyed him, but with a final sigh, eventually turned around on the blanket. James and Peter were on their knees a second later, leaning in to get a good look at the bald patch at the very base of his skull. After three weeks the hair had grown back sparsely, but at least the skin didn’t look raw anymore.

“Oh Sirius, mate,” James whispered, “you gotta come back with us. You gotta tell my parents.”

“I didn’t even want to tell you,” Sirius grumbled, turning around again.

“I know,” James said, the pain clear in his voice, “but we’re thankful you did.” He reached over and took both of Sirius’ hands in his own. It was an intimate thing, but Remus wasn’t a bit jealous. He loved James too.

“Everything’s gonna be okay,” James promised. “Screw school, then. There doesn’t have to be a timeline—no expectations. We’ll figure everything else out as we go.”

Pressing his lips together, Sirius squeezed James’ hands back. Then they smiled at one another, brothers in all but name, and it was enough. Sirius simply took up his guitar and James settled back into his spot on the blanket, renewed and the same all at once.

“If it’s what you want, then I’ll talk to them,” Sirius murmured, setting his fingers to the cords.

James nodded. “Thank you, Sirius.”

Remus didn't say anything; he didn't need to. He and Sirius had their own ways of talking to each other, but James and Sirius were a beast of their own nature. Only James could get through to Sirius that way. Remus tried to tell himself that it was normal to be jealous. He just wished he could see Tomny, or at least stop missing him.

While the rest of them continued to eat their lunch in relative peace, Sirius began to play. It was Remus’ song, the one they’d practised in the park. Remus could hear all the words in his head.



When those two kids found each other,

Heaven opened up and cried,

Dear lovely children, come to me;





And so our Johnny found his lover,

He felt a light that they couldn’t see,

He prayed away the heartache on his knees;





The Mary-Anne her mother once knew,

Never left her childhood street,

Instead she found her answers in her dreams;





Head held high, never cry,

Our lady’s love is nigh;

Hear our Lady of Conceptual Hope’s sad lullaby…



“What’s that tune?” James asked, over another mouthful of sausage and chutney.

“Moony’s new song.”

“It’s a work in progress—show you later,” Remus said, before anyone could ask him to start singing.

“Glad to see you’ve been doing some homework,” Peter said wryly. “But are there any more surprises we should know about? Like, neither of you are suddenly getting hitched, right?”

“No, Wormtail,” Sirius smiled; “Though I wouldn’t put it past Prongs and Evans.”

“Oh, I dunno. That probably depends on how Lily’s going to take the news of James and Farrah Fawcett,” Remus sniggered.

“You’re all wankers,” James said, already moved on to the trifle.





* * *





To no one’s surprise, it turned out to be much harder for Sirius to get the words out in front of Mr. and Mrs. Potter. He and James waited until that evening when all of them were sitting around the table and playing cards. Mr. Potter had already kicked their arses at whist and they’d just moved onto blackjack when Mrs. Potter had strolled into the dining room with drinks for all of them. They’d been having so much fun together that Remus had almost forgot the biggest purpose for their visit, but Euphemia kindly reminded him when she asked the fatal question:

“So, are you boys excited to return to school?”

Immediately, all four of them exchanged a look, but thankfully it was James who spoke first.

“Mum, there’s something we have to tell you.”

Their eyes connected—kind eyes—and just like that, the entire mood shifted. James hadn’t needed to say anything else, it was an automatic. Just the faintest look and all that was left was… poor dears.

Under the table, Remus gave Sirius’ hand a squeeze.

While the rest of them retired to the parlour for evening tea, Mrs. Potter took Sirius into the study to talk. Remus sat back with Peter while Mr. Potter prayed at the shrine—James joined him, though he looked much more sombre—and as Mr. Potter was ringing his bell, he sent up a silent prayer of his own, to no one in particular.

Whoever might be listening, please just let this work out. I don’t think I could let him go.

When the Aarti ceremony was over, they tried watching the telly. A game was on, Arsenal vs. Newcastle United, but not even James could pay attention. While his father sat back in his armchair and smoked a pipe, James paced the room, peppering him with reasons why Sirius couldn’t be sent back until he sounded downright whiny.

“You don’t get it, Dad—they’re evil! They hate everything and force him to obey every single stupid rule, and even when he does he’s punished! I know they made sure he couldn’t contact us for help! They wanted him to feel alone!”

“Your mother is talking to Sirius right now,” Mr. Potter said, the picture of calm. “We can’t jump to any conclusions. Afterwards, we’ll figure out how to contact his parents.”

“NO!” James shouted. “You can’t call his parents! If you do, that witch’ll show up and drag him out by his hair just like last time!”

“It won’t be like last time, beta, ” Monty assured him.

“But you saw his hair, didn’t you, Dad? They mutilated him! And there’s bruises all along his neck like he’s been strangled!”

Remus bit down on the edge of his teacup. He wasn’t sure it would help very much if he told James that the bruises were actually from the three weeks he and Sirius had spent snogging from dawn till dusk.

Mr. Potter tapped his pipe out on an ashtray. “Your mother will know what to do, James. Give them time.”

Bitterly throwing himself back into the sofa, James crossed his arms and sulked. Peter ended up offering him a mint from the bowl on the coffee table but he just shook his head, glaring at the television. Remus understood how he felt perfectly; it wasn’t fair. Finding Sirius at that Devon port made him more sure than ever that if he returned to Bath they’d never see him again. Even if Sirius eventually decided that he wasn't interested in bringing their summer fling back to school with them, it didn’t matter. Sirius was his friend before anything else, and if it came down to leaving him behind while the rest of them returned to Hawkings, then Remus was sure they’d smuggle him in first.

Halfway into the match, with Arsenal leading 3 to 1, Sirius emerged from the study looking tired and grim.

“She wants to talk to you, Mr. Potter,” Sirius said, though he’d never called Fleamont anything other than ‘Monty’ or ‘pops’.

Mr. Potter stood up from his chair and moved past Sirius into the hall, pausing only to set a reassuring hand on his shoulder.

“Chin up, son,” he told him, and Sirius gave a half-hearted shrug. After Mr. Potter had gone, Sirius slumped down on the sofa next to Remus, who had to restrain himself from reaching out and taking his hand.

“What’d you tell her? What’d she say?” James demanded straight away.

“She’s gonna call my mum,” Sirius murmured lifelessly.

“No! Didn’t you show her everything, and tell her about Belgium and—and how you got your scars?”

“ ‘Course I did,” Sirius snapped, “but what’s it matter? I’m just a stupid kid who can’t do anything on their own.”

James was on his feet in a second. “Fine then. I’ll just go talk to them.”

“James, no,” Sirius said, reaching out and taking his arm, “I’m not gonna argue with your parents.”

“Then let me argue for you!”

“Look, I know you mean well but they’re your parents.”

“And they should be yours too!” James huffed, nearly whimpering. “No one deserves parents like that or a family who hates itself so much.”

“He’s right, Sirius,” Remus said. Sirius turned on him, giving him an incredulous look that said ‘who are you to talk?’ He knew that were they alone, Sirius would’ve said as much aloud, but Remus didn’t care. “It’s okay to ask for help," he told him. "You asked for mine, right?”

Sirius sagged, and his hand on James’ arm slid free, letting James march down the hall toward the study.

“Don’t you want to stay?” Peter asked from his own couch. “James wants you to stay. We all do.”

Sirius smiled sadly. “I know, mate.”

“We could be a real band if you did. We’ve been practising, right, Moony?”

“Yup.” Remus gave Sirius a sideways glance. “It’d be a shame if you gave up on us now.”

Sighing, Sirius set a hand on Remus’ knee, squeezing it tightly, and this time Remus did not pull away. To anyone else it might have looked like a friendly gesture, but he understood. It was as close as they would ever get to be in front of others.

Neither James or his parents emerged from the study for a long time. Because he could be kind sometimes, Sirius distracted Peter with talk about his new drum kit. All too eager to be the centre of attention for even a moment, Peter began rattling off the kit’s specs and everything he’d managed to play half-decently since school had gotten out. Sirius listened with his entire body—recognising Peter’s worth and giving him the consideration he deserved in that subconscious way of his. It was one of the things Remus admired most about him. He wanted so badly to kiss him.

When James finally returned he was fuming. He marched back into the salon with his fists clenched and threw himself down on the sofa next to Peter.

“How’d it go?” Sirius asked cautiously.

“Fucking terrible,” James growled. “They keep saying they have to notify your parents otherwise they could be charged for kidnapping since you’re still a minor—can you believe that? Bloody kidnapping?!”

“That can’t happen!” Sirius gaped, surely horrified by the idea that the two adults he admired most in the world could be punished for his indiscretions.

“I agree, so change of plans—we’re gonna kidnap you!”

“What?” Peter chirped.

“Yeah, it’s our backup plan! We just need to hide you until school starts. We can go somewhere and hide until the first, and then we’ll take the train north and sneak you into school. At least there we’ll have plenty of time to figure out what we’re going to do.”

“That’s such shite, where would we even go?” Sirius asked scornfully.

“Moony’s maybe?”

Remus bit his lip. Hiding Sirius was one thing, but keeping four Marauders?

“We can’t go to Moony’s,” Sirius cut-in; “His dad’s no better—no offence.”

Remus did not feel offended.

“What about the tree house?” Peter suggested.

“You mean in the backyard?”

“Oh yeah!” James gasped. “It’s brilliant! No one ever uses it anymore, Dad can’t even get up the ladder most days because of his knees! We could bring you food at night, it’s genius!”

“Okay sure,” Sirius scoffed, “but what’ll you tell your parents? They're gonna ask where I went.”

“We’ll tell them whatever—tell them you ran off because they refused to help! Maybe then they’ll feel guilty enough to actually do something.”

“No, this is insane,” Sirius said, “I’m not going to lie to everyone and hide out in your bloody treehouse just so your parents’ll feel guilty!”

“Would you rather go home? Because that’s exactly what’s gonna happen if they call her and your mum shows up on our doorstep!”

“You could call Andy,” Remus suggested, making Sirius glare at him again.

“No—”

“Yes!” James agreed. “Andy—that’s brilliant!”

‘Stop saying everything’s brilliant!” Sirius lashed. “I’m not gonna risk getting Andy in trouble just so I can avoid my parents—her they’ll actually sue! You don't know how they are with family.”

“But she said to call her if you needed anything,” Remus interjected. “And I think this qualifies as needing something.”

“You talked to her then?” Peter asked.

“Not just talked—we ran into her and Ted this morning.”

Sirius punched him in the shoulder. “Stop spilling all my secrets!”

“You saw her?!” James practically shrieked. “You mean you actually saw her in person and you didn’t say anything?”

“Been a bit distracted, in case you haven’t noticed, Prongs. Besides, she doesn’t need to worry herself over some fight between me and my parents.”

“ ‘Some fight’? Ugh!” James smacked a sofa cushion in frustration. “I swear to god, you’re never dramatic when we need you to be!”

“It’ll be alright,” Sirius insisted again. “I’ll find a job or something to tide me over until November. It’s just two months!”

“You sound like you’ve already given up,” Remus hissed. “Don’t you want to come back with us?”

“Of course I do, but it’s not that easy! I need a guardian’s signature just to get back onto school grounds, so the money’s obviously not our only issue here!”

“We can forge the signature!” James cried. “Pete can!”

“I can!”

“And what if my mum shows up at school—what then?” Sirius demanded.

“Well… we—we could…” James rubbed at the back of his neck sorely. He glanced at Peter desperately, but apparently neither of them had considered that Sirius might not want to return to Hawkings because that’s exactly the place his parents expected him to be.

“I’ll take the train with you,” Sirius started, more softly now, “but you have to let me figure the rest out. It’s not as scary as you think it is.”

Remus wanted to correct him, of course it was scary, but he couldn’t.

If I stopped worrying about every threat my mum spat out, I’d never feel brave again. Sirius had told him that once. And though it’d been before everything, Sirius still found it within himself to be brave now. Remus supposed he owed it to him to be brave too.

“Okay,” he said, making Sirius look at him, “we’ll do whatever you want, Sirius. Just don’t ask us to let you go. We need you.” I need you. “We… need our Padfoot.”

Smiling sadly, Sirius nodded. Then he reached down and took Remus’ hand, making his heart jump until he reached out the other to James. James took it without hesitation and extended the same to Peter before forcing his face into that friendly James Potter smile.

“We’ll figure this out,” he promised.

Sirius nodded again, more firm this time, but just then a door slammed open down the hall, rattling every photo frame on the wall. A few seconds later, Euphemia Potter burst into the parlour, waving her hands frantically while her husband brought up the rear.

“I cannot believe it!” She seethed. “Oooooh that WOMAN! I swear I’ll—”

Mrs. Potter launched into a series of expletives only James and Mr. Potter understood while waving her hands about furiously. Her loyal husband followed her about the salon, wincing and trying his best to calm her.

“C’mon now, Effie,” Monty said, “let’s not do this in front of the boys.”

Undeterred by the obvious show of rage, James jumped to his feet, looking delighted. “So how’d the call go, Mum?”

“That—THAT—WITCH!” Mrs. Potter let out another frustrated wail while her fists trembled at her sides. “How could she say such—and about her own—!” Stopping short, Mrs. Potter took a deep breath and passed right by her son, instead stepping up to Remus and Sirius’ sofa. Remus couldn’t decide if she looked like she were going to scream or burst into tears, but then it didn’t matter anymore. Mrs. Potter had already knelt before Sirius on the rug and clasped his hand in her own, making the bangles at her wrist twinkle.

“Sirius,” she started, “would you like to stay here for the rest of the summer?”

Sirius’ eyes turned to dark saucers.

“Well, I-I—”

“I know it’s only a few short days until your term starts,” Mrs. Potter rambled, “but I want you to know you are welcome here, beta, and that you may stay however long you wish.”

It was possibly the first and only time Remus had seen Sirius without words. When several more seconds had passed and Sirius still had not said anything, he nudged him pointedly. Sirius blinked as if his entire body were resetting, and then coughed, turning red all over.

“I…”

“You don’t have to, of course,” Mrs. Potter continued, “but if you’d like to, I want you to stay with us. From tomorrow until forever, if need be.”

It wasn’t a question, not even a suggestion. She wanted him. It was crystal clear then how Sirius had become so taken with the family, despite only ever having visited the one time. The Potters did not wait for you to want them in return, they simply expelled their love, and waited for you to collect it. And Sirius, who so desperately craved being wanted, could not deny them.

“Yes,” Sirius said, voice small like a child, “yes, I would like to stay… ma’am.”

And just like that, Mrs. Potter straightened up, a relieved smile on her face. “Wonderful! I’ll call the school in the morning and we can get everything sorted! We’ll have to get you some new clothes, and all of your school things, of course, but we haven’t started that for James either so we’ll just do it all together!" She prattled, stopping just long enough to place a kiss on either of Sirius’ cheeks. “For now I think I’m going to start clearing out the spare bedroom right next to James’ room. We thought to put you up further down the hall since Monty’s been using it for storage and lord knows he hasn’t cleaned up in there in months, but that just won’t do, will it? Hmm, yes, I quite thought so! But until then, you boys just relax, okay? Oh-kay!”

Stopping to kiss Sirius once more, Euphemia Potter smoothed back her dark hair and promptly strode back into the hall towards the staircase, humming in a tight voice as she went. James looked to his father, mouth still agape.

“Dad…? What happened over the phone?”

“Let’s just say the call did not go how she expected,” Monty surmised, before reaching over and patting Sirius on the shoulder again. “Like Effie said, you’re welcome here, son. For now or for forever, there will always be room for you here.”

Sirius looked on the verge of tears. “Thank you, Mr. Potter.”

Smiling, Monty tucked the end of his pipe into his mouth. “Oh, so now it’s ‘Mr. Potter’, Sirius?”

Sirius cracked a bashful smile. “I mean, thanks, pops.”

Chuckling now, Monty pat Sirius on the shoulder. “Welcome home, beta.” He nodded at each of the boys and then set off after his wife, humming more gently than she had as he ascended the staircase. Watching him go, Remus now fully understood just how James had come to be James Potter.

“So, Sirius?” James started. “Whatchu you thinking?”

“I think I have the best friends in the world,” Sirius grinned. “And that I don’t half bloody deserve ‘em.”

“I think you just have great luck,” Peter said sarcastically, making Sirius sniff happily, before jumping up from the sofa to catch him in a headlock.

"Oh, how I love you, Wormy!" Sirius declared, grinding his knuckles over the shorter boy’s head while he wailed. Remus laughed at both of them, but he was inclined to agree, and as he leaned his head back on the sofa and watched his friends, it occurred to him that maybe his own luck wasn’t all that bad either.

'Aggro' is slang for deliberately aggressive or provoking.

'Roundhouse' and 'Dingwalls' are both live music venues near Camden Lock.

The 'chokey' is slang for prison.

A 'pram' is a baby stroller.

'Trifle' is a dessert. It's like the fucking best.

'Beta' is an Indian pet name meaning something like 'son' or 'baby'. (Thank you to mendokayalways for the correction ^^)

Chapter 70: If Wishes Were Horses...


Chapter Summary

Remus wishes... and he wishes... and he wishes...



Chapter Notes

C/W: Smoking, illicit drugs & a bad trip (LSD), allusions to mental illness (Remus/Hope), homophobic language (internal monologue), and severe internalized homophobia—mostly triggered by an internal event. There are NO hate crimes or the like.

But I repeat, this chapter goes HEAVILY into Remus' subconscious. Remus experiences a BAD TRIP. If you are at all sensitive to drugs or internalized struggles or don't care to see the development of this PARTICULAR queer identity from the ground up then perhaps this fic isn't for you. (And that's okay.) This struggle (drugs/his sexuality) will not follow Remus in the same way forever, but it will be something he contends with for much of his life. This aside, struggling with your own internalized guilt/prejudices doesn't mean that you are hopeless and/or incapable of honest love. I hope you'll understand that I'm trying to portray the story in a way I feel is honest to myself and the characters I've built, and that this is a transformative chapter. Transformation isn't always nice or easy. Peace and love <3
