Holy Moses, I have been removed,

I have seen the spectre, he has been here, too;

Distant cousin from down the line,

Brand of people who ain’t my kind;

Holy Moses, I have been removed…

- “Border Song” Elton John, 1970



The time they spent at the Potters was short but soothing, and when two days had passed and Walburga Black hadn’t shown up on the doorstep breathing fire and screaming blue murder, Sirius was finally able to relax some. This meant that his friends were able to relax, and eventually the gentle lull of the house had soothed all of them. Every evening when Mr. Potter arrived home from work, they played football in the back garden while Mrs. Potter took photos or busied herself by hanging laundry on the line. The house was considerably busy, since Peter had elected to stay over as well and Mrs. Potter was working from home at the moment, but Remus was used to sneaking around. In front of others, he and Sirius were as normal as they’d ever been. It was only when they were alone that things became different.

They learned quickly how to recognise the patterns of their fellow inhabitants so that they could steal away for those precious few cheeky or otherwise chaste moments. Everyday around eleven o’clock, Peter would lose himself in some day-time comedy show and James would phone Lily. This guaranteed them at least a half an hour, which they never wasted. The minute their friends were securely distracted, Remus would meet Sirius somewhere they could be alone; in their bedrooms, but also behind the garden shed, or in the upstairs bathroom, or even the hallway broom cupboard where that hoover had fallen over onto Remus’ ankle and left him limping for the rest of the day. It was a bit thrilling, but also entirely terrifying… and whenever Sirius turned those wicked eyes on him, Remus could not bring himself to resist.

The days were good, and Remus was enjoying himself, but he couldn’t deny that the in-between moments—like his dreaded shit-all hour—felt slightly Spartan. He’d always had a tendency to drift off into thought; when he was twelve a teacher had even given him the strap for day-dreaming through an entire test, but something about the soft, ambience of Potter Cottage brought out the worst of it. The summer air wafted through open windows, shifting the sheer curtains of every room like merry ghosts. Perhaps that was one of the reasons why James was so James; even his ghosts were happy.

The daydreaming didn’t always prove an inconvenience, but more than once it’d unearthed a memory Remus hadn’t even known he’d had. These mostly materialised in the tiny moments, like watching Mr. Potter read his morning newspaper. He bobbed his foot while he did so, and every so often the soft flapping of paper flutter would fill the air as he tapped the pages straight on his thigh. Remus almost always thought of Giles, but occasionally an echo of Lyall would slip through—of him sorting through document after document at the breakfast table. No meal in front of him, only coffee and that morning’s briefs penned by some nameless assistant. How vast the table between had felt then.

‘Remus, sit up straight,’ the memory went; ‘You’re a boy, not an animal.’

It was somehow worse with Mrs. Potter; she had a sing-song quality to her voice that was simultaneously comforting and yet all too jarring. Despite her friendly disposition, she was still a mother, and she was constantly going after James for the state of his hair or the perpetual grass stains that were always showing up on his trousers.

“Honestly, I should just cut them off at the knee! Leave you looking like an abnormally tall boy scout!” She grumbled that morning, after striding out of the utility room to shame her son for another pair of ruined slacks.

“ ‘s not meh!” James said over a mouthful of toast. His mother’s eyes narrowed and he swallowed very quickly; “Sirius wore those yesterday! Honestly Mum, you’d think he gets dragged around by raging bulls for fun.”

“You Judas!” Sirius gasped scandalously. “That’s merely the evidence of all the time I spend on my knees.”

James just about choked on his fork. “Doing what?!”

“Praying, obviously. Get your mind out of the gutter.”

“Ha! Could've fooled me!”

“You calling me a slag? At your mother’s breakfast table? Why I oughta…” Looking no less than delighted, Sirius then used the end of his fork to flick a sausage in James’ direction. Unfortunately he overshot and it landed in Peter’s teacup, making the poor boy shriek as hot tea surged over the sides of his cup.

“There you go, now you’ve stained the table cloth too!” James cackled.

“It’s too damn early for this,” Peter moaned, using a fork to scoop the sausage out onto the aforementioned table cloth.

“Oops! Sorry, Pete,” Sirius chittered. “Just think of it as your daily source of protein. Better than anything Potter’s offering up.”

“Eugh!” James howled, absolutely tickled pink.

As Peter began dabbing sorely at his lap, Mrs. Potter tossed the dirtyv tousers up over her shoulder. “Oh, you boys,” she huffed; “What am I to do with you?”

She marched away, leaving them to giggle like they were twelve and not about to be eighteen. Even Peter found it funny after James ‘accidentally’ fumbled the sugar bowl onto Sirius’ eggs, but Remus wasn’t really paying attention. He was off on his own; lost and drifting.

‘Remus, darling, you’ve a hole in your trousers. Did it happen while you were playing outside? Ah well, take them off so Mummy might mend them.’

It was a stupid memory—he didn’t even know if it was real. He couldn’t recall ever having seen Hope Lupin thread a needle. Her hands were always shaking, at least when he’d known her.

Silly, I used to mend your clothes all the time, Hope said into his mind. You were so tiny, nothing ever seemed to fit right. Your father wanted them to be tailored professionally, but how could I let anyone else touch my baby’s clothes? My sweet, sweet baby… My lovely darling boy…

Remus wasn’t sure when the voice had warped into hers. He wasn’t even sure it was her. Every time he thought too hard on it, the idea would come apart and the voice would fall silent, like smoke through his finger tips. He just wished it would all stop.

“So whadda think, Moons?”

Remus looked up. He couldn’t even tell how long he’d been out of it.

“Er… ‘bout what?”

James was picking his teeth with a fingernail. “Croquet. Dad pulled the set outta the garage yesterday. You game?”

“I dunno know how to play.”

“You knock the ball into the hoop,” Sirius said wryly. “Surely you can manage that, sports star?”

And because even Remus could manage that, they spent most of the afternoon in the garden, knocking colourful plastic balls through less colourful plastic hoops. As it happened, Remus found that he wasn’t entirely terrible at croquet; he and James won the first two rounds, but then they switched partners and it became quickly apparent that the victories had just been a combination of James’ skill and beginner’s luck. After lunch Lottie made the trek over, sporting a pretty blue dress and sunhat that was so wide-brimmed she could’ve fit an elephant beneath it. Her appearance turned their group of four into a group of five, which apparently meant that one of them would have to sit out. Remus tried to volunteer, but in the end it was Peter who grudgingly flopped down on the shaded picnic blanket so his sister could play.

“Don’t you have any of your own friends to hang out with?” He grumbled, sitting cross-legged with his cheek pressed into the side of his mallet.

“None who are as mindlessly unoccupied as you four,” Lottie answered coolly, adjusting the brim on her ridiculously large sun hat. “Mary’s still in Paris, and Marlene and Lily are decidedly unavailable. There’s always Bethany, though she’s in Croatia visiting family. And Anette’s taking a sculpture course in Florence. And Pernilla’s in Sweden again, though she just wrote me and—”

“Alright, we get it! Take your shot already.”

Lottie crossed her arms. “It’s Sirius’ turn.”

But Sirius wasn’t listening. For the last several minutes he’d been creeping closer and closer to Remus on the other side of the hoops, a look of sceptical concern on his face.

“You sure you’re okay?” He asked, for perhaps the dozenth time.

“Yes,” Remus replied, “just tired.”

“Did you not sleep well or something?”

“S’fine. Must just miss my own bed, I guess.”

Sirius wiggled both eyebrows. “I miss your bed too.”

“Stop,” he hushed, just as James thumped his croquet mallet into the lawn to get their attention.

“Black! S’your turn!”

Eager to advance the game, Sirius left Remus and scuttled over. He’d already drawn his sleeves up and promptly knocked his black croquet ball through the second hoop, immediately whooping with glee. As he lined up to take his awarded second shot, James let out a spectacular ‘LOOK OUT!’ and Sirius flubbed it all, sending the ball sideways several metres to rest by the old oak.

“Whoopsie, must’a been seeing things,” James sniggered.

Sirius whipped his head around; “You toff! We’re on the same team now!”

“Oh… right.”

“So immature,” Lottie sighed, shaking her head. “Really, you boys should be more careful. No girl’s going to want to marry any of you if you don’t grow up some. Like I met this guy recently, and—”

“I knew it!” Peter cried suddenly. “You didn’t want to come hang out with us, you just needed someone new to brag to!”

Lottie gasped, offended. “I wasn’t bragging! Hmph—honestly Petey, far from me to want to include my own brother in my wedding plans.”

Peter clasped both hands over his ears. “I’m not listening—I’m NOT LISTENING!”

“Lot!” Sirius gasped, his jaw practically dragging the dirt; “You mean you’re actually engaged?!”

“No way,” James said, equal parts aghast.

Lottie twisted an innocent blonde curl around one finger. “Well, I suppose not yet. But it’s only a matter of time.”

“I didn’t even know you were dating someone,” Remus said, practically overcome with chills at the idea of being married at seventeen.

“She isn’t!” Peter shouted, hands still over his ears. “She’s just deluded herself into thinking some guy she’s met twice is in love with her!”

“I thought you weren’t listening?” Lottie scoffed. She recovered a second later, looking pleased as punch as she dropped her croquet mallet down and lined it up with the yellow ball. “His name is Roger, and I’m going to marry him—even if he doesn’t know it yet.”

With a fine clatter, Lottie sent her ball whizzing over the grass, right through the third hoop. Sirius whistled and then clapped for her, before leaning casually on the top of his mallet.

“So where’d you meet this prince charming?”

“At Daddy’s office. I was filing some paperwork for him. Almost refused—it’s terribly dreary in there—but the secretary called in and I knew the system so I sort of thought, why not?”

“Sounds like the best ‘why not’ of your life,” James said. “What’s he do for work?”

“Oh I dunno, must be something important. He wore a suit and Daddy just about tripped over himself to shake his hand.”

“Did you actually talk to him at all?” Remus asked.

“Obviously, I’m not a total lunatic. The first time we got to chatting about the business, and other stuff like my nails—he complimented the colour. Then the second time I saw him he brought me the loveliest bouquet of flowers.”

“Which you said he plucked from the vase in the hallway!” Peter bleated.

“Shush. It’s the thought that counts.”

“Wow, Lot,” Sirius mused; “Sounds like you found yourself a real keeper. What’s he look like then? I at least hope he’s fit.”

Peter smacked the picnic blanket with an open palm. “Stop encouraging her!”

“Oh yes,” Lottie grinned, lining up her second shot; “Very fit.” She took the shot, which sailed across the lawn and went straight into the fourth hoop, and celebrated by giving Remus a tight hug around the middle as her teammate. As Remus patted her on the back in congratulations, James just sighed and looked sadly at Sirius’ ball, still adrift beneath the oak tree.

“Next time, I’m her partner.”

Sirius flipped him the bird.

“You should knock Remus out,” Lottie instructed the next round, when Peter had gotten up for his turn.

“Which daft idiot let you in here?” Peter grumbled, before ignoring his sister and trying for the hoop instead. He missed, and huffed vexingly before allowing Remus up to take his shot.

“Yeah, go Moony!” Sirius cried apathetically from the picnic blanket. He was lying down with his sunglasses over his eyes and not even paying attention, but did raise his fist as a show of moral support.

Licking his lips, Remus drew back his mallet and struck the ball. He was aiming for the hoop, but alas, he only managed to clip the edge. Immediately the ball spun wildly off course, knocking Peter’s aside with a mournful thwack!

“Told you,” Lottie said, as Peter groaned.

“Nice clear!” James said from the other side of the hoops.

“Oh! Did he get it in?” Sirius demanded, lifting his head. “Good show!”

“I was aiming for the hoop, honest,” Remus said to Peter, who just waved him on while scowling at Lottie.

“Go on, take your shot, Remus,” Lottie said. He obediently lined up the mallet, trying his best to aim while James, his partner this round, flapped his arms up and down enthusiastically.

“Yeah, you can totally sink it!” He called. “Straight on through the middle—don’t blob it! You want it right offside, yeah?”

“I had sports jargon,” Remus grumbled, drawing the mallet back. He’d just about sent it when another voice called out;

“Might want to move your hands up ‘a bit.”

Remus stopped dead and looked up to find Simeon Pettigrew strolling out the Potters’ back door. He looked tanner than Remus had last seen him, and the sun had turned his flaxen hair a deep honey blonde. He was wearing a navy polo and beige slacks like he’d just come from the country club, which he very well could’ve. On anyone else Remus might’ve found the attire entirely unappealing, but on Simeon it just worked. Maybe it was the earring…

“What are you doing here?” Peter asked, squinting at him.

Simeon flashed him a dazzling smile. “Mum sent me to pick you up, it’s almost tea. You guys been out here all day?”

“We’re ‘taking the air’,” Peter drawled, just as Sirius bolted upright on the picnic blanket and raised the sunglasses from his eyes.

“Oh shit—Sim!”

Simeon waved. “Alright, Black?”

Rather than answer, Sirius jumped to his feet and raced over, taking Simeon’s arm fondly while they both clapped each other on the back. “How’s Oxford?” Sirius asked.

“Eh, you know how it is. Just ‘a bunch of wanna-be philosophers crammed into the same five-by-five cubicle. But what about you, eh? You lot look good. Who’s winning?”

“Lottie,” all four of them said at once.

“Figures,” Simeon said, as Lottie took a commemorative bow; “only one person’s ever been able to beat my little sister at croquet.”

“Who?” Sirius asked.

Simeon crossed his arms, looking smug. “You’re looking at him.”

And that was how they ended up getting their arses handed to them on a silver platter for the remainder of the hour. Peter gave up early, hating anything that might pit him against his brother, but Sirius was all too eager to fill the gap and the rest of them cycled on and off as they so pleased.

“I was so close that time!” Sirius insisted, after his ball missed the hoop by only a hair and skipped out of bounds.

“Close only counts in horseshoes,” Simeon answered, poking him with the end of his mallet.

Having given his mallet up to James that round, Remus stood back on the sidelines and watched. Simeon’s sudden entrance had left him feeling a bit joltish, and though he was happy to see him, it was much easier to let Sirius take the brunt of the attention. Under the impression that a cigarette or two might help calm his nerves—he hadn’t had one since that day in the park with Sirius—Remus had just begun to entertain the thought of sneaking off when Mrs. Potter came strolling out the back door, announcing carved watermelon and lemonade for everyone. As they all jumped up and made a beeline for the porch, Remus hung back to pat his pockets, but he’d forgotten his cigarettes in the house.

“Moony, come get some lemonade,” James called, flagging him down from the porch. Remus nodded back, and started across the grass, but then Simeon fell into step with him and he promptly fumbled his croquet mallet.

“Hellooo there,” he drawled, staring at him with those baby blues.

Swallowing thickly, Remus bent over to pick up the mallet, and when he straightened up he found Simeon waiting for him, stopped in the middle of his path to the porch. “Hi…”

“Lose something?”

He glanced over Simeon’s shoulder, toward Mrs. Potter, who surely wouldn’t approve of the smoking. “Er… nah.”

Simeon’s eyes tightened curiously at the corners. “I didn’t happen to spit in your tea last time we met, did I?”

“What—no.”

“Why are you ignoring me then?”

“I was just… playing the game.” Remus gestured meekly to the mallet in his hand.

“Hmm… alright.” Simeon looked him up and down. “You got taller.”

It was true; Remus could look Simeon right in the eye now. In fact, he might’ve had a few inches on him—gangly inches, like a half-stuffed scarecrow.

“Maybe you just shrunk,” he said. Simeon chuckled, biting his lip over a smile.

“Forgot you were funny. There aren’t many funny people at Oxford. Tolerable, but too priggish for their own good most of the time.”

“Why do you go then?”

“Expectations, I suppose. Why do you go to school, Lupin?”

“Moony!” James called again. He was holding up a glass, but nearly dropped it when Sirius poked him in the bum with the end of a croquet mallet. Lottie let out a happy shriek as the two of them tousled, while Peter dove to save the plate of watermelon.

“Them,” Remus said, straight away. “Because of them.”

Simeon followed the look. “Ah… good reason, that.”

When he turned back to him, Remus felt his stomach drop a few feet. Simeon may not have spat into his tea, but he’d definitely been avoiding him. He couldn’t help being nervous, Simeon was so effortlessly cool. And he admired him—more than admired him. It was a queer feeling, he now realised. He wasn’t just a Siriusexual then—he was an entire queer.

“Are you staying for a while?” Simeon asked.

“A few days. We go back to school next week.”

“Right, right. Got any plans?”

His heart skipped a beat. “James mentioned a football game… and—uh, band stuff. Mostly writing, but we’re just gonna hang around I think…”

Simeon nodded thoughtfully. “Well, I’ll be in and out. Trying to visit as many people as I can before heading back for the term. Alice lives in Wembley now, and Cass’s gone off to Enfield. Might pop the train to go visit him, but…” Simeon leaned in; “try to keep Sunday night free.”

“What’s Sunday night?”

“Nothing, yet. But the week is young, and you’d be surprised what people can throw together by Sunday.”

“Oxford people? Thought you said they were all prigs.”

“Oh, they are. But the parties aren’t all bad.” Simeon winked, and Remus felt queer all over again.

Sirius, he told himself. Sirius, Sirius, Sirius!

“You save us any ‘a that?” Simeon called, already steering away from Remus toward the porch. Halfway there, Mrs. Potter reappeared and called out to him;

“Oh Sim, dear, your mother’s quite upset you’ve been gone for so long. Might be a good idea to get along.”

“Yeah, we’re going,” Simeon replied, jumping up the porch steps and grabbing Peter by the shoulders. “C’mon, little bro, get your things together! Just let me know if you need help tying your shoelaces!”

“Gerroff!” Peter grunted, batting his brother away. “I’m going!”

“What was Simeon saying to you?” Sirius asked, after James and Mrs. Potter had gone to see the Pettigrew siblings off.

“Ha, curtain-twitcher,” Remus said, stuffing his face with watermelon.

“I am not a curtain-twitcher! I just asked what he said to you.”

“… Nuffin’.”

“Didn’t look like ‘nuffin’,” Sirius grumbled.

Remus swallowed and turned to him. “He only asked vague questions and made vaguer statements. Probably just wanted to seem ‘cool’.”

“Mhm, sure.” Just then Sirius reached around, copping a handful of Remus’ bum. “Just remember, I had this first.”

“Hands off!” Remus hissed. He was just in time too—a second later Mrs. Potter rounded the back door.

“Boys, Monty’s just rung me and he says he’ll be getting off early tonight. Shall we head into town to get you some new things, Sirius?”

Tucking his hands behind his back, Sirius began to worry at his bottom lip. “Sorry, Mum, but I… don’t have the money.”

Effie frowned at him, then smiled. “Don’t worry about that, beta. Both of you just get your shoes.”

She vanished again, as quickly as she’d come, and Sirius flashed Remus a bashful look. “Don’t be jealous, but I think I’m in love.”

Remus shoved him.





* * *





The car almost felt crowded with five people. Mr. and Mrs. Potter rode up front of course, and after folding himself into the two-door coupé, Remus found himself pressed against the driver’s side window, with James and Sirius crammed next to him. They were excited, and even tried playing a round of bumps until Effie snapped at them to cut it out. Remus thought briefly that this must be what it felt like to be a part of a normal family; to have two parents that liked each other and prattled on about new school clothes and sensible footwear, and to have brothers who couldn’t help but get themselves in trouble and never really meant any harm by it. That was, if you were shagging one of them.

They went first to the tailors, the same shop where the Potters had been ordering James’ uniforms since he was in year two. It’d taken quite a bit of coaxing on Mrs. Potter’s behalf for Sirius to fess up just how little he had, but his general lack of anything—let alone an appropriate uniform—had been apparent since their arrival. It cost an atrocious amount to have the uniforms rushed in time for September 1st, but Effie didn’t bat an eye. She simply wrote the tailor a cheque and that was that.

“Remus, shall I put in an order for a uniform for you?” Mrs. Potter offered kindly. “Just in case you’ve grown at all over the summer?”

“Thank you, but I’m sure my dad’s got it covered.”

She nodded, but plucked a light blue dress shirt off one of the tailor’s racks. “How about this then? To wear on your off days?”

That would look wonderful on you, darling, Hope whispered. It’ll bring out the blue in your eyes.

Remus tried to stifle the voice. I don’t have blue eyes.

Of course you do. You were my perfect blue-eyed angel.

“No thank you, ma’am,” he managed. “I’ve got clothes at home.”

Effie held his gaze a moment, smiling in understanding and returning the shirt to the rack. “Don’t mind me then,” she told him, “but if you’re in need of anything—even a pencil—make sure you let Monty or I know.”

Remus nodded. He wanted to reply in the same kindness, but the short interaction had exhausted him. Retreating like a coward, he hung around at the front of the shop until Sirius and the Potters were finished, all the while desperately longing for a cigarette.

Afterwards they drove all the way into Fitzrovia, where Mr. Potter escorted them to his personal barber. The empty patch of skin on the back of Sirius’ head had mostly grown over by now, but it’d left a wonky hairline in the back, and Mrs. Potter insisted that it would be better to have the entire thing cleaned up before they returned to school and some nasty teacher complained of disorderly uniform and tried to cut it with sheep’s shears.

“But what if they cut all my hair off? What if they leave me bald?!” Sirius fretted, as they made their way down the street toward Winmore Barbers and Co.

“They’re just gonna fix up the back,” James reassured him. “Moony, tell him he’s worrying for nothing.”

“You’re worrying for nothing.”

“There! See—”

“Wigs exist, after all.”

Sirius shot him a venomous look, but when Mrs. Potter held the barber shop’s door open for him, he reluctantly plodded inside.

“We’ll meet you back here at half past,” Mr. Potter called, before ushering James and Remus back down the street. They stopped outside a large two-floor bookshop, and Mr. Potter pulled James’ return to school letter from his pocket to squint down at it from behind his thick glasses. “Let’s see if we can tackle some of this reading list before supper’s come and gone, eh boys?”

Remus, for one, was more than relieved to be back in a bookshop. He hadn’t had the chance to visit one for weeks, not since Sirius had arrived, and almost said as much to James when he commented on the sudden improvement of his mood. He caught himself when he realised that Sirius wasn’t supposed to have been staying with him for so long, and afterwards Remus resolved to be more careful. He still wasn’t exactly sure what the ‘this’ was between them, but he was positive he wasn’t ready to tell anyone.

As Mr. Potter followed a clerk around the shop, piling James’ arms high with class reading and A-Level exam workbooks, Remus gave the excuse that he needed to use the loo and slipped away on his own. He wanted to try and find something that might help him make sense of what he was feeling, but for all the times he’d been in a bookshop, Remus had no idea where to start looking for literature of such a queer variety. There was no way he was going to ask one of the clerks, and so he stumbled along on his own, doing his best to avoid James and Mr. Potter, until he eventually made it into the Philosophy and Cultures section. From there he was right and truly lost. Half the section was made up of tomes the size of his forearm, with titles that he probably would’ve had equal chance of deciphering were they in Latin. There was a small section dedicated to ‘lifestyle’, and Remus began to silently thumb through the covers, running keywords through his mind as he did so.

‘Homosexual’ felt the most academic. But there was also queer… gay… Poofter… Shirt-lifter—Bender—Arse Bandit—SISSY—QUEENIE—FREAK!

Hunched over, Remus put his head in his hands. He hated himself.

He hated himself.

Sirius, I’m sorry, he pleaded. I don’t know if I can do this…

You sure you’re not just lying to yourself, the voice said. Not Hope—the vicious Moony. He was back.

Hmm? Did I go anywhere? Or did you just become more deranged?

I hate you too, Remus thought.

Remus pulled his hands down to his neck, releasing a long sigh. This was what was exhausting him, he knew, the nonsensical unsurety of it all. But as chance would have it, when he opened his eyes again he found exactly what he was looking for: a small journal titled, Early Recollections of Homosexuals as Indicated by Lifestyle.

Ripping the book off the shelf, Remus glanced around to make sure he was alone before flipping it open to the introduction. It read;



This book is a collection of academic studies performed and founded in the science of psychology, created and curated by the finest minds within the field. Although a number of studies have sought to determine the homosexual problem at its root, few have looked toward its ongoing circumstances; that which help the problem persist. By examining the homosexual lifestyle, we seek to answer but two questions, how is the common homosexual related to its fellow man, and does there exist a common measure of lifestyle?



Remus could feel every heartbeat thump in his ears. Lifestyle? Problem? ‘It’?!

He flipped several pages deeper and kept reading;



To begin, it is helpful to translate how one might have a tendency to choose the homosexual lifestyle in the first place. It is worth noting that children who choose to become homosexuals are either those who have developed a feeling of weakness and inferiority toward the opposite sex within the environment they have found themselves, or alternatively, have been so petted that a very early desire for being protected and coddled takes on an intensive form. This can be true for both pampered and neglected children, for both extremes feed and intensify the child’s longing to attain a future in which he/she will remain entirely untouched by life’s difficulties. If additional familial difficulties do persist, they are likely to seek out the familiar, and this becomes no more apparent than in that of the attraction to the same sex.



This was worse than he could’ve imagined. It was a total mistake. He’d been looking for answers, just a single word that might help him make sense of it all, and rather he’d found condemnation—contempt. Remus wanted to stop reading, but it was as though his eyes were glued to the page. On and on the book went, reducing people’s lives to that of uniformed trauma. He didn’t want to fit these boxes, but he checked them all. Tick, tick, tick.

And then the real kicker came;



Homosexuals by nature, may be distinguished from heterosexuals by the following descriptions: weaker self-identity, lesser degree of initiative or motivation, or general lack thereof; greater degree of dependence, lack of religious association, effeminate tendencies, strong sense of the world as a hostile and dangerous place, issues with temperament, familial despondency, physical deformity and/or mental disorders, and more severely impaired gender identity.



Remus felt his heart break. It was just one book—one book in thousands—and yet it was enough to reduce him to what? To nothing.

His arms sagged as though they were failing him, and the noise that left his mouth with the next breath sounded more akin to a whimper. Then he realised;

A man was standing beside him. He was looking at him. Looking at him up and down.

It was not with kindness.

Wearing a tailor suit, with a smart-looking hat and briefcase, the man’s frown deepened, drawing deep crevasses across his aged face. He shuffled away in expensive loafers; he’d seen what Remus was reading, and he was disgusted.

Remus snapped the book shut and raced from the aisle. He did not leave the book where the man could find it, instead he shoved the book into the display case beside the shop’s front door, and whipped out onto the street into the hot evening sun.





* * *





To his credit, Remus did not run the entire way home. But he had to be away somewhere, so he took a lap around the corner and back, and after choking down no less than three cigarettes, he returned to find James and Mr. Potter desperately searching for him outside the shop.

“Sorry,” he blanched, “saw a friend, got caught up chatting.” James gave him a look, and Remus saw it for what it was immediately. “… Not Tomny.”

With two sets of fresh texts weighing them down, they made their way back to the barber where Mrs. Potter was having tea in an outdoor café with a freshly trimmed Sirius sitting across from him. The barber had not mangled him, but Remus had never seen Sirius’ hair so short. The crisp black waves were now clipped just below his jaw, with the bits on top shorter and more tousled to give what Mrs. Potter determined was ‘more body’.

“Does it look alright?” Sirius asked, appearing genuinely nervous.

For a moment, all Remus could think to do was begin applying homosexual signifiers to Sirius. Effeminate tendencies, issues with temperament, familial despondency—

He could’ve kept going, except it was Sirius looking at him. Sirius.

“You look great,” he told him, genuinely; “You… It suits you.” Everything suits you.

Sirius smiled, still shy, and Remus wished he could’ve looked at it forever. He wished he’d never gone looking for that book. He wished the word queer did not exist.

By then it was getting late into the evening, and Mrs. Potter determined the rest of the errands, such as securing Sirius new school shoes, could wait for another day. After piling back into the coupé, they made their way back to East Finchley and to Potter Cottage, where they cleaned up the back garden and Mrs. Potter served up a wonderful dinner of paneer butter masala.

“Don’t worry, Sirius, I think you’ll be able to handle this dish,” Mrs. Potter teased, as she served up his plate with more than double Sirius’ usual helping.

“I still don’t understand how you managed to make yesterday's dessert spicy,” Sirius moaned, making the entire table dissolve into laughter.

Remus ate quietly for the most part, and when it’d become clear that he wasn’t going to be able to keep up with conversation or stomach the rest of Mrs. Potter’s delicious cooking, he apologised and asked to leave the table early.

“Are you not feeling well, beta?” Mrs. Potter asked, reaching over to press the back of her hand to his forehead. “You don’t feel warm.”

“Just tired. Probably gonna tuck-in early.”

“You did spend a lot of time in the sun today,” she said, then; ‘Alright, you head on upstairs. I’ll wrap up your supper. Make sure you take a glass of water with you.”

Remus nodded and untucked himself from the table.

“See you tomorrow, Moony,” James called. “Remember, it’s the Arsenal scrimmage.” He flashed two thumbs up, and Remus responded meekly, before turning for the hall. He did not look at Sirius, too afraid that if he did, he’d see right through him.

Remus’ room at the Potters’ was spacious and clean. He found his small bag of things waiting for him amongst the fine furniture; one large bed, an ottoman, and a wardrobe hutch carved delicately in the shape of peacock feathers. The wardrobe itself was a beautiful piece, but at night he’d found that the feathers would turn into a hundred eyes, each of them silently watching and judging as he slept. The sun hadn’t even set yet, but as the yellow glow came through the bedroom’s window, it cast a shadow over the hutch, and one hundred eyes turned on him. What would those eyes say if they had a mouth? He wondered.

Get a load of this queer, probably.

Because he couldn’t stand any of it, Remus marched over to the window and threw it wide. The window’s view overlooked the back garden and also happened to let out over the porch’s roof, an ideal place to sit and mope and not be found. He didn’t even bother to test his weight; he was feeling rather reckless anyway. Shimmying out the window, he sighed against the warm summer air and leaned back against the side of the house. It wasn’t the most comfortable perch, but it was private enough.

That night was the first time Remus considered running away from the Potters’. As much as he knew he loved Sirius, Remus missed who he’d been before. He missed spending summers at the flat, where he could wrestle with his mates and not have to worry that anyone might think he had more shameful intentions. He missed not feeling guilty for being attracted to someone, girl or boy. Nowadays it was both. Attracted to Sirius and he was queer; attracted to girls and he was what—a cheater? Were they even in a relationship in the first place? … They’d said the fatal ‘I like you’, but things didn’t feel all that different from when they’d just been hooking up.

Remus lit a cigarette. Maybe they were just hooking up. Sirius didn’t want whatever he’d had with Miles… whatever that was. Hmph—this or that. What a horrible way to think about it.

Somewhere distantly below him, the sound of the Potters’ happy dinner conversation drifted up through an open window. First it was just chatter, then laughter, and then miraculously, Mss. Potter began to sing. It was a song Remus didn’t know, in a language he couldn’t understand, and yet he still felt sentimental.

I used to sing to you too, Hope said. Everyday. I was much better than her.

You were sick, Remus replied, in that place that did not exist; You made me sick too.

Shall I sing to you now?

Just shut up.

Oh, where have you been, my blue-eyed son?

Shut up!

Where have you been, my darling young one?

“FUCKING SHUT UP!”

“Woah—haven’t even said anything yet!”

Remus whirled to the window to find Sirius already halfway out onto the roof, hands raised in surrender. Fuck.

“Are you alright?” Sirius asked, appearing genuinely concerned. And why shouldn’t he be? The guy he was hooking up with was shouting at nothing like a raving lunatic. Embarrassed, Remus rubbed his nose to hide his flush and took another sharp drag from the cigarette.

“Sorry… just a bit out of it.”

“I could tell,” Sirius said, crawling the rest of the way out the window to take up space next to him. “Told the others I needed to use the loo, but thought it best to come check on you instead. Mind if I sit?”

“You’re already sitting,” Remus grumbled.

“Convenient.” Sirius reached over, grasping Remus’ hand by the wrist and bringing it towards his mouth. He smoked the cigarette right off his fingers, and after he’d exhaled the smoke, leaned in to kiss him.

Because they were alone, Remus kissed back. He was a weak man, and Sirius was oh, so beautiful.

The kiss progressed slowly, mostly due to Sirius. He leaned up into Remus, nibbling his bottom lip in wordless ask and when Remus opened his mouth for him, Sirius pressed in deep. They breathed heavily out of their noses, chests turning to chests, hands reaching to graze hungrily at neck and jaw and cheek.

“You’re trying to distract me,” Remus mumbled.

“Heh.” Kiss. “Is it working?” Kiss, kiss.

Remus broke away. “Sirius, I can’t.”

“Sure you can,” Sirius said, nipping playfully at his ear; “You just open your pretty mouth, and I’ll—”

“No, I mean I can’t do this.”

Sirius snorted as though he assumed they were still playing, but then he caught sight of Remus’ expression and his entire face fell. “And by ‘this’ you mean…?”

“I don’t think I can be queer,” Remus said shamefully. “I just… it’s not me. I can’t be…”

Sirius’ full lips flattened into a severe line. “Can’t be… or don’t want to be?”

And because he was cruel, Remus almost laughed. “Same thing, innit?”

Sirius wasted no time; he leaned back and popped to his feet, barely stumbling on roof tiles at all as he backed away. “Fine. Guess we’ll just stop all of this then.”

Wait—no! Don't stop!

“Hold on!” Remus quickly stubbed out his cigarette, trying to desperately beckon him back. “I never said I wanted all of it to stop!”

The look Sirius gave him when he turned back around was absolutely incredulous. “Bloody—what?!”

“I just meant that I can’t be that, Sirius. That—that word."

"Queer?"

"Yes! I’m not like—that. I’m… I’m not.”

“Well then, what are you?”

The question was like being flattened dead by a tumble of stones. What are you? What are you? What are you? Remus wished endlessly that he had an answer.

“I like you,” he said instead.

“Fuck you.”

He supposed that was fair. “I’m sorry if I hurt you.”

Sirius just shook his head at him, squaring up his shoulders like he was readying himself for a fight. “James told me about the girls, y’know. Yeah, that’s right—girls. As in plural. You told me it’d been one, so why’d you lie?”

“I–I don’t know!” Remus spluttered.

“I thought you were lying because it’d been a mistake! That shagging those girls was just your way of getting it out of your system. You saying it wasn’t? Am I the fuck you just have to get over?!”

“No!” Thinking of the family sitting just a few metres below them, Remus scrambled to his feet, only to botch it and nearly send himself flying off the edge of the porch roof. “I like you,” he said again, crouched over the ground and surely looking quite pathetic. An ineffable beast, Sirius stayed decidedly upright, stepping over the tiles with all the grace of a trapeze artist.

“I’m not sure you do,” Sirius answered venomously. “If you did, you wouldn’t be saying any of this.”

“I’m trying,” Remus swore, keenly aware of the open kitchen window just below them. “I haven’t had as much time as you to sort through all of this, have I?”

At that, Sirius eased a bit. Relief coursed through Remus, and he grappled for it.

“Maybe it’ll just take more time, but I never meant that I wanted to stop.”

“What’s the answer then? You’re not queer but you like me?”

“Yes…? I dunno—I’m just… I don’t know if it’s that easy.”

"Who ever said any of this was going to be easy?"

Remus frowned. He wanted to apologise, but he didn't know how. "Would you rather I just say I'm queer, even if I don't mean it?"

A muscle in Sirius' jaw twitched. "That's not fair."

"I.... I know." Remus dropped his head.

They were at an impasse, it seemed. Queer, but not queer enough. Thank god these things had always felt more clear for Sirius.

“Fine. Couldn’t you just be queer for me then?” He said simply, slapping his hands against his thighs in a shrug. His tone might’ve been nonchalant, but he was still frowning. Too bad Remus was too shocked to notice.

“ ‘Queer for you’?”

“Why not? I mean, s’not like we’re gonna be telling anyone anyway. So… maybe you can just be queer when it’s us.”

“Is that what you are?”

Sirius’ hands flexed at his sides. “Erm… no.”

“So you’re—”

“—Fully queer, yeah.” Sirius almost gasped when he said it; “Erm… Most of the time anyway.”

The last part felt like a lie, but Remus was hardly the person to call him on it. Sirius always saw things in black or white; one or the other, with no middle ground. If you weren’t a friend, you were an enemy. It was just another extrapolation of his passionate nature, his Shakespearean methodology of life.

“But I’m not blind,” Sirius said stubbornly, “I appreciate the human form too much to not have the occasional tryst.”

Impossibly, the corner of Remus’ mouth tugged upwards. Perhaps he was more fickle a creature than he’d thought. Sirius was telling him he was queer—queer—and yet he wanted to laugh.

“ ‘Occasional tryst’?” He surmised.

“I don’t think you can talk anymore,” Sirius replied haughtily. “Prongs seems to be under the impression that your body count now rivals mine.”

“Impossible.”

“Naturally. Told him as much myself.”

“ … Slag.”

“Tart.”

Relieved for real this time, Remus slumped back down. “I’m sorry,” he said again. “I think I just got a bit spooked coming back here.”

“Well, I get that,” Sirius said, settling back into his spot next to him. “We had it pretty good, hiding out at yours. Almost miss it.”

Remus took his hand. “Almost. S’pose there are a few upsides to being here.”

“Yeah, like not having to eat your cooking anymore. I was growing tired of burnt eggs and beans on toast.”

“I was talking about our friends. And beans on toast are an English delicacy, you uncultured twat.”

“I’ll have you know that I am a cultured twat. I speak four languages.”

“As if I could ever forget.”

“Je t’adore, mon chou. Sollen wir rein gehen und ficken?”

“Was that German?”

“Mhm, and a bit of French.”

“Oh. Gesundheit.”

Laughing, Sirius jumped up and tugged Remus on with him. “Allons-y, Moony! La notte è lunga!”

The dots connected for Remus just as he fumbled back through the window and Sirius began tugging at the bottom of his t-shirt. “What—now?! You told them you were going to the bathroom!”

“I’ll just tell them my stomach felt a bit funny,” Sirius smirked. “Won’t be a complete lie.”

Sirius finished ridding Remus of his shirt, before grabbing him by the chain around his throat and hauling him back for another kiss. The back of Remus’ legs hit the bed a second later, and as they fell back onto it, chest to chest, there really wasn’t much room left for argument.





* * *





The next morning was better. Remus did not think of the queer book or the voice of his dead mother, nor did he have to worry much about how close he and Sirius had sat at the breakfast table. They were in agreement; any queerness would be reserved for those special alone moments. In front of others they would remain normal friends. In the closet, Sirius had called it later. He’d said it with light disdain, but Remus couldn’t bring himself to care, even now. The closet was safe. The closet was blissfully unaware and made more sense than anything else at all. Revere the closet.

The evening before, after Sirius had emerged from his prolonged bathroom break with a rather sheepish-looking Remus in tow, James had forgiven the odd behaviour straight away. After Remus had assured him that he wasn’t feeling tired any more, James sprung the bright idea of ‘lifting Moony’s spirits’ by indulging Remus’ newfound love for all things gore and gruesome. Much to Sirius’ apparent horror (apparently he was more squeamish than Remus had thought), they stayed up late to watch The Exorcist on BBC1. Because it was a TV showing they only got to watch the first hour and half, but Remus was rewarded anyway when Sirius used his discomfort as an ‘excuse’ to slip into his room after everyone had headed off to bed.

The next morning, Peter arrived bright and early for breakfast and James and Mr. Potter came downstairs already proudly sporting red polos in favour of Arsenal. Remus hadn’t forgotten that he’d agreed to attend a real football match, he’d just hoped that if he didn’t bring it up it wouldn’t happen. As if.

“It’s such crap that you have to take the train alone,” James said to Remus over breakfast. Sirius’ rush-order uniforms that arrived that morning after Peter, and they’d all been engrossed with talk of school ever since. Remus, as a prefect, would be the only one leaving on the thirty-first, but he wasn’t worried. At least once he got to school he’d have Lily and the next day all his friends would join him and everything would be just fine.

“Can’t help it,” Remus said. “Pete, pass the butter?”

Peter did so. “Gonna be so boring though."

“I don’t really mind if it’s boring. Give me a chance to actually do some real reading. I promised Marlene I would finish her copy of ‘Ringworld’.”

“You didn’t read much over the summer?” Asked James.

“Not really… Just got busy.”

Only if it makes you the—Remus wanted so badly to say it, but their friends were around and so he bit his tongue and glared at Sirius, who smugly popped a grape into his mouth.

“We don’t have to hang out with him,” Peter said indignantly, “we can just crash his party and drink his booze.”

Sirius looked to James. “I’m gonna hang out with him.”

“Where’s this party, Pete?” Remus asked.

“I dunno, Windsor or something. Sim said he’d drive if we met him back at the house.”

“Lottie coming?”

Peter rolled his eyes. “No, she has a date.”

“Roger. And he’s a dick.”

In answer, Peter pointed his butter knife at Sirius’ nose threateningly.

“Yes!” Sirius cheered. “Gonna be a good day.”

“Two hours?” Remus sat back in his chair and groaned. “Just when Peter had given me hope.”

“So it’ll just be us in the entire stadium?” Sirius asked excitedly.

“Basically, but some others come too! Other fans and Dad’s work mates. Sometimes we’re there the whole afternoon.”

Remus smiled sarcastically. “Brilliant.”

As unexcited as he was to spend the next several hours sitting in a plastic stadium seat, Remus couldn’t deny that Highbury stadium itself was rather spectacular. Mr. Potter led them in a back entrance after shaking hands with the doorman like they’d known each other their entire lives and suddenly they were in another world. The stands looked incredibly large without any people in them, extending at least a hundred feet high every direction.

“They can fit over seventy-thousand people in here!” James tittered excitedly as they filed in behind the team’s benches along with a few other families. Mr. Potter knew them all, and introduced James and Sirius with equal parts of pride while Remus and Peter hung back in their seats.

“Sim didn’t care to come?” Remus asked, watching disinterestedly as the different teams warmed up across the pitch.

“Sim hates football,” Peter said, marking jersey numbers down in a notebook.

“Explains so much,” Remus murmured, missing the older Pettigrew brother all over again.

“Look alive, boys,” Mr. Potter called, shuffling back into their row with James and Sirius in tow; “they’re about to decide who gets opening kick-off!”

True to Mr. Potter’s word, the teams flipped a coin and Chelsea took kick-off, which was met with much moaning from James and Monty. It was clear that just like his son, Mr. Potter was a die-hard football fan. When the first foul of the game went to Arsenal he jumped up onto his feet and hollered at the top of his lungs that the referee must’ve left his eyes at home. James, Sirius, and Peter all killed themselves laughing of course, but Remus just shrunk further into his seat, somehow embarrassed. As he did so, he noticed a girl about their age sitting four rows ahead. She’d turned around to gawk, and was now busy giggling at Monty’s incessant shouting, but when she noticed Remus staring she flashed him a shy wave. Only slightly unsettled, Remus turned his attention back to the field and scanned the green for the ball only to realise at the last second that he was looking on the wrong side. While he did, Chelsea scored a goal.

“Aw, man, what are they doing?” James groaned.

“I told you, you’d be whining today, Potter,” Sirius cackled, putting his feet up on the seat ahead of him. Mr. Potter immediately chided him for bad stadium etiquette and Sirius dropped his feet, grinning guiltily. Unbothered, Mr. Potter held a rumpled ten pound note out to them.

“Here, at least one of the concessions should be open. How ‘bout one of you go fetch us some drinks and a meat pie or two?”

“Me. I’ll go,” Remus said eagerly, taking the money and jumping up from his seat.

“I’ll take a coke, Moons!” James called.

“Two pasties for me!” Peter added.

“And I’ll take a pint!” Sirius said, making Monty reach over and playfully bat him over the head.

“One pie, Remus,” Mr. Potter laughed, “and you can keep the change.”

“In that case, make it two pints!”

Making his way to the refreshment stand, Remus ordered everything, getting a coke and a Mars bar for himself. Once the clerk had passed him a box towering with drinks and meat pies, he did his best not to drop it while turning around, only to almost run headlong into the girl from the stands.

“Sorry!” She chirped, helping grab the food before it toppled over. “Didn’t mean to get in your way like that.”

“S’fine, don’t worry about it,” Remus mumbled, reaching out to right James’ coke.

“Do you need any help?” She offered, and Remus looked her over. She was short, only coming up to his shoulder, with long brown hair tied off in a ponytail and eyes large and green enough to rival Lily’s. She was pretty, and if he were the same person he’d been only a month ago, he might’ve entertained it, but not now.

“I’m good,” Remus said, stepping away.

“Not many people come to the practice matches,” she continued, seemingly undeterred. “My brother plays for Chelsea—number ten. Stephen McFry. Do you know anyone off the team, then?”

The name-drop might’ve worked for James or Sirius, but she’d picked the wrong Marauder. “Nope,” Remus answered, “just here with some friends.”

“Oh, well I’m Megan.”

“Er… Remus.”

She smiled sweetly, like she’d won a prize. “Do you know your way around, Remus? I could give you a… tour of the stadium? Watching them practice can be so boring sometimes, and these things usually run for a while, so…”

Remus almost faltered. All of sudden he remembered why he’d never liked attention like this. Girls like Megan always saw him for more than he was. Exciting or dangerous, maybe. Stupid really, since Remus only ever saw an awkward, lanky git when he looked in the mirror. Perhaps that was why he liked Sirius so much—he saw all of the awkward and liked him anyway.

“I really don’t mean to be rude, but I’m sort of with someone,” Remus said staunchly. “So… no thanks.”

Megan’s smile fell instantly. She sort of just gaped at him for a while, but before Remus could say anything else, she turned and fled in the other direction. Satisfied, albeit a little embarrassed he’d just been run from, Remus made sure he had everything and finally returned to his own seat, passing the food and drink out to his friends.

“Who’s winning?” He asked, eyeing Megan, who had reappeared in her seat with her back firmly turned to them.

“Still Chelsea,” Sirius answered, sipping his coke and not bothering to complain that it wasn’t a pint. Remus watched him and Sirius finally caught on, flashing him a smirk around his straw.

“Got something on my face, Lupin?”

“No,” Remus said quietly, “you’re just pretty.”

Face turning instantly red, Sirius glanced down the row before tapping James on the shoulder. “I’m gonna show Moony where the bathroom is,” he told him, before standing and ushering Remus back towards the stairs.

“Kay,” James answered, eyes never leaving the field. “… Wait, do you even know where the bathroom is?”

“James Potter, you boys are going to miss your movie!”

James dashed to his bedroom door, opening it and sticking his head out. “We’re on it, Mum! Pete’s gonna call!”

“Just make sure you don’t keep Simeon waiting,” Mrs. Potter returned from the bottom of the stairs.

James shut the bedroom door.

“You try telling her we’re headed to a ’college’ party,” James snapped, “she’d be burying us in the garden before we even made it up the drive.”

“Not all of us,” Sirius corrected. “Remember, you only need to be faster than the slowest runner.” He pointed at Remus from behind his other hand and Remus retaliated with a pillow in the gut.

“It wasn’t even a real league match. Hardly a loss.”

“Keep telling yourself that, Potter.”

James turned away like a scorned housewife. It was fitting since he was already going about the room, scooping up Sirius’ clothes from the floor. “If you’re gonna wear my clothes, the least you can do is make sure they make it to the laundry bin,” he said.

“Stop it, you toff,” Remus muttered, pushing him away.

“Why? I’m just showing off my favourite jeans. You wanna feel them, Moony? Oh, they’re sooooo soft.”

“Stop torturing him and come get your shit,” James called. He’d just picked up the trousers Sirius had been wearing the day before. From the back pocket, he pulled a piece of rather dingy-looking paper. It looked like an old napkin that’d been doused in coffee then put through the dryer and hung to dry outside. James began to open it, innocently curious, but Sirius was there in a second, leaping off of the bed and racing over to snatch it up.

“That’s private,” he snapped, carefully sliding the paper into the inside pocket of his jacket.

“Sorry,” James apologised, “didn’t mean to snoop, assumed it was rubbish.”

”What is it?” Remus asked, not as innocent.

”Nothing. S’just a song—haven’t finished it yet.”

Sirius cleared his throat, chancing a quick glance in the direction of the door. They might’ve been able to push him into saying more on the subject, had the phone not begun to ring downstairs.

“Suppose that’ll be Pete,” Sirius smiled then, the picture of decorum. “Shall we get our party on, lads?”

As odd as Sirius’ behaviour was, neither Remus nor James mentioned it. Aside from their friend’s general lack of interest in talking about the mysterious paper, there really wasn’t time. It was a short jaunt down the road to the Pettigrews’—past the country club and down a short side road that was so gnarled and bumpy it could’ve taken a tire off the Rolls. What they found at the end of the lane was a true cottage, modest and suburban, with a brown picket fence and several more cars lined up in the driveway. Simeon and Peter were already waiting for them, loading several crates of beer into the boot of Mr. Pettigrew’s Humber Sceptre. Peter was looking very modest in a pair of jeans and a faded Cream t-shirt, but next Simeon, who was wearing flared trousers with a collared shirt open almost to his navel, he appeared quite homely.

“I see you two raided the offie,” James said as they strolled up the drive, gravel crunching underfoot.

“Ho, lads,” Simeon called back. “Just stocking up. Does this mean you’re ready for the best night of your puny teenage lives?”

“Why? Are we gonna meet Mick Jagger?” Sirius asked, streaking on ahead to smack his palm against Simeon’s in friendly greeting. “Or have you come to tell me that my mother took a long-awaited trip to the sea and turned up dead in the water?”

“Nothing so spectacular, I’m afraid.”

Sirius shrugged, and Simeon lifted a single bottle of beer out of the car’s boot and raised it high in the air. “Gotta christen the night,” he said, before pulling a bottle opener from his pocket. It was conveniently hanging from his key ring, which Remus thought had to be a decent investment. Save him from using his teeth at least, though that was mostly a party trick anyway.

After popping the cap, Simeon drank deeply from the bottle and passed it along. By the time it made it around to Peter it was empty, and Simeon took the bottle and tossed it away across the lawn.

“I’m not picking that up in the morning,” Peter said.

Simeon sighed. “Just get in the car, Petey.”

And so in the car they went. Sirius called bagsy and none of them fought him on it, but thankfully the Sceptre had more room in the back seat than Mr. Potter’s sedan so Remus’ knees weren’t horribly cramped the entire way. The party was taking place in the historic parish of Harrow on the Hill, which meant that the home and the family it belonged to was surely to be affluent.

“Just don’t act lame and maybe you’ll manage to fool one of these university girls into going home with you,” Simeon told them as they were passing through Wembley.

“Not us! Pete and I are already off the market,” James said. “Guess that just leaves the two of you!” He clapped Remus on the shoulder enthusiastically, and Remus tried not to notice the look Sirius gave him from the front seat.

They arrived when Simeon pulled the Sceptre up to a manor estate with an already full driveway. The lawn was also packed, creating a checkerboard of expensive cars as far as the eye could see. The entire property, which was made up of the manor and several outbuildings, was surrounded by a nest of trees that cut it off from the rest of the village. Remus might’ve actually believed they were in the countryside had they not passed a roller rink and a Woolworths on the way in.

“Remember, just be cool,” Simeon said, as they unloaded the car’s boot. “Oh, and if someone comes up to you with a silver chalice and starts gabbing about ‘initiation’, run the other direction.”

“Silver chalice?” James murmured, as he hauled a crate of beer up to his chest.

According to Simeon, their hosts were a pair of brothers named Guy and Hugh. Both were econ majors at Oxford and shared several classes with him, but considering they looked identical, Remus gave up on trying to tell them apart the moment Simeon pointed them out from across the lawn. Not that it mattered; there were enough people at the shindig that he could’ve been introducing himself all night and still not have had the time to meet everybody. The party itself wasn’t even going on inside the manor, instead Simeon had had them carry the heavy crates around the side of the building and out into the back garden, which boasted an incredible lawn and courtyard, a stone porch-way, and of all things, a pool.

“Who the fuck has a pool in London?” Remus said, watching as hordes of kids lounged around the brightly lit water, some fully clothed, others wearing little more than bikini tops and swim shorts.

“Probably costs a bomb to heat it,” Peter added.

“I want one,” Sirius said straight away.

Across the courtyard, a sound system the size of a small house had been set up, playing top hits and the likes of Boney M. and even more Donna Summer. Kids swayed along, drinks in hand, and with the sun long gone from the sky, there were endless shadowed corners left for the more promiscuous couples to sneak off to. This was usually one of the more eventful parts of a party—seeing who hooked up with who—but this wasn’t Hawkings. All around them were strangers, and the four Marauders seemed to watch on in a slight daze, as though none of them could decide what to do next.

“Stop standing there gawking,” Simeon teased, strolling up and passing them each a fresh beer. “Go. Mingle—make friends. It’s the only real way to find the good stuff.”

James’ eyes widened. “And by ‘good stuff’ you mean…?”

Another person called Simeon’s name from across the courtyard and he turned away before throwing up an arm in greeting as a pair strolled up to them. Remus recognised the girl instantly; Alice. She was wearing a black mini skirt and silk top under a heavy leather jacket, and with her mod-looking bob and thick Edie Sedgwick eyebrows she looked straight out of an Andy Warhol film. Beaming, Simeon leaned in and kissed her on the cheek before clasping the shoulder of her male companion.

“Was wondering when you were going to turn up,” the guy said. He had long hair gathered into a ponytail at the nape and a thick moustache that made him look twenty and forty all at once.

“Got weighed down some,” Simeon said fondly, before gesturing to the rest of them. “Lads, you know Alice. This here’s Robbie. Alice, Robbie—I present to you, my brother, Pete, and his friends, James, Remus, and Sirius.”

“Haven’t seen any of you for a while,” Alice mused, looking them over. “Unlike you to be so generous, Sim.”

“I’m plenty generous, ask anybody,” Simeon said. “Thought I’d give ‘em a taste of a real university party.”

“Nah, ain’t real unless someone ends up streaking across the quad bare-arsed,” Robbie said. “Which the four of you might just have to do, considering you’re not even initiates yet. Fresh meat gotta fry, right?”

Robbie elbowed Simeon suggestively and Simeon nodded. “We could have them try bobbing for dead rats, like the cricket team did with their newest recruits.”

“Don’t let these two idiots psyche you out,” Alice cut-in, as the other two stepped back to laugh. “Most of us don’t even go to uni, we’re just leftover private school kiddies. Everyone’s chill.”

“Avoid the blue cups though,” Robbie said, holding up a blue plastic cup of his own. “Or you know, don’t.”

The three of them began to snigger at the obvious inside joke, but by then someone had called Robbie’s name and they were already shambling off. Almost making to follow, Simeon spun around suddenly like he’d forgotten they were there.

“Kay, so… drinks are over there—take what you want, no one cares. Someone usually tries to start a fight or two but they’re basically all talk so don’t worry about it. If anyone comes up to you asking for ‘Barbra-Ann’, they’re looking for molly. If someone asks for ‘Molly’, they’re looking for barbs—backwards, I know. Let’s see, what else… Erm… Don’t take any stardust if you want to be able to breathe in the morning, watch out for the chick that calls herself ‘Stardust’, she’s not that great a lay. Oh and remember—always wrap your willy. Kisses.” With that, Simeon began strolling off in the direction of his friends. “And mingle!” He called sharply, before rushing to meet Guy or Hugh—Remus couldn’t tell which—and leaving them to their own devices once more.

“Alice is pretty… pretty, don’t ya think?” Peter said after.

“I was merely being observant! I never said that I thought she was pretty!”

“Alright, you lumps,” Sirius interjected; “You heard the man—get to mingling. If it’s Moony’s last night of freedom before he’s to be ‘Pecky Prefect’ for the rest of the year, then I think we should all be sufficiently gassed.”

Briefly, Remus considered pushing Sirius into the pool.

None of them knew it at the time, but being a party where no one knew your name was quite freeing. Eventually there would come a time that this would no longer be the case, the party would be thrown by an acquaintance on their payroll, or by a company head looking to make connections amongst different agents, stars, and producers. Then the parties would be thrown for them, in celebration of their first, second—dozenth chart-topping hit. Suddenly people would be asking for them, looking for them. Amongst a sea of money and fame, everyone would know their names. But for now they were nobodies; just another handful of insignificant kids that showed up because of a friend of a friend.

“Think they rented it?” James asked, when he and Remus had stopped to take in the stacks upon stacks of ugly black boxes that made up the party’s sound system. The music itself was still pop-y, but the sound was almost garbled, like it’d been squeezed through a drinking straw. Remus had seen similar speakers being used on stage by the likes of the Who and Deep Purple.

“Must’ve,” he replied, wincing when more Donna Summer came on. He really hated radio sometimes.

A group of girls stood a short ways away, dancing on the grass. They held each other’s hands, spinning this way and that. As he watched, Remus thought bitterly how easy it was for girls; no one would ever judge them for holding their friend’s hand, or snuggling together on the couch. If they kissed one of their girlfriends on a dare it was hot, if a guy did it, it was gay.

These were university girls, he reminded himself, they were used to batting their eyelashes and getting what they wanted.
