Remus nodded. “Yes.” Yes, oh yes. He couldn’t help it. He thought of the man in the bookshop, and the way he'd looked at him. Then he thought of their friends, their classmates, their teachers. He wasn’t sure he could handle them looking at him like that. Even if they weren’t looks of hatred or revulsion, there would still be looks. It would always be there, in the front of their minds. If he said those words he’d be different forever, no matter how good they were to him. He and Sirius may have loved each other like anyone else, but they would always be… other. And after a lifetime of looking for a place to fit in, Remus wasn’t sure he could take it. Not just yet.

“Right then, school's off-limits. Nothing in public,” Sirius said again. “I suppose that’s that.”

Remus got a bad feeling. He stifled it. “Well, you know… we’re not at school yet.”

Sirius looked up. “Right…” Then he licked his lips.

Emboldened by their newfound confessions, Remus snaked an arm around Sirius’ waist and drew them close together under the soft morning light of the bathroom. He kissed him deeply, and Sirius responded in kind, opening his mouth into Remus like it was the only thing left to do. Their kiss was a needy one, but not like any they’d had in the beginning, when they were so desperate to have one another. This kiss was delicate because it might as well have been the last. Alone they could be whatever this was, but in front of others, they would be Remus and Sirius. Two parts of a single whole. Yes… that was exactly it. As far as anyone else was concerned, they were best friends, simple as that. And come the following morning, no one would ever know about what had happened during their summer together.

For now though, all Remus wanted was to feel Sirius against him and to commit every curve and line of his body to memory. Commit it to life. Make it real.

One more, he told himself, as Sirius traced his hands over his bare chest and pulled at his own clothes.

One more.





* * *





It was late afternoon by the time Giles had arrived to fetch him. As the old man hung back in the driveway to admire Mr. Potter’s Aston Martin and talk cars, Remus let himself be seen off by Mrs. Potter and her two—loving—sons.

“Now don’t you worry, Remus,” she told him kindly, “we’ll take good care of Sirius, just as you have been.”

“Oi, I took care of him too,” Sirius interjected, before shooting Remus a suggestive look. “If this tosser had it his way he’d eat beans on toast for every meal.”

“Explains the height,” James teased, shoving Sirius fondly; “All that protein.”

“Have a good train ride to school, and we’ll see you at Christmas, just like we talked about,” Effie said.

Remus nodded. “Thank you, Mrs. Potter.”

She hugged him, because that’s what mothers do, and Remus accepted it without any fuss. Afterwards he turned to his friends and offered James a hand.

“C’mon, none ‘a that!” James scoffed, before pulling him into a hug even tighter than his mother’s had been.

“You’re just the worst sometimes,” Remus grunted.

“The best-worst!” James added, pulling away.

Remus smiled softly and then it was time to turn to Sirius. He almost hugged him—raised his arms and everything—but Sirius just smacked his palm and grinned.

“Try not to enjoy your night alone in the dorm too much!” He said.

“Right…” Remus forced his smile to go wider. “Well, see you at school.”

As the others waved him off, Remus ignored the heavy feeling in his gut as he trudged down the driveway.

“Ready to go then?” Giles asked, ducking out of the front seat of the Aston.

“Mhm,” Remus answered blithely.

“Really is a handsome beast you’ve got there, Monty,” Giles said, shaking Mr. Potter’s hand in congratulations.

“You flatter me, Giles!” Mr. Potter turned on Remus and held out his hand. “Remus.”

He took it, and was immediately enveloped in another hug.

“Be well, son,” Mr. Potter told him.

Remus peeled himself away from his friend’s father, feeling the last of his patience chip away. “You too, sir.”

He tried to avoid looking back as the car pulled away from the drive, but in the end he couldn’t help himself. Just before Giles set off down the road, Remus turned around in his seat to find the small family of four standing on their stoop, Mr. and Mrs. Potter still waving goodbye. They were too far for him to make out their exact expressions, but Remus suspected Sirius’ was just as conflicted as his own.

“See you at school…” he murmured to no one.

“So,” Giles asked later, as they made their way back through the city toward home; “How was your stay?”

“Good.”

“Nice people, them Potters.”

“Yeah. Real nice.”

“You don’t seem very chatty today. What, still hungover?”

“M’fine.”

“Hmph. Would’a thought you’d be happier leaving your friend’s place. Hope it’s not school that’s got you in such a mood.”

Remus began fiddling with his thumb nail. “Gil…”

“Mm?”

He took a breath, not really believing that he was about to ask such a thing. It'd been years since she'd gone from the world, and he'd never cared before. Remus wondered if it made him a bad son, erring so vastly on the side of caution. But really, who wanted to know that their own mother was crazy?

“You remember how my mum was before she died?" He started; "How she would sometimes hear or... or see things that weren’t there?”

Remus didn’t look up, but he could sense Giles watching him in the rearview. “Whatchu mean, lad?”

“Well, I know she was sick, but… aren’t there different kinds of sick?”

Appearing reluctant to answer, Giles cleared his throat. “You see, Remus, your mum, she…”

"She had a lot of doctors," Remus cut in. "Not just cancer doctors, either. I know what they said about her, I would read their notes."

"You were ten," Giles replied sharply. "What were you doing reading such things?"

"She was my mum. She was what I had."

The driver's shoulders slackened in the front seat. "Oh boy," Giles muttered. Then he sighed; "Alright, so you have questions. I dunno how knowledgable I'd be, it's really something you ought to talk to your father about, but don’t you mistake none either, your mum was a good woman. She had a lot going on near the end, what with her sickness and all those stints in the cancer ward. Things like that can really take a toll on a person—on everyone. Change is expected, and she… Well, she always tried her best, didn't she? Some days were better than others, but your father never blamed her none for it. In fact he took care of her, right 'til the end.”

“And before I was born? Was she normal then?”

“Pfft. What’s normal? Nothin’ I know. We’re just people, lad, each trying to find our own way.”

“I don’t need you to comfort me,” Remus said; “I just want to know if I should be worried.”

“Why would you need to be worried?”

Remus looked out the window. “Never mind.”

Giles hummed a bit like he wanted to say something else, but thought better of it. “Hey,” he called instead, “why don’t stop somewhere? Pick up lunch, whatever you'd like."

"No thanks, not really that hungry."

Giles frowned, but then perked up again. "I know, how 'bout we turn on the radio? This car could use some good tunes.” Reaching for the dial, Giles flipped it into the first station and has the music filled the car, he flashed Remus a thumbs-up in the mirror. "See! Much better!"

Remus couldn't quite agree.





'Ooh, I feel love, I feel love,

I feel love, I feel love,

I feel love…'





The irony, he thought, as he dropped his head against the window.

“Augh, dammit,” Giles grumbled later, as the road ahead of them turned up closed for construction and traffic began to pack in behind them like dominoes. “Always gotta be doing something new, this bloody city. Them bloody ringways can’t be ready fast enough. Hold on, gonna take the route through Westminster,” he said.

In the back seat, Remus was only half listening as he flipped through a book of mediaeval poetry Mrs. Potter had given him. James and Sirius had thought it horribly swot-like, but Remus still needed a topic for his summer essay and was hoping he could finish the entire thing on the train. Sirius, naturally, hadn’t bothered with his.

The sun, the sister of the moon, from the south, the translation read; Her right hand cast over heaven’s rim; No knowledge she had of where her home should be, The moon knew not what might was his, The stars knew not where their stations were.

Remus hadn’t the faintest idea what it really meant, but as he read, the words stuck with him. He was already several pages along when he flipped back to them, reading them over and over again. Sirius would like this, he decided, if he just gave it a chance. But Tonya—she would’ve loved it. She’d have read it and understood every word straight away, and yet if you’d have asked her what it meant, her answer would undoubtedly be her own. Remus could almost hear it now; And the sun's the roaming heart who's lost her lover. She's clearly begging the stars to bring her love back to her, but they're lost to eternity too. It's a story of two soul-bound lovers doomed never to meet, and the bleeding hearts who watch from far away.

She was a storyteller, that Tonya, or she had been. Sort of like Sirius. Remus wasn’t a storyteller, he was merely a listener, and if Tonya had told him that she was the sun and he was the moon, he would’ve believed her. So would have Tomny, he suspected. Once.

Remus shut his book.

He did not miss Tonya’s letter, but maybe if he’d kept it, he’d have an excuse for what he was about to do.

“Gil, can you stop the car?” Remus pleaded suddenly, leaning forward in his seat.

"You feeling peckish now?"

“No, but there’s something I gotta do. If you'd just let me out here, I can meet you back at the house later. Won't even take long.”

In the rearview, Giles gave him an incredulous look. “Let you out—pardon me?! Absolutely not, I only just got you back. Nah, we’re gonna go home, and then you’re gonna get yourself sorted so you can actually make your train on time this year.”

“Please, I swear I’ll—”

“You can stop your whinging now, I ain’t letting you step foot outta this car until we’re back on Lupin property. Now you best just sit back and enjoy the ride ‘cause that’s my final word on the matter.”

Remus slumped back into his seat feeling frustrated. Outside, the city flew by, illustrated by all its hustling and bustling. In a few minutes they’d be over the River Thames and his best chance will have slipped away. He knew he shouldn’t want to push his luck, it’d already been sliced so thinly, and he had real responsibilities now, to both his friends and school. But he couldn’t leave without trying one more time. One more.

“So tell me,” Giles started, as the car rolled to a stop before a red light; “What’s your schedule this term look like?”

Wrenching off his seatbelt, Remus threw the door open. “SORRY, GIL!” He hollered, as he leapt out onto the road and swung the Roll's door shut after himself. He only just caught the tip of Giles’ flabbergasted sputter, but before he could be stopped, Remus was streaking down the middle of the street. Slipping past cars filled with surprised passengers, he finally scooted round the pavement, dodging pedestrians as he ran. Giles wouldn’t chase him, but he’d surely box his ears when he returned. It was a consequence he’d deal with later—for now he needed to find the nearest tube station.

After hopping the gates, he took the circle line toward Aldgate, and from there he walked. Being there, in that old neighbourhood he’d gotten himself lost in all those years ago, brought back a rush of memories, some more painful than others. He passed the shops where he and Tonya would buy bread daily the summer before and remembered her dancing in the street. Most days they didn’t even have the money to buy anything, it was just about finding something to do, and Tonya had had a knack for making even the most mundane things magical. After passing the shop, he happened upon the all-hours corner shop where they’d buy their fags whenever they ran out in the middle of the night. He could remember the time he and Tomny and Doss had made the trip over, only to be mugged not five feet from the shop doors. It'd been a bitter memory for a long time, but eventually they'd laughed about it. Remus might’ve stopped in to pick up a carton of cigarettes as a peace offering, except that he’d left everything behind in the Rolls, including his wallet.

Jump me then, he told his ironic fate. Rob me, beat me. I’ve nothing to give you.

But no one bothered him, and he carried on. The streets he knew like the back of his hand, but even more so, he knew that entertaining the idea of some miraculous return was stupid. Tomny had told him himself not to come, he’d been crystal clear, but Remus was too busy feeling sorry for himself to care. As he shuffled up the familiar streets he made a solemn promise that if Tomny could tell him in person that they were done, he’d leave and never come back. He just needed to see his face when he said it.

The building that housed Tomny’s flat looked the exact same when he finally stopped outside its rusted front gate. Most of the apartments had their windows open—desperate for some relief from the heat—but the window to Tomny’s place still had the air-con from last summer fitted in place. To anyone else it was an old aluminium box. To Remus it was a memory.

Pushing open the squeaky gate, he started up the pavement, stepping over the weeds that had burst through the cracks in the cement. A kid, maybe eleven or twelve, was sitting on the front steps, fanning himself with one hand and smoking a cigarette with the other. They eyed each other but Remus just approached the door buzzer and hit the flat’s number. There was no accompanying buzz which meant the ringer was broken again. Sighing, he turned to the kid and jutted his chin out.

“You live here?”

The boy took a stubborn drag on his cigarette, which was longer than any of his fingers. “Who wants tah know?”

“Right. Tomny still live ‘ere?”

“Who wants tah know??”

Remus set his jaw. It unsettled him that this child might know Tomny—that he might’ve been recruited into the group like anyone else or picked up because he was pitiful. It’d been easier to excuse a lesser age when they were all small, but they were grown now.

“Lupin. Tell him Lupin’s come to see him.”

The kid looked away. “Tell ‘im yerself. He’s out.”

“Gee, thanks,” Remus scoffed, turning away and dropping down the steps. While trying to decide what to do next—did he really have the time to sit and wait while just hoping that Tomny would show up?—he noticed a single flower that had broken through the cement with the other weeds, its pure white petals shining in the sun. Feeling the urge to reach out and pick it, Remus stopped before the weed and stared at it until another voice called out. It was not with kindness.

“What you doin' ‘ere?!”

When he looked up, Remus found Lee standing next to the gate. His brown mop of curls were gone, shaved nearly to the skin and giving him a more gaunt, skull-like appearance. Despite the heat, he was wearing jeans and heavy leather boots. His shirt was missing both sleeves and torn over the left side of his chest, though it was just as likely to be for aesthetic purposes than anything unfortunate.

“H-Hey, Lee…” Remus felt a surge of happiness rise in his chest; “Hey!”

“Don’t ‘hey’ me,” Lee scowled; “I asked what you were doin’ ‘ere!”

Before Remus could even begin to answer Lee had looked past him, practically spitting as he yelled;

“Darry! Get yer sorry arse inside before I crack ya a new one. And stop stealin' those fags!”

Instantly the boy was on his feet, abandoning his half-smoked cigarette as he opened the building’s front door and scuttled inside.

Looking anything but satisfied, Lee rubbed a hand across his face.

“So? Don’t tell me you’ve gone mute.”

“Uh…” Remus swallowed. “I—I came to see you guys. You know, for the summer…”

Lee checked an imaginary watch, the only hint of the boy he once was that Remus had witnessed so far. “I’d say you’re pretty late then.”

“Heh, yeah… my bad, I guess. Is—uhm… Is Tomny around?”

Eyes tightening, Lee pushed open the gate slowly and the metal screamed in protest. “What you want wiff Tom?”

“I’ve just got some things to ask him.”

“What sort 'a things?”

Remus felt his jaw begin to tremble. Stop being such a namby, he told himself; This is Lee for Christ’s sake!

“Look Lee, I don’t know what you’ve heard but—”

Lee started up the path, stopping with barely a foot of space between them. “And what would I have heard?” He demanded sharply. “Oh, c’mon now—don’t tell me we're still keepin’ secrets? All this time and all that bullshit and we’re still not fessin’ up to one another, Lu?”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Fucking hell—jus’ cut the bullshit!" Lee barked. "I know everything! Yeah, that’s right. How long did ya think Tomny could stand keepin' it a secret? Always covering for you and your scrawny arse. You know, it made a lot more sense when he finally told all of us. Everything from Christmas and the bleedin’ summers before that—all the favouritism! All the coddling! And then you up and betray us. Did you sell us out, Lu? Did ya?!”

Remus scrambled for a response, but it was as though his brain had short-circuited. He had no idea what Lee was talking about, but if he was this angry then perhaps it was just best to roll over and admit to all of it.

“Lee, I’m tellin’ you," he pleaded; "I never meant to fuck anyone over. All that stuff with Tonya, it was just—”

Lee’s eyes shot wide very suddenly, appearing almost cynical. “Woah, ‘Tonya’—haven’t heard from that bitch in a while," he sneered. "Most of us thought she’d up 'n run off wiff you. But that couldn’t be true because well, yer you and she’s just bottom of the barrel scum like the rest of us.”

Remus was stupefied; “Wha—”

“Must be so hard lovin’ the town bike. Did you take her for a ride, Lu? How’d that cunt taste? Was it rich enough for you—or was her flavour of whore too much for your precious palate?”

The suddenness of Remus’ rage nearly choked him. He grabbed Lee by the front of the shirt and yanked him forward; “DON’T—!” He snarled; “T-Talk about her like that again and I’ll—”

Lee met his anger with the flick of a knife. He whipped it out of his pocket in one smooth move, and the next thing Remus knew he had a switchblade pressed to the centre of his cheek.

“You’ll what?!”

Oh god. Remus released his hold of Lee's shirt immediately and tried backing away, but the other boy only got closer, reaching around the back of his neck to fist the hair there and pin Remus in place against his blade.

“You gonna kick my ass, Lu?! Gonna put me in my rightful place? Don’t you know who’s neighbourhood you’re in, ya fucking fairy?!”

Remus squirmed, but the knife was pressing a groove into his cheek, seconds from breaking skin. Any closer and Lee’d take his eye.

“Get off me!” He cried, attempting a push. Lee barely shifted his weight, and bore down on Remus even more, squeezing his neck tight enough to draw a cry from his lips. Lee laughed then, like a rabid animal pushed to the brink.

“Should I give you a scar to match the one Benny’s boys gave you?” He seethed through his teeth. “Send you home to Daddy with one eye? See how well-received you are then?! Or I know, how ‘bout we real dig deep—see if you fuckin' bleed blue? Couldn’t blend in with us mongrels then, could ya? Nah—we bleed red.”

“Lee, please! It’s bloody me!”

Lee shook him, and Remus felt the sting of the knife’s cut. “That’s the problem, don’t you see?!” Lee barked. “You’re a betrayer, Lu, and you know what happens to betrayers in the East End… That's right..."

Remus felt something trickle down his cheek. Please.

"You should’a never come back here, Remus Lupin.”

He took a breath; he held it. Lee’s eyes were pin pricks; his mouth twitched feverishly. Then he bared his teeth, like he might rip Remus’ throat with them. Unable to do anything else, Remus closed his eyes. He wished he were somewhere else, anywhere else.

Shall I sing to you, darling?

Save me, Remus pleaded. Someone save me.

“Don't be a fucking pansy, open your eyes! Look at me!"

He thought of Sirius, of how they’d confessed their love for one another just that morning. Was this the price? To gain his love he had to lose another’s?

"LOOK AT ME, LU!"

You’re the whole bloody sky, Sirius had said that to him once. Had he loved him then? ... Remus hoped so. He wondered if this was how it’d felt for Sirius to face down his mother. To face someone who ought to love you, and to have no means of satiating them. To be utterly alone.

“Open your fucking eyes, you fucking prick!"

Save me, Sirius, he begged. Save me.

"Last warning... You better open your goddamn eyes or I swear I’ll take this knife and pluck 'em out myself—!”

“LEE!”

For a moment Remus thought his prayers had been answered. That Sirius had somehow followed him all the way from Finchley, and had appeared in his defence like a knight with a sword. But Sirius didn’t know the End, and Sirius didn’t know Lee.

“Fucking let go of him!” Tomny snarled, jumping the gate entirely and rushing toward them. He faltered slightly when he saw the knife, and presumably the blood cascading down Remus’ cheek, but not enough to back down. “Lee, that’s enough!” He ordered. “Put down the knife.”

“No!” Lee wailed breathlessly, wrenching Remus’ head back further. “He’s a liar, Tom. H-He—ones like hims are the ones who—”

“You’re strung out, Lee,” Tomny said firmly. “You don’t know what you’re saying. That’s Lu, your friend.”

“No!” Lee hissed again, each breath like a laboured shudder. “He’s a rat—a f-f-fake!”

“He’s a kid. Now let ‘im go… before I beat your fuckin' arse into the dirt.”

Like a predator turned prey, Lee ripped the knife away from Remus’ cheek, pointing it straight at Tomny’s chest. “STAY AWAY!” He shrilled, but Tomny wasn’t fazed. The moment the blade had left Remus’ cheek he stepped up to them and grabbed Lee by the wrist. He wrenched it terribly, until Remus was sure the bone would snap, but Lee only gave a yelp and dropped the switchblade onto the pavement with a clatter.

“No!” Lee screeched, diving for the knife and taking Remus with him. He’d almost gotten it too, until Tomny used his boot to punt it across the lawn. With his entire body, he grabbed Lee around the middle and for a moment they wrestled, Remus still caught between them.

“Let ‘him—go!” Tomny grunted, before delivering a sharp punch into Lee’s stomach. The other boy immediately folded around his fist, finally releasing Remus, and Tomny caught Lee as he fell. Remus, with no strength left in his legs, plummeted back onto his arse in the yellowed grass, shaking all over.

“There, go on then,” Tomny sighed, as Lee doubled-over on the ground and threw up. He was crying—whimpering really, and after his stomach was empty, Lee turned to Tomny’s legs and held them, sobbing into the frayed hems of his trousers like a wretched child.

“I’mm’sorryyyyy,” he slurred. “I’mmmm’sssoooorrryyyyyy…”

Remus could only watch. He thought he might be crying, but when he touched his cheek he found it was blood. He wasn't even shocked, there was so room for it. Seeing Lee, who was normally full of such light and happiness, reduced to such a state; it was like a nightmare made real.

“I know,” Tomny muttered, rubbing Lee’s back roughly. “I know, mate.”

Nothing happened for a long time. Remus simply sat there, frozen, and Tomny comforted Lee the only way he knew how. He did not look at Remus, and when Lee’s cries had finally filtered off into little more than pitiful moans, he straightened up.

“Darry!” He called. “I know you’re there. Come on out.”

Remus wrenched his head around. The boy from before reappeared in the building doorway, looking weary-eyed and guilty. Tomny beckoned him over, and Darry quickly scuttled down onto the path, moving around Remus like he was afraid he might reach out and bite him.

“Take Lee inside,” Tomny told him, hauling his friend to his feet. “Make sure he stays there, right? Lock ‘im in the bedroom if ya have to, at least until he’s over the roughest bits.”

Darry nodded and meekly let Lee drape an arm around his small shoulders for support. It took some time for the pair to hobble to the end of the front path, and more still to get up the stairs, but eventually Lee and Darry made it through the front door, and it shut behind them with a creak. Remus stared after them for a long while, clutching the front of his shirt and trying to slow his out of control heartbeat. Then suddenly, a body blocked the sun from his face and Remus turned back to find Tomny offering him a hand.

“Stand up,” he said gravely.

Tentatively, Remus reached a shaky hand up and Tomny grabbed him. His hand was as warm and strong as he remembered, but the moment Remus was on his feet again he let go and stuck both in his pockets.

“What are you doing ‘ere, Lu?” Tomny asked. He sounded tired, which was somehow worse than if he'd sounded angry.

“I… Lee, he—”

“Lee didn’t call you 'ere,” Tomny cut-in, mercilessly. “Lee’s too strung-out on oxys to do much of anything these days.”

“When?” Remus asked, heart breaking. “Why?”

“You mean when did it happen? Or why did he start wanting to mark you up like an old tire? He wouldn’t have, if you hadn’t ‘a come.”

Remus felt a lump form in his throat. “I’m sorry,” he said sadly. “But I couldn’t just leave.”

“Why not?”

“ ‘Cause I made a promise…" He half-whispered. "I couldn't let you stay angry.”

Tomny let out a long breath, almost softening. “ ‘ere,” he said, before drawing a plaid handkerchief out of his pocket and passing it over. “For your… cheek.”

Remus let Tomny stuff the fabric into his hands. He balled it up at first, embarrassed somehow, before pressing it to his cheek. It smarted against the cut, but when he winced he was rewarded by Tomny closing the distance between them.

“Doesn’t look too deep,” he mumbled, tilting Remus’ face up by his chin. He withdrew quickly enough, and when Remus was sure he’d wiped most of the blood from his face, he passed the handkerchief back.

“For you to remember me by,” he said snarkily.

Impossibly, the corner of Tomny’s mouth lifted into a smile. It was gone a second later.

“I knew you would come,” he said. “Seeing you last night, I jus' knew it.”

“I don’t really remember what I said,” Remus told him after, “but I knew that I saw you. And I couldn’t go back without saying my piece.”

“And what’s that?”

“That I’m sorry. I am, Tom. You gotta believe me.”

Glancing around, Tomny scratched the side of his head. For a moment Remus thought he might rebuff him again, but then he was nodding. It was solemn, but it was something.

“Orright,” Tomny muttered, “let’s just get ya out of 'ere then.”

Giving a little grunt that meant ‘follow me’, Tomny turned and started down the pavement, straight out the gate. After a final glance at the flat, Remus had no choice but to follow.

Lee's right, I made a mistake coming back, he thought as he trailed behind his friend. Tomny hadn’t said a single thing to him since the flat and suddenly Remus was worried that he’d never get to tell him the things he’d come to say. More than anything he wanted Tomny to know how sorry he was; sorry if anything he did or didn’t do lead to Tonya’s departure and sorrier still that the only letter she’d left was for him rather than the man she was supposed to be in love with.

Seeing Lee so angry had changed something else within Remus too. He’d expected anger from Tomny, but not the others. As they walked he wracked his brain for meaning of what Lee had said, and when the realisation finally hit him, it hit like a train. Lee knew he’d been lying about everything; where he’d grown up, his family, where he went to school, how much money he had. He knew—and Tomny had been the one to tell them.

Does this make you the betrayer, or the betrayed? Vicious Moony asked. You should be angrier, should you not? Is it not your turn? Have we not been dealt enough injustices?

Remus ignored it. There was absolutely no ‘we’.

Ahead of him, Tomny stopped walking and cleared his throat. “ ‘ere.”

Looking up, Remus found that they’d made it to a caff. The words ‘Workman’s Cafe’ were written across the front window in chipped paint and a neon sign hung over the door, though most of the bulbs were busted as though someone had taken a bat to it ages ago.

“What are we…?”

“Well?” Tomny said, holding the door open for him impatiently. “You want to eat off the road or off a plate?”

Eyeing his friend (friend?) Remus slipped past him and walked inside. There was only a few other patrons inside, sitting amongst the cracked leather booths and checkerboard flooring while they sipped their coffees or read the paper. A radio was humming quietly in the background and everyone was keeping to themselves for the most part, not bothering to give them a second glance as they strolled in to the sound of a door chime. They took a seat in a corner booth and not long after a man wearing a grease-stained apron around his rather thick middle came out from the kitchen and leaned over the counter.

“Whatchu want?” He grunted across the cafe.

Tomny glanced at Remus briefly before answering; “Two chocolate shakes and a round 'a chips.”

“Oh no, I don’t have any money,” Remus said.

Tomny arched a single brow. Then he turned back to the cook. “Yeah, that'll be two shakes and the chips.”

Leaning back into his seat sheepishly, Remus kept quiet as the cook shuffled back into the kitchen. “Tom, what are we doing here?” He asked finally.

Plucking a toothpick from the tin at the end of the table, Tomny set it between his teeth and crossed his arms. “Figured ya wouldn’t show up on my doorstep after all this time if ya didn’t want to talk. So I brought us 'ere—now talk. Why’d you come back, Lu?”

It still hurt to hear Tomny speak so coldly, but Remus was done playing meek.

“I came to make things right,” he said firmly. “I’m tired of everything being so wrong.”

“What things? What’s wrong?”

“Everything’s wrong!" He exclaimed, before wincing and lowering his voice; "We’re all so messed up—I mean Lee just held a knife on me, what the fuck was that about?”

Tomny looked away, absent-mindedly chewing on his toothpick. “Some stuff’s happened, innit.”

“What stuff?”

“What’s it matter?”

Remus took a deep breath. “Look Tom, I know you didn’t want me to come back and I’m sorry about Tonya, I am—but I’m really tryin’ here. If you could just tell me something—anything—then maybe I could understand. And if after we’ve talked, you still don’t want me here, well… Well then I’ll leave and you’ll never have to see me again. I swear it.”

Tomny gave him a hard look. “I told everyone about you,” he confessed suddenly. “Where you come from, how you tried to hide it… I told them.”

Betrayed, the voice seethed. Betrayed—betrayed—betrayed!

Remus forced it down. He was hurt, but being hurt had never helped him solve anything.

“I… I already know that, Tom," he said quietly. "Lee, he—he said some stuff…”

“So what, yer not mad?”

“Would it change anything if I was? If I said I wasn’t mad would you forgive me for Tonya?”

Tomny reached up and pulled the toothpick from his mouth before rubbing his face and giving a low moan. “Ahhh, Lu… for Christ's sake, I’m not mad at you for Tonya.”

“Then why’d you tell me to stay away?" He demanded. "Why’d you say you didn’t want me around?!”

“ ‘Cause I didn’t know what else to do.” Withdrawing his hands, Tomny sniffled a bit and shook his head. “Orright, so I admit it. I was mad in the beginning—angry that she would leave an explanation for you—someone she should've barely known—and not me. Me! All I got was a bloody note pinned to the fridge asking me to post it to you and I was fucking pissed off! Not even ashamed to say that I almost burned it, but then fate had a good laugh. I hadn’t paid the gas bill 'n couldn’t find a fucking lighter in the entire flat. Tonya had started hiding ‘em.”

Remus almost laughed himself. He almost felt like telling him that the letter had been burned anyway. “It’s okay.”

“No, it's not,” Tomny said grimly. “I was jealous—jealous of your connection with her. Jealous I could never give her what she wanted while you just made it look so easy. Didn't really think I was before, but… yeah.”

“I’m sorry,” Remus said again, because what else was there to say when your friend was hurting so? “But you have to know Tom—she was your girlfriend! You loved each other and I—I might’ve liked her but I would never—”

Tomny put a hand up to silence him. A moment later the cook shambled over with their milkshakes and a basket of chips and left them on the table. He'd eaten nothing all day and still Remus wasn’t the least bit hungry.

“I know nothing happened between you,” Tomny said finally; “I know. I wasn’t jealous ‘cause of that. I sort of… fuck. I dunno, I'd gotten it into my head that she’d said something or told you something she wouldn't tell me! I thought that maybe you knew she was gonna leave and you didn’t bother saying anything.”

“I didn’t know,” Remus swore. "If I had, I would've done anything to make her stay."

“Yeah, I know." Tomny pulled the toothpick from his lips again, flicking it away. "But you were gone and I couldn’t be sure. It was coward’s shit—but then when I thought of how it would feel to see your face and think of her, I… I told you to stay away because I was a coward, and I’m sorry too. But I think it was probably for the best now anyway.”

Remus sat back in the booth. He knew what Tomny meant.

“What happened with Lee, Tom?”

Tomny began stirring his milkshake with his straw, but didn’t drink any of it. “Ian died,” he said stiffly. “Last May. It was an accident—or it should’ve been. Lee’s been pretty fucked up over it since.”

“How’d he die?” Remus asked, the skin of his arms turning to gooseflesh.

“Got jumped in an alley. Basic shite, really.” Tomny smiled sardonically, but it become a deep frown a moment later. He looked out the window, eyes glassy. “You remember when I told you he got someone a few months ago? He didn’t mean it, but that someone must’ve been important to someone else, who knew someone else and…” Tomny took a breath. “These things tend to snowball around ‘ere. It’s always an eye for an eye, tit for tat. The papers and those fucks in government like to make it sound like it’s one great free-for-all with everyone killing each other all the time, but there’s rules! You can’t just take someone out and not expect retaliation—even if it was just a stupid fuckin’ mistake. You don’t start flingin’ bullets unless you have the muscle to back it up, and Ian—he was just another dumb kid. I thought it would be better to get ‘im out of the city, but he didn’t want to go without Lee and Lee kept insisting that we could protect him until everything blew over.”

“Lee asked you to hide him?”

“S’not an unfair thing to ask, innit? Not from someone you supposedly take orders from.”

Tomny leaned his forehead on one hand, looking haggard. Remus looked away. Someone had carved out a smiley face on the surface of the table. “So Lee blames you…”

“… ‘e blames himself mostly, but yeah, me too. Lee was there when Ian was shot. He had to hold him while he bled out. I guess when he died something just… switched in him. It was like the whole world had become his enemy. It took everything—” Tomny smacked the table’s surface; “to keep him from going after the guys who’d shot Ian, but if he had it would’ve jus’ started up another fuckin’ endless cycle until everyone was just—just fuckin’ dead. Throwing ‘imself into work wasn’t enough, he needed someone else to be mad at—something to distract him—so I… I told him about you.”

Though those that are betray’d, do feel the treason sharply, yet the traitor stands in worse case of woe.

It wasn't the voice this time, but a memory. The quote was Shakespeare, one of the plays in his First Folio. Remus had read it in his classics class last term. It’d originally struck a chord with him because of Regulus, but he’d never brought it up out of fear of upsetting Sirius further. Hearing that your betrayer being in the worse situation is not something one wants to think about when they’ve been betrayed, but Tomny wouldn’t have understood it anyway, so again Remus kept quiet.

“I’m sorry, Lu,” Tomny said, after Remus had been quiet for some time. “I did wrong by you. I promised I’d look after you, and I failed.”

Despite himself and all of his anger, Remus shook his head. “Can't look after everyone, Tom."

"Hard lesson."

Remus ached. Ached for Lee, and the brother he'd lost. Also for Tomny, who'd clearly lost some part of himself that he couldn't place. He ached for Sirius, who deserved better than him, and then he ached for himself, for Remus Lupin, the nameless queer, not queer enough boy that had everything and nothing all at once.

"How are the others?" Remus asked stonily.

“Seesaw and Vint are fine. They’re still kickin’ around.”

“Yeah, saw them in Camden.”

“They were probably on a job.”

Remus bit his lip. Jobs, stabbings, deaths, he knew nothing about any of it.

“And Doss?”

“Doss got out. Moved to Cardiff with that girlfriend of his. ‘er family runs a sheep farm there.”

“He’s a farmer now?”

“Guess so. I think it suits him some though, don’t you?”

Remus smiled meekly and finally pulled his milkshake toward him. It was more milk than shake but it was cool when he sipped it and the chocolate was comforting.

“I’m sorry I betrayed you, Remus,” Tomny said. “I’m sorry I took the easy way out and told everyone your secret and I’m sorry I took everything out on you before that.”

Swallowing, Remus looked up at him—at the man he’d loved and admired for so long. “You know, Tom, people keep telling me they’re sorry. So many sorries. So fucking many that I’m getting real sick ‘n tired of hearing it. I’d rather we just be friends again.”

“I think I’d like that too,” Tomny said softly, then; “I really missed you, Lu.”

“I missed you too.”

Tomny smiled and picked up a chip, popping it into his mouth. Then he wiped his hands and pushed the entire basket aside. “What d'ya say we get outta 'ere? Do something fun—for ol’ time’s sake?”

Remus took one final gulp of his milkshake before doing the same. “Definitely.”

Grinning, Tomny threw a few quid on the table and they got up, and just like that they were practically chasing one another out of the caff. Remus had forgotten how easy it was to go from strangers to brothers in the End. It was almost refreshing.

At first they just roamed, picking off the memories one by one until they just felt like moments again. The corner shop, the closed down bowling alley three streets over that'd been busted into so many times it was practically public property now, the mattress store with bars over its windows and a cut out of a half-naked lady laying on every bed to entise potenial customers into coming inside. It was enough for Remus just to walk, but eventually Tomny was leading him into an alley where he dipped behind an old skip bin and came back with a milk crate full of spraypaint.

“You just keep these here for emergencies?” Remus ragged, already sorting through the old and dented cans.

“They’re Lee’s from a bygone era. He hid ‘em ‘ere after the city kept painting over that mural he’d done over on Quaker Street. Not sure how much is left in ‘em, but figure we could do at least a bit ‘a damage.”

Remus shook one of the cans, hearing its metallic rattling. “What we waiting for then?”

They found themselves an empty brick wall in between the alley and a street of row houses and got to work. Only a few of the cans had any paint in them and most of the nozzles were clogged after months of sitting out in the elements, but Remus wasn’t an artist anyway. Using a bright piss-yellow, he painted the words ‘Mercury is God’ over the brick’s rough surface. Tomny opted for a more traditional approach, tagging the wall with a great big ‘T’ and the words ‘Rent is piracy’.

“Pink Floyd said that their ‘Dark Side of the Moon’ album was partly inspired by graffiti,” Remus said as they worked.

“Hm. Graffiti is kind of like music, innit?” Tomny said, pausing to admire the ‘Townshend wuz here’ Remus was finishing on his end. “Sort of like another language—like a secret code for the beatniks and the underdogs.”

“What do you mean?”

Tomny pointed across from them, to a wall on the other side of the alley that had already been tagged with layers and layers of paint. Everything from handprints to warped cartoons to peace signs inside the Star of David. ‘Free your mind’ the wall said, and ‘Wall Street is here if you say it so’. There was also a badly drawn portrait of John Lennon with ‘Lenin’ written beneath, and a large portion of the wall's centre was dedicated to the words ‘Realise’, ‘Real Eyes’, and ‘Real Lives’.

“When you see stuff like that, what does it make you think?” Tomny asked.

“That… whoever painted it did a lot of acid?”

“Ha, yer being funny, but I know you see deeper than that. That’s the kind’a shit those dickheads in government think when they see it. They don’t see the history there—history of people who can’t afford their fuckin’ rent or aren’t qualified for the jobs they say they’re creating. These people—they’re the ones dyin’ in their factories and going hungry jus’ so their kids can eat.”

Remus concentrated on a tag that read ‘limbo’. Above it was a single dove with an olive branch in its beak. Below it, a body falling into a black hole.

“I don’t mean to sound preachy,” Tomny said, turning back to his wall. “I don’t think you’re like that—no matter where ya grew up.”

“I get it now though,” Remus said, raising his paint can. As he drew he thought of all the friends he’d earned and lost over the last couple years. None of them were all that different really, even if others would’ve looked between them and said they were as separate as the light and dark sides of the moon. Each of them smiled when they were happy and cried when sad, and in between both, they all experienced the same myriad of emotions; pride, cheerfulness, irritation, rage, love. It was all there. He’d seen it.

Busy humming a tune under his breath, Tomny walked up behind him. “ ‘Marauders’,” he read; “What’s it mean?”

“Just some band. They’re pretty small so I doubt you’d know ‘em,” Remus smiled, finishing the tag beneath it.

“Mhm,” Tomny chuckled knowingly, “and how ‘bout that one—‘The Boys of the End’. That another band?”

“Nope, but maybe one day it’ll be a song.”

“Well, I at least hope it’s a good song.”

“Me too."

Suddenly a police siren looped behind them and a single officer got out of his car, barking at them; “Hey, you! Kids—vandals! Stop right there!”

Tomny whistled in smug amusement. “Oi, Bobby Blue, where were you when I nearly got jumped last week!” He shouted, throwing his spray can and hitting the front of the police car with a clang.

“Tom!” Remus gasped. “You can’t just throw cans at the cops!”

“Sure I can,” Tomny shrugged, pointing with his thumb, “jus’ did it.”

“ALRIGHT, AGAINST THE WALL!” The officer barked, but Tomny just snatched Remus’ can and threw that as well before taking his hand and pulling him into the alley.

“C’mon, Lu—run!” He wailed in glee. The siren whooped behind them, but Remus just held onto Tomny, pumping his other arm as they emerged out the alley’s side onto a dingy neighbourhood street. At the very end was a churchyard surrounded by huge hedges. They threw themselves over its low wrought-iron gate and sped off across the lawn until they were convinced they’d put enough distance between them and the cop, and were able to tumble gleefully against the soft grass.

“Reckoned we outpaced him by a mile, Lu!” Tomny howled, rolling around on his back. Wiping tears of laughter from the corners of his eye, Remus leaned up against a large oak tree, admiring the leaves Tomny had succeeded in getting stuck in his hair.

“It’s what we get for picking a place right out in the open,” he chuffed.

“Ah, well at least we left our mark.” Sighing contentedly, Tomny stared up at the tree branches hanging over them. He’d stopped right next to him on his back, his head nearly touching Remus’ thigh. “Man, I forgot how fun jus’ causin’ chaos was.”

“You should come back to school with me,” Remus teased, “there’s plenty of chaos to go around.”

Tomny slapped him on the thigh; “Ah, but before you know it you’ll be done and causin' chaos right back 'ere again, won'tcha?”

“That’s the plan.”

“And just when do you leave for this poncy school of yers?”

“Thirty-first. Few days from now.”

“I see. And when ya return you’ll be headed to university, I expect?”

Remus pressed his tongue to the inside of his cheek. “Dunno actually. My friends and I, we’re sorta thinking that we could give music a try.”

“Really?” Tomny raised his eyebrows.

“Well, we’ve mostly just been playing at the idea—and we don’t actually have any full songs yet, but what we do have it’s—uhm—well yeah, it’s pretty good.”

“I believe it,” Tomny told him, “but Lu, will you do me a favour?”

“Hm?”

“Remember me when you’re looking down from the top.”

Tomny winked, and maybe it was the thrill of running from the cops for the first time in ages, or the fact that the sun was peeking through the leaves just enough to light up the gold in his dishwater blonde hair, or that Remus had just come to terms with leaving this part of himself in the dark—in the closet. Whatever it was, it had him absolutely ruined. Without a second thought, Remus leaned over and pressed his mouth to that little scar on Tomny’s upper lip.

For a second, Tomny’s lips parted, and he could've almost believed that they were kissing, but then he felt a hand on his chest.

Pushing him away.

Remus came to his senses all at once. He bolted upright, horrified by himself—horrified by the entire world. Tomny didn’t say anything, which was worse than yelling, and as he sat up on the grass, Remus prepared himself for the reality that he’d just ruined everything they’d only just begun to patch up.

But when Tomny turned around, he didn’t look mad or repulsed. Instead he scooted back up against the tree until they were shoulder to shoulder against its trunk, both looking down at their laps.

“I love ya, Lu,” he said softly, “but not like that.”

“I’m sorry,” Remus breathed. Terrified. "I-I..."

Reaching out, Tomny took his hand and gave it a squeeze. “Hey, s’nothing to be sorry for.”

Tomny held his hand until he’d stopped shaking. It was cool in the shade of the garden and not even the typical honking of nearby London traffic could be heard among the hedges. It was as though they were the only two people in the entire world.

"I don't know what's wrong with me," Remus whimpered. "I'm not… but there's Sirius, and oh god—I just kissed you!"

"Worried about the posh boy, eh? I'm sure he won't mind."

"You haven't met Sirius."

Tomny chuckled. He was still holding Remus' hand and gave it a little squeeze. "No, but I have a feeling he'll understand."

Pulling his hand away, Remus covered his face. Fuck. Shit—Fuck!

“Remus," Tomny said fondly, "I also wouldn’t worry much if I were you.”

Reluctantly, he peeled his hands away. “… Worry about what?”

Tomny grinned at him, showing off both dimples. “Even if you're not my type, you’re still totally going to rake in a ton of ass when you become a sexy musician.”

Snorting embarrassingly, Remus dropped his head back against the trunk of the old oak. He thought he might cry out of relief, and then he realised he already was.

“In that case,” he wept, “you’re going to regret not kissing me back, ya fucking prick.”

Next to him, Tomny raised both hands up behind his head, smirking casually up at the sky.

“You’re probably right.”





* * *





31st August 1977 – Two days later…





The morning he was supposed to leave for school, Remus got a letter in the post. The return address was of number 38 Burtonhole Lane, London, home of Potter Cottage, and it was written in Sirius’ beautiful scrawl. The letter was everything Remus had hoped.





Dear Moony,

(or alternatively, a one Mr. Dean)

THERE! I’m finally writing you back now so take that, ya dickhead! Also, I cannot BELIEVE how fast post travels in London. I asked Prongs how long he figured it would take to post something to you and he said two days—TWO DAYS?!?! Pure insanity. Next thing you know we’ll be sending them in tubes through the air. Prongs thinks it’s a bit daft that I’m writing to you instead of calling now that I can do that too, but this is a goodbye letter, so it should be formal. And yes, you heard me right, this is last one. No point in sending post if I’m always around to regale you guys with my beautiful voice in person, right? Yessiree, September 1st marks our last year at school, Moons, and then you’re in for it. No more holidays apart for us. Just the rest of our lives, baby!

I know you already know this because you were there, but I feel like I have to tell somebody or I’ll explode. Effie and Monty have been good to me—far better than I deserve. They’ve offered to pay for my tuition and I’ve accepted. And because Prongs is tired of hearing it, I need you to know that I’m going to pay them back every penny the minute I get Alphard’s inheritance. They say I don’t have to, but you and I both know that I do. On the upside, Prongs makes a pretty good roommate, but you already knew that too. He called me his brother the other day and I think he really meant it. It just felt different this time. Don’t tell the handsome twat, but I might’ve cried. Oh and you were both right about Wormtail, he’s really gotten good on the drums. He can actually carry a beat now!

Speaking of music, did you hear that Elvis died? Like actually DIED—on the toilet, no less! Guess it happened while I was at yours—really, how could we have missed it??? (I’m only kidding—I know we were pretty busy.) But Elvis! Who's next? Mick Jagger? Marc Bolan? I fucking hope not. All I’m saying is that when we’re rich and famous, the toilet is not the way I want to go. Put me on a rocket and blast my bones out into space. Now that’s rock and roll.

I’m glad we talked the other day. Put some real perspective on all of this. You’re still my best friend, Moons, and I don’t want anything to change that. You’re too important to me, and after all, I still need a bassist if I'm to start my world-wide musical take-over. Loving you just might be an extra perk, one that's just for us. (Never said I wasn't a romantic.)

Don’t get too lonely in the dorm without us. Or do, just means you’ll be thinking about me. I'll see you soon, and tell all those perky-prefects hello from yours truly. They don’t have any idea what they’re in for, letting a double-agent into their ranks.

Yours in unequivocal adoration,

Padfoot.



There was something about the letter that felt slightly foreboding, but no matter how many times he read it over, Remus couldn’t quite put his finger on what it was—Mick Jagger's death maybe? Whatever, Remus told himself. Be thankful, the two of you finally understand one another. And Sirius had given him hope. Just for us, he'd written. It was an aspiration for whatever their relationship was going to be. Maybe they could do this after all. Perhaps it was as easy as just saying yes.

When Giles put the Rolls into park outside the station, Remus tucked Sirius' letter away into his pocket. He’d probably read it again later, but for now he had a train to catch.

“You’re sure you have everything?” Giles asked, fixing the shoulder strap on Remus’ bag himself. He was probably just relieved they’d made it on time at all; Giles hadn’t even given Remus a real punishment when he’d returned from Tomny’s that day. All he’d done was shake his head at the cut on his cheek and mutter that his uniforms had arrived. Remus was definitely going to miss him.

“Yes,” he answered. “Just like I had everything the last twenty times you asked.”

Giles chuckled as the train’s whistle sounded behind them from down the platform. “Who would’a thought though,” he gushed, “our Remus going back to finish his A-Levels—and as a school prefect to boot! It’s enough to make a man start choking up.”

“Shall I find you a tissue?”

“I just want you to know how proud of you I am.” Giles took him by the shoulders. “And that your mum would be very proud of the man you’ve become too.”

“Thanks, Gil,” Remus said lightly.

Humming over a smile, Giles released him and took a step back. “Okay, remember what I told you the first time we did this—be good, and if you can’t be good…?”

“Be smart.”

“Ah, but you already got that covered, my little genius!” Rubbing the top of his head with several thick knuckles, Giles laughed while Remus batted him away. “Alright then, time for me to be off. I’ll see you at Christmas.”

“Bye, Gil. Miss ya already.”

“Miss you already too, cheeky blighter.” Still grinning, Giles tipped his hat and began walking away, waving over his shoulder as he did. Remus watched him go, silently thankful, before grabbing his trunk and turning back to the train.

“Don’t I get a sappy goodbye too?”

Remus just about jumped ten feet. Straight ahead of him, Tomny had appeared in the middle of the platform, looking cheekier than Remus had ever seen him with his same battered jeans, faded t-shirt, and a smile.

“TOM!” The disbelief was clear on Remus’ face. The two of them had already said goodbye that day in the End, and he hadn’t been expecting to see him again so soon. “What are you doing here?”

“Seeing ya off, a’course,” Tomny said, raising his arms. “S’yer last year after all, never gonna get the chance again.”

Unable to deny him, Remus rushed his friend, enveloping Tomny’s broad chest in a greedy hug. Tomny hugged him back of course, patting Remus on the back one with one hand all the while.

“How’d you know I’d be at this station though?” Remus asked as he pulled away.

“Lucky guess,” Tomny shrugged. “You did say you left on the thirty-first. Where’re yer friends at?”

“Oh, they’re not leaving for school until tomorrow. I—er… I have to go a day early.”

Tomny squinted. “Why's that?”

“Because I’m a—er… I’m a… nghschoolprefectmmnnhnn…”

“A what now?”

“I'm a school prefect!”

“Wow! That’s, er…” Tomny started to laugh; “Im-pres-sive, heh!”

“Shut up!” Remus cried, punching him in the arm; “I didn’t ask for it!”

“Oh yeah, sure, whatever you say, m’good sir.”

“You’re the worst.”

Tomny winked. “Yeah well, try not to miss me too much.”

Remus smiled. Never a day of rest with his friends. “I'm glad you came.”

“Me too. Feels a bit special knowin’ I get tah be the las’ one to see you off. Also, I may have picked up somefin’ for yeh.” From under one arm, Tomny pulled out a brand-new album, the Clash’s self-titled. “I asked around at the record store after you told me about that punk show you and yer friend went to. Bloke there said these guys were promisin’.”

“Thanks,” Remus said, admiring the cover; “Can’t wait to listen to it.”

“I know, and these are for when you do.” Slyly, Tomny held up a pack of cigarettes and tucked them into Remus’ shirt pocket. Glancing down at them, Remus suddenly felt very overwhelmed. Before he could start crying, he threw his arms around his friend again, making Tomny gasp and then laugh in response.

“Ah, Lu,” he hummed, patting him on the back, “m’gonna miss ya.”

“You keep saying that,” Remus said into his shoulder, “but I won’t be gone forever. I’ll be back, Tom.”

Tomny pulled away; “And I’ll be here,” he tsked, before picking up the handle of one of Remus’ trunks and wheeling it toward the train. “C’mon, let’s get you on board then.”

After lifting the trunks up into the train, Remus paused and looked back. He couldn’t leave without saying it. “Tom, about what happened the other day in that church yard. I need you to know that—”

“No you don’t,” Tomny said first. “ ‘Cause I understand. Maybe you surprised me a bit, sure, but you’ll always be my Lu, wont’cha? Nuffin’s gonna change that.”

Remus sighed. “Yeah,” he said, while Tomny pulled his hands from his pockets. He took Remus by the head and kissed his forehead fondly, before ruffling his hair.

“Go on then,” he told him. “Go kick that poncy school’s arse.”

With nothing else to do, Remus boarded the train. He dragged his trunks down to the first empty compartment and found Tomny already waiting outside the window. He rapped his knuckles to the glass to get his attention and Remus rushed to open the small window at the top, just to hear him again.

“Almost forgot—for luck!” Tomny said, before stretching up and passing a small object through the opening. Remus took it, and as he turned it over in his palm he realised that it was a lighter. Just as crappy and dented as the first one Tomny had given him.

Smiling, Remus broke open his pack of cigarettes and lit one up like a small victory. Tomny remained outside the window, looking like a nobody with his hands in his pockets, until the final whistle blew signalling the train’s departure. No one else knew just how important they were to each other, but when the train car began to move, Tomny proved it by kicking up into a jog, which quickly turned into a run as he tried to keep up alongside the locomotive.

“I love you!” Tomny barked through the glass, pointing furiously at Remus. “I love you! Kick its ass! Kick its ass!”

Remus slapped his palm to the window, like he could reach through it and touch his friend. “I love you too, Tom!” He cried back. “I love you!”

And then, as the platform neared its inevitable end and the train sped up to take Remus back to school, Thonas Armstrong fell out of sight.





* * *





Saying goodbye to Tomny at the station had left Remus’ heart feeling full for the entire, lonely ride back to Scotland. Unused to the quiet of an empty compartment, he read and napped and pigged out on snacks he’d bought off the trolley, and even found it in him to finish the rest of his summer homework. When the train finally pulled into the Highland station and he boarded the bus that would take him to Hawkings, Remus was more than a little travel weary. He knew from the prefect’s itinerary McGonagall had sent that he’d be expected to attend a meeting in preparation for the other students’ arrival the following day, but at least he’d have Lily to complain to and eat dinner with afterwards. It bummed him out that he hadn’t seen her on the train, but she could’ve just taken the other line from Liverpool. It was on him for forgetting to call first and check.

After he’d lugged his trunks all the way to Godric and dumped them in the empty 4A dorm room, Remus made his way up to Rowena and stuck his head in, catching another girl as she came down the staircase.

“Have you seen Lily Evans around?”

She glanced about in consideration. “I hav’nae, sorry,” she replied in a thick Scottish accent. “Are ye heading tae the prefect’s meeting?”

“Yup.”

“Cool, so am I.” She held out her hand; “I’m Patricia, year twelve, but ye can call me Trish.”

“Pleasure to meet you. I’m Remus, year twel—or I mean thirteen, I guess.” He shook her hand sheepishly. “Are you sure you didn’t see Lily upstairs?”

“Na, don’t think so. But a group o’girls have already left for the hall. Maybe she was with ‘em. We can walk over together if you’d like.”

“Sure, why not.”

Smiling kindly, Trish let the dorm's front door fall shut behind her and came down the rest of the stairs to join him. At her side, Remus spent the entire walk to the Great Hall glancing around himself at the campus. It felt like ages since he’d been there last and the breeze in Scotland was much cooler than it had been in London. Trish was friendly but she didn’t talk at a million miles an hour at least, which he appreciated. When they finally were filing in, another student had them sign their names on an attendance sheet and Remus stopped to scan the list for Lily’s name, only to realise that there was no ‘Lily Evans’ in attendance.

“Does Lily not have to sign this?” He asked the prefect, who shrugged in response.

Passing the clipboard along to Trish, Remus shuffled into the room and looked around for a glimpse of fiery red-hair. After turning up with nothing once more, he began to feel a seed of doubt bloom in the back of his mind, which he had to squash immediately.

Relax, Lily would never miss a prefect meeting. She’ll be here.

As he went back to scanning the rest of the prefects’ faces for any sign of his friend, Remus ended up locked eyes with not Lily, but Regulus Black, who was glaring at him from the other side of the room.

“Don’t think that’s a look o’admiration,” Trish said, appearing at his elbow.

“What? Oh, you… know Regulus?”

“Sure, he’s in my year, after ‘ah.”

“Right…”

Quickly breaking eye-contact, Remus turned away and shuffled toward another corner where he knew he’d have better luck avoiding the youngest Black brother. If he were being honest, Regulus had possessed very few of his thoughts throughout the summer. He'd wondered only with a small twinge of anger if Regulus knew what had actually happened to Sirius, but now that they were face to face, he could hardly blame him for the scowl. Not after what they’d done at the end of last year.

“I hope this doesn’t go on ah’evening,” Trish said, raising her arms over her head with a yawn. Remus agreed, only slightly bewildered as to why she’d stuck around, and thankfully Professor McGonagall appeared at the top of the stage of the Great Hall, clearing her throat to address all of them.

“Hello prefects, so happy to have you back with us for another year here at Hawkings School,” she said. “First of all, I wanted to thank you personally for your continued dedication to the school and upholding its rules and regulations. I know it’s been a long day of travel for all of you, but you’ll have plenty of time to gather your wits before your fellow students arrive tomorrow. In a moment I’m going to start listing off your perfect partners for the term and then afterwards you may mingle amongst yourselves and get to know one another in preparation for student arrival tomorrow. You’re going to be working together after all, might as well get used to it.”

“Remus!” A voice trilled quietly.

Lily! Finally…

Remus spun around, only to have his entire face fall when he found Jillian Stewart pushing through other students instead. “Sorry,” she said to Trish, before pointedly side-stepping her and getting between them.

“Dinna fash yerself,” Trish mumbled, before casting a questionable look at Remus, which he ignored out of pure embarrassment.

“It’s so nice to see you!” Jillian gushed. “You never told me you were going to be a prefect!”

“Oh, you neither, heh…”

"Jesus," Jillian swore suddenly. "What happened to your cheek?"

Remus touched the butterfly stitches Giles had outfitted over his cut. It'd be healed soon enough, without a scar most likely.

"Oh, you know... took a tumble."

Jillian's eyes flashed greedily. Dangerous, they seemed to say, like she were delighted.

“Well, I missed you over summer. It was so nice to get your letters.” She took his arm and held it so tightly to her chest that he could almost feel the outline of her bra through her school shirt.

“Man, people really gotta stop missing me,” Remus winced.

As Professor McGonagall began reading names of her list, Jillian continued to beam up at him. “Psst, Remus. Notice anything different?”

He looked around in question. “Er…”

“About me, silly! Look—I got my braces off.” She smiled again and Remus nodded slowly.

“Oh yeah, looks great, Jill.”

“Don’t they? It’s such a relief to have them off. Snogging is going to be so much easier now.”

Next to them, Remus heard Trish snort and he just about caved in himself. Where the fuck was Lily?

“I’m so glad you’re a prefect this year,” Jillian said, seemingly unruffled. “I always thought being stuck with one partner all year was terribly dreary, but wouldn’t it be so great if we got to be partners?”

Please god, no, Remus pleaded, anyone but you.

“Er—Jillian, have you seen Lily at all?” He asked nervously.

“Hm? You mean Lily Evans?" She chuckled faintly. "Why would I have seen her?”

“Because she’s supposed to be here. I didn’t catch her on the bus or at her dorm but—”

“Silly Remus, Lily’s not a prefect this year!”

Remus’ jaw dropped open. “What?”

“Yeah! She told everyone at the end-of-the-year party that she was switching her classes around and didn’t have the extra space in her timetable.” Jillian blinked happily. “Didn’t she tell you that?”

“No…” he half-wheezed, “no, she didn’t.”

“Oh, well that’s okay. Suppose she can always tell you herself tomorrow.”

“Miss Stewart,” Professor McGonagall called sternly from up on her dais; “Is there something you would like to share with the room?”

“Sorry, professor!” Jillian squeaked, clutching tighter to Remus’ arm as though he could save her from the Headmistress’s wrath.

Clearing her throat again, McGonagall went back to her list; “Stewart, Jillian,” she read, looking unsurprised.

Turning on him, Jillian held up two fingers. “Finger’s crossed!”

Silently, Remus began to pray.

Please! Please! Please! Not me! ANYONE BUT JILLIAN!

“—and MacDuff, Patricia.”

“Bugger!” Jillian frowned. “We’re not partners, Remus… tch.” She shook her head bitterly. “At least we’re guaranteed to run in the same circle as prefects, right?”

Remus just nodded, busy having his own celebration inside his head. Next to them, Trish looked as though she’d just swallowed a lemon. Remus could hardly blame her. Trish was a year younger, he doubted Jillian even knew her name.

“Remus, are you doing anything tonight?” Jillian asked, as McGonagall continued down her list of partners. “We’re supposed to be meeting again, but we could always sneak—”

“Lupin, Remus!”

Jillian fell silent immediately. Remus wasn’t thick—she was probably just trying to figure out who her competition was going to be, but if he wasn’t to have Lily, then Remus just hoped that his partner ended up being even moderately tolerable. He glanced quickly around the room. The options weren't horrible, there was always—

“—and Black, Regulus!”

Immediately, a dull roar of whispers broke out amongst the other prefects.

"Lupin and Black?"

"Wrong Black, looks like."

"No shit! Lupin better watch out, Regulus is out for blood."

“Regulus?” Jillian echoed sceptically. “That's Sirius’ brother, isn't it?”

She looked to him as though it was some grand revelation, but Remus couldn’t even hear her anymore. All around them, kids who remembered the horrible prank from the term before were craning their heads to get an eyeful, and when Remus finally spared a glance Regulus’ way, he found a look of pure venom waiting for him.

Be ready, it said; because I’m going to kill you.

Remus felt like the Titanic as it sank to the ocean floor. That ill-tempered fate had dealt him a foul hand yet again, it seemed, and left him sure of only two things:





He was going to throttle Lily, and;

He was so bloody fucked.





Chapter End Notes

'Bog' means toilet.

'Lorry' means truck.

Giles' meaning of 'ringways' refers to the ringway roads around London, precursors to the M25 motorway.

The poem Remus reads is called ‘Völuspá’. It is the most well-known poem from the ‘Poetic Etta’. It tells the story of the end of the world and its subsequent rebirth in Norse mythology.

A 'caff' is a small, inexpensive restaurant or coffeehouse; cafe.

Trish uses 'dinna fash' as in Scottish slang for 'don't worry about it'.
