Me and you and you and me,

No matter how they toss the dice, it had to be;

The only one for me is you, and you for me,

So happy together;

I can’t see me lovin’ nobody but you,

For all my life;

When you’re with me, baby the skies’ll be blue,

For all my life…

- “Happy Together” The Turtles, 1967



They had to be more careful at school than they’d been over summer. There were more people around to catch them, and few were strangers. Someone was bound to notice if they were constantly sitting with their legs pressed up against one another ankle to hip, or eyeing each other suggestively from across the room when they were supposed to be concentrating on class work. Luckily, Sirius had always been a flirt, so they did get away with some things in public.

“C’mon, Moony, take it!” Sirius crooned, mumbling around the baby carrot he was dangling in front of his face with his lips. Remus pushed him away by the cheek, but stole the carrot and snapped it in two with his teeth, making Sirius purse that perfect mouth wryly and look away.

He was glad they’d talked. More than glad, even—Moony was over the moon. Since making up Sirius had been as bright and sunny as ever, back to teasing his friends with fervent pleasure. Remus wasn’t really sure where they were going to end up, but as long as it was somewhere together, he was content. And he liked this Sirius—he liked the Remus he could be with this Sirius. Even if it had him missing summertime, unable to wake up and witness the way the morning sun dusted across his dark eyelashes.

“James said he’s glad you’re out of that ‘funk’,” Sirius told him, the first time they’d stolen away to the astronomy room together. “He told me yesterday in class. Asked if I knew anything about it.”

Unable to deny his ‘funk’, Remus hesitated in the dark. “And so did you…?”

“I told him it was something to do with your London friends, but that I didn’t know what. He pretty much let it rest after that.”

Well, it wasn’t entirely un-true. He still wasn’t sure what to make of Lee, and then there was the kiss with Tomny—which was totally over and done with, as far as Remus was concerned.

“He’s been more curious lately,” Remus said. “Yesterday he wouldn’t leave me alone at lunch. I think he’s noticed how much time we’re spending together.”

“He’ll get used to it,” Sirius reassured him. “Keep telling him we have detention or something.”

“And how long do you figure that’ll work?”

“Long enough to come up with a better excuse.” Sirius turned toward him, smoothly sliding one leg across Remus’ thighs until he was straddling his waist. “You’re making a liar out of me, Lupin.”

“And you’ve already made a thief out of me,” Remus said, leaning in. “I’d say that makes us even.”

“Hmm... Sounds like we’re a bad influence on each other.” Sirius pressed his lips against the corner of his jaw. As he did, Remus reached down and took Sirius’ wrist, pulling him closer until they were entirely chest to chest, lips moving against one another in slow, thoughtful movements.

“Mhm,” he murmured around Sirius’ tongue, “the worst.”

Remus would’ve been lying if he said it hadn’t taken them a bit to warm up to one another again, but once they were over the shy coddling and nervous reassurance, they’d thrown themselves at each other like they had that very first night on the Underground. In front of others they had to be careful—coy—but any chance they had alone was a free-for-all. They tried to keep it out of the dorm room, but the afternoons James had practice and Peter was busy with club activities were just too tempting.

“Got a light?” Sirius would ask after each time. Having a post-romp fag became a way to keep things grounded in reality. It was the switch from Remus and Sirius to just, Remus and Sirius. And despite the fact that Sirius most definitely had a light, Remus would always lean over with his zippo and light the cigarette for him. Occasionally the intimate closeness of the otherwise trivial gesture would lead to another pointed glance, and after checking the clock to make sure they had the time, Sirius would stub out the cig and pull Remus back in behind the bed curtains.

Their equal enthusiasm was comforting. Despite his initial concerns, Sirius seemed to need his touch just as much as Remus craved his. He was respectful, never going any further in front of others that couldn’t be explained away with a simple excuse or Sirius’ generally coquettish disposition. When they were alone he liked to lead, and Remus was more than happy to let him; but that didn’t mean he didn’t get his end-away either. It would usually start with kissing, then touching—fisting each other’s clothes until they were all but tearing them off one another. Things were always aggressive and fervid, but Remus didn’t mind. It made things harder to over-think, easier to lose himself in.

And when ‘get on me’ began to feel like old hat—oh the things they said to each other.

It wasn’t just the hooking up that had Remus relieved either. Once he and Sirius had gotten over their joint ‘funk’ (“It was joint and you know it.”) they were also free to be with their friends.

“Ah, finally joining us, are you? What was it this time—did you glue all of Filch’s brooms to the ceiling?” James had said, when they’d reappeared after an afternoon spent hidden beneath the football stands.

“No, but that would be a good one,” Sirius said, falling into him on the common room sofa. It was only natural that James be slightly overbearing. He’d never said it, but Remus got the sense that he now fully considered himself to be Sirius’ keeper. They were almost real brothers now—the Potters were Sirius’ family as much as they were James'. After their first week Effie had sent them all care packages, but she’d signed Sirius’ card with ‘love from Mum and Dad’. Sirius had denied it, but Remus was pretty sure he’d cried over it later.

They’d spent Peter’s birthday with just the four of them, crowded around a telly in the AV room and playing Pong on the Atari system his parents had sent as a gift, as he couldn’t really get much use out of the drum kit while at school.

“You said it was a sports game!” James wailed, after losing his third game in a row.

“It is! It’s like tennis! All you gotta do is bounce the little dot back,” Peter cackled.

“Well, if this dial weren’t so damn sensitive! It acts like my nan when you tell her she looks any older than thirty-five.”

“Who would’a thought we’d see the day that Pete would beat you at a sport,” Sirius cackled, promptly missing the dot and making the telly beep in displeasure.

“We should do a prank,” he said later, as they were sneaking their way back across the campus. In continued celebration, they’d broken into the dining hall and lifted a plate of biscuits, several mini chocolate mousses, and an entire pint of mint chocolate chip ice cream. They’d justified the theft on birthday grounds, but Remus had seen James leave a few quid taped to the freezer with a short note of apology.

“What sort of prank?” Peter asked, carrying the ice cream with one hand and munching on a biscuit with the other.

“A good one. One that’s bound to be noticed. Our reputation’s on the line, after all.”

“But Moony’s a prefect now,” James pointed out. “And you’ve already gotten him enough detentions this term.”

“We told you—that was Snape.”

“You mean to say that all of those detentions were Snape’s fault?”

Of course they weren’t all Snape’s fault—the detentions in question weren’t even really detentions at all. They were just excuses to get away together. Knowing this, Remus nudged Sirius from behind. “Any ingenious pranking ideas then?”

Sirius smirked. “I may have a few…”

“I just hope it doesn’t involve Regulus this time,” James ragged. Scoffing, Sirius snatched the ice cream from Peter and pressed it to the back of his friend’s neck, making James howl in surprise.

“Get back here!” He lashed, as Sirius tossed the ice cream tub back to Peter and took off across the lawn. Remus watched them, falling into step with Peter and imagining all of the devious ideas Sirius was hatching in his brain. Even if the two of them were now officially a secret item, it was still fun to be stupid with their friends. Music, pranking—it didn’t matter. The pleasure came from knowing that even when they weren’t able to be together as Sirius and Remus, they were still together as Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot, and Prongs. As Marauders.

It was the best.

Sunday 25th September 1977





“It’s the fucking worst,” Sirius hissed, as they shuffled into their pews for Sunday mass. “Five quid says they spent my entire year thirteen tuition on it.”

“I can think of a million other things to spend that kind of money on,” Remus agreed scornfully.

“Like a car. Like a debut album. Like a bloody cool motorbike. Fuck, the things I could do if my entire family wasn’t on Satan’s payroll.”

“It certainly is ‘in your face’ enough,” James replied, from his spot next to Sirius.

“Speaking of faces, is his supposed to look like that?” Asked Peter.

All four of them tilted their heads to the side, peering quizzically at the freshly-carved statue of Christ standing behind the heads of the student choir. The ten foot tall carving was a new addition to the church, one generously commissioned by the Black family, as thanks for ‘the school’s continued dedication to corrective instruction and established education’. It had appeared just the Sunday before and Sirius had wasted no time making fun of the garish sculpture—comments that only got worse once he’d found out that his family was the one to donate it in the first place.

“You guys staring at the new kid in class again?” Lottie teased, shuffling down the pew with the other girls in tow. Lily quickly slipped down the line, taking a spot between James and Peter and giving her boyfriend a quick peck on the cheek in hello. After she’d passed, Sirius threw a hand out, scoffing;

“It’s positively hideous. I mean, if they’re going to find a way to rub their money in everyone’s faces isn’t there a better way to do it than dangling a half-naked bloke in front of all our noses?”

“I think the son of God is a lot more than some ‘half-naked bloke’,” Marlene said pointedly.

Sirius shrugged his shoulders. “Whatever. Didn’t think you cared all that much for western religion after your trip down south, McKinnon. Didn’t you discover Ghandi or something?”

“Not Ghandi—Allah. Plenty of Moroccan people follow Islam, Sirius. And no, I’m not suddenly converting.”

“What about you, Mary? Still Buddhist?” Remus asked.

Mary winked. “Only on Sundays, love.”

“I bet if they had it their way, it’d be me nailed to that cross instead,” Sirius continued, grumbling loathsomely.

While the other girls all frowned in sympathy, Lily reached across James’ lap to take Sirius’ hand. “You don’t have to worry about it anymore, you’ve got us now,” she said comfortingly.

“Yeah,” Sirius mumbled, squeezing back, “yeah, I do. And besides, we won’t have to look at the ugly thing for much longer. At least not for today, anyway.”

“What do you mean?”

“Oh nothing,” he smirked.

Lily pulled her hand back suspiciously, turning on her boyfriend. “Potter?”

“Sorry, Daisy, I’m not saying anything.”

“What have you lot done now?” Lottie asked, nudging Peter.

“No idea,” he answered dumbly. “Moony, any thoughts?”

“No, not really. But I did wake up to find my private stash a bit light today. Anyone know anything about that?”

James and Sirius both swallowed their smiles.

“Oh, this ought to be good,” Mary scoffed playfully, crossing her arms over her chest.

When all the other students were settled and Professor McGonagall had stood up to call order, the priests filed in for their entrance procession followed by the altar bearers, each of them swinging the heavy metal thuribles ahead of themselves. Remus watched as the smoke from the censer burners wafted between the rows, purifying the students and raising their prayers up to Heaven. It was subtle, but as they reached midway down the aisles, one of the altar boys reached up to rub at his nose. Steadily, more and more kids began to blink in the light haze, expressions of recognition coming over each of them that ranged from confused to aghast to amazed.

“Nice,” Remus sniggered, once he’d gotten a whiff for himself.

Next to him, Lottie whirled around in the pew, her eyes wide. “It smells like—”

“WOAH! WHO BROUGHT THE WEED?!”

The amused cry went up very suddenly, making every priest and teacher shoot up in their chairs. What followed was a cacophonous roar of laughter as the procession came to an immediate halt, the head priest shooting down the aisles toward the confused altar boys, snatching the smoking metal pots from their hands. But it was too late. By now the entire room could smell it, and Marlene gaped at Sirius and James, who were falling into themselves with smug laughter.

“You didn’t!” She trilled.

“Of course we didn’t,” Sirius snorted, clearly lying.

She smacked him.

“James!” Lily blagged.

“He just said we didn’t do it! … But if we did, it would’a been real funny.”

“Real funny,” Peter agreed, knocking his fist against his best friend’s happily.

“I can’t believe you guys,” Marlene gasped. “You’re so going to get caught.”

“Why? It’s not like Sheila’s around to pin it on us. She's stepped out this weekend,” Sirius said smugly. Leaning back with his hands behind his head, he put his feet up on the pew ahead of him while the priests fled the church with the stinking censers in hand and the room continued with its chaos. Remus eyed him, before turning back to a very blanched Marlene.

“Yeah, Cherry, don’t worry, they got no real proof anyway.”

“Agh—! Damn it…”

Hissing, Remus pressed the tip of his thumb into his mouth before withdrawing it to examine the small cut. The silver thuribles had edges that could cut glass, and the little notched holes in the side that were meant to allow the smoke out acted more like the blades of a cheese grater. He might’ve thrown more of a fit, had the prank not worked out so masterfully. Though McGonagall must’ve thought herself pretty smart to choose him out of all the prefects to stay and clean up; if she couldn’t directly pin it on all four Marauders, then the single prefect among them would have to do. Remus was just thankful Regulus wasn’t asked to stay. He didn’t need any more animosity where he was concerned.

“Fuck this,” Remus griped under his breath, tossing the charcoal-smudged rag at the pile of metal censers they had left to clean. The metal bowls went down with a grand clatter, scattering themselves across the front dais of the church. Behind him sat the chancel in all its golden glory, and beyond that—the Blacks’ statue of Christ. Remus glared at it, flipping the crucified man off for good measure.

“Well, that was rather dramatic,” Trish drawled, appearing out of the vestry hallway with two more thuribles tucked under each arm. They were to clean every piece of silver in the entire church, it seemed. Déjà vu all over again.

“This feels like detention,” he scowled, kicking away one of the censer lids that had rolled toward him and turning to dangle his long legs off the side of the raised dais.

“This is pretty normal prefect stuff, actually. They always get a couple o’ us tae sweep up after mass.” Trish set down her load, before pushing up onto the edge of the stage next to him. “Ye’v just added to it.”

“It’s still shit,” Remus grumbled. So much for not throwing a fit.

“Meh, it’s not that bad.”

“Why are you even here, Trish?” He asked. “McGonagall didn’t force you to stay—why the hell would you volunteer?”

“Maybe because I actually did have prefect duty today, ‘n I’d rather be ‘ere than chasing kiddies around the primary campus with Jillian breathing down my neck.”

“Oh, so you just wanted to get out of other prefect stuff?” He asked gingerly.

“Yep.”

“No… other reason?”

“Na, why?”

“Well, you just… you don’t happen to… have a thing for me do you? Because—er—it just wouldn’t work.”

Trish gave him a deep frown before bursting into laughter. “ ‘A thing fur yeh’? Whit? No offence, Loonarny, but I barely ken who you are—you could be an axe murderer for all I know. Or some stuffy loud-mouth with an Adderall addiction.”

Remus hung his head, horribly embarrassed. “Oh. Wow—um… Yeah, sorry. That—That was weird… hah…”

“Are you that used tae strangers openly declaring their love for ya?”

“What? No, I—”

“Ah mean, I guess you’re braw enough, though that might just be the fact that you look like yer related to a tree, but—”

“It was weird!” Remus interjected. “I’m sorry. I just… bad track record lately, that’s all.”

Trish gave him an amused look. “With Jillian, right? She’s said a lot o’ stuff about you.”

Embarrassed, Remus picked up one of the rags and began absent-mindedly polishing one of the thurible pieces. “Yep…”

“She really had a thing fur yeh.”

“I know. Didn’t think the two of you got along all that well, actually.”

“S’a girl thing,” she giggled. “She’s bearable on her own. Yer a lad, so you wouldn’t get it.”

Remus thought of Regulus, who hated him whether they were alone or not. “Yeah…”

“So…” Trish mused, “how’s that ‘fiancée’ o’ yours then?”

“You heard about that, huh?” Remus snorted.

“Aye. Heard she was a solid ten outta ten actually. Real 'peng'.”

“Really?”

“Mhm, oh yeah—absolutely gorgeous. French, with locks down tae her bum ‘n a real affinity fur English bad boys.”

“Jesus Christ.”

“Canny, or he’ll hear you,” she sniggered, pointing at Sirius’ favourite ugly statue. Remus looked back, smiling and a bit amused by her.

“Look,” he started, “don’t tell anyone, but I’m not actually engaged.”

Trish gasped sarcastically. “Nah, ye don’t say!”

“Ha, ha. Yeah, it was just something my friend Lily came up with to let Jillian down easy, so keep it to yourself?”

“Meh. She’s dating that jimmie in my year, Roy Nilssen, anyway now, so I wouldn’t worry about it.”

“He on the football team?” Remus asked, trying to recall his face.

“Na, that’s Troy Michaelssen. Roy’s on the rowing team.”

“Oh. I see...”

“Suddenly feeling jealous?”

“No!”

Trish grinned evilly at him. She reminded him a bit of Tomny, but that might’ve just been the accent. She rolled her ‘r’s just like he did, though Tomny’s brogue wasn’t ever as pronounced.

“On the subject o’ lying,” Trish started, before turning away and rummaging around in her blazer’s pockets; “I may have had an ulterior motive for staying behind in church—one that doesn’t have tae do with yer handsome puss anyway.”

Intrigued, Remus straightened up to get a better look, and Trish came back with a joint tucked between her lips, which she lit off a pocket lighter and puffed to life.

“Trish!” He gasped, whipping around to make sure they were alone.

“Whit?” She blagged. “No one’s here—everyone cleared out after you and those muckers o’ yers tried hotboxing God’s living room.”

“You knew it was us?”

“Everybody knew it was you. Ye’ve actually got quite the reputation, Remington.”

Remus scoffed. “Please enough, I do not need any more nicknames.”

Trish let out a breath of smoke. Then she held her hand out to him. “ ‘ere, think this belongs tae ya.”

He glanced down, letting her drop the item into his palm. “My lighter!” He exclaimed, turning it over and pressing his thumb to the engraving there.

“Did’nae mean tae nick it,” she said. “Found it in my bag ‘n couldn’t remember who it belonged to. Luckily Black has your initials memorised.”

“Oh, well, you could’ve just given it to Sirius then.”

“Na, meant Regulus.”

Remus blinked. “Regulus?”

“Mhm. I did have ‘a go trying to give it to him actually, but he’s gey stubborn.”

“Right…” Remus pocketed the lighter. “We aren’t exactly friends.”

“Hey, I get it.” Trish took another drag. “So… how’d you do it?”

“You mean the prank? Well, the hardest part was just not getting caught really. We did it this morning before anyone else was awake.”

“You must be tired then.”

“Always.”

Looking him up and down, Trish took another long puff on the spliff before reaching over and offering it to him. “C’moan,” she teased, “not like anyone’s gonna notice the smell. Not until they start airing the place out anyway.”

He eyed her a moment and Trish shook the weed pointedly. “Well? Don’t tell me yer frigid?”

Smirking lightly, Remus took the joint from her and brought it to his lips. “You’d be surprised by the things I’ve done, kid,” he told her. Then the delightful smoke was enveloping his throat like a warm blanket—nothing like the dry, nasty stuff they’d used on the thuribles. Sirius had had to bribe that crap off some random tenth year just to avoid draining their entire stash, and the stuff tasted like it’d been left in a sock drawer for a decade.

“That’s some nice hash,” he said immediately, blowing smoke out his nose before handing it back.

“I know, right? Got it from my cousin, Clyde. He lives in the village actually. Every now ‘n then he brings me his maw’s cooking, but sometimes it’s the fun stuff.”

“He taking on clients?” Remus asked. “I’m in the market for a new fence.”

“Nah, not really. He’s a bit stingy.” Trish passed him the joint again. “But I’m sure I can put a good word in.”

She winked, and Remus accepted the weed with humble gratitude.

“You know, Trish, I kept thinking this school couldn’t surprise me anymore. I think I might’ve been wrong.”

“Oh, Remington, is there really any point in a life that can’t surprise ye?”

“No,” he said lightly, puffing on the end of the joint, “no, I suppose there’s not.”

She smiled at him, before tossing a rag at his head. “Okay, time tae get back to work, naughty boy.”

By the time they’d finished, they’d smoked and scrubbed themselves right through lunch. Father Minsin, the priest who’d caught them the prank’s first time around, had been pleased with their progress when he’d finally returned, but Remus was still given a week’s detention for the stunt and the smell it left. He wasn’t bothered. It’d been a good day nonetheless.

“Pretty sure that silver’s ne’er been so clean,” Trish said, stretching her arms out above her head as they skipped down the chapel’s front steps.

“Moony!” Sirius barked. He jumped up from beneath an oak tree across the courtyard, waving both arms over his head, James and Peter at his side.

“I’ll see ya later then,” Trish said, “ ‘n don’t worry, I’ll make sure to pass yer name on to Clyde.”

“Thanks, Trish,” Remus said, breaking away from her and crossing the lawn, hands tucked into his pockets.

“Who was that?” Sirius asked, staring after the twelfth year.

“Trish. She’s a prefect.”

“Did you get detention too, Moony?” Peter asked.

“Yeah. I think McGonagall's actually starting to regret making me a prefect. She gave me a whole week.”

“That’s bollocks, we got two,” James snorted, rolling an apple between both palms.

“Favouritism,” Sirius scoffed.

“Favouritism, my arse,” Remus said. “Just look at my hands, they’re rubbed raw from punishment.”

“Here, I’ll kiss ‘em better.”

Sirius made a grab for him but Remus just side-stepped, accidentally tripping the other boy and sending him sprawling into the grass.

“You wanker!”

Remus smirked in Sirius’ direction. “So, what, you guys have detention or should we practice tonight? I wanna get a jump on Sirius’ new song.”

“We could…” James started, glancing at a smiling Peter.

“Or—”

“—We could neglect our future careers just long enough to do something fun!” Sirius declared, springing up from the ground. “Moony, you drive, yeah?”

“You know I can, I—” Remus stopped short. “Why would I need to drive anywhere?”

Sirius ignored the question; “Cool! Potter’s been around the block a few times too, havent’cha, Prongs?”

“Yep, Dad took me out over the summer,” James surmised.

“But Pete and I,” Sirius smirked, “we’re total virgins.”

“Ugh, why do you have to say it like that?” Peter squirmed.

“Oh, get over yourself, you ninny. We all know you and Moira finally got your end away this summer—about time if you ask me—I meant driving.”

“Why would we need to drive anywhere?” Remus asked again. “Where would we even go?”

“Don’t get your knickers in a twist, Moons—just around the lake and back.”

“Oh-kaaay, in what car? Or are you planning on taking one of Kettleburn’s ponies out onto the road?”

“Ha, no.” Smugly, Sirius held up a small ring of keys, each one glinting in the fresh afternoon sun. “While you were busy shining silver with Penny Prefect, McGonagall had us helping Stan replace the tires on one of the trolleys in the garage.”

“You stole Stan’s keys?”

“Borrowed,” Sirius eased; “bor-rowed. And besides, they’re the spares! He had me hold ‘em and then forgot to ask for them back! So you see, it’s perfectly legal.”

“Define ‘legal’ for me!”

“I thought it was insane too,” James interjected, “but then Stan practically dared us to do it.”

“Wha…?”

Peter held up one finger in imitation; “ ‘As if any of you posh poncers could drive such a beast. You’d likely just ram ‘er into a tree as you would run a stop sign’. Can you believe it? There aren’t even any stop signs on school property.”

Remus could picture Stan saying the words perfectly; though his trolley wasn’t all that bigger than a milk float and could hardly be considered a ‘beast’.

“So you see, Moony? He was telling us to take it,” Sirius insisted gleefully.

“This is how people end up in prison.”

“Oh, excuse me for thinking you wouldn’t be adverse to a little grand theft auto.”

“That—” He drew up short. “That was different. And this doesn’t count as a prank.”

“So it’s not a prank.” Sirius dangled the keys in the air again, letting them chime. “That mean you don’t want to go for a nighttime joyride?”

Remus sighed, and while sensing his crumbling resolve, the boys crowded in.

“It’ll be fun!” Sirius grinned.

“Just one teensy-weensy whip around the lake!” James prodded.

“We’ll even go the speed limit!” Peter added.

“I don’t even know why you’re acting like you need my permission! I’m a prefect not your mother.”

“No, you’re right, that’s Potter,” Sirius nodded; “You’re our Moony. Can’t do a thing without our Moony.”

I hate you, Remus thought. I hate you and I love you and I hate you.

“We’re gonna be in detention until Wormtail’s next birthday.”

“Probably!”

“We could crash.”

“Maybe!”

“Stan’ll kill us.”

“Absolutely!”

“This is a bad idea.”

All three of them grinned. “PLEEEEEAASE, MOOOONYYY?”

“Alright!” He cried. “Alright! Just shut your gobs before someone overhears!”

“YES!” Sirius tossed the keys in the air in celebration. “You hear that, lads? Moony’s gonna teach us how to drive!”

“That was definitely not what I said.”

“I like to read between the lines,” Sirius said, “saves time. And besides, there’s no way you’re going to resist barking at us from the passenger seat anyway.”

“There is no passenger’s seat in a bus!” Remus shouted, but the lads were already off—racing back toward their dorm in earnest glee.

Because they weren’t total thickheads, they waited until midnight and once James had finished his nightly rounds as dorm monitor and the common room had emptied out, they snuck out into the darkness and the prank-not-prank was on. After making sure the coast was clear, Remus got the garage door open and they slipped inside, weaving between the small fleet of trolleys until they found the one their set of spare keys belonged to. Pushing the bus doors open, James bounded up the steps and dropped down behind the wheel, pattering it with his fingers.

“This’s gonna be great!” He announced. “A few turns around the lake and back, just like we agreed on!”

“Yeah, yeah,” Remus sighed, trodding up the steps after Sirius. “Just keep the headlamps off until we’re out of the garage and try to keep the noise to a minimum.”

“Us, noisy? Really, Moons, who do you take us for?” Sirius asked, before dropping a portable cassette player down on the bus’s dashboard.

“Where’d you get that?” James asked in awe.

“Borrowed it off some twelfth year kid over at Crowley House named Fergus. Thought our first drive together deserved some ambiance.”

“Can’t believe he just gave it to you.”

“Of course he did, I’m cool like that. Oh and by the way, we owe him a date with Mary.”

“I think you need to reevaluate that ‘we’,” Remus scoffed, before turning back to James. “Make sure you’ve got your feet on the clutch and break before you turn it on.”

Gingerly, James glanced at the pedals before sticking the key into the ignition and giving it a sharp turn. The bus rumbled to life beneath them, yellow lights striking on. They immediately illuminated the huge garage doors, as well as Peter, who was waiting by the wall switch to open them up.

“Damn!” He cried, throwing his arm up over his eyes. “Warn a guy next time!”

“Sorry, Pete,” Remus called, reaching over James for the right dial and turning the lights off.

“Kay… right, let's do this,” James breathed, grabbing the gear stick.

Remus stopped him; “Hold on, you forgot to make sure you were in neutral first.”

“I need to do that?”

Remus swallowed. “We can’t go upstairs.”

He glanced back at the dorm, its windows turned a golden orange with all of the vibrant life going on inside. Distantly, he could hear laughter. There would probably be questions later if they just disappeared…

“You got those from my drawer,” Remus scoffed.

“Obviously. You’re the best at rolling ‘em.”

“Thief.”

That was certainly convincing enough. Remus popped to his feet. “I hope it involves swallowing it.”

“Guess that depends on what it is I’m swallowing,” Sirius mused, already skipping down the rest of the steps with eager glee. Remus followed, and they’d just made it to the end of the lawn when a voice hollered after them;

They spun around. James was standing in the dorm’s doorway, arms raised in question.

They made real haste, scarpering around the side of the lawn and up the road toward the rest of campus.

“You might want to tone it down,” Remus said, once they’d stopped and he’d had time to catch his breath. “At this rate he’s bound to get jealous or something.” Or notice.

“What, Prongs? Nah, he’s cool,” Sirius said, gently toying at Remus’ hand with his pinky. “He knows we’re friends—me and you. It’ll be fine. I’ll make it up to him, you’ll see.’

“If you say so.” Glancing down at Sirius’ wanting hand, Remus took it. It was dark enough now, and the smile it put on Sirius’ face was worth all the risk.

Friday 28th October 1977





Somehow between classes, band practice, and the frequented snogging sessions, October had flown by. There’d been little time leftover for pranking, which was probably a good thing, since McGonagall had launched what appeared to be a very real investigation into the missing trolley. As the resident prank masters extraordinaire, she’d grilled every Marauder individually on its whereabouts, but not even Peter managed to break. Now, with the headmistress of their back and less than three days until Halloween, the boys of room 4A had plenty on their plate. There was to be a massive party, and if Sirius was to have his way, then they'd be playing not only hosts, but also entertainment. So far none of the teachers seemed to have caught on, and so all that was left was to remain casual and make it through the rest of their lessons for the week. This, of course, was easier said than done, at least where James Potter was concerned.

After spending half the lesson drilling them with notation and endless rounds and canons, Sheila had parked herself in front of the piano and ordered James to sit next to her. There she patiently let her fingers dance up the scale, singing while he stared at her like a dead fish.

“Do-re-mi-fa-so-la-ti-do! Now James, what note did I hit on ‘fa’?”

“F.”

“And on ‘do’?”

“C.”

“Good.” Sheila pointed to a note on the sheet music on James’ music stand. “And what is this note?”

“A… squiggly line.”

“Yes, but what does the squiggly line mean?”

“Do... not pass go, do not collect two hundred pounds?”

Remus and Peter broke down in laughter as Sirius spun his chair around backwards and dropped down between James and the piano. “Sheils, you’re wasting your time, really. It’s his ears that do all the work, not his brain.”

“Oi,” James scoffed, offended. “I know it’s an ‘F’ because of how it looks in here.” He tapped his skull. “That’s brain-power! Now you tell me how this squiggly line is supposed to make any more sense.”

“It just does!” Peter said.

James crossed his arms, uncharacteristically bitter. “Yeah, well it’s stupid.”

Sheila pat him on the shoulder comfortingly. “Considering you all have a quiz on musical notation next week, I suggest we keep at it, Mr. Potter, no matter how stupid.” With a warning smile, she stood up from the bench and strolled off across the room, to where Debbie McGuire was tripping her way through a concerto piece on her clarinet.

“It almost feels like you’re getting ‘em wrong on purpose now,” Remus said, making James glare at him.

“I’m not! I just don’t understand how you can keep it all straight! Quavers, semiquavers, demisemiquavers—it’s worse than maths, it’s mental!”

“Don’t forget the infamous ‘demisemihemidemisemiquaver’,” Peter snorted.

“The what?! You've gotta be fucking joking me."

“Cool it, Potter. You’ll do fine,” Sirius said, replacing Sheila on the piano bench. “Just remember your note rhymes, EADGBE— ‘every alter-boy deserves God’s big erection’.”

Peter grimaced horribly. “What’s wrong with ‘every amateur does get better eventually’?”

“I’m partial to ‘every acid dealer gets busted eventually’, meself,” Remus said.

Seemingly unimpressed, James slumped back in his chair, his ‘69 Stratocaster still draped across his lap. “What’s it matter anyway? We agreed to play rock music, not symphonies.”

“Nah, can’t think like that,” Sirius said, kindly reaching over and balling up James’ sheet music, tossing it over his shoulder; “What are ‘Kashmir’ and ‘Achilles Last Stand’ if not symphonies?”

“Bloody hard to play, that’s what,” Peter mumbled, already scribbling repeating music staffs in his notebook to study.

Stretching out his legs, Remus leaned back in his chair and raised his hands up behind his head. “So that means we’re practising later, yeah?”

“Hell yeah, gotta be ready for Halloween,” Sirius winked. “If we’re to put on a real show, that is.”

“You mean we’re still doing that?” Peter asked, glancing at Remus nervously. Remus did have some sympathy for him. Sirius had been chattering about throwing a Halloween bash for days now, but he wasn’t sure when talk had shifted from simply getting drunk to getting drunk and also performing live in front of their classmates. Just like Peter, the idea both thrilled and terrified him. He didn’t think he had stage fright, but then again he’d never been on a stage.

“Obviously!” James said, more enthusiastic than before. “We’re totally ready! I’ve never heard a group of amateurs sound so good.”

“Only covers though, right?” Remus pressed. James was already nodding, but Sirius sighed.

“Come onnn, I still think we should play some of your songs.”

“No, they’re not ready.”

“You mean you’re not ready.”

“Same difference. Everyone’s gonna be pissed anyway, do you want to be booed off stage?”

Sirius crossed his arms with a haughty expression, but luckily James Potter was to the rescue. “Let Moons off the hook this once,” he said. “He's right, and besides, we don’t want to push him too hard, lest he quit the band before it’s even started. Artists are sensitive like that.”

Now everyone break out ‘Newcastle March’ and we’ll see how that run-through’s going—and yes, Mr. Potter, that means you too.”

“Have some mercy, Mrs. Buchanan,” James moaned, dragging his music folder out as Peter popped up from his seat and went to sit next to the rest of the percussion students.

Peter kicked the song off, lazily tapping his snare and symbol along to the tempo they’d been practising since the beginning of term. Remus didn’t mind it as much, it was upbeat and loud, but it was far too easy for his friends, who all danced through the chords and beats with more ease than a greased-up seal. They were lucky that Sheila allowed them so much time for solo practice. A more stringent teacher would have driven the group of Marauders up the wall long ago.

“He’s already got a stable job. I could drop out and move in with him tomorrow if I really wanted to,” Lottie blagged. Lily appeared about ready to throttle her.

"Really, really."

"Are you sure? I already told Prongs we’d sort those Halloween costumes after dinner. Figure out the party.”

“Whatever I want.”

Remus had expected—and Sirius had probably hoped—that it would be one of their friends who discovered them first. It’d been easy to assume, what with his generally happy childhood, that he was without faults entirely, but that was simply not true. For all intents and purposes, James Potter had everything, and when one was used to having everything, losing even a bit of it tended to feel catastrophic.

The spat made living within the same five by five space much harder than usual. Any time all four of them were in the same place the air began to feel distinctly stifling, but James had made it a mission to spend as little time around Sirius as possible. He accompanied Lily to the library in the mornings, and made sure to sit at a different table for every meal. At night he camped in the girls’ room, which came as an initial shock to everyone.

"The lengths you two will go to avoid apologising, honestly," Lily huffed, when they'd all met for that Sunday's mass.

"I don't owe him anything," Sirius scoffed.

"Oh yeah, nothing at all! Not like I was your best friend or anything," James sneered. "Guess that's what I get for being concerned."

"Try being concerned for yourself for once!"

"A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back," Marlene ground out, with heavy bags beneath her eyes. "Proverbs, chapter twenty-nine, verse eleven."

"Hear that, Potter? That's bible-thumper for get a life."

"Hey Marlene, got any quotes about being a massive twat?"

On the bright side, James' abdication of their bedroom and all things Sirius Black meant that Remus got his boyfriend's full and undivided attention. With one less roommate to worry about, the two of them had even more opportunities to do the unthinkable in the comfort of their own beds. They spent the weekend sleeping in and during the afternoons when Peter was off with Moira, they had each other. Again and again. When James ditched them to camp out in the girls’ room for the third night in a row, Sirius had snuck over and slipped in behind Remus’ curtains with him, where he stayed for most of the night. Remus wasn’t worried, Peter was a heavy enough sleeper.

“You have to take him back,” Marlene said, come Monday morning. It was finally Halloween and McGonagall had cancelled the following day's lessons to allow them to recover from whatever hijinks they were bound to get up to come nightfall. That year, it was Godric hosting the party, and even without its two most infamous pranksters out on the prowl, things were bound to get messy.

“It’s been awful,” Marlene continued, busy untangling the paper streamers they’d nicked from the art room. “He snores and Lily refuses to stick her fingers up his nose to get him to shut up. Next time I’m just gonna suffocate him with a pillow.”

“James is nothing,” Remus said, untangling the other end; “You should hear Peter.”

“Yeah, well my snoring’s still better than hearing you moan and whinge all night,” Peter scoffed from behind the couch, where he was painting a life-sized Headless Horseman across a paper banner. “You actually sound as though you’re in pain sometimes. Like someone’s choking you in your sleep.”

With a sputter, Sirius released one of the balloons he was blowing up and it zoomed across the room, smacking into the common room’s grandfather clock with a great thwack! Two couches over, several ninth year boys they’d recruited to help tittered and let go of their own balloons, creating a whizzing flurry of colourful rubber. Watching, Remus couldn't help but grimace. Perhaps Peter wasn’t such a heavy sleeper after all.

On their other side, Mary uncapped a metal thermos and poured a suspicious amount of clear liquid into the jar of mixer she was currently concocting. Lottie was next to her, furiously stuffing orange slices into a jug of her own. It appeared to be some sort of cider, but judging from the vodka to juice ratio, they were all in for it.

“Remus’ sleep-moaning aside,” Mary began; “You guys have got your costumes all sorted for tonight, yes?”

Remus nodded. “Think so.”

“You still doing The Beatles?” Marlene asked.

At that, Remus deferred to Sirius, who was stubbornly stretching out a fresh balloon. “Of course, you think we slaved over those ‘Sergeant Pepper’ costumes for nothing?”

“You got the sewing club to make those,” Peter pointed out, “and they still look like one of my mum’s nighties.”

“Stuff it, Wormtail, you’re wearing the dress.”

Peter shrugged and popped to his feet with the freshly painted banner in hand. “Whatever. I get to be Ringo.”

“I think they’re going to look pretty great on stage,” Lottie complimented, tossing an orange rind forward and succeeding in getting it down the back of Peter’s shirt. The ‘stage’ in question was really more of a roped off corner of the common room, which they’d cleared out to allow space for their instruments. It'd certainly been an onerous task to lug Peter’s drum kit all the way from the Bellchant building, but as Remus glanced at the little set up, complete with amps and all, he felt a bit giddy. They’d all agreed upon sticking to cover songs, too nervous to play anything of their own creation, but they’d already spent weeks practising. It was bound to be great, so long as James and Sirius got their shit together long enough to slog through a single song.

As if on cue, James and Lily strode into the common room, carrying a box of extra decorations between them. Lily was already wearing her Wonder Woman costume, but had added a pair of trackie bottoms underneath to keep warm.

"It looks fantastic in here!" She cheered, as she and James set the box down next to one of the sofas.

"It was all Marlene," Peter called. "She's been bossing us around for hours."

Marlene raised her arms; "Your guys' idea of decorating is slapping a few streamers on the wall and calling it a day. Someone had to step in."

“Still, you guys really did do a great job,” James commended, stopping to admire the streamers she and Remus were currently hanging over the doorway.

“Yeah, no thanks to you,” Sirius quipped, appearing through archway with a stereo speaker in both hands.

“We brought your fake spiders, didn’t we?” James scowled after him. "Bloody had to dig for them in that theatre room."

"Yeah, and it only took you an entire hour."

"For your information—there was also an emergency dorm monitor meeting... Apparently McGonagall thinks we’re planning something.”

“Well, she’s right about that,” Remus said, jumping down from the ottoman he’d been standing on. “What’d she have to say? She's not shutting us down is she?”

The corner of James’ mouth quirked upwards. “Just don’t break anything.”

They knocked fists, and Remus did his best to ignore the look of irritation that Sirius was giving them. Across the room, Lily pulled her nose back from Mary's cider with a grimace.

“Oh my god. What did you guys put in this stuff—bleach?”

“Don’t be such a fuddy-duddy,” Mary told her. “It’s Halloween, and since we're decidedly not headed into the woods this year, I figure it's only right that we get absolutely trollied. Lot, did you remember to grab that bottle of Cointreau?”

“Left it in the room,” Lottie said, nibbling on an orange slice. “I’ll run and fetch it.”

As Lottie disappeared out into the hall, a group of sixth form girls from the baking club arrived, carrying with them tray after tray of baked goods. Lily and James directed them into the kitchenette like the helpful dorm monitors they were, and Remus took the opportunity to slip over to the far side of the room, where Sirius was currently hooking up the stereo. He wasn't going to mention anything to do with James, but unfortunately Marlene had followed him, and was determined to say her piece.

"I really think you need to cool it," she told Sirius, as he continued plugging cable after cable into the right slots. "It's been three days."

"Christ, why's everyone acting like it's the end of the world?" Sirius snapped. "Can't Potter and I have it out every once in a while?"

"I'm not saying you have to suddenly give up the ghost, you prat, but how're you supposed to play at the party tonight if you're still all up in arms?"

"I don't have to like him to play with him, McKinnon. Just look at Pink Floyd."

Marlene sighed and looked to Remus for support, but he had nothing, and eventually she left them to their plugs and records. It was still early in the day, and after a weekend of hassle Remus didn't much feel like playing mediator anymore, but he'd have been lying if he said he weren't worried for the evening's show. It was their first time playing in front of a real group of people rather than just each other, and with two of their members so horribly off-kilter, it was beginning to look like Marauders was headed the way of every other dwindling pipe dream of the 1970s.

With no small amount of teamwork, they'd managed to hang most of the rubber spiders from the ceiling by the time Lottie returned. She flounced back into the common room with her bottle of Cointreau in one hand and a well-chuffed smile on her face, as though she'd just won some sort of prize.

"Remus," she called. "There’s someone at the door looking for you.”

“Who?” He asked, climbing down from a precarious tower of ottomans. She shrugged, hooking a finger into her mouth as she stepped back out into the hall, and Remus reluctantly followed her out, stopping only to throw a cotton cobweb over Sirius’ hair. There he found her waiting in the dorm's entry way, standing next to a broad-shouldered guy Remus had never seen before. He was wearing a heavy work trench and matching boots, with a five o'clock shadow that couldn't have belonged to any sort of sixth form student, let alone someone from their well-to-do college. Just peaking out of the collar of his jacket, Remus could spot a tattoo in the shape of a swallow. It felt like hardcore stuff, and he was reminded of Doss.

“Here he is, the man of the hour,” Lottie said, presenting Remus to the stranger. He offered his hand when Remus approached, and Remus took it, though sceptical.

“Uh, hey. Can I help you?”

“I think ye mean, 'can ye help me',” the stranger said, in a thick Scottish accent. “My cousin Trish tellt me ye were lookin’ for a bagman. The name’s Clyde.”

Remus could hardly believe his ears. “Trish sent you?”

“She told me, aye.”

“And uh—how… How’d you get onto school grounds?”

“I do the deliveries,” Clyde said, jutting a thumb over his shoulder to where a large lorry was indeed parked out front of the dorm. “Trish tellt me tah keep edgy for a 'Remus Lupin'. Said I'd ken it was 'im when I found mesell staring at a guy that looks like a nose taped tah a fence post. Guessing that's you?”

Lottie gave a little giggle, and Remus managed to swallow his shock. “Er—yeah, I’m Lupin. And you’re definitely Trish’s cousin, alright.”

Clyde nodded. "Charlotte here's been telling me about you and yer mates. Said you got most o' yer stuff from Xeno, richt? He was your guy for everything?"

Remus looked to Lottie, who covered her mouth shyly. "Guess Charlotte has been busy."

"Aye well, I was Xeno's source anyway. You fandans been keeping the local circuit in business for years."

"Oh shit." Remus glanced around cautiously. "So you'll cut us in then?"

"He's thinking about it," Lottie mused. "Though I doubt he would've came all this way just to turn you down, Remus."

"I might have something oan me. Whit are ye using it fer?"

“It's Halloween, what else? We're throwing a party right here in the dorm."

" 'n whit's yer costume?"

"It's a surprise. If you want to know you'll have to come."

Clyde looked no less than pleased by the idea. He spared Remus a glance, before nodding his head in Lottie's direction. "She your girl?”

“Oh no." Lottie shook her head. "I consider myself more of a baby-sitter, where this one's concerned."

“Hm. Tall baby.”

“A bit too tall if you ask me. I tend to like my men about—” Lottie drew her hand up slowly, stopping just ahead of Clyde’s forehead; “Yeah, right there looks about good.”

“N’ere I thought all those Hawkings girls were wi’out any sense o’humour at all.”

“It’s dangerous to lump women together, you know. We start to realise how unfunny you blokes are.”

Remus raised a brow in judgement. Luckily Lottie caught the look and quickly raised her hands in surrender.

“Alright, I’m going. Mary'll still be waiting on her liquid courage anyway." She raised the Cointreau in accord and began backing up toward the common room. "Catch you later, Highlander."

"Definitely," Clyde replied, looking smug. Remus cleared his throat after, only mildly uncomfortable.

"So, uh—don't take this the wrong way, but you're a lot more... forthcoming than most of the other dealers I know."

"Ken many 'a us, do ye?"

“You'd be surprised."

“I trust Trish," the bagman said. "She wouldn’t send some jobbie my wey.”

“Cool. You got anything on you now then?”

“Always keep some hash in the truck—but ya didn’t hear that from me. Might have something else too if you’re guid fur it.”

“Can you get us more booze?”

“Aye, definitely.”

“And you can keep it coming after Halloween?”

“Offer’s guid til’ June s’long as you are.”

Remus quirked a smile. “Yeah, sounds ace. And if you can deliver like this we’ll make it worth your while.”

“Got a list?”

As Remus began shuffling through his pockets for a pen, Clyde’s gaze drifted up over his shoulder, toward the common room.

“And a’… yer bonnie, blondie friend—she single then?”

Later that evening, with enough hash and booze stowed away to choke a horse, Remus came out of the bathroom dressed head-to-toe in scintillating McCartney blue. The trousers were about six inches too short around the ankles, and his typically unthreatening biceps felt about ready to burst the fabric along the seams, but the get-up had been a favour of the sewing club, made mostly for their show anyway. Hopefully come midnight when everyone was well and truly bladdered, he could abandon the outfit for something more comfortable.

"You look fucking amazing!" Sirius crooned, the moment he'd gotten a look at him. Remus wasn't so sure he agreed, but he didn't object when Sirius began scribbling a rather unconvincing moustache across his upper lip using an eyeliner he’d “borrowed” from Mary.

“You’d probably be able to grow this yourself if you stopped shaving,” he suggested, holding Remus still by the chin. Trying not to smile, Remus batted at one of the shoulder tassels on Sirius’ equally-tacky costume. Though, the Lennon tea-shades were really selling the look.

“You saying I should grow a beard now?”

“I'm not saying you should come out as a member of ZZ Top, but you might look cute with a little lampshade on your top lip.”

“Maybe you should try it," Remus said, admiring the fake handlebars drawn across Sirius' mouth.

“Nah,” Sirius said, capping the liner; “ ‘fraid I’ll look like my dad. You’re lucky you don’t look much like yours.”

Remus nodded meekly. “Mm…”

Sirius turned away and came back with two glasses with a shot of vodka for them both. “Cheers,” he said, but before Sirius could down the shot, Remus placed his hand over the cup.

“It’s Halloween."

"I'm aware?"

"Tonight's the show. You know what that means.”

“Ugh. Moony—”

“You’ve got to talk to James, Sirius. Even if you don't make up tonight, it'll be your birthday in a few days—do you really want to spend it without James?"

"I've got you!"

"Okay, maybe I want to spend your birthday with James."

Sirius scoffed and took the shot without him. After he'd grimaced and recovered, he set the glass aside and straightened out his military dress.

“I don't care about my bloody birthday, Moons. Like I keep telling the rest of 'em, it’s not that big of a deal. If Evans can be pissed at him for a whole year, I don’t see why a few days is so diabolical for me. And besides, what would I even tell him? I can’t say anything about us—not that I want to—and he doesn’t believe me when I say it’s anything else."

"You really don't want to tell him about us?"

"Do you?"

Remus bit his lip. "I asked you first..."

Sirius gave him a very hard look, but then shook his head. "If I did tell him, it should be on my own terms, shouldn't it? And I—well, I don't want to tell him my biggest secret when we're... like this." Sirius voice grew fainter; "What if it... makes it worse."

Remus didn't really have an answer; he'd been thinking the same thing ever since the two of them had blown up on each other, but he was relieved to hear that Sirius wasn't thinking in extremes.

"Anyway," he huffed, "he’s just being paranoid.”

“He misses you,” Remus said. “And I think you miss him too."

"It's been three days. I don't need to miss him."

He shrugged, haplessly. "Alright. But I know us spending so much time together has James worried. I think he feels as though he’s losing his best friend.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“Is it? Remember how you felt when I was dating Marlene? ‘Cause I certainly remember how it felt watching you date Chastity.”

Sirius scowled off to the side like he often did when he knew he’d lost an argument. “I never got jealous when he started bunking off with Evans.”

“James has liked Lily since year seven. I’d say you got a bit more time to get used to it.”

“Fuck you for always being right.”

"Easy." Remus leaned in, brushing the hair from Sirius’ face and kissing the corner of his mouth. “Just try saying something before you’re too off your trolley to walk straight.”

As if to spite him, Sirius stole Remus' shot and downed that too before kissing him back. He felt the vodka burn his lips, but kissing Sirius always felt a bit like fire.

“REMUS! SIRUS!” Peter barked through the bedroom door, hammering it with his fist; “Something’s wrong with the stereo! Can one of you come down already and fix it?”

“You go?” Remus asked, putting his hands together piously; “Gotta use the loo.”

“Alright, sure. I'll catch you downstairs, rock star.” Backing up, Sirius gave him one more once-over before smirking devilishly. "Oh, and Moons? Don't look now, but I can see your nob through those trousers."

"You never did!" Remus gasped, but Sirius had already gone—slipping out into the hall with a laugh.

Once he'd made sure that he was adequately covered—"Knew he was lying..."—Remus made his way downstairs to dorm's ground floor, where the party was already in full-swing. Kids were arriving in droves, carrying booze and pumpkins, and all wearing a hotchpotch of costumes scrounged together from whatever they could find when so far from home. Peter Frampton was blaring across the room from the stereo, and the entire room was alight. Soon they'd either be cheering for them or booing them off stage, but that was the least of Remus’ worries anyway. On his way to get himself a drink, he heard familiar shouting from the kitchenette and followed the noise. There he found his boyfriend staring James down, a small crowd of curious students encircling them. Only Lily dared get closer, and was twisting back and forth between them, looking heated in her Lynda Carter get-up.

"Come on, you two, can't this be over with already? Just apologise to one another!"

Both boys ignored her, too viciously scorned to be of sound mind and reasoning.

“You’re a right twat, you know that?” Sirius hissed.

“I just assumed it wouldn’t be happening,” James shot back. “You know, since we’re not friends anymore.”

“Not even five minutes,” Remus sighed, already shoving his way through the crowd.

"Alright, that's enough. I thought we were here to party?" He grabbed Sirius' shoulder to pull him back, but Sirius dug his heels in. He had a point to prove, it seemed.

“Look at him!” He growled. “Can’t even commit to a fucking outfit!”

James crossed his arms. “I said I’d still play.”

“And how would that look, huh? Three Beatles and a—whatever the fuck that is?!”

Remus took a moment to look James up and down. He was not wearing his George Harrison/Sergeant Pepper get-up, and instead had changed into a... businessman?

“It’s Clark Kent, obviously,” James snapped, aggressively pointing at his glasses. He pulled his shirt back to reveal a crudely drawn 'S' for 'Superman' on his vest beneath, but Sirius remained unconvinced.

“You look more like you’re on your way to a fucking cubicle at your nine-to-five,” he lashed.

“Thought it was all about the music, Black. Or was that something you made up too?”

“Oh, fuck you!”

Chitters went up from the other kids and Lily waved her Lasso of Truth between them threateningly.

“Enough! God, I still don’t understand what this stupid fight is over!”

“ ‘ASK HIM’!”

“Hey, hey!” Mary trilled cheerily, shoving her way into the crowded room. Like Remus and Sirius, she was dressed up in shiny regalia, though her costume was an ode to Cher and featured an entire swan's worth of feathers rather than golden epaulettes. “When’s that show supposed to start?” She asked. “Lottie’s been telling people on their way in—they’re all excited to see Hawkings’ very own Marauders!”

“We’re coming,” James grunted, eyeing Sirius up scathingly. Sirius returned the look, tenfold.

“Guess it’s a good thing we changed the name to a ‘concept’ after all, Potter, since you don’t look like much of a ‘Marauder’ to me.”

“Let’s just get on with it, choir boy,” James replied cuttingly.

Looking indignant, Sirius spun on his heel and marched out, leaving James to glance sorely at a disapproving Lily and follow him.

“Was it something I said?” Mary asked after they’d gone.

Remus sighed. “I really wish it was, Mary.”

And then, because it was Mary, she handed him a drink.

“Bottoms up, darling. Night’s young yet.”

With a small smile, Remus accepted and knocked the side of his paper cup against hers before downing the entire thing. Afterwards he followed her out into the hallway, which was even more crowded than before. There they happened across Jillian and her new beau, Roy, who were both done up in matching sailor outfits. She waved, drink in hand, but simply passed him by on her way out of the common room.

“Solved that problem, did you?” Mary teased, wrapping an arm around his waist.

“Yes, despite what others might have to say, I’m not entirely hopeless.”

She threw her head back to laugh as they emerged into the bustling common room and a few of the silky feathers she’d clipped into her hair went up his nose. Remus sneezed, toppling sideways gracefully in the process, and just before Mary could reach out and help steady him he knocked into someone—nearly upsetting their drink.

“Oh shit, my bad.”

Trish turned around. “Na harm done—oh.”

Remus straightened up, suddenly very sorry. He and Trish hadn't spoken since that day he'd snapped at her outside the science building. He still felt bad, but between the JamesandSirius debacle, he'd yet to find time to apologise.

“Er—hi…” he said, while Trish pursed her lips, looking like she'd prefer to be anywhere else.

"Hi..."

Uninterested in their sombre affair, Mary tapped Remus on the shoulder. “Stefan D’Arcy is giving me the eye,” she announced; “This’ll only take a few. Meet you by the stage.”

She kissed his cheek and just like that was off—leaving him to his awkward fate.

“Whit are ye wearing?” Trish asked eventually.

“I’m supposed to be Paul McCartney,” he said, feeling stupid in the head-to-toe, iridescent polyester. “And you’re…”

Trish looked down at herself. She was wearing what appeared to be a white bed sheet and had wrapped a wreath around her head made out of real leaves. Over her chest was a red stain that looked a lot like cranberry juice. “I’m Julius Caesar,” she said. “After he got ‘imself stabbed, that is.”

“Cool! Nice... execution."

"Was that supposed tae be a pun?"

"No! I just meant—you know—the blood... You must really like history.”

"Oh," she looked down at herself and shrugged. “Not really. Just ken the feeling o' bein' stabbed in the back, is all.”

Remus Lupin, curse your big, fat gob.

At his silence, Trish turned to go, but Remus got ahead of her first. “Hey, I just wanted to say thanks!" He chirped. "Clyde came by today—helped us pull the rest 'a this together. You didn’t have to pass my name onto him, but you did, so—thanks.”

“No need tae thank me, Clyde was already making the deliveries."

“I know, but I was right awful to you. So you can…er—You can hit me if you want! I’d deserve it.”

She squinted at him. “Hit you for what?”

“For what I said,” he winced again. “It was gross—terrible. You caught me at a bad time, but I was still a right arsehole. I didn’t mean what I said. I'm real sorry.”

“Aye, you were an arse.”

“Yeah, so you can hit me—to make up for it.”

“That sounds like a cheap way tae make yerself feel better, not me.”

“Ha… maybe you’re right.”

Trish exhaled, shoulders relaxing as her usual frisky attitude returned. “Aw, Loonary, dinnae fash yerself. I wasn’t all that bothered by what ye said. You really think some walkin’ hooter on a stick can hurt my feelings? Not half-likely.”

Somehow the jab made Remus feel a bit better. “Do you really think my nose is that big?”

“It ain’t small.”

He smiled. “Well, thanks anyway. You’re a fucking cool one, Trish.”

“I know.” Trish held out her hand, and Remus made to smack it fondly, but she pulled back at the last second and socked him in the stomach.

“Yer right, Remington, that did make me feel better. Good luck on stage, by th’wey. Should be worth a good laugh.”

She left him behind, which was well deserved, and after a long moment of rubbing his ribs and smiling to himself, Remus made his way across the common room toward their little fenced off corner. Peter was already set up behind his drum kit. Moira was in his lap and Peter had his arms around her, using her hands to gently beat at the snare and cymbals as she giggled. James was standing next to them, sullenly fiddling with his guitar as he murmured back and forth with Lily. Sirius remained firmly on the other side, fiddling with the knobs on their amplifiers just to keep his hands busy.

“Where’d you disappear to?” Sirius asked when he approached.

“Sorry. Got caught chatting up Trish.”

“Trish...? Oh—you mean that prefect. Peppermint Patty or whatever.”

“Be nice. It’s just Trish—you’re Patty, ‘Pattycake’.” Remus pulled their set list out of his pocket and slapping it down over one of the amps.

“Ready to get this over with then?” James asked, strolling forward and picking up the plug for his amp.

“Try being a little less excited, why don’t you?” Sirius replied sarcastically.

Resisting a groan, Remus strolled back to the wall behind Peter’s drum kit and picked up his bass. After a quick kiss, Moira fled her boyfriend’s lap and Peter leaned over.

“They still…?”

“Yup.”

“Fan-tastic.”

Up ahead, Sirius shoved James away from him and spun the microphone around in the air. A light screech of feedback echoed, making James and everyone up front flinch, but Sirius didn’t so much as bat an eye. He cleared his throat and somewhere across the room, Mary cut the music.

“Oi, alright, so you all know us, but for tonight we ain't any ol' individuals—we’re Marauders."

The crowd’s response wasn’t any more enthusiastic than Sirius’ introduction. Kids shuffled about, but no one seemed to know what to say or how to act. Most of them had probably never been to a concert in their life.

“We’re gonna be playing a few songs for ya. Y ou might know ‘em, so try and sing along if you want, and er—happy Halloween, I guess.”

“Could you be any duller?” James scoffed, prompting Sirius to flip him off about ten millimetres away from the end of his nose. The gesture got a few people up front to laugh, but the joke was short-lived, and Remus found himself praying that they just made it through the set unscathed.

“This is ‘Communication Breakdown’," Sirius rumbled into the mike, and a moment later James had kicked off his fervent guitar riff. A few heads started to bob, and then it was Peter's turn. He came in with a crash, stumbling along until he matched James somewhat in rhythm, but Remus was so shocked by the initial disarray that he'd missed his own count by four bars. Cursing, he jumped in away, but by then the first verse had come and gone and Sirius had missed it.

"You gonna sing or not?" James called.

"Maybe I'll sing when you start sounding half-decent!"

Remus felt his his fingers begin to freeze up with apprehension. It was one of the most difficult songs they knew and it always took them a few moments to find each other in the rhythm, but they'd never been off in actual communication too. Already the song was proving an insurmountable challenge, and they were only thirty seconds in.

Please, you fucking toffs, he silently begged, get through it!

But there was no need to worry after James. Whether he saw the music as Sirius' challenge or as a whirlwind of thrashing colours inside his mind, he spun around to Peter's drum kit and stepped up to him with his guitar until they were playing side by side and matching frazzled rhythms. The gesture seemed to comfort Peter, who took a breath and finally started over at the beginning of the next bar. The moment he heard the drums level-out, Remus was able to find himself again in tempo, and he looked to desperately Sirius, who'd been observing them all from the front while swinging his microphone around lackadaisically.

"Right!" Sirius called, catching the mike out of the air. "Now that's what I'm talking about!”

Oh thank fuck.

As Sirius spun to face the front, igniting a few cheers, Remus finally exhaled. The longest intro in "Communication Breakdown" history, and just like that they were really playing.





“Hey girl, stop what you’re doin’!

Hey girl, you’ll drive me to ruin!”





Sirius might've sang with the same bluesy twang as Plant, but a bleating statue he was not. He gathered the microphone chord around himself so that he could skirt around the front of the stage, getting right up with the kids who stood to watch.



"I don't know what it is I like about you, but I like it a lot,

Won't you let me hold you—let me feel your lovin' touch!"





Maybe it was their initial flop, or even the song itself, but whatever it is, most of the Hawkings' crowd remained rooted to the spot. They didn't know what they should be cheering for—the singing or the music? Both seemed so at odds. Sirius flitted around James and his guitar like he were an electric fence, both of them playing chicken with one another.

“But I don't get it, what does ‘LE’ even mean?”

“Oh? You mean you didn’t realise?” Lottie hummed.

Slyly, each of the girls looked to Lily, who was back to blushing into her tea.

“It stands for ‘Lily Evans’ of course.”
