Chapter 80: Repercussions


Chapter Summary

Crazy girls. Magic mushrooms. Extortion. Dead bodies...? Just your average Monday, honestly.



Chapter Notes

This felt a bit like a "transitionary" chapter. Lots of tiny moments merged into one. I hope you get a few good chuckles out of it though.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



What would you think if I sang out of tune?

Would you stand up and walk out on me?

Lend me your ears and I’ll sing you a song,

And I’ll try not to sing out of key;

Oh, I get by with a little help from my friends,

Mmm, I get high with a little help from my friends,

Ooh, I’m gonna try with a little help from my friends...

- “With a Little Help from My Friends” The Beatles, 1967



Sunday 19 th November 1977



That morning, Remus Lupin awoke to the sounds of his friends’ whispering.

“What d’you think it is?”

“A dead body, probably.”

“But it’s broad daylight. How could you dig up a body in broad daylight?”

“I dunno. I've never actually done it myself, Wormtail.”

“Reckon they were murdered?”

“Totally. Ever hear about them twelfth year kids that went missing like ten years ago? Supposedly most of ‘em were found floating in the lake, but alas, the last body was never recovered…”

“You’re so full of shit, Sirius.”

Remus sat up in bed, pushing his curtains aside. “What are you twats on about now?”

His friends spun around. All three Marauders were crowded around the window between James and Sirius’ beds, apparently engrossed in whatever was going on outside.

“Sorry, Moons. Did we wake you?” James asked.

“Yeah.” Remus paused to yawn. “But that ain’t much different from any other day.”

Eager as ever, Sirius bounded across the room toward him. “Come take a look! Filch’s digging something up behind the dorm.”

“What is it?”

“Who knows? Just come look!”

Remus let himself be pulled, blinking in the morning’s bright light. He didn’t have to crane his neck much to be able to see the deep pit that was now taking up much of the green space on the dorm's back lawn. He saw no sign of Filch, but every now and then a shovel would reappear, tossing dirt up onto the pit’s ledge.

“Old codger must’ve been at it for half the night,” Peter said. “The ground’s almost frozen and that hole must be over ten feet deep.”

“I wish I knew what he was looking for,” Sirius said.

“I think your wish is about to come true, Padfoot!” James said. “Looks like Filch is done digging.”

A few moments went by, and all four boys leaned in even closer, practically climbing onto Sirius’ hutch and stereo to catch a glimpse. Rather unceremoniously, Filch reappeared from the pit on a wooden ladder, bringing with him a large metal canister about the size of a small dog. Sirius was instantly disappointed.

“That’s it?” He moaned. “All that digging for a bloody rubbish bin?”

“It could still have a body in it!” Peter suggested.

“Oh yeah? You show me the psychopath who bumped off a sprog.”

James gave a yawn, stretching one hand up to the sky and scratching his stomach with the other. “Not very exciting, oh well. Let’s just get dressed before we’re late for church.”

“I’m gonna go grab some fresh towels for a shower since Black used them all again,” Peter said, starting for the door. He’d only been quiet for a moment before; “Mooooony, they’re back again.”

Remus’ stomach sank. He’d just wrestled his night shirt up over his head and when he tore it away, he found Peter standing next to their bedroom door. Pinned to the outside wood were several dozen notes, each one printed in pretty pink lettering, cut into the shape of hearts and penned for him personally. It wasn’t even that they were suddenly in love with him—they wanted to tease as much as the guys did. The only difference was how much more determined they were to get his attention.

“These bloody girls,” Sirius huffed, stepping forward and pulling one of the larger love notes down. “ ‘To Remus, I just adored your poem. Would you write one to me sometime? Love Audriana, Bronte House’.”

Remus marched over. “Give me that.” He tore the note in two.

“Harsh,” Sirius said, the word ‘pleased’ written all over his face. He plucked down another, but when Remus made a swipe for it, he pulled his hand away.

“Uh-uh. You’re in your casanova era now, if I didn’t get any privacy then neither do you.”

“You never wanted any. You're like a bloody exhibitionist!”

Sirius cackled, then peeled down a handful of the love notes and threw them up in the air. “Better grab a coat, Moons, looks like there’s a chance of snow.”

“Ugh!” Remus grunted, batting the notes away as they fluttered down around him. “This is so stupid. They’re doing it on purpose.”

“Obviously, but some of them are actually pretty good,” Peter said, busy sorting through a handful of notes on his own. “Like look—pretty sure this one’s quoting Shakespeare. And this one here almost makes it sound as though you’re dating her.”

“I’m not dating any of them,” Remus said sternly.

“Of course you aren’t, Moons,” James announced, pulling his own shirt over his head and tossing it into the laundry bin by his bed. “I think I’d know if one of my best friends was dating someone.”

Sirius snorted, and then quickly covered his face with the love note to hide it. He lasted about half a second before he was recoiling over a cough. “Eugh! She’s bloody perfumed it!”

Peter and James began to laugh, but Remus wasn’t feeling very jolly.

“Enough of this nonsense,” he ordered, stepping forward and shoving both of his friends aside. He ripped the love notes down with vicious speed, letting them fall to the ground like broken birds’ wings. Majorie, Audriana, Cindy, Kelly-Anne—all of them, broken hopes only meant to badger him. It’d been like that since Friday, an incessant string of teasing that followed him everywhere. Literally followed. He’d been expecting the mockery from other guys, but the girls were by far the worst. On Saturday, they’d tailed him and Sirius across the entire village as though he were John Lennon at the height of Beatlemania. It hadn’t even mattered that Remus was without a penny to his name—there was no time to spend it. They’d tried going on down to the record shop, only to be swarmed by girls clutching Rita Coolidge and Elton John albums to their chests. Now it was Sunday, and they'd be expected to brave the horde for that morning’s mass. Remus had never resented religious institutions more.

At least his actual boyfriend was taking it well, he reminded himself. It could’ve so easily become a fight, but almost predictably, Sirius thought the entire thing was hilarious. After the mess at the music shop, they spent the remained of their village trip hiding out in some farmer’s barn. Which meant they were alone at least.

“It’s like you’re already famous. Imagine how they’d react if they really knew the truth,” Sirius had mused, while lounging across a hay bale like some barn cat. Alternatively, Remus had remained camped out by the doors, peeking out to make sure they hadn’t been followed.

“Hey.”

Remus turned around. Sirius had his shirt unbuttoned to the navel, a piece of straw sticking out of the corner of his mouth.

“What are you…?”

“Hay,” Sirius said again, cheekily waving a handful of straw at him. “It’s pretty soft, you know. Maybe even soft enough to…” He turned over arching his back until he was just peeking over his shoulder at him. What came after was enough to make Remus glad he’d latched the door. Now, he was staring at Sirius and reliving the memory in his head. You certainly can’t do that in London…

“Hey. Hey, Moons?” Sirius snapped his fingers at him. “You-hoo…?”

“Yep,” Remus replied, dumbly. While he’d gotten left behind thinking of Sirius’ behind, his friends had already moved on.

“I still don’t know how they’ve been getting inside without anyone seeing,” he heard Peter murmur, as he stepped out to retrieve his towels. James had already taken the opportunity to disappear into the bathroom, leaving Remus and Sirius on their own, still buried up to their ankles in pretty pink paper.

“You’re sure we can’t bump him off?” Sirius asked.

Remus blinked, alarmed. “Who?”

“Reg, obviously.”

Oh. “We’re not bumping off your brother,” he sighed. “Besides, don’t tell me you’re already done laughing at my pain.”

“Not by half. But just because it’s funny watching you run around like a chicken with its head cut off doesn’t mean I don’t want to bury that little shit six feet under.” Sirius smirked and shut the door. “It’s like, my entire life Reg’s been on my arse for rocking the boat, and now he’s managed to get my boyfriend about a hundred girlfriends overnight. It’s utter blasphemy.”

“I think you’re exaggerating a bit.”

“Am I?” He bent down to pick up one of the love notes. “ ‘Cause this one says she wants to have your babies.”

Remus pinched the bridge of his nose. “I wish I’d never written that fucking poem. Letting Flitwick fail me would still be better than this.”

“Well, I dunno about that.” Turning the note over, Sirius began peeling it apart as it's sparkled seams. It had a piece of his poem glued inside. “You never really said… but I wouldn’t be all wrong if I assumed that you wrote this for me, would I?”

Remus snatched the note away. “You were never supposed to see it.”

“Hm. Sounds like a waste.” He leaned in, and Remus knew it was going to be a kiss.

“BLACK! You been using my toothpaste again?”

They jumped apart, turning to glare at the bathroom door.

“You said I could!”

“I know, but at least put the bloody cap back on, man!”

Sirius rolled his eyes. “Idiot.” He passed Remus by, leaving a quick peck on the corner of his mouth as he went to the stereo and flicked it on. It was the Ramones album—the one James had mercifully picked up while on his date with Lily the day before. All girls aside, Remus had enjoyed himself; going around Craigtyre, pretending as though they could be on a date the same as their friends… it was nice. It made him think of summer. It made him long. Remus had never known what real longing was before Sirius.

He looked down at the love note in his hand. At the piece of his poem, just a scrap really, all made up of longing.



How wonderful it would be

To one day feel your love and care

On a public street





“Oi.”

Remus glanced up. Sirius was still by the stereo, a lit cigarette in one hand.

“Found the perfect place to hide the body,” he chaffed, gesturing out the open window with his thumb, toward Filch’s pit. “Just in case you’re coming around to the idea.”

“I’m still paying for your last great idea where Regulus was concerned.”

“Well, in that case, prepare to be paying for the rest of your life.” Sirius smirked at him and began scratching behind his ear. He snorted then, before unweaving a thin piece of straw from his hair. “Hey—more hay.”

Remus smiled—hopelessly.

"You idiot."

Sirius winked, holding the cigarette just before his lips. "Love you too."





* * *





Remus waited outside during breakfast. He did not want to deal with the chorusing ‘hi, Remus’ so early in the morning. Luckily he had Sirius who was willing to brave the fight for him. He emerged through the dining hall’s back doors with a buttered crumpet in one hand and a styrofoam cup of tea in the other.

“Audriana Vane practically throttled me just now. She’s still trying to figure out who you wrote the poem for,” he said, handing the food over. “Apparently word’s out of the bag about Farrah. No one believes you saved a stunning French model from the Seine anymore, Moons.”

“How will I ever recover?” Remus replied sarcastically, scarfing down the crumpet.

“Maybe we should just skip commmunion,” Sirius said, watching him.

Remus was ready to agree, but just then the doors behind Sirius burst open and several girls rushed out. Among them was Audriana Vane, who saw the two of them and immediately lit up. Remus was pretty sure she hadn’t even known he existed before all of the nonsense began—but then again, he’d never paid her any attention either.

“Reeeemus!” She keened. “So glad we found you, did you get our letters this morning?”

Remus sipped his tea awkwardly, resisting a grimace when it burnt his tongue.

“He got them, alright,” Sirius answered instead.

“Do you want to walk over to the chapel together?” Audriana offered, while the girls behind her giggled furiously. “You can come too, Sirius.”

“How generous,” Sirius said. “But Lupin and I were just—”

“There you are!” It was Marlene, emerging through the doors with Nicole beside her. “C’mon, you lazy sods, we’re going to be late for church.”

As embarrassing as it was, Remus was thankful for Marlene’s interruption. She and Nicole walked them over to the school church, arm and arm with him and Sirius. Their presence alone seemed to deter the girls, who walked several paces behind and whispered to one another furiously.

“Perhaps they're thinking that you and Moony got back together, McKinnon,” Sirius said, Nicole clutched onto his other arm.

“That’d be their mistake then,” Nicole said. “And Marlene’s, considering what she’s said about how Remus used to kiss her.”

“I only said you were shy!” Marlene laughed, when Remus rounded on her.

“I don’t think he’s very shy,” Sirius smirked. “In fact, just yesterday when we were in the village—”

Nicole held up a hand. “I don’t wanna know.”

The girls left them outside the church, where they managed to find James and Peter amongst the rabble waiting to get inside. Remus hated the cold, and therefore had bundled up in several layers, but he’d also brought a book with him in hopes that it would deter anyone from talking to him. It did not.

“That a new book of poems, Lupin?” One boy called. Remus flipped him the bird.

“Hi, Remus,” another girl cooed, before she was promptly chased off by Audriana and her friends. The group had insisted on hovering nearby, and made sure to glare at any girl who dare get too close. At one point Audriana happened to catch him staring and flashed him a dazzling smile, but it was not her Remus was looking at. Just over her shoulder, Regulus Black was waiting his turn to get inside. He’d also brought a book, and though Yaxley was trying to say something to him, Regulus kept on reading—blocking him out as though it were as easy as breathing.

“I’m just saying,” he drawled. “If we’re all gonna go out one day, we might as well make a big show of it. When’s the last time you heard of a rock star dying peacefully in his sleep? And I don’t mean from an overdose—mean, old and wrinkly, smelling of farts.”

“People die of natural causes all the time,” Peter reasoned. “Doesn’t make them boring.”

Sirius ignored him; “Ooh! How ‘bout a plane crash? You know, like Buddy Holly and Richie Valens. Think of it, they could call it ‘the day music died—again’!”

“Planes not your style, Potter? Okay, how ‘bout electrocution? You could just touch the mike stand with wet hands or something! Happened to the lead singer of the Yardbirds, and he got a candle-light vigil!”

“No way,” Sirius scoffed. “I ain’t going out like Elvis or Morrison, choking on my own vomit on the bathroom floor. Put me on a motorbike and send me off the edge of the M25. That’s how one of the Allman Brothers died.”

“Morrison died in a bathtub,” Remus corrected, without looking up from his book.

“I thought they just found him in the bathtub.”

“So you think he died, got up and then got into the tub?”

“… Alright, touché, Lupin.”

Remus glanced up, feeling sly. “If you don’t like bathtubs, you could always wrap your car around a tree like Bolan.”

Sirius clapped a hand over his heart. “Ooof. Still too soon, Moons. We’ll see who’s laughing when one of the Who up and keel over.”

Remus shrugged, unbothered. To him, dossers like Pete Townshend and Keith Moon felt as close as you could get to being immortal. People would be playing their music forever. Or, people with taste, anyway.

“Still warding off your many admirers, Remus?” Lottie teased.

“Alright, Potter.” She smiled, and then kissed him.

“Class. We’re supposed to have it read by Monday but I’ve been putting it off.”

“Doesn’t sound like you.” Sirius reached over, taking the book. “ ‘Medea’. Oh shit, this the one we’re supposed to read for Bilshin?”

She slumped back into the pew, arms crossed over her chest. He knew Mary could be covetous when it came to her friends, but it was even more so with her bestest and oldest friend. She’d probably thought she’d never have to worry about Marlene leaving her, since she was so rarely interested in other people. Remus couldn’t find it in himself to be sympathetic; if Mary was allowed her ever-revolving group of darlings, then Marlene deserved someone that liked her that way too.

“OOOH! Look who it is!”

A voice rang out from the pew behind them. It was Michael Baelish, a thick-headed idiot who’d never gotten higher than an ‘acceptable’ on any essay he’d ever written. No one seemed all that impressed when he began making a scene, but he’d certainly gotten enough kids to turn and look.

“What’s that,” Michael taunted again; “Remus Lupin—here? Why… shouldn’t you be off signing your many manuscripts?”

“Do you even know what a manuscript is, Baelish?” Sirius scoffed.

Michael ignored him, turning instead to his best friend and the equally as thick, Eli Barbary. “Barbary, mate—‘shall I compare thee to a summer’s day’?” He said. “Or I know, I’ll just ask Lupin to tell you that ‘your eyes are like diamonds, your arms a brace to hold me when I feel ill’!”

“Stop! Please don’t, my heart simply cannot bear it!” Eli wailed, before getting to his feet and dramatically ‘fainting’ over Remus’ back.

“Back off, Barbary!” James barked.

“Yeah, get the fuck away from him!” Sirius grunted, as he and Remus pushed the other boy back into his own pew. Eli didn’t seem to mind much. He simply sat up and laughed along with several other kids until Sheila strolled up the row, carrying a small armful of sheet music for the choir.

“Eli, Michael,” she smiled. “I was just looking for someone to help me carry these papers. They are so dreadfully heavy. Will you join me at the front of the hall?”

Eli and Michael both looked reluctant, but all it took was a bit more prodding to get them moving. They went first up the aisle, and Sheila stopped at the end of their pew just long enough to slide a single paper from her stack and pass it along to Remus.

“I’m not your English teacher, but if I were, you’d have gotten top marks.”

Remus gaped. As she left, he turned the paper over to find a copy of his poem with the words, ‘Absolutely brilliant!’ printed along the bottom. He was horrified.

“I heard even McGonagall got a copy,” Lottie whispered. “But don’t worry. She said it was entirely inappropriate to acknowledge such admiration from a student. Think that means you’re in the clear.”

“Gee, thanks a lot, Lot.”

“You can come back to our dorm after church,” Lily offered. “Marlene’s gonna meet me there. We were gonna study.”

Remus reluctantly glanced in the direction of Audriana and her friends.

“They aren’t in our House,” Lily said, catching the look. “We’ll smuggle you back under the blanket if need be. No one’ll tease you there.”

“Okay,” Remus nodded.

“And what about us?” Sirius protested. “You’re not going to offer James and I a chance to study?”

“You know the rules, Black. Neither of you are prefects, and asking you to study is like asking you to pull your own teeth out.”

“Studying is a made-up concept. Like time. We just exist—what happens to pass through my brain and get stuck is none of my business.”

“I think A-Levels would disagree.”

After communion got out, Remus promptly ditched his friends to follow the girls back to their place. He was happy for the peace and quiet, but that didn’t mean Sirius wasn’t going to try and badger. He’d gotten around Lily’s stringent House rules by standing outside the open common room window and leaning his arms against the sill. It let the cold in, but Remus couldn’t resist it when he’d call him over.

“We could drown him,” Sirius suggested. He was back on his rousing parenthesis from that morning, newly invigorated by all the ways they might get back at Regulus for his gross betrayal.

“No.”

"We could slightly maim him?"

"No."

“We could… spank him like the naughty boy he is?”

Remus considered. “Maybe.”

“Really?”

“No.”

Sirius huffed, dropping his chin down on the windowsill. “I hate when you’re like this.”

“No, you don’t,” Remus said, a wry smirk on his lips. “You think it’s charming and it gets you hot and bothered. That’s why I do it.”

Sirius bit his bottom lip, looking amused. “Tart,” he said, smirking right back. “Still, you were so mad when it happened—what’s changed?”

What’s changed is I found out Regulus did it.

Remus pinched his forehead. “Starting a prank war with Regulus isn’t going to turn out well for any of us—especially me. Did you forget I still have to spend the rest of the year as his prefect partner?”

“Of course I didn’t forget. You remind me every day. I just wish I knew how the tosser did it.”

“I know how he did it—prefects have access to the photocopiers. Ten quid says he skipped out on music lessons with me to steal the poem off Peter, then got his slimy friends to distribute them.” And really, Remus couldn’t even bring himself to hate him all that much. The entire plot was genius—a social murder, if you would; something he’d initially thought beyond the morals of a one Regulus Black. But he should’ve known better.

Never underestimate a Black.

“We need to get him back,” said Sirius

“We did get him back. Last June.”

“Ugh! I miss angry Moony—sensible Moony’s no fun. That little prat really fucked you up, you know.”

“Did he? Didn’t notice.” Remus sighed, dropping his head forward. “I just want to forget about it. It’ll be holidays in a few weeks anyway, then Regulus’ll be old news.”

Sirius set his jaw, like he wanted to argue but couldn’t find the right words. “Come away with me,” he said finally, fingers just brushing the cuff of Remus’ sleeve.

“I’m studying,” Remus answered, though not entirely untempted. “You should try it. We do have mock exams starting next week, you know.”

“Stuff the studying. They’re called ‘mock exams’ for a reason, let's go mock 'em. You’re smart enough to ace any bloody test without even trying.”

“Sirius—”

“Please…? Come on! Come away with me, and we’ll plot a horrible prank to get back at that miserable brother of mine. It’ll be brilliant.”

Remus was almost considering it, but then Lily appeared over his shoulder and thrust a pencil at the tip of Sirius’ nose to ward him off.

“Not a chance! We are studying! And if you’re not also here to study, then you’re here to distract. So off with you, Romeo.”

Sirius teetered back onto the grass with a laugh, one hand over his wounded heart. “ ‘O, sweet Evans, wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?’”

That was it for Remus. He pulled away from the window, already shouting; “Please, no more fucking poetry!” And Lily beamed proudly.

“You heard him,” she told Sirius, grabbing the window latches and pulling them closed. “Bye bye, baby!”

“ ‘Good night, good night’,” Sirius called woefully, “ ‘Parting is such sweet sorrow, that I shall say good night till it be—’”

The window shut, and Lily pulled the curtains together for good measure before stopping to dust off her hands. “There, finally some quiet.” She came to join him on the rug, their things already spread out on the coffee table between the sofa and fire. They were alone save the other girls distantly scattered about the room with studying of their own. This included Marlene, who was tucked up on a nearby sofa, long legs and Spanish homework set across the other cushions.

“I see he’s feeling needy today,” she teased, tossing a knowing glance in Remus’ direction.

“He wants to get back at Regulus.”

“Can you blame him? That was cold and underhanded, what Regulus did. Not cool at all.”

“I know.” And he did. Already Remus had pictured what it might be like to take Regulus apart piece by piece. The little git probably had a shrivelled up prune for a heart.

“But you aren’t really going to do anything to him, right?” Lily cut-in. “I feel bad for Regulus most days, and besides, going after him now would only put you on the same depraved level.”

“Nothing wrong with being a little depraved,” Marlene mused. “As long as no one gets seriously injured, I don’t see the problem.”

“Who are you and what have you done with Marlene McKinnon?”

Marlene uncapped her middle finger like a lipstick and drew it across her lips. Lily gave her a dirty look for the gesture—then giggled, muttering the words ‘you’re horrible’ before shaking her head and returning to her work. In answer, Marlene capped her finger again and winked at Remus.

“Nicole and I overheard those guys really having a go at you in church. You holding up alright?”

“I’m over it,” he lied.

“Oh? Does this mean you’re finally enjoying your newfound popularity?”

Remus flicked his rubber at her. “Popularity can kiss my arse.”

“Aw, poor Remus. You should beat them up. Show them how romantic you can be while pounding their faces in.”

“Yes, I’m sure that’ll solve all my problems.”

“It’ll solve a few.”

“No, it won’t,” Lily said, barely glancing up from her notes. “You’ll just be giving them exactly what they want. They wouldn’t be so entertained in the first place if you hadn’t lost your head in the dining hall like you did.”

Remus grumbled; “Do you have to start every conversation with an ‘I told you so’?”

“I’m only saying that if you act like you don’t care then they’re bound to lose interest eventually. I’d give it a try if I were you.”

“That might be good advice, except someone has to give them something more interesting to talk about first,” Marlene added snidely.

“In that case, shall I chat-up Chastity?” Remus quipped, making her scowl lightly as she licked her thumb and turned the page.

“Alright, Remus,” Lily started, reaching over to pluck his notes from his hands; “What started the War of the Roses and what repercussions did it have on feudal England at the time?”

If he’d been really listening, he might have been able to answer, but just then Lottie guided a weeping girl into the room, quickly bringing an abrupt end to their studying for a second time.

“Don’t listen to him, Prissy!” She cooed, before ushering Marlene’s legs off the sofa so the two of them could sit. “He’s a fool for treating you so badly—a right cad! I’ll bet he comes crawling back on his hands and knees before the week’s even out, you’ll see!”

“I don’t want him back!” The fitting girl howled. She looked about fifteen, but had enough makeup smudged beneath her eyes to rival a raccoon.

“What’s wrong, Priscilla?” Lily asked, scooting closer on the carpet. Remus, adversely, slid further away.

“Prissy and Spencer had a row,” Lottie explained quietly, as Priscilla continued her sobbing.

“I hate boys!”

“Join the club,” Marlene muttered.

“That bastard!” Priscilla groaned, turning on her. “Did you know, he left me waiting outside in the freezing cold for ages and then had the audacity to say that I was the one who was overreacting—but he didn’t even remember that it was my birthday! My own boyfriend!”

“Perhaps you should trade him in for a different model,” Marlene offered. No one seemed to find it funny.

“Have you tried telling him how it made you feel?” Lily suggested.

“Obviously, but Spencer’s a guy! And guys don’t care about feelings. They’d rather skip out and talk about stupid things, like business and billiards!”

"And boobs," Marlene added.

“There, there.” Looking sympathetic, Lottie cast her gaze toward Remus and instantly perked up. “Remus! Now there’s a man with some real emotional breadth. Remus, come tell Priscilla that dossers like Spencer Whitmore aren’t worth their weight in salt—or tears.”

Feeling the inevitable weight of another problem that was not his to deal with, Remus tried edging even further away. “Er, sorry, Lot—I’m not really not sure this is my forte.”

“Of course it is—you hate everybody!”

She had a point.

“What is it about November that turns guys into such pigs?” Priscilla moaned.

“I think it’s the name,” Marlene suggested; “Noh-vehm-berrr—just not very satisfying. Now October on the other hand…”

Ignoring her, Lottie threw out an arm. “You’re a guy, Remus, so what’s the answer? Why’s it so hard for boys to be decent to their own girlfriends?”

“Entitlement?” He suggested meekly.

“Yes!” Lily agreed. “Remus is completely right. It’s all that priggish entitlement. They expect us to be the ones crawling back to them—except they can’t even remember to wash their face at night and cry when we pluck their eyebrows!”

Remus leaned in; “James lets you pluck his eyebrows?”

Before Lily could answer, Priscilla gave another wail; “So I guess we should just throw out the lot of them then!”

“Not Remus,” Marlene said reassuringly; “I’m not much sure on his bathing habits, but he’s actually quite helpful… When he wants to be, that is. And he’s such the romantic.”

He flipped her off, and Marlene blew him a kiss in return as Priscilla raised her tear-stained cheeks from her hands.

“That’s right. I read your poem, Remus,” she sniffled. “It really was quite beautiful. If only Spencer were capable of half that level of romance. Oh… what do you think I should do?”

Oh FUCK no.

Remus looked desperately to Lily, but she appeared only too ready to listen. Lottie was of no help either, only motioning in a sort of ‘go on’ gesture. And Marlene—well, she’d raised her book in front of her face and appeared to be trying not to laugh.

“C’mon, Remus!” Lottie prodded. “What do you think?”

“Yeah, Remus, tell us,” Marlene chittered.

He scowled, but then Priscilla sniffled again, all while staring at him with those big girlish eyes, and Remus had no choice but to answer.

“Well... If you ask me, I—I’d say Lottie’s right. I mean, no guy who forgets your birthday and makes you cry this much is worth sitting in the fucking cold for… right?”

“You really think so?” Priscilla whimpered.

“Yes, Remus is absolutely right!” Lily said. “You should find someone who would wait out in the cold for you. Like… Like Remus! He’d stand in the freezing cold for anyone—especially a girlfriend. Just ask Marlene!”

“Oh no, Remus and I are ancient history,” Marlene laughed, waving her hand. “Love him, but no.”

Lottie leaned into Priscilla with an eager grin. “I know just what you should do, Prissy. Tell Spencer you’re interested in Remus and I swear he’ll be begging you to take him back.”

Remus pressed his palms into his eye sockets. “Mercy—please. Have I not suffered enough this week?”

The girls erupted into a fit of giggles, but by then Priscilla had stopped crying and things were finally starting to look up again. She and Lottie were already on their way out—to go make Spencer Whitmore sorry he’d ever been born, surely—when Priscilla spun back around and looked straight at him.

“Remus, I hope it’s alright to ask, but who was it who inspired your poem?”

He opened his mouth, then shut it.



“I just read a lot…”

Monday 21 st November 1977





“So that’s it, huh?”

“Seems like it.”

James squinted behind his glasses. “Definitely not a body.”

Remus wasn’t really sure what it was they’d expected. Though the pit Filch had dug out behind their dorm was unreasonably deep, all he’d uncovered was a small metal case. The item in question had turned out to be a time capsule, buried in the earth by a group of leaving students and their professors. Now the contents of the capsule had been put out on display to give everyone a glimpse at what life was like at school fifty years before. It held photographs and newspaper clippings, as well as several class photos and official documents. It had also preserved several more personal items; an old wallet, a deck of dingy playing cards, cinema tickets from a bygone age, family photos, and also a calcified package of Gold Flake cigarettes. It was all stuff that must’ve felt important to someone once, but had become little more than dirty antiques for the new generation to ogle.

“Reckon those guys in the photos are still alive?” James asked.

“Probably,” Remus answered. “They wouldn’t be much older than your grandparents.”

“They could’ve fought in the war though. Died.”

“Oh. Yeah, guess they could’ve.”

“That is so not a ‘rock and roll’ way to die,” Sirius said, then; “I’ll bet someone snuck at least a few nudie photos in there. McGonagall’s just too ‘fraid to show us those bits.”

“I’m betting on weed,” James sniggered. “You think they fit a little baggie inside the lining of the wallet? I know that’s where Lupin keeps his.”

“Oi, you always keep a little on you for luck.”

“And how’s that going for you, Shakespeare?”

Remus scoffed, pushing him lightly.

“What d’ya think fifty year-old weed even tastes like?” Sirius asked, stroking his chin.

“Dirt,” Remus answered. “You can’t get high off weed that old.”

“Of course you’d know," James finished. They all leaned in a bit closer after that, until Sirius finally straightened up, wearing that clever look of his.

“Maybe we should bury our own time capsule. Leave a piece of us behind for whatever losers find themselves in our places fifty years from now.”

“What—you gonna put your own naked photos in it if we do?”

“Maybe I will, Potter. You think Evans would be my photographer if I asked?”

“Dickhead!” James grabbed Sirius in a headlock and the two of them began tussling back and forth, other kids weaving around them in the hall, completely unbothered by the usual antics.

“Hey, Remus—over here!”

All three of them glanced up. Peter was waving at Remus from down the hall, looking ecstatic. Beside him stood three other boys. In contrast, they all appeared nervous and awkward.

“So that’s where Wormy went,” Sirius grunted, still wrapped in James’ headlock. Their friend had been missing all lunch hour, and Remus found it odd that he’d be turning up now with strangers in tow.

“Come on,” Peter said to the others, before leading them forward. “Remus, these lads and I have a business proposition for you.”

“What sort of business?”

“The poem sort.”

“Oh no, you don't!” James said suddenly, freeing Sirius and getting between Remus and the three strangers. “Pete, I don’t know what you’re on about but Lupin’s done with these bloody jokes, so you guys can just move on!”

“Yeah, enough taking the piss!” Sirius scowled, rubbing his neck. "Only we get to rag on Moony, them's the rules."

“They’re not here to take the piss,” Peter insisted. “They just wanna talk. Now could you two give us a moment? You can return to being Lupin’s bodyguards after.”

James and Sirius both deferred to Remus, who pursed his lips and gestured for them to go on. They do so, reluctantly, and as his friends shuffled up the hall, Remus crossed his arms.

“You better not be messing with me, Pete. I’m really not in the mood.”

“Just hear them out,” Peter pleaded, before clearing his throat. “Lads, this is Remus. Remus, these are the lads! Ashton Hyde, Francois Martin, and Spencer Whitman.”

“It's Whitmore,” Spencer grumbled.

Remus looked the boy up and down. “You’re Spencer?”

“Uh… yeah.”

Not much to go off of at all, huh, Prissy, Remus thought candidly.

He uncrossed his arms. “Alright, so whatchu want?”

Before any of the others could answer, Peter slid back in. “You see, Lupin, these here lads are having some issues of the 'feminal' sort."

"That's not a word."

"Right. What I mean is that they’ve got trouble at home—the honeymoon’s over—their favourite birds have flown the coop—they—”

“So what do you want from me?” Remus asked, looking straight at Spencer this time.

“My girlfriend fell in love with that bloody poem of yours,” he said. “Apparently it’s the best thing since sliced bread, and now she’s threatening to break up with me if I don’t come up with something just as foppish.”

“Didn’t Prissy already break up with you?”

Spencer gave him an odd look. “How’d you know about that?”

“Uh… word travels fast.” Remus cleared his throat. “So what—you all want me to write poems for you?”

“Well, we can’t bloody do it, can we?”

“Have you tried?”

Before Remus could put his foot in it any further, Peter slid in; “They’re willing to pay for it. You just whip something up, they pass it along to their girls—and boom! Everyone’s happy.”

“Pete, I’m about three seconds away from smacking the shit out of you.”

“As long as you thank me for this brilliant opportunity afterwards.”

Remus sighed. He wasn’t sure what had gotten into his friend, but if all it took to buy his own fags was a few cringe-inducing lines of script then maybe…

He turned back to the group. “Do they have to be long?”

Spencer shrugged, glancing at the others. “Nah, just enough to make her bawl a bit.”

“Alright… but it’ll cost you up front.”

“How much?”

“Twenty.”

“Twenty?” Francois yelped. “For a fucking poem?!”

“Each.”

The boys gaped.

“I’ll give you five quid,” Ashton said.

Remus picked at his teeth with his nail. “Ashton Hyde… Isn’t your dad a lord?”

The boy puckered.

“How ‘bout we split the difference?” Peter suggested. “Ten each and he’ll write like the wind. Your girlfriends’ll think they’ve woken up to new men.”

Ashton, Francois, and Spencer all looked at each other sorely.

Excited by the chance to woo their own girlfriends, the boys pulled out a pen and a paper each, quickly scribbling down what was needed. They split after that, and Remus let out a long breath, wondering how long it would be until all of it blew up in his face.

“Have I made up for accidentally letting Barty steal your poem yet?” Peter asked, looking smug.

“Nice try, Wormtail, but I’ve been burned before. We’ll see how this pans out first.”

Peter nodded, understanding, but still with a kick in his step that was distinctly un-Peter-like. When the ball rang, he strolled off with such a grin on his face that Remus found he couldn’t even be irritated anymore.

“They didn’t give you any trouble?” Sirius asked later, when he finally reappeared for Classics.

“Nah. Opposite, even. Tell ya later.”

Sirius raised an eyebrow in question, but already Professor Bilshin was calling out over the class.

“Alright, since some of you have gotten a little too comfortable recently—” He slapped a ruler down on a pair of desks up front, where a girl named Verity Wilkenson was currently straddling her boyfriend, both of them locked together at the lips. The pair burst apart, but did not look happy about it.

“New seat arrangements,” Bilshin barked. “Find your name on the board and park it, we’ve work to do today.”

Without even looking, Remus knew his chances of being sat next to Sirius were slim to none, but apparently the fates were shining on him today; he and Marlene had been given a pair of desks by the window.

“Finally!” She grinned, as he pulled out his chair and sat. “I’ve missed sitting beside you.”

“And what am I—chopped liver?” Sirius said, as he stopped by their desks.

“Liver with a side of day-old tripe,” Marlene answered, sticking out her tongue. Sirius made a play at trying to grab it, before instead picking up Remus’ copy of Medea as he pulled it from his bag.

“What’d you two think of today's play?”

“I loved it,” Marlene said automatically. “Let me guess, you never finished?”

“I skimmed,” Sirius said, flipping through the book. “Enough to know that Medea was a badass. ‘Cept she reminded me a bit too much of my mum. Maybe it was all the filicide.”

“I hope you’re being sarcastic."

Sirius gave Remus a snide look and passed the book back. “What’d you think of it?”

“It was okay. She was better in Ovid though.”

“Ha. You’re so cute when you talk like a swot.” Sirius crouched down. “Hey, get this—Prongs and I came up with a way to get back at Reg and his miserable comrades for what they did to you.”

“Does it involve any chemical warfare?”

“Just a little. But I’d hardly consider flour and bicarb soda real chemicals.”

“Bicarb soda? It isn’t more stink bombs, is it?”

“I’m offended that you even had to ask. We don’t repeat pranks. This one is brand new, and much sweeter. Call it a present, if you’d like. And the best part—all of Salazar’s gonna get a taste.”

Bewildered by all of the obscure hints, Remus opened his mouth in question only to be cut off when their professor ordered Sirius back to his desk. Winking at him, Sirius obeyed and dropped down into his seat, two desks away. His seat partner, a girl named Amanda, immediately started undressing him with her eyes, obviously delighted she’d gotten placed so close by. Remus wasn’t worried. The only one actually undressing Sirius Black was him.

“Shall I fetch you a camera?” Marlene murmured under her breath. “Bloody queer.”

Remus snorted into his palm, feeling familiar.

“Oi, pen any new poems lately, Lupin?”

It was Snape, naturally. The déjà vu must’ve summoned him. He’d been moved two rows behind them and seemed just as happy as Remus that the two of them were finally separated. Unfortunately his new seat partner, Verity, did not look all that pleased.

“Just ignore him,” Marlene advised, taking Remus’ shoulder and turning him around. “He’s only trying to get a rise out of you.”

She was right, and Remus calmed himself with thoughts of Sirius’ mysterious prank. Snape was in Salazar House; with any luck the revenge would extend to him as well.

“Alright, settle down!” Professor Bilshin called. The class quieted a few moments later, and he turned to write the title of their most recent play on the board. Out of the corner of his eye, Remus saw Marlene lean in, as though she were a tiger getting ready to pounce.

“ ‘Medea’, one of Euripides’ more notable tragedies which I’m sure all of you read to completion.” The professor eyed his students pointedly, and Remus glanced over at Sirius who gave him a sarcastic thumb’s up. Professor Bilshin didn’t seem to notice; he turned around and added the word ‘Themes’ to the board.

“Now, as an intro to our unit, who can suggest to me one of the themes present in our text?”

Marlene’s hand shot up. “Feminism.”

“Oh, here we go,” someone muttered. Remus glanced up sharply, and found Wells Lewis already sniggering with another boy near the front of the class. Wells was Verity’s boyfriend and a right dickhead when it came to most things, but Remus had never had class with him until that term.

“Alright—feminism.” Bilshin added it to the board. “Anything else?”

“Marriage,” Verity called, making Marlene roll her eyes.

“Good,” Bilshin said, scratching ‘marriage’ across the chalkboard. “Explain.”

While Marlene soured at not being given the chance to extrapolate on her point, Verity perked up in her seat. “Well, the whole plot hinges on it. Medea and Jason are married yet he’s fallen in love with the other princess so she wants revenge.”

“Oh my god—love?” Marlene said loudly. “Did we even read the same play? Jason doesn’t love Glauce, he wants her father’s kingdom.”

“A friendly reminder to raise your hand in class, Miss McKinnon,” Bilshin sighed. “Now, if we were to compare these two themes—marriage and feminism—what does the text say about them?”

Marlene raised her hand, but the professor picked Verity.

“That marriage is natural, but you have to be a good wife first. Medea loved Jason but she thinks she’s better than him. Who would want to stay married to someone like that?”

“She doesn’t think she’s better—she thinks she’s equal!” Marlene exclaimed. “Medea says it in the opening of the play, that marriage is intrinsically tied to a women’s reputation and therefore is just another example of the power imbalance between genders! Jason can divorce her and he’ll be fine, but she has to go into exile. It’s pure misogyny.”

“Hand, McKinnon,” Bilshin ordered. “Can anyone else name a theme?”

Wells Lewis raised his hand. “Revenge. The creepy bird murdered both her kids just to get back at her cheating husband.”

“Figures that’s what you’d take out of it,” Marlene protested quietly.

“Yes, but what drove her to that decision?” The professor urged.

“Pride,” Marlene said. “The Greeks were obsessed with hubris, and Medea’s too clever for the rest of her counterparts, but because she’s a woman, no one will take her seriously. To everyone else she’s just a villain.”

“Didn’t she cut up her own brother and throw his body parts into the sea?” Verity called.

“Exactly! She knew her father would have to stop to collect his son’s body so it helped Jason and the Argonauts get away with the Golden Fleece. It was a brilliant counter move.”

“I’d hate to be your brother,” Wells sniggered.

“Medea’s passion and suffering made her into a monster,” Marlene continued, ignoring the ridicule; “But how can we say for sure that her story is inherently worse than any other? Hercules also murdered his own wife and children and he’s still considered a hero. Medea’s automatically condemned because we’ve all been brainwashed into thinking that a mother’s only duty is to care for her children. But she was powerful, and Jason tried to make her subservient. If anything I feel bad for Medea.”

“Well, there’s a shocker,” Snape mused. “The suffragette feels bad for the witch. Someone call Hansel and Gretel.”

Half the class began to laugh until Professor Bilshin silenced them with a stern clap of his hands. “Alright, so suffering, a strong theme to be sure.” He wrote it on the board. “Lupin, I know you’ve read the play—what can be said about Euripes’ treatment of his characters in relation to this theme?”

“Uh, well…” Remus glanced sideways, where Marlene was staring at him with desperate eyes. “I think Marlene’s right. The play’s all about society versus women, and what it means to take charge of their own bodies. It's—uh… Well, it’s suffering.”

“And what’s the cost of your body, Lupin?” Wells’ seat partner called. Laughter erupted again, but Marlene had the support she’d been seeking.

“Medea suffers because she’s ‘othered’," she called. "Because people are afraid of her! It’s proof that she’s powerful. Jason would’ve been nothing without her magic, and yet the moment they arrive home he throws Medea aside and calls her a barbarian.”

“Maybe she was just ugly,” Wells reasoned. “I wouldn’t want to snog someone whinging about their problems all the time—especially if they had the face of a horse. Sound familiar, Lupin? You and McKinnon dated, yeah?”

A paper ball hit Wells in the back of the head and he turned around to find Sirius scowling at him. “Watch your mouth, mate.”

"What? I'm just making an educated guess. Thought you'd be able to relate, yeah, Black? At least you know how to pick 'em."

While the class sniggered at Sirius, Marlene scowled.

"Pig. At least Sirius—”

“That's quite enough," Bilshin cut in. "We're discussing themes, not the issues of beauty versus morality. Now would anyone else care to play the field?”

“Not McKinnon,” Wells drawled. “She’s much too busy being a bitter rug-muncher to take a swing at anyone.”

“Better than sounding like a worn out hose-bag with a silver spoon so far up his arse you’d think he’d fucking choke on it!”

“And that is detention, Miss McKinnon!”

Sirius sat up in his chair very quickly. “Hold on, that toff just called her a ‘bitter rug-muncher’ and McKinnon’s the one that gets punished? That’s fucked up.”

“That is detention for you too, Mr. Black. After school—my office.”

“Fine,” Sirius huffed, before cupping his hands around his mouth to holler across the classroom; “Looks like it’s a date, McKinnon! You prefer red wine or white?”

“Sirius Black, hallway—now,” Bilshin snarled. Shrugging, Sirius got up and made his way down the aisle of desks. Just as he passed Wells, his elbow came up, clipping him in the back of the head.

“Go to hell, Black,” Wells hissed.

Sirius waved mockingly before shooting a wink in Marlene’s direction and joining their teacher in the hall. There was more sniggering, but as Remus turned to Marlene, she simply turned her face to the window, head bowed low over her book.

“You—uh… handled that pretty well,” Remus told her, after the lesson had ended and they were making their way out of the classroom.

“I’m so sick of how women are treated at this school,” Marlene scowled. “We had to fight just to get our own football team, and then they told us we couldn’t compete in any official tournaments. And now this bloody-fucking time capsule.”

Sirius slid an arm around Marlene’s shoulders. “Oh? You heard about that, yeah?”

“Unfortunately.”

“You should see the hole they left behind our dorm. Apparently those older codgers thought it would be funny to bury it ten feet under. Not even Moony could crawl outta a pit that deep.”

Remus took a light shot at the back of Sirius’ head before deferring to Marlene. “What was wrong with the time capsule, Cherry?”

“I’ll tell you what’s wrong—that time capsule is from 1927, that’s fifty years ago!”

“Okay. Yeah…?”

“Do either of you know when Hawkings started admitting female students?”

Both of them shook their heads ruefully.

“Fifty-four years ago! Women were here four years before that capsule was buried, and there isn’t a single hint of their existence in the entire thing! Not in the school photos, or the certificates—none! It’s all memorabilia of men. Every photo and list and bloody artifact—men! But women were here—women were contributing to this college, and there isn’t a shred of evidence of that! We have no idea if they had clubs or organisations or what classes they enjoyed or how they spent their time. It’s tragic.”

Remus exchanged an ashamed glance with Sirius, who shrugged and offered an alternative;

“We were going to trick Salazar into eating a bunch of weed brownies if you wanted us to drop some off for Wells and Verity too."

“No,” she grumbled. “I think I’m just gonna sulk a bit more. See you in detention.”

Marlene pulled away and made her way down the hall to her next class, and Sirius sidled up to Remus and slung an arm around his shoulder instead. It was more of a reach, but Sirius didn’t seem to notice.

“Such a trooper, willing to take on some of society’s biggest quandaries,” he said, turning them the other way. “Think this is her first detention ever?”

“Probably... Is that really what we’re doing to Salazar? Weed brownies? That’s not a punishment, it’s a gift.”

“Not if they don’t know they’re eating them,” Sirius smirked. “And not if the gift comes on the same day as mocks.”





* * *





Sirius had kindly filled Remus in on the prank idea between final period and study hour, and even he had to admit that it was brilliant. As long as they made it tempting enough, the lads of Salazar House would wake up to a royal treat meant to motivate them on their first day of mock-exams. They wouldn’t put enough weed in the brownies to do any real harm, but sure as the wind blows, they’d be feeling it come exam time. The Marauders would have to wait a few days for the timing to line up, but that gave them plenty of time to start stewing. Lily had already refused to give them her personal brownie recipe, but Sirius had found a cookbook in the library that would do the trick. Remus was pleased; he couldn’t afford to get back at Regulus personally, but an all-House attack was a strong alternative. As long as he ate the bloody things.

Once Sirius and Marlene had disappeared to serve Bilshin’s detention, Remus made his way across campus alone. He had prefect duty, and though it was with Regulus, they were only filing paperwork in the office. Hopefully they’d be able to come to a wordless understanding to ignore one another, and then leave and never speak again. Hopefully.

As he walked, Remus began to feel that familiar empty feeling in his hand. His fingers felt twitchy, and though he knew logically that it was brought on by the anxiety of having to deal with Regulus again, he still searched for something to sedate it. So often lately, he’d been able to fill that empty feeling with Sirius; just a touch, or even a kiss if they were lucky enough to be alone. It was a lovely occurrence, but as it was, Sirius was in detention, so he could only reach for his cigarettes.

They were tucked at the bottom of his bag, buried beneath school texts and exam notes. He managed to reach them—his zippo as well—but as he withdrew the carton, the zipper of his pencil case got caught on the button on his shirtsleeve and came tumbling out, hitting the pavement with a clatter and scattering pens and pencils everywhere. Remus sighed, and stooped over to collect them. He’d just picked up his rubber when he noticed them.

It was Audriana, along with her group of friends. The girls were walking up the pavement arm in arm, with giddy smiles on their faces. They might’ve just passed him by, said hello, or stopped to fulfil another purpose—one that was innocent and not at all driven by ulterior-motives—except that Remus was never that lucky.

He hurried to collect his things, and then shot to his feet. It was stupid, he knew, to be running from a group of girls, but he wasn’t actually running so much as hastening in the other direction. Every so often he'd chance a look over his shoulder and each time he found they were still there, smiling at him and giggling to one another. They weren’t even waving—they knew he’d seen them, and now it was a game. A cruel game that only a girl (and probably Sirius) would find funny. But that wasn’t all. Around the fourth or fifth time he glanced back, Remus began to realise the true circumstances of their game. The girls weren't just following him.

They were getting closer.

Remus urged his legs to go faster, without fully breaking out into a run because that would be embarrassing and a lot like admitting defeat. Instead he pumped his arms, all while experiencing a shrill feeling that had come over him. He’d thought it might be enough to give them the slip, but when he looked back again—there they were! The girls had also upped their speed; no longer arm in arm, but rather scurrying after him at the same pace.

Oh god. They were chasing him!

Remus whipped his head around, searching desperately for a way out. He was approaching the science block now, and just beyond that would be the dining hall and its surrounding berms. If he could just make it past them then Castle Hall would be a straight shot, but every time he looked back the girls were somehow closer, moving so briskly it was as if they secretly had wings on their school shoes.

Fuck it.

Remus had reached the science block, and the moment he disappeared around the corner of the building, he was off. Running to—running from—it didn’t matter! All that mattered was that he put distance between himself and those crazy girls.

“There he goes!”

There were screams—he couldn’t tell if they were in despair or delight, all he knew was that he was now sprinting across campus with a wild throng of sixth form girls chasing after him. It was worse than that day in the village, at least then he’d had Sirius to laugh at him—and they hadn’t actually been running, they’d just been hiding! Now he was running—running with only the open berm to save him. He passed other kids, most of them appearing completely flummoxed to find their classmate being chased around the side of their school buildings. It was mortifying, but also terrifying. Every time Remus turned a corner and spotted the group out of the corner of his eye it seemed to have grown—more girls had fallen in with the others, throwing their hat into the ring! He should've known; girls were pack animals, and like wolves they would chase their prey when given any opportunity.

He skirted the dining hall, thankful indeed that it was not yet time for supper and very few were around to witness his shame. The girls kept coming.

“THERE—GET HIM!”

“SOMEONE GRAB HIM!”

“HE’S HEADING FOR BASTION!”

They were right. Directly behind the dining hall and across from the skip bins was a tiny building known as Bastion Hall. Generally students were not allowed inside, since it was mostly offices anyway, but that meant reprieve. Remus’ lungs were burning, and his bag kept walloping him in the gut as he ran. After skirting around a lorry parked out behind the cafeteria’s loading zone, he made a beeline for the tiny hall. The doors were open—thank god— and he rushed inside, slamming it after him. There was no visible lock, but he could still hear the high-pitched shouts coming from the girls outside. Panicking, Remus turned around and made to dash down the main hallway, only to nearly punt Mrs. Norris across the linoleum as she came streaking out of a random office. He just managed to miss her, and in doing so, collided headlong with a rubbish bin, taking it down to the ground with a horrible crash.

“WHAT’S THAT MAKING ALL THE NOISE?”

It was Filch. He came thundering out of his office wearing his usual mouldy-looking trench and heavy, steel-toed boots. His quivering jowls became a nasty grin when he spotted him, as though he’d yet to fulfil his quota of terrorized students that day.

“What—What are you doin’ in ‘ere, eh?” He wheezed. “Students aren’t allowed in ‘ere!”

“It was a mistake!” Remus insisted. He scrambled to his feet, trying to right the bin while chucking pieces of rubbish back inside. “I–I just tripped over the cat, and—”

“You hurt my cat?!”

There was a shout, this time from outside. The girls had crowded around the door and appeared to be pressing their noses up against the frosted glass.

“I think I see him!”

Remus abandoned the rubbish bin and all of its mess. The furious caretaker screamed after him, but there was no way he was going to stop. Remus wasn’t sure what was worse; being caught by the girls or submitting to Filch and spending the next several hours shovelling horse dung in the school stables.

Dodging a secretary as he ran, he burst out of the office building on the far side, letting out a moan of relief as Castle Hall finally fell into view. After making it across the road, he snuck in the back door and found himself alone at the end of Castle Hall’s ground floor hallway. His chest was heaving, and he couldn’t fathom how he was going to explain such a thing to his friends later on, but at least he’d made it.

Once he'd caught his breath, Remus straightened out his bag strap and made his way down the hall toward the main offices. Most of the secretaries and administrative workers would’ve gone for the evening, but that didn't mean he was lucky enough to be awarded peace and privacy. When he strode into the front office, he found Regulus Black standing along the head counter, busy sorting through files and replacing them in their correct cabinets.

“Finally decided to show, did you?”

Remus was instantly furious. There he was, stuck running from a problem that he’d created in the first place, and Regulus had the gall to snark.

“I’m not here to talk,” he snapped, dropping his bag down on a random chair; “I’m here because I have to be. So if we could just ignore each other properly, I’d appreciate it.”

“Fine by me. Just stay out of my way.” Regulus kept sorting, while Remus reached out toward his back to mimic strangling him. Finally he settled on flipping him the bird with both hands, and huffed strongly before marching over to the far side of the room to begin his busy work. He’d just taken off his coat and hung it on the hook by the office’s front window when a secretary marched back into the room, carrying a box that looked as though it’d been sitting in brown water for a decade.

“Oh! Boy, am I glad I caught you two. These books are being donated to the school in the village, but they need all our stickers peeled off. The prefects in the library were busy with a group of third years, so I figured we could lend a hand over here at the office.” She set the box down on the counter next to Regulus’ files. “There’s more on the trolley in the hallway when you finish those!”

As the woman left, her heels clicking on the tile, Remus strode over to the box and opened it. The mildewy smell of old books had just hit him when Regulus yanked the case away. He was already digging into it by the time Remus realised that it was meant to be a slight, but rather than give Regulus the satisfaction of blowing up, he stomped out into the hall to retrieve a box of his own.

“Little git… right fuckin' piece of… cheeky arse-hole…!”

Remus kept grumbling under his breath even as he returned to the office, dropping the box of books down on the counter opposite to his prefect partner. At least he got the window. While peeling the stickers off of each book, he stared out at the early evening sky. It was getting darker much earlier now, and they were due for a snow fall or two. Hopefully the weather would hold out until after exams. He didn’t much fancy lugging himself across campus during a snowstorm.

Pushing the stack of cleaned books aside, Remus reached into the box for another. As he did, movement beyond the window caught his eye, and he glanced up—just in time to see Audriana and her group of girls approach the Hall’s front steps.

He fumbled the book, ducking out of sight below the counter. Instantly his heart was in his throat. How had they found him? Why hadn’t they given up? Were they really just coming into the hall for shit’s sake?

“There’s odd, Lupin,” Regulus said, having turned to stare at him; “And then there’s you.”

“Piss off!” Remus hissed, before wrenching his head up to peek out the window.

“Looking for someone? Like your fan club, maybe?”

Remus couldn’t take it anymore. He jumped to his feet, thrusting a finger beneath Regulus’ nose. “Honestly, where do you get off?! You'd think you'd have some sense of self-preservation—I am seriously four seconds away from annihilating you!”

“With what? Your extremely quick wit? Good luck trying, I’m not afraid of you.”

“You’re gonna wish it was wit I hit you with when I’m done! Do you even know how it's been for me since you stole that poem?”

“Not my fault Pettigrew can’t keep track of his things,” Regulus replied coolly.

“—Crap!” Remus howled. “It’s been four days of absolute crap, and it’s all your fault! You fucked me over!”

He’d been expecting another dismissive jab, or maybe a snide remark or two—something that would ‘put him in his place’, but what Regulus did next was ten times worse.

He smirked.

"And how's it feel, Lupin?"

“All I was trying to do was help you!” Remus bellowed. “Since the day I got here, you and Sirius have been trying to pick away at each other like fucking pigeons and I never took a side! He’s my best friend and I defended you when he stepped outta line!”

“Well, thank heavens for that!” Regulus exploded. “You may be so generous, but I never asked for your ‘help’! And I never asked to be friends with that girl either!”

“It’s always ‘I never asked’—‘I never asked’, but that’s what nice people do, Regulus! And Trish is nice! She’s nice and you don’t deserve her friendship—I’m not sure you deserve anyone’s!”

“Go then! I never wanted to be stuck with you then, and I certainly don’t now! Why don’t you go find my brother and make yourselves useless somewhere else!”

“I will! God, if you put half as much effort into being a decent person as you do being miserable, then we might’ve solved world hunger by now!”

Regulus scowled very deeply. Remus almost thought it might try to hit him, like that day in October when they’d fought, but Regulus was smarter than that. He knew he couldn’t beat Remus in a fight, so he did the one thing Remus couldn’t defend against. He marched over to the office window and threw open the latch.

“HEY! GIRLS! YOU LOOKING FOR LUPIN?”

Remus’ stomach dropped. No, no, no…

“HE’S IN HERE!”

“What are you doing?!” Remus shot forward, pushing Regulus out of the way of the window. Just outside, he could see the girls, and they’d spotted him as well.

“You should really stop blabbing about your own weaknesses, Lupin. Someone might try using them against you.”

“You little—” He rounded on Regulus, grabbing him by the collar of his shirt. “You fucking cunt!”

Regulus flinched violently, and then grabbed onto Remus’ hands to try and push him away.

“Y–You’re a cunt!”

Remus had never wanted to smack someone more in his life, but the alarmed look on Regulus’ face and the fact that his time was wasting was enough to give him pause. He could already hear the girls’ excited shrieks and thunderous footsteps on the stairs outside. And so, in true fight or flight fashion, he released Regulus’ collar, grabbed his jacket, and his bag, and left him to whatever miserable brooding he preferred.





* * *





He lost them by the lake. Perhaps it was too cold, or maybe they’d just tired of the chase; but either way, as Remus half collapsed against the side of the rowing team’s clubroom—wheezing and coughing up a lung—he was relieved. The other Marauders were never going to let him live it down.

“That you, Lupin?”

He jumped—making his ribs twinge painfully. “Who’s there?!”

“Just me.” Trish came around the side of the clubroom, adjusting her muffler around her neck.

“Trish? What are you doing all the way out here?”

She pointed at the building with her thumb. “This place ne’er gets used in the winter. I come out ‘ere tae smoke sometimes… What's happened to you?”

“Oh.” He let out a long breath. “It’s a long story.”

She shrugged, indifferent or uninterested, he wasn’t sure. Then she pulled a baggie from her pocket. “Haven’t started yet. Feel like a walk and a smoke, wee bawbag?”

He did. Anything to avoid going back before the cover of nightfall. Together they left the clubroom behind and made their way down to the shores of the icy lake. Trish was an eager enough sharer, which Remus had to appreciate. She was a bit of an acquired taste, sure, but she was always real with you, and could definitely be counted on in a pinch.

“Yeah, I got a brownie recipe,” she said, as they walked along the edge of the Dubh. “Call 'em 'hash browns’. I’ll write it out fur ya—see if Salazar likes the taste. They should, I spent all last summer perfecting it with my cousin.”

“Clyde?”

“Na, got loads ‘o cousins, me. No siblings though.”

“Me neither.”

“Well, there you go. Us only bairns gotta stick together.” She stopped on the edge of the bank, next to a large boulder big enough to use as a make-shift table. “Here looks like an alright spot.”

She got to rolling, while Remus kept his back to her on look out. The wind had decided to be merciful, and only a light breeze was blowing off the water. They chatted, mostly about normal things, and eventually things turned to talk of Sirius.

“He actually called me a hippie? Smug bastard,” Trish mused, while sealing up her first joint and passing it along.

“He’ll call anyone a hippie. Think it’s just part of that age-old rocker versus flower-child rivalry.”

“I remember what his hair used tae look like when it was all long and flowy—he’s more ‘hip’ than he thinks. ‘n besides, I’m more like a stoner socialist anyway. A narcotist nonconformer, if ya will. Look here.” As if to illustrate her point, Trish passed him her thermos, which Remus stared down at quizzically.

“What is it?”

“It’s tea—or, a kind of tea. Go on, try it.”

Shrugging lightly, Remus tucked the spliff behind his ear and twisted the lid off the thermos. He took a swig, and the smell hit him about half a second too late. It left him instantly sputtering—almost gagging as the garish taste flooded every corner of his mouth with the rich flavour of rotting earth.

“Eugh—tastes like fucking dirt.”

Trish let out a cheeky snort. “It’s ‘cause it’s made with mushrooms.”

Remus frowned at the idea of drinking liquid fungus. “I’m guessing you don’t mean the average sort.”

“Nope, these are of the magical variety. Don’t worry, I never make it strong enough tae start seeing shit, just enough tae leave ya a bit floaty for ‘a while.”

“I gotta say, that’s pretty ‘hippy’ of you, Trish,” he said, before taking a second swig, grimacing, and handing the thermos back.

Trish took it and chuckled, looking out over the calm lake waters. She’d finished three joints, and tucked the leftovers back into her coat pocket. “What’s the hippiest thing about you, Remington?”

Remus considered. “I have a tattoo.”

“Na wey! Can I see it?”

He tapped his chest sarcastically. “Too cold. Should’a kept me inside if you wanted to strip me down.”

She snorted again. “I ken a few people who’d kill me for trying.”

“Ha, like who?”

“Half o’ yer wee fan club for starters.”

"Please, don't bring it up."

Trish looked pleased. “Alright, ya hippy—What’s yer tattoo of?”

“It’s Lily’s initials.”

“And just why do ya have Lily Evan’s initials tattooed on you?”

“Let’s just say I was heavily coerced on Halloween. I think your cousin was involved too.”

“Ohhh,” Trish smirked, “Halloween, huh? I remember, ‘n I have ‘a few guesses as tae who it was under that sheet by the wey.”

Remus bit his lip. “Oh yeah…? Er, who?”

“I’ll let’cha know when I figure it out for sure.” With an impish grin, Trish glanced down and suddenly came to a startling halt. “Oh my god!” She bent down, coming back with a stone she held up to her eye. Remus could just make out the warm brown of her iris through it. The stone had a small hole in its centre.

“It’s a hag stone!” She trilled.

“A what?”

“You know, a witches stone. In Gaelic we call them gloine nan druidh—‘druid’s glass’. They’re supposed tae ward off evil charms and prevent bad things like nightmares. They’re really rare.”

Remus stepped up to peer through the stone from the other side. “That's cool. Could always use more ‘evil charm’ protection.”

“I collect rocks actually,” Trish said, pocketing the stone and sipping her mushroom tea; “That’s my hippie thing. My dad always complains about how heavy my bags are when he comes to pick me up at the end of term.”

“That’s… sort of fitting,” Remus smiled.

“I know, right? Let me know if ya have any nightmares and I’ll let ya mooch it,” she teased.

They continued walking, passing the magical fungus tea between them until they’d made it all the way around to the eastern edge of the lake, near the storage buildings that were all shut up for the season. It’d be dark soon, but the sun was still a rich orange colour in the sky. Nice evening for a walk.

“Fancy a swim?” Trish asked, as she plopped down on one of the metal benches meant for watching the rowing teams.

“No thanks, I’ve felt those waters in the winter. Not nice.”

“Och aye, I remember hearing about that last year. Reginald told me.”

“You mean Regulus,” Remus replied, with a hint of distaste. Trish caught it, and set a hand over her brow, squinting up at him.

“You're mad at him, aren’t ye? For what he did.”

“Aren’t you? What he said to you before wasn’t exactly nice.”

Trish dropped her hand. “Guess I don’t really mind all that much. I know he’s hurting inside, and when ya hurt in here, it feels better to bring that hurt out. Sometimes others just get caught up, that’s all.”

Remus slumped down on the bench next to her, feeling a bit flighty from the tea, but also troubled. “I didn’t realise that the two of you were... close.”

“We aren’t really. Just in the same year. Sort of ran in the same circles as prefects, but he’s ‘a tough nut to crack, that one. Not that I havena’ tried. It’s stupid, but I always end up thinking that the best people to have around are the ones that want nae to do with me. It’s my hamartia.”

Remus looked down at his feet—at his boots caked with mud. Hamartia; a fatal flaw.

“That why you started talking to me?” He asked.

“Like’lie. You’ve got so many rumours around ye, Remington, it's almost exciting.”

“Eh. Mary starts half of them.”

Trish began toying with her lighter, clicking the spark wheel over and over again. “So this must mean that yer pretty bothered by whit Reginald did with your poem then.”

“Are you saying I shouldn’t be?”

“Na, but ye might be looking at it the wrong way… How many people have told ya that they like yer poem?”

“Enough.”

“Did ya listen tae any of ‘em? I mean really listen?”

“Sirius liked it,” Remus said, quietly.

“Oh? And what did the great Sirius Black have to say?”

“He said… Well… He said that it was like seeing himself again. But through—” My eyes; “—Someone else’s eyes.”

“That’s nice,” Trish smiled. “I bet if ye listened a bit more, you’d hear the same thing from other folk too. It’s like those songs of yours. People want to see themselves in ‘em. And the girls at this school, they just wanna feel something tender. Like yer poem. Don’t ya ken… Boys are mean, Remus.”

Remus was surprised. He didn’t think he’d ever heard Trish use his real name. Somehow it reminded him just a little of Sirius.

“I’m sorry for what Regulus said to you.”

“Eh. It’s all water under the bridge,” she shrugged. “He’s the one missing out, not me.”

Remus smiled. “You’re actually really smart, you know that, Trish?”

“Naturally. Dinnae tell me it took ye ‘til now tae notice?”

He laughed then, wondering how it was possible to feel so good after feeling so bad. Mental illness, probably.

“Does everyone have a hamartia?” Remus asked.

“Mm… maybe. Do you think you have one?”

“I dunno. Can I think about it?”

“Yeah, sure.” Trish pinched her lighter between two fingers. “In the meantime, want to share that spliff now?”

Remus sat up. “Yeah, go on. I’ll spot you when we get back to the dorms.”

They lit up together, the pot-heads, and passed it back and forth until they were thoroughly baked. Not even the cold could touch them.

“If you were a rock, what kind ‘a rock would you be?” Trish asked, flipping a smooth lake stone around in her hand. They’d since abandoned their bench and were throwing stones across the dark water, trying to hit a large boulder that was sitting several yards away and was just barely skimming the surface. They’d yet to hit their target, but Remus had faith.

“A grey one,” he answered blandly.

Trish began to splutter. “Not what colour—what kind? Like obsidian or—or basalt.”

He bent down and scooped up another stone. “What kind of rock is this?”

“It’s probably just shale.”

He threw the rock, watching it plop into the water’s surface next to the lake boulder. “Then I’d be shale.”

“So much for exciting.”

“What? Shale’s great. There’s so much of it—” He threw his arms out across the lakeside for emphasis; “Sounds great too. Shale. Shhhhhaale. Shale-shale-shale.”

Remus kept saying it until the word lost all meaning in his mouth and they were both laughing.

“Fine then,” Trish said. “If you’re shale then I’m schist.”

“No, you just made that up.”

“I did not! Sch—” She snorted and had to try again; “Schist is a type o’ metamorphic rock just like shale.”

“Schist is what people say when they stub their toe.” Remus illustrated by pretending to ram his boot against a large stone. “ 'Oh schist'! See?”

They both began cackling, the sort of laugh that occurred when you were too far gone to remember where the boundary was between funny and just plain stupid. They were laughing so hard that they didn’t notice it when they were run up from behind. Luckily, it was not Audriana.

“Moony, what the hell?”

Remus glanced up to find Sirius standing next to the bench, arms tucked in either armpit to ward off the cold. He had a vague look of irritation on his face, but Remus only thought it looked handsome.

“Oh,” Trish smiled, “Shale look, it’s yer boyfriend.”

“Hey, boyfriend,” Remus grinned dopily.

Sirius gave a start, blinking at them and opening his mouth before quickly closing it. If Remus wasn't so off his arse he might’ve noticed how he was blushing up to his eyebrows.

“Are you two stoned?”

“Yes, he's shale and I'm schist," Trish sniggered. Sirius gave her a bewildered look, before an icy chill whipped past them and he winced.

“Christ. It’s fucking freezing out here, you even missed dinner. Come on, Moons. Evans said we’re studying tonight and we got other shit to fry if we want to take down Reg and his minions.”

“He means ‘schist’ to fry,” Remus said to Trish, who immediately broke down giggling again.

“You were supposed to save some of the hash for Salazar,” Sirius grumbled, coming down to the water’s edge and grabbing Remus’ coat sleeve. “How high are you exactly?”

With a smile bordering on smug and stupid, Remus held his free hand up over Sirius’ head and passed it over him several times. “About five inches higher than you, short-stuff.”

Trish howled behind them, but Sirius only shook his head.

“Ha-ha—very funny. Do you know how long it took me to track you down, you tall twat?”

“Maybe you’d be warmer if you didn’t insist on wearing nothing but a leather jacket in December, Moooom,” Remus blagged, sassily pulling his arm out of Sirius’ grasp.

“So you got jokes then? Alright.” Sirius made to grab for him again but Remus shot backwards, holding up a finger snootily.

“It’s my arm! No touchy!”

Astonished, Sirius nearly laughed. “Moony, I ain't playing games. Now get back here.”

“Uh-uh!” Remus snorted, dodging his boyfriend for the second time.

“You cheeky shit—I am not doing this. We got actual pranks to plan!”

“You’re the one chasing me!”

“I’m not chasing you!”

“Are too!"

Sirius stopped short on the bank, giving him a stubborn smile. “Fine, come here then.”

Remus pretended to consider, taking a few steps forward until he was just an arm’s reach from Sirius.

“Good. Now are you done acting like a—”

Remus shot past him, smacking Sirius on the shoulder. “You’re it!”

“Ugh. Fucking prat,” Sirius scoffed, falling for it and finally giving way to an exciting game of cat and mouse. They tore across the banks, slipping past one another and laughing.

“Trish, stop him!” Remus wailed eventually, after Sirius had nearly caught him for the dozenth time.

“Nah, yer on yer own, schist-head,” she quipped, scanning the bank for more rocks.

The joke was enough for Remus, who—in a fit of laughter—turned very sharply and ended up on his back on the rocks. Sirius skidded to a halt next to him, bending over and grabbing him by the front of his jacket.

“There! Caught you!” He panted.

Remus might’ve kissed him right there in the open—even licked his lips in anticipation—but suddenly a sharp clang sounded from across the water, and they both turned to find Trish with her hands thrust into the air in triumph.

“I hit it!” She cried. “Remington, I hit the boulder!”

Sirius straightened up, staring past her at the lake with a look of absolute shock. “No fucking way.”

“I did! I did! Look, I’ll do it again.” Trish grabbed another rock and threw it. It fell just short of the ‘boulder’, but on the second toss her aim was true, and another clang echoed across the lake, making all of them perk up.

“That didnae sound like ‘a boulder,” she murmured in sheepish realisation, before holding a hand over her eyes and squinting. “In the name of the wee man, I think it’s a trolley!”

Remus stood up and stumbled down to the edge of the water with them. He’d been too dazed before to realise it, but there was no denying it. The seasonal cold had lowered the water level, and where the lake used to cover it entirely, the corner of Stan’s missing trolley now stuck out of its surface like a tiny floating island.

Sirius checked an invisible watch on his wrist, then whistled innocently. “Wow. Wonder how that got there…”

Remus lost it. By the time Trish and Sirius had managed to drag him back up the bank toward home, he was still laughing.
