Chapter 81: Hamartia


Chapter Summary

Exams have come to Hawkings. Remus plays business mogul. A prank goes wrong, and then oh so right.



Chapter Notes

No CW for this chapter. Also, I'm dedicating this one to Anastasia, because I know she'll never see it and I love that for her.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



‘Cause I’d rather stay here,

With all the madmen,

Than perish with the sad men roaming free;

And I’d rather play here,

With all the madmen,

For I’m quite content they’re all as sane as me…

- “All the Madmen” David Bowie, 1971



Friday 2nd December 1977





In reality, Trish had had the right idea all along. People did like his poems. They even liked them enough to pay. More than a week had gone by, and in some pinch of luck, Regulus’ grand joke had turned itself into a real financial venture. Eventually the girls had given up chasing him, and life returned to normal somewhat.

“We should call you the Poem Pusher,” Peter said, as Remus got up from the library table. He gasped, then; “The Substance Sonneteer!”

Remus let out an apprehensive chuckle. “Careful, Pete, your poor eyebrow’s only just grown back. Wouldn’t want it to go missing in the middle of the night.”

Peter covered both eyebrows with his hands. “You’re quite right, Moony. I reckon the ‘Blitzed Bard’ is ten times better anyway.”

“Somebody hold me back before I kill him.”

“Go on already,” Sirius laughed, pushing him on. “Don’t want to leave your two o’clock waiting.”

Remus smirked back. He was in the best mood he'd been in ever since Regulus had dropped that bomb on his life; they still found time to practice and write music, and soon exams would be over altogether. Then they’d be free to return home for the holidays, where he and Sirius could meet up in that little beach-themed bathroom as many times as need be. Yes, it was the simple pleasures, that's what Remus Lupin was after these days. Good friends, good music, and a good snog.

With his hands in his pockets, Remus left the small study room their little group had cloistered themselves in and made his way down the library’s centre aisle. He was looking for something—or more accurately, someone—and found them waiting for him in the Anthropology section, looking twitchy and nervous. Remus wasn’t nervous, rather, he felt brazen. He had the entire thing down pat. No holds, no exchanges, and certainly no I-owe-you’s. All payment was to be made up front, and if his buyers didn’t have the cash, then they would just have to look elsewhere, and now that word of his exploits had finally spread (thank you Barty) looking elsewhere was certainly easier said than done.

“You said ten, right?” The mousy boy warbled, staring nervously from behind glasses too big for his face. He was a tenth year, far too young to have such girl troubles, but money was money, and Hawkings was full of it.

“Price’s gone up actually. Now it’s—”

Reluctantly, Remus drew up short. The kid was white-knuckling his books and staring at him with brown eyes as big as a girl’s. He had a tenner peeking out of one hand.

“… Ten. Ten’s fine.”

A smile split his rosy face, and he raised the ten pound note, handing it over. Remus pocketed the money and then pulled out a tiny notepad and a pen.

“Who’s it for?”

The boy blinked at him. “Huh?”

“The poem. What’s her name?”

“Oh, uh… Sam.”

He wrote it down. “Hair colour? Eye colour?”

“Brown. B-Both brown.”

“Mhm. And what do you like about her?”

“Uhm… Do you think you could just write something nice? I–It doesn’t have to be too specific.”

Remus clicked his pen impatiently.

“Don’t you want it to be more... special? She’s already gonna know I wrote it.”

This was true. Everyone knew. What had started as a few boys looking to keep their girlfriends from breaking up with them had quickly ballooned into a school-wide fad. Every girl wanted a Lupin poem, it was like a new status symbol. Maybe they couldn't have their own personal tennis court or a leopard-skin bed with a mirror on the ceiling, but they could certainly cop a dingy limrick. He’d already written half a dozen for Chastity Bell alone, and though it always bothered him, he was at least able to charge those poor sods double.

“It’s okay if she knows,” the tenth-year insisted. “Put whatever you think would be nice."

"Does she at least have a favourite song? Band...?"

"What? Oh! Yeah, sure. She—er… She likes Pink Floyd a lot! And—uhm… The E-Eagles. It's an American band.”

Remus smirked. "I know who the Eagles are. Your girlfriend’s got good taste."

It might've been a trick of the light, but Remus could've sworn he saw the kid blush. Pretending not to notice, he cleared his throat and gestured back to the notepad.

"Alright, should only take a couple days. What’s your name and House so I can get this to you when it's done?”

“Oh, don’t worry about it!” The other boy chirped. “I’ll come find you!”

He took off down the aisle like he was scared of him, and a few seconds later Remus heard Ms. Pince’s reedy wail from across the library;

“Samuel Sheridan, you stop that running this instant!”

It didn’t take Remus long to put two and two together. He glanced down at his notepad, a funny feeling in the pit of his stomach, and—almost secretly—added ‘Sheridan’ after Sam. Then another voice was calling out to him through the shelves.

“Psst, Lupin! You still writing those poems? How much?”

Remus covered his mouth with a yawn.

“Twenty-five.”

Ten minutes later, Remus returned to the study room and found the rest of his friends exactly where he’d left them. They’d been there since breakfast, and in that time Lily’s hair had grown to twice its usual size simply from running her fingers through it while stressed. Lottie sat quietly next to her, listening to Spanish books on tape and chanting different verbs and their conjugations under her breath while Mary battled her way through an overdue psychology essay. On the boys’ side of the table, James had his Physics notes spread out around him as though a tornado had ripped through his school bag, but he wasn’t quite crying yet. Peter, on the other hand, had already wept twice over his Maths, and was currently copying out Lily’s notes from last term as though his life depended on it. Only Marlene had remained fully quiet—secluding herself on the far corner of the table and writing what appeared to be a very long essay of her own.

As he sat down at the table, Remus tugged his school bag toward him and pulled out a fresh notebook. There he began brainstorming all of the potential ideas for his newest customers, while Sirius—the only one of them that had managed to resist studying altogether—leaned over to snag a peek.

“Another score then, Moony?”

“Shush. It’s still working hours, Black,” Remus said, a smile still playing on his lips.

“I don’t know how you keep up with it all,” Mary asked, looking up from her essay. “How many of those poems has it been now?”

Remus shrugged indifferently. “Around forty-three.”

“Forty-three?!”

“Give or take.”

“That’s insane!”

“Shhh!” Lily hissed. She was flipping through her flashcards with such speed that she could’ve rivalled a street magician.

“It is insane,” James agreed quietly. “I don’t know how he writes ‘em so fast... And uh—speakin' a which, Moons, you finished with that thing we chatted about the other day...?”

Not even bothering to look up from his work, Remus reached into his bag and pulled out an envelope, which he passed onto James.

"Brilliant!" His friend grinned, before turning in his chair. "Hey, Daisy? Guess what, I've a little present. Now I know it's a bit early for Christmas gifts, but I think you'll like this one. It's 'eau de Lupin'."

" 'Eau de'?" Mary giggled. "Water of Lupin?"

"Huh? I thought that meant 'from'?"

Not one to be interrupted, Lily took the poem and added it to her stack of study papers with an air of indifference while James tried not to look too crushed.

"Is there any for me in there?" Mary asked. "I told Greyson I'd give him another chance if he stepped up his game a bit. And Jason's been dropping hints about some 'surprise' all week."

Huffing, Remus returned to his bag once more. "Here," he grunted, retrieving four different poems, each commissioned by a different guy. Mary lit up when she saw them, eagerly snatching them from Remus' hands.

"Shouldn't the guys who paid for those be the ones who give them to you?" Peter asked, having observed the entire thing from a safe distance.

"Of course. But how else am I supposed to know which one I'm going to like best if I don't see them all first? I'll give them back—let them think they're a step ahead."

Peter snorted, and then glanced at Marlene. "Can you believe that?"

"Mhm... sure," Marlene murmured, eyes boring into her paper. Remus was about to ask what class it was for, when Sirius reached over and nudged him.

“Oi. Where's my poem?"

"I only work on commission. And I’m backed up on orders as is.”

"Hmph. Stingy."

Remus smiled to himself, while Lily arched an eyebrow at him from across the table.

“You should be studying for your exams,” she swore, adding several more flashcards to her stack. “Not writing poetry just to make a bit of money on the side. It’s almost extortion.”

“You show me the legal definition of 'extortion' and then we'll talk,” Remus retorted. “This is simply supply and demand.”

Lily shook her head like he was hopeless and returned to her flashcards.

In all honesty, Remus might’ve been more worried about his marks had he not stayed up most nights studying on his own. It was fine to study then, in the hours he couldn’t sleep, but he’d already ixnayed poetry after dark. It always made for soppy messes, and was no good for writing with other people in mind. Now the daytime—that was when the poetry became easy, and once he'd figured out how to remove the him and Sirius aspects from it, the words began to flow like water. Remus had already amassed enough money for fags and booze to last him until the end of the year, and even had a bit leftover for some Christmas shopping. With his goal reached, he was now hoping to earn enough to make a small cash donation toward the flat. He knew Tomny’s pride would force him to refuse the gift, but Remus was determined. It would mean repaying Tomny for all the times he'd rescued him in a pinch—even if he had to shove it up his arse, Tomny would take the money.

“Ugh, I can’t take it anymore,” Lily huffed after a long while. “Sirius, will you quiz me?”

She handed the cards across the table and Sirius took them, clearing his throat.

“ ‘What must be present for a system of judicial precedent to work’?”

“The identification of the binding parts of the judgement, an agreed hierarchy of the courts, and… a sound system of law reporting.”

“Brilliant. A bit scary, but brilliant.” Sirius flipped another card. “ ‘To what extent has the principle of Parliamentary sovereignty and the role of the judiciary been affected by the UK’s entry into the EEC?’ … Jesus, Evans—you put entire essay questions on your flashcards?”

“You never know what they’re going to ask!”

“Alright then, I have a question for ya. What do they call those wigs all the judges wear in court? Do you know?”

“Don't—”

“A bob-wig, ha!”

“Sirius!”

“Fine,” he grumbled, raising the cards again. “What are the three types of delegated legislation?”

Lily sat back with her hands in her lap, looking confident. “Orders in council, statutory regulations, and local by-laws.”

“Ooh, so close. The card actually says ‘statutory instruments’.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“Not according to the card.”

“Sirius Black!”

“Careful,” James warned. “Push your luck any more and she might actually murder you.”

“Yeah, straight threatened my life this morning when I buggered up ‘House of Commons’ and ‘House of Lords’,” Peter added pensively.

“They’re completely different systems!”

Peter whistled innocently. “Whatever you say…”

They continued like that for a while, and when Lily looked close enough to reach across the table to throttle his best friend, James humbly took over. Without the job of quizmaster, Sirius turned his full attention to Remus. He started with subtly grazing his hand along the outside of his thigh beneath the table, before growing more emboldened and trying for a full grab. Remus ignored it at first, confident that no one else would notice. He was too busy trying to think of a word that rhymed with ‘irresistible’, but there truly was no ignoring Sirius Black. Eventually his fingers slid higher—then deeper, toward the inside of Remus' thigh. Remus put a hand on his wrist to stop him, and Sirius began stroking with his thumb, sending shivers across his skin.

Remus looked at him. “Black, you’ve a spider on your shoulder, did you know?”

Sirius seized, clapping a hand to his shoulder immediately, but when it came away clean, Sirius scowled at him.

“Dick.”

“Don’t you dare mention spiders,” Mary threatened. “There was one in our room just this morning. Marlene had to kill it with a slipper, right Marls?”

Marlene gave a little mumble, still barely listening. She’d moved on from her essay, and was now tracing lines across another paper with her ruler.

“What are you studying for?” Remus asked.

“I’m not.”

"What was the essay then?"

"It wasn't an essay."

Attention caught, Sirius turned to them with a raised brow. “Marlene McKinnon not studying for exams? Someone call the paramedics.”

“It’s a petition,” Marlene said haughtily, drawing back from the table to reveal a cleanly drawn-up list of values. “I’m tired of the blatant disregard for equality at this school. Hawkings claims to be a forward-thinking institution—it’s time they prove it. We're the ones hosting the year-end tournament this time around, and I can't think of a better way for Hawkings to showcase it's supposed 'ethos of equality' than by letting the girls play too."

“Wow,” Lily breathed, snatching her flashcards back from James; “You’re making a petition for a girls tournament?”

"No, not a girls tournament—I want the girls to play in this tournament. Same as the boys."

"THAT'S A WONDERFUL IDEA!" Lottie called, headphones still on and shouting through her Spanish tapes. "Muy bien! Estupendo!"

A few of them laughed, and Mary craned her said to get a look at the petition.

“I think it’s a good idea too," she said, "but do you really think old McGonagall’s gonna go for it?”

“That’s what the petition’s for, numpty." Marlene straightened up, cheeks splotchy with nerves. "If I can get enough kids and faculty to sign this then she’ll have to take me seriously. And besides, she’s a woman in a man’s job. It’ll happen, just you wait.”

Somewhat eagerly, James stood up from his seat and reappeared over Marlene’s shoulders to read the petition over. “I think it’s a great idea too,” he said finally.

Marlene appeared flummoxed. “You do?”

“ ‘Course. I’d kill to have some of you girls on the team. The guys get complacent thinking no one’s better than them, but then they turn around and pull crap like refusing a scrimmage match because they ‘don’t play girls’. It’s bloomin’ tosh."

"Oh... Well, they're just afraid they'll lose anyway."

"Too right," James grinned. "McKinnon, If you’d let me, I’d like to be the first one to sign your petition.”

A look of utter shock crossed her face, but slowly Marlene moved aside so James could lean down and scribble his name just below hers.

“Hand it here, Prongs,” Sirius called after him, before adding his name to the list and passing it along to Remus. The paper went around the table until all eight of them had signed and Marlene was left positively weepy.

“Thanks guys,” she said, holding the paper against her heart.

“We’re with you, Marls,” Lottie smiled, headphones now strung around her neck. “Anything to get out of more studying. Any more verb conjugations and I'm going to top myself. Juro por Cristo.”

“Agreed,” Sirius said, already moved on to making card towers out of Lily’s spare flashcards.

“I’ll give a copy to the other prefects if you’d like,” Remus offered, making Marlene beam.

“That would be great! The more people who see it the better. Mrs. Brady in the admissions office has already agreed to let me make as many copies as I want.”

“We could make it a group thing,” James suggested. “Pair off and take turns every lunch hour or something.”

“Yeah!” Sirius agreed. “Make it a contest—whoever gets the most signatures before holiday break wins.”

“You always have to make everything a competition,” Lily scoffed.

"How else do you make life fun?"

“Well, what’s the winner get?” Mary leered. “A lap dance from all the other losers?”

There was a chorus of moans turned laughter that Lily silenced with a wave of her arms. “I think the winner should get the satisfaction of knowing they helped their dear friend Marlene with an issue that was very close to her heart.”

Sirius blew a raspberry at her. “Boo. Boring. Lap dance is better.”

“Tell you what, Sirius,” Marlene said, “you get the most signatures on the petition, and you can have a lap dance from anyone you want.”

Remus glared at her, but Marlene remained purposely oblivious. Sirius wasn’t cheeky enough to make eye contact, but he did squeeze Remus’ left arse cheek from under the table.

“Deal, McKinnon.”

Delighted, Marlene went back to her petition and Remus knocked Sirius’ hand away before returning to his work. As he did, Sirius subtly slid him a spare flashcard. His perfect handwriting was all over it.

Better start brushing up your dance moves, it read.

Remus narrowed his eyes and stole Sirius’ pen.

You wish.

Sirius took the pen back promptly; I’ll even get Mary to lend you an outfit. Fancy a skirt?

Crumpling the note, Remus shoved it into his pocket and Sirius smugly turned back to his card tower.

“I need one of those,” Lily said, snapping her fingers at him a moment later.

“Only if you give us that brownie recipe of yours,” Sirius said, concentrating hard on placing another card on top. Unimpressed, Lily stole one of the bottom cards and the whole thing came tumbling down with a flourish.

“You’re positively wicked, Evans.”

“And you’re not getting my brownie recipe. Potter told me what you were planning and I’m not helping you sabotage an entire dorm right before exams just because Regulus was a little nasty.”

“A little?!” Sirius shot his best friend a glowering look. “Utterly whipped, you are.”

“I couldn’t help it,” James whined. “She’s top of our law class, which means she’s very convincing.”

“It’s alright,” Remus said kindly. “Trish gave me her recipe last week. She’s even got the hash oil. We can start baking on Sunday.”

“Brilliant!” James cried, while Lily covered her face and groaned.

"The things you four could do if you applied yourselves to something good for a change."

“But it is for a good cause!" Peter reasoned.

“Which is?”

“A... wicked prank?”

Lily rolled her eyes and went back to studying.

“Nice, Wormtail."

“Well, I’m not top of the law class…”





* * *





The next day, the Marauders got straight to work. Not on their pranking—that could wait another day—but on the petition. After all, there were stakes now. And though Remus had very little desire to actually win himself, he couldn't very well lose. He and Lily had volunteered to take the first lunch shift, and after Marlene had delivered them a stack of fliers, they took to the dining hall’s main corridor, attempting to catch anyone who was coming or going.

“Really, I’m sur—prised,” Lily grunted, while slamming her hand down on the stapler in an attempt to attach one of Marlene’s petitions to the hallway notice board. “Trish was so unassuming last year… ugh… Damn thing.”

Remus took the stapler from her, unjamming it. “You’re too aggressive, staplers are sensitive. They need a gentle touch.”

“Har har.”

He passed the tool back. “And Trish is still unassuming. It’s how she gets away with everything.”

“You're right. I don’t think she’s ever had a detention.”

Lily returned to hanging the petitions, while Remus stood by awkwardly with a clipboard of his own. He’d been eager enough to volunteer, but when it came to actually collecting signatures, he was proving to be a bit shit. Lily’s preferred method ended up being grilling any unsuspecting student who happened to walk past until they either signed or fled in terror, but like expected, Remus wasn’t really all that cut out for campaigning. He didn’t have her brazen drive, and was starting to realise that there was a very real chance they’d all be giving Lily Evans a lap dance come end of the term.

“Wouldn’t you like to sign a petition allowing women to play alongside men in this year’s football tournament?” She demanded of a group of passing eighth years. The young kids exchanged unsure glances but before they could scurry away, Lily was pressing her clipboard into their faces. “Equal right to play on the same field! No one should be denied the chance to show off their skills just because of their gender, don't you think? Or are you for discriminatory school sports?!"

Intimidated by her instant lecture, the kids passed around the chipboard and rushed off, leaving Lily with a pleased look on her face. “I think I might have a knack for this,” she boasted.

“Maybe," Remus said, "but one of them signed as ‘A. S. Muncher’.”

Lily raised the clipboard and groaned. “Whatever. We’ve already gotten like seven ‘Seymour Buttz’. Whatever helps Marlene, I suppose.”

“I dunno, I thought ‘Pierre Pants’ was pretty good.”

As Lily stifled her laughter, she spotted another girl making her way up the hall toward them and immediately shoved Remus ahead of herself. “There! Ask her!”

Remus swallowed, regretting everything, but like Lily had said—whatever helped Marlene.

“Hey—erm... Wanna sign a petition?” He babbled, drawing the girl to a stop in the middle of the hall. She looked at him, surprised at first, before drawing all of her hair onto one shoulder.

“Maybe. What’s the petition for?”

“To let the girls play alongside the guys at the end of the year football tournament.”

“Hm." She looked him up and down. "Strange to see a bloke crusading for a women’s football team of all things.”

“It’s a favour for a friend—” he started, before rushing to correct himself; “But girls should be allowed to play football wherever they want too!”

She considered for a moment before holding out a hand expectantly. Acting quick so she didn’t have time to suddenly change her mind, Remus passed the clipboard over and she left a big loopy signature at the bottom. “Is your name on here?” She asked, scanning the list.

“Oh, I signed a different page.”

She nodded and gave him a sly smile before handing the clipboard back. “Good luck with the petition.”

She left with a quiet flourish and Remus proudly looked at Lily, who was watching him with her arms crossed.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“What? You told me to ask her!”

“She all but left her phone number, Remus.”

“You know, Sirius actually got a phone number yesterday. I’m afraid he might be winning.”

“Figures.” Sighing half-heartedly, Lily tucked her clipboard under one arm and began fiddling with the stapler. “Hey, so James told you guys that I’m going back to his for Christmas, right?”

“Yeah, told us a while ago."

"And you're going too, right?"

"Mhm. My dad and Sandra’ll be vacationing in the French Riviera for Christmas so Giles is letting me stay at James’. Peter’s just next door and Sirius basically lives there now so it should be great."

"I've never been to London. We were gonna go for Pet’s birthday one year, but she decided to go to Cardiff with her girlfriends instead."

"You'll like it," Remus said. "Plenty of libraries. You won't even run out."

She smiled, before nervously twisting a lock of red hair around one finger. "Listen Remus, I’m only telling you this because you’re my best friend.”

Interest piqued, he turned to her in question. “Yeah…?”

“I’m a bit nervous,” Lily confessed all at once. “It's just... I’ve only ever spoken to James’ parents over the phone a few times—and they were always kind! But… it’s not exactly the same as meeting someone in person, is it?”

“You think they won’t like you?”

“Well no, but—" She stepped in closer. "What if they don't like that James and I are dating? What if they don't like that I'm not Indian or a Hindu, or—or that my family is working class? I don't have anything to offer him, I'm just... me."

"Lils..."

"It's not an ethnicity thing," she amended sorely. "I don't care that James isn't white, I never have... But I really want his parents to like me, and what if they'd rather he date someone else? A nice girl with a good background. Someone who takes tea in the garden and has a personal tailor and whose dad doesn't have to choose between thatching the roof or mending the fence, and—"

"Lily," Remus tried, more forcefully; "You have nothing to worry about. Who gives a shit about background—you're literally the smartest person I know. Besides, there's no way James would ever let anyone put you down for something as crap as a busted fence. You're amazing, you are!"

Lily sighed. "Remus, I know you're trying to be kind, but you don't get it. I'm not like you, all I have is school."

And she was right. As othered as Remus had begun to think of himself, he would never know what it was to be outclassed by someone he loved. He and Sirius might've been queer behind closet doors, but they were lucky as far as material wants went.

"It's not that I don't trust James," Lily went on; "It's just that a part of me's always wondered if maybe he was keeping it hush. That maybe his parents were worried and he didn't want to kick up a fuss while we were at school."

"I'm sorry," Remus said. "I didn't mean to dismiss your feelings. But I swear, Lils, that's not James. You must know it's not. And it ain't the Potters either. They're going to love you, especially because you're always grinding their son's gears."

She smiled bashfully. “You really think so?”

“I know so! The Potters—blimey—they’re amazing. They took Sirius in without a second thought, right? And they always considered him a son, even before that. They’re incredibly smart, and they support James with our music too. I’m... Well, I'm a bit jealous, to be honest.”

“You never know, maybe they could adopt you too."

“As much as I’d love to be your future brother-in-law, I don’t think it would work out,” Remus said, trying not to imagine what it would be like to be Sirius’ adoptive brother and dating him at the same time.

“Well, alright," Lily said, untucking her clipboard from beneath her arm. "I suppose I should stop worrying about what they're going to think of me and start worrying about what sort of gift I should bring.”

“I know James’ mum likes these little sweets that taste like pears—he’d probably know the name. And I’ll bet Monty would love to hear about your parents’ botany. He’s got a great garden, if that helps.”

“It does, thanks. Reminds me to be less nervous. I think I’m gonna go hang a petition up in the girls’ loo upstairs. Marlene figured it would be a good idea to put them where we know other girls will see them. Head to lunch with me after?”

"Yeah, go on."

He handed her a stack of petitions and the box of staples from his pocket and Lily started for the staircase. She was halfway up when she around and called back to him;

"Remus? You're pretty amazing, yourself."

Remus smiled. "Meet you back here."

As Lily turned and skipped back up the staircase, Remus began happily rocking back and forth on his heels. Their conversation had put him in a good mood—confident, even—and he made sure to put it to good use. While scanning faces as they passed him in the hall, a group of guys approached and Remus raised the clipboard.

“Sign a petition?”

They didn’t stop, but the group after them did. And the one after that. Eventually Remus realised that it was much easier to catch people heading into the dining hall, rather than out, where they'd inevitably have some lesson or meeting to get to. He was just finishing up with a few kids from his English Lit class when he was approached by a few more girls. They were headed by Priscilla, the one he'd witnessed crying into Lottie's shoulder the week before. She was beaming—grinning at Remus like he'd hung the moon himself.

“Hi, Remus.”

“Oh, hey… Priscilla, right? You know Lottie.”

She nodded fervently, while her two friends tried to hide knowing smiles.

“I haven’t seen you around since that day in the dorm, but I wanted to thank you,” she said. “You helped me realise that Spencer wasn’t worth my time—or my tears, as Lottie put it. I dumped him right after. But not before he gave me this.”

She held out a piece of paper, one of his poems. It looked rumpled and worn—well-loved, he realised.

“Glad you got it,” he said. “But no need to thank me, really.”

“I heard you and Jillian went on a date earlier this year,” Priscilla said. “But you told her that you were already gone for someone else.”

“Er… yeah.”

“And are things still like that?”

He nodded. “They are.”

“She’s lucky then, the girl you’ve fallen for.”

Remus smiled, genuinely. “Not as lucky as I am.”

The girls squealed—actually squealed—and Priscilla turned back to them to join in, before carefully tucking her poem away.

“What’s that you’ve got there?” One of them asked.

“Oh!” Remus felt stupid for nearly missing his chance. He passed the clipboard over. “It’s for one of my friends—Marlene McKinnon? Anyway, she’s captain of the girls football team, and she’s trying to petition the school to let them play in the tournament at the end of the year.”

“Oh my god, I love that,” Priscilla said. “Who says only boys can play sports?”

“Yeah, it’s complete bollocks,” he agreed. “Would you consider signing?”

He'd hardly needed to ask; one by one the girls went around and added their names to the list.

“Would you like us to take a copy?” Priscilla offered. “Val and I are on the dance team and Katie’s in the art club so we could get you a lot of signatures.”

“Yeah, that’d be great! Thanks so much.”

“No, thank you,” they giggled, each taking a spare copy of the petition and slipping past him.

“And don’t be a stranger, Remus! Let’s meet for lunch sometime,” Priscilla called. “I wanna hear more about your mysterious girlfriend.”

“Yeah. Yeah—totally!” Pleased, Remus looked down at the petition before an idea suddenly occurred to him. If that many girls knew his name, then it stood to reason that they might not object to giving them theirs.

Whispering a silent apology to Lily, Remus left his post in the hallway and ventured into the dining hall. There he began going table to table, interrupting other students until it wasn’t even scary anymore. He even approached Audriana, who had since cooled whatever crush she’d been brewing.

“You’re just too fun to tease, I think,” she cooed, before signing the petition and taking an extra copy to hand out among her theatre group.

When he’d exhausted all of the filled tables, Remus snagged an apple from the fruit trays along the far wall and scurried back out into the hallway. Fully ready to brag to Lily about his feat, he didn’t notice the interruption heading his way until the clipboard was tugged from his hands.

“Collecting donations for the poor and buggery, Loony?” Barty sneered. He waved the clipboard around as if to taunt him, while Regulus stood by beside him, looking indifferent. Remus might’ve reacted badly, had he not had over a week to put Regulus Black from his mind. He pulled the apple from his mouth and squared his shoulders, ready to take the pair head-on.

“Just give it back, Crouch.”

“You know those girls won’t actually be able to keep up in a real tournament,” Barty goaded. “No amount of signatures can change basic biology.”

“Sounds like exactly the sort of misogynistic bullshit I disagree with. Now hand it over and piss off before I write you up for harassing a prefect.”

“Ah, that’s right, ‘Loony the Prefect’—we all best run or else risk detention and a broken nose.” Barty pinched his and moaned mockingly before ripping the stack of petitions off the clipboard and flapping them in Regulus' direction. “Lookie here, Reg. This list’s only got girls’ names on it. Should’ve known since all Lupin's good for is stealing girlfriends.”

Remus crossed his arms. “Wouldn’t have thought that that would bother you much, Crouch, since you hardly have a girlfriend to steal.”

Barty’s sneer turned into a bitter scowl, and with one sharp toss, he scattered the petitions across the floor, throwing the clipboard down for good measure as he retreated up the hall. The pen he chucked the other direction. Afterwards he gave Remus a look that was worthy of a good pounding and began flouncing up the hall.

“Come on, Reg, let's go before we catch a case 'a the queers. Good luck with your silly round robin, Loony!”

Grinding his teeth together, Remus bent down and began collecting the papers, wincing as other students stepped on them and left dirty boot-prints behind.

“Here.”

It was Regulus. He bent down over Remus, holding out a stack of petitions. Remus eyed him sceptically, before taking the papers and adding them back into the pile.

“Shouldn’t you have gone already? Think your crap friend's calling for you.”

“Barty doesn’t tell me what to do.”

Remus scowled further, fetching his clipboard and standing up to tower over the other boy. “Yeah well, I know you’re hard to figure out on principle, but why you’d ever want to hang around him is truly beyond me."

"Yes," Regulus said, "it is beyond you."

He bent down to pick up a few more petitions, passing them over, but Remus turned his nose up.

"What's that you're always saying—'I never asked for your help'?"

"Do you want them or not?"

Huffing, Remus snatched them back. "What’s with the sudden friendliness?”

“I’m not being friendly. We aren’t friends.”

“But we could’ve been, couldn’t we? I thought we might’ve had a chance there. For a while anyway...”

“You’re delusional. We can't be friends, you’re already my brother’s… friend.”

“You’re really starting to sound like a broken record,” Remus snapped. “Hear me now, Regulus Black—I decide who I’m friends with, that’s it. There’s no ‘convenience’ to it. I’m not friends with people because I share a room with them, or lessons—I’m friends with them because I like them. And I even liked you for a while, ‘til you showed your true colours...”

Regulus’ eyes traced the ground. They stayed there for a long time, and eventually Remus had had enough. He turned to go.

“Why does it make me any worse?” Regulus asked suddenly.

“Worse than what?” Remus demanded, whipping his head around.

“Than him.” Regulus’ eyes came up. Hard, and grey. Almost familiar. “I was angry,” he said sternly, “so I got you back. Tell me, how does that make me worse than my brother?”

Remus drew up short. He’d been prepared for another fight—more quippy remarks accompanied by aloof undertones; but for all his wisdom, he’d somehow forgotten. Despite the cold exterior, despite the viper-like tongue, Regulus was still only a sixteen year-old kid.

"It doesn’t.”

“Then why would you want to be friends with him and not me?”

“I didn’t think you wanted to be friends with me, Regulus.”

Regulus seemed to remember himself. He raised his chin. “I... I don’t!”

“That doesn’t sound very convincing.” Remus sighed again, and reached up to scratch the back of his head. “You know, you really messed me up there for a while. What you did really fucking sucked.”

“Guess that makes us even.”

No, it's your fault! Your fault, your fault!



Remus closed his mind off to the voice. He didn’t want it affecting his decisions. He thought about leaving. A part of him even wanted to, but Remus had always been nosy when it came to Sirius and his problems. And whether either of them liked it or not, Regulus was one of Sirius' problems.

So, Remus extended his hand one final time.

“Even, then?”

There was a moment of silence. Maybe it was shock; like Regulus couldn’t believe he was offering him a second chance. It almost looked as though he was going to decline—Remus told himself to expect it. But rather than push it away, or even take it, Regulus gestured to the petitions.

“Have you got a pen?”

Now it was Remus’ turn to be shocked. He'd lost the one Barty had stolen, so he desperately searched his pockets and came back with one of the biros Lily had supplied him with, dubiously handing it over. Regulus took the pen along with his clipboard, stunning him further when he left his name printed neatly beneath the others. He held onto the petition for a moment longer, reading it over, before finally passing it back, the picture of good manners.

“Even.”

“You’ve surprised me,” Remus said.

“Is that good thing or bad thing?”

“Good,” he smiled. “Definitely good.”

Regulus nodded pensively while Remus tried not to let his relief show on his face. To hide it, he glanced down at the petition and remembered the mess that had gotten them there in the first place.

“Look, maybe it’s not my place,” he started, “but just one word of advice?"

"I'm not going to talk to Sirius."

"Ha, no… But you should talk to Trish."

Regulus puckered a bit. Guilty.

"She won't talk to me. Not after what I said."

"Nah, you see, I think she will. It's her hamartia."

It earned him a funny look, but Remus only nodded earnestly.

"Just try apologising to her. You don’t have to be friends or anything, but I know it’d mean a lot. She thinks you’re really cool.”

Regulus hesitated, and suddenly his proud demeanour vanished in favour of that awkward, shy kid Remus had only just begun to notice beneath the surface.

“Alright, I’ll apologise to her. But not because you told me to. For your information, I was going to apologise anyway."

"Of course," Remus smiled. "Oh, and one more thing. Whatever you do, don’t—well… If you see a brownie from now until Christmas, it’d probably be best to avoid it. But you didn’t hear that from me.”

The barest hint of a smile crossed Regulus’ features. Remus counted it as a win.





* * *





Sunday 4th December 1977 – The Night Before Exams…





That evening, they finished their final round of studying early and even skipped dinner. It was all part of the plan; anyone who happened to follow their nose to the Godric kitchenette would’ve found only four boys, innocently cooking a batch of brownies ahead of a long week of exams. In reality, they were plotting—plotting while simmering the ground up hashish in a pot of melted butter. And though it seemed almost a shame to waste good product on sods as sour as Severus Snape and Barty Crouch, all four of them were optimistic.

“I don’t endorse this sort of thing,” Lily said as she passed an armful of dinner boxes and canteen napkins to James, “but dinner is important.”

“Love you too,” James grinned, kissing her forehead and making his girlfriend scoff while she dusted the cocoa powder from the front of his jumper.

Once the brownies were securely in the oven, Remus retired to the common room with a book. He tried reading, but his head kept thumping in rhythm with the grandfather clock and he couldn’t manage more than a page before feeling dizzy. Somehow he’d managed to wake that morning feeling poor and lethargic. It was probably a result of all of his late-night studying, but there was so much to know! And with the poems… ugh.

He tried not to complain. None of the other Marauders seemed to be under the weather, and Remus didn’t want to risk being left behind during the prank. As he finished gorging himself on lukewarm lamb and potatoes, courtesy of Lily, Sirius came to join him by the fire.

“You feeling alright or are we gonna have to postpone?” He asked, pressing a hand to Remus’ forehead.

“Can't postpone,” Remus said, batting his hand away. "Tomorrow's exams."

"We could always wait until another day. Don't matter to me whether Reg fails his chem or maths exam."

Remus shook his head. He'd purposely neglected to tell Sirius that he'd tipped Regulus off to the prank. Better to avoid a fight and let him think his brother had outsmarted them. Even if he hadn't known, getting Regulus to eat anything so suspicious had been a long shot at best.

“Don't worry about it, I’m fine now. You three all finished in the kitchen then?”

Sirius held up a plate of wrapped brownies, grinning slyly. “By tomorrow morning, half of Salazar’s going to be taking their exams while severely off their trolley.”

James and Peter appeared in the doorway of the common room, puffer jackets in hand. “Dorm rounds are done,” James grinned, while Peter clapped his hands together. “Let’s get to messing, lads.”

Not bothering to be very sneaky, they went out the front doors and were rewarded by immediate teeth-chattering cold. It hadn’t snowed yet, but the forecast was calling for it, and the overnights were already dipping below freezing temperatures.

“I hope you saved a few of those for us,” Remus said, eyeing the brownies as they made their way up the dorm’s front path.

“We don’t get stoned on the job,” Sirius said, holding the plate of edibles out of reach.

“I didn’t mean for tonight, you twee idiot, I meant for after exams when we—”

Up front, James spun around on his heel and pushed them both back. “Abort! Abort!” He cried. “It’s Filch’s car!”

“Shit,” Peter hissed, as they all turned to see the caretaker’s rusted lorry creep up the road, headlamps casting a harsh glow like two great yellow eyes.

“We can go around back!” Sirius hissed. "Quick, cut between the Houses!"

Quickly they all turned and booked it back around the side of their dorm where the December frost crunched loudly beneath their boots. There Remus could feel the haze of his breath just in front of his face, but it was a cloudy night and without the moon or the street lamps to illuminate their path it was as though they were walking blind. He stumbled more than once on the uneven lawn, which was treacherous enough in daylight, covered with ice puddles and the occasional molehill. They could still hear the distant bang and rumble of the caretaker's truck, as though warning them to keep their wits about them or risk detention all the way into the new year.

“I can’t see anything back here,” Peter complained. “It’s like walking with a bloody sheet over your eyes.”

“Should we go grab the torches?” Asked James.

“Don’t bother,” Remus said. “Let’s just get on with this so we can get back.”

“Easy for you to say, wolf-man,” Sirius teased. “You can probably see in the dark.”

“I think it would be more ironic if Lupin turned out to be a vampire or something,” James mused. “I mean, he never sleeps.”

Peter chimed in; “What are you talking about? Moony sleeps all the time now. Can’t hardly get him up in the morning.”

“That’s just the morning,” Sirius said haughtily; “At night he’s actually very—”

Remus went to pinch him. He’d just found Sirius’ arm when suddenly the ground came out from underneath him. Literally.

With a surprised yelp, Remus plunged downwards in a short free-fall which ended several feet down on a stiff cushion of dirt. On impact his knee jabbed him in the chest sharply, momentarily winding him as his friends cried out in shock up above.

“Moony!” Sirius shouted. “Holy fuck! Are you okay?!”

Groaning, Remus looked up. A circle was impressed into the inky sky, all of the stars blotted out by clouds. The hole around him had to be at least nine or ten feet deep, but he could just make out the round shape of his friends' heads peering in on him.

“Yeah, m’fine,” he grunted. “Dirt broke my fall, I think.”

“It’s the bloody hole they dug looking for the time capsule,” James’ voice called. “Can’t believe they haven’t filled it in yet! I swear this school’s trying to kill us.”

“Don’t shout,” Peter warned. “Filch is probably still around... Can you reach us if we hold our arms out, Moony?"

In answer, Remus began feeling around for the walls of the pit. It was slimy, covered in dirt and muck, but he managed to find a short tree root lodged into its side. Grabbing hold of it, he reached up and for the barest of moments managed to brush a set of finger tips before the root gave way and he collided back down into the dirt on his arse.

“Shit... Too slippery. Frost has practically turned the bottom to mud.”

“We could get a rope—pull him out,” James suggested.

“There’s also that ladder in the kitchen cupboard,” Peter added.

“Okay. Well, you two go on then, I’m gonna stay with him,” Sirius said.

“Alright, be right back. Hang in there, Lupin!” James chirped, before the sound of shuffling feet began to fade into the distance.

“And be quick!” Sirius shouted after them. Remus shook his head lightly. There wasn’t a version of Sirius Black that came in ‘quiet mode’.

With nothing else to do but wait, Remus tried his best to survey his surroundings. The hole was pitch black, the kind of dark that began to look like grotesque faces when you focused on one spot for too long. He could tell just by puttering around that the bottom was at least a couple of feet across, enough space for him to sit comfortably at least, which he did and instantly regretted as the freezing dirt squelched beneath him. Whatever, he was already covered in muck; he could feel it seeping up his shirt sleeves from his hands and across the knees of his trousers where he fell.

“Moony, you sure you’re alright?” Sirius called from up above.

“Yeah,” Remus called back. “Believe it or not I actually think it’s warmer down here.”

“Well duh, no wind down in a hole.”

Remus smiled to himself and crossed his arms over his chest, glancing up. The sky had begun to clear some, and he could just see the beginning twinklings of stars peaking through.

“It’s like another world down here. You can actually see the stars shining,” he said. "Hey... How's that one John Lennon song go?"

A little snort. “... Are you high?”

“Ha, I wish. Would probably make this a lot more funny. C'mon, you're the one with the perfect memory, tell me how it goes.”

"Superior memory, not perfect."

"That mean you don't know it?"

Another snort. " 'And we all shine on... like the moon and the stars and the sun'... That the one?"

"Yeah." Remus hugged his knees. "That's the one."

There was silence for a moment, and then Sirius began to whistle the tune. Finally he stopped;

“Just you wait, Moons. We’re gonna get you out and finish this prank. You can laugh then.”

“S’long as I get first shower privileges tonight.”

“Of course. You think I’d let such a filthy man crawl into bed with me?”

“You’re impossible.”

Sirius’ head appeared over the edge of the hole, like a dark silhouette. “No, I’m improbable. Unexpected.”

That you are.

Remus kept on staring up. He couldn’t be sure, but he thought Sirius might be smiling. From down below, it was as though he were in the sky—floating amongst the stars like the Sirius for which he’d been named. It was so like him; Sirius was like the sky.

Remus was cold, and wet, and yet somehow content. Sirius was his sky.

“Say,” Sirius started, after a while; “how many of those poems have you written now?”

“Uh, maybe fifty or so?”

“Damn.”

“Yeah. Think I’m gonna stop soon though. I’m running out of adjectives to describe girls’ eyes. There’s really only so many times one can use the word ‘dazzling’ before it loses meaning altogether.”

There was a short chuckle, then; “So... you’re gonna stop soon?”

“Probably, yeah. I’d like to focus on our songs a bit more, I think. At least that way we’ll have something to show James and Pete’s parents over Christmas.”

“Oh. Well, that’s… That’s smart.’

The way Sirius answered made Remus think he wasn’t saying all there was to say, so he squinted up in the dark again.

“Sirius.”

“Hm?”

“Out with it. What’s the matter?”

“Nothing.”

“Sirius.” Remus grabbed a clod of dirt, throwing it up at the edge of the pit.

“... You missed.”

“Out with it!”

There was a great sigh, and then a flourishing hand appeared over the edge of the pit. “I just don’t know how I feel about it, s’all. You… writing love poems for other people.”

“But they're not my love poems."

"I know that! But you're—you're complimenting them. Making them feel good... I just sorta thought you'd only want to do that with me."

"Oh."

“It’s not like it's that big of a deal or anything,” Sirius said quickly. “Not even that much different from songwriting, right? And people paid Wilde and Shakespeare to write for ‘em so… You’re good at it too! It’s why they like them so much. A-And they're nice. Genuine, even. In fact, yesterday Cindy Carlisle showed me hers, and—”

“Sirius—”

“I don’t want you to think I hate them! Because they’re so beautiful. And they’re so 'you' too, and I love you, so...”

“Sirius!”

“… Yeah, Moons?”

“I’m sorry.” Remus frowned deeply. Such an idiot, he was. “I didn’t realise writing those poems would bother you.”

“They don’t! It’s not the poems… it’s… the other people.”

“It’s alright, I understand now,” Remus said. “I’ll stop writing them. Right now—I’m done. I was finished with ‘em anyway.”

“No, you don’t have to stop,” Sirius replied. “It’s good practice, and good money too, obviously. You don’t have to stop just ‘cause it bothers me.”

“Of course I do. We’re dating—why would I ever want to bother you?”

Sirius fell quiet then, as though he hadn’t been expecting such an answer. Because it made him nervous, Remus sat up a bit more, craning his head as though he could catch a glimpse of his love in the darkness.

“Sirius, you can tell me when things bother you,” he called. “I want you to tell me when things bother you. I’m not as good as you—I’m not a mind-reader. But I think this—talking bit... Talking about the things that bother us—well, it’s what a relationship is supposed to be, innit?”

“... You suck.”

“Huh?”

“How about beguiling?” Sirius said suddenly. “ ‘And her eyes were like a beguiling labyrinth, deep and without end’.”

“I—” Remus stopped to let out a chuckle. “I can’t keep up with you.”

“There’s always the classic ‘ravishing’. Ooh, yeah, tell her that her eyes were ravishing. That’ll really get a girl going.”

“How about ‘glorious’ instead?" Remus supplied. " ‘And glory was in the skies, reflected in those grey, storm cloud eyes’. What’d you think—any good?”

He’d meant the rhyme as a quip, but when Sirius said nothing, Remus grew nervous again.

“Sirius…? Come on, I was only teasing. You’re still there, right? … Sirius?”

There was no launching cry—no ‘bombs away!’ —Sirius simply sailed down into the pit in front of him with a heaving grunt, nearly landing directly on top of Remus’ ankles.

“Oh shit—that was way deeper than I thought!” He gasped, wobbling in the muck. Remus gaped up at him, half frozen from surprise.

“What—What the fuck are you doing?!”

Sirius gave him a wry look. “Oh, you know… Figured you’d be lonely down here by yourself. Thought I'd 'drop in'—heh!”

“But you’re supposed to be up there so they can find us in the dark!”

“… Oops.”

“Oh for fuck’s sakes.”

“You’re right though—s’cozy down here,” Sirius said, plopping down next to Remus in the dirt so they were shoulder to shoulder. “Whaddya think, should we cuddle?”

“Shut up.”

“C’moooon, you know you want to. And you were being so romantic a second ago—my little poet.”

“Shove off. James and Peter—”

“Would probably find it very hot and want to join in. We can just tell them we were cold. That we’re staving off fever.”

Remus smiled to himself and rolled his eyes. “Only we would end up stuck in a hole the night before exams.”

“That’s why we’re going to be rock stars and everyone else is going to be ordinary,” Sirius sassed.

Remus reached out and took his hand. Even in the dark—even covered in as much filth as they were—he knew every line and curve of the beautiful pianist’s fingers that instantly opened up and intertwined with his own. It made sense—he had spent the better part of the last two years zoning out on them.

“You sure seem to like Trish,” Sirius said eventually.

“I do,” Remus answered, then when Sirius was quiet again; “What, no quippy jokes?”

“I’ve…” He took a breath. “I’ve decided I wasn’t going to be jealous anymore.”

“Blimey, when’d you decide that?”

“About four seconds ago.”

“Prime timing, that.”

Sirius’ free hand came up, swatting him lightly across the nose and leaving a smudge of dirt behind. “What’s the point of being jealous when all you do is go around making everyone like you so bloody much?”

Remus snorted, wiping his face on his sleeve. “I do like Trish,” he said. “But I think I like her—well—because she reminds me a bit of you.”

“Really?”

“Yeah. So did Tonya, actually. I sort of… look for you in other people.”

“Why would you need to do that when you’ve got the real thing right in front of you?”

“It’s my hamartia, I guess.”

Sirius hummed in delight. “Careful, you start saying stuff like that and I might actually fall in love with you for real.”

Maybe it was the darkness, or the fact that he couldn’t see Sirius’ face and expressions in their entirety. Whatever it was, it cushioned him enough to let the words flow out like a river.

“I love you,” Remus said softly. “More than anyone.”

There was the barest sound of an inhale, and then Sirius’ mouth came up and he settled his lips along Remus’ lips. Remus could practically taste his smile. Hotter than any fever, it burned like the enduring passion of a star. It singed and warmed him all at once.

“I love you,” Sirius said between kisses; “The most.”

“I love you, Sirius,” Remus said back, because he couldn’t stand not saying it. "Always."

I love you, I love you. I am in love with you, Sirius Black.

Heedless of the dirt or the muck, they clung to each other in the darkness. In his head, Remus was already constructing the lie that got Sirius into the pit in the first place when he spotted the familiar yellow of a torch cutting across the top lip of their filthy prison.

“Sirius,” he mumbled against his lips; “Sirius, they’re back—James and Pete.”

Sirius broke away immediately and jumped to his feet, arms flailing. “Here!” He cried. “We’re down here, Prongs!”

Standing next to him, Remus jumped too, both of them shrieking until finally their saviour was bearing down on them with a torch trained viciously in their eyes.

Hand shielding his brow, Sirius swore; “Fuck Wormtail, mind turning your light that way a bit? S’not like we’ve been sitting in the bloody dark this entire time or anything.”

The torch whipped away and Remus blinked around the sun spots in his vision. Then his stomach sank to his knees.

“Ooh, dear, we are in trouble,” Filch sneered, grinning with teeth as yellow as his torch.

Bollocks.





* * *





Probably against his better judgement, the sour caretaker did agree to get them out of the pit. When Remus finally climbed out, covered head to toe in muck, he found James and Peter standing off to the side, both looking rather sorry and glum. They’d been caught on their way back out on their rescue mission, and rather than risk leaving their two best friends to freeze to death overnight, they gave up the ghost and told Filch everything. Though they conveniently left out the part about the weed being in the brownies.

“I’m telling you—they’re a surprise for a friend’s birthday. We were gonna leave them outside their door,” Sirius scowled. Filch had them lined up in front of their dorm, marching up and down the line like a drill sergeant.

“Likely story comin’ from a couple ‘a pumpkin heads out after hours,” he scoffed. “No, I’m confiscatin’ the lot as contraband.”

All four boys exchanged an unsure glance, but Filch had already set the plate of sweets aside. “Now, turn out yer pockets—all of yeh. Let's see what else you've managed to sneak in illegally.”

They did so bitterly, handing over everything from wads of pre-chewed gum (“That’s right nasty, Pete.”) to a near-full pack of cigarettes. Remus lost his second lighter to Filch, and was contemplating his odds of being able to slip his hand into the caretaker’s pocket to get it back when they were all ordered to lift their arms so they could be patted down for any other possible ‘illicit goods’. None of them had any weed on them, but Remus realised too late that his pockets weren’t quite so empty.

“You ruddy mop-sticks hide all sorts of rubbish under these bleedin’ coats—” Filch was saying, before his gnarled fingers fell across the hard shape tucked into Remus’ breast pocket; “What have we ‘ere, ‘ey?”

Before he could stop him, Filch ripped the lapel of Remus’ coat away and shoved his hand down, snatching up his song journal in one fell swoop.

“Oi! Give that back!” Remus cried. He’d forgotten that he’d left it in his coat pocket and seeing Filch’s slimy fingers all over it made him thrum with fury.

“If this little book were so important to yeh, then you shouldn’t have been caught out after hours!”

“You can’t just grab a student like that!” Sirius lashed. “It’s practically assault! We have a right to autonomy and privacy!”

“Rule breakers forfeit all rights to privacy!”

“But you can’t just take our things! What does one little book have to do with being out after curfew?!”

“I’m reviewing it for contraband! Who knows what sort of dirty messages are written in ‘ere!”

“It’s a bloody notebook!” James hollered.

“One more word out of any of you’s and I’ll have yeh muckin’ stables ‘til June!”

Sirius managed a swipe at the journal, but Filch caught him by the wrist.

“Try that again and I’ll break yer fingers,” he threatened, before throwing Sirius back and grabbing Remus by the collar to haul him out front. “Now march, ya bleedin’ ingrates! You’ll head straight to Professor McGonagall's office in the morning!”

Filch slogged them all the way up to the fourth floor of Godric House, muck and all, and left them in the doorway of their bedroom with a final threat; “I see any of you’s out again after hours and I’ll make yeh wish you’d never been born!”

The moment the awful caretaker had shut the door and stormed off, Sirius charged it, wailing on the wood with his boot. “Fucking—DICK!”

“That’s enough, Black,” James sighed. “You’re gonna wake up the whole dorm.”

After stripping out of his dirty clothes, Remus slumped back on his bed. Beyond the embarrassment that Filch might possibly read his songbook, he was left more than a little depressed. The notebook had everything; “September”, his version of Sirius’ “Wag the Dog”, "Tonya’s Song", and even the beginning drabbles of “Hard to Be a Teen”. Every shred and scrap of his songwriting was in there. Now it was all gone, and unlike Sirius he didn’t have the musical memory to replace it.

“Fuck,” Remus hissed, aiming a light kick of his own at his wardrobe.

Instantly Sirius was at his side on the bed. “I’m sorry, Moons. I know what it was that bleedin’ codger took.”

He sighed, holding his head which had begun to ache. “Whatever, I’m tired. I’m gonna go take a shower.”

“It can’t be that bad,” Peter reasoned, while Remus rifled through his hutch for a fresh towel.

“Says you, Wormtail,” Sirius snapped. “You didn’t have much to say when Filch was robbing us blind.”

“Well, I just assumed we’d get it all back."

This gave the other three boys pause.

“You mean break into Filch’s office?” James started.

“Yeah, duh!”

“Pete, we tried that—in year ten. Twice! Filch had us cleaning out the crawl spaces above the science buildings for weeks.”

“I still get nightmares about all the dead squirrels,” Sirius shuddered.

“We didn’t have Moony back then,” Peter reasoned; “And—Filch hadn't confiscated an entire plate of edibles right before either.”

“Oh my god, he’s right,” Sirius said, perking straight up; “In a hour that son of a bitch is gonna be out cold. Christ, this kid might be a genius after all!”

While Peter crossed his arms haughtily, Remus slowly looked up from his hutch.

“Do you really think he’d eat them?”

“Do I think he'd resist eating an entire plate of freshly-baked goods? We’d have a better chance of finding a giant squid in the Dubh,” Peter scoffed. “Nothing ever comes out of Filch’s office, especially not sweets.”

Sirius leapt up from the bed. “This is brilliant! That tosspot doesn’t know there’s weed in them—which means the prank worked after all! By the time he wakes up he’s not even gonna remember what year it is, let alone that he gave us detention!”

James, ever the voice of reason, chimed in; “As much as I want to stick it to Filch, we do have exams in the morning, you know.”

“Oh c'mon!” Sirius cried, surging toward his best friend and clasping him over the shoulders; “What would you rather be known as, Potter? The guy that got a good night’s sleep before one of his boring law exams—which he’s been studying for religiously anyway—or the guy that broke into Filch’s own bloody office when he was utterly caned?!”

The answer was obvious on James’ face, but it was Remus he looked to.

“Well, Moony? It’s your book, and you’re the one who’s gonna have to pop the lock.”

As his friends rounded on him, Remus glanced at the clock on his bedside. He was tired and filthy, and still had a headache… but it wasn’t shit-all hour yet.

“Alright. Let’s go rob the bastard.”

That was all the permission the others needed. Bundling up in whatever mucky coat they could find, they quickly slipped back out into the night. Four boys with a bone to pick.

Filch’s office was located in a tiny building tucked away behind the cafeteria called Bastion Hall, though over the years it’d affectionately earned itself the moniker of ‘the Bastille’, since anyone going in was certainly about to be punished. Remus had only been inside twice, the first time after Filch had caught them setting off firecrackers on Sirius’ sixteenth birthday, and the second just last week when he'd been fleeing the clutches of Audriana and her pack of girls. He’d never made it all the way into the caretaker’s personal office though, and for that he was thankful.

Being one of the older buildings on campus, the Bastille felt more like the Shrieking Shack’s more straight-edged cousin. The floor tiles were chipped and worn and all of the walls had a certain shade of yellow to them, earned from years of age and smoking indoors. Together they snuck in quietly, their hearts thrumming with the excitement of getting to stick to one of Hawkings’ oldest bullies. Sirius, who naturally had the most experience with Filch's office due to his many detentions, took the lead, brandishing them onward in the dark.

“It’s this way,” he whispered, glee and anticipation clear in his voice.

"Remember," James said, "this is a covert rescue mission. We're only taking back what's ours."

"And what we can carry," Sirius sniggered.

They made it to the office door, which had a cross hatch window complete with curtains drawn behind it and a small plaque bearing Filch's name. James and Sirius leaned their heads together to peek through the small slit between each curtain before drawing back with big smiles on their faces.

“He’s in there, alright. Looks like he’s asleep,” Sirius said.

“Did he eat the brownies?” Peter asked.

"Can't be sure. Try and keep quiet with the door, alright Moony?"

Remus nodded, pulling a few pins from his pocket and kneeling down before the doorknob. Its insides were worn down from years of use, but he managed it quick enough, grinning when that familiar tick and click echoed from its joints.

“Thought you said this was going to be hard,” he quipped snidely.

“ ‘Fraid that’s not the only door we gotta get through,” Sirius smirked, making Remus’ smile falter a bit.

Once he’d moved out of the way, James slowly rotated the doorknob. All four of them held their breath as it dropped open, squeaking painfully on its hinges until finally they had a decent view of the grimy man through the gap. Filch was slumped back in a seemingly ancient leather chair with his eyes closed and his feet up on the desk. Next to them, the desk lamp was still on, illuminating a half-eaten batch of Marauders-certified weed brownies.

“Oh fuck yeah,” Sirius breathed, fist-bumping James.

“Make sure he’s really asleep before you start celebrating,” Peter warned as they all straightened up and slipped soundlessly into the room.

“How many d’you figure he ate?” Remus asked.

James squinted at the brownies; “Looks like at least six.”

Creeping up to the caretaker’s side, the Marauders peered down at him. Filch’s eyes were closed and he was buried up to his nose in his heavy winter coat, but he was unmoving—completely still.

“You think he’s dead?” Sirius murmured grimly.

“No way, you can’t die from too much weed,” James said, before his face fell; “Right, Moony?”

“I don’t know, I’ve never tried it!”

They leaned in closer and slowly Sirius held up a single finger. Before Peter could even attempt to stop him, he poked Filch in one wrinkly cheek and the caretaker gave a hoarse snort, making them all wheel back in fright. Though by either sheer dumb luck or the brownie’s effectiveness, Filch stayed asleep, now snoring horribly.

“And what would you have done if he had woken up?” Remus grumbled.

“Ask if he’d like another brownie. Duh.”

"Just don't touch him anymore," James shot, as they all spread out to start their search.

The office itself was covered in clutter; stacks upon stacks of old newspapers and magazines covered every surface, coffee-ringed mugs and overflowing ashtrays littered between it all. One wall was made up entirely of rusted filing cabinets overflowing with files and other bits of paper and there was a coat rack in the corner piled so high with jackets an entire person could’ve been buried beneath. There was only one window in the entire room, which was covered in dead flies with its exterior barred and coated in an endless array of spitballs—some of which were certainly courtesy of Sirius.

“Moony, over here,” James called, ushering Remus over to another door on the room’s far side where they’d all gathered. One look at it told him everything he needed to know about his friends’ first failed attempt to storm the office; the door had at least a dozen locks of varying styles, some that were definitely going to need to be pried off.

“I think I’m gonna need more than a few bobby pins,” he winced. "Anyone see any keys?"

"He always keeps 'em on him," Peter winced, turning to look back at the dozing man. James joined him, scratching his head dubiously.

"Moony, you wouldn't happen to make a good pickpocket too, would ya?"

“Don't bother. It's a good thing Filch always comes prepared,” Sirius grinned, scooping up a crowbar that had been unceremoniously left in an umbrella stand next to the desk.

Once Remus had rid them of the locks he could handle and James had taken a pair of bolt cutters to the thin door chains, Sirius slid the edge of the crowbar up under the final bolt and gently pressed his weight against it. The door gave a deep groan, making them all wince, but still did not give.

“Prongs, come help me out with this.”

With the two of them at it, the bolt began to pry back, millimetre by excruciating millimetre.

“So close!” James grunted, before finally the lock snapped back with a sharp bang and they fell against each other in one big pile. Horrified, Peter and Remus whirled on Filch. The caretaker gave a low grunt through his snores, but kept sleeping, and they relaxed as Sirius tossed the crowbar away with another clatter and popped up to his feet.

“Open sesame,” he grinned, throwing the door wide.

Inside was a mountain of confiscated goods. Boxes towered over one another, dingy from dust and neglect, and there were cabinets full of liquor bottles, glass pipes, and other drug paraphernalia. There was a trunk of prohibited clothes in one corner with a rusted, metal shoe rack next to it, piled high in the same risqué heels worn by the corner girls that came out at night in Soho’s red-light district. Above that was an entire shelf dedicated to banned books and dirty magazines, and as it so happened, a crate of what looked to be spray paint. Just beneath that was several plastic tubs full of water pistols, which must’ve been confiscated from the largest water-battle ever hosted. The room was absolutely a delinquent’s treasure trove.

“How much you want to bet there’s a family of rats living in here?” James asked, pulling the string on the only free-hanging light bulb in the entire room.

“Smells like mould and moth balls,” Peter commented, eyeing a tub randomly overflowing randomly with rubber ducks.

“Oi lads,” Sirius called from next to the trunk of clothes, “think Filch plays dress up?” He held an ugly old bra the size of his head up over his shirt and James snorted.

“I think that belonged to your grandmother, actually.”

“And how would you know that?” Sirius asked, whipping the brassiere at the other boy’s head.

“C’mon Padfoot, you know the old ladies love him,” Remus smirked. James scooped the bra up from the floor and threw it at him in return.

“Alright,” James ordered once they’d stopped laughing, “let’s get our crap and get out of here.”

“What’s the rush, Prongs? Even if ol' Filchy wakes up he’ll be in no fit state to do anything. I want to look around,” Sirius said, pulling open a drawer and inspecting its contents. “Holy fuck—jackpot!” With a triumphant look, Sirius pulled out several roman candles, waving them around and making shooting noises at his friends. James instantly joined him, rifling through eagerly.

“There are some of Bob’s firecrackers in here!” He said gleefully. “Think of what we could do with all these.”

“Burn down the entire school, likely enough,” Peter added, though he didn’t look any less excited as he opened his bag and began filling it with all sorts of explosives.

On a more personal mission, Remus began sorting through his own share of drawers and boxes in search of his songbook. As he did, he ended up coming across an impressive array of tapes and vinyl LPs, which Sirius practically drooled over until James reminded them that they were only to take what was absolutely necessary. (The fireworks, in this case, were absolutely a necessity.) Remus thought he'd found what he was looking for when he unearthed a box of tattered notebooks and journals, but all that was there was a collection of assorted class notes and diaries older than himself. Unsatisfied, he pushed the box away.

Across the room, Sirius beckoned Peter over; “Wormy, get a load of this—” before promptly opening a can of rubber snakes in his face, making Peter jump back and nearly topple a stack of cardboard boxes that was taller than he was.

“At least someone’s having fun,” Remus muttered to himself, before glancing back toward the main office. There was a chance Filch hadn’t bothered to sort through everything he’d taken off them earlier in the night before sitting down to enjoy his stolen midnight snack, which meant that he could’ve still had Remus’ songbook and lighter on his person. The thought didn’t bode well, but he had to try.

Leaving his friends to their nonsense, Remus made his way back into the office and pushed up his sleeves. He’d just rounded Filch’s chair when he spotted his first obstacle; sometime between getting the storage door open and heading inside, Mrs. Norris had taken up residence on the sleeping caretaker’s lap, her yellow, lamp-like eyes staring back at him as though she were daring him to try anything funny.

“Nice kitty,” he breathed, slowly sliding closer. “I’m not gonna hurt you, I just need to…” Biting his lip, Remus slipped his hand into the side pocket of Filch’s coat, feeling around. He didn’t dare take his eyes off of Mrs. Norris, afraid that the moment he did she would come flying at him with her claws extended or worse—wake her master.

Remus’ rifling was rewarded with his personal carton of Embassy cigarettes, which proved well enough that Filch had yet to empty his pockets. He tucked them away for safekeeping before moving on to the next pocket, in which he found Sirius’ cigarettes and three lighters, one of them being his own.

“Moony!” Sirius called suddenly, his voice a strained whisper. “What are you doing?”

Remus looked back to find all three of his friends standing in the storage room doorway, utterly gawping.

“Are you mental?” Peter hissed.

“Just hold on,” he told them, before slowly reaching up to the collar of Filch’s jacket.

"You're gonna get yourself killed!"

Remus ignored the warning. He was so close. Only one more pocket left.

“That’s it, nice Mrs. Norris…”

The cat made a small noise like a trill and he froze, but all Filch did was snort and shift slightly in his chair. When the old man had settled again, Remus pressed on. He was holding his breath and would’ve bet anything that his friends were too, but when he finally managed to slip his hand into the inside breast pocket of Filch’s coat, his fingers brushed the smooth edges of his journal and he was able to grab hold of its cover.

Giddy with victory, Remus pulled his hand back and let out a sigh of relief. “Got it,” he grinned, holding up the book.

“Yeah, Moony!” James cheered quietly, then in perhaps a moment of oversight, he clapped his hands together and that was all it took to spook Mrs. Norris. The cat skittered off Filch’s lap with a yowl and each of them gasped in horror. Instantly a gnarled hand clamped down around Remus’ wrist, squeezing so tightly it threatened to crush his bones like a bird’s. Remus’ stomach launched into his throat as Filch turned his head, slowly opening one eye.

“What... time is it…?” He lurched in that scraggly voice of his.

Remus was speechless at first. It felt like a joke.

“H–H–Half past one."

Filch narrowed his beady eyes before swallowing like he’d tasted something fowl and dropping his head back against the chair. His grip loosened on Remus’ arm, and Remus ripped away, scrambling backwards until he slammed into Sirius' knees. It was only then that he realised that Filch was not in fact getting up to throttle him, but rather had fallen back asleep in his chair.

“Holy shit. You just might be the luckiest son of a bitch I’ve ever met in my life,” Sirius said, helping Remus to his feet.

Remus shook his head grimly. "I think I'm gonna be sick..."

“Glad you got your book back, Lupin,” James said, patting him on the back. “Now let’s get out of here before the old fart actually wakes up.”

With their pockets and school bags full of all sorts of banned bits and bobs, they took the remaining brownies and fled the hall, feeling richer than kings.

“Got all sorts of stuff perfect for pranking,” James was telling Remus while they skittered up the sidewalks. “Rubber snakes, explosives, fart in a can—the works! Padfoot here, even found some of his own tapes that Filch had confiscated after our stereo prank in eleventh year.”

In answer, Sirius held up the tape and kissed it. "Rock 'n' roll is back, baby!"

“We’re so going to get expelled,” Remus grinned, lighting a victory cigarette. Just then Peter shouted from up ahead;

“Hey lads, don’t look now but it’s snowing!”

They all glanced up at the night sky. It was bright and Remus could see the tiniest flickerings of little snowflakes as they drifted down to earth.

“First snow fall,” he mumbled. “Always unexpected.”

“This is great,” James declared, batting Sirius fondly and not looking the least bit tired; “We got everything back and then some and in less than two weeks we’ll be heading home—all of us, together. We should make more plans! Maybe try and see a live show—catch a glimpse of our futures, yeah? Is that new song of yours ready yet, Lupin?”

Remus pat his breast pocket, where his newly-returned songbook was securely tucked away. “Almost, Prongs.”

“Brilliant! S’all brilliant!”

“So brilliant we should celebrate,” Sirius suggested, before drawing to a stop under one of the buzzing road lamps and reaching into Remus’ pocket himself and withdrawing his lighter. He tossed it at James, who caught it with a questioning look.

“You mean…?”

Sirius smirked, and at the same time, both boys said;

“Roman candles.”

“Oh hell yeah!” Peter cried, dropping his bag on the icy sidewalk as he and James eagerly began to root through it.

Remus stood back, content with his fag, but as he watched Sirius just turned around in front of him and blocked the view.

“Here," he said, holding up another zippo. "To make up for the one I just stole. And the one I lost...”

The lighter was silver, made with cheap plate metal that was already tarnishing on one side and turning brassy. Remus recognised it instantly. Utterly stunned, he reached out and took it, turning it over in his hands. It was the one Tomny had given him the day before eleventh year, the same one he'd lost to Filch ages ago. He was suddenly trembling, and not from the cold.

“You remembered!” Remus exclaimed, looking up at Sirius.

“ ‘Course. It meant a lot to you, I couldn’t very well leave it behind." Sirius grinned, then bit lip giddily. "That’s the right one, right? I had to sort through about a million of those little fuckers.”

"Blimey..." Remus’ face split into a smile, even though he felt like half-crying. “It’s definitely the right one. It’s Tomny’s actually. He—er… he gave it to me before I came to Hawkings.”

“Oh, well in that case—” Sirius made a grab for the lighter, but Remus pulled his hand back in time.

“What? What are you doing?”

“Can’t have you thinking ‘bout that toff every time you light up. My pride couldn’t take it.”

Remus laughed, unable to help himself. “I thought you were trying to be less jealous?”

“Of girls. I said nothing about other guys.”

“Shameless, you are.”

Sirius opened his mouth to deliver what was undoubtedly another clever quip, but suddenly a loud pop sounded from behind them, followed by a spectacular show of red as James aimed one of the roman candles up at the sky.

“Oi, Black,” he called, before dropping his arm and training the firework in their direction; “Think fast.”

Sirius tilted his head. “You wouldn’t—”

Oh, but he would.

The candle fired and Remus and Sirius had to dive apart to avoid it, hitting the grass with two low groans. They looked up in time to see a second shot—this one green—arc over their heads from Peter.

“You’re mental!” Sirius shouted. "And so dead!"

Cackling, James and Peter loped away across the frozen lawn while Sirius tossed Remus a firework of his own, quickly fumbling with a lighter and the fuse.

“This is how people end up in the hospital!” Remus warned, grappling for the roman candle before narrowly avoiding another green burst. “Motherfu—! You’re gonna regret that, Pete!”

“Bring it on, Moony!”

“Marauders, ATTAAAACK!” Sirius cried, racing after James with his candle pointed ahead of him like a magic wand. It blew red, lighting up his laughing face in the darkness.

No one, in fact, ended up in the hospital.

It was a good night.
