For my Lily bloom in J—”





In a sudden fit of protest, the tape recorder began shrieking with the tell-tale sounds of jammed plastic, and James’ singing came to an abrupt halt.

“Bugger,” Remus hissed, hitting the eject button and ripping the 8-track tape from its slot. The slight smell of melted PVC followed, making them both wrinkle their noses in distaste. “Must’ve gotten caught up inside the machine."

“Damn. I knew I wouldn’t sound magnificent or anything but that just stings,” James snorted sarcastically.

“You sounded great,” Remus amended, squinting the tape. “It doesn’t look all that damaged. Will probably still play actually, though I wouldn’t risk trying to copy over it now.”

Shrugging, James took the cassette from him and flipped it around, sliding it back into its slot and hitting play. This time instead of recording, it played the song back to them in all its raw and genuine goodness. At the very end, there was a little rippling sound and then Remus could be heard muttering ‘bugger!’ before the tape cut off.

“We could get another one from the AV room,” he offered. “Though we might have to wrestle it off Pete.”

“You know what, I sorta like it this way.”

“You don’t think you weren’t dragging the bridge a bit? … Ha—just taking the piss.”

James scowled; “I was gonna say that now it’s got a bit of both of us.”

“Then you’re a sap.”

“Guess I am.” Smirking slightly, James yanked the 8-track from the machine while Remus handed him a felt pen. He quickly scribbled the date across the cassette's back. The front he finished off with ‘To Daisy, all my love, JP’.

“You really think she’s gonna like it?” He asked after.

“No,” Remus answered, “I think she’s gonna love it.”

James grinned down at the tape, all dimples, and Remus suddenly felt disappointment surge over him. Not at James, but at himself.

“Hey James?”

“Mm?”

“You care about Sirius, right?”

“Like my own brother," James supplied, before furrowing his thick brows furrowed together in question. "Why? Is something the matter with him?”

“No, sorry. I was only thinking about something he said earlier.”

“Which was what?”

Remus bit his lip. “Prongs, do you believe in keeping secrets?”

“Depends. In third year Simeon tried to convince all of us that babies came from space. Said it was a secret only adults knew."

"Did you believe him?"

"Only for a few years." James smiled, and tilted his head. “Has something happened, Moony?”

“No… not really.”

"Would you tell me if it had?"

Remus took a deep breath, straightening his back and giving James his best Janus-faced smile. “I’m fine, Prongs. Don’t worry about me. Just got caught up thinking about how it’s gonna feel not being with the guys for Christmas.”

"You mean your Tom friend and them."

"Yeah..."

“Well, don’t be too sad, you've got us to keep you company after all. And if you’re really missing the ambience, we can just set something on fire. Like a rubbish bin. S’long as it’s outside, of course. Mum would have a fit otherwise.”

Remus smiled, despite himself. “Thanks, Prongs. You’re a real mate.”

James set a hand on his shoulder, squeezing it kindly. “Anything for the world's most dangerous Marauder.”





* * *





It wasn’t always hard. Sometimes imagining a life with Sirius was easy.

“Plants! We should get loads of plants. Big ones! The kind that climb right up to the ceiling and ruin all the walls.”

“Do you even know how to take care of a plant?”

Sirius would smile. “Can’t be any harder than taking care of you.”

And Remus would melt, just a little bit. “In that case we’d need a lot of light.”

“Yes!” Sirius agreed. “We’ll find a place with big windows—or maybe a skylight. They have those in London, yeah? And your books can go there!” He swept an arm out, toward whatever imaginary wall he was picturing. “We’d have to display my records too of course. Find a great set up for the stereo. Think we could build one?”

“You and me? Not likely. But we could hang a photo of Mick Jagger over the dining room table.”

“And Hendrix in the toilet, with a claw-footed tub!”

“Isn’t that a little tacky?”

“Of course, but who’s ever lost out to a little bit of ‘tack’?”

Remus chuckled to himself, the feeling of Sirius’ hands curling into his hair. It was a Thursday and nothing exceptional spectacular had happened, but somehow, it felt like they were the only two people in the entire world. Like Sunday.

“How ‘bout Clapham?” Sirius whispered later that night, after he’d snuck into Remus’ bed. They were so close, Remus could feel the tip of Sirius’ nose brushing against his own.

“Sure, if you like being knifed on your way home,” he murmured back, only half lying.

“How stirring. I hear Hyde Park is nice in the winter, maybe we should look for a place with a view.”

A sudden snore cut across the room. Peter.

“Ngh… no, James… you’ll set off the burrito trap early… not enough… nghh… salsa…”

Sirius snorted into his hand, then; “We’re totally gonna be stuck with these tossers forever.”

“Yeah,” Remus murmured. “But a view would be nice.”

As their friend’s breathing evened out, Sirius drew a finger up the side of Remus’ cheek, tracing the shape of him. “I am going to buy so many shitty leather jackets.”

“Mm…” Remus kissed his finger. “And what else?”

“A new pair of Doc Martens.”

“Yeah?”

“Mhm. And then I’m going to beat the shit out of them for no reason at all. We’ll get you some new trainers too. Like those red Chucks we saw in Camden.”

“You want to dress me up?”

“Ha. If I had it my way you’d be naked all hours.” Sirius smirked devilishly in the dark. “Also, m'gonna buy a motorbike and use it to wake up all our neighbours when we come ripping home from a show at the crack of dawn.”

“Just don’t come to me with any injuries. Blisters or otherwise.”

“You mean you wouldn’t want to nurse my wounds? What happened—"

"Shhh!"

Sirius laughed noiselessly. "What happened to that dashing Moony in the bathroom—the one who bandaged all my wounds for me?”

“He found some sense. I think I baby you too much, Padfoot.”

“You never know, maybe I’d like being babied by my baby.”

They kissed, and when they were tired, they slept. Or, Sirius slept. For Remus, sleep still felt impossible. He couldn’t decide if he were up or down. These moments with Sirius made him feel up, but the uncertainty of each day and night wore on him, and it wasn’t just because of exams.

It felt good that Sirius wasn’t retreating from him at least. After their talk, Remus had been afraid that he’d shut him out, but whether it be because he had real faith in him, or because he couldn’t stand the quiet, Sirius remained familiar. There were no cold-shoulders—no resentment—and eventually Remus was able to relax a little. There were things to look forward to during the holiday, after all. The two and a half weeks at Potter Cottage were sure to be warm and friendly and genuine, but there was no astronomy tower in East Finchley, and James had a big family. If the rumours were to be believed, then even the hall cupboard would be packed with a cousin or two. Sirius had his own bedroom at the Potters now, but that would be given up for Lily and the room Remus had stayed in was being occupied by Effie's great aunt Binita. The woman was apparently a hundred and two and slept with the fireplace raging even during dead summer.

“So you two are gonna be bunking with me,” James offered kindly, as they continued going over plans for the trip home. Peter still had maths to revise for and therefore was missing, but Lily had completed their humble group of four in his honour. With her in tow, they'd met up in the Godric common room, as Remus had started running a fever and didn't much feel like leaving the dorm.

“Dad’s still got the old cots we used for camping, so at least you won’t be on the floor," James continued. "Might just have to wipe the dust off."

“Oh sure, we get it. We’ll be on the cot in Potter’s room,” Sirius said snidely, elbowing Remus with a suggestive wink. "We don't mind a little camping do we, Lupin?"

“What are you on about now?” Lily asked with a tone of annoyance.

“Nothing—Lupin and I will be totally bunking with Potter. Gooooot it.”

James’ eyes shot wide while Lily’s cheeks burned. “If Mum catches Lily and me in the same room she’ll hang me on the wall like mistletoe.”

“Oh? How nice. I hear mistletoe’s good for snogging.”

Lily moaned. “You’re horrible.”

Sirius winked in Remus’ direction again, while Remus just sipped his tea. He wasn’t about to fight it—if James and Lily caved then it meant they’d get a room to themselves for an entire holiday. He just hoped the door had a lock.

“Don’t pretend you’re not excited, Evans,” Sirius started up again.

“Of course I’m excited, it’s Christmas.” Lily pushed her hair from her face, looking haughty. “And it’s the first time I’m spending the holiday away from home. You should’ve heard the fit Pet threw. Mum and Dad never let her stay away for so long when she was our age.”

“The woes of being an older sibling,” Sirius sighed. "You young'uns have no idea how easy you've got it."

"Does this mean you've talked to Reg again then?" James asked gingerly.

"You mean since you pulled that little saviour stunt of yours? No, as a matter of fact, I haven't. I mean, did you really think that the tosser was gonna give me the time of day twice in one week?"

Sniffling slightly, Remus leaned in, getting the feeling that he was somehow out of the loop. "I don't understand, you mean you actually talked to Regulus?"

"Aren't you listening? I said I tried. If the little git doesn't want to talk to me, it's on him."

"What did you say?"

Sirius rolled his eyes. "Ask Potter. Practically breathing down my neck, he was."

"Only because you refused to do it on your own," James rebuffed. "I just thought it would be nice to tell Reg our plans. See if he'd like to... y'know, tag along. It was only to be nice, of course!"

"That was nice of you," Lily agreed. "Pet and I don't always get along, but I would hate going home without her. It wouldn't feel like Christmas with one of us missing."

Sirius thumped his palm against the common room table. "Thanks for that stirring addition, Evans, but my brother took one look our way and told us to fuck off. Little Reg would rather swallow his own tongue than follow us back to Potter's, and I say, more power to him. Maybe now he'll finally get to be the only child he's always dreamed of being, ha!" He looked at Remus then, probably expecting a smile, and when he didn’t get one, Sirius straightened up in his chair with an air of dismissal.

“No matter. This is still going to be a great holiday. Family be damned.”

“Don’t jinx us now, mate,” James said. “Still got a few exams left.”

“No, it is,” Sirius insisted; “I can feel it.”

It didn’t seem like an intentional jab, but Sirius’ remark had gauged a deep crevice into Remus’ confidence. He didn’t think Sirius would offer him an ultimatum, Either you tell them or I will; but the only other alternatives he could think of were breaking up or living a lie, and he didn’t want that either. So, Remus sought the advice of the only person he could think of.

His ex-girlfriend.

“No, I haven’t told anyone else aside from you and Sirius,” Marlene said, when he’d asked a day later. They were alone together on a bench outside the cafeteria, the snow-covered lawns stretching out in front of them like shimmering fields of ice and crystal. Sometime near the middle of exam week, Remus’ light malady had mutated into a persistent cold. He felt gross, but apparently wasn’t beyond the realm of snoggability quite yet. Sirius still laid with him every night, dreaming of their imaginary flat. Those moments were easy, it was the days that sucked.

“It’s just me and Nicole,” Marlene went on, breath coming out in a haze; “And Chastity, I suppose, but she ain't likely to tell anyone. She’s back to dating Tristan Thomas now anyway.”

“You’ve thought about telling the girls though, right?” Remus said, coughing into his elbow. “Or even just… I don’t know, Mary?”

“Well fuck, of course I’ve thought about it, but am I gonna say anything? Not a chance. Not now anyway.”

“Why not? Are you still afraid of how they’d react?”

Marlene covered her face with her hands. “Remus, I’m sorry, but I really can’t talk about this right now. Not right before we go home.”

“Oh.” He tucked his hands into either armpit. “Right. Sorry…”

There was a sigh, and then Marlene was looking at him sadly. “Things are more complicated than just telling people, I think,” she said. “It's hard not to wonder who they might tell. And I... Well, things feel a bit different now. Like, I can’t imagine myself with a man anymore."

"Really?"

She shook her head. "I’ve tried. It was easier when I was a kid, but now we're more grown and—"

"Sirius said the same thing..."

"He understands."

And I must not then, Remus thought bitterly.

"When we dated," Marlene started, "I thought it might work out with you. That I could like you the way I like girls, but it just didn’t end up like that. And I’m not sure how to tell people that without making it sound like I’ve changed. It’s like, I’m still me, I’ve just… grown up some.”

Remus nodded, and Marlene slid her hand along the bench in offer. He took it, and squeezed her gloved fingers.

“There’s something else, isn’t there?” She asked timidly. “Is it Sirius then? Has he said something?”

It was as though a breath had turned to ice and lodged itself in his throat. Remus coughed again, trying to clear it away, but the sob built up and up until his eyes were pricked with tears.

“I like him so much, Cherry,” he swore, “but what if I’m wrong about all this?”

“What do you mean, love? Are you thinking that maybe you don’t like guys after all?”

He hung his head. “No—I know I like guys, but Sirius, he—he’s so sure. So sure about everything! ... What if I’m just dragging him along behind me?”

Marlene sighed and leaned into his shoulder, hugging him tightly. “You gotta talk to him, Rem. Before you implode.”

He wondered how to tell her that talking was the very problem. They talked so much that they just ended up going in circles. He didn’t want to be angry with Sirius for doing something that he needed so desperately, but he couldn’t help but feel like Sirius was leaving him behind. Remus wished he had Tomny to talk to, or even Tonya, who he’d sparsely thought of in recent months, but both were miles away, and he wasn’t sure he could stomach the conversation over the phone. So rather than talk, he did the next most impulsive thing he could think of. The first chance he had alone with Sirius, Remus initiated one of the most intense snogging sessions they’d ever had.

Sirius was more than surprised—they were in the corner stacks of the library, barely out of sight—but he never pushed him away, and Remus just kept up. If he couldn’t say the words, then maybe there was a chance he could make Sirius understand with his actions.

Every moment they had alone together following his and Marlene’s conversation were spent snogging; holding each other up against the first available surface and doing just about anything time would allow. They had more close-calls during this short whirlwind of affection than ever before, but a desperate sense of recklessness had already taken over. It was as though he had to prove that their relationship was worth having even if no one else knew about it—because it was the only thing that made sense. But if Remus had been allowed a shred of omniscience, he would have seen himself spiralling, and might have had the time to realise that the faster he fell, the harder the crash back to earth would be.

“Remus?”

He lifted his chin from the top of his guitar case to find Sheila walking toward him down the hallway, her heeled Beatle boots clicking on the tile. They’d finished their music exam ages ago, but Remus had stuck around, telling the other Marauders he had prefect duty. He didn’t really, he just wanted to be alone for a while.

“What are you doing here?” She asked, stopping beside him. “Shouldn’t you be at supper?”

“Wasn’t feeling very hungry.”

Sheila glanced at the wall across from them—at her and Hope’s photograph. She sighed a little, and it was almost wistful.

“Come with me then, hey?” She nudged his arm fondly. “We’ll have some tea.”

He followed her back to the room, but rather than make them sit in the tiny office, Sheila poured him a cuppa and together they set up along the orchestra risers. As he waited, Remus thought of the exam. James had done brilliantly on his recital, although he’d been quite worried about his results of the written component afterwards. Peter had done less spectacular during the practical, but scored near top of the class on the written. And of course Sirius had breezed through it all.

“You’re the same age now as we were then, in that old photo,” Sheila recalled, as she handed Remus his cup and came to join him on the risers. She was wearing a flowery white blouse tucked into red gingham slacks—quite tame for her, all things considering—but she’d made sure to match the red to her hair scarf. The entire ensemble made Remus think she looked a bit like Audrey Hepburn.

“Funny how people age and photos don’t,” he answered blithely, sipping his tea. Sheila eyed him, but only stirred hers with a spoon.

“I thought you were wonderful during your mock-recital today. You’re really starting to get to know your way around that bass. Have you given any thought to trying out a different instrument?”

“Guitar,” Remus said quickly. “I’m learning a bit of guitar.”

“Oh?”

Before he could stop her, Sheila was up and moving again. She quickly zipped across the room to her office, and after a short clatter, reemerged with an instrument case in hand.

“Might need a bit of a tune-up, but she’s a personal favourite,” she said, setting it down in front of Remus. The case itself was worn—smoothed over by years of love and use—but when he flipped the snaps up and lifted the lid, what was inside took his breath away. It was a Martin acoustic guitar in pristine condition, made of a rich mahogany colour and polished to a shine. Bob Dylan played guitars like this. David Gilmore. Eric Clapton. Legends.

“Go on then,” Sheila prodded. “Show me what you’ve got.”

He didn’t have much, but the instrument was too beautiful to keep in its case. Remus withdrew it carefully, quickly tuning each string while Sheila watched, her chin balanced on one hand.

“I’m not gonna sing or anything,” Remus warned.

“Oh no, never,” she smirked. “Know any scales?”

“Yeah.”

“Alright, give us a C major then.”

He did as she asked, and with no mistakes to boot. Pleased, Remus glanced up and Sheila nodded.

“Good! Now D minor?”

He knew that one too. Apparently there was a point in practice. Take that Sirius.

“That’s brilliant, Remus, just watch out for that pinky… Can you show me any more?”

“Uh… E major, maybe?”

She gestured for him to go on, and Remus looked back down at the guitar but this time as he set his fingers to the keys, he messed up.

“That’s alright, try it again,” Sheila encouraged. He did so, and she nodded him on. “Faster.”

So, Remus went faster.

“Again. Faster.”

He went faster.

“Faster!”

On his third loop around, Remus’ index finger slipped, creating a loud thwang! that had them both wincing and laughing.

“I’d say that’s pretty good for a beginner,” Sheila mused, before holding her hands out. “May I?”

He passed the guitar back, and Sheila kicked one leg up over the other. She found herself in the strings quickly, and the next thing Remus knew, she was singing.

“ ‘Don’t it always seem to go, that you don’t know what you got ‘til it’s gone—paved paradise and put up a parking lot…’”

She kept playing, mostly humming and poking fun at the melody, and finally Sheila clapped her hand over the strings and grinned.

“Admittedly, I’m not much of a singer. Your mum was leagues better than I ever was. She used to be able to—as they say—charm the birds from their trees.”

Remus dropped his gaze to the guitar, and Sheila must’ve caught it, because she handed the instrument back for him to pluck at.

“I hear you don’t have much in the way of plans for university?” Sheila prodded. When he raised a brow, she shrugged innocently. “We teachers do talk to one another, you know.”

“I suppose you’re going to try and talk me into applying then?”

“No, not really. The world's too vast to be hung up on institutions forever. And I knew your mum, and she had no real desire to go to school either. At least not the traditional sort.”

She uncrossed and then recrossed her legs, and when Remus said nothing, seemed to take his silence as permission to continue;

“Hope only wanted to play piano. She would’ve played it from dawn until dusk if you’d have let her—even had a dream of doing it professionally. But when her parents suggested she get married, she gave it up.”

Because he was surprised, Remus finally asked; “Couldn’t she have been married and also followed her dream?”

“That was her plan actually. She’d even accepted a seat in a top conservatory to begin training, but in the end she backed out.”

“Why?”

“Because she found out she was pregnant.”

Remus didn’t even have it in him to be shocked. He simply clutched the guitar’s neck more tightly, glaring down at the floor.

“So what—she couldn’t have a dream because she had me instead?”

“What? Oh no. Remus, please don't think..." Sheila sighed, then leaned forward to look him in the eye. “You've misunderstood me. Hope loved you, Remus, truly. There was only one thing in the entire world she wanted more than music.”

“And what was that?” He asked miserably.

“To be a mum.”

Remus could’ve clawed his own eyes out. They betrayed him—instantly burning with seventeen years worth of unwept tears. If Hope Lupin had wanted to be a mother so badly, then why hadn’t she stuck around long enough to do it?

“Don’t you see, Remus?” Sheila said. “You were her dream come true.”





* * *





Friday 17th December 1977





It was with great reluctance that Remus phoned home. He’d waited until the second-to-last day of term to do it, and although Effie had been so kind to pre-arrange everything with Giles herself, Remus still figured he owed it to the old man to let him know his plans.

“I should tan your hide,” Giles’ stern voice rumbled through the phone. It was morning and Remus was god-awful tired, but he always enjoyed their friendly back and forth.

“Think you can reach it from London?”

“I see you haven’t lost any ‘a that sass… How did your exams go?”

“They were only mocks.”

“And?”

“And they went great, thank you."

“Great? Not just ‘fine’?”

“I could just hang up, you know.”

Giles chuckled, and somehow Remus found the sound soothing. He wouldn’t have said so—that’d be embarrassing—but either way the chance was taken from him when his body was suddenly wracked with coughs.

“Blimey, you alright, son?”

“Yeah,” Remus wheezed. “Just a cold. I’ll get over it. But I was calling to tell you that I’m gonna stay at James’ for the holiday.”

“And you're just telling me this now?"

"Does that mean I can't?"

A gruff sigh. "You sure you’re feeling up to it?”

“Mhm.” He couldn’t stand being home anyway. Not now. Not after Sirius and Sheila and… fuck.

“Alright,” Giles said, “but you should come home at least once. See the dogs, have a meal or two. Your father and Sandra have already left for the Riviera. It’ll just be the two of us—and the lasses in the kitchen, if you’re lucky.”

“I dunno. You might ask me more questions about school, and—eugh—university.”

“Promise I won’t.”

Remus smiled, wiping his sleeve beneath his nose. “I’ll phone ya. Swear.”

“I still get to be the one to pick you up from the station, right?”

“Wouldn’t have it any other way, Gil.”

Another chuckle, and then Giles grimaced. “Ugh. This damn heartburn. Doc says I’m not allowed to eat fatty foods anymore. No more steak or bacon, can you believe it? Dunno what he’s on about—I’m as healthy as a horse.”

“A forty year-old horse, maybe.”

“Exactly! Not a day over forty—it’s what I keep telling him.” Giles gave a laugh that descended into another bout of hawking. Remus supposed it made them both disgusting and ill.

“Oh!” Giles said suddenly; “Reminds me, I found some old trunk in your room the other day. White outside, brass handles, practically falling apart—sound familiar?”

Remus let out a breath. Hope’s trunk. He hadn’t brought it that term. Ever since blending his records in with Sirius’ collection, there’d been no need.

“Yeah. S’just an old thing. You can get rid of it.”

“You sure?"

"Yeah, don't use it anymore anyway."

"Understood. Now you enjoy that ride home tomorrow. I’ll be there to pick you up when you and those lads ‘a yours arrive.”

“Kay. I should go anyway, I’ve got prefect stuff.”

“ ‘Prefect stuff’? Oh, if only that therapist ‘a mine could see you now.”

“Shove off. As if you have a therapist”

They said their goodbyes then, and Remus hung up, immediately bursting into another coughing fit that left his entire chest sore. It’d started with the fevers, then a runny nose, and now this. At least Sirius hadn’t seemed to catch it. A miracle, considering how often they’d been snogging lately.

But there wasn’t time to be sick, he was going home tomorrow, and today... Well, today he had a prefect partner to contend with. If being with Sirius was like plunging down on a never-ending rollercoaster, then trying to navigate Regulus Black was like trying to climb a mountain with no peak. Sirius was never silent, he was loud and obnoxious and gloriously free. But Regulus was none of those things. In the beginning Remus had just thought him quiet—quiet and bitter and unwilling to change. But he knew better now. He knew that silent and quiet were not mirror images of each other. Instead they were two sides to the same coin; you could be silent, or you could be quiet. Sirius was never quiet, but he could be deafeningly silent. He could be that kind of silence that seemed to say all the things words couldn’t. And it occurred to Remus, as the two of them were cleaning up after the Hawkings staff holiday party, that Regulus Black had his own iteration of silence as well. He hadn’t tried snapping at him for the amount of mop suds Remus was dripping across the floor, and neither had he made any sarcastic remarks about the festive decor or the small collection of liquor bottles someone had tried to hide at the bottom of the rubbish bins. He was simply withdrawn, moving about the room like a ghost.

“So, how’d the fifth years' little concert go?” Remus asked finally, desperate to fill the emptiness. “Sorry I couldn’t make it—had a history exam.”

Regulus dropped a tray of half-eaten fruit cake into a large rubbish bin. “It went fine,” he said numbly. “They got through most of the song at least.”

“Oh, that’s—well, that’s great.”

“Mm.”

Remus stretched awkwardly. “The kids—they’ve really started to like you, hey?”

“If you say so.”

“Charlotte clings to you.”

“She just likes the violin.”

“She called you magnificent three times the last time we were there. Said your playing was ‘really-super-uber good’.”

Regulus kept his back to him, slowly collecting the last of the paper plates and throwing them in the bin, and Remus felt defeat wash over him like a wave. He and Regulus may have managed to put their general differences behind them to get through their prefect duties, but they were far from friends. Perhaps he was expecting too much.

Sighing, Remus turned back to his mop.

“They asked me if we’d do it again next term,” Regulus said suddenly.

Remus’ head snapped up. Regulus wasn’t looking at him, but he’d turned, clutching a small tower of styrofoam cups in his hands.

“You mean like keep teaching the kids?”

“Yeah, but only a few times a month.” Regulus tossed the rubbish in the bin. “It was Buchanan’s idea. She—er—she came to see the show.”

It was unlike Regulus to stumble with his words. It made him sound more his age—more human, perhaps. It made Remus soften.

“I hope you said yes. We still haven’t gotten to ‘Für Elise’ after all.”

There was that fleeting smile again. It graced Regulus’ mouth—so like Sirius’ mouth—but was gone a moment later as he turned his gaze to the window. He looked forlorn; tired. Sirius had always looked the same way right before leaving school. There had be an alternative.

“Hey Regulus, have you ever given any thought to staying at school for Christmas?”

“Why would I do that?” Regulus retorted sharply.

"Lots of people stay over the holidays. Mostly to study, but... You just seem like like something’s bothering you."

"That's none of your business, is it?"

Remus sighed awkwardly. "Well, do you really want to go home? I know Sirius talked to you and all but—"

"Please, not that again. You and your incessant obsession with my brother is really starting to wear on me."

Temper momentarily ignited by the quick dismissal, Remus threw the mop to the ground—creating a clatter so spectacular that Regulus jumped and turned around again.

“You didn’t answer my question,” he said sternly.

“I never agreed to answer your bloody question!”

“So you’re a coward then?”

“Why don’t you just fuck off, Lupin?!”

Remus mentally punched himself. “I didn’t mean it like that. I just meant to say that you don’t have to go back if you don’t want to. There are things you could do instead.”

“Such as following somebody home like some stray? Follow you? Sorry to say that not all of us are blessed with our own personal delinquent.”

“Does that mean you actually want to go back there, to the ‘Ancient and Most bloody-fucking noble House of Black’? All by yourself?”

“What else am I supposed to do? It’s home.”

The answer told Remus everything he needed to know. Slowly he picked up the mop, clutching it with both hands. “My house never felt like home,” he said plainly. “Never. I don’t think I even knew what ‘home’ was supposed to feel like until I left. And I may not know much, but what I do know is that home isn’t where other people say it is. Home is the one place you can be yourself. A front door and a bedroom don’t give you that—people do. People you love.”

“Love? Is that what you told my brother to get him to leave?”

The accusation rocked him to his very core. “Regulus, I didn't do anything! Your parents sent Sirius to Belgium. He had to run away from another fucking country! He didn’t—He didn’t leave you!”

“You don’t know anything!”

“Then try explaining it to me!”

“It’s so easy for him!”

“What’s easy?”

“Everything!” Regulus shouted. “He has everything! Everything comes to him with such ease—it’s damning! What with his friends and his talent and marks and even that fucking boyfriend and—”

Regulus froze instantly, eyes boring into the floor tiles as though he were searching for a way to take the words back. It was regret on his face, clear as day, and Remus could hardly believe it.

“The what…?”

Regulus visibly paled, and Remus knew the look. Like he'd said something he shouldn't have.

“Forget it. This is stupid. Let’s just finish this and be done with it.” Regulus spun around, looking for something else to clean, but the tables were clear, the chairs stacked. There wasn’t so much as a piece of tinsel left to distract him, and so he began ringing his hands, looking back and forth as though he were craving another distraction. Remus wouldn't give it to him.

“Regulus, do you mean…?” Miles. The name hung in the air like a storm cloud, and afterwards Regulus dipped his head, squeezing his shoulders in very tightly as though he could make himself disappear.

“Of course he told you…”

“How do you know about that?” Remus demanded, even more firmly this time. There was a short silence, but finally Regulus set both hands on the table before him, spreading his fingers as though he were grounding himself. When he began his confession, he seemed to Remus small and frail.

“He… He was always getting these letters when we were at home. He never let me read them, of course, but I knew he was sneaking them in. So one day I waited for the kid that was always bringing the post and I... Well, I fucking took them. Then I made him swear he wouldn’t tell Sirius, said I would rat him out to our mother—get him fired. I had no idea when I opened it that he was… well.” Another pregnant pause, and this time Remus caught the flash of Regulus’ shoulders as they trembled. “I knew what she would do if she found it, so I burned it. I never snooped again, I swear.”

Remus swallowed thickly, looking at the ground. “And Sirius, does he…”

“Know it was me? Of course not. And I never told anyone either. They’d have disowned him ages ago if they did.”

“And what—you didn’t want that?”

Regulus whipped around, a look of excruciating hurt across his face. “Why would I want that?”

“I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to—”

“I know how you all think of me. That I’m just some carbon copy of everything Sirius hates. That I’m the worst of him.”

“Reg—I–I mean, Regulus, no—no, we don’t think that.”

“He does. But I guess it doesn’t matter now anyway. He’s got a new family… And a new boyfriend.”

Remus felt his blood run cold. Suddenly he couldn’t see Regulus at all. It was just that dark pit, with endless mud clinging to ever inch of him—burying him. Blocking out the stars.

“… How did you find out?”

“Figured it out myself. Wasn’t that hard, once I started paying attention.”

He might vomit. He would vomit. The room was spinning.

“Regulus—”

“Just stop, Lupin. I’ve had enough. He’s left and that’s that. But I’m tired now, and I’d like you to go. You can just leave the mop. And don't worry, I'm not going to tell anyone. There’s no one left to tell anyway.”

Remus didn’t have any words left to argue with. He retreated quickly, setting the mop back into its bucket and snatching up his coat. As he did, a small rattle echoed from the pocket and Remus was suddenly reminded of what was inside. With shaky fingers, he reached inside and withdrew a small 8-track tape of Miles Davis’ greatest hits.

“Happy Christmas, Regulus,” Remus murmured, leaving it on one of the tables on his way out.





* * *





Later that night, as he was lying in his bed and wheezing from shortness of breath, Remus added Regulus Black to his list of things he was trying not to think about. It was getting rather long now; Hope, Lyall, Sirius, Tonya leaving, Tomny stuck in the End, Sirius, addict Lee and his dead brother, Sirius, his marks, the band, London, Sirius—all the usual stuff. Regulus was an unwelcome addition, but an addition none the less.

He managed to push the list of worries away long enough to make it through the following morning, where he and his friends all rushed about, furiously packing and chittering over the things they were most excited to do over Christmas. James wanted to take Lily ice skating and to see the lights in Hyde Park. Peter was looking forward to practising on his own set of drums back home and had agreed to go see a stage show with Moira, who would be in London visiting extended family. Marlene was going to be spending every other evening volunteering in a soup kitchen. She kept talking about some film she was excited to see called Star Wars, but Remus thought snidely that the plot sounded rather ridiculous and long-winded. She'd gotten Mary to agree to go with her though, provided she concede to several days worth of shopping around Carnaby and Oxford Street.

Remus had made no plans. Nor had he called Tomny. He'd been too busy, and now was simply content enough to just let things fall into place. If the others’ busy schedules meant he and Sirius had the time to sneak out and catch a show themselves, that was just fine by him. He didn't want to think about New Years.

With their things all packed and ready, they met up with the girls and made their way down to the dining hall for supper. The tables were packed, it being their last night, and the food was already getting cold, but his friends were determined to put on a show. They'd come up with the idea the day before, and though Remus had never really really been one for Christmas carols, none of them seemed all that deterred.

“On the seventh day of Christmas, my true love gave to meeee!” Lottie sang; “Seven Lily’s fretting!”

“Six of Mary’s exes!” Lily chanted.

“Five failed math tests!” Mary keened.

“Four tea sugars!” Peter cried.

“Three boring swots!” Marlene trilled.

“Two stinky trainers!” James crooned.

“And a Moony in a really bad moooood!” Sirius wailed.

It was brilliant and horrible all at once—brilliantly horrible! They went on down the line like lunatics, all seven of them screaming out in the middle of the dining hall and practically forcing other kids to join in. Remus might’ve felt more left out, had they not dedicated the song to him in the first place.

“Do we really have to do this twelve times?” He demanded.

“ ‘YES’!” They all shouted back, before starting up again. On and on it went, until they reached the final day, all nearly out of breath.

“On the twelfth day of Christmas, my true love gave to meeee—twelve drug dealers!”

“Eleven busted lighters!”

“Ten damn detentions!”

“Nine girls I fancy!”

“Eight pissed off teachers!”

“Seven Lily’s fretting!”

“Six of Mary’s exes!”

“Five failed math tests!”

“Four tea sugars!”

“Three boring swots!”

“Two stinky trainers!”

“AND A MOONY IN A REALLLLYYY BAAAAAD MOOOOOOD!”

He let them finish and then clapped begrudgingly along with the rest of the room. A few of the lunch ladies even cheered for them and there was some whistling, but Remus just shook his head in disbelief until the clamour finally died down. He glanced around for Regulus, wondering what he might’ve thought about the whole thing, but did not find him at his usual table. It worried him enough to make his stomach twinge.

“Well?” James cried. “What’d you think?!”

“Why you would want any of those things for Christmas, is beyond me.”

“Yes, but did you like it though?” Lily asked, still breathless.

“ ‘Like’ is a subjective term.”

“What an ungrateful bastard!” Marlene snorted from her seat next to him. She poked him in the arm with the end of her fork and he flicked a carrot at her.

“Come now, no need for that, Macdonald. Everyone knows it's only a defence technique,” Sirius said from across from them. “He’s so humbled by our amazing singing that he doesn’t know what to do with himself, so he resorts to half-assed quips and sarcasm.”

“Cheers to that,” Mary said, raising her glass. As his friends shared in a toast, Remus joined in too, though rather unenthusiastically. He’d sat across from Sirius on purpose, hoping that a lack of closeness would deter him from his relentless thoughts. Rather, all it’d done was make things worse. His boyfriend was a few precious feet away, beaming with the excitement and thought of returning to London the next morning, and all Remus could see was Regulus’ face, impressed onto his brother’s with that same expression of calm worry. He knew Regulus didn’t want to return home—he saw it in the soft moon-grey of his eyes. But either out of reluctance or fear, the proud Black son would not admit it.

And then there was the fact that Regulus knew everything.

He knew.

Unable to stop thinking about it, Remus kept going back and forth over whether he should tell Sirius. On the one hand, Sirius might be able to do something if he could only see the camaraderie of it. Regulus had kept their secret after all. Maybe he could use it as a launching point—offer his brother a real way out like James had done for him and ensure his silence by way of ally-ship. But Remus knew better; the chances of the two brothers reconciling before their departure time on Saturday morning were rather slim. And besides, he wasn’t sure it was entirely fair to ask Sirius in the first place. Why should he have to feel guilty over the fact that he was finally free to do as he pleased with his chosen family while Regulus had to return home to the one they’d been left with? Sirius had done his time—dealt with the consequences—and when push came to shove he’d defended Regulus. He’d gotten scars doing it.

Did Regulus not defend him also? He burnt that letter. It must count for something.

So formal, the voice had become. Remus almost missed the crudeness.

Get fucked.

That was more like it.

Do you even believe in karma? You called Regulus the coward, but the only real coward here is you. Not telling anyone is as good as hurting him yourself.

You’re wrong, he thought after. I’m not Regulus’ keeper, and he doesn’t want me to be.

No, I’m exactly right. You’re always sticking your nose in where it don’t belong but then as soon as you hear something you don’t like you piss off. You just don’t want to feel what they feel. This is exactly what Lyall was talking about. You’re selfish. You’re a brat. You. Don’t. Care.

I care about Sirius! He doesn’t owe anybody anything! And if I push Regulus anymore than this he could tell people! We’d be ruined.

Nah, if you really cared, you’d tell Sirius the truth. You could help Regulus. You’re hiding it because you’re a coward.

Shut up! I've enough to deal with without you butting in too.

Telling your own brain to shut up. You are loony.

“Moony, earth to Moony?” James said from his other side. “You good, mate? ”

“Yeah,” Remus croaked, shaking off the unease.

“We should’ve called you ‘Moony’ because you’re always drifting off into space,” the dark-haired boy chuckled, before dropping into a whisper; “So what d’you think, should we play the tape for Lily tonight?”

“Er—I thought you were gonna give it to her on Christmas?”

“Well yeah, but then I thought it might be nice to play it with all of us together. You definitely gotta be there at least. What—bad idea?”

Remus shook his head. “I'm sure the others will want to hear. And I know you just wanna show off.”

James grinned guiltily. “You should be a cop. You always know what people are thinking.”

Remus wished it were true. Maybe then he could tell Sirius with utmost confidence that Regulus truly needed his help. Without it, he was just banking on pure intuition, and he’d been plenty wrong before.

“Alright, alright, finally the moment you’ve all been waiting for!” Marlene declared, hopping up from her seat. She whipped out a piece of paper and cleared her throat formally. “I’ve collected the petitions and totalled up all the signatures, and I'm proud to announce that we finally have a winner for our battle for gender equality!"

"Who?!" Mary and Sirius demanded.

"First... Drumroll please!”

They all started hammering their hands on the tabletop, filling the room with commotion.

“And the winner is... No one—it’s a tie!”

They all baulked for a moment and Sirius leaned in. “Between who?!”

“Lottie and Remus!”

James reached over and clapped an arm around Remus’ shoulder. “Way to go, Moons!”

“How?” Lily demanded. “I mean, Remus I get—practically had an entire army of eighth year girls behind him, but Lottie?! You didn’t pass out a single petition!”

“Not at Hawkings she didn’t,” Marlene grinned.

“I just mentioned to Clyde that it might be cool if he took Marlene’s little appeal around the village a little,” Lottie shrugged. “For tiny townsfolk they’re really quite progressive.”

“You’re still seeing him?” Peter gaped.

“We meet for tea on occasion.”

“I can’t fucking believe it,” Sirius said, sounding genuinely impressed. “Only you, Lot.”

She blew him a kiss as Mary leaned across the table. “Wait, does this mean they both get a lap dance?”

As tempted as Lottie seemed to be by the idea, they did not all break out into a suggestive caper at the cafeteria table. Remus still couldn’t look Sirius in the eye as they made their way back to the dorm, but he blamed it on his fatigue.

“I still think you should let Ms. Pomfrey take a look at you,” Lily was telling him. “It’s been days—that’s far too long. If your fevers still haven’t gone away it could mean an infection. You could get sepsis.”

Remus shook his head, burying his face in his muffler and trying not to slip on the icy path. “S’fine. It’s just a cold, it’ll go away.”

“You should at least lie down,” James said. “ ‘Pops’ isn’t even on until seven anyway.”

That he could agree to. Casting a rueful glance at Sirius’ back, he decided he needed a break anyway, and some time alone in the dorm room would be a welcome relief.

You’re selfish and vile.

Piss off, he told the voice.

When they got back to Godric, all of his friends peeled off their winter kits and shuffled into the warm common room while Remus excused himself. Sirius, not one to just accept and move on, stopped him by the stairs.

“Are you really not feeling well? ‘Cause I could—”

“Nah, go on. I’m just gonna lie down for a bit. Maybe take a bath.”

“Okay, I’ll come get you when the show starts.”

Checking to make sure they were alone, Sirius quickly kissed him before slipping away. With him gone, Remus made the climb to the fourth floor alone where he peeled off his clothes. Too tired for a bath, he took a damp towel to the winter sweat clinging to his neck and torso and collapsed into bed instead. Not long after his teeth began to chitter with fever and he drew the covers up to his nose to ward off the chill. He wasn’t sure when he’d fallen asleep, but when he awoke he was slick with sweat again. A quick glance at the clock told him that seven had come and gone, leaving him even more lightheaded and exhausted than he’d been before his nap.

“Feeling any better?” Sirius asked, making Remus jump. He was lounging back on his own bed across from him, a piece of paper in front of his nose, which he set aside as Remus blinked awake.

“You were supposed to wake me up," Remus said. He sat up, clutching his forehead as all the blood rushed to it. "What happened with the show?

“Didn’t want to wake you. You didn't miss anything anyway. Biggest name was Wings, but Elton John co-hosted and he wasn’t entirely terrible.”

Remus nodded at the run-down. “What’s the paper for?”

“Oh this?” Sirius drew the paper back from his nightstand, casually fanning himself. It looked like the same one from days before, Remus recognised the crest now. The Blacks. “This is old-hat, my good Moon. Had it for a while now... Just can't seem to get rid of it."

Remus tipped his head in question, and Sirius shrugged haplessly.

“It's a letter from my parents, letting me know that I’ve been officially and forthwith ejected from the Ancient and Most Noble House of Black.”

“You mean—?”

“Yep, arrived on my birthday with the post! Took me several weeks to open it though. Apparently since I’m eighteen now, there’s no more rule saying they have to take care of me. So that's that. I’ve been officially dis-owned. And you know what? Good riddance.” Straightening up, Sirius scrunched the letter into a tight ball and tossed it toward the wastebasket sitting outside the bathroom. The ball bounced off the rim and rolled away, and Sirius clicked his tongue in disappointment.

“He shoots, and he sucks…”

Remus stared at the ball. From his position it was just peeking out from the corner of James’ bed—like a badly hidden secret.

“Sirius, there’s something we should talk about…”

Sirius hopped up from his bed and crossed the room, using the posts of Remus’ bed to swing himself onto its end with a cheeky look. “What’s that—you trying to cash in on that lap dance already? Figured you’d want to wait until you were properly awake, but I might be persuaded.”

“It’s about Regulus.”

“Ha. Good luck getting a lap dance out of him."

“Enough with the bloody lap dance!"

Sirius’ smile vanished. He crossed his arms.

“Fine, since you’re so up in arms already. What's the matter with him then?”

“It’s just—he’s been telling me some things… Or he hasn't, but he's... I think it's bad, Sirius.”

“Go on then, don't keep us in suspense."

Remus knotted his fingers together in his lap. He felt a bit woozy, and sticky all over from sweat, and with Sirius looking at him the way he was, he was starting to wonder if bringing Regulus up at all had been a fatal mistake.

“I’m not sure what it is, but I think there's something seriously the matter with him."

Sirius snorted lightly. “Well, that’s nothing new. Suspect there’s plenty to diagnose, sour as he is.”

"He misses you.”

“Ha! That's a good one."

“Okay, so he didn't say that exactly, but I can tell that he doesn’t want to go home for Christmas.”

“Alright, so why’s he talking to you about it?”

“Huh?”

“You!” Sirius snapped. “Why’s he telling you all this over me?”

“Sirius, this isn’t about me. I think you should be the one to talk to him, that's all I'm saying. Make him see that you care. Not—Not take on any extra burdens, just… maybe say something that might comfort him?”

“Reg doesn’t talk to me,” Sirius scowled. “He won’t—I've tried! Little git only turns away when I do.”

“What if I were to go with you then? We could head over to Salazar right now. Make him listen!”

“Or what, bury his head in a snowbank? Potter’s right—your brain’s on the moon, Moons.”

Remus resisted the urge to groan. The more he spoke about Regulus, the more urgent everything seemed to feel.

“He needs someone, Sirius.”

“What he needs is a therapist. We all do. Forgive me, but I don’t see how this is my problem.”

“It just is! He’s your brother!”

“Yeah? And what has he ever done for me?”

“He kept your secret!”

Sirius drew back like he’d been slapped and Remus snapped his teeth together, forcing a huff out through his nose.

“Regulus knew about you and Miles, Sirius.”

“How?” Sirius’ voice was breathless; staggered with shock. Guilty, Remus dropped his head and stared down at his hands.

“He found one of your letters.”

“You mean he stole it.”

“He was a kid.”

“He’s a liar!”

“Oh come on, Sirius! Stop taking the piss!” Remus reached out to grab him, but Sirius just pulled away. Hurt but undeterred, he plunged on. “He kept your secret for years—didn’t tell a soul!”

“He told you, didn’t he? Was probably cracking up just thinking about it. Me and Miles—hell! Must've been calling us fudge-packers to those fucking friends of his every time we turned around.”

“He didn’t! Literally no one knows! Don’t you think Barty would’ve told the whole world by now if he had? Told everyone about us?”

He realised his mistake a second too late, when Sirius’ eyes shot wide, turning more white than grey.

“You told him about us…?”

“No, he guessed! He guessed because he knew about Miles, I was just trying to reassure him—”

Sirius ripped away, practically falling off the bed in his haste to put as much distance between the two of them as possible.

“WELL, GREAT!” He roared; “AS LONG AS REGGIE’S REASSURED!”

Now he’d done it. How could he be so bad at this? Desperate, Remus threw off the covers and pushed to his feet. He staggered, but Sirius wasn’t about to wait for him to catch up. He had to chase him across the room, and even then Sirius wouldn’t look at him.

“Sirius, I know what it’s like to not feel at home with your family,” he said—begged; “I know what it’s like to—”

“How?” Sirius snarled. “How could you possibly know, huh? You think your dad resents you because—what? You hate going home? Because you’ve got delinquents for friends, and you've been kicked out of a few schools for setting some rubbish bins on fire? You don’t know anything—how could you ever know how this feels?!”

Tell him, the foul voice keened; Tell him right now. Throw it in his spoiled face!

“Sirius, I’m not—”

“I am such an idiot!” Sirius laughed, turning to pace back and forth before James’ bed. “I am so stupid! And to think that I actually thought you were coming around! That you were gonna tell me you were ready! New Years—HA! What fucking rubbish! Thought that maybe—”

“Sirius!”

“—We could finally cut all the bullshit and just start living like everyone else! I–I thought that what with McKinnon knowing—oh! But I should’ve known, really! It figures my own boyfriend would have an easier time talking to my brother about my past relationships than he does talking with me about OUR current one! That—That it’s fine for you to talk to others about us but when I even think about it I’m emotionally crucified—!”

“Sirius, this isn’t fucking about us!”

“Of course it’s about us! It’s about the fucking fact that you can’t admit to yourself what we are—WHO we are—but you’ll just spew whatever convenient bullshit to get my brother on your side!”

“ ‘Side’?! Sirius, what fucking side?”

“Whatever bloody side you’re on! Which clearly ain’t mine! God—I tried to talk myself out of it, you know! Told myself it would be useless to just wait around until you’re done bloody denying it!”

“Denying. What.”

“Us!” He lashed. “Denying us! You still don’t get it—we’re not Lily and James, just nervous to tell our friends because it would be a little embarrassing—we’re gay! Bent as a nine bob note! A couple ‘a fairies lost in the closet!”

“I’m not gay, Sirius!”

“Oh yeah! So you’re not gay—whatever! You’ve still done some pretty gay shit anyway.”

It cut—cut like a knife to the bone. And Remus seethed.

“You’re not making any sense,” he growled. “You’re pissed because I’m gay but then not gay enough? Make up your bloody mind!”

“I don’t care!” Sirius spun around with a hiss. He was clutching one of the records, arms shaking like he wanted to throw it but couldn’t quite bring himself to. “Be whatever you want, but I told you! I refuse to be someone’s secret! I won’t do it again, not even for you!”

“But before you said—”

“I know what I said! But maybe—just maybe—I want what Lily and James have! Maybe I want all of it—everything! But we can’t have everything, can we, Remus?”

“Why do we have to have everything anyway?” Remus whimpered. “Why can’t we have this much?”

“Because,” Sirius started, his voice deadly low, “because I’m selfish. And when I think of my life, I want everything. I want what everyone else has! I want my love to be painted in the sky—I want a legendary love!”

“You want that more than you want me?”

He could see the way Sirius ground his teeth together, straining the muscles in his neck. Finally, he turned away, pressing both hands on top of his stereo and leaning into it. “Yes, that is what I want,” he whispered.

Remus stared after him, aching all over. “But I love you,” he said.

“Oh, you love me, really?”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like it’s small… Like it isn’t worth anything.”

“You said it, not me.”

For a split second, Remus forgot himself. It was a vicious anger, one that demanded to be felt, and to drain it all, he turned toward Sirius’ bed and kicked the baseboard so hard, the wood cracked. It might’ve helped him feel less, had Sirius not flinched so badly that he dropped the record. The vinyl disc hit the ground with a clatter, escaping its cover and rolling across the floor to rest by Peter’s bed. Remus stared after it, ashamed.

“Sirius—”

“No. No more.”

“You can’t—” Remus ached. “You fucking… You told me that I was the sky!”

There was a flash of a shiver in Sirius’ shoulders, but he would not look at him. Instead he turned back toward the stereo, one hand clasped to the side of his neck.

“I guess that’s the thing… You never agreed to be my sky.”

At a loss for words, Remus looked blindly toward the bathroom. The distance between them, which while fighting had felt wider than any canyon, suddenly felt too close to breathe. He stumbled toward the doorway but as his hand clasped over the knob he felt the inexplicable feeling of dread wash over him. If he left things as they were now, he was afraid everything really would be over.

“Sirius, please don’t do this—”

There was a sudden knock, and a second later the bedroom door opened and James popped his head inside.

“Everything alright, you two? What was that banging noise?”

It was Sirius who answered first.

“Moony tripped,” he replied coolly. “What’s going on, Potter? Where are the others?”

“Downstairs still,” James said. “We’re finished with cards I think, but Pete wants to crack into that bottle of Tokay he's been saving and Mary keeps going on about a game of questions. I told them to hold off for a bit though—see how Moony’s doing first.”

“He’s fine,” Sirius snapped, facing James with his arms crossed; “Been all busy barking his head off.”

James appeared confused and came into the room a bit further, but Remus stopped him with a hand.

“It’s fine, James, I’ll come down in a second. Just… gonna shower first.”

“Alright…” he said, then; “Black?”

Sirius waved him off harshly, before advancing on the door and ushering his best friend out. The door clicked shut behind them, and Remus was left alone. With nothing else to do but make good on his word, he yanked the bathroom door open and stripped out of his pant bottoms. He could weep in the shower.

The water he kept cold, which quelled the burning in his skin but only worsened the trembling in his core. He thumbed the chain necklace looped around his neck. He'd never taken it off—was now the time? What did one do with such gifts during a break up? Was this even a break up? Remus didn’t know. He didn’t know anything.

When he was finished he avoided looking in the mirror, disinterested in the solemn, dark-ringed expression he would find. Eventually Lily came to check in on him, concerned, and the only way he think of distracting her was to agree to join her downstairs with everyone else. The stairs sucked as usual, but it was getting late and the common room was already reasonably sparse. His friends had sequestered the set of sofas in front of the hearth—as was their right as leaving students—and waved when they spotted him slogging over.

“You feeling better then, Remus?” Lottie called, and he nodded to her while taking a corner seat next to Marlene. He didn’t look at Sirius, who was sandwiched between James and Mary with a beer in one hand.

“You’re just in time for the good stuff!” Peter grunted, fighting against the wine stopper of his bottle of Tokay. Lottie eyed him before snatching the bottle with a sharp ‘give me that’ and whipping the cork out of its neck. They all cheered as the liquor began to flow, and Marlene handed him a mug.

“Here, put some real hair on your chest.”

Remus hummed in response and sipped. It tasted like plums.

“Everything okay?” Marlene asked quietly, reading his mood. “Black’s been sour as a grape ever since he came downstairs.”

“Sorry, Cherry, but not now.”

She puckered lightly but nodded and turned back to the group as Mary took control.

“So! Twenty-one questions, right—we’re all in agreement?”

“Yesssss!” Lottie trilled.

“You don’t have to play if you don’t want to,” Marlene whispered. Wordlessly, Remus nodded and she smiled softly before tilting her head onto his shoulder. “Go on then, Snatchy, ask your question!”

Mary glared at her. “Alright, fine! My question’s for the pétasse over there! Marls—how’s Remus in bed?”

“Not that it's any of your business, but he’s an absolute stag in the sheets!” Marlene declared, holding Remus’ hand up and kissing it for good measure. Mary laughed, but nodded fairly and gestured for Marlene to ask her question.

“Lottie! Did you or did you not hook up with that drug dealer in town—what’s his name—Colson?”

“WHAT?!” Peter shouted, making his sister shove him quite sharply.

“His name is Clyde, and I did not,” she answered haughtily, “but that doesn’t mean I wouldn’t.”

“You mean Clyde peddled that petition for nothing?” Mary leered.

“ ‘Nothing’? You and I have clearly never snogged.”

Everyone moaned with laughter and Remus took another sip of the Tokay. It warmed his insides some, but it was taking all of his concentration not to let himself shiver with fever next to Marlene.

“My turn,” Lottie announced. “Sirius, is it true Kimmy asked you to father her child last year?”

“Are all these questions going to be about sex?” Lily blagged.

Sirius ignored her. “No. She asked me to father child-ren. The crazy bird wanted three. Even had the names picked out. Bradford, Constance, and Eldric.”

“Thank god she dumped you first,” James quipped. “Those are horrible names.”

“And what are you and Evans planning on naming your first sprog? ‘Prongs Junior’?”

“At least that has some ring to it. ‘Eldric’ is just begging to have his head flushed down the toilet.”

“Hear, hear, Potter!”

The two clinked glasses and drank, while Remus watched. It made him vehemently jealous—how easy it was for Sirius to put on his mask in front of others and pretend it was all okay.

Then Mary reached over and slapped Sirius’ knee. “Your go, Black!”

Sirius cast his eyes about the room, swirling his cup.

“Alright. What’s something you’ve never told anyone else?”

There was a pause and then Peter leaned in. “Who're you talking to?”

“I’m talking to Lupin, a’course.”

Suddenly Remus’ heart was thundering in his ears. Marlene perked up, quick to come to his aid.

“Remus isn’t playing," she said.

“He never said so,” Sirius retorted, staring directly at him now. “Can’t chicken out once the question’s been asked.”

“Remus isn’t feeling well,” Marlene insisted. “Ask someone else.”

“Thanks, but I’m asking Lupin.”

Remus was afraid to open mouth, else he might scream. His hand had seized over the rim of his cup, threatening to shatter its flimsy edges with the strength of his panic. He knew what Sirius was doing—what he wanted to hear him admit. It was purposeful.

“C’mon, Padfoot, try Pete instead,” James prompted, but Sirius would have none of it. He only leaned in further, his every limb taunting.

“Tell us, Lupin."

No.

"What's the one thing you’ve never admitted?"

Stop it.

"The one thing you’ve never said out loud?!”

I won't say it.

"Go on, fess up!"

Marlene threw herself to her feet. “That’s enough, Sirius! I told you, Remus isn’t playing—”

“I’m not my father’s real son.”

He felt frail saying it, but his voice carried, abruptly silencing Marlene’s rant and making every one of his friends turn to look. Suddenly it all felt very silly—this one thing. The secret he’d been too afraid to say aloud since that last day with Hope in her hospital room; when she’d told her eleven year-old son that the real reason his father didn’t love him was because he wasn’t his father at all.

Ah. Karma.

Lily spoke first, but it was just his name. He could hear the sympathy in her voice. The pity. He couldn’t stand it, so in a fit of self-destructive rage, he ripped the wound open further.

“Yeah, that's right! I’m a bastard!” He sang, ironically up-beat. “My dad hates meee, and it’s because every time he looks at my face, he sees some other bastard’s kid… And—And get this! When he doesn’t see that guy—whoever the fuck he was—he sees a reminder of his dead fucking wife! Who apparently everyone thinks killed herself. So that's cool, yeah?”

Vos non lupus, baby.

Remus laughed venomously and downed the rest of his drink. His friends still sat stunned, but he refused to look at Sirius. He wouldn’t.

“You’re all staring with your gobs open but this is great for me—really! Finally get to admit it, don’t I?! That’s it, everyone! That’s the last ‘a the Lupin secret stash! Someone call the papers! Alert the media! It's all out now!"

Marlene slumped down on the sofa next to him, frowning, with tears in her eyes. It was clear she knew exactly what had just happened, but he refused to accept her pity either and pulled his hand away when she reached for it again.

“Lu—” James stopped himself, then; “Remus, we didn’t mean to—”

“Nah, don’t sweat it, Prongs, all’s good in love and war, innit. My turn then? Alright! Mary, how do you get away with wearing your year nine skirt to every French lesson? Is it to boost your marks, or is Mr. Dupont just that much of a pervert?”

The quip wasn’t fair to Mary, but she didn’t so much as look bothered.

“Remus, it’s alright if you—”

“God! Why’s everyone so bloody nervous all of a sudden? Black asked a question and I answered it! There—the one truthful thing I’ve never said aloud. And now you all know. Actually feels good… Yeah, feels good to come out with it.”

No one relaxed, and as he glanced around he caught the expression on Sirius’ face. It looked to him like horror, but then there was that pity again.

“I’m going to bed.”

Pushing up from the couch, Remus slammed his cup down on the table next to him and all but ran from the room. He just wanted to be angry, but he could feel the sobs building up in his chest, the kind that would ache and leave him breathless for hours. It’d been so long since he’d felt them—Sirius’ influence—but now there was nothing left to keep them at bay. Behind him, he heard his friends whispering.

"Sirius, how could you?"

"I didn't know! ... I-I… I didn't know..."

By the time he made it to his room, Remus was biting his lip to hold back the screams.





* * *





That night Remus dreamed. Or whatever the verb was for ‘nightmare’. It all felt the same.

He was back in the hospital, which he hated. It always smelt too clean, the lights too bright, and people were always telling him which way to go, where to sit, when to keep his voice down. All he wanted was to see his mum, and sometimes they would say he couldn’t even do that. Then Giles would have to lead him back out of the too-clean, too-bright corridors, sometimes calm, other times kicking and screaming, which he only did because he knew he wasn’t allowed.

This day wasn’t like one of those days. He was eleven now and hadn’t kicked and screamed in ages. Except for that time a few months ago when that horrible Butler Frederick had taken the radio away. That was well deserved, of course. It was his mother’s radio. Frederick had no right to remove it, the bastard. He was gone two weeks later anyway.

No, today wasn’t like then. Today the hospital had called. Remus hadn’t been able to make out all of what his father was whispering to Giles before they caught him eavesdropping, but he managed to overhear some of it.

Bad night. Treatment’s not effective anymore. This is it.

He didn’t understand, mostly because he’d yet to imagine a world where the treatment wouldn’t work. To him, there was only a world where Hope was healthy, at home all of the time and throwing wonderful Sunday teas at which Remus would get to stuff his face with however many jam tarts as he pleased. There was also a world where she was sometimes confused, and thought a Thursday might be a Saturday, or forgot that she lived in their house, or that she’d left the kettle boiling and let it burn one of the kitchen staff. Finally, there was the world where Hope was in and out of the hospital. Where wires and tubes covered her arms and body and she was sometimes too tired to open her eyes, but would squeeze his little hand to signal that she knew he was there.

But a world where there were no jam tarts or kettles or tubes? That world didn’t simply exist.

She was awake in her hospital bed when they arrived. She had a silk scarf wrapped up around her head, hiding the spots where her beautiful blonde hair had come out in clumps from something Giles called ‘radiation’. It always sounded terribly frightening to Remus, but it was supposed to make her better, so…

The radio was playing next to her bed. It was a hospital radio, so the speakers would sometimes crackle like the cap of a fizzy drink, but he still recognised the song. It was one of Hope’s favourites.





Oh, where have you been, my blue-eyed son?

And where have you been, my darling young one?





There were a few tubes, but not enough that she couldn’t speak, which was good because she had plenty of things to say. Perhaps if Giles had stayed in the room with him or Lyall hadn’t had that meeting to make, then she wouldn’t have said them at all. But they were both gone, and she was there, and he was eleven.

“I’m sorry, my darling. I’m so, so sorry…”





* * *





No one tried to wake him. They didn’t have to. At shit-all hour, Remus got up, dressed, and carried his trunk as quietly as he could down to the common room. There he rolled a cigarette and smoked it to ash near an open window, and when that was done he rolled another. He repeated this until sun-up, when his lungs felt so singed he doubted he could speak if he tried.

No one bothered him and his friends never came looking. At eight o’clock he picked up his trunk and began lugging it down to Castle Hall, where he found a small crowd of eager students, all of them excited to return home for the holiday. As he stood off to the side and watched as the haze of their breaths floated up into the sky, he imagined what it would be like telling James that he couldn’t stand coming to his for Christmas anymore. There would be a bit of fruitless arguing—promises of apologies on Sirius’ behalf—but he would eventually give in, and then Remus would be left to go back home. At least the estate would be empty. But empty meant quiet.

No, not quiet—silent.

Agony. That’s what it felt like. He so badly wanted to throw his friends’ kindness back into their faces, but a dam had been broken—all of his secrets were spent. He felt hollower than hollow, as though the entire world were seeping into his chest cavity, dispersing everything that made him ‘Remus Lupin’ and splitting his matter up into a million different pieces until he was nothingness all over again. Aside from Giles and the dogs, the estate had nothing that would help put him back together again. All that was left of him was there—with his friends, with Sirius.

He could go to Tomny. He should. Tomny would understand. But then again, Tomny was in the East End, and there was Lee… and the Potters had been so kind and… shit—shit! It was all shit.

Across the berm, he spotted his friends waiting by one of the buses. James and Peter waved tentatively, and he nodded back. Sirius was drawing circles in the snow with the tip of his boot. Unbothered.

So go then, Vicious Moony seethed. Go and make his life miserable too. Show him how it feels.

Yeah, maybe he would.

“Hello, Remus.”

Sheila’s voice was soft when she said his name. It felt like a hug from a mother almost, but then again he couldn’t remember what that felt like, really. He turned to her, and Sheila beamed at him while wearing an effervescent orange peacoat. She looked like a smiling traffic cone.

“Are you excited to be going home for the holidays?” She asked him. “I hope your father’s taken some time off.”

It was almost ironic.

“Yeah, loads. Enough to vacation in the Riviera with his new wife.”

Instantly Sheila’s good mood vanished. It might’ve been the rawness in his voice or the fatigue on his face, or perhaps after two and a half years of seeing each other every day, she was just able to tell what his misery looked like.

“I didn’t know Lyall had remarried.”

“Yeah, last autumn.”

She frowned at him. “Are you alright, Remus? What’s wrong?”

“Did you know?” He asked her, finally forgoing any needless pandering and cutting straight to the bone. Just like Sirius.

“Did I know what?”

“Did you know that Thaddeus Dean was my dad when you gave this to me?”

She looked down, to where he’d pulled the rumpled photograph from his pocket. Remus hadn’t looked at the thing in months, and yet the image felt as familiar as the back of his hand.

“Remus, I…”

“Don’t lie to me.” He thrust the photo at her again. “Did you know?”

She seemed to shrink away from it this time, like the truth might bite her. When she spoke, her voice was a reedy whisper. Thin.

“I wasn’t entirely sure. Hope never said and… But when I saw you that first day in my class, it was uncanny." She let out a shaky breath, her voice snapping. "It was like seeing him again. After all these years—Tad. A bit taller, skinnier in some places, but the same nose—same eyes.”

He felt the trembling return, but without fever.

“Why did you give this to me…?”

His teacher’s mouth fell open with unsaid words, but they were just excuses, and so he shoved the photograph back into his pocket.

“Remus—” Sheila said quickly, “there’s something else I should tell you.”

“No, thank you,” he ground out, turning toward the buses. “Goodbye, Mrs. Buchanan. Happy Christmas.”
