Chapter 83: Coda


Chapter Summary

Coda /ˈkōdə/ noun

1. The concluding passage of a piece or movement; an expanded cadence.

2. An ending, with the freedom to start again.



Chapter Notes

The irony of the song opening this chapter just kills me, idk.

And a note to everyone who was worried about Remus' health, he is FINE lmfao. He does not have cancer or any other terrible illness you lot have been dreaming up. I don't like angst that much.

No C/W for this chapter, but it's not exactly uplifting either. Hang in there *smooches forehead*



See the end of the chapter for more notes



I’m on the top of the world, lookin’ down on creation;

And the only explanation I can find;

Is the love that I’ve found, ever since you’ve been around,

Your love’s put me at the top of the world…

- “Top of the World” The Carpenters, 1972



Mrs. Potter had just about passed out in the foyer when she saw James and the bleached skunk stripe lining his sweeping fringe, but it was nothing compared to the look she gave Remus.

“Remus, beta, are you alright? You look positively ill.”

He didn’t deny it, and neither did any of his friends. James and Lily had been silently fretting over him since Scotland, passing him handkerchiefs to dab the sweat on his forehead and stuffing him with hot tea from the train’s trolley cart. Only Sirius remained stoic; Remus didn’t care—let him sulk.

“Just tired from the train,” he said. Then he wobbled while taking his boot off and James had to reach out and steady him.

“Giles is still in the drive talking cars with dad,” he said, eyeing his mother uneasily.

“M’fine, James."

Mrs. Potter stepped forward anyway. “May I?”

Remus nodded reluctantly, allowing her to press the back of her hand to his forehead.

“Arey baap re… You’re burning up. Perhaps we should have Giles take you home until you’re well.”

“No, please. I’m fine, really!" He insisted. "No one else has caught anything, I’m just tired—just need some sleep, and I… I would rather not go home.”

Effie looked at her son warily before sighing. “Alright, but it’s straight upstairs with you. You’ll take James’ bed while I prepare something that’ll warm you up. And we’ve a neighbour two houses down, Dr. Ostrowski, we’ll have him take a look at you.”

Remus didn’t fight it. He’d already decided on the train that anything was better than returning to that empty estate.

“Here, let me get your trunk,” James said, ushering Remus out of the way while Mrs. Potter retreated into the kitchen.

“And you should take your jacket off, it’s wet from the rain,” Lily insisted, already peeling it off him by the collar.

“Guys, I told you I’m fine—” He’d meant to step over James’ guitar case, but like the klutz he was, caught his toe on the edge and nearly sprawled on the foyer carpet for a second time. He might have gone down on his face had a hand not shot out and steadied him. Alarmed, Remus turned sharply to find Sirius holding his elbow. They locked eyes for the first time since their fatal game of questions, and Sirius quickly released him, turning away to fumble with the buttons of his coat.

More affronted than he would’ve been had Sirius just let him fall, Remus drew himself up to his full height and turned for the stairs. He’d already told himself that should he choose to stay, Sirius was not his prerogative. Not his problem. He was there for his friends, and Sirius Black was not his friend.

No less than ten minutes later, Remus lay curled up under the covers of James’ fourposter, staring up at the poster of Farrah Fawcett he’d yet to remove from the roof. He knew he should be happy Mrs. Potter had agreed to let him stay, but lying there, in an unfamiliar bed, made him feel suddenly panicked. Cagey. Like he needed to flee. Idiot—coming back to the Potters’ had seemed like such a good idea on the train, when the mere thought of returning to the Lupin Estate had left him rushing to the toilet to vomit. (Though that could've just been courtesy of Lily’s personal mixture of turmeric and ginger tea—heavy on the turmeric.) Now he felt guilty. Who was he to weasel his way into his friend's home and ruin everyone's holiday? Just because he and his boyfriend had had a nasty break up...

Had he and Sirius broken up? It felt like it. Remus had never been more angry with anyone in his entire life, save perhaps his parents. Why couldn't Sirius ever listen?! If Remus was the walking time bomb then Sirius was the match ready to set him off. Maybe they were bad for each other after all. Maybe they should've just stayed friends. Though really, Remus couldn't remember what it felt like to just be Sirius Black's friend.

"Effie, have you seen my boots anywhere? Should need to salt the drive, I think."

"In the hall cupboard, dear!"

"Right, right... Effie, have you seen my muffler anywhere? Bit nippy out."

"On the stairs, dear!"

"Yes, yes... Effie, have you seen my spectacles anywhere? Can’t bloody—"

"On your head, dear!"

"Oh my..."

Potter Cottage was a big house, and in big houses sound tended to carry. As he laid awake, listening to the distant hum of happy reunions and novelty holiday tunes playing off the radio, Remus could feel a familiar itch to disappear creep back in. He imagined them all downstairs, sat down by the warm hearth and sharing all the bits of themselves Effie and Monty had missed since September. The girls' prank on Halloween, Sirius' birthday, the time capsule and Marlene's petition. He could hear laughter, the occasional motherly condemnation. James' good-natured reply, Lily's timid agreement. Sirius.

Remus couldn’t take it anymore. The entire thing had been a mistake. Sirius wasn't miserable, he was happy! Happy to be home with family in a space big enough that he didn't have to look at Remus all hours. Remus' plan had failed, he needed out.

Throwing off the covers, Remus sat up in bed and reached for his jumper. He'd have to leave his trunk, it was too heavy to lug down the street with him, but what good were books and things anyway if you didn't even know where you were going?

It got noisier as he emerged into the hallway. Already out of breath, he wheezed lightly as he descended the stairs, but could still hear the sound of Lily and Mrs. Potter's happy voices drifting up from the kitchen. The others were clearly in the parlour, and he briefly caught word of a football match being discussed. Trying his best to block it out, Remus searched the hall cupboard for his scarf and coat. He’d just finished lacing up his boots when James came skittering down the hallway, heading for the stairs. With a tray of homemade soup balanced in his hands, he’d almost swept past him, but froze at the last second. Foot on the first step, James looked surprised—and disappointed.

“Moony, what are you doing?”

Remus sighed, like a burglar caught in the act. “M’gonna head out.”

James only blinked at him.

"Huh?"

"Gonna go... now. I'm leaving, James."

"You're leaving now? Without telling anyone? What... Did you call Giles or something?”

Remus shook his head, utterly shamefaced, and the look James gave him was horrible.

“Where were you even gonna go? To the East End?”

He opened his mouth to answer, but James just cut him off;

“Remus, are you mental? It’s dark out—gonna be real late soon!”

“Shh!” Remus groaned, desperately. “S'fine. I know my way around.”

“That’s not the problem!” James huffed, setting down the soup tray. “What’ll I tell Mum? Or Lily?”

“Just tell them that I got Giles to come get me or something. That I was too sick."

“Mate, you are sick.”

“Then don’t tell them anything. Say you never saw me.”

“You actually expect me to lie to them? Not a chance. Just stay, we’ll—we’ll figure something else out.”

“James, I can’t.” I can hear him laughing and I thought I could handle it but I can’t. It’s killing me.

“Moony, if this is about what happened yesterday, Sirius has already told me he’s sorry. Sorrier than anything. He didn’t mean to push you into… whatever that was. None of us knew anything about your dad."

"I know, that was sort of the point."

James frowned deeply, and took a step forward. "I don't know how it's been for you," he said, "and I won't pretend either. But Remus, if you thought for even a second that we’d think any less of you because of it—then you’d be dead wrong.”

It was good of him, but Remus had never been as good as James Potter. He stepped back, closer to the door, and raised a hand to ward him off.

“James... Please. I can't do this tonight."

“You can't go! People are gonna be coming around for the holidays soon. People who want to meet you guys! My cousin Ajay’s coming back home to visit and he’s got all these crazy stories about America. It’ll be a good distraction, and when you’re better, well… Then we'll do it your way. Heck, we’ll even go find Tomny together if you'd like.”

“No offence, Prongs, but I don’t want to sit around listening to Ajay talk about the Red Sox and the Yankees. I need to—”

“Don’t be a shit friend, Remus.”

It was the nastiest thing James had ever said to him, but it didn’t matter. His dark eyes softened immediately and he stepped forward, placing a hand on Remus’ shoulder to give it a gentle squeeze.

“Stay,” James said again, “stay and get better.”

He wanted to say no. He wanted to throw his friend’s kindness back into his face—be that shit friend who ran out on them the moment things went bad, but if the situation had been reversed, Remus couldn’t see himself doing any different.

So, Remus allowed James to help him out of his coat, and together they made the long trek back upstairs. He ate the rasam Effie had prepared and only bothered James once about Farrah, before changing into his night clothes and slumping back in bed. James hadn’t dawdled after that, a small mercy, and when he left he turned on the radio.

“Just try and relax some,” he told Remus, before shutting the door. Remus stared after it, mentally comparing its size to that of his bedroom door back at the estate. It was a horrible feeling, but at least the radio helped some.





‘It’s a livin’ thing,

It’s a terrible thing to lose;

It’s a givin’ thing,

What a terrible thing to lose…’





Lily appeared sometime later, setting a cup of water on the bedside table and carefully laying down beside him overtop the covers. She noticed the poster immediately, but before she could comment on it, Remus spoke.

“He’s still got one of you up over his bed at school. Kisses it every morning… Sirius put it up.”

“I remember,” she said, smiling up at the roof of the four-poster. “Funny, that Sirius. Though not always…”

A dour feeling came over him.

“Lils.”

“I know you're sick, so we don’t have to talk about it if you don’t want to. But I can tell that all this has been on your mind for a while now. You've been a bit odd lately, Remus.”

Odd like a cuckoo clock.

He pushed the memory away. It felt like a lifetime ago. “Yeah, well—sorry for being so odd.”

“I didn’t mean it like that.”

“I know.”

She took his arm.

“Remus, I know what Sirius did was not kind, but I wish you’d talk to us. You don't have to take on everything alone, you know. You've got people here who want to help."

"Thanks, Lils, but I really don't want to talk about it."

She nodded solemnly, and then slid her hand further until it was cradling his palm. Her fingers were soft, and Remus just felt clammy.

“I didn’t come up here to badger you. I just wanted to let you know that the others are getting ready for bed. Monty wants them up early to help rake the leaves from the lawn. If you’d like, you can sleep in the guest bedroom with me. We don’t have to talk about it.”

As she spoke, Remus cast his eyes over the cots, already set up for what might have been a fun night of boyish antics. Could’ve been, had he not cocked it all up so badly. He could barely look at Sirius now—being in the same room with him for even a moment would just send him running again.

With a wordless nod, Remus sat up in bed and allowed his friend to help him hobble out into the hall. That night, he laid awake thinking about how Lily’s hair looked like dark whips of fire as it spread out across her pillow. It felt almost odd to see her sleep—the closest he’d come was the time she’d nodded off in James’ lap in the common room, and then also that night in the girls’ room, after she and Snape had had their final falling out. Funnily enough, Sirius had preoccupied his thoughts during both instances; and now, despite the slightness of her frame and the quiet kitten-like breathing, he had to keep reminding himself that Lily was not Sirius. The constant pang was a sorry reminder that without even saying the words, he and Sirius were over. They hadn’t so much as glanced at each other on the train—hadn’t said a word in either’s direction since the fight in the common room. How long had it been since they weren’t able to look at one another’s face and read everything written there?

Guess you both got what you wanted, the vicious Moony said. No more hiding now.

No, Remus thought, as he turned his back on Lily so she wouldn’t wake up and see the damp on his cheeks.

Not like this.





* * *





Remus spent the first several days of holiday in bed—Mrs. Potter’s orders. He was fed soups and masalas that could’ve cleared even the worst sinuses, and James and Peter came by frequently to add to the growing pile of records they’d left next to the beside turntable. They didn’t ask him about what had happened back at school, and he saw neither hide nor hair of Sirius. It was a boring existence but at least he wasn’t being forced to go home. He'd rather let Lily play nurse than any of the maids back at the estate. At least at the Potters' no one was a stranger.

Though she was not happy to hear that they were sharing a room, Lily had managed to convince Effie to let Remus stay. She tended to him like an army medic until he'd finally snapped and said he could dab his own sweaty forehead. When Dr. Ostrowski arrived on their second day, Effie had shown him upstairs where he introduced himself in a deep Polish accent. He used a tongue depressor to check his throat and waved a narrow light across his eyes for so long that Remus was sure he’d go blind.

“Any discomfort or tightness in diaphragm?”

“No.”

“Hm. Try deep breath.”

Remus did so, and stubbornly resisted the twinge in his sternum. He did wheeze a bit on the exhale however, and the doctor peered at him sceptically.

“Have you been coughing up phlegm?”

“Yes.”

“What colour?”

“Yellow,” Remus answered, before coughing sharply into his elbow.

“He’s been coughing going on a week now,” Effie added, while she and Mr. Potter stood by the door. “Fevers every night.”

After taking a moment to listen to his heart beat, Dr. Ostrowski pulled the stethoscope from his neck, turning back to the worried couple.

“He has chest infection. Probably started as cold, then mutated. I will give prescription for bacteria. If is viral, should resolve on own.”

Effie’s shoulders slackened with relief while Mr. Potter fit the end of his pipe into his smiling mouth.

“So I don’t have to go to the hospital?” Remus asked anxiously.

“Not now. Keep eye on symptoms. If get worse, let me know.”

Snapping shut his medical bag, the doctor stood up from the bed and allowed Mr. Potter to show him out.

“Never thought a chest infection would be good news,” Mrs. Potter said, coming forward to change the damp flannel on his forehead. “We’ll send the boys out to pick up the prescription.”

“I can go myself,” Remus insisted.

“I hope you’re joking.” She drew the covers up, then leaned down and kissed the top of his head. “Drink your tea, and make sure you eat up all of that soup. I’ll be back to check on you in a little while.”

And that was how it went for Remus. Endless rounds of doting friends, antibiotics, and warm meals. Just dreadful, really. Despite the fact that he was mostly bedridden, he could tell when Potter Cottage began to get a whole lot busier. The front door would open every now and then to the sound of cheerful greetings and pattering boots. Cousins came in from all over the countryside, filling up the home until every nook and cranny was occupied. He finally met the infamous Ajay, who arrived the same day he’d flown in from Boston and strode straight into the room with James while wearing a Harvard University pullover.

“Sorry you’re feeling so crap,” Ajay said, after Remus had shot upright in bed and nearly keeled over trying to make himself look presentable. “Cuz told me you like music though. You heard of Van Halen?”

Ajay was cool, Remus decided. He brought James several records, most of them by American bands none of them had even heard of. Remus listened to each one on repeat for hours. Later, when he was feeling halfway decent, he even managed the occasional trip downstairs to mingle or share a meal. The Potters’ dining table had extended ten-fold to make room for everyone, but Remus always made sure to sit opposite to Sirius for meals. Unfortunately, this often meant contending with James’ younger, less tactful cousins.

“How did you get that scar?”

“Hamsa!” One of James’ uncles hissed; nearly choking on his supper. He said something in Hindi that sounded a lot like ‘behave yourself’, but Remus wasn’t fazed. He turned to the girl, rubbing the bridge of his nose pointedly.

“Picked a fight with a samurai. Nasty stuff. But don’t worry, I made sure to get him back. Took both eyes out with a single chopstick.”

She squinted like she didn’t believe him while everyone else at the table shared a chuckle. Remus spared a glance at Sirius, but he was not smiling. Instead he nudged James, and asked him to pass the butter.

As nice as meeting the Potters’ extended relations had turned out to be, Remus was not out of the woods entirely. The cough had ebbed, but his fevers returned with vengeance in the days leading up to Christmas. Lily continued to come and go from their bedroom with copious amounts of tea in hand, as did James’ vast family.

"Mummy says rock music melts your brain," Arun said. He was only eight, but seemed to consider himself very knowledgable in most things.

"Oh, it does," Remus agreed. "Sometimes I have plug up my ears just to keep it from leaking out." He stuck both pinkies in either ear and puffed up his cheeks, making Arun and his six year-old sister giggle.

"You two aren't supposed to be in here," Lily said, emerging through the door with a tea tray and a book tucked under one arm. "Remus is still sick. Do I have to tattle to your parents?"

Quickly, both kids leapt down from the bed and shot out the door, giggling some more and they slammed it behind themselves.

“Sounds like a circus down there,” Remus called.

“It is. More of James’ aunts and uncles just arrived,” Lily said, as she set the tray down on the bedside. “Did you know he has two cousins named Aarush? And three named Stephen! Anyway, they all say to get better soon. They’re saving you a portion of the driveway to shovel whenever it decides to snow.”

“As if London gets any real snow.”

She smiled and passed him a cup of tea. Remus matched it meekly, and stopped in inhale a much needed whiff of Mrs. Potter's famous chai. He had no idea what that wonderful woman put in the stuff, but it worked magic where sleep was concerned.

“You should go and visit,” he told Lily, while sipping the drink. “I’m not dying of tuberculosis, you don’t need to tend to me like a wilted daisy.”

“Nonsense. Monty lent me a book and I thought you might like it, that’s all. Now shut up and drink your tea while I read to you.”

He appreciated her, but could tell that the hovering was just Lily's way of keeping track of him. There was no way that James hadn’t told all of them about his disappearing attempt, and though it made him feel like a coddled child, he didn’t fight anymore than necessary. The alternative meant going home, and though he would certainly be left alone at the estate, it wouldn’t mean peace.

On the forth morning, Giles arrived to check in.

“Remus, darling,” Mrs. Potter called through the door; “Giles is here.”

She stuck her head inside, but Remus only pretended to be asleep, and after a bit more cooing, he began to hear their hushed voices in the hall.

“Should we wake him?”

“Don’t bother, Effie. Best to let the little blighter sleep. Thought I might take him home ‘cause he’s been so sick, but now that I know… He’d probably rather stay.”

He did. He couldn’t go back to that house. Not now, and not ever. Vos sunt non lupus. He did not belong.

In the end they didn’t bother him, and Mrs. Potter left a thick envelope on his bedside, along with an assortment of gifts to be opened on Christmas. A few were from Giles, but most were from his father and Sandra. Remus resisted the urge to glare at them, but he did chance upon opening the envelope, which turned out to be a card showcasing the beautiful Monaco beaches and several hundred pounds in cash. Sandra had written a short note wishing him happy Christmas, but there was no note from his father. Just a swirling set of initials; L.L. Apparently Remus hadn’t the need to hustle his classmates with his poetry after all.

Trying not to let the chilly gift turn his stomach, he tore the card in half and shoved the money into the deepest pocket of his coat. Perhaps he’d burn it later.

If overhearing Giles and Mrs. Potter’s conversation had done anything, it’d proved his suspicions; for a long time Remus had wondered if Giles knew that he was not his father’s legitimate child. He’d never had the courage to ask—couldn’t even stomach imagining the face he’d give him—but now that the answer was clear, he wasn’t sure whether to be hurt or angry. So… he became neither. Remus simply pushed the thought away, along with all the rest of life’s disappointments.

While sitting alone in his and Lily’s bedroom, he carefully took stock of the presents Giles had brought. Not all of them were for him, in fact a good portion were gifts. Most had been picked from a catalogue; a guitar strap for James, a new camera case for Lily… simple things, really. He’d paid for all of them himself using the money from his poems, and now they all sat at the foot of Remus’ bed, swathed in red and gold wrapping. One of them, perhaps the largest, felt all for naught now. He tried not to think about it.

It became easier to avoid Sirius as the house grew more crowded. While James’ uncles helped Mr. Potter change burnt out Christmas lights or salt the drive, the mums puttered around the kitchen like a flock of busy hens, speaking Hindi to one another and English when Mrs. Pettigrew came around. There was no mistaking her for Peter and Lottie’s mum, not with her stout stature or head of peach-blonde hair. She greeted all of them enthusiastically, shaking Remus’ hand and dubbing him the ‘handsomest stalk of wheat she’d seen in all her years’. She was kind, with eyes like Simeon and the same sort of vivacious mettle as Lottie. Perhaps somewhat predictably, she was not one to hold her tongue, and like her children, seemed to let loose any and all thoughts that popped into her head.

“I never did much care for that old Jim Callaghan, but this Thatcher woman… I shudder to think what she’ll have to say if she ever gets into office.”

Yes, she was rosy and predictable, but if there was one thing Remus was not expecting from Mrs. Pettigrew, it was the whole-hearted encouragement with which she had for their music.

“Now, I’ve been talking to Rod,” she said one morning, after rushing over to help Effie decorate several cakes; “that is, Charlotte and Peter’s father—and I think that having you boys perform at the New Year's party would be spectacular! Christmas is for thanks and carols—good food and all that fuss, but I don’t see why we shouldn’t have a little live music to ring in the new year, hey?”

It’d surprised them to say the least, but as word got around that the home-grown ‘Marauders’ would be making a special guest appearance on the final night of the year, they had no choice but to acquiesce.

“I think it’s a champ idea actually. We haven’t played anything outside of a practice since Padfoot’s birthday,” James said, once they were all crowded around the kitchen table together, using a needle and thread to string coloured popcorn onto garland.

“And Sim’s gonna be back by then,” Lottie added. “He’s spending Christmas at his girlfriend’s, but he says he wants to see you all play.”

Girlfriend—sure, Remus thought to himself; Nice cover, Sim.

“You mean he wants to see us make fools of ourselves,” Peter grumbled, fighting to get his needle through a particularly stubborn kernel.

“You won’t make fools of yourselves,” Lily insisted, as James leaned past her and smacked a hand on the table.

“Daisy’s right! This is our chance to show our parents we’re serious. If we put on a good show, then they’ll have to give our gap year some thought.”

“Lupin doesn’t even have his bass,” Sirius said blandly, speaking about Remus as though he weren’t sitting a mere two seats over. “What are we even gonna do with two acoustics and no microphone?”

The revelation seemed to dampen James' spirits a bit, and he glanced at Lily.

“Is there nowhere we can borrow what you need?” She suggested. “Maybe find a rental shop?”

“This close to Christmas?” Remus echoed, looking anywhere but at Sirius. “S’fine. I’ll just sit this one out. You guys can get by for one performance without a backing bass.”

“No way,” James scoffed automatically. “Marauders go on as a whole, or not at all. We’ve still got a few days until everything’s shut up, maybe we could… Oh! Ajay used to have tons of mates into music—one of them’s got to have a bass lying around somewhere.”

“You could ask one of them to lend it out!” Lily agreed.

“Yeah, and in the meantime, you can just play rhythm guitar, Moons. You’ve better timing than me anyway.”

“Problem solved!” Lottie cheered, as Remus nodded along in indifference. Next to him, Peter flicked the stale popcorn kernel away and picked up another, this time licking his fingers and shutting one eye.

“Guess we best get to practising then,” he said, before promptly stabbing the needle into his thumb.

The holiday busyness kept them distracted at least; when they weren’t liberating Peter’s parlour and driving Mr. Pettigrew mad with all their noise, there was always party prep to be done. Someone new to meet. A meal to be shared… And on those mornings where James was away on some lovesick adventure with Lily, and Peter was off visiting Moira, Sirius and Remus made sure to sequester themselves in different rooms.

Remus also tried not to let this bother him. After all, he’d never felt so angry with someone in all his life—a sentiment he made sure to repeat to himself on the daily. He and Sirius had continued to brush each other aside at every meal and practice and every time Remus was reminded that no matter what he’d promised him, Sirius’ impulsive anger had gone too far this time. He’d all but dared him to publicly confess to something he’d told him—he’d told him—wasn’t true.

Why’d you do that? He’d asked the Sirius in his head, over and over again.

Why’d you do that?

Why’d you do that?

Why’d you DO THAT?

Why is it never enough for you?!

Enough… It was almost laughable now. Sirius Black did not know the meaning of the word ‘enough’. It did not exist within his vocabulary, and if it did, it certainly did not apply to him. It was never about enough, it was always more. Not enough to be bisexual—just gay. Not enough to have this—to need everything. And in his bitterest moments, Remus came to realise that that was all it was. Sirius had accepted that his boyfriend could be ‘bisexual’ because it was more than he’d been before, but eventually that must’ve just felt insufficient. It wasn’t a sin to be one or the other, but to be stuck in between? To be insufficient? Well… that was just not good enough.

He did not know whether or not Sirius had made good on his word to tell James he was gay, and he did not ask. Instead Remus waited, expecting some sort of change—even just a subtle shift at the way James looked at his best friend—but in the end there was nothing. He couldn’t decide if that meant James knew and did not care, or that Sirius had held back. It was maddening. He wouldn’t have ever imagined that not knowing whether James knew, would somehow be worse than him actually knowing. It made him want to run away again. He had no more secrets to punish them with, and no matter how many times James apologised on Sirius’ behalf, no matter how many times Peter or Lily told him they were sorry—Remus was not. The only thing Remus was sorry for was how long it’d taken him to realise that whatever he and Sirius had been was doomed from the start.

You could just leave. Find Tomny. What’s really stopping you?

He didn’t really have an answer. Maybe he needed a push, but James had already told him not to be a shit friend, hadn't he?

Well, I think that ship’s already sailed, mate.





* * *





Friday 23rd December 1977





“Are you sure you won’t come ice skating with the rest of us?” Lily asked, as she stood in the doorway of Remus’ bedroom, a concerned look upon her face.

“I can barely walk on my own two feet—now you want to put me on ice too?”

“I would’ve thought you’d be good at it! Long limbs and all…”

“Go already, before I sneeze on you,” Remus threatened, ushering her out of the room. They got about three steps before Lily had whipped around again, grabbing him by the shirt sleeves.

“Okay, but—Marlene’s already told me she managed to get us all tickets for that ‘Star Fight’ film or whatever.”

“You mean ‘Star Wars’.”

“Yeah, that’s the one! Technically it’s not out until the twenty-seventh, but there’s this cinema in Mayfair that’s doing a special holiday showing tomorrow on Christmas Eve! Lottie and Peter have already said they can’t come—they’re making the drive to collect Simeon, so promise you’ll go if you’re feeling better?”

“Promise. Now let me nap, woman.”

She smiled, but paused once more, this time with her palm on the doorknob. “James played me your guys’ song last night, by the way.”

Remus sighed, already embarrassed. He knew James had wanted to play ‘Lily Bloom’ for her on their last night at school, but then he’d gone and buggered the whole thing up.

“Hope it wasn’t too lame.”

“ ‘Course not! I only meant to say that it was brilliant.” Lily threw herself forward into a hug. “Thank you. It’s the nicest thing anyone’s ever done for me.”

Blushing, Remus murmured a shy ‘you’re welcome’, and then as they pulled apart; “You made sure to give James a kiss too, yeah?”

“Many kisses.”

“Oh, s’good then.”

Lily’s expression softened. “Remus, are you sure you’re alright?”

“It’s just a tiny infection, Lils.”

“I don’t mean you being sick. I mean… here.” She touched the place over her heart, her green eyes sad and soft. “None of us blame you for not telling us about your dad, but it’s been days now… And you and Sirius are—”

“There is no ‘me and Sirius’,” he snapped. “I need you to stop asking.”

“I would, except now Sirius refuses to talk about it with anyone. Even James.”

“Sounds like a him problem then.”

Oh, Remus—he could see it in her eyes. Thankfully she didn’t say it. Instead she just gave him another hug, and whispered into his shoulder;

“Just know that when you’re ready to talk about it, we’re here.”

She was kinder than he deserved, they all were, but all it took was another stilted dismissal and Lily finally left him be with his radio—promises of their prompt return following her on her way out.

The house was quieter after that, what with most of James’ relatives off on final holiday errands. It was a brief lull; in mere hours every inch of the Potters’ cottage would be stuffed with merry well-wishers and party-goers. For now though, it was just his moping self and the queen of the house, who eventually did come knocking.

“Remus, dear, may I come in?”

He sat up, mumbling in the affirmative while tucking away the book he’d been reading and turning down the radio’s volume. A second later Mrs. Potter was sticking her head inside.

“Still feeling a bit peaky?”

“S’not so bad anymore,” he said. "Cough's almost gone."

“Oh, good.”

Mrs. Potter slipped inside wearing her kitchen apron, her hair up and out of her face as always. She glanced over the single gold-wrapped present still sitting on the foot of his bed before perching herself on top of the covers and drawing it into her lap to toy with the bow. Remus tried not to look so earnest. Most of the gifts Giles had dropped off had already been placed beneath the tinsel-clad tree in the salon, courtesy of James, but he’d kept one, wondering if he should give it at all. He knew what was inside. A brand new pair of Doc Martens. Size nine. Too small for himself.

“All ready for Christmas then?” Effie asked, eventually setting the present aside.

“Yeah. Did you need any help in the kitchen then? I probably shouldn’t touch the food, but I could do dishes or—or something.”

“Oh no, don't worry yourself, dear. We spent all day yesterday prepping. Should be a good turn out for the party tonight. Which you are invited to attend, by the way, provided you’re feeling better.”

He sniffled for effect. “Maybe, yeah…”

Mrs. Potter smiled kindly and pat his leg. “Don’t feel pressured. You just focus on getting better. I did wonder though, if you're feeling up to it, would you mind if we had a little chat? Just you and me.”

“About what?”

“Well, to be frank, it’s about what you said when you arrived. I wanted to wait until you were well again, but since this sickness of yours insists on sticking around I thought now might be good, considering we finally have a bit of quiet around here.”

He looked down at his lap uneasily, but Euphemia Potter was hardly the dithering type. She looked him in the eye whenever she spoke, and did not allow for cowering.

“James told me a bit about your fight with Sirius,” she started. “He said it was spurred by something you said about your father. Is that true?”

Well, it wasn’t wrong.

Remus nodded reluctantly.

“And is your father the reason you don’t want to go home?”

Suddenly the dots were starting to connect.

“It’s not like that.”

“Hm. Like what?”

He struggled to find the words. He didn’t want her to misunderstand. “Like… Well, I’ll be eighteen in March,” he tried instead. “Won’t matter after that.”

She gave him a smile that felt a lot like a frown, and Remus knew he’d said the wrong thing.

“Remus, beta, I make it a habit not to pry, but is there anything you'd like to tell me? Or anybody? … I know how hard it was for Sirius to talk about his family but—”

“I’m not like Sirius,” he answered sharply. “My dad, he… Lyall doesn’t hit me.”

Another smile, and Remus wanted to top himself.

“I understand.” She stroked the bed covers gently. “But you know, there are other ways people can hurt us that don’t leave any exterior wounds. They can hurt us with words, or ignore us when we really need them. They could... take advantage of our love, or forget us. And it can happen to anyone, even very strong people. Even those who might seem well cared for. It’s called neglect, Remus.”

Neglect. It was an ugly word. It seemed to hang in the air long after she’d said it, and yet Remus couldn’t bring himself to agree. He wasn’t neglected, he had everything. He had so much, that he’d had to lie about having nothing just to fit in. He’d worn their clothes, shaped his mouth to fit their words, and yet he’d still gone home to gilded window panes and marble floors. Remus Lupin wasn’t a have not, he was a will not.

"I'm not neglected."

"Remus, beta—"

"I'm not!"

Aren't you?

No, no, no... Go AWAY!

How many times have you wanted to scream at him... All those times... Look at me.

No.

Please, look at me.

No!

LOOK AT ME!

"Remus."

She moved toward him, using that soft, motherly tone he was not used to, and Remus flinched. He hated himself for it the moment he saw the reaction of it reflected in her face.

“I’m sorry. I-I didn't mean to—”

“No, I’m sorry,” Mrs. Potter said firmly. “I believe I may have overstepped. I didn't mean to panic you.”

“He doesn’t neglect me,” Remus said again, because what else was there to say? “He raised me. Kept me, even after she died… And he never hit me, either. Not once. He just—He wants to make good on his investment.”

“Remus—"

Oh no.

"Children are not investments.”

He hated that. The way she said his name. Remus, Remus, Remus. He wished she would stop—that she would go away.

“He only took away my allowance," he blabbered. "I was angry—I was being a brat.”

“Everyone’s a brat sometimes.”

“Not me. I'm bad all the time. I tell him I hate him—all of the time. He got remarried and I hate her too, even though she doesn’t deserve it. I make life hard on purpose—I run away. I lie, all of the time. And I smoke cigarettes and take drugs. I’m a bad friend to James, I won’t go to university, and I don’t care about any of it! ... If you were smart you’d kick me out.”

Effie shook her head. “No, Remus. It’s not your fault.”

Remus. Remus. Remus.

Remus, my darling.

Remus, my baby.

Oh, where have you been, my blue-eyed son?

And where have you been, my darling young one?



He put his head in his hands, curling in on himself and yanking on his hair just to feel something. He should’ve gone after all—should’ve run away—told James to fuck off. He hated all of them, especially her, and now Effie was ruining all of it. She slid from the bed and knelt down beside him, not touching but close enough to make him tremble.

“It isn’t your fault.”

Stop. Please stop.

”Do you understand, beta? It’s not—”

He couldn’t. He wouldn’t.

“—your fault.”

“Stop!”

It took every ounce of him to say it, but when he whipped his head up only meaning to swear at her some more, he was instantly shattered again. It was her eyes. So like James’ eyes and yet for a moment… oh… right. This. It was this—this feeling. Remus had forgotten what a mother felt like. Not to be looked at, but looked after.

He was come apart instantly.

“It’s not your fault. You’re a good boy. It’s not your fault.”

For so long she held him, repeating these words in his ear as he cried into the front of her apron. She stroked his hair and kissed his head, murmuring these words. Through it all she smelt of Christmas and home cooking, of teakwood, P&G detergent and poinsettia flowers. She was kind and it killed him and he hated her but she held him anyway; sitting on his sweaty bed sheets and rocking him back and forth like she might a baby. She sang to him too, and though the words were in Hindi and he did not understand, Remus wept. How he’d missed lullabies.

Afterwards he felt only numb. The embarrassment crept in slowly, but she didn’t release him until he could sit up on his own without sniffling. There she stroked his face some more; patting the damp from his cheeks while Remus stared down at the covers.

“Thank you. I’m alright now,” was all he could think to say.

She kissed his forehead. “Of course."

“I’m sorry for making you take care of me like this.”

“No. Do not ever apologise. You are welcome here. Monty and I always talked about having more children—siblings for James. I’m glad to know that he went out and found them for himself.”

Remus had no words to that, and so she smiled kindly at him and pat his leg over the covers as she stood. Beneath the shame, he was grateful—she knew when her job was done and did not dawdle. Another coughing fit overcame him as she approached the door, and Effie shook her head.

“I’m going to send up some more tea for you. See if we can’t knock that cold right out of your system. You took your medicine already, yes?”

He nodded.

“Good. Then you just relax. Let me know if there’s anything you need. Anything at all.”

“… Thank you, Mrs. Potter.”

“You’re welcome, beta.” She pulled the door shut behind her and Remus sagged back into the pillows, grinding his palms into both eyes. He felt rubbed raw, and his runny nose was worse than ever. He wondered if seeing him cry had made her feel better—like she’d accomplished some great thing in getting him to acknowledge a pain he’d only ever sought to ignore. He felt guilty for not trusting her, but such was instinct. She was an adult, and adults had caused most of his problems—or they used to. Lately he was doing a fine enough job on his own.

But neglect? That was a new one.

Mrs. Potter clearly didn’t know what she was talking about if she’d thought he’d been actually neglected. If she could’ve seen the way Tomny or the rest had grown up then she would’ve seen that Remus walked on a carpet of clouds. He’d always told himself he was better off—that he’d never wanted for money or food or clothes. A dad was a luxury, and he had enough of those anyway. He was fine.

After about twenty minutes of trying to sleep while the radio hummed distantly on his bedside, Remus finally sat up and tossed off the bed covers. He sneezed into his elbow, and as he did, the disc jockey’s voice filtered through the speakers;

“And that was ‘Silver Lady’ by David Soul. Now coming at you with some ABBA! Here’s ‘Take a Chance on Me’! ... 'If you change your mind, I’m the first in line! Honey, I’m still free, take a chance on m—!’

“Oh shut up.”

Remus clapped his hand down on the radio’s off switch, before tugging a jumper over his head to ward off the chills that never seemed to leave him. He reached for the box of tissues on the wardrobe dresser, but found it empty. Grumbling, he trudged over to the bedroom door and threw it wide, only to narrowly avoid running headlong into Sirius.

“Sorry—!" He wiped his face quickly, desperate to not let Sirius know he'd been crying. "Was gonna use… the… loo…”

Sirius recovered quickly. He was holding a tea tray in his hands while worrying at his bottom lip. “Effie said you were napping… Guess she lied. But she asked me to leave this next to your bed.”

Remus looked down at the tea set, which smelled strongly of mint and peppercorn. Sirius pressed it into his chest and he took it, suddenly aware of his ragged bedhead and the frog in his throat. “You didn’t go out with the others?”

Sirius shook his head. “Been working on something. Didn’t want to disrupt the flow. And besides, I’m not much one for skating anyway. Too cold.”

“Oh. Do you mean a song?"

"Maybe."

“Is it... any good?”

Sirius shrugged, looking sheepish. “Maybe.”

“Cool...”

Neither of them said anything for a long moment, and after glancing at the floor, Sirius turned to leave.

“Wait.” Remus clutched tightly at the tray. “Don’t you want to talk or something?”

“Talk about what?”

Ugh. “Any of it?”

Sirius crossed his arms over his chest. “Didn’t seem like you wanted to talk,” he replied sharply. The reaction made Remus bristle a bit.

“I didn’t.”

“Why bother now then?”

“Because you were outside my door? And because it’s… convenient?”

The corners of Sirius’ mouth turned up humourlessly. “ ‘Convenient’. What an apt choice of words.”

“I take that to mean you’re still angry.”

“Yeah, I’m still angry.”

“Well, I’m still angry at you too,” Remus countered.

“Fine. No one said we had to be sorry to play in a band together, but I’m not playing stupid apology games anymore.”

Remus ground his teeth together. “So where does this leave us?”

“Guess we’ll find out.”

Sirius turned again, but Remus wouldn’t allow him the last word. Not after everything.

“You told James’ mum about my dad,” he said suddenly. Sirius stopped dead at that, and seizing his opportunity to sink teeth into flesh, Remus set the tea tray aside and stepped out into the hall. “You told her about the things I told you in confidence. About my dad.”

“You didn’t just tell me about your dad,” Sirius said stonily. “You told all of us.”

“Not that,” Remus growled. “I mean the rest—Lyall. All the stuff he’s said.”

“Oh. Yeah, I guess I did. Are you pissed off over that too then?”

“I should be, shouldn’t I? She thinks I was bloody neglected now!”

“Weren’t you?”

Remus swallowed thickly. “Not like you.”

“Oh, is it a competition now?” Sirius mocked. “The age-old game of ‘who’s daddy likes them the least’?”

“In that case, I wouldn’t bother if I were you. You’re a sore loser, and I’ve got two dads that don’t want me.”

“You said it, mate, not me.”

It was like watching a trapeze artist teeter on a tightrope. Remus couldn’t look away, even as the rope trembled and he was left holding his breath in anxiety. It was that roller coaster plunging down, down—only now, he could see the rocks at the bottom.

Unwilling to crash, he turned back to his room.

“Lupin.”

He almost ignored him out of sheer stubbornness, but Sirius had always commended every shred of his attention. When Remus stubbornly looked back he found Sirius with his back turned, a hand reached out toward him with its palm upturned, open and seeking. He wouldn’t look at him, but it was his hand he offered. Like a truce. It almost made Remus nostalgic.





Take me back to July,

Bright, beautifully bold;

Now it’s December,

And I’m turning cold…





He’d written the song for both of them. For so long it’d meant everything, and then when they’d fought it’d begun to ring hollow. And yet there they were anyway.

Looking away, Remus reached back and took his hand. Sirius gave it a gentle squeeze; so faint, more like a caress than anything else. Then he was gone, descending the stairs and dropping out of sight to the floor below.

That evening, Remus did not venture out of his room. Instead he opened the bedroom window, feeling the December cold ice his bones and remembering what I’d been like to sit with Sirius on this corner of the roof. It was not a fond memory, no matter how many times Sirius had let him kiss him or what had come after.

“Bloody freezing in here,” Lily hissed, when she’d come in for bed. She fetched a spare blanket from the hall cupboard and buried them both under its plush warmth before turning out the light.

“How was your day?” She whispered, hair haloed against her pillow. “Did you talk to Sirius at all?”

Remus shook his head at the question. “How was skating?”

“Good. We went to Hyde Park. I wish you could’ve come. Potter always claims to be a sports god, but he fell three times.”

“Bet you had a laugh.”

“Me and half the rink. It’s what he gets for showing off.” Lily hummed quietly. “Are you feeling any better?”

“A bit.”

“Does this mean you’ll go out with us tomorrow?”

He considered. It would be nice to see Marlene, and at least with that many of them, he and Sirius could avoid getting stuck together.

“Alright.”

She grinned at him. “I love you, Remus.”

“Love you too, Lils.”

Lily fell asleep quickly, tired from the day’s events, but Remus remained all too awake. He waited until the house had finally settled and all of its occupants were sure to be sleeping, and then grabbed the present Lily had moved from the bed to the top of the wardrobe and crept downstairs. Outside, he found that the staircase’s railing had been encased in tinsel and the soft glow of the tree lights could be seen before he’d even stepped into the salon. Beneath the real Fraser Fir, which Mr. Potter had cut down himself on the edge of the property, was a large array of presents, all lovingly wrapped and bound, just waiting for the morning they’d be torn open by eager hands. Remus went to place the gold-wrapped gift amongst them, but stopped short at the last second. He peeked at the tag.

To Sirius, From Remus.

He ripped it away, crumpling it in his palm. Then he tucked the gift back under the tree.





* * *





Christmas Eve, 1977





Mrs. Potter sighed, examining her thermometer. “You still have a slight fever. Perhaps we should take you to the hospital after all. See about some stronger antibiotics.”

“No!” Remus urged. “I’m fine, I don’t need a hospital.”

“Remus, it’s important to take care of your health.”

“I’m practically all better. Honest.”

She scowled like she didn’t believe him, but by then James was already grabbing Remus by the shoulder and shaking him vigorously.

“Come oooooon, Mum,” he moaned. “Moony's been stuck in bed since we got back and it’s just one evening! After tonight you can stuff him with kadha ‘til it leaks out of his ears.”

“Thanks for that image,” Remus scoffed, before looking back at Effie. “I’ll be alright, Mrs. Potter. Thank you for looking after me.”

“You promise to dress warmly? Not like this one…” She eyed Sirius, who had decided upon his leather jacket without so much as a pair of mittens.

“You can’t wear a muffler with this, Mum, it’d totally kill the look.”

“No hanging outside in the cold,” she ordered Remus. “Don’t want you sniffling come Christmas.”

“Promise.”

James swooped in a second later; “Don’t worry, Mum, it's only a matinee—we’ll be back before your Christmas Eve party turns into a pumpkin.”

Mrs. Potter remained sceptical, but in the end the tickets were already bought and not even her overbearing kindness would keep Remus from missing out.

“Here, take Monty’s scarf, it’s much warmer!” She insisted, as they all donned their coats in the foyer. Remus let himself be bundled, while James and Lily stood by, trying to hide their sly smiles.

“What?” He asked Sirius, mumbling through the wool; “No jokes?”

Sirius looked him up and down. “I had some. Don’t much feel like giving you the satisfaction now.”

They finished by scoffing at each other, and then followed each other out to the driveway where all four of them piled into Mr. Potter’s sedan. He was kind enough to drive them to the nearest tube station, which was already bustling with last-minute holiday shoppers and those just looking to get home. From there they took the train the rest of the way into the city and hurried down to the icy London pavement to meet Mary and Marlene outside the theatre in Leicester Square. Both girls were bundled up tight and standing close together to avoid being jostled by the hundreds of other fans waiting in line to get a chance to glimpse the film taking the sci-fi genre by storm. Despite the weather, some were even in costume, and everyone was yammering excitedly about ‘death rockets’ and ‘sky-walkers’ and whatnot.

“It’s like a bleedin’ rock concert,” Sirius whistled, as they slipped in line behind the girls.

“Hey, no cutting!” Someone shouted.

“Bite me, Suspender-Stanley.”

“Don’t you look snazzy,” Mary commended, “and not at all like you’re about to freeze your bollocks off.”

“Be a mate and lend me your pockets, Macdonald?” Sirius begged, too cold to argue. Mary obliged, and he slipped his arms around her, pushing his hands into her coat pockets as though he were holding her from behind. Mary seemed pleased enough at this, and even smirked at the pair of young girls ahead of them who’d turned around to ogle the handsome boy in the leather coat.

Remus was not bothered. He’d fallen into step with Marlene, who seemed to be shivering as well, but upon closer inspection, was actually bouncing up and down on the spot from pure excitement.

“How’d you swing the tickets for this anyway?” He asked her.

“My brother!” Marlene exclaimed. “He’s got a friend who works at the theatre. It’s my Christmas gift.”

“You didn’t need to spend your Christmas gift on us,” Remus frowned.

“As opposed to what—going alone?” She shook her head. “This is way better anyway. Last year Michael got me these god-awful earrings from Biba.”

“Earrings are nice…?”

“Only if you’ve got the holes to match.” Marlene lifted the edge of her wool cap, revealing bare earlobes. “Anyway, how’re you doing?”

“Fine. Chest thing's almost gone.”

“That’s good, but I sorta meant what happened with Sirius.”

Remus took a deep breath. There was a throbbing behind his eyes that was just shifting from a mild discomfort to a gnawing affliction. “It’s done, Cherry,” he told her.

“You talked then—made up?”

“No. We’re done.”

"Is that why you're still wearing his necklace?"

Alarmed, Remus pressed a hand to his throat, but the necklace was covered by a jumper and a coat, not to mention Mr. Potter's scarf.

"How did you...?"

"I guessed." Marlene dropped her gaze, looking sorry. “Has Sirius at least apologised?”

“We’ve moved on," Remus huffed sharply. "I'm over it."

“Shit, Remus. You can’t just forgive him! He—” She dropped her voice; “He tried to get you to out yourself. Before you were ready! I mean, who even does that?”

Her vexation toward Sirius placated him momentarily, but then that same surge of guilt rose in his gut. Briefly, he considered telling her about all the times Sirius had made his own feelings about coming out crystal clear, only to dismiss them without a second thought; but really, Remus didn’t fancy rehashing the conversation in public.

“I don’t care anymore. I just want to forget about it.”

Marlene looked like she wanted to argue, but then an excited cry went up in front of the theatre, and the line finally began to move.

“Here we go!” Marlene said to the rest of them. “Best be quick or we’ll get stuck at the front and have to stare up at the screen the entire time.”

“God forbid,” Sirius drawled; “I can’t wait to see nerd history in the making.”

Most of them went into the dark theatre with very low expectations and when it was over, all filed out again, the booming film score practically chasing them up the aisle by the heels.

“Well, that was surprisingly… not terrible,” Mary said.

“Just admit you liked it and move on,” Marlene blagged.

“I wouldn’t say I ‘liked it’, but that Solo fellow wasn’t too hard on the eyes. I might be coerced into seeing a sequel if we get at least one shirtless scene.”

“You’re such a…” Marlene scoffed. “Fine. What about the rest of it then? What about Leia?”

“The whiny princess? Meh.”

“She wasn’t whiny! She was a soldier—a rebel! Honestly I'm amazed a man wrote her character. Competent and beautiful.”

“My god, did it finally happen? Did you fall in love, Marls?”

“Oh shove off.”

“I liked the laser swords,” James said, waving his hand around with a whirring noise and playing at chopping Sirius’ arm off at the shoulder. Playing along, Sirius clutched his arm and moaned terribly, before bouncing back and shooting finger guns in James’ direction as he fled through the throng of giddy movie-goers.

“I’m gonna go find the lav. Meet you outside,” Remus said to Lily, before excusing himself to the theatre toilet. He hadn’t said anything (mostly because Marlene would’ve crucified any of them for chatting over the film) but somewhere between the exploding planet and the exploding spaceship that looked like a planet but was decidedly not a planet, his fever had crept back in full force. It left him hunched over a bathroom sink, breathing hard as he tried not to throw up. Everywhere smelt of stale popcorn and BO, and he felt light-headed just from standing. At least the theatre had been dark, but Remus was not look forward to the chilly ride home on the tube.

“Don’t be a bloody jessie,” he told himself; “you just need to make it back. You can pass out in your room, fucking toff.”

When he finally emerged from the bathroom—nearly running head-long to a man wearing green face-paint and a pair of antennae—he found his friends waiting for him across the dark street. Despite the late hour, people were still bustling around, most of them avid fans or loiterers looking to pick a pocket or two. Even in the dim light given off by the theatre, Lily must’ve noticed how pale he was, as she turned to him and peeled off a glove to check the temperature of his forehead.

“You ninny, you’re burning up again. That’s it, we’re taking you to the hospital.”

“You mean you’re still sick?” Mary gaped.

Remus groaned and pushed Lily’s hand away. “I’m fine. It’s Christmas Eve, let’s just get to the train and go home.”

“I can ring dad from a booth and ask him to come pick us up from here,” James offered.

“No, don’t bother, I can make it. I’m not—” he surveyed his friends, counting only four. “Where’s Black?”

“Maybe you should look into the hospital,” Marlene pressed, taking his arm quickly. “It’s on our way, Mary and I will take you! Come on, let's go!”

Marlene meant well, but it was too late. He’d already spotted him a short ways down the street, standing on the corner. Sirius—talking to a girl. A pretty girl. She must've come from the film as well, but she didn't look like she smelt of popcorn or BO. She wore a long coat and a winter hat, dark hair braided down her back. And Sirius... he was standing in that self-possessed way of his—all legs in his dark jeans. And he was smiling. Then when the girl reached out to bat playfully at his arm, he didn’t move away.

Suddenly Remus missed the annoying robots and the dark corners of the theatre. His hands seized at his sides and everything began to ache, especially his head.

Sirius was talking to a girl.

Sirius, who was gay, was talking to a girl.

Sirius, who he’d been in love with and dreaming of moving in with up until a week ago, was talking to a girl.

Now he knew he was going to throw up.

“There he is,” James said, spotting Sirius a second too late. “Five quid says she complimented his jacket or something. Hold on while I go get the tosser. Oi, Black!"

As James started his merry way down the pavement, Remus began backing up in the other direction. Marlene clung to him, her platform boots scraping the pavement as she tried to pull him back.

“Remus—Remus, come on. Don't worry about that, he’s just being stupid!”

“What’s the matter?” Lily demanded, the picture of concern.

But Remus couldn’t speak. He was turning over in his grave and he wasn’t even dead yet. He was so not done moving on. He hadn’t even packed yet. He was still wearing Sirius’ bloody necklace, for Christ sake. Why hadn’t he taken it off?!

“I—I need to go,” he stammered.

“What you need is to go to the hospital!” Marlene pushed. She kept a tight hold on his wrist, but Remus was still looking at Sirius. Sirius who was turning as James approached, holding out a hand in gesture to the girl, speaking as though he were introducing them.

Oh god, he knows her name.

With a sharp twist Remus had freed himself from Marlene’s grasp and turned, marching away.

“Remus!” Mary cried after him. “What the—come back!”

Lily shrieked too, wailing his name like it was a curse;

“Remus Lupin, where do you think you’re going?!”

But Remus only covered his ears, taking the first corner he came upon and high-tailing it up the lane. He wouldn’t be caught—he refused. He would not be the person Sirius looked to after being chatted up by some random girl off the street.

Without being fully conscious of where he was going, he caught a train from Charing Cross to London’s east side and never looked back. As a result, he’d gotten on a no-smoking car by mistake. Irritated, Remus began instantly searching his pockets for a desperate fag anyway and nearly shat himself when he whipped out a wad of cash Lyall had given him and scattered half of it on the train floor. The notes scattered and he scrambled to collect them, before promptly switching cars. West of the Strand you’d likely get shivved for carrying that much dosh on you. Not that he wasn’t already making about a dozen other mistakes. He was already out walking alone after dark, half-delirious with a fever while the other half of him was delirious with Sirius. And he was wearing a coat worth more than a month’s wages at any dock along the Thames. The money in his pocket felt like a small burden in comparison to the rest, but at least if he got jumped he could throw the money one way and run the other.

As he made his way up the twisting streets, Remus realised with proper irony what a circle his life had become. Before Hawkings he would’ve done just about anything to return to the End, and he had. But he’d never imagined how often he’d be slinking back.

When he reached it, the flat’s building looked the same—crumbled, rusted, and wet from the December rain. The light over the front door’s entryway was out, but he buzzed the flat’s number and was relieved to find that the ringer actually working again. Then a girl answered and Remus nearly stopped breathing.

“ ‘ello, wotchu want?”

It was like hearing Tonya’s voice all over again, except this girl sounded sing-song, the voice of someone high on more than just life. Tonya never sounded like that, even after a dozen lines, she was too charming.

"Helloooo...? Th is Maxie with the hash?"

“No," he croaked anxiously. "I'm not Maxie, I'm... M'lookin’ for Tomny.”

The intercom clicked off and Remus briefly considered cutting his losses and taking off. He wasn’t sure he could get away with another confrontation with Lee fully intact.

“ ‘oo’s this?”

Not Lee. It was Tomny’s easy brogue that cut through. Hearing him nearly made Remus lightheaded with relief.

“It’s me, Tom."

There was some silence, undoubtedly Tomny collecting every thought that had just shot out of his head, then; “Meet me under the balcony.”

Remus did as he was told, skittering down off the front steps and rounding the front of the building, staring up at the dirty second-floor balcony as he rocked back and forth on his heels. It was hard to make out Tomny’s expression as he slid the door open, but he could see his breath coming out in little puffs of haze under the moonlight. Noise followed him out, the sound of plenty of people partying it up inside. Remus kicked himself—it was Christmas Eve. Of course he’d have people over.

“You’re mental coming ‘ere in the middle ‘a the night,” Tomny lashed at him from above. “How’d you even get past Stepney?!”

“You know how it is... No one bothers with a skinny kid.”

“Wish that were true.” Tomny sighed, before rubbing his shoulders harshly. “Fuck—s’cold out ‘ere. You come all the way from Blackheath?”

“No, Finchley.”

Tomny swore again and Remus felt a pang of guilt.

“I know you got people here, a–and I’ll go if I need to. Just needed to get out and cool my head, really. Didn’t know where else…” He winced; “… sorry.”

Tomny pinched his forehead, but waved him off. “No, don’t go. Jus’ stay out of sight for a sec. I’ll get rid of ‘em.”

“You really don't have—”

“Shaddup!” There was the noise of shuffling feet, and then; “Don’t freeze, posh boy.”

Obediently, Remus hunkered down in the shadows off the side of the front yard. It took about twenty minutes, during which his breathing had gone from slightly laboured to sounding as though he’d just run half a marathon. He was sweating an obscene amount inside his coat, but by then people had started to pile out of the front of the building. The rowdy group shambled out the door together, laughing and swearing as they kicked open the rusted gate and made their way up the lane. Remus thought he might’ve caught a flash of Seesaw among them.

“Nerve ‘a that Tom!” One of them cried. “Kickin’ us out on Christmas like fuckin' tweakers on his doorstep.”

“You are a tweaker, tweaker."

"Fuck off!"

"M'gonna head over to Geddy’s. You wankers comin'?”

“Oh shit, yeah! He’s got the good stuff anyway…”

Their chatter receded with them as the group trudged further up the lane. Remus was almost tempted to follow, if just for the chance to overhear something familiar, but then Tomny was there, nervously calling out for him in the dark.

“I’m here,” Remus rasped, rounding the dead blackthorn bushes that lined the front garden.

“Blimey,” Tomny cursed, coming down the wet steps in naught but his socks. “You look like death if he got hit by a train.”

“Try a Boeing seven-thirty-seven.”

“I don’t even know what that means.” He took Remus by the arm. “M’on then, little swot. You’ve already ruined my high, might as well getchu inside.”

Every single floorboard in the building creaked as they made their way up the stairs to the second floor. It was what happened to old, unkempt buildings in the winter. Frost had made its way inside, covering window sills and door hinges. They passed the row of post boxes, painted over with graffiti tags. A dead plant sat at the base of the stairs, its pot filled with more cigarette butts than dirt. Remus hadn’t realised how weak he’d become until he had to practically let Tomny carry him up the stairs. It was slow-going, as he had to stop every fourth step or so to catch his breath.

“What’s a’matter witchu, Lu?” Tomny grunted; “You actually get jumped on the way over or sumfin?”

Remus took another step and winced. Even his lungs had started to ache out in the cold.

“Ngh—sick. Got a chest infection.”

“Fuck. You taking any meds?”

“Mhm... Left them behind.”

“Bollocks.”

Remus grimaced, nearly missing the next stair. “Sorry for interrupting your party.”

“You didn’t interrupt anything,” Tomny huffed. “Those guys been ‘ere goin’ on three days now. I was getting ready to chase ‘em out. Feelin’ a bit ‘humbug’ as of late anyway.”

That makes two of us, Remus thought bitterly.

They managed to get inside eventually, and thankfully it was warm. The flat smelt of stale cigarettes and the musk of many bodies, but Remus didn't care. Tomny carried him across the threshold and dropped him on the living room sofa—which was dingier than he remembered—before squatting down in front of him and reaching up to lift his eyelid with the pad of his thumb.

“You sure you ain’t tweakin’?”

Remus shook his head. “S’just a fever.”

Tomny tsked and checked his other eye. “And what was it you were doin’ in Finchley?”

“Friend’s place. Had to get out. Some… stuff’s happened.”

With another heavy sigh, Tomny released him and leaned back. “Can’t believe you came to me for medical help. Thought you public schoolboys were s’posed to be smart.”

“Jus’ wanted to see you,” Remus said honestly.

Tomny gave him a long look, like he couldn’t decide what insult fit him best. In the end he said nothing at all, just dropped his head and began unlacing Remus’ boots for him.

“Missed ya too, plonker.”

Feeling a bit weepy, Remus stared down at the top of Tomny’s head. The gold had faded from his hair as it always did during the cold months, leaving it soft and brown like a fallen leaf in autumn.

“Orright, up yeh go,” the older boy said, once he’d gotten both boots off. Snaking a hand under his armpits, Tomny pulled Remus to his feet and helped guide him down the hall toward the bedroom.

“Thanks,” Remus wheezed, as he collapsed down on the edge of the bed.

“You should drink something,” Tomny said as he straightened up. He left and came back with a coffee mug, passing it over with a little smirk. “Hope you still like the taste of London tap water.”

Remus gulped it down. “Tastes like home.”

Tomny nodded awkwardly and pressed his hands into his back pockets. “Well, you can stay ‘ere until yer feelin’ better. I’ll take the couch. No problem.”

"I don't mean to take your bed."

"You gonna make me tell ya to shut up again?"

“In that case,” Remus smiled meekly, “I hope you at least cleaned the sheets."

Tomny flicked him on the forehead. “You’ve clearly got jokes so guess that means yer gonna be jus’ fine.” Taking the empty mug, he mumbled something about medicine and turned to the door.

“Thank you, Tom.”

Tomny froze in the doorway, looking back at him. “You still got that scar, I see. S’not going away. It’s stubborn… like you." He chuckled quietly. "You know, you could'a called first."

"I know," Remus nodded. “I’m sorry if I let you down.”

“Nah. You know me, don’t expect nuffin. Can't let me down if I'm expectin' nuffin, yeah?"

“Then I let the others down. I’m a shit friend.”

At that, Tomny turned around and strode back into the bedroom. He stopped just before Remus, and placed a hand on his forehead, smoothing his hair back. “Be a shit friend then. You can fix the rest in the morning. When you're feeling better.”

"Not sure that's how the world works."

"No, it is. Don't cha know? I know everything." Smirking, Tomny pushed him back onto the covers. “Sleep. I’ll be right out ‘ere.”

He disappeared into the hall, leaving the door open a crack so that yellow light from the kitchen’s hob could spill onto the floor. There was a light clatter of glassware on metal, then rushing water from a tap. Eventually Remus heard the faint sound of someone humming, and recognised the tune immediately.

"Mmm... You say goodbye, and I say hello… Hello, hello… I don’t know why you say goodbye, I say hello..."

A lump formed in the base of his throat and Remus drew up the covers up to his nose. It was warm, comforting. The radiator was buzzing. Everything smelt familiar—like Tomny.

You say goodbye... I say hello...

Remus shut his eyes. Before he knew it, he was asleep.



Chapter End Notes

The first song on the radio is "Livin' Thing" by Electric Light Orchestra, 1976.

Rasam is a South Indian soup while kadha is a variation of chai or black tea. Both are considered effective against sickness!

Biba was a women’s fashion store in London.

'The Strand' is a major thoroughfare in London.

Chapter 84: Christmas, 1977


Chapter Summary

Back at the flat for Christmas. Some has stayed the same, and much has changed.



Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for more notes



No one knows what it’s like,

To be the bad man;

To be the sad man,

Behind blue eyes;

No one knows what it’s like,

To be hated;

To be fated,

To telling only lies;

But my dreams, they aren’t as empty,

As my conscience seems to be;

I have hours, only lonely,

My love is vengeance that’s never free…

- “Behind Blue Eyes” The Who, 1977



If you’d have asked, nine times out of ten, Remus Lupin would've told you that he did not dream. This was a lie of course, because everyone had dreams—Remus just barely remembered his. Every morning he woke up with the wisps of the night’s recital slipping away into the forgotten void, and he would go about his day thinking he had not dreamed at all. And really, this was how he preferred it. He had no interest in imagining that he could fly, or that he’d lost all of his teeth at once, or woken up in a room full of people completely starkers. In his later years, it’d even become a point of pride not to dream.

But you know what they say, the more you chase a high, the harder it is to achieve.

The memories came all at once as they tended to, tugged to the surface on an invisible line made of sickness and drugs. It was as though admitting his deepest secret had drawn them forth like an angry mob to the hanging. They came to him in night visions—cruel and lonely dreams built to fuck with his head. On those nights, he might have preferred the impossible. He’d have taken any hideous monster or man-made horror over the trudged up memories of his tiny, helpless self. It was like a trick—he was getting pranked by his own brain and he couldn’t even find the words to describe it afterwards. He simply woke up, memories made of the shape of his shirt buttons or the smell of a cooked meal dancing behind his eyes. Going from darkness to light as though he were leaving the theatre of a film without any meaning.

Just as a sad, sad film.





* * *





“Here, darling, open this one next. ‘To Remus, love Mummy and Daddy’.”

He took the gift eagerly. His fingers were small and round. Young, then. Inside the wrapped box he found a pair of gloves, made from hairsheep leather and fitted especially for those tiny fingers. He tried them on, mostly to make his mother happy, but when Hope slid the next present toward him, Remus quickly tossed the gloves back into their box to be forgotten.

“This one is from Mummy,” she grinned. It was a fully transistorised record player, complete in his own little plastic carrying case.

“It’s got five records even,” Hope preened, pointing to the outside of the box; The Four Seasons, Petula Clark, Herman’s Hermits, Peter and Gordan, and yes!—The Beatles.

“He’s never going to sleep now. He’ll be listening to that thing all night,” Lyall said, sitting behind them in one of the salon's expensive carven armchairs. He had a glass of sherry in one hand. Remus stared at it, and the glass winked at him in all the colours of the glittering Christmas tree.

“Music is enriching,” said Hope, as Remus forwent the winking glass and began tearing into the turntable’s box. She was sat on the rug beside him, hands folded neatly in her lap like a true lady. She looked pretty too, with her hair and makeup all done-up despite the early hour. It was astonishing, considering she'd only left the hospital the week before. Remus couldn't remember how he knew that.

Parallel to his wife, Lyall wore well-fitted slacks and a dress shirt, suited like he was ready for a day in the office rather than a holiday off. He was handsome too. Remus hoped he'd be handsome like that one day. For now all he had to wear were pyjamas with cowboys on them. After all, it was Christmas morning and he was only nine. Nine... It was to be expected.

“Are you happy, darling?” Hope smiled, as Remus fiddled with the player’s plug. He nodded, surveying the rest of his gifts. None of them came close to the turntable.

“Can I play it?” He asked, raising the Beatles’ 45. Lyall got to his feet a second later, his sherry glass empty.

“In your room,” he said, but when Remus scrambled to his feet to do so, Hope stopped them both.

“Hold on, darling, there’s one more!”

Remus could hardly believe it. There was more?

As Lyall slowly returned to his seat in the armchair to observe, Hope slipped across the room. “It’s a secret present!” She called, before pushing a large box out from behind the salon chaise. It was wrapped in all red, with a large gold bow on its top. Remus was elated instantly, and as his mother dragged it over the rug toward him, his fingers itched to release the gift from its paper prison.

“Who’s this one from, then?” Lyall asked.

“My aunt,” Hope answered simply, before depositing the gift down in front of Remus. “Go on then, darling. Open it!”

Remus wasted no time. He tore into the wrappings, eyes immediately shot wide. “A car!” he exclaimed, admiring the pictures along the front. “It’s a car!”

Hope joined him on the rug once more to admire the toy, folding her legs primly beneath her so as to not crease her skirt. “An RC car, how exciting!” She said. “And look, it runs on petrol, just like Giles’.”

Unable to wait anymore, Remus wrenched open the top of the box and began digging through the cardboard inside. He was excited—he was always excited on Christmas! But if he’d been paying any attention, he might’ve noticed the sceptical look on his father’s face as he inspected his empty sherry glass.

“Which aunt of yours was it then?” He asked Hope. She did not look at her husband, just continued to pet Remus’ hair.

“Aunt Justina.”

“Your mother’s sister?”

“Mhm, yes. The one who lives in Holyhead.”

“I remember. Just didn’t think Justina recalled much of Remus. He must’ve been, what—three months old the last time she visited? Certainly never sent gifts before.”

Hope’s voice turned tight; “Maybe she saw it and thought of him. He’s already ten.”

"You mean nine?"

"Yes, what did I say?"

Lyall sighed. “I just don’t understand how Justina could’ve arranged for such a thing. Not after being diagnosed with dementia four, five? Years ago…? Is her hospice in Holyhead as well then? Odd, considering I send the cheque to Blackpool every month.”

Remus looked up at his mother to find Hope’s expression to be very severe. She was smiling, but it did not quite reach her eyes. “Call it a Christmas miracle,” she replied, before grinning eagerly at her boy. “Remus, do you like it? Shall we race it around the garden?”

“Don’t be ridiculous, it’s freezing out,” Lyall said. “Remus, go play your records in your room. I need to speak with your mother.”

Remus might’ve argued, but he was having a hard time deciding which present he liked more. In the end he was quite agreeable to the record player, but just as he went to shut the lid on the RC car’s box, he noticed a little note slipped just between the inner wrappings.

“Remus, what’s that?” Hope asked, as he withdrew it.

“A card,” he said. “It’s got my name on it, Mummy.”

When he awoke again it was already nighttime. He’d slept through Christmas, but somehow, Remus wasn’t all that bothered. A snore echoed from beside him. Turning over, Remus found Tomny asleep on top of the covers next to him, still in his clothes and hair completely sleep-mussed. He wasn’t the same sort of beautiful sleeper Sirius was—he was drooling a bit—but he was familiar.

Immediately Tomny’s eyes shot open, making Remus’ heart seize up. He squinted at him in the darkness, before his hand came up—unceremoniously slapping him on the forehead.

Remus blinked. “Ow?”

With a weary grunt, Tomny turned over and Remus was left to stare at the broadness of his back. His shirt was frayed along the collar and his shoulders clung to the fabric. He was fair, even a bit freckled. Familiar.

Remus slept.





* * *





This time he was fourteen, sitting outside the headmaster’s office and glaring at the floor. There was a thick knot in the floorboard between his feet, and when he shut his right eye it looked a bit like Giles’ when he was angry. To pass the time, Remus switched back and forth, shutting one eye and then the other to see the expression change. The game was mindless, but it at least helped to distract from the twinge in his knuckles. Normally he’d be given some ice, but relief was reserved for misunderstood boys—not violent ones. Fuck you, fuck you, FUCK YOU!

There was silence, and Remus ground his teeth together. Lyall was going to buy his way back in, of course he was.

“Be that as it may, Mr. Lupin, my hands are tied,” said the crotchety Headmaster; “Professor Wright has been with this college for many ‘a year, and is a well-respected part of the academic community. The silence that followed sounded a lot more like the pounding of a gavel. He’d been sentenced, and the sentence was exile.

Good riddance.

The office door opened, and Lyall Lupin stalked out into the hall. He shut the door after himself, before stopping next to Remus’ chair. Even with his head bowed in misfortune, he was still a ginormous man.

“Get up.”

Remus didn’t so much as play at hesitating. He’d gotten what he’d wanted since September—a first class ticket out of the stuffy boys’ college—but that didn’t mean he was out of the woods entirely. He followed his father down the hallway, then the looming staircase, where they finally crossed the hall’s foyer and passed beneath the painting of Jesus and Saint Joseph that hung over the school’s front doors.

By then Remus was dragging his feet. He could see Giles at the head of the school's drive, standing stoically beside the Rolls with his hands crossed in front of him. Remus hadn’t seen either of them in weeks, and as they descended the school's front step, he imagined the ride home to Blackheath and the words just came tumbling out.

“It’s not my fault! That teacher’s dirty. He makes us slam our fingers in our desks or stand the entire day if he catches us talking out of turn. Remus blanched. He wanted to keep shouting, but the grip his father had on his shoulders was tight enough to bruise.
