Lyall Lupin did not wait. Instead he trudged down the gravel drive toward the silver Rolls-Royce, where Giles was waiting with the door open. Remus hung back, rubbing the soreness from his biceps. He’d nearly missed it, but then the hair on the back of his neck stood on end, and he turned around to find several boys watching him from the school’s windows. They looked like ghosts. Well-dressed, cherub-faced ghosts. In their eyes they wore a glazed layer of judgement.

You never belonged here.

Freak.

Get lost.

Remus raised a hand, and flipped every one of them off.





* * *





When he woke again, he found Tomny bent over the bedside table, cutting a small line of white powder with a razor blade. It looked like Tonya’s stardust, but when Remus nudged him, wanting a hit, he was met with a shake of the head.

“Nice try. This tosh s’off limits to toffs.”

Rolling his eyes, Tomny licked his finger to wipe up the rest of the powder and rub it along his gums. "Just go on, sleep sum'more. You need it."

Tomny stared at him for a moment, with pupils the size of a ten pence, then reached for the bedside drawer. He pulled out a fresh bottle of pills—downers, with the label torn off.

Remus took three, and was asleep again before his head even hit the pillow.

This time, there were no dreams. No Hope, no Lyall, no pitiful boy caught between the two. The sleeping pills succeeded in knocking him out for almost another full day, and when Remus finally stirred again, it was to the shrieking of the flat’s phone.

“Those fuckin’ cunts,” Tomny groaned, dragging himself out of bed and leaving Remus to turn over drowsily. He could faintly hear him in the living room, grumbling haggard answers before finally slamming the receiver down and reappearing in the bedroom’s doorway.

Remus loved Tomny, he did, but the man couldn’t cook to save his life.

“How do you live like this?” He demanded, throwing away an entire bag of potatoes that had sprouted in one of the bottom cupboards. A mixture of relief and amusement spread across Tomny’s features. “Yeah, orright. In the meantime, how d’ya feel about Chinese?”

Together they bundled up and skipped down to the nearest take-out shop, which had supposedly opened sometime over the summer. Remus remembered the building as a laundrette and it still had the same chipped tile flooring, only now was dressed up in all red with cheap paper lanterns hanging from the ceiling and dragons and pandas displayed across every surface.

But since neither he nor Tomny were packing one of 007's pistols, it could only mean bad news.

“I thought that was you, Armstrong," the guy crooned. "What's the craic, ya wee dryshite?"

“Nice to see you too, Benny,” Tomny answered stoically. The gangster smirked at his tone, before glancing at Remus like a predator eyeing up his next meal. His two guys stood quietly behind him, and for a brief moment Remus thought he recognised one of them, but before he could place the face, Benny had already leaned in and placed a hand on the table between them.

“Yeah, we’s spotted you through the window. Thought it only courteous to drop in and say ‘ello. Happy Christmas, n' all that... So who’s this—yooer new girlfriend?”

“He’s a kid,” Tomny replied staunchly. “And we’re about to eat dinner, so how ‘bout we do this later, maybe?”

“Ah, but like me mam always say, there’s really nathin’ like discussin’ business over a fine meal. Boys—saddle in, maybe?”

Before Tomny could object any further, the group had crowded around the end of their booth and Benny had dropped down next to him with a satisfied grin. The other two stopped briefly on Remus’ side, indicating with a jerk of their heads that he should stand. Remus reluctantly did so, only to be pushed back down into his seat, now sandwiched between the two of them.

“Skinny one, aren’t ya?” The familiar one chuckled from his left side, dropping an arm along the back of the booth. Remus didn’t dare look him in the eye now; even his voice made the hair on the back of his neck raise.

“So, Army!” Benny clapped his hands together. “I ‘eard through the auld grapevine that you talked to Scotty earlier.”

As he spoke, Remus remembered the phone ringing—Tomny’s exasperated voice.

“Then you’d know that we’ve already been over everything,” Tomny ground out. “We worked out a deal. He’s gonna get his share and then some, and the rest goes to you. We just need another few days to move the leftover merchandise.”

“See, s’funny you’d say that though, considering we’s also ‘eard that chu went by Mikey’s place yesterday.”

Remus didn’t know who ‘Scotty’ or ‘Mikey’ were, but judging by the way the colour drained from Tomny’s face, he doubted either news was all that good. Benny on the other hand didn’t seem to notice, and their waitress arrived, glancing warily between the newly enlarged group as she set their food down.

“Thanks, cailín,” Benny grinned. “And if you don’t mind, I’ll get some o’ dahse fried noodles—the ones with the lettle shrimps on ‘em.”

She nodded before shuffling quickly away, and Benny picked up one of Tomny’s chopsticks to stab it crudely into a piece of pork and pop it into his mouth. “So, where was I,” he chewed; “Ahh yeah, that’s right—our lettle birdy said you’d already worked out a deal. Sahmethin’ like—ah, what was it—twenty KG’s? Tell me Armstrong, ‘ow’re you and yooer boys gahnna move twenty feckin’ KG’s of snow for Mikey when you’re s’posedly still workin’ on that ten for us?”

Tomny set his jaw, fists clenched on top of the table. “There’s no deal with Mikey. Twenty KG’s? That’s impossible—must be some sort of joke. I mean, Christ, we had to wait for the cops to stop sniffin' around just to get your shit back on the street.”

“Oh yeah…? Bad for business, those gardaí.” Benny leaned back and began fumbling for something inside his jacket pocket. For a single terrified second Remus pictured him pulling out a blade, but when Benny drew his hand back, it was just a carton of cigarettes. He peeled the cover back and stuck one between his teeth before offering them to Remus. “Want one?”

“He doesn’t,” Tomny clipped.

“Shut up, Army. Let the kid answer for ‘imself,” Benny scoffed. “You deaf, kid?”

“That means you answer,” the thug on Remus’ left growled. He raised a hand, shoving his head forward, and Remus swallowed.

“… No thanks.”

“S’all you ‘ad to say,” Benny replied casually, tucking the cigarettes away. “Got a light dere, wee pup?”

He nearly declined again, but something in his gut and in Tomny’s gaze told him not to make both of them liars. With the thugs watching his every move, Remus slipped his hand down into his pocket and withdrew the first zippo he found—the silver plated one from James and Sirius. Forcing his hands not to shake, he reached across and held the little flame to the end of the gangster’s cigarette before clicking the lid shut.

“Ah,” Benny exhaled. “So you say there's no deal, Army—alright. S’a bit contradictory from what I’ve ‘eard but sure, I’ll believe ya. I’m all about givin’ me boys the benefit o’ the doubt. S’long as they’re contrive and all that.”

“Contrite,” Remus said automatically.

“What’s that?”

“You mean contrite. You want them sorry. Repentant.”

Benny raised his eyebrows and shot a look at Tomny, who looked about ready to keel over. “Well, look a’dat, Armstrong. You got yooerself one wiff some brains this time! Where’d you find ‘im, eh? The Queen’s palace?” He leaned in to Remus. “You some lettle runaway, gobshite?”

“I told you he’s just some stupid kid,” Tomny tried again, more forceful this time; “He’s got no hand in any 'a this, so if you want to talk to fucking business then bloody talk!”

The corner of Benny’s mouth jerked and he sat back up, smiling warmly. Then he snatched Tomny up by the throat and pinned him to the booth.

Remus bolted upright from his seat in defence of his friend, but both thugs had him by the shoulders in a second, pinching him so tightly he nearly cried out. He would’ve fought them—he would’ve—had Tomny’s arm not shot out, stopping him. The look in his eyes was not fear for the hand wrapped around his windpipe, but a warning for him; Don’t.

"Watch it, kiddo," Benny cautioned, squeezing Tomny's throat tightly in his fist. "I think yer forgetting jus' who's house you moved into..."

Feeling useless, Remus had no choice but to slump back against the cheap leather booth. He opened his hand on the table top, dropping the wooden chopsticks he’d been clutching like knives, and Benny smirked.

“There's a smart boffin,” the one on his left snarked. Remus looked at him then, fully and up close, and finally he recognised him. It was the blue eyes that tipped him off. They were clear as glass—the exact same pair that had stared him and Tonya down in that dirty alley. Suddenly Remus felt as though he were breathing through a straw again. The scar over his nose throbbed.

“Army, Army, Army..." The gangster's voice was deadly low, even as Tomny struggled against him. "We give you and yooer boys three weeks to get the job dahne—yeh don’t—and then you lip me in front o’ a kid?”

“You’ll get yer money!” Tomny wheezed.

“For feck’s sake—no apology? Are you actually bein’ mouthy again?!” The gangster bellowed. “Dahn’t you even know who I am, you lettle motherfucker? I will put you in the ground before you even ‘ave the chance to start pissing yooerself—if I don't get what’s due! You hear me?! I'll feckin' burst ya, I will!”

He punctuated the threat by slamming his free hand on the table hard enough to make the glasses shatter. Somewhere else, Remus heard their waitress shriek.

“Tom!” Remus cried, straightening against Blue-eyes’ hold on him; “Just give him the money already!”

Tomny shook his head as best he could while pinned, mouth forming a silent plea to get Remus to shut up. Enraged, Benny shook him.

"Where's my fucking money, Armstrong?! What do you got?"

“Tomny, just fucking give it to him!”

“Shut up, you!” Blue-eyes hissed after, raising his fist. Remus flinched, waiting for the incoming blow.

“Alright!” Tomny’s cries cut between them like a strangled yelp, and he gestured desperately to his pocket. “Th—ere!” He gurgled; “T—ake it!”

Looking slightly astonished, Benny used his free hand to reach into Tomny’s coat and withdraw the thick fold of notes, courtesy of Lyall and now bound together with a rubber band. It stung to see the money clasped in the gangster’s fat fingers, but not as bad as it did watching Tomny go blue in the face in the middle of a fucking Chinese restaurant.

“Colour me surprised. Where’d a ponce like you get dis much dosh? You selling your arse now?” Benny look across the table. "You selling his?"

“Who cares?” Remus growled. “It’s yours now. Call it interest on whatever he owes. Just let him go—you’re choking him!”

Benny glanced back at Tomny like he’d quite forgotten the iron grip he had around his throat and slowly relaxed his fingers, letting Tomny spin away and cough sharply.

“Tell you what, Armstrong—since you’ve got yooer puppy so well trained, imma let you off ‘fer the night.” He pat Tomny on the shoulder in a friendly manner, and Tomny quickly scrambled out of the booth.

“Lu… Lu,” he panted, gesturing desperately for Remus to join him. Remus went to stand, but was pulled back into his seat as Benny wheeled on him.

“You seem like a smart one, kiddo. A word o’ advice though—I’d drop the pox bottle. Because next time I’m naht coming back for the interest, I’m comin’ back for the whole thing." Grinning, Benny extended an arm and traced a line down the side of Remus' mouth. "Let me know if you're ever looking for a new gig, eh?"

Remus wrenched his face away, disgusted, while the gangster continued to leer at him. He stood first, and turned on Tomny sharply.

"And you Armstrong," he smiled, picking a piece of lint from Tomny's jacket. "Go n-ithe an cat thú is go n-ithe an diabhal an cat. You know what that means? Means, you get my money, or mark me words, I'll be spittin' on yooer grave. Understood?"

Tomny scowled. "Yeah."

"Sorry? Don't think I heard you. I said, do you understand?"

"Yes, I understand."

"There's a good laddie." Slapping Tomny lightly on the cheek, Benny finally turned away and Remus was roughly pushed into the aisle as the three men strode out of the restaurant, the door chime clattering after them. For a second neither of them breathed, and then Tomny was rushing him.

“You okay, Lu?” He demanded, helping him to his feet.

“Yeah,” Remus murmured, “Yeah, m'fine, Tom...”

"That fucking Benny... I didn't—shit."

Tomny bit his lip hard before turning his face away and pinching his forehead. Feeling suddenly exhausted, Remus looked around to find their waitress and the kitchen staff gaping at them from the back of the restaurant.

“Bill please…”

They walked home in silence, their shoulders occasionally bumping into one another as they swayed. It took Remus almost four streets to realise that Tomny’s silence wasn’t in favour of any forlorn sulking, that rather he was too busy looking out for their surroundings—his eyes trained on every dark corner and crack just in case Benny and his guys had doubled-back to wait for them. He relaxed some when the flat’s rusted gate came into view, and together they dragged themselves up the stairs to the second floor, stomping along as though their feet were encased in cement.

“Well, that was fun,” Remus said blandly as he pulled his boots off and Tomny threw the bolt into place. He wouldn’t look at him, and Remus felt a zap of anger.

“I’m only kidding—that was fucking awful.”

“I hope you’re still not planning on being a therapist,” Tomny mumbled, shucking off his coat and running a hand through his wild hair. “M'gonna crash, I think. Make sure you eat—and take your meds. Don’t want yer fever coming back.”

“You mean we’re not going to talk about what just happened? You're really just going to fuck off, just like that?”

“What’s there to say?”

“How ‘bout—what the fuck, Tomny?! Who were those guys?”

“C’mon, Lu,” Tomny scoffed, taking a package of cigarettes out of his back pocket and lighting up in the middle of the living room; “Thought you were supposed to be the smart one?”

“I’ll kill you if you make a joke out of this.”

“Good. Saves Benny the trouble."

Remus could have thrown something. Then he realised where he was—a second later and the lo mein was decorating the wall over Tomny’s shoulder.

“Orright,” Tomny said, peeking at the wall; “That’s your share.”

“Tomny, just talk to me! Tell me what I can do to help!”

Out of all the things he could’ve said, this was perhaps the worst. Remus wished he’d insulted him—pushed him—made him angry, but instead all he’d done was beg. And Thonas Armstrong did not beg.

“There is no fucking ‘help’, Lu!” He exploded, pelting the oppsite wall with his cigarette carton. “Life does’na always get fixed jus’ ‘cause you want it to! No matter how good you are, or how badly you want things to go yer way—it ain’t mean you’ll get it! Because life’s just shit! And you need to get over this idea ‘a yours that you’re—that you’re gonna fucking save me, or something! Because you ain’t! This is fucking reality, so get with the bloody program or GET THE HELL OUT!”

It was agony to hear, and Remus dropped his head, lips trembling as he clamped them shut. Tomny stood across from him, jaw clenched tightly, hands fisted at his sides. His pupils were huge again, though this time it couldn’t be all drugs.

“Who are we?” Remus whimpered. “What’s done this to us...?"

Tomny lifted a hand, wiping beneath his nose. When he breathed it was laboured, like yelling had taken everything out of him.

“Can’t all be winners, mate... Some of us just get participation ribbons.”

That night they laid in bed next to each other, and the space between them might as well have been an infinite chasm. Tomny had forgotten to leave the hob light on, pitching in them darkness, and the radiator kept switching on and off sporadically, leaving the entire flat in a chill. Neither of them had said anything since the argument, and Remus could feel himself sinking—going crazy in his own head, just as Sirius had said he would.

He resents you. They all do. Teachers, parents, friends…

Not Tom, Remus told the voice; Never Tom.

Even in his mind, it felt like a lie. Remus would resent him, had their situations been reversed. Even Saint Joseph himself would’ve been hard-pressed to find the space in his heart for such forgiveness. But as far as rough, street-raised, drug dealers went, Tomny was pretty saint-like.

“Tom… are you awake?”

“… Yeah, m’awake…”

Remus could’ve cried.

“I’m sorry.”

For a while there was nothing, until a hand slid across the bed in search of another. When Remus found it, he held on tight.

“… Me too, Lu.”





* * *





“C’mon, Lu, dance wiff ‘er!”

Even dreaming, Remus felt as though he might throw up.

“No way, you dance with her, Lee!”

“Bloody fuck—if you two're gonna blather on for this long then I’ll dance with ‘er,” Tomny said, pushing past both of them toward the blushing, doe-eyed girl that’d been steadily drifting closer and closer throughout the evening. Remus wasn’t the least bit bothered; Tomny was tall and fit, and he was gangly and awkward. Not to mention he was only thirteen; girls still scared him a bit.

“Ah, don’t worry none, Lu,” Lee hollered, dropping an arm around his shoulders. “You’ll get yer end away one ‘a these days.”

Remus bristled a bit, embarrassed, but the room was noisy enough that no one else had overheard. It was sweltering inside the hall, it being July, but they’d all eagerly piled into the dance anyway, its cement-covered walls and fluorescent lighting the only indication that they were actually in an old garage. Someone had turned those off though, in favour of flashing lights that turned the entire room into a strobing rainbow. There was a stereo in, playing music loud enough to get drunk to. Kids filled up every crevice, dancing and leaning against one another in a shared haze. It was pure party madness.

“Here, Lu!”

Someone passed him a flask. He didn’t even know what it was, but it burned going down and afterwards they handed him a spliff. Round and round the circle it went, and when they were finished there was always more. Remus was off his trolley, knackered to the nines. He was up! Up, up, up! And with his judgement so severely impaired, Lee even managed to wrestle him into dancing with another girl with braids in her hair. It was a slow song, and he held her waist awkwardly as they swayed. She was taller than him too, maybe a bit older, but Giles had said that he was due for a growth spurt any day now. Hopefully.

“Yeah, go Lu!” Lee cried, as he and Doss stood on the hall’s sidelines, a girl on either side of them. “Now lips ‘er!”

"Don't be so crude, Lee!" One of the girls scoffed. "He's just a baby."

"No, 'e ain't! He's a man, aren't cha?! Go on, Lu, slip 'er the tongue!"

Remus’ eyes bulged, but when he looked back to his dance partner, he couldn’t tell if her expression meant she was expecting it or too nervous to suggest it herself. In the end he settled for asking her name. Mweer-in. He didn’t even know how to spell it. Oh god—was his first kiss going to be with a girl whose name he couldn’t even spell?!

Giving Mweer-in a tight smile, Remus glanced back towards his friends in search of solace only to find that Lee and Doss had both gone, effectively leaving their dates alone on the side of the dance floor. Pulling away from his partner, he spun around, and finally spotted his friends near the back of the hall. They had Tomny between them, heads tucked tightly together with a deep glower on each of their faces. Others had joined them, familiar boys and older guys that Tomny knew. Remus had only just begun to get acquainted with the rest of the gang, but he knew the group well enough to know that things were not right. They were staring, then pointing at something—or rather, someone. A lot of someones.

Another group, this one smaller than theirs and all but foreign to Remus, had gathered across the room. They were glaring back with their hands in their pockets, the tell-tale sign of unwelcome party crashers. The dance was happening on claimed territory, and territory was all about reputation. The weak lost out, while the strong stood their ground.

Ditching the dance mid-song, Remus quickly shoved his way through the crowd. He reached his friends just as Tomny and Doss broke off from the group and challenged the ones up front. The threat was clear; get out or get beat.

For a second there was hostility; the invading boys fought back—we’re just here to have a good time, mate!— and Remus began to see knives come out, clutched by those willing to go down for their leader and their turf. But it was unnecessary; the enemy was outnumbered five to one, and the entire dancehall had come to a standstill just to watch. They were muscled out by Tomny and his boys easily enough, and once the threat was finally gone, the party resumed. Remus went to Tomny, interested and concerned, and the dark mask Tomny had worn lifted instantly.

“Lu, baby! You snog anyone yet?”

He almost said yes, just to get the tosser off of his back, but then suddenly the window to their left exploded in on itself. Rocks and dirty beer bottles were hurled through the glass, shattering each of the hall's window's with a deafening crash. The music cut out, and for a while there was only screaming and shouts of confusion and anger. When the shattering finally ceased, everyone stood around, stunned. Some had been cut by flying glass—a girl was holding her hand over her eye while blood leaked out between her fingers. Remus paled seeing it, and that was when he felt the warm trickle drip down the side of his neck.

"Aw, shit. Lu!"

While Lee and Tomny crowded around him, Remus raised his hand to the shell of his ear and felt a sharp sting. He'd been cut, a shallow graze along the top of his left ear. It smarted terribly though it probably looked worse than it was. He couldn't be sure, before Tomny could check it out, another boy ran in.

“WOTCHER, SISSY LADS! COME ON THEN, SHOW US WHATCHU GOT!?”

He finished his shout with the resounding smash of another beer bottle on linoleum. It might as well have been a war cry. It was their ‘Tongs ya bass’. It was a challenge, and they were naught but stupid kids.

All of them started running at once, eager to exert their aggression on another. Even Tomny, as charismatic and as friendly as he was, was not immune. He led his angry mob straight out of the hall where more boys were waiting with large stones and heavy sticks in hand. They fled quickly enough, but by then it’d become a chase.

“Fuck your Hamlets, peaky bitch!” The enemy wailed. “Fuck your Ends, sodding wastemen!”

It was terrifying and exhilarating at the same time. Remus had never been so close to such action, and he ran like his life depended on it, in too deep to stop. He didn’t know that the chase would end the moment the other boys crossed back into their territory—he had no idea where his territory even stopped and theirs began. He was drunk, high, and thirteen, and the blood was coating his neck. He did not hear his friends when fell behind, shouting and whistling at him, desperately trying to get him to stop.

“Lu! Where ya going, ya daft cunt?”

“Get back ‘ere! You’ll get yerself killed, you will!”

He’d outrun most of them, his skinny arms and legs carrying him up the bricked lane. If he were thinking, it’d probably be something along the lines of how proud Tomny would surely be when he caught their assailants—but there was no catching them. He was a kid in over his head, and he didn’t realise how fucked he was until it was too late.

He'd chased the small group all the way into a council estate, where he plunged deeper and deeper into the cement kingdom, flying up and down stairs and walkways layered in spray paint and gang signs. They were warnings—stay away—and Remus did not listen. As he threw himself around a final bend, there they were. At least twenty boys lying in wait, each wearing their bovver boots, carrying a knife or a lead pipe with nasty expressions on their faces. Fresh meat, the looks seemed to say. Easy kill. No problem.

“That’s peak, tiny man,” said the one in front. “Why don’t ya come ‘ere a moment?”

It was not an open invitation. He stepped back.

"Oi, where you going?"

Another step.

"C'mere, little sop!"

"Yeah, we won't hurt ya!"

Another.

"Didn't cha fuckin' 'ear 'im? C'mere!"

Remus did the only thing he could think of—he turned and ran. Ran like a scared rat with his tail between his legs. In only a few seconds, he’d gone from the hunter to the hunted, and this time he was going to be gutted for it. His ear ached—stung as it was whipped by the wind. He was afraid.

“DON'T JUST STAND THERE! FUCKING GET ‘IM!”

In the dream, it was as though he was running for hours. He couldn’t breathe, every time air went in, his lungs just about collapsed getting it out again. He could hear the boys at his back, screaming like a pack of wolves. A bottle smashed by his ankles, a stone hit him in the back. They’d rip him apart if they caught him—they wanted to hurt him. And all because of some stupid dance.

“LU! OVER 'ERE!”

The cry went up like an alarm, and suddenly boys were rushing past him—toward the fray. The immense relief that came with seeing his friends again had Remus collapsing onto a patch of grass off the side of the pavement, his legs complete mush. All around him kids were barking and wailing on one another, using everything from bricks to broken bottles as weapons. Remus could only wheeze, doubled over and looking around desperately for Tomny. Then someone came up from behind and socked him with a pipe. It only clipped his shoulder, but the pain was instant, and Remus howled, clutching his arm. For a while there was only noise, and then when things started to drift away, a set of hands grabbed him.

“NO! NO! LET ME GO! TOMNYYY!”

“Fuck! It’s me, ya wee cunt!”

Remus opened his eyes. Their attackers were gone—fought off—and only his friends were left. It was Tomny who was bent over him, bleeding from the temple and grinning ear to ear.

“Boy, you sure can run, Lu,” Tomny panted. “But I found ya… I’ll always find ya…”





* * *





When he woke up, Remus had no idea what day it was. The clock on the bedside was busted as well, but it felt about midday. Tomny was still asleep beside him, and as he watched his chest rise and fail, Remus thought only of his friends. He lifted one hand up, tracing it along the shell of his ear. There was a scar; how had he never noticed it before?

You’re a betrayer, Lu.

Lee's voice came at him like that metal pipe. It hurt worse somehow, but he was in for it now.

Did ya make a mistake, Remus?

Don’t be a shit friend, Remus.

You make me happy, Remus.

I can't talk about this, Remus.

You’re the sky, Remus.

Do you cry, Remus?

But we can’t have everything, can we, Remus?

Remus covered his face—moaned.

“Shit…”

He knew it wasn’t a good idea, but he left the flat anyway. Without Tomny. He could live without the milk, but when his cigarette carton turned up empty his day was already decided for him. The only thing that had changed about the local corner shop was the bloke behind the counter, and when Remus walked out clutching his shopping bag of fags and bottled milk, the sky over the East End was grey and cold. He wasn’t entirely sure why, considering it was December, but he ended up taking the longer route back. It took him past even more council housing, where he spotted countless haggard-looking residents sitting on their patios, their pipes and cigarettes drifting smoke up into the dull air. Some read the paper, others glared at him as he passed. None seemed happy to see him.

Remus remembered what it was that had made him take that particular route in the first place when he came across the little dilapidated park in all its rusted glory. It was the place where he and Tomny had first met. Felt like ages ago now, and as he stopped to admire the ice collecting on the pavement, Remus found his legs unconsciously carrying him onto its gravel turf.

The climbing frame was the same—rusted over and likely to slice a palm open as soon as used. The swings were also the same. Only one was usable, so he sat on it, feeling the icy chains bite into his palms. Eventually Remus pulled out the cigarettes and lit one up. He thought of almost nothing while he did it, and for a moment it felt like peace. Nearby sat a phone booth. That was new—but its walls were already tagged all over with graffiti and the door had been half-busted in.

He should call Giles. Or James. Someone at the Potters’. They deserved an explanation, even if he didn’t really have one. Would Sirius answer? No, probably not… Even if he did, what could they possibly have to say to each other? 'I'm sorry?' But Sirius was done playing apology games, he said it himself. Maybe that meant they were done for good. What shite that would be come January.

A footstep crunched behind him, followed by many more, and Remus cursed himself. While he’d been stuck in his own head, he’d allowed himself to be walked up on. There were only three of them, but they wore their caps down low, and their jacket collars high. They looked about his age, but it was clear they’d grown up around the area. Here were the local neighbourhood thugs, just looking for a score.

“Hey-up,” the first one said. “ ‘aven’t seen you around ‘ere before.”

Remus arched a brow. “You must’ve not looked hard enough then.”

It was a weak come-back at best, but it was enough to make each boy pause. The one in front ran his tongue across his front teeth, like he’d just found his favourite meal sitting warm on the pavement.

“Bum a fag, mate?”

“Sorry, fresh out,” Remus said, tucking his carton away and taking a poignant drag.

“That’s cute, but I wasn’t really asking.” Without missing a beat, the guy pulled a switchblade, popping the blade open as he and his friends took several measuring steps toward him.

“You sure are quick to the draw,” Remus remarked, eyeing the blade warily. “Normally I get at least a few more quips in.”

“Yeah, but we’re in a bit of a hurry, ya see. So I’ll let you pick, hand over what'chu got or we beat you 'til yer sniffin' blood. Your choice, innit."

It was in his nature to argue, but Remus Lupin was not built entirely out of stupid. He knew not to play with knives, especially in such a neighbourhood as Tomny’s. So, while the boys crowded in on his swing, he pulled out the cigarettes and tossed them at their feet.

“Yeah, that’s right,” the boy leered, scooping up the box. “Now be a good bitch ‘n turn out the rest ‘a yer pockets.”

“You just took my brand-new fags and now you’re gonna mug me too? Tell me, do they give thug training at the local community centre these days? Or is that only for the to the thick and stereotypical?”

“We're gonna do worse than mug ya if ya don’t turn out yer fuckin’ pockets, cheeky cunt!” One of the others trilled.

Remus sighed. He stood up, still clutching his shopping bag, and began rifling around in his pockets. The others waited impatiently, shifting their feet from one foot to the other.

“Hold on, I know I’ve got a few quid on me somewhere. Where's that darn wallet...” Remus cleared his throat, still patting himself down. Finally, he glanced into the shopping bag. “Oh! Here it is. S'all in there.”

He started to hand the bag over, and the first guy reached for it, only to scowl when Remus pulled the bag back very quickly.

“Sorry, lads, I just have one question before you finish mugging me.”

“And what’s tha’?”

“Can you catch?”

He smiled, genuinely. And then with all of his might—Remus threw the bagged bottle of milk. It slammed into the face of his first attacker with a hollow ring, surprising all of them. The guy cried out, dropping his knife to cup both hands over his face, and Remus didn’t waste a moment. Instead he turned and bolted straight for the street.

“DON’T JUST STAND THERE, YA FUCKING IDIOTS! GRAB THE BITCH!”

Now, Remus had always been fast. It’d saved him on more than one occasion, but what he made up for with speed, he lacked in coordination. As he ran, his boot came down on a particularly nasty patch of ice, and just like that he was sprawling. The boys were on him a second later, jamming him in the back with a knee and landing a nasty shot along his jaw. He thrashed beneath them, but throwing the milk had only given him a few seconds’ head start, and he’d bottled it.

“Get ‘im up!” The first one snarled. “Yeah, now hold 'im still. I’m gonna see how mouthy he is while I'm carving 'im up…”

Remus struggled, but they still managed to haul him to his feet. At least there he got the pleasure of seeing Milk-face’s bloody nose as it dripped down onto the front of his tracksuit.

“Looks like I messed up your jacket,” he grunted. “My bad, mate.”

“Don’t worry,” he said, spitting blood. “When I’m done wiff you, I’m gonna take yours.”

Remus jerked again viciously, but the two on his arms had a tight grip. As he leaned in, Milk-face’s scowl quickly turned into another grin. He used his blade to trace the scar over Remus’ nose, right up into his eyebrow.

“Looks like we ain’t the first ones to fuck you up, princess. I’m almost disappointed.”

“Just do it then!” He snarled. “If you’re gonna do it then just fucking do it, you spineless shit-eating bastard!”

"Shut up!"

One of them decked him from behind, snapping Remus' head forward hard enough that he saw stars. His teeth rattled and he might've bit his tongue, but Milk-face was grinning enough to distract him. He had a chip in his left front tooth, cut sharp on an angle. Must've been painful when it happened. Now all Remus could do was focus on it as they crowded in around him.

"Orright, little cunt. You just hold still then, or I’m gonna—”

“Yer gonna what, Ticks?”

The boys all froze; even Remus was surprised to see him. Tomny came around the corner with both hands in his jacket pockets. He had deep bags under his eyes, and his lips were dry and cracked, but he walked as though he were King of the World. To these poor, shocked boys, he might as well have been.

“Tomny…” Milk-face gawked; “What are you...?"

“You know, Ticks, if I was gonna gut somebody, I wouldn’t spend all day talkin’ about it beforehand. I’d just gut ‘im. I think you’ll find it saves time.”

“This guy mouthed off,” Milk-face—now Ticks—blabbed. “We’s were gonna teach ‘im a lesson about what happens to cheeky cunts when they try taking the piss.”

“Yeah, ‘cept this one’s spoken for. So let him go before I take your fucking thumbs instead.”

Ticks appeared reluctant, but with blood still running down his face, he didn’t look all that ready to take Tomny on. He stepped away, and a second later the other two had released Remus’ arms.

“Good lads,” Tomny said. “Now what don’t you give the kid his fags back and we’s can all go on home? In fact, if I’m rememberin’ right—you boys still owe me. Where's my money?”

Ticks visibly paled. "I... Well, we's hadn't finished getting it yet, that's all."

"Oh? So rather than get out there and do yer fuckin' jobs, you're here—harassing randos for plonk change?"

"We'll get it!" One of the others assured him. "We're good 'fer it, Tom."

"Better be, or it's your arses I'm handing over to Benny. Now hand over the shit."

Remus had never seen somebody scowl with their entire body, but somehow Ticks managed it. He wrenched the cigarettes from his pockets and held them out, but when Remus went to grab them, he was pulled in close.

“I dunno who you are, but know one thing, you fucking ponce. Big bro Tom ain’t always gonna be around to protect ya. Eventually it'll be just you and us, and then you'll regret mouthing off. You hear me, you little b—”

“Did you not just hear what I fucking said?” Tomny demanded, cutting between them both. “I said piss—the fuck—off!” He punctuated the statement with a sharp head-butt, slamming his forehead directly into Ticks’ already bloody nose. There was a sickening crunch, and Ticks crumpled instantly.

“AUGH! My fucking nose!”

“Get ‘im outta ‘ere,” Tomny ordered, wiping Ticks’ blood off of his face. The other two didn’t hesitate, and after a bit more moaning from their friend, the group quickly disappeared around the park’s cement wall.

“Got a hanky?”

Remus looked back at Tomny. There was blood between his eyebrows. He was grinning.

“What the fuck are you doing here, Tom?”

“Just out for a little stroll…” Tomny bent down, grabbing the knife Ticks had dropped. He stopped long enough to check his reflection in the blade, before folding it up and pocketing it. “Good thing, too. You have this habit of getting yourself into the messiest shit, Lu.”

“And I suppose you’ll always be there to find me, and dig me out again?”

“Too right, I will.” Smirking, Tomny grabbed Remus’ face in his hands and turned him this way and that for an inspection. “They didn’t actually cut ya, right? ‘Cause if they did you know I’ll blind ‘em.”

“They didn’t get the chance!” Remus snapped, batting him away. “Now what are you really doing here?”

“Looking for you, wanker. Figured if ya weren’t at the shops that you might’ve gone down this way. Lucky I was right.”

“Well, aren’t you just the brightest bulb in the box.”

“Heh. Far from it.” Tomny pat him on the cheek. “C’mon, toffy. Let’s getchu home. I’ve still got a few beers in the fridge. And a surprise even, if ya behave.”

Remus was quiet on the way back to the flat. He’d lost his milk, but didn’t feel like stopping for another. Doubted Tomny would agree to it anyway. He walked ahead, shoulders hunched in his thick donkey jacket and hands in his pockets. He was watching the streets, Remus knew, just in case they were to come across someone who might be looking for them. They’d gotten lucky with Ticks and his boys. But who knew who they’d tell, especially considering Tomny had broken his nose. Every now and then Tomny would glance back, as if to make sure Remus was still there.

“For someone wiff such long legs, yer sure draggin’ your feet.”

Remus flipped him off, and Tomny winked at him. Bastard.

“If you start whistling, I’ll kill ya.”

“Should I sing instead?” Tomny mused, then sung anyway; “‘Did you ever see a lassie—a lassie, a lassie? Did you ever see a lassie, go this way or that?’”

Remus caught up, yanking his friend by the back of his collar until he grunted. “Stuff it.”

Tsk. “Thought musicians were supposed to like music?”

“Maybe I’m not a musician then.”

Tomny gave him an annoyed look, but said nothing else. From then on, they walked side by side, all the way back.

“Here,” Tomny said, cracking a beer and handing it to Remus. It was cold, but so was the rest of the flat. They had to wear their jackets inside.

As Tomny retreated back into the kitchen with his own beer, Remus drifted further into the living room. He considered turning on the telly, even if just for the noise, but he was distracted soon enough.

With his beer in one hand and a rolled up fiver in the other, Tomny did a line. Remus watched and wondered how much a bump like that might cost, and how much of Benny's ten KG's Tomny had snorted himself.

“Just… give me a few,” Tomny breathed, while sinking back into the sofa. “I’ll be good in a sec…”

Remus didn’t know what else to do other than wait. As Tomny got busy getting high, he sat down on the end of the settee and he waited. Waited for something—anything to happen. The plate that he'd used to pour the coke onto still had a small scattering of white powder at the edges. Too curious to resist, Remus glanced at Tomny, who had his eyes closed, and scooted forward on the couch. He licked his finger and then ran it along the plate before pressing the tiniest bit against his gums the way he'd seen Tomny do before. The numbing effect was instant, but the bitter taste it came with was horrid. Rushing into the kitchen, Remus spat several times into the sink and held his mouth under the tap. The ammonia-like taste stuck around afterwards, but as he made his way back out into the living room, he spotted Tomny smiling lazily at him with one eye open.

“Hey, Lu... Tell me again why you ain’t going to university.”

“Because I’m gonna be in a band.”

“A musician after all, eh? Wow… s’cool… a band… You—uh… still doing it with that Sirius-bloke? The one you's broke up with?”

Remus let out a shaky breath. He couldn’t answer, so he changed the subject instead.

“Who were those guys at the park, Tom?" He slumped down on the sofa, tonguing the numbness from his gums. "You said they owed you. So what—that mean they work for you? Or are you their personal ‘Benny’?”

“I ain’t like that fat fuck, Benny,” Tomny grumbled, eyes sliding shut again. “They just run for me, s’all. We’re all a part ‘a the system, Lu. Working men—working cogs. It’s like the… circle ‘a life… You’s get… used to it…”

“Why won’t you ever tell me about it, then?”

Tomny was silent then, and Remus turned on him. “Hello...? Tom!”

Tomny’s eyes stayed shut, and for a moment Remus feared the worst. He threw himself forward, tapping his mate's shoulders firmly.

“Tomny? Are you alright?”

There was no response, so Remus pressed his ear to Tomny’s chest. Then, when he began to hear the telltale thumping of a heart in rhythm, his alarm turned to anger. He wrenched away, already fuming.

“Fucking arsehole—wake up! Fucking wake up, Tomny!”

But Tomny didn’t, and Remus growled, slamming his beer bottle down and throwing himself up from the sofa. He marched into the kitchen and picked one of the dirty glasses from the sink, filling it with water. Then he sped back out into the flat’s living room and doused the bastard with it.

“WAKE UP!”

Tomny stirred, even gave a little moan—but his eyes stayed shut, and Remus felt his temper boil over.

“FUCK YOU, TOMNY!” He wailed, smacking Tomny across the face with an open palm. “Get—UP!”

He had to smack him once more, but finally Tomny stirred. He moaned a bit louder, and just as Remus raised his hand a third time, Tomny shot upright on the sofa.

“Fuck!” He cried. “Shit—ow!? Did you really have to hit me, Lu?”

“It was the only way to wake you, ya fucking skaghead! What’s a’matter with you, huh? What if you’d died?!”

“I’m not gonna die!”

“Seems likely enough! If all you’d rather do all day is get high, then no wonder Tonya fucking left!”

Tomny had always been an immovable thing—unfazed and serene no matter what came across his path—but the moment Remus said Tonya’s name, he flinched.

“Just smack me again, why don’t you?” Tomny whimpered. “Think I’d prefer it.”

Hearing him like that, so small and fragile—Remus instantly broke. He slumped down on the sofa next to him, head in his hands.

“I can’t do this, Tom. I can’t… Like—I’m supposed to be the fucked up one. The one with all the issues. You’re the one who holds it all together.”

Tomny glanced down at himself, peeling his wet shirt away from his chest. “That’s not fair, you get everything. Rich twat.”

“I hate you. And I’m not gonna laugh.”

“Why not? Laughing’s easier…” Tomny chuckled weakly, then slid closer to Remus when he noticed him sulking. “Aw. I’m sorry, Lu. I know you’re disappointed. Didnae wan’ you to see all ‘a this…”

“Don’t. I can’t be the good guy, not when I’ve fucked up so badly. I just need you to be good, Tom.”

“ ‘Cause that’s not a crap-ton ‘a pressure or anything… What the fuck’s ‘good’ nowadays anyway? Didn’t think there was such a thing in this world.” Tomny ran a hand through his choppy hair, before grinding out a hiss. “Augh—fuck. High’s practically down the drain… Guess we might as well have it out.”

Remus raised his head, and he found Tomny staring at him. There were bags under his eyes. Deep ones. A blood vessel had burst in the left. He’d never looked so tired.

“I think I’m just embarrassed by it, right?” Tomny said, his voice low and hoarse. “It’s the drugs and everyffin. Used to be embarrassed by the thieving—breaking into cars, the petty robbery. And now it’s this shit. Should be normal for a bloke like me—hundreds ‘a people doing the exact same crap to survive, but it’s different with you. I just… don’t like telling you.”

“Why?”

“Because!” He snapped. “Because as far as I’m concerned, you’re the good one. And I still don’t want you to look at me any different—I can’t take it. So please, stop asking. Jus’ let me have this one thing. Okay, Lu?”

Remus looked down at his hands. Secrets, secrets. Why did they insist on following him everywhere?

“I get it, Tom,” he said quietly. “Why you’d keep it a secret. It’s not the knowing that’s the hard part—it’s everything else. Not what people’ll say—but what they’re thinking inside. That’s the worst fucking part, isn't it?”

Tomny sighed. “Yeah. That’s the worst part.”

They were quiet for a while, just two broken kids on a patched sofa. Couldn’t have had a more different start, but there they were… at the End.

“You were right,” Tomny said, head tipped back and zoning out on the ceiling. “Every time you asked about Tonya, you were fucking right.”

Remus’ heart clenched. “I’m sorry.”

“Nah, no more sorries. No more secrets...”

With a heavy exhale, Tomny sat up and turned to Remus. He sniffed a bit, wiping below his nose.

“Listen, I was a right fucking wreck after Tonya left. I lost my bloody mind, innit. But I could see how the others were looking at me, so I put it all away. I wasn’t ready to let go ‘a her, but she was gone. Couldn’t do nothing about it. Instead I tried taking control of what I could—the drugs, the money. And at some point… I dunno, wasn’t enough. I couldn’t stand being ‘ere without her—in my own home. So one night I lost it. Trashed the whole place. Ripped it apart and smashed up everything. 'Specially everything that reminded me of 'er.”

“You didn’t...”

“Fucking rights, I did. Threw the entire stereo out the window and everyffin. Figured, no one’s gonna come looking for it… Still, couldn’t tell anyone. Felt too pathetic. I was really down back then, but I’m better now. Swears. All the shit with the drugs—it's nuffin’.”

Remus knew better than to believe him, but he was at odds with every other person in his life. He couldn’t be at odds with Tomny too.

“Just please tell me you didn’t toss her copy of ‘Abbey Road’. It was an original pressing.”

“Dunno. Was that the one with the banana on the front?”

“Nico too? Oh Tom… What’d rock ‘n roll ever do to you?”

Tomny smiled and reached for his beer, sipping it. “Secrets fester, I think. They become bigger than they are—and then suddenly they’re not just secrets anymore, they’re problems. I mean, hey, look at me? I got rid of all of it, even felt a bit better—but I tell ya… still miss her music sometimes…”

“I miss her too," Remus confessed. "So much. And I—I thought it would go away, but it never does.”

“Yeah… Well, when grief’s all you got, sometimes it hurts worse to let it go.”

The words hung between them like a hook on a line, and Remus knew they were the truth. For so long he’d been searching for a way to let go of all the anger—all the hate—but who was he without it? Was he Remus Lupin because of that anger, or was he angry because he was Remus Lupin? Seventeen years, and he still wasn’t sure.

“Hey.” Tomny knocked his knee against Remus’ kindly. “Don’t stay sad. I told you I had a surprise for ya, yeah?”

“Don’t know if I can handle anymore surprises, Tom.”

“Ah, but you’ll like this one. Wait here.”

With an excited little kick, Tomny threw himself up off of the sofa and whipped down the hall toward one of the bedrooms. He was gone only a moment, and when he reemerged, he was holding not just any old gift—but a guitar. A bass guitar.

“Happy late-Christmas, lovely tosser.”

“Tom, no,” Remus moaned, “you didn’t.”

“Sure, I did,” Tomny beamed, coming forward and setting the pristine instrument over Remus’ lap. “The guy in the bob-shop called it a Teisco. Said it was almost brand new—hardly ever been played!”

Remus ran his fingers up the neck of the bass, almost forgetting how to breathe. He flicked his thumb along one of the strings and felt it vibrate neatly. It was no 1951 Fender Precision, but it was perfect for a dumb kid with very few aspirations.

“I got it on-offer, so I know it’s nuffin’ special,” Tomny rambled, “but figured if anyone could do something wiff it, it’d be you. S’better than letting it hang in the window of that shop getting bleached by the sun, right?”

“It’s amazing, Tom. You shouldn’t have—really.” He punched Tomny in the arm sharply. “Stop wasting your bloody money on me!”

“Wasn’t even my money!” Tomny protested. “Used some of that dosh your dad pushed on you.”

“You absolute spanner—I told you to use it on yourself!”

“Yeah, and then you went and gave the rest of it to a cock-jockey like Benny. Nothing to be done now. Can’t get the money back from him and the shop’s sign said no refunds, so... go on! Might as well play the bloody thing. Oh shit—wait! I gotchu one of those new-fangled amps too, though I 'spect it’s old as dust. Dunno how it’ll sound.”

Tomny jumped up once more and rushed from the room, coming back with a decently worn-out amplifier that he dropped on the floor next to the sofa. “Was a real bitch lugging this thing up the lane, y'know. Hope you make it worth my while.”

"It's great, Tom."

"Great enough to play, innit."

Suddenly feeling very shy, Remus made to set the instrument aside. Tomny caught hold of the neck at the last second.

"What you doing?"

"I don't even know what I'd play?"

"You fucking cares? Play something—anything. Play those fucking secrets of yours.”

Remus bit his lip. "That sounds mildly cheesy."

"Just play, wanker."

If Remus could have collected all of the time he’d wasted on hesitating, then he’d have been left with half a lifetime. It killed him to think about, and so for once, he allowed himself to stop thinking altogether. While Tomny graciously plugged in the amp, he fit the chord into the end of the bass and carefully turned the Teisco over in his lap. He strummed down roughly, feeling the rebound of its unstretched, untried strings, and bit his lip again. They were out of tune. He’d have to fix them—wear them down until they moved exactly how he wanted them to. It’d be almost like starting over.

As he moved his fingers along the stiff strings, not bothered by his lack of flow or general rhythm, he began to feel more free. Tomny had no idea what went into making a song, which meant anything could be a song, and since it was just the two of them there no one was left to question it when he began to sing.

“You say you want answers, everything and more. And I got the answers—oh, I got secrets-galore…"

Tomny laughed, nodding his head in another ‘go on’, and Remus shook his head.

He didn’t know where the words were coming from, he’d never even written it. He just kept playing, and the stupid chant spilled out of him like water.

"How ‘bout—I fuckin’ hate football? Or… any sport at all, really… And I fell in love with my best friend, though this might be the end, clearly. ‘Cause I can’t come out of the closet, locked up… like a—like a safe-deposit! And that’s kinda sad… So there’s a few secrets, finally said ‘em aloud, and I ain’t done yet. How ‘bout—my dad’s not my dad, and that’s kinda sad… Yeah, my dad’s not my dad. Would’a thought I’d be glad… that my dad’s not my dad…"

A sharp inhale, then; "Fuck. Tom, my dad, h-he...”

Remus filtered off, his chunky licks becoming little more than slams on the strings as he descended into tears and Tomny sharply pulled them together on the sofa.

“I hate them,” Remus sobbed into his shirt. “He hates me because he’s not my dad and she—and she never told me! Or—Or she did, but then she just fuckin’ went off and died!”

“I know,” Tomny whispered, patting his head soothingly; “I hear you now.”

“I ruined everything. It’s all so messed up. Sirius hates me now—James and Lily must hate me! It’s all ruined… and I don’t even understand why it’s so bloody difficult! I left them with no word—no reason, just fuckin' ran off! I dumped them to come here like I always do. And I lied—again and again!”

“People lie, Lu. They jus’ do. S’a part of being human. And you’re not any lesser for havin’ a shit dad. It’s on them—on those deadbeats—no one else.”

“I hurt him, Tom,” he whimpered. “I hurt Sirius. I was so focussed on making sure no one else noticed that I forgot all about him.”

“Sounds like something you gotta tell him then.”

He knew Tomny was right, but more talking? It felt impossible. What if things got even more messed up? What if they missed each other again? Him and Sirius—sometimes it felt like they were speaking in different tongues.

“Hey—hey." Tomny pulled away, forcing Remus to look at him. "You think I’d lead you wrong on purpose?”

He shook his head pathetically, and Tomny smiled.

“Then what 'chu so worried about?”

Dear god, Remus thought. This was a man he’d do anything for, he was sure of it.

“I really love you, Tom. You’re like my brother.”

“Always wanted a lil’ brother," Tomny chuckled. "Didn’t count on ‘im being taller than me though.”

"You’ve probably just gotten shorter in your old age..."

"Cheeky shit." Tomny laughed again, and then wiped the damp from Remus' cheek. For a moment they were just staring at each other, two boys with nothing left to lose. Tomny's eyes were red along the whites, and bluer than Remus had ever seen.

Anything, he swore. Anything.

Tomny cleared his throat. “Hey, Lu—”

There was a sudden knock on the door, loud enough to make both of them start.

“Stay here, it’s probably just someone tryin’ to drop in,” Tomny said. He stood up, already starting away before turning back. “But just to be safe—maybe hide.”

Remus didn’t need telling twice. Feeling a lot like a spineless milksop, he ducked out of sight behind the sofa while Tomny made his way toward the door. The front door creaked as it opened and Remus held his breath, releasing it only when he heard Tomny sigh in relief.

“Lee? What the f—why didn’t ya buzz the flat?”

“Piece of shit intercom’s out again,” Lee scoffed. “I swear s’like somebody unplugs it.”

“How’d you get inside then?”

“Dezzy from downstairs let me in. Now where you been? No one's heard from you in days.”

There was a light thump like Lee had tried to push the door open.

“Sorry, can’t come in—I’m… entertaining.”

“Oooh, I get it. S’that Boots girl again, innit? You been hunkered down and enjoying yourself, you randy bastard.”

“None’ya business. Now bugger off, don’t want her fainting at the sight ‘a your ugly mug. Put a real dent in my evening.”

“Easy now. I should at least say ‘ello, shouldn’t I? So where is she—bedroom?”

“Lee.”

“Orright, orright. I can tell when I’m interrupting. But you’d best come out soon or else I’m haulin’ ya off her perky arse meself. You coming out to Vint's for New Years?”

“Yeah, I’ll be there.”

“Good. Can’t mope around ‘ere all the time. Cheryl’s been on watch for you, ya know. Best get out there before she realises she’s got better options.”

“Better, as in you?”

“You know me, I’m a beast, Tom. Can’t keep me down.”

There was a short chuckle—Tomny—and then a clap of hands. “Orright. See ya later then, dickhead.”

“I’ll save ya a bump. Ta.”

The door shut and Remus finally peeked out from behind the sofa. It stung a bit, to have heard Lee sound so much like his old self and know that everything had changed. So, Remus did what Sirius would do, and he cracked a joke.

“Does the Boots girl have a name, you slag?”

Tomny smirked wryly, hand still on the doorknob. “Never thought to ask actually.”

“You idiots wouldn’t last five minutes with Marlene.”

“Ah, yes, your lesbian girlfriend. Tell me about her next.”





* * *





Over the next day and a half, Remus told Tomny everything.

Every gritty detail.

He left not a shred out no matter how bad it made him look, and by the time they were finished they’d gone through all the beer in the flat and the three bottles of scrumpy Tomny had been saving for only the most desperate of occasions. Even then, their throats were dry from talking, but Remus felt better. In the beginning he’d assumed that Sirius was used to the secrets because he’d been living one for so long, but it was different for him. For Remus, secrets felt protective—like an iron wall he’d built up around himself. They kept some distance between him and the hardest parts of being Hope Lupin’s son, safeguarded him against Lyall’s resentment, and helped him find a place in a world that would’ve otherwise considered him too opulent to welcome. For Sirius, secrets were only an unfortunate circumstance of life. He found no comfort in them.

At some point they’d put the telly on, but ended up talking over the program. Tomny put the drugs away, even though it probably would’ve been easier to not, and instead they played cards, cooked a modest supper, changed the linens. Keeping up with the mundane things made talking easier, and eventually the radiator kicked on again and warmth began to seep back into their bones. On the 29th they took a trip to the laundrette to clean those changed linens and Remus had to hide in the toilet when a pair of local kids spotted Tomny through the window. One of them was Brecker, the jerk who’d gone with Tomny to the party last summer. It took a while to shake them, but when Remus emerged from the filthy lavatory, Tomny gave him a lopsided smile and any unfortunate twinge was quickly forgotten.

“So what yer saying is, that you’re really not—” Tomny grunted as he yanked the phone cord from the wall; “—queer?”

Remus shrugged from his place on the floor, the Teisco strapped across his lap. “More like halfway. I’m a halfer—girls… and guys.”

“Blimey. Didn't much think that was an option, meself.” Shrugging, Tomny tossed the phone aside. It’d been ringing off its hook all evening and he'd ignored it every time. Fuckings sods, they’re interrupting Lu time! He’d say.

“Tell me then,” Tomny said, picking up a fresh beer bottle and slouching down on the couch. “What’s it about this ‘Sirius Black’ that’s got you so sprung?”

“If you saw him you’d know.”

“He that pretty?”

“Well, I think every girl at school’s swooned over him at least once.”

“Heyyyy,” Tomny grinned, knocking Remus’ shoulder with his beer; “And he’s with you, huh? Handsome dog…”

“I dunno if he’d consider us ‘together’ anymore.”

“Mm—nah. You know what they say, don’t count your pretty, rich boyfriends before they hatch.”

Remus smiled despite himself, and then looked down, busy tightening his A-string. Tomny watched happily, sipping away. It was the first day in weeks he hadn’t woken up just to get high, and Remus could see it in the bouncing of his leg—the pin-point sweating along his collar. Tomny tried to play it off, but he could tell he was suffering.

“So what’s it like then, being with a girl and then a guy?” Tomny prodded. “Don’t it get confusing at all? I mean, you probably wouldn’t forget what to do when… you know. That part’s all instinct—heh—but what happens when they want different things?”

“You mean like different things… in bed?”

“Yeah! But also, you know how a girl wants to be protected, and—er… a guy, protects? Whadda do then?”

“It works the same. We take care of each other.”

Tomny nodded thoughtfully. “And in bed then? I mean, since you brought it up..."

Remus scoffed, hands dropping from the bass. “I’ve only ever been with one guy. My experience isn’t exactly vast.”

“Not true! You kissed me that one time.”

“Shut up, we’ve already been over that. It was a mistake. Won’t happen again.”

“Right.” Tomny twiddled his thumbs. “So… does this mean you were ever in love with me?”

“Sod off!”

“I was just asking! Christ, don’t need to bite my head off. Never met a ‘bisexual’ before, alright? M’trying to put myself in yer shoes.”

“Right. Let me put it this way then, if you were a girl, would you still have fallen in love with Tonya?”

“Nah, don’t think so,” Tomny mused.

“Really? Why not?”

“I’d be too busy falling in love with you. In all your manic-toff glory.”

“Fuck you, Tom.”

“Yep, that’s right. Could’ve had my Cinderella moment.” Tomny sighed, sipping his last beer with one hand and tucking the other behind his head. “Bet it’d be mighty comfortable, being ‘Mrs. Remus Lupin’.”

“I think the Lupin track record would disagree.”

“What about the guy in the photo—your real dad?”

Remus glanced to the coffee table, where the creased picture of Hope and her friends sat amongst a collection of coins and pocket lint. He’d showed Tomny the photo and for the first time, he had not been ashamed. It was a part of him, but it was not the whole of him.

“Don’t know anything about the guy,” Remus said. “Mum never mentioned him really, but when Sheila gave me that picture and said they went to school together I just sorta connected the dots. He probably doesn’t even know that I exist.”

“Does that bother you?”

“It should, shouldn’t it?”

Tomny shrugged. “I never thought having a dad was all that. Usually they’re only made of shit 'n disappointment.”

“Right…”

“But hey—if you do, well orright then.”

“No… I dunno.” Remus sighed glumly. “I’ve known about this guy for six years now and never even said his name aloud. He's not my dad, he’s basically a stranger. Guess I always thought that not meeting him at all was better than doing it and finding out he doesn’t want me.”

“Hm. And now?”

“And now… I think I’m still afraid.”

“Well,” Tomny pursed his lips in consideration, “I wouldn’t worry about it, mate. You can always change your mind later.”

“You think?”

“Sure. Seesaw didn’t meet his dad ‘til he was seventeen. And then he turned out to be an alcoholic dickbag working in some meat-packing plant. Yours is some posh bleeder with a name like ‘Thaddeus’. Even if he is an utter waste of a personality, you might still be able to get some money out of it, yeah?”

It was supposed to be a light joke—comforting, but what did Remus need with more money? He was going to live with his friends in some crummy corner flat in Soho and make crummy music and drink crummy beer, provided he got his shit together first.

Man… he really needed to call Giles.

“At least he ain’t bad looking,” Tomny said, picking up the photo. “Mum always used to say that my old man looked like a toe come to life. Ha. Bitter hag.”

Remus burst into laughter, and Tomny joined him. Eventually talk shifted again—Doss and his new family, brimming with promise.

“He’ll make a good dad,” Tomny said firmly. “That kid’s gonna have a chance.”

A chance. Remus had had plenty of those, and he’d squandered them all. Would Tad have been like Doss, young and inexperienced but with a heart big enough to try anyway? Or would he be more like Lyall, drowning in money and promise and somehow still dissatisfied with life. Maybe he could’ve been like Mr. Potter, kind and warm with bad jokes that everyone knew were bad but laughed at anyway.

But no. Remus’ luck had never been that good. He could only hope Tad was somewhere in the middle, not that it really mattered if he never planned on meeting the guy.

God, he missed Sirius. It would be so easy to explain all of it to him. He’d get it before he even got the words out, and then the solution would just materialise in front of them. Remus liked talking to Tomny, who was understanding and patient, but no matter how familiar he was, it just wasn’t the same.

On the 30th, five days after running off on his friends without word, Remus told Tomny about the New Year’s party at the Pettigrews'.

“They actually want your band to play? Wow. That’s a lot of faith.”

“We’re actually pretty good, I’ll have you know!”

“Sure, I know,” Tomny laughed. “Been listening to you going on two days now—you’re good, Lu. I guess that means you’ll be headin’ home then.”

“I don’t want to leave,” Remus said earnestly.

“Ah, but you made a commitment. Can’t go back on your word, it ain’t manly. Jus’ do me a favour, play a few more songs before you go.”

So he did. Remus played every song in his repertoire, including the ones he’d written for the band. He let Tomny peruse his songbook and read all of it, even the really bad stuff.

“Tell me, Lu, what emotion were you trying to evoke by rhyming ‘disintegration’ with ‘refrigeration’?”

“I was going for chilling, obviously. I’m just surprised you can read a word that big.”

“You callin’ me thick?”

“Don’t worry, it’s charming.”

“I like it when you flirt, Lu.”

“Ha—that’s not flirting.”

Tomny arched one handsome brow and flipped to the next page in his songbook. “Oh? Then what is?”

His heart gave a little jump and Remus quickly glanced down at the bass to hide it. “Nice try, but I ain't falling for that. Flirting with you feels too much like emotional incest.”

He’d expected another quip, but when that didn’t come, Remus looked up. Tomny wasn’t smiling anymore, but rather than staring at him, his attention was caught by the song book. Curious, Remus leaned in to get a look at the page he’d turned to and instantly deflated.

“Oh… That’s—”

“ ‘Tonya’s Song’,” Tomny finished, before cracking a wry smile. “Of course you wrote her a song.”

“I never finished it exactly,” Remus answered, slightly ashamed. “The words never felt right. Couldn’t pin it down.”

“Yeah well, could never pin ‘er down in person either. I expect trying to capture her with words is even worse.” Tomny touched his fingers to the page. “ ‘Raven-haired… Midnight dancer…’ This is… wow.”

Remus bit his lip, but he’d had no need to be nervous. Tomny just sat up, eyes bright, and passed the book along.

“Will you play me whatever it is you have? I’d like to hear it.”

The request left him anxious again, but he’d already decided that would’ve done anything for Tomny. He could do this.

The song was simple, just three verses. It hadn’t changed since he’d written it.



You can stay up all night,

Figuring out what to do next;

Everything seems alright,

‘Til you run out of cigarettes;

Raven-haired,

Midnight dancer;

If I could give you everything,

Would you ask for me?

Star of those rainy nights,

And now our night is through;

You’ve asked your questions,

I’ve asked for you.



Once he’d finished, Remus set the bass aside. His skin felt tingly—his face hot. Everything was buzzing and his fingers were trembling, but when he looked up, Tomny was staring at him from his recliner, lips parted. He still had that little scar on his top lip.

“Blimey," Tomny murmured. "You’re amazing, you are."

For once, Remus couldn’t find it in himself to disagree.





* * *





This dream would be the last. Somehow, it made sense that it would be her.

In this dream he did not feel ill, nor did he feel lost or unwanted. It was the first to comfort him, and the last he’d remember having for a very long time. He felt her touch and panicked at first, half-worried she were someone else. But then he realised.

No one sang like she did. No one had ever held him like she had.

“Let us cling together as the years go by, oh my love, my love… In the quiet of the night, let our candle always burn. Let us never lose the lessons we have learned…”

Remus felt the burn of unwept tears. She was stroking his head, singing to him, so beautifully. Enough that he wanted to live in it—cling to the dream and never let her go. He had to look, had to, but he was afraid. What if she vanished before his eyes again?

“Remus.”

Please stay. Please stay with me.

“Remus, sweet love. It’s time to wake up.”

No. No, please. I’m so tired.

He felt her beautiful hands on his face, and her beautiful lips on his cheeks, and after she’d kissed each of his lashes, Remus finally opened his eyes.

“I miss you,” he said. “I wish you hadn’t gone.”

Tonya smiled at him. “I love you, Remus,” she said. “You are so loved.”



Chapter End Notes

[To have someone] 'sectioned' is to forcibly admit them to hospital (thanks Becca, lol).

[To] ‘bottle it’ means to get so close and then mess up. Tripping at the finish line, if you will.

'What’s the craic?' is like 'what's going on?'

'Cailín' is an Irish word meaning 'girl'.

'Gardaí' is the Irish word for police.

'Dryshite', 'gobshite' and 'pox bottle' all roughly mean fool or useless person.

The Gaelic phrase/insult 'go n-ithe an cat thú is go n-ithe an diabhal an cat' translates to 'may the cat eat you, and may the devil eat the cat'. Creatively meaning that the cat should do you in, and then the devil will do you both. If you're curious for pronunciation, here's an intimidating rendition.

'[Tongs] Ya Bass' is a sort of war cry for Scottish youth gangs and the like. Gang members would shout their gang's name and 'ya bass' to rally before a fight.

'Peak' is bad luck.

'Randy' means horny.

'Scrumpy' is a harsh home-brewed cider. Also a brand.
