“Now that ain’t true,” James pressed. “Pete’s as much of a Marauder as the rest—”

“No one asked you, Potter! You’d follow this idiot off a bridge if he marched you there, so you tell me, why should I support my boyfriend when he’s so insistent on acting like he walks on water just because you three have put this silly fantasy in his head?!”

“Because he will walk on water some day,” Sirius said. “At least to some people. Pete’s an artist, and pretty soon he’s gonna have those around who see that. Who appreciate him for it. And all you’re gonna be is the whiney girl he dated in sixth form that was too blind to see what was right in front of her.”

The girls gasped, and Remus instantly regretted not stepping in sooner. Before he could, Moira screwed her face up very tight. She looked like she might actually kill Sirius, but instead she merely snatched Prongs Jr. from his hands and slammed the darling baby down on the floor of the dining hall with a great plume of floury dust.

“Junior, no!”

As James threw himself to his knees and began scooping handfuls of Prongs Jr. back into its tattered bag, Moira pointed a finger beneath the tip of Sirius’ nose.

“You can tell Peter that until he’s ready to wake up and see what an arsehole you are, I am not interested in anything he has to say.”

While the rest of the dining hall stared, Moira and her friends gathered their lunch trays and marched off. Remus was mortified, though not as mortified as Peter when he appeared beside them.

“What the fuck did you say to her?!”

Remus glared at Sirius, who only shook his head.

“Personally, Wormy, I think you dodged a bullet. Not a shred of maternal instinct in that one at all…”





* * *





For three days Peter hardly spoke to them, which was no less than they deserved really. He was slightly more lenient with James, as they still had McGonagall’s home-ec project to complete, but even that never went past apathetic chit-chat. It left James in a mopey mood, which meant Sirius was in a worse one. In forms the three of them sat around, hardly even caring when Barty threatened to use the flour bags as target practice for all the office supplies he’d nicked from other people’s desks.

“Go away, Crouch,” Lily ordered. “Unless you’d like Remus to give you your fourth detention this week.”

He didn’t listen, and so Lily got Professor Bilshin to give them permission to use the classroom next door. When they sat down, she reached over to brush a patch of flour from the front of James’ jumper.

“I don’t understand why you guys don’t just leave them behind at the dorms,” she said, eyeing the half-deflated bag of flour in his lap. “They aren’t even real.”

“Can’t,” said James, flipping open his law text. “McGonagall’s has all the teachers in on it. She gets them to take attendance for the flour in every lesson.”

“That is insane.”

They all grunted in agreement. Clearly their headmistress was just having a laugh.

“It's worse for him,” Sirius said, pointing at James while chuckling lightly. “He’s practically a single mother now.”

“Yeah, no thanks to you.”

Sirius’ smile vanished, and Lily scooted her chair forward.

“Yes, you’re all miserable, we’ve covered that. But have any of you tried fixing it? Apologising, maybe?”

“ ‘Course we have,” Remus answered. “Pete won’t—”

“I meant to Moira.”

“No way,” Sirius replied. “I’d rather cut my own ear off than apologise to that snooty bint.”

“At this rate you might have to, that is if you ever want Peter to speak to you again.”

He scoffed, but it seemed James was not entirely opposed.

“Daisy’s right. You should apologise to her, Padfoot.”

“Why me?”

“Because you’re the one who called her a whiney nobody!”

Lily turned on him. “Sirius! You did not.”

“Okay, so maybe I did!” Sirius snapped. “But we were all thinking it! She’s hated us since ninth year, and you know all she does is bad-mouth us to Pete when no one’s around. Sorry that I’m the only one with the balls to say something…”

“It’s not worth it if it hurts Peter too,” said Lily. “You can’t treat him differently and get down on him for who he dates.”

“Now hold on, we may not be the socialist utopia everyone wants, but we treat Pete the same as anyone!”

“No, not the same as me,” James said. “Not the same as Moony.”

Remus felt his shoulders grow tight, while Sirius slumped in his chair and scoffed.

“Oh, come on. That’s different.”

“Different how?”

“You really gonna make me spell it out, Potter?”

James shut his textbook with a smack. “Fine, maybe it is different! But Moira could still be right. You’re my best friend, Sirius, and Moony, well he’s your…”

“My boyfriend,” Sirius answered curtly. “You can say it, Prongs. He’s my boyfriend.”

“No one’s not saying it, Sirius,” Lily sighed, “but Peter doesn’t even know.”

“Christ, where’s McKinnon when we need her? Moony and I don’t owe an explanation to any of you. Potter’s just upset ‘cause Thurnberg called him a sheep, but it’s our relationship! A secret one, I might add. And Peter Pettigrew couldn’t keep a secret if all our lives depended on it!”

“That’s not fair,” Lily scolded. “Not when you haven’t even given him a chance.”

Sirius gaped at both of them, and then whirled on Remus.

“What about you? Don’t try telling me you don’t have an opinion?”

Remus winced. “Call me a hypocrite—”

“You’re a hypocrite.”

“—But … I think maybe Lily's right. We should at least try to tell him.”

“You really want Peter to know? ... You?”

“I just think we owe it to him to be honest, like we have with the others. And if we want the band to work then…”

Sirius looked back to James, who had started picking at a hole in Prongs Jr.’s head rather than make eye contact. Finally he groaned.

“Fine! We’ll tell him… But after the Craigtyre trip! … Don’t need any shitty rumours messing up what could be our last good day.”

They all agreed on that at least, and Remus tried to not give in to the black hole that was slowly eating him from inside out. It’d been there ever since Sheila left, and got bigger each and every time he thought about that photo from his baptism.

It was another hitch; another hitch in the tragic pattern that was his life. Realising it made Remus feel like a stoppered bottle shaken to its bursting point. He wanted to scream and yell, to beat them with his fists, but everyone he felt the need to punish was long gone.

Where are you? Came the anger, often. Why are you all such cowards?

He put it away.

On Saturday, all upper-sixth students met their buses outside Castle Hall as usual. It was their final weekend with the flour children, and luckily for them Professor McGonagall had been kind enough to let all of the would-be parents off for the evening. Uninterested in toting the heavy bags around off campus, nearly everyone had left them back at the dorms—but not James Potter. He still had his flour bag in a sling across his front, though Prongs Jr. had been looking worse for wear ever since Moira exploded him across the dining room floor.

“I have a gift for you,” Lily said, before unceremoniously pulling out a blue baby cap. James took one look at it and lit up from top to bottom.

“Oh, Daisy! It’s great!”

“Thought you might like it,” she said, as he kissed her hair and fit the cap over Prongs Jr.’s head. “One of the girls in Rowena is like a knitting machine.”

“That is so embarrassing,” Sirius grimaced. “At least you know he’ll be loyal.”

“Look, Potter,” Lottie cooed, “now Junior and Francois are matching.”

She showed off her own sack of flour, which had a pink bonnet fitted over its top. Remus had forgotten that Lottie was in Sheila’s choir class until she’d appeared with baby Francois the next day. Though he tended to avoid looking at it; the extra lipstick and fake eyelashes were a bit unsettling.

“Petey, will you help me with my bag? It’s got Francois’ dummy in it.”

“Now you’re just taking the piss,” Peter grumbled, fetching his sister’s bag for her anyway. Remus watched, but when Peter caught him staring, he was not impressed.

“What? Do I have something on my face?”

“Er—no…?”

Peter spun away, and Remus tried not to let it bother him. As they moved up the line, nearly ready to board, he spotted Trish with her clipboard and got an idea.

“Oi, where’re you going?” Sirius called, as Remus stepped out of line.

“Just to talk to Trish! Be two seconds!”

“You’ll miss the bus!”

The crowd of kids was already thinning by the time he reached her, most having sorted themselves onto their allotted buses. A few honked, ready to pull away from the pavement, and Remus could hear his friends calling out to him from behind.

“Best get a shift on, Remington, else ye’ll miss yer bus.”

“I know, Trish, I’ll be quick—nice hair by the way.”

She reached up, touching the wisps of hair that had been shorn short like Liza Minnelli's.

“Whach'ye want then?”

“Can you tell me what bus Moira Thurnberg is on?”

She glanced down at the list. “Uh… Bus three.”

“Cool, thanks. Say hi to Regulus for me.”

Her cheeks reddened, though that could’ve been the cold, and she smacked him—“Say hi to him yerself, lavvy head!”—but Remus had already legged it. By the time he made it back down the grass to his bus, Sirius was hollering at him out the window.

“Hurry up, Evans asked the driver to wait!”

“Actually I’ll meet you in town!”

“What?!”

“Just gotta do something first!”

“You nutter!”

Flashing Sirius a thumbs up, Remus watched as his boyfriend ducked back into the window and slammed it closed. A second later the bus honked twice and began pulling away from the curb. Luckily for him, when he made his way aboard bus three, it was Stan sitting in the driver’s seat.

“Sorry, Stan. Missed my bus.”

“Just get on, Lupin,” the man yawned, pulling the door shut after him.

He found Moira sitting near the middle with her friends, and only began to regret every decision he’d ever made when he started down the aisle and was met with three piercing glares. He stopped beside Moira’s seat, only slightly intimidated by the look her best friend Rachelle was giving him.

“Uh… Hey, guys."

The girls merely glared.

"Uh... so, Rachelle, would you mind switching seats for a moment? I just would really like to talk to Moira…”

Rachelle crossed her arms. “Yeah, right. You’re thicker than I thought if you think I’m moving, Lupin.”

“You can sit here, Remus,” Hannah said, adjusting her glasses. Both Moira and Rachelle spun around in their bus seat to accost her for it, and she shrugged shyly. “What? Everywhere else is full…”

He sat, and though Moira tried her best to ignore him, he was tall enough to see over the back of her seat.

“Moira, what Sirius said was—”

“Save it,” Rachelle hissed. “She isn’t taking Pettigrew back.”

“But Peter—”

“Really should be here himself if he meant it,” Hannah finished.

Remus sighed. He wasn’t going to get anywhere unless he changed tactics.

As the bus started up and set itself down the cobble path leading out the school gates, Remus raised his voice and addressed the best friends instead. Appeal to the masses, and all that.

“I get it, you guys have full rights to be pissed off. I would be too. Sirius was a total dick, and James and I—”

“Said nothing—”

“Did nothing.”

“Yeah… But look, I can’t say anything for whatever happened between the two of them over Easter, but you guys should know that Pete is really torn up about it. Regrets it and everything. His—uhm… His brother… Yeah, he told him to… to give Moira space! That’s the only reason he hasn’t said anything before now. But he’s really, really sorry. And we are too, if it counts for anything…”

The girls shared a glance, and then deferred to Moira, who’d kept her arms crossed and was still glaring out the bus window.

Hannah nudged him, nodding urgently; Keep going!

“You wanna know what Pete said? He said that… That Moira was the only one for him. No one better, and no one who knows him better… Not even us.”

The bus kept on rumbling, banging off the rough dirt road as it headed into the valley. For a while it seemed as though Remus’ efforts were all for naught.

Then Moira turned around.

“Did Sirius put you up to this?”

“What? No… I mean, he’s sorry too, if that’s what you meant.”

She pursed her lips. “You’re going to regret it if you get stuck cleaning up his messes forever.”

“Yeah, but sometimes he cleans up mine too.”

She didn’t look impressed, or like she believed a word he’d said, but neither did she spin away in a huff. Remus told himself it was something.

“Fine, Lupin. You win. I’ll talk to Peter, but Sirius can stick his apology up his arse.”

It was more than something then—it was a win.

"Fair enough."

Sirius wasn’t impressed when they got off the bus in the village, but he understood when Moira approached Peter and asked if the two of them could go off together.

“You sneaky bastard, you really are the best-worst matchmaker there is.”

“Trust me, it’s not for a lack of trying,” Remus moaned.

Because everyone wanted their alone time—and because Sirius couldn’t bear to be seen in public with Francois and Prongs Jr.—they arranged to meet back at the broomsticks as a group later in the day.

“It’s just so dumb,” Sirius was ranting. “Baby-this, father-that. I don’t get it.”

“You’ve been in a bad mood since McGonagall set the assignment,” Remus said, the two of them walking shoulder-to-shoulder as they started up the village’s high street. "Wanna tell me what that's about?"

“What, like you’re actually enjoying yourself? Don't tell me that you want to be a parent all of a sudden?”

“No, but it’s only two weeks. And it’s just a bit, anyway. James is only making fun.”

“Yeah it's a bit—it’s a bit annoying. And it’s insensitive.”

“Insensitive how?”

“Insensitive like—you! You just found out about Sheila! That you had a whole godparent out there who knew everything and still didn’t tell you! And then Pete goes off the rails, and you’re also dealing with your bloody dad—or dads—I mean, parents are just shite all around, who would ever want to be one? All they do is let you down...”

He could sense Sirius’ own hurt leaking out around his words. Perhaps he’d gotten a bit too comfortable when it was them, Regulus, and Mary. Their friends’ arrivals, the assignments, the jokes—maybe it was a bit much. But hating James and lashing out at Peter wasn’t fair either.

Purposely slowing their walk, Remus looked up at the grey-blue sky. It’d rained that morning, and puddles were still collecting around the roadside. A small lorry drove past, scattering their surfaces and rumbling all the way up the street. He finally stopped on a corner, and had Sirius do a turnabout to face him.

“Do you think Sheila loves me?”

“Huh?”

“Do you think she could love me, even after all this time?”

“Well... Who wouldn’t love you?”

It was such a Sirius answer. So lovely and simple.

“I care about you so much, nothing else should matter. It doesn't matter. So if you’re feeling bad, Sirius, you can talk to me. You know that, right?”

Sirius wiped beneath his nose, a bit like a child. “You hypocrite. You never tell us your problems.”

Remus laughed and fit his hands into his coat pockets. “Yeah, guess I deserve that.”

“Does that mean you forgive them then? Sheila and—and your parents…?”

“Dunno,” Remus shrugged. “Might never forgive ‘em. But I’m not going to let them take the things I want away from me anymore.”

Sirius’ lips parted in further surprise. He thought for a moment, and then he smiled. The sort of smile that creased every inch of his face and had made Remus fall in love with him that very first day.

“You know, just this morning Mary was ragging on me," he said. "She said I had the emotional range of a teaspoon. Do you know what I told her?”

“That it’s closer to two teaspoons?”

“I said, ‘that’s okay, Moony’s deep enough for the both of us’."

Oh.

"And you are. I could drown in you. Couldn’t imagine a better way to go, actually.”

Now that’s a song, Remus thought.

Swelling with happiness, he surged forward, hugging Sirius first and then dropping an arm around his shoulder as they walked. To anyone else it might’ve looked casual, but to the two of them, it meant so much more.

After a quick pit-stop for whisky and cigarettes, they stopped in at the record shop, where Sirius badgered Graeme to put on some T. Rex and Remus sorted four crates of stock just to leave with a slightly-battered copy of The Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan.

“Not that I’m questioning your taste,” Sirius said, as they left the shop and started toward the pub; “but… Nah, I’m questioning your taste.”

“It’s got a certain song on it,” Remus said, peering down at the back of the album sleeve. “Haven’t heard it for a while. I’d know what all the fuss is about.”

“It’s that good?”

“No. Pretty sure it’s shit, actually.”

They shared a smile.

When they arrived at the Three Broomsticks, they found their friends already waiting for them. Remus had to duck to avoid cracking his forehead against the drooping sign hanging above the pub’s doorway, but the inside was as warm and inviting as always. Near the back, James, Lily, and Marlene were set up at their usual table, a small forest of glasses already spread out in front of them.

“Oi, Padfoot!” James cried when he spotted them. “Come over here! I think I’ve finally figured out what’s got you so cross lately.”

“Oh yeah?” Sirius asked, sliding in next to James, Remus right behind.

“Yeah, completely my fault—I forgot how much the title meant to you! So here, say hello to your first godchild!” James gestured to Prongs Jr., still wrapped up in his lap. Next to him, Lily shook her head hopelessly.

“I told you it wasn’t a funny joke.”

“No?” James frowned. “Padfoot? … Dadfoot…?”

Sirius slumped back against the booth, and finally groaned. “I hate ya, Prongs. I love ya, but I hate ya.”

This made everyone laugh, and just like that, things were alright again. They ordered more drinks and the Broomstick’s landlady, Rosie, came over to prattle them about being nearly finished with school. Marlene told them that Lottie was visiting with some girlfriends a few tables down, and so far Peter was still missing in action after going off with Moira earlier on. Remus hoped it was a good sign, and not because she’d drowned him in the lake.

Eventually Mary made an appearance, shrugging off her winter coat while grinning ear to ear. She shoved in next to Marlene with news that she’d just refused a date with Jason Barnes, arguably one of the fittest boys in their year.

“Why’d you say no?” Marlene asked her. “You told me he’s been making eyes at you for weeks.”

Mary smiled coyly, popping a few pub peanuts into her mouth for good measure. “I almost did, but then I thought to myself, in less than two months we’ll all be going off—doing new things, in new places! And I just sorta thought that it would be nice to spend the rest of my time at school with my friends.”

Remus and Sirius shared a glance. Not even the dim lighting could hide the rosy twinge in Marlene’s cheeks after that.

Remus was relieved when Peter and Moira finally showed up. Peter stood awkwardly at the end of the table, but Moira didn’t seem interested in backing down. While James quickly cleared space for them, she regarded Sirius coolly.

“Thurnberg.”

“Black.”

This time, Sirius did not need a swift kick beneath the table. He straightened up in the booth, and raised a nod to her. “I respect anyone who can speak their mind like you did, Thurnberg—no holding back. And for what it's worth, I’m… sorry, for what I said.”

Moira glanced at Peter, softly, and nodded. “I accept your apology.”

“Moira and I are dating again,” Peter smiled.

The girls all congratulated them, and when the two were sitting, Lily leaned over and pat the girl fondly.

“Don’t ever pay any attention to what Sirius says. He’s a sour thing, especially when his friends like anyone more than him.”

“Only ‘cause it must mean they’ve gone mad! There aren’t many people more likeable than I am.”

“I can name a few,” Marlene said, counting off her fingers; “Charles Manson, Ivan the Terrible, Filch…”

It made everyone laugh, and Sirius raised his glass with a scoff. “Alright, everyone yack it up. See if you’re laughing when it’s this face that’s paying your mortgages, then you’ll all be desperate to have me—”

“Lily?”

It surprised Sirius, enough that he almost fumbled his pint. When he looked up to see what it was, he let out a heavy sigh.

“Christ, I can’t believe no one’s put a bell on you yet. What do you want, Snivellus?”

Snape miraculously held his tongue, though he did look a lot like he’d swallowed a lemon.

“Lily, I just came to offer my congrats.”

Looking surprised to be called upon, Lily raised her head and nodded cordially. “Erm, thank you, Severus… but for what?”

“I spoke with my mother this morning, and she told me the good news. She said she was chatting with your parents this morning when they mentioned that you’d gotten into Oxford.”

A round of gasps went up.

“Oxford, Lils?” Marlene demanded. “You mean you heard back from them already?”

“I–I… uh…”

“Daisy, that’s amazing!” James said. “For real? Blimey, why didn't you say anything?”

Lily was still stammering. “I—I only found out the other day. They moved me from ‘conditional’ to ‘accepted’ after Professor McGonagall wrote to them on my behalf. I was going to tell all of you tonight, I just… couldn’t find the right moment, really.”

“Yeah, it’s proper brilliant, except Snivellus, here, ruined the surprise,” said Sirius.

“It’s fine, Sirius, really—”

“Because it’s still amazing,” James said.

“It’s more than amazing,” Snape interjected haughtily; “it’s remarkable. To get into Oxford is a top achievement. In fact I was accepted as well for chemistry—”

Mary interrupted, raising her glass. "To Lily!" She cried, and they all matched it, cheersing while Lily turned red in her booth.

“Thank you, everyone. And you too, Severus. It still doesn’t quite feel real, but... I’m afraid I’m not going to Oxford.”

“What?” They all echoed.

“Why not?” Asked James.

“Because… I’ve already accepted a different seat. At the University College of London.”

For a moment everyone was silent, until James connected the dots.

“So you’ll be in London...?”

“Starting in September, yeah!”

James nearly leapt up from his chair—only Prongs Jr., still sitting in his lap, kept him seated. “Oh, bloody hell—yes!” He cried, taking Lily and kissing her several times on either cheek. Their friends had just begun to celebrate when the good news was unfortunately interrupted once more.

“You can’t be serious,” Snape fumed. “You mean you’d actually give up a spot at the most prestigious university in the country just to chase after—after these bastards?!”

“If you wanna get technical then only Moony’s a bastard,” Sirius said, making Remus punch him in the arm.

“It’s my choice, Severus,” Lily said calmly. “Please tell your mother I said thank you. But I’m only going back home to Liverpool to gather my things, then I’ll be moving to London.”

Snape began to sputter; “What—? Why?! I… I cannot believe you!”

“She didn’t ask for your opinion, Snape,” James snarled, leaning over his bag of flour threateningly.

“And just what exactly are you possibly going to learn in London? How to fare-dodge and avoid the puddles of piss on the pavement?”

“Oh yes, some of life’s greatest lessons, naturally,” Sirius cackled. “Add in a little debauchery and hedonism and you’ve got our entire summer itinerary.” As if to prove his point, Sirius untucked a cigarette carton from his pocket and lit one up right there, blowing the smoke in Snape’s direction.

Nostrils flared, Snape remained at the end of their table, practically vibrating with rage. “This is pathetic,” he snarled. “You’re throwing so much away and for what?”

“It’s her choice, Snape,” Marlene hissed.

“It’s a stupid choice!”

“Alright, I think we’ve all heard enough,” James said firmly. “You didn’t get what you wanted, but we’re not interested in the fight you so badly want to pick, so just shove off.”

“You’ll drag her down, Potter. She's only going because you—"

“Enough!” Lily shrieked, surprising all of them. “I won’t do this anymore, Severus! No more name-calling or bickering or fighting. This is my choice, and I’ll not have you belittling me or those I care about! Now please, leave!”

“But Lily, you're making a mistake!”

“You’re not hearing her!” James lashed. “You have nothing to do with this, Snape. Now get lost before I have to—” In a beat of protective anger, James had made to stand—except the argument had distracted him, and as he got up, Prongs Jr.’s sensitive paper wrapping got caught on the table edge and tore straight down the middle.

They all yelped as flour flooded the table top, dousing drinks and spilling into laps. Desperately, James went to grab for the bag, but there was no helping it; Prongs Jr.’s powdery insides slipped out between his fingers in vain.

“Oh—not again!” He wailed, as the rest of his friends were caught between moans and crazed laughter.

“Now you’ve gone and done it, Snivelly!” Sirius howled, holding his cig aloft and flicking flour at him. “You’ve killed a child! Lily’s adoptive son, no less! I hope you’re happy with yourself.”

Looking repulsed, Snape shot one final glance at Lily before storming off.

“It’s not in my hair, is it?” Mary fretted, desperately trying to wipe the dust from her shirt-front.

“No,” Marlene giggled, “but it is right there—!” She finished by poking her friend on the tip of the nose, leaving a white outline behind as Mary scoffed.

As other patrons turned to watch them scoop handfuls of flour out of their laps, Rosie reappeared at the table-side, a rag in both hands and disbelief written across her face. “Jesus Mary and Joseph—what happened?!”

“I killed my child,” James sobbed, leaving white handprints across his face.

“It’s just flour,” Remus clarified. “School assignment. The bag ripped.”

“Yes, well it’s going everywhere,” the landlady grimaced.

“We’ll clean it,” Lily assured her, wiping flour from her chin with one hand and comforting James with the other.

“Sorta sad, isn’t it?” Sirius said to Remus. “I was barely a god-dad for an entire hour. If you ask me, the whole thing was completely half-baked.”

“Was that supposed to be a pun, Padfoot?”

“Did’ya like it? I got more. You really bread my mind, Moony. Now I’m on a roll. Or how ‘bout—” He dipped his pinky finger into the flour and licked it; “the kid was a real raw talent.”

“You’re terrible.”

Sirius began to snigger, and then stubbed his cigarette out in one of the tiny white mountains on the table. “Maybe. Call the whole thing a recipe for disaster.”

“Oi.” Reaching over Remus, James clapped Sirius in the back of the head, sending flour everywhere. “Where’s your compassion, Padfoot? That was your godson, it was.”

With his dark hair sprinkled white, Sirius just shrugged. “I’m already numb. Forgot to tell ya, but Knobby might have taken a tumble out of a third floor window this morning.”

Remus gaped at him; “Might have?”

In answer, Sirius dug a hand into his pocket and pulled out a single baggie of flour. “Reckon half a cup will be enough to earn us decent marks with McGonagall, Moons?”





* * *





They ended up staying late, scrubbing flour from the cracks in the Broomsticks’ floorboards for so long that they had to make a run for it just to make the final bus. James had to carry what was left of Prongs Jr. out in a shopping bag, and when Lottie saw them all covered head to toe in white, she laughed so hard she nearly dropped Francois.

“At least one good thing came of today,” James said wistfully, indicating toward the back of the bus, where Peter and Moira were stowed away, grinning and smiling and positively made-up.

“You know what this means, right?” Sirius asked. “We’re gonna be stuck with Thurnberg ‘til we die.”

“Little victories, Padfoot, little victories.”

Back at the dorms, James didn’t even bother showering. Instead he made straight for the kitchenette to perform what he was calling ‘emergency surgery’ on what was left of his son. Too tired to make fun of him and too weirded out to help, Remus and Sirius made their way upstairs before anyone else could catch an eyeful of their ghostly get-up.

“How the fuck did it get into my belly-button?” Sirius mused, looking down at his bare chest as Remus emerged from the toilet, freshly showered.

“It was behind my ears too,” said Remus, rubbing a towel over his head. Sirius glanced at him, moving to prop himself up on his bed with his elbows.

“Are you sure you don’t want to hear the story of how Knobby ended up falling from the Priori Block’s third floor?”

“Save it for McGonagall, we’re gonna need a decent sob story if we don’t want to fail,” Remus said. He pulled the towel from his head and came forward, bending down so he could lock Sirius’ lips with a kiss.

Suddenly the door flew open and Peter raced inside, making the two of them jump apart as though they’d just been given an electric shock.

“Hey lads!” Peter cried, barely glancing their way as he beelined for his own bed.

“H–Hey Wormtail,” Sirius started. “Said goodnight to Thurnberg already?”

“Not quite!”

“Things are going well then?” Asked Remus.

“Yeah, brill!” Peter threw open the hutch at the end of his bed and began digging through it. “I told Moira I was sorry for the way I acted over Easter—I was a proper dick. But I think she’s even coming around to the idea of the band! You think we could still get into the campus gardens at this time? I wanna take her out and explain everything properly. ”

“Probably, if you’re quick about it.”

“Sorry for freezing you guys out earlier,” Peter said, tugging on his spare trainers. “I was just upset about Moira.”

“We get it, mate,” said Remus. “We’re just glad you’ve made up.”

“Thanks. You two done with the shower then? I gotta piss but I don’t want to keep Moira waiting too long.”

“S’all yours,” Sirius called, and Peter nodded at him before disappearing inside.

“Well, glad that’s over with.” Reaching for the ashtray on his bedside, Sirius picked up one of his unlit cigarettes while Remus sagged against the floor next to him.

“Sirius… we gotta tell him.”

“What—like right now?”

Remus pulled the cigarette from Sirius' lips, leaning in until they were nose to nose. “Sirius, it’s time.”

“Okay,” he sighed, snatching back the cigarette. “How d’ya wanna go about it then? ‘Hey, Pete, just so you know Moony and I are dating and while you were fighting with your girlfriend, we spent all of Easter shagging on the common room floor. But don’t worry, we never touched your bed’.”

“Very funny.”

“Should be, I got the rug burns to prove it.”

Remus shook his head. “There’s gotta be an easier way. How’d we do it with James and Lily? I can hardly remember…”

“That’s ‘cause you were too busy having a fit,” Sirius snorted; “We could always tell him about Sim. About how he tried to kiss you on their front drive.”

“Not a chance.”

“You’re right, imagine the fallout.”

“It’d be catastrophic.”

“More like cataclysmic.”

“I think you mean calamitous.”

“Mm… God, I love that big brain of yours, Lupin.” Then Sirius leaned in and kissed him.

“Hey, Sirius, I think I found your—” Peter stopped dead outside the bathroom doorway. “What are you doing?”

Remus pulled back, turning to look at Peter with eyes like saucers. “Pete! We were just—uhm—!”

“Snogging,” Sirius said, very boldly. “We were snogging.”

“… Why?”

Sirius glanced at Remus, then back at Peter, and shrugged. “Because we… love each other?”

A look of floundering confusion crossed Peter’s face, then what could’ve been realisation. For a second Remus almost thought he’d gotten it—before his mouth split into a dismissive smile.

“Right, sure. Very funny, you daft tarts,” Peter said, crossing the room toward them. “Here’s your ring, Black. You should keep better hold of it, I just about knocked it down the drain.”

“Oh shit, that’s mine actually.” Remus reached out and took the ring, slipping it back onto his own finger as Sirius gaped at him.

“You took it off?!”

“Only ‘cause my hands were still covered in flour! Must’ve forgotten it on the side of the sink… Cheers, Pete.”

At the thanks, Peter gave Remus a funny look. “You sure? It’s got Sirius’ initials inside.”

A beat passed between them, and Remus looked at Sirius again, who carefully sat up on his bed. “Yeah... and it’s Moony’s ring."

“Why would Remus be wearing a ring with your initials in it?”

Both of them leaned forward pointedly, and Sirius beckoned Peter on with his hand. “Because we’re…”

It was as though the gears began turning behind Peter’s eyes. “You’re—”

“Buggering each other, yeah.”

“Sirius! I’m going to push you out of a third floor window.”

“What? You said you wanted to tell him!”

“I did, but—shit…”

Peter continued staring at them with disapproving eyes. “You mean the two of you are actually…?”

“We meant to tell you with the others,” Remus urged. “But then things got complicated and we were worried that… well…”

“Others? You mean James knows?”

Maybe it would’ve been better to lie, but it would’ve done nothing in the end. And so they nodded.

“Since January.”

“January?!” Peter half-shouted. “You guys have been doing th—this?!—since January?!”

“A bit longer than that…” Remus confessed. “But yeah.”

“So the two of you… In our room?!”

“Yeah, our room,” Sirius shot defensively. “As if you haven’t done god knows what with Thurnberg in here.”

“That’s different! Moira’s a girl, and Moony, he’s a—he’s a—!”

“A guy?”

“Yes!”

“Blimey!” Sirius cried. “Moony you never told me that!”

“Sirius, don’t.”

“Why not? Macdonald didn't have such a reaction, and she found out the same way.”

“You told Mary?” Peter demanded. “Who else knows then?!”

“Evans,” Sirius answered. “And McKinnon, though she sorta figured it out on her own.”

“No, I told her,” Remus rebuffed.

“You did? I thought she called it.”

“No, Lottie was the one who figured it out on her—” Remus covered his mouth quickly, but the damage was already done.

“You gotta be fucking joking,” Peter said. “Does everyone know but me?!”

“It wasn’t intentional.”

“Bollocks!”

“We figured you wouldn’t want to know,” Sirius said. “That you’d rather be blissfully unaware.”

“Not when everyone else knows! Not when you guys are having a great laugh behind my back!”

“We weren’t laughing, Pete. We were—”

"Screw you!"

Before Remus could even finish, Peter had gone from the room. Just marched straight out, without another word. Dread welling up inside of him, Remus jumped to his feet and made to go after him, but faltered before he’d even made it halfway to the door.

“Well, now he knows,” Sirius said, solemnly flipping the cigarette around in his hands.

“Do you think he’ll tell anyone?” Remus murmured, still staring at the door.

“No. But that doesn't mean he’ll ever talk to us again. Maybe Marauders will be looking for a new drummer after all.”

“He didn’t seem offended,” Remus tried meekly. “That we were both blokes, that is. Just that we didn’t say anything.”

“A poison dart frog doesn't seem poisonous, either.”

And with that, Sirius turned over on his bed.

Neither of them ventured out, and Peter didn’t return. Remus wanted to stay close to Sirius—to let them comfort and reassure one another—but he was too wound up. In the end they stayed on their own beds, not talking. Near curfew, James finally returned with a half-sellotaped Prongs Jr. under one arm and his shirt and trousers still covered in flour. He seemed breathless, like he’d taken each set of stairs at a run.

“Hey,” he panted; “Have either of you seen Pete? I saw him walking out and he seemed kind of off.”

“We told him, Prongs,” Sirius said, completely blasé. “He knows about Moony and me.”

“Oh… Oh shit.”

“Yeah.”

“O–Okay. And I’m assuming it went…?”

“Swell,” Remus answered from his own bed, nose tucked into a book.

No one said anything for several seconds, and James simply stood in front of the door, chewing his bottom lip nervously.

“Well hey, i–it’s okay, right? I’ll talk to him. He’ll come around, I know it.”

“Glad you’re so confident,” Sirius said, popping up to set a record on the turntable.

Still appearing antsy, James started across the room and set Prongs Jr. down on his bedside. “There’s, erm… There’s something else too.”

“Oh no, has the Queen died?” Sirius asked sarcastically. “Or no, wait—it’s not John Lennon is it?”

“No.”

“Paul McCartney? He always was the most insufferable Beatle.”

“No!” James turned around, and looked straight at Remus. “It’s Buchanan. She’s back.”



Chapter End Notes

As far as I’m aware, bleached flour wasn't banned in Europe until the 90s.

'Delia Smith' was/is a famous British baker. She actually baked the cake that was on the front cover of the Rolling Stones’ “Let It Bleed” album.

'Gaffer tape' is just duct tape.

A 'dummie' is another name for a pacifier.

The Bob Dylan song Remus is talking about on the 'Freewheelin' Bob Dylan' album is "A Hard Rain’s A‐Gonna Fall" -- the song that was playing in Hope's hospital room the last time he spoke to her, and the song that's caused him so much trauma consequently. I like to think this is his first step toward healing, and ofc Sirius was there to see it <3

Chapter 92: Blue


Chapter Summary

"What sort of blue?"



Chapter Notes

Note: This chapter picks up immediately following the end of chapter 91. Apologies to any people who have to wait until late in their evenings for these Sunday chapters to be released, lol. I'm in the PST timezone so I'm quite far behind the majority of readers.



Massive Trigger Warning for this chapter: Mental illness involving adults and children as well as strong intrusive thoughts (Remus) and mental trauma. I will say it loudly for those in the back This chapter touches heavily on Hope Lupin's poor mental health.

Here is a tumblr post I made a while ago stating what Hope was experiencing, however this has been a theme throughout Cadence and should not come as a shock, though I understand why it could be read as upsetting.

Trust me when I say I don't take any of these themes lightly, nor should any reader. Poor mental health is a hard topic to handle within media, but just because someone has poor mental health does not mean they aren't capable of being a good person who is worthy of care and love. If you are at all sensitive to this, please do not read this chapter or come to my tumblr to ask for a summary. As long as I'm active, I will always give it, no matter how long it's been. Thank you.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Don’t let me down,

Don’t let me down;

Don’t let me down,

Don’t let me down…

- “Don’t Let Me Down” The Beatles, 1969





Sheila was beloved. Remus had always known that. She looked for the troubled ones, the lost causes, and accepted them even when they shouted obscenities right in her face. She was kind, often too kind… too patient. But she was beloved. And as much as he hated her for what she’d done, Remus couldn't help but love her too.

Do you think she could love me, even after all this time?

“You don't have to go," Sirius told him. "Not if it'll make you sad."

I am sad. I'm always sad. I have been sad for eighteen years.

And who's fault is that?

The thought came violently; intrusive and punishing. He hadn't had one in so long—Sirius' influence, probably. Stupid Remus... And here he'd thought it must've meant that he was getting better.

You don't care! It rang, like some sick children's song. You don't care, you don't care, you don't caaaaaaaaare!

"Moony?"

Your fault, your fault!

“I’m going to see her, Sirius.”

“… Alright then.”

Remus had never been to the teachers' quarters before. Considered out of bounds to all students, the brick and mortar building sat just behind Castle Hall and boasted the largest car park on campus save the trolley depot. They had to scale the main gate to get inside, but it was easy enough for the two seasoned pranksters.

Unsurprisingly, James had gone after Peter. Remus had no idea whether it would help or what James even planned to say to him, but he didn’t have the energy to argue. If Peter wanted to be angry with them then he could be angry, but Remus could only tolerate one relationship imploding at once. Maybe it was selfish, but if Sheila really was back then he wasn't going to wait. Not until he got his answers.

"Shit... Fuck!"

Remus threw his hands down, hearing the sharp ting as the bobby pins disappeared into the dark. He'd been working on the front door's lock for ages, but it was heavy and the wrong kind—harder to pick than the usual pin-and-tumbler ones scattered about campus.

"What if we just knock on her window?" Sirius suggested, standing behind Remus and looking antsy.

"We don't know which window is her's."

"Eh, maybe we get lucky."

Remus sighed, haggardly. Even if they did manage to somehow get inside, there was no guarantee they'd even be able to figure out which door belonged to her. One wrong move and they could be in detention for the next month.

"We could wait until Monday," Sirius said, pressing a hand on his shoulder. "At least that way you know she'll be—"

"I don't want to wait until Monday, Sirius!"

The shout had poured out of him on accident, and Remus was instantly sorry. "I'm sorry," he murmured, standing up beneath the buzzing yellow entry light. "Sorry..."

"You don't have to be sorry." Sirius raised a hand, pressing his palm to the side of Remus' neck. It was cool; comforting.

"You can go," he said. "I'll figure it out on my own. No need for you to get caught up too."

"Not a chance. I'm here, Moons. Always."

Remus smiled, agonisingly. What would I ever do without you?

Just then the gate surrounding the building's car park gave a loud buzz. It began rolling back and a van drove through, its headlamps reflecting off of the first floor windows as it pulled up to the curb, cornering them on the front doorstop.

"Quick!" Sirius hissed, stumbling away from the doors and practically pushing Remus into a thatch of the nearby bushes. Had they dawdled for even a second longer they would've been caught by the delivery man pushing a heavy laundry cart from his van into the building.

"We have to do our laundry and they get theirs delivered?" Sirius whispered harshly. "Oh, that is so not fair."

"Shh!" Remus hissed, elbowing him to be quiet. Luckily the delivery man didn't seem to notice. He whistled as he passed their hiding spot, a large silver keyring jingling on his belt. It was the perfect opportunity, but in his hurry to hide, Remus had gotten his shoelaces caught up in the lower brambles of the hedge.

"Sirius, the door!" He moaned, as the delivery guy pushed his cart inside and the door began to shut behind him.

"Yeah, I got it!" Sirius grunted, pushing free of the hedge. He caught the edge of the door at the last possible second, sliding his fingers in between the gap. After freeing himself from the bush, Remus joined him in the doorway. He had several leftover leaves in his hair, and brushed them away while Sirius smiled. "You missed one," he said, picking a stray twig from the front of his jumper. Remus caught his hand and kissed it, trying to keep his own from shaking. Sirius only looked at him sadly.

"Are you sure you wanna do this, Moons?"

"I'm never sure," he murmured into his knuckles, "but I'm tired of waiting."

There was not much to be said after that. Together they slipped soundlessly into the building. It was already past supper time, but unless every Hawkings professor made it a habit to retire at eight o'clock Saturdays, then they still ran a high risk of being caught. Thankfully they were not left to wander around aimlessly for long. The building's lobby was brightly lit, and next to a wall of tiny post boxes they found a directory that was most likely meant for deliveries. They scanned the list until they found her; S. Buchanan, 3F9.

"So..." Sirius raised his arms for a stretch; "Elevator or the stairs?"

They took the stairwell, which was made of cement and echoed horribly, and ran the risk of being caught only once when Professor Bilshin stepped out to collect his post.

"I could'a gone my whole life without seeing old Bil' in a robe," Sirius shuttered, when they finally emerged on the third floor. "Reckon he was naked under it?"

"I don't really want to think about it to be honest," Remus murmured, busy scanning the golden door numbers as they rushed down the hallway. Sirius had to practically skip to keep up to him, but Remus was hardly paying attention. He counted the flat numbers as they went; F4, F5, F6—

Just as they were nearing a hallway corner, Sirius grabbed Remus by the front of his coat and pinned him to the wall.

"Watch it!" He hissed. "Laundry dead ahead."

They flattened themselves against the wall, and Remus peeked around the corner to find the laundry deliverer from earlier. He was standing in front of one of the flats—3F9.

He should've expected the smile when she answered. Sheila always smiled.

"Oh, Linus. Hello. Final round of the evening, is it?"

"Yes'm. Just get in yourself?"

"About a half hour ago, yes."

It was like hearing her again for the first time. Remus didn't know if he wanted her to hold him, or to scream in her face.

Stop that. Don't be kind—I hate you!

Outwardly she looked no different from the way she always did, and yet something was off. From his hiding spot, he forced himself to look past the vibrant purple dress, the polka dot tights, the golden butterfly clip in her hair. What he found was dullness and exhaustion. The bags under her eyes had darkened, and the faint stripes of grey at her temples had grown more pronounced. Beneath her colourful shell, it was as though she’d aged ten years in only a few short weeks. Still she smiled.

"Apologies for bothering you so late, Mrs. Buchanan, but I got that laundry you sent out before you left," said the delivery man as he began digging around in his cart. "Figured you'd be wanting them clean linens for when you got back."

"My, that's very thoughtful of you." She took the linens as he passed them to her, and afterwards, she handed him a small package wrapped in paper. "And, just before you go... This is for you. I thought you might enjoy it."

"For me?"

"Yes, I was digging around in some boxes back home, you know, trying to clear up the clutter? Anyway, it's just a little book on bird watching. Colin once got it into his head that he might pick it up as a hobby, but I'm afraid neither of us quite had the patience for it. I thought maybe you'd get better use out of it."

Linus peeled back the wrappings like a kid on Christmas. He softened once he'd gotten a look at the cover, and finally pulled off his cap.

"That's very kind 'a ya, m'um. And... Apologies for your loss. Your husband was a smart man, picking you for a wife."

She placed a hand on his shoulder, and Remus felt his own twitch.

"Thank you, Linus. You're very kind."

It was agony waiting for the man to move on, even more so to see her smile and wave—stop it, stop it, stop it! Your fault, your fault!—but then Linus rolled his cart out of the way and she finally looked up. He knew instantly that she had spotted them by the way her smile vanished.

There, Remus thought bitterly; You finally see me.

"Moons...?"

Sirius was prodding him gently on the back, but Remus couldn't see anything but her. He watched as she looked sadly down at the stack of linens she was holding and ran her hand across the soft lace. Then she nodded, and stepped away from the open door—disappearing back into her home. It was an invitation, Remus knew. And it scared him.

"I'm gonna go in," he mumbled, still staring at the flat's open door. Ever the brave one, Sirius nodded and began marching straight for it.

"Right. Let's go in then."

Remus caught his arm.

"Sirius, I-I love you, but... I think I..."

It didn’t matter if he could hardly form a coherent sentence; as always, Sirius was reading his mind. “Hey,” he whispered, reaching up to hold Remus’ cheek; “Don't worry about me. I already had plans anyway. Gonna go see if Bilshin's itching for company. Heard he makes a mean cup of tea."

Remus chuffed, like a laugh that turned sad at the end, and Sirius, the liar, hugged him tightly.

"I’ll be right here if you need me, Moons."

Remus held him for a long time, relishing in the comfort. Then he went to face his fears.

There was no missing the flat as hers; there was a coat rack stood by the door, draped in at least half a dozen patterned rain coats. On the wall hung a portrait of Duke Ellington, and every inch of the floor was covered in some eye-catching rug or other. There were stacks upon stacks of books, music sheets, and records piled everywhere—most of them jazz—and photographs sat strewn about in frames, though Remus tried hard not to look at them. Instead he stared at the boxes, an obvious addition to the room. Some were labelled; kitchen, bath, bedroom...

Colin's things.

Distantly he could hear the sound of her tinkering in the kitchen, and when she returned she was carrying two mugs of tea.

"Excuse the mess," she said. "I thought we might have tea while we talked."

"You mean you actually want to talk?"

"Don't you, Remus?"

He glared at her, but she was used to such things as angry children. Smiling meekly, she set the mugs of tea down on the coffee table, using a book on music theory for a coaster. She gestured to the sofa chair across from her, but Remus didn't trust himself enough to sit. Better to be uncomfortable; he had plenty of uncomfortable things to say.

"Do you want to tell me how you got in here?"

"Snuck in after the laundry guy."

"Hm. Clever thing," she hummed, stirring her tea. "And where has Mr. Black gone? I hope he's not out causing too much trouble."

"I'm not here to talk about Sirius," Remus snapped. "I'm here to talk about you. And me. 'Cause it's a related thing, isn't it?"

It was harsh, but no less than she deserved. With a slow sip, she swallowed and set down the tea cup.

"Would you like to sit?"

"No."

She sighed. "I understand why you're angry."

"No, you don't." Remus felt his lower lip begin to tremble. "Where were you—where did you go?"

"Glasgow. It's where our home was."

"Was...? You're back to stay for good then?"

“Mhm, yes. I love Hawkings, and I love teaching. I think I would miss it if I never came back.”

“So does this mean your husband…”

She nodded, hands folded tightly in her lap. “Colin’s passed away, yes. We had a service for him in early April. It was beautiful, but I needed to take some time.”

The sudden urge to lash out rose inside Remus. No one had ever given him time. “I don’t want to feel bad for you,” he said lowly.

“I understand.”

“I’m angry with you.”

“I… understand.”

“Furious, even. I hate you. There are so many things I want to say to you. Things that you… That you deserve!”

“You can say them. I promise not to be angry.”

He almost wished she was. At least if she were angry then they could shout at each other, be equals. As it was, he was still just the angry kid.

Your fault, your fault!

"Remus, I am sorry for everything I’ve—"

"SHUT UP!" He wailed, resisting the urge to slam his fist through the nearest pile of books. “You knew what you were doing! You put that photo there to fuck with my head, and you didn't even care! How long did you think it would take me to find it? A week? A YEAR?!"

"Remus..."

"You didn't even care!" He said again. "You left that photo in there hoping that by the time I found it, you'd already be long gone. That I'd be grown up and you wouldn't have to worry about taking responsibility anymore! Like some sick fucking fantasy!"

"No! No, never."

"Liar! You're a liar—in fact, you're worse than a liar! Because you couldn't even tell me the truth yourself! You... You're a coward, just like her. You let me find out that you’re my fucking godmother and then you disappeared. But you—you were supposed to be better! I believed in you!”

As his voice began to shatter, Sheila’s mouth parted in pain. She stood up from her chair and started towards him, but Remus only stepped away, too afraid to let her close. She stopped then, and covered her mouth to hide the shakiness in her voice

“Remus, what I-I did to you… was so indescribably wrong. You can’t imagine how sorry I am.”

“I don’t care how sorry you are!” He swore, losing his patience and slamming his hands into the back of the sofa chair ahead of him. “You know Linus the bloody laundry driver better than you know me! But I was owed! You owed it to me—all of you! I don't care if you were in fucking Scotland with a sick husband—I could’ve used you! I might not have wanted you—probably would’ve hated you, but dammit—I could’ve used you. You’re my godmother, it was your job to protect me and you threw it away! And now… Now people pity me… I have everything—a home, friends who love me—and yet I’m pitied because the people who were supposed to want me—didn’t. And it’s YOUR FAULT!”

“Oh, Remus—”

“No! Don’t you ‘oh Remus’ me! Just tell the fucking truth! I’m eighteen! Tell me why you did it! Why you never told me who you really are—TELL ME!”

He was come apart all over again. Confronting her was more terrible than he could’ve ever imagined, but they were both in it now. It was obvious in the way Sheila covered her face—hiding the tears that had started trailing down her cheeks with her hands.

“I’m so sorry,” she pleaded, over and over again. “Sorry—so sorry. What I did—I’m so sorry, Remus…”

“Tell. Me.” He croaked. “Didn’t you… Didn’t you want me?”

“Yes,” she whimpered, “yes, oh yes. I swear, Remus, I wanted you from the first moment I held you in my arms. You were so precious, and I loved Hope more than anything. And then when I saw you in my classroom, I thought that maybe… but you..."

"But what?"

"You didn’t know who I was, Remus. I was a stranger to you, and for a while I thought it was for the best. You had your family, and I’d already promised your father I wouldn’t tell you anything.”

“You mean Tad didn’t want—”

“No.” Sheila shook her head sadly. “Not Tad. Tad—he... Oh Christ, we were so young. Hope, me—all of us. Just young and stupid. I’m sorry, Remus, but I haven’t spoken to Tad in years."

Remus felt his heart lurch, but it was what he’d suspected. “Lyall then.”

Sheila’s entire face creased into a horrible sob, and she dropped her head in shame. “Yes... it was Lyall. You see, when Colin and I met we were still in college. He was so brilliant back then, he could play anything under the sun. But he got in on scholarship, and his family was poor. So when I told my parents we were getting married they disowned me.”

“What does this have to do with me?”

“Everything,” she wept. “Colin was an aspiring musician in London, and I was just a simple school teacher. We had no money, and when he became ill and couldn't work anymore, I had to stay home and take care of him. I never resented it, never, but life can be cruel, Remus. We were drowning and Colin needed more than what I could give him. I went to your parents for help, but Hope wouldn’t see me. She was still so angry... Your father had to go behind her back to help us, and in the end he agreed to finance all Colin’s hospice care as long as I never tried to contact either of you again.”

“… Why?” He couldn’t think of anything else to say. He wished he’d listened to his gut and just run away.

“Because I knew about Tad, and he wanted you to be a Lupin. He wanted to keep his wife and son, no matter what.”

Suddenly Remus felt like he was drowning too. Couldn't get a breath in. His brain wouldn't shut up—I hate him! I hate him! I wish he was dead.

The thought was too much. He staggered, enough so that he had to grab onto one of the sofa chairs just to support himself. Immediately Sheila came forward, but Remus simply threw an arm out. “Don’t,” he hissed, before fisting the front of his shirt to help himself calm down. She flinched, but did not back away. Nor did she try to touch him again.

“Remus, you're right. I am a coward,” she said, with all the sadness of a thousand lonely nights; “I took the money your father offered and moved Colin and I back to Glasgow. I told myself it would be better for everyone. Hope would get better, as would Colin, and you would grow up loved.”

"Do you hear yourself?" He echoed. "Loved? No, all you did was keep more family from me. You kept yourself from me.”

Sheila nodded, unable to deny it. “I’m so sorry.”

“It's not enough, not by half. The world may not be fair but I deserved better, from all of you. So I want to know. I want to know why the two of you fought. You and Hope."

She stared at him, then her eyes fell to the floor.

"No more secrets," he said gravely. "If you lie to me now, I’ll know it, and I will never forgive you. Not for as long as I live.”

A beat passed between them, and Remus suddenly regretted ever sending Sirius away. It would've been easier to have him there to hear it, rather than have to say the words himself again later.

"Alright, I will tell you," Sheila said finally. "But first you have to sit down."

He wanted to say no, but couldn't find a good enough reason to throw it back in her face. He needed to know, and like her, he was tired.

"I need you to understand just how sick your mother was," Sheila started, once they were both sitting quietly across from one another. She thumbed her mug of tea anxiously, and often glanced at the photograph of a man sitting on the mantle. Remus didn't have to ask whether it was Colin or not.

"It was not a good situation for anyone, Remus, let alone a baby."

"I don't care what you thought about the 'situation', I want to know why the two of you fought. Why didn't I grow up knowing about you?"

She sighed. “Because I was the one who told Lyall she needed help.”

"... You?"

"Yes," she said grimly, wiping a few stray hairs from her face with shaky fingers. “Hope—she... She would have these breakdowns, just scream herself hoarse. It started about a year before you were born. Some days it was about Lyall, other days it was about Tad, some—nothing at all. She would just scream, Remus… And then you were born and for a while she seemed well again. She was so happy to hold you, hardly ever put you down. We thought it was over..."

"You're saying she was crazy?"

"No, not always. Most days were wonderful, you would've never known the difference. But then you were born, and she became fixated on you. She wouldn’t let anyone near you, not even Lyall. Then her outbursts got worse and I... Well, I told Lyall he should have her looked at, just for her own safety. At first they just chalked it up to pregnancy and mood swings, a traumatic after-birth. Later when the symptoms persisted the doctors started calling it, ‘severe mental depression’. It was rubbish of course, nobody really knew what that meant. They just stuffed her with medications, hoping something would fix it. When it didn't, the depression became ‘mania’. I didn’t want to believe it at first, but how could I not? One moment she was laughing and speaking to you clear as day, and the next she’s throwing herself down the bloody stairs—!”

She lapsed into silence for a moment, clutching her cup hard enough that her knuckles went white.

"I'm sorry... I didn't mean that. It's just... we were worried. We didn't want her to hurt herself, and it almost always became worse whenever you were involved. I didn’t want to believe she could actually hurt you, but one day, during one of my visits she was rocking you in your nursery. I got up to make us some tea and—and when I came back she was... She was trying to smother you in your crib. Oh Remus..." She shook her head, looking ragged. "That was the first time she was committed to the hospital. Lyall swore me to secrecy, he didn't want them to take you away from her. But Hope blamed me for telling him, and I couldn’t even argue. But she was so sick, Remus, I swear.”

He knew she was telling the truth. Even now, at eighteen, Remus could still remember the weeks his mother used to go on her ‘holidays’. She'd be gone and no one could tell him what it was she'd left him for, and whenever she returned she'd always felt... empty, somehow. Like she wasn't really there. She could see him, hear him, but she wasn't the mum he knew.

"Your mother deserved better than those doctors," Sheila told him. "She was a good girl. And she loved you, she... She just needed more help."

"Did you know then that Tad was my real father?" Don't lie, don't lie. "Did she tell you?"

Sheila shook her head. "I knew the two of them were having an affair and that she was probably in love with him, but I think things changed when she found out she was pregnant. She was probably very scared, Remus."

"Scared enough not to tell her best friend the truth?"

She shrugged, sadly. "She wanted her baby to grow up with a father."

"No, she wanted her lover! She was always changing her mind. I remember how she used to follow him around like a lost fucking puppy, she didn't care!"

"She cared, I know it. We're all just selfish in love."

He was still angry, and he didn't want her words to bother him, but they did. Remus knew exactly what it was to be selfish. His selfishness had almost doomed him and Sirius from the start; it'd never solved anything. When he was in love, only one thing had ever helped.

Remus raised his head.

“I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to forgive you, but I'm glad you told me the truth."

"I am too," she said. "You are so brave, and I swear, Remus, I will never lie to you again. You deserve better, just like your mum did. And if you'd let me, I would like to be in your life. Even if it's just as your music teacher."

And so, Remus Lupin was at a crossroads. He could go right, and live unhindered by the past he so resented, free from any bonds made by so-called family. Or he could go left, and begin his trek through poisonous jungles of hurt and anger and resentment all while not knowing if it'd even be worth it in the end. Those were the choices; go right, alone, or left, with her. It almost seemed like an easy solution for someone who'd never put much stock into any adult, but she'd said she wanted him. And in the end that's all anyone could really hope for.

"I can't forgive you for what you did," he said, "but I don't want you to go. I want you in my life, if you're willing."

The look on Sheila's face was like blue skies after a month of rain. "Oh," she sobbed, "yes. Yes, please. I would like that very much.”

"No more second chances though. I... I can't do it again."

"I know. I swear it."

He nodded, and then noticed a ticking on his cheek. Reaching up, he touched his fingers to his face only to have them come away wet. It scared him slightly to wonder how long he'd been crying, and whether his tears had influenced her decision. That thought—that one—was the one that broke the camel's back.

He began to cry, for his mother, but also for himself, and as he wept she came to him. She held him, and he did not push her away.

“I love you, Remus,” she whispered. "You are so loved."

They clung to each other for a long time, and through it all Remus was reminded of Mrs. Potter, and how it'd felt to be held by her. A motherly rock, a gentle hand over the forehead. Perhaps Sheila hadn't had as much practice, but there was time. There was always time.

When the tears had ebbed, Sheila released him and crouched by the foot of the chair. "You're okay," she told him, "You're okay."

He nodded, feeling like a used tissue, and using her thumbs, she wiped the tears from his cheeks as they both sucked back several sniffles.

“Guess this means we’re family,” he croaked.

“Guess so,” she answered.

“I don’t know a thing about you,” Remus confessed. “I mean, I know you like music and have questionable taste in fashion, but… not much else.”

She beamed; in all her beloved kindness. “How about we start with something small then?"

"Like what?"

"Like... I hate parsnips. I love tomatoes. And my favourite colour is orange, like a sunset. Now you go.”

"I... I like sweet things."

"Oh yes, I knew that."

"Yeah, and—uhm, I don't really like mushrooms."

She stuck her tongue out. "They're just fungus anyway. And your favourite colour?"

“Blue.”

“What sort of blue?"

Remus thought. Sirius, Sirius.

"A very specific kind."

He had waited for him. Of course he had. The dear idiot.

He’d fallen asleep on the bench in the hallway, head tilted back against the cinder brick wall. Remus bent down in front of him to wake him, and gently squeezed Sirius’ shoulder until he’d jolted awake.

"Ngh—I'm not out of bounds!"

“It's me.”

"Moons...?" Sirius wiped his eyes. "Shit... didn't mean to fall asleep."

"Surprised you could, what with all my shouting."

"You were shouting?" He sounded concerned.

"Only a little."

Sirius peered at him. Then he brought his hands up and gently traced beneath Remus' eyes with the soft pads of his thumbs. “You’ve been crying.”

“Yeah,” Remus said honestly. “I was sad.”

“Are you still sad?”

“A little. But I’m glad I did it.” Leaning in, Remus pressed his mouth to Sirius’, who kissed him back. Slowly their lips parted, but rather than coming apart, they simply dissolved into a tight hug. Sirius slipped down from his bench so they could be even closer, straddling him and wrapping his arms tightly around Remus’ neck.

“M'proud of you,” he murmured, as Remus’ shoulders began to tremble.

They held each other like that for a while, uncaring if anyone were around to see it. But it was late anyway, and when Sirius finally peeled himself away, Remus had no tears left in the bucket.

“Come on then, let’s get you home," Sirius said, picking him up off the floor. "I think a nice, soothing bath is in order."

“Sorry for making you take care of me all the time,” Remus mumbled.

“Don’t be stupid. We take care of each other.”

Despite the late hour, James was waiting for them back at the dorm. He glanced up from his A-Levels text and smiled hopefully, but Remus only had enough energy left to collapse down onto his bed.

“Where’s Pete?” Sirius asked cooly.

James’ smile faded. “Just needs some time, I think. You two proper spooked him, doing it the way you did.”

“I’m sorry our relationship is so shocking, but he’s the one who ran off."

"Sirius, do we have to do this now?" Remus asked. Sirius glanced at him and shook his head.

"Sorry."

Across the room, James sat up on his bed. "I didn’t know you'd told Mary and Lottie."

"Potter, Moony's asked for quiet."

"But you should've said something, don't you think?" James reasoned. "Even just helped him understand a bit more, instead of laughing at him. I mean, hell, I was shocked when you told me—not that I have an issue with it or anything... But you didn't think he'd be upset to be the last to know out of everyone? Wouldn't you be upset?"

"That has nothing to do with any of this," Sirius said staunchly. "It's not as if we planned the order on purpose. Mary was by accident. Lottie figured it out on her own. It's not our fault Pete's too thick—”

"Don't be a twat, Padfoot!"

The shout was so sudden, especially for James. Probably very unused to it, Sirius peeled off his coat and marched into the toilet. Remus watched him go and sighed, thinking about how he could really use a month-long nap.

“I didn't mean to shout," James said, guiltily thumbing his textbook.

"I know, Prongs."

"I'm just worried. I agreed on this band stuff so that we could stay together, but if this is how it's gonna be, I don't think we'll last."

Remus' stomach sank like a heavy stone. "You're probably right..."

"You don’t have to explain yourselves to me," James called. "But will you at least talk to him? For me?”

“Sure, Prongs."

James' shoulders seeped with relief and smiled at him again. “How were things with Buchanan? Did you sort it?”

“Mostly. I promise to tell you everything later.”

He nodded in understanding. “Okay, Moons.”

Trying not to appear sheepish, Remus kicked off his boots and followed Sirius into the bathroom. He hadn’t locked it, and when he strode inside he found Sirius already filling the tub, muttering darkly to himself;

“Acting like he’s the one who’s been wronged… little rat…” Sirius straightened up when he saw him, and turned around with a hand to his forehead. “I’m sorry,” he muttered, “you’ve already had a shit night and here I am going off.”

"Wasn't all shit," Remus shrugged, and then gestured to the tub. "May I?"

"Huh? Oh. Yeah, drew it for you."

"Will you stay with me too?"

Sirius didn’t need any more asking than that. Quickly he stripped himself down and crawled into the tub, spinning around in the old porcelain tub to hold a hand out to Remus. “Here. Think I’m gonna hold you today.”

Oh, yes please.

Remus didn’t feel the least bit shy as he peeled out of his clothes and slipped one leg over the edge of the tub, followed by the other. Both he and Sirius knew what the other looked like on the inside, down to their very bones, and that was ten times uglier than whatever could be found on the surface anyway. Against his back, he could feel the rough shape of the burn scars that laced across Sirius' chest. He was growing out of them just as the doctors said he would, but it was still slow going. Good thing Remus adored every part of him, even the sad ones. Inside the bath, the water was warm, but Sirius was by far the warmest part. Remus' legs stuck out the other end by a good half, but he couldn't be bothered to complain as Sirius hugged him from behind and pressed small kisses along his hairline.

“Bit ironic, isn't it?" Remus murmured.

"Mm..." Kiss, kiss. "What's ironic?"

"My life. Shit's like a fucking kitchen sink drama. Dunno where all the nonsense comes from.”

“You mean that's just occurring to you now?”

Remus smiled, reaching up and pulling one of Sirius’ hands to his mouth to kiss. “I don’t think I can ever be without you now, you know.”

“You won’t be.”

“Ever? You swear you won’t go anywhere?”

“Never. You’re stuck with me, Moons. I’m like gum on the bottom of your shoe. Handsome gum.”

Remus kissed his hand again. “Tell me we’re gonna fix things with Peter. I really want this—all of us, in London, together.”

Sirius exhaled and Remus felt it tickle the back of his neck.

“Fine, alright. If he’s willing to come around, I will too... Of course I will. Can't risk losing James, I think I've come to like Wormtail's stubborn push-back. Who knows, might win us a Grammy one day.”

Remus chuckled, dipping further under the water, while Sirius leaned over him and smirked.

"What? You think we can't do it?"

“If there's anyone who can do it, it's you, Sirius."

Sirius gave a low hum and buried his face in the crook of Remus’ neck. “Not on my own… Need my Moony, don't I? After all, you’re our good luck charm.”

Remus shivered. “How do you do that, Sirius Black? Make me feel so good when all I want is to feel bad?”

Sirius lifted his face to whisper into his ear.

“Magic.”

Chapter 93: Stayin' Alive... Stayin' Alive...


Chapter Summary

Oooh, the girls are fighting... hehe. I love arguing :^)



Chapter Notes

CW: Alcohol and drunken shenanigans, including a brief cheeky bit in a broom cupboard. (These boys have no idea of the meaning of 'subtlety'.) If sex talk isn't your thing, pay attention to the '>>>' and '<<<' to skip over it.
