Thursday 15th June 1978 — The Final Day of the Tournament

As promised, the Hawkings football team beat out their second opponent in a nail-biting 2 to 1 match. The team from Aberdeenshire was still guaranteed a spot near the top of the podium, but no one was celebrating yet. To win, Hawkings' first-ever co-ed team would have to beat out Brentford in the final game. The boys team had managed it the year before with no meagre amount of effort, but so far Brentford had been dominating on the field, with a startling 6 to 1 win over their previous opponents. Now with a few girls now thrown head-first into the fray, the championship game went from being about school pride to self ego—which in their current state, was worth far more than any ruddy trophy anyway.

Unfortunately, ego often made sickly monsters out of everyone.

“It’s bloody ridiculous. A mockery of the sport!"

“They can’t even place! Who would give up the chance for a first place trophy just to have a bunch of manky girls on the team...”

“Brentford’s gonna ground those henpecked bastards into the dust.”

“Bunch of bloody contrarians... They must think it's gonna get them noticed, but no league scout wants a player who’s gonna break the rules just to for the hell of it. Pointless...”

“Yeah, plus they all look like blokes!"

“Ha! Maybe these lads like blokes.”

“Heh! They should change their name—instead of Hawkings they can be ‘Arsemongers’.”

Remus wasn't entirely sure but he almost thought he could feel his blood boiling. The slander had been going on ever since their school's team had taken to the field the day before, but now that it was confirmed that Hawkings was to be playing in the final game, all bets were off. Every player in the tournament—loser or not—had come out to watch, and the stands were packed nearly to their bursting point. As James and Marlene led their team in a warm-up, Remus stood off to the side of the players' bench with Peter, helping him as he refilled water bottles. Down from them, a group of boys from another school had formed a circle at the edge of the pitch, mostly to shit-talk the other teams. And Remus might've been able to handle it, were they not speaking loudly enough that anyone within a twenty feet radius could hear them.

"If you had to pick one, which would it be?"

"Mm, one on the end I think, with the brown hair."

"Her? She's got shoulders bigger than my Pa. And no tits."

"Alright then, the one next to her. Though, might have to put a bag over her head first—heh."

If Remus had sleeves, they would've been pushed up to his elbows by now. Peter must've noticed this, as he came around the bench and got between Remus and the boys.

"Don't listen to them, Lupin. They've already lost, they just wanna run their mouth."

"Yeah? And how easy d'ya think it'd be to run their mouth with two fat lips?"

"There's like five of them and one of you, plus you know James'll kill you if you got kicked off the field for fighting right before their final match."

"I like my odds." Remus ground his teeth together. "And 'sides... Potter's halfway across the pitch, what he don't know won't kill him."

"Oh c'mon, Moony..."

As Peter sighed, one of Marlene's girls, an eleventh year named Summer, came trotting up to the bench for a sip of water. When she was finished, she set the bottle aside and returned to the field, only to be jeered and whistled at by the rival team on her way.

"Yeah, go on girl, bit faster! Can't quite see those knickers under those shorts!"

"If you aren't gonna give us a show then you could at least turn around so we can see the front!"

Poor Summer baulked, shame-faced as she covered her chest with her arms. She ran the rest of the way back to her team with the boys' laughter nipping at her heels, but the final straw for Remus was when one of the boys turned around and smirked.

"Ha... Frigid bitch."

They went on mocking her, holding their hands to their chest and poking their fingers outward like a pair of nipples as they laughed. Summer was sixteen, she just wanted to play football.

"Right, that's it." Dropping the armful of water bottles he'd been clutching, Remus side-stepped Peter, who tried meekly to haul him back. "Oi!"

“Shh! Lupin, don’t—!”

“OI!”

It got their attention.

As Peter hung back, looking around nervously for a teacher, Remus strode right up to them.

"What do you want?" The first of them asked, looking up at him with a disinterested scowl on his face.

"I wanna know what it is you think you're doing," Remus spat.

"Nothing."

"Nothing? You call harassing a bunch of girls 'nothing'?"

"It's just a bit of friendly pitch-talk," said another. "If you Hawkings freaks can't handle a little laugh, then maybe you shouldn't be playing in our tournament."

The boys all shared a smirk, as though they were waiting for Remus to concede defeat in lieu of their cleverness. Too bad Remus never really did learn how to quit.

"Can I borrow that?" He asked, pointing to the football one of them had tucked under his arm. The kid glanced dubiously at his friends before ultimately handing it over. They watched as Remus took the football and spun it between his hands several times.

"Do you even know what you're doing with that?"

"Nah, not really. Not all that good with my feet, to be honest." Remus stopped the ball, looking up. "But I am good with my hands... Know a game, even. Wanna know what it's called?"

The group shared a look, and then all jumped as Remus surged forward and grabbed the front of the first boy's sports shirt in a single fist.

"It's called, you piss off, or I'm gonna be shoving this football so far down your throat, you'll be shitting it out in an hour."

"Now that sounds like a fantastic game! I always did say these things didn't do enough to help us get to one another. Pity."

The voice came from behind them, and a second later Remus felt a pair of hands snaking up his back and over his shoulders.

"Hello, lads," Sirius purred. "Having a good time, are we?"

No one said anything, and finally Sirius smirked and gestured to the boy Remus had by the collar.

"Lupin, you can let go of him now."

He didn't want to, but the slight squeeze Sirius gave to his shoulders told him that he probably should. To the boy's credit, he was brave enough to try and take his football back, only to recoil when Remus flinched sharply toward him.

"There, that's better, isn't it?" Sirius grinned. "I recognise your shirts. You're from 'Cow-poo', aren't you?"

"It's Caldew," one of them moaned.

Remus sniggered quietly, and each of the rival boys shot him a dirty look.

“Listen," sighed Sirius, "I did overhear one of you using the word ‘contrarian’ correctly, so I suppose not all of you have brains falling out your arse, but I’d still watch out if I were you. "Long enough!"

Sirius shook his head. "I don't think so. You see that scar on his nose? He didn't get that fighting a bunch of teenage brats from Dalston and Cumbria. You see, Lupin here, is our headmistress's big rehabilitation project. You take a kid from the streets and give him a place to live, clothe him, feed him 'til he's strong, then you release him back and hope he's learned enough not to kill anyone. Doesn't always work though... Sometimes they reject the education. Sometimes they've just got too much of the ol' killer in 'em."

None of them seemed eager, and either because they believed him or because Sirius' ramble had bored them enough to lose interest, each of the group finally turned away. The last, the one who was missing his football, waited a second longer until Sirius had snatched the ball from Remus and held it out.

"You want it? Fine. Go—get it!"

With a purposeful smirk, Sirius kicked the ball straight up into the air and let it soar toward the edge of the stands. The Caldew boy chased it for a moment, until he realised just where it was going to land. All morning, Filch had been shambling across the field, collecting rubbish and muttering to himself about the 'lazy, ungrateful ingrates' he was forced to pick up after every day. When the football came down over his head, it smacked him dead-on, nearly knocking the nasty old caretaker right off of his own knobby knees. When he'd recovered enough to look up to see who'd hit him, Filch spotted the guilty-looking boy and let loose a well-deserved shriek.

"You! Get over ‘ere now!"

"That was quite the speech back there," Remus said, after they'd turned and made their escape toward the middle of the stadium. A few kids who'd watched the entire affair from their seats, cheered as they passed, and Sirius threw his arms up to receive them.

"You loved it!" He called, still waving excitedly as they started up the metal staircase. The crowd was huge now, supplemented by the addition of various classes from the elementary campus and all of the teams that had been knocked out before the finals. Lily and the girls had taken their seats in the dead centre—even Sam was there, trying to flag Remus down like a jet on a runway. The field was fuller now too, and as they got higher into the stands, Remus could see that the Brentford team had already taken to the pitch for warm-up, led by their annoyingly handsome captain.

“I told James to kick Brentford’s arse today, right?” He called over the noise.

“Yes! About three times before breakfast.”

“Good. I hate them.”

Sirius laughed and pat his shoulder. “Okay, Moons.”

They’d reached the midway point of the open-air stands, and Remus shot a wave at Lily, who had joined Sam in trying to get their attention. “Remus, here!” She shouted, gesturing to the two empty spots next to her.

He went to follow, already muttering an ‘excuse me’ to the kids at the end of the row, when suddenly Sirius had grabbed his arm, pulling him back into the aisle.

“Hold on, Moons, your almost-brawl nearly made me forget. I have a genius idea.”

"For what?"

"A prank, of course."

Already intrigued, Remus stepped in close and watched as Sirius slid a small cassette out of his pocket, holding it up for him to take. “Found that behind my bed yesterday when we were packing up the rest of our crap,” Sirius said. “It’s Mary's, thought I’d lost it ages ago.”

Carefully dodging a few kids on their way further up into the stands, Remus turned the tape over. “The Runaways?"

Sirius nodded keenly. "You've listened to them then?"

"Yeah, once or twice. But why’re you showing it to me now?”

“Turn it over, ya numpty," he tsked. "Read the first track.”

Remus did as he was told, and a second later he felt a bemused smile spread across his face. “Really? Bit on the nose, don't you think?”

“I think it's perfect, actually! And the band’s made up of all chicks. American ones. Think McKinnon will like it?”

“Maybe. Or she'll bash your head in."

"That's a chance I'm willing to take." Humming gladly, Sirius plucked the tape from his fingers. “I thought we could play it as the team takes the field. Really amp up the crowd—like how they do it during the Cup.”

“Alright, but your stereo’s a bit quiet to be heard over the crowd.”

“Who said we were gonna use my stereo?” Smirking, Sirius jutted his head to his right, and Remus glanced up to spot the announcer’s box sitting at the top of the stands.

“Oh no. They’re never gonna let you do that.”

“Well, we won’t know unless we try, right?” Elbowing him, Sirius turned and quickly began skipping up the steps. Taking a moment to glance back at Lily, who had her arms raised in question, Remus shrugged and followed, catching up to Sirius at the very top. It was colder at the top of the stands, and so high up that peering over the backside of the stands made Remus feel a bit woozy. Down below they could see the referees begin to clear the field.

"Best be quick if we want this to work," Sirius called.

“But how are you even going to convince them to let you play it?”

"Do you really have so little faith in me?" Sirius scoffed, then flashed him a wink; “Watch and learn, love.”

Sliding tape out of its plastic case, Sirius opened the door to the press box and strode inside. The interior of the tiny room was covered in wires and control panels, each of them snaked around each other in a never-ending tangle. Remus’ only had about a foot's worth of clearance over his head and the entire thing looked like a fire hazard, but luckily for them, there was only a single other person inside. His name was George Kelley. He was sitting in the announcer's seat when they walked in, scribbling urgently in the margins of his notes. The three of them had taken nearly two years of forms together and George had always seemed nice enough, even if he was a bit of a suck-up.

“Hey Georgie,” Sirius called, as the heavy door slammed behind them. In answer, George spun around in his chair, his headphones sitting idly around his neck.

Remus had to swallow his own smile as Sirius shot him a delighted look and quickly passed the cassette along to the other boy.

“That’s right! Pete mentioned you were even named president this year. So cool... What’s this one do?” Sirius pointed to a set of dials.

“Kinda… except we’re not recording anything here. It’s all about output.”

“I see, I see. And that knob there?”

“It’s the microphone’s gain. Means volume.”

“Wow, you are so knowledgeable, really. Does that mean it’s separate from the stereo’s?”

“Yeah, the stereo’s gain is here. But don’t touch it. Everything’s carefully balanced. Even a single nudge could throw it all out of whack.”

“No, of course. Hands to myself... Now what’s that button over there do?”

As George kept on, all too happy to show off his vast knowledge to his upperclassman, Sirius shot Remus a pointed look and gestured his head in the direction of the controls. Remus didn’t need to be a mind-reader to understand what he wanted.

“Hey Georgie,” Sirius interrupted, “you sure you put the tape in correctly? Looks backwards.”

“What?” George wheeled the chair back over to the stereo. As he did, Remus reached forward and dialled the stereo’s volume up to max, before quickly putting his hands behind his back again.

“Oh sorry,” Sirius said, when the tape turned out just fine, “my bad. You clearly know what you’re doing, I’ll stop pestering ya now.”

George waved him off and checked his watch before cursing; “Game’s about to start. Remember, no talking.”

Sirius nodded, zipping his lips and throwing the invisible key over his shoulder. Pleased, George returned to his seat and set his headphones over his ears, pulling the microphone towards himself. It truly was a wonderful view. Soon the players would be taking the field, Remus just hoped that they'd find what they were about to do as funny as they did.

A few moments later, a timer began to chime loudly, and George silenced it before clearing his throat, one hand on his papers, the other on the microphone. When he was ready, he took a deep breath, and hit the button on the mic’s base.

“GOOOOOOD MORNING, FOLKS! And welcome to the final game of the 1978 Inter-School Cup! Today’s match may not be deciding who takes home the trophy, but it will determine who has bragging rights for the following one-hundred and ninety-two school days! Now please put your hands together to help me welcome our visiting team—BRENTFORRRRD!”

The team began to take the field, and George listed off their names and numbers while the crowd whopped and clapped excitedly.

“Good show! Good show! And rounding out the Brentford team, we have its loyal captain. Number four and defensive midfielder, Captain Cal—”

“AH-CHOO!”

George spun around in his chair, and Remus wiped beneath his nose, giving a rather convincing sniffle. “Sorry, allergies.”

Downright sputtering into his hand, Sirius bent over to hide his laughter while Remus wiped the smug look from his face and George turned back around with a huff.

“Ahem—that’ll be Captain Callum McAllister… And here they are, taking to the pitch. Good show, lads! Now let’s all put our hands together in a great Hawkings welcome to the Brentford team!”

As the crowd cheered, Sirius nudged George from behind.

"The tape, Georgie, the tape!"

"Jesus christ, I know!" With one hand covering the mike, George reached over to the stereo and let his finger hover over the play button. “Now, guys and gals, let’s get ready to welcome today’s home team to the field—let’s hear a great cheer for HAWKINGS!”

The button was pressed. The stereo gave a great purr, and then a single click echoed, before the entire stadium was assaulted with the sound of an electric guitar. The stands rattled in face of such volume, while bodies flinched and hands flew to cover sensitive ears. Those closest to the press box spun around in their seats just in time to see Sirius wrestle a horrified Georgie from his chair, Remus standing delighted behind them. The entire crowd had turned rigid out of shock, and their friends on the field had become statues as they gaped up at the speakers.

It was marvellous.

“HELLO DADDY, HELLO MOM—

* * *





In the end, Hawkings took the game in another decisive two-to-one win. Both teams had been clinging desperately to a tie since the second half had begun, but it was Marlene, their best striker, who’d ultimately broken it within the last twenty seconds of the game. Backed by James and several others, she'd charged the Brentwood team and made one final, heroic leap toward the goal that sent the football rocketing into its upper corner. The crowd had gone absolutely mad, screaming so loudly that George’s announcement could barely be heard.

“THERE YOU HAVE IT—MARLENE McKINNON SCORES IN AN ALL-TIME NAIL-BITING FINAL MOMENT! HAWKINGS WINS! HAWKINGS TAKES THE TOURNAMENT!”

Afterwards, while the team was doing their celebratory sweep of the grounds and the girls had gone off to prepare their additions to the time capsule, Remus and Sirius were ordered to serve their punishment by clearing up the stadium stands of all leftover rubbish. The June sun was sweltering, and bending over the benches to collect the rubbish was turning his back achy and his mood grim. They didn't look suspicious, though every now and then Trish would say something that made Regulus smile, and he would hide it by turning his face away so as to not let anyone know he was actually enjoying himself.

Mum'll probably take them when he goes home, but I thought he should have something to remember me by, since I'm leaving and all."

Another sigh, and she'd turned for the stairs. “You boys are going to do great things one day," she called, "I just hope that for your sakes, your children will take after their mothers, rather than their fathers.”

“Oh, I don’t think you have to worry much about that one, Minnie!"

Later that night...

It was their second-to-last night at school—ever—and Remus could feel the nerves and excitement radiating off of his friends like stink off a boys' changing room. After dinner, they’d all agreed to finish any last-minute packing and then meet back at Godric just after curfew, where they could then head out together to bury their time capsule. They’d already scoped out the perfect spot; just a little ways into the trees, in the same place they'd managed to pull off the most magnificent Halloween prank known to man. (Or the worst, if you were to ask the girls.)

The ground where they'd chosen to plant the capsule was soft and it’d been easy enough to dig through the damp mulch. Originally their main worry had been how they were supposed to store the capsule so that it'd stand against any elements it might encounter while underground, but when Peter had had the bright idea of “borrowing” the school’s capsule from its exhibit in Castle Hall, they’d all pitched in to help nick it. It’d taken less than an hour to smuggle the metal canister back to their dorm, and now all that was left was to bury the memories and forget about them for the next twenty years.

After spending the better half of the evening packing their things away into it, James had just returned from his nightly headcount when a knock on their door made everyone look up.

“I’ll bet it’s Minnie!” Sirius cried, throwing himself over the stolen time capsule as though his body alone could hide it. "Knew she couldn't resist me for long. She must've come back to accept my proposal."

“Or to expel you on your final night!" James said, doing the same. “She's found out what we did and has come to stop us!”

“You guys are so lame,” Remus said, getting up to answer the door himself. He opened it just a crack at first, and rather than finding an angry, capsule-less Headmistress, he was met with another boy, yawning and holding out a letter.

“Post for you, Lupin."

Remus took the envelope and shut the door. He noticed strangely that there was no return address, but his name had been neatly printed across the front, and the stamps were all marked correctly.

“Who’s the letter from, Moony?” James asked, shoving Sirius off the time capsule and tugging it to the edge of his bed.

“Dunno… Giles, probably.”

“That driver of yours worries more than both of my parents put together,” Peter said, shutting the capsule’s lid and tossing a sheet over it as a poor disguise.

“You can call him in the morning," Sirius said, grunting as he and James lifted the heavy capsule between them. "Meanwhile, our ladies await."

Remus turned the letter over in his hands. Up until a moment ago, he’d been completely ready to rush out into the night with his friends, but now he found himself hesitating. The lack of a return address had made him suspicious. Could it really be? Could it actually be from Tonya?

Quickly, he hid the letter behind his back. “You three go on, I’ll catch up. Just need to use the loo.”

For a split second he let himself hope, but when he unfolded the top half of the first page, he did not find a letter from a lost love. Remus’ breath caught. Slowly he unfolded the letter the rest of the way.



Dear Remus,

We have received your application to The University of Manchester’s Faculty of English Language and Literature, and are pleased to offer you a seat for the incoming 1978-1979 school term. Competition for September’s intake has been fierce, but we were highly impressed by your strong application and clear plans for the future. Below you will find a concise outline for what must be completed in order to secure your seat for this term’s intake. We look forward to your arrival.



Remus lowered the letter. To his knowledge, he had not made any application—and certainly not any plans for a future at the University of Manchester.

Furiously, he tore open the second letter.

I debated fiercely whether or not I should write you this letter, but after pulling some strings with the head of admissions at Manchester University, I decided it was worthwhile. I know you and I have never had the best relationship, but I want the best for you, and I would see it done if I can. I had never envisioned a life for you as someone who reads books and argues ethics as a career, but if it is to be that or a life without point, then I would have you in school. I implore you to look past any feelings you have for me and see sense. Remember, I do this for you, and I swear to not ask anything else of you if you agree to attend.

The world wants you, Remus. Don’t let it down.

Lyall Lupin.



He’d signed the bottom, as he might’ve signed a notice to another legislator. Two great swooping ‘L’s, wrapping up a string of ‘I’ statements that made his stomach turn. ‘I debated’, ‘I decided’, ‘I implore’ … Despite the bitterness, the letter might’ve been the kindest thing Lyall had ever done for him.

And Remus hated it.

Not just because he was angry, but because it made him hesitate.

While his classmates had attended lessons and informational sessions on how to properly apply to and navigate university life, he had found every excuse to skive off. He hadn’t wanted anything to do with any of it. All he’d wanted was to be Remus Lupin of the Marauders. Not "Remus Lupin of Manchester University". But he could be now—couldn’t he? He’d be in Manchester after all. Two-hundred miles between him and anything that might trigger even the slightest memory.

You could leave it all behind, that traitorous voice said; Be a completely new person. Actually make something of yourself.

Why would I ever want that? I have a place here. People that I love.

Sure, they love you now, but what about when all that rubbish about a band fails? What about when they realise that it's all a fool's errand and everything blows up in your face? What about when they become bitter, and angry? And when you start fighting—go your separate ways like all adults do? What will you have left? We can do this, he swore. We can! I want this band.

For now…

Remus squeezed his hands into fists, crushing the twin letters in his grip. He knew he should burn them—try to erase all of it—but there wasn’t time. Before he could decide what to do next, Sirius was opening the door, stepping in expectantly.

“Neither… Pointless.”

He wasn’t sure how it was possible, but Remus instantly felt better.

“I said no, obviously.”

“Yep. Called dad over dinner.”

“And surely he shouted some sense into you?” Peter demanded.

James just shook his head. “Maybe he was a bit disappointed, sure, but he told me to do what I thought was right. And that he’d support us no matter what we chose.”

“Wow…” Mary said. “Is he looking for a daughter?”

James laughed then, but it was Sirius who stepped forward. “You do know that Liverpool’s been in the top three teams of the division for the last six years running, right?”

“ 'Course I know, but what do I need with a top three English football team? I’m gonna be in the biggest band in the world.”

Sirius paused, and then raised a knuckle to his mouth to hide his smile. “Aw, alright—c’mere, you bleedin’ tart!” Throwing his arms around him, Sirius clung tightly to best friend while the pair of them laughed, and all it took was a single beckoning hand for all eight of them to be hugging again. As he held his friends, Remus pushed all thoughts of Manchester and university from his mind. He didn’t need it, and he didn’t want it.

Everything he wanted was right there.

When they eventually broke apart, Lily kissed James on the cheek (as did Sirius, though his was much more passionate) and they picked up the sheet-covered capsule to trek further into the trees. Guided by the light of the girls’ torches, they walked until the path started to look familiar again, and soon enough the darkness gave way to a small clearing with a large pit dug out in its centre.

“Let’s make a pact,” James suggested as he and Sirius set the capsule down at the pit’s edge. “Even if we aren’t friends anymore, we’ll all agree to come back and open this thing together.”

“What if by then I hate your guts?” Sirius teased, wiping sweat from his brow.

“You still have to come, it’s part of the pact.”

“We could always drag him back by his hair,” Mary suggested, setting down her own bag. "That'd get him moving."

“Won’t have to drag me back,” Peter said, unzipping his school pack and pulling out a large handful of comic books—copies of Eagle, Spider-man, and Captain Britain among them. “Man, I’m really gonna miss these issues.”

“I’m still not convinced they’re gonna be worth any money,” said Lottie.

“Shows what you know. One day they’re gonna start making these into movies or something, and then you’ll be eating your words.”

“Guess we’ll find out in twenty years,” Sirius interjected, stepping between the two squabbling siblings to tear away the sheet, revealing the old metal capsule.

“Oh my god,” Marlene gasped straight away; “Is that…?”

“Oh, that’s right, you girls didn't hear. We may have snuck out and robbed your favourite display over at Castle Hall, McKinnon. Kept the capsule for more personal reasons though.”

“What’d you do with the rest of it?”

“It’s perfectly protected, don’t worry. Filch’s office makes for a great storage space.”

“Figure it’ll take them years to find it in there,” James grinned.

Lily’s mouth dropped open into a very shocked ‘o’. “You mean you actually stole from the school?!”

“As if it was the first time,” Peter snorted.

“That time capsule was half a century old! It was part of history!”

“Sexist history!” Sirius rebuffed. “Or were you not there when McKinnon was having kittens over the whole thing?”

“I was there,” Lottie chimed in, making the rest of them snigger.

“We made sure to dig through it first though,” James said, busy rooting through his pocket; “Even managed to find this.”

Extending his hand, James gave Marlene a faded piece of an old school article, dated all the way back to November of 1927. While the other girls crowded around, Mary slipped in a small patch of mud and nearly dropped her torch.

"Fucking woods... Can't see anything out here!"

"Just read it aloud, Marls," Lily urged.

Taking a second to clear her throat, Marlene raised her torch; “ ‘This year, the top student award in an academic standing goes to Margery "Midge" Williams, who shattered over five academic records that had been previously set by her peers. Miss Williams is described by her professors as a 'brilliant mind with limitless potential' and is on course to attend Oxford University this coming September, where she will be studying medicine in hopes of being among the first female graduates to pursue surgery. Pictured below is Miss Williams, holding her certificate while shaking hands with Headmaster Dippet’. Good work... Midge'.”

As Marlene lowered the notice, she found Sirius and the other boys grinning at her.

“We thought you should see a bit of female Hawkings history for yourself," he said. "Do you like it?"

Marlene nodded, before sniffing and wiping her eyes. “God—I think I’m gonna cry.”

“Awe, Marls!” Mary hugged her, and Marlene held her arm while sparing Remus a sheepish glance.

"Look at me while I'm crying and I'll punch you."

Remus shrugged, and hugged her too.

“Okay, I'd say it's about time to get this show on the road,” James said later, when Marlene had recovered enough to dole out several punches. “Time to load ‘er up, ladies.”

One by one, each of the girls stepped forward and began pulling small items from their bags. When it was her turn, Lily produced an entire photo album, of which she stopped to show Remus—pointing out a small series of photographs featuring four boys with flowers in their hair.

“I made sure to make copies,” she told him, “but I think it’ll be nice to open this up when we’re older and see our younger selves again.”

"Our 'younger selves'? Way to blow my mind, Lils.”

Mary added several items herself, such as the Rowena patch from her old school jacket and a collage of her favourite celebrities that she'd made out of glitter and magazine clippings. Marlene included the game line-up of the final tournament as well as Midge's article and a diary she’d been keeping throughout the year, and Lottie slipped in a letter she’d written to her future self, a list of every boy she’d ever kissed and their rating out of ten, as well as a tiny clay sculpture of the Goddess Aphrodite, which she’d made in art class when she was fourteen.

“What the hell you putting that in for?” Peter asked.

“To remind me of the beauty of the female form.”

“It looks more like a gnarled tree trunk with a face.”

“Tell you what, when we take it out again in twenty years, I’ll celebrate by smashing it over your head.”

It went on like that—letters, photos, a single badly produced demo track—until the case was nearly full. At one point, James remembered that he'd left something in his other pocket, and pulled out a blue baby bonnet, along with a torn stred of a label bearing the words Baker's Favourite Bleacher Flour.

"Poor Prongs Junior," he moaned, kissing the paper label. "Gone, but never forgotten."

He tossed the label and bonnet in, while Sirius rolled his eyes. "And now for something actually worthwhile..." With no further prompting, he produced the single 8-track tape they’d made and held it aloft for all of them to see. “Here's to the music,” he said, “and to all of our favourite songs.”

“You mean we’re really not going to play it?” Lily asked, sounding disappointed. Sirius tipped his head wryly in her direction and smiled.

“Have faith, Evans. I'm sure when you listen to it, it'll feel like no time's passed at all.”

And then he tossed the tape into the capsule with a short clatter. It was full after that, officially completed with a part of each of them. To Remus the capsule felt like an accumulated treasure trove; a collective effort of who they were, much like how all the best songs and albums they would go on to produce would surely feel, though they didn’t know it then.

Equal parts of all of them, equal parts in the charade, equal parts in the end.

With the capsule full, James went to shut its lid, and Remus remembered what he’d been hiding in his back pocket.

“Hold on, Prongs. Got one more thing.”

Untucking the letters from his pocket, he smoothed them out in his hands and felt his fingers begin to shake.

"Remus, what's that?" Lily asked, laying a comforting palm on his arm.

A chance? He wondered, then;

No.

A cage.

"My dad wants me to go to school," he told them, passing the letter around for each of them to take a look. "More than anything else, he wants me to make something of myself. He would rather me buy my way into a decent life than take the risk of an extraordinary one... But he's never understood me, don't think he's ever really wanted to. And I don't hate him for who he is to me—he can't help it any more than I can. But... I want different things, and I'm gonna do it my way, not anyone else's."

"I think that's an admirable thing," Lottie said softly, passing him back the letters. Remus stared down at them for a while, doubting—until he remembered Lily's hand on his arm, and the thought of all of his friends' faces washed it away.

Remus took a breath, and on the exhale, he tossed the letters inside the capsule and watched as James shut the lid up tight.

They struggled a bit getting it into the hole, and it took a while to rebury, but as Sirius pat the final shovelful of dirt into place, Remus knew he'd made the right choice. As they all dusted the dirt from their clothes, Mary and Marlene began passing around tiny styrofoam cups from the dining hall, which they filled generously with whisky from Sirius’ flask.

“To us!” Sirius declared, raising a toast.

“To friends!" James added. "To love and care and all the other bits!"

“And to staying together,” Remus finished, giving Sirius a very fond look.

“ 'TO STAYING TOGETHER'!”

They knocked their tiny cups together over the freshly-buried hole, toasting each other and themselves, and polished off the booze.

“Whoooo… burns so good,” Sirius coughed, before crushing his cup in his hand. “Now I suppose it’s a good time to tell you all about my plan for a final prank.”

" 'Prank'?" At least three of them echoed.

"Woah, don't all start applauding at once."

“What do you mean 'prank', Sirius?" Lily exclaimed. "I thought that thing back at the tournament was your final prank!”

“What? No, are you crazy? A final prank has to involve all of us, or it’s not a Marauders’ prank at all.”

Lily covered her face, but James and Peter looked on, appearing far too eager.

“What’d you have in mind, Padfoot?”

Sirius began stroking his chin thoughtfully. “McGonagall’s holding our grand end-of-school send-off in the Great Hall tomorrow, right?”

They all nodded.

“Great. Now how many chickens do you reckon it’ll take to make her rethink her choice of location?”

As Sirius’ smile turned absolutely wicked, Lily peeked out from behind her fingers;

“Oh no.”

“I think you mean, oh yes." Sirius wiggled his eyebrows, before slinging an arm around James and Peter and drawing them in close. "Ladies, lads, best drink up, ‘cause we ain’t sleeping tonight…”

Chapter 96: The Great Last Day


Chapter Summary

I am dedicating this chapter to all of you who love music as much as Remus Lupin. To all of you who are as kind as James Potter, and as wild as Sirius Black, and as dear as Peter Pettigrew. To everyone who's kept up with this story for as long as they have, and for all of you who've just discovered it.

This one is most certainly for you <3



Chapter Notes

There is really no reading this chapter without the music.

None.

Zip.

It won't work.

And so I advise you to resist until you have a moment alone, where you can play our songs and think about these boys in all of their foolish loveliness.

HERE is a link to a “tape” of songs the characters will be listening to in fic. My advice: have it queued for the final scene of this chapter, when all the students have moved back down to the football pitch. I promise you will not regret it.

Also, one very special shout out to Anita, who came to me all the way back in April and asked if I could put the song "Ballroom Blitz" into the fic. Even then, I had the wonderful pleasure of telling her, that I already had <3

PS: A lovely tumblr follower has also decided to start translating the fic into Russian. You can find that linked here.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Two of us wearing raincoats,

Standing solo in the sun;

You and me chasing paper,

Getting nowhere on our way back home;

We’re on our way home,

We’re on our way home,

We’re going home…

- “Two of Us” The Beatles, 1970



He was far too drunk. How could he not be? It was the eve of their last day at school ever.

Ever.

The thought hit him like a train. Once he would've killed to say as much; back when he was younger, angrier. Back when all he wanted was to live in The End with Tomny and be anyone else. It'd been easier then, in some ways. Less rules, less people to disappoint. Less friends to hold him when he was feeling ill. And he had been ill, for a long time. Wouldn't find out how ill for a long time yet, but still... they made things easier.

After they'd buried the time capsule and christened the earth with their empty bottles, all eight of them set themselves to Sirius’ plot of insanity. It took nearly all night, but when they were finished Remus and the boys shambled back to their dorm with their hearts thrumming in anticipation. It was an unspoken truth that they'd be alone; that the girls would depart on their own for a few precious hours longer in the room they’d grown up in. There'd be plenty of opportunities to fall together in a drunken pile later on, for now everyone had their own memories to say farwell to.

"Goodbye bed," James blubbered, pressing his face into the maroon curtains. "Goodbye side table, goodbye lamp. Goodbye mysterious piece of gum that's shaped like Winston Churchill."

"Go on, Pot," Sirius said, swaying dubiously as he helped his friend into bed. "There'll be other beds."

"Not like these," James whimpered, still clinging to the curtains.

"Here, then."

Sirius peeled the stale wad of gum from the bedpost and handed it to James. At first the expression on his face had read as horror—the gum had been an unspoken companion for as long as they'd lived in the room—but then James simply started crying again.

"Sirius, you're so nice," he whimpered, as Sirius nodded mechanically and brought the covers up over him. "I love you, man. Really!"

"Yeah, yeah. You too, mate."

"Sirius, will you tuck me in too?" Peter moaned, legs half hanging off of his own bed.

"Bloody christ... Do I have to do everything around here?"

As Sirius wobbled drunkenly toward Peter's bed, Remus sat crouched beneath his own. He had his mother's case open again, and was gently moving the last of his belongings from his bedside into it for safe-keeping. He hadn't meant to leave things to the last moment, but life had just been so busy lately. As he packed away the tapes boxes and the cigarette boxes—some of them empty—he eventually came across the final photo in his collection, still rumpled and creased from the days it'd spent living in his pocket, and all the lives it'd lived before that.

Finished with Peter, Sirius turned around and gently nudged Remus' thigh with his foot.

"What about you? Need tucking in?"

"I'm okay."

Sirius crossed his arms. "Well? Aren't you gonna ask me if I need tucking in?"

Remus shook his head, regretting it only when the room began to spin. "Be there in a tick."

Sirius retreated genially, and Remus turned back to the tiny white trunk and the photograph in his hand. April 23rd 1954, it read. They smiled at him, the same way they had the first time he'd ever held it. It'd almost burned him back then. It didn't anymore. Yes, the ache was still there, but like most hurts, it'd grown dull over time. Perhaps eventually it wouldn't bother him at all.

"Mooooooony..."

"Coming, Pads."

He held the photograph for a moment longer, and could swear he was lighter. For the first time he thought that yes, he did look like him. Tad. Once that would've bothered him too.

It didn't anymore.

I don't need you, he thought; but I'm glad you exist.

Before shutting the trunk, he slid the photograph into one of his books. He'd forget come morning which book, but it'd be protected and that was all that mattered.

Peeling away the day's dirty clothes, Remus lifted Sirius' bed covers and climbed in next to him. Sirius' arms were warm around him. His hair, like spilled ink, was dark on the pillow.

Remus buried himself in it; the warmth, the dark, and shut his eyes.
