Friday 16th June 1978 - The Last Day of Term...





"Right, now it's two o'clock, and you all know what that means. I'm afraid our final music lesson has reached its end."

There came a chorus of groans—twenty-five unhappy nine year-olds, each disappointed by the idea of having to let go of the only cool teachers they'd ever had. Little Dominic Henley honked his trumpet indignantly, while the whole of the percussion section began banging their drums and ringing their bells in protest.

"Come on now," Remus tried, shouting over the noise; "Surely you wouldn't want our last day to end on such a sour note?"

He surveyed them, their tiny, forlorn faces, and felt pride begin to bubble up in his chest.

"I never thought I would miss this, but I will. And that's okay. You all have come so far, if you keep practising then I'm sure you'll be blowing Bach out of the water one day. You should be very proud, all of you—well done."

He clapped for them, and they clapped too, but it was clear what they were all waiting for.

Or who they were waiting for.

"Any parting words of wisdom, Mr. Black?"

Despite Remus' speech, Regulus did not look impressed. He stood behind the teacher's podium with his usual uniform of Salazar green and a frown.

"Honestly I'm disappointed," he said. "Eight months and not a single one of you can manage the introduction to ‘Für Elise’. You've no discipline, lack general motivation, and there's simply no relying on you to do any of the work on your own. It's almost as if you think people play music for fun. Well, you wanna know what I have to say to that?"

The entire class baulked as Regulus turned to the tiny drummer boy sitting off to his left.

"Jacob, tell them what I have to say!"

The boy raised his drumsticks dubiously, and then brought them down again in three sharp strokes;

BA-DUM-TSSS!

"I say job well done."

The children erupted into fitful bouts of laughter, each squealing their delight. They came to him in a rush—first the girls, then all the rest—hugging his legs, begging him to stay. They loved him; even with all the prickly demeanour he could muster, they loved him. And Remus loved to watch.

When the chairs had been stacked and all the instruments had returned to whence they came, Remus tucked Sheila's guitar back into its case. He'd kept the photograph of her and his baby-self at the christening, and now it hung taped to the inside of the lid. Little victories...

"They have gotten better," he called, smiling down at the guitar. "Mrs. Bean told me they're the best sounding class of fifth years she's ever had."

"Not best behaved, though."

"Yes well, who'd take 'well behaved' over smiles like those."

There was a pair of snaps as Regulus shut his violin case. He had his back to him, but Remus imagined him smiling too. Just a little.

"You're really very good with them," he said, leaning casually back against one of the desks. "Think you'll do it again next year?"

"Without you?" It was a scoff more than it was a question.

"Why not? I think you'd be good at it. Good enough to be a teacher yourself, if you really wanted."

Regulus turned on him then, and where Remus expected dismissal, he found hesitation.

"I'm not the one who's good with them, you are," he huffed. "You're the patient one, I just know all the notes. If you're seriously telling me that that's the only thing you need to be a qualified te—"

Remus held up a hand, head shaking. "No, you're right," he mused. "It takes far more than just knowing a few notes to run a music class. You've got to keep them in line, make sure they listen. Then you've also got to excite them—make them want to learn. You have to comfort them when they struggle, celebrate them when they overcome... And that's exactly what you've been doing, Regulus. Now, I'm no expert, but I'd say that makes you more than qualified."

A flush began to creep up beneath Regulus' collar. "But you're the one who started it," he said, busying himself by tapping the stack of sheet music into a neat pile; "They follow you."

"Maybe. But look, you can be as 'sacrificial lamb' as you want about this, but you didn't need me, Regulus. Not for the important bits. Those you did all on your own, for eight whole months. You can be proud, you know."

"My father always said pride is man's number one downfall."

"Mine always said I was his kid. Parents can be liars."

The look Regulus gave him was incredulous, but Remus only shrugged.

"Makes it easier if you joke about it."

They lapsed into silence, and Remus glanced at the clock hanging on the classroom wall. Already the others would be down at the church, setting up what would be the final show of their entire school-career. It'd been hard going in the beginning, but with the help of Bobby and the other lads, the plan was shaping up to be the prank of the century. Best get a move on before one of them accidentally blows their fingers off.

Picking up his guitar, Remus wrapped his school bag over one shoulder and prepared his goodbye;

"I'll see you later, then?" He called. "For the party and the tour with the new seventh years?"

Regulus nodded. "Remember, we're meeting at the dining hall, then outside the Great Hall for the tours. Don't be late."

"Wouldn't dream of it."

Smirking, Remus turned away but stopped just short of the door. When he glanced back, he found Regulus staring down at the stack of sheet music.

"You can be whatever you want, Regulus," he told him. "But I think you'd make a pretty great teacher too."

Regulus looked up at him, his usual aloofness having returned.

"Yes, well... I suppose if you could do it, anyone could."

Remus shrugged. "You got me there. See you."

Outside the sun was shining. Heaps of kids had taken to the lawns, playing games and enjoying what was to be their last full day on campus. After supper McGonagall was set to give her leavers speech, and come morning, the class of 1978 would be parting for good. That wasn't to say they weren't going to get a few good laughs in first.

On his way to the church, Remus passed by the Great Hall in all its exuberant finery. Normally the hall was reserved for large events, such as exams and the odd theatre performance; all other days it tended to sit empty, but not this day. Today it was mayhem, and everyone knew it.

Chickens! Chickens everywhere!

They were spilling out of the hall's main doors like flood water, squawking and preening for what might've been their first and only taste of real freedom. As it turns out, the barnyard fowl had mysteriously appeared in the Great Hall overnight, leaving behind a mess that could've turned even the strongest of stomachs. The stench was foul, and Remus could see teachers and school workers holding handkerchiefs to their noses as they ran about, desperately trying to corral the beasts. Feathers and muck scattered the lawn, and while a large group of students stood by to gawk, Professor McGonagall hung furiously around the top step with a very pursed look on her face.

"I don't understand where they all came from, Minerva!" Professor Flitwick cried, letting out a strangled yelp as one of the chickens soared overhead and clipped him with its feet.

"Tricky things, chickens," came Professor Kettleburn, the old agricultural teacher with only one eye. "They've been known to open doors, you know. Why, once in the middle of the night, I found one swimming in my bathtub, I did! Figured a storm blew its coop open."

"This was no storm," Professor McGonagall thundered.

Quickly, Remus turned and legged it the opposite direction.

It was still mid-afternoon by the time he made it down to the chapel. He'd had to dodge a few passing priests on their way out of the parsonage, but after they’d advanced to the other end of the courtyard, Remus creeped up the church's front steps and slipped inside. The main foyer and the sanctuary were both empty, but Remus made sure to keep quiet as he cut across the back of the room and darted up the balcony’s staircase. It felt a little silly to be sneaking around in broad daylight, but he wasn’t there to confess his sins. If anything, he was orchestrating them.

Flinching at every groaning stair, Remus finally emerged on the balcony’s landing, where hence he found James and Sirius arguing over how to fit the stage platform together. It’d taken them nearly all night, but somehow they’d managed to haul everything from the music room up to the church’s second floor veranda. All of their instruments sat piled up along the balcony’s far wall along with the several speakers they’d borrowed from the AV room, though they all paled in size when compared to the church's mighty pipe organ. A tool in their initial prank all the way back in Remus' first year, the grand instrument was now perfectly outfitted to play the backdrop for their final one.

Remus could hardly wait.

“No, no, no—you gotta put the pin in one notch higher,” Sirius hissed, as he and James struggled to fit two brackets of the stage together.

“I’ll notch you,” James grumbled back. “Why don’t you lift the bloody thing higher then? Maybe that way I could put the pin in instead of supporting the whole thing myself.”

“I am lifting it!”

“Are you sure? ‘Cause the lack of strain in your bicep says otherwise.”

“Fine. Ugh—This enough for you?”

“Is that you actually flexing?”

“Oh fuck off.”

Remus almost laughed. Clearly the lack of sleep was getting to them.

“Oi,” he called, “be any louder and the Heavenly Father Himself might overhear you.”

Not expecting to find anyone behind him, Sirius nearly dropped his end of the platform, causing James to hiss as his fingers got caught beneath. “MOTHERF—NGH!”

There was a clatter as James dropped his end and wheeled away. Remus winced just watching.

“Oops. My bad."

Huffing, Sirius set his half of the bar down and went to his friend. “Sorry. Your hand okay?”

“Yeah, s’fine,” James said, grimly sucking on his thumb. “You finished with your kiddie lessons then, Moons?"

"Yeah. Regulus says hi."

"Really?"

Remus made a face. "No?"

James turned away, still sucking grumpily on his thumb, while Sirius stepped up and took Remus' guitar from him.

"This place is looking good," Remus said, glancing at the stack of amps behind stage-right. "Think it'll be ready for later?"

"Only if Pete can sort the electrical on time," Sirius said. "He's downstairs, working on that ancient plugboard in the cupboard. Say, you got that...?"

In answer, Remus raised his wrist, showing off one of the hair bands he'd pawned off of Mary that morning.

"Ah, bless'm," Sirius said, removing the hair bauble and kissing Remus' wrist on the way. “I didn’t even hear you come up the stairs," he said, mumbling around the elastic as he gathered the rest of his hair into a ponytail. "You think we should be keeping watch?"

"If you haven't been caught so far then I'd say we're alright. They found the chickens, by the way."

Sirius lit up. "Really?! How'd it go? We've never used that many chickens before—was it a total mess?"

"Worse. I'll wager that if McGonagall spots any of us she'll let Filch skin us and wear our hides as a coat."

"Well, I think I'd make a very handsome hat, don't you?"

"Yeah. I think that hair of yours would just about pass for raccoon fur."

Sirius smirked bashfully, and just then a tremendous blast of noise came soaring out of one of the amps. When they spun around, they spotted James with his guitar strapped across his chest, leaning down over the balcony railing.

"SOUNDS GREAT, PETE!"

"Potter!" Sirius lashed, rushing forward to slap his hand over the amp's off switch. "Are you trying to get us skinned alive?"

James threw his hands up, offended. "What? Gotta test the equipment before the show, don't we?"

As the two set back to bickering, Remus adjusted the strap of his bag and began backing toward the stairs. Sirius caught him just as he was about to slip away;

"Off so soon, Moons? Suppose you've got your perky little prefect party to attend."

"Just say you're jealous, Padfoot!"

"Pull my own teeth out first!" Sirius hollered. "Have fun with MacDuff and my brother, traitor! We'll be here, setting up the prank of a lifetime!"

"Miss you already!"

"Wanker. Oh, and don't forget—the field! Tell everyone you see the party's happening on the field! After the show!"

Remus waved behind himself, dropping down into the foyer below. As he did, he heard James hiss;

"Oi, Black, what happened to being quiet...?"

"Don't be a hypocrite, Potter. You used to moan from the back of the classroom during silent study."

"That was always your idea!"

It was hard not to laugh. Even when the days of exams and pranks were long behind them, would those two always be so JamesandSirius, Remus wondered?

He hoped so.

It was harder to avoid any teachers and staff on his way back toward the dining hall. When he walked in, Remus half expected to find Professor McGonagall waiting for him with mediaeval shackles in her hands, but instead all he found were the other prefects, each of them dressed nicely and swarmed around a table ladled with cake and pudding. There was music going—a lot of Wings and Paul McCartney—but no one complained when he showed up in plain slacks and his Sex Pistols t-shirt. In fact, judging from their reaction, they’d expected it. Word must've already spread regarding the chickens, and Remus was immediately bombarded with questions regarding the stunt and whatever else the Marauders had planned for that evening.

"Is it true we're throwing the leavers' party on the football pitch?" Asked one of them.

"Yeah, so tell all your friends,” answered Remus.

"Was it really you guys who put the chickens in the Great Hall last night?” Demanded another.

"Now where'd you hear a rumour like that?"

“I heard you were the ones who put the trolley in the lake!”

"Er..." The questions were coming faster now.

“Is it true you nicked more equipment from the AV room again?”

"No way, where'd you put it?"

“Yeah, do you need help hiding the stereos this time around?”

"I want in!”

“Remus, are you really leaving school to be in a band? Like really, really?!”

He could barely keep up; but it was good to know that his friends had succeeded in spreading the word. Remus just hoped that none of the teachers had caught wind; it would've been disappointing to put a stop to a party before it'd even started.

“Just make sure you bring all of your stuff down to the pitch tonight,” he hushed to everyone. “Tell everyone in our year to bring blankets and torches."

"And bug spray," sniggered one.

"Can people in other years come too?" Whispered another.

"Yeah, 'course. It's just for fun anyway."

In truth the camp-out had been James’ idea, but even Lily had gotten behind it in the end. They’d all agreed that sleeping out under the stars seemed the perfect way to end their final day at school, and judging by the looks of fascination Remus was getting from the other prefects, they were right.

When he was halfway through his pudding, he was approached by a friendly boy named David Alcott. Remus had only ever spoken to David a handful of times, but he seemed perfectly eager to be in on the plot when he strode up to Remus and tapped him on the shoulder.

“I heard another little rumour going around, Lupin. Word is, that you and yours are hosting a private concert, that true?”

“Ask me after church later.”

“Why, what’s happening in the church?”

Remus swallowed the giddy instinct to blab, and instead did something very un-Remus-like; he pulled David in close, as if they were friends, and smiled. “Can I trust you to keep a secret, David?”

The consensus was positive and Remus eagerly bent his head in closer so that he might begin explaining everything. Afterwards he and David shared a fist-bump, and Remus withdrew his arm.

“Remember, get as many kids into the centre aisle as you can. Tell others if you like, so that we can fill it up. We don’t want any of the teachers or fathers to catch on too early otherwise they'll ruin everything. When it's over we'll all meet down at the pitch.”

“You can count on me, mate. Can’t wait to see this—it’s gonna be absolutely legendary!”

Smiling, Remus had just turned away when a camera flash caught him across the face, leaving him momentarily incapacitated.

"Sorry, Remus," Jillian cooed, flapping the fresh polaroid through the air. "I just needed proof."

"Proof of what?" Remus grumbled, rubbing his eyes.

"That I knew you before you were a famous rock star. This could be worth a lot of money someday, you know. After all, not all prefects can get away with having piercings and tattoos.”

“It’s one tiny tattoo, which I received against my will. How do you even know about that anyway?”

“Girls talk,” she shrugged, before popping her chewing gum. "Now chop-chop. We've still got a few kiddies to show around campus."

It was cutting it close, but Remus didn't have a proper excuse to get out of doing the tours. He figured that at least if McGonagall were to find him there, she'd have to consider his generous contribution to the school when sorting out a punishment.

“This—is the Great Hall!” Remus hollered, stopping his group of seventh years just below the hall’s main steps. “You’ll write all your examinations here, but they also use it for drama lessons, team-building exercises, and all the other stuff no one cares about.”

There was a second holler as one of the kids through their arm out in a point;

"CHICKEN!”

Sporting several fresh scratches to his face and neck, Filch had appeared at the top of the hall’s steps with a single chicken tucked under one arm. He scowled when he saw the kids, and the bird promptly pecked at his shrivelled, old hand. It made the caretaker yelp, and he promptly dropped the bird, only to have to chase it back into the hall again.

“Oh, well yes,” Remus said, as everyone laughed. “Apparently it's a popular spot with chickens too.”

They continued on with the tour, passing Castle Hall and weaving in and out of the science and arts blocks. A few of the more dutiful eleven year-olds were scanning their campus maps as their guides called out to them, while others just drifted this way and that, looking about as excited as Sirius in detention. Near the back, Regulus had busied himself with regularly scolding a pair of boys who had thought it funny to use the side of every building as target practice for their spit wads. A small group of girls stuck close-by, whispering to each other and hiding small giggles behind their maps. Regulus didn’t seem to notice.

“You’re becoming popular,” Remus said to him, when they made a tour toward House Lane.

“You’re crazy,” Regulus said, then, more boldly; “I’ve always been popular.”

“Oh my god, was that vanity? Coming from our Edge?”

"I can’t wait until you leave Hawkings, Lupin.”

Regulus went on ahead, ushering the students past one of the main trolley depots and doing his best to help them understand the different routes. While he did so, Remus fell into step with Trish, who was lagging toward the back and absent-mindedly balancing an unlit cigarette between her nose and top lip.

"Well, if it isn’t the great Remus Lupin," she mused, moving the cigarette behind her ear, "breaker and mender of hearts."

"I don't remember breaking your heart, Trish. Does that mean you have one for me to mend?"

He’d meant it as a joke, but after seeing the smile slip from Trish's face, he instantly grew to regret it.

"He's not that good-looking," she muttered, eyes trained on the front of the group. Remus didn't have to ask who she meant. "Looks more like a bastard, if you ask me. A gommy, self-important little bastard."

"Shit, Trish... I'm—"

"Ah, shut yer puss, Remington. I'm not killing ma'self over it. Just a bit upset, is a'h."

"Did he say something to you? Was he rude—"

"Nah, nah. Now it's last day, dinnae fash yerself."

"How can you say that? If he said something foul, then you deserve a chance to return it, tenfold!"

"But he didn't." Trish smiled quietly, kicking a stone from her path. "I told him I fancied him, 'n that dobber... That fucking dobber... He said that I was the prettiest girl he'd ever had the pleasure of talking to."

"He did."

"Mhm."

"Then why...?"

"Because." And then she looked up at him, voice almost a whisper; "Ain't it obvious? There's someone else."

Oh.

Trish looked him up and down sceptically, before finally sighing and moving the cigarette down to her lips. "So I told him how I felt 'n he didnae feel the same, big whoop. He could've laughed at me, but he didn't. Instead he..." She cleared her throat. "Have ye got a light, my dear gowk?"

He did, and so as the tour group grew further away, Remus bent down and lit the cigarette for her.

"He never said wha 'twas, in case ye were wondering," she muttered, almost dismissively. "Just that it couldnae work. Guess we're both losers in love."

"You're not a loser, Trish. You're..." He looked down at her; her tartan dress and gleaming dress shoes paradoxed by the large tear in the knees of her stockings. "Well, you're..."

"Go on, dinnae break your neck."

"You're cool," Remus amended. "I mean, I like you, so..."

"And that's supposed tae be a compliment because, what—you dinnae like anyone?" She laughed then, heartily, hand over stomach. "I should be so humbled. Too bad you're about as sprung as a daisy in June."

"What's that supposed to mean?"

"Oh come on, Remington. You... Black..." She made a 'go on' motion with her hands. "I ken I have a funny accent but I'm not an eejit."

Suddenly Remus felt a lot like pitching himself off of a roof.

"You think that I...? That me... That Regulus and I could ever—?!"

"No! Fuck, in th' name of the wee... I meant older Black! Bigger Black! Wolloping Sirius!”

"Ah."

Trish laughed again, nearly dropping her cigarette. "Dear Loonarny, you always did have a habit o' assuming people were in love wi' you."

"How'd you find out?" He asked, grimly. "Was it... obvious?"

"Obvious? Nah. Nae until ye straight told me, that is."

"I, what?"

"You told me! Dinnae ye mind? It was that day down by the loch. We were talking 'n then Sirius showed up. I was mostly joking, but you—you cried him yer boyfriend! Figured ye meant it, what wi' the way you two are always going along."

He laughed awkwardly. "I don't remember... Did you happen to give me any drugs?"

"Is that a trick question?" Smirking, she passed him the cigarette, and Remus took a long pull as they continued ambling down the pavement.

"Regulus knows," he said, almost surprising himself. "He figured it out too. Actually, pretty sure he figured it out before I did."

"Clever cunt."

"Yeah... But listen, Trish, you can't tell anyone."

"I ken. Figured your band's plan o' world domination might be hindered if it came out that th' lead singer 'n the bass player are doing each other behind the speaker stacks."

"Thanks for that image."

They walked on a bit further, nearing the back of the tour group just as they came to a stop ahead of the first set of dorms. Jillian was at the head of the group, lecturing about the history of each house while most of the kids meandered unenthusiastically around the lawn.

"Listen tae her," Trish chuffed, "she'd lecture to a wall if given half th' chance."

Remus passed the cigarette back, before rocking back and forth on the balls of his feet. “So... Does this mean you and Regulus are still friends then?”

“What? Like I'd just let him drop me? Nah, I spent months working on that bugger. Besides,” she ruminated, “I’m nae so easily deterred.”

“You’ll take care of him then?” Remus asked. “Sirius won't admit it, but he's worried about leaving him behind."

“Yeah, tell Black number one not to worry. I’ll stick so close, Reginald’s gonna think I’ve started growing off o' his arse.”

“Thanks, Trish.”

She took another drag, and then promptly punched him in the arm. Even as he rubbed the soreness from his new bruise, Remus knew that he would miss her too.

"That reminds me," Trish said, as she kicked another stone onto the lawn. "Find me after the assembly, I have a gift for you."

"A gift?"

"Just a wee something. You know, for luck."

Remus shrugged genially. "Oh. In that case, could always use more luck..."

"Hey! Who said you could have a smoke break?" It was Regulus, come to chide them for being useless dregs to society. "Don't think you're getting out of this so easily!" He called, practically shaking a fist at them.

"Who's smoking? I'm not smoking," Trish said, grinding the cigarette out on the bottom of her shoe. "Remington, were ye smoking? Tsk-tsk."

Regulus crossed his arms, and Trish came forward, tapping him fondly on the chest. "Dinnae be such a wee clipe, Reginald, I’m coming."

She twirled around him, humming cheekily, and when she was gone, Regulus gave Remus the eye.

"Did she say anything to you?"

Remus shrugged. "Dunno. She talks so funny I can't understand her half the time."

It was enough to earn him an indifferent eye-roll, and as Regulus marched to the front of the group, Remus followed feeling distinctly pleased.

“This is Byron House,” Regulus called out; “It’s a boys’ dorm. Next door is Finch House, for girls. The secondary campus has a total of ten dorms, and next year you’ll be living in one of them with three other roommates. And you better learn to like them because they're the only ones you're going to get. Now, if you’ll follow me, we’re going to have a tour of the inside so you can get an idea of where you might be living for the next seven years. Girls, follow Stewart and MacDuff into the ladies' dormitory, boys, follow Lupin and me. And don't try and sneak off. If you do, we'll know."

The kids all eagerly followed, and Regulus stopped to hold the door open while ushering them inside. Remus made to do the same, but drew to a halt when he felt a gentle tug on the back of his jacket. Turning around, he found one of the boys had hung back behind the rest and was watching him with an anxious expression. His name tag read, Milton.

Already feeling sorry for the kid, Remus knelt down.

“Feeling okay there, mate?”

Rather than answer, the boy glanced around nervously and gestured for Remus to come even closer. “The other man said we’d have to share a room,” he murmured.

“Yeah, you’ll have roommates, but no more than three," Remus said, counting each off on a finger. "I was nervous too when I first came, but my roomies ended up being pretty cool. Reckon you’ll like it eventually. And if anyone gives you any trouble, you can always talk to Professor McGonagall. She’s pretty nice, I'm sure she'll help you out.”

This didn’t seem to make Milton feel any better. He continued fretting with his fingers, and finally leaned in to whisper in Remus’ ear.

“What do you do if you still wet the bed?”

“You… oh.” Remus cleared his throat. "Milton, do you mind if I go get my friend Regulus? 'Cause he's really good at dealing with stuff like this..."





* * *





Later that evening...

Sirius’ plan had worked, it seemed. With the entire Great Hall smelling of chicken faeces, the whole of the secondary student body was shuffled into the church pews for their final assembly. The crowd seemed rowdier than usual, though most of it was chalked up to the anticipation of summer holidays. Remus couldn’t help but think that they’d also had something to do with the open secret currently rushing from student to student, but that was no one else's business really.

Upset that their precious sanctum of supplication was being bombarded so late in the day, the priests insisted on holding a short service before McGonagall was able to take her place behind the podium. Unlike normal mass, no one had bothered taking roll-call, and so therefore no one would be noticing the four missing boys from room 4A. Rather, Remus got to watch from his hiding spot on the organ balcony, peering through the gaps in the railing while his heart thundered restlessly in his ears.

Th-thump! Th-thump! Th-thump!

Was this what it would feel like—being on stage in front of hundreds—no, thousands of people? Maybe not, considering the entire thing was a prank and they weren’t even supposed to be there... Bleeding christ—he wished he hadn’t let Sirius talk him into wearing makeup, and that he’d told Lottie to buzz off when she’d started layering those curlers in his hair. They'd just left him looking like Bob Dylan, and not even the cool weed-smoking Bob Dylan from his electric days. More like the hippie turned born-again Christian—ugh! And where did Mary even get these slacks?! They were leather, at least a foot too short around the ankles, and were so tight he was sure his bits would fall off come the end of the night.

Glancing back over the railing, Remus was positive.

He was going to throw up.

“I think I’m gonna throw up,” he whispered to James, who was hunkered down next to him, clinging to his guitar for dear life.

James shook his head furiously. He was also wearing trousers two sizes too tight, but that was because they belonged to Sirius. His gelled-up do had returned from the summer prior, though now it was longer and the frantic curls looked about three seconds from bursting free.

“N-Nah, s’good, we’ll be jus’ f-fine,” he stuttered. “W-We jus’ hang tight for S-Sirius’ signal and… Oh god, I’m gonna throw up too.”

“Do us a favour and don’t vomit over the balcony,” Peter murmured, appearing from behind them and almost making Remus jump. Throwing himself down next to James, Peter squinted to get a look at the crowd down below.

“Are Bobby and the lads in place then?” James asked, busy flapping the collar of his jacket. He wasn’t even wearing a shirt beneath—Sirius had convinced him that if Jimmy Page could go shirtless in a bedazzled suit jacket, so could James Potter.

“Yep,” Peter answered, “they know their cues. Should be a real blast.” He chuckled at the pun, before calmly stretching out his neck. Like the rest of them, Peter wasn’t exactly dressed for the usual sneaking or pranking either. He’d refused any eyeliner, but Lottie had somehow swindled him into wearing one of her blinding gold lamé shirts. Remus didn’t say it, but he looked a bit like a walking Christmas tree topper.

“Do you think people will actually cheer for us?” Peter asked.

“Forget cheering—we’ll be lucky if they don’t throw rotten tomatoes,” James yammered nervously. “How are you so damn calm anyway?”

“I did some breathing exercises before the show.”

Remus began to laugh, and then covered his mouth to stifle it.

“Breathing exercises, right…” James peeled his hands away from the guitar neck and flexed his fingers. “Oh god… What if I forget all the notes? What if I forget the words?!”

“Then Sirius'll remember enough for all of us," Peter reassured him. "Stop worrying, Potter. We’ve been playing this song for weeks, way longer than we’ve been planning this.”

“But what if everything gets all jumbled up in my head? What if Sirius can’t even make it up here in time?”

“Then we play until he does,” Remus interjected quietly. All of the fears James was just now realising felt like old hat to him—of course they were bound to forget something, but wasn’t that just one of the many woes of live music?

Fuck, this was so insane.

“How much longer?” He asked, inevitably growing antsy again. Down below, McGonagall had just finished congratulating all the students who’d made top marks on their A-Levels. Remus’ name had been called, though he hadn’t been around to stand up and receive the applause. Suspicious.

James checked his watch. “Should be any second now. Sirius said to start near the end—when McGonagall starts thanking everybody.”

Remus crawled forward slightly, peering through the railing’s bars to get a look at the backs of all of their fellow peers’ heads. Their Headmistress still stood behind her podium at the front of the church, with all the priests and choir kids lined up behind her. Beyond that stood the covered-up statue of Jesus, its white sheet completely still and inconspicuous. If Remus were to tilt his head just right, he would be able to make out the large music amp they’d hidden behind the church’s altar for a certain someone’s grand entrance. They knew from the beginning that they'd only have time for the one song before Bobby's grand finale, which was probably for the best anyway. With the way James' hands were trembling, Remus worried they'd barely get through the first verse.

Busy squinting to see if he could get a glimpse of the white sheet moving, Remus had just managed to spot the girls when a head turned and he found himself making solid eye contact with Davey Gudgeon through the bars of the mezzanine.

“Oh shite!” He yelped, pulling back to face his friends; “Davey just looked right at me. He totally knows we’re up here.”

“Yeah, a‘course he knows, James told the entire football team,” Peter said.

“No, I didn’t,” James whispered back.

“You said you did!”

“I told them about the camp-out, not this. I thought that that’s what we’d agreed upon?”

“Well, I told the prefects,” Remus baulked.

"You did? Moony!"

"Only a few! Sirius said to make sure everyone knew to head down to the field after...”

“You really didn’t tell people about the concert?” Peter asked James.

“No! Did you…?”

Peter cringed slightly. “Uh… yeah. I may have told some people.”

James gaped at him; “How many?”

“Erm… many…”

“Oh, Wormy…”

“Too late to turn back now,” Remus said, peering through the balcony railing once more. The longer he watched, the more kids began to turn their heads. It was like a falling row of dominoes—one would turn to whisper in their neighbour’s ear and then suddenly a fresh pair of eyes would snap back toward the balcony. Some even waved. Remus couldn’t decide whether it made him more nervous or less.

I hope you know what you're doing Sirius...

“Well, Black may not be here, but that don’t mean we can’t cheers to each other,” James said, pulling a small flask from his back pocket and popping the top. “Good luck, lads,” he said, before taking a swig and passing it along to Peter.

“To not choking on stage,” Peter said, raising the flask and taking a swig. “Eugh—fuck, James, you know I hate bourbon.”

"It was all that was left after last night."

Peter handed the bottle to Remus, who paused long enough to swish the booze around and raise it for a quiet toast. “To hopefully getting paid instead of punished for this one day.”

“Here, here!”

James shushed them, and Remus grinned as he tipped the flask back. The alcohol had only just hit his tongue when his gaze passed over the front of the church and he made eye contact with one of the teachers. It was Sheila. She smiled at him—right at him—and then raised one finger to her mouth in a silent shh .

Remus spat bourbon everywhere.

“EUUGH—!”

James slammed one hand down over Peter’s mouth to stifle his moan of disgust, while using the other to gently smother Remus as he coughed and sputtered.

"Oh my god, was that vomit?” Peter groaned, peeling James' hand away. “Try giving us a bit ‘a warning before you spew everywhere.”

“S—Sorry,” Remus wheezed, trying his best to swallow the rest of his coughs.

“Here, take another sip,” James instructed, holding the flask to Remus’ mouth himself. Remus gagged heavily as it went down, but afterwards he was able to breathe again.

“Guys… I think that—ahem… Sheila—”

James grabbed him by the shoulder. “Hold that thought, Moons. I think McGonagall’s finally finishing up!”

They all craned their heads to get a look, and Remus found that James was right. Far below, Professor McGonagall was wiping beneath her eyes and clapping her hands together fondly.

“And I want each and every one of you to know how proud we are of you. You are truly a force to behold. And thank you so much to everyone who—”

Suddenly, a short whistle-screeched echoed from the back of the church, cutting off the headmistress mid-speech and making everyone jump. It was Bobby—or one of Bobby's lads—setting off the tiny whistle-cracker that was to be their cue. The end was upon them, the curtains had been raised;

Their coordinated attack had begun.

“That’s the signal!” Peter cried, already making a mad dash toward his drum kit. Remus and James did the same, scrambling for their guitars and rushing to plug them into the amps. The moment they did, a reverb echoed around the church like thunder, making everyone jump in their pews for a second time. Heads snapped skyward—even those who'd been in on it were surprised.

What in god's name—

“This is it, Pete,” James tittered, stepping up in front of his microphone and covering it with his fist. “S’all you mate!”

Peter, who was normally the first one to be shaking in his boots during any prank, had somehow come alive. He was literally vibrating with excitement, swinging his drum sticks around and clashing a single symbol loud enough to turn every head in the room. From his place on their makeshift stage, Remus now had a full view of every priest, teacher, and student in the house. They all gaped back at him, some more disturbed than others, but there was no stopping it. It was a waterfall, and they were going over.

Peter leaned into his microphone; “ONE—TWO—THREE—FOUR—!”

Just like that they were off to the races. Peter began his drum intro all on his own, a high-intensity fill that seemed to get faster and faster the longer it went on. Kids stood up from their pews to get a better look—teachers covered their mouths in shock, but nothing compared to the moment that Sirius’ voice came shooting through the speakers at the front of the church.

"Are you ready, James?”

James leaned into his mic; “Uh-huh.”

“Remus?”

“Yeah.”

"Pete?”

“Okay!”

“Alright fellas… let’s GOOOOOO!”

In one deft move, the sheet that had been covering the busted statue of Jesus for nearly half of term was ripped away, revealing a single leather-clad, makeup wearing, nail polish adorned, Sirius Black.

He sprung off of the statue like a trained gymnast, bubbling with all the energy he’d been so desperately keeping under wraps throughout the entire service. People screamed when they saw him, to cheer or to condemn; Sirius didn’t care. He had a microphone in one hand, attached to the longest audio cord they could find in the AV room, and he swung it around like it was a trophy. No one else had dared make a move toward him so far—they were too stunned to touch—and Sirius bobbed his head and whirled around the altar like it was a stage made with him in mind.

And when he sang?

Glorious.

“Oh, it’s been getting so hard, living with the things you do to me…"

Remus couldn't believe it. It didn't matter if he could barely feel his fingers, their plan was working. It was bloody working!

"—My dreams are getting so strange, I’d like to tell you everything I see…”

Sirius flashed a smile and one of the girls near the front screamed, throwing her arms in the air as if she could reach out and touch him. By then one of the priests had broken free from his horror-stricken trance and shot forward, attempting to reach the star-streaked boy as he danced around the altar.

“Oh, I see a man in the back as a matter of fact—" Sirius pointed at Professor Bilshin; "his eyes were as red as the sun! And the girl in the corner—lets no one ignore her,” then Ms. Hooch, blowing her a kiss; “ 'Cause she thinks she’s the passionate one!

"OHHH YEAH!”

“Mr. Black! Mr. Black!” McGonagall began to cry out, flapping her arms wildly as she flung herself to her feet. Undeterred, Sirius streaked away, skirting around the far end of the pew until his microphone cord had pulled all the way taunt.

“—And the music was soothing! And they all started grooving!"

“MR. BLACK!”

"—YEAH-YEAH-YEAH-YEAH!”

It was a ballroom blitz. Like flying, Sirius had launched himself over the back of the first pew, only to land straight in the laps of his peers. Hands grabbed him—hauled him to his feet—and a second later he was up again, racing down toward the aisle, straight for their headmistress. The room moved with him—McGonagall had no choice! When Sirius fell into her, she caught him suddenly in her arms and the split-second of disarray allowed Sirius to plant a firm kiss directly on the headmistress's cheek.

The church was a wildfire.

Everywhere they chanted;

“BALLROOM BLITZ! BALLROOM BLITZ! BALLROOM BLITZ!”

He must've stunned her with his candor, as when Sirius stood up to take his place out front again, Professor McGonagall did not stop him. A priest tried to lunge, but Sirius only fell back to be instantly swallowed by the crowd. Kids whooped as he ultimately abandoned the microphone and began racing down the middle aisle toward the balcony’s staircase. Then they swarmed the aisle after him, blocking the way of his pursuers.

As the crowd came apart down below, Remus spared a glance to look down at himself; his fingers were buzzing—flying across the strings of his bass guitar as though the song's rhythm was a second heartbeat. Next to him, James was absolutely wigging out; he swung across their make-shift stage, not with Sirius' grace but his own rabid desire. He shredded that electric guitar, and when it was time to sing again and Sirius was nowhere to be found, James leaned into his mic to dazzle them with a voice of his own.

Remus wondered what colours he saw.

“—Ohh, I softly call you over. Then you appear, there’s nothing left of you…”

And then, grabbing the microphone tightly, James began to howl;

“And the man in the back is ready to crack, as he raises his hands to the sky! And the girl in the corner is everyone’s mourner—” James pointed and Remus just knew it was at Lily; “She could kill you with a wink of her eye!”

“OHHHHH YEAH!”

Sirius had burst up at the top of the stairs right on cue, fresh mic in hand and a look on his face that was higher than any drug.

“And the band started leaving—‘cause they all stopped breathing!”

Coming together in the centre of the stage, James and Sirius began to wail into the same microphone. “

And the man at the back said, ‘Everyone attack’—and it turned into a ballroom blitz! And the girl in the corner said, ‘Boy I want to warn you—it’ll turn into a ballroom blitz’!

"BALLROOM BLITZ!”

The pair blew apart as if electrified and Remus took over completely, the weight of his bass notes vibrating the very floor beneath them. Down below it was as if the entire church was inhaling all at once, just waiting for the beat to drop again. No teacher had managed to get close to the balcony—there were too many students in the way. When he looked up, heart beating out of his chest, Remus spotted Lily and the rest of the girls standing on top of the pews, screaming and hollering like all the rest. Just beyond them was Barty, looking utterly stupefied, and—THERE! It was Trish—riding the shoulders of a very stressed out Regulus.

How she convinced him, Remus had no idea.

“OHHHHH YEAH!”

“It was like lightning—"

LIGHTNING!

"Everybody was frightening—"

FRIGHTENING

"And the music was soothing, and they all started grooving!"



YEAAAAH! YEAH-YEAH-YEAH-YEAH!

“Fucking go, Pete, GO!” James screamed, striking his chords as Sirius took front of stage again, clapping a tambourine in time with the beat. The crowd followed, and the clapping became a thunderstorm. Poor Professor McGonagall had all but given up reaching them—too caught between the sea of romping bodies to even make it through to the stairs. Though, Remus barely noticed;

He was too busy waiting for the real boom.

“It’s—It’s a ballroom blitz!”

One.

“It’s—It’s a ballroom blitz!”

Two.

“It’s—It’s a ballroom blitz!”

Three!

“YEAHHHH—it’s a ballroom blitz!”

And then off it went.

BOOM!

BOOM—B—B—B—BOOOOM!

BOOM! BOOM! BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

The screams were deafening. They drowned out all sound of the music, so loud that the noise shocked even the four Marauders up on their stage. They dropped their instruments in an instant and convened at centre-stage while kids and teachers began to scatter. The shock—and maybe fear—was obviously very real, but none of them would’ve ever risked their friends’ safety for a gag. The firecrackers were only going off behind them, at the front of the church that had already been expertly vacated thanks to the most spectacular distraction Hawkings School had ever seen. No one was in any real danger, but as little Bobby Johnson and his friends of would-be pranksters continued to let off the cheekiest explosives they could cook up in the tenth year science classroom, Remus looked over the church and knew that they’d won.

“We love you, Hawkings!” Sirius shouted into the mike. "We will never forget you... honestly. Never."

He dropped the microphone with another boom, and just like that, began pushing Remus in the direction of the balcony stairs. It was easy enough to throw themselves into the chaos going on down below,and after a strategically planned separation—in which James and Peter went left and he and Sirius went right—Remus found himself by the row of church offices, where they could conveniently make a sharp left and sneak straight out the back doors.

“HOLY SHIT!” Sirius shouted the moment they fell out onto the grass; “HOLY SHIT!”

“I KNOW!” Remus screamed back, still trembling with euphoria. They were alone, and so he grabbed Sirius by either cheek and pulled him in for a single victory kiss. After that they were falling into each other, already losing their heads with laughter.

“Did you see, Bilshin’s face?!” Remus howled.

“He was nothing—you should’ve seen Snape!” Sirius replied.

“I can’t believe that worked!”

“Me neither!”

“Man—I totally fucked up the bridge!”

“Are you joking? Not even! I forgot the lyrics ten seconds in—pretty sure I just shouted nonsense up there!”

“Oh my god—what if I just threw up right now? ‘Cause I think I’m gonna throw up!”

“HA—I already did!”

Remus grappled Sirius into another fierce hug. Yeah, this was it. He could definitely do this forever.

“Where the fuck are Prongs and Wormtail?” Sirius demanded after, while peeking around the side of the church. “They were supposed to meet us—AHH!”

Sirius leapt backward as Sheila Buchanan swept around the side of the building, arms already crossed over her chest. Behind her, they could still hear the flurry of kids pouring out of the church. The fireworks had long since ran out, and Remus hoped Bobby and the others had escaped unscathed. Even if they hadn't, he was too preoccupied worrying over the look of severe rage on Sheila's face to be of much help.

"Do you have any idea what you've done?" She demanded. "Any idea?!"

"Yeah, we've just made history, Sheils," said Sirius, completely brazen.

"Did you, now? And would you happen to know if anyone got hurt while you were off making history?"

"The firecrackers were at the front of the church," Remus insisted. "You all were at the back—"

"Yes! Watching you! You and that insane—I mean, that stunt was just... And you! Oh, you boys! You are in so much…” She took a breath; “In so much—oh hell, I can’t even be angry!”

With a great sigh, Sheila pressed a hand to her forehead, grinning as though she were in pain. Across from her, Remus and Sirius shared a look of disbelief.

“You two idiots,” she moaned. "What were you thinking pulling a stunt like that on your last day?”

Slowly, the disbelief turned to relief. And Remus finally let out a breath. He was sure he'd never seen Sirius so proud.

“It’s because it’s our last day, Sheils! Had to do something big, didn’t we?”

“You certainly covered ‘big’! I mean, Jesus F. Chopin… Please just tell me that you’re finished now?”

“Almost,” Remus winced, happily; “We did tell everyone in our year that we’re camping out on the football pitch tonight, but that’s more an event… than a prank…” He stopped because she was squinting at him very harshly, but Sirius just threw an arm around his shoulders.

“So what’d you think? You’re our music teacher and you just watched the whole show—we were pretty great, huh? That's your legacy—think we really have a shot of making it one day?”

She opened her mouth, then smiled and shook her head hopelessly.

“I feel I should hand over my teaching license just for saying this… but yes, you boys were pretty good. Doesn’t mean you won’t be punished, though.”

“Are you going to let McGonagall expel us?” Sirius sniggered. “Because the main idea was that she can’t expel what she can’t find.”

“I should, shouldn’t I? It’s what any other sane teacher would do.”

“But you just said you’d hand over your license, so…?”

Sheila gave them both a very hard look. “You’ll have to clean it up.”

“We will!” Remus nodded.

“All of it! The instruments, the explosives, the Christ on a cross—”

“You can count on us, Sheils,” Sirius said, giving her the two-finger salute. “It’s just… Do you mind if I change first? These leather pants are giving me a major front-wedgie.”

Remus cringed a bit, but Sheila only began to laugh. And then she did something Remus would not have expected in a million years following a prank—she reached out and hugged both of them.

“I’m going to miss you boys dearly,” she said. “Perhaps this isn’t the proper moment, but I am so proud of you.”

Remus spared a glance at Sirius over his godmother’s shoulder, and the look Sirius gave him was almost weepy. He smiled, shyly, and they both hugged her back.

“Now off with you,” Sheila ordered, sniffling slightly as she released them. “Enjoy your last day.”

Remus peeked back into the church. “But I thought you wanted us to clean—”

She flapped her hands at him. “Go before I give you a real detention!”

“You heard the lady, Moons,” Sirius declared, taking his arm and dragging him backward. They kept going, until Sirius came to another stop and whirled around. He was holding Remus’ hand now, and Sheila didn’t even blink.

“Hey, Sheils! Seeing as you and Moony are practically related now, will we be seeing you around the holidays?”

Remus pinched him—embarrassed—but Sheila only smiled.

“Goodbye, Sirius Black," she said. "I cannot wait to see all the things you will accomplish."

They turned from her then, waving their goodbyes, and as they cut across the church's back garden, Remus kept hold of Sirius' hand and gave it a little squeeze.

Me neither.





* * *





Remus did not remember paying much attention to the sky as a kid. He’d always been able to see the stars from the estate, and though their twinklings got harder to see the further he went into the city, he never once missed them.

But he would miss these stars.

They floated by like a blue river, juxtaposed to the daunting black background that made up the rest of space. It made Remus feel small, but in a good way. The night that fell over Hawkings was so vast; there was no horizon, not really, there was only sky and that place where sky gave way to treetop and blissful rolling hill. In an effort to keep things as obviously secret as possible, they’d turned off the stadium lights all save one and left the night sky alight with all its many constellations. He could’ve counted forever and still not named them all; but if the stars were to count back, then they would’ve found several hundred students, all mulling around each other on soft green turf and living out what would be their final days of youth.

“Here, Remus, in case you get cold.”

Lily knelt down next to him on the grass and draped a crochet blanket over his middle. It was June, so of course it wasn’t cold, but Lily would always be Lily.

“Do you reckon you and James will get married someday?” He asked.

She cocked her head, then gave him a funny look that was probably well deserved.

“Maybe. Why?"

"Just wondering."

"Oh, Remus." She scooted closer, until she was lying by his side. She took his arm as well, and let her head rest against his shoulder. "Don't worry. I'm pretty sure everyone's feeling a bit contemplative tonight."

"Suppose lying under the stars will do that to you."

She giggled, then; "Oh, look! Leprechaun cloud."

The party grew more rambunctious as more and more kids began to trickle down from the dorms, toting blankets and belongings and otherwise acting very excited. Some groups had chosen to set up camp on the football stands, but most took to the field and ended up scattered, waving their torches through the air like hundreds of little fireflies.

After lying with him for a while, Lily had gotten up to rejoin her circle of girlfriends, who were all sitting together and passing a thermos of sherry between themselves. Moira had joined them as well, and beyond that, James, Sirius, and Peter were kicking a football around with several other lads in their year. Remus was mostly content to watch. The pitch was full of friend groups just like theirs, with not a teacher in sight; girls huddled together to swap secrets, boys winning and losing to each other in dare games and arm-wrestling. He caught glimpses of kids attempting handstands or else dancing around with jump ropes and hula hoops, others with midnight picnics spread about the grass. There was a girl knitting, a boy with his French horn, kids blowing smoke rings, passing bottles, making daisy chains, stargazing. He saw a pair of bicycles, a tent, a girl lovingly reading her copy of Jane Eyre aloud, several mattresses, and a… a goat?

Okay, that one was unexpected.

Remus turned over onto his stomach, squinting dubiously, but the goat was real—standing several feet away and quietly munching on the grass, entirely minding its own business.

“Wonder where that handsome devil came from,” Sirius said, grinning at the look on Remus’ face as he slid in next to him.

“Could you have had anything to do with it?” Remus mused.

“Me? Nah.”

“Right."

“I’m serious! ... Heh. Pretty sure some of the tenth years busted him out for the night. Feels good—knowing that we’re leaving a legacy behind.”

“Because the time capsule wasn't enough.”

Sirius’ face split with a grin. “Speaking of that..." He began rooting around the pockets of his jacket, pulling out a lighter, his cigarettes, Mary’s eyeliner pen which he definitely had no intention of returning. Suddenly suspicious, Remus sat up on the grass.

“Is this another prank? I'm not saving you from Sheila this time.”

"I'll have you know that Sheila's love for me 'saved me from Sheila'," Sirius scoffed. "But here, since you asked…”

With a mischievous look, Sirius plunged his hand into his back pocket and pulled out a tape. Instantly Remus was appalled.

"You git, is this our demo?"

"No," Sirius replied staunchly; “That I left for whoever we are in twenty years. It's too shitty to listen to now, so if you're done accosting me, take a better look."

He handed him the tape, and Remus turned it over in his hands. Across the front was a label, bearing the words; Marauders and Co., 1978.

"It’s the tape we made with the girls," Sirius said softly. "You know, the one with all our favourite songs."

"You mean you didn't bury it?"

"Oh, I buried it, alright. After I had one of the lads in the AV club make us a copy. Even got him to mix up the order for a bit of fun. Now it's one big surprise..."

Remus scoffed. "You sneaky bastard. You told the rest of us we weren't allowed to listen to it."

"So? Maybe that makes me a liar, but aren't we all liars in love?"

Remus clutched the tape tightly, and then held it to his heart. “What songs did everyone choose?”

“Dunno, I haven't listened to it yet. But if you're that curious, we could always play it now.”

Looking sly again, Sirius jutted his head toward the stands on the far side of the field, and to the press box containing the controls to the stadium’s entire speaker system.

“No…" Remus started; "No, you’re mental. With everyone else here?"

"They seemed to like it well enough last time," Sirius sneered. Then he sighed wistfully, taking the tape back and holding it up to admire. "Though, I suppose we could always just throw it in the bin... Wait twenty years to listen to it, until we've all forgotten what our favourite songs even were... Your choice, really. But if it was me? Well, I always tend to think that nights like these are better with a bit of music.”

“You dick.”

They smirked at each other for a while, and Sirius pointed toward the press box again.

"Come on, Moony. I already checked, the door ain't even locked..."

Before Remus could give in, James' voice called out;

“Oi, Sirius! Lupin! Come over here.”

Exchanging a glance, Sirius tucked the tape back into his trouser pocket and together they meandered over to their friends. Just as they reached them, Marlene threw herself over James, taking him down to the grass in a single solid heap.

"Give-them-to-me!" She shouted, furiously scrambling for whatever James was holding in his hand. Unfortunately for her, Sirius didn't miss a beat. He swept toward James, who naturally opened his palm and let him take it. Lottie and Mary whooped, laughing while Sirius took a graceful bow and Marlene raised her fist at him.

"Black, you give those back," she said, still pinning James face-down in the grass with her other hand.

"But what are they?" Sirius pondered, holding up what appeared to be a cardboard box no bigger than a matchbook.

"They're—ugh—smelling salts," James grunted. "McKinnon lifted them from the medical tent during the tournament.”

"I did not!" With a huff, Marlene gave up trying to bury James' head in the dirt and got to her feet to dust herself off. "I was helping clean up the first-aid tent after the game and they fell out of the kits. I picked them up for safe-keeping and just forgot to give them back, that's all."

"Likely story," heckled Mary.

"And just why would I steal smelling salts?"

"For the rush," Sirius grinned, opening the tiny box and taking out one of the glass capsules.

"Don't," Marlene warned. "They're not toys."

"Sure, strictly speaking."

"They smell awful."

"Only for a second." Satisfied, Sirius tossed a second vial at James, who grinned as he caught it out of the air. Lily gaped at him, whipping her torch around.

"You aren't actually going to sniff that, are you?"

"Why not? I've always wanted to try it," James said. "Hooch once had to use it on one of the lads after he ran head-first into the goal-post. He was a beast after—said it was the best rush he'd ever had."

Lily threw her hands up hopelessly, while Mary and Lottie began to chant; "Do it! Do it! Do it!"

"There's one more vial," Sirius declared, holding it out on offer. "Moons?"

"I'm good, thanks," Remus said, pulling out a cigarette.

"Wormy?"

“Nah, I choose life,” Peter scoffed, slumped down on the grass next to Moira.

Mary and Lottie's chant carried, and suddenly other voices from nearby groups had joined in; "DO IT! DO IT! DO IT!"

"They don't even know what they're cheering for," Marlene huffed, as James and Sirius sniggered wickedly.

“So how do we do this?” Sirius asked. "Break it with your teeth?"

“Do not put that in your mouth!” Lily screeched. “Honestly, you’re both such idiots—hasn’t anyone told you that you don’t have to attempt every stupid idea that comes into your thick heads?”

“But then how would we ever have evolution, Daisy?” James laughed. “You’re supposed to hold it under your nose and break it with your fingers. Like this.”

Following James’ lead, Sirius held the little tube beneath his nose and tried pinching it. “Bugger. Can’t get it.”

“Yeah, tough thing,” James agreed. “Oh hold on, I think you’re supposed to crush this part right—EUGH!”

It was as though James’ entire body had turned to jelly. He wobbled for a second, his eyes rolling backward as he flopped down to his knees on the grass. He wasn’t exactly choking, but the noises he made were like listening to a dead fish as it flopped on the shore of a lake.

“Siri—neugh—Sirrr-us, don’t do it—”

James began coughing horribly while other kids crowded around, laughing and cheering for him. This, of course, only fed Sirius' desire to do it himself.

“Don't be such a pansy, Potter,” he laughed, still trying to break the vial beneath his nostrils. "It can't really be that bad—EOH GAUD!”

The gagging came next, and suddenly Sirius had fallen back on his arse like a dead weight. As he fell into James, both of them flopping back and forth miserably, Lily and Marlene jumped up and gave them a chorusing round of "I told you so's".

"O-Oh my god," James warbled, “I think I just smelled in triple-dee."

“It’s 3D, you moron,” Peter said, finally succeeding in making all of the girls laugh.

Then Davey Gudgeon appeared behind Remus and crowed straight into his ear-drum; "Gee, what's wrong with them?"

Annoyed, Remus shrugged and handed Davey the remaining vial of smelling salts as he took a pull on his cigarette. A few moments later, there was a little snap and Davey had joined James and Sirius on the ground.

"I think that counts as poisoning, Remington."

He turned around. "You gonna rat on me, MacDuff?"

"Not today." Smirking, Trish stole his half-smoked cigarette and began rooting through her own pocket. "Got something for you."

"Right. My 'gift'."

"Just a wee one." She winked, then gestured for him to hold out his palm. Into it, she dropped a small stone with a hole in its middle.

"Your hag stone,” he said in awe.

" 'Gloine nan druidh'," Trish corrected. "To keep away yer nightmares. And fur a bit o' extra luck."

Remus closed his hand around the stone, still warm from her pocket. "Thanks, Trish."

"I'm gonna miss you, ye bloody giant. Send me a ticket tae one o' yer shows, promise I'll bring a better present."

"Deal."

He was half sure she was going to punch him again, that was until Barty Crouch had called her name.

"Fucking hell, MacDuff! You bloody coming or not? Just 'cause you're it, don't mean you can skive off!"

"Ach, yer maw!" Trish hollered back. "Get your knickers out o' a twist, lollyhead, I'll just be a second.”

The insult made Barty scoff, and he turned around to his friends, Regulus and Yaxley, arms waving at her as if he meant to say 'you see?'

"Don't mind them," Trish said to Remus. "They wantae play tiggy in the trees. Wouldn't happen tae have a spare torch, would ya?"

He gave her his, and she slapped him hard—but fondly—on the chest.

"See ya around, Loonarny! And you—best run, ya fucking bawbags!"

She set off after them, giving another war-cry loud enough to spook Barty and the others back into the trees. It was dark, and Remus couldn't be entirely sure, but he hoped that the look he saw on Regulus' face was a smile.

Tapping out another cigarette, Remus went to collect his blanket and shuffled back over to Lily, who was sitting at the end of the girls' row.

"Where's Sirius?" He asked.

“Guess."

Turns out he didn't have to. The music came first, shooting out the vast speaker system and filling the entire stadium with a sharp reverb. The song was not forgiving—a blast of noise that made everyone jump. There were no firecrackers this time, no live band bursting forth from beneath the legs of a seven foot-tall Jesus statue, and yet that didn't stop the kids from cheering. It was a Blondie song, which Remus only knew when he watched Marlene leap to her feet.

"He didn't!" She screeched. "He wouldn't!"

But then he did.

Up above, Sirius and James burst out of the press box and started rushing back down the stands again while the speakers played "X Offender" at full volume. Kids, who no doubt, had been waiting for this very moment, began to point and whoop for them. The pair made it to the ground at a tie and rushed back to their friends, Sirius falling down before Remus and half-tackling him round the middle.

“Whaddya think, Moons?!”

"I think..."

'I know you wouldn't go—

You'd watch my heart burst,

Then you'd step in!'



"... I think you're amazing."

Sirius beamed at him, and was very suddenly accosted by Marlene. "You!" She cried, happily. "You stole this album from me."

"Think again, McKinnon!"

She wheeled back, turning to the other girls as realisation dawned on her face. Lily and the others still hadn't seemed to catch on, but James was grinning like the cat who caught the cream. All around, kids were dancing—having fun! And when the song changed and became a heavy blue-rock, James thrust a finger at Remus.

"Yours!" He cried. "This one's yours, right?"

"Not mine!" Remus laughed.

'Well, come on! Come on! Come on! Come on!'

Lottie screamed. Actually screamed.

"It's the tape!" She hollered. "It's my song!"

Sirius clapped his hands together. Janis Joplin was singing to them, and the girls were in disbelief.





'—But what I'm gonna show you, baby, that a woman can be tough!

I want you to come on! Come on! Come on! Come on and TAKE IT!

Take another little piece of my heart now, baby!'





Sirius looked up at Remus.

"Moons, I'm so happy."

Oh… how badly Remus wanted to kiss him just then.

It really was their tape. Disjointed, moody, eclectic, and as odd a mix as they were. Take eight different people, with eight different personalities, and one was bound to get something interesting. First it was Marlene, then Janis Joplin for Lottie—and then a Who song started and everyone once again pointed fingers at Remus.

"I-It's not mine!" He bleated, almost embarrassed.

"It's mine!" Peter declared, standing up proudly. "You guys think Moony's the only one with good taste?"

It was flooring. James leapt up to pat Peter on the back, and together he and Sirius strummed air instruments while Moira and the girls did their best to sing along. Remus might've joined in—he should've, really—but it was harder when he realised which song Peter had chosen.

Won't Get Fooled Again...

Remus shrugged it off. It was merely a good song, surely Peter didn't mean anything by it...





'Pick up my guitar and play,

Just like yesterday!

Then I'll get on my knees and pray...

We don't get fooled again!'



Mary’s song came just as quickly after that anyway. And as expected, it was ABBA—though not just any ABBA... As the song began to play, Remus recalled an old memory;

Send off your grandma with ‘Hasta Mañana’ and I guarantee there won’t be a dry eye in the room.

There was truly an ABBA song for everything.





'Hasta mañana, say we'll meet again,

I can't do without you...

Say you forgive, the sooner the better!

Hasta mañana, baby!

Hasta mañana, until then...'





"You bitch," Marlene moaned, wiping her face furiously as tears leaked from the corners of her eyes. Mary hugged her, and they rocked gently along with the song until its very end.

"Who's song is next?" Lily asked, poking Sirius anxiously. He shrugged, then glanced up at Remus, who was sitting with his arms around Sirius' waist.

"Dunno. Got the lad who helped me tape it over to mix up all the songs. Why, what'd you pick, Evans?"

Lily covered her mouth, a blush rising in her cheeks. "I didn't think everyone would hear it."

Sirius launched upright, nearly bashing Remus in the chin.

"Now I'm intrigued!"

He needn't be; as it turned out, James and Lily were next.

An old married couple before their time, the two of them had unknowingly dedicated their own choices to each other in one final show of serendipity. Without ever being sure she’d hear it, James had picked a Mamas and Papas’ song, just because he knew how much Lily loved them. And then after, it turned out that Lily had gone with a Kinks’ song, James’ own favourite.

Everyone began to laugh when they’d realised what had happened, but then James invited his girlfriend to dance and it didn’t even matter. It was still dark, but Remus was pretty sure he’d watched James whisper the song lyrics into Lily’s ear as they swayed.

* * *





They played the tape twice more that night, and each time they enjoyed it more. Kids danced, kids sang, kids lost their minds.

And they made their memories.

Later, when the songs had ended and the world fell still again, Remus turned to Sirius beneath the stars and took his hand. Distantly he could hear the sounds of James and Lily as they muttered lovely things to one another. Mary was humming, Marlene was grumbling at her humming, Lottie kept asking if they could hear the crickets, and dear Peter was singing 'mama mia' in his sleep.

"Are you alright?" Sirius whispered, gazing at him in the dark. "You look... nervous."

Remus shook his head. "I'm happy."

"You're sure?"

"Yes." But; "Everything's ending now, isn't it? It's all going away... Or, we're going away."

"Yes. To London." But; "I'm as old as Tomny was when I left and now it's all over. You know, I used to think that was all I wanted, but now it's here and I'm already forgetting things. Maybe I'm not ready for it all to end."

Sirius leaned up on one arm, his black hair falling down over his face like a curtain.

Oh...

“Too good to be true, actually." Sirius laughed. "Probably be completely manky inside."

"Probably."

"Still... Do you want to go with me?”

“Yes," Remus said, drawing Sirius toward him and kissing his soft lips. "Anywhere with you.”

Any way the wind blows...

Overhead, the stars watched and wished they were them.

Chapter 97: #43 Knoxbridge Lane


Chapter Summary

You're a starfucker, starfucker, starfucker, starfucker, star!



Chapter Notes

TW: Brief mention of suicide by hanging—in reference to war-induced PTSD.

Oh my god, mot actually posted a chapter early???? must be witchcraft. (or a terrible fucking sleep schedule, you decide)

Anyway, it's the start of a new era! Our gap year!! *Pause for dramatic effect 👀*

I have no promises for gap year, it's pure chaos. It started out as a much smaller thing, then naturally grew in chaos (and size asfjk) the deeper in I got. In fact, I'm barely finished, so if there's some inaccuracies, I hope to be able to catch them later.

For now, on with the show!!



See the end of the chapter for more notes



This will be an everlasting love,

This will be the one I’ve waited for;

This will be the first time anyone has loved me,

I’m so glad you found me in time,

And I’m so glad that you’ve rectified my mind;

This will be an everlasting love for me…

- “This Will Be” Natalie Cole, 1975



They moved in at the beginning of July. It was a two story London maisonette in the middle of Shepherd’s Bush that overlooked a busy street filled with shops and greengrocers. It would’ve been too small if it weren’t for the attic that'd been converted into a small bedroom and toilet. That space would become their sanctuary; their little piece of the pie.

Their very first home.

It was the corner flat—Remus smacked Sirius the first time he called it a 'townhouse'—leaving them with just a single set of neighbours to their left, which suited them just fine, what with all the noise they were bound to make. There had been no asking price listed on the advert Sirius had shown him and so Remus had been sceptical, but it was a decent area, and as wonderful as the Potters had been to them, there was only so long he could stand free-loading before he ended up renting some seedy guest house in South London.

"You're lucky you caught my ad when you did," said the landlady, as she showed them around the ground floor. "I was going to divvy it up into separate flats, but I bloody hate dealing with contractors."

"We'll need the space anyway," replied Sirius, as he ran his fingers along the faded wallpaper in the front entryway. The landlady meandered after them keenly. She appeared glamorous, with long, painted eyelashes and a waist nearly the same size as her neck. The advert had been listed to a "Margaret" but when they'd arrived she’d introduced herself as “Peggy”. She seemed very pleased indeed when Sirius reached out to kiss her hand—even more so when he’d flashed that dishy grin at her. Remus thought the act a bit superfluous, but anything to get a roof over their heads.

“My third husband, Paul, tried to have the entire thing gutted last year,” Peggy went on. “Only got as far as the floors before he croaked, but everything’s been freshly painted."

"I can see that," Remus said, picking at a half-inch nail sticking out of the kitchen doorway that'd been painted over in a rather foul shade of beige. Peggy kept close on their heels, smoking a cigarette and looking them up and down as if she were still trying to decide whether or not they were wasting her time. Perhaps she doubted their ability to pay, judging them for their age and choice of dress like any wary forty-something with an unresolved bone to pick with the world.

"I’m looking to get at least one-forty for it," she said, pointedly.

"That's kind of steep."

"Market's facing a rent shortage, you know."

"Yeah, has been since 1965."

Sirius elbowed him. The flat was perfect, enough space for all of them and their instruments and wasn't even completely manky. Best to not bottle it.

“So you’re firm on the price?” Remus asked, testing the waters.

“Price’s firm.”

He glanced around, wondering what their odds were of being scammed. Not that he knew anything about buying a home. The walls were high—much higher than the ones back at Tomny's place. There were no water marks on the ceiling either, and all the lights worked.

“Does it get cold in the winter?”

“Oh, no. It’s all central heating ‘round here nowadays,” Peggy said. “Fridge’s been replaced too. I’m willing to let out to students but I’ll need at least three months rent upfront. Plus a deposit for anything you might break.”

"And how much is that?"

She eyed Sirius' heavy boots. "Ninety pounds."

"That's more than half a month's rent!"

"It's a proper sought-after area, you know."

Turning back from the main windows, Sirius gave her a winning smile. "Don't worry, Peggy, I'd say ninety's more than fair."

It must've surprised her, as she nodded dubiously and pulled the blue-wrapped Vogue cigarette from her lips. As Sirius flounced toward the open kitchen, Remus replaced him by the front windows and peered outside. Down below, the main thoroughfare dragged by, noisy and alight with life. It was only a three minute walk to get to the Central Line, and they’d passed a corner shop and two separate newsstands on their way over. There was a grocer’s across the street too, as well as an off-licence and a post office. Everything they needed, right within reach.

As Remus was busy watching an old woman hobble up the street with a yappy Yorkshire Terrier on a lead ahead of her, Peggy came up behind him with two fingers still primly poised around her cigarette.

"He mentioned you were looking for space," she pondered, blowing smoke from her cherry-red lips. "Space for what?"

So she was suspicious then. Or rather, she hadn't stopped being so.

"There's five of us actually. We're looking for somewhere to rent together."

"All of you men?"

"Four guys, plus our friend Lily."

"Lucky girl." She took another drag, and Remus couldn't decide if she were being sarcastic. “What’d you say you kids did again?”

Now she was veering dangerously close to the truth. When they'd returned from school, Monty had warned them how tough it would be to find somewhere in the city with enough space for five plus a rock band, but at least they all had one thing going for them now.

Real jobs.

“Sirius works the evening shift at a pub,” Remus answered truthfully, “and I’ve got managed a gig over on Denmark Street. Our friend Pete works for his dad, and the other—James, he's got a job lined up as a server. We’re not bums.”

“Or students, apparently?”

“Uh, sort of… Took a gap year.”

“He’s just being metaphorical, Peg!” The cry came from Sirius as he threw himself back down the staircase and rounded into the living room. He had his hands on his hips as he proudly announced; "We happen to have our own band."

Remus was instantly horrified. Peggy's eyes had gone narrow with sudden suspicion, and he imagined her next move would be to put them out on the pavement like the guilty dogs they were. He’d begged Sirius not to bring up the band, especially not after every other place they'd looked at had fallen through the moment the landlords heard of their less-than-reputable career intentions. No one liked a noisy neighbour, and four boys with guitars and amplifiers didn’t exactly scream ‘trustworthy tenants’.

Still, Sirius was stubborn. He took a stance of complete transparency—screw any crotchety old fools! If they were going to complain anyway, might as well get it out of the way early. Remus just wished he’d stick a sock in it until they’d signed the bloody lease.

“We won’t be a bother,” he reassured the landlady. “We’re looking for another space to practise, even. Like a—a garage! This’d just be somewhere to lay our heads at night.”

“My second husband was in a band,” Peggy said sourly. “Useless bastard. Never brought in a penny. Then he up and died of a heart attack at thirty-seven.”

Sirius gave her a smug smile. “Well, we’re only eighteen.”

Would his suffering end if he simply threw himself out the window, Remus wondered? Luckily for him there was no need. A hint of a smile traced the corner of her mouth, and Peggy hid it with another deep draw of her cigarette.

“You any good then, boy?” She asked Sirius.

“Better than good. We're the best.”

“Play anywhere I’d know?”

“Not yet.”

“Then how could you possibly know that you’re the best?”

“Because we’re mental,” Sirius smirked. “And mental makes art.”

“We’re good tenants!” Remus yelped, rounding Peggy to get between her and his menace of a boyfriend. “Won’t give you any trouble… I swear it.”

Peggy exhaled, the tart aroma of her cigarette drifting across the room toward them. The purse in her lips told Remus that she wasn’t entirely convinced, but that she was at least willing to play along.

“I happen to own the place next door as well," she told them. "For the most part, I’m a bit of a night owl. I don’t mind staying up as long as my mornings are quiet. I like going out, but I love a nice lie-in twice as much. And you’re cute, all things considered.”

The two of them shared a hesitant glance while Peggy took another drag, burning the cig down to its filter.

“There's a basement beneath this one,” she said, tapping her heel on the wood floors. “It’s unfinished, but it’s got cement walls, so I reckon it'd be quiet enough. I’d be taking a risk renting to you, but if you can come up with the full three months beforehand, and you're willing to double that tenancy deposit, then I might just be tempted to give you a go.”

Sirius’ eyes widened. “No shit—for real?”

“Mm.” The landlady pulled out a silver cigarette tin, tapping her ash into the corner and sticking the leftover stub inside. “The world needs more artists, Mr. Black. And I say, let ‘em come.”

“Holy—cheers, Peg!”

Remus smacked him for being overly familiar, but Peggy was already pointing at them like a threat.

“I’m still firm on the rent though. You miss one month and that's it—you’re out on your rear.”

“You don’t gotta worry about that,” Sirius swore, “we’re all in. Even got the cash now if you really want.”

She smiled faintly, and snapped the tin shut, returning it to the pocket of her impossibly-tight jeans.

“Then it looks like we have a deal.”

Afterwards Peggy left them to fetch the paper work, and just like that, they were newly-born renters selling their souls to capitalism. Remus did a turn about the room, imagining what it would look like lived-in. A bookshelf here, Sirius’ stereo there, Peter's artwork and a few of Lily's favourite plants…

“A whole fucking house—I can’t believe it!” Sirius called. He was in the kitchen, opening and closing every cupboard like he might find a secret world hidden inside. He’d just darted across to the fridge when he hollered; “We should celebrate!”

“Got that bottle of jack back at the Potters',” Remus said.

Sirius let the fridge fall shut, and then rushed back into the empty living room. He launched himself into Remus, who caught him, and turned his face up.

“Moons,” he whispered, only for them; “We’re home.”

Home.

Remus had never thought the word could sound so good.
