That was four months ago now, but Remus could still remember their first night in the flat like it was yesterday. It’d rained, and Sirius had opened the window to listen to its gentle city thrum. They were lying on a bare mattress in the converted attic of their new flat. Peggy hadn’t been lying—the bedroom was a walk-up, with only a single set of narrow stairs and a door that shrieked on its hinges every time it was opened, but they’d chosen it for the privacy. It was a small room, less than half the size of their old dorm room, with an attached toilet made up of powder blue tiles and a single grey sink. And it was all theirs.

“Shall we find ourselves some seashells to go with?” Sirius had said, very snidely. "Perhaps a fuzzy rug for a shower mat?"

"You'd like that, wouldn't you?"

They'd forwent the seashells, and the rest of the room they’d filled sparsely; a wardrobe with nicks in the varnish that they’d picked up from a car boot sale, a set of on-offer night tables, and an atrocious rug that smelled faintly of wet dog. It was rubbish, all of it, but it was theirs!

The bed was the only thing they’d sprung for. Even after all those years at school, Sirius didn’t like the idea of sleeping on a mattress that had been used by someone else. Barely an hour after they’d gotten the keys, they’d gone on down to Bensons for Beds together and picked one out. They’d earned themselves a few dubious looks from the sales clerks, but Remus found he didn’t care all that much. The poor sods worked on commission and wouldn’t dare risk losing a sale, even if the customers were a pair of questionable-looking teenagers.

Yes, it had rained—enough to turn the air hot and sticky, but Remus had been hardly bothered. He was too busy lying next to his love, composing another song in his head. The words came together like puzzle pieces, in the slow rubato of their new home.





Of all the bad things I did,

The best of them was you;

Of all the sad things we hid,

The worst of them, we saw through,

And if I had three wishes,

I wouldn’t ask for a dime;

I’d weave myself a symphony,

Begging for you, yourself, and time…





He’d thought about writing it down, but everything they owned was still boxed up by the front door, so instead he filed the words away. Even if he somehow forgot them, he’d remember them eventually. They weren’t going anywhere; they were home.

“Whatchu thinkin’ about, Moons?”

Remus turned his head back, to where Sirius was lying, hugging him from behind. His mouth was tame, but his eyes were smiling.

“How happy I am,” he told him. “And how much I love you.”

“Aw… you poof.”

Now it was October, and each of them had found their own way to settle into city life. Thanks to his dad’s connections, James had managed to snag a job at waiting tables at some posh hotel in Marylebone. The gig was a straight shot along the metro line and the pay was well worth it, so James couldn’t have cared less that he was waiting on the same sort of people they'd been going to school with their entire lives. Often he would tack an extra half hour onto his commute if it meant he could escort Lily to her classes at the college.

Peter was doing well enough too. He’d moved into the single room just off the kitchen, while James and Lily had taken the second floor bedroom for themselves. Moira had been by to visit a few times, having settled on attending a women's university in Stratford. Without a set of classes of his own to distract him, Peter’s father had insisted he come work at the publishing house. Mostly it sounded like complete drivel, but there were some perks.

“Guess who they’re putting on page three of tomorrow’s paper,” Peter called, as he trudged across the flat’s entryway that evening, ripping off his tie.

“Who?” James answered, busy fixing himself and Lily a cup of tea.

“Lovely Linda.”

Peter slapped the newspaper down onto the kitchen table and they all crowded around to get a look at glamour model Linda Lusardi in her page three headshot, sans shirt.

“Dad’s trying to keep up with ‘The Sun’,” Peter said. “Says naked girls are about all people willing to pay for these days.”

“He’s right about that,” Sirius snorted. “Blimey, just get a look at those nipples. Could poke an eye out, don'tcha think, Potter?”

Next to him, James just stared on dumbly. “I dunno… She looks sorta… nice. Like she's a... nice girl.”

Sirius gave Remus a look that said ‘get a load of this sucker’ and just then Lily strode into the kitchen, arms raised as she gathered her hair into a ponytail at the top of her head.

“What're you guys looking at?” She asked, mumbling around the hair bobble between her teeth.

“Nothing!” James yelped, snatching the paper up from the table.

Not stupid enough to ignore the obvious ploy, Lily let her hair drop and ripped the elastic from her mouth as she crossed the room toward them.

“Hand it over.”

They did, only because they were all afraid of the consequences should they refuse, and Lily scoffed before unceremoniously stuffing the paper into the kitchen bin.

“Demeaning!” Was all she hissed at first. “It’s demeaning to women, and utterly priggish—sexist!—behaviour!”

“Evans, I hate to break it to you, but you live with four blokes now,” Sirius shrugged haplessly. “Bound to be a few sexy prigs mixed in. Admiring naked women is in our nature.”

Peter gave him a look. “Aren’t you gay?”

“ ‘Aren’t you gay?’” Sirius mimicked, flicking him in the forehead. “Idiot.”

As far as sexy/sexist prigs went, the four of them did pretty well with an added girl in the mix. Not that she was going to put up with being treated like a maid. It came as quite a shock when Lily found out that none of them knew how to properly clean a toilet, but by week two she’d assigned all the tasks that'd needed doing, and the rest of them made quick to comply. While Remus, James, and Peter handled the more frivolous chores such as emptying the bin and covering the weekly shop, Lily and Sirius had made up an unlikely team of their own. The kitchen became their territory, and there they argued about what suppers to make and how long they could keep a potato once it’d sprouted.

“I knew you could cook a little, but I had no idea you were actually good at it,” Remus said once, when he’d come downstairs and caught Sirius making a cottage pie in the middle of the day.

“I used to spend a lot of time in the manor kitchens," he shrugged. "It was the only place Mum wouldn’t bother to go looking for me, and I enjoyed hearing the cooks mouth off when she wasn't around. Guess I just picked up a few things.”

"The cooking or the mouthing off?"

Sirius smirked. It nearly made Remus blush.

“I feel like I’m always learning new things about you," he said.

“Suppose that’s what keeps it exciting.”

Now he was surely blushing.

“Here, budge up. I wanna help.”

Yes, they’d all settled in nicely. It had taken until Lily had arrived for them to spring for any real dinnerware—they’d spent the first week eating porridge from mugs and sipping cider straight from the bottle—but her influence and womanly touch had set them straight quick enough. Work and band practice came neck-and-neck as far as priorities went, but none of them felt like skiving off. The basement set-up they had going was perfect, and every day they were sounding better and better. Remus didn’t even think about the estate anymore, and though Tomny was still stuck in Ipswich, he’d return eventually, once the frozen docks and cold weather had properly chased him back home.

Yes, in just a few short months, the flat at number forty-three, Knoxbridge Road had become their oasis, and every day Remus lived within its walls, he felt more and more invincible.



* * *





Saturday 21st October 1978





It was warm for October. Remus could feel the sun slightly singeing the back of his neck. He didn’t mind so much; Sirius liked counting the freckles.

“You seem well,” Sandra told him, while sampling her cappuccino with prime, little sips. “Healthy. Happy, too.”

“I am,” he answered.

“You are?”

“Yes.”

She seemed to let out a breath of relief. They were sitting amongst a cafe’s outdoor patio along Mayfair; not his idea, but hers. Sandra had tried insisting that he order something, but Remus had graciously declined and was instead lounging casually in the patio chair, legs crossed at the ankles. He had a shift soon anyway, and had only agreed to meet on the condition that she did not “mother”. Sandra seemed to find this agreeable enough, and so far had managed to avoid all mention of Lyall, interjecting with only the occasional tidbit about Giles or the dogs.

“You're not at the Potters' anymore," she recounted, "where is it you’re living now?”

“Shepherd’s Bush. Been there since July.”

“That’s a nice area. And you’re living with friends, are you?”

“Mhm, yeah. We split the rent, but Sirius has his uncle's inheritance so he covered most of the costs up front."

“You mean it’s just the two of you?”

He shook his head, not really interested in sharing many details, and she began tracing the edge of her teacup. Feeling awkward, Remus checked his watch. He was due at the shop in a half-hour. It was still enough time to make it even if he walked, but before he could make an excuse and slink away, Sandra jumped back in.

“Get this—a new litter of pups were born last week! Zenyatta’s third. Such a lovely girl, she did so well.”

“That’s good. Suspect dad’ll be retiring her soon then. Sent out to pasture and all that.”

He meant it lightly, but the words made Sandra’s smile vanish, and Remus instantly wished he could take them back.

“I was only joking. If there’s anyone he does right by, it’s his dogs, innit.”

“Your father still worries about you as well, Remus,” Sandra said, after a long pause. “He worries about whether you’re taking proper care of yourself.”

“Dunno why he’d bother, s’not like he’s ever worried before.”

“You know that’s not true.”

Remus said nothing, for once not interested in the usual argument. Sandra leaned forward in her chair. He knew straight away what she wanted; it was the only reason she'd asked to meet him in the first place. To pry.

“I think you should visit. Have a little chat with him, that’s all. No arguing, no judgement, and I promise neither of us will mention school either. Just tea. Would you consider coming home for tea?”

It's not my home. The thought was bitter with pride, and so rather than answer, Remus looked off to his left where a young mum was sitting, sipping her coffee and reading a book. She had a pram next to her, and whenever the baby began to fuss, she’d simply reach out and rock and carriage a bit. She didn’t even glance at the kid, but the act itself was care enough.

“Sandy, do you know who Keith Moon is?”

She perked up, as though she thought he might finally impose some sort of willingness to make peace with Lyall.

“I’m afraid not. Is he a friend of yours?”

Remus smiled to himself. “He was one of the best drummers in the world. And he died last month.”

“Oh, well that’s too bad.”

“My mother would’ve known who he was—is. She didn’t know much, but she would’a known that.”

Sandra set her teacup down, and Remus felt the clink of its glass like a stern reprimand.

“Remus, this isn't about you and me,” she began. “You’re going off on your own now, and that is so dearly exciting, but we still worry. We worry if you’re eating enough—sleeping enough. You’re only eighteen, that’s still very young to be taking on the entire world on your own.”

“I'm not on my own. I’ve got my friends. We take care of each other—always have. Now is there anything else I'm forgetting? Something left to worry about? Because if not, I have somewhere to be.”

“You’re right, I’m sorry,” Sandra nodded; “I don’t mean to chase you off. I know I promised not to bother you with fretting... But I have something for you actually. Thought you might want it, now that you’re moved out on your own.”

She reached for her bag and withdrew a small parcel swathed in tissue paper.

“Your father had it framed,” she said as she passed it over. “He wanted you to have it.”

Remus stared at the gift, suddenly nervous. He thought he should decline, but she pressed it into his hands anyway. When he unwrapped it, he found the smiling image of his mum staring back at him. She was younger, sitting on the floor of the estate’s parlour and bouncing a baby Remus on her knee. She seemed bigger than he remembered—not small like a teenager, nor frail from age and sickness—instead fuller in the cheeks and hips. There was no colour to the image, but even in black and white, she looked warm. A whole woman.

Remus covered the photo with the tissue paper, and then tucked it into the large outer pocket of his coat.

“That’s nice,” he murmured. “Thanks.”

“I thought it was such a darling photo. You and Hope.”

Remus nodded stiffly, before reaching into his inside pocket and pulling out his wallet. He left a tenner on the table, more than enough for Sandra’s cappuccino, and stood.

“Oh, now what are you doing that for?” Sandra tutted immediately, trying to hand him back the note.

“It’s fine. Tea’s on me today.”

“But you didn’t even order anything!”

“Can’t I buy my step-mother a drink every now and then?”

She softened at that—step-mother, Remus had never said it in front of her before—and he took the opportunity to tuck away his wallet and stand up from the table.

“Better scat now. Don’t want to be late for work.”

Sandra quickly perked up in her chair. “You’ve gotten a job then? That’s fantastic! Where at?”

Remus stepped past the table, buttoning up his coat. He suddenly felt more playful.

“Job—what job? Didn't you know, Sandy, I’m only a good-for-nothing musician.”

It boggled her for a moment, then he heard her laugh, hopelessly, and that was the last Remus saw of her for a good, long while.

As he walked, he counted the hours in his head. One eight-hour shift at the music shop, and then two hours until they’d be on stage. Not a literal stage—more like a slight raised platform corner of the pub Sirius had gotten a job in. They’d all been lucky to get something, what with the way English businesses were shutting down left and right and centre. It felt as though if a factory weren’t closing, then its workers were going on strike, lobbying for more pay and better working conditions. The autoplant Ted had worked in since he was seventeen had just shut its doors, leaving him and three hundred other men without a job to feed their families. When he’d heard, Sirius had gone over to Islington to visit, but according to him neither Ted nor Andy had been all that worried. There will be more jobs, she’d told Sirius, and more chances to be sacked from those too!

They’d only ever met once, but Remus admired Andy and Ted. Young parents, just trying to make their own way and love each other. It was more than he could say for most people.

As he walked, the city moved about him, full of life and also its usual misery. He passed a man sleeping in a doorway, with a sign by his feet saying "will work for meals". His coat was ragged, having seen too many winters, and his boots clung to the bottom of his feet like cardboard. Silently, Remus rooted around in his pocket for the bit of spare change there, and left the coins in the tin can set out by the man’s feet before carrying on. Around him the air smelt like the sea, but also not—a salty scent more akin to the brackish water of the Thames. There was a woman sitting on a bench, letting her terrier lick from a takeout box while she flipped through the paper. A cop was barking at a pair of kids who flew past him on their bicycles, pulling faces and shouting things like “fascist pig” and “tory tart”. Every time he got close they’d speed off, before circling back around like baby-faced piranhas. They probably didn’t have a clue what it was they were saying, it was mere words on a loop. It felt like summertime.

The shop where Remus worked was on Denmark Street, otherwise known as Britain’s very own “Tin Pan Alley”. Less than a decade before, music-makers and lovers alike used to flock to the street in search of the next best thing. They crowded into the various shops, buying and peddling their trade. The windows remained adorned in everything from records to mandolins, to costly electric guitars and dingy old fuzz boxes. But that was only half the fun.

Up above, overlooking the pavement like gods themselves, there were various flats where music publishers and studio-owners had once run the promised land from right behind their own office desks. All day they flapped their coattails and entertained the best in the business; Stones, Hendrix, Kinks, Sabbath, Bowie—they’d all been there, recording their demos that would go on to become life-altering albums. The street had declined much in recent years due to a boom in big studio tech, but a few of the more stubborn shops had stuck around down below, peddling their wares to the average passer-by. It was disheartening to know that he'd missed the prime days of such rock and roll, but Remus always made sure to count the windows on his way to work, as if he might one day catch a glimpse of someone special peering back at him.

“Hasn't your mummy ever told you it's not polite to stare? Perhaps you should start singing. Then they might open their windows, thinking you're a pretty bird.”

“Or an air-raid siren.” Remus turned his gaze ahead, toward the pavement outside of his shop where she was waiting for him. “Hey, Cas.”

“Hey, handsome,” she grinned. “Come here often?”

“Only to see you, love.”

Dorcas—or Cas, as Remus knew her—laughed as he cut between the pair of tables sitting in front of the cafe next door. Her beaded earrings caught the sun and glittered as she pressed a hand to his chest in mock fondness. She was dressed in typical form—a Stylistics t-shirt slashed high above her waist and jeans low enough to show off her entire midriff. She had the music shop’s A-board sign balanced against one hip, and several albums meant for restocking on the other, which Remus took from her on approach. She muttered a thanks, before pulling her long brown locs onto one shoulder and flapping a hand to ward off some of the heat.

“Decent day so far?” He asked, as she straightened out the shop sign.

“Would be, if Phil could get his head outta his arse for five minutes.”

"I've never known a manager to be that flexible."

"Ha! Me neither."

Behind them, a group of young teens still in their school uniforms were busy digging around the albums in the fifty-pence bins.

“I better not catch any ‘a you stuffing none of those into your bags again,” Dorcas warned. “I know you’re good for it, ya posh public school brats.”

The kids all gave her a dirty look and quickly shuffled into the shop, the doorbell twinkling after them. She glared a moment longer, then waved Remus over to the messy bins teetered high with cheap, on-offer singles and old albums that no one ever wanted but were in a constant state of disorder regardless.

“C’mon then, stud. You’re already late, might as well help me with this.”

Remus objected; “I have another five minutes before my shift starts,” but ambled over to the bins with her anyway.

“How was your morning?” Dorcas asked, fanning herself with a tattered copy of The Yardbirds while she went through sections T to Z. She had a necklace around her neck bearing the Star of David, which she played with in her free hand.

“Fine. Saw my step-mum for a while. Not much else. How’s the shop been so far?"

“Bit slow for a Saturday, to be honest. Had a few people coming and going, plus that weird guy with the parrot came by again. But Phil keeps riding my arse about getting that leftover stock out. I'm pretty sure he's a robot, but I've yet to find the bloody off switch.”

“Dunno why he's so insistent,” Remus grumbled. “It’s all German synth. And what do they have? Kraftwerk.”

“Mm… Reckon you’ll be sad you missed him actually.”

“Who—Phil? Please tell me he died.”

“I wish. Guess again.”

“The parrot guy?”

“No! … Well, maybe. I like it when the parrot tells other customers to piss off. But there was someone else! He came by to take a look at that Les Paul Special hanging behind the counter. But oh—you probably wouldn’t know him…”

Remus nudged her, too curious. “Come on, Cas, don’t leave me in suspense. Who was it?”

“Oh, you know… just someone named 'Ronson'. You know, white guy—plays guitar—got Ziggy Stardust and Aladdin Sane on speed dial.”

Remus’ jaw dropped, and Dorcas gave him a cheeky look.

“You mean, Mick Ronson?" He warbled. "As in the Mick Ronson that produced 'Transformer'? The guy who toured with Lou Reed and Bob Dylan—the guitarist who helped shape Bowie’s entire career?! You mean that Mick Ronson?!”

“Yeah, that’s the one, ya anorak.”

“And you’re just telling me this NOW?”

“He’s long gone already!” Dorcas laughed. “You’re the one who didn’t want to work early mornings.”

Remus covered his face and groaned. “Man, Sirius is gonna go mental. Like shit—Mick fucking Ronson, how cool is that!?”

Suddenly someone was clearing their throat pointedly and they both looked up to find their manager, Phil, standing in the shop’s doorway. Remus wished he could say that Phil was an alright guy, but really he was just a dick. A true music snob without the added benefit of any taste, and a mullet that looked more like he’d taken the tail off a dog and stapled it to the back of his head. Most days Phil was so intolerable that it was all Remus could do not to strangle him with an amp cable. He would’ve quit on the first day, had the job not had a few obvious perks.

“Hey there, cats and kittens,” the manager drawled; “Mind helping me out inside and—oh, I dunno—doing your job?”

“You said you wanted the bins reorganised,” Dorcas said, dropping Yardbirds back into its slot.

“Yes—to you. Not him! Now let’s get a move-on, lover boy. Those 1968 Martins won’t re-string themselves.”

As Phil turned and marched back inside, Remus tossed a glance at Dorcas, who rolled her eyes indifferently and turned back to the stacks and stacks of albums.

“I need all of these done before your lunch break,” Phil ordered, after he’d led Remus to the back of the shop, where no less than a dozen guitars were waiting, each stacked up on top of one another like dominos. “Need ‘em restrung, and don’t forget to check the bleedin' necks. A few of them have raised bridges too—oh, and change out the pickguards on this one, this one—and that Yamaha! I don't like looking at the scratches.”

As Phil blabbered, Remus stopped to pick up the guitar in front. A beautiful Gibson J-45.

“You sure you want me to change this one out?” He asked. “I think it looks fine as is.”

“I didn’t ask you for your opinion, Lupin, I asked you to fix ‘em! Just got the whole stock in from some estate and I wanna have them ready for sale by tomorrow, so chop-chop—hop to it! Gotta love it when those decrepit old collectors start pushing up daisies.”

The door chimed as more customers filed in, and while Phil left him to upsell some dad out buying his kid his first guitar, Remus huffed and took a seat behind the repair counter. Next to him sat Bo, an old repairman who’d been working at the shop since it was managed by Phil’s father. Remus liked Bo. He was chatty about himself but rarely pried, and had the wildest stories of all sorts of musicians that'd come into the shop over the years. He'd once told Remus that he'd been around when Denmark Street was just a lane, and while it was surely an exaggeration; the things Bo had to have seen in his hayday—blimey.

“Don’t mind ‘im,” Bo said, half bent over a stack of pickups he was rewiring; “He’s been cheesed off ever since Ronson came in looking for that Les Paul. Said the neck had a slight bend in it. Now everything’s gotta be checked twice-over.”

“You saw Ronson too, then I take it?”

“Ya snooze, ya lose, kid.”

Remus sighed, and Bo pat him fondly on the arm as he turned the guitar over.

“I dunno what he’s on about, the neck’s fine.”

“Already told him as much,” Bo nodded.

“Fucking Phil… Guess he would’ve blamed you for the Les Paul.”

“Nah, we didn’t touch that guitar, and ‘sides, I know Ronson. Did some custom work for him a few years back. I think Phil’s just crumbling under the pressure. Has been ever since his father retired.”

“Does crumbling also make you a dick?”

“Sometimes.”

As Bo dropped his magnifying glasses back down over his nose, Remus turned to his work for the day. He wasn’t really sure how he’d ended up in repairs and services, but when Phil had given him the job back in September, he would’ve been willing to sweep the pavement outside, just so long as he could hang out where the music was.

The music, he told himself, as he picked up the perfectly good Gibson and began clipping its strings; Do it for the music.

“Hey, kid,” Bo grunted, “want to learn how to replace the frets on this old strat?”

Remus glanced up, to where Phil was arguing with a guy over the price of a second-hand Telecaster. He’d barely finished the conversation before he was spinning around and harping at a young boy who was testing out one of the other guitars.

“No, no, no! You don’t play ‘Stairway to Heaven’ in here, don’t you know any shop etiquette?!”

Remus shook his head. “Don’t you think our fearless leader will have a fit if we don’t finish everything else first?”

“Maybe,” Bo shrugged, “but he can’t afford to sack me. So what’ll it be?”

Remus smiled. He really liked Bo.

“Yeah, go on.”

Bo was a patient teacher, and over the months he’d spent working beside him at the repair counter, Remus had gotten to know him quite well. He reminded him of Giles, who also tended to gab when he worked. Bo told him all about his childhood growing up as a black kid in Hackney; how he and his four brothers had all slept in the same five by five room, how his mother supported them by washing and mending other people's clothes, how he’d had his first drink at eleven, and kissed his first lady at thirteen.

“And you wanna know what? Twelve years later, I married ‘er,” he’d bragged. “And I’ll be damned if she ain’t still the finest fox I’d ever done seen.”

Bo’s father had been a veteran of the Great War, and then a drunk afterwards. Used to beat his mother, but then when his older brother Joseph—“Jo and Bo we’s used to be.”—had gotten old enough, he started beating back until they’d kicked the evil man out altogether. And then when Bo was just eighteen, the world went to war with itself for the second time.

“Egypt,” he’d said. “They’d shipped me on out to Egypt. I tried telling ‘em, I’m not that sort ‘a African, mate, but they’s wouldn’t have it. At fourteen I'd already learned to drive thanks to this Italian mate who lived in our building—name was Tomasso. He had this little coupe he'd brought over from Valle D'Aosta. Then when the war started, they interned Tomasso at the Isle of Man and repossessed his coupe for the metal. By then I was already off-continent. All day I’d drive them big officers around in my little buggy, choking on dust. But it wasn’t all bad, got to play cards with the boys in the evening, and Cairo was a handsome enough city, 'least before the Jerrys came.”

Remus knew the story well enough by now. After his base in Cairo had been captured, Bo had spent three years in a POW camp until Hitler put a gun in his mouth and the subsequent liberation allowed him to return home to his sweetheart and pop out a couple of kids. As it turned out, both of his younger brothers had been conscripted after him, though only he and Joseph had returned. Then in ‘47 Joseph hung himself in their childhood bedroom and 'Jo and Bo' had become just ‘Bo.’

“Jo was the musician, not me,” Bo said, as he traced his worn fingers over the neck of a beautiful Les Paul Custom. “I just tuned the strings for him.”

Whenever things eventually circled back around to Joseph, Bo tended to filter off. He never went into much detail, which Remus appreciated, but he was always very pragmatic. Said he quit smoking while interned because it was either trade your Red Cross tobacco rations to the Germans for a few raw potatoes or starve to death. Hadn’t touched a cigarette since. Remus had tried to relate to him, but Lyall had never been to war, and though he’d never met his paternal grandfather, he knew he’d managed to avoid being drafted when his own father sent him to Belfast for "business".

But Giles had been to war. He’d come of age in the middle of it all, and as the son of a factory worker, had nothing to keep him from conscription. When he was eighteen they’d shipped him off to France, and when he was twenty, Singapore, because the wound wasn’t already deep enough. Giles rarely talked about it, but Remus knew that he’d lost people too; an older brother and friends he’d grown up with in South London. It was an experience Remus would never know, so long as the world kept its shit together, and—reminisce of his days in the End, or perhaps because he was desperate to relate to someone real in his new environment—Remus lied to Bo about it anyway.

Just once.

“My—er... My dad did a tour in France, actually.”

“Ah, nasty business that. What’s he do now?”

“He’s a driver.”

“Good for ‘im.”

Old habits die hard, as they say.

Remus never brought up Giles or his service again after that. He felt guilty for lying, and it’d been too easy. Bo talked to him like a person—like Lee and the rest of the boys before they’d found out. He had no idea what sort of person his real dad was or how much money he made, and as far as Bo was concerned, they were the same, save maybe their age and the colour of their skin. It was that belonging again; the legacy of that miserable little boy who'd so desperately wanted to belong.

The best thing about Bo though—he did not dwell. Naturally chatty, he jumped from topic to topic with little care, and that almost always meant there was something to learn. The old expert seemed to know everything there was to know about guitars, recording, and music, though he’d never set foot on stage himself. Any and all dreadful managers aside, Remus enjoyed the work, and learning from Bo was a definite upside. His other coworkers were generally likeable as well, but he worked most often with Dorcas, who’d been hired just a few months before he had and was still a bit of a mystery. All he knew about her was that she liked music enough to put up with Phil’s bitching and that she was a part of some sort of local activist club that met half a dozen times a week and organised events like sit-ins and demonstrations outside local council meetings. She never deigned to mention any more than that, which Remus supposed was fair, considering he’d shared so little about himself. So far he’d resisted telling everyone apart from Bo that he was in a band—though it was more like he didn’t want to jinx it.

“There, make sure it’s in there nice and snug,” Bo said, observing Remus as he hammered the final metal fret into place.

“Well, well,” Dorcas mused, appearing and leaning over the counter to get a look; “Ain’t you just a regular dab hand.”

“He’s a natural,” Bo complimented, while checking over his work. “Yup, looks about ready for strings now.”

They both stood by and watched Remus restring the guitar, and afterwards Remus held it across his lap and played a quick cord to ensure everything was properly in tune. It was, and he was rewarded with an impressed clap from Dorcas.

“You gonna finally admit to me that you can play thing that too?” She teased. "Or do you only know how to play funky bass lines that no one else ever gets to hear?"

“Play it?!" Bo exclaimed. "Shit, how about he finally admits to more than just—”

“Thanks, Bo,” Remus cut-in, “but I think this is yours?”

Bo took the mallet as Remus offered it and snatched the guitar back with a knowing look before getting up from the repair bench to return it to his hook on the wall. As he did, Phil appeared from around the corner and threw his arms up.

“Oi, Grace Jones, your shift’s not over for another half-hour and I ain’t paying ya to disco with the lads. Get back on the floor!”

“I’ll be right there,” Dorcas called, before rolling her eyes in Remus’ direction. “Fucking prick. Ugh, I’ll see you later.”

He waved to her as she split, and then felt a nudge from behind as Bo returned to his stool.

“Nice girl, that Dorcas. Knows her stuff too.”

“Yeah, she does.”

“So have you asked her out on the town yet?”

“What?” Remus baulked. “No! I’m not—I mean, she’s great and all, but she’s—”

“Got bigger balls on her than you?”

“Thanks for that." Suddenly Remus felt like hitting himself over the head with the mallet. “We’re just pretty different, her and I. 'Sides, I doubt she’d be interested in me anyway.”

Bo shrugged and returned to his collection of mis-wired pickups. “Try telling her about that band of yours. Young kids like you should be bragging about tosh like that. Maybe you ain’t looking for a girlfriend, but another fan—even a friend? Couldn’t hurt.”

Remus wasn’t so sure about that, he’d had more than enough people get the wrong idea after he played it friendly, and wasn’t looking for another storm. Good thing Dorcas came with more surprises than he’d bargained for. Remus was behind the front counter when her shift had finished, busy ringing up a set of strings for a young guy. He couldn’t have been more than sixteen, but he was staring at Remus with all the scrutiny of an old woman.

“Okay, so for the nickel strings… that’ll be two quid, mate.”

“Hey… don’t you play at the Shoestring?”

Remus blinked.

“Huh?”

“Yeah, I remember you now!” The guy started. “I’ve seen you! You're Marauders—you do covers. Me and my mates watched you play there last week. Heh—the Shoestring’s the only place that’ll serve us juice under the table before six.”

“Oh. Right… er—yeah. S’my band…” Remus cleared his throat awkwardly, but the boy didn't seem to notice.

“You guys are good," he grinned. "We wanna do that someday—play in the pubs. What sort ‘a kit you got?”

“Uhm… s’a Teisco BS-36 but—”

“Right! The Teisco. My first set was a Teisco Del Rey too, actually. I’m playing on a Telecaster now, but hey, you make the Teisco sound great.”

Remus was still trying to decide if he’d been insulted when Dorcas strolled up to the counter, her jacket swung over one shoulder. The kid took a look at her and suddenly grew a bit less bold, smiling shyly as he passed the money across the counter and swiped his package of strings.

“Thanks for this,” he said. "We’ll drop by again—see you play! Rock on, mate!”

"Yeah, rock on..."

The kid flashed Remus a final wave as he left and Dorcas leaned across the counter, peering dubiously at them both.

“That was cute. What was he on about?”

“I… I think I need to upgrade my kit.”

She gave him a funny look, and then snapped her fingers toward the drawer beneath the register. “Pass me my lip balm? Just there.”

He did so, and she coated her lips in it before sticking the tube away in her pocket. “Right, I’m off. See you tomorrow, babs.”

“Uh—hold on, Dorcas, do you actually have a sec?”

She spun back around, snapping her fingers again. “Sure, but I’ve gotta catch the train in a few so be quick about it. My cuz’s giving me the big chop tonight.”

She mimed at snipping off her locs and Remus nodded quickly. After sparing a final glance around to ensure that neither Phil or Bo was within ear-shot, he leaned over the counter toward her.

“Would you be interested in coming out with me and some mates tonight?”

Her eyes widened. “With… you?”

“Yeah.”

“Aw shit, Remus, I… Look, you’re a total dish, but I’m not really…”

“Uh?” It took a moment, but then Remus’ eyebrows shot up upon realisation. “Woah, woah—no! This isn’t—I’m not asking you out, Cas.”

“You aren’t?”

“No.”

“Christ!” Dorcas bent over at the middle, hands on her knees like she was relieved. “Oh thank Christ… Scared me there for a moment, Lupin. I dunno what I would’ve done if you were actually fucking serious.”

"Huh. Poor choice of words..."

"What's that?"

Remus shook his head, stifling a smile. “Judging by your reaction, I’m guessing vomiting all over the floor was in the cards.”

Dorcas caught the sarcasm and laughed at him again. “Don’t be offended, you just aren’t my type, is all. Now what is it you really wanted to ask me?”

“I wanted to know if you’d be interested in coming to a show. It’s out in Lambeth. Know it’s a bit of a ways, but it’s a live band.” Remus gulped. “My… band.”

“Actually?” She straightened up then, eyes narrowing. “You stingy little shit, you never told me you were in a band. What d'you play?”

“Bass.”

“I know you play bass, you prat. I meant, what kind of music?”

“Oh—rock. Covers mostly right now, but we’re trying to convince the manager to let us play more of our own stuff. Like I said, the pub's out in Lambeth. It’s kind of seedy but the food ain’t all rubbish, and the beer’s decent. My—My roommate, Sirius—he works there. Can usually snag us a few pints on the cheap too.”

“I see.” She tapped her nails on the countertop, before snapping her fingers toward one of the pens next to the register. “You said tonight, yeah? Gimme the address, I’ll see if I can pop by. Lambeth don’t scare the likes ‘a me.”

“I don’t imagine much does.” Remus scribbled down the pub’s address, before handing it to her. She took it, smirking.

“Mind if I bring a friend along? It's just my boy, King. He's cool, I promise. In a band himself, even.”

“Yeah, totally. The more the merrier.”

“Aw, don’t you sound posh.” Smiling, Dorcas used the pad of her fingers to dab at the sheer balm on her lips. When she was finished she brought out a pair of dark sunglasses and set them on the bridge of her nose as she backed herself toward the shop door. “See you tonight then, Bootsy Collins,” she called. “Can’t wait for you to blow my mind in one of those cute slipovers of yours.”

“Comfortability is paramount,” Remus replied. Then just before she could go, a thought occurred to him; “Hey, Cas? Out of pure curiosity, what is your type?”

Dorcas lowered the sunglasses. “Blondes.” Then she raised them again and tossed him a final wave. “Toodle-oo, babes!”





* * *





They'd given themselves a year. One year to conquer an industry that got more and more saturated with every waking moment. At least they weren't hurting for money—a fact that would come back to bite them when people started asking how they could dare take up space in a coterie that'd had to fight tooth and nail just to feed itself. Back then they were still nobodies and therefore it didn't matter. They'd have to get used to the mob and their pitchforks, but that was a problem for a future marauder.

There would be the occasional upset, maybe a fight or two, but for the most part, those were the good ol’ days. The patient days. They were what it meant to simply exist. To be. Later, Remus would look back and miss them, but that was only after he'd forgotten dreary, monotonous moments, where all they could do was labour toward the things they wanted. You see, before fame, all one wants is for everyone to know their name, but the moment it happens, there’s no longer a steady being. You’re no longer a nobody—you’re a somebody, and somebodies never rest.

If any of them could’ve done it all over again, they probably would’ve said not to rush, but they’d given themselves a year, and a year proved to be all that was needed in the end. If they had gone back and done it differently, maybe they would’ve missed their shot. Maybe nothing would’ve ever come of ‘Marauders’. No way to tell, really. In the grand scheme of things, fame was about luck, not talent, and somehow the universe had granted them enough of both.

As Remus turned the key in the lock and nudged open the flat’s heavy front door, he was met with a call coming from the kitchen.

“Potter, is that you?”

“Just me, Lils.”

“Oh good! Well, food's almost ready.”

Humming in contentment, Remus stopped to pick up the letters that had been shoved through their post slot. Most were bills and local shop adverts, but the final envelope was different. It was a letter, labelled in tidy penmanship and addressed to him. Setting the other post aside, Remus tore open its top.



Dear Remus,

I’m so glad to hear things are going well with your new job. And your band! How exciting… I hope Mr. Black’s been keeping up with those vocal exercises. Wouldn’t want him to strain his tenor before twenty.

Things are going just fine up here, though I have to say, we’re two months into the term and somehow it doesn’t quite feel the same. Too quiet, maybe. Every now and then I wake up with a feeling that something is going to happen, like I should be expecting smoke bombs in the teacher’s lounge or rock music in church. Imagine my disappointment when the biggest excitement of my day turns out to be a bloody nose or Mr. Filch’s cat getting stuck up a tree. I am happy to report that Regulus is doing very well in music, though that might not come as a much of a surprise. Sometimes I even wonder to myself if he isn't the one teaching me. He did shock me a bit when he decided not to take up the violin, and I'm sorry I can't tell you what it is that he's chosen. Apparently I've been sworn to secrecy.

Thank you again for writing to me, Remus. Being your teacher has been one of the greatest joys of my life, and now that is done, I'm grateful to be anything more. I know that you and your friends will do magnificent things, but don’t forget the little ones either. And send me a photograph of your new flat. I’d like to see for myself where it is you now call home.

With love,

Sheila A. Buchanan





Remus smiled to himself. He could already picture what he would write back—we never put smoke bombs in the teacher’s lounge, though now I’m thinking it was a wasted opportunity—but by then Lily had appeared in the entry way, holding a mason jar full of water.

“Have a good shift, did you?” She asked.

“Mhm, and your day?”

“Oh, my lectures were fine. I’m finally getting used to being on campus anyway.” She smiled and handed him the jar. “Can you take this upstairs with you and water Remus? James and Peter have gone to get the van, should be back any minute.”

“I’m sorry,” Remus said, perplexed and tucking Sheila’s letter under one arm, “but water… Remus?”

“The plant—the one I put in your bathroom?”

“And apparently named after me. Why?”

“Well, I already have a James, Peter, and Sirius.” She gestured to the hallway table, which was supporting a very large fern. “This is Marlene, isn’t she beautiful?”

“Stunning. And why, per-say, is she named after our very human friend?”

“I dunno. Just seemed like a Marlene.”

With a light shake of his head, Remus took the jar and began up the stairs to his and Sirius’ bedroom.

“Make sure you get changed beforehand,” Lily called after him; “The boys are gonna need help moving the equipment into the van, and Sirius is already over at the pub, working!”

“Yes, Mummy-dear, I sure will!”

He heard her huff before returning into the kitchen, but by then Remus was already one flight up. One more and he was pushing aside the creaky door leading to his bedroom. It was just after seven, and they were due to go on stage at The Shoestring at half-past eight. Plenty of time to load up Mr. Pettigrew’s van with their amps and instruments and scarf down a few precious bites of food.

After pouring the mason jar of water into the leafy plant Lily had propped up on the corner edge of their loo window, Remus set the jar aside and emptied his pocket contents onto his wardrobe hutch across the bedroom. Shrugging off his coat, he quickly found himself collapsed back on the bed, mid-evening lull hitting him hard.

Now, Remus almost always slept on the right. He wasn’t sure when it’d happened, but sometime since moving in, that spot had simply become his. Though every now and then he’d roll over and bury himself into the rumpled sheets on Sirius’ side, just to breathe him in. It was almost odd; they slept in the same bed every night, and yet the left side was just so Sirius. He did it now, curling into Sirius’ side and groaning into the pillow. Fuck a job—they should’ve just gone with Sirius’ advice and played the part of the nugatory artist living off of inheritance. They’d have certainly gotten more sleep that way. Sometimes Remus really hated being a functioning member of society.

When he could finally bring himself to move again without groaning, Remus pressed up from the bed and peeled out of the day’s clothes. He’d just pulled a fresh t-shirt over his head when Lily’s voice came wailing up the stairs once more.

“REMUS! THE BOYS ARE HERE!”

“Coming!” He hollered back, tossing on his coat and shoving his wallet and keys back into his pockets. His finger jammed something hard and he hissed, only then remembering the framed photograph Sandra had given him.

Withdrawing it, his eyes scanned over the crumpled tissue paper and for a moment he considered unwrapping it and setting it upon the hutch. But then he imagined looking at it every day—and because that sucked too much, he slid it into the top drawer with his socks instead. Maybe one day he’d be able to stomach looking back on vivid memories like those, but for now, it was enough just to know that they existed at all.

Scarpering down the stairs, he found Peter and James in the kitchen, inhaling the casserole Lily had so graciously made for dinner. James looked like usual—fit without trying in a plain white t-shirt and slacks—while Peter had dressed up a bit in a wide-collared shirt and open waistcoat.

“Wotcher, Lupin!” Peter said, as Remus came in.

“Good day, lads?”

“Oh yeah,” James replied, swallowing. “As my manager would say, ‘the rush never ends at the Ritz’. It’s mental, truly. Some big-wig parliament member came in today, chap ordered bitters and tonic water.”

“That’s actually supposed to be very good for an upset stomach,” Lily interjected, pushing a plate of food in front of Remus. “Here, eat. Can’t have you passing out on stage.”

He took a seat at the table obediently, and began shovelling food into his mouth alongside his friends. “Everything go alright with the van?” He asked around bites.

“Yeah,” Peter answered; “Though I think Dad’s getting tired of lending it out. We’ll probably have to get our own soon.”

“I’ll talk to Sirius about it.”

“Sorta hate that he’s the one always footing the bill,” James grunted.

“Don’t bother,” Lily said, leaning up against the kitchen counter and bringing a cup of tea to her lips. “I think he secretly enjoys being everyone’s sugar daddy. Some more than others.” She winked at Remus, who rolled his eyes over a mouthful.

“Despite what the rest of you might think, he does not foot my bills."

"What about that new amp?" Asked James.

"That was his idea! Same with those pedals of yours, and Peter's new toms as well!"

James shrugged, muttering; "I don't mind having a sugar daddy."

“Honestly, you always have to have a chip on your shoulder, Moony,” Peter snorted. “Anyone else would just let themselves be spoiled, but not Moony—nooooo.”

They all laughed, even Remus, and Lily glanced at the clock on the wall. “Best hurry up if we’re to make it in time for a sound check.”

“Aren’t you just becoming the little band manager,” James mused, standing up to drop his plate into the sink’s soapy dishwater.

“Someone’s got to keep you lot on track,” she said, smacking him on the arse.

“Christ,” Peter grimaced. “Let the pair of ‘em move in together and all of a sudden it’s foreplay by the kitchen sink.”

“Peter!”

Remus grinned wryly, spooning his last few bites of dinner into his mouth. By the time he’d washed up and set the dishes out to dry, James and Lily were already reaching for their jackets—Peter, the keys.

“Alright,” James called, once they had carried all of the equipment up from the flat’s basement and piled it onto the curb. “Tonight’s show—scale of one to ten. I say seven. You, Pete?”

“I’m betting on a five,” Peter said, struggling with two of their biggest amps; “Ngh—Just feels like a five-kind of night.”

“Them's poor odds. How about you, Lupin?”

Remus considered. They’d been playing their ‘rate the show’ game for a while now, ever since Ray, manager of The Shoestring, had agreed to let them play a weekly gig. It was an easy way to quell the nerves, and the loser bought drinks after, no matter how bad.

“Nine.”

“Whoo-hoo,” James whistled. “Moony’s feeling optimistic. And Moony never feels optimistic. Must mean we’re in for a good night after all.”

“Maybe he’s just invited someone he wants to impress,” Lily added, handing Remus his bass. Remus took it, carefully placing it into the back of the van.

“As a matter of fact, I did.”

They all blinked at him in surprise.

“You did?”

“Just a coworker. Her name’s Cas. She’s cool.”

“Oh my god, are you actually making friends?” Ragged James.

“Piss off.”

“I think it’ll be nice,” Lily interjected. “The others are coming too. Marlene’s got the night off and Mary’s gonna head over after some rehearsal-thingy for her voice lessons. Only Lottie’s a maybe, but that’s just because she was supposed to take the train and see Roger.”

“Can’t stomach not seeing him for one weekend, can she?” Peter griped.

Lily put her hands up. “She’s your sister.”

When they had everything loaded up, the four of them climbed into the van and set off across the city toward the rundown district of South Bank. James drove, since they’d all agreed ages ago that he was the steadiest behind the wheel. Lily sat beside him, window down so the cool evening air could rush through her fire-red waves. It was kind of Mr. Pettigrew to lend them the van, but Sirius continuously griped about how rolling up to a concert in a van with the words ‘Daily London Local’ blasted on its side did little for their image. Though if he'd had it his way, they'd be carting their instruments over to gigs on the back of a motorbike.

The Shoestring Pub wasn’t exactly a high-flyer’s favourite hangout. Rather, it was a seedy hole in the wall lying just across the river. The location was central enough, however, meaning that plenty of locals tended to pop in after the dockyards closed up shop for the day. Normally their band only ever played on Tuesdays, which were much slower and tended to favour the more down-on-their-luck type of crowd, but the group that had held the Saturday evening slot had recently lost their drummer, leaving behind a hole in the ranks. Sirius had been quick to snap up the opportunity, and because Ray could grudgingly admit to liking him, he’d agreed to give them a shot on the condition that they made sure to name-drop the drink-of-the-day ahead of every show and, of course, agreed to play covers.

Only covers.

“Crowds like covers!” The manager had said, when he was outlining his conditions. “They can sing along to covers, and where there’s singing, there’s booze. It’s just the way of the world, lads.”

Remus still thought this was complete crap, but Ray was right; beggars couldn’t really be choosers.

As James pulled up to the pub’s corner, they were met with a cloud of cigarette smoke courtesy of the drifters hanging out outside.

“Remember, don’t bother locking the doors,” Peter grumbled. “We’re taking it all with us anyway and dad says he'd rather them root through the empty glove box than break a bloody window.”

Piling out of the van, they each grabbed a section of gear and carted it toward the back alley, proceeding past a drunk patron who was already passed out on the pavement. At least—they hoped he was passed out. Setting down Peter’s bass drum, James did the honourable thing and nudged the guy with his boot. He grunted and turned over in the dirt. Yup, still alive.

“Ray!” Remus cried, wailing his fist on the metal of the pub’s back door. “Ray, open up!”

A few seconds clicked by, and the door was eventually opened by a burly guy with a permanent glower plastered across his face. He was wearing his usual uniform of faded slacks and a Hawaiian shirt, the apron hanging over top stained more yellow than white.

“Playing cook tonight too, Ray?” Remus asked.

“Lonnie didn’t show up,” the manager growled. “And I thought I told you buggers to use the front door.”

“Last time we did that Pete got pickpocketed on his way in.”

“Happens to everyone at the Shoe. Think of it as an initiation.”

“Come on, Ray,” James complained. “Don’t make us lug it all around front again.”

He seemed about likely too, before craning his thick neck sideways and letting a friendly smile grace his lips. “Orright, but only ‘cause you brought me flowers.”

As the ‘flower’ in question, Lily giggled at the obvious attempt at flattery and squeezed in between them with Peter’s cymbals in hand.

“Thank you, Ray,” she said, as the manager stepped back to allow her inside before the rest of them. Remus went next, bowing his head in thanks and trying not to drop the pair of amps he was carrying.

"You only encourage him when you do that, you know,” Remus chaffed as he and Lily squeezed through the grimy kitchen.

“You don't know what it's like," Lily tsked. "Everyday I watch Potter get hit on by 'sweet old ladies'. One compliment from Sirius’ manager every now and then isn’t going to kill anyone.”

Remus glanced back at James, who was giving Ray a friendly clap by the door. The manager took one of the guitars from him, and even helped him carry it inside.

“No, I suppose it won’t,” Remus chuckled.

Inside, the Shoe was already busy—patrons sidling left and right with full pints in hand. The pub boasted a small platform on its right side for the entertainment to set up on, but all the equipment was self-supplied by the bands, save for a single piano in the corner that looked like it’d survived a bombing in Mile End. The lack of house speakers or amps made for a taxing set-up, but once those and Peter’s kit were organised, they really only needed to plug in and play.

“I’m gonna tell Sirius we’re here,” Remus told the others, when they’d dropped their gear beside the stage.

“Grab us a bevvy, wontcha, Moons?”

Remus gave James the two-finger salute and started back across the pub. He was about halfway when some old codger with foam in his beard and an empty glass reached out and grabbed his sleeve.

“You the new band in?”

“Part of it, yeah,” Remus flubbed.

“Good, good. Couldn’t stand those other muppets. Too much moaning into the mike. Have us a good show, will ya, boy?”

Remus just nodded along, used to the drunken spiel, and the guy finally released him long enough to reach the bar.

“A round of pints for the most kick-ass band from here to Hollywood, if you’d be so kind,” he said, leering over the side of the counter. Sirius spun around immediately, looking good in his plain white vest, despite having already worked a full shift. The velvet slacks that flared at the bottom and the leather choker around his neck were a bit much, but Remus was more interested in the fading burn scar, which peaked out proudly beneath the vest’s right-hand strap. He'd gotten so used to seeing it over the months they've been dating that it'd become like nothing to him, but Remus was glad Sirius wasn’t as conscious over it anymore.

“Don’t you sound smug,” Sirius smiled, already reaching for a set of glasses. He drew up short when he noticed what Remus was wearing—and Remus knew this, because Sirius always spoke his mind.

“Christ, what are you wearing?”

Remus glanced down at himself. Jeans, a plaid button-up hanging open over a Bad Company t-shirt. Normal dress for him.

“What? It’s clothes. And I think you’ll find that you’re the odd one out among this crowd. Those trousers are tighter than Mary’s.”

"That's because they are Mary's."

"You've got to be joking me."

"You wish. Wanna come kiss it?" Wickedly, Sirius smacked a hand down over one of his back pockets. Before Remus could dignify it with a response, someone had gone to the jukebox and put on the Rolling Stones.





'Baby, baby, I've been so sad since you've been gone,

Way back to New York City,

Where you do belong!'





Instantly Sirius was humming; " 'Honey, I missed your two-tone kisses—legs wrapped around me tight. If I ever get back to Fun City, girl—I'm gonna make you scream all night!'"

Tossing aside a pint glass, he reached over the bar for the front of Remus' shirt, only to have his hand batted away. But he was still singing, and might've done worse had Ray not come pushing out of the kitchen's saloon doors with a basket of chips in either hand.

“Oi, Black! Finish those orders and take a mop to the loo before you’re off, will ya?”

Sirius spun round indignantly, jerking a thumb toward the beer taps. “Can’t you get Marshall to do it? I’m on bar tonight.”

“Marshall’s gonna be covering you at the bar, now get!”

“Fine, fine,” Sirius huffed' “But listen, Ray, about what we were chatting about earlier—”

“The answer’s still no. Beers, toilet, mop—now.”

As the manager split off to deliver the food, Sirius turned back to Remus and rolled his eyes. “Still won’t let us play any originals, the sodding gaffer.”

“Guess he wants us to prove ourselves first. Mop that toilet to a shine and he just might let us.”

Sirius scoffed at him, and then finished filling the rest of the beers. “Right, here’s a few pints then. I’ll be over to help set up after I mop the fucking toilet.”

“Don’t worry about it,” Remus said, pulling his cigarettes from his pocket and handing them over. “You’ve worked hard, take a little break after. We got set-up covered.”

Sirius snatched up the cigarettes and smiled. “Have I ever told you how much I love you?”

“Only when you want something.” Remus took the pint and sipped it as Sirius leaned over to take another woman’s order. It was almost hot to see him behind the bar, his neck slick with sweat. He’d picked up bartending quick enough, though you’d be hard pressed to find anyone around the Shoestring who’s go-to wasn’t a cloudy cider or a mug of Heineken.

“Another round, Starboy!” One of the tables not far off called. Sirius pointed at them fondly in return and reached for a bottle of cheap Amaretto before catching sight of the cheeky grin on Remus’ face.

“Don’t.”

“It’s a cute nickname. You would’ve liked it once upon a time.”

“How do you know I don’t like it now? If I’m ‘Starboy’ then you know what that makes you, right?”

“No, but please enlighten me.”

Rather than answer, Sirius smiled to himself and held a finger up as if in wait. Then he pointed to the jukebox, and the chorus of the Stones’ song hit its peak.

“ ‘You’re a starfucker, starfucker, starfucker, starfucker, star—yes you are’!”

“Har-har, very funny.” Thinking it was about time he got back to the others, Remus scooped up the tray of beers and turned back toward the stage. Then in a moment of curiosity, he remembered Sheila’s letter and set the tray back down again—too curious not to ask.

“Hey, did Regulus mention to you that he isn't playing the violin anymore?”

Sirius looked up from the beer he was pouring. “He’s not?”

“Not in music class anyway.”

“So what’s he playing then?”

“Dunno, Sheila never said. But I got another letter from her today.”

“Ah, and how is the amazing god-mummy?”

“She’s fine, and I wish you’d stop calling her that.”

Sirius shrugged, flexing those wonderful biceps as he poured another drink. “Reg is old enough to do as he likes. I think it’s great that he’s trying new things. Bet he’d look good on an oboe.”

“How do you know it’s not something cooler? Like a guitar, maybe? Hm?”

“Because he's my little brother,” Sirius snorted. “Reg takes pride in not being cool. I’ll call him later, you’ll see. He’s probably picked something odd and foreign—like the didgeridoo.”

“Yeah, yeah.” Again, Remus picked up the tray of beers. “I’ll see you in a few.”

Sirius blew him a kiss, and then grinned at another guy already approaching the bar. “Angus! Two jack and cokes, I presume?”

Pints in hand, Remus swung back around and headed for the stage. James and Peter had the mikes and drum kit just about set up, and sometime between leaving them for Sirius, Mary and Marlene had shown up as well. No Lottie, which must’ve meant she’d travelled to Reading to visit Roger after all.

“Hey, you,” Marlene said, wrapping her arms around him the moment he’d set the drinks down. He kissed her cheek and when she pulled away, Marlene pinched his nose between two knuckles.

“You were supposed to call me.”

“Right!” Remus pulled his face away. “Sorry, got a bit busy. Sirius and I were up late last night working on a new song.”

“You sure that’s not all you were doing?” Mary mused from her table closest to the stage.

“What is this, national 'take the piss outta Remus day'?” Remus shook his head, then feigned a frown. “Forgive me, Cherry?”

“It’s fine,” she said. “Ended up staying late at the office anyway. Who’d have known a group of radicals would need so much fucking paperwork.”

“Does that mean you’ve been neglecting your civil duty to set any and all cop cars on fire the moment they enter your periphery?”

“Unfortunately. A zealot’s job is never done.” She smirked and reached up to finger a piece of hair that had fallen into her eyes. It’d grown longer since she’d chopped it off before their final year, and she now wore it in a rough shag, cut short around her ears and forehead. Mary had compared it to a street dog when she’d first seen it, but somehow Remus doubted that she was the type Marlene was looking to impress nowadays. The rest of her was dressed as it usually was—oversized jacket, jeans with purposeful holes cut over the knees, heavy boots that’d likely kill a man with the right amount of blunt force trauma. Beautiful, cut-throat Cherry.

“Shall I grab you a pint?” Remus offered, but Marlene just waved him off.

“Nah, I’ll go. Got a bone to pick with Black as well. I know it was him who vomited in my boots after that night out at the Roxy last week."

"If it makes you feel any better, he fell asleep that night with his head in the toilet."

"Thanks, it does. Back in a tick.” She kissed him on the cheek in return and then stepped away, just in time for James to throw his amp cable at him.

“You gonna tune your own bloody guitar, or am I to do that too?”

Remus rolled his eyes, gently whipping James in the thigh with the end of the cord as he set to plugging in his amp. The Shoe’s stage was without any lights, but they usually just dimmed the bar’s overheads and went from there. Standing on the raised platform, he could already see the pub’s patrons sizing them up, no doubt wondering whether they were going to be shit or not. As James went about adjusting the height of his microphone, and Peter quietly fussed over their impending set list, even more people began to gather; young and old squishing into the pub on the busy Saturday night.

“And how have you been?” Remus asked Mary, plucking anxiously at his D string. “Haven’t seen you since you came by the flat last time.”

Sitting off to the side of the stage, Mary set down the pint she’d been nursing and blew a corkscrew curl out of her eyes. “Things have been alright. Finally got myself moved out of my family’s place, though Marls still refuses to come with me. She says the rent’s too high. Don’t know why she’s got her knickers in such a twist over it though, I told her that she wouldn’t have to bother with it since Daddy’s already agreed to foot the bill 'til I'm out of school.”

He didn’t say it, but Remus had a feeling that was exactly why. At the beginning of September, Mary had settled into a resplendent little flat in Bloomsbury, not five minutes from Birkbeck University where she was studying the French language and culture. Similar to Lily's UCL, Birkbeck was a subsidiary college at the University of London. The area was less posh than she was used to, but she claimed to enjoy the intellectual atmosphere, and often she and Lily were able to meet each other for lunch. She was still taking her vocal lessons on the side, but remained very much casual about them whenever anyone asked.

Unlike her best friends, Marlene had elected not to carry on to university. Instead she had left home almost immediately following the end of upper sixth and picked up casual work for most of the summer before finally settling into community outreach at some local not-for-profit. She got paid in pennies but was happy enough with the work, and far too proud to let any of them pay her way—even Mary.

“It's a breeze mostly,” Mary continued. "My professors seem right pleased with me though. A few have asked me if I'd consider studying abroad for a year in Montpellier or Paris. Wouldn't that be a sight."

"And your voice lessons? How are they going?"

"Oh, you know..." She gave him a simpering smile. "My instructor says I might have what it takes to sing Baroque. Bit naff, but it's supposed to be a compliment. If you’re ever in need of that or a bel canto singer, just let me know.”

“We might have to,” James said, strutting up behind Remus; “if Sirius doesn’t feel it necessary to show up for his own gig. Christ, where is the tosser?”

“Had to mop the toilet,” Remus said. “Told him to cop a fag after. I’d cut him some slack too, you know what this place’s loo looks like.”

James sighed, unable to argue, and Peter appeared next to him, wringing out his drumsticks nervously.

“Is it just me, or are there more people here than usual?”

Remus glanced out over the crowd again; there were certainly more than their accustomed Tuesday audience. In the time since he’d left Sirius to set up, the din had turned to a full-blown clamour, and he expected they’d have to turn up the mike and amps a few decibels just to be heard over the noise. He’d gone to do just that when a familiar face caught his eye, and Remus lit up all over.

Handing James his bass, he stepped off the stage and surged forward. His arms were up before he realised it, but Dorcas had never really struck him as a touchy-feely person. She stepped back from him just as they met up in the crowd, turning the hug into a high-five and laughing awkwardly.

“I think you’re gonna have to buy me a drink first, ya hunk.”

“Sorry!” Remus chirped, surprised by himself. Since when did he hug people?

“Your hair looks great,” he said, gesturing to Dorcas’ newly buzzed scalp, mostly to hide his nerves. “Hell… I can’t believe you’re here!”

Smiling, Dorcas peeled off her jacket and threw it over one shoulder. “Yeah, well, when your awkward coworker invites you out to see his band with the questionable name, you go.”

“Ouch. I never told you our name.”

“Saw it on a sign on the way in. Marauders, right? It’s—uh… questionable.”

“Suppose that’s you being kind.”

“You know it,” she smirked, before stepping back to introduce the man standing next to her. “Brought you that friend I was talking about. This here is my boy, King.”

King was a tall guy, broad shouldered, with hair as wide and fierce as Jimi Hendrix. He wore sunglasses inside, and had a single gold earring in one ear, but when Dorcas introduced him he pulled the glasses off and nodded in friendly greeting.

“It’s Kinglsey,” he said, offering Remus his hand. “But my friends call me King.”

“Thanks for coming to the show, man,” Remus said, taking it. They shook, and subsequently Dorcas nudged Kingsley in the arm.

“King’s something of a musician himself,” she boasted. “He and his band play out in New Cross every weekend, and they’ve got an evening spot at Ronnie Scott’s twice a month.”

“I know that place," Remus nodded. "Jazz club, right? Killer tunes.”

Kingsley nodded, returning his sunglasses to the bridge of his nose. “You guys should come by sometime. See about jamming. Dee swings by all the time, mostly to mooch the free scotch. Sometimes it’s like we can’t get her to leave.”

Dorcas punched King’s arm. “Oi, not in front of the coworker.”

Remus chuckled, but it was as though a hint of some forgotten memory had trickled through to the front of his brain.

“I’m sorry,” he said, “but did you say ‘Dee’?”

“It’s just a nickname,” Dorcas surmised. “Cas, Dee—call me whatever you want, can’t be arsed anyway.”

“But she’s been Dee since we were kids,” Kingsley finished. “Little Dee-Dee.”

“King, I swear to god…”

“Sorry,” Remus nodded, brushing off the strange coincidence. “It’s just a friend of mine once knew—”

“Moony!”

It was Sirius, bounding through the rabble like a spark plug on speed. He stepped past Dorcas and Kingsley and grabbed Remus by his shoulders, already steering him for the stage.

“C’mon, let’s get this show on the road before the rotten fruit starts flying.”

“Hold on, Sirius, I want to meet—”

“Sirius!”

Now it was Marlene, pushing through with a drink in either hand.

“You forgot your beer, you dickh—” she started, but then she realised who they were with, and just like that, the moment became one of those infallible instances of utter providence. Marlene looked at Dorcas, and Dorcas looked at Marlene, and both drinks hit the floor.

A cry went up instantly as the thick pub glasses clattered against the boards, spattering the ankles of a few nearby patrons. It was enough to break Marlene’s spell, as she leapt backwards and gaped over what she’d done.

“Shit! Ooh—I’m so sorry!” She said to Kingsley, whose flared trousers had suffered most of the fallout.

“Don’t sweat it. A little spilt juice never hurt no one.”

Despite the pardon, Marlene snagged a handful of paper napkins and dove for the floor. Sirius went to help her, muttering something about how the floor was sticky enough anyway, but it was Dorcas who got there first. She bent down next to Marlene and righted the glasses, which thankfully had not broken.

“Wow. Never thought I’d see you again, blondie,” she said. Marlene looked up at her immediately, a blush enveloping her entire face.

“You…” She laughed suddenly, and it was a bit like a sigh. “You changed your hair!”

“Uh, yeah. Just today actually.” Almost looking shy, Dorcas ran her fingers along the cropped hair at the base of her skull. “Gonna take a bit of getting used to, but I think a little change is good for us, don’t you?”

Marlene’s mouth fell open, helpless and dazzled, and from their position a few feet away, Remus and Sirius exchanged a look.

“Did you…?”

“No, no idea…”

Marlene glanced at them, and quickly popped to her feet, fisting the dirty napkins. “Guys, this is Dee. We… We met in Morocco.”

"It's actually Dorcas," Dorcas amended. "There goes my grand overseas persona."

A laugh slipped out, and Marlene quickly slapped a hand over her mouth to stifle it. Luckily for her, Sirius knew how to draw a crowd.

“Oh!” He crowed. “So you’re the infamous Dee?”

Dorcas rounded on Marlene. “Been talking about me, have you?”

Remus didn’t think it was possible for Marlene to blush any harder. He nudged Dorcas, partly still in disbelief himself.

“I can’t believe you never told me you went by Dee.”

“Like I said, can’t be arsed. He just called you 'Moopy', wanna explain that for me?”

"It's Moony, actually."

"Oh, 'cause that makes much more sense."

“Oi!” Ray grunted, appearing behind them all. “Practically begged me for this Saturday night spot, didn’t cha? Now are you four gonna get up there and play or not?”

“We’re going!” Sirius trilled, already pushing Remus ahead of himself. Marlene, Dorcas, and Kingsley all went over to the girls’ table, fitting in between Mary and Lily. From his spot on stage, Remus couldn’t hear what was being said, but he knew when Marlene had introduced them from the gaping looks of surprise on Mary and Lily’s faces.

“Who’s that with Marlene?” Peter asked.

“It’s Dorcas,” Remus said. "My coworker."

“Yeah, otherwise known as ‘Dee’,” Sirius added keenly.

“Holy shit. As in…?”

“Yup. Looks like Moony’s been holding out on us.”

“We just work together,” Remus scoffed. “I had no idea she and Marlene had met before today.”

James shook head. “I’m telling ya, lads, it’s like the world’s getting smaller and smaller each day.”

“You’re right,” Sirius said, as grasped the mike; “So let’s make it a little bit bigger, hey?”

Remus looked at Sirius standing before his microphone, and could’ve kissed him. It would become a common enough feeling later on, once people had begun to chant for them rather than a stiff pint and some noise, but even then there’d be nothing he could do about it. So instead, began practising the move he’d be doing for the rest of their lives; he picked up his bass guitar, plugged it into his amp, and got ready to play his heart out.

Sirius turned to the microphone;

“Hello, everybody, nice evening so far!?”

The audience’s clamour died slightly as Sirius addressed them for the first time. They all turned to get a look at the skinny kid with the microphone and velvet trousers, but Sirius wasn’t the least bit shy. He worked every crowd for its last drop of enthusiasm, and tonight was no exception.

“I know you’ve probably realised already that we’re not your regular Saturday evening entertainment,” he said; “but I think you’ll find we’re a little more fun.”

A hoot went up from Mary, and she raised her glass as several others joined her.

“This is James Potter, our lead guitarist. He could’ve been a lawyer like his dad, instead he’s here with us ingrates. Everyone say thank you. And that there is Peter Pettigrew on drums, our resident lady-killer—just don’t tell his girlfriend.”

Peter slammed his bass pedal several times and Sirius saluted him humbly.

“And this here is Remus Lupin, our big bad bastard on bass.”

"Very funny," Remus called, as the crowd hooted and Dorcas punctuated the moment with a primely timed wolf-whistle.

“Mhm,” Sirius crooned; “I’d watch out for that one, he’s got teeth.”

Remus grabbed his own back-up mike; “Just introduce yourself already so we can bloody play!”

“Alright, alright. No need to get frisky, Lupin—that’s the audience’s job.” Sirius smoothed his hair back out of his face. “My name is Sirius Black, and together we make up Marauders. Best remember that, ‘cause one day your girlfriends are gonna be shouting our names.”

The audience laughed, and this time a woman did call Sirius’ name, just in time for him to wink and Peter to finish counting in on his sticks, and James to hit his first major riff.

“Alright, ladies and gentlemen, let’s go for a ride, shall we?”

From then on, Sirius had them. They’d played the same list of covers on Tuesday nights to moderate applause, but it was nothing like playing to a full house. In a room filled with cheering people, even a cow bell could sound cool—though, it might’ve helped that they were playing Zeppelin.





“In the days of my youth,

I was told what it means to be a man;

Now I’ve reached that age,

I’ve tried to do all those things the best I can—”





James played from his waist, sauntering up and down the stage reminiscent of Page. Peter slammed his daddy-bought cow skins so fast he was off-tempo, but it worked for the dirty song so none of them had ever said anything. Down among the throng, Marlene and Dorcas were standing hip to shoulder, screaming the lyrics and sparing chance looks at each other whenever they could. Remus was delighted—it wasn’t hard—but if he were being honest, he was paying more attention to Sirius than anything else.





“Good times, bad times—you know I’ve had my share;

When my woman left home for a brown-eyed man—

Well, I still don’t seem to care!”





God, it was bloody distracting! Remus capitalised on his fleeting bass solo, and yet all he could see was Sirius. Sirius!—as he ripped the microphone from its stand and whipped it around, snagging it out of the air just before the next lyric.





“Good times, bad times—you know I’ve had my share;

When my woman left home for a brown-eyed man—

Well, I still don’t seem to care!”





Luckily for Remus, all the audience seemed to see was Sirius as well. They loved him, even the old guys who never had anything decent to say about anyone. They raised their glasses to him, then their fists, and when that wasn’t enough, they stomped their feet and sang along until God Himself had no choice but to listen as well. The Shoestring was an old building, built before the war, bombed, and built again. It didn’t have the structure to support such madness. The floor groaned and the lights flickered, and no one was a drop sober.

“Come on, South Bank,” Sirius urged; “I wanna hear you scream!”

Their set was forty-five minutes, and they were due for another after ten o’clock, but as their final cover came to a close, Sirius swooped in, barely finished singing.

“We should play one of our songs!” He hissed, fist over mike.

“What?” James demanded. “But Ray’s already said no.”

“The crowd loves us, but we could still lose ‘em to beer and chips in a second! Just think of it, we got an entire set left—even if we suck, we can win ‘em back then!”

“I agree with Sirius!” Peter said, chiming in from his drum kit.

“I dunno,” Remus fumbled. His fingers were numb and as were his lips, though that could’ve just been the alcohol. “We’ve never sung our songs in front of anyone we didn’t already know.”

“No time like the present!” Sirius grinned. “All we just have to do is pick one and play it!”

“Easy for you to say, you’ve only got to remember the lyrics!” James said.

“I see appreciation for your lead singer knows no bounds, Potter.”

“We should play ‘Hail Mary’!’ Peter called.

“We’ve just barely finished writing ‘Hail Mary’!” James moaned.

“You remember the notes, don’t you?”

“Well, sorta—”

Sirius smacked him on the arm. “Sorta's all we need, mate! Half the people in ‘ere aren’t even gonna know that it’s not a cover!”

At Sirius’ words, Remus looked at the audience. Most people, the girls included, were peering at them with dubious expressions.
