Unlike the news van, the Volkswagen had seats enough for all of them, and Remus’ head didn’t touch the ceiling when he sat up front.

“I think it’s marvellous,” Lily insisted. “Tons of bands travel like this nowadays, and now everybody’s gonna know exactly who it is whenever you pull up to one of your gigs!”

“Yeah,” Sirius hissed. “They’re gonna go, ‘here comes Marauders in their nancy-mobile.’ I mean, come on, Evans—it’s bloody purple!”

Remus had to agree with Sirius there. The colour was certainly in your face enough; a bright electric purple with white rims. The bus’s hood ornament was missing from its front, leaving behind only a faded outline of the iconic ‘VW’, but... it was cheap.

“Here,” he said, handing Sirius the leftover cash in its envelope. “Buy yourself something nice to make up for it.”

“Maybe I will,” Sirius grumbled, pocketing the money. “Like a fucking Ducati. God knows we’re not getting anywhere in a reasonable time while driving this thing.”

With a stern grunt, Peter hopped down from the back of the van and practically shoved James’ amp into Sirius’ arms. “Considering it’s here and we have a show to play, maybe you could help us get the rest of this gear inside and worry about your van’s paint job later, hey?”

Amp in hand, Sirius spun away and stalked off, muttering words like 'bloody purple' and 'so lame' under his breath. Lily was shaking her head at him, but it was James who laughed as he shut the van’s doors.

“Don’t worry, he’ll come around the moment he realises this van’s much more conducive to shagging.”

“What a keen observation, Prongs,” Remus said, shouldering his guitar case.

“It's got the shag carpeting for it,” Peter sniggered.

“Honestly, you boys.” Huffing, Lily went after Sirius, and together they lugged the rest of their things into the pub. There they found the Shoestring’s regular Saturday night hustle waiting for them, complete with several friendly welcomes. More and more regulars were starting to take notice of them these days, and with every new gabbing mouth, their odds of stumbling across that golden opportunity seemed to be creeping closer and closer. Remus knew—all it took was the right person. After all, it’d been Brian Epstein who single-handedly raised the Beatles up from underground Liverpudlian clubs to the world’s stage, and all he’d done was take a cheap chance on one of their shows. Demos and deals aside, the Marauders needed their own Epstein, and the best way to find that was to make more noise than anyone else.

And if there was one thing the Marauders were good at, it was making noise.

“Busy tonight,” Remus said as he peered over the jam-packed bar.

“Some local group was having a football match just up the road. Guess they’re out and looking to drown themselves now,” Sirius explained, while plugging in his microphone. He went to the pub’s rolling piano next, which looked worse for wear but still played in tune. It always took Sirius a few minutes to psyche himself up before taking to the keys, but even he couldn’t deny the dimension it brought to their music. Songs like “Downtown Girls” just weren’t complete without it. And Sirius glowed—absolutely glowed when he was playing.

“Alright, come get your juice,” Ray called, appearing at the edge of the stage with a tray of drinks. They may not be getting paid for the shows, but there was never a shortage of free beer. While James and Peter rushed them, Remus held back and nudged Sirius on the arm.

"Beer, Pads?"

“Be there in a sec,” Sirius answered. “Got this tune I wanna get it down on paper before I forget it.”

Remus nodded, understanding, and watched as Sirius pulled a tiny notepad from his pocket. He was rarely without one these days. He set it on the piano’s shelf and kept the pencil tucked between his teeth as he gently tapped the piano keys. He couldn't hear it over the busy bar—doubted Sirius could either—but he knew Sirius would play it for him later if he asked.

Dropping down off the stage, Remus scooped up his gin and tonic minus the tonic and joined his friends by the girls’ usual table. Lily and Marlene were loyal and came almost every Saturday—Mary too so long as she didn’t have a date. Lottie was getting harder and harder to pin down these days. According to Lily she’d taken a leave from her secretarial program to stay with Roger in Reading, a horrible decision in Lily’s mild opinion. Remus hadn’t bothered to point out that while Lottie was living with one man fresh out of school, she was living with four. He had a feeling Lily wouldn’t have appreciated the jest anyway.

“I don’t know why you’re being so stubborn about this,” Mary was ranting. “If you’d just come and live with me then we’d have loads more fun than whatever’s going on in that bloody dosshouse.”

“It’s not a dosshouse!” Marlene countered sharply. “It’s a shared flat, no different from the boys’ place. And it’s nice. We all work together too, and downstairs there's this single mother who—”

“Your mother would have a heart attack if she saw the state of the hall toilet.”

“And an aneurysm, what’s your point?”

Mary groaned; “You’re impossible.”

Remus mostly tuned out after that. He was used to the renting debate where Marlene and Mary were concerned. For them, it was an ongoing crisis. Marlene wanted her independence and Mary wanted to keep her friend close; neither of them were wrong, just simply not in agreement.

Eventually Dorcas appeared, surprising him. She was alone today, though Remus had come to like Kingsley well enough. He was a real whizz on the sax—Regulus would’ve loved it. They’d gone down to see his group play at Ronnie Scott’s several times since meeting him, and Sirius had just about jumped at the chance to chat-up their pianist. It's all about collaboration, he'd told him.

“Didn’t know you were coming tonight,” Remus said, as Dorcas knocked her glass against his in lieu of a greeting.

“Why? Was I uninvited?”

“No—I only meant…” he sighed with a chuckle. “You know, you really need to stop doing that.”

"Busting your balls, you mean?" Dorcas smirked, sipping her drink. “Heads up, you’ve got a few wannabe skinhead pricks over by the bar. They’re hounding all the girls, and talking a lot ‘a shit about the band.”

Immediately Remus looked up. It wasn’t hard to pick out the group she was talking about. Those sorts tended to travel in packs, but even a few of them could be deadly enough. Tomny used to say that for every one skinhead, there were two steel-capped boots. For now, Remus counted twelve boots. They’d congregated near the large tables at the back, and were making more than half the bar’s usual noise.

“Sirius said a local match got out up the road,” he grumbled. “Must’ve come from there. They didn’t say anything to you, did they?”

She waved him off, clearly indifferent. “If I stopped to entertain the likes of every racist prick that crossed my path, I’d never get anywhere. They’re losers, don’t bother yourself.”

It didn’t sit right, but even if the group seemed to be not much more than teenagers themselves, it was still early. Remus wasn’t quite looking for a fight yet.

When it was finally time to take to the stage, Sirius took over with all of his usual vigour. They used to have to introduce themselves before they started, but nowadays people already knew who they were. They didn’t want long-winded introductions, they just wanted to jam. So Marauders opened as they usually did; with a cover that was guaranteed to get people into the mood. This time the song they’d chosen was slightly out of their comfort zone—a funk rock number that’d been stuck in Sirius’ head for days.





“Once I was a boogie singer,

Playing in a rock and roll band!

I never had no problems—yeah,

Burning down the one-night stands…”





There was the laughter—not directed at them, but rather at Sirius’ ridiculous show—and that really got the rest of them going. While James wiggled his hips suggestively, Sirius sauntered up and down the tiny wood panelled stage like he owned it, dressed in a white singlet with a neckline that dipped so low it might as well have been hanging past his leather-clad waist. He reached forward into the audience for Marlene, who made a play of fainting into Dorcas’ arms, while Mary leaned past her for a kiss. Sirius gave it to her, and every other girl in the room shrieked in envy. Remus didn’t mind, it was all part of the gimmick.





“Yeah, they were dancing and singing—

And moving to the grooving!

And just when it hit me,

Somebody turned around and shouted—

Play that funky music, white boy!

Play that funky music riiiiight!

Play that funky music, white boy,

Lay down the boogie and play that funky music ‘til you die!”





James loved the guitar solo. Not to be one-upped by Sirius and Mary, he polished it off with a kiss of his own that left Lily red from top to bottom. Yes, Remus decided, after watching the way the crowd rocked and flowed to the rhythm like a single sea; I can get behind funk.

On the outro, Sirius played it up, thrusting his mike out to the audience. They were delighted; their singing loud enough that the speakers managed to pick up the entire room. It really was just that good.



“Play that funky music!

Play that funky music!

Play that funky music...”





Each of them were sweating by the time they’d finished, but no one noticed. It was part of the show.

“You guys really know how to rock with it,” Sirius applauded into the mike. He was received by his usual cheering, the occasional friendly heckler, but today the crowd was extra rowdy. As Sirius launched into the usual spiel and preamble, he was joined by jeering voices from the back of the pub.

“Is this all the Shoe’s guid fer nowadeys?” One of the teen thugs barked. “Bunch ‘a sissies singing on a stage?”

“Yeah, what happened to fine drink and piss all?” Called another.

“It pissed off,” Sirius drawled; “Though if you’re really that interested, ladies, I hear the spritz is to die for.”

More laughter went up, as it often did when Sirius got the better of his hecklers. Very rarely did these things bother him, and even rarer still did their noise ever become louder than his microphone.

“Bloody poofter… Oi, did yer mum make you that skirt?!”

“No, yours did. Turns out she’s a real wiz at multitasking. Don’t know many other birds who can wank a guy off while still managing to keep her lips ‘round my prick the entire time!”

The guffaw grew, and though Remus was enjoying himself, he could tell Sirius was stomping on thin ice. The crowd’s amusement quickly died down as the skinheads got louder—shouting obscenities until Ray was bristling behind the bar. Sirius gave it right back to them ten-fold, the microphone imbuing him with confidence, but if he kept it up much longer, they’d probably end up getting jumped on their way home. Luckily James was often the sensible one. He stepped up to Sirius and whispered in his ear, playing his role as anti-devil’s advocate. Unluckily, Sirius had already had about five beers and enjoyed getting the better of people worse than himself far too much.

“Oh, what’s that, Potter? You’re saying we shouldn’t tell them their sisters called? That they already have dates this weekend? Damn. Looks like you’re out of a shag tonight, lads!”

“Fucking ponce! Fucking shitebag!” The thugs wailed;

“I’ll gut cha!”

“You and your pet ponce start high-tailin’ it back to fucking Canterbury!”

“Fucking do ya in, I will! Straight batter ya!”

“All of youse!”

The room was a clamour after that, with strangers leaping to their feet to defend their house and house band. It was frightening, but not even the threats of real gangsters could deter Sirius. Drink or not, on stage he was king. He was untouchable. It didn’t matter how English they were—this king never backed down from a fight.

“Wanna start throwing names, lads?” He shouted back. “Alright, why don’t you try meeting us outside and see where that gets you? That is if you’re done suckin’ each other off behind the rubbish bins!”

Fists pounded the air in threat, each of them eager to get a piece of the mouthy boy.

“I’ll break yer fucking legs, ya nasty poofter! Let’s see ya try twirling around like a bloody fairy then!”

With an angry cry, Sirius charged the front of the stage. He might’ve gone after them too, fuelled by the drink, had James not grabbed him round the waist. As it was, all he could do was kick out like a fitful bronco as the other men handled their assailants. Still behind his kit, Peter had started up a rolling beat on his snare drum that made every pulse in the room hammer, while the girls remained off to the side of the stage, protected well-enough by the crowd but still looking nervous and uncomfortable. Deciding that he'd heard enough, Remus unstrapped his bass and jumped down from the stage. He’d crack the poor thing over the first sucker’s head if need be.

“Yeah, fuck you too!” Sirius was shouting, having lost hold of his microphone. “Your mum’s seen more bell-ends than weekends, fucking wankers!”

It was chaos for a while, until Ray and a couple of the burlier guys from the kitchens came out wielding field hockey sticks. They waved them at the skinheads but never actually got close enough to take a whack, that would mean retaliation.

“Get out of my pub! Get the fuck outta my pub!” Ray was screaming. “Go—GO! Fucking beat it, before I call the cops on all ‘a you sorry excuses for men!”

There was more yelling, but the room had come together with Ray as its figurehead. Eventually the thugs were ejected by a group of working men, already hardened by years of dealing with smart-assed hooligans just like them, but not before the group’s ringleader had turned and pointed directly in Sirius’ direction.

“I’ll be lookin’ out for you, queenie!” He hissed. “I’ll kick yer fucking head in!”

“Oh yeah?! Well, up yours, shitebag!”

There was hooting—for Sirius or the promise of a fight, Remus wasn’t sure—but the men left, and finally everyone inside could pause for a much needed breath. It took several minutes for the crowd to settle, and by then Ray had stormed the base of the stage and grabbed hold of Sirius’ pant leg, furiously shaking him back and forth like an idiot of a rag-doll.

“My pub!” He barked. “My bar! Whatchu think you’re on about, hey?!”

High off of his own idiotic show of bravery, Sirius swallowed an obvious smile and looked out over the crowd, which was hanging on every word. Most were probably still hoping to catch a glimpse of their promised violence, but savagery or no, they couldn’t look away. They were starved of him.

Sirius grabbed the mike.

“Rock and roll, am I right, fellas?”

For a moment there was nothing, and then—just like that—they all lost their minds. The crowd cheered until Ray had no choice but to release them. They wanted more—of Sirius or the violence, it didn’t matter. People simply mobbed closer, until the stage was surrounded and Lily and the others had to fight just to remain nearby. Women, men—all of them wanting a piece of London’s newest and stupidest rock band.

On all accounts, it was their best show yet. They reopened with a Black Sabbath cover, because it was loud and the crowd wanted to be heard. The floor shook along with the thump of the bass, and James was a powerhouse on his guitar. Sirius didn’t just sing, he belted, and for the first time, Remus could see people sing along to more than just the covers. Their own songs were starting to catch on, and hearing the lyrics in that tiny pub on the Thames, Remus imagined what it might be like to hear them sung by a crowd of thousands.

Glorious, probably.

“I still think you’re absolutely mental—going after those guys like you did,” Mary said after, as they were climbing off stage with their entire upper-bodies soaked in sweat. “They’re like cue balls with teeth. If they wanted to, they could’ve snapped you in half.”

“I thought it was hot,” Dorcas retorted. "If not also completely stupid."

“It was hot, wasn’t it?” Sirius teased, attempting to sling an arm around her. Dorcas dodged it, but Sirius recovered easily when she handed him a fresh beer instead. Heart still racing from the set, Remus thought he might just pass out if he didn’t get out of the sweltering room.

“I’m gonna step out for a bit,” he told Marlene. “Fancy a fag?”

“Yeah, be out in a sec,” she replied, slipping away to join the rest by the bar.

Making his way outside, Remus pulled his cigarettes from his pocket while he set to joining the pub’s usual nightly rabble. The usual regulars stopped to congratulate him on the set and a couple even offered to buy him a drink or two. He humbly rain-checked, content to just stand back and have his cig, and it was a relaxing enough break until a loud bout of obnoxious jeering caught his attention. Glancing down the pavement, he managed to spot the same jerks from earlier all crowded around each other outside the pub’s corner entrance. Apparently Ray’s threat was enough to get them out of the bar, but not gone completely. The thugs were smoking and generally doing piss-all, but every time a pub patron accidentally stumbled too close they got the same nasty treatment as the band had. Girls were whistled at and taunted, while anyone deemed too old or ugly to shag were abused with various obscenities. It made Remus’ blood boil.

Now, now, his foul little voice said; What would Tomny do?

Nothing, he’s too busy shopping for nappies and baby bassinets.

But what would the old Tomny do? Those fuckers came after your mates.

Yeah... they did.

They did! And you know the rules—no one comes after our mates. Maybe it’s time to pull up your sleeves after all, nancy-boy.

Despite the chill, Remus did just that. It could’ve been the beer, or the joint he’d smoked on the ride over, but all of a sudden, all he wanted was a good fight. An excuse to vent his anger. He felt ashamed for not coming to Sirius' defense, and angrier still for reasons he couldn't quite place.

Weaving his way through the crowd of smoke and people, Remus stopped only when he was standing a few feet behind the first burly sack of shit that had shouted at them earlier. The group was yammering on about something, but Remus didn’t bother to eavesdrop. Instead he flicked his cigarette butt away and tapped their main antagoniser sharply on the shoulder. He spun round immediately, looking up at Remus as though he were a very tall piece of gum he’d just scraped off the bottom of his shoe. He already had a shining bruise on the top of his cheek, which Remus could only assume made him feel very tough.

“Whaddaya want?” The bruiser grunted.

“You were inside earlier.”

“Yeah."

“Wasn’t a question."

The skinhead scoffed; "You got sumffin' you wan' say to me, pansy-shit?"

“Only that I remember you. You and your mates said some nasty things about my band. And my friends.”

“Oh yeah? And whatchu gon’ do about it, ya fuckin’ pillow muncher?”

“Nothing. But I think you owe us an apology.”

The look the guy gave him was incredulous. Too bad Remus was pretty sure he couldn’t have spelt ‘incredulous’ to save his balls.

“I’ll tell ya,” he spat, “you fuck off right now, mate, before I put your head through this ‘ere brick wall.”

Remus smirked lightly. By now they’d amassed a small crowd of onlookers. He knew that the tussle from before wasn’t already forgiven, but that didn't mean that the crowd wasn't looking forward to seeing him get trounced by a bunch of teenage skinheads.

“You're right, s'my bad,” Remus amended. “I’ll go. Before I do though, mind if I pinch a fag, mate?”

“Nah, I ain’t telling ya again—fuck off!”

Remus raised his hands in surrender, but just then one of the other skinheads stepped forward, face wrinkled with a look of mischievous delight.

“I’ll allow it,” he said. “ ‘ere. You sure got a pair on ya, don’t chu? For a skinny poofter…”

He plucked the cigarette he’d been keeping behind his ear and offered it to Remus, much to the chagrin of his friends. Remus accepted, and then turned back to the first dosser, eyebrow raised.

“Got a light?”

Either to save face or because he was looking forward to beating the shit out of him afterwards, the thug acquiesced and handed Remus a metal lighter. As Remus lit the cigarette, he leaned in with a nasty look on his face.

“Hey, since we’re mates an’ all now, think you could hook me up with one ‘a them girlfriends ‘a yers? Usually I’d go for the ginger, but that fucking queen singing on stage weren’t half bad either!”

It was practically an invitation. While the others howled in laughter, Remus flicked the zippo shut and held it out. He smiled—his whole face—and when the guy went to take the lighter back, he dropped it between his feet.

“Whoops.”

“Fucking prick, whadda ya think yer—”

Remus drew a hand back—and drove it straight toward the bruiser’s nose. There was a crunch, then a very noisy grunt, as the guy flew backwards into his friends. They caught him—barely—but it was enough to ignite the feud. Instantly Remus was surrounded, but he knew where he was. The Shoestring was a rough crowd, and most of its patrons were just as itching for a fight as the rest of them.

It became a brawl in less than five seconds. Fists were flying, and Remus caught more than one of them upside the head. He got in several fine shots on the bruiser, who—despite being barrel-armed and thick in the chest—was at least a head shorter. All Remus had to do was pull back in time to avoid his shots and bring his fist up in an arc the way Tomny had taught him when he was twelve.

Punch and dodge, Lu! And watch them elbows—deadly they are!

He wasn’t sure where the memory had come from; he could barely recall it over the swarm, but the moment he did, the thought began to slip away. Like that inevitable stone beneath water.

“JUST WHAT DO YOU THINK YER DOIN’?!”

It was Ray. With a field hockey stick clutched in one hand, he grabbed Remus by the collar of his shirt and hauled him backwards—out of the fray built of clubbed boots and back toward the pub doors where his friends were waiting for him. They caught him, and Remus found himself hauled back inside the Shoestring before he could blink. A crowd had formed around the doors, but James and Sirius pushed right through them to where Lily was waiting with a rag in hand. She forced it up under his nose, practically sucker-punching him herself, and Remus pulled away, wincing, before realising that he really was bleeding from both nostrils. It smarted a bit, the rag, but not enough that his nose was broken.

“Christ, Moony! Are you trying to get yourself stabbed?” Sirius gasped.

“No,” he said through the scratchy fabric, “I leave the stabbings for Mondays through Thursdays, obviously.”

“Check his shirt, just in case,” Peter shrilled, gesturing downwards to a small tear in Remus’ t-shirt. Sirius was on him in a second, yanking it up to reveal a small slice in his abdomen. It wasn’t anything serious—a surface wound at best—but it was clearly a slash from a blade.

“You fucking idiot!” Lily wailed after. “You—You absolute bollocking imbecile!”

“What she said!” Sirius cried. Unable to help it, Remus smirked into the rag. He could hardly feel his injuries, and he’d only sort of been knifed. As far as he could tell, he was up.

“Rock and roll, am I right, lads?”

They all stared at him, before finally breaking down into little fits of their own. Even James had tears in his eyes from laughter, and Peter howled so hard he stumbled into a table and knocked over several glasses. Only Lily didn’t seem to find it funny, though that was to be expected.

Ray got everything handled eventually, and allowed Remus to remain despite the fight and his better judgement. They still had one last set to do before the night was over, but his hockey stick combined with the crowd of loyal pub-goers had been enough to drive the thugs away. No need to even ring the bobbies. Which was good, considered Remus was only half sure the Shoestring had a valid liquor licence at all.

“You’re trying to ruin your nose again, I know it,” Lily chastised, as she drew a wet napkin across Remus’ face to get the blood off. “You should know that the NHS doesn’t cover nose jobs.”

“What do I need the NHS for when I've got you to snap it back into place for me?"

She smacked his thigh, and then turned back to the bar top to grab the bag of ice as Sirius handed it to her. “Stupid boy.”

“That’s me.” Remus ran his tongue across his upper lip, tasting copper, and then glanced sideways to find Sirius staring at him, a bottle of gin in one hand. “Shall I fetch you a camera?”

“I’m trying to decide if it was attractive watching you lose that fight, or pathetic.”

“I didn't lose. It was a draw."

"That's what losers say."

"And? Have you decided?"

At that, Sirius didn’t say anything. He simply smirked and leaned over the counter, rolling his tongue in Remus’ ear. “If only Jillian Stewart could see you now,” he said. “She’d have jumped your bones leagues ago. As it is, I’m already holding back.”

“Clearly,” Lily snapped, reminding them of her presence. Remus snorted then, which hurt his nose, and Sirius followed it up with another scandalous purr, silenced only by Mary’s arrival.

“That’s quite enough of that,” she said, perching herself on the bar stool on Remus’ other side. She snapped her fingers and Sirius poured her a shot of Haig, along with one for Remus. “I can’t believe it. A girl leaves to go to the lav one time and she misses all the action.”

Having finished tying off the ice bag, Lily pressed it against Remus’ face and made him yelp. “Fuck—ow? ... Thanks for that, Lils.”

“It’s your own fault. Idiot.”

Remus turned to Mary. “Where’s Marlene?”

“She left,” Mary replied, polishing off her shot and swiftly raising her fingers into singular air quotes; “With ‘Dee’. Didn’t even stick around to watch your rousing show of masculine foolishness.”

“Don’t be jealous just ‘cause McKinnon’s getting some tonight and you’re not,” Sirius said. Mary rolled her eyes, and just then James and Peter came to join them, having collected their leftover pints from the table near the stage.

“Think you’re gonna be fit to go on stage again, hey Rocky?” James asked, passing Remus his half-empty pint. “Or should we let you go a few more rounds with Ray first?”

Remus took the drink, finishing it in a single go, along with the shot Sirius had poured him.

“How ‘bout you try putting ‘em up, Potter?” He retorted after, wiping his mouth.

“Oh yeah?”

James cackled as he raised his fists, jokingly sending several shots toward Remus’ busted face. Remus retaliated with his left hand, still holding the ice against his mouth and nose with the other, and eventually Sirius and Peter had joined in, leaving them all bouncing around the bar like a bunch of kooks. Mary and Lily reprimanded them fondly, but even they were distracted enough not to notice the stranger that had approached them from behind.

“ ‘ello there, lads!”

The fun died out immediately and Remus watched as Sirius stopped playing at feeding Peter a knuckle-sandwich and shot upright. When he spun around on the bar stool himself, Remus found a stout little man grinning back at them. He was wearing a brown suit over a horrendous paisley shirt, and was so bald that the top of his head looked like one of the shiny cue balls that were always going missing from the Shoestring’s billiard tables. He might’ve fit in with the earlier group of thugs, had he not been about twenty years too old and three feet too short.

“So this is the Marauders!” The man exclaimed, much too eager for Remus’ liking.

“Actually, it’s just ‘Marauders’,” Sirius said snidely, making James and Peter snigger into their beers.

“Ah, I gotcha. Like ‘em ‘Talking Heads’—very mod.” He paused long enough to rub both hands together, showing off the golden rings he wore on both pinkies and thumbs. “Marauders… hm, yes… Well, I’ve ‘eard plenty about cha ‘a course. Not much gets on round ‘ere without ol’ Fletch hearing ‘bout it. And what I ‘eard is that you four are the freshest things since sex, drugs, and rock ‘n—blood. Blimey son, you know yer bleedin’, ey?”

“Am I really? Why didn’t any of you tell me?” Remus grumbled, pressing the rag tighter to his nose.

With his obvious accostment out of the way, the stranger turned to the rest of his friends and continued to look them all over, like a fat hyena with a fresh carcass.

“I was told this was the place to find new talent. ‘Shoestring on the Thames’—s’got quite the ring to it. Classic origin story, stuff! Let me guess. There’s four of ya, so… I'll wager that you must be Sirius Black?”

“What gave it away?”

“Something about the look of ya!” He gestured to Sirius’ leather trousers and lack of functioning shirt sleeves. “Like a tight little Don-juan wrapped up in all the right duds!”

Sirius peered at the rest of them. “A what…?”

“I’m sorry,” James cut-in, “but do we know you?”

“Oh! Apologies, where are my manners…” The stranger snapped his thick fingers before taking the gin bottle and pouring himself a drink in Mary’s leftover glass. “Doug Fletcher, at your service.”

It didn't tell them much, and so Peter’s brow creased as he stepped forward. “And you're a friend of Ray's?”

"Weeeeell, I wouldn't go that far. He and I only met today, innit." Grinning again, Fletcher knocked back the shot neat and fumbled to pull a card from his suit pocket. It was a simple thing; reasonably business-like with his name all embossed and an office address and the words ‘A&R Manager, EMI Records’ written across the front in bold lettering. When Remus read it, he just about fell off the bar stool.

“You see, I represent the arts and repertoire for a very reputable record label,” Fletcher went on. “It’s my job to head out into the world—ontae the ‘scene’, if you would—and find the next big thing. And I think that you boys might just be that next big—massive—thing.”

Peter and James peered over the business card together, mouths hanging open so far they were practically drooling. When Sirius snatched it from them, it was with great astonishment.

“You represent EMI?” He demanded, almost white-knuckling the business card.

“That’s what the card says, don’t it?” Fletcher poured a second shot, but this one he didn’t drink. Instead he just held it up ahead of himself, like he were CEO of a multi-million dollar company, negotiating over a fine glass of sherry.

“Now I’m tellin’ ya, you lads come on the scene at a pure, prime time! Music’s ‘a changin’ an’ the studios are starving for some fresh sounds. Sham 69, The Undertones, Pistols—all of em, young guns, just like you! Heh—no pun intended. But they’re the ones changing the scene, right? The rest of the industry, they’re all doing the same thing. Radio hacks, I call ‘em. All synth this, electronic that. But real rock—now that’s sex itself. You heard ‘a Van Halen, eh? How ‘bout Whitesnake? Cock Sparrer? Or Christ—what’s the new one… The Police!”

“Aren’t they the group doing all that white reggae?” Sirius asked, while the rest of them exchanged a dubious glance. “Might as well ask us to jam with the Dire Straits. Fancy being the next ‘Sultans of Swing’, lads?”

“Alright, forget the bloody Dire Straits!” Fletcher hissed. “Too folky anyway. My point is—you’s already got the songs, I ‘eard ‘em. Great stuff! Bleedin’ hits in the making! But more importantly, ye’ve got the look! And ‘tis look that I can sell. I mean, hell—I love it! You’re visceral—seismic! Caustically likeable! People want fresh—gritty. Punk rock’s backsliding, and all ‘a us wee folk are tired of the huge stadium bands. We want new fish, and you lads are it, I’m telling ya. You’re like little unsung entertainment juggernauts!”

“I dunno, they just sorta seem like a bunch ‘a virgin nobs to me,” Mary said, making Lily snort into her drink.

“Ah! And I see you’ve already got yourself a couple ‘a lovely ladies to tag along,” Fletcher grinned. “Inspiration central! Nothing makes for a number one hit better than heartbreak. Not that you’ll ever be hurting for company. Just wait until you tour the Balkans, that shite’s as easy as Jagger with his fly undone!”

Fletcher nudged Remus pointedly, but when none of them laughed, the manager quickly cleared his throat.

“So, you lads got a demo then?”

Now it was their turn to be nervous.

“It’s a… working thing,” James blabbed.

“As in…?”

“We’re working on it,” Remus finished.

Fletcher nodded sympathetically. “Ah, I get it. First step’s always the ‘ardest, ‘specially for up and comin’ groups such as your good selves. We used tah think that making the entire album was the ‘spensive part, but nowadays, all ‘a it’s gone through the roof. Poor buggers don’t stand a chance, not without being signed first. And well, no one’s gonna sign ya without a demo, will they? ‘Fraid that’s life, lads. Nah money, nah fame…”

“It’s not that,” Sirius interjected. “We have the money, it’s the studio space we don’t got.”

“I see.” The manager stroked his chin, suddenly more invigorated. “In that case, I might be able to get you guys in over at De Lane.”

Remus' jaw dropped. "As in De Lane Lea Studios?”

"Way to go, dork," Sirius teased. Remus smacked him for it, but Fletcher only looked keen.

“Ah, you know it, eh? Well, would I be right tah assume that you also know who’s recorded there?” The manager leaned in very close, like it was a secret he’d been dying to share. “All four ‘a them Beatles sat at those mixing tables. Pink Floyd used to have it out in the booths too, same with the Who. Legend has it that studio two’s still got a hole in the wall after Pete and Roger got a little too rowdy and one of ‘em put their fist through it. If it were me, I’d bet on Townshend. Why, I even had a similar conversation with Jagger once, but he’s always favoured Roger. Said he was real spazz that way. Speakin’ a which… none ‘a you would happen to be Queen fans, would ya?”

Fletcher could’ve been asking them to sign their own death warrants; they were in it now. Utterly drooling over the idea of recording in the same place their heroes had once stood. Hook, line, and sinker.

“Payment’ll be upfront ‘a course,” the manager told them, “but I got a guy. Works the late shifts at the studio. Can probably get you in after hours. You ain’t bound to see anyone else while the studio’s shut up for the night, so don’t get yer hopes up of running into no bloody Keith Richards, but we’ll see if we can getchu all set up, we will.”

“So you really want us to—to…” For once, Sirius was at a loss for words. James had to smack him on the back for him to spit the words out; “You’re gonna let us cut a demo in your studio?”

“You said it yourself, all you’s need is a place to record, right?”

“Yeah...”

At that, Fletcher raised his tiny glass of Scotch. “So whaddya say, lads? You wanna make an album?”





* * *





The next morning, Remus would not remember their answer to Fletcher’s million dollar question. Yes, obviously, but anything else—negotiations and the like—would be lost to the whirl of celebratory drink that had followed. Sirius had announced the good news to the entire pub at the head of their second set, and afterwards some kind well-wisher had offered each of them a bump in the men’s toilet.

They’d accepted, of course. They were rock stars now—or at least on their way. They’d have to get used to things such as strangers openly offering them drugs. Up until then Remus had never tried cocaine, Tomny had kept all of that private, but he found the experience not all that different from being drunk. When he was drunk things that usually bothered him tended to fall away; everything was funny, and he was more confident. Up. Cocaine made him twice that. It was the perfect social lubricant. He took to the stage like he’d been born on it, and as a result, had strangers pour themselves out to him.

Remus poured right back. A social waterfall.

“Man, you guys are amazing!”

“Thanks, man!”

“Heard you were making an album?”

“Guess so!”

“Will I see you on ‘Top of the Pops’ someday?”

“Maybe!”

Fletcher bought them drinks on credit. Even James, who was supposed to be driving the van back, gave in after he offered to send a car for them. The instruments would survive until morning. Fletcher talked and talked about brands and companies, and all the bands he’d met and signed—Did you know that Rod Stewart only ever wanted to play football? Now he’s got nine number-one albums!

The Marauders ate up every word.

“And just wait ‘til you start getting fan mail—up to the ceiling, it’ll be! We’ll work out a post box later, after you’ve signed all the contracts. Got a dream venue? Somewhere you’ve always dreamed of playing?”

“Madison Square Garden!” Sirius exclaimed. “We want the Garden within four years. Wembley in three. Hammersmith Odeon in two. I don’t fucking care where else.”

“Right. No tall order then.”

“And ‘Top of the Pops’,” James added, having spoken to the same shrill party-goer as Remus. “Debut on the ‘Pops’ would be cool. We wanna be national.”

“I’d like to see Japan,” Peter finished. “And Canada. People tour Canada, right? They’ve got mountains.”

“And you?” Fletcher turned on Remus, fresh whisky in hand. “What’ll it be for our killer bassist?”

Remus blinked at him. His nose and throat were numb from a second bump. Ray had put on Roxy Music over the bar’s speakers and he imagined the song was theirs.

“I want Marauders to be the biggest band on Earth.”

Fletcher grinned at him.

“Then I guess we’ve got some work to do.”

They clinked glasses, and it sounded like diamonds. Sirius was staring at him like he’d hung the stars himself. James hugged Peter close, called him brother. Remus asked Fletcher for a pen. He handed him the one from his suit pocket—gold plated—and he wrote a lyric on his palm.





I’m the disappointing kid, bred of them upper class

Dad paid to get ahead, I say ‘finish last’





He’ll have sweat it off by morning.

They ordered another round, this one on the house, and before the drinks even arrived they were being cheered back onto the stage for an encore. Lily and Mary had already gone, tired from their long day spent at school, but they had new friends. Fans. Ray and Fletcher stood by the stage, clapping with a fat cigar in hand. It’d be late soon, well past the 11PM British pub hours. Not that it mattered.

They were rock stars.

They were on their way!

And not for one moment did it occur to them that they were being completely and utterly scammed.

Chapter 99: "Wotcher!"


Chapter Summary

The boys start their first step of becoming real rock and roll stars, and boy is that step a doozy.



Chapter Notes

CW for THIS chapter: Intrusive thoughts and BPD triggers in the first scene. He makes some bad decisions and says things he doesn't necessarily mean, so if this is at all triggering for you, please don't hesitate to come over to my tumblr (@motswolo) and ask for a summary of the first scene.
