Wednesday 6th December 1978





They met up in a tiny greasy spoon cafe near Whitechapel, off the corner of Cable Street and not far from Tomny's flat. Its front windows were decorated in twinkling lights and cotton made to look like fake snow, and there was a flyer pasted on the front door advertising visits from Santa Clause at the nearby shopping centre. Remus would wish that he’d picked somewhere nicer the moment he sat down, but Tomny had insisted—nowhere fancy. They were not fancy folk, as he said, and even if they were, no one did a good fry-up like the average working-man anyway.

When Remus arrived he’d found Tomny smoking outside on the pavement. For a split second he imagined what it might be like if he were just meeting his friend to catch up. Would they batter each other around a bit? Go find some half-empty paint cans and get to tagging the streets? Maybe they’d pop a lock or two, rob a corner shop—have some real fun. There certainly wouldn't be any talk of jobs or babies. Remus missed it, but he knew by the way Tomny looked at him that there was no going back.

Thonas Armstrong had made up his mind, and Remus was just going to have to get used to it.

“I feel a bit bad,” Tomny said, “making ya come all this way.”

“I live in Shepherd’s Bush now, not China. I think I remember my way around St George's East. Best watch out or it's you who's gonna turn amnesiac, ya old fart.”

“Cheeky shit. Fine, c'mere.”

Tomny hugged him tight. Remus hugged back.

“Aw, Lu... I’m glad we’re finally doing this."

“Me too.” As they pulled apart, Remus tucked either hand into an arm pit to ward off the cold. “So… Where is she then?”

“Skylar? Oh, she’s inside already." He raised the cigarette meekly. "Says being around all the smoke is bad for the baby. M’gonna try and quit, maybe. Might even save meself a few quid, innit.”

And the coke? The dealing? Remus wanted to ask. Have you managed that already?

“Gonna need the money for nappies anyway,” he said instead.

Tomny chuckled, and then flicked his cigarette butt down a nearby street drain.

“Shall we?”

She was waiting for them in a corner booth, the red vinyl seat off-setting the dark navy of her winter coat. She waved when they came in, and Remus’ stomach plummeted. Skylar was pretty. Perhaps if she weren’t he could’ve compounded a poor appearance with the fact that she was up the duff without a penny to her name and created some real pity for the girl. But it was not to be. Dishwater blonde, same as Tomny, with eyes the colour of melted chocolate. She had a few moles, charming ones, with a pouty little mouth. A true countryside princess, with an Essex accent.

“It’s a pleasure to meet youse,” she said, after he’d sat. Then she offered him her hand. The other she kept cradled around the base of her stomach like it was this great weight to bear. Remus didn’t know why; he’d asked Lily and with her due date set for late April, the baby couldn’t have been bigger than a lump of dryer lint. But Remus shook her hand anyway, and introduced himself properly, determined to make a half-decent impression. It was just one meal. He could make it through one meal.

"Oi, Bruce," Tomny called, instantly garnering the attention of one of the guys in the kitchen; "cup of coffee for this one and three of your best fry-ups. Just put it on my tab."

"Ain't got no tabs 'ere," Bruce replied.

"Not even for me?"

There was some grumbling, but Remus could tell it was in good faith when Bruce ambled out of the kitchens with a fresh pot of coffee.

"Thanks, Brucey. Throw in some extra bacon and I'd say that favour you owe me's settled."

Tomny tossed him a wink, and after Bruce had gone, turned to Remus.

"Don't worry about Bruce. Food's cheap and he only spits in the eggs on odd days."

"Actually I thought I'd get your breakfast today," said Remus. "You know, as a shitty congratulatory."

"Don't play daft. I told you today was my treat, and so it shall be." He pushed one elbow up onto the back of the booth and tucked a lock of Skylar's hair behind her ear for her. "You can buy me a real present later."

"Yeah, alright," Remus scoffed, wrapping his hands around the warm coffee mug. So far Skylar had said very little, and Remus had almost pegged her for shy until she set her own mug down and leaned in.

"I'm not being funny, but I was expectin' a bit more of ya," she giggled. "Tomny said youse were posh. Half-expected you tah kiss my hand when you walked in 'ere."

"He's been known to do it once or twice," Tomny said snidely, while Remus ignored him and stirred several sugar packets into his coffee.

“Tomny says youse are in a band?” Skylar said genially.

"Yeah, I am."

"And you sing too?"

Tomny smirked over the rim of his own coffee, and Remus resisted the urge to kick him beneath the table.

“No, I just play bass. We have our singer, but you really shouldn't bother yourself with Tom, Skylar, all he spouts is rubbish.”

“Nah, nah, I stand by that one,” Tomny grinned. “Go on then, tell ‘er about the band. ‘Marauders’, innit?”

Remus shook his head sheepishly. “It’s just a thing.”

“Now that’s fuckin' pish.” He looked to Skylar. “Back-breakingly modest, ‘e is. Any'fin you wanna know about music, this guy 'ere knows it. He used to park ‘imself in front of the radio all hours. Sometimes I’d find him asleep on the floor, hugging the thing like a teddy bear.”

“Sod off,” Remus said, flicking a plastic fork at him. Tomny laughed, picking up the fork and using it to pick his teeth.

“You guys playing in any big name clubs yet?”

“Not really. Got a thing over at this pub in South Bank—one I told you about."

"Aye, right."

"But we’re looking to cut a demo soon.”

“What’s a demo?” Skylar asked.

“S’like a resume... For music," Remus pandered. "Comes before the album. It’s where I’m headed after this actually. Gonna meet the guy organising it for us, see if we can’t pass the tape on to some studios after.”

"That sounds exciting," she replied, as Tomny tossed the fork aside and went on sucking his teeth.

“So that getaway plan of yers was for real then? Thought you jus’ didn’t want to hang out with me.”

“You know it’s not like that," said Remus. Tomny waved him off, playful, while Skylar glanced between them both. She popped a fried tomato into her mouth, chewed, and then straightened up in the booth.

“So you two grew up together then?” She asked.

“Er, not really.”

“Sure, we did!” Tomny exclaimed, sounding offended. “I’ve had you goin’ on six years now.”

“Off and on… S’not exactly like we were neighbours or anything.”

“Pish,” Tomny said again. He gave Remus an odd look, then turned sideways in his seat to look at Skylar. “I found 'im in a park. Little sod was crying like a girl 'til I came around. After that he used to run away and visit us all the time. Straight turned up outta the blue most days. Had to bribe him jus’ so's he'd go home. And ‘e had this driver—more like a parole officer, really. His name was... Oh, bollocks—what's the fella's name again, Lu?”

"Giles."

"Giles! We's shared custody, me and 'im. Lu was too much of a handful for anyone else to tolerate. Still rings true today."

While Remus rolled his eyes, secretly pleased, Skylar clapped her hands together in great realisation.

“Oh, I know 'oo you are now! You’re that Lu, aren’t cha? Tomny's told me about you... You’re the one that grew up in the big 'ouse with all the dogs and them. You went to that poshy school! ... Your dad’s some sort ‘a fancy minister or something.”

Suddenly the coffee felt thick on Remus' tongue.

“Yeah, that’s me…”

“I used to know someone 'oose dad sorta did that too," Skylar went on, "but 'e was only a parish rep—not even a real priest—so 'e made shit money. How does your family do it then?”

Again, Remus shifted uncomfortably. “My grandfather owned a lot of land. Sold most of it before he died, and my dad didn’t have any siblings so…”

“Christ, you never told me that,” Tomny gaped. “I'll wager that’s a fat inheritance.”

Afterwards, Skylar swatted him on the shoulder. “Tomny, you nob—why didn’t 'oo tell me he 'n Lu were the same person?”

“Didn’t think I had to. Lu’s Lu, Sky. Does it look like I got many poshy public school kids stuffed up my sleeve?”

He waved his jacket sleeve for emphasis and Skylar only shoved him by the arm. She kept her hand there afterwards though, and Remus stared at it, lost in an unformulated thought.

“You must have a lot going on then,” Skylar said, snapping him from his daze. “Or, I’ve heard lots anyway. Tomny talks about you plenty. You knew Lee and them.”

"You've met Lee?"

"Oh yeah, 'e's come round the flat a few times, innie. A bit of a dosser but nice enough so long as Tomny don't ignore 'im for too long. Gets a bit frazzled otherwise, d'ya know what I mean?"

The comment stung, more so for the fact that she could’ve known ‘Lee and them’, but thankfully Tomny got there first.

“Sky, I told you that’s off limits,” he said lowly. “Lee is—”

“I remember, I’m not thick,” Skylar replied curtly. “But they were friends once, now I can’t even ask about it? It’s not like he’s offering much to the conversation…”

The couple shared a sharp look, and Remus got the feeling that it was an argument they’d had before but hadn’t really had a chance to finish. He wished they’d stop talking about him while sitting right in front of him. In fact he wished he’d never come at all, but he was godfather now—or would be, in four and half months. Christ.

One meal, Remus thought, Just one meal.

“So how’s work coming, Tom?” He asked finally, clinging to every word. He was rewarded when Tomny champed at the bit, probably just as desperate to take the heat off.

“It’s orright! Better than I thought, at least. Burrin’s already got me working with him on the books.”

“Gambling?”

He shrugged. “I just count the bets, mate. Working the books, it's honest enough work, innit. S’usually slow down at the tracks this time of year, but there’s always work to be had. It’s a fucking hike to get there though.”

“Thought you were gonna get a car?”

“We did. S’a 1963 Hillman Imp. Runs like a can ‘a shite though, jus' like the name. Overheats at ten degrees and I think that petrol tank is a bottomless pit.”

They shared a chuckle, but Skylar didn’t seem all that amused. She sipped her coffee and then placed a firm hand on Tomny’s shoulder.

“Remus, did Tomny tell you we’re thinking of moving?”

Remus’ smile faltered. “Moving…?” Like, for real?

“Yes, out of the city—”

“She means out of the hustle and bustle,” Tomny cut-in. Skylar gave him a tight look for it, but still smiled at Remus.

“We hope to find one of them row-houses eventually,” she said. “Get out of council housing. Nothing huge, just someplace big enough to park the car—a nursery for the baby, you know.”

Suddenly alarm bells were starting to go off in Remus’ head. Abort! Abort! But Skylar and Tomny were looking at him. He had to say something.

“You’re gonna leave London? Just like that?”

“No, never,” Tomny replied. “I ain't going anywhere. Maybe jus'... Havering or something. Still counts.”

“But it ain’t in the city.”

“I think Southend-on-Sea would be nice,” Skylar interjected. “It’s not too far, and plus there’s always a pier that Tomny could find work—”

“So what? You’re gonna work on a pier for the rest of your goddamn life?”

The comment was sharp, perhaps sharper than Remus had meant for.

“No,” Tomny scoffed. “But it’d be nice to be somewhat closer to work. No room for dog or horse racing 'ere, mate—all the decent tracks are out yonder.”

“So you're gonna give up the flat.”

It wasn't a question, but Tomny answered like it was; “Not entirely. I’m thinking ‘a letting one of the other lads take over the lease for a bit. You know I can’t afford two rents, but 'least the flat's cheap.”

Calm down, Remus told himself. You can’t lose it over a fucking address.

“Right,” he managed. “Well, that’s… You, er—You really sound like you’ve got a plan going.”

“We do,” Skylar smiled. “And that’s not all. Tomny’s promised 'e's gonna get ‘imself clean so that we’ll all be ready when the baby comes."

Instantly Tomny was chiding her. "Lu don't wanna 'ear about that, sweetheart."

"Why not? You should be proud." She looked to Remus; "He’s been going to AA. Two weeks clean already, isn’t that brilliant?”

Remus was stunned; he barely heard the rest of her sentence.

“AA, as in… Alcoholics Anonymous, Tom?”

“Jus’ a few meetings,” Tomny said sheepishly. “Thought I’d give it a go. It's not that serious.”

“Really? Just—give it a go?"

Don’t.

"Boy, don't you sound committed.”

Stop.

“You're sure it's not ‘Narcotics Anonymous’?”

He's just embarrassed.

Remus leaned forward; “Or do you plan on keeping the blow on the down-low while you’re changing nappies and coaching football practices?”

“Oi!”

A line had appeared between Tomny’s brow, furrowed in hurt and confusion. It should've been enough for Remus to stop, but part of him didn't want to. Instead he was a bucket tipped; the anger swept forth like toxic oil down a river, and this time he went with it.

“I’m just saying, seems like a lot all at once. A year ago you would’ve rather cut off your arm than move out of the city. Very well couldn’t, not with all your customers being—”

Tomny slammed a hand down on the table, making the dishes rattle and Skylar jump.

“That’s enough," he swore. "No... No need to dredge up the past.”

“Oh? I didn’t realise it was ‘past’.”

“Yeah, it is. So leave it already.”

Remus clamped his lips together, and it ended in a stare down. He barely saw Skylar. And then that nasty voice crept back in with vengeance.

He's always calling the shots, isn't he? it hissed. It’s his fault she left so where’s his punishment? 'We don't care—we don't care'? How 'bout he doesn't care!

One of the salt shakers had upended itself when Tomny slammed his hand down. Remus watched as Tomny traced a finger through the mess absentmindedly. He thought he could hear him mutter the words "bad luck" under his breath, but the whisper was gone a moment later when Tomny brushed his hands off and took a deep breath.

"How yer dad then? Still busy being a pompous sack of shit?"

Under normal circumstances Remus would've accepted the jab as an insult meant only for Lyall and not a reflection of his own character, but he was feeling spiteful all of a sudden.

"I thought we came here to discuss your family," he scoffed. "You know, the one you're lying to."

"Lu." Tomny cocked his head. "Don't."

“Don’t what? I mean, really, Tom—don't you think Skylar should know everything about you if she’s gonna be sticking around? I mean, you made a baby with her, after all. Reckon that means you're alright with her picking through the rest of your dirty laundry.”

Before Tomny could lash out at him, Skylar cupped both hands around her boyfriend's bicep. “I know about the drugs, Remus," she said, looking earnest. "And I want you to know that I don’t care. Everyone makes mistakes, but Tomny's gonna right them. He's gonna come out better, just like I did. Hell, when I met Tomny, I was drinking a bottle a night jus' to get to sleep and going wiv' any guy that'd so much as look at me twice.”

“Yeah, well... I imagine it’s a lot more lucrative to forgive your drug dealer.”

“What'd you say to her?" Tomny echoed. "Lu, you need to shut the fuck up right now.”

“What? You mean to tell me that you haven’t sold any dope since coming back here, Tom? Yeah, right.”

"He hasn't," Skylar insisted. "He told me he hasn't."

"Nah, just look at him. He's lying to ya, Sky."

A vein bulged in Tomny’s neck. Remus had never seen him so angry, and though he was alarmed, a part of him revelled in it.

“Didn't he tell you, Sky? Suppose it feels like a lifetime ago now... But he did it. For years. All the way from Limehouse to Shoreditch—Tomny had it all. Uppers, downers, blow, barbs, smack! Whatever fits your fancy, really. Didn't he tell you any of that? Did he tell you about all the times we got high together? Or—Or the fights he got into? And how about Lee’s brother, hm? The one who was knifed in an alley? Or me? Or... Or Tonya! Don’t tell me he forgot to tell you about Ton—”

“REMUS!”

The shout was loud enough to draw the attention of the entire restaurant. Like before, Remus and Tomny barely noticed, it was only Skylar who flinched. She looked down at her lap to avoid the strangers' stares and began fidgeting her fingers with red, burning cheeks. Across the table, Remus had both hands fisted together so tightly he could feel the bite of his nails in either palm. The look Tomny was giving him was absolutely deplorable, and he deserved every second of it.

I’ll hate her, he'd told Lyall once, I’ll make her hate me too.

“I think I need to use the lav,” Skylar murmured.

“Yeah, think I’ll step outside for another fag,” Tomny said flatly, his eyes never leaving Remus’ face. “Lu was just leaving anyway.”

Skylar stood up, pretty mouth puckered, and set her napkin down on the table. “It was nice to meet you, Remus," she said, and then she left, shapely hips swaying on her way.

Hate her, the voice said.

“Get your fucking coat,” Tomny told him. “You’re done.”

Remus didn’t even have it in him to be sorry. He followed Tomny out onto the icy street corner, shoving his hands into his pockets as Tomny rifled around for a fag. It was cold outside and the pavement was empty apart from a few passing pedestrians and the occasional car. Remus would be due at Fletcher’s office soon—he was meeting the boys. What a fucking mistake all this had all been.

“You crossed the line,” Tomny told him, when he finally had the cigarette lit. “You did it on purpose. You wanted to fuck this up for me.”

Remus shoved his hands in his pockets bitterly. “Guess I just thought I’d save you the trouble of doing it yourself.”

“Oh fuck you, Lu! What’d I ever do to you to deserve this?”

“You brought me here!”

“ ‘Brought you here’— ha! That’s rich! Forgive me for wanting my best friend to be even the least bit involved with my life! You know, you really are just some spoiled, pampered prat. You think you can take your anger out on Skylar just because you have abandonment issues? Welcome to the fucking club!”

“Only assumed she’d want to know about what it is you really do, but I guess I was wrong," Remus blabbered. "I just don’t know what makes her so fucking special that you’d hold off from telling her the truth.”

“She’s having my kid!” Tomny wailed. “She’s gonna be the mother of my child, you fucking bellend!”

“You sure about that? Said it herself, didn’t she. Are you sure this kid’s even yours, Tom?”

It was too far. Remus knew it the instant the words left his lips. And he didn’t blame Tomny for a second, even as he brought his fist up in one fell swoop. The punch was solid, catching him on the jaw and slamming his teeth together with a painful snap. Remus went sprawling to his knees on impact, but he’d saved his teeth and tongue. Lee had once told him a story of a guy who’d made that mistake during a fight. Ended up severing the muscle clean off. Mute ever since.

“You're lucky,” Tomny hissed, shaking out his fist; “that was my left.”

Remus raised his head, icy pavement biting through the fabric of his jeans. Tomny's punch coupled with the wet ground had zapped him of all his anger, leaving him feeling only miserable and ashamed.

What have I done?

“Fuck... Tom, I—”

“No," Tomny groaned. He looked ill, like he might vomit. "You... You just shut your fucking mouth. I can’t—I... Fuck! Fuck—shit—FUCK!"

He punctuated the cry by spinning round and kicking out at one of the rubbish bins the cafe must've set out that morning for rubbish collection. Luckily the bin was empty, but it did bounce several metres down the pavement, nearly taking out the knees of a well-dressed man walking the opposite way. He glared at Tomny as he passed them, and Tomny raised him the single finger salute and bellowed a sharp: "Who you think yer lookin' at?"

Afterwards there was no one left to yell at or kick but each other. Anxiously, Remus got to his feet, fists clenched at his sides.

"I'm sorry, Tom."

"No, you don't get to be sorry," Tomny hissed, pointing a vicious finger at him. “ You ..." A shaky breath; "You just don’t get it, do you? I needed to make this work.”

“For who—her? For the kid?”

“For myself, you right bastard!”

Aching deeply, though in no way worse-off than his friend, Remus took a step forward. He wanted to apologise again, but he watched as Tomny retreated from him and knew that another "I'm sorry" would get him nowhere.

“Please, Tom,” he begged instead. “Tell me how I can make it up to you.”

“This ain’t about making it up to me! I brought you here because I wanted you to meet Skylar. Cause—Cause I wanted you to like her. And then you go and pull this shit! Like fuck, Lu! … And to mention Tonya? Christ, why’s it so hard for you to be proud of me?”

Remus almost whimpered.

“I am proud of you, Tom.”

“Yeah, well it ain’t enough.”

And perhaps it wasn’t. For three years Remus had feared only being left behind, and now that Tomny truly had gone ahead he’d become hysterical. It was his own fault. Tomny had offered him a hand— come with me, be a godfather— and he’d ruined it. He could see it in Tomny's eyes, and felt it as he watched him turn away.

"Where you going?" Remus asked.

"Away.”

"No. No, you said you weren't going anywhere."

"And you said you were happy for me... Guess that makes us both liars."

"So that's it?" Remus demanded. "We're done? Just like that?"

Tomny stopped, his shoulders collapsed inward like a child's. For a long time Remus didn't think he was going to turn around, but then he did, and Remus regretted it all over again.

“I think you should go, Lu,” Tomny told him, calmly stubbing out his cigarette on the cafe wall. “Just… Good luck with all your band shit or whatever. M’sure I’ll hear it on the radio someday.”

And then Tomny moved past him, back into the cafe. The door jingled and a corner of the Santa Clause flyer fluttered in the wind. It would be warm inside, Remus knew, but he didn't deserve the comfort. He deserved only the ice in his bones.

Turning, Remus started up the street toward the nearest tube station where he might be able to catch a cab. Did this mean he was relieved from all future godfatherly duties, he wondered?





* * *





When Remus fully came to again, he was sitting in the back of a cab on his way to Fletcher’s office. The address he'd given them was situated along Coventry Street, just off Leicester Square in Soho. It was a unique area, for lack of a better word—one that felt seedy in the daytime only to come alive with bustle and neon the moment the sun dropped below the horizon. Handing the cabbie a fiver, Remus clambered out of the cab's back seat and found himself knee-deep in Chinatown likeness. Adverts for take-out and call-girls littered the damp street corners, while air stinking of exhaust and local cuisine floated overhead. Across the street lay the iconic Prince of Wales Theatre, dull orange bulbs advertising its in-house comedy show. ‘Too funny for words’, its marquee read; ‘If you don’t laugh—sue us!’

All around him people shambled on by, out to catch an early matinee or else pop into one of the many couture shops or peep shows lining the strip. Remus found his friends standing outside a sex shop bearing the name ‘Tunnels of Love’, sharing a cigarette between the three of them while they waited. It was Peter who spotted him first, pushing the fag onto James and rushing forward, nearly slipping on the slick pavement.

“Moony—Finally! We were starting to wonder if you were ever gonna show.”

He shrugged, hands in his pockets. “I’m here now. Why didn’t you guys go inside?”

“Couldn’t very well go in with three-fourths a band, could we?” James replied, stubbing out the cigarette. “Feeling ready then?”

“As ready as I’ll ever be.”

"Good," said Peter, "I'm tired of freezing my balls off out here."

If James or Peter picked up on his lack of enthusiasm, they didn’t mention it. It wasn’t until they’re rung the building’s door buzzer and were making their way up the set of interior stairs adjacent to the sex shop that Sirius mentioned the meeting with Tomny.

“So, how’d it go?” He asked, keeping his voice low so it might be muffled by the creaking sound of their boots on each step.

“Fine,” Remus replied, before realising he was going to have to try a bit harder to keep his curiosity at bay. “Tomny got a new job down at the dog tracks.”

“And the girl?”

It was James who saved him from having to answer. “Are you sure this is the right place?” He called. They’d emerged on a wooden landing that felt more ‘shabby Soho flat’ than ‘EMI music producer extravaganza’. As they filed in next to each other, one of the doors closest to them opened and a middle-aged man tottered out. He gave each of them a dark look, punctuated by a five o’clock shadow and a terrible underbite, and then gruffly pushed his way through to get downstairs.

“He smelt wonderful,” Sirius said tersely. “Like stale hops and cat piss.”

“Keep it up and he might just come back and stab you with a blunt blade,” James mused.

“Maybe he will. It'd give me something to write about, at least.”

“It’s down here, wankers,” Peter called, having moved further up the landing than the rest of them. “Number three.”

The rest of them followed, stopping outside a dingy panelled door without any windows. It was the same as all the others, except this one had a golden plaque hung up outside. Doug Fletcher. Arts and Repertoire, EMI Music Publishing.

Sirius flicked the plaque with his finger. It tinged like plastic.

“Well,” he said, glancing sceptically at the rest of them. “We did come all this way…”

And so, with a deep breath, Sirius raised his fist and knocked.

The door flew open before he’d even finished, revealing a grinning Fletcher in a pin-striped suit and pink satin cravat, bald head polished to a shine. He’d forwent the over-sized golden rings today, and instead had several silver bangles on either wrist that jangled like a cat’s collar whenever he flourished his barrel-shaped wrists.

“If it ain’t my three o’clock! Or should I say, London’s next hardest and heaviest group ‘a thrashers! Come in, lads, come in!” Ushering them inside, Fletcher pointed across the room to where a lanky guy with thick-rimmed glasses sat in a cushioned arm chair. “This ‘ere is my man, Albert Wilson. He’s going to be the one helping you record in-studioso . That is, in the recording studio. Heh.”

They nodded eagerly, each without a peep to split between them. For all the uninspiring exterior, they were certainly in awe now. With large street-facing windows shrouded in beaded blinds and rugs that looked like they were fresh off the boat from Persia, Fletcher's office appeared to be dressed up even more fabulously than the man himself. Albert sat on a small loveseat in the corner, legs crossed at the ankles as he looked them up and down. Ahead of him sat a single leather office chair and a large oaken desk decorated with a heavy crystal ashtray, a rolodex, and a golden statuette of what appeared to be a naked women’s bust. The wood-panelled walls, though still marred with the building's general dinge and water damage, were covered with placards advertising EMI and all its signed acts. Several more golden records hung framed over an upright piano. Remus peered at each of the band’s names closely—Muggle & the Martyr, The Crookshanks, Abra Kadabra—none sounded familiar.

“Ah, I see you’ve noticed the high-achievers board,” Fletcher said, coming up behind him. “Abra Kadabra’s ‘Goblets of Ire’ went platinum just last month, as a matter ‘a fact. Haven’t got the record in the mail yet. Bad luck, that.”

“I've never heard of them," Remus replied. "You said they went platinum in the UK?”

“No, in Bangladesh actually.” Fletcher thumped him on the back. “Here's hoping the next gold-plated record I’ll be getting is yers, eh?”

Remus got the feeling he was supposed to laugh, but thankfully the manager had already moved on. He ushered him back to a large leather sofa that sat across from his desk and Remus squeezed in beside James and Peter while Sirius perched himself on the arm rest. Once he was seated behind his desk, Fletcher eased back into the creaky leather chair and put one foot up on the desk.

“So let’s just start by covering the basics. Which of ya writes the songs?”

“Lupin does,” Sirius answered, without a hint’s hesitation. Remus scoffed and thumped him in the leg.

“We all write the songs.”

“Hm, group effort, is it? Makes things a bit messy in the accounting department, but s’nothing we’s ain’t used to. Make sure's you keep record of who wrote what, that way we can divvy up the royalties as needed.” Pointing a finger at them assuredly, Fletcher pulled a cigar tin from his pocket and used one of fat cuban cigars to gestured toward Albert, who’d already begun scribbling away on a notepad. “Put Lupin down as the principle then," he ordered. "The other’s we’ll sort out as we record.”

“Yeah, and when do you think we’ll record?” Sirius pressed. “ ‘Cause we been working on the songs like you said, and we got more than enough to—”

“Hold on now, hold on,” Fletcher eased; “We’ll get there, son, I promise ya. But before we do, what I needs to know is what sort of image you lads wanna portray. Who do you’s want people tah see when they look at you—what should be the first thing that pops intae their heads when they hear the name ‘Marauders’.”

“Good ol’ fashion rock ‘n’ roll,” James answered simply.

“Yeah,” Peter added, “we’re a rock band. Like the Rolling Stones or Cream.”

“You want people to think of the Stones when they come ‘n see ya?”

“No,” Sirius cut-in, giving Peter a pointed look, "we ain’t the Stones. We're better."

“Now that,” Fletcher applauded, “is what I wanted to hear. That's a record I can sell!” He paused, long enough to light the narrow cigar off a lighter plated in the same shimmering gold as his records. “You lads have the gusto—the zeal—but if you’re missing anything it’s a goal. Simply saying you want to be the ‘biggest and best’ ain’t enough no more.”

Peter leaned in; “But you said—”

Fletcher snapped the lighter shut, exhaling. The smoke instantly stung Remus' eyes, reminding him of Lyall.

“Being big is great, you need ‘big’ to be the best," Fletcher told them, "but whatchu also needs is a certain uniqueness—a sui generis, if you will. You need something that sets you apart from all the rest ‘a the acts on the circuit. I think this attitude of yours could be it, so long as you can back it up with your sound, that is.”

“And how will we know if we've managed to 'back it up'?” James asked.

Fletcher shrugged. “ ‘Fraid that’s on you, but I suggest you do it fast. Punk’s a dying art, my friends. It was rock’s eleventh-hour shot to take back power. Now that it’s failed, we need a new angle. Mosh pits are out and dance parties are in. So you tell me, where are you going to land…? Empty mosh pits, or menagerie dance floors filled with silk-wearing dolly birds?”

“Neither,” Remus said, making all of them turn on him. “We’re not punk. And we sure as hell aren’t doing whatever those new wavers are into."

"So...?"

"So we ain't gonna cave. Instead we’re gonna do it our way, just like the guys before us but better. We’re gonna find all the ones that punk and synth left behind and we’re gonna play our music for them. Not the music they want, but the music they don't know they should be... be wanting.”

He'd trailed off towards the end, suddenly chock full of self-doubt, but he must've said something right, for the others were already grinning at him in agreement. As James reached over to slap him fondly on the arm, Remus caught Fletcher and Albert exchanging a purposeful glance.

“You guys live together?” Albert asked.

“Yeah,” answered Sirius. “Got a flat in Shepherd’s Bush.”

“Daddy paying for the demo then?”

“No, we work for your information,” Remus snapped, thinking of Tomny.

“Alright, alright,” Fletcher cut-in, “I think it's time we get this show on the road, don't you? I told you four the first time we chatted that I wasn’t gonna take any money for meself from the get-go. I know, s'generous of me. Most new acts don't get such a sweet deal, but to save us the hassle of all that paperwork I say we negotiate contracts once the demo’s recorded and in our hands. From there we can start taking it to distributors. Until then, you’re only paying for studio time. Sound fair?”

“Fair,” they nodded dubiously.

“Brilliant. I’d say that makes this a done deal, lads. If you’ve got the money on you today, Albert can work out a date for you to record down at De Lane. What say you?”

The other Marauders all glanced anxiously at Sirius, who slipped off of the sofa arm and pulled open his Glastonbury coat. Reaching inside, he untucked an envelope of cash and passed it over the desk. Fletcher peeked inside and before giving Albert a quick nod of approval and slipping the envelope into one of the desk drawers.

“Next Sunday work for ya?” Albert asked. “We’ll have to do it at night, when the studio’s closed. S’all they’ll allow for student bands, but at least no one’ll be around to bother us. Should give me enough time to cut it all together and get you that demo before the holidays too.”

“Yes!” Sirius exclaimed, looking excitedly at all of them. “The sooner the better really. Can’t wait forever.”

“What, got a flame licking that skinny behind ‘a yours?” Fletcher teased.

“No,” Peter started for him. “But we told our parents we’d go back to school if nothing came of the band thing, and it’s already been several months.”

“Aw, I get that.” Fletcher stood up from the chair. He was admittedly not that much taller on his feet. “Parents just want what’s best for ya. But you let them know that your good pal Fletch’s got it allllll sorted. Demo’s practically a done deal, just gotta hit record! But do your ol' pal a favour, would ya? If anyone else tries to sign ya before we've gone to EMI, you let Fletcher know. Got's to make sure you're not getting a sour deal. Only honour amongst friends, ain't there?”

With that, they made their way to the door, herded out into the hall by Fletcher and his foul cigar smoke.

“Oh, and one more piece of advice, lads!” He called, just as they’d stepped out into the hall. “Get some posters made. Start painting the town in your image. People can’t come to see ya if they don’t know you exist. Who knows, maybe one ‘a them’ll turn out to be your biggest fan.”

The door shut with a slam, and barely a beat had passed before James and Sirius were throwing themselves at each other in jubilation.

"I can't fucking believe it!" James sang. "We're getting our own demo—holy shit!"

"Holy shit!" Sirius agreed. They continued dancing around each other all the way back down to the ground floor, where the next door sex shop's sign was still flashing out its window.

"Don't you reckon we're celebrating a bit early?" Peter warbled as the four of them emerged onto the street and James began grinding his knuckles into the top of Sirius' head in jovial congratulation. "We just handed him everything we have and we've still got nothing to show for it. That was nearly five months' wages, you know."

"And a good chunk of my inheritance," Sirius said, freeing himself from James and poking out his tongue playfully. "Don't worry, Wormy, if the demo fails I promise to buy you out. Maybe you can start up your own art studio."

Peter didn't appear contented, but just then James separated himself from Sirius' side and declared that a round of drinks were in order and that they should make their next mission to find the nearest possible pub to get royally pissed in. With all of them in agreement, Remus followed on obediently, keeping silent as Sirius eventually fell into step with him.

"So I've been thinking, should we open the demo with 'Hail Mary' or 'Doomed Generation'? 'Hail Mary' would be a real punch in the throat, but maybe we wanna start off more with something more modest—you know, build up to the real heavy stuff. What do you wager, Moons?"

Remus didn't answer at first, and Sirius had to tap him.

"Moons?"

"Something was off about Fletcher."

Sirius tipped his head back to groan; "What, you too?"

"No, no... It's just something that he said." Remus peered down at the wet pavement beneath his shoes. " 'Honour amongst friends', that's what he said, but he's wrong. It's 'no honour amongst thieves', that's the saying."

Sirius bit his lip, looking temporarily deflated. The expression was gone a second later.

"Who gives a shit what barmy idiots like Fletcher have to say? We're only using him to get the demo. Old fool didn't even make us sign any contracts, right? The way I see it, if he turns out completely useless then we just get our tape and get out. Find another way into EMI. I'll bet there's loads of tossers just like Fletcher. It's all 'a part of the game, remember."

Remus nodded. "Maybe you're right."

"Of course I'm right. I'm like so right it's wrong—that's the best part. Now c'mon, I can feel a stiff pint calling your name, Moons. With luck, it'll be the last one you ever have to pay for outta your own pocket."





* * *





Christmastime, 1978

In the nearly two weeks that’d followed their meeting with Fletcher, the Marauders worked harder than ever before, dedicating every waking hour not spent at work to honing their craft. Remus told himself to be thankful for the lack of free time; it meant less hours would be wasted languishing over Tomny. He hadn't heard from the would-be father since their spat outside the cafe, and since Remus had made no effort to reach out either, he assumed that Tomny simply wanted the space and resigned himself to a waiting game. Things would be alright eventually, Remus told himself. He and Tomny had had falling outs before—this wasn't the first time and he doubted it'd be the last. Even if Tomny didn't call first, eventually Remus would come slinking back, begging for forgiveness, and Tomny would give it to him as he always did. For now, all Remus needed was to be patient.

On the upside (or down, depending on who you asked,) Sirius had somehow managed to wrestle the rest of them into performing the back-up vocals on a couple of their more pop-rock tracks. Normally James was the only one who had the courage to sing back-up to Sirius while on stage, but they'd all agreed that the songs didn't sound as whole without it.

"Why don't you just layer more of yours and James' vocals on top of each other?" Remus had asked. "You can do that, you know. In the studio."

"I know, but I wanna hear it like this first. Now let's cut the whinging and take it from the top, shall we?"

It went okay at first, but then Remus' voice cracked on the second verse and he'd been forced to pummel Sirius with his fists until the arse stopped fully-belly laughing. This went on for several days.

It was clear that the Marauders had really hit their stride as a band during those few weeks. It was then that Remus really discovered how good Peter was at harmonising with Remus' bass. Practically reading his mind, the two of them bounced beats off one another all day and all night until they were creating rhythms just as complementary as any Jones-Bonham composition. Of course James and Sirius had proved as formidable a duo as always. Together they penned a rather explosive composition involving an experimental sort of reverb they could only achieve by placing two amps side by side and swinging the guitar around in front of them in a windmill-like motion. It looked rather stupid in practice, but anything for the art, Remus supposed.

When it’d finally come time to record the songs in-studio, they’d taken turns pinching each other just to make sure they weren’t dreaming. They were due to be up the entire night recording, but still Remus hadn’t been able to sleep. Instead he laid awake, staring at the radio and ruminating in his own jitters.

“Just think of the album cover,” Sirius had told him, muttering sleepily into the side of his neck. “I’m… mmm… finally gonna get you into a pair of those leather trousers… swear it.”

When that fateful Sunday finally came, they waited until near-on nine o’clock at night to load everything into the van. Lily had wanted to come as a show of support, but it was the end of term for her and she had an exam in the morning. Without their favourite ginger tag-along, James and Sirius took the front seats while Remus and Peter rode coach with the instruments.

“I’m starting to think getting Minnie was a good idea after all,” Sirius said, tilting James’ rearview mirror to grin back at them. “I mean, you two look so cosy back there.”

“Would you stop with the stupid name already?” Peter moaned. “It’s a car not a golden retriever.”

“I still don’t get it either,” James said, twisting his mirror back. “Why did you insist on naming our van after our old Headmistress?”

“Because,” Sirius sniggered. “Now it’s a Minnie- van.”

They all groaned.

James took the A40 over to Holborn, where they found themselves knocking on the loading bay doors of none other than De Lane Lea Studios. There they waited, practically vibrating on the spot for reasons that were entirely unique to each of them.

"You're sure we're in the right place?" Peter asked.

"Yes, we're sure," Sirius snapped, hands pressed tight to his chest to ward off the chill. "Do you see another building around here with the words 'De Lane Lea' written out front?"

"You don't need to be a prick about it."

Before Sirius could answer, the back door swung open, revealing Albert in a pair of matching white shirt and slacks. Remus recognised the faint smell of antiseptic permeating the air around him. Albert didn't seem to notice.

“Come on then,” the sound tech grunted briskly, shoving a brick beneath the door to keep it propped open. “Let's get that gear inside before you wake up the whole bloody neighbourhood.”

Albert was strictly to the point, Remus noticed early on. He refused James' request for a quick tour of the studios, citing strict time constraints and a lack of free studio space. After overhearing the sound of what appeared to be voices coming from the end of one hall, Remus became almost sure that they weren't alone as Fletcher promised, but before he could inquire further, Albert had them corralled into one of the control rooms, the sight alone impressive enough to make Remus forget all about any possible gate-crashers. The control room itself was very clean and sleek-looking, not at all like the shag-rug and wood-panelled recording booths Remus had seen snippets of in the likes of NME and Cream magazine. To him, the control table and surrounding area looked more like something torn straight out of one of Marlene’s science fiction novels. A spaceship maybe, or a robot assembly line.

In a clear hurry to get going, Albert kindly helped lug their things into the studio's booth, and from there they got straight to work. Not a single moment was wasted, apart from those spent sorting out the issues with the tape. Of which there were many.

“I got it, I got it! Just let me do it!” Albert prattled, after the machine had tangled for the third time, ruining Sirius’ near-perfect take and prompting all of them to emerge from the live room to see what was the issue. Remus didn’t say anything, for fear Albert would somehow overhear them through the booth's speaker playback, but it appeared to him that Fletcher’s ‘right hand man’ was very new to the whole ‘recording’ business. He supposed it was to be expected; they were still quite green themselves.

With only one hour left until sun-up, the Marauders were nearly depleted. There was Peter, half-asleep at his drum kit, and James who had downed about twenty-seven cups of black coffee, and finally Remus who was quite literally begging for fag. Only Sirius seemed to come with limitless stores of energy, as to be expected.

“Just a bit longer. We still have that last song of yours to record first," he insisted, sliding his headphones back into place and giving Albert the 'okay' through the booth's main window. "Al, cue up a fresh tape, would ya?" He called. "We're gonna do Lupin's ballad."

“No, don’t worry about it,” Remus said into his own microphone, painfully tired and exasperated. "We don't need it."

“What?!"

Sirius' voice came through the speakers along with a horrible sequel of feedback, making all of them with headphones flinch and Peter spring awake from the floor beside his bass drum. "Sorry..." He muttered, adjusting the microphone, then; "What d’you mean ‘don’t need it’? It’s your song.”

“Yeah, and I just don’t think it’s the right fit for the album anymore, that's all.”

“Moons.” Sirius gave him a look that was half sleep-deprived irritation, half forlorn sympathy. “It’s a good song. It should go on the album.”

Remus shook his head. No.

Not that song.

Not “Tonya’s Song”.

Not anymore.

“None of the others are acoustic. It’ll sound out of place.”

“Sod that. It’s our best love song.”

Love song. He almost flinched when Sirius said it.

"I won't do it. I said no."

“Fine then, be a stubborn prat about it,” Sirius huffed, already reaching for his guitar. “We’ll have Potter play your bits instead—”

“Sirius, why don't you just fuck off!?”

At the sound of his raised voice, Peter sat upright and James lowered his twenty-eighth cup of coffee-in-a-styrofoam-mug. Remus knew that Albert would also be keenly listening in from his place back in the control room, but he was too proud to look. And too proud to apologise. It appeared as though it was becoming a bad habit of his lately.

“I don’t want to," he said solemnly, in place of a defence, "please, Sirius.”

At Remus' pathetic attempt to appeal to his compassionate nature, Sirius deflated some, his pale shoulders falling slack as he tipped his head back to frown at the ceiling. Remus could tell he was more than a little disappointed; he’d always loved “Tonya’s Song”, enough to look past the fact that it was clearly a love song Remus had written for someone else.

“Come on, Black,” James said, chiming in reasonably. “We still have Moony's other ballad, ‘How Nice It Could Be’. It’s ‘love’ enough, yeah? Let’s sort that one next.”

“You also said that we still need to stack a few more vocals for ‘Downtown Girls’,” Peter called, muffling a yawn.

The look Sirius gave him made it obvious to Remus that he wasn’t satisfied, but he didn’t push anymore and for that Remus was grateful. Going through the motions and simply playing the chords was the easy part, but either due to their unwavering friendship or general exhaustion, there were no more arguments to be had in the booth. Come seven o'clock, they were stood around the futuristic sound board with Albert, listening to what would go on to become the scrap pieces of the Marauders' very first album. The recording was messy; rough-hewn and clearly amateur—and yet Remus had never felt so proud of anything he’d help create in his entire life.

On their way back to Shepherd’s Bush they passed a bottle of Jack around in hard-earned celebration. They got caught up in traffic along the way, but were already on their second or third wind of the night and couldn’t be bothered to give a crap. These were morning commuters, all of them on their way to the boring mundane desk jobs that paid for their boring mundane lives. They were eighteen—and they had just finished recording a studio demo. Soon that demo would be passed on to the execs at EMI, and if all went well there, they’d hopefully be signing contracts within the coming New Year. Invigorated by this knowledge, (and the whisky) Remus looked out the window at a bus full of morning pedestrians and flipped them the victorious bird. Life was good.

Of course they all crashed the moment they arrived home, barely having the energy to bring the gear back inside with them to avoid being robbed. It wasn't until several hours later, at around four o’clock, when Remus awoke to Lily knocking on their door. Regulus had called.

Sirius immediately leapt out of bed, and when Remus eventually found the energy to follow, he found him draped over the kitchen phone, regaling his brother with all the fantastical realities of being a real-life recording artist.

“No, seriously, it was amazing! The studio was damn impressive, they had an isolation box and everything… No, not like in prison. It’s meant for—well, if you knew what it was meant for then why bother taking the piss? … Mhm… Ugh. I still don’t know why you’d bother, it’s not like anyone ever has a good time at those fucking parties, least of all us... Sod Mum—why don’t you just come out here for Christmas? Potter’s parents are putting everyone up and there’s plenty of room. “I’m not giving up my faith,” she’d assured Remus, the first time he’d asked; “but it’s like, you start seeing the world differently when you don’t have the same neighbours around to tell you how everything's just supposed to be. I'm glad my parents sent me to Hawkings. Otherwise, I'm afraid I would've ended up just like them.”

And because he could, Remus had hugged her just a bit tighter that day.

While the addition of Mary and Marlene to the party's already growing guest list was hardly cause for calamity, Remus still couldn't quite understand how the Potters did it. Ever the gracious host, Effie was pleased by the arrival of every new face, and no matter how many appeared in her entry way, she was always able to magic up room for them to rest their feet. Potter Cottage was always a bit extraordinary like that.

After supper, the eight of them congregated in James’ childhood bedroom for some much needed friendship overhaul, and Remus was struck by the realisation that he’d quite missed seeing all of their faces in the same place. Their flat at Number 43 Knoxbridge Road was home now, but there was something nostalgic about cramming into a tiny bedroom with tiny bottles of sherry they’d nicked from their parents' stores. They passed the bottles around until they were all suitably inebriated and afterwards, drew straws to see who got to choose the music. Lily had won most recently and has surprised all of them by putting on a Stevie Wonder album. Perhaps the worst lightweight among them, James had grown drunk off his dad’s Guinness early, and had promptly began singing every track aloud to her.

“Isn’t she loooovely? Isn’t she woooonderful?! Isn’t she precious! Less than one minute—”

“With Potter?!”

“No! Just—getting all the attention.”

Mary shrugged, handing her back the beer. “Naturally. Who doesn’t like a bit of attention? It’s the gooeyness I can’t stand.”

"Well, we're already both women, so it's not like we can get married even if we wanted to. Dee and her little sister converted after her mum met her step-father. She was only six, but she's got two older brothers and they're agnostic." Marlene began picking at her thumbnail. "Both of our religions denounce homosexuality as a sin, but I know there's more liberal-minded folks out there. Even a few in here, if you know where to look."

"You're welcome," Sirius said, teasing her with a bow. Everyone laughed, and Marlene knocked his shoulder fondly with one fist.

"No, it's just nice to know that we're not alone. Reform is hard, but," she sighed and looked at Lottie, "I guess you could say we're working on it."

”Oh, I’m sure we do,” Sirius said out of the corner of his mouth. Mary didn’t seem to notice.

“And eyes.”

“Nah, she’s right, you know,” Sirius said. “Effie’s just so—blimey. I'm not usually one for Oedipus—mostly 'cause my own mum's a fucking hag—but I swear, Potter, if I were any straighter you'd be calling me Dad."

Sirius peeled the pillow back, looking devilish. “Oh, I know.”

“Hey, Lottie,” Lily called, already suitably curled up on the carpet with her head propped up on one of James’ thighs. “When are you gonna tell us about this ‘big surprise’ of yours?”

All heads turned, and Lottie flushed slightly as she made herself busy straightening her skirt. “Well, I wanted to save it for Christmas. Tell everyone all at once, you know?”

“Yeah well, we’re your friends and I’m your brother so out with it,” Peter insisted.

“You’re not pregnant, are you?” Mary asked, making all of the boys seize up. “ ‘Cause if you are, I know this darling shop over on St James’s that makes the cutest babygrows. Kara-Ann used to dress Gigi in them all the time.”

“No, I’m not pregnant!” Lottie snapped. “I’m… I’m getting married!”

For a moment no one breathed. Remus could've heard a pin drop, if not for the party noise going on downstairs. "So just to be clear," she started, "you're not pregnant?"

"Oh Mary!" Huffing and rather than show them a ringless finger, Lottie stood up from the carpet and scooped up her purse, which she'd left lying on James' bed. From inside, she produced a small velvet box. “I couldn’t very well wear it, Mummy’s like a hawk with these sorts of things and I wanted Roger to be there when we told everyone,” she explained, opening it and revealing a diamond the size of Remus’ front tooth. “It belonged to his mother," she crooned. "It’s a family heirloom.”

"Now that's a fucking rock," Sirius gaped. Lottie smiled and slipped it on, and from there the girls crowded around, admiring the ring and showering her with compliments. As the girls celebrated, Remus looked to Sirius, who—with an indignant frown—had reached for Remus' right hand and found it empty.

"Oi, where's your ring?" He hissed quietly. In answer, Remus raised his left hand, showing off the silver band.

"Thought it might keep some of the aunties downstairs at bay if I wore it over here tonight."

"Aunties—bah," Sirius scoffed. "What you should be worried about is keeping me at bay."

He grabbed the front of Remus' jumper, bringing him in for a kiss that left butterflies twirling in his gut. The moment may have stayed a blissful one, had Peter not shot upright on the carpet.

“Married!?” He cried, making all of them jump. “You’re seriously getting married?!”

Lottie looked up from her girls’ huddle. “Don’t get your knickers in a twist, Petey, it’s not like I’m telling you to go out and propose to Moira tomorrow.”

“But we’re eighteen! And Roger’s like—twenty-five!”

“Twenty-eight, actually,” Mary corrected. “He’s an Aquarius with an Aries moon. Very spontaneous, that.”

“Don't start that, Mary, I thought you hated love!”

“Oh, I love love, Peter. It’s the happiness I can’t stand.”

Mary's sarcasm aside, Peter threw his arms up and the others turned back on Lottie once more.

“When did he pop the question, Lot?” Asked Marlene.

“Yesterday."

"YESTERDAY?" Peter bleated. Lottie ignored him;

"I was getting on the train back from Reading and Rog pulled me aside and he never wanted to be apart again. I didn't realise how the distance was affecting him—I thought it was only me. But then he got down on one knee in front of the whole platform and asked me right there! Even the train whistled for us..." She blushed, pink as a little girl; "He kissed me out the window as it was pulling away.”

“Ugh!" Mary wheeled back, hand to her forehead. "The romance of it all!”

"And he's the one then?" Lily asked. "He's the one you want?"

"Couldn't imagine anyone else."

“Then I say congrats, Lot,” James called over to them, already opening his arms for a hug. Beaming, Lottie went around the room to embrace all of them one at a time. Last of all was Peter, who did not so readily open his arms in congratulations and merriment. Instead the two siblings squared off, their expressions so similar it was a wonder they weren't looking in a mirror.

“You really aren’t going to say that happy for me?”

“You want me to lie to my own sister?”

“You could at least pretend then.”

Peter’s nostrils flared. “And do you such a disservice? You don't want to marry him, Lottie, you’re only saying yes 'cause you want to play house. Because without him you don't know who you really are, and you can't be arsed to figure it out on your own.”

Lottie slapped him.

“Screw you, you stupid fucking wanker!" She howled. "Wanting to be loved isn’t a bad thing, Peter! You’re just afraid that no one’s ever going to pick you like Roger’s picked me. Just because Moira’s family has decided that they don't like you doesn’t mean you get to take your pain out on me!”

She stormed out, and with a shared look of anxiety, the rest of the girls inevitably followed. Remus, meanwhile, didn't know what to say. They all shifted their weight uncomfortably while Peter stood by, rubbing his sore cheek and clutching a bottle of Guinness against his chest. Finally, he flopped back down onto the rug and met James' eye.

"Don't say it."

“I think you were a bit harsh there, Pete,” James replied anyway.

"A bit?" Echoed Sirius.

“Oh come on, everyone was thinking it! It's not my fault I'm the only one with balls enough to say it." Peter snarled, then waved the bottle of Guinness toward the door. “She’s never even been on her own! Always had to have a boyfriend, telling her what to do and where to go! Now what—she’s just gonna get married and play housewife forever?”

“If that's what she wants," Remus said.

“Aren’t you listening? She doesn’t know what she wants! She doesn't know who she is.”

“She seems to know enough about you though, didn't she?” Sirius prompted. “C’mon, Wormy, what’s the real reason you've flown off the handle? Is it really something to do with Thurnberg?”

“None of your business!”

“Pete.” James sidled over, placing a comforting hand on his friend’s shoulder. “You can tell us, mate. You know you can tell us, right?”

It didn’t take much more than that. Peter had never been one for keeping secrets to himself, and as James bared his familiar sympathy, the explanation came tumbling out.

“You know how Moira and Lottie sometimes hang out?" He moaned. "Well she told Lottie that her parents don’t want her seeing me anymore. They don’t think it’s smart, right? What we’re doing with the band... And now that we’ve left school I guess they don’t want their daughter dating some bum.”

“Man, fuck them,” Sirius retorted. Remus gave him a sharp look for it, then;

“Did you talk to Moira yourself about it?”

“ ‘Course I talked to her about it.”

“And…?”

“She says she doesn’t want to break up, but if it comes between me and her family, I dunno what she'll choose.”

The words 'not me' seemed to hang in the air, and Sirius gave Remus a look that said ‘I told you so’. Ignoring it, Remus leaned in;

“Have you told her about the demo? How Fletcher’s gonna introduce us to EMI?”

“That’s just more promises. She's tired of promises and I don't blame her.”

“Maybe you should get her to come to a show then,” James offered instead. “It’s been so long since she’s come out to one. Lots has changed since then! Who knows, maybe seeing us actually do something in front of a crowd’ll bring her more on board.”

Peter pursed his lips. “Maybe…”

“And you should apologise to your sister,” Sirius added. “Otherwise she might not invite you to the wedding. Miss all the cake.”

“She never apologises to me,” Peter griped. “Give it a day, she’ll calm down.”

There was a knock at the door, and Simeon stuck his head inside.

“Ho, boys. I know I just arrived and all, but does someone want to tell me why my baby sister’s downstairs crying her pretty eyes out?”

Simeon’s entrance marked the true beginning of the holiday season as far as the Pettigrews went. The next morning the two families came together for a stellar Christmas brunch, and for the first time Remus found himself willingly intermingling with a slew of adults. They asked him things like what he’d been doing since school and what he thought about the housing market and current rate of inflation. When he professed that he didn’t pay much attention to such things they laughed and wrote it off as adolescent charm. It made him wonder how long he’d be able to get away with it.

After they’d all eaten and presents had been opened, James and Sirius managed to corral several of James’ cousins and uncles into a game of footie in the back garden. Marlene joined in of course, as did Mr. Potter, who proved surprisingly spritely for a man who’d woken up complaining of a crick in his neck. It still hadn’t snowed, although Effie appeared hopeful for some come the evening.

After having spent most of the day avoiding others, eventually Lottie reappeared without so much as a puffy eye in sight. Not long after Roger made his grand entrance and everyone welcomed him, apart from Peter that was. No, Peter stared at Roger like he was a wad of gum stuck to the floor of the Underground. But they all knew Lottie, and she’d never made a habit of asking permission from anyone; Lottie simply did as Lottie pleased. Now, on Christmas Day, Roger had barely managed to get a glass of Mr. Pettigrew’s famous mulled wine into his hand before she was gathering the entire house together to make her big announcement.

"We just wanted you all to know," Lottie called, "that Roger and I... are getting married!"

The excitement was immediate; the shriek of joy Mrs. Pettigrew let out could’ve been heard from space.

“I hope this means you’re next,” one of James’ aunts cooed at Simeon afterwards, as he and his new girlfriend Lorraine stood by to congratulate the happy couple. A humble raconteur himself, Simeon gave an off-hand dismissal and distracted the auntie with talk of his days at Oxford. Remus had only just met Lorraine, but she didn’t appear to him all that jealous at the attention Lottie was getting. He could only assume that Simeon picked his girlfriends very meticulously.

“I’ve never seen such a big Christmas,” Lorraine said to him, after the two of them had convened by the buffet table on sheer happenstance. “So many people.”

“It’s pretty normal around here. You get used to it.”

Lorraine cocked her head. “I hear you’re in a band.”

Remus smiled. Never ending, that.

As the evening slid into night, Remus watched as all of the ‘proper adults’ traded fruity cocktails for Remy Martin Cognac and expensive red wine imported from France. Mr. Potter broke out his personal stash of cigars, which he offered to each of the boys despite his wife’s griping.

“Don’t just keep it in your mouth,” Simeon instructed. “You gotta bring it down into your lungs. Nice and deep, like this.”

He set the cigar against his lips and breathed in, while Peter nodded sharply.

“I know how to do it, I’m not an idiot.”

Peter inhaled, and promptly began to hack up a lung.

“Oh Petey,” Simeon chuckled, smacking his brother on the back.

“Here, have one of mine,” Roger said, offering a packet of Senior Service cigarettes. Peter took one look at him and declined out-right. On Roger’s other side, Lottie shot him a nasty glare.

“Think he’ll ever get over it?” Lily asked Remus, having apparently been spying as well. They were both sitting across the room, a sofa away from where James and Sirius were playing their own version of “Jingle Bell Rock” to entertain all the little cousins. As they strummed their guitars, Mary appeared behind each of them and fit a Santa hat over their heads. Neither complained.

“Eventually,” Remus answered. “I think he’s just upset she didn’t tell him first.”

“I know how it feels.”

“Petunia?”

Lily nodded. “Petunia.”

He fit an arm around her, cigar poised in the other. He knew things between Lily and her older sister were complicated, and had been ever since Lily left home for her scholarship at Hawkings, but very rarely did she get down about it. Remus resolved that it was good of her. No way he could’ve tolerated such a sour bint for a sister.

“Looks like you’re going to be buying two bridesmaid dresses next year, huh?”

“Looks like it,” Lily sighed. “Pet’s vicious too. She’ll probably have me in some hideous colour. Like chartreuse.”

“I dunno, I think you’d look quite good in yellow.”

"Chartreuse is more green."

"Even better."

"Are you?" Lily leaned back to look at him; “Alright. Remus, would you consider coming to meet my entire family at a wedding where you'll be forced to smile and dance with me all night while my wonderful sister judges the fact that your suit isn't perfectly pressed?”

“Sweet talker." She fit her head onto his shoulder. "Have you given any thought to what you and Sirius’ll do while we're away?”

“Work, probably. Write some more songs.”

“Sirius bought that couch.”

“I didn’t mean to make you sad, Remus. I only wanted to know how you felt about it."

"S'fine."

"No, I’m sorry… Have you not heard from him at all?”

“No.”

“Have you tried calling?”

“Once.”

“And?”

“He didn’t pick up.”

She returned her head to his shoulder, so close that the top of her Santa hat was tickling his cheek. Then she took his hand and squeezed it ever so tight.

“It’ll be alright, love,” Lily said. Her hands were warm.

Across the room, one of the young cousins that had been listening to James and Sirius play suddenly leapt up from the carpet and ran headlong toward the nearest window, screaming for his father to join him.

“Baba, look! Snow!”

The entire room moved at once. A true white Christmas hadn’t been seen in London in almost a decade, and so when everyone pulled the curtains back to reveal the thin blanket of snow covering the back garden, a cheer of awe and excitement went up. Potter Cottage’s back garden boasted a wonderful hill just beyond its fence, and they raced around under the blue-cover of the waxing moon. It didn’t take long for the first snowball to be thrown either, and from there on out it became a full-on battle. Remus took a nasty shot to the back of the head, courtesy of James, but was avenged by Lily when she feigned in close only to shove a handful of powder down the back of James' jacket. Remus had no time to gloat; already he was being forced to flee as Sirius began pelting him with several snowballs of his own. He managed to outpace Mary easily, who was struggling not to trip in her heeled winter boots while being chased by a small troupe of James' baby cousins.

“No, no, no! I’m Switzerland!” She shrieked, dodging most of tikes. Unfortunately, Marlene had also followed, and her aim was true—snowball bursting over the back of Mary’s head in one glorious shatter of white.

Remus could feel the sweat that had begun to gather on his back. He’d stopped running long enough to watch James and Peter race down the hill on toboggans, only to come colliding with the frosty ground as Sirius tackled him from behind.

“Moony!” Sirius gasped, pushing his snow-speckled hair out from his eyes; “I’m out of fags. Come get some more with me?”

Remus nearly laughed. It was Christmas, and near-on midnight. Nowhere nearby would be waiting with its lights on to sell them a packet of Silk Cut.

“Here.” He rolled over, pushing Sirius off. “Have some of mine.”

Sirius looked down at the carton Remus offered, then back up at him with an arched brow.

“I said— I’m out of fags. Now come get some with me.”

“Ah.”

They helped each other up from the snow, and after checking to make sure no one was paying attention, made a beeline back toward the house. “You two are in a rush,” he mused.

“Forgot fags inside,” Remus lied, at the same time that Sirius said; “Need to use the loo.”

Looking between them both, Simeon simply smirked and tipped the bag of marshmallows in their direction before stepping past without another word. "This way!" Sirius hissed, grabbing Remus by the arm.

“You’re crazy,” Remus laughed, as he was practically dragged through the house and shoved inside one of the hallway cupboards. It was dark and fully crowded with winter kits and the like. Remus was practically tripping over the sea of boots strewn about the floor, but Sirius was already tugging at his clothes—ripping his jacket off of his shoulders with eager fingers.

“Curse you and your infernal hatred for all things cold,” he hissed, while fighting with the thick fleece jumper Remus was wearing underneath.

“Why aren’t we doing this in our room?” Remus demanded, busy feeling around the wall for a light switch.

“Too impatient. Need you now.”

“It’s just upstairs.”

“C’mon, Moons. Where’s your sense of adventure?”

“Absolutely mental, you are.”

“Fuck. You always know just the right things to get me going.”

"I can't bloody see anything."

There was a little click, and Sirius had turned on the single free-hanging light bulb over their heads. He had a right smirk on his face, and when Remus glanced up, he spotted a single bushel of mistletoe wrapped around the bulb.

“Wow," he smirked, "wonder who put that there.”

“You did.”

“Did not. Must’ve grown on its own. Like Christmas magic.”

“I think it’s a fire hazard.”

Sirius tugged off the light.

“Better?”

Remus kissed him. Hard and deep, until they were fully stumbling over the mess around their feet. They were alone, but the house still thrummed with life; they could hear laughter, the call for more firewood, a Christmas album playing off the lounge stereo. The closet smelt of dust and damp, simultaneously wrapped up in cinnamon and cloves of Effie's home cooking. Remus pushed his hand up into Sirius’ hair and he felt the remnants of leftover snow tickle his skin. When Sirius spoke, it drove shivers down his spine. It blocked out all other noise, until it was just their bodies and the hazy breaths they traded in the dark.

“Shit, Moony. Little to the left—”

“Fleamont Potter—”

“Oh, fuck. Right there—”

“I don’t care if you’re hot as the devil himself—”

“Want you—”

“You’re going to wear that jacket— oh my!”

For a moment they were blinded by the yellow of the hallway light. Mrs. Potter had swung the closet door wide, looking for a jacket only to come across a pair of boys attached at the lips instead. To her credit, she did not scream, but the look on her face was clearly that of astonishment. Ripping his hand out of Sirius' trousers, Remus leapt away as if electrocuted, lucky they’d really only gotten as far as their dishevelled shirts.

“Hello, dears," she chirped. "Is there any particular reason why you’ve chosen to coalesce in the hallway cupboard?”

Try as he might, Remus could not come up with an excuse for the life of him.

“This isn’t what it looks like, Mrs. Potter!” He cried.

“It isn’t?”

“No, we—!”

“Yeah! I—I–I mean, we… We just—!”

It was Sirius who’d finished stammering. He continued on like this for several seconds while Effie simply stared at him, and only shut up when Mr. Potter’s voice came hollering down the hall.

“It’s the blue one, Effie! The blue one!”

“The blue one…” Mrs. Potter murmured to herself.

“Mum—” Sirius drew up short, flinching as though saying the word had brought him physical pain. Then he opened his mouth again, as if to offer some further desperate explanation, but Mrs. Potter only pressed a single finger to her lips. Slowly she drew the cupboard door toward herself while also reaching into the closet between them. With a sharp tug she freed a blue duffle coat from its hanger and draped it over one arm.

“The blue one,” she said, nodding gently. Then, with a knowing smile, she shut the door. For a moment neither of them said anything—as if waiting for the dreaded gotcha!

It never came.

“… Moony?”

“… Yeah, Sirius?”

"Did that really just happen?"

"Y-Yeah... I think it did."

"Oh..."

"Mm."

"Moony?"

"Yes, Sirius?"

“Happy Christmas.”

A hand reached across the darkness and found Remus’ wrist. He followed its slender fingers, right down to the softness of its palm, and squeezed. Remus smiled.

“Happy Christmas, Sirius.”
