January 1979





New Year’s that year had fallen on a Sunday, and thanks to the British Parliament’s great Sunday Observance Act, this meant that there was very little to be done in lieu of partying. The Pettigrews’ still hosted their usual get-together, but it was much more subdued compared to the grand ball they’d put on the year before. To respect the sabbath, they served only red wine in tiny crystalline glasses and people mostly mulled around, chatting and smoking in pairs. Mrs. Pettigrew still begged them to perform, and even gifted them a brand-new Marshall amp that helped blow James’ old sound out of the water. The songs she suggested were rather drab for a group of wannabe-rockers on their way to the world’s stage, but of course they played them for her anyway.

When the holiday lull was over, replaced instead by a blisteringly cold January, the Marauders returned to their home in Shepherd’s Bush and got straight to work. Predictably, Lily had made near-on perfect marks in her first term at UCL and rather than drinks, celebrated with a brisk trip to the library to review everything she'd managed to get wrong. Sirius meanwhile had gotten it into his head that if they could excite the studios with their first demo, keeping enough material in their back pocket for a second debut would surely impress. Remus wasn’t confident that all of their new tracks would be a hit—Sirius’ latest song was called “Wag the Dog” and was really just a thinly-veiled allusion to oral sex with an unsavoury title—but there was something to be said for the effort. When Fletcher called, they’d surely be ready.

Except that Fletcher never called.

Day and night they waited, hoping for even a single scrap of news. When nothing came, they tried phoning the office directly, but they never got anything more than the telephone answering machine and its cheery reel-to-reel tape message.

“ ‘ello! You’ve reached your ol’ pal Fletch, managerial-extraordinaire! ‘Fraid I can’t take your call at the moment, but m’sure I’ll get to it whenever I’m back in me office. Cheerio!”

They’d left so many messages that the machine inevitably over-flowed, and after finally coming to the conclusion that they weren’t getting through, the Marauders were forced to return to their excruciating waiting game. To James this was dismal news; he’d had to spend all Christmas dodging his family's incessant questions about work and future plans for university. Peter was also in a tizzy, though that could’ve been chalked up to his similar problems with Moira.

“We just have to be patient,” Sirius told them, each day they went without any word.

It was laughable of course; Sirius Black had never been patient a day in his life. Despite his stubborn confidence, Remus hadn’t missed the way Sirius would jump every time the phone rang, racing to make sure he was the first one to pick it up. Mid-way through January, James had bitten every nail down to the quick and Peter had struck up the annoying habit of drumming his hands against any available surface at all hours. Even Remus was beginning to feel the burn of it. Each of them had developed a rather poor sleep schedule, working all day to support themselves only to stay up writing and practising through the night. They were smoking all hours, whether it be fags or hash, which led to one late, red-eyed session where one of them had tossed a still-burning roach into the garbage and accidentally started a small bin fire.

In attempts to cull any further acts of arson while also ‘maintaining and expanding their creative minds’, Sirius managed to get his hands on some magic mushrooms from one of the Shoestring’s regulars. While waiting for them to take effect, James had a brilliant breakthrough on one of the riffs he’d been working on. The lyrics came to Remus instantly and while he scrambled to put pen to paper, Sirius grabbed his guitar and Peter picked up his sticks and just like that they were blessed. It was the best song they’d ever written, Remus was sure of it, but then the mushrooms kicked in and everything went black.

When they woke up the next morning, the paper containing Remus' lyrics was missing, save only a few leftover scraps as though a dog had gone at it. With no ferocious animal in sight, they were forced to come to the unfortunate conclusion that one of them must’ve eaten it.

It wasn’t all bad though. Later Remus would look back and reminisce, wishing they hadn’t rushed themselves so badly. It all felt rather menacing, the idea that only a few precious months lay between life as an immutable rock and roll idols or a boring nine-to-five. Perhaps the reason James and Peter had thrown themselves into the work head-on was because they couldn’t bear the thought of reapplying for unis or spending the next four years in lecture halls; their need for stardom would always appear lesser when compared to Sirius’, but that didn’t mean they didn’t want for it.

“I just don’t get why we can’t go over there ourselves,” Peter huffed. “Fletcher promised us that demo weeks ago! You gave him the money, Sirius, so where is it? He said it’d be a done deal by now.”

“We know what Fletcher said, Wormtail. We were all there,” Sirius grumbled, draped across the sofa with an arm over his eyes. It was a Wednesday—or a Thursday. None of them had slept, and if they had it’d been fitful and unproductive. Lily was cooking breakfast, and James was fighting with the coffee machine while Remus flicked through the morning radio, hoping to pick up one of the pirate stations that sometimes floated down the Thames.

“Fletcher said these things take time,” James reasoned, coming out of the kitchen.

“It’s been time! No where’s our bloody record contract?”

“How ‘bout this, if we don’t hear from him by next week then we’ll head over there ourselves?” Sirius offered.

“NEXT WEEK?!” Peter smacked his hand down on the sofa arm. “Oh that’ll make a real difference. Better yet, why not just wait for Easter, or the Queen’s next bloody jubilee?!”

With a frustrated grunt, Sirius swung himself upright on the sofa. The anger in his expression might’ve culminated as something he’d certainly regret saying, but just then the phone rang, making all of them flinch.

Sirius was on his feet in a second—leaping across the room in a few short strides.

“Hello?!”

For a few seconds Remus was hopeful, but then Sirius’ glower returned and he was shouting down the line;

“No, we ain’t interested in your bloody election! You can take your Iron Lady and shove ‘er up your arse!”

He slammed the receiver down, just as Lily came around the kitchen counter, unfazed by the anger as she offered him a cup of coffee.

“Sirius, maybe it is time you guys pay that manager of yours a real visit.”

Sirius took the coffee and stared down at it before finally raising his head in Remus’ direction. Having already given up on the radio, Remus met his gaze, and nodded.

“Doesn’t feel like there’s much else we can do. I'm sure one visit wouldn't hurt.”

“Fine,” Sirius relinquished. “But I'm gonna call again first. If he doesn’t pick up, we’ll go over to the bloody office ourselves.”

All of them seemed to find this agreeable, and Sirius began punching in the numbers, leaving the phone on speaker-mode as the rest of them waited anxiously, clinging to the edges of their seats. At first the line just rang. And rang. And—

“Wilson, that better be you! About time, been waiting on you all day! Now where’s my bloody van? You think this ruddy piano’s gonna move itself!?”

Sirius’ mouth dropped open, and he quickly shut it.

“Fletcher…? Fletcher, it’s me, Sirius Black.”

Silence echoed through the phone, and then a short clatter, as though someone had dropped the receiver.

“Blimey—Sirius!” Fletcher cried a moment later; “Didn’t realise it was you, son. I was just—er… Waiting on this repair guy! Piano’s gone outta tune, gots to get it checked. What can I do for ya?”

“We—uh…” Glancing back at his friends, Sirius cleared his throat. “We’ve been trying to contact you, Fletch. For ages. It’s about our demo. You promised us that—”

“Ah, right, right, the demo! Sorry ‘bout that, lads, went outta town for the holidays. Then the missus made a massive stink about going up to visit her parents. They’re getting old, you know. Can’t hardly get outta bed on their own nowadays, and the government won’t do nothin’ tah support ‘em. You always know a society’s gone downhill when it stops taking care ‘a its elderly.”

The never-ending speech felt like Fletcher’s usual harangue, but they were tired and too hungry for answers to entertain it. Luckily Sirius wasn’t a complete fool.

“Look, Fletcher, you promised us that demo before Christmas—we paid you for the lawyers’ fees for EMI, so what’s going on?”

“Tell you’s what, how ‘bout you and the boys come by my office sometime this week and we can talk all about it? After that we can get the show on the road quick ‘nuff, you’s jus’ got a few more papers to sign, s’all.”

“Papers? What papers —Fletcher, we haven’t signed anything!”

“What’s he talking about?” Peter demanded.

“Er—that's right!” Fletcher cried, still upbeat and dreadfully personable. “Can't do anything wif'out signing them papers first! Gotta set it all straight before we head over to EMI, don’t we? Show the big boys we mean business. So let's say you lads come over sometime next week and we’ll sort it all out then, yeah?”

“How about today—”

“No!” The manager yelped, before giving a very hearty laugh. “Ahem —I mean, today’s no good for me, lads. Got lots of meetings lined up with the studio. Plus I gotta sort out that piano, y’know? In fact—I, uh—I think that’s Al with the van now! So I’ll see you lads next week, let's say 3 o'clock Wednesday. Sounds great to me. Now ta!”

He hung up very quickly, and they were left to stare at one another. No one said it, but it was clear they all had the same bad feeling.

James reached for his coat, hanging on the back of one of the dining room chairs.

“Right. Who’s got the van keys then?”

BUZZ! BUZZ! BUZZZZZZZ!

“Sirius, he isn’t answering.”

“He’s gonna answer!” BUZZZZ! BUZZZZ!

Remus sighed, turning away from the door.

“Let me try!” Peter insisted, pushing Sirius away from the ringer. He tried several times to no avail, and finally James took a turn. BUZZ! BU–BU–BUZZZZZZZ!

Irritated by the noise, Remus retreated across the pavement and lit a cigarette. Cars passed him by, as did the people, most of them shuffling along quickly so as to avoid the chilly wind that was cutting through Soho like a knife. The next door ‘SEXX’ shop’s neon sign was out, it being before randy-hours, and a bum was sleeping in the doorway opposite the street from them. The whole thing felt as grey as the sky, and not for the first time, Remus got the feeling that their ‘too-good-to-be-true’ moment had finally reached its end.

“Maybe he’s left for the day,” he overheard James say.

“Or maybe he’s still trying to pull the wool over our eyes,” Peter said, ringing the bell once more. With an unhappy grunt, Sirius shoved him out of the way and began hammering his fist against the bell. BUZZ! BUZZ! BUZZ!

“UGH! Moony, come see if you can pick the door!”

“I don’t have a pin or nothing on me,” Remus said, ambling back over. “C’mon, let’s just come back later.”

"He could be in a meeting," James suggested.

“You really believe that shite, Potter?”

“Don’t you? I know you would’ve this morning.”

Sirius scowled at him and turned back to the door. “I don’t care if Rod Stewart and the bloody Queen are shooting a porn rag in his office, he’s—” BUZZ ; “gonna—” BUZZ ; “answer!”

B–BUZZ! B–BUZZ! B–BU—

“Bloody—ALRIGHT!”

It was a woman. She opened the building’s front door with a vexing hiss, revealing hair that was bleached to a fry and a robe that was little more than a bit of black lace with a wrap around her middle. She might’ve been pretty once, but a combination of age and poor luck had left her face looking saggy and tired-looking, smudges of mascara impressed beneath either eye.

“Can I fucking help you?” She shrilled, mouth drawn up to reveal uneven, yellowed teeth.

“We’re here to see Fletcher.”

“Who?”

“Doug Fletcher,” James clarified; “The music rep.”

The woman slumped against the doorway, raising a cigarette to her lips. “Sorry, boys. No ‘Doug Fletcher’ ‘ere.”

“Yes, yes there is!” Peter insisted. “There were two of them, Doug and Albert! Second floor, office three!”

“Nuh-uh. No offices ‘ere either.”

“But we were just here last month!”

She drew a deep breath and blew the smoke up over their heads. “Listen, I manage the whole building, and I’m telling ya, I didn’t rent to no ‘Doug Fletcher’.”

“Who’s in number three then?” Sirius snapped.

“Can’t say. M’sure it goes against some sort ‘a renter’s agreement or clause or whatever.”

“How about if we made it worth your while?”

Shoving his hand into his pocket, Sirius withdrew a pair of rumpled tenners and held the money up. The landlady eyed them sceptically, before reaching out and snapping up the notes, which she tucked into her bra.

“You said flat three? That was a short term rental, only asked for a couple month’s lease. Paid in cash too. Guy’s name was Mundungie.”

“ ‘Mundungie?’”

“Somethin’ like that, yeah.”

“Do you know if he’s in now?” Urged James.

“Unfortunate if he were, what with the way you four were wailing on the bell, but no. He and his skinny boyfriend moved out this morning.”

“This MORNING?!” They all exclaimed. Unfazed, the woman ashed her cigarette on the doorway and shrugged.

“Bad luck, boys. But hey, maybe you can still catch one of ‘em. I saw the skinny one carrying things out into the alley earlier. Normally I don’t let out to those who I figure are buggerin’ each other, but these days I can’t really be arsed. A tenant’s a tenant, s’long as they pay on time and don’t bring the work home. Are any of you looking for a place then? I could … OI!”

None of them had stuck around long enough to even hear her offer; they were off like lightning the moment she mentioned the alley. Like with much of London, they were forced to leg it all the way down the street, where they looped the corner and found an entrance to a long, grime-encrusted back lot. There they kept running, racing past back doors that lead to various businesses and the steel bin lorries set outside. As they neared the end, Remus nearly tripped on a manhole cover that was left to teeter precariously off to one side. While he was busy having flashbacks to that night in the pit back in Hawkings, Remus heard Sirius give a deep bellow;

“ALBERT!”

Looking up, he spotted Albert near the end of the alley, loading boxes into the back of a large white van.

“Oh shit!”

Scrambling to toss the rest of the boxes inside, Albert threw the van’s doors shut and ran to jump in the front; too bad for him, Sirius got there first. He grabbed Albert by the back collar of her jacket just as he was climbing inside and threw him up against the side of the van, pinning him in place with arm across the base of his throat.

“Talk!” Sirius hissed. “Before we rip your arms off and beat you with them!”

“Alright, alright!” Albert keened. “I’ll talk, just—just don’t hurt me!”

“You little fucking wanker!” James yelled; “You thought you could take our money and just run off? Where the hell is Fletcher?!”

“I–I don’t know!”

Sirius slammed a fist against the side of the van next to Albert's head. “THINK!”

“Okay! Okay! He’s gone, not like, dead or anything, b-but he ain’t here anymore!”

“Where is he then?” Remus barked.

“I dunno, I swear! He dropped me, same as you! Scam’s no good once people start figuring it out so he never sticks around in the same place for long.”

“So it was a scam!” Peter huffed furiously.

“ ‘Course it was a scam! You really think a guy like Mundungus Fletcher had ties to one of the biggest music labels in the country?”

“Mundungus?” Remus echoed. "You've got to be fucking joking me."

Albert shrugged haplessly. “Can’t help what our parents name us, right?”

The Marauders all shared a defeated look. Fuck.

“Look,” Albert rasped, before straining his neck to lessen Sirius’ grip on it; “You seem like nice kids, so I’m gonna do ya a solid and fill you in— eugh!”

“Stop talking,” Sirius growled, bearing his weight down further; “You’re gonna tell us the truth, and you're gonna tell us where our money is, or we're gonna be using your face to scrub the fucking pavement.”

“Alright, poshy, alright. Just ease up a bit, okay? Can’t hardly breathe ‘ere!”

Remus reached over and grabbed Sirius by the shoulders, slowly walking him back until he’d released his grip on the miserable man. Still wheezing, although laying it on entirely too thick, Albert took a moment to massage his windpipe before straightening up.

“It’s a common scam for those who know their way around the industry, innit. You take a group of wannabe rock stars and you promise ‘em big things. Recording contracts, houses, cars, girls, drugs—it don’t matter. They always fall for it, because we're all just as desperate for a piece ‘a the pie as everyone else.”

“You’ve done this before then” James scowled. “Tricked honest people out of their money.”

"They ain't all honest," Albert griped. “It’s easier with young guys—guys like you, fresh off the mummy-daddy money train. You think you know how the world works but you don’t. You think anyone would bend over backwards to make you happy. Give you the shirt off their backs if you only asked for it.”

“I'd be careful not to insult us,” Sirius warned, “or you’re gonna need an extra shirt just to mop up all the blood after we cut you open and sell your kidneys to make up for our losses.”

Albert shrugged, running a hand over his jaw. “Fletch’s been doing this a long time, kid. Longer than you've been around. Hell, even did it to me and my band a few years back.”

“He scammed you too?” Peter asked. “Then why are you working with him?”

“Money’s money. You think you can survive on a janitor’s wage?”

“You’re a janitor? But what about EMI?” James echoed. Then it dawned on him. “You don’t really work at EMI… do you.”

“Sure, I do,” Albert said. “I’m the night janitor. Or I should say, I was the night janitor. Got sacked last week when they found out I’d let you guys inside. Quite enjoyed the sound stuff though. Think I could make a real career out of it one day?”

Looking about ready to explode, Sirius turned away and aimed a sharp kick at the alley wall.

“ FUCK!”

“Nah, don’t sweat it,” Albert said dismissively; “I know exactly how you feel, lads. But my piece of shit band wasn’t gonna get anywhere anyway—realised it when I figured out what Fletch had done. You want my advice? Get out while you can. You boys don’t have a snowball’s chance in hell of making it anywhere. The music industry’s gonna take one look at 'chu, bleed you for all yer worth, and leave ya for dead. Hopes and dreams? That’s all bunk. And you’re gonna realise it one day when you’ve woken up feeling like you are dead, wishing you were, and working on crap because the whole world’s crap and you’re the crappiest crap of all and then maybe—!”

Albert never got to finish. Before he knew what he was doing, Remus had stepped forward and swung at him. He caught the janitor upside the chin, felt the scruff of his stubble against his bare knuckles, and watched as Albert went down beside the van’s front tire like a bag of bricks.

“Aw shit, Moons!” James moaned, as they rushed to check that he hadn’t done any worse damage. Fortunately, Albert was still breathing. He sat up on the dirty cement, holding his jaw and looking up like he couldn’t believe Remus had actually hit him.

“Wha’ the ‘ell, man?”

“You should’ve stayed scared of us,” Remus said lowly.

Wincing, Albert pulled his hand away and gently tested his jaw. Since it was clearly not broken, he reluctantly stood up and began dusting himself off. “Alright, I can see you’re very serious about all of this, so you might as well get what you paid for. Mind if I step back into the van for a moment?”

“Nice try,” scoffed Peter. “You tell us what it is we’re looking for, and we’ll get it for you.”

Rolling his eyes, he gestured toward the back doors. “Blue box. Tiny one with the handle.”

Eagerly, Peter sprung into action. He went around the side of the van and after a few seconds, came back with a tiny PVC case, filled with various unlabelled tapes.

“What’s this?”

“Whaddya mean 'what's this?' That there’s your demo.”

Four jaws dropped. The contents of the box was little more than a mess of tapes—there had to be at least twenty of them, and most appeared to be wound incorrectly or else had bits of film sticking out. It was a far cry from any professional demo recording.

“You’ve got to be joking,” James said, peering over Peter’s shoulder to get a look.

"You keep saying that," Albert remarked. "Sorry lads, but if you wanted something better maybe you shouldn’t have hired the janitor to do it.”

Already fuming, Remus jumped toward him a second time and Albert fell back into the side of the van with a loud thump, hands up in surrender. “Sorry!" He yelped; "Not funny—not funny at all. My bad, really. Bad Albert, bad! S’just… at least you have something now, right? S’more than any ‘a the other poor sods got.”

“Have what? This is just a pile of crap,” Sirius hissed.

“ 'Pile of crap'?” Albert crossed his arms indignantly. “That crap got me fired, I’ll have you know. You’re lucky you got anything at all. Fletcher’s never gone so far for one of his scams before. Getting you in at De Lane was totally unnecessary, if you ask me. Most don’t even make it to the office, though I guess that just means he thought you were worth your salt after all. Maybe you should take it as a sign. Maybe you could be that diamond in the rough! That is, if you remember to sign a contract first.”

Sirius grabbed hold of Albert’s collar again. “We want our money back, shite-for-brains!”

“Hey, I hear you, I really do. But my wallet’s empty, mate. Check for yourself. Search the entire van if you must. All you’re gonna find is a busted piano and some plastic gold records."

"We should take him to the police," said James.

"You could, but really, what’re they gonna do? You have no proof, just little ol' me. I'll bet they don't even hand you a tissue.”

“We could crack your damn skull open,” Sirius threatened.

“Couple ‘a posh school prats like you? Nah, you don’t have the guts.”

Remus growled; “Try us."

At that, a wide grin split across Albert's face, this time with blood in his teeth.

“Alright, go ahead, beat me into the dirt. But it ain’t gonna get you your money back. Ain't gonna bring good ol' Fletch out of hiding. You ain't rock stars, and you ain't no diamond in the rough neither. You're nobodies, and like every other nobody in this Godforsaken city, you four got scammed. So best wake up, lads, 'cause you got about as much chance of making it as rock stars than I do of becoming the Queen of fucking England.”



Chapter End Notes

A 'rolodex' is one of those desktop card index used to record names, addresses, and telephone numbers.

A 'live room' (also known as the 'recording booth') is the room in the recording studio where all the sound happening. On the 'other side of the window' would be the recording computers and the sound tech.

A 'babygrow' is like a sleep suit for babies, obviously.

'Footie' is just short for football.

A 'roach' is the butt of a weed/hash cigarette.

De Lane Lae Studios is a real recording studio. It used to be located in Holborn but was moved to Wembley in the early 70s. Lots of big names recorded there, including Jimi Hendrix, Pink Floyd, Queen, and Deep Purple.

The 'Sunday Observance Act' was an act of Parliament in Great Britain that essentially prohibited the use of any building or room for public entertainment or debate on a Sunday. While not necessarily enforceable in private homes, it was generally frowned upon to hold big gatherings on the "Lord's Day". It was repealed in 2005.

Also this probably doesn't need to be added but in the UK the "ground floor" is the equivalent of the first floor in North America, so a "first floor landing" is technically one floor off the ground, ie. "second level".

Ellen Barrett was the first [openly] lesbian priest in America, ordained in 1977 following the Episcopal Church approved the ordination of women. America's first openly-gay rabbi was Allen Bennett, who declared himself gay in 1978. He was the rabbi who would later officiate the funeral of Harvey Milk later that same year.

The first night of Hanukkah would've indeed fallen on Dec 24th in 1978, and although it's not the most important holiday to the Jewish community, it felt important to me that Dorcas would've been spending the night with her family. Also it probably [very likely] didn't snow in London on Christmas Day in 1978 but I'm pretending it did.

Okay that's all for my notes, see you guys next week on the 18th for the first day of 2022's Hanukkah!

Late February 1979





It would’ve been easy to pretend as though Fletcher hadn’t gotten to them. As though his scam and subsequent betrayal hadn’t knocked the wind from their sails and left them stranded in a sea of doubt. Remus imagined it as headlines:

Armageddon: London Band Strikes Fool’s Gold!

Verdict’s Out on Marauders—‘Mental Makes NO MONEY!’

Messers See Themselves Out: What’s next for this band of willfully ignorant twats?

They each laughed when one of them made a joke about it, but eventually the laughter would filter off into unease, and then came the restlessness. What was next for Marauders? Could this really be it? They'd promised their parents one year... Was fate finally telling them it was time to throw in the towel now? After all this time?

“Bollocks!” Sirius would growl. “It’s just a setback, all bands have ‘em! We’ll work harder—practice every day. Eventually we'll get into a real studio! And fuck managers, they’re all money-grubbing bastards anyway. We’ll do it ourselves, no one knows Marauders like we do. No one knows us like we do.”

And for a while they believed him, but then life began to creep back in—as it tended to—with its usual responsibilities and when no grand opportunity had presented itself on either the real or metaphorical doorstep, the Marauders were finally forced to admit that their music might be taking a back seat. All of their friends were busy these days; Peter had quit working in the basement of his dad’s paper company to go ink illustrations for the comic artists upstairs, and James had been promoted to head waiter at the restaurant. Still madly in love with her fiancé, Lottie continued splitting her time between London and Reading, planning her wedding around train rides and taxi fares while Marlene continued working hard at the non-profit and on her relationship with Dorcas. Out of all of them, Mary was the easiest to pin down. So far she had invited them to several showcases at her conservatory. Being generally busy and not really that big a fan of opera, Remus had only gone to the one, but even he couldn't deny the fact that Mary was brilliant. In just one year she'd managed to expand her voice enough to garner her own solo.

"Brilliant!" Sirius declared, once the concert had ended and they'd all gathered in the lobby. "Assolutamente fantastico! Best contralto in the county."

It was as close as Sirius came to being upbeat since the Fletcher incident. They'd all taken it hard, but Sirius more-so, perhaps just because he'd been the one to vouch for Fletcher the most.

Humbling accepting Sirius' praise, Mary kissed his cheek as Lily handed her friend a small bouquet of roses. Then she beckoned another man over. He was handsome; Remus recognised him as her partner in one of the duets.

"Everyone, this is Claude."

Claude was gone a week later. Last Remus heard Mary was dating some Austrian guy now she’d met while clubbing in St James, but she'd dumped him too the minute things started getting too serious. As far as Remus could tell, Mary quite fancied most of the men she dated, but she knew how to call it quits when they inevitably began pushing for more than she was willing to give. If only they could all be so pragmatic.

Still nursing the gaping wound Fletcher's betrayal had left on his pride, Sirius insisted they made use of every moment the four of them were home together to work on their music. While Lily was busy with school or otherwise fielding phone calls from Lottie as she fussed over wedding caterers and floral arrangements, the Marauders were downstairs in the basement, hard at work. Perhaps too hard. Sirius had deemed their usual 'jam routine' practice-style a futile effort, with too much time spent on haphazard drivel and not enough on overall cohesion. He came at James like a drill sergeant, and Peter like a prison warden—viciously instructing them on their own instruments and not accepting anything less than perfect.

It was unlike them to argue during practice, but after Sirius had spent an entire afternoon meticulously scrutinizing their latest composition, James slumped down on the basement couch with an irritated huff.

"I don't get it," he moaned, "the song's already finished, and I say it's fine!"

"It's badass," added Peter. James nodded, one arm thrust outward in ready agreement.

"Yeah, it's... Shit, it's punk."

"Haven't you been listening?" Sirius snapped. "We're not punk! Tell 'em, Moony!"

Remus said nothing, cravenly plucking at a string on his bass and making himself look busy as though the instrument was ever anything less than in-tune.

"Punk is in," James rebuffed.

"And already on its way out! God, I swear we walked into Fletcher's office and you were staring at the ceiling."

"Who gives a fuck where I was staring, he conned us!"

"Yes, and maybe if we stopped looking at it as just a bad thing, we could learn something!"

"Dunno what you're gonna learn," Peter grumbled quietly. "That demo tape we got back was all rubbish. Not a bit of it was usable."

Sirius ignored the comment, as he did with most things that refused to go his way, and went to stand in front of his mike stand.

"Now again, and bloody do it right this time!" He barked, loudly enough that the feedback from the microphone made all of them wince.

One didn't have to be a genius to realise that Sirius was buckling under the pressure. He had been ever since Fletcher, but Remus knew the real reason for the fire that'd been lit under his arse hit a lot closer to home. Near the end of January, a letter had arrived for James stamped with the University of Exeter's seal. They'd all puzzled over it initially, but when James refused to let any of them read it, Sirius' contemptuous side began to rear its ugly head again.

“Exeter? What’s Exeter University doing sending you post? Are they that desperate for a decent football team?”

James didn’t rise to the bait, and so in answer, Sirius leaned over the back of his dining room chair and snapped the letter up. James was on him in a second, but already Sirius’ teasing smile had vanished.

“They’ve accepted you,” he said, clutching the letter hard enough that his knuckles turned white. “Faculty of Business and Economics… What the fuck do you know about economics, Prongs?”

“It’s just an admissions letter,” James replied bitingly. “Dad has an undergraduate degree in economics, right, so when I applied I just thought that—”

“You applied?!”

“No, I deferred, you nob! Last year. It’s just that time, I expect…”

Sirius laughed humourlessly. “So will you go then? Be a good boy and head off to college just like Mummy and Daddy expect?”

“Sod off. I’m here, aren’t I?”

“For now.”

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

Sirius ignored him. “Did you say yes?”

“No. But could you really blame me if I had?”

The tone in James’ voice was deadly, and Remus could tell by the way Sirius flinched that he felt it too. Desperate to fuel his anger, he whirled next on Peter, who’d been quietly scribbling in a notepad as though he couldn’t be bothered with any of it.

“And you?” He demanded. “Have you gotten any fancy letters you’d like to share with the class?”

Confused, Peter faltered, and Sirius snatched the notepad from his hands.

“What is this anyway, huh?! More illustrations for work? Work—work—bloody work! When’s the last time you put some real practice in on the drums, huh?! I thought you wanted to be the next Ginger Baker, not Walt fucking Disney!”

James got between them;

“Come off it, Black—leave Pete alone!”

“I’m only saying, he’s been real quiet!”

Things might’ve gotten worse, had Remus not reached over and snatched the letter and the sketches away from Sirius himself.

“That’s enough, Pads. I think it’s probably time we all take a break… Cool down a bit.”

The look Sirius gave him could’ve turned a lesser man to stone, but off he went—ashamed and still entirely pissed off. They heard every stomping step on the staircase, and after that—the slam of a bedroom door. Quietly, Remus mourned. He'd never been exiled to the couch before, but he supposed there was a first time for everything.

“I’m not going to Exeter, Moony,” James said later, when Sirius still hadn’t come down.

“I know, Prongs.”

“Sirius just thinks he wants it more than anyone else.”

Out of loyalty for his boyfriend, Remus nearly found himself telling James that he was right—that Sirius did want it more than anyone else. The band had been Sirius' dream for longer than Remus had even known him. Once Remus had asked him who his favourite was. He'd been expecting Bowie, maybe T. Rex or Roxy Music, but Sirius had shot them all down.

My band, he'd said, because my band's gonna be the best.

Remus hadn't believed him then, but he'd believed him a month ago, and he wanted to believe him now.

Only, he hadn’t anticipated what that really meant.

No one brought up James' Exeter letter after that night, and eventually days—and then weeks, had passed altogether. They continued with their Saturday gigs at the Shoestring, but it was clear something had changed. All of their naive enthusiasm had been traded for frustration; the Marauders were tired. Any frequenting fans they’d managed to garner before Fletcher had been put off when they’d realised that their once beautiful singer had been replaced by an angry boy too obsessed with perfection to bother with a simple pint during working hours. As a result the band’s showmanship was suffering. They barely had the energy to play their instruments anymore, let alone interact with their audience. Not all days were tough though, just most of them.

Remus’ nineteenth birthday was set to fall on a Saturday that year, and a sure cause for celebration. Though the ridiculousness of his eighteenth would be hard-pressed to be outdone, the anticipation of an entire pub of inebriated strangers, all singing directly to him, made Remus want to crawl into the deepest, darkest hole he could find.

It was one week to the day of his approaching humiliation when the Marauders arrived in Lambeth for their usual gig. The night had started alright, but then quickly spiralled out of control. James’ new amp kept losing power and Sirius’ microphone insisted on screeching feedback into the audience’s ears, and the drinks they’d downed to help with their hangovers wasn’t doing anything for their general playing. It was mortifying to see the room jump with every squeal of the mike, but not so mortifying as the face Sirius made when the first bout of heckling reached his ears.

“Christ, give us a break already, why don’t cha?”

“Yeah, get off the stage! Send up someone who can actually play something!”

And that was all it took. No less than three seconds later, the entire pub was bearing witness to the great eschaton that was Sirius Black's temper.

“FUCK YOU! If you think you can do better then how ‘bout you peel that crusty arse of yours outta that chair and give it go, fuckin’ tosspot!”

The enraged men stood up and Sirius leapt down to meet them, backed up by an equally inebriated James and a heavily frustrated Peter. The girls were there too, with Dorcas and Mary screaming threats and Marlene about ready to smash her beer bottle over the head of the first person who dared call Sirius a ponce. Ray managed to break up the scuffle before either group could really start battering the other, but he wasn’t very impressed that they’d driven off paying customers when the night had barely begun. After their set he pulled them aside and gave them the grave news. Ray was cancelling next week’s show, as well as the one after that, and Sirius was to go on an immediate holiday.

“What the hell, Ray?!” Sirius demanded. “You’re sacking me?”

“Don’t tempt me, princess. You four were an utter disgrace up there tonight. This is a pub, not a bloody boxing ring! Now the show’s been cancelled, so do yourselves a favour and take the time to get your bleedin’ act together.”

It was another defeat, this time from someone they admired, and they were all thinking it;

Go home, you’re not good enough today. Come back tomorrow. Or never.

Deep down Remus knew that Ray had good intentions, but none of them dared say anything in his favour as they packed their instruments into the back of the van, and especially not after Sirius screamed and hurled a glass bottle against the brick wall of the alley for good measure.

“Well, I for one think it’s a good thing,” Peter grumbled on the drive home. “Could use the practice anyway. We sound like shit.”

“We sound fine!” Sirius snarled at him.

“Yeah, well since when has ‘fine’ gotten anyone a record deal? We’re all out of sync. You can’t decide what key it is you’re singing in and half the time it’s like the rest of us are playing completely different songs.”

“Then maybe you should take a look at the setlist for once, Wormtail, instead of getting off your face on Ray's free Guinness!”

“You can piss right off, Sirius! You’ve been like this for weeks, always slagging off. You used to be cool about everything—or most things, anyway. Now it's like you've gone and turned into your bloody mother."

Remus had to hand it to Peter, he always did know how to go for the throat.

As Lily spun around in the front seat, face engulfed in abject horror, Sirius pulled the sweat towel from around his neck and whipped it at Peter's head.

"Here, Pettigrew, have mine! Since you're so intent on throwing in the bloody towel! Boy, you and Ray sure are a pair!"

Remus groaned, trying to reach between then; "C'mon, guys, that's enough."

"I ain't throwing in the towel!" Peter cried, snubbing Remus completely. "And neither is Ray! He only told us to take a break—”

“WE DON’T NEED A BREAK!”

“Enough!" Lily wailed, slamming her hand down on the passenger's side armrest. "Keep it up and you're going to make Potter drive off the bloody road! What the four of you need is sleep. Sleep and some actual rest. No more killing yourselves over all this, and for God's sake, no more fighting! Now… James and I are going away for Pet’s wedding in a few days, and I think the rest of you should do the same.”

“Ah, and I suppose that means dear Petunia’s extended a few more plus-ones?” Sirius drawled.

Lily's eyes narrowed vexingly. “No, I only meant that you should get out of the house for a while and stop moping around like miserable, squabbling children. Lottie’s wedding is coming up too, and I won’t have you ruddy idiots ruining it by being in such a mood.”

“And where would you suggest we go, o’ wise one?”

“Well, Peter’s going to Moira’s, for example.”

Sirius shot Peter a nasty glare. “I’m sure Stratford’s just idyllic for taking the air.”

Before Peter could fire back a retort, Remus reached across the van’s bench and took his friend's shoulder. “He doesn’t mean it, Pete.”

“Don’t talk for me,” Sirius snapped. “You’re not my sodding mother.”

The comment left a sour note in all of their mouths, and no one spoke any more of of mothers or weddings until they’d passed from Kensington back into Shepherd’s Bush.

“Maybe a holiday would be good for all of us,” James suggested haggardly. “It's like Daisy said, she and I are going up to Liverpool, and Pete’s off with Moira. Moony, Black—the two of you could take the van and go anywhere you wanted. How 'bout Devon? The house there is always empty this time of year. It’ll be chilly, sure, but I’m sure Mum and Dad wouldn’t mind lending you the keys.”

“Oh, yes, Devon!” Sirius sang tersely. “Where the young go to cry and the old go to die. I’m sure there’ll be plenty to do. We can go to the pub with all the locals—dip our toes in the ocean and see how long it takes them to fall off.”

“I’ve never been to the sea,” said Remus, blandly. This was apparently quite the revelation, as Sirius and Peter whirled on him very suddenly. Up ahead, James was already adjusting the rear view mirror while Lily craned her head around as well, mouth open in a tiny ‘o’.

“Never, Remus?”

“Well… Maybe once when I was really young, but I don’t remember it.”

"You came all the way to Dover to get me," Sirius pointed out.

"Yes, and I was a bit too preoccupied to go hunting for seashells, if you didn't notice."

Sirius looked away, but in the front seat, James was practically doing a jig.

“There then!” He declared. “Black, why don’t you take Lupin to the sea? It’ll be like an early birthday trip. You can take the van—make a road-trip out of it if you'd really like. I'm sure Moony can swing the time off work, hasn't very well asked for any time off before, have you, Moons?”

Not wanting to step on any toes, Remus glanced warily at Sirius. He didn't look excited by the idea, but at the risk of sounding like an absolute arse, Sirius simply turned his cheek into his shoulder and muttered a quiet, "Whatever."

Remus tried not to let it show, but secretly he was glad they were getting out of town for a while. Ever since Fletcher, the flat had taken on a rather dismal disposition. Dishes had started to pile up in the sink, and more than once they’d missed putting the bin out on the curb for pick up. It wasn’t that they’d all suddenly become slobs, more like there was so little time for anything else. Work, band—no play. Lily did her best to stay on top of things, but none of them had ever considered her a maid, nor would she tolerate being treated as such. That evening, when they returned to an entryway in desperate need of a mop, Lily turned on them and said just three words.

“Clean. Then pack.”

No one argued.

The next morning, Remus called Dorcas and begged her to cover his shifts at the music shop. She agreed, only after much bribery and enough begging that Remus swore his pride would never be the same again. Come Tuesday, when James and Lily were set to leave on a train from King’s Cross, the rest of them gathered their things together and said their goodbyes. Peter had already caught the early train to Moira’s, and Remus was just getting ready to give his friends a lift to the station when Mr. Potter made an unannounced visit. He’d been kind enough to drop off the keys for the holiday house and even offered to drive the happy couple to the station himself so that Remus and Sirius could get on the road at a reasonable hour. Positively buzzing, he stood in the entryway pouring over an A to Z road map that was probably as old as they were.

“Effie told me of your plans last night, and I think it’s brilliant!” He declared, in the same up-beat tone as his son days before. “The house itself is in Dawlish, remember, but Exeter’s just a half hour up the road if you get bored. Sometimes the power gets a bit finicky right after winter, so if it goes out just flip the circuit breaker in the garage. Much easier than when I was a boy—they were all real fuses back then. If you have any questions you can always give Effie and I the bell. Though… I suspect the two of you will be just fine.”

He gave them a sort of cheeky side-eye, and Remus was left with the feeling that Effie had let him in on more than just their spur-of-the-moment holiday plans.

“Thanks, Dad,” Sirius said, wrapping his arms around the older man. Remus hugged him too, albeit less firmly, and afterwards Sirius nudged him, already turning for the stairs.

“I’m gonna go get out bags,” he said, folding up the map. He passed James and Lily on his way up the staircase, and while Lily simply embraced Sirius and left a kiss on his cheek before carrying on down, James took a moment to pull him aside.

“It’ll be good,” Remus heard him murmur; “Just try and relax.”

If Sirius said anything in reply, Remus didn’t catch it. Already Lily was approaching him and Monty, suitcase in one hand, handbag in the other.

“Lily!” Monty cried. “You get lovelier every time I see you.”

“Hello, Monty,” Lily smiled, setting down her bags so she might hug him also. “Thank you so much for offering to drive James and I to the station. We really could’ve taken a taxi.”

“Nonsense, it’s no problem at all. Is this everything then?”

“Yes, should be. James is just bringing his suit down now.”

“So what’s the verdict, Evans?” Remus asked. “Are you wearing chartreuse?”

“Worse.” Bending down, Lily opened the top of the suitcase to reveal a pastel yellow dress covered in frilly satin flowers. “I’m considering spilling wine on it halfway through the ceremony just so I can change.”

“If you really want to stop the show you could just spill the wine on Petunia instead."

Smirking, Lily began to rifle through her things. “Here,” she said, pulling out a tiny vinyl bag and pushing it into his hands. “My camera. Thought you might want to take it with you.”

Remus stared at the device dubiously, afraid any sudden jostle might break it. “Your camera? But don’t you want it for the wedding?”

“Knowing Pet, there’ll be plenty of cameras around already. And besides, she’s got me on child-rearing duty the entire time anyway. Vernon’s got cousins coming in from the countryside and she's invited all the neighbours... Now there’s two full rolls of film in there. It should work fine so long as you don’t drop it into the sea or something.”

“No promises," Remus smiled, but he clutched the device protectively.

With a quick kiss on the cheek goodbye, Lily zipped up her suitcase and made to carry it out the door. Remus went to help, but was instantly rebuffed by Monty as he gathered Lily’s things in one arm and used the other to walk her down to the flat’s front steps.

“All ready then?” James chirped, flouncing down to the main floor with a garment bag over one shoulder.

“Yup. That your suit then?”

“Mhm. Freshly tailored, matter-of-fact. Had to let it out a bit in the waist… I think I've gained weight, Moons.”

“You mean since secondary school?" Remus gave him the quick once over. “Think it's normal, mate."

“You're probably right. 'Sides, Lily says she likes it. More padding to cuddle.” James pat his gut fondly. “We’ll be back next Sunday. Now are you sure you and Sirius are going to be okay on your own?”

“ ‘Course. I’ll feed and walk him twice a day.”

“That’s my boy.”

They embraced, and after a quick check to see that he had his keys, James blessed Remus with his final goodbyes and slipped out the front door. The instant he’d gone, Sirius’ voice echoed down from the floor above.

“Moony! Did you see what happened to that copy of ‘NME’ I left on the dresser table? I just bought it…”

“I packed it!” Remus called back. “Thought you might like to have it on the road.”

“Oh. Good thinking.”

Sirius descended the steps a few moments later. He brought with him their largest trunk—their! Felt a bit crazy to think about—as well as a familiar leather guitar case, still just as worn and chipped as the day Andy had gifted it to him.

“Are you sure you want to bring that?” Remus asked, eyeing the guitar warily. “I think the whole purpose of this is to… you know, get away from it for a while.”

“We have to practice, don’t we?”

“You’re not going to get rusty in one week.”

Sirius looked down at the case, lips pursed stubbornly. Remus was already readying himself for a row, when Sirius sighed and set the guitar down against the entryway wall.

“Ready then?”

Remus blinked, trying not to seem too stunned.

“Er... Y-Yeah! Let’s get going…”

They met each other on the threshold of the rug, and there Sirius turned his head up for a kiss. Remus nearly melted. He knew Sirius' chronically bad mood hadn't entirely dissipated, but he’d never been so looking forward to a real holiday in all his life. Perhaps Mary was wrong; maybe romance wasn’t so intolerable after all.

“I’m driving,” Sirius said, as they stepped out the door.

“Oh, you are so not driving…”

They got into Dawlish just a few minutes shy of midday. It was a straight-shot along the M4, then down toward Exeter, and it rained the whole way, beating the van’s front windows until Remus was half-sure they’d be swept off the motorway.

“Do you feel like stopping at all?” Remus asked. “Monty said Exeter’s got all the decent pubs.”

“No,” Sirius replied, busy glaring out the window.

Remus kept on driving.

The downpour had lightened by the time they were pulling onto the seaside town’s main road, but the day's previously poor weather had cleared the pavement of all pedestrians anyway. They passed rows upon rows of sleepy houses coloured in worn white, yellow, and blue, and retaining walls made of original brick and mortar. Just over the rooftops Remus could make out the dusky blue waters of the English channel. It was exciting; he’d never wanted much for the ocean, but now that they were there, he could feel the swell of it in his chest. When he cracked his window the briny sea-smell of it seeped in like the rain, clearing his sinuses and giving him the first real breath of fresh air he'd taken since leaving Scotland last June. He'd read once that those who lived by the ocean tended to live longer. Seeing it—smelling it—Remus now understood why.

“Should be your next right,” Sirius said, squinting down at the A to Z and turning it around several times.

“You sure? Your last right almost took me to Glastonbury.”

“Are you gonna sass me or are you gonna turn right?”

“Aye, aye, captain—turning right.”

They arrived at the house when the sky was only drizzling, and there on the corner of the lane that overlooked the sea, they found a mini Potter Cottage sitting idly, just as quaint and as sleepy as the rest of its distant neighbours. The summer house had a private drive for the van, with an attached garage, white stucco walls, and a terracotta roof. All of its windows were framed white as well, with several of them bearing panes made of the most dazzling stained glass. The key stuck in the lock a bit but when it finally gave way, it revealed a cosy living room made up of light pine furnishings and cashmere rugs. Attached to it was a kitchen, with cupboards painted grey and adorned in matching rainbow glass. The rest of the interior was modest—or modest for its means, anyway. There was no television, but there was a radio. The bottom floor was split up between the kitchen and dining room as well as an office that doubled as the guest room, while the upstairs held two bedrooms and the single bath, all decorated identically to the little beach-themed bathroom the Potters’ kept in their home back in London.

“It’s nice,” Remus said, peeling out of his winter coat. “Ceilings are a bit low though.”

“You’re just too tall,” Sirius mused, stretching up to brush his fingers along one of the wooden ceiling beams. “At least it’s not completely freezing inside. Flick on the radiator will you?”

While Remus did so, Sirius shook the damp from his hair and strolled into the kitchen. He went to the fridge first, opening it and sighing. Empty, as expected.

“We’re going to have to make a shop run for dinner. How’s the weather?”

“Think the rain’s mostly stopped," Remus replied, peeking out the lace curtains.

“Might as well go now then. Just let me change first.”

Sirius grabbed their trunk and headed down the hall for the guest bedroom, and Remus continued peering out the window. The cottage itself was just a few kilometres from the sea, situated on top of one of the majestic cliffs the town was known for—making for the most amazing view. It being early March, the beach was mostly empty, but he could just make out a few wandering gulls soaring down over the shore.

Letting the lacy curtain fall back into place, Remus strolled back over to the radiator to warm his hands. It was then that he noticed the small wall hutch hung up over the dining room table. Covered top to bottom in photographs, the hutch bore memories from every summer James had been alive; James in the garden, no taller than Monty’s waist, James without his two front teeth, wearing swimming bottoms and a woman’s sunhat, James on the end of a pier, holding a crab bigger than his head. There were other family members Remus didn’t recognise, even a few of Peter; his chubby arm wrapped around James’ shoulders while James grinned his very James Potter grin and held two fingers up behind Peter’s head.

“Ugh, just look at them and their happy childhoods,” Sirius drawled, strolling up from behind while tying his hair into a half-knot behind his head.

“Sorta makes you want to punch an eight year-old in the face, don’t it?”

“Just a bit.”

Remus snorted, turning to look at him. “Oi… That’s my jumper.”

Sirius glanced down at the burgundy knit jumper he’d pulled over his t-shirt. “Obviously. Now are you ready to go?”

They walked instead of taking the van, and though it was chilly, Remus appreciated it. It was the air—the smell of it, the clarity; like his lungs were breathing for the very first time. Overhead the gulls cried, and when they reached the promenade he made Sirius stand at the edge while he fumbled with Lily’s camera.

“Do you even know how to use that thing?”

“Just shut up and smile.”

He snapped the photo and as it was printing, Sirius came forward and snatched the camera for himself.

“Let’s take one together.”

While Remus bent down next to him, Sirius raised the camera. He smiled, but for several seconds there was nothing.

“Aren’t you—”

KA-CHICK!

“Moons, you ruined it!”

“And I think you’ve blinded me. Ugh…”

As Remus straightened up and rubbed the flash from his eyes, Sirius gave a snort and ripped the spoilt photo from its spout. “Here,” he said, raising the camera once more, “give us a little snog this time.”

“A snog?"

“Yeah, why not? It’s not like anyone else’s around.”

That was true enough. They’d only passed two people on their way down from the house, a man pruning the dead branches from her front hedges and an old woman walking her dog. Now that they were there, a quick glance in either direction told him that they were the only two on the promenade. They might as well have been the only two in the whole world.

“Alright,” Remus said, secretly giddy. “But only one.”

Sirius smiled and leaned his face back in. They met in the middle, and one more flash and shutter sound later, he was waving the fresh photo through the air.

“You better not show anyone that,” Remus warned, taking the camera and hanging it around his neck by the strap.

“No, I’ll save it for the grandchildren.”

They made their way down onto the beach, past the craggy stones and onto a soft brown sand that clung to the soles of their boots. Remus regularly found himself sinking into the mud holes and little tide pools, but Sirius danced along like it was nothing—winter scarf billowing behind him in the wind. Not far off they could see a family enjoying themselves near the very edge of the shore; every now and then the kids would shoot into the water up to their ankles, scream, and rush out again. Eventually their mother bundled them up into little towels and they retreated back toward the stone stairs, until they were naught but tiny specks in the distance.

“I used to love coming to the sea,” Sirius said, busy kicking up sand as he stared out over the horizon. He had a far-away look in his eye Remus could relate to, like he was thinking about somewhere else.

“Wasn’t aware the great city of Bath had a sea,” Remus called, raising the camera. He snapped a photo of Sirius impressed in the creamy orange glow of the early sunset and afterwards Sirius turned around to smirk at him.

“It doesn’t. Our governess, Gisela—”

“The one who ran off with the gardener?”

“And don’t forget the twenty-thousand pounds from my dad’s safe,” Sirius added keenly. “Before she split she’d sometimes take us over to Bristol in the summertime. They had this nice beach over in Portishead, bit different from here, but—well, I can’t remember much, really… Used to come home with my feet all cut up from walking on all the barnacles though.”

“Didn’t you swim?”

“ ‘Course, but Reg hated it. Hated the whole thing, to be honest. Though, s'probably my fault. See, I used to dig up the tiny crabs and put them down the back of his shirt… Once I even brought one back with me and left it on his pillow for him to find. Told him it must’ve crawled into his ear and drove all the way home with us.”

“You are an absolute terror. No wonder he hated you.”

“Yeah, maybe... We’re better now though."

In a moment of vulnerability, Sirius looked up from the sand and Remus saw all the memories impressed onto his face like a tattered mask.

“I never really was a very good brother,” he murmured. “Just… left him there, didn’t I?”

“You were a kid,” Remus said, overcome with a sense of déjà vu.

“So was he.” Sirius sniffed, his cheeks rosy from the cold. “I was a bad brother… Think I waited too long to fix things. Now I’m here and he’s there—"

"Regulus is at Hawkings."

"For now. But what about after? He's almost finished with school, and sure—he could go to some fancy university far away, 'cept Mum's never gonna let that happen. He's all they've got now... What if he never gets out?”

Remus shuffled closer, bending in so he and Sirius were nearly nose-to-nose.

“He will.”

"And if he doesn't want to?"

"Then he'll have to decide that for himself." Remus sighed, touching their foreheads together. "Regulus is smart, Sirius. And you two are more alike than you think.”

Somehow, it was enough for Sirius, and he smiled quietly while accepting the quick kiss Remus offered next. Afterwards he raised both hands up above his head, giving a long stretch before a brisk wind came and left him trembling beneath his coat.

“Fuck—alright. That’s enough beach for today. Let’s head over to the shops before they close, I'm starving.”

They turned together, setting sun at their backs as they made their way back toward the concrete promenade. Halfway there, Remus glanced down at Sirius’ hand, his knuckles red from the cold. When he reached down to take it, Sirius snapped his face toward him.

“We’re holding hands in public now?”

“Why not? It’s not like anyone else’s around.”

“Mm… Clever you.”





* * *





Wednesday 7th March 1979



Reading by the seaside was better than reading anywhere else, Remus had decided—save maybe the middle of the night with Sirius sleeping beside him and the sound of rain pattering against their bedroom window. He learned to love the sound of the waves rolling in, and the wind as it whistled off the water. For the first time in his life he was waking feeling fully rested—eager to get out and breathe the fresh air.

“Maybe we should get a house on the beach,” he said the next morning.

“Yeah, like in Santa Monica,” Sirius replied, busy brushing sand from their blanket while munching on one of the butteries they’d picked up for an easy breakfast. “We’ll get ourselves a big place, with a killer view. Throw massive parties—Prongs can even invite Farrah Fawcett. It’ll be a blow-out.”

Remus didn’t hate the idea, but he returned to his book anyway, pretending not to notice the antsy way Sirius was bobbing his leg. His fingers too, were incessant. It'd been less than twenty-four hours and yet they were constantly tapping or flicking, as though he was just desperate for a set of strings to set them against. He tried reading—the Potters kept an impressive collection, even way out in Devon—but it was clear that it was mostly for Remus’ sake. Sirius held the book, considered its pages—but just appeared bored. Remus wished it were summer, so that they might actually find something to do other than sit in silence or listen to Radio 1’s Top 40.

“Feel like heading over to the pub for supper?”

“Sure,” Sirius shrugged. “Could use a pint.”

So dinner was settled, but they still had an entire day to kill. When the wind inevitably started to pick up again, they fled the beach for warmer accommodations only to find that the power had gone out back at the cottage.

“Monty did warn us this might happen,” Sirius sighed, as Remus smacked the radiator and found it cool to the touch.

A few rolling arpeggios later and the rapture was through. For several seconds no one did anything, there was silence among the mob. Remus waited for the applause they were used to—the hollering that accompanied every one of their London performances—but there was nothing. Finally, when Sirius looked about ready to flee the piano altogether, a man up front leaned forward.

“Well? You gonna play another, son?”

The breath of relief Remus gave mirrored Sirius’, and when he smiled, everyone began to cheer and clap. Between them, Sirius looked at Remus and matched his giddy grin. It’s good! Remus mouthed back, flashing him a thumbs up and a subtle 'go on'.

Someone came forward and set a pint on the edge of the piano, which Sirius snatched up immediately.

“Rule number one!” He called, with all his usual Sirius-vigour. “Never put a drink on a piano. Do that, and it’s bound to go end-up.”

Then he knocked the glass back and finished it in a single breath. The pub cheered, and after he’d wiped his mouth, Sirius set his fingers back on the keys.

“Gonna take it back with this one. See if you know the words… ‘The warden threw a party in the county jail! The prison band was there and they began to wail! The band was jumpin' and the joint began to swing! You should've heard those knocked out jailbirds sing—"

Let's rock!

Everybody, let's rock!

Everybody in the whole cell block—

Was dancin' to the jailhouse rock!

They left in a hurry, as all good stars do, with bellies full of beer they hadn’t paid for and grand smiles on their faces. The barkeep had told Sirius to come back anytime; apparently the drink sold better with a show. Who would've thought it?

“God—I missed this!” Sirius exclaimed, as they emerged from the pub and the crisp midnight air hit them dead in the face. “We should do more shows! A few nights a week at the Shoe ain’t enough to get us anywhere.”

“We could try somewhere new! Like Soho! Or—Or Camden!” Remus suggested, more than willing to humour him after what he'd just witnessed. “Maybe one of the local universities will like us.”

“Whaddya talking about, everyone likes us!”

“It’s a first step.”

“Yeah okay, but we’ll want bigger! Remember—Madison Square Garden in four years!”

“Let’s start with a few polytechnics first and see what happens.”

Sirius laughed, then stumbled—barely able to stand up on his own anymore.

“Bugger, we should’ve drank more! S’not like we were the ones payin’ for it.”

“You’ve drunk enough,” Remus told him, clutching the arm Sirius had slung over his shoulders. “Here, wanna stop for some fags.”

They turned into a passing corner shop and while Sirius slipped down the sweets aisle, Remus went for the front counter, pressing the bell until the attendant appeared out from the back office.

“One packet of Embassy Golds, please.”

“We’re out. Got Players.”

“Eh… Yeah, that’ll do.”

As the guy rang him up, Remus noticed a radio playing from inside the office. He recognised the voice as the disc jockey from that morning’s pirate station, but it was what he was talking about that really interested him. Every now and then he caught a word—“London”, “concert”, “clash”.

“Can you turn that up, please?”

The attendant glanced at him, and then drifted back into the office, raising the volume loud enough for Remus to overhear.

“Yes, you heard it here first, folks!” The DJ trilled. “The Anti-Nazi League’s hosting a rally in Westminster in protest of the Metropolitan Police’s lack of support following several attacks within the city, and rocking punk act The Clash—fresh off their Pearl Harbour tour—have volunteered to play in support. The attacks are thought to be a result of the rising influence of far-right groups such as the National Front and it is the hope of those participating to force those negligent MPs into direct action! All proceeds from the concert go toward local charities and supporting those affected by the violence, so YOU too can catch the Clash live Friday—tomorrow night, at the Lyceum Ballroom in the West End. Be there, or be a sodding bigot.”

Remus’ hand shot out.

“Sirius! Sirius, come over here!”

Sirius wandered over, chewing on an open packet of giant coke bottles. “Wha...?”

“The guy on the radio says that the Clash are having a concert. They’re playing in the Lyceum tomorrow night.”

“But that’s in London.”

“I know.”

Sirius squinted at him, still chewing. “Tomorrow's your birthday. You think we should go?”

“Why not? We can do what we want with our own holiday, can’t we?”

“I suppose so.”

“Are you gonna pay for those?” The shop attendant asked, appearing in front of them and pointing at Sirius’ coke bottles. Remus sighed and snatched the sweets, setting them on the counter.

“This, and the pack of Players.”





* * *





Saturday 10th March 1979





Despite the night’s excitement leaving him absolutely wired, Remus slept hard. When he woke, he turned over to find that Sirius had already gone from their bed. He could still feel the warmth left on his side of the covers, as well as the tail-ends of what might’ve been a dream weighing on the forefront of his mind. Already he could feel it slipping away from him, no different from all the others he woke up forgetting, except that this time, all he could remember was Tomny.

They'd been talking. Just talking. About what, Remus couldn't recall. Happy birthday, Lu—had Tomny said that? Maybe. But then a baby started crying, and well…

Remus pushed the thought away. They were going home today, no need to get weepy with a four hour drive and an entire rock concert ahead of them.

“Sirius?”

There was no answer from downstairs, and when he came into the kitchen Remus found the dishes washed and sitting in the drying rack. Scratching the back of his head, he went to the backdoor and opened it to the brisk Devon chill.

“Sirius?”

Again, no answer; but this time Remus could hear the distant sound of radio music coming from inside the garage. He was just in time to witness the local dust lorry as it rumbled up the road toward the next house. Stuffing his feet and pyjama bottoms into his boots, Remus scuttled down the driveway and picked up the now-empty tin bin, carrying it back to its place amongst the heap of rubbish that had been left piled next to the garage. He couldn’t remember putting it out the night before, but clearly one of them had been sober enough to do it.

“Sirius?” Remus banged on the outside of the garage, once he’d wrestled the bin into place. “Are you alive?”

“Yeah, in here, Moons!” Sirius hollered back. “Mmm… 'Mommy’s alright, Daddy’s alright, they just seem a little weird… Surrender! Surrender!”

It might’ve been Sirius’ singing that’d distracted him, or just his own horrid luck. Either way, Remus turned for the garage doors and got his boot caught on a dirty old tire that’d been left out to rot in the rain. He stumbled, cursing, and straightened up to give the tire a sharp kick—sending it rolling backward and straight into the rubbish bin. A colossal crash sounded as the bin took a tumble of its own, and then the radio cut out.

“Moony, you okay?”

“Fine,” Remus huffed. “Dropped the bin.”

Grumbling under his breath, Remus righted the bin as well as the old tire. He’d just fit the lid back on when he noticed something sticking out from behind the rest of the rubbish. It was vinyl, like the cushion from a car seat, only much thinner. Too wide for a bike, it was… oh.

“I’ll assume the bin said something particularly nasty to you to earn such treatment,” Sirius said. He was crouched down beside his precious motorbike despite the early hour, a predictable smear of grease on either cheek.

“It deserved it,” Remus replied, wiping his hands on his trousers. “You look busy. Did you decide that we aren’t going home today after all?”

“No, no! Just thought I’d give Gisela here one more tune up before we go.”

“You’ve named the bike after your old governess?”

“What can I say? I’m nothing if not sentimental.” Sirius tapped a screwdriver against the metal body, before tossing it away and popping to his feet. “You’ve got perfect timing though, I was just about to see if I could start her up. I fetched the petrol myself just this morning, now stay right there!”

Not entirely convinced it’d work, Remus crossed his arms and leaned against the garage doorway. He watched as Sirius swung his leg over the sports-bike, hovering over the uncomfortable lack of seat.

“First you turn your fuel line on,” he said, moving slowly like the bike might buck him off. “Then you press this here to see if the fuel’s coming out—it’s called the tickle.”

“Imagine if you’d studied for your A-Levels like you studied this bike.”

“Ha-ha… Now, ignition on.” He flicked another switch on the body. “And finally—the firing stroke!”

With one foot on the throttle and one on the ground, Sirius grabbed the bike by both handlebars and threw himself up—then down. There was a striking sound like a thousand matches being lit and suddenly the motorbike was thrumming beneath him; a dead thing brought back from the brink.

“Holy shit!” Sirius exclaimed. “I–It turned on! Moons, she turned on!”

“I see that.” Remus pushed off the doorway, genuinely impressed despite himself. “I didn’t think you were gonna get that thing to so much as purr.”

“Well, she’s purring now!” Sirius cranked the handlebars this way and that, flashing him with its single headlight. “C’mon, let’s take her out for a spin. You and me!”

“Sirius, you know we can’t.”

A beat, and then Sirius deflated. “Yeah… you’re right. Don’t even have—”

“I mean we can’t…” Remus smirked, picking up the dirty old seat, “without this.”

Sirius’ mouth fell open. “You found it!”

“It was out with those old tires. I guess Monty meant to get a new one.”

“Aw, dunno why he’d bother. This one’s a beaut already!”

Leaping off the back of the bike, Sirius took the bike seat and set it over the garage bench table. He took a rag to it, wiping away the layers of dirt and grime that’d been collecting for months. The vinyl was cracked in several places and even missing a chunk out of the back, allowing cotton to burst out like a wound, not that Sirius seemed to mind. It only took him a few minutes to slide the seat back into place and screw it down.

“Ah! Feels good,” he sighed, practically bouncing up and down. “So whaddya say, Moons? Feel like taking her out for a birthday spin?”

"Oh? Is it your birthday?"

"Aw, please?"

He’d probably regret it, but the look on Sirius’ face was too bright to dampen. After rushing back inside to change, Remus met him out on the road, where he found the bike purring and Sirius blowing dust out of an old helmet.

“Found this inside. Here, put it on.”

“What about you?”

“Haven’t you seen the films? The good-looking guy never wears a helmet.”

“Forgive me if I’m not convinced.” Pulling on the helmet, Remus swung his leg over just as Sirius showed him, and nervously wiped the sweat from his palms. “Right. You can go now.”

“Aren’t you going to hold on?”

Oh!

He slid closer until he could feel the elegant curve of Sirius’ back forming to his chest. They were so close, Sirius might’ve been able to feel his heart thumping through his jacket.

“Feet up, Moons, just like I showed ya!”

Remus did so, squeezing even tighter as he felt the bike lurch beneath them. “A-Are you sure you know what you’re doing?”

“Nope!” Sirius revved the engine. “But that’s half the fun, innit, delinquent boy?”

He only had time to mutter a quick prayer before the bike was moving, curving down the cobble road and onto the main thoroughfare. It might’ve been alright, had Sirius not jumped the stop sign and immediately cut off an oncoming lorry.

“Oops!”

“Sirius! We are going to die!"

“Everyone dies, Moons! At least we'll die in style!"

With the honking lorry at their backs, Sirius put on a burst of speed, and just like that they were off.

For the first several minutes, Remus didn’t dare raise his head. The bike's revving made his stomach hurt and the wind rushed his ears like a slapping tidal wave. The only thing keeping him from being swept away completely was the feel of Sirius’ leather jacket lashed between his fists. They hit a pothole and suddenly all Remus could picture was their mangled bodies as they flew through the air, Sirius’ brains splattered across the roadway like a Jackson Pollock painting. Not so handsome now, are you, Remus the ghost would say.

“Moony, you big ninny!” He heard Sirius shout. “Have you looked up even once?!”

“You’re going to kill us!”

“Better men have tried, believe me!”

Remus resisted the urge to punch him in the gut, fearing a crash.

“What’s that?” Sirius called. “Something’s in the road!”

“Shut up!”

“Oh god!” The bike wobbled sharply. “Moony, look out! We’re gonna—”

“SHUT UUUP!” Remus wrenched his face up, his heart in his throat, and found nothing—only open road ahead of them.

“Knew you could do it,” Sirius sniggered.

Right, Remus thought, now I’m going to kill you.

As maddening as Sirius was, he’d released him from his fear—however temporarily. The wind still rushed them, only now Remus could feel the tickle of Sirius’ hair as it whipped around and kissed him fleetingly on the face and neck. The bike was sturdy on its wheels, and with them aboard it went roaring down the country road, never straying far enough from the sea that they couldn’t see or smell it. The sky was ice blue and the air was colder now, but Remus didn’t even care. He was reminded of being back in Sandra’s fancy coupe, racing around every bend as fast as the engine could handle. It was as close to flying as he’d ever felt.

Up and down they went, yielding to every bend and racing down the straightaways like lightning. Sirius read the road better than someone on a first ride should’ve been able, but Remus had already gotten used to being surprised by him.

“I love you.”

Sirius leaned his head back. “What was that, Moons?”

“I said—" and he took a deep breath; "I LOVE YOU, SIRIUS BLACK!”

“OH! HA! I love you too! I love you, Moony—I LOVE MOOOOONY! WAH-HOO!”

Remus tightened his hands around Sirius’ waist, heart thumping all over again. Sirius put on another sharp burst of speed, and then looked back at him and smiled.

"I love you more than anything. Happy birthday, Moons."

Remus blushed beneath his helmet.

“Sirius, you’re really such a—YOU FUCKING IDIOT, EYES ON THE BLOODY ROAD!”

“HA-HA!”



Chapter End Notes

Getting "off your face" is just drunk.

If someone "slags off" they're criticizing or mouthing off.

The "A to Z" is a popular road map in the UK.

"Butteries" are a type of bread roll.

Songs featured in this chapter:

“Hit Me with Your Rhythm Stick” by Ian Dury & the Blockheads, 1978 (It was the band’s number 1 single); “I Fought the Law” by The Clash, 1977; “Vienna” by Billy Joel, 1977; “Jailhouse Rock” by Elvis Presley, 1957 (ever heard the Queen version ? 👀); and finally, a quick cameo from “Surrender” by Cheap Trick, 1978.

Fun fact: In the original version of "I Fought the Law" by Bobby Fuller the line is "I left my baby and it feels so bad" but the Clash changed it to "I killed my baby". You won't find it on any recordings except for the original live version of them at the Lyceum theatre, found here, but it was this cover (and this choice) that really helped get the band noticed in America.

Chapter 101: All the Young Punks


Chapter Summary

I’m King ‘a the dock! I’m King ‘a the dock!
