I don’t know how I’m gonna tell you,

I can’t play with you no more;

I don’t know how I’m gonna do what mama told me,

My friend, the boy next door;

I can’t believe what people saying,

You’re gonna let your hair hang down;

I’m satisfied to sit here working all day long,

You’re in the darker side of town…

- “That’s the Way” Led Zeppelin, 1970



“Say it—SAY IT!”

How had this happened? It was just supposed to be a concert…

“Didn’t you hear me? I said say it!”

He couldn’t think. Didn’t know what to think. Where was Tomny?

“I’m gonna give you one last chance… Either you say it, or things are gonna get a whole lot nastier.”

I’m King ‘a the dock! I’m King ‘a the dock!

He would not say it.





* * *





Earlier that night…





It was a hard sell trying to convince Sirius that they couldn’t just leave the van and ride the motorbike all the way back to London. Sirius finally relented after Remus pointed out that he didn't actually have a motorcycling licence, and that he didn't fancy dying a miserable death along the M4 on his birthday, but it took promising to return for the bike come proper weather to get his stubborn ass into the van. So long as Monty didn’t mind a little sharing, that was.

“You’re sure we can park the van here?” Remus asked, wrenching the gear shift into park. It was just after six and they were in the West End. The streets seemed lively enough, though how many were on their way to the same place as them, Remus couldn't be sure.

“It’s fine, stop worrying!” Sirius called, practically leaping from his seat and slamming the van's door after himself. “We don’t have time to go all the way home anyway. Now c’mon, we’ll miss the opening act!”

Undoing his seatbelt, Remus slid out and came to join Sirius on the pavement. He noticed a smear of grease on his left temple, the only remnants of their wild morning spent zipping up and down the Devonshire streets. “At least you’ll blend in with the dirty punks,” he teased, using his thumb to wipe it away.

The Clash were playing at the Lyceum Ballroom, an old theatre that’d been made over and revamped more times than Bowie’s career. They had to hurry just to make it there on time, but upon arrival, they found a crowd big enough to rival any one of James' covetous football games. There were punks and Jamaican rude boys and mod revivalists with their mopeds. As promised, the Anti-Nazi League had congregated themselves along the Strand with their small rally of banners and bullhorns. There were other tables set up, mostly bearing the names of sympathetic council members and various other trade unions, and along the street a large gathering of police officers had taken it upon themselves to help direct traffic. Remus could tell by their dour looks that they were not as excited to be there. A few were carrying riot shields, pacing uneasily; the only thing standing between the League and those taking offence to their being there in the first place.

Despite the looming presence of police, another throng of people had assembled across the street, these ones carrying boards and placards bearing various slogans in support of the National Front and all their fascist-favouring allies. Through megaphones of their own, they shouted obscenities and foul abuses to all that were gathering. Thankfully the nearby streets were so loud that the noise of the traffic and crowd's eager yammering all but drowned them out. Remus doubted they'd be putting up with the snub for long, but the police were out in force, and they had a concert to get to.

After dodging a few trades activists (and only getting suckered into signing one petition) they managed to shove their way toward the front of the queue. Remus paid for the tickets—a meagre two pound fifty—and while they waited for the usher to rip their tickets, Sirius picked up one of the boot-tramped fliers from the ground and waved it in Remus’ face.

“ ‘The only band who matters’,” he read. “It’s certainly bold enough.”

“It’s a lie. Tossers haven’t seen us yet.”

If Sirius hadn’t been broken of his musical blues already, he certainly was now. He grinned at Remus and suddenly a crash sounded as a window somewhere nearby shattered, causing both of them to flinch and duck. The mob was throwing rocks now.

Inside the Lyceum opened up like a palace, everything everywhere gilded and shiny, just ripe for use. The punks stood out as juxtaposed against the historical venue, not that they seemed to care. Egged on by the crowd’s inherent competitiveness, Sirius managed to elbow his way into the stage’s very front, tugging Remus along without care. The usual velvet seats had been removed in favour of bodies packing themselves into the pit, and it was so hot Remus could feel the sweat already gathering along his spine.

"Prongs is gonna kill us, you know," Remus said to Sirius, half-shouting in his ear just to be heard.

"Eh, let him! Punk waits for no one."

Many times Remus had wondered when it'd be that they'd get to see heroes like David Bowie or the Rolling Stones perform, but they were all off touring the likes of America and Japan. Besides, that was music, sure—but this? This was culture.

They knew the show was starting when the lights came down and a guitar could be heard echoing feedback through the sound system.

The band itself was a riot. Joe Strummer was a frontman for the history books, a complete legend in the making. They played punk rock as it was supposed to be; not angry and self-righteous, but valiant and unafraid, willing to say all the shit that needed to be said—damned be the consequences! They wore shirts with the collars popped, and were decorated head-to-toe in studded belts, zippers, safety pins, with the traditional bovver boots that could curve a head in. Their hair was slicked at the temples like the teddy boys of old, but their voices were powerful, teeming with youthful rage. The ruling establishment, police, alienation, boredom—they condemned all of it. They were provocateurs, yet nothing about them read as a cry for help. They weren’t unclean animals champing at the bit, nor were they pretentious shit-bags just looking for a reason to whinge.

The crowd fed into them but never did itself in. No one was spitting at each other as they had in the basement of the 100 Club while watching Sid Vicious play an unplugged bass guitar with blood dripping down his face. The throng simply moved as one, ebbing and flowing like a great metal-studded sea while the band came alive ahead of red and yellow stage lights.





‘He's in love with rock'n'roll, whoaah!

He's in love with gettin' stoned, whoaah!

He's in love with Janie Jones, whoaah!

He don't like his boring job—NO!'





Sirius leapt up and down for the entire set, pounding the air with his fist. With his unkempt hair and leather jacket he could've almost passed for a punk. No one gave him a second glance as he used Remus’ shoulder to hurl himself skyward with added velocity. Toward the end of the show when a large guy in a sleeveless leather jacket began to jostle him unfairly, Remus stepped in and told the prick to fuck off. It didn’t work, and while the encore started and the band began to thrash harder than its audience, Sirius took his arm and together they escaped toward stage-left. They ended up in front of one of the stage monitors, not ten feet from where the guitarist was ripping into his Les Paul. He could’ve sweated on them and Remus would’ve thanked him.





‘Hanging about—down the market street,

I spent a lot of time on my feet!

When I saw some passing yabbos,

We did chance to speak!’





“THINK I SHOULD TRY IT LIKE THAT?” Sirius yelled in his ear.

“TRY WHAT?” Remus yelled back, too busy watching the band and getting battered by the crowd to be paying much attention.

“PLAY THE GUITAR ON STAGE! LIKE STRUMMER! I COULD DO THAT!”

“I’M SURE YOU COULD, PADFOOT! JUST—HA!—JUS’ LIKE ‘IM!”

“WANKER! I SO COULD!”

Remus threw his head back and cackled, nearly butting the guy behind him in the forehead. They were packed in like sardines, sweating through their leather and fever-driven to teenage madness. Remus’ head felt like it was in an oven, but he wasn’t even conscious enough to complain. The music had hold of him; every drum fill was a punch, every riff a stab to the gut. He was sober but he might as well have been on speed.





‘All the young puuuunks!

Laugh your life—

'Cause there ain't much to cry for!

All the young cuuuunts!

Live it now—

'CAUSE THERE AIN'T MUCH TO DIE FOR!'





The entire thing finished with one final sweep of the drums, and just like that, the Clash were forever impressed on Remus’ subconscious. He’d be humming the likes of “Clash City Rockers” and “Tommy Gun” under his breath for years.

As the band left the stage and the theatre lights went up again, the crowd continued to rally. They were desperate for anything more, even the tail wisps of a show well-done. Cupping his hands over his mouth, Remus whooped and fed into the fever until he felt Sirius tugging on his arm. He was pointing furiously at a wall along the side of the stage, where the concert’s previous lack of light had concealed a single inconspicuous door. At first Remus was confused—he didn’t want to leave, the high was there! But then, as he blinked at him dazily, he began to realise just what Sirius was alluding to. The door was painted all black to blend in with the stage, but if they’d come in from behind, then moving forward could only mean one thing.

They had to wait for a short lapse in the security. As the men in black cut-off t-shirts began shepherding everyone out, Sirius slipped past the flimsy barrier and reached the door in a single stride. Then a miracle happened—the door was unlocked.

“Christ, I can’t believe that worked!” Sirius gasped, the moment they were through.

“Stupid luck,” Remus agreed, nodding and still breathless. The hallway they'd found themselves in had walls made of brick, lacquered in a peeling white paint. There were countless doorways cutting through it like Swiss cheese and behind them they could still hear the sounds of life—celebrating fans, endless cries and whistles, the clattering of stage equipment already being packed up. No broken windows, though if the situation outside hadn't improved in the last two hours then Remus imagined it was only a matter of time.

Without any preamble, a roadie came flying out of one of the doorways, wheeling along the usual stack of flight cases. Remus and Sirius just about fled in the other direction when they saw him, but the guy barely glanced their way, rushing past in cargo shorts and a t-shirt with dark stains under either armpit.

Watching him go, Remus glanced at Sirius. Sirius glanced back. Wordlessly, they both descended into a fit of laughter that lasted just long enough for—

“OI! YOU TWO GET BACK ‘ERE!”

They’d been spotted. Their great conquest of the Clash's backstage foiled. Before Remus could even beget an apology, Sirius slapped him in the gut and sprinted away.

“Leg it, Moons!”

They took off together, the security guard roaring at them to return or face the consequences. Within a few seconds they’d caught up to the roadie from earlier, who gaped the moment he realised who was overtaking him. Not willing to give up so early, Remus stayed tight on Sirius’ heels and squeezed past the trolley of flight cases, only to get his jacket pocket caught along the edge of the middle case. It tugged free all at once, taking the rest of the black boxes down with a thunderous clatter and nearly sending the roadie flying over the handles.

“SORRY!” Remus yelped, as Sirius threw his head back and cackled.

The mess slowed down the guard some, but by then the hallway had widened into a full underground passage, complete with stacks of crates sitting idly by. Countless wires lined the floor just waiting to be tripped over. They might’ve been able to take advantage of the head-start, had the noise of the falling cases not drawn the attention of every other person within ear-shot.

As two more members of security turned and darted straight for them, Sirius grabbed Remus by the elbow and yanked him through a doorway off to their left. It led to a concrete stairway that smelt of mould and damp. With little light apart from the glowing yellow lamps mounted on the wall, there was no telling where it might lead.

“Up or down?” Remus demanded, still aware of the shouting out in the corridor. Next to him, Sirius looked frantically at each staircase.

“When in doubt!” Was all he said, before he was wrenching Remus down and further into the heart of the theatre.

They raced over either step, hearts launching into their throats as they heard the door they’d come through slam open and heavy boots fill the stairway above.

“Bloody run, Moons!” Sirius hissed, taking the steps two at a time.

“I am!”

Thankfully they managed to find another door just one floor below. This one merged into a different corridor, packed with theatre hands as well as crates upon crates of different stage equipment. Speakers sat piled against the wall across from them, along with several pieces of a drum kit and a soundboard larger than their entire bed back home. Remus might’ve stayed longer just to admire it, had Sirius not already been pulling on his arm.

“C’mon! We just—”

“Pissing sod—outta the way!”

They’d turned directly into the path of several men, and the one in front—who was perhaps no taller than Lily—waved his hands in their faces frantically until they jumped apart. “I don’t care what the fucking lawyers have to say, the lawyers know piss-all about what fucking punk is!” He was howling at the guys; “Someone sort it out! We’re in Canterbury next month and if I have to hear Topper whinge one more time that his stash’s been cut, I’ll have ‘em all sacked!”

“Blimey, you sure?”

“Uh-huh!”

“Wicked.”

Too star-struck to realise how long they’d dawdled, Remus was almost tempted to follow Rhodes down the crowded hall until the door leading to the stairway flew open behind them.

“YOU! STOP RIGHT THERE!”

“You blokes just don’t bloody give up, do you?” Sirius floundered, practically leaping several feet backward in surprise. They were headed straight for a crossroads, but the security guards were only an arm’s length behind, and they did not sound happy.

“Oi, you see a kid running around here?" Someone called distantly. "Bloody berk jumped the barrier.”

A cardboard sign hung from it, tipped the wrong way. When he turned it around it read; Door handle busted, use south exit.

Typical.

All other options spent, Remus turned to the door the Siouxsie-girl had gone through and slipped inside. It was clear it was a dressing room, but if only he'd known beforehand just who it belonged to.

“So Joe, what d’ya think about the bootleg LPs of the Clash that are going around? I mean that’s bound to be taking money out of your pocket, right?”

Joe…?

“I say good luck to it, ‘cause we ain’t hit anyone wiff a live LP like we should’a. Like they expect, innit. But we ain’t like th’ other bands ‘a our standard—we’re trying to do sum'ffing new. Show up the other groups, say ‘this is what a proper group does’. Not sell old rubbish that ye’ve already bought.”

Remus quite literally froze. His eyes were watering furiously from all the cigarette smoke but he would’ve had to be blind to miss who was leaning up against that dressing room counter. His face was on the bloody tour poster—and every half-decent copy of NME of the last year. It was Joe Strummer, lead singer for the fucking Clash.

“So these bootleg people, I say good luck to ‘em,” Strummer went on. “It’s a pirate business and we’re watching. So if we catch ya, we smash the microphones—we smash the tape recorder, and we wrap th’ tape ‘round yer ‘ead. But good luck to ya, right. If you can get it onto vinyl then I’m not gonna start chasing ya.”

The interviewer nodded methodically, holding the microphone almost directly beneath Mr. Strummer’s nose while Siouxsie-girl passed him her cigarette.

“Joe, is there a message behind what you write that makes it a little more special than anything else on the scene? You call it either ‘the dole or rock ‘n roll’, but do you really think the working class understands you?”

“ ‘Course they understand, and what we’re saying to the working class is… You okay there, mate?”

Remus blinked. He almost looked around to see who Strummer was talking to. Then it hit him.

No way. No way Joe Strummer was actually talking to him!?

The singer arched a brow, glanced at the Siouxsie-girl, and pointed with his cigarette.

“Toilet’s just there, mate.”

Remus couldn’t believe it. Joe fucking Strummer just told him where the bathroom was.

Holy shit!

Before he could do anything else—like sob or soil his trousers—a pair of hands slammed down onto his shoulders.

“Gotcha!"

It was the security guard. He pinched Remus around the neck uncomfortably, fisting the back of his collar and leaving no room for an escape.

"Thought you could take off and run wild back ‘ere, didn’t you, greasy bleeder!" He shouted, then; "Apologies, folks. I’ll get ‘im outta your hair now…”

There wasn’t time for anything else. The guard hauled Remus out of the dressing room faster than he’d arrived. As he marched him back up the hall, grumbling about the ‘other miserable git’ that could’ve only been Sirius, Remus couldn’t help the smile that’d spread over his face. In the back of his mind, he’d already won the night. He could still hear the concert. Or wait—someone somewhere was playing the new Clash record like a hail Mary.



I want to move the town to the clash city rockers,

You need a little jump of electrical shockers!

You better leave town if you only want to knock us,

Nothing stands the pressure of the clash city rockers!





At one point, just after the furious guard had finished swearing up and down that he was going to spend the night in the nick for such a stunt, another man dressed in all black with a stage pass hanging around his neck appeared and complained of a brawl that’d broken out in front of the theatre between several punks and a group of National Front thugs that’d come to crash the party.

“You best be thanking your lucky stars tonight, boy,” the guard told him, as he threw Remus out into a back alley by the scruff of the shirt. It was surprisingly busy outside, the alley filled with plenty of other kids, all mulling around and waiting to see if they’d manage a glimpse of the famous rockers through their back door. A few of them glanced at Remus venomously on his way out, as though they too had dreams of breaking in to get even a whiff of Strummer’s presence. Remus didn’t care. The feeling of being on speed was back, and lasted even as Sirius threw himself at him from behind.

“Moony, you made it!” He cried, as Remus turned to face him. “Been missing you. Thought I was going to have to spring you from the nick.”

“They threw you out too, huh?”

“Caught me by the stairs,” Sirius grumbled. “But I almost made it onto the stage! I was trying to snag one of the mikes but they beat me to it."

"Bad luck."

“You didn't.”

“SHHH!” He hissed, covering Remus’ mouth with both hands. “You trying to get us mugged?”

“Group of skinheads at the end of the alley.”

“Sirius, you generally aren’t supposed to talk to the fascists at the anti-fascist rally.”

“But all the socialists had was pot.”

They slung an arm around each other and started for the end of the alley, stepping over dirty puddles and piles of rubbish. The other punks watched them but paid no mind for the most part, too busy standing around and smoking.

“Prongs and Wormtail really are going to be so miffed they missed it,” Sirius was saying. “Maybe we should take ‘em to a show. Hey, the Damned's just made a comeback! And I hear Rat Scabies likes to challenge people in the audience to get up and play for him. Think Pete would go for it?”

“Truthfully I think Peter'd have a heart attack if someone like Rat Scabies so much as looked at him.”

“Ha! Probably. Couldn't very well blame him. Man, we should get over to America! I’d like to see Van Halen—and the Cars,” Sirius said, busy gawking at a girl with hair spikes sharp enough to poke an eye out. She flipped him off for it, and he finished by blowing her a kiss.

“Few times. Mum used to fly Reg and I to Germany every other summer to visit our grandmother. Bitchy old cow. Then another time for my cousin Bellatrix’s wedding in Marseille. Also a bitchy cow. Have you never been on one then?”

Remus shook his head. “Mum always said she hated flying. And I don’t have any cousins.”

“None at all?”

“Not that I know of.”

“I can think of a few things.”

Smirking, Sirius slipped an arm around his waist. “Flying ain’t that bad anyway, but hey—if you get nervous, I’ll let you sit in my lap for moral support.” He sniggered while Remus steered them past a set of skip bins covered in graffiti. As they neared the end of the alley, one of the skinheads that'd been loitering caught up with them, hands and neck buried deep in his bomber jacket.

“Looking for a score, lads?”

“Nah, we’re done for the night,” Remus said.

Remus felt himself sigh. They could probably handle a few pricks looking for a fight—provided they didn’t pull a knife, that was—but he knew from the sound of heavy boots down the alleyway that Perry’s shouting had already drawn the attention of others.

“Here.” He tossed them what was in his pockets; a few rumbled notes, his cigarettes, a cheap lighter, nothing worth losing an eye for. He tried to hide the drumstick, but Whacker noticed it first and snatched it. Then he leered at Remus, waving it in his face and playing at taking an eye out before growing bored and pitching it down the alley. It hurt a bit to hear the distant clatter, but not enough for Remus to throw a punch.

“Now there’s a good boy,” the skinhead jeered, once Sirius had managed to resist throwing himself at him. Remus was thankful. Lily had hidden a key beneath a stone in the flat’s tiny garden ages ago, they could leave the van for one night. Better to just get away with all limbs intact.

“And how will you pay our fee?” Another voice called. Remus spun around instantly, furious and about ready to lose it himself.

“What fucking fee—”

“Our handling fee,” Lee grinned. “The one you pay to avoid being handled.”

It was like being stared down by the barrel of a gun. Remus staggered slightly, enough that Sirius looked over at him with concern. But he was there alright, really there. Lee. He strolled up with the rest of his crew, flicking away a cigarette butt as he adjusted the collar of his coat. It wasn't the boy he’d once known, but an angry man, looking to settle a score.

“Hello, Lu.”

Dammit.

“You know these toffs, Lee?” Perry called.

A round of scornful laughter echoed from the group at Lee’s back. More jeering, this time accompanied by a sharp smack to Remus’ shoulder courtesy of Whacker. “Fuck—you... LEE!”

“Yeah, you’s always were a half-decent scrapper,” Lee chuckled, before flexing his hand and driving it straight into Remus’ stomach.

“Stop it!” Sirius wailed, pinned in a headlock of his own. “Let him go! Stop hitting him—Remus!”

“Ha. Fought best with a damsel to save too!”

The fist came down again.

“Stop it!”

Again.

“STOP IT!”

Again.

He took each shot to the ribs, then the stomach; might’ve vomited had they not kept his head up. As he retched, Lee stepped back for a breather and wiped the sweat from his brow.

“Well! Nothing like letting off some good ol’ steam. And now... Well, now I'm gonna break every single one of those little fingers. Someone hold 'em up for me, would'ya?"

His hand was captured, and no matter how Remus pulled the arm around his throat just got tighter. He gave up when he began seeing black spots in his vision, and by then Lee had him around the wrist, ready to snap his thumb at the joint.

"Shall we say a countdown?"

"Stop it!" Sirius said. "You fucking bastard—let him go!"

"One."

Remus wheezed.

"Two."

He shut his eyes.

"Thr—you know what? I've a better idea."

The entire group of them exhaled, even those of Lee's guys that'd been anticipating the celebratory snap of bone. Releasing his hand, Lee crouched down over Remus again.

"Now I got’s an idea for ya, Lu," he cooed, poking Remus tauntingly in the cheek. "How 'bout we let'chu both go? That’s right—you and princess there, can waltz on out all on yer own. Hell, we’ll even give you yer shit back. All you’s got to do is one little thing. Can you do that for me, Lu? Just one teensy-weensy little favour?”

“Don’t listen to him, Moony,” Sirius croaked, earning himself a sharp jab to the stomach from Whacker and Perry each. Remus cried for him, practically spitting, but he couldn’t move with the bicep around his throat. Every time he struggled the skinhead squeezed tighter, until everything began to blur together again. A distant ringing had started in his ears like a far away telephone. He couldn’t feel his toes. Were they cold?

“Oi, careful not to kill ‘im Keg. Still need the bastard awake…” Lee whistled, then smacked Remus on both cheeks. “C’mon, eyes on me, Lu. You ain’t done your penance yet. All’s you gotta is repeat after me, then we’ll let cha go, orright?”

I’m tired.

The thought came to him slowly, like a leaf drifting downstream. He was so cold.

“Just three little words: ‘I’m a ponce’.”

It’s cold out. I’m cold.

"I don't 'ffink he's listening, Lee."

Another smack.

“Jesus Keg, fucking let the man breathe, would'ya?! Can’t say shit with your fist in his throat.”

There was a sudden release, and the breath surged in all at once—filling Remus' lungs to the point of discomfort. For a moment he almost believed they were somewhere else, but then his eyes fell on Sirius, still struggling with an arm around his own throat.

Sirius…?

“Cute show, Lu, but you ain’t done,” Lee goaded, close enough that Remus could feel his breath on his cheek. “Go on, you gotta say it. ‘I’m a ponce’.”

He wanted to humiliate him. For all he'd done, Lee wasn't a killer, but he was hurt. And he wanted to take that hurt out on Remus.

“ ‘m… not a ponce…”

Lee’s lip lifted viciously, revealing a sharp chip in his left canine. Remus thought he recognised it. Back when they were fifteen, Doss had bet Lee that he couldn't make the jump across two of the floating docks in the Shadwell Basin. Naturally Lee tried it anyway, and he made it across, only to crack his face open on the way back. It earned him a split lip and a nasty goose egg, but for those few precious moments he’d done it. Lee had bested them all.

Take that! Take that, you shitty tossers! I’m King ‘a the dock! I’m King ‘a the dock!

“Fucking—pay attention!” Lee snarled, driving another fist into Remus' stomach. “This is your last chance, Lu. Either you say it, or things are gonna get a whole lot nastier... Now SAY IT! ‘I’m ponce! I’m a dirty little queer who'd lie to his own friends' fucking faces!”

“You miserable bastard!” Sirius kicked his legs out, like a fitting horse. “Don’t touch him!”

Lee grabbed Remus around the jaw.

“SAY IT! OPEN YOUR GODDAMN MOUTH!”

And because he couldn’t refuse anymore, Remus did open his mouth, just like Lee wanted him to.

Then he spat in his eye.

Take that! Take that! I’m King ‘a the dock! I’m King ‘a the dock!

Lee wheeled back, wiping at his face hysterically. His hands were shaking. Drugs or rage, Remus didn’t know.

“You little…" He dissolved into a laugh of disbelief. "Oh Lu... fuck—I warned you.”

I can take it, Remus thought proudly. You can’t break me.

And maybe he could’ve stayed proud like that, were it just him, but as Lee wiped the spit from his eye and turned to look at Sirius and he knew just how wrong he was.

“Perry, break his arms.”

There was a hint of hesitation probably along the lines of 'Both of them?' but it was quickly dismissed. Perry grabbed Sirius’ wrist and braced back against his own forearm, ready to snap it at the elbow. Remus could see the alarm in Sirius’ face, the way he stared at his own arm as though it was already taken from him. As though he were already a lost cause. And as Perry got ready to shatter it all, Sirius squeezed his eyes shut.

“NO!”

The cry ripped free of him like an organ from his chest. In a fit of strength, Remus tore his right arm free and grappled onto Lee’s trouser leg.

“No, no, please—please, Lee—PLEASE!”

“Gerroff.”

“Please, please stop it! Don’t do this, you can’t do this!”

“I told you!” Lee roared. “I told you to say it! NOW HE PAYS!”

It was like watching in slow motion. He could see the tightening of Perry’s hand, the strain on Sirius’ face as he waited for the inevitable snap of his arm. It’d kill him, not having his arms. They were already mourning their first failure. If Sirius couldn’t play anymore, it’d all be over. They’d never come back from it.

So, Remus turned everything off.

"I'm a—!"

He never got to finish. Like the hiss of hose, a great noise echoed from out on the main street, whistling through the air and ending with a horrible bang. Everyone turned to look, even Lee, and suddenly the sound of yells and rushing books were coming toward them.

The crowd pushed their way down the alley together—anti-fascists and National Front members alike. Marching forward, Lee caught hold of another nearby skinhead and shook him for answers.

"It's the bizzies!" He cried. "Police started shooting off gas bombs like the fucking Provos!"

"Lee, I can't be arrested again, I only just got out!" Said one of the guys. The fleeing man pushed free of Lee's hold, and Lee took a harsh shouldering from another runner. Nearby they could hear the wail of an ambulance, and more hiss-and-bangs as the police culled whatever riot had started beyond them.

"Come on, Lee," Perry said, throwing Sirius into the alley wall and grabbing his friend by the front of his Ben Sherman in a panic. "Forget these fuckin' packers! We gotta go!"

Perry might as well have been asking him to shake hands. Forgetting his revenge, no matter how misconstrued, he couldn't take it.

A police whistle cut through the air, closer than before, and more and more people plunged down the alleyway looking for an escape. Smoke filled the air, enough to make Remus cough—but then he realised it was just the arm around his throat. He stared at Lee, gurgling deep in his throat and begging him with his eyes. You hold all the cards.

"Lee! ... Lee!"

Agony. That was what Remus saw in Lee's face. He was so close. Where was the satisfaction?

"Let him go," Lee growled, "fucking... let him go."

Remus was released immediately, kicked for good measure, and nearly trampled as the boys all turned in the opposite direction. Sirius was by his side in a second, so fast Remus nearly lashed out at him when he felt his hands on his ribs.

<<<

"This ain't over!" Lee was screaming, as his friends half-dragged him toward the end of the alley. "I see you again, and I'll kill you! I'll kill you, you hear me?!"

They were swallowed up by the crowd, and Remus could hear Sirius' voice as he rasped sharply in his ear.

“Remus. Moony, are you alright? Come on, you have to get up. Can you stand?”

He would have to. Gritting his teeth, Remus rolled over and allowed Sirius to haul him upright. Water had seeped in through his trousers and the front of his shirt; his throat felt raw from screaming.

"Did I say it?" He croaked.

Sirius shook his head, confused. "Moons, you're in shock."

"No!" Remus yelped. " 'I'm a ponce'—did I say it?!"

"No. No, you didn't say it."

I...

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be sorry, idiot. We've got to get out of here."

Tugging Remus’ arm over his shoulders, Sirius turned and began leading Remus to the end of the alley. It was slow going, and every scream and pop of a smoke grenade made them flinch.

"You know, for a skinny guy you sure do weigh a ton," Sirius was mumbling. Remus leaned on him just a little bit more for the next few steps, and Sirius responded with an exasperated laugh. "I don't know how you do it," he grunted; "attracting drama everywhere you go—it's mental. Starting to think you're a bigger attention whore than I am."

"No one's a bigger whore than you, Sirius."

"Oi! I'll have you know that I am a single dick kind of chick. Or is it the other way around..."

Remus started to laugh and then seized up. "Ow! Shit... don't make me laugh."

"Laughter's the best medicine anyway, and by the looks of things, you need it. You're hurt bad, Moons. I should take you to the hospital."

"No hospitals," Remus grunted. "Let's just get home."

Stopping just long enough to readjust his hold on Remus' arm, Sirius grumbled something under his breath that sounded a lot like 'bloody predictable' and continued walking. Remus couldn't be bothered. His entire body hurt, and he had to breathe through a sliver in his teeth just to keep himself from wincing after every step.

The idea had been to move away from the fighting, only they hadn't anticipated just how far the rally had broken down. Emerging out of the alley, they found what could only be described as a state of pure calamity. War had broken out ahead of the Lyceum, with police and civilians scattered everywhere. Sirens razed the night while hordes of Metropolitan police were arresting punks and skinheads alike. Down came the rally signs for the National Front and the Socialist Workers Party and anyone who so much tried to stand their ground was beaten into submission with heavy batons.

A group of kids had managed to light flares and were using them to ward off arresting officers while several others had climbed on top of cars, stomping their windows in as well as beating back anyone bold enough to try and stop them. Others clung to the theatre’s front steps and massive stone columns with megaphones in hand, screaming their agendas at the top of their lungs.

Everywhere people were running—away or toward the fighting, sometimes Remus just couldn't tell.

"This way," Sirius hissed. "I see an ambulance."

"N-No! Don't need no bloody ambulance—find the van!"

“There’s blood on your face.”

“It’s cosmetic. Stole it from Mary.”

“Wanker. Look who's making jokes now.” They stepped down a curb and Remus’ ankle nearly buckled.

“Shit… Sirius, I'm—”

"Don't talk anymore then," Sirius hissed. "Just walk. Look around for the keys if you can.”

As the two of them stumbled along, several police ran past with riot shields and batons, blowing on whistles shrill enough to make their ears seize. The air was thick with smoke, and as they coughed, a bottle soared over their heads and burst against the building wall next to them. Sirius did his best to shield him from the raining glass, but it'd happened so quickly Remus barely had the time to register it.

"FUCKING WANKER!" He heard Sirius bark, though no one came forward to take credit for the act. Across the street, they spotted one of the skinheads roughing up a young punk girl, violently shoving her into a wire fence as she spit and pummelled him with her fits. Sirius was off in a second.

“Get your hands off her, you thick fuck!” He cried as he tackled the skinhead from behind. It was enough to rip the guy off of her and send both him and Sirius sprawling, allowing the girl enough time to bolt. Remus rushed to his aid, but was beaten to the punch by a pair of officers. They wrestled Sirius and the skinhead apart, instantly wrenching their arms behind their back.

“Get off me!” Sirius grunted. “Get your hands off me, ugly prick! Shitty fucking cozzer!”

Then he punched the officer, straight in the nose.

“Sirius!”

Remus took one step—two! He grabbed the cop from behind, ready to rip his arms off should he refuse to release his Sirius. Only he hadn’t seen the other officer come up from behind and raise his baton. It came down over Remus' head like a lead pipe, turning his feet to flimsy paper beneath him. As he collapsed to the pavement, all Remus could remember thinking was that being bashed in by a cop didn’t feel any different from being bashed in by Lee's thugs.





* * *





Remus woke up a few hours later in a holding cell without windows. It was dark inside, the sort of dark that stripped away all time and space. He’d been relieved of his coat, forced to endure the horrible chill that had since settled deep into his bones. When Remus tried to lift his head up off the hard-as-stone bed, he found Sirius sitting across from him in a little ball, forehead resting on his knees. His head was up before Remus had even finished groaning.

“Moony!”

Sirius rushed him in a second, clambering onto the prison cot and cupping Remus' face with either hand. “Shit… Fucking pigs really got you, you’re going to have one hell of a lump. Are you alright, does your head hurt at all?”

“Ngh… No worse than usual.”

Sirius frowned horribly. “Shit, I dunno how to check for a concussion... Here, how many fingers am I holding up?"

Remus blinked. "I'm thinking of a number between two and..."

Scoffing, Sirius pulled away before he could finish, accidentally letting Remus' head slam back against the cot.

"Shit, sorry! Didn't mean to give you another bruise."

“Oh yeah, just add it to the collection.” Remus winced again as he tried to sit up. He needed Sirius’ help to do it, but eventually they were both settled back along the cell wall, shoulder to shoulder against the cement.

“And you?” Remus asked him. “Are you alright?”

“Me? Oh yeah, never better. Always wanted to see what the inside of the nick looked like. Bit dreary. Could use a rug.”

“Hollywood says we get one phone call if you’d like to give Mary the bell.”

Sirius grinned weakly. “One of the assholes that brought us in came by earlier. Said they were gonna hold us for the night, release us in the morning. Honestly, I was expecting worse.”

“What—You think participating in one riot’s gonna get you a trial? You’re not that famous yet, mate.”

“Yeah, but I sure socked that cop though.”

"Knew you were gonna bring that up."

"So you did see!" Sirius chuckled dryly. “Man... Prongs and Wormtail are never gonna believe us. Lottie’s wedding is next week, think she’d find it funny if I made my speech in handcuffs?”

“You're not getting a speech."

"Truly a missed opportunity."

It was so stupid. There they were, talking to each other as though they hadn't just been beaten to a pulp by one of Remus' ex-best friends and promptly arrested and thrown into prison afterwards. Remus nearly called it for what it was, but then Sirius was leaning his head against his shoulder. It was a nice feeling, but the weight was enough to make Remus groan a bit.

“Sorry!” Sirius chirped. “Wasn’t thinking… How’s your body feeling?”

“M’alright, nothing feels broken. Lee was pulling his punches—trying to show off. None of them really stuck.”

“Fucking prick. We should’ve curbed his miserable face in.”

“There were two of us, and almost a dozen of them. Nothing we could’ve done.”

“Still, if I ever see that fucker again, I swear I’ll…”

Remus shook his head. “Don’t think about it anymore. Do you know what time it is?”

“No. Past midnight at least."

"Oh good, so it isn't my birthday anymore?"

Sirius winced as a reply. "You were out for a while... Sorry to say all you have to show for it is a black eye.”

“Better me than you.”

“Oh, because you’re so tough?”

“No. ‘Cause you’re the face. How’re we gonna put you on the cover of the album with a black eye?”

“Ah.”

Quietly, Sirius reached over into Remus’ lap and took his hand. He was warm—the warmest thing for miles. Off in the distance Remus could make out the sounds of other offenders as they paced back and forth in cells of their own; snoring, moaning, or else the occasional curse directed to the officers, God—even their own mothers. It all felt rather stereotypical. But dark rooms were to dark thoughts what lungs were breathing, and despite telling Sirius not to stew on it, Remus couldn’t help but think of Lee.

The evening’s events came back into him like a wash of ice. Just… all of it. The concert, the drugs, Whacker, short and rat-like, and Perry, with a face like a decomposing toad. Lee.

Say it!

“Sirius… I…”

I’m a fucking ponce!

“It’s not your fault,” Sirius cut-in, already reading his mind. “It’s not. You were their friend.”

“Once.”

“Once is enough. Once matters.”

And maybe it did… once. But things were different now. If Lee was to be believed then Tomny was on the outs too. Maybe he and Skylar had already headed up to Havering—hell, maybe the baby was already here. He didn’t know, he and Tomny hadn’t talked in…

“Stop that,” Sirius ordered. “I can see those cogs moving inside your head. You can't think about that—you can’t. We don’t mourn the people who’ve hurt us, Moony.”

"I miss James," Remus said, pathetically. "And Lily, and Peter and Marlene."

"Me too."

"I wish none of this had ever happened. I wish I'd never met Tomny."

"Don't say that."

"It's the truth. Maybe if we'd never met then none of this would've happened."

"Maybe, but then you never would've come to Hawkings, and I..." Sirius bit his lip. "We aren't our parents, you know. I don't care what Lee says. We are not them."

And because Sirius needed to believe it as much as he did, Remus did not argue.

Neither of them spoke for a long time, and eventually they laid down next to each other on the tiny cot, Sirius' back pressed against Remus' chest, their arms wrapped around one another. Eventually Sirius' breathing had become so level that Remus thought he'd fallen asleep. Then Sirius whispered into the dark;

"Moony?"

"Mhm."

"I'm sorry for what happened tonight."

"... Don't think about it. It was my idea to go."

"I know, but I wanted you to have a good birthday. Shit I... I should've found you something better than that stupid stick. I should've—"

Remus leaned forward, burying his face in the crook of Sirius' neck. He still smelled of sweat and the cloying scent of police smoke grenades, but Remus didn't care.

"Tell me something happy?" He asked.

Sirius was quiet for a while.

“Remember last month when Sid Vicious died?"

"Jesus. I said happy, not depressing."

"No, no." Sirius chuckled. "He died and it was in all the papers, right?”

“All of them,” Remus relented. “Even Sheila heard about it.”

“You still write to her?”

“Sometimes. She's a bit more forceful over the phone.”

“That’s nice… You deserve someone to write to.”

“Sid Vicious,” he prompted, when Sirius grew quiet again. “You were talking about Sid Vicious.”

“Right, right. Easy to forget... And that’s the problem, ain’t it? The guy’s been dead—what, a month? And it’s like the whole world’s forgotten about him."

"Not quite. They're saying he murdered his girlfriend."

"I don't believe it," Sirius said, before squirming a bit. "Or maybe he did, I dunno. Not like it matters anyway, it's already old news. Everyone’s too busy interviewing Paul McCartney and wondering what colour knickers Rod Stewart’s wearing these days.”

“Leopard print, for sure.”

Sirius chuckled quietly. Then he reached for Remus hand, drawing it tightly across himself and lacing their fingers together.

“I’m not gonna end up like Vicious, Moony. Getting so far only to throw it all away... When I go out, people are gonna remember me.”

“And what is it they’ll remember you for, Padfoot?”

Sirius squeezed his hand.

“… All of it.”





* * *





Sunday 11th March 1979 — The Next Morning...



“On your marks, gentlemen!”

They both started awake, shooting upright on the cot in a hurry. For a split second Remus almost forgot where he was. Then he heard the rattle of the keys in the cell lock and it all came flooding back. Sirius sat next to him, looking disoriented while he blinked the sleep from his eyes.

“Ngnn… What time is it?”

“About half-past five,” the officer answered, swinging open the cell door.

“In the morning?!”

“Just in time to catch the first train. Now on your feet!”

Sirius waved him off, clearly irritated to be woken before any reasonable hour, and turned on Remus, eyes suddenly shooting wide.

“Shit Moons, we fell asleep! How’s your head?”

Remus groaned, recounting the day before. Clash City Rockers. DMT. Lee. I’m a ponce! Lee, again.

“Well, I’m not dead, so…”

They were released, along with a stern warning to stay away from any further rallies—fascist, socialist, or otherwise—and a warning that if the guard ever caught them sharing a cot again he'd have them arrested under the Sexual Offences Act.

"Homophobic bastard," Sirius grumbled, shrugging on his jacket outside the station gates. "We weren't even doing anything! Try telling a straight couple they have to wait until twenty-one to share a bed."

Remus had no energy to agree; after a night spent in the cells, every inch of him felt like it'd been hit by a train. Still, he swallowed the aches and any urge to complain. He told himself that they just needed to make it home where he could assess the damage properly and sob in the shower should he really feel the need. It was a fine plan, only it fell apart slightly when they returned to the street where they’d left the van the night before and found it missing. After a few stressful minutes of wandering, they discovered that in their hurry to get to the concert, they’d parked in a taxi rank and the van had been undoubtedly towed.

“Man, that Joe Strummer really fucking owes me,” Sirius lashed, after they’d jumped the turn-stalls and took the Tube the rest of the way home. “A van and a microphone. They can keep their bloody drumsticks.”

“Oh yeah, you can ask him when you’re famous,” Remus replied blandly, busy counting the building numbers as they turned onto their street.

“So how’s it feel? You’re nineteen and officially a felon. Bet Sheila would love that phone call.”

“You tell Sheila,” Thirty-nine, forty, forty-one; “and I’m telling Effie.”

“Bastard.” Sirius shoved him, ignoring the way Remus groaned. “Okay, who’s telling Evans then?”

“No one. Let her think we were in Devon the whole time.”

“And the van? They’re gonna be back soon—and the sign back there said the tow yard’s closed on Sunday-Mondays.”

“Then we'll just say that the van hasn’t been towed. That it’s… being lended out.”

“Riiiight. Good one.”

“We can just tell her that Dorcas needed it,” Remus said. “Or that Kingsley called and—oof!”

Remus' chest twinged. He had a curse on the tip of his tongue and was ready to unleash it upon Sirius for daring to stop right in front of him, only they'd made it to the front steps of their flat, and Remus—being much taller—merely had to glance up to see what had stopped Sirius so soundly in his tracks.

“Holy fu…”

Remus could not believe his eyes. It was—

"Regulus?"

He was sitting before their front door, looking young in his school clothes and jacket, his trunk tucked up behind him as though he’d been dozing against it. He looked weary, and when he stood up it struck Remus that he’d grown—that his hair had grown! For a moment he looked so much like Sirius that Remus began to wonder just how hard he’d hit his head.

“About time you got back,” Regulus said, dusting the dirt from his trousers. “Where have you been then—prison?”

They were too flabbergasted to laugh. Sirius held a hand to his forehead, then dropped it as he rushed up the stairs to embrace his brother. Regulus let it happen, wincing only slightly when Sirius began to bark into his ear.

“Reg! Holy shit, what are you doing here?! Scratch that—how’d you get here?”

“I took the train, of course. Had to see you.” Regulus pulled away and regarded Remus with a nod. “Lupin.”

“R-Regulus.”

“You little shit, you told me you weren’t coming!” Sirius smacked his brother lightly on the shoulder. “Out for Easter break then?”

“Sirius, Easter isn’t for two weeks.”

“Oh... Then why’re you here?”

Regulus glanced down at his feet. “Something’s happened back home," he murmured, meeting Sirius' gaze again as his brother went a rough shade of white.

“What is it?” Asked Sirius. "What's wrong?"

“It's father, Sirius,” Regulus said. “He's gone. The funeral’s tomorrow.”



Chapter End Notes

Welp, it was about time they got arrested 🥴 Did you catch Regulus 'prison' pun?? Lol.

Slang for this chapter:

The National Front is/was a far-right, fascist political party in the United Kingdom. In the 1970s they were very focused on "keeping England white". Disgusting stuff, but very real.

'Flight cases' are the durable black/silver cases that music and film equipment are often shipped in

'Sacked' means fired.

A 'berk' is a foolish person.

'The dole' is the UK's version of unemployment benefits; jobseekers allowance.

The 'nick' is prison.

'Miffed' is annoyed.

'Skip bins' are dumpsters.

Ben Sherman shirts were popular amongst the skinhead culture but had nothing to do with anyone's political views, as skinheads had a wide culture and could be either left or right leaning (see: white power skinhead).

Saying 'that's a gas' or 'that's gas' means you heard something funny.

'Telling porkies' is slang for telling lies.

A 'cozzer' is a police officer.

'Bizzies' are police.

The 'Provos' is a slang term for the Irish Republican Army.

The Sexual Offences Act of 1967 declared that while the age of consent for heterosexual couples remained 18, it was illegal for anyone under the age of 21 to engage with homosexual acts. This discriminatory law was not repealed until 2003.

Songs mentioned in this chapter: "Janie Jones" (1977), "All the Young Punks" (1978), & "Clash City Rockers" (1977) all by The Clash.

The conversation between Joe Strummer and the interviewer is pretty much plagiarized from THIS interview. I still feel a little bit "ehhh" about putting words into real rock stars mouths, so this is just one way I like to get around that.

Chapter 102: Sunk


Chapter Summary

"You went into the water. Please don’t come out the same.”



Chapter Notes

- “Mother” Pink Floyd, 1979



When he was six years old, Remus watched as his father took a dog behind the family barn and shot it.

They’d left that morning to hunt foxes near Oxfordshire. Remus hadn’t gone, he was too young. Instead he'd gotten to stay and have tea in the garden with Giles and his mum, but he’d seen them leave; twelve of his father’s best hounds, all trained to perfection, along with several colleagues from work. There had been excitement in the air, jovial handshakes interlaced with the incessant barking of dogs all desperate to be freed from their kennels. Only one of the dogs appeared weary enough to give pause. A juvenile called High Strung, aptly named for its skittish nature, had just been deemed fit for a first run. Normally this would have taken place on private property, with a fence and game birds and all the like, but Lyall wanted to test the dog’s limits. The breeding bitch had been brought all the way across the Atlantic, desired for the sleekness of her black coat. Back home she’d produced champions, and when her first litter was born on English soil, it was clear that High Strung was that champion. They praised him for his strong legs, the nobleness of his face. Surely he’d be the perfect hunting animal—he’d win awards!

But then came the accident.

Unused to the sound of a gunshot, High Strung bolted first chance. One of the men foolishly tried to grab him, but the ground was uneven; they caught the side of a ravine. Both master and dog fell.

The man was sent to hospital for his injuries, but the dog they brought back to the estate. There was no hospital for living investments, or at least not ones so far gone. The handlers had taken one look at High Strung’s shattered pelvis and declared him a dead dog breathing.

It’ll be lame forever, Lyall. Best to put the beast out of its misery.

He’s my dog, I’ll do it.

Remus didn’t understand; when he heard his father’s answer he felt a swell of pride for having such a responsible father. Lyall didn't know that Remus had followed him from the garden, that he was watching as he pet the dog’s flank and set a pistol to its skull.

Goodbye, poor beast.





* * *





Monday 12th March 1979





“Moony?” Sirius’ uneasy voice drifted through the door; “How’s it looking?”

Remus didn’t answer at first. His eyes were glued on the mirror that hung over the chipped bathroom sink. Lee pulled his punches—that’s what he’d told Sirius. A lie, then. Barely a day later, and the skin over his stomach looked like the flesh of a bruised apple.

“Not that bad, actually,” he called, dropping the hem of his shirt. Good thing too; Sirius came striding in a moment later with a tie in either hand.

“Black or navy, do you think?” He held either tie up to his throat. “I know black is more traditional, but personally I think nothing screams ‘I hate my dead son-of-a-bitch dad’ more than looking miserable in navy blue.”

Remus pointed weakly to the black, and Sirius sighed, tossing both over his shoulder.

“Almost ready to go then? You’ve been in here for ages.”

“Yeah, yeah…” Rubbing along the back of his neck awkwardly, Remus resisted a twinge. Sirius had been very short with him all morning, his usual sarcastic attitude dialled up to a nine. Not much had been shared between him and Regulus the day before, save for a few details about the funeral. Regulus drifted around the flat like a nervous ghost, while Sirius behaved more like a cornered dog—likely to bite the moment he felt threatened.

The service was being held that morning at some fine church in the city, with a subsequent celebration of life taking place at the historic Black manor later in the afternoon. With no car and no way to get one so early in the morning, they'd been forced to concede defeat where the service concerned. Regulus appeared antsy at this, but if anything Sirius only looked relieved.

“Are you doing alright?” Remus asked him, as they stood facing each other in the bathroom. “You seem…”

“Upset?” Sirius sucked his teeth, revealing a sardonic smile. “You think because my father died and my own family didn’t even care enough to tell me they were holding a funeral that I’d be upset?”

“Sirius—”

“Or because my little brother ran away from his train home ‘cause he couldn’t stomach the idea of going back there on his own, despite the fact that he hasn’t asked me for anything in over five years? Or—Or that the only way I can help him is by going back to that fucking place despite the fact that I swore I’d never go back! That’d I’d never see them, or speak to them, or even mention their names again? Ha! No—No, don’t be silly, Moony, I’m not upset at all.”

“It was a stupid question,” Remus amended sorely. “Forget I said anything… Is Regulus at least doing any better?”

“Dunno. Tosser still hasn’t said much.” Sirius crossed his arms. “Half expected to wake up and just find him gone, y'know. It's like, why’d he bother coming to me? He knows what I’d tell him…”

Don't go. It was written across his face like an angry plea, and Remus nodded, understanding.

“You could tell him not to, ‘cept the moment you tell him not to do something, he’s just gonna wanna do the opposite. He’s too much like you, Pads.”

“Yeah,” Sirius scoffed, “it’s how I know the only thing left to do is to follow him. At least if I’m there I can assure that the only person doing something they’ll regret is me. If it were just Reg, he’d probably let mother convince him to do something epically stupid. Like agree to a marriage pact. Or join a cult.”

“Didn’t you once say that your family’s basically a cult already?”

“So you understand the risk? Good.” Sirius glanced back toward their bedroom, where Remus knew a pair of dark suits would be laid out over the bedcovers. They'd been hanging in the back of the wardrobe for ages—a bygone remnant of what had once been their lives. Seeing him now, Remus didn’t have to ask to know what Sirius was thinking.

“Don’t worry,” he promised, stepping up to hold him from behind; “I’ll go with you. I’ll never leave your side.”

There was a shuddering breath, followed by a single forlorn sniffle, and then Sirius turned his head back to face him. His eyes were glassy, but his mind was made up.

“Well, Moony… once more unto the breach, shall we?”

It was a sordid morning. Regulus had been ready for hours by the time the two of them were both dressed and making their way downstairs. He was reading the newspaper, but rushed to hide it the moment they came into the room. Remus didn’t have to ask what article, he’d read it himself that same morning.



MILLIONAIRE BUSINESS AND OIL MOGUL, ORION BLACK, DEAD AT FIFTY

BATH—Well-known investor Orion Black died in his family home last Wednesday, aged fifty years. While a cause of death was not immediately available, spokespersons for the family’s estate were able to confirm that a heart attack and subsequent heart failure was to blame for the patriarch’s premature passing.

Various prominent business leaders and politicians alike have expressed their condolences over Black Sr’s death. The Somerset-born magnate had succeeded his family’s business and all related assets in 1961 following the death of his father, Lord Arcturus Black III . Though the Blacks are notorious for being private when it comes to their affairs, it is open knowledge that the family garnered its immense monopolies via various industrial and scrap metal industries founded in 1892 by the then family head, Lord Phineas Nigellus Black.

Commissioned by Lord Black near Oxfordshire in 1902, the largest of the estate’s metal-work factories saw a great boom throughout the First and Second World Wars, expanding into automotive and watercraft construction. In 1924 the family expanded into the oil business, thus further contributing to their already massive wealth. It is not known which direction the Blacks plan to take their endeavours in the coming future, but spokespersons for the estate have said that the family has no intent of slowing down. Orion Black is survived by his wife, Walburga, and son, Regulus. The private funeral has been scheduled for this coming Monday, March 12th. The family is requesting privacy during this period of mourning.



It was startling almost, how an entire life could be summarised in three short paragraphs. That’s funny, Sirius had said when he read it, they didn’t mention anything about his massive gambling habit, or the gout, or the many, many mistresses. I would've at least expected to see something about the sweatshops in India or the deforestation in Bolivia, but nah, these tossers didn’t do their research at all.

Regulus didn’t have much to say on the subject, and even if he did, he certainly wasn’t about to share it with them. After accepting their offer of the couch he'd awoken with deep bags under his eyes that refused to go away no matter how much he rubbed at them. There were hardly any wrinkles in his dress shirt, though he still worried over them with frantic little motions. No one seemed all that interested in breakfast, and so Remus put a pot of coffee on, which they shared in rather unenthusiastic silence. Sirius refused to come out of the kitchen, meanwhile Regulus had taken up residence at the dining table, stirring his coffee several times clockwise, then an equal amount back again.

“I know what you’re both thinking,” Regulus said unexpectedly. “You think I shouldn’t go. That going back there again would be a mistake. All the extended family will be there…”

Remus, who had been sitting on his own at the nook, glanced gingerly back at Sirius, who was leaning one hip against the kitchen counter and staring stubbornly down at his coffee, obviously listening anyway.

“I think you should do… whatever it is you came here to do, Regulus.”

Regulus looked up at Remus, then over at his big brother.

“One more time then?”

Sirius tapped the side of his coffee mug thoughtfully. Then he set it aside and produced a small silver flask that he began filling with the first bottle of liquor he found amongst the cupboards. Afterwards, Sirius turned and raised the flask to them.

“One more,” he said, before tipping it back against his lips.





* * *





You little shit, you’re in it now,

I hope they throw away the key!

You should’ve talked to me more often than you did—

But no, you had to go your own way,

Have you broken any homes up lately?

- “The Trial” Pink Floyd, 1979





Remus could still remember how it’d felt to be barred from his mother's funeral. Back then he would’ve given anything for an older brother who could just tell him what it was he was supposed to do. What he was supposed to feel—what to do next. Watching those two brothers, he almost felt a sting of envy, as though the eleven year-old inside of him still hadn’t learned how to forgive. But after they’d gathered their boots and coats, Sirius took his hand and squeezed it tightly, and Remus knew then that whatever he’d missed when Hope had died, he would be that for Sirius now.

Bath was a good two hours away, and with no hope of springing the van from the tow-lot until Tuesday, they’d decided to rent a car out of Ealing. The surcharge to rent to anyone below the age of twenty-one had been horrible, but they’d managed it—a cheap Morris Marina that’d left another unfortunate dent in their now dwindling rainy-day fund. Sirius would’ve never complained about money, but was forced to dismiss Regulus’ worries over it when he began insisting on paying him back in the future. As it was, Regulus had brought very little cash with him and had spent most of it on his train ticket into London.

“You didn’t just try to train-hop?” Sirius had asked.

“I’m not a lunatic,” Regulus had replied.

So there were still a few differences between the two then.

The Black family manor was much too large to be located in and around the main city, and instead laid on the outskirts of Bathford, a civil parish some three miles from the Bath’s city centre. It was the ancestral home of the Blacks, and while not all of Sirius’ cousins lived nearby, they were expecting a decent turn-out.

“No doubt Bellatrix will be there. She'd have brought that shitty husband of hers, Rudingus or whatever.”

"It's Rudolphus," Regulus mumbled quietly.

"Still a cunt." Sirius chuckled to himself. “Suspect Uncle Cygnus and Aunt Druella'll be by too. And of course Narcissa… she'd be married now, yeah? Gross. Think Aunt Belvina will be bringing a new boy-toy, Reg? How old was the last one you wager—I'm thinking somewhere between eighteen, and eighteen and eleven months.”

There was no answer from the back seat, and so Remus took it upon himself to fill the air;

“I forgot how insane your relative’s names are.”

“Oh, you mean like Bellatrix? That’s nothing. Our mum’s father had a cousin named Eridanus. Though she never seems to find it funny whenever I ask for stories about our dear ‘Uncle Anus’.”

Remus swallowed his smirk, and suddenly Sirius was shooting upright in his seat, pointing out the window.

“There, just over that ridge is Brown’s Folly. It’s this useless old tower on the hill that was built by some lord for his squire or whatnot. Reg and I used to go there when we were kids. Snuck out all the time, didn’t we, Reg?”

Again, Regulus said nothing. Sirius didn’t seem to notice.

“Mum used to threaten to send dogs after us,” he went on, sniggering again. “We’d stay out in the woods for hours—Reg was always getting us lost.”

“You mean you were getting us lost.”

“Yeah, alright, but I always got us out again though, didn’t I?”

More silence.

“Remember how Kreacher was the only one who could ever find us? Hell, that dog was so old and decrepit it pissed dust. It’s a wonder something didn’t just come along and eat him first.” Sirius leaned his head back. “Bet you’re looking forward to seeing him again, hey?”

“Kreacher died. It was last Christmas.”

“... Oh.”

Sirius was decidedly less chatty after that.

Eventually they’d turned onto the private road that would take them to the manor. It was initially forested on either side, but eventually opened up to reveal sprawling green hills, somehow perfectly manicured despite its egregious size. There were animals lounging amongst the knolls that Remus initially took for cattle, but upon closer inspection, turned out to be a herd of small deer.

“They’re fallow deer,” Regulus explained. “They come around in the spring and early summer when the fawns are being born. During the winter months they migrate south toward Southampton. But they always come back.”

“At least someone still enjoys the idea of coming home,” Sirius mumbled.

There was no missing the manor when they saw it; a large baroque country house, made of a white limestone and built in one long row. There was very little landscaping save for a stone wall surrounding the property and a massive front drive, now decorated with every sort of lavish car one could imagine. The Morris Marina stuck out terribly with its chipped dandelion-yellow paint job, though there were very few left around to witness their arrival.

“It’s late in the day by rich sod's standards,” Sirius observed, peering up at the cloudy sky; “Reckon they’ve already retired to the drawing room to lament over our father’s greatness.”

Remus had pulled the car into park next to a very lavish black Cadillac, and not for the first time, began to feel massively out of his depth when it came to the Blacks. His grandfather had inherited land thanks to a series of good business dealings following the war, and Lyall had always had a stern grip on his own finances; Remus had come from easy pickings, he knew better than to deny it, but this—this was old money.

“That’s my old bedroom there,” Sirius told him, pointing to a top corner window along the houses’ eastern side. “Always wanted to bring a guy over. You know—a quick shag or two, just to scandalise Mum.”

“Sirius.”

“Yes, yes, Reggie, don’t get your knickers in a twist.” Smirking, Sirius adjusted the front of his suit. “I already promised—no squabbles, no causing a scene, no telling Bellatrix she looks fat in her new funeral dress. No giving Mum any reason to rip someone’s head off—namely ours. You know, truthfully, it’ll probably be the most boring funeral our family has ever had.”

With a look of plain distrust, Regulus stalked on ahead and Sirius took the opportunity to wink at Remus. He raised his hand, revealing a pair of crossed fingers.

“He knows it’s an impossible promise. On a good day, our family makes the Borgias look like saints.”

Somehow, Remus was not all that comforted.

They followed Regulus up the drive toward the manor’s looming front doors, but Sirius stopped them when they grew near the trimmed hedges.

“What are you doing?” Regulus demanded, as his brother took his arm and began dragging him away.

“You’re not just going to waltz into the front door, are you, Edge? You’re an honorary Marauder now—where’s your sense of adventure?”

Regulus didn’t seem too pleased at the idea of becoming any part of Sirius' grand schemes, but did not fight as he was led around the side of the vast house. Together they stopped below one of the manor's protruding ground floor windows and Sirius started by asking Remus for a boost. Balanced on the tip of Remus' knee, he pulled a single trusty hair pin from his pocket and began shimmying the long end in between the gaps in the window.

“We shouldn’t be out here,” Regulus hissed. “That’s father’s study, we aren’t allowed.”

“And who’s going to stop us? His ghost? ”

Regulus baulked slightly, but Sirius paid him no mind. With a giddy “A-ha!” he’d managed to wiggle the pin all the way inside and lift the old brass latch, allowing the window to swing open toward them.

“There,” he mused, tapping Remus’ shoulder to indicate what a good job he’d done; “I know I’m no burglar extraordinaire—like some people—but I don’t think I’m half bad at this.”

“Oh goody. Just what you needed, an even bigger head.”

Sirius grinned as Remus helped hoist him inside. After he’d given the okay, Regulus came next. Making sure to grab hold of as little of Remus as possible, he continued grumbling about the idiocy of having to break into his own home until had shimmied himself over the edge of the window and his skinny legs had passed out of sight. It took both Black brothers to haul Remus inside, and what they found was an interior just as grand as its out. Sitting pretty at nearly three times the size of their flat's living room, the study spread out before them in an opulent row, with oak panelled walls and shelves on every side. A desk sat at one end, paired with a luxurious leather armchair and one of those fancy standing globes gilded in real gold. Beyond the desk hung a portrait of a man with a thick moustache and a white rose in his lapel. Remus didn’t have to ask if they were related; his black hair and stern expression gave it away.

“Ah, great-great-great grandfather Phineas!” Sirius exclaimed, throwing himself down into the leather armchair and spinning around to face the portrait; “How I missed your ugly mug staring me down from beyond the grave. Not so smug now, are you? Say, how’s Dad? Has he invited Hitler to play a round of golf in all nine circles of Hell yet?”

“Sirius, we shouldn’t be in here,” Regulus said again. He’d crept over to the study door and was standing next to it, squeezing his palms together as he often did when he was anxious. Outside Remus could hear the telltale noises of others gathered; no laughter, but plenty of lull and chatter.

Ignoring his brother's plight, Sirius spun around in the desk chair and began stroking his chin in an exaggerated manner. After reaching forward, he knocked the lid off of an ornate cigar box and pinched one of them between his two fingers, taking a pretend draw off of one end.

“I've been thinking of growing a goatee myself, Moons, what do you think? Facial hair's been ruined on me, on account 'a the family resemblance, but if I'm going to Hell anyway then I figure a few whiskers wouldn't make that much of a difference.”

Abandoning the door, Regulus stomped toward the desk. “Enough,” he snapped. “No one's laughing, and I didn’t bring you here so you could poke fun and get us thrown out first chance.”

“If I remember correctly, it was us who brought you here. Right, Moony?”

Remus held up a hand, not interested in being fodder for Sirius’ reckless spat, and finally Sirius tossed the cigar aside and stood up.

"You think everything I do is pointless, don't you, Reg?"

Regulus' nostrils flared, indignant. "I wouldn't, except you always have to take the piss about everything."

"True. Fine, then. Think what you want, but you should know that I do have a reason for coming here.”

With a haughty look, Sirius began pushing his father’s chair up against the back wall. Then he climbed onto it.

“Moony, help me with this, would you?”

Remus didn’t fully understand until he was helping Sirius lift his great-great-great grandfather's portrait off of the wall. The portrait itself was immensely heavy, though nothing compared to what they found underneath. It was an elaborate steel safe, inset directly into the wall and complete with a spinning dial lock.

“Big enough, isn't it?” Sirius said proudly. “If there was anything Dad was good at it was playing the role of the overly pretentious, clichéd malefactor.”

“What are you doing with Father’s safe?” Regulus asked uneasily.

“What does it look like I’m doing? I’m getting you your inheritance. If you’re gonna come all this way for his bloody funeral then you might as well get something out of it.”

Taking hold of the dial, Sirius leaned his ear against the side of the safe to listen to the mechanisms click. “What do you think? Surely he wouldn’t be stupid enough to use his own birthday.” Sirius spun the dial, grinning, but when he reached for the handle, the safe did not budge. “Hm… Oh, I know! How about his and Mum’s anniversary, hey?”

Regulus slapped both hands down on the desk. “Sirius, stop it.”

“Tsk! No cigar. Should’ve known. But hey, how about the day he met Adeline? Everyone knows she was his favourite mistress.”

Click, click, click—nothing.

“The year the war ended?”

No.

“The day his father died?”

No.

“The day we struck oil down in Venezuela!”

All of the codes were wrong. Huffing, Sirius stood back with his hands on his hips. He looked as though he were playing a part, while Regulus merely looked woebegone—like a kicked dog.

“No way he made it as simple as one-two-three-four.” Sirius stroked his chin again; “Oh! I know—how about your birthday then, Reg?”

Regulus scowled deeply as Sirius turned back to the safe. Remus had read once that avalanches sometimes made these great cracking noises, like the creak of old wood beneath a heavy boot, as its first sign of impending danger. Seeing Sirius now, he could almost hear the cracking begin in real time.

After entering the numbers correlating to Regulus’ birthday, Sirius leaned back to pull the safe handle sharply with both hands; no give.

“Darn. Really thought I’d had him with that one. Favourite son and all… Hm. Should we try mine then? Just for fun, of course.”

This time when Sirius spun the dial Remus was sure he could hear the cracks. He could see them too, displayed across Regulus’ face in a look of horror. Don’t, it seemed to say, but even just deep down, Regulus knew how alike they were too. The moment anyone told Sirius not to do something, he was only going to do the opposite.

“Moony, I might be in need of your expert lock-picking skills in a moment,” Sirius teased, taking hold of the handle; “ ‘Cause I can’t possibly figure what the code would be if not—”

Because he was sure he would fail, Sirius had yanked the safe door open with all of his strength, simultaneously losing his balance and sending himself sprawling backward when the door unexpectedly fell open.

Luckily for him, Remus’ reflexes weren’t all rubbish.

He caught Sirius before he could body-slam himself against the floor, but the force of the catch carried the both of them sideways and into the wall, where they collided with the portrait of Phineas Nigellus. The painting teetered for a moment, before falling forward and clipping the legs of the massive standing globe that’d been resting next to the desk. What followed was like a failed chain reaction, and Remus found himself recalling that night back at school, when they'd set off the smoke bombs in Salazar House only to fumble massively.

With the heavy portrait as its trigger, the antique globe fell to the ground, shattering its wooden stand and effectively releasing the globe's sphere like a pinball machine. It hit the bottom of the window with a hollow thunk and ricocheted into a nearby floor lamp. Regulus did rush to save it, but proved too slow, and the lamp teetered dangerously before finally over-turning and smashing into a million pieces against the wooden floor. The crash was legendary.

Afterwards you could’ve heard a pin drop. Sirius sat up, pushing Remus’ arm off. He was gaping—not at the lamp or his brother, but at his father’s safe. It was clear that whatever game Sirius had been playing, he had not expected it to open for him.

"After all this time...?"

His words were a whisper, one instantly swallowed by the rush of noise coming from outside the study. Already Remus could hear Regulus’ distress.

“Sirius, you idiot! You promised—look what you've done!”

The study doors burst open, and in swept none other than Walburga Black. She was flanked by four others; two men, one of which was older and had the same unsmiling expression as the man in the portrait, as well as two women, one blonde, the other a curly-haired brunette.

“You!” The brunette woman screamed, pointing a vicious finger at Sirius. It made him turn over, his confidant façade still stifled by the shock of the safe.

“Bella," he bleated, “Cissy, Uncle Cygnus—you’re all here.”

“Of course we're here,” Bellatrix hissed. “What are you doing here?”

“I…” Sirius faltered for just a moment, then; “Heard we were throwing a party at the main house. Figured the invitation must’ve just gotten lost in the post, but if you're here to give me the bollocking of my life, then go ahead—let's hear it.”

“You wretched, little brat. Why we should have you arrested—”

Walburga raised her hand, silencing Bellatrix instantly. “Rudolphus, the door if you wouldn’t mind.”

Remus had a feeling he knew which one was Rudolphus. He was Bellatrix’s husband and the only one among them that didn’t have the Blacks' aquiline nose and glass-coloured eyes. He went to the door and shut it, cutting them off from any other guest bold enough to come spying. Afterwards Remus had expected Walburga Black to burst into flame on the spot—ready to damn them and send them straight to hell for even daring to set foot into her house. But she didn’t. In fact, she didn’t even look at them.

Hands clasped tightly ahead of her black dress, she moved across the room toward Regulus, who stood flinching by the remains of the shattered lamp.

“Regulus, darling, are you alright? We were so worried when you didn’t arrive home on the train yesterday.”

She might as well have been speaking Chinese. Regulus floundered, as he always seemed to in front of his mother, and glanced very quickly at Sirius before looking away again.

"I'm sorry," he mumbled; “There... was a mix up at the station...”

Walburga stroked her son’s head, caressing the curls that had grown just past his jaw. “Then why didn’t you call us?” She asked, smiling as though she found it all very silly. “We would’ve arranged for you to be brought home.”

“I didn’t want to bother you. Not with Father…” Regulus trailed off uneasily. “I didn’t mean for things to happen this way.”

“He’s lying,” Sirius whispered, quietly enough that only Remus could hear. In an attempt to keep him from saying it again, Remus took his hand; only he could tell by the sharp turn of her head that the blonde woman—Narcissa, Remus remembered—had caught the gesture.

Slowly his hold on Sirius’ fingers weakened.

Across the room, Walburga pressed her smiling lips into a thin line. She was still petting Regulus’ hair, only her fingers had tightened on the ends, turning almost white at the knuckle.

“I do wish you’d cut your hair like we discussed at Christmas, darling. It is so…” Then she, too, trailed off. “No matter. You’re home now.”

With arms thin like a spider’s, she smoothed a wrinkle from Regulus’ suit and promptly embraced her son. Over her shoulder Remus saw Regulus’ face turn ashen. He wondered if now Regulus regretted coming, but why should he? He was coveted, if not just merely cared for.

One by one the other Blacks came forward to hug their cousin and nephew. Regulus hugged back sparingly, but when Bellatrix swept in for a cuddle Remus spotted the blatant look of satisfaction she was giving Sirius. Afterwards Walburga gathered Regulus to her side. She stared for a long time at the broken lamp and at the state of the opened safe, but her expression was calm; collected.

“I suppose thanks are in order.”

“Thanks?” Bellatrix echoed. “Aunt Walburga, you should have them arrested for breaking and entering!”

“For attempted robbery,” agreed Rudolphus.

“Sister, I too, think it highly irregular to allow for such a…” Cygnus licked his lips, “transgression. And at your husband’s funeral, no less. The proper authorities should be contacted.”

“In that case I would call Officer Digby at the Charing Cross station,” Sirius said. “Just spoke with him myself yesterday and if we’re gonna go this route then I’d prefer to expedite the process, if you don’t mind.”

Regulus visibly grimaced, but Walburga’s poised expression never faltered. Even if she held no love for her eldest son, seventeen years of practice was helping keep her emotions in check.

“Thank you,” she enunciated clearly; “for bringing my son home. Now I must ask you to leave.”

The gratitude felt more like a slap in the face, which Sirius took stoically.
