“Alright,” he nodded, tongue pressed between his bottom lip and teeth; “Reg is back where he should be, we were just leaving anyway.”

With his hands shoved into the pockets of his suit, Sirius sauntered forward.

“For what it’s worth, I really am sorry about Dad. Heard it was quick. Pity... Suppose you would've preferred a more drawn-out, agonising ordeal. Something to milk the papers."

It was Bellatrix who reacted; “Get out! Get out!” She screamed, but by then Sirius had already moved past his family and kicked the office door open. Skirting around the desk, Remus followed nervously while Rudolphus reached around and kept hold of his fitful wife. The self-effacing gesture must’ve brought something mean out of Sirius again, as he turned and hollered at the top of his lungs;

“Nice dress, by the way, Bella! I heard Rudolphus isn't even stealing your panties to wear into the office anymore. Oops—I hope that wasn't still a secret!”

The crowd that had gathered outside the office began parting around Sirius like the Red Sea, as though his disownment were an illness to be caught. Behind them Bellatrix continued to rage, cooed at gently by her sister and husband. Ignoring Bellatrix's fury, Sirius glanced openly to his left, where an old woman was glaring at him from beneath the rim of an enormous black silk hat.

“Aunt Belvina! Oh, I told Reg you’d be here.” He swept in to give the woman a grand kiss on either cheek, to which she shrieked and began batting him with her oversized purse. Sirius bowed out graciously, before leaping toward another relative.

“Cousin Leo! Blimey, I thought you were dead. Did you not break your neck in an awful polo accident a few years back? No, just the tailbone? Lucky, that. Though I imagine the healing time sucked ass… And Aunt Margery, how lovely to see you again! Is it true you’re still pumping the stem cells of poor, orphaned children into your face to avoid wrinkles? Well, it’s not working very well, is it? And holy—you’re shitting me—is that the old prime minister? Tell me, Mr. Wilson, when you were drafting that Lavender List of yours, did you consider putting that Oswald Mosley chap on the list? I have a feeling he’d have appreciated the title of Knight Commander of the British Empire.”

It was like watching a spectator sport where the only goal was to insult as many people as possible in the least amount of time. Sirius went around to all of them, digging up dirt people didn’t even know they had. Finally, Walburga had had enough. She marched out of the office, with Regulus tight on her heels and gestured to her brother;

“Cygnus, call the police.”

Sirius’ hands shot up in surrender. “Hey, I’m going, Mum—I’m going! You can’t very well blame a guy for wanting to catch up with his family. After all, it’s been sooo long. And to meet again under such terrible circumstances—tsk. Why, it just gets me so choked up.”

As Sirius made a show of wiping away imaginary tears with his middle fingers, two more guests came up behind him and grabbed him by the arms. Remus was moving instantly, but as it was, Sirius did not need his help. He removed both sets of hands by completing a quick duck and slide manoeuvre, getting behind both men and pushing them forward into a stumble with a quick slap over the back.

“Nice try,” he tsked, “but you really shouldn’t be putting your hands on the Black heir in his own home.”

It was the straw that broke Walburga Black’s back. Instantly she was fuming, making everyone leap half a foot into the hair when she shouted;

“Regulus is the heir—you are disinherited!”

Sirius yawned, feigning disinterest. “Mm, right… forgot about that bit. Ah well, I can still try and show my appreciation for the old man after his death, can’t I?”

There was no need to wonder what Sirius meant. He turned and flounced back through the crowd, into a grand atrium-like room with tall floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the back courtyard. The crowd followed like a swarm of pigeons, too curious about the train wreck that was quickly unfolding in front of them. The entire room was outfitted in tables decorated with buckets of iced champagne and bouquets of red and white carnations. There was a large portrait of Orion Black arranged on a pedestal at the far end, and just before that, an impressively sleek grand piano.

Sirius stood before the beast, and then flapped the back of his suit jacket as he took a seat at its bench.

“No!” Walburga screamed, coming into the room behind Remus with the rest of her family. “I forbid you from touching grandfather’s piano! I forbid it!”

“He may be your heir,” Sirius shouted back, pointing directly at Regulus; “but no one can do what I can do. So just this once—all of you can shut up and listen.”

They might as well have been back in the office, whispering about portraits and inheritance. The room fell deadly silent as Sirius lifted the piano’s key lid, and Remus recalled that the last time many of these people had seen Sirius take to a piano, it was likely when he was pouring 100-proof vodka across it and lighting it on fire. What Remus wouldn’t give to have seen it.

Sirius chose Beethoven. The piece was probably easily recognisable for anyone who enjoyed ‘real music’ as the snobs would have it, but Remus only recognised it thanks to a few weeks spent in twelfth-year music when Sheila had attempted to rally the class together for a formal symphony. It hadn’t ended well—there was very little room in Beethoven’s finest for a bass guitar and they'd only had a single competent violinist—but Remus remembered:

Symphony No. 5, written in C minor.

The piece was polyphonic, derived from a fancy Greek word meaning “many sounds”. In a formal orchestra it could feel as though you were listening to two warring tides, pushing and pulling against one another in endless tandem. Messing up even a single harmony would ruin all of that, and that was what made the piece so difficult to play. But Sirius didn’t need to worry about pushing or pulling; he was only one man and thus the only thing he needed to harmonise with was the war raging on inside his own head.

Watching Sirius, it was clear the song was weighing on him. He bent over the instrument's keys like some grotesque, twisted thing; nothing like the boy who'd sat needle-straight and kissed him over their school's piano all those months ago. He came at Beethoven with all the bloodlust of a ravenous hound—striking the theme’s iconic first notes; dun, dun, dun, dunn! Dun, dun, dun, dunn! It was awe-inspiring, but Remus knew that what came after was Sirius’ true bread and butter.

The soft transition started, and his cadence slowly increased like rolling thunder clouds spreading out over a sparkling green meadow. His fingers pounded against the keys, doing the job of an entire orchestra. Where Remus imagined his own fingers would have begun to ache, Sirius only grew faster; faster and faster until it just didn’t seem human anymore. Around the room, his spectators were slack-jawed. Even Regulus appeared shocked, but Walburga Black was not impressed. She stood by the doorway with a severe purse in her lips. Hearing it—seeing her—Remus felt anger swell inside his chest.

“Do you finally hear him now?” He demanded, having to shout just to be heard over Sirius’ climactic performance. A few in the room managed to tear their eyes away from the piano long enough to glare at him, but Walburga wouldn’t dare. Regulus stared at the floor.

“You’re monsters!” Remus wailed, driven by the staccato-like fury in Sirius’ music. “You’re all monsters, and I HOPE YOU ROT!”

A few women gasped into their champagne flutes; some of the men gave dirty looks that said they wanted to knock him on his ass. Remus would have welcomed the fight just about then. He could feel Sirius’ coda like a rush in his blood, working and playing double-time at a speed that should not have been humanly possible. And when the coda came—well, that was that the most beautiful ‘fuck you’ Remus had ever heard.

With a final slam of his fingers, Sirius was finished. He sat huffing on the piano bench, sweat pouring off of his face and neck. Remus could feel his heart hammering from across the room, but it didn’t stop Sirius from turning to address his audience.

“Sorry for rushing,” he panted, “can't seem to break the habit.”

No one said anything as Sirius stood up from the piano and went to one of the nearby tables, wrenching a fresh bottle of champagne from its silver ice bucket. Remus was already at his side, grasping Sirius’ arm and feeling the way his hands shook.

“Are you alright?” He whispered.

“Peachy.”

Back with the others, they watched as Regulus made to step forward. He might’ve said something to Sirius—for Sirius—but his mother never gave him the chance.

Swiftly abandoning the rest of her family, Walburga stormed straight toward them. She only came up to Remus’ shoulder in the end, but he knew from experience that she did not need to be able to reach all of someone to cut them deeply.

“You are a disgrace.”

“Oh," Sirius cooed, "I love it when you’re so thoughtful, Mummy.”

“You may have your hooks in Regulus now, but trust me, it will not last. One day you’re going to lose it all, and when that day comes…”

She never finished; she didn’t need to. It was enough for her that Sirius knew he wasn’t invincible, and that he would never have her approval.

“You will leave this house now,” she said, deadly low, “and never come back.”

Sirius held up a pinky in promise, and then pried the cork out of the champagne bottle with his teeth and spat it across the room. There was a loud pop as he did so, and the chilled champagne sloshed across the marble floor at their feet. Walburga jumped backwards, lest he soil her dress.

“Now that you’ve all witnessed what will surely be the only moderately interesting thing that’ll happen to any of you for the next twelve months, I think we will be bidding you adieu.” Sirius went to turn away, but stopped at the last second; “J’espère que vous brûlerez tous en enfer.”

Remus had no idea what he said, but judging from the vein bulging in his mother’s forehead and the gasps of shock going up from the rest of the room, it wasn’t exactly a fond farewell.

Champagne in one hand, Remus in the other, Sirius strode straight out of the atrium, making faces at his family and blowing kisses at the rest. They didn’t stop for Regulus, nor did the brothers say anything as they passed each other; Sirius simply kept walking.

“Are you sure you want to just leave?” Remus asked, as he was pulled toward the front door and adjoining main staircase.

“You mean Regulus," Sirius said stiffly, then; "I think the clever git can last a few minutes on his own. After all, they like him. We should do our own thing for a little while—in secret.”

Remus hadn’t the chance to ask what the secret was before Sirius was tugging him away from the door and up the massive stairway. They emerged on the second floor, then the third, passing crystalline windows and marble statues and—was that a suit of armour?

“Sirius, where are we going?”

“Don’t you remember?” Sirius giggled. “I said I've always wanted to shag in my own room.”

To say that Remus was surprised would’ve been an understatement, but he didn’t stop Sirius as he led him down the manor’s labyrinthian hallways. No one was around to stop them, but the walls had eyes enough. Portraits of other Black family members followed them everywhere, as well as the occasional baroque painting of a flower scene or whatnot.

“My great-grandmother collected hundreds of paintings from the great Dutch masters,” Sirius explained. “ ‘Girl with a Pearl Earring’? That’s on loan to The Hague from the Black family’s personal collection.”

“Bloody hell.”

Sirius sniggered again, and suddenly they were standing outside a single door. It didn’t look any different from the rest, save for the name plate reading “Sirius” and the massive “ROCKS” carved haphazardly into the wood beneath it.

“Reg’s says ‘sucks’,” Sirius confessed, before grasping the door handle. “Shit. Mum must’ve locked it.”

“I didn’t bring anything with me,” Remus said, patting his pockets. “You still got that hair pin from earlier?”

“No need,” Sirius said proudly; “I know this door. You just jiggle the handle a little to the left and—got it.”

The door fell open with a faint creak, revealing a handsome bedroom with velvet curtains and a vast four-poster bed.

“You have a chandelier in your bedroom...?”

“You act like it was my idea.”

Sirius pulled him inside and shut the door. It was dark with the curtains drawn, but it wasn’t hard to make out the poor state of the walls. Bits of shredded wallpaper and what appeared to be posters of scantily-clad women went all over the room. Remus didn’t have to ask; Sirius had told him the story about the nudie magazine ages ago. He’d thought it proper funny then, but now—seeing it up close—Remus felt a chill.

“I’ll bet Mum wanted it locked up for good. Old cow... Did you notice how she didn't even say my name? It's like she couldn't. Or wouldn't... I suppose.”

Sirius turned and began running his finger over one of the bed posts. It was unusually cool inside, and there was a fine layer of dust on everything. Remus wouldn’t have been surprised if some of the books on the bookshelf had begun to mould.

“It’s cold in here.”

Sirius took the observation as a challenge.

“Well then, allow me to warm you up.”

Taking him by the shoulders, Sirius spun Remus around until his back was to the bed. He didn’t push him down until they’d cleared away the grimy covers, but afterwards Sirius relieved him of his suit jacket and together they fell upon the bed.

“Are you sure?” Remus asked between kisses. “Mhm—your family is downstairs.”

“Fuck ‘em. I need to feel something.”

Perhaps that should’ve been the first indicator that something was wrong. Sirius was the most feel sort of person Remus knew. He was always feeling things—good or bad. Sirius had enough feeling inside him to sink a warship, if only he knew how to direct it.

Remus wouldn’t lie, getting busy below the waist in his boyfriend’s childhood nightmare room felt rather unsettling. He couldn’t imagine ever wanting to do the same in his bedroom back at the estate, but—as he stupidly remembered—they had. Over and over and over again. Back then it was about feeling like they were the only two people in the world, and now it felt like they were there just to get back at Sirius’ parents, dead or alive. Despite that, Remus didn’t complain. He knew what he was like at his lowest, and if this was Sirius' way of lashing out then so be it. After all, he and Sirius had never been cut from the same cloth; they simply matched each other, and that was enough.

They took things slow, coddling each other with feverish touches and tender kisses that made Remus feel like he was coming apart at the seams. Sirius stitched him back together again every time, kissing along his jaw while twisting two fingers into the chain at his throat. At some point Remus thought he could feel him trembling, but every time he went in search of the source, Sirius would capture his hands and pin them back against the covers.

Sirius’ tongue was as deft as it usually was, dividing his lips like wildfire and making Remus want to beg for more in a language he couldn’t even put words to. Without his shirt, the planes of Sirius' torso were smooth and flushed with heat. Only his left side bore any real texture, the burn scars he’d carried since he was eleven—now fading—having left him more blighted on the inside than he was on the out. With gentle kisses, Remus made his way down Sirius’ torso, caressing every uneven ridge and divot with his tongue. He had always loved Sirius’ scars for what they were; a reminder that he had survived horrible things and made it out the other side better—not made it out for them or because of them, but because Sirius had decided that that is what he would do. Seeing him now—touching him—Remus was sure he’d never known a braver person.

Brave, even as he shook himself to pieces in his hands.

“Sirius?” Remus leaned away, attempting to pry Sirius off of his neck. “Sirius… Sirius, stop. You’re shaking.”

“I’m not,” came a mumble. Remus felt a tongue skim along the edge of his ear, but when he went to grab Sirius by the hips he felt him flinch.

“Sirius, what’s wrong?”

“Who says anything’s wrong?”

There came another nip at his ear, and this time it was Remus who flinched away. When he turned to look at Sirius, he found tears streaking down his cheeks. They caught the faint blue light peeking through the bedroom's heavy curtains, turning his face pale and white.

"Sirius—"

"I don't care," Sirius warbled, his voice becoming raspy and thin. "I don't... I don’t care if I’m bloody shaking, I don’t care if the whole damn world is shaking—I don’t want to do this anymore.”

Remus cupped his cheeks for him, wiping away tears with the pads of his thumbs.

"Then don't."

It was like a curtain had come down over Sirius' face. Relief, despair—Remus didn't know. But he recognised the far away look in his eye, and knew that everything from the summer before their final year to Regulus showing up alone and cold on their doorstep, had been building to this single moment.

"I hate him, Moony," Sirius said softly, shutting his eyes as if he could visualise it. "I fucking hate him... I hate the whole lot of them. Every day I wish that they'd burn, that they'd poison each other to death. They tell me to get over it but I can't, and even if I could, I wouldn't. So why...? Why now? Why make my wish come true now?!"

And then Sirius opened his eyes, red-rimmed and bluer than a winter's sea.

"Why'd he have to go and die now? Him—He was supposed to live! Live and be miserable. Live and see that I can do shit all on my own—that I don’t need them or their arrogant, elitist fucking family! He was supposed to live so that he could see that I belong to me! That I'm untouchable. Because when I'm out there, where everyone can see me—they can't even get close! He was supposed to see that—He was supposed to live!"

Sirius was shouting now, but at least he was starting to make sense. In his fitting he'd pushed Remus' hands away, reaching up to knot his fingers in his hair himself and pull from the roots. Aching, Remus went to cup his face again—and then again when Sirius pushed him off the second time.

“Hey, hey! Sirius, it’s alright… I'm here.”

But Sirius was still shaking, and now he had angry tears in his eyes;

“Nah, now he's dead! And all those fucking people downstairs, I hope they die too. I hope they all get onto a boat and that that boat sinks and they all fucking drown! I wish that Regulus had never come to me—I wish he’d never bothered to ask for my help.”

“You don’t mean that,” Remus urged, getting flashbacks of the two of them stuck in that jail cell. “Regulus came to you because he trusts you.”

“Dunno why. All I do is fuck things up for him. Or—make him heir, I suppose. Shit... Such ironic bullshit!”

A second lapsed between them, in which Sirius turned and punched his old headboard. It must've hurt, as he groaned through his teeth, cradling his fist to his chest. Scooting closer, Remus took his hand and placed a gentle kiss along his knuckles.

"I used to wish for it too, you know," he confessed, slowly stroking the red flesh. "When I found out my mum was dying, a part of me wished she'd just hurry up and go. Like it'd make it easier or something... Then when she was gone, I wished it'd been my dad instead. I told him that... That it should've been him."

"Maybe it should've," Sirius said lowly. "He ruined your life... S'only fair."

Remus shrugged. "I know I blamed him for a long time, but really I think now that it was just a way to avoid blaming myself. It's like, if I could be so mad at him that I wanted him dead, then maybe there wouldn't be any space left to hate myself. It worked for a while... but hate rarely works forever. There's always a bottom, Sirius."

"Is that what this is? Bottom...?"

"It's you, torturing yourself for something you're not responsible for. You gotta stop."

"Responsible," Sirius echoed—sardonically like a bad joke. "Sorta like how you’re not responsible for Lee turning out to be a complete waste of oxygen?”

It felt like left field, but then Remus followed Sirius' gaze down to the splotchy bruises that mottled his stomach. Seeing them, Remus began to smile sorely, sadly.

“... What a pair we make, huh?”

Sirius chuffed lightly, his running nose making spit strings between his perfect lips. He reached out to touch the bruises, and Remus held in a breath.

“This is supposed to be a dream come true," Sirius whimpered, wiping the snot from his upper lip. "Why don’t I feel happier?”

“Because..." And Remus covered Sirius' hand where it lay against his own stomach, knotting their fingers together; "Because you’re human. And you're in mourning.”

Sirius shook his head. “No... No, we’re not supposed to mourn those who’ve hurt us.”

“Yes, well... Mourning’s never been for the dead anyway.”

Despair surged forth and suddenly Sirius was moaning;

“Oh... Oh god.”

It took a long while for Sirius to calm down. In that time, Remus held him, stroking his long black hair and kissing his face until his shoulders had finally stopped trembling. They laid together on those cold bed covers, imagining all the ways fate had dealt them a poor hand.

"You know what's gonna suck the most?" Sirius whispered; "They're gonna think we had it easy."

"Who?"

"Them—everyone. The whole world is going to see us as proper little rich boys with nothing left to want. They're going to call us industry plants, and try to say that we don't belong. That we had everything."

Remus thought of his old friends; of Lee.

"We did."

"Yeah... and it's not fucking fair."

Life rarely was, it seemed.

“You were there earlier,” Sirius said eventually, breathing into the skin of Remus' collarbone; “Back at the piano. How did I sound?”

“Brilliant. If not a bit mental.”

He felt Sirius’ shoulders move with a chuckle. “You didn’t try to stop me.”

“Yeah, it felt like your moment. I couldn’t be the one to stop you.”

Sirius sighed, turning his face so that Remus got the feeling he was also staring up at the underside of the ornate four-poster.

“I hope we never have to come back here again.”

“Next time we’ll just torch it to the ground. We can start with that awful office and work our way out. Make it so every last piece is unsalvageable.”

He’d been expecting another witty retort, maybe an offer of agreement followed by some harebrained idea they’d never actually see through to fruition, but instead Sirius merely unattached himself from Remus’ embrace and sat up.

“I’ve just remembered something.”

He was off the bed in an instant, rushing to the far corner of the room where he collapsed to his knees next to the window. Remus sat up in alarm.

“Sirius?!”

“I know it’s here somewhere.” Sirius began pushing his hands against the floor until one of the boards eventually gave way. He stuck his arm in, but came up empty. “Ugh. Figured she would’ve cleared it out, but I bet she missed one thing…”

Lowering himself until he was almost completely flush to the floor, Sirius gave a little grunt and continued straining his shoulder until finally he was sitting back up on his heels, a single photograph clutched in his hand.

“Stuck it to the underside of one of the boards, just as a little precaution,” he explained. Dusting himself off, he brought the photo back to the bed for Remus to have a look. There Remus found himself staring down at an image of four happy boys, no older perhaps than thirteen or fourteen. Each of them were covered head-to-toe in mud, but they beamed back at the camera proudly anyway. There was Sirius, with his tongue out and two fingers dragging down his lower eyelids in a taunt; James with an arm around a fair-haired Peter, both yet to lose the baby-fat in their cheeks; and a fourth boy Remus recognised only by omission.

“Is that… Miles?”

His tone rose at the end, honestly surprised, and Sirius took it as permission to smile.

“Yeah! You see, we’d just gone on a hike for gym class, ‘cept it was March so it’d been raining the entire week and the whole path was soaked in mud. We—er… well, I can’t really remember who pushed who first, but we all ended up belly-sliding down the hill.”

“Bet it was you who pushed first.”

“Ha… probably. Hooch was furious when we got back to the school. Gave us a week's detention each.”

Remus clutched the photograph tightly. It was hard to tell because of all the mud, but he thought Miles’ hair might be brown. His cheeks were ruddy and he stood taller than Sirius but shorter than James. There was no way of knowing whether it still rung true; several years had passed since the photo had been taken, and in all his time at Hawkings, Remus had never once gone in search of evidence of Miles' existence. James had once told him there was a team photo hanging in the gym atrium from the single term Miles had tried out for the football team, but Remus had told himself that he needn’t bother. Miles was gone, and no amount of 'oohing' and 'awing' over old pictures was going to magically bring him back.

And that was perhaps the only reason Remus didn’t feel bad as he passed the photograph back to Sirius.

“I’m happy you found it,” he told him; “It sounds like a good memory.”

Sirius smiled—one of the handsome sort, concentrated out of the corner of his mouth. Then he leaned forward and kissed Remus softly.

“Don’t ever go anywhere,” Sirius whispered, when their lips parted.

“Never.”

Their clothes were wrinkled and dusty by the time they’d retrieved them from the floor, and when it was time to leave, Sirius did not bother giving the room a second glance.

“Can’t wait to be out of here,” he said, rubbing his arms as if he felt a sudden chill up his spine; “This place has always given me the heebie-jeebies, 'specially when the portrait's eyes follow you. Truthfully, I think it’s haunted. Gotta be, what with how many of my family members died within its walls.”

“Let’s just not think about it anymore,” Remus said, purposely not making eye contact with a nearby painting. They were making their way back down the main staircase when they were finally caught, though thankfully this time it was only by one Black.

Standing firm at the base of the staircase, Narcissa crossed her arms and scowled prettily at them. Remus knew she and Sirius must be related, as only the Blacks could scowl prettily. Sirius had spotted her first and nearly yelped, before sagging into Remus out of relief.

“Cissy! Wow, am I glad to see you. It’s been so long! Loving the new hair colour by the way—they say aviation blondes are all the rage in Europe these days.”

“You were supposed to be leaving,” Narcissa said, her tone less shrill than her sister’s, but not any less foreboding.

“Yes, well, we were just picking up a few things,” replied Sirius. “Now we are, in fact, leaving, so if you could so kindly step out of the way…”

She did not move, but rather came towards them. Every stair she took made Sirius shrink slightly, until she was standing directly below them and yet still at eye-level.

“I want you to do something for me, Sirius. A favour, you might call it. And I forbid you from speaking a word about it to anyone.”

“At all?”

“At all.”

“So what’s this then, like—a secret favour?”

Narcissa scoffed like he was no more than an irritating child. “I need you to take these letters to Andromeda for me,” she said, producing a small bundle of letters from the clutch purse she carried. Sirius eyes the letters suspiciously at first.

“Why don’t you just take them?”

“I haven’t spoken with my sister in years. But you? You must see her all the time.”

“Not all the time,” Sirius admitted, rubbing the back of his neck. “More like… every other month or so?"

Narcissa's eyes narrowed.

"But yeah—totally! Ooofff couuuurse I can do that for you. But I am a bit curious as to what’s inside them...?”

“That’s none of your business, and if you don’t want me going to Aunt Walburga so that she can have you arrested for trespassing then I suggest you take the letters to my sister—unopened.”

“Right...”

Sighing regretfully, Sirius held out his hand and let Narcissa push the envelopes into his palm. Then she lingered a moment longer.

“Your shirts are misbuttoned.”

Remus and Sirius both looked down, alarmed to find that she was right. At least two of Remus’ buttons were misaligned, and Sirius had mistakenly clasped his suit jacket with the interior buttons facing out. As Sirius rushed to fix them, Remus glanced back at Narcissa, who was peering at them with the same scrutinising look as she had back in the office.

“Goodbye, Sirius," she said. "I doubt we’ll be seeing each other any time soon.”

Sirius nodded, jacket hanging open as he tucked the letters safely into his breast pocket. “Have a lovely rest of the funeral, Cissy." He winked. "You always were my favourite cousin.”

“And you always were a liar,” said Narcissa, as she turned and began marching primly down the stairs to rejoin the party.

“Not gonna lie,” Sirius laughed, as the pair of them burst out onto the manor’s front steps, “thought we were goners back there for a moment. But I should’a known—Cissy’s always been good in a pinch. So long as she wants something, a’course.”

“Speaking of wanting something, what do you think is in those letters?”

“Dunno. Maybe Uncle Cygnus and Aunt Druella are trying to disinherit Andy again. Can you disown someone twice?”

Remus shrugged, busy digging around in his pocket for the car keys.

“All I know—!” Sirius declared, raising his hands to the sky in an effort to soak up the sun that had just started to peek through the clouds; “is that this is the best I’ve felt while visiting home in a long time. Maybe we should do this more often—a biannual family get together where we’re not just celebrating some dead relative we all secretly hated.”

“And if that’s too hard you could always just start murdering your family members on the regular,” Remus suggested. “I’d start with that awful grey-haired bloke that was standing behind Bellatrix in the atrium. He smelt like if mothballs could rot.”

“You mean Uncle Cadmus? Nah, he's only related by marriage so he's got no real money. If you’re really gonna bump someone off then it should really be Aunt Bel—AH!”

They’d been rushing to get back to the car, a hurry they soon came to regret the moment they rounded the side of some fancy Italian coupe to find Regulus sitting on the hood of their rental car.

“Where are you going?”

“Home!” Sirius babbled; “Back to London where we belong, thought it'd be obvious. What about you—what are you doing out here?”

“I knew you couldn’t have left if the car was still here," Regulus mumbled. "I went looking but Narcissa said you’d gone out to the gardens.”

“Yeah? Well, Cissy’s a liar. We weren’t in the gardens we were—” Sirius faltered slightly and Regulus rolled his eyes.

“You were doing something you ought not to be doing—yeah, I figured.” Regulus pushed off the car lazily. He had something in his hands he was playing with, and Remus realised with no small amount of surprise that it was one of the cigars from his father’s office. “I also figured that if I asked to come, you’d take me with you.”

Sirius blinked in confusion. “You... You want to come with us?”

The question seemed to stump Regulus. A year ago, he might’ve refuted it outright, but they’d all done some growing up in that time. They were different people now.

“I don’t want to stay here," he said, twisting his hands over the cigar. "I told Mother I was leaving. With you."

"You—You did?"

"Yes. And I also told her that she was wrong about you. That you're a good brother."

"You're shitting me."

A trace of what might've been a smile grazed the corners of Regulus' mouth. "I'm not you, Sirius. Hoping that it'll all just work out no matter the consequences."

"But you'll try?" Sirius asked.

Regulus licked his lips. "I could maybe... be somewhat convinced to try, yes."

It was a Regulus sort of answer, but it was enough, and Remus knew without asking that Sirius was already sold on the idea.

But that didn’t mean he wasn’t going to tease...

“You sure?” He grinned, shoving his hands into his pockets and leaning over Regulus tauntingly. “ ‘Cause there’s no backing out later. When you become a Marauder you’re in it for life.”

“I’m not joining your stupid band, if that’s what you mean.”

Sirius covered his heart. “Ouch. You know if you’re going to be our roadie then you’re going to have to show a bit more enthusiasm than that.”

"Not a roadie," Regulus corrected, cheeks flushed. "This is temporary. Just until I go back to school."

"Okay, so you want to hang out with your big brother for a few weeks, I get it. But then what?"

"Then... I guess I just hope that it all works out."

There wasn’t a hint of Sirius that could’ve refused him. Grinning ear to ear and entirely too pleased for words, he took his brother by the shoulders.

“You can stay for as long as you like.”

Regulus nodded, his lower lip giving the barest of quivers, and then he passed Sirius the cigar. Beaming, Sirius set it between his teeth and turned back to Remus;

“Well, Moons? Ready to go home?”

“After meeting your family?" Remus replied. "Yeah, think I could use a stiff drink.”

“Oh, then what the hell are we waiting for then?” Sirius exclaimed, wrenching open the Morris’s passenger side door. He ripped off his tie with the same motion and tossed it across the windshield of the Italian coupe. “Come on, lads, let’s go get disgustingly drunk!”



* * *





Feel the bile rising from your guilty past,

With your nerves in tatters,

When the conch shell shatters;

And the hammers batter down your door;

You’d better run!

- “Run Like Hell” Pink Floyd, 1979



It took Regulus almost the full two-hour drive back to London to realise that they had no plans to go home straight away.

“But what about our clothes?” He asked, as Remus pulled the Morris back into the rental yard.

“We’ll get new clothes. Ones that aren’t going to make you look fresh off the Prada runway.”

It was an exaggeration, but as Regulus frowned, Sirius twisted around his seat looking nothing but eager.

“Come on, Reg! Haven’t you ever wanted to see the city for yourself? I mean, really go where the culture is?”

"Culture and crowds are not synonymous."

"You see, Moons? Told you he was smart. He's onto us already."

Remus put the car into park. "Ah, well. To Portobello Road then?”

After getting rid of the car, they hopped the tube—actually hopped the turnstiles, Regulus was horrified—toward Notting Hill and Ladbroke Grove, where they had plans to take the London-newbie through the nearby market stands. They got a few looks for their formal dress, though most seemed to dismiss them as a few fresh-out-of-business school wash-ups merely late getting into the office.

It was a Monday, and already being late into the day, the market was slowing down. Early morning shoppers had come and gone, leaving behind picked-through vegetable stands and a cafe dinner rush that smelt of fresh bread and coffee. It wafted out onto the street to merge with the smell of tarmac and nearby perfume vendors, making Remus’ stomach growl and his nose itch at the same time. Around them there were Sikh families running stalls stuffed full with glimmering silk and cotton caftans, next to awning-covered shop fronts selling t-shirts of American sports teams Remus had never heard of. They passed street musicians and weary men peddling tables ladened with tarnished silver, as well as brick walls covered with every sort of poster and flyer one could imagine.

Weaving through the cars and people, Remus almost felt nostalgic. His fondest memories of Portobello were that of the times Tomny had brought him. Back then it was like a game between all the lads—who could fill their pockets the quickest and with the best stuff without ever being caught. Remus partook occasionally, of course he did, but he was never as bold as the rest of his friends. He still had Giles’ wrath to fear back then. Now he was grown, and had since made new memories there with Sirius. They’d filled their kitchen cupboards with old china bowls purchased off a kindly Korean woman that spoke almost no English; their bathroom rug had come from one of the charity shops and Remus had spent hours poking through the volunteer-run bookshop on the corner. It was a bit jarring to think of how differently his life might’ve turned out had Lyall not decided to send him north to Scotland as a last-ditch effort to clean up his son’s act, but that was the funny thing about fate—sometimes things tended to work out where you’d least expected them.

“Mmm, take it all in, Edge!” Sirius said, taking a deep breath for emphasis. They’d passed beneath the A40 Westway into the north end of the market and a lorry rattled overhead like thunder, making Regulus jump.

"Take what in? The pollution?"

"Would it kill you to not be so literal for once?"

Ignoring their grumbling stomachs, the first task at hand was to find something decent for all of them to wear. Regulus had whinged over returning to the flat so he could retrieve his trunk, only Sirius had refused to let him wear anything that required a decent pressing beforehand. Instead they took to the busy streets, wandering through the stalls until they’d found themselves standing outside an old charity shop with its usual array of well-loved toys, picture books, and ‘famine relief’ adverts displayed in the front window. A bell chimed as they walked inside, and Remus caught the familiar whiff of dust and musky old clothing. A shop attendant was going through boxes of old hoover parts up by the front desk and there was a rack of over-stock sitting by the door, mostly made up of men’s winter coats priced as low as two quid. Moving up the rack, Regulus paused before an old bomber jacket with orange and yellow stripes and began thumbing one of its sleeves. It only lasted a few seconds before he caught them staring.

“What?”

“Nothing,” Sirius said with a small smile. “See anything you like?”

Regulus rolled his eyes at them, then turned and stalked further into the shop. After he’d gone, Sirius went to the bomber he’d been eyeing and pulled it off the rack. “Just in case,” he told Remus, winking.

Because he had no real preference for style, it didn’t take long for Remus to find himself something to wear in the cluttered shop. Sirius repeatedly tried to pawn various items off on him, muttering things like ‘imagine how it’ll look on stage’ and ‘you and your half-a-mile long legs’, but Remus rejected most of them on the grounds that he didn't feel like dressing up as an Elton John impersonator for the rest of the night. Sirius was not impressed.

When he was finished, Remus had traded his suit for a pair of canvas trousers and a faded chore coat. Once paid for, he found Sirius browsing the shoe section, Regulus nowhere in sight.

“Please tell me you’re not thinking of buying this?” Remus held up a paisley-printed dress shirt he’d plucked from the pile Sirius had amassed next to him. Sirius scoffed and snatched the shirt back.

“Piss off, it’s camp. Not that I’d expect you to know what that means.”

“I know camp,” Remus maintained. “Like Bowie.”

Sirius shook his head, "Hopeless," then he looked him up and down. “Is that really all you found? You look like you’re on your way to the glue factory.”

“So like the average Londoner, then.”

“There is nothing admirable about being ‘average’.”

Deciding that this was not the hill to die on, Remus glanced around. “Where’s Regulus then?”

“I dunno, he was in outerwear.”

On cue, Regulus came tearing around the end of the aisle, nearly knocking over a stack of half-dressed mannequins as he raced back towards them.

“I think I saw a rat,” he gasped. “O-Over there! It was hiding inside those disgusting fur coats.”

“It’s quite possible,” Remus said; “Pretty sure they come inside when it rains.”

Regulus was clearly appalled.

“You said this was a charity shop, not a refuse.”

“Try dialling it back on the negativity just a titch, okay, Reggie?” Sirius sighed, moving away from the shoes to hold a shirt up against Regulus’ torso. “Sometimes you can find some really cool stuff in here.”

“Yeah, like syphilis.”

"Don't be a snob." Sirius switched the shirt for a pair of jeans. “Now these might not be too bad. Why don’t you try ‘em on?”

“These look like they haven’t been washed in years.” He checked the tag; “And they’re women’s.”

“Don’t knock ‘em ‘til you try ‘em.” Sirius grinned, then began piling several more pairs into his brother’s arms. “Here, take these. Dressing rooms are that’a way, there’s a good lad. And don’t you worry, I’ll keep looking. We’ll have you a whole new wardrobe before we’re finished.”

Regulus went—with no small amount of grumbling—and Sirius turned back to Remus, who’d been leaning over an empty rack with an unlit cigarette dangling from his lips.

“You did look good in those jeans."

“Knew you were looking at my arse," Sirius smirked. "Here, found something for you too, even.”

With a victorious smile, Sirius held up a pair of crimson-coloured Chuck Taylors, size eleven. One of the laces was broken but aside from that they fit perfectly. As Remus was testing them out, Regulus came back out of the dressing room, looking awkward in a pair of baggy jeans and his undervest.

“You’ll need a belt,” Sirius nodded, “but look here, I’ve found you the perfect shirt.”

He held it up and Regulus’ eyes widened.

“No. No way.”

“Aw, don’t be such a fuddy-duddy, Reg! This is just the thing for what we have planned next, trust me.”

When it came to clothing, Remus was pretty sure Regulus didn’t trust Sirius as far as he could throw him, but either to make his brother happy or because he couldn't stand spending another moment inside the manky shop, he took the shirt.

By the time they were finished, Sirius had outfitted his brother head-to-toe in second-hand chic and had even found a new stylish Harrington jacket for himself. When Remus began complaining of starvation, the three of them popped into a local cafe for a spot of supper. Mostly Regulus appeared weary of city's preference for fusion cuisine. Watching Sirius attempt to coax him into taking a bite out of one of his pakoras was like observing a mother as she tried to convince her picky eater of a child that eating solely chips for supper did not make for a well-rounded meal.

“Quick,” Sirius urged after, hurrying them toward the nearest entrance to the Underground; “I wanna get out there before the sun sets.”

"Out where?" Regulus demanded.

"You'll see."

It was another short ride, for which Sirius sat on one side of the train and insisted on playing a game of footsie with Remus across the aisle. Every now and then one of them would pause long enough to gauge Regulus’ reaction, but if he was bothered, he never let them know with more than a light scoff. Instead Regulus watched; not them, but others—people on their way home from work, teenagers on their way home from school. He stared at those folk who’d fallen asleep drunk on station benches and peered at the back of newspapers as others read the periodicals. Watching him watching other people, Remus would’ve given just about anything to see what was going on inside Regulus’ head.

“I don’t get it,” the younger Black brother said later, when they’d reached their next destination only for it to turn out to be little more than your average zebra crossing. “They just stood there for a photo, and now it’s like some sort of national monument? What a waste of time.”

“I swear, you’re so uncultured,” Sirius huffed, ushering Regulus into the middle of the crossing. “Stand there and act like you’re having fun.”

“Why do I have to be in the photo?”

“Because, Potter’s never gonna believe me without any proof. Now smile.”

“Don’t forget to show us your shirt,” Remus called, raising the instant camera he’d borrowed off a Japanese tourist. Regulus scowled at him, but there were other people waiting for their chance in the famous crossing and Remus refused to take the photo until he’d opened the bomber jacket Sirius had gotten for him and showed everyone what was underneath. When he finally did, several nearby tourists began to snigger, and a passing woman in a green peacoat gasped scandalously. Sirius only grinned.

Teens want Beatles, the shirt read, not Jesus!

“Right. Now say, ‘Helter Skelter’!”

In answer, Regulus raised his middle finger and Remus took the photo while laughing. It felt like a culmination of sorts, but there was so much to see, and they were only just getting started.

“Come on, Reg, run!”

They tore across the pavement outside of Regent’s Park, dodging pedestrians and cackling as the sun set over the tops of the buildings. Their bus was leaving without them and they were determined to catch it. Remus reached it first, hailing himself aboard the back platform of the double-decker. He was followed swiftly by Sirius, who’d taken a running leap and nearly landed straight on top of him. Still panting, they turned around to find Regulus running full-tilt behind the bus. They screamed at him, waving their arms;

“So close—”

“Just a bit more!”

Reaching his hand out, Regulus grasped the silver pole and—with one final oomph!—dragged his skinny arse onto the bus’s rubber platform. He nearly wobbled when he went to stand, but Remus caught him by the shoulders—Sirius by the front of his jacket. Behind the bus, the bike-bound police officer that’d been pursuing them since Regent’s Park blew his whistle indignantly. For a moment it looked like he might actually catch them, but he was foiled after being caught in a pedestrian crossing. Sirius was already celebrating.

“OH!” Regulus exploded; “You just HAD to spit in the fountain!”

“It’s a cultural thing,” he cackled. “Think of it like a rite of passage.”

“Everyone does it,” Remus said, as the bus dinged to its next stop.

They rode it back into the city, arriving not long after the sun began to set. What they were left with was the twinkling lights and buzzing neon that the more popular high streets were known for. Unused to such a busy place, Regulus eventually got better at dodging the crowds and taxis, remaining silently enamoured with it all. They made sure to tease him every time they happened across one of the less savoury sex shops, and for supper it was fry-ups, straight from the nearest greasy spoon’s grill. Regulus seemed dubious over the fact that they were still serving breakfast foods so late, but he was hungry and tired enough not to complain.

“So what next?” Asked Sirius, sipping coffee as he spread a sightseer map he’d nicked from a local newsstand. “All the touristy places’ll be closing soon I suspect, but there’s always always the theatre.”

“Hyde Park’s just around the corner too,” Remus mused, “we could see if the pigeons are up for a photo.”

“No!” Regulus huffed, busy ham-fisting his fork. “No more bloody photographs… Christ, when you said we’d go around the city, I thought you meant we’d do something exciting.”

“What—running from the cops not exciting enough for you?” Sirius said.

“Exciting and illegal are not mutually exclusive.”

“Maybe not where you’re from.”

While Regulus began complaining that he and Sirius were, in fact, from the same place, Sirius leaned over to Remus and whispered in his ear. He was not expecting him to propose such a mad idea, but in hindsight, Remus knew that Sirius had been obsessed with the idea ever since he'd told him the story of how Tomny had talked him into it at just fifteen.

"You do realise it was one of the single stupidest things I’ve ever agreed to?" Remus said. "We were pissed to hell when we did it.”

“He said exciting!" Sirius urged. "Can't think of anything more exciting than that."

Or prone to accident, Remus thought.

He glanced at Regulus, who was still shovelling spoonfuls of beans and fried tomato into his mouth. What Sirius was suggesting was idiotic and reckless, not to mention dangerous. If they got caught they’d certainly be arrested, but Regulus had said exciting, and well…

They had to make their way back toward Shepherd’s Bush to get there. On the way they stopped back in at the flat to warm up and to share in a bit of liquid courage. Frustrated that neither would tell him what they were up to, Regulus initially turned his nose up at the hooch.

"Trust me," Sirius said, pushing the bottle into his hands, "you're gonna want this."

It was late by the time they'd reemerged, and knowing what they were about to do, Remus kept expecting to turn a corner and find an enraged Lily ready to tell them off for such an idea. She was so going to kill them when she got back...

Arriving at their destination, Sirius paid the cabbie and then began skipping along the pavement, pulling a full flask from his jacket pocket for yet another swig. Already shivering in his jacket, Regulus walked along beside him and groaned dramatically when he realised what it was they'd come all this way to see,

“You mean you spent ten pounds on a cab just so that we could come see some barmy old bridge?”

“Calm down, it was only like three quid,” Sirius replied, passing the flask along to Remus, “And this isn’t just any bridge. This is the Barnes Railway Bridge.”

Regulus didn’t look any more impressed at the declaration. He glanced over the entrance to the bridge’s footpath, peering at a scratch of graffiti that read things like ‘BOB FENDER IS A CUNT’ in big, bold lettering. Smirking, Remus offered him the flask, which he rebuffed at first.

“We already had a full bottle back at the flat.”

“I know but I reckon you’re gonna need a bit more.”

Regulus sighed and took the booze, hands fidgeting at his sides. Further down the bridge, the sound of a zipper could be heard as Sirius undid his trousers and began pissing off the side of the footpath into the shallow water below.

Regulus choked around the flask, covering his mouth; “That’s fucking disgusting.”

“Wow. I never thought anyone could be a bigger prude than Moony,” Sirius sighed. Once he’d finished relieving himself he zipped up his trousers and wandered back over, slapping Regulus on the arm encouragingly. Regulus gagged in reply, and Sirius got a sharp punch in the arm for it.

It was pitch dark when they finally made their way out onto the bridge. Aside from the moon, the only light came from the windows lining the row-homes off the street running alongside its southern end. The air was chilly, but not unbearable when one was suitably drunk, which Remus supposed they would have to be to even consider the stunt they were about to pull. He hadn’t been to Barnes Bridge in years, not since Tomny had set down proper roots in the End. Back then he’d have run amuck with just about anyone, desperate for a thrill and a good time. The most famous of them was named Patrick, but everyone had called him Plucky after one of his favourite pastimes—playing chicken with the oncoming trains out in the Clapham rail depot. Remus had never gotten to witness it himself, but according to Tomny, Plucky could be seen taunting up to five trains a night. It was all a very neat party trick, but then one evening the lads went down to the rail yard after having a bit too much to drink and Plucky forgot to lace up his boots.

After hearing the story, Remus had never looked at a Battersea train the same way again.

“Ready to do this?” Sirius asked, practically jumping up and down in place. Remus laughed, too nervy to do anything else as he peered down the adjoining train tracks expectantly. Doing so, he was reminded of Plucky, but told himself this wasn’t nearly as dangerous because they wouldn’t be running, only... "hanging". Meanwhile Regulus was watching the river, humming to himself and still sipping from the flask, apparently unbothered.

“What are we waiting for?” He asked. "Hope it's not for you the two of you to grow a brain. In that case we'll be out here all night."

“Oh, you’ll see, brother dear,” Sirius drawled, leaning against the wrought-iron railing that separated the tracks from the footpath. Remus figured they’d have no issue climbing over it; it was what came next that was the tricky part.

“Do you guys do this a lot?” Regulus prattled on. “Come to the middle of nowhere and wait for nothing?”

“As a matter of fact, I’ve never even been here before,” Sirius told him. “But I’ve wanted to come ever since Lupin told me about it.”

“Right—Lupin. You’re just full of exciting stories, aren’t you?”

“I’ve been known to dabble. Why? Are you curious?”

Regulus stuck his tongue out, and Remus chuffed. He watched as the younger boy turned back to the water, lazily reaching his arm out and tipping the smallest bit of booze out of the flask to watch it fall onto open air.

“Don’t waste it,” Sirius chided, taking the flask. “You wanna drop something, you use your spit—OH! That’s it! We can teach you how to spit!”

Regulus made a face. “I know how to spit.”

“No, you don’t,” Sirius laughed, already steering the both of them toward the railing. “Go on, Moons, show him how it’s done.”

Tipsy and entirely too eager to please, Remus took hold of the railing with both hands and hocked a large wad of phlegm straight out over the water. Sirius clapped for him, but Regulus looked about as offended as a sixteenth century woman asked to show off her petticoats.

“Your turn now, Edge. Give it a try,” Sirius encouraged, welcoming the dirty look it earned him.

“I am not spitting in the river.”

“You have to! You didn't do it back at the fountain and it’s a rite of passage. Lupin taught me my first ever time in London.”

“No, not happening.”

“C’moooooon!” Sirius nudged Remus, and together they took up a chant; “SPIT! SPIT! SPIT! SPIT!”

“God—FINE! Just shut up already!” Elbowing Sirius out of the way, Regulus readied himself on the edge of the railing.

“Oh, and don’t feel too bad if you’re awful at it,” Remus added. “Sirius couldn’t get past the tips of his shoes the first hundred times.”

“Shuddup, Moony.”

Flashing them his favourite glare, Regulus relaxed his shoulders and leaned as Remus had. Then he coughed deep in his throat, and with a sharp thrust, spat an impressive loogie straight out over the canal. It flew several feet before disappearing down into the darkness, and by then Remus and Sirius were already cheering.

“I knew you could do it,” Sirius keened, shaking his brother by the shoulders. “My little hooligan!”

“Yeah, yeah, just pass me the booze.”

Together they shared another round, and when the flask was mostly depleted, Sirius tucked the little bottle away and clapped his hands together.

“Right. We’ve waited a decent while, figure it’s about time to get this show on the road. Moony, if you’ll please.”

Remus linked both hands together, creating a little platform for Sirius to fit the bottom of his boot into. Regulus eyed them, shuffling closer.

“What are you doing?”

“Going over the railing, what’s it look like?”

“You’re going to jump into the river?!”

“Not that railing, silly. This one!”

With a sharp ‘oomph’ Sirius had hauled himself over the wrought-iron and onto the edge of the train tracks. He wobbled a bit before finding the correct footing, and Remus reached through the bars to grab him.

“Careful. Mind the gaps.”

“I got it,” Sirius assured him. “You coming over?”

“Yep.”

As Remus carefully stretched his long legs up over the bars, Regulus grabbed hold of the railing and began to bark at them;

“What are you doing? Get back here!”

“C’mon, little bro,” Sirius grinned, reaching an arm out to steady himself on one of the vertical beams. “Where’s your sense of adventure?”

“You’re going to get hit by a train!”

“Do you hear a train?”

Regulus blanched, and Remus held out a hand to him.

“Here. I’ll help you.”

It wasn’t in his nature to accept help—from anyone—but either because it was late and they were drunk, or because he’d already thrown caution to the wind just by coming with them, Regulus accepted.

“There,” Sirius said, when all three of them were on the other side. “Isn’t this just exciting?”

“Thrilling. Now can we get off?!”

“In a bit.” Sirius began skipping up and down the track, open air hovering dangerously between every joint. Remus kept close, unsure if he would even be able to catch him were he to fall. They'd survive if that were the case; it was only about a fifteen foot drop to the water below, twenty at most now that it was winter, not that Regulus seemed comforted.

“You okay, Edge?” Sirius called, when Regulus refused to let go of the bridge’s main arch. “Don’t tell me you’re scared of heights now?”

“I’m not scared of heights!” Regulus snarled. “But I’d rather not drown in a filthy, sewer-ridden river!”

“You won’t drown, you’ll just get a little wet. Now come over here. Let go, you won’t believe how good it feels. It's a total rush.”

Regulus flipped him off, only to panic when he realised that he no longer had two hands on the metal beam. Watching him, Remus stepped onto the same joint as Sirius so they were shoulder to shoulder.

“Maybe we should stop here.”

“No way,” Sirius whispered. “He’s braver than he thinks he is.”

Remus didn’t have much to say to that. He hung back as Sirius trotted back toward the railing and stopped right beside his brother, leaning in so their foreheads nearly touched and their dark curls melted into one another under the light of the moon.

“Reggie, listen to me. Just take a deep breath. You’re alright—you can do this, you only need to let go.”

“No, I’ll—I’ll fall.”

“You won’t, promise. You won’t, cause I’ve got you.”

Sirius offered his hand, palm up, and Regulus eyed it with a reluctant expression. Several seconds passed, but when he finally reached out and took it, Remus exhaled.

“D-Don’t let go!” Regulus babbled.

“I won’t,” Sirius promised again, already carefully guiding him out onto the middle of the rails. “There—just there. Put your foot there… Good! You’re doing so well.”

Regulus winced, the wind lapping at his hair and gently pushing it across his pale forehead.

“Shit… Fuck, I-I’m doing it!”

“Well done!”

Regulus smiled, then caught the tip of his boot against the next joist. He flinched sharply, but Sirius was there to steady him, just as he said he would be.

“There," he said, as they both straightened up. "Not so bad, now is it?”

Slowly, Regulus released his brother's hands and was able to stand upright, breathing deeply. “Hell," he panted, "I can’t believe you idiots do this every night.”

“That’s a bit generous,” Sirius chuckled. “We try to save the really exciting stuff for special occasions. Like funerals and blood moons.”

Regulus laughed, giddy like a kid on his first rollercoaster. Up, up, up!

“So what now, we just stand here?”

“If you’d like. I expect the waiting’s the worst part, ain't it, Moony?”

“Waiting—what waiting? Waiting for what?”

“Shh!” Remus pressed a finger to his lips; “Do you hear that?”

An unsettling feeling overcame all of them, and Remus glanced down at the metal rails beneath his feet. They were quivering slightly; somewhere down the tracks, a faint rumbling had started that was getting more noticeable with every passing second. Then, the loud blaring of a horn burst through the night, and Regulus’ question was answered.

Honestly, he should've seen it coming. What went up always came... down, down, down.

“Fuck! We gotta go!” Regulus gasped, whipping his head around. “W–We gotta get off the tracks!”

“We will,” said Sirius, “just gotta hang tight first—heh.”

“ ‘Hang tight’?!”

“Moons, how d’ya do it?”

“This way.” Remus bent down, carefully shifting himself around so he was sitting on the metal joist, his legs dangling down over the river below. Sirius matched him, and they both turned to look at Regulus. The train horn blared again, louder this time. Closer.

“Well? Hurry up, Edge!”

“Sirius, a train is coming! We stay here and we’re gonna die!”

“We're not gonna die! Not if you do as you’re told, anyway. Now just sit down on the bar like we are. Don’t worry, Lupin’s done this before.”

Once, about five years ago, Remus thought dismally. He watched as Regulus glanced between Sirius and the safety railing, as if measuring the likelihood of death as it hurtled down the tracks toward them. He must’ve decided it was too far a distance to risk on his own, and so he squatted down on the bar next to his brother and slowly got his feet beneath him.

“Sirius, if we die out here I’m gonna kill you!”

“Now that’s just cliché.”

“Just stay calm, Regulus,” Remus told him. “You gotta stay calm.”

"Oh, fuck you, Lupin!"

Another blaring horn, and Regulus looked about as far from calm as one could get. All around them the bridge shook while the now-visible headlamp of the train’s engine reflected around their backs like a glowing full-body halo. They had a minute at most, and then the iron beast would be right on top of them.

“Both of you, listen to me!” Remus called over the noise. “Now you’re going to see another rung just beneath the joist ahead of you! Lean forward and grab onto it, and then when you’re ready, slide off and hold on tight!”

“Hold on?! LUPIN, ARE YOU CRAZY?!”

“Do what he says!” Sirius bellowed. “It’s either that or jump!”

Another horn call, and this time Regulus screeched with it.

“AH! I–I CAN’T REACH IT! SIRIUS, I CAN’T REACH IT!”

“Just lean forward a bit more!”

“AH-UGHH! AH—I got it! I–I got it!”

“Good! Now let go!”

They fell like dominos, one after the other. First Remus, then Sirius, and finally Regulus, until they were all dangling over the canal by the skin of their fingers. For a moment it was easy, but then the adrenaline inevitably wore off and Remus remembered how it felt to wake up that morning, battered as though he’d been laid out by a road sweeper. This was twice as bad and every bruised muscle screamed out in protest, though none as loud as Regulus’ bellowing.

“I HATE YOU!” He screeched. “YOU’RE AN IDIOT, SIRIUS—YOU’VE MADE ME INTO AN IDIOT!”

“YEAH, EDGE! WAAH-HOOO!”

The train was upon them before Sirius had even finished his victory cry. It rattled overhead like a jet on the runway, so loud that Remus could barely hear himself think. Sirius kept screaming, as did Regulus—though his sort was distinctly less enthusiastic. It occurred then to Remus that he had no idea how long these London freight trains could go on for. He’d once heard Lily say that the passenger trains like the ones they’d rode into school on could get up to a half a mile long. How long would half a mile take to cross over a single thirty-foot bridge? Longer than they could hold on for, surely.

“Sirius! … SIRIUS!”

“Yeah?”

“I may have forgotten one tiny little detail about the first time I did this!”

“And what was that?”

“That I walked home in wet clothes!”

He could only see the back of Sirius’ head so he couldn’t be sure, but if he wasn’t crying, then the sound Sirius was making was certainly laughter.

“Right—well! That’s brilliant! My advice is to try and avoid the warm spots, ‘cause I might just piss myself!”

As the seconds ticked by, Remus began to feel his arms grow more and more tired. Ever since the charity shop he’d been more aware of his injuries, and hanging off the bottom of a bridge certainly wasn’t doing anything but aggravating them. Aside from having to bear the strain of his entire body weight, the metal bars they were clinging to were freezing and every passing train car shook the bridge to an unvarying degree. They’d set themselves up for failure—glorious, glorious failure.

“I can’t!” Regulus was moaning. “I can’t do it anymore, Sirius!”

“Hold on, little bro! Just a bit longer!”

Emboldened by Sirius’ surety, Remus tried to calm himself by counting the cars, but his brain was muddled from the pain and it was all he had just to cling on. Then, when it seemed as though he couldn’t bear a second longer, the final railcar passed overhead and just like that, the noise fell away.

“We did it!” Sirius cried. “Ha! We did it! Reggie, you did it!”

“Okay, but now what?!”

“Moons?”

“Uhh…” Remus looked around—even stupidly checked his feet; nothing but dark water. “We just have to—er… pull ourselves up!”

“We can’t do that!” Regulus yelped. “My arms are gonna rip out of their sockets!”

“Well, gentlemen, looks like there’s only one thing to do.” Sirius let go of the bar with one shaky hand, raising it to his forehead in a salute. “It’s been a pleasure hanging with you.”

“Sirius, no—!”

And just like that, Sirius Black was flying—straight down into the drink.

There was a splash but Remus barely heard it. He too, had already let go. The soles of his shoes hit the Thames with a great slap and instantly he was seized all over. Water rushed him like a zap, invading his mouth and nose as his legs flailed desperately beneath him. When his head finally broke the surface it was met with all the aches and pains of his injuries as well as a chill wind that licked up off the water. He felt as though he'd gotten flatted by the road sweeper all over again, and yet the adrenaline made up for all of it.

“Sirius?" He called, splashing through the pitch-coloured water; "… SIRIUS!?”

“I’m here, Moons!”

A shape moved toward him in the darkness—Sirius, with his black hair plastered to his cheeks and forehead in inky rivulets. He paddled forward with a grin not even chattering teeth could tarnish, and together they reached for each other.

“Where’s Regulus?” Remus demanded. In answer, Sirius pointed up toward the bridge overhead, only to gape when he realised that Regulus was gone as well. Suddenly frantic, the two of them whipped their heads around, splashing through the surface of the water as though Regulus might appear out from under them.

“Reg?! Reg, where are you?”

“Regulus!”

Somewhere not far off, a voice had begun to wail. They paddled forward to find Regulus flailing near the banks, face screwed up and chin barely out of the water as he moaned.

“No more! No more!”

“Reg! Reg, ya big ninny, open your eyes!”

“I can’t!” He moaned; “I can’t!”

“Yes, you can! You’re an utter ledge! You did it, now open your bloody eyes or your big brother’s gonna have to—!”

A sharp splash caught Sirius in the face, leaving him sputtering.

“I don’t have a brother!" Regulus wailed. "I have an insurance liability!”

It was somehow colder on the shore, a revelation Remus had while he was dragging himself over the rocks and fighting against stiff clothing and stiffer limbs. The taste of dirty bilge water lingered in his mouth and his hair dripped down into his eyes with an icy sting. Fuck—His entire body hurt. Next to him, Sirius was still laughing, lying back on the shore with his feet barely out of the water. Was mania a side effect of hypothermia, Remus wondered? Regulus certainly wasn’t fairing much better, though he was on his feet at least. On his feet and panting like a dog.

“You…! You fucking… LUNATICS! You should be medicated—both of you! We could’ve—we could’ve fucking died! OOH—It’s a wonder that… eugh… That you’ve even lasted this long! How you haven't been arrested for endangering the public, I'll never know!”

“Arrested? HA—Where do you think we spent the night yesterday, Edge?”

There was a lapse in Regulus’ shouting as he took in the information, obviously trying to deduce whether Sirius was lying or not. Before he could come to his conclusion, Sirius had rolled over and staggered up the bank.

“Here, Edgie,” he said, pulling the flask from his pocket; “Take the ‘edge’ off a bit.”

Regulus did take the flask, but rather than open it, he wrenched his arm back and flung it into the canal. Remus watched it disappear with a splash, and frowned.

“Cool… Wasn’t like that was mine or anything…”

“Oh fuck off!” Regulus slumped back down on the rocks with his head in his hands. He looked so pathetic, all sopping wet; Remus almost felt bad. “I think I've become stupider,” he moaned. “I can actually feel myself losing brain cells by the minute. Christ, mother's gonna kill me. I have to go back there soon, and when she finds out I… crap, shit—fuck!”

“Sod this.” Sirius kneeled down on the shore, wobbling as his wet shoes slid along the rocks. “You don’t have to go anywhere you don't want to. Especially not back there.”

“Easy for you to say, it’s not expected of you. You—Sirius—live in this great fucking bubble, content as long as you can play your shitty music and see your shitty friends. What responsibilities could you possibly have?”

“I could be responsible for you. Come live with me, Reg.”

Sirius might as well have dunked him in the river again, for all the look Regulus was giving him.

“What?” He blanched. “No! No, don't be ridiculous, I can’t live with you!”

“Why not? It's not like we've never lived together before.”

“I have school to finish, for one.”

“Alright, I’ll pay for it," said Sirius firmly. "Then you come and live with me. I’ll let you do whatever you want—anything. You can go to university, you can work—I don’t care! As long as it’s what you want.”

“And what if I don't want to live with you?"

"You don't?"

Regulus' snappy retort died on his tongue.

"I can’t,” he whimpered. “I can't live with you. You and me—we just don’t… And there’s still mother—”

“No,” Sirius swore. He fell forward, clasping his brother by the shoulders. “This isn’t about what she needs. It’s about what you need—what I need. I need my brother, Reg.”

“And what if I’m not your brother anymore?” Regulus demanded, throwing off his hands. “What if I never was? I’m not just some little kid anymore. I’m not just gonna follow you around forever—I mean, what if I’m not everything you want me to be?!”

“Then I won’t ask you to be anything! Just be here. And if you can tell me honestly, that you’d rather be back there, with all those people who don’t give two shits about the real you—then fine, I won’t ever ask you again. But you have to say it here, right now—to my face!”

There was a sharp silence, in which Regulus dropped his head once more. When he looked up, his eyes found Remus as he stood silently just over Sirius’ shoulder. Seeing him wet and pathetic, it was like he was fifteen again. Fifteen and stealing Sirius’ Black Sabbath tapes in hopes that it would get his big brother to look his way for even a moment longer.

“You went into the water, Reg,” Sirius pleaded. “Please don’t come out the same.”

Slowly, Regulus’ eyes shifted back. Remus didn’t know what it was he found there, in those grey eyes so alike to his own, but whatever it was, it must’ve been enough.

“I don’t want to go.”

A relief. An exhale. A sad smile—and Sirius was nodding.

“Okay.”

“I don’t want to go back.”

“Okay.”

“You’ll be disappointed eventually," Regulus whispered. "You’ll be ashamed…”

At that, Sirius shook his head.

“That’s what they never told us, Reggie… No one’s ever died from a little bit of shame.”

With a miserable sob, Regulus buried his face in his knees. He shook for a little while longer, but once Sirius had moved up the bank to hold his shoulders, Regulus slowly lifted his head.

He wiped a hand beneath his nose.

"... I’d like to go home."

It was enough for Sirius, who took his brother’s arm and pulled it across his shoulders to help carry him across the stones. As the brothers started their wobbly ascent up the bank, Remus came in close and took up Regulus’ other arm. They were almost to the stairs that lead back up to the street when Regulus spoke again;

“Sirius?"

"Yeah, Reg?"

“Please, no more bridges…”

“You're really tying my hands there, Edge, but alright. No more bridges.”

“Lupin? Black? I’m home! … You’re here, right? The two of you didn’t murder each other, did you?”

Peter rounded the corner into the living room with his bags, and found Remus standing in just his pants and vest, an extra-large mug of coffee in one hand.

“Hey, Moony. How was the holiday—”

“Shh,” Remus whispered, finger to his lips. “Still sleeping.”

He pointed to the sofa, where a head of black hair could just be seen peeking out from beneath a blanket.

“Blimey, what’s he doing? It’s past noon.”

Remus shrugged, and Peter began pushing up his sleeves.

“Oh! Step back then, Moony. I got this.”

It was hard not to laugh while watching Peter creep steadily up to the top of the couch. He started by leaning over the sleeping bundle, fingers splayed and at the ready.

“C’mon, Black. Time to rise and sh—”

Regulus turned over with a haggard scowl, and the next thing Remus knew, Peter had fallen backward over the coffee table.



Chapter End Notes

'Rushing' in music is when you play the tempo of a piece faster than it is written.

The 'Lavender List' was a satirical name for Prime Minister Harold Wilson's controversial 1976 Resignation Honours; PM's could bestow titles and honours upon people of their choosing when leaving office, and this list caused controversy as many of Wilson's chosen recipients held political views that went against his own Labour Party (think right-leaners and capitalist bastards).

'Pakoras' are a deep-fried vegetable dish originating from India and often sold by street vendors and restaurants in the UK. Sooo delicious.
