End of March 1979



In a timeframe that would’ve made any sane bride dizzy, and with the fervent help of Mrs. Pettigrew and a slew of other hired hands, Lottie had gotten the grand wedding she’d wanted. They’d picked a Wednesday—the first Wednesday of April—and though it felt like an odd day for a wedding, all of the Pettigrews’ closest friends and family would be in attendance. Remus was informed later that it was the only day they could book the venue on such short notice. Naturally, he felt that the entire thing felt more than a bit rushed, but since only Peter seemed to share the sentiment, he kept the thought to himself.

The girls were very busy those days; Lily appeared to have run herself entirely ragged between all the dress fittings, hen parties, studying, and classes. Sirius of course teased her over it, loudly anticipating the day it’d be her walking down the aisle in a lovely white gown of her own, but Lily was abstinent. She was far too busy to even consider such things. If she and James did get married, it would not be for a long, long time.

And so, as his friends went about settling back into their usual routines, Remus steeled himself to do the same, only now the Marauders had their eyes on a bigger prize.

It’d started with their triumphant return to the stage. Ray had called—the Shoestring needed its favourite act back, and they were hardly in a position to deny him. Coupling as a slightly-belated birthday celebration for James, the five of them plus Regulus all piled back into the Minnie van with their instruments and made the short trip across the city. Despite the excitement, the atmosphere inside the old Volkswagen had turned anxious before they'd even made it to the opposite bank of the Thames. After all, it’d taken less time for bigger bands to be forgotten by those who'd once cheered their name, and they were still newcomers on the scene.

"They probably won't even care," Peter anguished, making Remus recall their earliest days at the Shoe, where they'd played to audiences of as little as four people merely there to drown themselves in their pints. But then, if there was anything a small, local pub was known for, it was the loyalty of its patrons.

Upon their arrival, Ray met them at the back doors and they were welcomed back by the kitchen crew with open arms. Ray offered them drinks to celebrate—just the cheap stuff—and when they emerged into the rest of the bar with their gear, plenty of people craned their heads to get a look. Some friendly faces tapped their pint glasses approvingly, others cheered—finally a good show!

Just like that, Remus knew they were home.

“This is really where you play?” Regulus asked warily, peering around the spit-n-sawdust pub as though a disease might leap off of the nearest bar stool and bite him.

“Expecting a concert hall, were you?” Sirius leered, stopping to dramatically breathe in the smell of cigarette smoke and spilt hops. Regulus didn’t reply; it was clear by his scrutinising expression that the Shoestring was not what he'd been expecting. After nearly a week in London, he’d given up on the stiff black slacks he’d brought from home and had instead taken to borrowing whatever pieces from Sirius’ wardrobe that offended his eyes the least. Now, with a pair of plain jeans and his usually neat hair hung loose around his face and ears, he was starting to look like any other seventeen year-old kid.

They found their usual table near the stage empty and waiting for them, with their name and the word ‘reserved’ written clumsily across a paper napkin. One of the r’s was backwards, turning it into ‘RESEЯVED’. When Sirius saw it, he scooped up the napkin and offered it to Remus.

“Could make a half-decent song.”

“For a great big industry plant like us?” Remus smirked. “Maybe.”

By the time the Marlene, Dorcas, and Mary had shuffled in to join them, it was peak hour and the bar was slammed. Drinks had been pouring for hours, and would continue to pour until Ray gave last call, which usually waned later, considering it was a Saturday. After organising their gear and doing a quick sound check, Remus stepped off the stage with the others and found Mary practically throwing herself over Regulus out of excitement.

“Oh, I missed this handsome face!” She simpered, clamping both hands across Regulus’ cheeks and mashing them together like playdough. “You came to see me, didn’t you? Oh, just say it. I’ll forgive you for forgetting to call—you cheeky thing!”

As Regulus almost toppled off of his chair, begging for sense and personal space to reassert itself, Sirius leaned over and shoved his hands between them.

“I’m sensing some blatant favouritism,” he pouted—before Mary took a threatening swipe at his cheek that left Sirius to leap away or else risk ruining his pretty face.

“Oh, shut it you. I can look at your smug gob whenever, but this one—oh. You really know how to keep a girl wanting for more, don’t you, Regulus?”

Remus had never seen someone go so red without passing out first, but luckily for Regulus, the girls’ drinks had arrived and Mary was suitably distracted. As she offered him little sips from her cocktail, Dorcas shuffled over to Remus with a fresh pint.

“Right, so do you want the good news or the bad news?”

"There's bad news? Blimey, start with that then, I suppose,” Remus replied, already feeling dour over the unfortunate smirk she was giving him. He didn’t know what it was he should be expecting when she leaned in to whisper in his ear, but it certainly wasn’t—

“Sacked?” Remus gaped at her. “What do you mean I’ve been sacked?!”

“Sorry babs, but Phil asked me to pass word along. Apparently he didn’t take too kindly to us switching shifts. Call it a wounded ego if you must, but he’s already hired one of his mates to replace you. Some bell-end named Geordie.”

“That prick,” Remus growled. “He’s never cared when we’ve switched shifts before. Five quid says he was probably just looking for a reason to get rid of me… buggar… I knew he never liked me! Ain’t my fault he can barely string a guitar.”

Dorcas leaned in, pinching his mouth and jaw together with two fingers. “He never liked you because you’re tall and good looking. It was starting to piss him off—seeing as half the customers came in just to ogle you."

"They did not."

"Ha. Right. Well, if you ask me, there are worse things to lose a crappy job over.”

“You gon' tell me the good news now?”

She smiled, releasing his face and tapping him fondly on the cheek. “I’ll do you one better. Come by the shop on Monday during Phil's lunch break and I’ll show ya.”

Remus drank the pint she’d offered—bitterly—and by the time the glass was empty, couldn’t give half a shite anyway. Since the incident with Fletcher, he’d managed to squirrel a small bit of money away, though it was nothing to live off of. He’d meant to put it toward a second amp to boost their sound, or maybe a decent wah-pedal for James to use on stage so they could finally get their riffs to start sounding like the way they did in Remus’ head. For now it’d have to be collateral, but at least as long as he was unemployed he’d have more time to focus on the music. He could tell Sirius and the others later.

Just before they were scheduled to take the stage for their first set that night, Lottie arrived wearing a beautiful satin skirt and a blouse with a Chelsea collar. She appeared a bit overdressed when compared to the pub's other patrons, but didn’t seem to notice as she weaved through the inebriated throng. With T-minus three days until the wedding, she’d nearly backed out of coming, but had made the effort to clear her schedule when Lily had informed her of Regulus’ sudden arrival.

“No, you must come to the wedding,” she gushed, going as far as to take both his hands in hers for dramatic effect. “It’ll be such a party, I swear you’ll have fun! You are Sirius’ brother, after all, and that makes you family. Oh, please say you’ll come!”

Regulus didn’t stand a chance. He'd caved almost immediately, and even Remus had felt some semblance of pity for him. Lottie was hard to say no to on a good day, but ever since getting engaged she’d become even more sure of herself. More… nubile, almost. She often went out with Roger’s mother—first as a guest, and then slowly as a member of all the high society circles she’d been dreaming of since she was a little girl. Combined with that and the new demure style of dress, it’d quickly become obvious; Lottie wasn’t just preparing for a wedding, she was in training to become a wife.

“You sure you don’t want Marauders to play on your big day, Lot?” Sirius asked, as he leapt up onto the edge of the stage in preparation for their incoming set.

“Yeah!” James called, already above them and swinging his amp cable around. “We could totally do it. I’d even acquiesce to some Elvis. Presley or Costello—take your pick.”

“Sorry, boys,” Lottie hummed; “Maybe if the four of you hadn’t been so busy tearing pieces off of each other, Roger and I would’ve considered it, but I’m afraid the act’s already been booked.”

“It’s not that Rod Stewart impersonator you were talking about, is it?” Peter grimaced, appearing behind her from the direction of the loo.

“He’s not a—Petey, your fly is down—he’s not a Rod Stewart impersonator! He just happens to look a bit like him.”

"And sound like him," Peter scoffed. “If you ask me, I say that if it acts like a duck, dresses like a duck, and quacks like a bloody duck… Well, then it’s probably a Rod Stewart impersonator.”

“Good thing no one’s asking you!”

Peter shrugged indifferently, setting his drumsticks between his teeth long enough to do up his zipper and clamber up on stage. Finishing his second pint, Remus stood up to join them. Already the crowd was pushing in, growing louder; he could taste their excitement and he wanted more.

As he followed his friends up onto the stage, Remus overheard Regulus shouting to Mary over the crowd’s noise;

“Where’s that Evans’ friend of yours? Figured she would be here for Potter’s birthday.”

“Lily had a late meeting with one of her lecture groups today!” Mary hollered back. “They finish their term in April so she’s been really busy. She’ll be by later though… She said she’s bringing a surprise!”

Regulus nodded, then looked upwards at Remus. He hadn’t realised he’d stopped with one foot on the stage.

“What are you staring at, Lupin?”

"Nothing. Just didn't realise you'd missed Lily so much."

"What's this about Lily?" James asked, appearing between them.

"Regulus was just worried she was going to miss your birthday party, Prongs."

"Shut up, Lupin!" Regulus snapped. "When are you two going to start this ridiculous show of yours?"

Suddenly the pub's overhead lights began to dim.

"Right about now, I suppose," James grinned. "Try not to cheer too loudly for us, Regulus. Get's distracting."

It might've been the lighting, but Remus thought that Regulus' face had somehow turned even redder. Could Regulus have a thing for Lily, he wondered? No, certainly not. If he did then it couldn't have been anything more than a school yard crush. What was it they said—distance makes the heart grow fonder?

"Come sit over here, Regulus!" Mary called.

Watching him stalk away, Remus tried to recall an instance where he’d witnessed Regulus and Lily interacting with one another, but nothing came to mind. Surely he was just reading too much into things.

As the lights continued to dim, Remus looped his guitar strap over his head and felt the familiar weight of his bass settle over his right shoulder. The crowd whooped—anticipation for what was to come—and Sirius began looping the microphone cord around his wrist. What came next was James and Peter—launching themselves into a boisterous cover of a Thin Lizzy song just to get the audience hooked while Sirius played his role as frontman perfectly, rousing the audience from whatever daze had accompanied them along their everyday lives. He already looked the part, wearing a red military jacket he’d picked up at a costume store and a pair of white trousers that felt distinctly Freddie Mercury-esque. Sirius was looking more and more like a queen every day now; not that anyone would’ve gotten away with insulting him for it.

After they’d wrapped up the cover song, Sirius swung his mike around and caught it mid-air. He was panting, but Remus knew it was from excitement.

“Shoestring," he bellowed; "have you missed us?!”

Cheers went up, an answer;

Yes!

“Now I know you can do better than that—SOUTH BANK, HAVE YOU MISSED US?!”

YES! YES! YES!

“Now that’s more like it! How’s everyone doing out there? You alright? You staying cheeky, hm…?”

Some replied—YES!—and a few more made fun of the posh way he pronounced every syllable. It was a common enough reaction, one that Sirius accepted wholeheartedly. He played with them, loved on them, and they adored him right back.

“We missed you too,” he told them.

“Took a little break, is all.”

“But we’re back.”

“—Better than ever.”

“In fact we have a new song for you.”

“Would you like to hear it?”

Yes!

The room began to clamour.

“You would?”

Yes!

"I'm not so sure."

YES! YES!—More!

“Well then... Let’s have some fun, shall we!?”

It started with a clap. Then a stamp. Then a thundering that reached all the way inside of Remus’ rib cage.

They’d never played the song in front of the audience, it was too new. You wouldn’t have found it on those butchered tapes from Fletcher. Here, they were delving into new territory—if anything it was a chant. One to clap along to, one to stomp your feet.

One that could fill an entire stadium.

Fuck Fletcher.

And that was the end. The entire pub cheered for Peter as he shattered his cymbals, and for James as he slid up and down his strings with a final flourish. A girl reached for Sirius and he bent down to kiss her hand. Her friend did the same, begging for another, then another. Remus had never enjoyed the feeling of sweat on his back so immensely.

After their first set, they stumbled off the stage feeling haggard and vibrant. They wanted to go again—they would go again—but first, alcohol.

Their drinks were paid for—by who, Remus didn’t know. Marlene made him scarf down some food so he wouldn’t throw up, but then one of the kitchen lads had some dexies. Remus took two, which was probably two too many, but he’d missed the feeling. It was like drinking thirty cups of coffee all at once. It made the sad things less sad, and the happy things euphoric. They were due for their second set to start any minute when Remus found himself drifting back across the pub. The booze had turned him sentimental, while the uppers made him dauntless. There was only one callbox at the Shoe, and he had to wait his turn before he could use it. Stupid; there weren’t enough drugs in the world to make him forget that number.

I’m sorry—he could start with that. And also; I’m an idiot. I don’t even know why I said it. You’re totally right. I’m a stupid fucking prick. I miss you. Skylar didn't deserve it. Forgive me?

The telephone line fell silent, unanswered. Unreplied.

Tomny didn’t have a messaging machine.

As it turned out, Sirius had been trying to inform him that Lily had arrived. She came into the pub with her full bag of school things, though it was the girl trailing closely behind her that had them instantly all curious.

“Didn’t miss too much, I hope?” Lily said, brushing her wind-ragged hair from her face as James helped her out of her jacket. When she was suitably presentable, Lily stood back to introduce her new friend.

“Everyone, this is Sybill. She’s part of my surprise.”

Sybill was a flighty thing, that much Remus could tell. She had hair the colour of wheat that sprung up from behind a beaded headband like she’d stuck a fork in an electrical socket when she was very young, and she wore glasses so large that her eyes seemed to bulge out like a cartoon character. Standing next to Lily, she kept a colourful folder clutched tightly to her chest as though it might shield her from whatever fallout might come. Not that she needed it; the girl wore so many crystals and talismans around her neck, it was a wonder she hadn’t fallen over from the weight of them.

“Sybill and I met in our media law class,” Lily went on. “She’s studying journalism. And in her free time she—”

“I also make zines!” Sybill burst out, thrusting the paper folder toward Sirius while simultaneously falling into a near ninety-degree bow. Sirius glanced at the folder dubiously before taking it and flipping it open.

“What’s a ‘zine’?” Lottie queried, getting up on a chair so she might take a glimpse over Sirius’ shoulder herself.

“A zine is a small, curated publication of just about anything,” Sybill recited, still bent over at the waist. “But I—” She raised her head, only her head; “make zines to expose hypocrisy and supply my audience with all the tools required for revolution and anarchy.”

"And music, on occasion," Lily added cautiously.

Weirded out, and perhaps standing a bit too close to the strange girl for comfort, Remus wandered over Sirius and squeezed in with the rest of his friends. Inside the folder, Sybill had stuffed several tiny pamphlets ranging in size and severity. Most were printed in black and white, with their letters hand drawn or else cut from other magazines like some murderous ransom note. The titles were absurd—Windsor Poo, Erectile Conjunction, Slasher Chick—but they were nothing compared to the content.

“People actually pay for these?” Regulus muttered, as Sirius flipped open to a page that seemed to feature John Lennon’s head pasted onto the body of the Virtruvian Man, the words ‘We Can Wank It Out’ scribbled across his chest.

“They only ever make enough to go toward the next issue,” Sybill tittered honestly, finally straightening up. “Most of those are collaborations with local artists, but with your permission, I’d like to feature your band in this month’s issue.”

“Us?” James echoed in disbelief.

“Yes. You see, I’ve actually seen you play before. I was going to do a feature on you anyway—purely for research purposes—but then Lily told me she knew you personally."

"It was quite serendipitous," Lily nodded.

"You’re not exactly the normal sort we’d feature," Sybill went on. "To be honest I'm not sure how well our audience will take to you, but I like keeping things fresh. And you four are particularly bombastic.”

She seemed to say this with pure wonder in her eyes, or maybe it was just the unintentional bug-eyed effect of her glasses. Either way, Sirius passed back her folder and Lily swooped in;

“We have one more surprise actually,” she said, shooting a keen glance in the eccentric girl’s direction. “Sybill, here, is actually the vice president of the events committee at UCL, and if you’re interested, she’s said that she can probably get you guys into the rotation. See about letting you play on campus.”

“You mean you want us to play a concert at the university?” Peter gaped.

“Lots of up ‘n coming bands do it,” Sybill said, blinking off in the direction over Peter’s head as though she’d suddenly found the wall more interesting. “We hosted the Human League last month. Before them it was the Spandau Ballet, then Dick Damage and the Dilemma… Next week Duran Duran is showing.”

Sirius made a face, before mumbling under his breath; “What the fuck kinda name is ‘Duran Duran’?”

"Sounds like an aftershave," James agreed.

“They say, having breezed right past ‘Dick Damage’,” scoffed Dorcas, making Marlene snigger into her palm.

“Well?” Lily urged. “I know it’s not the Marquee or anything, but it could be a stepping stone. Haven’t you guys been saying you wanted to play more shows anyway?”

Lily was right. Sybill might’ve been a bit odd, but she had connections, and aside from general know-how, connections were the only things the Marauders were in dire need of.

“Best birthday gift—EVER!” James announced, after he’d swooped in to lift Lily straight out of her shoes. “God, I love you.”

The comment made the hairs on the back of Remus’ neck stand on end, but when he turned toward Regulus, he found him hesitantly flipping through Sybill’s zines, while the bushy-haired girl sat next to him and pointed out the political context for every eerie collage and cartoon. He would’ve expected anyone who had a crush on Lily to be more perturbed seeing her so in love, but Regulus didn’t seem to care much at all.

Almost disappointed, Remus felt his shoulders deflate before one of them was being poked by Sirius.

“Hey, who was that you were talking to on the phone?”

Remus nearly started. The almost-phone call already felt like a lifetime ago.

“Uh… no one. Couldn’t get through.”

Sirius nodded, though it was obvious he didn’t believe him. “You ready to get back on stage then?”

“Yeah. Yeah, go on.”

The second set went might like the last, albeit slightly sloppier and more sloshed ‘round the edges. Not that their audience seemed to care; they too were pissed off their asses, all save for Lily who’d volunteered to drive the van back to Shepherd’s Bush.

“You know us, we know you,” Sirius had recanted into the microphone; “but for those who’ve just arrived, I’ll do one final introduction.”

Pete began with a drumroll, to which everyone cheered. The crowd was familiar to them now, and no longer shy. They pleaded for noise and fever. No—they demanded it.

“On drums, we have the Marauders’ effervescent everyman, Peter Pettigrew!”

Whoo, Peter! Yeah, Peter!

“On guitar, you’ll find the illustrious James Potter, poster child for Huggies nappies and boy scouts everywhere.”

Ow-ow! Hey, Potter! Nice arse, Potter!

“The unassuming brooding giant with the bass guitar is our dearly beloved Remus Lupin, lover of sappy songs, boring books, and married women everywhere. Better lock up your mums, everybody, this one’s dangerous.”

Remus! You can have me, Remus!

"And finally, your main course for the evening, my name is Sirius Black, and we are—Marauders.”

The night finished without a hitch, their first in many months. The audience screamed and chanted and knew their names and for a while Remus couldn’t decide whether it was real or just some lucid dream he was having. Such an obvious success with the promise of more had him finally reassured, but when the show was over and the lights had turned on, Remus finished his final pint and went home to his bed in busy little Shepherd’s Bush. The next morning when he remembered the dexies and the zine and the almost-phone call, he was left feeling sick.

For once, he was glad Tomny had not picked up.





* * *





Monday 2nd April 1979





Remus wouldn’t realise it until later, but being sacked from his job at the music shop along Tin Pan Alley would come to be one of the most insignificant moments in his entire musical career. When Dorcas told him of his sudden loss of employment Remus’ first inclination had been anger. The drink he’d sunk at the Shoestring had led him next to acceptance, but as he rode the tube over to Tottenham Court Road, his acceptance quickly turned into trepidation. He didn’t want to have to rely on Sirius or his friends for money, and with all the strikes still going on in everything from private unions to public sectors, job prospects within the city were bordering on slim to none. He’d be lucky if he could find work in some meat processing and packing plant. What a swell gig that ought to be, coming home smelling like the inside of a cow's intestines every day. God—Sirius would never kiss him again.

“Look, Remus, ya know I like you. But I can’t just let employees do as they please all the time. I’m your boss! I need to be respected. And I needed you here last week to help with those new shipments, but where were you? Nowhere to be found apparently.”

“Come on, Phil,” Remus urged, following his old manager further into the shop. “I got Dorcas to cover all my shifts, and you and I both know that she’s loads more useful than I am. If it’s the repairs that’s the problem, then Bo can easily handle—”

Phil swung around; “Bo called in three times last week on account ‘a his back! As far as I’m concerned he's on bloody probation. I’ve got orders piled out the back door, and customers breathing down my neck twenty-four-seven! And don’t even get me started on the bloody manufacturers… Those bastards are only late on shipments until we’re behind! Now I’m sorry, Lupin, but I’ve made up my mind and them’s the breaks. I mean, hell—I’ve already found your replacement.”

Phil gestured languidly toward the store’s guitar wall, where a peaky-looking guy in a Che Guevara t-shirt was sitting on a stool and polishing one of the sunburst Ibanezes. He waved when Remus turned around, and the guitar nearly took a header into the wood panel floor. Phil made a yelping sort of noise when it happened, but the guy only sat back on the door and gave each of them a half-witted smile.

Remus turned back around. “You’ve got to be joking.”

“Er… Geordie’s still in training.”

“Oh come on, Phil! You’re shitting me! That guy looks like he’s got an order against him saying he can’t be within a hundred feet of any school or public park. I mean does he even know anything about music? Does he know how to restring a bloody guitar?”

Phil did not look amused. He puckered sourly, then crossed both arms and Remus knew he was finished.

“You can pick up your final cheque from Grace Jones on your way out,” he huffed, already turning away. “Oh, and tell your little friend there, our policy is you break it, you buy it.”

A few feet away, Regulus turned away from the six-piece Ludwig drum kit he’d been admiring and flipped Phil the finger. Phil looked astonished, but when he turned on Remus expecting some reprimand, Remus only shrugged.

“Them’s the breaks, Phil.”

There was not much left to be said after that. Once Phil had returned to his office, old Bo came out from behind the repair counter to shake Remus’ hand and offer his condolences.

“We’re gonna miss you ‘round here, kid.”

“Me too.” Remus glanced bitterly toward the office; “Most of it, anyway…”

“Want my advice? Forget Phil, he’s a right little cunt. Always has had it in for the handsomer lads.”

Remus smiled, bashfully; "Dorcas told you to say that," and Bo pulled him in for a friendly clap on the back.

“Make sure you come back and visit,” he told him. “Maybe I’ll do some custom work for you when you’re big and famous. Blow those mass-market hacks outta the water.”

“I’d like that, Bo.”

When he meandered back to the front of the store, he found Dorcas waiting for him by the cash register.

“I see you brought the spare along,” she mused, gesturing to Regulus, who was drifting back and forth between the stacks of amps.

“Yeah. Promised Sirius I would babysit seeing as I’m out of a job and all. But don’t tell Regulus that.”

Dorcas smirked and slid the drawer to the cash register shut. She had a lolly in one hand, which she fit back into her mouth as she turned to him.

“Right, so let me get this straight then. Your boy’s little brother shows up on your doorstep after the two of you had just gotten out of the clink, but he’s supposed to be six-hundred miles away, going to some whoop-dee-doo school in the middle of Scotland—‘cept their dad popped his clogs, so really he was on his way to the funeral and just couldn’t bring himself to go any further. Which wouldn’t be so worrying, save for the fact that he and Sirius get along about as well as two squirrely cats in a rubbish bin. So now he’s freeloading for who knows how long, ‘til he either decides whether he’s going back to the posh school where his she-devil of a mum can get her claws in him, or stays here and lives on your couch. That about right?”

“Don’t forget about Lottie’s wedding. She already made him promise to go. And to be a flower girl. Though, I might’ve dreamt that bit.”

“Oh, Lupin. Someone should write a book about you. They’d make a mint.”

"Nah, no way anyone would ever pay to hear about me."

Dorcas smiled, leaning her elbows on the counter. "How's the kid doing then? Looks miserable."

"Regulus? He's always miserable. But his school's gonna be going on Easter break soon. Reckon he'll decide what he's gonna do after that."

"Have you invited him to join the band yet?"

"Twice. But he doesn't seem to fancy Sirius' offer of letting him play the harmonica."

“Could you two idiots please stop talking about me as though I’m not standing right here?” Regulus snapped, glaring at them from behind an aisle of music books. “It’s bad enough Lupin’s been dragging me around town all day. When are we going home?”

“Oh, it’s ‘home’ now, is it?” Remus smirked, glancing back at him. The look Regulus gave him was venomous, but before he could lash out again, Remus began rifling around in his pocket for some loose change.

“Here, Edge, why don’t you pop over to the shop on the corner and buy yourself something sweet. I’ll meet you there when I’m finished.”

Regulus snatched the money, then flipped Remus off for good measure and promptly turned for the door. They waited for the tell-tale chime to come before laughing, and by then Dorcas was slipping her lolly back behind grinning teeth.

“Mouthy little thing, inn’he? Can’t get over how much he and Black look alike though.”

“I keep doing double-takes myself,” Remus agreed, as Dorcas slid his final pay stub across the counter for him to sign.

“It’s gonna be such shit without you,” she said, grumbling around the sweet. “Pretty sure Geordie’s got about as many brain cells as a ceramic garden gnome. Did you know that yesterday I asked him to receive one of the incoming shipments while I handled this customer? Well, when I came back he was organising the fuzz boxes by the number of knobs.”

“At least you know he can count.”

Dorcas sighed, haggardly, then pressed her tongue to the side of her cheek in a poor attempt to hide a smile. “Yes, well, considering I’m the only one around here who knows how to handle the bloody shipments, I don’t feel so bad giving you this.”

Remus cocked his head in question as Dorcas peeked back toward the office—assumedly to check if Phil was spying—and then disappeared below the shop counter. What she came back with was a large box, big enough to make a heavy thump when she set it down in front of him.

“What’s this?”

“It’s the good news from the other night,” she smirked. “Consider it a belated birthday gift. For you and Potter.”

Already intrigued, Remus began inspecting the box keenly. It was black, with what looked like a picture of a very large calculator on its front. Then he spotted the metres, along with the dials and multi-tracks.

“Is this… Is this what I think it is, Dee?”

“It’s better,” she told him, before swinging the box around so he could read the label. “What you’re looking at is the best in brand-new, top of the line technology. They call it the ‘Portastudio’. This American company just put them out on the market for professional use—you can’t even buy these in the shops yet! They let anyone record up to four different tracks right at home and cut and mix your own tapes directly onto any cassette. All you need is a pair of headphones! Look, I found it here.”

With an eager thrust, Dorcas handed him a copy of a print catalogue, already flipped open to an advert displaying the same machine. Introducing the first at home 15” by 18” recording studio, it read; The TASCAM Model 144 Portastudio is built for the musician on the go! Add special effects or fix a flat note from anywhere in the world, all with the ease of smooth, multi-track recording.

Remus was speechless.

“How did you get your hands on this?” He demanded, flipping the page to find layers and layers of different control specs.

“I do all the ordering, duh. All I had to do was put the shop’s name on some list and the company sent one right over. It’s supposed to be a display model—you know, so we can sell them—but Phil doesn’t even know it’s here so I figured he wouldn’t mind if I leant it out to you first.”

“This is amazing… Do you know how to work it?”

“Ha, no,” she snorted. “You’re on your own with that one, babs, but there’s a manual. I’m sure if you put those four public school brains together you’ll figure it out eventually. Five—if you count your new stray.”

Remus beamed down at the Portastudio. “This... Shit, this is amazing! Thanks, Cas. You don’t know what this means.”

He reached across the counter to hug her—something Remus Lupin would never have done in any regular circumstances—and Dorcas accepted, albeit awkwardly.

“Go on then,” Dorcas said after, ushering him out; “before Phil comes back from his third lunch break and we’re both out of a job.”

"I'll be seeing you at the wedding then?" Remus called.

"Wouldn't miss it."

It was raining when Remus walked out of the shop, arms clasped tightly around the Portastudio's awkwardly-large box. Having unfortunately adapted Sirius’ poor habit of never bringing an umbrella with him anywhere, he cut quickly down the street and slipped into the nearby corner shop before the rain had had time to seep into his hair. The shop attendant gave him a funny look when he walked in with his armful, but said nothing as Remus shuffled toward the magazine racks, where he found Regulus passively flipping through a copy of the New Musical Express. Regulus didn't bother giving any indication whether he noticed him, rather he turned the page in his magazine;

“Evans’ weirdo friend writes better music reviews than this shite. ‘The revolution will be dyed in peroxide’? What a load of bollocks.” Huffing, Regulus set the magazine back on the rack and then did a double-take at the Portastudio. “What’s that?”

“Our golden ticket,” Remus grinned.

Regulus rolled his eyes. “Whatever. Are you finally ready to leave? Traipsing across the city in the rain wasn't on my to-do list.”

“Yeah, just gimme a sec. Wanted to pick up some more fags before we go. Sirius finished off my pack last night. You want any?”

Regulus just looked at him.

"Right."

Adjusting his grip on the Portastudio, Remus turned and approached the shop’s front counter. “Packet of Embassy Number One’s,” he grunted, setting the large device down on the counter.

The guy fetched the cigarettes, punching in the numbers on his register. “Nice typewriter,” he said, eyeing the large box as he doled out Remus’ change. After pocketing the coins and fags, Remus took the heavy device in his arms again and spun around, only to narrowly avoid running into a man who’d come upon him from behind. He was dressed in an expensive-looking overcoat, with a thick moustache and goatee. He barely glanced Remus' way as he mumbled a quick pardon as slipped past. It might’ve been the end of the interaction, had Remus’ jacket sleeve not caught on one of the pick ‘n’ mix displays, successfully knocking a large bucket of fruit jellies to the floor. The sweets promptly scattered in every direction, and he heard the attendant behind the counter give a moan.

“Sorry! Sorry, my bad…”

"You're gonna have to pay for that."

"Uh—right..." Remus looked for a place to set down the Portastudio.

“I’ll pay for the kid’s gaffe,” the other man said impatiently, before pulling a twenty-pound note from his wallet and slapping it down on the counter. “Just give me a double pack of JP Special, I’m in a rush.”

Torn between apologising and thanking the man profusely, Remus began backing up toward the door, his face red with embarrassment. He might’ve fled the shop entirely had Regulus not grabbed his arm and pulled him down the front aisle toward the magazines.

“What are you doing?” Remus hissed, stumbling after him and almost taking out a second display.

“Saving your stupid career, idiot!” Regulus shoved his earlier copy of NME in his face. "Look!"

Remus nudged the magazine aside with his chin, struggling to keep a hold of the Portastudio. “Jesus christ, Reg—What’re you on about?”

“You told me before that this used to be a famous street, right? So that stands to reason that famous people would sometimes come here, yes?”

"I... I guess!"

“And do you know who Gaz Spectre is?”

Remus scoffed; “ ‘Course I know who Gaz Spectre is. He was the guy who discovered Jeff Beck. That was until the Yardbirds came along and—”

Suddenly Regulus was smothering him with a hand. “That was a rhetorical question, you fucking dolt,” he hissed, flapping the magazine in his face once more. “Here. Shut up and read the first few lines.”

Remus obeyed—albeit reluctantly—and Regulus dropped the open magazine down over the top of the Portastudio’s box. It was just a small article really, tucked in between the likes of ‘The Secret Life of Captain Sensible’ and ‘The Sins of Siouxsie Sioux’.

But there it was;





Indomitable producer, Gaz Spectre of Spectre Records, retains his title as ‘producer with the world-wide reach’ after the company’s latest signing of new Australian rock band Rosencraft. The band’s first single, “Poor Excuses” has been steadily rising in chart popularity since its February release, while their debut album is set to hit shelves and stations in early September. This addition of the ‘New Boys Down Under’ comes as a follow up to the label’s already impressive lineup, which includes various modern power-houses such as the Swedish punk group Ultraculture, as well as London-based groups The Weird Sisters and De Facto Regime. When asked for comment, Spectre only had this to say: “I don’t sign bands, I sign phenomena.”





“So he sounds like a nob," Remus drawled; "so what?”

“So what?” Regulus hissed. “That nob just paid for every little sweet you knocked on the floor, shithead!”

It took several seconds for the words to register, and by then Remus had already glanced back down at the magazine article. What he found was a photograph of Spectre, hands folded neatly as he glared at the camera lens from behind a huge studio desk. He wore aviator sunglasses like Elvis and there were at least half a dozen gold records hanging on the wall behind him. When he squinted, Remus could just make out a package of John Player Superking cigarettes lying open next to the ashtray.

Holy shit…

A sharp door chime drew Remus from his stupor. It was like getting hit over the head with one of those gold-plated records.

Gaz Spectre! Triple-gold standard record producer Gaz Spectre was strolling down the corner shop aisle!

Holy shit!

Unaware of the shock and turmoil that had overcome them, Spectre glanced at Remus and Regulus rather indifferently, popping a raspberry fruit jelly into his mouth as he passed. There was another chime, and the shop’s door inevitably fell shut behind him. Gone.

“Hey…” Called the attendant. “You have to pay for that magazine, you know…”

Suddenly Remus couldn’t breathe.

“What are you doing?” Regulus seethed, practically shoving him. “Aren’t you gonna go after him?”

“A–And say what?”

“How about, ‘hello, my name is Remus-shitface-Lupin and I have a shitty band you might want to sign to your shitty fucking music label that’ll make both of us a bunch of shitty fucking money’?!”

“Is this really your idea of a pep-talk? Because you suck, mate!”

Groaning at Remus’ obvious incompetence, Regulus turned and grappled onto the edge of the shop’s window display. What came next was a Spectre play-by-play;

“He’s lighting a cigarette… Now he’s walking down the street… He’s—He’s getting into a car! Lupin, it’s now or fucking never!”

Shit. Shit. Shit—fucking—shit!

The attendant had come around from the counter. “Hey, you have to pay for that—OI!”

But there was no stopping him. Before he could realise what it was he was doing, Remus had half-tossed the Portastudio at Regulus and swept out of the corner shop. It didn’t occur to him that he was still holding the magazine until he was outside and being lashed about by the heavy rain. What started as that morning’s simple April shower had quickly turned into a torrential rainfall, soaking Remus down to his skinnies. Up ahead, he could see Spectre stopped next to a lavish black sedan. He had a driver next to him who was holding up an umbrella as the producer lingered on, smoking his cigarette. Remus was still twenty paces away by the time he flicked the ash and butt into a nearby puddle. Then the driver reached for the door, and Remus felt his chance begin to slip away.

“Uhm, pardon me, sir? … M–Mr. Spectre, sir?”

The man in the black coat didn’t turn around, and in his nervousness, Remus nearly gave up. What if Regulus was wrong and he was just chasing after some random guy?

No—he pushed the thought aside and called out a second time, and when that did nothing, Remus took another step forward and forced himself to swallow his fear. Better to be wrong than to miss out on the chance of a lifetime.

Marching up to the side of the sedan, he planted his two feet and raised the magazine up over his head to block the rain.

“Excuse me," he called in a wobbly voice; "but are you Gareth Spectre? As in ‘Gaz Spectre’ of–of Spectre Records?”

"Maybe. Who's asking?"

"You don't know me, but my name is Remus Lupin and I've been following your work for a while now. M-My friend saw you back in the shop? I knocked over the sweet display..."

A pathetic beat passed, then;

“Sorry, kid, but like I said earlier, I’m in a rush.”

It was a dismissal, and yet still a shred of hope had bloomed in the centre of Remus’ chest.

“But you are Gaz Spectre!” He gasped, as the chauffeur opened the door and the man readied himself to climb inside. “You’re the producer who signed—”

Suddenly the chauffeur rose up, looming toward Remus with shoulders like a bull’s. “Don’t touch the car!” He roared, nearly sending Remus spiralling as he pushed him back toward the pavement.

“John!” Spectre yelled; “What’d I tell you about shoving ‘em? Do I look like I need another lawsuit?”

“Sorry, boss…”

“I have a band!”

If it were any other moment Remus might’ve keeled over from the embarrassment of it, but as it was, he was desperate. His cry made both of the men give pause for only a second, but that second was all he needed.

“I have a band,” he repeated breathlessly, spitting rain from his mouth as it poured down the sides of his face in fat rivulets. “We’re really good! We—We write our own songs and everything—we started it in school. We can show you, all I need is a few minutes."

“And this band of yours,” Spectre mused, like a cat toying with a ball of yarn; “I suppose you think you’re the greatest thing since Christ came back to life to make a watered down chardonnay?”

“Well, I–I…”

“There’s a million bands out there,” the producer scoffed; “So many, there ain’t enough stages in the world to fit them all. Now the radio's full, kid—I don't need any more bands."

"That's shite."

The comment slipped out before he could stop it, and Remus clamped his mouth shut as Spectre whirled on him.

"What was that?"

Screwed and completed out of his depth, Remus glanced down at the soaked magazine. It wrinkled under his hand, and he imagined walking back to Regulus with nothing else to show for it. He could do that. He wouldn't.

Remus squinted down at the blurry words.

"Phenomena..."

Spectre took a step forward, shouting over the noise of the rain; "Speak up, man!"

“Phenomena!”

Spectre blinked, and with nothing else, Remus threw up the magazine.

"You want a phenomenon, don't you? Well, the Marauders are a phenomenon. Just listen to us play once and you’ll know! We’re a family—we need each other more than we need the air in our lungs, and we're good. Our lead singer, Sirius, you—you haven’t seen anything until you’ve seen him! And James, our guitarist, he sees colours—like actually sees them. We have a drummer too that'll knock you on your arse and me—I'm...” Remus sighed, furiously wiping the rain from his face. “Look Gaz—I–I mean, Mr. Spectre, sir… I swear—you take a chance on us…? We won’t make you regret it.”

He was panting by the time he'd finished, and the reaction he got was little more than dismissive. Remus watched as Spectre sighed and brushed away the drops of water that had slid down the umbrella and onto his shoulders.

“ ‘Marauders’, huh? … S'a shit name.”

“You once signed a band calling themselves ‘Body Pyle’,” he grumbled. “And if memory serves right, you only got the one single out of ‘em before the lead singer was arrested for dealing heroin outta his mum’s basement.”

“Do you deal heroin?”

“Nah… kicked the habit.”

It might’ve been a trick of the light, but Remus thought he saw Spectre smirk.

"What'd you say your name was, kid?"

"Remus. Remus Lupin."

“And what sorta music do you play, Remus Lupin?” He looked Remus up and down appraisingly. “Are you a punk?”

“Not really.”

“Yeah, didn’t have the look about you… New wave?”

“No.”

“What then?”

“We’re…” Remus glanced at his hands, hapless. “We’re rock.”

Spectre shook his head. “Nice try, tosspot. You see, that used to be worth something—used to. Now everyone’s gotta have a shtick.”

“We don’t have a shtick, we're just us,” Remus said, with as much conviction as he could muster whilst looking like a drowned alley cat. If he'd had to guess, he would’ve assumed he’d botched it already. He was good at getting second chances, but first ones? Now those were a bit harder to come by. He waited while Spectre smoked his second cigarette, knocking ash into the puddle between his feet once—twice—three times—

“That was a shit pitch,” Spectre said, then; “You got a tape for me?”

Remus felt the air leave his lungs all at once.

“N–Not on me, but—”

“Then how am I supposed to know if you’re so ‘good’?”

“Come to a show! We play at the Shoestring pub out in—”

This time it was the driver—or bodyguard, Remus couldn’t tell.

“You think Gaz has time to wander around some waster’s pub?” He demanded, then; “Go on, piss off, kid. You’re done here.”

He shoved Remus again, albeit more gently, but this time Remus wasn’t taking the abuse sitting down. He grappled for the driver’s arm, holding on as if it was a life raft, and rejection was the sea he would otherwise drown in.

“We can get you a tape!” He begged. “Just give us a week!”

Spectre shook his head, brushing rain from his suit jacket. “I fly to New York on Wednesday, s’gotta be sooner than that. Can you get it to the office by noon tomorrow?”

No, Remus thought.

“Yes,” he said.

“Fine. Johnny,” he jutted his head toward Remus; “give the idiot my card.”

Johnny didn’t look too happy to be doling out his boss’s card to a nobody kid on the streets, but he did it without complaint and afterwards Spectre flicked away his final cigarette and got into his car. He stopped his chauffeur just as he went to shut the door, and raised a single finger toward Remus in warning.

“Listen here, tosspot, you should know the only reason I stopped to hear you out is because you look so pathetic standing there in the rain, but I don’t tolerate anybody dicking me around. I ain’t no Danny-fucking-Fields, right? You drop that tape off and it turns out shit—I’m throwing it in the bin and billing you for my wasted time.”

Remus nodded, positively thrumming from head to toe, and watched as Spectre gave him a final side-eyed glance, as though he were still working out if he’d made the right decision. Either way, he gestured soundlessly to the chauffeur, who shut the door and left Remus to stare back at his own sopping reflection in the window's glass. By the time the car was pulling away from the curb, Regulus had come out of the shop to meet him, trainers splashing through puddles as he struggled to balance his umbrella and the Portastudio.

“Well? What’d he say?!”

Remus grinned down at the damp business card in his hand. “He told me to bring a demo to his office by noon tomorrow.”

“Do you even have a demo?"

Remus shook his head. “But we've got something better."





* * *





There was quite literally no time to waste. Before he’d even taken off his wet clothes, Remus was shooting toward the flat's phone and calling around to each of his friends’ places of work. He ordered them to get their sorry arses back to the flat as soon as possible, and when they asked why, Remus told them it was an emergency. To no surprise, it was James who arrived first, tired and out of breath after running the entire way from the tube station.

“ALRIGHT—” He wheezed; “WHO DIED?”

“I’ll tell you what died, Prongs! Your parents’ hopes and dreams of ever seeing their only son become a lawyer!”

“... Huh?”

Remus confessed to everything, and could tell by the look on his face that James didn’t entirely believe him. When they finally made it home, Sirius and Peter were also sceptical, but if Regulus’ corroboration wasn’t proof enough, Spectre’s business card certainly rid them of the rest of their doubts.

“A demo?” Sirius echoed, as the three of them fought over the card. “Where are we gonna get ourselves a whole fucking demo in less than twenty-four hours?!”

“From this!” And he planted the unboxed Portastudio down before their feet. Flummoxed, Sirius looked at James, who then looked to Peter, who asked;

“Why did he just hand us a plastic suitcase?”

It was not a suitcase, and from the moment Remus explained himself, nothing else mattered aside from the demo. Knowing that they were going to be up working until the sun rose again the next day, James and Peter both called into work feigning colds, whereas Sirius simply called Ray up at the Shoestring and shouted down the line; We’re making a demo, can’t make it into work tomorrow, don’t sack me!

It was a new step in the journey, that was for sure, and Lily appeared supportive—general concern notwithstanding.

“I just don’t want you to put all your eggs in one basket again,” she cautioned, as they ripped into the Portastudio later that night. “Remember what happened last time?”

“Don’t worry, Daisy,” James told her; “At least this way we’re making our own demo. If Gaz Spectre don’t want us then we’ll just go over his head. Who knows, maybe EMI will still want a taste.”

Despite what Dorcas’ catalogue had claimed, the Portastudio quickly proved to not be as user-friendly as they were expecting. There were four tracks, but Remus couldn’t for the life of him figure out how to switch between one without copying over the work he’d just finished on the other. As he attempted to scan through the horrendously complicated manual—metres, faders, and overdubs, oh my!—James and Sirius went blundering ahead on their own, as per usual, messing around with the microphone tracks and record button.

“Testing, testing,” Sirius drawled, nearly yawning into the microphone. He’d just discovered the master faders when his face lit up for a second time; “Oh shit, look! This button plays it backward.”

He stamped a finger down over the right button, and what followed sounded a lot like his voice set to helium, unintelligibly muttering the words;

'Gnit-set, gnit-set!'

“I wanna try!” James grabbed the microphone. “Prongs is the best Marauder.”

‘Re–nar-arm tss-eb eht-si sig-norp!’

“Wicked.” Sirius held the mike out to Peter. “Hey, Pete, think you can let one rip?”

It turns out that a fart played backward sounds a lot like a fart played forwards, but to four immature boys it was still worth a few cheap laughs. After that Lily ushered them out of her living room, claiming a need to study, and the boys excused themselves to the basement without argument. Setting the mini record studio aside for a while, they got to work on their songs, tweaking every strum and note until they had something polished enough to be proud of, but not too polished as to not belong on a rock and roll record.

Early on, Regulus had reluctantly joined them downstairs. He slumped back into their dingy band sofa with a book in his lap, pretending as though he weren’t interested and occasionally called out helpful directions such as “You’re dragging,” and; “One of you’s off tempo, five pounds if you can guess who it is.” After about three hours of this, Sirius picked up the heavy Portastudio and dropped it at Regulus’ feet.

“We get it, Edge, you’re very funny, but we have less than twelve hours to get this thing done, and believe it or not, your little voice-over isn’t helping! So here, why don’t you actually make yourself useful and sort this headache out for us.”

Regulus gave him an eye-roll, but eventually picked up the thick yellow manual. It took him less than an hour to know the machine inside and out, and after that they were forced to listen to him as he dictated orders like an unofficial sound tech.

“Have you even decided which songs you’re going to put on this thing?” He asked, scribbling notes in the margins of the Portastudio’s manual like he was studying for A-Levels.

“Reckon all of them,” James called optimistically.

“All of them? You don’t put all your songs onto a demo.”

“He’s right,” Sirius said. “I don’t know how he’s right… but he is. Fucking Fletcher had us doing everything wrong. A demo’s supposed to be a taste—a piece of what we can do, if you will. There’d be no point in paying us if we just handed them the entire cake for free.”

“Then which songs?” Asked Peter.

At that, they all seemed to defer to Remus.

“Well… ‘Downtown Girls’ for sure. It was our first real song, and I stand by it.”

“ ‘Hail Mary’ should be on it,” James added. “I never get tired of that one.”

“Put down ‘It’s Hard to Be a Teen’,” Sirius told Regulus. “And ‘Doomed Generation’. We’ve just finished it—make it a grand ol’ ‘fuck you’ to Fletcher.”

Regulus glanced up from his notes. “That’s four. Reckon more than five would be pushing it.”

“We still need a ballad,” Peter pointed out. “Should we do ‘How Nice It Could Be’?”

No one said anything, and again all eyes were on Remus. He knew exactly what they wanted.

“No.”

“But Moony—”

“It’s not a good song.”

Sirius bent down before him, grasping the neck of Remus’ bass. “It is a good song, Moons—I swear… It’s not just your feelings for her in there, it’s you. You think I could stand it if it weren’t? If you really hate it, then we’ll never bring it up again but…” Sirius sighed. “It’s a good song, and I think it deserves a spot on our first album.”

Remus hung his head. Dammit.

For so long, accepting that song had felt like accepting defeat. That she was really gone, and at the end of it all, she’d never really cared for him in the first place. It stung more after his falling out with Tomny—turned the defeat into mindless shame. But what came after shame?

Acceptance?

Compassion, a tiny voice said. It wasn't hurtful, or angry. It felt like her, and Remus ached. Maybe it was time then. Maybe with this, he could finally put Tonya's memory to bed.

“It can’t be called that,” he swore. “It needs another name.”

Sirius thoughts for a moment. “ ‘Midnight Dancer’.”

It felt right, and slowly Remus nodded his head in permission.

“Fine… but I’m gonna need a drink first.”

Staying long enough to kiss Remus over his hair, Sirius stood and gestured to Regulus and the Portastudio.

“Well? Blimey, what are we waiting for? Someone get this man a fucking drink so we can record these songs!”





* * *





Tuesday 3rd April 1979 — 11:14 AM





Someone was shaking him.

“Lupin! Wake up! Lupin! Augh… Sod it.”

SMACK!

Remus awoke with a start, shooting upright on the sofa so quickly, he nearly slammed his forehead into Regulus. Clamping a hand over his throbbing cheek, which now burned from the force of Regulus’ slap, he moaned;

“Blithering fuck—Regulus, did you just hit me?”

“Yes. And do you even know what time it is?” Regulus snarled.

“Time for you to work on your bloody bedside manner, I’d say.”

“It’s past eleven, you nob. Shouldn’t you four be on your way to deliver that tape? Or did you stay up all night working on it for nothing...”

Like shaking off the cobwebs, it took a moment for Remus to understand the gravity of what Regulus was telling him. He looked out over the basement, where his friends had all passed out, empty beer bottles and dinner plates strewn out between them. Horrified, Remus made a grab for Regulus’ wrist, turning it over so he could see his watch.

“Shit… OH SHIT!”

“That godmother of yours called again, by the way,” Regulus told him. “She left a message on the machine. I think she was looking for me.”

“Hope you said hi then,” Remus grunted, “save her the trouble of yelling at me.” He began scrambling for his socks and shoes, which had somehow ended up across the room. As he tugged them on he gave James a gentle tap on either cheek to get him going and eventually they were able to rouse both Sirius and Peter and get them on their feet as well.

“I don’t understand—how could we all have fallen asleep?!” Peter bleated as Remus rushed to free their homemade demo from the Portastudio’s tape deck.

“Who cares? We’ve got thirty fucking minutes to get this tape across the entire city!” Came Sirius, as he desperately attempted to tame the bed head he’d received from falling asleep with his head against the wall.

“I’ll get the van keys,” James said, only to come to a startling halt when Regulus raised the key ring on a single finger. “My hero!” He moaned, before snatching the keys and smacking a fat kiss on Regulus’ forehead. The move startled Regulus horrendously, but not before James had time to smile and disappear up the basement stairs, a quick ‘Thanks darling!’ following him out.

Unwashed, exhausted, and probably a little hungover, the other three Marauders hung close to James’ ankles, racing down to the corner where they could throw themselves into the old Volkswagen van. Poor Peter barely had the side door shut before James was ripping away from the curb.

“Where am I going?” He demanded. “I don’t bloody know where I’m going!”

“Moony—card!”

After struggling with his pocket, Remus reached forward and slapped Spectre’s rumpled business card into Sirius’ palm. “It says Barnsbury,” he told them. “Head toward Fitzrovia, Potter, it’ll be faster!”

James did so, and they whipped along London's Westway for a good while, but when the two lanes inevitably became a one-lane and they found themselves stuck behind a slow-moving milk float, Sirius nearly had a fit.

“For Christ’s sake, Prongs—GO AROUND HIM!”

“And where shall I go, Padfoot—up onto the pavement?! Shall I drive into the row of parked cars? Or I know—is there a magical flying van button on the console that’ll I’ve somehow missed? ‘Cause if you could kindly point it out I’d much appreciate it!”

“Shut up!” Remus bellowed. “There’s no point in ripping each other’s faces off, we’ll get there when we—”

But Sirius wasn’t listening. From the passenger’s side, he’d waited until he saw a gap in the parked cars along the road, then he reached over and grabbed the steering wheel, yanking it to the left. Everyone screamed—including Sirius—and James swerved around the milk float, narrowly avoiding slamming into the back of a taxi parked at a forward taxi rank.

“YOU IDIOT!” James wailed, beating Sirius with one fist and clinging to the steering wheel with the other. “YOU COULD’VE KILLED US!”

“Glory at any cost, Potter!” Sirius cackled.

They made it to North Barnsbury with little more than three minutes to spare, and after the quickest parallel park of James’ career, the four Marauders began scurrying down the street with only Spectre’s business card to guide them.

“Forty-four,” Sirius said, “we’re looking for forty-four!”

James counted the addresses; “Twenty-eight, twenty-nine…!”

“Uh, not to be a downer, but we did actually manage to finish the tape, right?” Wheezed Peter. “I can’t remember anything after Sirius’ sixth ‘Hail Mary’ overdub.”

“No point in worrying now, Pete,” Remus told him, with a similar feeling of unease in his gut.

It was quite miraculous that they actually managed to make it on time. They found the studio office on a very fine street, in a building that was made up of several floors and a spectacular amount of windows all interspersed with carved stone columns. The door marked “Number 44” was painted green, with an expensive knob that fell open under their hands like butter. They looked ragged and out of place when compared to the lobby's plush velvet furniture, but the secretary was away from her desk and thankfully no one stopped to question them as they legged it toward the nearest lift.

“Guys, I think I’m gonna vomit,” James moaned, bending over at the waist as the lift doors slid shut ahead of them.

Sirius groaned; “You always have to vomit."

“Try some deep breaths, James,” offered Peter.

"Ugh..."

Sirius sniffed the front of his t-shirt. “Moons, do I stink? I feel like I stink… Blimey, I can’t meet Gaz Spectre like this. I smell like a skip bin!”

“Everyone just shut up!” Remus snapped, hands in his hair and fisting it by the root. His stomach seemed to be dropping down a floor for every one the lift went up, and he had to pull the tape from his pocket just to keep his hands busy. On the front was the flat’s address and phone number, and on the backside was the band's track-listing:





MARAUDERS, APRIL 1979

03:14 Downtown Girls

04:37 Hail Mary

02:37 Midnight Dancer

03:22 It’s Hard to Be a Teen

04:03 Doomed Generation





It felt odd to see it spelt out so clearly. Three years of hopes, dreams, and work, all for one tiny tape. Madness, actually.

When the lift's bell dinged to signal their arrival, the doors slid open to reveal a long hallway interspersed with various offices bearing words like ‘management’ or ‘publishing’ or 'communications' on tiny metal plaques. Secretaries fluttered around like moths to a porch light, carrying stacks of paper and fresh pots of coffee and paying them little mind.

Unsure of where else to go, the four Marauders began moving warily down the hall. There they stopped before one of the first offices, where they could overhear someone shouting on the phone. There was a man inside pacing back and forth in front of the desk, practically strangling himself with the telephone cord.

“No—No! Now you listen to me, we paid for that airtime! Mr. Spectre signed a contract with the BBC at the beginning of the year that states—what? … No! Listen… either you put my boys on the air, or you’ll be out of a fucking job, right! You wanna know how many names I got working over at your bloody BBC? Enough to—bloody hell… Just—Just hold on…”

They’d been spotted. The man marched over to the door and might’ve imparted upon them a few choice words not appropriate for one's typical office setting. Only, he had forgotten to set the receiver down, and instead yanked the entire phone right off the desk with a glorious clatter.

“FUCK!” He spun on them; “Would you please—piss off?!”

The door slammed in their faces, each of them leaping back to avoid getting smacked in the face.

“Gee, sounds like someone’s having a bad day,” mumbled Peter, making all of them crack up.

They found the main office of Spectre Records—unsurprisingly—waiting for them at the very end of the hall. The room smelt of wood and cigarette smoke—not that far off from the musty smell of the catalogue rooms back at the Hawkings library. There were several cubicle-like desks, each taken up by a different office worker and their type-writer. As the chorus of clicking keys filled the air, Remus found himself drawn to the vibrantly-coloured paintings of various rock idols that hung on the walls. They had Jimi Hendrix, and Jim Morrison, and every member of the Beatles.

Across the room, sat what appeared to be the main desk, where a young guy in a black turtleneck was going through a box of files, sorting them into different wire baskets. Behind him sat one final office, with a door bearing a single window made of translucent glass and the name ‘Gaz Spectre’ written across it in gold letters.

“At least we know we’re in the right place,” Remus murmured, as the four of them plucked up enough courage to go forward. They were spotted before they even made it to the desk, and the guy looked them up and down with a condescending brow before returning to his files.

“What do you want?” He muttered, clearly not that interested. None of them said anything until Sirius shoved Remus ahead of them like some half-assed sacrifice.

“Er, hi. My name’s Remus Lupin, and uh… Mr. Spectre asked me—or–or us to drop off a tape for him. It–It’s a demo… for our... band...”

He felt stupid—Why did he always choke at these things?—not that the guy seemed to notice.

“Right,” he said blandly; “Well, you can leave it there with the others.” He gestured languidly at a wire tray sitting atop the desk, already piled high with discarded tapes and envelopes that looked as though they hadn’t been touched in weeks. Seeing them, Remus baulked a bit and glanced dubiously at his friends.

“Sorry, but I think Mr. Spectre meant for me to give it to him directly.”

There was a short chuckle;

“The day Gaz Spectre wants some Woody Guthrie wannabe to hand him anything is the day he promotes me to company director—now if you don’t mind, we here at Spectre Records are very busy. Leave the tape if you want, but please go away.”

“Isn’t there any way we could meet him?” James urged, candidly. “Just for two minutes?”

“Even if I wanted you here for another two minutes, there’d be no point. Mr. Spectre flew out for New York this morning.”

The news was like a punch to the gut, and Remus instantly had his hackles up. It was one thing to stutter, it was another to take a shot lying down.

“He said he wasn't leaving until Wednesday,” he snarled. “We were up all night working on this damn thing. If you could just bloody give it to him then we—”

The guy had slapped the lid onto his filing box.

“Look, you can leave the tape there and go, or you can toss it in the bin for me and I’ll have security throw each of you out onto your rears. Now what’s it gonna be?”

Perhaps it was the lack of sleep, or the fact that he’d promised his friends salvation in the form of Gaz Spectre—whatever it was, Remus was about three seconds away from knocking that smug head off the top of his stupid fucking turtleneck. If not for the grace of Sirius, he might’ve. As it was, Sirius stepped forward and grabbed Remus by the shoulder. Eyes connecting, Sirius gave him a slow, knowing nod as he took the tape and dropped it unceremoniously into the wire basket.

“Thanks for the opportunity, mate,” he said, saluting the other guy before guiding Remus away from his own doom. Retreating back toward the lift, Remus could tell that whatever morale they’d walked in with was already fading. And it was all his fault.

“Now what are we gonna do?” Peter grumbled, as they rode the lift back down to the lobby.

“We’re gonna do exactly what we’ve been doing all along, I suppose,” sighed James. It made Remus want to punch him too.

“How is it you’re always so goddamn optimistic all the time?”

“Would you rather me be all dour and moody like you?” James asked, before reaching up and ruffling the hair at the back of Remus’ skull. “There’ll be other chances. That girl Sybill just got us on to play at the university last week, right?”

He was right, but because Remus wasn’t good like James, he turned around and nudged Sirius.

“You were unnaturally quiet in there.”

“I just figured letting you punch the guy and going to jail wouldn't be as conducive to meeting our goals.” Sirius smiled meekly, then stepped back to wrap his arms around Peter and James’ shoulders. “C’mon, lads, let’s not waste our time on sods like these anymore. We’ve got a wedding to get to.”

The lift bell dinged as they arrived at the ground floor, and all of them nodded respectively, though it was hard not to notice the air of disappointment that followed them out on their heels.





* * *





You’re gonna tell me sweet things,

You’re gonna make my heart sing;

And I’m gonna hear bells ring,

‘Cause I’m gonna love you too, oh!

- “I’m Gonna Love You Too” Blondie, 1978



Wednesday 4th April 1979 - Lottie's Wedding Day…





Sirius banged his fist against the bathroom door.

“Reg, come on, mate! I’m all for having a cheeky wank every now and then but do you think it can wait until after? We have somewhere to be, you know!”

“Fuck off! You did this on purpose!”

“And just how was I supposed to know the cleaners were gonna shrink your suit? Come on, mate… Pal…? Buddy…?!” Another bang. “Shit, Reg—quit being such a whinger! It’s too late to go get another suit anyway, so put on those big boy trousers and come on out here like a man!”

“I said, piss—OFF!”

Sirius sighed, shaking his head haplessly, before glancing down at Regulus’ ruined suit.

“Did the cleaners really shrink it?” Remus whispered, lifting one of the cuffs.

“Ha—no,” Sirius snorted, before lowering his voice. “I paid the tailor to take it in a few inches in the chest and sleeves.” He turned the jacket over, showing off the fresh seams. “Can’t very well wear a suit that doesn’t fit, now can he?”

Remus scoffed, dropping the cuff and mouthing; You’re evil.

Sirius winked. Then he banged his fist against the bathroom door a few more times.

“C’moooooooan, Reg! Let’s see the suit! You and I are blood—I know it looks good.”

The door flew open, nearly taking off the tip of Sirius’ nose. As he leapt out of the way, Regulus Black stormed out wearing none other than a powder blue suit, complete with a ruffled jabot collar and matching white loafers. Sirius had clearly outdone himself on the spectacular get up, but the look on his brother’s face did not appear to be all that grateful.

“You know, I think I like it,” said Remus. “You look like Bowie.”

He and Sirius shared a cheeky glance, and then both burst out laughing as Regulus began to seethe.

“Oh, shut up,” he snarled, tugging viciously at the collar. “You two are really taking the piss if you think I’m wearing this out in public. I look like if Liberace and a tube of toothpaste had a baby.”

“Don’t be so dramatic,” Sirius scoffed. “It doesn’t even have rhinestones. If you really want to look like Liberace, you should try this.”

With a flourish, Sirius tossed him what appeared to be a plain black silk jacket. The suit might’ve been alright, if it weren’t for the embroidered inferno of bedazzled red flames and ostrich feathers zipping up its back.

“I cannot believe you wear this shit out in public," Regulus spat, throwing the suit aside with all the rest.

“Don’t be silly. Most of the time I just put it on and give Moony little fashion shows while he sits on the bed in the nude.”

"It's very breathy on the bits," Remus agreed, slouching back on their bed. Regulus scowled at him.

“I don’t even know why I have to go to this bloody wedding. It’s not like it’s my friend who’s decided to get married at eighteen.”

“You have to go because we’re going,” Sirius said, reaching forward to straighten out his brother's shoulder sleeves for him. “Can't very well sit around here by yourself all day, I won't allow it. Now Lottie’s been kind enough to invite you, so let's put on a brave face and go show everyone how spectacular you look in my clothes."

"One day, Sirius... One day I will strangle you."

Just then the bedroom door opened, and James strolled in wearing full black-tie. “Hey lads, just about ready to—CRICKEY! Wow, Regulus, you look great!”

For a moment Remus thought he could see steam coming out of Regulus’ ears. Shoving Sirius’ hands down, he bolted for the bathroom and slammed the door after himself. It made James baulk a bit, but by then Sirius was already hammering his fist on the door again.

“What the bloody hell are you doing now? It’s only Pot—”

“PISS OFF!”

It took some finessing, but eventually Sirius did manage to get Regulus out of the bathroom. He was not pleased to know that the rest of them would be wearing black, but didn’t have much other choice; Sirius was the only one closest to his size, and the only one with a spare suit at home.

By the time the car arrived, each of them was freshly showered and dressed, with their hair combed and faces neatly shaved—on Lily’s orders, of course. The ceremony was being held in a lovely church just outside St Albans, with the reception set to commence at a nearby country club straight after.

As they were arriving, Remus spotted Dorcas talking to one of James’ cousins in the church’s atrium. Rather than a dress, she had opted for a deep emerald pantsuit, with a fashionable neckline flared hem. She waved when she noticed them, and broke away from her previous conversation with ease.

“Nice suit, Meadowes,” said Sirius.

“You too.” Dorcas began fiddling with one of her earrings. “Blimey, has anyone got anything to drink? If I’m to spend the next six hours surrounded by this many rich old white people, I should think I’d need to be pissed first.”

They didn’t, it being a church, and Sirius smirked as he wrapped an arm around her.

“Hang in there, love. Plenty of time to get pissed later. And hey, I think the wine’s kosher too!”

Moving from the atrium and into the nave of the church, they passed several ushers handing out ceremony programs, as well as those waiting to escort the few older guests to their seats. Despite their close personal proximity to the bride, the only task the four Marauders had been given was to show up and make sure Peter made it through his reception speech, though that in itself was proving harder than anticipated.

“I dunno…” Peter stammered, as they filed further into the church with the other guests. He turned to look at Moira on his arm; “M–Maybe Simeon should do it, after all.”

"Don't say that, Petey."

“Yeah, isn’t Sim already doing the best man speech?” Sirius drawled. “You know, since Roger doesn’t have any friends of his own? You’d think that’d be ten times worse.”

Moira glared while Peter’s shoulders slumped, but it was James who leaned in with encouragement;

“Ignore him, Pete. Lottie asked you to give a speech because there’s no one else in the world she’d rather have speak at her wedding than her twin brother.”

“You don’t know that, maybe she asked me and I said no,” Sirius snarked, earning himself a sharp flick to the ear from Dorcas. He sighed then nodded at Peter; “Don’t know what you’re worrying for, Wormy, you’re gonna do great. Hell, you’ve been practising that speech of yours for days now.”

“Sirius is right,” said Remus. “Lottie’s going to love it.”

Peter nodded, albeit apprehensively, and just then Mrs. Potter came rushing up the aisle.

“Oh, boys, there you are!” She chirped, holding a hand to her chest and looking beautiful in a burgundy silk gown. “Petey, your mother’s still with the girls, but here’s your buttonhole. Take it and go to the back of the church with the other groomsmen, Simeon will help you pin it on.”

Nodding quickly, Peter took the little flower pin and shot back the way they’d come, leaving Mrs. Potter behind to catch her breath.

“Busy morning, Mum?” James asked.

“You have no idea.” She sighed and cupped her son’s cheek dotingly. “I do hope that you’ll give me more than just three months’ notice when you decide to get married.”

“Does this mean you’ve already popped the question, Potter?” Dorcas mused. “I should let Lily know.”

“Lay off, Meadowes,” James squeaked, obviously embarrassed.

“It's lucky for me, really,” chuckled Mrs. Potter. “Poor Jenny’s been barely sleeping, what with all the work it’s taken to get everything ready for today. She’s just lucky her daughter isn’t a pickier bride.”

“Well, I think it looks great,” Sirius said, turning his head to admire the church. “Whoever did the flowers bloody knew what they were doing. Moony, what do you think? Blue or yellow flowers for ours?”

“I think you’re lucky to have not burst into flames walking in here, Black.”

Smiling, Effie reached over and pinched Remus’ cheeks. “Oh, honestly! You boys get more handsom every time I see you. Remus, you’re as tall as a weed, and Sirius, your hair is truly a feat. And—And, who is this?”

They all came to attention at once, most of all Regulus, who Effie had stopped to stare at as though she were already dazzled. Adversely, Regulus looked as though he were ready to leap behind one of the pews, though that didn’t stop Sirius from reaching over and wrapping a proud arm around his shoulders.

“Mum, I'd like you to meet Regulus, my brother,” he announced. “Handsome tosser came as a spare. Bit last minute, but he cleans up well, right?”
