Later that night...



“Ah! … Augh… AGH, F—SHIT, EVANS!”

“Oh, stop whinging!” Lily hissed, busy capping the jar of ointment she’d been applying to each of Remus’ many cuts. She hadn't been happy to come home from class to find Sirius and Trish bent over him on the sofa with a rag in either hand, but of course that hadn't stopped her from barging in and taking over. Remus' back hadn't been faring well ever since taking on the bramble bushes; he felt like he'd been used as a scratching post for several angry cats. After the ointment was applied Lily placed a large stick-on bandage over top, making him wince all over again.

“Honestly, Remus, if you didn’t insist on getting yourself caught up in such asinine situations then I wouldn’t be here right now torturing you.”

“That’s what I told him,” Sirius sighed. Meanwhile he was across the room, tucked up on one of the sofas and already three drinks in. Remus noted with slight amusement that the beer he was drinking was the same brand Barty had cracked over Lee’s nose earlier, but it didn’t stop him from shooting Sirius the bird.

“You shouldn't have gone there at all," Lily scolded. "And don't you dare try and tell me you didn't talk him into it, Sirius Black."

"I didn't talk him into it! I just... didn't talk him out."

Lily's green eyes narrowed. "Honestly, I never thought I'd get stuck living with such fools!"

"You sure about that?" Regulus said out of the corner of his mouth. Inexplicably, it made Lily smile, and he quickly glanced away—a gesture that did not go unseen by Remus.

"Well," Lily huffed, “at least I have some good news.” Finished with his bandages, she tapped Remus on the shoulder while shutting the first-aid kid and Remus was able to spin round and face her at the kitchen table while lowering his t-shirt. “Sybill’s given the go-ahead on your guys’ show at UCL," she said happily. "That's right—come next Friday, you four are going to have your first ever live, head-lining concert.”

“No way!” Sirius shot upright on the couch, nearly upsetting Trish’s beer as she went in for a sip. “She really made it happen?”

“You mean real people are going to pay real money just to listen to you bang and whinge for a whole hour?” Barty demanded.

“Even better, Crouch” Sirius told him, “they’re gonna pay to listen to us bang and whinge for two whole hours!”

“Wow. Sucks for them."

Shoving his tongue between his teeth and bottom lip, Sirius tipped his beer toward Barty, who only crowded more closely into Regulus.

“Aw, what’s wrong Crouch? No ‘break a leg’?”

“I hope you break a leg, Black—in fact, I hope you break both of them!”

Not long after, the front door opened and Peter and James strolled in, their hands black with car oil and big smiles plastered across their faces.

“Good news,” James announced, “turns out Little Edge didn’t actually manage to ruin the van’s transmission, so it looks like we’re good to head out to Camden tonight!”

“Are you sure?” Lily asked, peering dubiously at Remus. “I think some of us have had enough excitement for one day...”

“I’m fine,” Remus replied stubbornly. He reached for his coat as he stood up, purposely resisting the twinge in his back.

“Just you wait, Edge,” Sirius said to Regulus as they all congregated by the front door to gather their coats and boots; “The Damned are sure to put on a good show. I know this guy from work, who swears their lead singer's like a fucking vampire or something. Said he even drank real blood on stage once."

"Don't be ridiculous. Vampires aren't real."

"Don't tell this guy that. It'd ruin the whole show."

Regulus rolled his eyes, and Sirius grabbed him by both shoulders, guiding him out the front door. "Ah, don't worry, Edgie. You haven’t seen anything ‘til you see your big brother up on stage anyway!”

With the brothers already out, James sidled up to Peter and playfully shoved a pair of his drumsticks into his hands. “Here, Pete,” he sniggered, “for when Rat Scabies dares one of the audience to take over for him on drums again.”

“As if,” scoffed Peter, tossing the sticks away. “He won't, and besides, I don’t fancy getting my head kicked in by a couple of punks when I don’t know all the notes.”

"I'd fancy it," Barty said snidely, before Trish had him by the ear.

They had to cram together in the back of the van just to get all eight of them to fit, and since Sirius insisted on sitting up front with James, Lily ended up riding the entire way to Camden in Remus’ lap.

“This's so exciting,” Trish exclaimed, her tiny shoulders crammed in between the two Salazar boys. Despite the fact that she’d travelled all the way from the Scottish Midlands to rip Regulus a new one, she’d packed rather poorly when it came to the general wardrobe department. Lily had offered to lend her a blouse for the concert, but in the end she’d gone with one of Sirius’—a cyanotype t-shirt they’d picked up along Portobello Market ages ago. It had Iggy Pop’s face on the front, layered with what appeared to be an x-ray of a very large ribcage. Overtop she was wearing Barty's jacket, of which she'd rolled up the sleeves just to make fit.

“Don’t tell me you’re nae completely buzzing,” she said to Regulus, who up until that moment had been staring out the window, watching as the bright lights of Camden High Street whipped on by.

“It should certainly be an experience.”

“Ugh, you’re like the grim reaper o’ fun.”

Regulus leaned his mouth into his hand, pretending not to notice, but Remus thought he’d managed to catch a hint of a smile in the light of a passing headlamp.

The Damned—or The Doomed, they were billing themselves now; it changed by the week—were playing at Camden’s Electric Ballroom. A bar and roller-disco most nights, the venue was occasionally transformed into a stage house meant to showcase the best and worst London’s rock scene had to offer. Remus had never been, but Dorcas called it a right of passage. You hadn’t lived until you’d seen the club’s bartender smash a bottle over a heckler’s head like it was a Greek wedding.

They parked the van a few streets over, making triple-sure to steer clear of any taxi ranks, before making their way over to Kentish Town Road where they found the club’s entrance already teeming with young fans. The concert being his idea initially, Sirius had generously offered to cover the door fee for each of them on the condition that should the lead singer turn into a vampire bat on stage, they’d all bow down and name him their new prophet. Remus didn’t know how likely that was, but when Dave Vanian took to the stage decked out in white face makeup and a billowing poet’s blouse, he began to think that Sirius’ odds of winning might not actually be that bad.

“He looks insane,” Barty said, before practically yelping as his shoulder came into contact with one of the “no wave” fans. This one was wearing a jacket with enough studded metal it could’ve been considered a lethal weapon. “Do they actually expect people to be able to dance to this noise?”

“Sure, you can dance, Crouch,” Sirius laughed, “just don’t expect to be given much room for pirouetting.”

The crowd was getting on great. Three fights had broken out before the end of the second song, but as none went so far as to draw any blood so most people remained unbothered. Instead they threw themselves skyward, bouncing up and down in place like highly-excitable and highly-inebriated children. An elbow caught Remus in the chin at some point, but when he looked to see who’d hit him, he couldn’t tell his neighbour’s arm from his own. They were packed in like sardines, spilling beer onto each other and practically tramping across their own shoes.





‘Go where you want to go,’ the song said, ‘don’t stay locked at home!

Don’t be a fool—

Don’t cry wolf!’





As far as Remus could tell, this was a people who’d come together purely to lose themselves in the noise. Unlike the Sex Pistols, there was no expectation to be the foulest couture-wearing dickhead in the room, and no one was foaming at the mouth for the chance of getting at some greasy blighter in a leather jacket that happened to share their own political epiphanies as they had while watching the Clash.

They were simply…





‘So come and have some fun, yeah!

And help us smash it up—’





There to enjoy.





‘Don’t be a fool—

Don’t cry wolf!’





“Not really your typical anarchists, are they?” Sirius called, shoving his way past a pair of head-banging girls in matching dog collars.

“They’re not anarchists at all!” Remus shouted back. “They’re just loud!” And better musicians than the Clash and Sex Pistols combined, certainly.

Smirking, Sirius then shrugged in indifference as he pushed a can of Skol lager into Remus’ hand. On his other side, James and Peter were taking turns shielding Lily from the more rambunctious members of the audience. When lead singer Dave Vanian began waving his tongue suggestively at them, Lily laughed and slapped James on the arm, probably suggesting that he start doing the same.

Of all of them, Regulus and Barty were predictably having the worst time. Remus had suggested earlier that the two of them hunker down by the bar and get drunk enough to take the edge off, but they’d declined then, and it only became obvious as to why when about halfway through the show, a beefy guy with hair stained vermillion and no shirt on indicated that he wanted to lift Trish up onto his shoulders. She almost accepted too, before Barty did the unthinkable and raised Trish onto his own shoulders himself. From there she had a prime view of the entire room, which she made the most of by shrieking every time the beret-clad guitar player came to the front of the stage to hammer out a solo.





‘Problem child, problem child,

We think you live much too wild!

Problem child, problem child,

When you get home—

Your daddy’s gonna tan your hide!’





It went on forever. At least, that’s how it felt. Back at the Shoestring they had to break in the middle of their sets—let sense reassert itself so that more booze may flow—but at a real concert, nothing else mattered aside from the music. Remus could see the sweat on the band’s face and chest and he knew—he knew—what it was to be there. To feel so out of breath you might pass out any moment, to be so in need of a drink of water you think that’s it, this is the end!

And yet the rush makes it all worth it.





‘Problem child, problem child,

We think you live much too wild!’





Things began to get real rowdy near the end of the show. An amplifier had been blown halfway through, creating a wonderful show of bang and sparks and the guitarist kept knocking over his microphone stand, usually battering some poor member of the front row in the process. If the crowd had been close to the stage before then they were practically breathing on the band now. Though she remained a good sport, James had eventually taken Lily to the back to get some air and Peter seemed to have made good friends with a punk couple who looked to be about in their mid-forties. Sirius was still going strong of course; he and Remus were on what had to be their third or fourth beer, though how Sirius found it so easy to slip in and out of the crowd at will, Remus still couldn’t understand.

Trish had since traded Barty’s shoulders for Regulus’ and—urging him forward with her heels as though he were a saddle horse and not a boy—had managed to gain Vanian’s favour, screaming loud enough that the lead singer eventually pulled what appeared to be a kerchief from one of his billowing sleeves and tossed it into the audience for her to catch. A pair of girls just in front had turned around to stare with envy, and Trish smirked as she kissed the silky scarf and tucked it in the collar of her t-shirt.

Somewhere between the raucous “Stretcher Case” and blustering “Neat Neat Neat” drummer Rat Scabies had lost his shirt, playing in only his trousers and a pair of sunglasses missing one lens. He seemed to favour the ‘dead behind the eyes’ sort of drumming face, but before Remus could finish the thought (or his beer), the song ended and half of the band threw down their instruments and stalked off stage. After that the bassist downed a beer and tossed the can in the audience only to meander off in sure search for more, and all they were left with was Scabies himself. He gave an impressive drum fill—characterised by enough bass drum to burst an ear-drum—and then Scabies stood up from his stool and pointed both sticks at the audience.

“Oi, which one of your sodding cunts has the bollocks to get up here and play? HUH?!”

The room cheered manically, but none were quick to volunteer. Scabies was known for the stunt, often luring an unsuspecting fan on stage only to let the crowd rip them to pieces the moment they were proven as anything less than astonishing.

As the drummer went on harassing them for tribute, Sirius slipped over to Peter and shoved him in delight.

“Go on, Wormtail! The bloke’s name is ‘Rat’, you’re practically cousins!”

“Piss off! That joke ain't even funny anymore!” Peter replied, looking a lot like he might throw up.

“Ain’t any ‘a ya got the balls?!”

"Come on, Wormy!"

“You do it then if you’re so brave!” Peter yelled, shoving Sirius toward the stage.

“Me? I can’t play the drums!”

“Lupin, then!”

“Sod off.”

Scabies roared into the microphone;

“No one!?”

It seemed like the angry drummer was not about to get his wish. A few guys near the left corner of the stage were playing at it, but every time one attempted to get on stage they’d wobble drunkenly and fall back down to be consumed by the mob. At one point Scabies began shoving them off stage himself, disappointed in their sorry state and obviously low-calibre. Some shouted for him to get back behind the drums and light them on fire—a favourite party trick of his Remus had always wanted to see up close. But Scabies would not have it. While his band mates were off, probably downing several shots and the odd cheeky bump or two, he stalked up and down the stage like a prison warden, shaking his sticks in the air and punting empty cans back into the crowd.

“Pete, you gotta,” James said, having appeared with Lily from the back of the venue. “It’ll be legendary!”

“Oh, go on, Peter! We know you’d be brilliant,” Lily encouraged, but Peter only shook his head again. Outwardly—and perhaps drunkenly—Remus was disappointed, but he couldn’t blame Peter for refusing. Getting up on stage with your own band was one thing—accepting the challenge of real label-signed punk rocker was another. If someone like Sid Vicious had even looked at him, he would’ve folded on the spot.

When several long, drawn-out minutes had passed and no one had risen to the bait, Scabies stormed back over to his kit and unceremoniously hurled his floor tom across the stage. The crowd ate it up, but it was clear not everyone was happy. Trish booed, still clinging to the tops of Regulus’ shoulders, and shockingly, Barty joined her. It wasn’t until the rest of the band reemerged on stage and Scabies took to one of the microphones that the mood finally shifted.

“Bloody pathetic! Since when did Camden Town become land of the fucking pillocks?!”

Initially Remus thought nothing of it. Scabies could only bleat for so long; eventually the band would pick up their instruments and finish out the show, and they’d all go home with their ears and brains rattled to mush. But then something happened that no one could’ve seen coming.

Again, Scabies hollered—“No one? Is there feckin’ no one!?” —and quietly, almost like a sigh, Remus heard a mumbled, “fuck it” coming from his left side.

A small yelp—and Trish had been dropped to the ground as Regulus started pushing past others like Barty, heading for the front of the stage. Like a sailor returning to land, Trish stumbled, and Remus scrambled to catch her as they were both jarred by the eager crowd. Together they watched as Regulus sifted through the sweaty bodies, his face tilted down but hand thrust high in the air so he could be spotted amongst the masses. Me, it seemed to say, I volunteer.

“No way,” blurted James, having somehow witnessed the whole thing over Remus’ shoulder; “He’s not doing what I think he’s doing, is he?”

Remus was without words. He could only gape as the crowd eventually began to catch on, parting obediently for Regulus the moment Rat Scabies noticed and pointed a single stick straight at him.

“A-ha! A sacrifice!”

The drummer crowed enthusiastically as he reached a hand down to help Regulus up onto stage. The minute Regulus’ feet touched that cheap vinyl platform, the audience went wild. A second later, Remus felt a hand grab his shoulder. Sirius.

“Am I seeing things, or did my baby brother just get on that fucking stage?”

“I think he’s doing more than just getting on stage,” Remus bleated back. They watched as Scabies righted the floor tom and directed Regulus behind the drum kit to his very own stool. The seventeen year-old kid moved robotically, like he couldn’t remember how he’d come to be on stage in the first place, and when Scabies handed him the drumsticks, Regulus stared at them like he’d just been given a live bomb to hold.

“What’s he gonna do up there?” Demanded Peter. “He doesn’t even know how to play!”

“What, ye think he just sits around in that bloody music room twiddling his bonny little thumbs?”

It was Trish. She and Barty had turned on the rest of them, a single smug look split between them.

“Uh—I don’t know about you, but I don’t think Scabies is gonna let him get away with playing Beethoven’s ‘Moonlight Sonata’ at a rock concert,” said Sirius.

“You mean he never told you?” Barty laughed. "Figures."

“Told him what?” Wailed James.

But Barty refused to say anymore. Sirius demanded it, even threatened to kick him out on the streets if he didn’t fess up, but Barty’s lips were sealed.

“Trish, is this for real?” Remus asked.

“You ain't dreaming, if that’s what you’re asking, Loonary.”

Remus looked at Sirius, who looked at James, who looked at Peter—and instantly they knew what was going on. It was unbelievable—the Marauders were had! Even Lily looked on in shock. Regulus—on the drums? Why? How?!

Sheila.

The thought must’ve occurred to Sirius the same moment it had Remus, for they looked at each other with equal parts shock and realisation. She'd never told them what instrument Regulus had picked up back in September, and now they were finally sorting it out for themselves—at a live concert, no less. Up on stage, Regulus was currently being zeroed in on by all four members of The Damned. The band’s guitar player, Captain Sensible, shoved a microphone beneath his nose so he could introduce himself, but when Regulus said nothing—merely staring out over the room as though his brain had short circuited—Remus had to swallow a laugh of disbelief.

“What’s yer name?” Scabies was shouting, to no avail. The sight of the large crowd had clearly dampened whatever reserve of mad courage it’d taken for Regulus to ignite the little stunt, but when Scabies simply answered with a swift, “Aw, who gives a fuck what yer name is! Let’s just feckin’ play!” and knocked the mike away, Regulus had no choice to comply. A perfectionist to his core, he straightened up behind the kit, readjusting the pair of sticks and began twirling them like a nervous gesture. Scabies leaned down to whisper something in his ear, but when Regulus shook his head, the drummer simply shrugged and stepped away, accepting a beer as it was handed to him by one of the stage hands.

“Right, let’s hear it for the nameless wonder!” Scabies hollered, no mike needed. The crowd roared for him—for Regulus—and eventually the noise died down, replaced by craven need. The rest of the band had their instruments, but it was clear they, like the crowd, only intended to sit back and watch as Scabies tortured his next victim. Already the room was growing restless again. Remus could feel it like the heartbeat in his ears.

Play. Play. Play.

“Well?” Scabies asked him. “You gonna play or not, kid?”

There was no answer; Regulus was frozen, staring down at the drums like they might swallow him whole. Remus heard the heckling start from the back, growing more and more bold;

“Bloody play something!”

“Kick him off!”

“What is he—thick?!”

But it was a different voice that cut through all of it;

“Go on, Edge!” Sirius barked, cupping his hands around his mouth; “Go on—don’t listen to these tossers, show ‘em! You can do it!”

“Yeah, Edge, you can do it!” James added.

“You can do it, Regulus!”

“Play, Regulus!”

“Hurry up, Reginald!”

“Fucking, show ‘em, Reg!”

“Go on! Take the plunge!”

“You’re fearless, Edge! You’re a beast!”

“Play—play!”

“Hell yeah!”

They’d all started. From Barty to Lily, they went down the line shouting their encouragement like a war chant.

Play! Play! Play!

“We’re here for you!” Sirius told him. “You’re my brother—you can do it!”

“Anything you want, Regulus,” Remus shouted, “you make the rules!”

“You're gonna kill it!” James insisted.

It was probably very embarrassing, but knowing Regulus, that was perhaps the only way to get him to do anything. He may have cringed behind the drum kit, but at least it snapped his mind out of its vegetative state. It took the band’s eyes off him, and it gave the audience something to listen to—and that, in itself, was enough.

The first hit of the bass drum was like an electric shock to the entire room. It was amplified immediately by a rolling clash of cymbals and a cascade of dropped jaws, though no one could’ve been more shocked than Sirius.

“Holy shit,” he muttered—and holy shit was right. Aside from the drums, the entire room had gone deadly quiet; like a jazz drummer, Regulus’ playing had started out as a series of beats meant to rock the tempo back and forth like a boat. He played with his left just as equally as his right, commanding every note with immense precision and growing faster and faster with every hit on the snare. Even just watching, Remus’ heart felt like it was in his throat. It felt like watching Sirius play the piano at his father's funeral—the tip of the waterfall, in which the subsequent plunge came faster and faster with every passing second.

Caught in a wave of awe no different than that of their audience, members of The Damned stood around like slack-jawed spectators; their instruments might as well have been lead in their hands. Rat Scabies himself had been finally outdone, it seemed. He gaped at Regulus openly, the beer in his hand all but forgotten, and when Regulus’ drum fill came to a shuddering close, he threw his arms up in a clap.

Only Regulus was not finished.

With a booming smash, he launched himself into a blinding fit—smashing his bass and cymbals simultaneously. It took a few seconds, but eventually Remus began to recognise the beat, and it was not jazz.

“Is that Black Sabbath?” Peter bleated.

“It’s ‘Paranoid’,” Remus answered in awe. Next to him, Sirius had his hands in his hair;

“HOLY SHIT!”

All Barty and Trish could do was cheer.

By now some of the other band members had started to catch on. It was only natural; Black Sabbath had set the bar for countless punk groups, and hearing them now, members like Captain Sensible were clearly invigorated.

Taking up his guitar, Sensible took a few seconds to tweak his tuning before joining Regulus in the opening riff. With the guitar it was everything. It broke the audience from their surprised daze and suddenly people were cheering again. They wanted more!

Dave Vanian picked up his microphone;





‘Finished with my woman—‘cause she couldn’t help me with my mind!

People think I’m insane—because I am frowning all the time!’





“FUCK YEAH—GO, REGGIE!”

Sirius bellowed louder than the rest, using James’ shoulders to leap high enough so that Regulus might be able to see him if he only looked up. But Regulus wasn’t paying attention to them. The band’s bass player had moved over to the drums, matching his tempo to Regulus’ in a great show of improvisation. It wasn’t a perfect cover—not by miles—but Regulus’ playing had already wowed everyone. He’d peeled himself out of his jacket, and now perspiration was shimmering off his face and bare arms under the hot lights. Across the stage, Rat Scabies may as well have been creaming his pants. He leapt up and down, nearly driving his knees into his own throat while the band’s guitarist, Captain Sensible, threw himself down on his back, playing upside down and looking like the possessed girl from the Exorcist.





‘All day long I think of things—but nothing seems to satisfy!’





The crowd roared.





'Think I’ll lose my mind—if I don’t find something to pacify!’





There was a crash as someone smashed a bottle over one of the stage monitors.





‘Can you help me?’





Rat Scabies picked up the broken bottle—





‘Occupy my brain!’





And drank from its shattered rim.





‘OHHH YEAH!’





It was like lighting a match and waiting for it to burn down the wick. Captain Sensible was a shit guitarist when compared to the likes of the real Black Sabbath, but no one cared. This wasn’t about paying tribute—this was as close to any of them got to God. The amplifiers seemed to get louder, the bass harder, and no one knew what to do. The crowd thrashed as one, fists pumping through the air and shoving coming from all sides. Here was this regular kid, plucked from the masses—a fan, just like them! They wanted a piece, and thankfully Scabies gave it to them the moment he tossed the shattered bottle aside and threw himself over the crowd. They caught him, after perhaps a few concussions, and he crowd-surfed across the entire room while Regulus—a skinny little punk—played his own drums for him.

If Regulus noticed what was going on within the crowd, he did not give any indication of it. Instead he kept his head bent down low, dark hair falling into his eyes like a shield. Maybe, thought Remus, if he couldn’t see them, it meant it didn’t matter what happened. If Remus could’ve told him anything just then it would’ve been that his mother would be very disappointed in how fucking cool he’d turned out to be.

When the song was over, Regulus finished them off with a fill that made you feel as though you were tumbling down a set of stairs. Where he’d learned how to do such a thing—and in only a year—Remus couldn’t fathom, but he’d done it. And he’d fooled them all.

Dave Vanian, the perfect punk-rock gentleman he was, congratulated Regulus with a kind handshake. He’d only just pushed his hair out of his eyes, and seemed to be looking around for somewhere respectable to leave the sticks, only Rat Scabies ha made his way back onto stage. As Regulus came out from behind his drums looking like a kid caught with his hand in the biscuit tin, Scabies slammed him on the back for his good work and finished by wrenching Regulus’ arm up into the air like he'd just won the Grand Prix. The following cheers were loud enough to shake the entire room, and they muffled Scabies’ words when he leaned in to ask Regulus something. Whatever it was, Regulus still did not seem interested; he shook his head for the second time, still breathing hard, and Scabies shrugged before giving him the sticks to keep as reward for his hard work.

Afterwards, when Regulus was free to rejoin the crowd, he was met with even more fans eager to share their congratulations. He had to fight just to make it back to his friends, who were all standing in the middle of the pit with stupid looks on their faces. Regulus’ nose was bleeding lightly, but Sirius merely took his jacket sleeve and began wiping it away for him before shaking him by either shoulder.

“You crazy bastard—you never told me you could do that!”

“You were so great!” Lily said.

"More than great! That was goddamn amazing!” James agreed. “Scabies looked likely to pass out when you started playing.”

“Thought I was going to pass out,” Regulus panted. Everyone laughed, even those nearby they did not know, and as Barty pointed and went on telling everyone that that was his best friend, Trish leaned in to give Regulus a kiss on the cheek.

“Aye, you were brilliant.”

“Must’ve felt amazing,” Remus said, giving him a light tap on the shoulder. “What was it you were thinking up there?”

Regulus glanced down again. His hands were trembling, but he just squeezed Scabies’ worn out drumsticks and slowly the shaking ebbed.

“I just… wanted it to be loud,” he said eventually. “When it’s loud, it’s like nothing else matters.”

“You weren’t worried you were going to sound awful?” Peter asked tentatively. At the question, Regulus finally raised his head. Then he looked straight at Remus.

“There are worse things than sounding awful.”

Remus smiled, but it was Sirius who hugged his brother. “I have never been so proud and so fucking pissed off at the same time. You... You little shit—You better not be keeping any more secrets from me!”

Regulus shrugged, and afterwards James reached over and raised his hand into the air the same way Scabies had. “Come on, I think this deserves a drink!”

Everyone cheered in agreement, and as The Damned began gearing up for a final encore, Remus and his friends turned for the bar. The music was instantly blaring again, and James looked at Peter;

“Isn’t it cool, Pete? Now you got another drummer to jam with!”

“Yeah… S’cool.”

Behind them the band's speakers roared;





‘Well, you used to hang around on the rails, yeah!

You know they was your patch,

But there’s a brand new kid in town;

Never gonna let you live it down, he’s gonna—

Stab yor back!

Stab yor back!

Stab yor back!

Stab yor back!’





“Oh, that reminds me!” Sirius called, after they’d reached the bar and ordered a double round of fresh beers; “What’d Scabies say to you up on stage just then?”

Regulus sipped from his can, grimacing; “He asked if I wanted to do ‘Speed,’ but I told him I didn’t know the song.”

Sirius glanced at Remus, and then began breaking down. By the time he'd caught his breath, his laughter had turned to real tears on his face.

“Oh, baby brother—you have so much to learn!”

A Few Days Later…





"Show me again?"

"No."

"C'mon, pleeeeease? Just one more time."

Regulus scoffed, but set his sticks back against the drums—one-two, one-two—showing off the basic intro to "Paranoid". James followed it with his eyes, enamoured, and when Regulus was finished he leapt up from his nearby stool.

"Oh, I get it. So it's like—" Instead of going for the sticks, he leaned over top of Regulus' shoulders and took both of his hands in his own. Regulus might've rebuffed him for it, had James not been doing the same thing all afternoon. Now he just looked mildly perturbed, hunched over Peter's drum kit with that dark fringe falling into his eyes. When they'd finished, James rattled the cymbal several times.

"Just one more!"

"Ugh..."

One-two, one-two!

Finished with my woman—‘cause she couldn’t help me with my mind!

People think I’m insane—because I am frowning all the time!

A small smile tugged at the corners of Remus' mouth while he watched them. One-two, one-two—"One more?"—One-two, one-two—"God, you're so annoying."—One-two, one-two—"Yeah, reckon you like it though."—One-two, one-two—"Shut up!"—One-two, one-two—

Not realising that he'd been staring, Remus snapped from his daze and glanced down into his lap to find the joint he'd been rolling had come apart in his hands. He was sitting across from Trish and Barty in the basement of their flat's pseudo-practice room, helping them make use of the last of Trish's London weed stash. Barty's rolls were twice as bad as Remus', with loose leaf spilling out either end—not that Trish seemed to notice. She did slap his fingers when he began tearing the extra rolling papers into little bits though. Barty only sneered at her.

"Sorry," Remus said, licking the side of the ruined joint in an attempt to save it.

"You were zoning out," Trish replied, sounding amused. "Feel like sharing with the class?"

"I just keep wondering whether I should tell James about it."

"Tell Potter about what?"

"Oh, you know. Just Regulus' crush on—"

He didn't even get to finish; instantly both kids' eyes shot up. Barty had even stopped ripping Trish's rolling papers into tiny pieces, and fisted both hands in his lap.

"How do you know about that?" He demanded.

"You mean it's really true?" Remus was shocked. "I only guessed."

"You want my advice?" Trish said, fitting a finished spliff into the corner of her mouth and lighting it up. "Dinnae say anything. Reginald's like a spooked deer—bring it up and he'll ne'er come within fifty feet o' ye again."

"And I'll have to kill you," Barty added keenly.

Remus rolled his eyes. "I wasn't gonna say anything," he said, setting aside the mangled spliff and reaching for another. " 'Sides, there's no hope for it. Everyone knows that Lily's totally gone for James."

"Which is why I'll kill you if you say anything," Barty insisted. Behind them, James and Regulus were still thankfully banging away and unaware, but Trish must've been worried, as she grasped Barty by the chin and held her lit spliff up to his lips.

"Here, bawbag, use this 'n' relax."

Barty did, but only while shooting a deep glare at Remus. It was unsettling, even for Barty Crouch. James was a good guy; if it did somehow come out that Regulus had a thing for Lily, he wouldn't do anything more than tease. Though for Regulus, teasing was certainly enough to push him over the edge.

The mood changed again when the door to the basement opened and Peter sauntered down the stairs. He'd already changed out of his work clothes and appeared rather worn out, but recovered the moment he spotted Regulus sitting behind his set of drums.

"Sirius said you guys would be down here already."

"Yeah, just messing around," James said kindly. "Good day at work, Pete?"

Peter shrugged, then licked his lips dubiously as he gestured to the dum kit. "Thanks for saving my seat, mate."

Regulus was up in a second, awkwardly palming the pair of sticks Scabies had given him. "Thanks for letting me use it while you're gone," he mumbled back.

"Any time."

Remus stood up from the floor, taking a moment to stretch as he called out to Peter; "Did ya see Sirius then, Pete?"

"Yeah, he's upstairs. You know the bloody girl in him takes forever to get ready."

"It's just band practice."

"Hey, he's your boyfriend." Peter tested the pedal of his hi-hat, before snapping his fingers in recollection; "That's right. Phone call for ya, Moony."

Remus shot a look at Trish and the others. "Let me guess, Sheila again?"

"No, it's that Skylar girl.”

Shit. “Was she crying?”

“Didn’t sound like it. Lily picked up. Told her I'd fetch you.”

James gave Remus a hopeful smile. “That’s good news then, right, Moons?”

Remus wasn’t so sure. Setting aside his bass guitar immediately, he passed Regulus, who'd gone to sit with Barty and Trish and had his head bowed as all three of them shared in whispered conversation. Their eyes met for a second, but Regulus' expression gave away nothing.

Upstairs, Lily was watering her plants, gently pruning the Marlene fern she’d moved into the living room window for more light. Her nose wrinkled when he walked in, and she stifled the overpowering smell with the collar of her shirt.

“Ugh, Remus, you need to stop smoking. I can smell you from here.”

“It’s all part of the process, Lils. Helps us get loose—'broadens the mind'.”

“How you four get anything done, I’ll never understand.” She hummed. “Phones for you.”

Nervously wringing out his hands, Remus fetched the phone. He braced himself for tears—was James right? Was it good news, or was Skylar just putting on a brave face?—and took the plunge.

After a while, he was underwater. He could hear her, but she was far away, like an echo.

Sky?

Hey, Sky…

It’s Remus.

You’re good? That’s good.

Say, I just wanted to let you know that I went back to the flat the other day and—what?

You found him?!

No, yeah—shit, that’s great news! Do—Do you think I could...?

He’s sleeping.

No—No, I understand! As long as he’s alright…

No, I get it.

Yup. Totally.

And hey, about the baby—

Yeah!

No…

Alright, I’ll call back later.

Take care of yourself, okay?

The phone felt heavy in his hand. He still hadn’t hung up, and he could hear the dial tone the same way he could hear Lily, calling his name in concern.

“Remus? Remus?”

There was a short thundering as someone—Sirius—came down the stairs in heavy boots. The front door opened at the same time, and again Remus was underwater. He heard their voices drifting around him;

"Hey there, Mr. Ringo Starr! … Oh don't make that face, you know you love it..."

“Right, I’m coming… Hold on, Edge, have you been smoking?”

“Piss off.”

Tomny was back.

Tomny was fine.

Tomny did not want to speak to him.



“Moonyyyyyyyyy—! Come on, Moony, we got a concert to prepare for! Shit, that's mental to say, isn't it? ... Eh, Moony?”

Tomny's fine.

He's fine.

Chapter End Notes

A 'flannel' is like a kitchen/dish cloth.

If someone has been 'slated' they've been publicly shamed/criticized.

'No wave' was a cultural movement that came as a response to “new wave”.

'Wimpy's' was/is a fast-food chain.

'Skol' was/is a brand of canned beer.

Technicaaaaallly, 1979 is not the ideal timeline for a Damned show, but it was important to me that I featured the Damned as long as I was going to feature the Sex Pistols and the Clash. So to any super punk fans out there, please allow me this one deus ex machina.

I based the Damned show loosely on THIS performance. Also Here’s the Sex Pistols version of "Friggin' in the Riggin'". As far as I know you can't find it on streaming services. (I used the Anthrax version on the Spotify playlist .)

Songs in this chapter: “Have You Ever Fallen in Love” by the Buzzcocks (1978), "Heart of Gold" by Neil Young (1972), “Don’t Cry Wolf” and “Problem Child” and “Stab Yor Back”, all by The Damned (1977). Also “Paranoid” by Black Sabbath (1970).

Saturday 21st April 1979





Sheila was still burning a hole in their phone bill, still intent on sorting out just when her precious students would be returning to school, but no one could be bothered to stop the fun long enough to explain. Regulus and the others would be taking the train back to Scotland in a few days anyway, and in the meantime Sybill had made good on her promise to host their next gig. The turnout was good, better than expected even. For whatever outlandish peculiarity she’d projected onto them during their first meeting, Sybill’s handle on the UCL student body was impressive. She ran the event seamlessly, directing her volunteers on how to best wrangle the waiting crowd, and she knew where all the plugs would be when it came time to set up.

“You have your own monitoring system?” She'd asked, when they came rolling up to the hall’s backdoors with their amps.

“No,” replied Sirius, “but I'll wager that if we sounded like utter shit, one of you would’ve told us.”

She hummed at him, then; “You can borrow ours, I suppose.”

It was quite the set-up, much more professional than anything they’ve ever had a handle on anyway. When Remus had first heard about the shows being put on by Sybill’s events committee he’d assumed they’d be small, empty ballroom-type things where a few students drifted in between astrobiology and liberal arts classes. As it turned out, these were major college events. Various clubs ran pub crawls for most of the day leading up to every show; even the most donnish student would skip out on an evening of studying to throw themselves around the basement of the university’s shabby venue for a few drunken hours.

“Now who’re those guys?” James asked, after they’d hauled their equipment inside only to find another group of boys standing at the top of the hall with instruments in hand.

“Student band,” answered Sybill. “They’re your opening act.”

It was startling. Perhaps even more startling than the eager crowd of kids waiting beyond the doors.

“Opening act?” Echoed Peter.

“Mhm. Calling themselves ‘The Disciples of Wonder’. They’re okay. Bit more ‘progressive’ than you four, but I figured it would be a better suit than anything with a bongo in the lineup. They’ll open, warm up the crowd a bit, and afterwards it’ll be all you. I’d say be ready by quarter to nine.”

Patiently, she stared at them—still bug-eyed behind her glasses—and the four Marauders shared a wary glance.

“What’s the matter?”

“It’s just… We’ve never even opened for anyone before,” James explained. “Seems a bit mental that all of a sudden we have an opener ourselves.”

“Now you’re complaining about not being the opening act? And here I thought I’d seen it all.”

She meandered off, her harem skirt swishing as she walked, and the Marauders had no choice but to be grateful. Admittedly, it wasn't hard.

They were serving drinks in the corner (mostly lukewarm cans of lager), and Sybill had taken the liberty to have one of Peter’s poster designs printed and made into a banner they could hang above the windows behind their stage set up. Opposite to the banner, leaflets advertising for all kinds of clubs and classes papered the walls and among them were the various show bills and fliers of all the different bands that’d come before. Remus recognised a few as one-hit wonders that'd only just managed to get on the radio—Moby Grape, The Knack, and the like—but most were unknowns. Scrubs and punks just looking to make it like everybody else. Eventually James pointed to one. Dick Very and the Headways.

“Holy shit! Now there’s a blast from the past… What was that, tenth year?”

“Eleventh,” Remus corrected. “I wasn’t with you guys in tenth.”

“Right, right. I haven’t heard about those guys in ages. Wonder whatever happened to that Dick Very.”

“I 'eard he shot himself in the face while staying in some boarding 'ouse in Dublin,” called one of the opening act guys.

"You're shitting me."

"No, he's right," said another. "His girl left him for George Harrison’s tour manager or something.”

James looked at Remus, appalled. “Now that’s fucking depressing.”

“A moment of silence for Dick Very,” Sirius said, appearing between them with a round of beers, to which he raised boldly in the air and announced; “To Dick!”

“To Dick!” James agreed, swigging the beer.

Later when the opening act was set to start, Sybill rushed the four of them into one of the tiny classrooms just off of the hall. According to her, they were only ever used for private study around exam time and she apologised for the lack of a proper dressing room, but they weren’t bothered. It was simply another luxury they’d never gotten the chance to miss. In fact, Remus would’ve needed five extra hands to count all the times he’d spent crowded around the Shoestring's bar, watching Sirius check his reflection in a jug of Heineken.

“What d’ya think, Moons?” Sirius called now, raising two coloured eye-liner pencils. “Red or blue?”

“Did you steal those from Mary again?”

“The word is borrow, thank you very much. … Bit harder now that we’re out of school.”

“But you still make it work,” Remus smirked, before pointing at the left pencil; “Blue.”

“Oh good. Then that must mean the red is for you.”

It incited a small scuffle, in which Sirius had bent himself so far over Remus with the red eyeliner that Remus nearly toppled from his chair. James ignored them, nervously fretting on his unplugged guitar, while Peter had sat in his own corner, drumming his sticks against an empty desk and tuning the rest of them out. (He had also popped a Valium, courtesy of his mum’s medicine cupboard, but they’d all taken one and were pretending that it didn’t count.)

“C’mon, Moons! Just a bit under the eyes!”

“Piss off!”

The classroom door flew open, and Trish wobbled in, eyes alight and both hands cradling a beer. “Christ, it’s an absolute rocket out there! Opening act’s a bit mince but they’re holding the crowd well enough. You lads should see it—think ye’ve got about a hundred people waiting to see you play.”

“A hundred?!” James gasped, while Remus shoved Sirius off and sat up in his chair.

“Give or take.”

James turned ashen and Sirius whirled on him.

“Don’t you dare throw up in here! It’s too small, it’ll reek! Go take the air if you need it.”

Trish, who was busy guzzling from her pair of pints, nodded as she brought the lip of the beer can down again. “Reginald and Bum-face are out back already if you wanna go see them. I’d avoid taking the front door though. Saw a few girls out there that looked pretty off their heads, if ya ken what I mean.”

Setting his guitar aside, James wobbled past her and Remus followed him to the door.

“Can ya believe the price of a beer ‘round here, Remington? Guy wanted thirty-pee just for a fucking can.”

“You know if you tell them you’re with us they’ll just give ‘em to you. We’re not making a wage for this so Sybill promised free beer.”

“I ken,” Trish laughed. “But Crouch paid. Just thought it would be funny.”

With her double-beers in hand, she slipped out after James and Remus turned to holler at Sirius, who was struggling with his eyeliner in one of Lily’s tiny compact mirrors.

“Gonna go have a fag before the show.”

“Hold on,” Sirius called, “can you help me with this first?”

“Ask Pete, he’s got a steadier hand than me.”

“Yes, but once Pete’s done touching up my makeup, I can’t very well give him the homoerotic kiss a moment of that calibre deserves.”

“Relationships between the drummer and lead singer rarely work out anyway,” Peter confirmed, snidely.

Remus groaned, letting the door fall shut as he meandered back toward Sirius. Grinning with victory, Sirius handed him the eye pencil and hopped up onto one of the desks, clapping his thighs as a means to beckon Remus in close.

“Be gentle, Moony. Eyes are the windows to the soul, you remember.”

“Shut up, ya bloody prat. And hold still.”

Sirius smiled, tipping his head back and looking toward the ceiling as Remus drew a blue line across his lower lashes. He struggled to keep the pencil steady, a task not made any easier by Sirius' incessant chattering.

“Don’t forget to smudge it a little with your pinky! Mary says it looks sexier that way."

"Is that right..."

"Oh yeah—it's the 'post shag' look. The sort that leaves you walking funny.”

“I told you to shut up,” Remus grumbled, doing as he was bid. He didn’t say it, but seeing Sirius with those long lashes of his now tinged in messy blue, he was almost inclined to agree with Mary. “Did you check the phone messages before we left today?” He asked, mostly to keep his head on straight.

“Mm-hm,” Sirius mumbled, as Remus moved to do the second eye. "I think Sheila's getting impatient with us. Careful, don't call her back soon and she might disown you."

Remus pinched him.

"Ow!"

"I meant—besides her."

Finished with his make up, Sirius sighed and looked down again. “And nothing—but who cares? We don’t need Spectre. That dickhead wouldn’t know ‘phenomena’ if it clapped him ‘round the arse.”

Remus tried not to be disappointed. It was easier, after nearly two weeks of nothing. In the wake of Lottie’s wedding, a part of him had still been holding out hope that someone at Spectre Records would see their tape and chance it a listen. Then he’d considered that maybe they had. And that maybe they’d just decided that Marauders weren’t worth their time.

Not good enough.

“Don’t look so pathetic, Moons,” Sirius told him, leaning in to kiss the tip of his nose. “Tonight we play London College. Tomorrow—who knows? Maybe Madison Square Garden.”

“And just what happened to four years?”

“Eh. I’m rounding down.”

Remus rolled his eyes, but the smile had already worked its way onto his face anyway. As Sirius began to tease him once again with the threat of Red Rocket eyeliner, Remus leaned in for a kiss. Eventually Sirius had him by the collar, two pairs of eager hands roaming southward in search of a convenient zipper. They were cut short when Peter threw one of his sticks at them.

“Oi, no shaggin’ in the dressing room! … Don’t want it to reek.”

Not five minutes later, Remus had managed an escape for that desperate cigarette. Pushing past the horde of sweaty university students, he wandered through the hall, bobbing his head along to the opening act and nodding genially at whoever happened to look his way. He stopped to pick up one of the room temperature cans of lager, and off to the side, managed to spy Lily sitting around a circle of milk crate bar stools with Sybill and several other girls. No Marlene tonight—she had a night shift at the women’s shelter—but Mary had arrived with them and spotted him straight away, promptly striding over with a black garment bag slung over one shoulder.

“Reeeeeemus!” She simpered—practically yelling to be heard over the sound of the opening band. “Where’s that boy-toy of yours? I brought him that pair of trousers he’s been whinging about.”

“First room off the hallway there. And don’t call him my ‘boy-toy’.”

Mary blew him a kiss, before pinching his bum quite rudely and rushing off. No one seemed to notice, and so Remus took his beer and began trudging his way toward the exit. Bodies parted indifferently around him, paying little mind and mostly just interested in the music. It was a diverse enough crowd for the area; he found hippies with their media arts degrees, philosopher punks aiming to start the next revolution, suits with undergraduate business degrees scheming for their chance at the Wall Street shuffle, and foreign students just looking to take it all in. The Disciples of Wonder were holding their own well enough with an electronic rendition of “Paint it Black”, but even then Remus could tell that the crowd was hungry. Was it for Marauders? Would they even be to their taste? One could only hope.

The air outside was the warmest it’d been all April and for once it wasn’t raining. Tapping a cigarette from its carton, Remus stood back against the hall’s exterior wall and set himself to the task of people watching. Most other students were on break from classes for the Easter holiday, but that didn’t mean they weren’t going to coalesce on the school quads to share a round of scrumpy and other illicits. Across the pavement he’d spotted a girl wearing a velvet blazer, its collar bedazzled with small crystal skulls. The flashy outfit was hard not to notice, and he paid for it when she caught him staring and returned the look in kind. But Remus was neither interested nor desperate enough for conversation. Adjacent to her, James was standing amongst a circle comprised of Regulus, Trish, and Barty. He was attempting one of Remus’ very own lighter tricks, which he sorted eventually—though at the risk of his own eyebrows.

“Wait until you get a load ‘a this one,” James said after, before whipping out a fifty pence coin. “Learned it in scouts when I was eleven.”

“Was that before or after they taught you how to bore people to death?” Barty asked, earning him a sharp pinch on the side from Trish. Regulus merely watched on, holding a beer in one hand and nibbling absentmindedly on his opposite thumb nail. Remus wondered if James would still be so friendly had he known about the obvious crush Regulus had on Lily.

“Alright, now keep your eyes on the coin, everyone!”

Who was he kidding, of course James would still be friendly.

With a quick flourish, the coin had vanished from James’ hand only to reappear a few seconds later behind Trish’s ear. She giggled, most likely due to the fact that she was at least five beers deep already, and James did the same to Barty, who flinched away and swatted at his own ear for good measure. Afterwards James turned to Regulus, but before he could reach out, Regulus had grabbed his arm by the wrist and revealed a second coin hidden inside the cuff of his sleeve.

James puckered, clearly put out to be caught in his own act.

“You’re not supposed to touch the magician…”

“Magician, or court jester?” Regulus snarked, flicking the coin back at James’ head. It made Remus chuckle. He might’ve gone to join them—stopped eavesdropping long enough to test out his own rusty sleight of hand—had the dark-haired girl from earlier not sidled up to him against the wall.

“Bum a fag?” She asked, with a voice as sweet as sugar cane. He passed her one, as was the generosity of addicts, and she leaned into his lighter while drawing her long, oil slick hair behind one ear. “I’m Christine.”

“Er—Remus.”

“Never seen you around here before. First show?”
