“Hold on, the Roundhouse has been empty for months now—Subway Sect just cancelled a show. They say the roof’s caving in. Care to explain that one?”

Gideon nodded pragmatically. “You’re right. No one’s used the venue since last summer when Siouxsie and her Banshees nearly brought the roof down. Literally. The whole thing’s needing a good refurbishment, but luckily for us, I know the bloke that used to manage it. His name’s Jeff Gilbey—he’s a good guy. Bought the place when it shut down and worked on the roof himself all summer, only now the floor’s rotting and it’s basically a write-off. Reckons he’s gonna sell it for the land to make up for his losses, but I got a couple other groups interested in playing there first. If you’re willing to share the stage for a night then there’s a small chance I could get you in, but only if you’re interested.”

“Is that safe?” Lily asked.

The manager smiled. “Who ever said rock and roll was safe?”

Before anyone could reply, Sirius leapt up off his stool;

“Band meeting!”

Despite several bystander’s sudden interest in the going-ons of the group, the four boys were able to segregate themselves off in a corner where they bent their heads together to parley.

“I dunno,” James started. “It sounds a bit too good to be true, don’t it?”

“It’s always gonna sound too good to be true,” Sirius rebuffed, “it’s the chance of a lifetime.”

“But he’s so charming and good looking. Aren’t you even a little bit suspicious?”

“Paying close attention to his face, were you, Prongs?” Peter drawled. James rolled his eyes, but the rest of them were already sniggering.

“I see he’s already charmed your girlfriend well enough,” Remus added keenly. Back across the room, they could see Lily and Mary giggling at something Gideon was saying. They each had a can of seltzer now and were sipping them as the fancy A&R manager leaned one elbow on the bar.

“Can’t very well blame her,” James grumbled.

The look Sirius gave his best friend read as bewildered, but before he could question it, Peter had already jumped back in;

“I think we should do it.”

“You do?” Remus asked.

“Yeah, he can’t be lying.”

“And how do you figure that?”

“I mean, it’s obvious, isn’t it? Gingers can’t lie.”

“ ‘Gingers can’t lie?’ Where the fuck did you hear that from?” Sirius demanded.

“Sim. He told me once—it’s like a rule or something.”

“A rule that only applies to gingers? What are you—four?”

"Shut up!"

James snorted into his palm. “Pete, mate,” he laughed, “I think your brother might’ve lied to you.”

Peter grumbled unkindly, cheeks turning red, and Sirius slapped him on the back. “Forget the gingers,” he said. “Moony, what d'you think?”

Remus pulled on his neck with both hands. “It’s an opportunity for sure… I think we’d be kicking ourselves later if we let it go just because the guy’s a bit ‘too suave’.”

“Oh, so you think he’s hot too, huh?”

"That's not what I meant and you know—"

"Yeah, yeah, I get it." Sirius sucked his teeth. "Right. I know my track record isn’t perfect, but I also think it’s a good idea. Like, that was our demo back there, and if those stinkin’ sods at Spectre Records liked it, then maybe this is it! Maybe this is exactly what we’ve been waiting for.”

“Sure, but not many bands make it at nineteen,” Remus mumbled pessimistically.

Sirius took his arm. “We’re not just any band.”

That was true, he supposed. It had to be.

"So?" James echoed. "What's the verdict?"

Soundlessly, the four Marauders looked at each other, and one-by-one, each nodded in full agreement.

“We accept your offer,” Sirius announced when they’d returned to the bar; “Just tell us what day we’re meeting Spectre.”

Gideon set down his can of seltzer, already primed with a laugh;

“Oh no, you’re not meeting Spectre. Gaz doesn't have time for every college band who manages to get a demo into his postbox. Nah, you guys are gonna play a show at the Roundhouse—a more than generous offer—and later, if I decide you’re worth it, then I’ll pass you onto Spectre. Deal?”

They couldn’t very well say no. If nothing else, Gideon was right; a show at the Roundhouse was an unbelievable opportunity.

Standing up from his stool, Gideon shook each of their hands while Lily and Mary clapped happily.

“This is so exciting," Mary said. "Our very own band of losers—about to become an even bigger band of losers!”

“C’mere then,” Sirius cooed, “give this loser a fat snog.”

She squealed, batting him away at first only to later take his face in both hands and leave a cherry-red kiss mark on the centre of his cheek. Just then Sybill reappeared, promptly congratulating them on the good news and henceforth scolding them for being late to start their second set.

"Look at you four, already in demand," Gideon gloated. After giving his hand another excited shake, James and Peter promptly scooted back toward their set-up at the front of the hall. Sirius followed a moment later, muttering something about needing to take a leak, but did linger long enough to watch Gideon finish his beer.

“You’re not gonna regret this,” he told the manager; “Marauders is gonna be the biggest band in the world, you know.”

"Yeah? And who said that?"

"Me. Just now."

"Well then. Let's not jinx it." And Gideon knocked his beer against Sirius’ in agreement.

Afterwards, with Sirius gone to piss, the only one left to see the big-shot A&R manager off was Remus. He walked him to the door, where Gideon clapped his shoulder genially.

“Sorry I can’t stick around for your second set. The Allman Brothers are flying into Heathrow tonight and I'm to meet them at the airport. It’s their first UK tour since the hiatus and Gaz wants ‘em treated well.”

“Right, but about the Roundhouse—”

“Relax, kid! It'll take a short while to sort everything out, but it'll happen. Just gotta be patient... In the meantime you lads got my card. Got yours too." Already backing towards the hall’s doors, Gideon pulled their demo tape from his pocket and waved it through the air. “Good luck, lads. Here’s hoping guys like the Allman Brothers are opening for you one day.”

Remus wasn’t so much an Allman Brothers fan, but he couldn’t deny the small thrill he felt as he watched Gideon leave the hall.

“You helped make this all happen, you know,” he told Lily when he returned to face her at the bar.

“Did I?”

“Yes. You got us the gig with Sybill. You’re the reason Gideon came at all.”

"You don't think he would've found you at the Shoestring?"

Remus shrugged. "Jesus, Lils, I'm only trying to say thank—"

“You're welcome, Remus," she cut-in fondly. "Anything for the object of my dearest affections. But I will be expecting a dedication at the end of your first autobiography.”

He hugged her, absorbed in her warmth, and when they pulled apart again Lily tapped his nose with her finger and continued sipping on her cheap cocktail. Somewhere between Sirius’ bold claim and Gideon’s subsequent departure a swift drum beat had kicked off from the front of the room. Figuring it for Peter, Remus didn’t pay the noise any mind until Mary reappeared on Lily’s far side, a look of astonishment plastered across her face.

“You guys so aren’t going to believe this.”

And maybe they wouldn’t have, had neither of them witnessed Rat Scabies’ temper tantrum back at the Electric Ballroom. Admittedly, Remus was still surprised. Based on the way Regulus had snapped at Sirius and James for yammering over the feat the entire drive home, he would’ve expected Regulus to never play a single note in front of them again; yet there he was, set up behind Peter’s drum kit and smashing away. Trish and Barty stood behind him looking thrilled, if not completely inebriated. Regulus himself would not look up at all; he kept his head bowed as if his long hair were blinders meant to block everything out.

“Bitches! Why didn’t anybody tell me Regulus could play the drums?” Demanded Mary.

“It’s a new thing!” Lily practically shouted so she could be heard over Regulus’ barrage of sound; “He didn’t tell anyone—not even Sirius!”

“Well, he’s good! More than good, if they’re anything to go by…”

She gestured toward the small crowd of students who had amassed next to the stage. Most were just bobbing their heads along to every thundering sixteenth note, but as the solo went on, more and more gathered, some even cheering and raising their drinks.

“Blimey,” Mary said, as Regulus began slamming on his hi-hat and crash cymbals; “Maybe you guys should put him in the band.”

There was no time to stew on Mary’s little joke. Already Remus spotted Peter as he stormed over to them with an apprehensive-looking James close on his heels.

“Moony, go on over there and tell Sirius’ baby brother it’s time he got himself back into line. If Gideon overhears this mess, it could ruin everything!”

“Gideon’s already long gone,” Remus blabbed. “Why haven’t you asked him to just stop?”

“I’ve tried! The cheeky cunt blew me off!”

“I dunno, I think Regulus is just playing around,” James reasoned. “Look at him—he’s clearly drunk or something.”

“Drunk enough to play that?” Peter wailed, gesturing to the cacophony of noise. “He’s acting like Keith Moon if he were half-bladdered on Adderall.”

Coming from another drummer it might’ve been a compliment, but Remus knew it wasn’t. Above all, what Peter admired in his own drumming was strict precision. He looked up to guys like Neil Peart and Buddy Rich—those known for their flawless technique. He didn’t care for showy solos or insane speed rounds, and for the most part the other Marauders had never complained. A drummer’s job was to keep time, a hard thing to do when based purely off of instinct. Peter had spent hundreds of gruelling hours nailing down every one of their compositions, often having to bend at Sirius or Remus’ every whim. He was a good team player when he wanted to be and probably deserved more compassion, but as it was, Remus was still riding the high of Gideon’s offer. He didn’t quite want to be brought back down to earth yet, and so instead he said;

“It’s just a drum kit, Pete.”

“Wrong!” Peter spat. “God, you don’t get anything, do you?”

He stalked off, and Remus and the others were left to flounder in his wake.

“Where’s he going?” James whined. “Sybill will murder us if he just leaves—we still got a whole ‘nother set to do!”

“We’ll go get, Peter,” Lily offered, taking Mary’s arm. “In the meantime you two idiots might want to think about getting Regulus off of Peter’s drum kit.”

It felt like getting a scolding in primary school. While James shifted his weight uncomfortably, Remus scanned the crowd for any hint of Sirius, of which there were none.

Regulus was still going by the time they’d made their way behind the drum kit toward Trish and Barty. A few girls had crept closer to the kit the longer Regulus played and appeared to be trying to speak to him. As far as Remus could tell, Regulus hadn’t said a word in reply—hadn’t even looked up. Luckily for him and James, Barty was all too willing to gab.

“Saw Puny-grew throwing a fit,” he simpered. “Poor bloke. Must be hard feeling so second-rate in your own band.”

“Shut your mouth, Crouch,” snarled James. “I know you were the one who put Regulus up to this, and it’s Peter’s drum kit.”

Barty raised his arms in mocking surrender before gesturing to Regulus in a ‘go ahead’ motion. Glancing warily at Remus, James moved forward.

“Regulus?” He shouted, leaning in only to swing his face out of the way when Regulus went for his crash cymbal. “Regulus! Edge—it’s me! James! Can you… I mean, could you stop for a moment?”

The crowd was booing before Regulus had even stopped, but he did—slowly, like he was caught in a trance.

“You good?” James asked.

“War Pigs…”

“Huh?”

“I said the song’s called ‘War Pigs’! Fuck, le'me alone!”

He was talking to James like he was one of the pestering girls, Remus realised. It was hard to tell if James had come to the same conclusion though; rather he looked almost hurt.

“Regulus, mate?” Remus called, coming in close. “Are you feeling alright?”

Regulus ignored him, slashing at the snare while tapping his foot against the pedal of Peter’s bass drum; thump-thump-thump-thump!

Remus turned to his friends; “How much has he had to drink?"

“Only about twelve beers,” yawned Trish. “And a little pinch 'a weed.”

“Isn’t that a bit excessive?” Griped James.

She shrugged. “Lollyhead almost never smokes it. He asked for some after your first set. Couldn’t think of a reason to tell him no.”

“Yeah? I can think of about twelve different reasons,” Remus scoffed. By now James had Regulus by the shoulders, and was slowly easing him out from behind the drum kit.

“There you go, champ,” he smiled, wrapping an arm around his shoulders. “Let’s get you some water.”

For the most part, Regulus appeared agreeable to this, but then some girl who’d been watching him play came up to his other side and took him by the arm. She’d only said about three words before Regulus was wrenching himself free, his expression similar to a kid who’d just stuck his fingers in a light socket and gotten burned.

“Sorry,” James apologised, “he’s a bit out of sorts right now.”

The girl stepped back disappointingly, but by then Regulus had recognised just who it was who was leading him.

“Potter…”

“That’s my name.”

“Get… gerroff.”

“Don’t be difficult, Edgie. Just gonna get you some water and then we’ll all be right as—”

“I said—get off!”

The cry was viscous, and James released Regulus before he could take a drumstick upside the head.

“I don’t need your help,” Regulus warbled. “Don’t… Don’t touch me.”

“Right,” James huffed, “you wanna tell me today’s date then? Or even your name? ‘Cause you look higher than a kite, mate.”

“Fuck off. Why don’t you just go find your perfect little girlfriend and leave me alone for once, you stupid prick!”

A few nearby watchers sniggered, and Remus got the distinct sense of deja vu.

“What are we, back at school?” He grumbled, walking forward. He took the drumsticks from Regulus, who didn’t fight, and then pushed him by the shoulder. “Walk on, ya bastard, or I’ll carry you.”

The look Regulus gave him could’ve curdled milk, but Remus didn’t care. He pushed him again, lightly, and looked back at James. “Sorry, Prongs. How ‘bout you just go find Peter and the girls? I’ll be right back with this one.”

James nodded, glancing once more at Regulus, who did not return the look.

“And you two—” Remus pointed at Barty and Trish; “Any more trouble and you’re sleeping in the rain.”

Trish blew him a kiss—as did Barty, though his was of the more crude variety.

Back at the make-shift bar, Remus sat Regulus down at one of the empty stools and pushed a cup of water toward him.

“James was just trying to help you out. You didn’t need to bite his head off.”

“Yeah? Well, Potter can get fucked.”

Remus rolled his eyes, tapping the drumsticks against the bar top in irritation. “You know, just because you have a small thing for Lily doesn’t mean you get to be a dick to James whenever you want.”

Regulus flung his cup over, nearly soaking the front of Remus’ trousers.

“What the hell—”

“You say anything like that again and I’ll take your eyes, Lupin!”

“Jesus… Where’d you even hear that—an Al Pacino movie?” Remus found a stack of old newspapers in the bin to his left, which he used to begin sopping up the water. “You’re going back to school in a few days,” he muttered, “are you sure you wanna leave on such a sour note?”

“Piss off.”

“You should really work on regulating that temper of yours. You’re starting to sound like a broken record.”

“Don’t psychoanalyse me. I pay people for that.”

Remus shook his head. Tossing the wet newspapers aside, he gestured for another glass of water. “Are you at least glad you came?”

“No, your first set sucked.”

“Cheeky prat… I meant London. It’s only been four—five bloody weeks since you got here.”

Regulus fell quiet, contemplating his water. “Sirius is worried,” he said after a while. “I can see it every time he looks at me.”

“ ‘Course he’s worried. You’re his brother.”

“No, he’s worried I’ll go back to school and end up doing everything our mother wants of me. He’s worried I’ll turn out just like the rest of our family—horrid.”

Remus turned his head away, disguising his obvious wince with a gentle scratch to the back of his head. He hadn’t anticipated any confessions.

“Well… will you?”

He felt stupid for putting it so plainly, but couldn’t come up with any other way to phrase it without beating around the bush.

“I don’t want to,” Regulus said. “And I… I don’t want to go to university either.”

It was a surprise to say the least, especially for someone as smart and talented as Regulus. But then again, Sirius had been the same way.

“Got any plans then?”

“No."

"None at all?"

Regulus mumbled something.

"What's that?"

"I said—that I… may like... being in London…”

“Oh?!” Remus tried not to sound smug. “Really?”

“Yes, but that’s not a plan.”

“Who says? You think we moved out here with jobs all lined up and the perfect flat just waiting for us? Nah. We figured it out as we went along, just like everyone else. We had help of course—Sirius’ inheritance, James and Peter’s parents—heh—Lily. But we did it. And you can do it too, if you’d like.”

Regulus rolled his eyes. “I hate your pep talks.”

“Yeah, I know.”

By then the bartender had come round again to offer Remus another beer. He abstained—for once—and instead asked for a water. When the guy brought it to him, he raised it to Regulus.

“To figuring it out.”

“You’re not really going to make me cheers with you, are you?”

“Go on, do it. Otherwise I’ll tell James you fancy his girlfriend.”

Regulus glowered, but reluctantly raised his cup and knocked it into Remus’. Feeling well pleased, Remus sipped from his cup—tipping it back just in time to glimpse Sirius bounding toward them from the back doors.

“There you are!” He cried, wrapping his arms around Regulus from behind. “Edge! Have you heard the good news? Your big brother’s gonna be headlining the Roundhouse.”

“Congratulations,” Regulus hissed, already pushing him off.

“It’s shit you’re gonna miss it.”

“He’ll catch other shows,” Remus said. "Won't you, Edge?"

Regulus rolled his eyes, picking up his water.

"Shut up, Lupin..."



* * *





“My teachers say I’ve got no clue! My parents don’t approve of you!” I first heard the lyrics in a little pub over in South Bank. When I started hearing it again in my head weeks later, I knew I had to go back. A week more and I was scribbling their name on every scrap receipt I could find. I paid a kid four and a half quid to write the lyrics on the walls of an Underground station, then I snapped a photo. It’s still in my wallet now, soon it’ll be printed on the front cover of this magazine.

MARAUDERS. It must be love.

It’s 1979 and punk is dead. “God Save the Queen” – the Queen is saved. There ain’t no more British pop and Bowie’s jumped ship to drop acid with Iggy in New York. All that’s left is new wave speed and inconsistent E flat shock chords. Not that anyone’s told MARAUDERS that. With melodic songs and near impeccable manners, this four-man band cannot claim to be the new Kings of Punk, nor do they care to. They are something else entirely. Something old, something new, something borrowed—full debut.

Can you hear them?





Remus lowered the copy of Sybill’s Slasher Chick fanzine. He’d lost count of how many times he’d read it since she’d dropped it off yesterday morning, but it wasn’t nearly enough. According to Sybill they’d already pawned off almost a hundred copies since their show just four days ago. They weren’t the only subject—she’d also managed to snag an interview with one of the Ramones’ ex-roadies and there was a controversial opinion piece on page nine titled “My Vagina’s No less ‘Holey’ than Yours” critiquing the Catholic church’s view on abortion—but there was no denying that the Marauders took front page. There wasn't much way of devising who said what thanks to the way Sybill had penned the interview, save for the fact that Remus had actually been there. Reading it back now, he could picture every word perfectly;





Sybill: How old are you?

Sirius: Twenty-one!

Peter: He’s lying, we’re nineteen.

James: Eighteen, in Pete’s case. He’s not nineteen until September.

Peter: Wanker.

Sybill: What have you been doing in London lately?

Sirius: Shagging as many hot women as possible, naturally.

James: No, don’t print that.

Remus: Potter’s worried his mum might read this.

Sybill: You can say what you want. We’re not aiming at the general public anyway.

Sirius: Yeah, that was a joke, but we say what we like…

Sybill: Now that the Pistols are through and the Ramones have gone back to New York, there’s a lot of curiosity about the London scene and what’ll come next… Do you expect to be next?

Peter: I wouldn’t say we represent the entire scene…

Sybill: Who do you represent?

Sirius: The sexy people.

Remus: You’re going to sound like a twat.

Sirius: *mimicking R* You’re going to sound like a twat.

Sybill: How do you feel about New Wave?

Sirius: No comment.

Sybill: Are you old school then?

Peter: Nah, we’re new school.

Sybill: Do you have any dreams to be distributed in America one day?

James: Oh, sure!

Remus: But we’d like to be distributed in the U.K. first.

Sybill: Any other groups in London you feel are any good?

Sirius: The Damned are the only one with a clue. It’s why they got left behind.

Sybill: How about the American bands?

Peter: Didn’t we just talk about the Ramones?

Remus: Iggy’s good, but his band sucks. And he should stop partying with Bowie – selling self-destruction as art doesn’t suit Bowie, and Iggy’s better on his own anyway.

Sybill: You’ve heard about Patti Smith?

Sirius: Yeah, and she talks too much.

Sybill: Takes herself seriously.

Sirius: Oh, course! She’s an artist.

Sybill: Do you think of yourselves as following the tradition of rock 'n' roll or going against it?

James: What’s the tradition of rock 'n' roll again?

Remus: Dying at twenty-seven.

James: Oh…

Peter: Against. Definitely against.

Sybill: What will your music be like in a few years?

Sirius: Interview us in a few years.

Sybill: Are you guys comedians or something?

(No answer.)

Sybill: Mods or punk rockers?

Peter: Mockers.

Sirius: You stole that from Ringo.

Peter: Sod off.

Sybill: Is this the worst interview you’ve ever done?

Peter: It’s the first interview we’ve ever done.

Sybill: You’re playing at the Roundhouse in a few weeks. How does that make you feel?

James: Don’t ask unless you’ve got a bucket.

Sybill: You each come from substantial backgrounds. Do you see this as a hindrance or an advantage?

Sirius: You said there’s no chance of our mums reading this?

Sybill: It’s not likely.

Sirius: Bollocks.

Remus: Right, we know what we look like. Four shit-eating toffs who’ve never done a hard-day’s work in their lives. And maybe we haven’t – we’ve been granted a lot. But we’re not looking to tell anyone how it is, or what it is they should believe in.

Peter: Lots of people have talent, just not the means of funding it.

James: That's right. Not everyone could afford to do what we did. Sometimes it's all you have just to wake up and put food on the table.

Sirius: We're not claiming to be the most self-aware. We were given a head start, we see it. Mostly we're just here for the art.

Sybill: And what would you say to those that might say you haven’t suffered enough for the art?

Sirius: You haven’t met my mother.

Peter: And art isn’t just suffering.

Sybill: What is it then?

Peter: It’s everything. It’s part of everyday life.

Sybill: So you’re not just posers?

Remus: Everyone’s a poser. You think Jesus wasn’t posing on that cross? We don’t just write what we know, we write what we feel. If they’re gonna hate us then that’s life, innit. Everyone hates you.

Sirius: Now who sounds like a twat?

(R shoves S.)

Sybill: Lupin, you write the lyrics, don’t you?

James: Is it that obvious? Our little Shakespeare.

(R shoves J.)

Sybill: Last question – If you could say one thing to London’s youth to wake them up, what would it be?

Sirius: That getting your prick sucked feels better when you’re awake.





They’d made fun of each other for hours afterwards—“ ‘everyone hates you, that’s life, innn-it, Lupin?’’—and in the end James asked Sybill for an extra copy to send to his parents.

Now it was late April, and Regulus and his friends were due back at school so that they could pass their exams and get on with their lives. Remus wasn’t sure what would come after, but Regulus had an open invitation to their couch, and—should he so choose—an offer from his big brother to support him at whatever university he should choose. With their first big-time show at the Roundhouse just on the horizon, it was all getting very real, very fast.

For now though, it was time to say goodbye.

“You’re sure that’s all of it?” Remus asked, while setting the last of the bags down by the front door.

“Should be,” Regulus replied, checking his trunk’s clasps. When he’d arrived the trunk had been relatively light. Now it was heavy, packed full with clothes, music magazines, and records Sirius had insisted on sending his brother back to school with. Culture, he’d called it.

“Excited to be going back?”

Regulus shrugged. “Where’s Sirius?”

“Still upstairs, I expect. I’m sure he’ll be down soon.”

This time it was a nod, and then Regulus let his gaze drift out the front door. Trish and Barty were already standing on the pavement with their bags, waiting on the taxi Lily had been kind enough to call for them. They were arguing about something—Trish making a face, Barty rolling his eyes. She’d just grumbled something very Scottish at him when Barty reached a hand toward her face, only to have his fingers slapped away viciously.

“Crazy bird! You had dirt on your collar—I was only trying to brush it off!”

“Brush your own dirt, Bawbag!”

“Bleeding Christ, you’re infuriating.”

“Wow, that’s a big word for you. Can you even spell it?”

Remus touched his thumb to his lip. “Are those two really…?”

“God, I hope not,” Regulus grimaced. “There’ll be no living with them.”

He smiled, then fit his fingers into his mouth for a whistle. "Oi, MacDuff! Got something for ya!"

Down on the pavement, Trish turned around and Remus tossed her the small object. Instantly Barty had crowded in to see what it was, but she answered with a cry;

"My hag stone!"

"Gloine nan druidh," Remus corrected, almost certainly butchering the pronunciation. "You were right. Turns out it is lucky, after all."

"Not 'lucky'," she scoffed, before setting a hand over her eyes. "Don't you want it?"

"Do me a favour and hold onto it 'til the next time I see you."

It drew a smile from her, and she clutched onto it. When Barty curiously reached out to touch, she swatted his hand. It would've been endearing, were it not Barty Crouch.

"God," Remus scoffed, turning back to Regulus. "What did you even manage to do with Crouch? Can't believe I'm saying this, but he might actually be less of a little dickhead now.”

“If you think I’m about to take all the credit, you’re daft.”

Chuckling, Remus reached out and pat Regulus on the shoulder. He rethought the gesture the moment Regulus began veering away from him, and rubbed his hands together afterwards to hide the awkwardness.

“So… We’ll be seeing you in the summer then?”

“Only if Sirius doesn’t come to his senses first.”

“He means it when he says he wants you here,” Remus promised. “And you’ll like London. It’s not exactly the city of dreams or anything... but it’s got some decent opportunities if you know where to look. You’ll say hi to Sheila for me in the meantime, yeah?”

“I didn’t know she was your godmother,” Regulus said. “It explains why she talks about you so much.”

Remus pressed his lips together, staunching a smile. “I’m gonna go get Sirius,” he told him, patting his arm once more—quickly this time, so that Regulus couldn’t avoid it. “Don’t go anywhere, Edge.”

Before he could even wink, Regulus had flipped him off, and Remus began backing towards the stairs. On the above landing, he ran into James, who was coming out of his and Lily’s room with a small tin under one arm.

“The others still here?”

Remus gestured back down the stairs in confirmation. “Those from your mum?”

“Yeah. I told her that Regulus really liked the kheer she’d made, so she wanted to send him back with some baking—you know, like how she used to do for us. Is Sirius down there?”

“Nah, looks like he’s hiding out. I’m gonna go get him right now.”

“Ha, bloody coward.”

“Don’t be too hard on him,” Remus smiled. “I think he’s just sad his brother’s leaving.”

James began backing down the staircase. “I swear, Moons, had you said that to me a year ago I wouldn’t have believed you.”

“I wouldn’t have believed me either, Prongs.”

Leaving James to it, Remus ascended the narrow set of stairs leading up to his and Sirius’ bedroom. He was half-expecting to find Sirius pacing the room nervously, and was fully ready to commit to his usual pep talk, only, when Remus walked into the room, it looked as though a bomb had gone off in one of the wardrobes. Clothes were strewn everywhere, carpeting the bed and floor with an unnerving amount of leather and spandex.

“Sirius, what are you doing?”

“What’s it look like?” Sirius grunted. He was on his hands and knees before their wardrobe, digging through the bottom of it as though it were a skip bin and he’d accidentally thrown out a box of takeaway that was still good.

“Dammit. I put it in here so I wouldn’t lose it, and now I can’t bloody find it!”

Stepping over a stray boot, Remus sat down on the corner of their bed, feeling the mattress sag beneath him. “Wanna tell me what it is you’re looking for?”

“My leather jacket—the old one. I had Wormtail update it for me. Wanted to give it to Reg as a going away present.”

“Stunning. ‘Cept it’s sitting right here.”

Sirius sat up so fast he smacked his head against the wardrobe’s door handle. After cradling his scalp for several minutes, he ceased his moaning and finally crawled back over to the bed, where Remus had unearthed the old jacket from beneath a pair of horrendous tartan trousers Sirius had procured over at the Spitalfields Market.

“You’re brilliant, you are,” Sirius said, giving Remus a quick peck as he stood up and raised the jacket. “Think he’ll like it?”

Remus didn’t get the chance to reply; instead Sirius turned the jacket around to reveal the name “EDGE” slashed across its back in white paint. A tiny “made in London” took up the rest of the space toward the bottom, painted in all the colours of the Union Jack.

“Do you like it?” He grinned. “Glows in the dark too.”

“Do you want my honest opinion?”

“Okay, so it was mostly a joke,” Sirius admitted, folding the jacket over one arm. “Just wanted to give him a reminder that he was here.”

“I don’t think he’s likely to forget.”

A beat passed, and Sirius had leaned back in for another kiss. This one was slow, thoughtful and nostalgic. When they broke apart again Sirius had shut his eyes and leaned their foreheads together.

“You know… When I found out Alphard had left me that money, I figured it would be for the both of us. He probably thought leaving it to me was the easiest way to keep Mum and Dad from getting their hands on it, but later, when Reg and I fell out… Well, just started thinking he didn’t care for my help anyway.”

Remus reached up, tangling his fingers in Sirius’ hair. It’d gotten even longer in the past year and was now hanging below his collarbones. He could still remember the time they’d been out Christmas shopping for Lily, and Sirius had been mistaken for a girl on his way out of some fancy boutique. Sirius had been embarrassed at the time, but puffed right back up again when Remus told him they only stared because he was so pretty.

“You worry too much,” Remus told him, kissing those pretty lips again. “Five quid says he wears it the entire train ride home.”

Sirius’ face became a grin. “I’ll take that bet.”

With a cheeky shove, he had Remus on his back on the bed, the jacket trapped between them as Sirius shimmied his way up Remus’ torso to straddle his legs. There was a rhinestone belt digging in between his shoulder blades, but it took a back seat to all the feelings of Sirius’ mouth on his. Tongue-n-tongue, they stayed that way until a distant honk had Sirius sitting up in alarm.

“Shit. Already?”

“That’ll be the taxi,” Remus nodded, wiping his mouth. “You should go on down, say your goodbyes. Maybe you can make him swear he’ll come stay for the summer.”

“Yeah… Yeah, alright! You go stall him."

"Why?"

"I left a pair of drumsticks sitting around and now I think I’ve lost them in all this mess.”

“How typical.” Kissing Sirius once more on the cheek, Remus picked his way back through the clutter and started down the stairs. Arriving on the first floor landing, he could hear voices coming from the front door.

“I’m sorry for snapping at you last night,” Regulus was saying.

“Don’t worry about it,” James replied. “You were drunk.”

“Yeah, but I didn’t mean it. What I said.”

“It’s cool. I told Lily, and she forgives you too.”

“Oh. Great…”

Inching down the stairs, Remus paused. The two were standing across from each other in the entryway; Regulus had Effie’s tin of baking in one hand, and was staring down at it dubiously. Was this it then, he wondered? Had James caught on to Regulus’ little crush on Lily at last?

“Sirius really enjoyed having you here,” James said eventually. “Sorry we’ll be missing your birthday.”

“It’s fine.”

“Well… You totally blew us all away at The Damned show! Last night too, before you stopped, that is. I’d never seen anything like it.”

Regulus glanced up, and Remus didn’t miss the hopeful look in his eye.

“Yeah?”

“Totally! I still think you could form your own band, that is, if you really wanted to. Sirius might have a heart attack—it’s always been his dream, right—but I’m sure he’d come around eventually.”

Regulus shook his head staunchly; “It’s just a hobby. I’ve got no interest in dreams.”

“That’s too bad,” said James. “You’ve sure got a lot of nerve. You could probably do whatever you wanted. All it takes is a few seconds of bravery. Sirius told me that once.”

“Bravery? Really…? ”

“Why not? It’s like—back at the concert, that was one of the bravest things I’d ever seen, yeah? You got up there when no one else would—it was mad! So, say all it takes is a little bit of madness, and boom—everything you want can come true.”

“So now it’s madness,” Regulus chuffed.

“They’re related,” James grinned. “But I find that when you want something, you can’t just wait for it to come along on its own. You just gotta do something a bit mad first to make it happen.”

And this was perhaps the moment Remus would be kicking himself over for many, many years to come. So far off the mark he’d been, that when Regulus pressed up onto his toes to kiss James on the mouth, he’d had the gall to be surprised.

A credit to James’ character, he did not leap away in shock. Instead his eyes bulged, and he reached up to grasp Regulus by the shoulders. This seemed to spur Regulus back to his senses, and he pulled back, his cheeks a violent red.

“I’m sorry, I… I just needed to do that. Just—Just once.”

And then Regulus was gone, scooping up his trunk and darting out the front door, Effie’s baking tin clutched tightly to his chest. It was clear James was dazed; when Remus finally descended down the rest of the stairs on rubbery legs, he turned to face him with an open mouth.

“Moony, did you see…?”

Remus nodded.

“But I–I didn’t—”

“I know, Prongs.”

James deflated, arms hanging limp at his sides. Down on the pavement, Barty was helping Regulus shove his trunk into the taxi boot. He harped at him, mostly complaining about Trish—not that Regulus seemed to be paying any attention. After muscling the trunk inside, Regulus slammed the boot shut and glanced back up at the flat. He must’ve seen them staring, as he quickly turned away and hurried into the back seat of the cab.

“I should probably tell Lily,” James said in a hollow voice. “That’s what you do, right? You’re supposed to—to tell ‘em.”

“It could be worse,” Remus gulped. “I mean, he kissed you.”

“Yeah. That’s right, he did.” A beat, then; “But maybe… don’t tell Sirius.”

Remus glanced at him, surprised, but before James could begin explaining himself, Sirius came thundering down the stairs.

“Useless cunts! What're you doing letting them leave?!”

He pushed past them and ran down to the street just as Barty and Trish were getting into the cab. Regulus rolled the window down for him, and Sirius shoved the jacket and drumsticks inside before taking a moment to lean both arms on the edge of the cab’s window edge. Remus couldn’t see Regulus’ face with him in the way, but he’d have bet a lot more than five quid that he wasn’t looking Sirius in the eye.

“You think he’d blow his top if he knew?” Asked James.

“Uh…”

“It was only the one time,” he went on babbling; “And it ain’t gonna happen again, so… Shit, Moons, will you please not say anything?”

Remus was at a loss. It felt wrong to be keeping such a secret, especially when everything was just starting to make sense. Of course Regulus had a thing for James— of course! Honestly, he was a proper spanner for not picking it out sooner.

“We don’t need anymore drama for the band,” James reasoned, mostly with himself. “And Regulus is going home now. So I suppose, what Sirius doesn’t know won’t hurt him. Right...?”

Great, Remus thought; now he’d gone and jinxed it.

"Sure, Prongs..."

James looked at him. “Shit. Please, Moons?”

Remus pinched his forehead, trying not to look at Sirius’ back as he leaned over the cab. Maybe James was right—it was only a kiss after all.

“Alright, James. Whatever you say.”

Visibly softening with relief, James grabbed him by the shoulder. “Thanks, mate. You’re a good friend. I’ll see you downstairs for a bit of practice, yeah?”

“I’ll holler when Peter gets back.”

Nodding, as if to psyche himself up, James let out a breath and then slipped out the front door, heading towards the exterior stairway that led down to the flat’s basement. He didn’t dare look at the taxi when he passed, but made sure to wish the others a safe trip back to Scotland and gave a genial wave. Even while watching, Remus couldn’t tell if Regulus had waved back.

After several minutes, during which they’d surely racked up a decent idling fare on the taxi meter, Sirius rubbed his brother’s hair and stepped back from the window to see them off. He remained there until the car had turned a corner at the end of the street, hands pressed into his back pockets.

“You okay, Moons?” Sirius asked when he strode back through the front doorway of their flat. “You look like you’ve seen a ghost. Say, you haven’t seen Sybill’s little magazine lying around anywhere, have you? Think I’d like to have it framed…”



Chapter End Notes

New character alert!! (I love Gideon Prewett) Also hello Regulus???? Boy moves in crazy ways. So proud of him actually.

'Mince' means like rubbish.

'Scrumpy' a strong cider drink.

A 'vest' is the same thing as a man's undershirt.

Mitch Mitchell was the drummer who worked with Hendrix in the Jimi Hendrix Experience.

An 'A&R manager' is someone who negotiates and signs new artists for record labels and music publishers.
