Chapter 106: The Roundhouse


Chapter Summary

The Marauders play to their very first concert audience.



Chapter Notes

No CW's for this chapter apart from brief mentions of addiction.

I use (as in Sirius sings) two songs in this one. The first is one I wrote to the melody of "Dazed and Confused" by Led Zeppelin (though I ignored 02:06 - 03:29 where Plant is just moaning while I wrote it) and "Five to One" by The Doors. Feel free to play both while reading.



See the end of the chapter for more notes



Buddy you’re a boy, make a big noise,

Playin’ in the street, gonna be a big man some day!

You got mud on yo’ face, you big disgrace,

Kickin your can all over the place, singin’—

We will, we will rock you!

We will, we will rock you!

- “We Will Rock You” Queen, 1977



Sunday 6th May 1979





The first time Remus had ever laid eyes on the Camden Roundhouse it’d reminded him of a wary and dilapidated version of Albert Hall, or perhaps a more industrialised rendering of some ancient Greek pantheon. Since then its exterior had changed very little, what with the chipped pavement and worn-out car park all chockablock with rain puddles and potholes. Piles of old roofing tiles had been mixed in with abandoned stage pieces at the far end of the property, all discarded from the venue’s previous life as a performing arts powerhouse. It was a huge building, originally built to house turntables for steam engines—but like the telephone box in Marlene’s beloved Doctor Who, its vast cement walls gave very little indication of the sort of volume it contained within. Now standing in the middle of the annular hall, Remus stared up at the surmounting set of glass windows at the roof’s peak and imagined a fall from that height would kill anyone. And they were supposed to play there, he thought? He wasn’t confident his ruddy little amp could fill a room half this size, let alone be heard over an entire crowd. But there they were; no going back now.

“You’ll be happy to hear that I’ve made the executive decision to have Marauders round out the show,” said Gideon. ”Get it? Round as in Round-house? God, I just kill myself.”

He sniggered as he strolled over to them, continuously tapping a clipboard against one hand. He'd yet to write anything on it, and Remus got the feeling he just held it to look professional. Not hard. His suit was pure-white with a navy shirt underneath and he looked a bit like a ginger-fied Marlon Brando, minus the cigarette and Sicilian accent.

“Also, just as a little tidbit,” Gideon threw in, “you should know that it’s a sold out show. Turns out Gaz was feeling generous. He put out a little advert in last week’s edition of ‘Sounds’.”

He said all this very keenly. The Marauders, meanwhile, had yet to pick their jaws up off the floor. Even the girls, who’d come early to witness their soundcheck, hadn’t a single quip to split amongst themselves.

In a shocking turn of events, Moira had turned up to show her support for Peter, making up for the loss of Lottie, who was still off on her glowing honeymoon with Roger. She had managed to find the time to send a postcard though; Congrats! Guess you idiots managed to prove Dad wrong after all. Love from San Sebastian!

“The Do Nuffin’s will warm-up the crowd, get everyone nice and loose,” Gideon said, pausing long enough to direct a set of stagehands rolling in a soundboard the size of their bathtub back home. “You’ll be following Modern English at nine-thirty. Show ends ten-to-eleven. Any later and the city’ll fine us for violating noise limits. Considering you lads don’t have much in the way of a cab fund, I wouldn’t risk it.”

“Cool—Cool…” James stammered, acting decidedly not cool. “Any other advice then?”

“Yeah. Don’t fuck it up.”

That was what they got: a wink and a warning not to ruin their first ever chance before it even started. Remus knew that by putting them up at the Roundhouse, Gideon had effectively given Marauders his personal stamp of approval, which meant that any chance of failure also ran the risk of marring his own industry name. And yet Remus couldn’t help but feel that they still stood the most to lose.

Despite Gideon’s warning, the soundcheck was a disaster. News of a sold out audience had turned any budding anticipation into full-out dread for the four concert-newbies. Thanks to the Roundhouse’s tiny modular stage, there wasn’t enough room for each of the band to have their own set up, which meant that sharing was the only way forward. They’d agreed to use Peter’s drum kit, but the amps and pedals were being provided by Modern English, a new-wave band from Colchester that sounded more akin to Genesis than they did Aerosmith or Led Zeppelin. Hearing their soundcheck, Remus thought the songs went too bad—no different from the verse-chorus-verse one might hear on the radio those days—but something about the band’s stage presence or general lack thereof felt unnerving. Mostly they just swayed ahead of their synthesisers, a style Sirius later mimicked during their own practice. He paired it with a droll rendition of the band’s only single, “I’m Drowning”, shambling ahead of his microphone like a zombie;

“ ‘ I’m drowning… dun-DUN-dun-DUN! Going underrrr… I’m drowning… ’”

He only stopped after Peter threatened to strangle him with his own microphone cord, lest the other band overhear him. They were already usurpers; it'd been clear from their first meeting that neither band wanted much to do with their new pals. The Do Nuffin’s had already been playing together for years and were therefore much more established on the local scene than Marauders could ever hope to be. Adversely, Modern English’s recorded single painted them as serious musicians with a real shot of making something of themselves. Though neither group was popular enough to be making any real demands, no one made a secret out of the fact that Remus and his friends were complete novices, and thus had swooped in on what could’ve been a big and very real opportunity for the rest of them.

“Tough,” Sirius said later, busy admiring his arse in one of the dressing room mirrors. “Suppose the hotter bird gets the worm.”

Dorcas tutted. "You say that now. Just wait until some hot young dish sweeps in to steal your limelight."

"Impossible. No one's that good-looking."

They ragged him for a little while, but Sirius' confidence had always been a bit contagious, and glancing around the tiny dressing room, Remus was quite sure they'd take what they could get just then.

With a bit of help from Mary, Sirius had turned out a show-stopping new look, complete with eyeliner, black velvet pants and red lamé matador’s jacket—of which he wore nothing underneath. He’d spent the better part of The Do Nuffin’s set complaining that the outfit would’ve looked better if he’d just had a few tattoos underneath—comparing ideas with Marlene and Peter—but Remus disagreed. Sirius looked already like a rock star. He looked like Jagger.

“Hope you’re ready, lads!” Gideon called, sticking his head in the dressing room’s door. “ ‘Cause you’re on in five minutes.”

He was gone a second later, just in time to miss James standing up from his seat, his face having turned a horrible ashen grey.

“I think… I need a bucket!”

"I'm starting to wonder if this isn't a medical condition we should be worried about," Lily winced, patting her boyfriend on the back.

As James made a mad-dash for the bin, Peter put down his empty beer bottle and gave a loud belch.

“I can feel it,” he rasped, still expelling air; “Tonight's gonna be a perfect show. A ten out of ten! Right...? What d’you think, Moony?”

“I say ten too,” Remus replied, barely glancing up from his bass guitar. Peter cheered.

“And you, Sirius?”

“Ngh—Eleven!” Sirius bellowed. He was across the room, doing a poor attempt of a hand-stand against a wall covered in faded Jimi Hendrix posters.

“Can you stop that?” Remus scoffed. “You’re going to break your neck.”

“I’m trying to evoke a natural rush,” Sirius said, his face already flushed. “Wouldn't have to if someone—ngh!—hadn't refused the sound guy’s offer.”

“This is literally the most important show we’ve ever played,” James moaned, cradling the plastic bin to his chest. “You’re not allowed to be high for it.”

Sirius grunted, folding forward off the wall. “Aren’t you excited, Prongs?” He simpered, creeping closer to James and his bin. “Just think of it… All those people out there, anticipating the show. Waiting for you—cheering our names! Just—Potter, Potter!”

James thrust a finger out. “I will vomit all over you, Black!”

The sound of a thumping fist came from outside the dressing room door, making them all jump and signalling that it was time to take their places. The girls shuffled out first to join the audience near the front door and afterwards, Sirius reached an arm down and hauled his best friend to his feet.

“Well!” He grinned, smacking James on the back; “Go on—get it all out now, mate, ‘cause for the next two hours, you’re not even going to have time to breathe.”

It was chaos outside the dressing room. Remus had never seen so many people running around in one place, save for maybe that time they’d snuck backstage for The Clash. Two weeks ago he’d been astonished by Sybill’s ability to gather a mere hundred people or so, and now—between those working the show and those attending it—there had to be at least a thousand bodies packed between them and the front doors. Apparently anyone who’d brought their copy of Sounds with the show’s advert in it had gotten in for free, and the draw of getting to see three bands for the price of none was well worth it. Even if they were complete shit, Remus doubted many in the audience would care.

But it wasn't just about playing their songs correctly, he reminded himself. This was about proving to blokes like Gideon that they were worth the shot in the dark. That Marauders could be the best band in the world. That they were not complete failures...

“For a bunch of sops, those Essex bastards sure can move a room,” Sirius said, peeking out to admire all the people hanging out on the upper balcony. One of the venue’s swivelling stage lights caught him dead in the eyes as he did and he flinched, only to turn back around with his hair glowing blue under the light and a beaming smile on his face.

“Holy shit.”

Remus nodded. “Holy shit.”

“Get it together man,” Peter was busy telling James. Like a little christening, they’d each been given a shot of whisky and a firm handshake when they approached the ramshackle staircase that led up to the stage. There they found Modern English finishing up their encore to the sound of roaring applause. It appeared as though their minimal stage presence was of little consequence to the exuberant crowd—not that James seemed to notice. He was too busy pulling at the collar of his ringer t-shirt and trying not to hyperventilate.

“Does anyone see Lily and the girls?” He wheezed, covering his mouth to force air in through his nose. The answer was no; it was nearly impossible to pick out anyone amongst the sifting crowd. If they wanted to see their friends, then they were going to have to get out on stage.

“Gear’s almost ready,” Gideon said, appearing out from behind a set of stage monitors. “You lads looking forward to your first big show?”

“Do you always do this?” Sirius asked instead. “You know, play babysitter for the bands?”

“Playing babysitter for spoiled little rock star cunts is my job. It’s not always glamorous, but it has its perks. A house in Costa Rica, for example.”

Before Gideon could brag any further, a man in all black with a headset on came up and nudged him from behind. He gave him the okay, and Remus felt his stomach hit the floor.

“The stage is all yours, gentlemen,” Gideon grinned. “You do remember what to do with it, right? Which end of the guitar is up?”

In answer, Sirius reached for the microphone a waiting stagehand had been cradling for him. “Best get that contract ready, Prewett,” he called, already walking up the stairs. “Wouldn't want another agency to beat you to the punch.”

Looking back on it, Remus would consider that instant as the moment Sirius Black sealed the deal on the rest of their lives. They didn't know it, but Gideon Prewett had already decided that very first night he’d seen them play that they had what it took to be a good band. Still, it was Sirius’ confidence—his no-fail attitude—that was what made Marauders truly great.

The lights were down when they walked out on stage for the very first time. As the audience swayed gently in anticipation, Remus focussed hard on trying to remember the set up; Peter’s kit toward the back, a microphone stand at centre stage, and a keyboard on the far right for Sirius' piano bits. His cheap Teisco bass would be waiting for him next to the stack of amps on stage left. There he felt for it until his fingers hit the strings in the dark. There was a faint rippling sound from the attached amplifiers as the low notes slithered through their stage monitors. Somewhere nearby Remus could hear the faint ticking of an amplified metronome, ready to count them in.

Tick–tick–tick!

He swung the bass’s strap over his head. This was it.

Tick–tick–tick!

Adjusted his E string. This was fucking it!

Across the stage, in pitch darkness, James Potter fit a guitar pick between his teeth and strummed down. Amp feedback echoed.

The crowd got loud.

Behind them, Peter Pettigrew drew a stick along the edge of his crash cymbal.

Tick…!

Remus Lupin struck a chord. Felt the sound tremor in his feet.

Tick…!

And Sirius Black wrapped the microphone cord around his wrist.

… Tick!

“Do any of you remember what magic feels like?”

The lights stayed low, anticipating the eager roar of the crowd as Sirius spoke into the mike. Remus felt every word like a caress over the skin of his arms and neck, but there was no time to be caught up in all of Sirius’ sensualities. With a gentle flick he began the descending bass line he’d built the song around. It was a love song in a way, and also a curse. He’d come up with the melody ages ago—admittedly during some stupid spat between him and Sirius he couldn’t even remember the reason for. But the drama was there, the lust was there. And when Sirius sang…



“ ‘I know that they’re here and we’re supposed to play,

A song that I wrote for you in happier days;

Sweet little mama, I’m caught under your spell,

Black magic woman, I fear I ain’t well!”





The lights went up with a great whoosh, and suddenly Remus felt like he was being blinded by a supernova. James’ guitar shrieked and whined—turning their ominous love song into the curse Remus had meant for in his anger. He felt stung and abused, scorned and what for? Sirius Sirius Sirius—but there was Sirius, with a single hand on the microphone and blowing out his entire chest;





“ ‘You knoooow it can’t be no more—

I think this man outta leave,

Ain’t got no more answers, baby, but you taste so sweet;

Run me around in a dark room—

Don’t know where I am,

Yeah, draw me in, baby, my heart’s growing weak!”





It was like dropping into the punch instead of dodging it. Peter kept them in line with the gentle tap-tapping on his snare and clash, while every shuttering twang of James’ guitar rocked them right back again. The audience ahead of them were hypnotised—they didn’t know whether they should be moaning or crying. James had called it the Zeppelin effect; seeing how their mouths dropped open and their eyes glazed over like they’d just been shown the white gates of Heaven. Sirius had that effect on people regardless, but his voice changed when he whined. It turned raspy. It turned them on.



“ ‘If being lost is a crime, then a sinner I’ll be,

I still love you, baby, you’ve got magic up your sleeve;

Praying for a woman shouldn’t be too much to need,

Can’t it be now, baby—

Please don’t leave me to grieve!”





Sirius tossed his hair back;





“ ‘Please don’t leave me to grieve!”





Peter brought down his sticks.





“ ‘Don’t leave me to grieve!”





James slashed his strings.





“ ‘Don’t leave me!”





Remus took a breath.





“ ‘DON’T LEAVE ME!”





Before Sirius had even finished his final scream, James had moved to the centre of the stage, rocking his hips forward as his fingers chased themselves up and down the strings. With Peter at his heels his song soared across the hall like a siren, and the wave of people down below surged up to meet him, crashing over the lip of the stage with desperate and longing fingers. All sound fell away except for them—and they didn’t know what they were doing, they’d made it up! The words were made up, the melody was fake—none of it mattered apart from listening to each other! Their first song at their first real show and it might as well have been one they’d never even heard before. It could’ve been—didn’t matter. The Marauders knew each other well enough to make any strange thing feel familiar again.



“ ‘I know that they’re here and we’re supposed to play,

I’ll make love to ya, baby—thinking of happier days;

And sweet little mama, I’m still caught under your spell—

Black magic woman, I’m gonna send you to hell!”





It was as though he could feel Sirius’ hands on him now. The microphone cord was wrapped around his throat, squeezing and squeezing until all that was left was that airy feeling that kissed your brain before you passed out. Maybe they shouldn’t have started with “Black Magic Woman”; they’d ascended and now there was nowhere else to go but back down.

Oh well…

Might as well make it a party then.

By the next song the crowd had been broken from its trance and with every slam of Peter’s drumsticks, and eventually their mindless thrashing had returned. Come the third song, Remus could no longer feel his fingers. It was an odd sensation—not the fingers, the captivation—but the audience had not acted this way for The Do Nuffin’s or for Modern English. They had played their music and struck a few cords but this was different. This was a carnal need for something more. Remus would’ve given it to them all night if he could, only the Marauders didn’t have enough of their own material to cover an entire hour and a half-long set. But they did have two things:

Sirius Black.

And Jim Morrison.



“ ‘Five to one, baby—

One in five;

No one here gets out alive, now—

You get yours, and baby,

I’ll get mine;

Gonna make it, baby—

If we try!”





Sirius hadn’t wanted to sing any covers, but there was something to be said for a song an audience could sing back to them. The people may have liked the originals, but they hadn’t had the time to get to know them yet. Jim Morrison had been dead for almost a decade, and dead Americans sometimes made for pretty decent art. Memorable art, anyway.





“ ‘The old get old—

And the young get stronger…”





The rasp was back like a growl, and Sirius kept both hands on the mike as he slid toward the floor at the front of the stage;





“ ‘May take a week—

And it may take longer…”





Eventually his velvet knees had hit the stage;





“ ‘They got the guns,

But we got the numbers…”





His head tipped back;





“ ‘Gonna win, yeah,

We’re takin’ over—

COME ON!”





Sirius draped himself across the black vinyl floor, arms spread open like he could absorb every inch of the madness tipping their metaphorical scale. Remus looked at him and he wanted him but there was something else too. He’d noticed it before that last bridge—and now James was playing again and he’d forgotten.

Remember!

Remember, dammit!

Remember where?

There…?

No—there!

Across the room, near the back bar and lit up by the black lights. He’d picked out Gideon by his white suit and hair, but it was the man standing next to him that Remus was really interested in. He’d only seen him the one time outside that corner shop along Denmark Street and now there were lights in his eyes, blinding him—but he was sure!

“It’s Gaz!” Remus shouted over the music, moving toward Sirius as he swung himself up from the floor of the stage. “By the bar—it’s Gaz Spectre, he’s here!”

Sirius’ eyes flashed greedily—hazily—but he saw him. Remus could tell by the way Sirius fit his microphone back into its stand that he’d hit whatever reset button existed within him. To change one’s tune mid-song was always a gamble, but Gideon had lied to them and brought Spectre anyway. If there was ever a time to finish with a bang, it was now.





“ ‘ Your ballroom days are over, baby,” Sirius growled;

“ ‘Night is drawing near…”

“ ‘Shadows of the evening,” Whined;

“ ‘Crawl across the years…”

“ ‘Ya walk across the floor with a flower in your hand,” Moaned;

“ ‘Trying to tell me no one understands…”

“ ‘Trade in your hours for a handful of dimes—” Keened;

“ ‘Gonna make it, baby—in our prime!”





The sound disappeared, and slowly, the crowd began to whisper;





Come together… one more time.





Peter’s bass drum thumped; ku-tss!





Get together… one more time.





James eased his slide down the strings;





Get together… one more time.





Remus held his breath.





Get together… one more time!





With a single deafening crack, Sirius kicked the mike stand over and slammed into the floor.





“GET TOGETHER—ONE MORE TIME!”





And that was all there was for it. They were together—the entire room was with them. Remus looked and looked and he couldn’t see Lily, but he knew instinctively that she was there. Her and Mary and Marlene and Dorcas. Could they feel it too? Remus thought so.

By the time they were thundering off stage, Remus felt like a million pounds that’d just been run over with a train. His ears were ringing—whose idea was it to not invest in ear plugs?—and he definitely couldn’t feel his legs.

“Good news!” Shouted James, despite the fact that he was standing right next to them. “I don’t have to throw up anymore!”

It was around this time that Remus realised James had lost his glasses. Maybe it'd helped—not being able to see the audience—but there wasn’t any time to look for them.

“Spectre!” Remus gasped, slamming Sirius in the centre of the chest and nearly winding him all over again. “He was by the bar—let’s go!”

But they were not allowed. Either because they were worried about their newest stars causing a riot out front or because they meant to hussle the four of them into the back to very violently coerce them into signing their lives (and future pay cheques) away for their brief five minutes of fame, the stage hands and small team of security Gideon had hired to work the event began ushering the Marauders back toward their dressing room.

“Alright, we’re bloody going!” Sirius snapped, before his mood shifted again and he was bounding forward to wrap his arms around James’ shoulder. “Holy FUCK—that was amazing. Did you hear us? I mean, did you fucking hear us?!”

“I don’t think I’ll ever hear anything again!” Peter shouted, apparently suffering from the same ringing in his ears as Remus.

They made it to the dressing rooms and Sirius burst through the door like a jack rabbit on speed. He only paused when they came face to face with Gideon, smiling around the lip of a cigarette as he leaned back against one of the dressing room tables. He said something that was probably very sly, but Remus could hardly hear anything over the ringing in his ears and James' shouting;

“WHAZZAT?!”

Gesturing, Gideon snapped his fingers and the door was yanked shut behind them.

"Let's talk, lads."

A few minutes later they’d all peeled out of their sweaty stage gear and were given several rounds of whisky and a cool towelette to drape over their necks and eyes. It felt like overkill, but when Remus began to notice the spots in his vision from the stage lights he acquiesced to the pathetic little towel and leaned back in his chair with his face covered.

“You boys did great out there,” he overheard Gideon profess. “Blew the roof off the joint. Almost literally.”

“I thought I saw a few ceiling tiles falling into the audience,” James snickered.

“And Spectre?” Sirius asked boldly. “We saw you two by the bar.”

“That’s a keen eye you got there. But I’m ‘fraid Spectre’s loooong gone. Sorry, boys. I tried to keep it quiet to avoid any possible disappointment.”

Remus didn’t have to lift the towel to notice that the disappointment was already in the room.

“I assume that means he hated us,” grumbled Peter.

“On the contrary, Pettigrew… Gaz says he wants to sign you.”

It was astonishing enough news to stump all of them for several seconds. Before Remus had even swung upright in his chair—towelette flying off his space at warp speed—Sirius was already on his feet.

“Are you serious?” He shouted. “He actually wants to sign us!?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You’re not just having us on, are you, Gid?” James babbled; “ ‘Cause if you are, one of us ain't gonna be leaving this dressing room in one piece.”

Gideon tipped his head forward in a chuckle. “No, Potter. In fact, I am happy to report that Marauders is officially the latest and greatest signing of Spectre Records Limited. Save a few pesky contracts, of course. You blew more than just the audience away tonight—you impressed Gaz. He thinks you could be exactly what you say you are, and he’s willing to give you a chance, so…” And then Gideon stood up from his chair, arms wide. “Welcome to the family, lads.”

It was an instant celebration. Peter threw his sticks in the air while James swooped in from behind and lifted each of them straight off the ground in a great bear hug. They embraced Gideon too, but Remus barely noticed. He’d already grabbed Sirius.

“We did it, Moons!” Sirius gasped, holding Remus’ face in his hands. “We got a record contract—we did it!”

Sirius was right—they did do it!—and like with every other major milestone they’d shared so far, Remus cupped Sirius around the back of his neck in a reflex and kissed him full on the mouth.

It took them a few seconds to realise what they’d done, and by then it was too late. Sirius sprung away from Remus as though he’d given him an electric shock, and they both found Gideon staring at them with a bewildered look on his face. For a while no one spoke, until finally James stepped up to Sirius.

"Yeah, whoo! We did it!" He cheered, before attempting to grab Sirius by the face and lay one on him. He never got so far; Sirius was pushing James away by the cheek before their lips got within feet of each other.

"Quit taking the piss, Potter!"

"I ain't! I'm cel—e—bra—ting."

The bold attempt to cover up for Remus' mistake still didn't stop Sirius from pushing away like a kid worried about catching cooties. Peter, meanwhile, had his head in one hand, staring at the floor as though he were questioning every decision that'd lead him up to that point.

"Valiant effort, Potter," Gideon said, before pointing between Remus and Sirius. “So this a thing then?”

“No,” Sirius answered, at the same time Remus replied with, “Yeah.”

Shocked, Sirius whirled around and Remus felt a small stab of guilt for being the one to go against him. He tried to make Sirius understand with his eyes—they were only safe as long as they decided who knew—but Gideon had his answer.

"This is gonna require some serious PR coverage," he mumbled, scratching his chin. He thought a moment longer before letting out a casual sigh. “Well, good thing PR’s my entire job.”

Sirius scoffed, like he didn't believe it. "You mean you don't care that you just agreed to sign a band of poofters?"

"I have a girlfriend," Peter said, raising his hand. It made Gideon smirk at least.

“What? You think you’re the first benders I’ve ever worked with? That’s a laugh. Nah, we’ll sort it. Get ‘chu girlfriends or something—you know, for show. Everyone does it.”

“Everyone…?” Peter gaped. “Even like—Led Zeppelin?”

Before anyone thought to answer him, a knock came at the door. One of the hired security stuck his head in.

“Oi, Gid, got some girls here to see the band. They all got passes…”

“Speaking of girlfriends!” James cheered. He rushed forward just as Lily and the other girls piled into the room, hair stuck to their necks with sweat and already yammering their praises.

“You were fantastic!” Lily cried, throwing her hands around James. “Ohmygod—it was spectacular!”

"Wonderful!"

"Truly amazing!"

"Next time you should all be shirtless."

Remus was still dazed. Eventually Gideon had wandered over to him and passed him another shot of whisky.

"Don't sweat it, Lupin. We've all got our vices. One and done—you got it out of your system. Now just make sure you play it smart and I'll make sure that none of this ever blows up in our faces."

His words gave Remus the distinct feeling of deja vu, but still—he clinked his whisky shot against Gideon's anyway, and told himself that he'd never make such a blatant mistake again.

As Lily embraced James and Moira raced to congratulate Peter, Remus set the shot glass aside to smile at Dorcas, who was striding forward with Marlene.

“I think you’ve actually managed to get better, Lupin,” she smirked, before delivering a cheeky punch to his bicep. “Guess getting fired from the shop was a blessing in disguise after all.”

“Funny how that happens,” Remus grinned.

“Just you wait,” said Marlene, “soon they’ll be whisking you off to posh places in fancy limousines and cars with blacked-out windows.”

“Yeah, you’ll be checking into the Savoy under pseudonyms just so your crazy fans don’t come breaking down the door," Mary cheered, her arms locked around Sirius' neck and lipstick marks now decorating both of his cheeks. Before she could give him another, Gideon was swooping in.

“That day might be closer than you think, ladies.” Then he broke the news to the girls for them, and was even kind enough to call for a bottle of champagne in celebration.

“You should come down to the office this Friday. You’ll have a meeting with Gaz, and he’ll decide where it is we go next. Don’t quote me, but I think he’s gonna get you on a tour.”

The boys all shared the same look of disbelief. James had both hands clasped over his head like he was going to puke again, and Sirius was about one glass of champagne away from doing another hand-stand. It was amazing! A whole tour? Suddenly their heads were being filled with ideas of where it was that they'd go. North—South—the whole country? But then Gideon made snide mention of 'America' and it was as though the Marauders could no longer think straight at all.

America...

Holy fuck.

In all their excitement, they'd somehow come to the conclusion that this was news far-deserving of a second round. It took some prodding, but eventually Gideon agreed to take them over to the Roundhouse's club and bar. Most of the crowd had dissipated by now, but there were surely a few left who'd recognise them.

"And remember, don't go around bragging about the record deal," Gideon warned them. "It's bad luck to count your platinum records before they've gone gold."

"Yeah, and we ain't even officially signed yet anyway," said James. Sirius smacked his arm for it.

"Don't jinx it, Potter!"

As they all turned for the door, Remus felt a tug on his sleeve.

“Remus, hold on. There's something you should know.”

It was Lily. She kept hold of him by the sleeve, nibbling anxiously on her bottom lip.

“What is it, Lils?”

“We weren't sure whether to say anything or not, but I know you'd want to know. It's... Well, Tomny. He was here—he... I guess he came to the show.”

Suddenly all the noise in the room evaporated.

“Tomny…?”

“Mhm,” Lily nodded, as Sirius and the others turned on them. “He was watching your guys' set.”

Suddenly Remus felt jaded. “Yeah, and the Queen was on the balcony,” he scoffed, unwilling to have his good mood ruined by whatever game Lily was playing at. Before he could pull his arm away, Lily was shaking him.

“No, really, Remus! I swear—I know it was him! He was standing right near us. We only noticed toward the end.”

“She’s telling the truth,” Marlene insisted. “We couldn’t get any closer, it was too packed."

"Where'd he bloody go then?" Sirius asked.

"I dunno. We lost sight of him after the lights went down."

It was a boot to the stomach. Remus’ heartbeat had begun to race again, different but not unlike the way it had up on stage. Desperate, he turned to Sirius.

“What are you waiting for then,” Sirius told him. “Don’t you want to see him?”

Now Remus didn’t care who was around. Heart swelling with pride, he leaned in and captured Sirius’ lips in a kiss a second time.

“He was by the east doors,” Mary called, as Remus threw the dressing room door open afterwards and nearly slammed into the back of the pair of security posted up outside.

“Wait, hold on!” Gideon barked. “You can’t go out on your own. Lads, bring him back.”

Ignoring his new manager’s wishes, Remus shoved past the bodyguards and threw himself down the hallway before he could be stopped. It was stupid to hope, especially considering he had no idea where he was going or if Tomny would still be there. Maybe Lily had made a mistake. Maybe it wasn’t even him after all. There were plenty of other blonde, scruffy-looking guys in London.

Weaving his way through the confusing hallways of the Roundhouse’s backstage area and out into the lobby, Remus began to imagine a stranger in Tomny’s place, stuck wondering just who this “Remus” idiot was and why four barmy girls were bothering him. Get a load ‘a them, he’d say, they think I know—

"Tomny!"

Bursting out the front doors, Remus found himself standing on a large piece of pavement. Cars and taxi cabs zoomed past on the dark street and crowded groups of people mulled around as they often did after concerts got out, smoking and sipping out of the occasional beer can.

Remus felt embarrassed for shouting. It’d garnered him several looks, a few of which were beginning to transform in front of his eyes. He began to hear the whispers;

No way.

Is that really…?

—I think it is!

“Hey, man, will you sign my shirt!?”

Remus jerked away, only to end up backing into another girl and accidentally trodding across her foot. She yelped in offence at first, but after looking up to see who it was, promptly forgot all about her scuffed boot.

“Hey, aren't you with the band?” She asked.

Frazzled and completely disoriented, Remus backed the other way and felt someone grab his arm.

“You’re with the band!”

“You’re in the band!”

“Hey—guys, look! He’s in the band!”

Fuck, fuck, fuck!

People began to press in from every direction. They didn’t even know his name, not that it mattered. They were undeterred by his height or general unfriendliness—desperate for whatever golden luck he had to rub off on them for even a moment. Looking into their many faces, Remus began to wonder whether crowds like this could smell fear.

“Sorry—I’m sorry,” he winced, trying to push his way through; “Please, just—just let me through! I’m looking for someone, alright—”

The words died on his tongue when Remus finally spotted him. He was standing off to the side, staring. Same sandy hair, same white t-shirt split at the collar, blue jeans—

“Tom!”

“It was so cool how you shredded the guitar at that part—”

“Do you really know Modern English?”

“Tomny!”

“What’s your name?”

“Are you going backstage?”

“TOM!”

The fans were packing in even tighter—with those on the outside unsure of who it was they were even fighting to see. Nearby a waiting police car whooped its lights, temporarily spooking them and causing Remus to lose sight of his friend. With no patience left, he began forcing his way through the wall of bodies before him. They followed, naturally, and what had started as an accidental run-in became a small chase. Was this how the members of Led Zeppelin felt?

It took a while before he was alone again, and in that time he’d circled all the way back to the venue’s far side and had found himself severely out of breath. He couldn’t see Tomny, nor had he spotted him again while eluding his—fans? Admirers? Insane groupies?

“Shit.”

Remus covered his face with his hands. He might’ve started crying out of sheer frustration, had a hand not come out of nowhere and slammed itself up against the back of his head. After practically face-planting into the dirty pavement, Remus spun around expecting a fight. But then—

“Yer lucky… That was my left.”

For a moment Remus thought he was going out of his mind. A chill came over him.

“Tom?” He echoed, breathlessly. “You… What’re you doing here?”

Tomny did not smile at him. Instead he crossed his arms over his chest, looking more irritated to be dealing with Remus’ shit again than anything else. The skin beneath his left eye was yellow like the leftover remnants of a black eye, and there was a split in his top lip that had scabbed over. His old scar had opened up again.

“Came to see the show, ain't it obvious?"

"Yeah, but... why? How'd you know?"

It was that boyfriend ‘a yers,” Tomny said. “Sent me a ticket.”

“Sirius…? You're saying Sirius sent you a ticket?”

“Innit.” Tomny glanced up at the stone wall that led almost fifty feet up to the Roundhouses’ roof; “His note said you were getting up to sumffin big. Gotta be honest though, didn’t expect it to be this big... Shit, you’re like a real rock star now.”

Remus felt his ears begin to burn. “We’re not making any money from it,” he mumbled, “it was just something we did to see if we could get a record deal.”

“Well? Did you?”

“Er… Yeah. Yeah, I think so.”

“Good. Reckon any bastard who tells you no would’ve have to be fucking deaf.”

It was nice; nicer than he deserved. Remus felt his resolve begin to crumble again. Tomny must’ve seen it in his face, as he immediately waved a hand through the air.

“Nah, none ‘a that weepy shit. I didn’t come to watch you blubber.”

Remus wiped his face, embarrassed. “Then why—” He cleared the whine from his voice. “Why did you come?”

Tomny pressed his hands into his back pockets, sucking on the inside of his cheek.

“I guess… because I missed my best friend.”

There was no stopping the tears then.

“Augh!” Tomny moaned, tipping his head back as Remus furiously scrubbed at his eyes and cheeks. “Stop it! ‘Ere, enough—cut it out.”

He thumped him again, upside the head and again on the chest.

“Don’t!” Remus moaned, embarrassed. “Piss off.”

“Make me, ya little shit.”

Another smack, this time across the face. Remus shoved his hands away.

“Stop it!”

“And jus’ what you gon’ do ‘bout it, princess?”

Tomny hit him again, and this time Remus came back with a swing of his own. He cleared the air before his nose, but Tomny was too busy gloating at the near-miss to notice the second set of knuckles heading straight for his jaw. It landed with a crack of teeth and Remus felt a small twinge of satisfaction, which only lasted about as long as it took for Tomny to recover and drive his fist into his stomach. From there it became a test of endurance, with both of them grappling for each other’s middle. They nearly had each other on the ground by the time the cop car pulled up and flashed its lights.

Tomny hauled him up; “Shit—go!” And together they took off down the street.

They ran until they’d made it around the corner of nearby Regent’s Park Road, where cars zipped through the intersection and people continued to pass them with no interest or inclination of who they were.

“Yeah... Yeah, I needed that,” Tomny panted, half-collapsing into the graffiti-coated brick. Remus followed, leaning his back up against the mucky wall and breathing hard. He pressed a hand against his rib cage and the gesture alone forced out a groan that left Tomny chuckling in amusement.

“Did I hurt you, hot stuff? You used to be able to hold your own when we were kids.”

“I’ve been going through it a bit lately, if you must know,” Remus grunted. “Hurt myself falling off the edge of your old balcony, right.”

“Is that supposed to be you bragging?”

“Fuck off, Tom.”

There was little bite in it, and Tomny just ended up chuckling again as a cab motored past, flashing them with its headlamps.

“Stupid sod… What’d you go back there for?”

Remus found a crack in the pavement to glare at. “You. What else?”

Tomny pressed his tongue to the inside of his cheek.

“And uhm—Lee, did he…”

“He threatened to kill me.” And not for the first time.

“Shit.” With a haggard sigh, Tomny ran one hand through his hair. “Look, if I had’a known you’d go back there then I would’ve—”

“What, picked up the phone?”

“You act like you were burning a hole in the phone-box.”

“Well, I was doing more than you, wasn’t I?”

This one did have bite, for which Remus was instantly sorry for. They both hung their heads—guilty—and eventually Tomny pulled a box of cigarettes from his pocket. He offered them to Remus first, who accepted only to place the cigarette behind one ear. Tomny didn't say anything.

“Skylar came by our place last month."

“Oh, aye?”

“She couldn’t find you.”

“That was sort of the idea.”

Setting a cigarette between his lips, Tomny began fumbling with his lighter. It only sparked, and finally Remus reached over and took the lighter. The flame caught a second later, and Remus capped the lighter with a crisp clink.

Tomny inhaled. “I ain’t proud.” Exhale. “Ran out on my girl when she was days away from having a baby, didn't I.”

Remus fiddled with the lighter, sheepish. “Where'd you go?”

“Oh, you know… Hung around.”

“And is that how you got all this?” Remus gestured to the black eye and the fat lip.

“Huh? Oh, nah. Got that when I went to visit Mum.”

“Your mum?”

“Mhm. She’s got herself a boyfriend, I guess… Fat ugly prick.”

Remus was astonished. “I don’t get it. You never talk about your mum. I didn't even know you found her.”

“Wasn't hard. She was still out in Plaistow, jus’ like I thought.” Tomny chuckled humourlessly. “Guess I’d somehow gotten it into my head that she should know about the baby, right? Shit, had this whole plan… She didn’t want to see me though. Jus’ took a sec to figure that bit out.”

"Jesus, Tomny... Why didn’t you just go home?”

Tomny pulled the cigarette from his lips. All they had in the way of light was a single buzzing street lamp, but even then Remus didn’t miss the way his bottom lip quivered.

“I dunno, Lu. I just don't know...”

Remus was grateful for the dark street when he pulled Tomny in by the head, hiding whatever frustrated tears he may be shedding into his shoulder. He wasn’t expecting Tomny to cry, much less hug him back, but his arms were fierce as he lashed them around his back.

“I fucked up, Lu.”

“S'okay, Tom.”

“I should never have left, innit... Now m'a piece of shit, jus' like my ol' man."

"That's not true. You went back. Skylar called me.”

There was a pathetic snivel. “Had to, didn’t I? S’my kid…”

“Yeah. Yeah, it is.”

Tomny squeezed even tighter, and with an ache in his ribs, Remus’ eyes turned downwards. Eventually he spotted the still burning cigarette now lying abandoned on the cement.

“Tom… You know I’m proud of you, right?”

Seconds ticked by, and slowly Tomny released him, keeping just one hand on his shoulder. Remus matched it, fisting him by the shirt.

“I’m sorry for what I said before,” he told him. “I’m sorry to you, and to Skylar. I’m sorry that I’ll never understand what it’s like. And I’m sorry for ever looking down on you. Even—Christ… even when I didn’t mean to. No—especially then. I was supposed to have your back, and I let you down."

"Shaddup."

"No," Remus insisted. "I fucked up, right? I was a proper cunt to you and Sky. But I swear, Tom... I’ve never been anything less than proud to call you my friend.”

It was the honest truth. When he was a kid, Remus had bragged to anyone that'd listen how cool and amazing his friend was. He didn't know when that had changed, and he was sorry for pissing off when Tomny had clearly needed him the most.

"You're a sop," Tomny told him. "And you ain’t my friend.”

Remus dropped his eyes.

“You’re my brother.”

The weight coming off of his shoulders was indescribable. Remus made a noise like he’d been punched again, and Tomny compensated by tapping him fondly on the cheek.

“I have sumffin for ya,” he said, reaching into his front pocket. The ‘something’ in question was small, silver in colour and about the size of a poker chip. Remus nearly dropped it when Tomny flicked it toward the centre of his chest. He held it up to the light.

“ ‘To thine own self be true’,” he mumbled aloud. “Twenty-four hours.”

“S’been a bit longer than that." Tomny smiled bashfully. “Few more days and it’ll be a month. Not a single hit in all that time—I promised Sky. It was the only way she’d agree to let me back in the house.”

“She must’ve really changed you then. You never did well with ultimatums.”

“You should talk.”

Remus chuckled, passing the sobriety token back; “I’m proud of you,” he said again, meaning it. It earned him a smile as Tomny returned the chip to his pocket. Nearby a series of honks drew Remus’ attention. He wondered what time it was and if his friends were still waiting for him. And Sirius… He’d sent Tomny the ticket. So much good in his life, and he had Sirius to thank for it.

“There’s one more thing, Lu,” Tomny said, drawing Remus’ attention back. He had something in his hand again. It was a photograph.

“Jus' thought you’d like to see your goddaughter.”

At less than a day old, the baby in the photo had a face like a potato, with a gummy mouth and the faint wisps of fair hair coming out of the top of her ill-shapen head. Remus could have counted every baby he’d come into close contact with in his full nineteen years on one hand. Seeing her—photo alone—he was absolutely bricking it.

“She… Holy shit. She’s… beautiful, Tom.”

“Eh, looks a bit like a smushed pumpkin to me,” Tomny said. “Don’t lie! I can see you thinking it too. Skylar damn near kicked me out of the delivery room for saying the same, but it’s the truth.”

“No, no,” Remus laughed, creasing up all over. “She’s beautiful, really. Reckon she’s got Skylar’s eyes.”

“You think? I sorta thought she had mine.” Tomny sighed mockingly. "Doesn't look all smushed now though. She was born back in April. April twenty-second, at nine-oh-nine in the morning... Most mental day of my life—just about hit the floor seeing her come out."

"Shit. Don't blame you."

"We named her Emma too. Emma Louise.”

“That’s a nice name.”

“Yeah, Sky wanted something simple, innit." Tomny pressed his hands into his pocket, looking almost nervous. "She was pretty set on Emma early on, but I… mayyyy … have told her a lil' sumfin about my favourite ‘Great Aunt Louisa’...? 'Bout how she made such a difference in my life, and how I always swore I’d name my first kid after her... Mm? Yeah, it was good though, she was totally sold after that.”

He should've caught on; Tomny was all but giving him the elbow and sly wink. As it was, Remus just turned the photo over. “I didn’t know you had a great aunt.”

Tomny smacked him over the head.

“Ow—!?”

“Honestly, for someone as smart as you, you sure are thick!”

“Right, so why d'ya hit me?”

“I don’t have a Great Aunt Lou-i–zah, you toff. Are you really gonna make me spell it out for you?”

It probably took longer than it should’ve, but slowly Remus began putting two and two together; Louisa... Louise... Louis... Lou—

“You’re shitting me.”

Tomny ran his tongue along grinning teeth. Standing across from him in disbelief, Remus smacked him in the chest.

“You actually lied to your pregnant girlfriend about some fake great aunt just so you could name your kid after… After—”

“If you said anything I’d deny it.” Tomny gave him a long look, and Remus felt himself soften.

“Look, Lu, I don’t got a dad to name no kids after. And I ain’t naming ‘em fucking ‘Thonas’, that’s for sure. You’re all I got… You're all I want. And now I reckon yer in it for life, sucker.”

"For life?"

"Innit."

Remus could have cried.

“Will you come back with me?” He asked. “I think the others would like to hear the good news.”

Tomny shrugged, hands in his pockets. “Eh, why not. Skylar’s already gonna take my balls just for being out so late—Emma’s a shite sleeper. What’s a few more hours?”

Endlessly pleased, Remus turned and together they began making their way back up the dark street. The pavement had since cleared out for the most part, but he doubted anyone would have recognised him as a Marauder now. The smile on his face was much too sappy.

“You can keep that one by the way,” Tomny said, gesturing to the small four-by-four photograph Remus was still clutching in his hand. “And you should come and visit. Sky’s invited you over and Emma—she deserves to meet her godfather.”

Suddenly Remus was bricking it again.

“Fuck. You know, it actually sounds mental when you say it like that.”

“You think that’s bad? Try Dad.”





* * *





Friday 11th May 1979





Remus knew they were in for it the moment James had appeared downstairs with his hair combed. They’d all woken up on time that morning on time, and had even spent breakfast going over a game plan of what to do should Spectre decide he wasn’t interested in signing them after all. (This mostly involved telling the award-winning producer where he could stick his gold records and slamming the door on their way out.) But however well-prepared they felt, it was hard to predict one’s van breaking down in the middle of one of the biggest thoroughfares in London.

“Switch gears, Pete! Switch gears!”

“I’m bloody trying, Potter!”

“Come on, Minnie. Hang in there, old girl!”

The van gave a lurch, shooting forward like a hoover that’d sucked up its own cord. Remus knew they’d been in trouble ever since Paddington when the engine had started acting up every time Peter pushed it over thirty miles per hour. Spectre’s office was in Barnsbury and now only a few short minutes away by car, but they’d gotten cocky with how much extra time they’d had—dawdling by the front door like they were The Rolling Stones and it was written into their contract to be fashionably late for everything.

“I told you we shouldn’t have stopped for those bloody sausage rolls!” James wailed, as the van’s engine gave yet another jarring shriek.

“They were having a two-for-one!” Sirius shouted back, offended.

Wiping the sweat from his brow, Peter lowered the van into first and let it putter along like a dying animal as other frustrated drivers on their way to work honked and swerved to get around them. Finally there was no use for it anymore, and they were forced to admit defeat after the van sputtered and died just two streets over from King’s Cross.

“This is just great!” Sirius hollered, after James had opened the van’s rear-engine cover and was hit in the face with a cloud of grey smoke. “The one time we let Pettigrew drive, and the van keels over in the middle of the road!”

“Me?” Peter snarled. “Why’s it always my fault—Moony’s the one who bought the damn thing!”

Standing further up the pavement, Remus fit a cigarette in his mouth; “I suppose this isn’t a good time to play the ‘Lily made me do it’ card.”

James shut the engine cover with a sigh, standing up and dusting his hands off on his trousers. “Well, lads, guess we’re walking.”

“How long’s that supposed to take?” Asked Peter.

In answer, Sirius reached out to a passing man, who’d stopped to let his terrier piss on a nearby tree.

“North Barnsbury, huh?” He echoed, scratching beneath his flat cap; “Well, you’re not far, lads. It’s only about a mile’s walk from ‘ere.”

“A mile?”

“Give or take. Should only take you about twenty minutes.”

They all glanced at James, who’d pulled back his jacket sleeve to check his watch.

“We have fourteen minutes.”

Shit.

“How is it we’re always fucking late?!” Peter moaned, as they each broke off into a sprint.

It was not an easy sprint. James, naturally, had no problem, and Sirius’ one-track mind helped him forget about the fact that he’d done little else besides smoke and drink for the last eleven months, but along with Peter, Remus eventually began to lag behind. His lungs were on fire before they’d even made it over Regent’s Canal, and he was only now discovering that the right heel of his trainer was not fully attached to the bottom of its sole. They made it with scarecely a minute to spare, and James stopped long enough to thump a palm on both Remus and Peter's backs as they approached the front doors of the building.

“Hang in there, lads,” he said. Sirius, meanwhile, wasted no time. He was giving their name to the lobby’s secretary when one of the elevator doors dinged from across the lobby, and out stepped Gideon Prewett in another one of his fancy Italian suits.

“Ah, smashing—you’re here! Was starting to wonder if you were gonna stand us up.”

“Sorry. Van broke down,” James said.

Gideon caught on as he glanced between their sweaty faces. “So, you—what, ran here?”

His answer was another ragged wheeze from Remus, and suddenly Gideon was grinning as he herded them into the lift.

“Gaz was really impressed with what he saw at the Roundhouse show,” he said, leading them down the long hallway on the top floor. A young secretary leapt into an open doorway just to avoid them, arms full of folder stacks. She puckered sheepishly when Gideon smiled at her, before glancing back to the rest of them.

“I was my brother Fabian who passed your tape along first, you know,” he went on. “I thought you sounded like a bunch of Zeppelin wannabes, but he was the one to convince Gaz and I to keep listening.”

“So why aren’t we here, thanking him?” Sirius drawled.

“Oh, you will be. He’s in the meeting. I handle the talent while Fab handles the finances. We’re a package deal, see, so do me a favour and try not to piss him off. He’s the one who makes sure you all get paid.”

The Marauders shared a giddy look. Paid for their music? That’d be the day.

Following closely on the music manager’s heels, Remus was surprised when the office with the rock stars’ portraits hanging on the wall turned up empty. “Gaz likes to get everyone out of the office when he’s meeting with new talent,” Gideon explained, gesturing to the empty typewriter desks. “Thinks all the extra noise can be off-putting.”

“You should tell him to check in with his staff sometime too,” Remus grumbled, still able to recall the rude guy they’d handed their demo tape off too.

Stopping before the door labelled gold with the words ‘Gaz Spectre’, Gideon knocked once and let them inside. It was a nice office, with deep leather furniture and glass covered bookcases bearing photographs and various awards and accolades. It wasn’t as flashy as Remus had been expecting, though admittedly his experience with real music producers was rather null. Fletcher had been putting on an act, and they, in their own naivety, had fallen for it. Gaz Spectre didn’t need an act, what he needed was fresh talent, and if Marauders didn’t live up to every bit of that expectation then they’d quickly be finding themselves put out on their rears all over again.

“Well,” Spectre mused sarcastically, as the four of them trotted in after Gideon, “if it ain’t my favourite group of phenomenons.”

He was sitting behind a tall desk, rocked back in his leather armchair with a fat cigar balanced between two fingers. His suit was crisp and there were smatterings of grey at his temples, though his moustache and goatee were decidedly black. He could've dyed it to look younger, Remus thought snidely. Behind Spectre, a man who looked almost identical to Gideon save for the closely-shorn way he wore his hair, was leaning up against a bar cart with an empty glass in his hand.

“Gaz,” Gideon started, as he began gesturing to the rest of them; “This is Remus Lupin, Peter Pettigrew, James Potter, and Sirius Black. Lads, this is Gaz Spectre, founder of Spectre Records. That there is my brother, Fab.”

Spectre nodded at them, while Fabian stood up from the bar cart and poured a generous amount of liquor into the empty tumbler, setting it next to Spectre’s ashtray.

“Bourbon?” He offered, raising the decanter. They each nodded timidly, and Fabian went around pouring them a drink. Spectre still hadn’t acknowledged his own, and so the Marauders glanced dubiously at one another, wondering if now was the right time to drink.

“Well?” Spectre raised his cigar. “You gonna sit or not?”

They rushed to obey, squeezing themselves into the leather sofa across from the desk. Sirius sat beside them in the remaining armchair, tapping the rim of his bourbon glass with one finger. Remus knew it was an anxious gesture, but Sirius was doing a pretty good job of masking his unease.

“You certainly don’t look like today’s average rock stars, I’ll give you that,” said Gaz. “You look about ten years too late.”

“Or more,” said Fabian.

"You mean you think we're... too old?" James asked.

"Not old—over. I'm calling you over. Finished. Ca-put. You look like you're waiting for the next great Woodstock, and I'm fresh out 'a hippies."

The comments made each of the Marauders look down at themselves. Hardly a cause for alarm, Sirius appeared much the same as he always did in his leather jacket and motorcycle boots, while James looked like an Indian John Lennon with his gelled-up hair and round glasses. Peter had opted for a coat Moira had gotten him as well as a bootlace tie; distinctly un-rock unless you were riding a moped and listening to skiffle. Not used to paying any attention to what he was wearing, Remus had dressed himself little more than a jean jacket and dark trousers, and—as he was now realising—had come out looking like the guy that sold newspapers on the corner.

“Don’t worry, we'd look better on an album cover,” Sirius said, earning himself a short chuckle from Gideon. As Spectre turned to look at him, Gideon leaned over James’ shoulder from behind the sofa and pointed down the line at each of them.

“I promised you rock, Gaz. And you saw it for yourself—these boys can deliver.”

“They can put on a half-decent show, sure,” Spectre nodded, “but that don’t mean they can sell out a stadium.”

“Who do you know who’s selling out stadiums in the beginning?” Peter asked. “The Beatles—”

“Sold over three-hundred million units before you were done wiping your nose, shortstack.”

“The Beatles had no competition,” said James. “The radios were too racist to play anything more than Liverpudlian pop—of course they came out on top.”

“Got something against scousers, kid?”

“No. My girlfriend’s from Liverpool.”

Remarkably, Spectre smiled. Then he pointed at Remus with his cigar and Remus felt his stomach drop.

“You know, when this one flagged me down in the street I thought to myself, ‘here we go, another fucking idiot who thinks his dreams are worth more than the piss on the pavement’. So colour me surprised when Fab, here, played me his tape. Got me thinking to myself, ‘holy shit, maybe he is worth more than the piss’.”

“Generous of you,” Remus mumbled, making Sirius snigger into his palm.

“So they’re clever—so they’re wily—big whoop. Rock’s a liability nowadays, lads. Everyone wants pop, and people ain’t just buying records ‘cause they like the way the music sounds anymore. Now you gotta appear to their ‘wider senses’. You need a show in everything—in the way you dress, drink, and act. If you ain’t covering yourself in shiny little sequins like you're Gary Glitter then they don't want 'cha."

"I don't think that's true," Sirius said boldly. "The Who spent all their time smashing up instruments and Ozzy just covered himself in blood. People still wanted them."

"Aren't you listening, spanner? Those guys are old. They've already secured their success. What do you have?"

"Heart," Peter said.

Remus could see it on Spectre's face; 'Heart'? You've got to be joking me.

"What more do you need than heart?" Sirius said in Peter's defence. "Real bands—real people have heart. You can't put heart into a button you press on a synthesiser. The people know it, they've just forgotten. They don’t know what it is they should be wanting anymore, and it’s our job to show ‘em. So you're right, Ozzy is old. Guys like him don't know what it’s like to be just another face in the crowd anymore.”

“And you do?”

“Sure, we do. Joe Strummer once offered to let Lupin use his toilet after we snuck backstage.”

James reached over and smacked Remus on the arm—“WHAT?”—and Remus waved him off.

“If rock’s so over," he said, "then why’d you invite us here?”

No one said anything at first. Spectre had begun sucking on the end of his cigar. Finally he nodded at Gideon, who leaned over the back of the leather sofa with a delighted sort of grin on his face.

“How’d you four like to go on tour… in America?”

The Marauders’ jaws dropped. Looking at each other, they might as well have popped another bottle of champagne.

“For real?” Echoed James. “You’re not just making this up?”

“Have you never heard of America, mate?”

James gripped the chair arm next to him, while Peter leaned over and began smacking Remus enthusiastically on the thigh. Sirius had gone very quiet.

“I’ll admit it is a bit backwards,” Spectre said, dabbing his cigar in the ashtray. “Normally we’d put you up for more shows while we work on getting a single out onto the radio. Then we’d see about a local tour, get you out at the universities, maybe a few shows up north to drum up interest in wider places, but it’s like I said—rock’s a risk. New rock, anyway. Ain’t enough to just throw money at an album—that’s a waste. And I ain’t in the business of waste.”

“So…?” Remus urged.

“So instead we flip the script. I’ve got a band over in Nevada that needs an opener for their latest tour and I think you’re the best ones to do it. Meanwhile, we’ll get your demo pressed as an EP—those we’ll distribute strictly to the radio stations. See if we can’t drum up enough interest for an album... You should know that Warner Brothers just did the same thing for Van Halen last year, so if you sorry sods can do enough to leave those fans foaming at the mouth and racing back to the charts, then I’ll put you on a three album contract.”

James was practically leaping out of his seat. “Three albums?!” He exclaimed, clasping Gideon by the hand. “You're lying."

“Good news, right?” Gideon grinned.

“Try blinding!”

But then, like an impudent devil on their shoulder, Sirius stopped tapping his bourbon glass.

“And then?”

Everyone whirled on him. Spectre merely scoffed.

“Whatchu mean 'and then'?”

“I mean, what happens when we blow Van Halen and your ruddy little Las Vegas band out of the water? 'Cause we’ll want more. Reckon you’ll want more, Gaz.”

The corners of Spectre’s moustache quirked. “Are you trying to sell yourself into slavery, kid?”

“Not at all.” Sirius leaned forward on his knees. “Just trying to show you what a real phenomenon looks like.” Sirius glanced sideways at his friends and winked. Then he lened forward and placed both hands on his knees.

“We want the Garden.”

The words seemed to hang in the air.

“ ‘The Garden’?” Fabian echoed. “You mean you want to play Madison Square Garden?”

“That’s right. In three years.”

“Th—! Three years...?”

Sirius shrugged. “Or less. Depends on how well you market us, I suppose.”

Gaz tapped the tip of his cigar into the ashtray. “That’s bold. In this business ‘bold’ means risky.”

“What’s a phenomenon without a little risk?”

Fabian pinched his forehead. “Do you know how few bands make it to a mid-level stadium? What you’re talking about is a coliseum—built for twenty thousand people.”

“Is that all? Best to put us down for three nights then.”

The Marauders all stifled their laughter. They may have been used to Sirius’ blithe conviction, but it was clear the music producers were not. Luckily they had Gideon on their side.

“Alright, cheeky,” he said, “Prove to us you can work a crowd in Denver, and maybe then we’ll talk about booking you into the most famous music venue in the world.”

Sirius and Gideon knocked knuckles, and afterwards they all turned to look at Fabian, who was measuring their frontman up for all he was worth. Then he gestured to James.

“You—Potter. Ever tried contact lenses?”

“Uh… no.”

“We’ll get you some for the tour. Rock stars don’t wear glasses.”

James scratched the back of his neck. “Seems a bit ableist but alright…”

“Lily loves those glasses on you,” Peter remarked kindly, just as Gideon strolled forward and clapped his hands.

“There’s this little saying we have in the industry, lads. ‘We want the girls in the audience to want to be with the boys in the band, and we want the guys in the audience to want to be in the band’. Can’t do that if you’re up there looking like Elton John.”

“Ha!” Sirius crowed. “Elton John wishes he looked this good.”

Eventually they’d all settled back down into their chairs, and Spectre finally raised his long-forgotten drink. “The British Invasion’s over, lads,” he declared, “you’ve missed the final charge. All we’ve got left ‘round here is born-again punks and crappy heart-less synthesisers. I’m afraid America’s all that’s left for you now.”

In answer, Sirius raised his glass. “Well then, let’s bring on the yanks.”

They stumbled back out onto the city pavement with the shock of Spectre’s offer still buzzing in their ears. You leave in a month, he’d told them, wrap up any other business before then, and Jesus-fuck, find yourselves something else to wear. American girls are different from English women, they care what your clothes look like before they start ripping ‘em off.

“Did that really just happen?” Peter demanded, as a London tour bus drove past and several tourists leaned out its windows to snap photos of them. As the bus drove off, Sirius wrapped a hand around Peter’s neck to pull him upright, and slapped him passionately round the middle.

“Yes, my dear Wormy—you just got signed to one of the biggest record labels in the entire country! Time to pack your bags and kiss your mummy goodbye, mate!”

They continued to celebrate, whooping at every bewildered pedestrian who happened to toddle past. James, meanwhile, had moved further up the pavement and was staring very intently into a sewer grate.

“Potter?” Remus shuffled forward, placing a hand on his shoulder. “Potter, are you alright?”

James looked up at him. “Peachy. Just wanted to get a good wiff.”

“Wiff of what?”

“Our shit. ‘Cause it don’t stink no more.”

“I really hope that was meant to be an attempt at a lame joke.”

James’ face split into a grin, and he took hold of Remus’ shoulder in return, just as Sirius and Peter came skipping over. “We did it, didn't we? We actually fucking did it.”

“We did!”

“Holy shit... We did it!”

“Better call Evans.”

James rocked back on his heels in disbelief. Then he threw himself skyward in a single great leap.

“PACK IT IN, BOYS!" He hollered at the sun, "‘CAUSE WE’RE GOING TO AMERICA!”



Chapter End Notes

'Chockablock' means crammed full with something.

'Sounds' was a music magazine that would've been read by fans of the era.

A 'cab fund' is just an account of extra money to be used by the band (usually on drugs, lol).

'Bricking it' means you're so scared you're crapping your pants.

An 'EP' is short for 'extended play'; shorter than a full album, with more songs than a single.

Also Modern English is indeed a real band.
