If you see her, say hello,

She might be in Tangier;

She left here last early spring,

Is livin’ there, I hear;

Say for me that I’m all right,

Though things get kind of slow;

She might think that I’ve forgotten her,

Don’t tell her it isn’t so…



During a particularly nasty wind storm in April of 1956, Cherie Anne Roberts gave birth to a healthy baby girl in a tiny council flat in the north end of Brighton. She was fifteen. She’d only known she was pregnant for eight weeks.

After the baby was born, Cherie’s mother agreed they could stay on the condition that—should anyone ever ask, the baby was adopted. She was only a distant cousin, a friend of the family’s—there would be no out-of-wedlock babies in her house. No cheap whores here, no sir.

Torn by guilt, Cherie stubbornly refused to give the baby a name. Or maybe she couldn’t. With nothing else her mother called the girl “Ruth." Cherie called her “Baby." This went on for two years, until Cherie’s mother died of a sudden heart attack and Cherie and Baby were left on their own.

Evicted from their flat and without a roof over their heads, the pair traveled further into the city, where Cherie would end up moving in with a man named Jack Riley. Jack worked construction, building council estates for the poor just like the one they’d been evicted from for being too poor. He also dealt drugs on the side, and would prove a good enough father to Cherie’s baby until 1961 when he was put away for involuntary manslaughter after one of his usual deals had gone sideways.

Following Jack’s incarceration, Cherie moved in with another man, also named Jack, who pimped her out to help pay the rent. During this time Cherie had fallen down two flights of stairs outside their building and broken her collarbone. A neighbour who had been partaking from a late-night cigarette on his balcony could've sworn she'd been pushed, but Cherie was adamant that she'd tripped. The nurse then told her that she was nine weeks pregnant, and had subsequently miscarried in the fall.

Six months later Cherie was pregnant again. She was excited for this one—more than willing now that Jack II had agreed to marry her and take the child on as his own. But it was not to be. Despite all Cherie's efforts, the baby was born already an angel. A blessing, in hindsight.

Of all Cherie’s children, only the first would remain stubborn enough to make it through early childhood. It had taken some time but eventually Cherie had named her Grace, after her mother—though there had not seemed to be much point to that either.

At six years old, Grace had fallen into a bush of stinging nettle outside their council estate and had to be dragged home by a neighbour when they discovered her hours later, playing in the street while covered head to toe in flaming red welts. The woman had much to say; how could someone let a child get this filthy? Are you even feeding her?

Embarrassed, Cherie stripped her daughter bare in the entryway of their home and spanked her. She called her stubborn—too stupid to cry. Then she washed and fed her.

After the incident with the stinging nettles, everyone inside the estate began to call Baby Grace “Nettles” and Nettles she remained until one day in early spring when the girl that was once a stubborn baby too stupid to cry packed a small suitcase and climbed out the bedroom window, never looking back.

She was two weeks shy of her fifteenth birthday.

In the beginning she’d still gone by Grace. Not after her grandmother, but after Grace Kelly, the beautiful American actress turned princess of Monaco. Ms Kelly had married her prince in April of 1956, the very same month and year Nettles had been born. On April 19th to be exact, but Nettles had been born on the 15th, four days too early. It was her first life-long disappointment.

After becoming Grace again, Nettles moved to Littlehampton, where she started going by the name Tracy, after the glamorous socialite Grace Kelly had played in the 1956 film, High Society. There she dreamed up all sorts of stories for herself; how she was born in St Petersburg to a loving mother and father, but had tragically lost both in a plane accident when they were on their way to Tibet for her father's research on Buddhist monks and their choice to undergo monastic silence. She was then taken in by an evil aunt, who only cared for the inheritance and would lock Tracy in the attic every time she spoke or did something out of turn. Some bought it, while others tried calling her bluff—it didn't matter. She was Tracy Lord from High Society, and they were little people from Littlehampton.

Littlehampton would end up being 'home' for seven months before she ultimately hopped the rail to Portsmouth, leaving behind both an abusive boyfriend and Tracy Lord. It went like that for a while—new city, new boyfriend, new name. In Southampton it was Amy—High Noon. Swindon, Frances—To Catch a Thief. Birmingham, Georgie—The Country Girl. Eventually Nettles had run out of names and cities. She’d been in and out of London for months. Fucked over and used by more boyfriends than rats in St Pancras station. She needed a change. And then it hit her.

Paris.

Maybe she couldn't be princess of Monaco, but surely France was the next best thing? Still, she couldn’t be Grace in Paris. And she certainly couldn’t be Nettles. She needed to be someone new.

As it turned out, the name ‘Tonya’ came to her while she was sleeping in the doorway of some pub in Watford. She’d missed the last train and a drunkard was wailing out for his wife, begging the night streets to help him win her back.

Tonya! Tonya! Tonya! I love you, baby! Tonya, baby, come back to me!

With her new name, Tonya hitchhiked down to the port of Dover, where she spent her final few quid on a one-way ticket to Calais.

Growing up she used to have a tape recording of this woman singing in French. She had no idea what she was saying or what the songs were about, and the tape was bootlegged so it didn't have a name or a cover, but there was a little bit at the very end where the woman said something in her pretty accent. Tonya (then Nettles) used to imagine it was a dedication to some lover—that that was who the entire album was for. She could do that, she told herself, all she needed was the accent.

Walking up to the ticket booth, the girl that was Tonya but used to be Georgie who used to be Frances who used to be Amy who used to be Tracy who used to be Nettles who used to be Grace who used to be Baby, put on what she hoped was the best French accent the guy working the counter had ever heard. She held up the line with her sob story of how she'd lost her passport to a pickpocket in Upper Clapton and did her best to sprinkle in the few French words she knew—oui, non, bonjour, poufiasse!

To her luck, the guy bought it. Either it was the end of his shift and he couldn't be arsed to call over a supervisor, or he was just stupid enough to buy the 'poor whimpering French girl' act. He was filling out the form for her ticket when he asked her for her surname and every thought of idiot ticket guys and French love songs flew out of her head.

"Oi, girl. I need your full name."

She looked up, mouth ajar, only to find a realtor’s advert pinned to the nearby noticeboard.

Call Benson and Barlow, everything we touch turns to SOLD!

Barlowe, she told him, with an ‘e’. Because that was sophisticated.

He stamped her ticket without thinking twice.

Paris wasn't so bad, once she'd gotten there, that was. She'd managed to stow away on the back of a dairy truck from Calais to Lille and from there was picked up by a band of French hippies that looked about four years too late for Woodstock. Their weed was shite and the guy she was sitting beside kept pretending to fall asleep on her shoulder so he could sniff her hair, but it beat walking. They arrived on the outskirts of the city that evening and from then on it was hustle, hustle, hustle.

Not that she wasn't used to it.

The French are arrogant but they've got big egos. All it took was a few nice words and boom—she had a sofa to sleep on for the night, maybe a shower and something fun to help her not think for a while. That's how she met Alain. He found her passed out on the floor of some strangers' salle de bains after one sleeping pill had turned into one too many sleeping pills. When she woke up, the first thing he said to her was;

"You know, that's how Jim Morrison died."

Actually he said it in French, but she was too busy vomiting a mixture of red wine and Vasparex over his shoes to care all that much.

Despite the vomit, Alain took her home. It was a reasonably nice flat in the Charonne Quarter of Paris where she would end up living for the next nine and a half months. It didn't escape her—afterwards—how nine and a half months was just enough time to have a baby. If it weren't for the wannabe bulimic prima-ballerina living one floor above them who preferred to trade her birth control for laxatives, Tonya could've ended up exactly like little fifteen year-old Cherie Roberts, giving birth alone on the floor of her one bedroom flat.

Nah, she had to give Alain more credit than that. He was a drunk with a bit of a mean streak (who wasn't) but more than that, he was an artist. Three nights a week, he and his band would perform down at some fancy jazz club often frequented by celebrities and all the finest the City of Love had to offer. Some nights Tonya would stay behind, smoking skinny cigarettes while flipping through French magazines (she still enjoyed the pictures) and listening her way through Alain's massive collection of American jazz and rock and roll. He had everything, and was very knowledgeable about it too. Plus he never made Tonya feel like an idiot for not knowing the name of this album or that guitarist. Sometimes Alain would act irritated by her inability understand him in French, but he knew enough English for the both of them, and often Tonya would get the feeling that Alain liked knowing she depended on him for more than just drugs and a roof.

On the nights Alain agreed to bring her down to the club for his gigs, Tonya would sit at the bar and order three dirty martinis with two olives each. No one in Paris drank a martini that wasn't just sweet vermouth over ice, but eventually she got good at convincing the bartenders to make her little American cocktails and let her live her little Parisian dreams while her boyfriend stood on stage and sang about fucking other women in a language she did not understand.

She was painting her toenails by candlelight one evening (between Alain's drinking and her candy habit they sometimes didn't have enough money to pay the electrical) when Alain asked;

"Hey, Tonya, how old are you again?"

Eighteen.

"... Hein."

She asked how old he was.

"Twenty-eight."

Huh.

She'd lied of course. She wouldn't be eighteen for another fourteen months.

Tonya would eventually leave Alain the same way she'd left home; pack a bag, slip out the fire escape window, never look back. Just like back then there wasn't any singular trigger—no big fight or bruise to nurse while lamenting over what to do next. She simply woke up one day and decided that was that. The course was run. Time to move on. She wasn't sure when Switzerland had become the goal. It probably had something to do with it being the closest. Plus the country's reputation of neutrality didn’t hurt.

Can't tag me, I'm Switzerland!

Tonya realised her mistake too late when the guy at the border turned her away for not having a French passport. He might’ve had her arrested as an illegal had she not welled up with tears, claiming to have left it at home. Up until that point, Tonya hadn't considered just how much she'd come to rely on Alain's satisfactory English-speaking skills, and so with nothing else to do she turned around and hopped the first train back to Paris with her tail between her legs.

Never look back, my arse.

She told herself that Alain would believe a story of her getting lost on the subway and spending a few nights at a friend's. (Anyone could be a friend—that bush over there could be a friend.) She even considered telling him she'd been kidnapped but had escaped after kicking her captor in the balls when he attempted to lift her out of the trunk of his car; only, she never made it as far as Paris. Halfway through her train journey the ticket inspector sorted out that she had not exactly paid the fare for entry, and Tonya "Barlowe with an e" was unceremoniously ejected from the train at the nearest station.

She slept on the station bench, and woke up to a woman nudging her shoulder. She was not high this time, and this woman was not some long-haired singer-songwriter with a Jim Morrison fetish. This woman was a nun—a French one, complete with the white collar and black veil and everything.

"Est-ce que ça va, mon enfant?"

Tonya struggled to recall any French she'd picked up from Alain. In the end she managed to tell her that she was cold and hungry and had nowhere to go. The nun said something else in a soft voice, and just like that three more of them appeared. They had a car and they were willing to take her with them. Tonya couldn't fathom a reason to decline.

The nuns belonged to a small convent just outside of Provins, France. They were almost entirely self-sufficient, growing most of their own food and even running a small winery off of the grapes they grew on one half of the church's land. They sold the wine to local restaurants in nearby towns and villages, and even had their own pop-up stalls at a local market. That was what they were doing when they found her; she'd been saved, and all because of a few bottles of Cabernet.

The one who'd found her was called Sister Hélène. She was well-educated, supposedly the only daughter of a good family before she joined the church, and—as it turned out—was quite fluent in English as well. She listened to Tonya's confession—the drugs, the drinking, the men she'd said no to, the men she'd said yes to, her hatred toward her mother for always failing to protect her, her hatred toward the world for failing to protect little Cherie Roberts as well. And afterwards, when Tonya had cried so hard she felt like throwing up, Sister Hélène held her and told her she could stay.

It wasn't easy. The nuns got up early seven days a week and they were only allowed one glass of wine at suppertime. The only man who frequented the convent often enough to be called a regular was an old farmer by the name of Monsieur René who brought them beef and pork in exchange for fresh eggs and a share of the nuns' successful potato crops. Even if Monsieur René was twenty years younger and looking for a quick shag, he didn't speak a word of English. Nor did most of the other sisters.

By her third week at the convent, Sister Hélène decided that all communication in English had come to an abrupt end. It frustrated Tonya, who already struggled to communicate in her own language and was about ready to strangle someone for a fucking cigarette. Sister Hélène squawked sharply at her every time she asked for something in English, reminding Tonya of the chittering jay birds that lived in the beech trees that lined the churchyard, but eventually her French did get better. And the more she spoke, the more her world opened up.

She was not the only woman at the convent who had yet to take any vows. Others dropped in unannounced looking for refuge or a warm bed and meal for a night or two. There were mothers, daughters, friends, and strangers. None stayed as long as Tonya, but all were just as grateful. It was a wayward home. Tonya wondered when exactly it was that she'd started to refer to it as such.

Now it was summer, almost half a year since she'd arrived at the convent strung-out and hopeless. The air was sweet and her hair was shorn short to the scalp, making her neck appear even longer than normal. On the days when they were feeling playful, the sisters called her pet names like 'Mademoiselle Hepburn' and 'Jean Seberg'. When they were scolding her, they called her ‘odd girl’, and ‘mon cher cœur’. When it rained they did chores, and on the days the sun shone they chased each other and took turns playing rounds of croquet on the lawn. They frolicked like they were little girls again, and at night they showed her all of their girlish secrets. A photo of a past lover, a scrap of fabric from their mother’s wedding veil, even—under sworn secrecy—a few Camel cigarettes to hold beneath the nose and enjoy on a blue moon.

She never knew what had made them like her so much, they always refused to say. But they'd welcomed her like a stray cat with unwavering devotion, and no matter what she did she would never have earned it. The girls adored her stories, especially the ones she made up, and she had never enjoyed eating apricots in the garden as well as when she was with them.

Perhaps there was something to be said for mothers and sisters after all.

On her fifth month of nun-ified respite, the boy came. He was nineteen—Monsieur René's son, sent on an errand for his father who'd fallen in the field while checking on a newborn calf and had unfortunately injured his back. The boy's name was Françoys, and he was beautiful. By their second meeting they were sneaking off behind the tiny barn to snog each other in between bales of hay. Of course they were discovered, and Françoys was promptly run off property by the offended sister as though she'd just caught Tonya breaking her vows to God.

She'd never agreed to be a nun, she howled. She'd made no vows of chastity. And so in a fit of embarrassed rage, she shoved her few meager belongings into the same rucksack she'd arrived with and announced her leave. Sister Hélène watched with no small amount of disappointment, flitting back and forth like the jays.

"Arrête! Sister Mary Celeste was merely shocked to find you in such a state. There is no need to run off."

'A state'? She was only kissing a boy. At least this one was finally her age.

Hélène sighed and set both hands on her shoulders. "Ma chere, calme-toi. You will explain yourself to Sister Mary Celeste, and all will be as it was."

She pushed the sister's hands away. No—

I think it's time I go.

It was always gonna happen eventually.

Forgive me.

And so she left; back to Paris where she sought out Alain. She only made it as far as the corner street adjacent to his flat before turning around. After that she wandered, considering what her new name would be. But she liked Tonya. People cried out at night for Tonya—missed her and marked the days until she would return to them. No, Tonya wasn't finished, although she did change her surname; 'Belova' after some Russian glamour model she saw on a paper advert for Paris's red light district.

The winter was rough. People tended to be more stingy with their sofas and showers when it cost that much more to heat them. The Summer of Love was over, and Alain had a new girlfriend anyway—an American. No way she was older than sixteen, she looked like a fucking baby doll version of Twiggy. Seeing her should've made Tonya want to claw Alain's eyes out, but all she felt was a familiar seed of self-loathing. She was almost nineteen now—too old to ask for a stranger's pity without expecting to give something in return. Alain was gone, and whatever bridge that had led her to the nuns was now burned. Her fault.

She'd run out of love in Paris, and so with nothing left, she hitchhiked back to Calais and bought a one-way ticket home.

Walking up that familiar path, she wasn't even sure what she'd find. Most of the street had been bulldozed to make way for gentrified city flats and a public rec centre. But she found it. And she found her, sitting outside the front steps of the council flat, smoking the same brand of cigarettes she'd smoked when Tonya had left.

Hey, Mum.

Cherie Roberts had gotten old. She had lines on her face where lines ought not to be, and her body was sunken in so much it looked like her collarbones might punch right through her skin like paper. Tonya wondered if she'd look like that one day; a washed up beauty queen with overgrown roots and dull gold band on a single narrow finger.

"What are you doing here?" She asked, arching a thin brow.

It was obvious wasn't it?

She'd come home.

"Home, huh?" Cherie inhaled her Kim Slimsize cigarette, smoke gliding straight up her nose. Finally she stood up from the steps.

"If you're staying, you're gonna work for it. You ain't just gonna have the run 'a the house no more, you'll have to pay your own way. You hear me, Grace?"

Actually her name was Tonya now.

If Cherie had heard her, she made no indication of it.

The flat was the same. Small, with fading yellow wallpaper and a crack in the bathroom window that turned any condensation to ice in the wintertime. The first thing Tonya had noticed was that in the four and a half years she'd been gone, Cherie had been blessed with another child. Rebecca, a cute little girl with a button nose and curly brown ringlets, spent most of her time in front of the television set, playing with off-brand Barbie dolls and rubbing her snot into the shag carpet. Cherie worked the front desk at a local nursing home and was sometimes called in to do double shifts when they were short nurses. On these days she often left the toddler locked behind a baby gate in the living room, occasionally coming home on her breaks but only if she got one that day.

It wasn't so bad at first. Cherie refused to call her Tonya, but had agreed to let her stay on the condition that she watched over her sister during the day. Rebecca had Tonya's old room now, and with her return the two had started sharing a bed, meaning that Tonya was the one who woke up when Becky started fitting from a nightmare. She would sit and rock her until she stopped crying, feeling the snot seep into the thin fabric of her t-shirt.

Shhh, baby, shhhh. It's alright.

It felt nice to know that someone was calling out for her again.

"I'm pulling a double today so you're gonna have Becky until eleven," Cherie called. Standing in front of the stove, she scooped out the eggs just before they could burn and left the steaming plate on the table while she ashed her cigarette in a leftover coffee mug from the day before. Rebecca immediately reached for the eggs but Tonya distracted her with little bits of toast, wiping her small face with a flannel before any peanut butter could get up her nose.

"Grace? Gracie, you hear me?"

My name is Tonya.

Cherie stuck a second cigarette between her lips. "You gotta watch her today."

But the off-license down the road was hiring. She was going to see if they'd give her an interview.

"As in today? What the fuck—no. I need you to watch Becky, I only took this shift because I knew you'd be here."

There was always Dom. Why not him?

"It ain't Dom's fucking responsibility, it's your responsibility." Cherie lit the cigarette, slapping the lighter down on the kitchen counter as she gestured sharply at the two girls with her long nails. "We agreed when I let you come back here—you watch your sister. Ain't Dom's problem... you hear?"

Yeah. She heard.

"Good. And for Christ's sake, eat something. You're too fucking skinny."

"I think she looks great," said Dom, as he came striding into the tiny kitchen with his boots on. "Not as great as her mother 'a course... Good mornin’, darlin'."

"Hi, baby."

They kissed, in which Dom held her mother against the counter top and Tonya did her best to get Rebecca to eat a piece of sliced apple. Cherie had to practically beat him off—giggling like a school girl all the while—and as she rushed off to get ready for her shift, Dom smacked her ass and took a seat at the breakfast table.

"And how are the rest of my girls, huh?"

Dom tugged his plate of eggs toward himself. He pat Rebecca on the head, but the baby girl didn't react. She never did. Hardly even spoke. Not around anyone but Tonya anyway.

Giving up on getting the four year-old to eat, Tonya wiped her hands and stood up from the table. She asked Dom to watch Becky while she showered.

" 'Course, princess. You go on. Oh and—" He took her by the arm, shoving several rumpled notes into her palm. "Buy yourself something nice today, eh? On ol' Dom."

She thought of Rebecca when he smacked her ass, and did not react.

The situation was always bound to break down eventually. Dom was straighter than any guy Cherie had ever been with (as in—he’d never been arrested or charged) and even ran his own garage on the south side of town. He wasn't Rebecca's dad but he put food on the table. And he had friends. Resourceful friends. Cherie's drug of choice had always been the drink, but when Tonya asked him to get her some painkillers Dom had come back with a hundred milligrams worth of hydrocodone. She asked him what he wanted for them, but Dom only smiled and kissed her hair. Anything for one of his girls, right?

But all generosity had its limits.

That night he’d been drinking, but Tonya knew enough to notice the signs. Men like Dom were cowards. Confront them with their own failings and they’ll crumble like a stale dog turd on the pavement. When Dom came into the bedroom she shared with Rebecca, Tonya screamed and screamed—threw shit and cursed him bloody. He was already running when she picked up the baseball bat Cherie kept near the front door for the local boys who sometimes came looking for a window or two to smash. She didn’t care which neighbours poked their heads out to see; Tonya slammed that bat into the headlights of Don’s crappy 1971 Ford Pinto and meant it.

"Crazy bitch! You crazy bitch! You’re gonna regret this!"

Go! Get out of here!

Rebecca cried for hours afterwards, but at least Dom was gone. And when Cherie got off her double shift later that night, Tonya came out into the living room fully prepared to tell her everything that bastard had tried to do.

Only... she hadn't expected Dom to drive out to Cherie's work to humiliate her by wailing on about her psycho daughter and subsequently dump her in the middle of the parking lot.

"You little whore! You came onto my man—I did everything for you, I sacrificed my body for you! Let you grow in me like a tumor—you whore! You whore! You whore!"

There was no staying after that. Even if Cherie could see sense, there was no way she'd ever go back. Maybe she should've taken Rebecca with her... But how could she? Tonya wasn't her mum, she could barely take care of herself. She just hoped Rebecca could forgive her someday.

Things got better when she met Tomny.

Of course she never took him seriously. He was just some goofy kid—younger than her by almost seven months and therefore completely unfuckable. But she had to hand it to him, he was...

Charming.

No, that's a lie. He was more than charming. She liked him from the very first moment they met. In another life she probably would’ve married him.

Sorry.

Late June 1979





If there was one thing she’d learned, it was that train stations were the same everywhere. London, Paris—no matter the day, now matter how pretty the architecture, all of them still smelt a bit like piss. It was one of life’s greatest ironies; you could build a beautiful thing, fill it with all sorts of great promises, and yet even beauty had to yield to the ineffable flick of the cigarette.

It took seven months to sort out her passport. One thing they don't tell you about being born: you need a piece of paper to confirm that you were, in fact, born. Conceived—birthed—shagged into existence. According to this silly little thing called the law, it's not enough to just appear somewhere and say 'hey, I'm alive'. It's enough to die though. You die—someone finds the body—and they write the proper documents right up. How's that make any sense?

In the time it took for the British Consulate of Paris to sort out that she was not a Russian spy (shot herself in the foot choosing a name like 'Tonya Belova', honestly) and instead just a silly girl who'd gotten good at finessing the ticket attendants at her local Port of Dover, Tonya could've almost had another baby. She didn't, of course, which was a good thing considering she spent half that time coming down from her worst withdrawal yet.

Eighteen months she'd spent loving Tomny, and there was not a single day she regretted. She was drowning in herself, and Tomny was the lifebuoy keeping her afloat. But Tomny couldn't be the one holding them up for air all the time. Tomny needed a buoy too. And Tonya was a sinking stone.

She needed to learn how to float.





'If you get close to her... —iss her once for meee. Always re... —spected her, for doin' what she did ‘n... gettin' free—'





"Ugh, damn thing!"

Bang! Bang!

"Vas-y, encore une fois. Peut-être que la radio s'excusera."

She huffed, looking up. "You need a new radio, Sister. This one's a piece of crap."

Sister Hélène smiled, and Tonya slowly set the broken radio aside.

"Have you gathered all your things?"

"Oui."

"And you have your ticket?"

"I'll buy it at the station."

The sister nodded. "I have this for you. Sister Marianne picked it up in town. It's in English. Just something for you to read on your journey."

She passed her the magazine, and then cupped her face. She cried—she couldn't help it. They'd taken care of her a second time—une étrangère, their odd girl. Their little runaway.

“S’il vous plaît écrivez-nous, ma chère."

Please write.

“Que Dieu veille sur toi.”

May God watch over you.

Until that moment, a small part of her had wondered if she might stay with those sisters forever. But she had never been so close to God, and she had plans now. She wanted to see all the places she'd lied about. Find 'home' again, and again. Maybe she still didn't know how to float, but she knew one thing; if you've never gotten to spend a summer living at a nunnery in the French countryside, sipping hand-pressed wine and eating apricots under the shade of the fruit trees, then you really haven't lived at all.

Standing in line ahead of the ticket booth, she began flipping through her English magazine. She read the names of all the rock stars Alain had told her about, and the ones she'd come to know on her own. She ogled their photographs, compared stops on their tours, wondering if she could catch a show or two—and it was there, in that little French train station, that she saw it.

It was the photo that caught her eye. She'd never have missed that brooding face anywhere. He was handsome now. Almost a man. He’d probably insist he already was, but that was just the stubborn in him. Oh, how she missed it.





THE CIVIL-MOUTHED YOBS!

THE ROUNDHOUSE, LONDON – “ROCK IS DEAD in Britain”, says Gaz Spectre, Head of Spectre Records and producer for the potential new rock band, MARAUDERS (pictured below), as he stands in the back of the famed venue watching his newest gamble bear it all to a crowd that didn’t know whether they wanted to be punk or rock. Without so much as a debut release, Marauders come on the scene as virtual unknowns—a gamble Spectre says he and his company are willing to take.

Oh Remus.

Look at you. You're all grown up.

My sweet, sweet love.

“Bonsoir, Madame. Comment puis-je vous aider?”

She looked up, surprised to find that she’d reached the front of the ticket line so quickly.

“Uh... Un billet,” she told the man behind the counter, quickly tucking the magazine away. She smiled; "S’il vous plaît."

“Bien sûr. Et où irez-vous ce soir?”

Where will you go?

She thought. Anywhere. Anywhere. It made her playful again.

“Ce soir? Mmm… Zurich. Demain? … Qui sait.”

“Je vois…” The attendant raised a brow at her. “You are American, yes?”

“Dieu non. Is my accent really that bad?”

“Non, c’est très joli,” he chuckled. Friendly for Paris. “Where are you from, madam?”

She shrugged, flicking lazily through her handbag.

Brighton. A tiny council flat. My mother’s c—

“St Petersburg originally, then nowhere. Then London, and then nowhere again. Most recently, a tiny convent en Provins.”

He eyed her clothing; the white t-shirt that lacked a brasserie, the jeans that hung low on her waist. Lips that had touched many, and surely would touch many more.

“You are a—eh… a nun?”

“If you say so, monsieur.”

She handed him Grace Roberts' passport.

"One ticket to Zurich, please. I'm meeting someone."

Can't tag me!

I’m Switzerland.

“Everything seems to be in order, Mademoiselle,” said the attendant, as he stamped the dead girl’s passport. “If you do not mind my asking, who is it you are meeting? Your husband?”

“Husband? Oh, no.” She took the passport and the ticket, and tucked both back into her tiny handbag. “Actually I'm looking for someone.”

“Who?"

“I'm not sure." She smiled. “But won’t it be so wonderful to find out.”
